payload.text:
## Twelve questions, one for each thing that matters

No new material in this lesson. This is the whole course, compressed: mechanics, the object model, scoping, generators, exceptions, modules, and the design trade-offs in the capstone. Every question is answerable from what you have already been taught, and every explanation is written to teach the answer rather than restate the option.

Take them without the notes. Where you get one wrong, go back to the module in the table below rather than memorising the letter.

## What changed about how you write code

The single biggest thing this course tried to do was move a set of reflexes from other languages into Python ones.

You used to think about *values*; you now think about **objects and the names pointing at them**. You used to assume assignment copied; you now check **what kind of object is behind the name** before you let a function touch it. You used to read a default parameter as a value; you now know it is **an expression evaluated once**, which is the difference between a correct signature and a bug that only appears on the second call.

You used to add a `for` loop; you now ask whether a comprehension, a dict, a set, or `itertools` already says it in one line. You used to catch exceptions broadly at the top; you now catch them **where you can do something about them** and let the rest carry a message. You used to optimise because the code felt slow; you now **measure, then fix one thing, then measure again**.

None of that is Python-specific style. It is what it feels like to know a language, and it is the part that transfers to the next one you learn.

## The six reflexes, and where each one came from

If you keep one thing from this course, keep these. Each is a rule that predicts behaviour you would otherwise have to memorise case by case, and each is the reason a piece of code that surprised you did what it did.

## What is deliberately not covered

Type checking at scale, async programming in depth, C extension authoring, web frameworks, packaging and distribution, and anything specific to a third-party library. Each is a whole field. The foundations here are what make those fields learnable rather than merely copyable — and most of them assume exactly the object model, the import system, and the testing habits you now have.

payload.code:
# The same function, written the way you would have written it before
# this course, and then the way you would write it now. The second version is
# not "more Pythonic" as a style rule — each change is one of the six reflexes
# above, and each one exists because a specific bug would otherwise happen.
from collections.abc import Iterable

WORDS = ["ant", "bee", "cat", "dog", "antelope", "fox", "owl"]


# --- version 1: the one you would have written first -------------------------
def unique_lengths_v1(items):
    result = []
    for item in items:
        if len(item) not in result:      # reflex 2: a list used as a set, O(n) per test
            result.append(len(item))
    return result


# --- version 2: the container that makes the test cheap ---------------------
def unique_lengths_v2(items):
    seen = set()                        # reflex 2: the container that makes the test cheap
    result = []
    for item in items:
        n = len(item)
        if n not in seen:               # reflex 6: O(1) test, measured, not assumed
            seen.add(n)
            result.append(n)            # reflex 2: never mutate a list another name holds
    return result


# --- version 3: what you would actually ship --------------------------------
def unique_lengths(items: Iterable[str]) -> list[int]:
    """Lengths of the given strings, first-seen order, no duplicates.

    Reflex 1 (a name binds to an object, not a box) is what makes the "seen" set
    safe to mutate here: the function owns it, nothing else can reach in.
    """
    seen: set[int] = set()
    result: list[int] = []
    for item in items:                  # reflex 4: lazy over whatever iterable is passed
        n = len(item)
        if n not in seen:
            seen.add(n)
            result.append(n)
    return result


print(unique_lengths_v1(WORDS))   # [3, 8]  correct, but O(n) per test
print(unique_lengths_v2(WORDS))   # [3, 8]  correct, and linear
print(unique_lengths(WORDS))      # [3, 8]  correct, and says what it accepts

payload.title: Six reflexes, and the module that gave you each one

steps.title: 1. A name binds to an object — it is a label, not a box (module 2)
steps.desc: `a = b` makes two names for one object. Nothing is copied, ever, unless you call a copy function. Every aliasing bug in Python, and the whole design of pass-by-assignment, falls out of this one rule.
steps.code_snippet:
a = [1, 2]
b = a        # same object, two names
b.append(3)  # a is now [1, 2, 3]

steps.title: 2. Mutation is the only thing that matters for data (module 5)
steps.desc: Lists, dicts and sets mutate in place; ints, floats, strings, tuples and frozensets do not. Which container you pick changes which bugs are possible, so pick the immutable one until you have a reason not to.
steps.code_snippet:
TUPLE = ("a", "b")   # safe to share
LIST = ["a", "b"]    # shared means your bug

steps.title: 3. Late binding is the default, and a default argument is evaluated once (modules 8 and 14)
steps.desc: A closure reads the variable, not a snapshot of it, so a loop variable seen by a callback is whatever the loop left behind. And `def f(x=[])` is one list shared by every call that omits the argument — the two most-reported Python bugs both come from these two sentences.
steps.code_snippet:
def f(x=[]):      # one list, forever
    x.append(1)
    return x

steps.title: 4. Laziness is a design choice with a cost, not a free win (module 9)
steps.desc: A generator consumes its source one item at a time and holds one item in memory, which is why it beats a list over a stream. Used twice, or indexed, or measured, it is slower. Reach for it when the data does not fit, not by reflex.
steps.code_snippet:
with open("huge.log") as f:
    lines = (l for l in f if "ERROR" in l)  # lazy
    first = next(lines)  # reads one line

steps.title: 5. Errors are data, and the message is the point (module 10)
steps.desc: An exception carries a type and a message and travels up the stack until something handles it. `else` for the happy path and `finally` for cleanup are the two clauses people skip and then wonder why. A traceback names the line: read it bottom-up.

steps.title: 6. Measure before you optimise, and structure before you micro-tune (module 14)
steps.desc: Almost every "Python is slow" claim is an O(n²) loop, a list used as a set, or a re-computed invariant. Fix the algorithm and the language stops mattering. Reach for a linter, a profiler and a test before you reach for a faster construct.

payload.text:
## After this course

The most common way people fail after finishing a programming course is stopping. The second most common is reading. What actually works is **building the next thing that is slightly too hard**, and writing down what you had to look up.

Concretely, in the order that tends to work:

1. **Rebuild something you already use badly.** A better grep, a script that renames 400 files safely, a cron job that fails loudly. Small, complete, and immediately useful.
2. **Take a real codebase and fix one issue in it.** Not write one — fix one. Reading other people's code, matching their conventions, and having your change accepted teaches more than any tutorial.
3. **Learn the toolchain you have been avoiding.** `git` properly, a real debugger, a linter configured to your taste, type checking with `mypy` even on code you never annotated. These pay for themselves within a week.

And one habit worth more than all three: **when a program does not do what you expected, do not fix it by guessing.** Print the values. Read the traceback from the bottom. Write the failing test. That habit is the difference between someone who is slowed down by Python and someone who is not.

questions.prompt: Inside a function, `print(x)` is on line 2 and `x = 1` is on line 4, and there is a module-level `x = 0`. What happens when the function is called?
options: It prints `0` and then creates a local `x`
It prints `0` and assigns 1 to the module-level `x`
It raises `NameError`, because `x` does not exist in any local scope
questions.explanation: Python decides a name is local for the entire function the moment an assignment to it appears in the body — not from the line of the assignment onward. So the `x` on line 2 is a local slot that has not been filled, and the read fails before `print` runs. Fix it with `global x` or, far better, by taking `x` as a parameter.

questions.prompt: When Python evaluates `obj.name`, and the class defines `name` as a `property` while the instance dictionary also has a `name` entry, which one is used?
options: The instance dictionary, because instance data is always checked before the class
The property, because data descriptors found on the type take priority over the instance dictionary
The class attribute, and the instance entry is silently ignored
questions.explanation: The full rule is: data descriptors on the type first, then the instance `__dict__`, then non-data descriptors and plain class attributes. Because a `property` is a data descriptor, defining one makes the attribute read-only no matter what is in the instance dictionary — while a plain function attribute loses to the instance dictionary. `__getattribute__` is the hook that implements the whole search.

questions.prompt: What does `nonlocal` let you do that `global` does not?
options: Rebind a name in the nearest enclosing function scope, so an inner function can update an outer function’s local without touching the module namespace
Make a name global from inside a class body
Remove the need for `return` in a generator function
Delete a name as well as assign to it
questions.explanation: `global` reaches the module namespace. `nonlocal` reaches the nearest enclosing *function* scope, skipping the current one. It exists for closures and accumulators — `def make_accumulator(): total = 0; def add(n): nonlocal total; total += n; return add` — and reading a name you never assign does not need either declaration.

questions.prompt: What does `gen.send(value)` do, and when is it legal?
options: It raises `value` as an exception inside the generator
It replaces the generator object with a new one
It resumes a suspended generator and makes the `yield` expression that suspended it evaluate to `value`
It returns the generator’s `return` value immediately
questions.explanation: The argument of `send` becomes the result of the `yield` expression that the generator is currently sitting on — which is what makes it the basis of coroutines. `send(None)` is exactly `next(gen)`, and calling `send` on a just-started generator raises `TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator`, because there is no suspended `yield` to deliver it to.

questions.prompt: Which of these builds the whole list immediately, and which defers all work until iteration?
options: `list(f(x) for x in data)` defers; `f(x) for x in data` is eager
`[f(x) for x in data]` is eager; `f(x) for x in data` is lazy
Both are eager, because both fully evaluate `f` before continuing
Both are lazy, because the parentheses are only grouping
questions.explanation: The brackets construct a real `list`, running every element right now. The parentheses construct a generator object that merely holds the loop. Over a large or unbounded source that is the difference between exhausting memory and holding a constant footprint, and `sum(f(x) for x in data)` avoids the intermediate list entirely. If you want eager, use a list comprehension — never `list()` over a generator, which is just a slower comprehension.

questions.prompt: Inside an `except` block, `raise TaskError(msg) from exc` does what?
options: Suppresses `exc` so that only the new error is reported
Retries the `except` block using the new exception type
Raises a new `TaskError` and sets its `__cause__` to `exc`, so the traceback shows both and names the new error as the direct cause
questions.explanation: Even without `from`, Python chains the two exceptions: the new one gets `__context__` pointing at the old one, and the traceback prints "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred". The explicit `from` sets `__cause__` instead and changes the wording to "The above exception was the direct cause". Use it when the new failure is *caused by* the old; leave it implicit when the old is only background context.

questions.prompt: Why does a `with` block call `__exit__` when the body raises?
options: The statement is compiled as `try`/`finally`; `__exit__` receives the exception info, and returning a truthy value from it suppresses the exception
`__exit__` is called before the body runs, so resources are ready in advance
The interpreter catches the exception, runs the block, and re-raises it afterwards
questions.explanation: `with` desugars to `__enter__`, a `try`, and a `finally` that calls `__exit__` with the exception info. A falsy return from `__exit__` lets the exception propagate; a truthy one swallows it. That suppression is the only way a `with` block hides an error, and returning `True` from `__exit__` to "handle everything" is a well-worn way to swallow a bug and debug it three hours later.

questions.prompt: A module inside a package `app` does `import data`, and there is both a top-level `data.py` and an `app/data.py`. Which one is imported?
options: `app/data.py`, because a package’s own directory is searched first
Neither — Python 3 raises `ImportError` for an ambiguous module name
The top-level `data.py`, because Python 3 resolves imports absolutely; you need `from . import data` for the sibling
Whichever was imported first, decided once and then cached in `sys.modules` forever
questions.explanation: Python 3 dropped implicit relative imports. Inside a package, a plain `import data` looks in the top-level namespace, not in the package directory, so the sibling requires the explicit relative form `from . import data`. The related trap is still live: the *script’s* directory is `sys.path[0]`, so a local `json.py` or `random.py` in your project really does shadow the standard library for that run.

questions.prompt: Why is `assert result == [3, 1, 2]` a weak test for a function that returns a list of ids?
options: `==` on lists compares identity rather than contents, so the comparison is meaningless
It pins the ordering into the contract, so a correct reordering fails a correct implementation — assert on a set, a length, or membership instead
`assert` cannot be used with lists at all
pytest rewrites `assert` into a form that only records the failure
questions.explanation: Assert the requirement, not one particular arrangement of it. If order matters, say so in a named constant and sort both sides; if it does not, assert on `set(result)`, on `len(result)`, or on membership. Separately worth knowing: `python -O` strips every `assert` from the bytecode, so assertions are for tests and internal invariants, never for validating user input in production.

questions.prompt: When does the single JSON file stop being the right storage choice for the tracker?
options: As soon as the file passes about 100 KB
When the program is installed as a package rather than run from a checkout
When you need concurrent writers, partial updates, queries across the whole dataset, or transactional guarantees
questions.explanation: The honest limit of a single JSON document is not size but access pattern. Whole-file read-and-write is O(n) per operation, which is fine for hundreds of tasks and wrong for tens of thousands, and it gives you no concurrency and no atomicity unless you build them. The migration path is a repository interface with two implementations — which is only possible if the CLI never touches JSON directly, which is exactly why that boundary exists in the capstone.

questions.prompt: The tracker is asked to finish task 99, which does not exist. What should the process do?
options: Print `no task with id 99` to stderr and exit non-zero, using the code `argparse` already uses for bad input
Print the message to stdout and exit 0, because the program itself ran successfully
Let the failure propagate as an uncaught exception so the traceback is visible
Print the message to stderr and exit 0, because no data was harmed
questions.explanation: Exit code 0 means success and anything else means failure, and both a shell and every CI system key on that distinction. `argparse` already reserves 2 for bad input, so using it for "no such task" is consistent, and stderr keeps diagnostics out of a pipeline consuming stdout. An uncaught traceback is a bug report about your program, not an answer to the user’s question.

questions.prompt: Why does `save()` write to `tasks.json.tmp` and then `Path.replace()` it over the real file?
options: It is faster, because a small file is written from the page cache
`json.dump` can only write to a file that does not already exist
The rename is atomic on POSIX and on Windows, so the data file is always either the old version or the new one, never half of each
It avoids holding the whole document in memory while writing
questions.explanation: This is the write-temp-then-rename pattern, and it is the difference between losing one command and losing the entire store. `Path.replace` maps to the atomic rename syscall on POSIX and to a replace-semantics `MoveFileEx` on Windows, so the target path is swapped in one step. Opening the real file for writing in place would leave a truncated file if the process died, filled the disk, or lost power mid-write.

courses.title: Resume + LinkedIn Building
courses.subtitle: The fastest first certificate — build a resume that survives the six-second skim and a LinkedIn recruiters can find
courses.description:
You do not need more projects to get an interview. You need the projects you already have to survive a six-second skim and a keyword search.

This is the shortest course on TieEdu on purpose. Four modules, eight lessons, two hours. It takes a resume that lists duties and turns it into one that leads with outcomes; it makes that resume readable by the applicant tracking systems that filter most online applications; and it rebuilds your LinkedIn so a recruiter searching "react intern" actually finds you.

By the end you will have a one-page resume you can defend line by line, a LinkedIn profile that is a searchable version of it, and a tracking sheet so your application season is a process instead of a hope.

**Who this is for:** any student, any branch, any year — who has applied to something and heard nothing back, or who has never applied because the resume felt unfinished.

**What you need:** your existing projects, even the tutorial ones. We will rebuild two of them into resume material.
outcomes: Restructure a resume to pass the six-second recruiter skim
Write a resume an applicant tracking system can parse and score
Turn duty-style bullets into outcome-led bullets with real numbers
Select and present two or three projects as experience, not an archive
Handle education, CGPA and certifications without filler
Rebuild a LinkedIn profile as a searchable version of the resume
Run a 15-minute tailoring pass and track every application
courses.about_course:
This course is built around one idea: a resume is not a document you write for yourself. It is a document written for a six-second skim and, before that, for a machine that does not care about your typeface.

Every lesson follows the same nine steps — an objective, a hook, the concept, a worked example, a practice task, the common mistakes, the exam or interview angle, a quiz, and a summary. The worked examples are real resumes, rewritten line by line. The practice tasks are things you do to your own resume in the next ten minutes, not homework for later.

The final module covers LinkedIn, because for most students the resume is finished and the profile is still the default "Student at college" headline that matches zero recruiter searches. And it closes with the pre-application checklist — the fifteen minutes that save more offers than any single bullet rewrite.
prerequisites: Any existing resume, even a rough one
At least one project, however small
A LinkedIn account (or willingness to make one)
audience: First- and second-year students preparing for internships
Final-year students who have applied and heard nothing back
Any branch, any year — this course is not technical
Anyone whose LinkedIn still says "Student at college"

units.title: Resume structure & the skim
units.summary: Recruiters skim in ~6 seconds. Four bones: header, target line, experience, education. One page for a fresher. Target line names the role, not "seeking opportunities".
questions: What are the four sections every resume needs?
Why does a fresher keep the resume to one page?
What does the target line say, and what does it never say?

units.title: ATS parsing
units.summary: Most large companies parse your resume before a human. Killers: two columns, header contact, icons, creative section names. Fix: single column, plain-text contact, standard headings. Run the Notepad paste test.
questions: Why does a two-column resume fail ATS parsing?
Where do contact details go for maximum compatibility?
What does an ATS primarily score on?

units.title: Bullets: action → task → result
units.summary: Strong bullets end in a result. "Responsible for X" is a job description. Find your number: time saved, scale, errors cut. No number? Use scope. Use I, not we, for your part.
questions: What are the three parts of a strong bullet?
Rewrite "Worked on the login module" as an outcome bullet.
How do you write a project nobody used?

units.title: Projects as experience
units.summary: For a fresher, Projects IS the experience section. Choose 2-3 you can defend for 10 minutes. Four elements: name+what, stack, your contribution, outcome. Group projects: name the team, verb YOUR part. Deploy it.
questions: What are the four elements of a project entry?
How do you present a group project without hiding your part?
What is the highest-leverage single upgrade to a GitHub project?

units.title: Education & certifications

questions: What belongs in a fresher Education section?
How do you handle a 6.8 CGPA honestly?
Which certifications are worth a line?

units.title: LinkedIn & applying

questions: What should the default LinkedIn headline become?
Where do projects live on LinkedIn?
What is the 15-minute tailoring pass?

Your CGPA is 7.1. How do you handle it, and why?

previous_year_questions.question: Tell me about a time you improved something measurably. Use a resume bullet structure.
previous_year_questions.solution: Action → task → result. Name the number. E.g. "Cut the report generation from 3 hours of manual Excel to a 15-minute automated script, used weekly by the team."

previous_year_questions.question: Why should we hire you over another fresher with the same CGPA?
previous_year_questions.solution: Do not restate the CGPA. Lead with one outcome-led project bullet the other candidate cannot match — a real number, a real user, a real deployment.

previous_year_questions.question: What is the one change you would make to your resume right now, and why?
previous_year_questions.solution: Name a real, specific improvement you already know you need (e.g. "my third bullet still starts with Responsible for"). Self-awareness plus the fix.

bank.prompt: A recruiter at a campus drive has 200 resumes for 40 seats. Roughly how long is the first skim of each resume?
bank.explanation: Eye-tracking studies of recruiter behaviour put the first pass at around six seconds — a filter, not a read.

bank.prompt: Which four sections are the "bones" every effective resume has?
bank.explanation: Header, target line, experience, education. The rest is optional dressing; these four carry the resume.

bank.prompt: Why does a two-column resume often fail in an applicant tracking system?
options: Most parsers read linearly, so the sidebar vanishes or interleaves with experience text
Two columns trigger a spam filter
It cannot be saved as PDF
bank.explanation: ATS parsers typically read left-to-right, top-to-bottom. Sidebars and text boxes either disappear or get mixed into the main flow.

bank.prompt: Where should contact details go for maximum ATS compatibility?
options: In the body, as the first labelled lines
bank.explanation: Headers and footers are frequently skipped by parsers. The body, labelled in plain text, is always read.

bank.prompt: An ATS primarily scores a resume against a job description based on:
bank.explanation: Keyword overlap drives the match score that decides whether a recruiter ever sees the resume.

bank.prompt: Which section title would an ATS most likely fail to classify as work history?
bank.explanation: Parsers match on standard headings. A creative title like "My Learning Journey" matches nothing.

bank.prompt: What are the three parts of a strong resume bullet?
bank.explanation: Action → task → result. The result is what recruiters quote in hiring meetings, and what most students omit.

bank.prompt: Which is the strongest rewrite of "Worked on the login module"?
options: Responsible for various aspects of authentication
Added password reset, cutting locked-account support tickets by ~30%
bank.explanation: It has a verb, a specific task, and a number. The others are all duty-style.

bank.prompt: You built a project nobody used. What is the honest way to write the bullet?
options: Invent a user number to sound bigger
Use scope: endpoints, lines of tested code, dataset size
Leave the project off the resume
bank.explanation: Scope is honest and specific. Inflated numbers are caught in interviews; adjectives convince nobody.

bank.prompt: Which verb is most honest and informative for a fresher?
bank.explanation: "Migrated" (and built/cut/fixed) are true at intern level and carry real information. Spearheaded and orchestrated imply leadership you may not have had.

bank.prompt: A JD asks for React, TypeScript and testing. You know React well, TypeScript a little, testing not at all. What is correct?
options: List all three to pass the ATS
List React with evidence; omit TypeScript and testing
List React and TypeScript; omit testing
List all three and explain in the cover letter
bank.explanation: List only what you can defend in an interview. Half-truths get past the filter and destroyed in the technical round.

bank.prompt: What is keyword-stuffing, and why does it backfire?
options: Listing too many skills — it makes the resume too long
Adding JD keywords you do not have — it passes the filter then fails the interview
bank.explanation: It is faking JD keywords. It works once, then the technical round ends the application.

bank.prompt: For a fresher, which section carries the most weight?
bank.explanation: Projects are the closest thing a fresher has to employment history, and they are where the decision is usually made.

bank.prompt: What are the four elements of a strong project entry?
options: Repo URL, commit count, stars, forks
bank.explanation: Name + what-it-is, the stack, YOUR specific contribution, and the outcome (a number). Most students omit the outcome.

bank.prompt: Your group project has four members. How should the bullet read?
options: "Built the booking module (Node, MySQL) for a 4-member team project used by 150 hostel residents"
"Worked with 3 others on a management system"
bank.explanation: Name the team context, then verb YOUR specific part with the stack and an outcome.

bank.prompt: Your CGPA is 6.8. What is the correct approach on a fresher resume?
options: Omit it and lead with strong projects
bank.explanation: Never round or inflate — it is caught in verification. Omit and compensate with projects, or show it honestly if the page is strong enough.

bank.prompt: What should a fresher's Education section contain?
options: Degree, college, CGPA (if helpful), graduation year
bank.explanation: Degree, college, CGPA (if it helps), graduation year. School marks are noise after year one of college.

bank.prompt: Which certification is most likely worth a line on a fresher resume?
options: AWS Cloud Practitioner, if the JD asks for cloud
bank.explanation: A genuinely hard or JD-required certification. Generic courses everyone has are not differentiators.

bank.prompt: What should the default LinkedIn headline "Student at college" become?
options: A keyword line: role, top skills, honest status
bank.explanation: The default matches zero recruiter searches. A keyword line is honest AND findable.

bank.prompt: Where should your best projects live on LinkedIn?
options: As Personal Project entries in Experience, plus Featured links
Nowhere — LinkedIn is for jobs only
bank.explanation: Experience is a structured search field; Featured is what a curious recruiter clicks. Use both.

bank.prompt: How much of the LinkedIn About section shows before truncating in the feed?
bank.explanation: About two lines. Those two lines must stand alone — what you are, what you want.

bank.prompt: How should a resume file be named for a SDE internship application?
bank.explanation: Name-Resume-Role. Recruiters download dozens; a named file is findable later.

bank.prompt: Before sending, links on your resume should be checked:
options: In an incognito window, confirming nothing sits behind your own login
Not necessary if they worked last week
bank.explanation: Incognito confirms it works for a stranger. A dead deployment is worse than no link.

bank.prompt: What is the correct use of a tracking spreadsheet during an application season?
options: Log applications after you get a response
Log the day you apply and the day anything changes; review at season end
Optional if you apply to fewer than 10 roles
bank.explanation: Update on apply and on every change. At season end it is the only honest picture of what works.

bank.prompt: A resume is submitted through a portal and marked "unable to parse". Most likely cause?
options: A layout the parser cannot read linearly — two columns or header contact details
bank.explanation: Non-linear layouts (columns, text boxes, header contact) are the classic parsing failure.

bank.prompt: Your best project has 300 users but no "impact" metric like revenue. What is the strongest honest outcome to write?
options: "Used by 300+ students; load time cut 4s to 1s"
"Won second prize at the college hackathon"
bank.explanation: Scale (300+ users) and a measurable change (4s → 1s) are both real numbers. Adjectives are claims; these are evidence.

bank.prompt: Which LinkedIn change will most immediately change how often you appear in recruiter searches?
options: Rewriting the headline as a keyword line
bank.explanation: The headline is a primary search field. "Student at college" matches nothing; a keyword line matches real queries.

bank.prompt: You followed a 4-hour tutorial and cloned Netflix. Can it go on your resume as-is?
options: Yes, a clone shows you can follow instructions
Only if you add stars to the repo
No — add a feature the tutorial did not have, deploy it, then it becomes a project
No, tutorial clones are never allowed
bank.explanation: As-is it is a learning exercise. One original feature plus a deployment makes it a project you can defend.

bank.prompt: When is the best time to apply to a freshly posted role?
options: After 30 days, when it is proven serious
Within the first 48 hours, before the shortlist forms
After someone you know refers you
bank.explanation: Many roles are reviewed rolling and closed once filled. Applying early is a free, real advantage.

bank.prompt: A recruiter searches "react intern bangalore". Which profile surfaces, and why?
options: The one with the most endorsements
The one whose headline, About and Experience all contain those keywords in searchable text
The one with the best photo
The one with the longest About section
bank.explanation: LinkedIn search runs over structured and text fields. Keywords in headline, About and Experience are what match.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain what a recruiter looks for in the first six seconds of a resume
Name the four sections every resume needs
Restructure a resume so the skim test finds what matters

payload.text:
A recruiter at a campus drive has 200 resumes for 40 seats and one afternoon. They do not read them. They skim them — top third, a few keywords, a decision. Research on eye-tracking puts the first pass at around six seconds, and in those six seconds they are looking for four things: who you are, what you want, what you have done, and whether you are worth a call.

Your resume is not a document you write for yourself. It is a document written for a skim.

## The skim has a shape

When a recruiter picks up your resume, their eyes follow a predictable path — not because they are lazy, but because they are fast. They start at the top-left of the page, take in the name and the role you are targeting, then drop to the first bullet of your most recent experience, then scan down the left edge for dates and employers, then check education at the bottom.

That path is why the order of your sections matters more than the polish of your typeface. A resume that hides your degree on page two, or buries your internship under a wall of coursework, is a resume that loses the skim.

## The four sections

Every resume that works has the same four bones, in roughly this order:

1. **Header** — name, phone, email, LinkedIn, city. Not "contact me if interested".
2. **Target line** — the role you want. "SDE Intern" or "Data Analyst Intern". This is what tells the recruiter which pile you belong in.
3. **Experience** — internships, projects, open source, research. This is the bulk, and it is where the decision is made.
4. **Education** — degree, college, CGPA if strong, graduation year.

Skills, certifications and achievements hang off those four. They are supporting cast, not the play.

payload.title: What the skim is looking for
rows: Which role this resume is for

payload.title: The one-page rule is not a suggestion
payload.text: A fresher with a one-page resume is telling the recruiter "I know what matters". A fresher with two pages is telling them "I could not cut anything". Neither is a good first impression.

payload.title: Restructuring a resume that fails the skim
payload.problem:
A second-year student's resume, as written:

- Name, "B.Tech CSE Student", phone, email
- "Skills: C, C++, Java, Python, HTML, CSS, JS, React, Node, MongoDB, MySQL, Git, Linux, MS Office"
- "Education: B.Tech CSE, ABC College of Engineering, 2023-2027"
- "Projects: College website (React), Student result portal (PHP), Snake game (Python)"
- "Certifications: Java (Coursera), Python (Udemy), Web Dev (Udemy)"
- "Strengths: Hard working, team player, quick learner, positive attitude"

The problem: nothing tells the recruiter what role this student wants, the skills list is a word cloud, the projects have no outcomes, and the whole bottom half is filler every applicant also has.

steps.title: Add the target line
steps.desc: Under the name, put the role. "SDE Intern — Summer 2026". This alone moves the resume out of the "generic" pile.

steps.title: Cut the skills list to what you can defend
steps.desc: Six skills you can talk about beat sixteen you cannot. Group them: Languages, Web, Tools. Drop MS Office — everyone has it.

steps.title: Give every project an outcome
steps.desc: Not "Built a college website" but "Built the college department site in React used by 300+ students; cut page load from 4s to 1s by lazy-loading the course list".

steps.title: Delete the filler section
steps.desc: No "hard working", no "team player", no "positive attitude". Every resume claims these. Prove them in a bullet instead.

steps.title: Move education down, keep it clean
steps.desc: Degree, college, CGPA (if above 7.5), expected graduation. Nothing more. No school, no 12th marks, no "hobbies".

payload.solution:
The rebuilt resume, top to bottom:

**RAHUL SHARMA** | +91 98xxx xxxxx | rahul@email.com | linkedin.com/in/rahulsharma | github.com/rahuls

**Target: SDE Intern — Summer 2026**

**Projects**
- College department site (React) — used by 300+ students; lazy-loading cut load time 4s → 1s
- Student result portal (PHP, MySQL) — automated result publication for 1,200 students, replacing a manual Excel process
- Snake game (Python, Pygame) — 400+ GitHub stars after a college Discord post

**Skills** — Languages: C++, Python, JavaScript · Web: React, Node, HTML/CSS · Tools: Git, Linux, MySQL

**Education** — B.Tech CSE, ABC College of Engineering, CGPA 8.2, graduating 2027

Same student. Same facts. One of these gets a call.

payload.title: Run the skim test on your own resume
payload.prompt:
Print your resume (or open it full-screen). Set a timer for six seconds. Look at it, then look away and write down, from memory: the role you are targeting, your strongest experience bullet, your degree and college, and your graduation year.

If you cannot recall all four, a recruiter cannot either. Fix whatever you missed — usually the target line or the first bullet — and run the test again.
payload.hint: The most common failure is the missing target line. If a stranger cannot tell what job you want from the top third of the page, you have not finished.

mistakes.mistake: Listing every technology you have ever touched
mistakes.fix: A skills list is a promise. Six skills you can defend in an interview beat sixteen you cannot — the interviewer will pick one at random.

mistakes.mistake: Putting your school and 12th marks on a fresher resume
mistakes.fix: After your first year of college, school marks are noise. Degree, college, CGPA, year. That is all an interviewer needs.

mistakes.mistake: Writing "hard working, team player, quick learner"
mistakes.fix: Every resume claims these. Delete the section and prove one of them inside a real bullet instead.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: In a campus drive with 200 resumes for 40 seats, roughly how long does a recruiter spend on the first pass of each resume, and what are they looking for?
payload.answer: Around six seconds. They are looking for four things: who you are, what role you want, what you have actually done, and whether you are worth a phone call. The skim is a filter, not a read.

points: A resume is written for a recruiter's six-second skim, not for you.
The skim path: header → target line → first experience bullet → left-edge scan → education.
Four bones every resume needs: header, target line, experience, education.
One page for a fresher. Cutting is the skill.
Delete filler attributes; prove them inside real bullets instead.

questions.prompt: What are the four sections every resume needs?
questions.explanation: Header, target line, experience, education. The others are optional dressing; these four are the bones.

questions.prompt: Why should a fresher keep the resume to one page?
options: Because two pages gets rejected by ATS software
Because a one-page resume signals you know what matters
Because there is a legal limit
Because recruiters refuse to read two pages
questions.explanation: It is a signal of judgement, not a hard rule. A one-page resume says you could cut what did not matter.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the target line?
options: "To use my skills for the growth of the organization"
"Looking for a challenging role in a reputed company"
questions.explanation: A specific role with a timeframe. The others are generic and tell the recruiter nothing about which pile you belong in.

lessons.title: ATS: writing for the machine first
lessons.summary: How applicant tracking systems parse your resume, and the four mistakes that get you filtered out before a human sees you.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain what an ATS does to your resume before a human reads it
Restructure a resume so an ATS parses every section correctly
Avoid the four formatting mistakes that fail ATS parsing

payload.text:
You apply online. Your resume goes into an applicant tracking system — Workday, Taleo, Greenhouse, Lever — and for most large companies, that system is the first reader. It does not care how good your typography is. It cares whether it can pull out your name, your email, your work history, and your skills into fixed fields.

If it cannot, your resume is either dropped into a "low match" bucket or shown to a recruiter as an unparseable mess. Either way, you never get the six-second skim.

## What the ATS actually does

An ATS parses your resume into structured fields: name, contact, employers, dates, titles, education, skills. It then scores the resume against the job description by keyword overlap. A human recruiter later looks at the shortlist, often sorted by that score.

This is why two people with identical experience can get different results — one resume parses cleanly and scores well, the other parses into garbage and scores badly.

## The four parsing killers

1. **Tables and text boxes.** Many parsers read left-to-right, top-to-bottom, ignoring visual layout. A two-column resume with your skills in a side column often ends up interleaved with your experience text.
2. **Headers and footers.** Contact details in the header are frequently invisible to the parser. Put them in the body.
3. **Images and icons.** A phone icon instead of the word "Phone", or a photo header, can break field detection.
4. **Creative section names.** "My Journey" instead of "Experience" means the parser does not know it is work history.

The fix for all four is the same: plain single-column layout, standard section names, text (not icons) for contact details.

payload.title: ATS-safe vs ATS-risky
rows: My Journey, Where I Have Been

payload.title: Save as PDF, but keep a .docx copy
payload.text: PDF preserves your layout for the human. Some older ATS parsers mangle PDF text layers. Having both ready lets you submit whichever the portal asks for.

payload.title: Fixing a resume an ATS could not parse
payload.problem:
A student applies through a company portal. The resume looks great in Word: two columns, skills as coloured icons in a sidebar, contact details in the header, a photo top-right, and a section titled "My Learning Journey".

Two weeks later, no response. The student applies again with a friend's referral and gets a call. The friend, who works there, checks: the original application was marked "unable to parse" and never reached a recruiter.

What broke, and how to fix it, section by section.

steps.title: Kill the two-column layout
steps.desc: Move everything into one column. The sidebar skills move under a "Skills" heading after Experience.

steps.title: Move contact details into the body
steps.desc: First line of the document: Name, then Phone, Email, LinkedIn, GitHub — each labelled in plain text.

steps.title: Replace icons with words
steps.desc: No phone glyph, no LinkedIn logo. The words "Phone" and "LinkedIn" are what the parser matches.

steps.title: Rename sections to standard names
steps.desc: "My Learning Journey" becomes "Projects". "Where I Have Been" becomes "Experience". The parser matches on the word.

steps.title: Write dates in a full, consistent format
steps.desc: Jun 2024 – Aug 2024, not Summer '24. The parser needs a month and a year to compute duration.

payload.solution:
The parseable version, same content:

RAHUL SHARMA
Phone: +91 98xxx xxxxx
Email: rahul@email.com
LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/rahulsharma
GitHub: github.com/rahuls

**Experience**
Software Engineering Intern, XYZ Pvt Ltd — Jun 2024 – Aug 2024
- Automated a manual reporting step, cutting 4 hours of weekly work to 15 minutes

**Projects**
College department site (React) — used by 300+ students

**Skills**
C++, Python, JavaScript, React, Node, MySQL, Git, Linux

**Education**
B.Tech CSE, ABC College of Engineering, CGPA 8.2, graduating 2027

Same facts. Now a machine can read them, and a human still can.

payload.title: Parse your own resume
payload.prompt:
Copy the entire text of your resume (Ctrl+A, Ctrl+C, paste into a plain text editor like Notepad). Read what you pasted.

If your contact details are missing, your skills are out of order, your dates are garbled, or two sections have merged into one paragraph — that is exactly what the ATS sees. Fix the source document, paste again, and stop when the plain text reads cleanly top to bottom.
payload.hint: The paste test is the fastest ATS check you can run. If it looks wrong in Notepad, it looks wrong to the parser.

mistakes.mistake: Using a two-column template with a skills sidebar
mistakes.fix: Most parsers read linearly. A sidebar either vanishes or interleaves with your experience. Single column, always.

mistakes.mistake: Putting your phone and email in the document header
mistakes.fix: Headers are frequently skipped. Put contact details as the first lines of the body, labelled in plain text.

mistakes.mistake: Inventing a creative section title
mistakes.fix: "My Journey" means nothing to a parser. Use "Experience", "Projects", "Education", "Skills" — the words it matches on.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A resume is submitted through an online portal and marked "unable to parse". What is the most likely cause, and what is the single most effective fix?
payload.answer: Most likely a layout the parser cannot read linearly — a two-column template, text boxes, or contact details in the header. The single most effective fix is a plain single-column layout with contact details in the body and standard section names.
payload.source: ATS parsing behaviour, Workday / Greenhouse / Taleo

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: For most large companies, an ATS reads your resume before a person does.
It parses you into fixed fields and scores keyword overlap with the job description.
Four parsing killers: two columns, header/footer contact, icons, creative section names.
Fix is always the same: single column, plain text contact, standard headings.
Run the paste test: Ctrl+A into Notepad. If it reads cleanly, so does the parser.

questions.prompt: Where should your contact details go for maximum ATS compatibility?
options: In the body, as the first labelled lines
questions.explanation: Headers and footers are frequently invisible to parsers. The body, labelled in plain text, is always read.

questions.prompt: Which section name would an ATS most likely fail to classify as work history?
questions.explanation: Parsers match on standard headings. "My Learning Journey" matches nothing.

questions.prompt: What does an ATS primarily score your resume on?
options: Keyword overlap with the job description
questions.explanation: Keyword overlap with the job description. Which is why tailoring the skills and experience wording per application matters.

modules.title: Module 2 — Experience bullets that survive a skim
modules.summary: Turning projects and internships into outcome-led bullets. The formula, the numbers, and the verbs that work.

lessons.title: From duties to outcomes
lessons.summary: The single rewrite that changes how a bullet reads: stop describing what you did, start describing what changed.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Rewrite a duty-style bullet into an outcome-style bullet
Apply the action → task → result structure to any experience
Find a real number for a bullet that seems to have none

payload.text:
Here are two bullets from the same internship:

- "Responsible for the backend of the company dashboard."
- "Rebuilt the dashboard's data layer, cutting the API's p95 response time from 1.8s to 240ms for 40 daily users."

Same work. Same person. The first bullet tells a recruiter nothing they can repeat to their manager. The second one is a sentence they can quote in a hiring meeting.

The difference is not vocabulary. It is that the second bullet ends in a result.

## The shape of a bullet that works

Every good bullet has three parts, and most weak bullets are missing the third:

1. **Action** — a strong verb. Built, cut, automated, migrated, designed.
2. **Task** — what you did it to. The system, the process, the codebase.
3. **Result** — what changed. Faster, cheaper, used by more people, fewer errors, less time.

"Responsible for X" fails on all three. "Responsible" is not an action — it is a job description. And there is no result.

## Finding the number you think you do not have

Most students say "my project had no measurable outcome". It almost always does. Ask three questions:

- **Time:** how long did this take before, and how long after?
- **Scale:** how many people used it, how many records, how many requests?
- **Change:** what was broken or slow or manual, and what is it now?

If the answer is genuinely "nothing changed" — you built a to-do app and nobody used it — then the honest number is the scope: "a to-do app for 3 courses, 12 endpoints, 800 lines of tested code". Specific beats vague even when there is no impact number.

payload.title: Duty vs outcome
rows: "Added password reset, cutting support tickets about locked accounts by ~30%"
"Automated the weekly sales report, saving 3 hours of manual Excel work each week"
"Wrote 60 unit tests that caught 4 regressions before release"
"Built the department site in React, used by 300+ students, load time cut 4s → 1s"

payload.title: If you truly have no number, use scope, not adjectives
payload.text: "A REST API with 12 endpoints and 800 lines of tests" is stronger than "a robust, scalable backend". Adjectives are claims; numbers are evidence.

payload.title: Rewriting three real bullets
payload.problem:
A student's project section, as originally written:

- "Made a college result portal using PHP and MySQL."
- "Worked on a movie recommendation system using Python."
- "Did an internship at a startup where I helped with their website."

Every one of these is a duty, not an outcome. None of them survives a skim. Rewrite each one.

steps.title: Portal: find the scale and the change
steps.desc: What did the portal replace? If results used to be published as a PDF on a noticeboard, and now students log in and see them — that is the outcome. How many students? 1,200. That is your number.

steps.title: Recommendation system: what does it actually do, and how well?
steps.desc: If it has an accuracy number, use it. If not, use the scope: dataset size, the algorithm, how many movies. "Cosine-similarity recommender over 5,000 MovieLens ratings" is specific.

steps.title: Internship: what did you touch, and what was the effect?
steps.desc: "Helped with their website" is invisible. What did you change? A bug, a page, a deploy process? If you only fixed small things, say so honestly with scope: "fixed 15 UI bugs across 4 pages over 6 weeks".

steps.title: Rebuild all three with action → task → result
steps.desc: Strong verb, the thing, the change. Read each one aloud. If it does not end in something that changed, rewrite the ending.

payload.solution:
The rewritten section:

- **Student result portal (PHP, MySQL)** — Built a login-based result portal serving 1,200 students, replacing a manual noticeboard process; result publication time cut from 2 days to same-day.
- **Movie recommender (Python, scikit-learn)** — Implemented a cosine-similarity recommender over 5,000 MovieLens ratings, evaluating 3 similarity metrics to pick the best; 78% top-3 hit rate on held-out ratings.
- **Web intern, ABC Startup (6 weeks)** — Fixed 15 UI bugs across 4 customer-facing pages and added a contact form that cut support emails by roughly a third.

Same person. Now a recruiter has three sentences they can repeat to a hiring manager.

payload.title: Rewrite your three weakest bullets
payload.prompt:
List every experience, project and internship bullet on your current resume. Find the three weakest — the ones that start with "Responsible for", "Worked on", "Helped with", or "Assisted in".

Rewrite each using action → task → result. For each, force yourself to write down one number, even if it is a scope number (how many users, how many endpoints, how many lines of tests). If you cannot find a number, the bullet is still too vague.
payload.hint: Start the bullet with a past-tense action verb: built, cut, automated, migrated, designed, shipped, fixed.

mistakes.mistake: Starting every bullet with "Responsible for"
mistakes.fix: Responsible for is a job description, not an achievement. Start with a past-tense action verb: built, cut, automated, migrated.

mistakes.mistake: Hiding behind "we" so your own contribution is invisible
mistakes.fix: "We built" tells the recruiter nothing about you. Say what you specifically did inside the team work.

mistakes.mistake: Inflating a small fix into a transformation
mistakes.fix: Recruiters smell inflation. "Cut load time from 4s to 1s" is great if true. If you only fixed a typo, say "fixed", and let the volume of fixes speak.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Rewrite this bullet as an outcome-led bullet: "Responsible for the backend of the company dashboard."
payload.answer: Any version with action → task → result. Example: "Rebuilt the dashboard's data layer, cutting the API's p95 response time from 1.8s to 240ms for 40 daily users." The key is ending in what changed.
payload.source: Standard resume-writing practice

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Every good bullet: action → task → result. Most weak bullets miss the result.
Find your number: time saved, scale reached, errors cut. No number? Use scope.
"Responsible for" is a job description. Replace it with a past-tense verb.
Use "I", not "we", for your own contribution inside team work.
Specific beats vague even when there is no impact number.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a strong resume bullet?
questions.explanation: Action → task → result. The result is the part most students omit, and the part recruiters quote in hiring meetings.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest rewrite of "Worked on the login module"?
options: "Added password reset, cutting locked-account support tickets by ~30%"
questions.explanation: It has a verb, a specific task, and a number. The others are all duty-style.

questions.prompt: You built a project nobody used. What is the honest way to write the bullet?
options: Invent a user number to sound bigger
Use scope: endpoints, lines of tested code, dataset size
Leave the project off the resume
questions.explanation: Scope is honest and specific. Inflated numbers get caught in interviews; adjectives convince nobody.

lessons.title: Action verbs and the words that get you filtered
lessons.summary: Which verbs carry weight, which ones are filler, and how to match the job description without keyword-stuffing.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Choose action verbs that match the level of the work you did
Identify and replace filler phrases that carry no information
Tailor resume wording to a job description without keyword-stuffing

payload.text:
There is a version of resume advice that says "start every bullet with a power verb" and then hands you a list of fifty: spearheaded, orchestrated, leveraged, synergized. Most of those words make your resume worse, not better.

"Spearheaded the migration of the user table" for an intern who ran a script once is a claim that collapses in the interview. "Ran the migration script for the user table, verified row counts, and rolled back a bad batch" is a claim you can defend.

The right verb is the one that is true at your level.

## Verbs that carry information

A good action verb tells the recruiter the *kind* of work you did. The useful families:

- **Built / shipped** — you produced something that exists now.
- **Cut / reduced / automated** — you made something faster, cheaper or smaller.
- **Migrated / upgraded** — you moved something from state A to state B.
- **Fixed / debugged** — you found and resolved a real fault.
- **Designed / architected** — you made the structural decisions (use carefully as a fresher).
- **Tested / validated** — you proved something works.

## Words that are filler

"Helped", "assisted", "participated", "involved in", "responsible for" — these are all attempts to avoid saying what you actually did. Replace each with the specific thing.

"Various", "several", "many" — if you can count it, count it.

"Robust", "scalable", "efficient", "user-friendly" — adjectives are claims. A number is evidence.

## Matching the job description, honestly

Read the job description. Note the three or four skills or technologies it repeats. If you genuinely have them, make sure they appear in your resume in your own words — in a project bullet, not just a skills list.

If you do not have them, do not fake them. A resume that matches on paper and fails the first technical question is worse than one that was honest and got a call for a different role.

payload.title: Filler → specific
rows: "Built 4 REST endpoints for the order service"
"Migrated 12k user rows from MySQL to Postgres, verified counts"
"Cut bundle size 1.2MB → 380KB by code-splitting the router"

payload.title: One true verb beats five impressive ones
payload.text: "Built", "cut", "fixed", "migrated" are the four that do the most work for a fresher. You do not need "spearheaded" or "orchestrated" until you have actually led something.

payload.title: Tailoring one resume to two different job descriptions
payload.problem:
Rahul has one solid project: a college department site in React, used by 300+ students, with a Node backend and MySQL.

He is applying to two roles:

1. **Frontend Engineer intern** — the JD repeats: React, TypeScript, CSS, performance, accessibility.
2. **Backend Engineer intern** — the JD repeats: Node, REST, databases, caching, testing.

He has one set of experience. How does he write two resumes that are both honest?

steps.title: Write the common core once
steps.desc: The facts never change: React site, 300+ students, Node backend, MySQL, load-time cut. Draft the bullets once.

steps.title: Frontend version: lead with the frontend facts
steps.desc: First bullet emphasises React, the load-time win, component structure. Backend appears second, briefly. Skills list puts React/JS first.

steps.title: Backend version: lead with the backend facts
steps.desc: First bullet emphasises the Node API, the database schema, the query that was slow. Frontend appears second, briefly. Skills list puts Node/MySQL first.

steps.title: Cut what the JD does not care about
steps.desc: Neither version mentions the Snake game or the Coursera certificates. They are real, but they are not what these two roles are hiring for.

payload.solution:
Frontend version, first two bullets:

- Rebuilt the department site in React, cutting page load from 4s to 1s via route-level code-splitting and lazy-loaded course data
- Designed a 14-component library reused across 6 pages, with keyboard-navigable menus meeting WCAG AA

Backend version, first two bullets:

- Designed and built the Node/Express API (18 REST endpoints) behind the department site, with MySQL schema normalised to 3NF
- Profiled and fixed the slowest query (result lookup, 900ms → 40ms) by adding a composite index and connection pooling

Same project. Same truth. Each resume answers the question the JD is actually asking.

payload.title: Tailor for one real job posting
payload.prompt:
Find one real internship or fresher job posting you could plausibly apply for. Copy the JD text.

Underline the three skills or technologies it mentions most. Now go through your resume and, for each one, write down where (if anywhere) you have evidence of it. Anything you have not actually done, strike off your skills list. Anything you have done but buried, move it up.
payload.hint: The goal is not to match every keyword. It is to make sure the three that matter are impossible to miss.

mistakes.mistake: Using "spearheaded" or "orchestrated" as an intern
mistakes.fix: These imply leadership you may not have had. "Built", "cut", "fixed", "migrated" are true at every level and carry more information.

mistakes.mistake: Stuffing the skills list with every word from the JD
mistakes.fix: Keyword-stuffing gets you past the first filter and destroyed in the interview. List only what you can defend.

mistakes.mistake: Sending the identical resume to every application
mistakes.fix: A resume tailored to the three skills that matter in a JD consistently outperforms a generic one. Same facts, different emphasis.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A job description asks for "React, TypeScript, testing". You know React well, have used TypeScript a little, and have never written a test. How should your resume handle this?
payload.answer: List React with evidence in a project bullet. Mention TypeScript only if you can defend it in an interview — a half-truth is a trap. Do not list testing at all; instead, if you have any testing-adjacent experience (manual QA, verifying outputs), describe that honestly. Never fake a skill the interview will probe.
payload.source: Interview screening reality

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: The right verb is true at your level: built, cut, fixed, migrated.
Filler words: helped, assisted, various, robust, scalable. Replace with specifics.
Adjectives are claims; numbers are evidence.
Tailor emphasis per JD using the same honest facts — never invent skills.
A resume that matches on paper and fails the interview is worse than an honest one.

questions.prompt: Which verb family is most honest and informative for a fresher?
questions.explanation: These are true at intern level and carry real information about the kind of work.

questions.prompt: What is keyword-stuffing, and why does it backfire?
options: Listing too many skills — it makes the resume too long
Adding JD keywords you do not have — it passes the ATS then fails the interview
Using the same verb repeatedly — it reads as lazy
Putting skills in the header — it clutters the top
questions.explanation: It is adding skills you cannot defend to match the JD. It gets you past the first filter and destroyed in the technical round.

questions.prompt: You are applying to a backend role with the same project as a frontend role. What changes?
options: The facts stay identical; the emphasis, order and skills list shift to backend
You delete the frontend work entirely
You add backend skills you have not used
questions.explanation: Same honest facts, different emphasis. The backend version leads with the API and database work.

modules.title: Module 3 — Projects and education, done properly
modules.summary: How to present projects so they read as experience, and how to handle education, CGPA and certifications without filler.

lessons.title: Projects as experience
lessons.summary: For a fresher, projects are the experience section. How to choose, structure and present them so they carry the resume.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Select the two or three projects that best represent your ability
Structure a project entry with the four elements recruiters look for
Present a project you did as a group without hiding your own contribution

payload.text:
If you are a fresher, your Projects section is doing the work that an experienced hire's Employment section does. A recruiter reading your resume for an internship is really asking one question: has this person built anything that worked?

Three projects, each with a clear stack, a clear outcome and a clear personal contribution, beat ten GitHub repos nobody has cloned. The section is not a mirror of your GitHub. It is an argument that you can build.

## Choose two or three, not ten

The projects on your resume should be the ones you could talk about for ten minutes each without notes. That means cutting. A project you abandoned in a weekend, a tutorial you followed, a "ToDo app" clone — these can live on GitHub. They do not belong on the page.

A good resume project has:
- A **real user** or a **real dataset** — not "for practice".
- A **stack you can name** — languages, frameworks, database.
- A **number** — users, records, load time, accuracy, uptime.
- A **thing that was hard** — the problem you hit and solved.

## The four elements of a project entry

1. **Name and one-line what-it-is.** "Student result portal — login-based result publication for 1,200 students."
2. **Stack.** PHP, MySQL, Apache. Or React, Node, MongoDB. Name what you actually used.
3. **Your contribution, specific.** What did you personally build? The schema? The auth? The front end?
4. **The outcome.** A number, a change, a scale. This is the part most students skip.

## Group projects

If it was a team project, do not write "we built" and leave your own part invisible. Write the team scope in one clause, then your part in the verb: "Built the authentication and session layer (JWT, 3 roles) for a 4-member team project serving 200 users."

payload.title: Weak vs strong project entry
rows: "TaskFlow (React, Node, MongoDB) — team of 3; built the drag-and-drop board and offline sync used by 80 hostelmates"
"Dept site (React, Node) — 300+ students; route-level code-splitting cut load 4s → 1s"
"Recommender (Python, scikit-learn) — cosine similarity over 5k MovieLens ratings; 78% top-3 hit rate"

payload.title: One project with a number beats three without
payload.text: A single entry that names a stack, a scale and a result is worth more than three tutorial clones listed side by side.

payload.title: Turning a tutorial clone into a resume project
payload.problem:
A student has these on their GitHub:

1. A Netflix clone (React, TMDB API) — followed a 4-hour YouTube tutorial.
2. A portfolio site (HTML, CSS, JS).
3. A weather app (React, OpenWeather API).
4. A calculator (Python, Tkinter).

They feel none of these are "real" enough for a resume. They are right — as written, none of them is. But two of them can be rebuilt into something real in a weekend each.

steps.title: Drop the calculator and the plain portfolio
steps.desc: The calculator is a tutorial exercise. The portfolio is a website, not a project — its own entry can be a line in the header if needed.

steps.title: Rebuild the Netflix clone into a real product
steps.desc: Keep the front end. Add accounts, a watchlist that persists, and a "continue watching" row computed from real watch state. Deploy it. Give it a URL.

steps.title: Give the weather app a reason to exist
steps.desc: Add something the tutorial did not have: 7-day hourly data, a saved-cities list, offline caching of the last fetch. Now it is a product, not a clone.

steps.title: Write each with the four elements
steps.desc: Name + what-it-is, stack, your specific contribution, outcome. For the rebuilt clone, the outcome can be "deployed, used by N friends" — honest and specific.

payload.solution:
Two projects, rebuilt:

- **CineStream (React, Node, MongoDB, TMDB API)** — Movie browsing app with accounts, persistent watchlist and continue-watching; built the auth layer and the watch-state aggregation endpoint; deployed on Render, used by 25 friends.
- **WeatherLens (React, OpenWeather API)** — Multi-city weather with hourly 7-day forecasts and offline caching of last fetch; rebuilt the data layer to batch 5 city requests into 1, cutting API calls by 80%.

Same skills. Now each entry reads as something a person built and shipped, not something a person followed.

payload.title: Pick and upgrade one project this week
payload.prompt:
Look at your GitHub. Choose the one project that is closest to being resume-worthy but currently undersells itself. This week, add ONE thing that gives it a real user or a real number: deploy it, add persistence, add a feature a real user would want, or run it against a real dataset.

Then rewrite its resume entry with the four elements: name + what-it-is, stack, your specific contribution, outcome.
payload.hint: Deploying is often the highest-leverage single change. A live URL is proof it runs; a GitHub repo is only proof it compiles.

mistakes.mistake: Listing every repo on GitHub
mistakes.fix: The resume is an argument, not an archive. Two or three projects you can defend for ten minutes each beat ten tutorial clones.

mistakes.mistake: Writing "we built" for a group project with no personal contribution named
mistakes.fix: Name the team size, then use the verb for YOUR part: "Built the auth layer for a 4-member team project..."

mistakes.mistake: Following a tutorial and calling it a project
mistakes.fix: A tutorial clone is a learning exercise. Add one feature the tutorial did not have, deploy it, and it becomes a project.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What are the four elements of a strong project entry on a fresher resume?
payload.answer: Name + one-line what-it-is, the stack you actually used, your specific contribution, and the outcome (a number: users, scale, load time, accuracy). Most students omit the outcome.
payload.source: Standard fresher resume practice

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: For a fresher, Projects is the experience section — it carries the resume.
Choose two or three you can defend for ten minutes, not ten clones.
Four elements: name + what-it-is, stack, your contribution, outcome.
Group projects: name the team, then verb YOUR part.
Deploying is often the highest-leverage upgrade: a live URL beats a repo.

questions.prompt: For a fresher, which section carries the most weight?
questions.explanation: Projects. They are the closest thing a fresher has to employment history, and they are where the hiring decision is usually made.

questions.prompt: You did a group project. How should the bullet read?
options: "Built the booking module (Node, MySQL) for a 4-member team project used by 150 hostel residents"
"Worked with 3 others on a management system"
questions.explanation: It names the team context but leads with YOUR specific contribution and the stack.

questions.prompt: Your project has no users yet. What is the honest outcome to write?
options: Deploy it and use the real number, or use scope (endpoints, lines of tested code, dataset size)
questions.explanation: Deploy first if you can — then the number is real. If not, scope is honest and still specific.

lessons.title: Education, CGPA and certifications without the filler
lessons.summary: What to include, what to cut, and how to handle a CGPA you are not thrilled about.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decide what belongs in the Education section and what to cut
Handle a low or middling CGPA without hiding or apologising for it
Select certifications that add signal and cut the ones that do not

payload.text:
There is a specific anxiety every fresher has about the Education section: "my CGPA is 7.1, is that going to get me filtered out?"

The honest answer is: at many companies, yes, a 7.0 is a cutoff for the first filter — and there is nothing you can write on the resume to change that. But at many others, including most startups and product companies, 7.1 is fine and what matters is what you built. The resume's job is to make sure that when a human looks, the CGPA is not the most interesting thing on the page.

## What belongs in Education

Degree, college, expected graduation year, and CGPA if it helps. That is the whole section for a fresher.

- **Degree and branch:** B.Tech CSE, B.E. ECE, B.Sc. IT — exact name as your university writes it.
- **College:** the full name. Not an abbreviation a recruiter outside your state will not recognise.
- **Graduation year:** expected, e.g. "Graduating 2027". Internship season is driven by this number.
- **CGPA:** include it if 7.5 or above. Below that, it is optional — see the strategy below.

## What to cut

School name and 12th marks. After year one of college, nobody is hiring you for your 12th percentage. "Hobbies", "Extra-curricular" as their own sections. A "Declaration" paragraph ("I hereby declare that the above information is true...") — this is a form-field convention, not a resume section.

## Certifications: almost always too many

Three certifications from Coursera/Udemy that everyone also has are not differentiators. They are the resume equivalent of a skills word cloud. The exception is a certification that is genuinely hard or genuinely required — a cloud certification the JD asks for, a competitive-programming rating, a national-level exam rank. Those go on. The rest can go in a single line or off the page entirely.

Optional. If the rest of the resume is strong, show it; if not, lead with projects and omit.
Usually omit. Compensate with strong projects, internships, or a competitive rating. Some companies will filter on it regardless — nothing on the resume changes that.

lessons.title: LinkedIn: the profile that gets found
lessons.summary: Headline, About, Experience and Skills on LinkedIn — how they differ from the resume, and how recruiters actually search.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write a LinkedIn headline that works as a search keyword and a pitch
Write an About section that a recruiter reads past the first line
Structure Experience and Skills so recruiter searches surface you

payload.text:
Recruiters do not only read resumes that arrive. They search. On LinkedIn, a recruiter searching for "react intern bangalore" is running a keyword search across headlines, about sections, experience and skills. If your profile does not contain those words in searchable places, you do not exist in that search — no matter how good your GitHub is.

Your LinkedIn is not a copy of your resume. It is a searchable version of it, with room for a voice the one-page resume does not have.

## The headline is not your job title

The default LinkedIn headline is your current role at your current company — which for a student is "Student at ABC College". That is a headline that matches zero recruiter searches.

Write it as a keyword line: "CSE Undergrad | SDE Intern aspirant | React, Node, Python | DSA". Each pipe-separated chunk is a term someone might search. "Aspirant" is honest; it does not claim an internship you do not have.

## About: first two lines do the work

LinkedIn truncates the About section after about two lines in the feed. The first two lines must stand alone. Start with what you are and what you want, not with a philosophical opener.

Then: what you have built, what you are learning, what you are looking for. First person. Three short paragraphs, not a wall.

## Experience and Skills are search fields

Experience on LinkedIn is structured data a search runs over. Put your internships, significant projects and positions of responsibility here — even unpaid, even short. Each needs a description with the same outcome-led bullets as the resume.

Skills: the first three are what recruiters see without clicking. Put your three strongest there. LinkedIn lets you take skill assessments; a passed badge is a small but real signal.

lessons.title: The pre-application checklist
lessons.summary: The final pass before you hit apply: what to verify, what to tailor, and how to track applications without losing your mind.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Run a complete pre-application check on resume and profile
Tailor an application to a specific job description in under 15 minutes
Set up a simple tracking sheet that survives a full application season

payload.text:
The most common application failure is not a bad resume. It is a good resume, sent badly: wrong file name, a stale LinkedIn URL, a cover letter addressed to the wrong company, or a application for a role that closed three weeks ago.

The checklist in this lesson takes fifteen minutes. It has saved more offers than any single bullet rewrite.

## The file and the naming

Name the file `Rahul-Sharma-Resume-SDE.pdf`. Not `resume_final_v3.pdf`. Not `Resume (1).pdf`. The recruiter downloads forty of these; a named file is findable in their folder a week later.

Always PDF unless the portal explicitly asks for .docx. PDF preserves layout. Check that the PDF's text is selectable (Ctrl+A should highlight text) — a scanned-image PDF is invisible to ATS.

## The links

Click every link in the resume and on LinkedIn, in an incognito window. The GitHub should not 404. The deployed project should not be down. A dead link on a resume is worse than no link — it is a broken promise in the first minute.

LinkedIn URL: claim a clean one. `linkedin.com/in/rahul-sharma-cse` not `linkedin.com/in/rahul-sharma-8a3b2c9`. You can set this once in settings.

## The tailoring pass (15 minutes)

1. Re-read the JD. Underline the three skills it repeats.
2. Make sure those three appear in your resume — in a bullet, not just the skills list.
3. If the role names a city or mode (remote/hybrid/onsite), and your resume or LinkedIn says nothing, add your city to the header. Recruiters filter on it.
4. If there is a named recruiter or a referral, use their name in the opening line of any note you send.

## Tracking

A spreadsheet. Columns: company, role, date applied, link, status (applied / screening / interview / offer / rejected / ghosted), next action, next action date. Update it the day you apply, and the day anything changes. At the end of a season, this sheet is the only thing that tells you which of your channels actually work.
