courses.title: Aptitude & Reasoning Mastery
courses.subtitle: Clear the OA round - the highest-frequency quant and reasoning topics from TCS, Infosys, Wipro and Capgemini, taught with the shortcuts that save minutes
courses.description:
Every campus placement and off-campus OA opens with an aptitude round. A learner who clears it reaches the coding round; one who does not never sees it. This course teaches exactly the topics that appear - no filler, no "advanced" chapters that never show up in an actual OA.

Eight lessons across four modules: number system and HCF/LCM, ratio-partnership-mixtures and profit-loss, speed-trains-work, then the reasoning half - series, coding-decoding, blood relations, direction sense and syllogisms. Every lesson uses the same nine-step structure: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, the exam angle, a quiz and a one-screen summary.

**Who this is for:** any student, any branch, preparing for TCS NQT, Infosys, Wipro, Capgemini, Cognizant or any other company whose OA starts with quant. Also useful for GATE/PSU prelims and bank exams.

**What you need:** class-10 arithmetic. No calculator needed - every technique is taught for mental or rough-paper calculation.
outcomes: Find any unit digit using the power-cycle method in under 15 seconds
Recognise HCF, LCM and "same remainder" patterns on sight
Solve ratio, partnership and mixture questions with alligation
Compute successive discounts and SI/CI differences in one line
Apply D = S x T with relative speed for trains, boats and opposite directions
Solve work-rate problems using the one-day-work method
Decode number series, letter series and coding-decoding rules
Draw family trees, compass diagrams and Venn circles that force the right answer
courses.about_course:
This course is built around one idea: aptitude is not about being "smart at maths" - it is about recognising a small number of patterns and applying the matching shortcut under time pressure. There are perhaps forty patterns that cover 95% of the questions asked in Indian campus OAs. This course teaches the highest-frequency half of them, with the shortcut for each, a worked example, and drills that build the recognition speed.

Quant (Modules 1-3) is taught with the techniques that replace calculator work: power cycles, HCF-of-differences, the alligation cross, the SI-CI difference formula, relative speed and work rates. Reasoning (Module 4) is taught with the diagrams that make wrong options visibly wrong: difference rows for series, position tables for coding, family trees for blood relations, compass grids for direction, and Venn circles for syllogisms.

Every lesson ends with a quiz graded on the server, and the course finishes with a 15-question timed exam drawn from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

No calculator needed - every technique is mental or rough-paper

Anyone taking TCS NQT, Infosys, Wipro, Capgemini or Cognizant OAs

units.title: Number System and HCF/LCM
units.summary: Unit digit = power cycle (period 1/2/4); reduce exponent mod period. Same-remainder pattern = HCF of pairwise differences. LCM - r for remainder questions. HCF x LCM = product (two numbers only).
questions: How do you find the unit digit of 7^256?
What is the "same remainder" HCF pattern?
When does HCF x LCM = product apply?

units.title: Ratio, Partnership and Mixtures
units.summary: Share proportional to capital x months. Mid-year joiner counts only their actual months. Alligation cross: ratio = (mean - cheap):(expensive - mean). Draw-and-replace: final = x(1 - y/x)^n.
questions: How is partnership profit shared when partners join at different times?
State the alligation rule.
What is the draw-and-replace formula?

units.title: Profit-Loss, Discounts and Interest
units.summary: Profit% on CP always. Successive discounts: a+b-ab/100. 2-year CI-SI difference = P(R/100)^2. Dishonest dealer: base is weight given, not claimed.
questions: Why are two 10% discounts not 20%?
What is the 2-year CI-SI difference formula?
What base is used for a dishonest-dealer profit %?

units.title: Speed, Trains and Work
units.summary: D = S x T. km/h to m/s: x 5/18. Same direction |S1-S2|, opposite S1+S2. Train+platform distance = L_train + L_platform. Work: add rates 1/a + 1/b. Worker leaves: fraction done, then remainder / remaining rate.
questions: Convert 60 km/h to m/s.
What distance does a train cover crossing a platform?
How do you combine two workers rates?

units.title: Series, Coding and Reasoning
units.summary: Always write the difference row first. Letters: convert to positions (A=1..Z=26), find pattern, convert back. Wrap-around past Z -> A. Coding: decode the shift from one pair, verify, apply. Blood relations: draw the tree. Syllogisms: Venn containment. "All A are B" implies "Some B are A", never "All B are A".
questions: What is the first analysis to run on a number series?
How do you verify a coding shift?
What does "All A are B" always imply?

important_questions: Walk me through how you would find the unit digit of a large power in an OA.
Explain the alligation cross with a milk-water example.
How do you solve a work problem where one worker leaves mid-job?
What is the difference between CI and SI for 2 years, and why?
How do you approach a blood-relation question under time pressure?
State the "same remainder" HCF pattern and when to use it.

previous_year_questions.question: TCS NQT: A 150 m train at 60 km/h crosses a 350 m platform. Time taken?
previous_year_questions.solution: Convert 60 km/h = 50/3 m/s. Distance = 150+350 = 500 m. Time = 500 / (50/3) = 30 seconds.

modules.summary: The arithmetic foundation: divisibility, power cycles, HCF/LCM patterns, percentages and alligation.

lessons.title: Divisibility, remainders and the power cycle
lessons.summary: The number-system shortcuts that turn a 90-second calculation into a 10-second one.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply divisibility rules for 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 11 without a calculator
Find the unit digit of any a^b using the power-cycle method in under 15 seconds
Compute remainders using modular arithmetic

payload.text:
TCS NQT first quant question: "What is the unit digit of 7^256?" Sixty thousand students saw this. Most tried to multiply 7 by itself and ran out of time.

There is a four-second method. Every power of every digit repeats its unit digit in a cycle of at most 4. Once you know the cycle, the question is a remainder, not a multiplication.

## Divisibility rules you must know cold

| Divisor | Rule | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | Last digit even | 348 yes |
| 3 | Sum of digits divisible by 3 | 471: 4+7+1=12 yes |
| 4 | Last two digits divisible by 4 | 1316: 16 yes |
| 8 | Last three digits divisible by 8 | 10576: 576 yes |
| 9 | Sum of digits divisible by 9 | 6354: 18 yes |
| 11 | Alternating sum divisible by 11 | 9182: (9+8)-(1+2)=14 no |

## The power cycle (unit digit)

The unit digit of a^b depends only on the unit digit of a, and it cycles with period 1, 2 or 4:

| Base unit | Cycle | Period |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0, 1, 5, 6 | itself | 1 |
| 4, 9 | 4 then 6, 9 then 1 | 2 |
| 2, 3, 7, 8 | period 4 | 4 |

To find the unit digit of a^b: take b mod (cycle period). If the result is 0, use the last element of the cycle. For very large exponents, reduce b mod 4 first (for period-4 cycles).

## Modular arithmetic essentials

- (a + b) mod d = ((a mod d) + (b mod d)) mod d
- (a x b) mod d = ((a mod d) x (b mod d)) mod d

These let you reduce any huge number to a one-digit calculation before you touch it.

payload.title: Always reduce the exponent mod 4 first
payload.text: For any base ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8, compute (exponent mod 4) before anything else. If it is 0, the answer is the last element of the cycle. This single habit removes most of the time pressure.

payload.title: Finding a remainder without a calculator
payload.problem: Find the unit digit of 7^256. Then find 7^257 mod 5.

steps.title: Step 1 - identify the cycle
steps.desc: Powers of 7 cycle as 7, 9, 3, 1 with period 4.

steps.title: Step 2 - reduce the exponent
steps.desc: 256 / 4 = 64 exactly, so 256 mod 4 = 0. A remainder of 0 means the last element of the cycle.
steps.code_snippet: 256 mod 4 = 0  ->  use 4th element of (7,9,3,1)

steps.title: Step 3 - read off the answer
steps.desc: The 4th element is 1. So 7^256 ends in 1.

steps.title: Step 4 - the second part: mod 5
steps.desc: 7 mod 5 = 2. So 7^257 mod 5 = 2^257 mod 5. Powers of 2 mod 5 cycle 2,4,3,1 with period 4. 257 mod 4 = 1, so the answer is 2.

payload.solution:
Unit digit of 7^256 = 1.
7^257 mod 5 = 2.

Notice the second part did not need the unit digit at all - reducing the base mod 5 first is faster when the modulus is 5.

payload.title: Five unit-digit drills
payload.prompt:
Find the unit digit of each, then check with the cycle:

1. 3^47
2. 8^2025
3. 4^99
4. 9^50
5. 2^303

Write down the cycle, reduce the exponent mod the period, then read the answer. Time yourself - each should take under 15 seconds.
payload.hint: For 8^2025: cycle of 8 is 8-4-2-6 (period 4). 2025 mod 4 = 1, so the answer is the 1st element: 8.

mistakes.mistake: Multiplying out the power instead of using the cycle
mistakes.fix: Never compute 7^256. Reduce the exponent mod 4 and read the cycle. The cycle exists precisely so you never multiply.

mistakes.mistake: Using the digit-sum rule for every divisor
mistakes.fix: Digit sum works for divisibility by 3 and 9 only. For 7, 11, 13 you need the direct rule or modular arithmetic.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that remainder 0 means the last cycle element
mistakes.fix: If exponent mod period = 0, the answer is the LAST element of the cycle, not the first. 256 mod 4 = 0, use 1 not 7.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is the unit digit of 7^256?
payload.answer: 1. The unit digits of powers of 7 cycle as 7, 9, 3, 1 with period 4. Since 256 is divisible by 4, the unit digit is the last element of the cycle: 1.
payload.source: TCS NQT / Infosys OA style

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Divisibility: 3 and 9 use digit sum; 4 and 8 use last 2/3 digits; 11 uses alternating sum.
Unit digit of a^b: find the cycle of a (period 1, 2 or 4), reduce b mod the period.
Remainder 0 from the reduction means the LAST element of the cycle.
Always reduce the exponent first - it is the fastest single step.

questions.prompt: What is the unit digit of 3^47?
questions.explanation: Cycle of 3 is 3-9-7-1 (period 4). 47 mod 4 = 3, so the 3rd element: 7.

questions.prompt: Which divisibility rule uses the alternating sum of digits?
questions.explanation: For 11: (sum of odd-position digits - sum of even-position digits) must be 0 or divisible by 11.

questions.prompt: What is the unit digit of 7^256?
questions.explanation: Unit digit 1 means remainder 1 when divided by 10.

lessons.title: HCF, LCM and the same-remainder pattern
lessons.summary: The pattern recognition that separates a 90th-percentile OA score from a 50th: when a question says "greatest number that divides", it is asking for HCF.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decide in one read whether a problem is asking for HCF or LCM
Solve the classic "greatest divisor" and "smallest multiple" OA patterns
Apply the same-remainder HCF-of-differences technique

payload.text:
Infosys OA: "Find the greatest number that will divide 43, 91 and 183 so as to leave the same remainder in each case."

Students who read "greatest number" and reach for LCM lose three minutes. Students who know the pattern solve it in fifteen seconds: take pairwise differences, then HCF of those differences.

The entire question is a test of whether you recognise the pattern, not whether you can compute an HCF.

## HCF and LCM in one sentence each

- HCF (Highest Common Factor) - the largest number that divides every number in the set. Also called GCD.
- LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) - the smallest positive number that is a multiple of every number in the set.

The identity that ties them (for two numbers only):

HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b

This holds for two numbers only. For three or more, the identity does NOT hold - a common exam trap.

## Euclid's algorithm (fast HCF)

Repeatedly replace the larger number by the remainder of dividing it by the smaller, until the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the HCF.

HCF(48, 18):
48 = 2x18 + 12
18 = 1x12 + 6
12 = 2x6  + 0
-> HCF = 6

## The "same remainder" pattern

If a number d leaves the same remainder r when dividing a, b, c - then d must divide (a-b), (b-c) and (a-c). So:

d = HCF(a-b, b-c, a-c)

This is one of the most frequently asked patterns in Indian campus OAs.

## "Greatest number that divides" vs "smallest number that is a multiple of"

- "Greatest number that divides X, Y, Z" -> HCF
- "Smallest number that is a multiple of X, Y, Z" -> LCM
- "Greatest number that divides ... leaving the same remainder" -> HCF of pairwise differences
- "Smallest number that when divided by X, Y, Z leaves remainder r" -> LCM(X,Y,Z) - r

payload.title: Pattern recognition cheat-sheet
rows: Smallest number that is a multiple of
Leaves remainder r when divided by each

payload.title: Always reduce to coprime before multiplying for LCM
payload.text: LCM(12, 18): factor out the common 6 first -> LCM = 6 x 2 x 3 = 36. Computing LCM as (a x b)/HCF is fine for two numbers but the factor-out method is faster mentally.

payload.title: The "same remainder" question, solved
payload.problem: Find the greatest number that will divide 43, 91 and 183 so as to leave the same remainder in each case.

steps.title: Step 3 - verify the remainder
steps.desc: 43 / 4 = 10 r 3; 91 / 4 = 22 r 3; 183 / 4 = 45 r 3. All leave remainder 3. Correct.

steps.title: Step 4 - state the answer
steps.desc: The greatest such number is 4.

payload.solution:
Answer: 4.

The pattern "same remainder -> HCF of differences" is the entire trick. Without it, students try random divisors and fail.

payload.title: Three classic OA patterns
payload.prompt:
Solve each, then check the pattern you used:

1. Find the greatest number that divides 20, 42 and 60 leaving the same remainder.
2. Find the smallest number which when divided by 35, 56 and 91 leaves a remainder of 7 in each case.
3. HCF of two numbers is 12 and their product is 6336. Find the LCM.
payload.hint: 1: HCF of pairwise differences. 2: LCM(35,56,91) - 7. 3: LCM = product / HCF = 6336 / 12 = 528.

mistakes.mistake: Applying HCF x LCM = product to three numbers
mistakes.fix: The identity holds for two numbers only. For three, compute HCF and LCM separately.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing "greatest divisor" with LCM
mistakes.fix: Greatest number that divides -> HCF. Smallest number that is a multiple of -> LCM. Read the verb, not the noun.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to subtract the remainder in the LCM - r pattern
mistakes.fix: "Leaves remainder 7" means LCM - 7, not LCM. If you answer LCM you are off by exactly the remainder.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Find the greatest number that will divide 43, 91 and 183 so as to leave the same remainder in each case.
payload.answer: 4. Take pairwise differences (48, 92, 140) and compute HCF = 4. Verification: 43, 91, 183 all leave remainder 3 when divided by 4.
payload.source: Infosys / TCS OA classic

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Greatest divisor -> HCF; smallest multiple -> LCM. Read the verb.
Same-remainder pattern: HCF of pairwise differences.
Remainder r on each divisor: LCM - r.
HCF x LCM = product holds for TWO numbers only.

questions.prompt: Greatest number dividing 43, 91, 183 with same remainder?
questions.explanation: HCF of differences 48, 92, 140 = 4.

questions.prompt: Smallest number divisible by 35, 56, 91 leaving remainder 7?
HCF = 12, product = 6336. LCM?
questions.explanation: LCM = product / HCF = 6336 / 12 = 528.

modules.summary: Allocation problems, profit-sharing, the alligation cross, successive discounts and SI/CI differences.

lessons.title: Ratio allocation, partnership and alligation
lessons.summary: How a total is split, how profit follows capital x time, and the alligation technique that turns a long equation into a line on paper.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Split a quantity in a given ratio and compute partnership profit shares
Apply the alligation cross to mixing problems
Solve the draw-and-replace mixture pattern

payload.text:
Capgemini OA: "A and B invest Rs 12,000 and Rs 18,000 in a business. After 8 months, C joins with Rs 15,000. If the annual profit is Rs 12,000, what is C's share?"

Every student who has seen the pattern knows the one formula: share is proportional to capital x months. Every student who has not, sets up three equations and runs out of time.

## Partnership: profit follows capital x time

When partners invest different amounts for different durations, each partner's share of profit is proportional to their capital x time (often written as "investment-months").

Share of X = Total Profit x (X's capital x X's months) / Sum(all capital x time)

If all partners invest for the same time, this simplifies to the ratio of capitals alone.

## The alligation rule

When two ingredients of prices (or concentrations) a and b (a > c > b) are mixed to get a mean price c:

Ratio of quantities = (c - b) : (a - c)

The difference on the opposite side gives the share. This is a weighted average written as a diagram.

Example: Milk Rs 20, water Rs 0, mean Rs 16.
c - b = 16 - 0 = 16; a - c = 20 - 16 = 4.
Ratio milk : water = 16 : 4 = 4 : 1.

## Removal and replacement

A container has x litres of pure milk. y litres are drawn off and replaced with water, repeated n times.

Final milk = x x (1 - y/x)^n

This formula covers the entire family of "draw and replace" questions.

payload.title: Always convert capital x time to the same unit
payload.text: Mixing months and days, or years and months, is the most common source of a wrong partnership answer. Convert everything to months before you divide.

payload.title: A joins mid-year - count only their actual months
payload.text: If C joins after 8 months of a 12-month year, C's time is 4 months, not 12. The question says "after 8 months" meaning 8 months have already passed.

payload.title: Three-partnership profit split and alligation
payload.problem:

Part B: Milk at Rs 20/litre mixed with water to get Rs 16/litre. Ratio?

steps.title: Part A Step 1 - capital x months
Part A Step 2 - simplify the ratio
Part A Step 3 - C share
steps.desc: Total parts 35. C = 5/35 x 12000 = Rs 1,714.

steps.title: Part B - alligation cross

payload.solution:
Part A: C's share = Rs 1,714 (approx). Capital-months 144k:216k:60k = 12:18:5.
Part B: Milk : Water = 4 : 1.

C only held the capital for 4 of the 12 months, so C's capital-months is 60,000 not 180,000. That is why C's share is small despite investing a large amount.

mistakes.fix: C joins after 8 months -> C time is 4 months. Always count the actual months the capital was held.

lessons.title: Profit, loss, successive discounts and interest
lessons.summary: The marked-price chain, why two 10% discounts are not a 20% discount, and the SI/CI difference formula.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute profit/loss percent from cost price and selling price
Apply successive discounts using the single-equivalent-percent method
Use the SI-minus-CI difference formula for 2 years

payload.text:
A shopkeeper offers two successive discounts of 10% and 10% on a Rs 1,000 jacket. Most students say "20% off, so Rs 800".

The actual answer is Rs 810. The first 10% takes Rs 100 off (leaving Rs 900). The second 10% takes 10% of Rs 900 = Rs 90 off (leaving Rs 810).

Successive discounts do not add. They compound - and the compounding is exactly the same mathematics as successive interest rates.

## The profit/loss identity

- Profit% = ((SP - CP) / CP) x 100
- Loss% = ((CP - SP) / CP) x 100

The base is ALWAYS cost price. A common trap: "sold at 20% profit then 20% loss" - the two percentages have different bases, so the net is a loss, not break-even.

## Successive discounts (the single-equivalent method)

Two discounts a% and b% are equivalent to a single discount of:

a + b - (ab/100)

For 10% and 10%: 10 + 10 - (100/100) = 20 - 1 = 19%. So Rs 1,000 -> Rs 810.

For 20% and 30%: 20 + 30 - (600/100) = 50 - 6 = 44%.

Alternatively, multiply the "pay fractions": 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81, so you pay 81%, meaning 19% off.

## Simple and compound interest

SI = P x R x T / 100 (linear growth).
A = P (1 + R/100)^T for CI (exponential growth).

For 2 years: CI - SI = P x (R/100)^2.

This single formula converts every "difference between CI and SI" question from multi-step algebra into one line.

## Dishonest dealer (false weight)

A dealer claims to sell at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Profit% = (1000-900)/900 x 100 = 11.11%. The base is the WEIGHT GIVEN, not the weight claimed.

payload.title: Profit then loss at the same % is a NET LOSS
payload.text: Sell at 20% profit then 20% loss on the same item: 120 x 0.8 = 96. You lose 4%, not break even. The bases are different.

steps.title: Part B - apply the difference formula

lessons.title: Speed, relative speed, trains and boats
lessons.summary: The one equation D = S x T, plus the relative-speed adjustments for trains, rivers and opposite directions.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use D = S x T confidently with unit conversions (km/h to m/s)
Compute relative speed for same-direction and opposite-direction motion
Solve train-crossing-platform and boat-in-stream problems

payload.text:
A 150 m train at 60 km/h crosses a 350 m platform. How long?

Most students convert units halfway, forget the train's own length, or add when they should subtract. The entire question rests on one idea: when the train clears the platform, it has covered its OWN length plus the PLATFORM's length.

Convert 60 km/h to m/s (multiply by 5/18 = 16.67 m/s). Total distance = 150 + 350 = 500 m. Time = 500 / 16.67 = 30 seconds. Three steps, no tricks.

## The master equation

D = S x T

Everything in this topic is this equation plus a unit conversion or a relative-speed adjustment.

## Unit conversion (memorise both directions)

- km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18
- m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5

60 km/h x 5/18 = 16.67 m/s. 10 m/s x 18/5 = 36 km/h.

## Relative speed

- Same direction: S_rel = |S1 - S2|
- Opposite direction: S_rel = S1 + S2

## Trains

- Train crosses a pole: distance = length of train only.
- Train crosses a platform: distance = length of train + length of platform.
- Two trains crossing each other (opposite direction): S_rel = S1 + S2, distance = L1 + L2.
- Two trains same direction: S_rel = |S1 - S2|, distance = L1 + L2.

## Boats and streams

- Downstream: S = B + W (boat + water)
- Upstream: S = B - W (boat against water)
- B = (down + up) / 2;  W = (down - up) / 2

payload.title: What distance to use
headers: Distance in D = S x T
rows: Length of train + length of platform

payload.title: Convert units FIRST, before you set up the equation
payload.text: Mixing km/h with metres is the single largest source of wrong answers in this topic. Convert everything to m/s (or everything to km/h) before you write D = S x T.

Part B: Two trains 200 m and 300 m long approach each other at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. Time to completely cross?

steps.desc: Train length + platform length = 150 + 350 = 500 m.

steps.title: Part B - opposite direction, relative speed
steps.desc: Convert: 72 km/h = 20 m/s; 54 km/h = 15 m/s. S_rel = 20 + 15 = 35 m/s. Distance = 200 + 300 = 500 m. T = 500/35 = 14.29 seconds.

payload.solution:
Part A: 30 seconds.
Part B: 14.29 seconds (500/35 = 100/7 = 14.29 s).

Both parts used the same structure: convert units, pick the right distance, apply D = S x T with the correct speed (absolute or relative).

Solve problems where a worker leaves or joins mid-job

payload.text:
"A can do a job in 12 days, B in 18 days. Together, how long?"

Most students try to find an LCM or set up a proportion and get tangled. The rate method takes one line:

A rate = 1/12 per day. B rate = 1/18 per day. Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per day. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

The shift from "days to finish" to "fraction finished per day" is the entire topic.

## The rate principle

If A finishes a job in N days, A rate is 1/N job per day.

To combine workers, ADD their rates. The combined time is the reciprocal of the combined rate.

## Two workers

A in a days, B in b days:
- Together: 1/(1/a + 1/b) = ab/(a+b) days
- For n days together then one leaves: compute the fraction done, then the remainder / remaining worker's rate.

## The LCM shortcut (mental math)

To add 1/12 + 1/18 without a calculator: take LCM(12,18) = 36. Convert: 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36. Reciprocal = 36/5 = 7.2.

## Pipes and cisterns

Same as work: a pipe that fills in x hours has rate 1/x per hour. A pipe that empties in y hours has rate -1/y. Net rate = sum of signed rates.

payload.title: One leaves mid-job: compute fraction done first
payload.text: A and B work 4 days together, then B leaves. Fraction done in 4 days = 4 x (combined rate). Remaining fraction / A rate = days A works alone. Never try to "adjust the total days".

steps.title: Step 2 - work done in 4 days together
steps.desc: 4 x 1/12 = 1/3 of the job done.

The rate method never requires you to "undo" the joint work - you always compute fraction-done, then divide the remainder by the remaining worker's rate.

modules.summary: The reasoning half of every OA: number and letter series, coding rules, family trees and Venn-diagram syllogisms.

lessons.title: Number series, letter series and coding-decoding
lessons.summary: How to read a series: differences, ratios, alternate terms, and the letter-position method that works for every alphabetic series.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Identify arithmetic, geometric and second-order differences in a number series
Decode letter series using forward (A=1) and reverse (Z=1) positions
Apply coding rules from a given word-code pair to new words

payload.text:
Find the next term: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ___

Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10. The differences themselves increase by 2. Next difference = 12. Answer = 30 + 12 = 42.

This is a second-order arithmetic series - one of the three patterns that cover most number-series questions in Indian OAs. The other two are geometric (multiply by a constant) and alternating (two interleaved series).

The skill is not arithmetic. It is knowing which three analyses to run, in which order.

## The three analyses (in this order)

1. First differences - subtract consecutive terms. If the differences are constant -> arithmetic. If the differences themselves have a constant difference -> second-order.
2. Ratios - divide consecutive terms. If the ratios are constant -> geometric.
3. Alternate terms - take every 2nd (or 3rd) term. Often two independent series are interleaved.

If none work, look for: digits changing independently, primes, squares, or Fibonacci-style sums.

## Letter series: the position method

Number the alphabet: A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26. Convert every letter to its position, apply the numeric pattern, convert back.

For reverse coding (Z=1, Y=2, ...), use position = 27 - forward position.

## Common letter-series patterns

- Constant step: A, C, E, G -> +2
- Increasing step: A, C, F, J -> +2, +3, +4
- Wrap-around: Y, Z, A, B -> continue past Z to A (mod 26)
- Alternating: A, Z, B, Y, C, X -> forward/backward simultaneously

## Coding-decoding: the three families

1. Uniform shift (Caesar cipher): every letter moves by a fixed number. CAT -> DBU is +1.
2. Reverse coding: A<->Z, B<->Y. New position = 27 - old position.
3. Position arithmetic: letter positions doubled, squared, etc. Convert to numbers first to see it.

The method is always the same: decode the rule from the example, verify on every letter, then apply blindly.

payload.title: Series analysis decision tree
rows: Every 2nd term is its own series

payload.title: Write the difference row under the series before anything else
payload.text: It takes 10 seconds and eliminates 70% of wrong hypotheses. If the difference row is constant, stop - you have the pattern.

payload.title: An interleaved letter series and a coding question

Part A: Find the next term: B, D, G, K, P, ___
Part B: If CAT is coded as DBU, what is DOG coded as?

steps.title: Part A Step 1 - convert to positions
Part A Step 2 - look at differences
Part A Step 3 - next difference and answer
steps.desc: Next difference = 6. Next position = 16 + 6 = 22 = V.

steps.title: Part B - decode the shift
steps.desc: C->D (+1), A->B (+1), T->U (+1). Uniform +1 shift. Apply: D->E, O->P, G->H. Answer: EPH.

payload.solution:
Part A: V (differences increase by 1: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).
Part B: EPH (each letter +1).

Converting letters to positions first makes the pattern visible; trying to "see" it in letters alone is much harder.

lessons.title: Blood relations, direction sense and syllogisms
lessons.summary: Drawing a family tree that eliminates wrong options, walking the compass, and testing syllogisms with Venn diagrams.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Translate a blood-relation sentence into a family-tree symbol and draw it
Track multi-leg direction changes and compute net displacement
Test syllogism conclusions with Venn containment diagrams

payload.text:
Pointing to a photograph, a man said, "She is the daughter of the only son of my grandfather." How is the lady related to him?

Grandfather's only son = the man's father. Daughter of his father = his sister.

Without a tree, most students guess between sister, cousin and niece. With a three-line tree, the answer is forced.

## Family-tree symbols (memorise these)

- Triangle = Male
- Square = Female
- Horizontal line + symbol = Spouse
- Vertical line down = Parent to child
- Siblings on one horizontal bar = Brother / sister

## Translation rules

- "A is the brother of B" -> A = male, same generation, sibling.
- "A is the wife of B" -> A = female, married to B.
- "A is the mother of B" -> A = female, one generation above B.
- "Only son of my grandfather" = my father (if my father was the only son).

## Direction sense: the compass method

Draw a small cross: N up, E right, S down, W left. For each leg of the journey, draw an arrow and label the distance. At the end, add the N-S components and the E-W components separately, then use Pythagoras for the net displacement.

## Turning conventions (read carefully)

- "Turns left" from facing N -> faces W. From facing E -> faces N.
- "Turns right" from facing N -> faces E. From facing E -> faces S.
- Keep a running "facing" variable. Update it at every turn before drawing the next leg.

## Syllogisms: the four statement types

| Statement | Venn diagram |
| --- | --- |
| All A are B | A circle entirely inside B |
| No A are B | A and B completely separate |
| Some A are B | A and B overlap (at least one shared) |
| Some A are not B | A has a part outside B |

## What definitely follows

- "All A are B" implies "Some B are A" (always true - the A part of B exists).
- "All A are B" + "All B are C" implies "All A are C" (chain).
- "No A are B" implies "No B are A" (symmetric).
- "Some A are B" does NOT imply "All A are B" - the "some" might be a proper subset.

payload.title: Always draw the tree - never solve blood relations in your head
payload.text: The tree takes 20 seconds and makes every wrong option visibly wrong. Students who skip the drawing score roughly half the marks on this topic.

payload.title: A three-leg direction problem and a syllogism
payload.problem:
Part A: Rahul walks 3 km north, turns right and walks 4 km, then turns right again and walks 3 km. How far and in what direction is he from the start?
Part B: Statements: All cats are dogs. All dogs are animals. Does "Some animals are cats" follow?

steps.title: Part A Step 1 - draw leg 1
steps.desc: Facing N, walk 3 km north. Position: (0, 3). Facing still N.
steps.code_snippet:
Start (0,0)
up 3 km N -> (0,3)

steps.title: Part A Step 2 - turn right, draw leg 2
steps.desc: Right from N = East. Walk 4 km east. Position: (4, 3). Facing E.

steps.title: Part A Step 3 - turn right, draw leg 3
steps.desc: Right from E = South. Walk 3 km south. Position: (4, 0). Facing S.

steps.title: Part A Step 4 - net displacement
steps.desc: From (0,0) to (4,0): 4 km due East. The north and south legs cancelled.

steps.title: Part B - Venn containment
steps.desc: Draw cats inside dogs inside animals. "All cats are animals" (by chaining), and "all A are B" always implies "some B are A". So "Some animals are cats" definitely follows.

payload.solution:
Part A: 4 km due East (north and south cancel).
Part B: Yes, "Some animals are cats" definitely follows.

Drawing each leg on a grid makes cancellations obvious. Drawing Venn circles makes syllogism answers visual, not verbal.

mistakes.fix: The tree makes wrong options visibly wrong. Draw it every time, even for "easy" questions.

mistakes.mistake: Turning the wrong way (left/right confusion)
mistakes.fix: Left from N = W; right from N = E. Write the new facing on the diagram at every turn before drawing the next leg.

mistakes.fix: All A are B does NOT mean all B are A. Draw the Venn: A inside B does not put all of B inside A.

points: Draw the family tree with symbols - never solve in your head.
"Only son of my grandfather" = my father.

Net displacement: sum N-S and E-W components separately.
Syllogisms are set containment - draw Venn circles.
"All A are B" implies "Some B are A" but NOT "All B are A".

courses.title: Engineering Mathematics I
courses.subtitle: The Year-1 maths every branch shares — limits and series, optimisation, integration, matrices and eigenvalues, taught with the exam shortcuts that save minutes
courses.description:
Every engineering branch starts from the same mathematics. This course covers the Year-1 syllabus that AKTU, VTU and MU curricula share: limits and continuity, series expansions, applications of derivatives, integration and its uses, and the linear algebra that later semesters assume without re-teaching.

Eight lessons across four modules. Every lesson follows the nine-step structure: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, the exam angle, a server-graded quiz and a one-screen summary. A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final exam; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** first-year students of every branch who want the maths to click once, properly, rather than re-deriving it under exam pressure each semester. Also useful for GATE/PSU aspirants revisiting the basics.

**What you need:** class-12 calculus and basic algebra. A pen and paper for the worked examples — these are not spectator topics.
outcomes: Evaluate limits and apply L Hospital rule only when the form justifies it
Expand any smooth function with Maclaurin and Taylor series
Optimise engineering problems with first and second derivative tests
Sketch curves completely using the five-step checklist
Integrate by substitution, by parts, and by partial fractions
Compute area, volume and improper integrals as applications
Find matrix rank, determinants, inverses and eigenvalues
Classify linear systems as unique, infinite or inconsistent from rank
courses.about_course:
This course is built around one observation: Year-1 maths is re-taught badly in most colleges, then re-learned under panic before every exam. The underlying ideas are few, and each one has a clear geometric or algebraic picture. Once that picture is solid, the exam questions become routine applications rather than puzzles.

Calculus (Modules 1 and 3) is taught with the standard limit laws, the four memorised series, and a technique-selection table for integration that tells you which tool matches which integrand shape. Applications (Module 2) emphasise the setup of optimisation problems and the five-step curve-tracing checklist rather than blind differentiation. Linear algebra (Module 4) is taught through rank and eigenvalues, the two ideas that carry into every later semester from circuits to control theory to data science.

Every lesson ends with a quiz graded on the server, and the course finishes with a 15-question timed exam drawn from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.
prerequisites: Class-12 calculus (derivatives, basic integrals)
Class-12 algebra (quadratics, simultaneous equations)
audience: First-year engineering students of any branch (AKTU / VTU / MU and similar)
Diploma students revisiting Year-1 maths
GATE / PSU aspirants brushing up fundamentals
Anyone preparing for campus placements that test quantitative maths

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Evaluate left-hand and right-hand limits and decide when a two-sided limit exists

payload.text: An examiner writes lim(x->0) sin(x)/x on the board and asks for the answer without a calculator. The ones who understand that the ratio of two quantities going to zero at the same rate approaches the ratio of their instantaneous speeds write 1 in five seconds. That speed difference is what this lesson builds.

A limit answers one question: what value does f(x) approach as x approaches a, even if f(a) itself is undefined.

**Two-sided limit exists iff:**
1. Left-hand limit lim(x->a-) f(x) exists.
2. Right-hand limit lim(x->a+) f(x) exists.
3. They are equal.

**Continuity at a:** the limit exists AND equals f(a).

| Discontinuity type | Behaviour | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Removable | Limit exists, f(a) differs or undefined | (x^2-1)/(x-1) at x=1 |
| Jump | Left and right limits finite but unequal | Sign function at 0 |
| Infinite | One or both sides shoot to infinity | 1/x at x=0 |

**L Hospital rule:** for form 0/0 or infinity/infinity, lim f/g = lim f'/g', provided the new limit exists. It does NOT apply to 0 x infinity or infinity - infinity without rewriting first.

steps.code_snippet: sin x / 2x   ->   0/0 again

steps.title: Apply L Hospital a second time
steps.desc: Differentiate again: cos x over 2. Substitute: cos 0 / 2 = 1/2.

payload.solution: The limit is 1/2. One application of L Hospital is not always enough. Re-check the form after differentiating; if still indeterminate, apply again.

payload.title: Evaluate these yourself
payload.hint: 1 and 2 are 0/0: L Hospital once each. 3 factors. 4: compare highest powers, answer 3.

mistakes.mistake: Applying L Hospital to a non-indeterminate form
mistakes.fix: lim(x->1) x^2 = 1 by direct substitution. Differentiating gives 2x = 2, wrong. Always substitute first.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to re-check the form after differentiating
mistakes.fix: After each L Hospital application, substitute again. If no longer 0/0 or infinity/infinity, stop.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing continuity with differentiability
mistakes.fix: Differentiable implies continuous; |x| is continuous at 0 yet not differentiable there.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Show lim(x->0) (tan x - x) / x^3 = 1/3.
payload.answer: Form 0/0. Differentiate: (sec^2 x - 1) / 3x^2 = tan^2 x / 3x^2. Still 0/0: differentiate again or use tan x ~ x near 0 to get x^2/(3x^2) = 1/3.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Two-sided limit exists iff left limit = right limit, both finite.
Continuity = limit exists AND equals f(a).
L Hospital: only 0/0 or infinity/infinity; re-check form after each application.
Differentiability implies continuity; the converse is false (|x| at 0).

questions.prompt: When does a two-sided limit exist?
options: When left and right limits are equal and finite
questions.explanation: Both one-sided limits must exist and agree.

questions.explanation: Directly only 0/0 and infinity/infinity; others need rewriting first.

questions.explanation: No break (continuous) but left derivative -1, right +1: no unique tangent.

lessons.title: Maclaurin and Taylor series
lessons.summary: Expand any smooth function around a point; use standard expansions as exam shortcuts.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write the Maclaurin series of a function from its derivatives at zero
State the standard expansions of e^x, sin x, cos x and 1/(1-x) from memory
Use substitution to expand composite functions such as e^(2x) or sin(x^2)
Estimate a function value with a truncated series

payload.text: The series e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + ... is how a computer computes the exponential. There is no magic exponentiation circuit; there is a loop adding terms until the change falls below a threshold. The same expansion turns many 0/0 limits into two-line subtractions.

A Taylor series rewrites a smooth function as an infinite polynomial centred at a. The Maclaurin series is centred at zero:

f(x) = f(0) + f'(0)x + f''(0)x^2/2! + f'''(0)x^3/3! + ...

**Memorise these four:**

| Function | Maclaurin series | Valid for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| e^x | sum x^n / n! | all x |
| sin x | x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ... | all x |
| cos x | 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - ... | all x |
| 1/(1-x) | 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ... | abs(x) < 1 |

Substitution is the common technique: expand e^(2x) by replacing x with 2x in the standard series. Always check the validity interval after substitution.

payload.title: Why factorials appear
payload.text: The n-th derivative of e^x is still e^x, so f^(n)(0) = 1 for every n. Dividing by n! keeps each term finite.

payload.title: Expand a quotient using a standard series
payload.problem: Find the Maclaurin series of f(x) = (e^x - 1) / x up to x^2.

steps.title: Expand the numerator
steps.desc: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2 + higher. Subtract 1: e^x - 1 = x + x^2/2 + x^3/6 + ...

steps.title: Divide each term by x
steps.desc: Every power drops by one: x/x = 1, x^2/2x = x/2, x^3/6x = x^2/6.

steps.title: Read off the answer
steps.desc: Series is 1 + x/2 + x^2/6 + ... so coefficient of x^2 is 1/6.

payload.solution: f(x) = 1 + x/2 + x^2/6 + O(x^3). Technique: expand with a known series, then multiply/divide term by term.

payload.title: Expand these yourself
payload.prompt:
1. sin(x^2) up to x^6.
2. cos(2x) up to x^4.
3. Use 1/(1+x) series to evaluate sum of (-1)^n / 3^n.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the factorial in the denominator
mistakes.fix: Every term x^n needs n!. Tattoo: power over factorial.

mistakes.mistake: Using the series outside its interval of convergence
mistakes.fix: 1/(1-x) is only valid for abs(x) < 1. Substituting x = 2 diverges.

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the O(...) notation too early
mistakes.fix: Write O(x^n) after every truncated series. Never equate approximation with identity.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Find lim(x->0) (x - sin x) / x^3 using series.
payload.answer: sin x = x - x^3/6 + O(x^5), so x - sin x = x^3/6 - O(x^5). Dividing by x^3 gives 1/6.
payload.source: VTU previous year

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Maclaurin = Taylor centred at 0: sum f^(n)(0) x^n / n!.
Memorise e^x, sin x, cos x, 1/(1-x) expansions.
Substitute to expand composites; re-check the interval.
Truncated series carry O(x^n); never treat approximation as equality.

questions.prompt: Coefficient of x^3 in Maclaurin of e^x is:
questions.explanation: General term x^n/n!, so for n=3 coefficient is 1/3! = 1/6.

questions.prompt: For which x is 1 + x + x^2 + ... = 1/(1-x)?
questions.explanation: Geometric series converges only for absolute ratio less than 1.

questions.prompt: lim(x->0) (e^x - 1 - x) / x^2 equals:
questions.explanation: e^x - 1 - x = x^2/2 + O(x^3); dividing by x^2 leaves 1/2.

modules.title: Module 2 — Applications of Derivatives
modules.summary: Optimisation, mean value theorems, and curve sketching.

lessons.title: Maxima, minima and optimisation
lessons.summary: Turn a word problem into a derivative test; classify critical points without a graph.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Find critical points by solving f prime(x) = 0 or locating non-differentiable points
Classify critical points using first and second derivative tests
Formulate an engineering optimisation problem as a single-variable extremum
State and apply the Mean Value Theorem with correct hypotheses

payload.text: A beam of given perimeter must enclose the maximum rectangular cross-section. The calculus answer is a square, and every structural design handbook says the same, because the optimisation is identical. Exams love these problems because they reward setting up the function correctly.

A **critical point** of f is any c where f'(c) = 0 or f' does not exist. Every local extremum of a differentiable function occurs at a critical point, but not every critical point is an extremum (x^3 at 0).

**First derivative test:** look at the sign of f' immediately left and right of c.

| Left of c | Right of c | Conclusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| + | - | Local maximum |
| - | + | Local minimum |
| + | + or - | Neither |

**Second derivative test:** f'(c)=0 and f''(c)<0: local max; f''(c)>0: local min; f''(c)=0: inconclusive.

**Mean Value Theorem:** if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there exists c in (a,b) with f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a). Rolle theorem is the special case f(a)=f(b), giving f'(c)=0.

payload.title: Word problems: the objective function comes first
payload.text: Express the quantity to maximise in one variable using the constraint. Differentiate only after substitution.

payload.title: Optimise an open box from a square sheet
payload.problem: A 20 cm square sheet has equal squares cut from each corner; flaps fold into an open box. Find the cut size that maximises volume.

steps.title: Define variable and objective
steps.desc: Let x be the cut side. Base (20-2x) by (20-2x), height x. V(x) = x(20-2x)^2, 0 < x < 10.

steps.title: Differentiate
steps.desc: Product rule: V prime = (20-2x)(20-6x).

steps.title: Solve V prime = 0
steps.desc: x = 10 (rejected: zero volume) or x = 10/3 cm. Endpoints V(0)=V(10)=0, so interior point is the max.
steps.code_snippet: x = 10/3 cm approx 3.33 cm

steps.title: Verify with second derivative
steps.desc: V double-prime = 8x - 160. At x = 10/3: negative, confirming local maximum.

payload.solution: Cut size x = 10/3 cm maximises volume. Maximum volume = (10/3)(40/3)^2 = 16000/27 approx 592.6 cm^3.

payload.title: Solve these optimisation problems
payload.prompt:
1. Two positive numbers, product 200, sum minimum?
2. 100 m fencing, rectangular plot against a river (no fence on river side). Maximise area.
3. Verify MVT for f(x) = x^2 on [1, 4].
payload.hint: 1: a = b = 10*sqrt(2). 2: width 25 m, length 50 m, area 1250 m^2. 3: c = 2.5.

mistakes.mistake: Stopping after critical points without classifying
mistakes.fix: x^3 has critical point at 0 that is neither max nor min. Always run the derivative test.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting endpoint checks on closed intervals
mistakes.fix: Global extrema on [a,b] occur at critical points OR endpoints. Evaluate f at all candidates.

mistakes.mistake: Mis-stating MVT hypotheses
mistakes.fix: Continuity on closed interval and differentiability on open interval are both required.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Cylinder volume 500 cm^3, minimum surface area. Find radius.
payload.answer: h = 500/(pi r^2). S = 2 pi r^2 + 1000/r. S prime = 4 pi r - 1000/r^2 = 0 gives r^3 = 250/pi, r = cuberoot(250/pi) approx 4.3 cm.
payload.source: Standard end-semester

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Critical points: f prime = 0 or undefined; not all are extrema.
First derivative test (sign change) always valid; second fails at f double-prime = 0.
Closed-interval global extrema: compare critical points AND endpoints.
MVT needs continuity on [a,b] plus differentiability on (a,b).

questions.prompt: f(x) = x^3 has critical point at 0. What is it?
questions.explanation: f'(0)=0 but no sign change: inflection point, not extremum.

questions.prompt: MVT for f(x)=x^2 on [1,4] guarantees f prime(c) equals:
Fixed perimeter, maximum rectangle area shape is:
questions.explanation: AM-GM or calculus: a = b = P/4 gives square.

lessons.title: Curve sketching and asymptotes
lessons.summary: Combine first and second derivatives into a complete qualitative picture of a graph.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Determine intervals of increase, decrease, concavity and inflection
Find vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes from limits
Sketch a rational or polynomial using the five-step checklist
Identify even/odd symmetry that halves the sketching work

payload.text: Before any CAD software draws a linkage trajectory, it evaluates the function at a grid of points. Curve tracing is the analytic version: understand where the graph rises, bends, or escapes to infinity, and a rough sketch becomes a reliable engineering diagram.

Curve tracing is a checklist, not an art. Run these five steps in order:

1. **Domain and symmetry.** Even (f(-x)=f(x), y-axis symmetric) or odd (f(-x)=-f(x), 180-degree rotational)? Sketch only the right half and mirror or rotate.
2. **Intercepts.** y-intercept: f(0). x-intercepts: solve f(x)=0.
3. **Asymptotes.**
   - Vertical: lim(x->a) f(x) = +/- infinity at points not in domain.
   - Horizontal: lim(x->+/- infinity) f(x) = L finite.
   - Oblique: lim f(x)/x = m finite nonzero, then b = lim (f(x) - mx).
4. **Critical points and concavity.** Solve f prime = 0 for turns; f double-prime = 0 for possible inflections; test signs in intervals.
5. **Endpoint behaviour.** For open intervals, describe the limit so the sketch knows whether to approach an asymptote.

payload.title: Trace a rational function completely
payload.problem: Sketch f(x) = x^2 / (x - 1). State asymptotes, turning points, inflection points.

steps.title: Domain and intercepts
steps.desc: Domain: all real except 1. y-intercept f(0)=0. x-intercept x=0 (double root: touches axis).
steps.code_snippet: Domain: R - {1}; intercept (0, 0)

steps.title: Asymptotes
steps.desc: VA at x=1 (denominator zero, numerator nonzero). Degree num > den: no HA. Divide: x^2/(x-1) = x + 1 + 1/(x-1), so oblique y = x + 1.
steps.code_snippet: VA: x = 1;  Oblique: y = x + 1

steps.title: First derivative
steps.desc: f' = x(x-2)/(x-1)^2. Zero at x=0 and x=2. Sign: + on (-inf,0), - on (0,1), - on (1,2), + on (2,inf).

steps.title: Classification and concavity
steps.desc: Max at x=0 (value 0), min at x=2 (value 4). f double-prime = 2/(x-1)^3, never zero; concave down on (-inf,1), up on (1,inf). No inflection.

payload.solution: Graph touches origin, max at 0, falls toward VA x=1 from left; reappears right of VA, min at (2,4), rises along y = x + 1. The division x^2/(x-1) = x + 1 + 1/(x-1) reveals every feature at once.

payload.title: Trace these on paper
payload.prompt:
1. f(x) = 1/(x^2 - 4): asymptotes and intercepts.
2. f(x) = x^3 - 3x: turning points and inflection.
3. f(x) = (2x+3)/(x-1): horizontal or oblique asymptote?
payload.hint: 1: VA x=2, x=-2; HA y=0; y-int -3/4. 2: max at -1 (2), min at 1 (-2); inflection at 0. 3: HA y=2.

mistakes.mistake: Setting the numerator to zero for asymptotes
mistakes.fix: Numerator zeros are x-intercepts. VA comes from denominator zeros after cancelling.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to cancel common factors
mistakes.fix: (x^2-1)/(x-1) = x+1 for x!=1: removable discontinuity at 1, not VA.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming every critical point is a turn
mistakes.fix: x^3 has f prime(0)=0 with no turn. Check for sign change of f prime.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Find the oblique asymptote of f(x) = (3x^2 + 2x + 1) / (x + 1).
payload.answer: Divide: (x+1)(3x-1) + 2. f(x) = 3x - 1 + 2/(x+1). Oblique asymptote y = 3x - 1; VA x = -1.
payload.source: AKTU 2023

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Five-step checklist: domain/symmetry, intercepts, asymptotes, derivatives, endpoints.
VA: denominator zeros after cancelling; HA/oblique: limits at infinity.
Oblique via polynomial division when degree num = degree den + 1.
f double-prime sign gives concavity; zero crossings are inflection candidates.

questions.prompt: Vertical asymptotes come from:
options: Zeros of the denominator after cancelling
questions.explanation: Denominator zeros (after cancelling common factors) are where the function blows up.
Factor: (x-1)(x+1)/(x-1) = x+1 for x!=1. Hole at x=1, no asymptote.

questions.prompt: Oblique asymptote exists when degree of numerator is:
questions.explanation: Degree num = degree den + 1 gives a linear asymptote found by division.

modules.title: Module 3 — Integration & Applications
modules.summary: The standard techniques, improper integrals, and area/volume applications.

lessons.title: Integration techniques
lessons.summary: Substitution, parts, partial fractions, and trig substitutions — pick the right tool on sight.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Recognise which technique (substitution, parts, partial fractions, trig sub) matches a given integrand
Apply integration by parts to products of polynomial and exponential/trigonometric functions
Decompose a proper rational function into partial fractions
Evaluate definite integrals using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

payload.text: Every signal-processing course reduces to integrals of the form sin(ax)e^(bx) dx. There is no single formula for that family, but there is a reliable technique — integration by parts applied twice, which returns you to the original integral and lets you solve for it algebraically. That trick (the circular parts loop) appears in half the end-semester questions on any engineering campus.

The indefinite integral is the reverse of differentiation; the definite integral computes signed area. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links them: if F prime = f, then integral from a to b of f = F(b) - F(a).

**Technique selection — learn this table:**

| Integrand shape | Technique |
| --- | --- |
| Contains f(g(x)) g'(x) | Substitution u = g(x) |
| Product of polynomial x exp/trig/poly | Integration by parts |
| Proper rational function | Partial fractions |
| Contains sqrt(a^2 - x^2) | Trig sub x = a sin theta |
| Contains sqrt(a^2 + x^2) | Trig sub x = a tan theta |
| Reduces by power reduction | Trig identity first |

**Integration by parts:** integral u dv = uv - integral v du. Choose u by the LIATE order: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. Whichever family is higher in LIATE becomes u.

**Partial fractions** require a proper rational function (degree numerator < degree denominator). If improper, divide first. For distinct linear factors: (px+q)/((x-a)(x-b)) = A/(x-a) + B/(x-b).

payload.title: Always try substitution before parts
payload.text: If the integrand contains a inner function whose derivative is also present (up to a constant), substitution wins and is faster. Parts on such integrands is wasted effort.

payload.title: Circuits in by-parts
payload.text: For integral e^x sin x dx, apply parts twice. The original integral reappears on the right; solve algebraically for it. Never loop forever — set up an equation.

payload.title: Circular integration by parts
payload.problem: Evaluate integral of e^x sin x dx.

steps.title: First by-parts
steps.desc: Let u = sin x, dv = e^x dx. Then du = cos x dx, v = e^x. Result: e^x sin x - integral e^x cos x dx.
steps.code_snippet: I = e^x sin x - integral e^x cos x dx

steps.title: Second by-parts on the remaining integral
steps.desc: Let u = cos x, dv = e^x dx. Then du = -sin x dx, v = e^x. The remaining integral becomes e^x cos x + integral e^x sin x dx = e^x cos x + I.
steps.code_snippet: integral e^x cos x dx = e^x cos x + I

steps.title: Solve for I algebraically
steps.desc: Substitute back: I = e^x sin x - (e^x cos x + I), so 2I = e^x (sin x - cos x), hence I = e^x (sin x - cos x)/2 + C.
steps.code_snippet: I = e^x (sin x - cos x) / 2 + C

payload.solution: integral e^x sin x dx = e^x (sin x - cos x)/2 + C. The circular trick: after two parts the original integral reappears; solve the linear equation rather than continuing to integrate.

payload.title: Integrate these
payload.prompt:
1. integral x e^x dx (by parts)
2. integral x cos x dx (by parts)
3. integral 1/(x^2 - 4) dx (partial fractions)
4. integral sin^2 x dx (power reduction)

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the wrong u in by-parts
mistakes.fix: Follow LIATE. For x e^x: algebraic (x) beats exponential, so u = x. For x sin x: algebraic beats trig, so u = x.

mistakes.mistake: Applying partial fractions to an improper rational function
mistakes.fix: If degree numerator >= degree denominator, divide first. Otherwise the decomposition is invalid.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the constant of integration on indefinite integrals
mistakes.fix: Every indefinite integral needs + C. Omitting it costs marks even when the antiderivative is correct.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Evaluate integral of ln x dx.
payload.answer: By parts with u = ln x, dv = dx: x ln x - integral x (1/x) dx = x ln x - x + C.
payload.source: Common end-semester 1-mark warmup that becomes a 6-mark multi-part

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: FTC: integral a to b f = F(b) - F(a) when F prime = f.
Technique table: substitution, parts, partial fractions, trig sub.
By-parts u chosen by LIATE; circular cases solved algebraically after two parts.
Partial fractions need a proper rational function; divide if improper.

questions.prompt: In integration by parts, LIATE stands for:
options: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exp
questions.explanation: LIATE ranks which factor becomes u: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.

lessons.title: Area, volume and improper integrals
lessons.summary: Apply definite integrals to plane area, solid volume, and integrals with infinite limits.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute the area between two curves by integrating the difference with correct limits
Find the volume of a solid of revolution using the disk and shell methods
Evaluate a Type-1 improper integral as a limit and decide convergence
Recognise the standard convergent integral of 1/x^p on [1, infinity)

payload.text: The capacitor discharge curve never truly reaches zero, yet the total energy delivered is finite. That paradox is an improper integral: the area under an infinite tail can still be a convergent number. Electrical, civil and mechanical engineers all meet this in first-year labs; this lesson makes the computation routine.

**Area between curves:** if f(x) >= g(x) on [a,b], area = integral from a to b of (f - g) dx. When curves cross, split at intersection points and take absolute value of each piece.

**Volumes of revolution:**
- **Disk method** (rotate around x-axis): V = pi integral f(x)^2 dx.
- **Washer method** (gap between curves): V = pi integral (R^2 - r^2) dx, R outer, r inner.
- **Shell method** (rotate around y-axis, integrate in x): V = 2 pi integral x f(x) dx.

**Improper integrals** have an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand. Evaluate as a limit:

integral from a to infinity of f(x) dx = lim(b->infinity) integral from a to b of f(x) dx.

If the limit is finite, the integral converges; otherwise it diverges.

**p-test on [1, infinity):** integral 1/x^p converges iff p > 1.

payload.title: Area between a parabola and a line
payload.problem: Find the area enclosed by y = x^2 and y = x.

steps.title: Find intersection points
steps.desc: Set x^2 = x: x(x-1) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 1. On [0,1], x >= x^2.
steps.code_snippet: x = 0 and x = 1

steps.title: Set up the integral
steps.desc: Upper curve y = x, lower y = x^2. Area = integral from 0 to 1 of (x - x^2) dx.
steps.code_snippet: A = int_0^1 (x - x^2) dx

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.desc: Antiderivative x^2/2 - x^3/3. At 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6. At 0: 0. Area = 1/6.

payload.solution: Area = 1/6 square units. Always find intersections first to get correct limits, and check which curve is on top between them.

payload.title: Compute these
payload.prompt:
1. Area between y = 4 - x^2 and y = x + 2.
2. Volume when y = sqrt(x) from x=0 to x=4 is rotated about the x-axis.
3. Does integral_1^inf 1/x^2 dx converge? Evaluate it.
payload.hint: 1: intersect at x=-2 and x=1; area = integral (-2 to 1) of (4-x^2 - (x+2)) dx = 9/2. 2: V = pi int_0^4 x dx = 8pi. 3: yes; lim b->inf [-1/x]_1^b = 1.

mistakes.mistake: Integrating the absolute difference without splitting at crossings
mistakes.fix: If f and g cross inside the interval, split the integral at each crossing and integrate upper-minus-lower on each subinterval.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an improper integral as a normal definite integral
mistakes.fix: Write the limit explicitly. Substituting infinity directly is not a valid step and earns zero method marks.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing disk and shell methods
mistakes.fix: Disk/washer integrates along the axis of rotation; shell integrates perpendicular and multiplies by 2 pi radius. Draw which radius you are using.

payload.question: Evaluate integral_0^1 ln x dx as an improper integral.
payload.answer: Unbounded at 0: lim(a->0+) integral_a^1 ln x dx = lim(a->0+) [x ln x - x]_a^1. At 1: -1. At a: a ln a - a -> 0. Result: -1.

points: Area = integral (upper - lower) with limits at intersections; split at crossings.
Disk/washer for rotation about x-axis; shell for y-axis when integrating in x.

modules.summary: Rank, elimination, determinants, inverses and eigenvalues — the linear algebra every branch reuses.

lessons.title: Matrix rank, determinants and inverses
lessons.summary: Compute rank by row reduction; find determinants and inverses without blind formula-chasing.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Reduce a matrix to row-echelon form and read off its rank
Compute 2x2 and 3x3 determinants by cofactor expansion and row operations
Decide invertibility from the determinant and from the rank
Find the inverse of a 2x2 or 3x3 matrix using Gauss-Jordan elimination

payload.text: A structural engineer writes 12 equilibrium equations for a truss with 12 unknown member forces. Whether the structure is stable, under-constrained or over-constrained is exactly the question "does this matrix have full rank?". The same rank test appears in circuit analysis, computer graphics and machine learning — one idea, every branch.

A **matrix** is a rectangular array of numbers. The **rank** is the number of linearly independent rows (equivalently columns), computed as the number of non-zero rows in the row-echelon form.

**Row operations** (all rank-preserving):
1. Swap two rows.
2. Multiply a row by a non-zero scalar.
3. Add a multiple of one row to another.

**Determinant** is a scalar attached to a square matrix. Key properties:
- det(AB) = det(A) det(B).
- det(A^T) = det(A).
- Row swap flips the sign; scaling a row scales the determinant.
- Upper triangular: determinant = product of diagonal entries.

**2x2 determinant:** det [[a,b],[c,d]] = ad - bc.

**3x3 cofactor expansion** along any row or column: det = sum of entry times its cofactor. Expanding along a row of zeros is the free speed-up.

**Invertibility:** A square matrix A is invertible iff det(A) != 0, iff rank = n, iff Ax = b has a unique solution for every b.

payload.title: Row-reduce before expanding
payload.text: A 3x3 determinant with two zeros in a row is a one-line cofactor expansion. Create zeros with row operations (keeping track of sign changes) before expanding.

payload.title: Rank and solvability of Ax = b (n unknowns)
Rank by elimination, then invertibility
payload.problem: Find the rank of A = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 5, 7], [3, 7, 11]] and decide whether A is invertible.

steps.title: Eliminate below the second pivot
steps.desc: R3 -> R3 - R2 gives [0, 0, 1]. Matrix is now upper triangular with three non-zero rows.

steps.title: Read the rank and determinant
steps.desc: Three non-zero rows: rank = 3 = n. Diagonal of echelon form is 1, 1, 1 so det(A) = 1 (operations R2-2R1 and R3-3R1 do not change det; R3-R2 also does not).
steps.code_snippet: rank(A) = 3;  det(A) = 1

payload.solution: rank = 3, det(A) = 1 (non-zero), so A is invertible and Ax = b has a unique solution for every b. Always row-reduce first; the echelon form answers rank and often det in one pass.

payload.title: Compute these
payload.prompt:
1. det [[2, 1], [3, 4]].
2. Rank of [[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]].
3. Is [[1, 2], [2, 4]] invertible? Why not?
4. Inverse of [[2, 1], [5, 3]] using the 2x2 formula.

mistakes.mistake: Applying row swaps without flipping the determinant sign
mistakes.fix: Each row interchange multiplies the determinant by -1. Track every swap in a side column while you reduce.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to divide by the determinant in the 2x2 inverse formula
mistakes.fix: A inverse = (1/det) [[d, -b], [-c, a]]. Omitting 1/det is the most common single-line error on 2x2 inverses.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing rank of A with rank of the augmented matrix
mistakes.fix: Solvability needs rank(A) compared to rank([A|b]). Only looking at A misses inconsistent systems.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Find values of k for which the system x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 10, x + 2y + kz = mu has (i) unique (ii) no solution.
payload.answer: Coefficient det = (2k - 6) after expansion. Unique solution iff k != 3. When k = 3, the augmented rank check decides: if mu != 14 the system is inconsistent (no solution); if mu = 14, infinitely many.
payload.source: Standard AKTU 7-mark question

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Rank = non-zero rows in echelon form; row operations preserve rank.
det(AB)=det(A)det(B); det(A^T)=det(A); triangular det = product of diagonal.
Invertible iff det != 0 iff rank = n iff unique solution for every b.
Ax=b: compare rank(A) with rank([A|b]) to classify solution sets.

questions.prompt: A 3x3 matrix with rank 2 has determinant:
questions.explanation: Rank < n implies the rows are linearly dependent, so det = 0.

questions.prompt: If det(A) = 0, then A:
questions.explanation: Zero determinant means singular: no inverse exists.
Every row is a multiple of [1,1], so only one independent row.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
lessons.summary: Solve the characteristic equation, and read eigenspaces for the 2x2 and 3x3 cases examiners actually ask.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Form the characteristic polynomial det(A - lambda I) and solve for eigenvalues
Find an eigenvector for a given eigenvalue by solving (A - lambda I) x = 0
Use the trace-determinant shortcut to check eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix
State the geometric meaning: eigenvalues stretch eigendirections without rotating them

payload.text: A vibration engineer needs the natural frequencies of a building. Those frequencies are the eigenvalues of the stiffness-over-mass matrix; the mode shapes are the eigenvectors. Every stability question in control theory, every principal component in data science, and every iteration analysis in numerical methods runs through the same two-step: characteristic equation, then null space.

A non-zero vector x is an **eigenvector** of A if A x = lambda x for some scalar lambda. The scalar is the **eigenvalue**. Geometrically: A stretches or shrinks x along its own direction; it does not rotate it.

**Finding eigenvalues:** solve the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. For an n x n matrix this is a degree-n polynomial with n roots (counting multiplicity, over the complex numbers).

**Finding eigenvectors:** for each lambda, solve the homogeneous system (A - lambda I) x = 0. The solutions form the **eigenspace** for that lambda; any non-zero vector in the space is an eigenvector.

**2x2 shortcut:** for A = [[a,b],[c,d]]:
- lambda_1 + lambda_2 = trace = a + d
- lambda_1 * lambda_2 = det = ad - bc

Use these to check your characteristic polynomial — a mismatch means an arithmetic error.

**Properties worth memorising:**
- det(A) = product of eigenvalues.
- trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues.
- A is invertible iff every eigenvalue is non-zero.

payload.title: Repeated eigenvalues
payload.text: A repeated eigenvalue does not guarantee n independent eigenvectors. A scalar matrix like 2I has eigenvalue 2 with multiplicity n and full eigenvectors; a Jordan block like [[2,1],[0,2]] has only one independent eigenvector. If asked "distinct eigenvalues", the geometric multiplicity question is the follow-up.

payload.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2x2
payload.problem: Find the eigenvalues and a basis for each eigenspace of A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]].

steps.title: Characteristic polynomial
steps.desc: det(A - lambda I) = (4-lambda)(3-lambda) - 2 = lambda^2 - 7lambda + 10 = (lambda - 5)(lambda - 2). Eigenvalues: 5 and 2.
steps.code_snippet:
lambda^2 - 7 lambda + 10 = 0
lambda = 5 or 2

steps.title: Eigenvector for lambda = 5
steps.desc: A - 5I = [[-1, 1], [2, -2]]. Row reduce: second row = -2 times first. Equation: -x + y = 0 so y = x. Eigenvector [1, 1].
steps.code_snippet: lambda = 5: eigenvector [1, 1]

steps.title: Eigenvector for lambda = 2
steps.desc: A - 2I = [[2, 1], [2, 1]]. Rows identical: 2x + y = 0 so y = -2x. Eigenvector [1, -2].
steps.code_snippet: lambda = 2: eigenvector [1, -2]

payload.solution: Eigenvalues 5 and 2 with eigenvectors [1,1] and [1,-2] respectively (any non-zero scalar multiple also works). Always verify with trace and determinant before writing the final answer.

payload.title: Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors
payload.prompt:
1. A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] (diagonal matrix).
2. A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]].
3. A = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] (swap matrix).
4. Verify trace/det checks for #2.
payload.hint: 1: eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 2 and 3; eigenvectors are the coordinate axes. 2: eigenvalues 3 and -1; eigenvectors [1,1] and [1,-1]. 3: eigenvalues 1 and -1; same eigenvectors as #2. 4: trace 2 = 3+(-1); det -3 = 3*(-1).

mistakes.mistake: Solving for eigenvectors of A - lambda I = 0 incorrectly by dividing a row to zero
mistakes.fix: Row-reduce (A - lambda I) to echelon form, then write the free-variable parametrisation. Never divide an entire row by zero.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that eigenvectors are only defined up to scalar multiples
mistakes.fix: [1,1] and [5,5] represent the same eigendirection. Any non-zero scalar multiple is a valid answer; state the equivalence.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming every matrix is diagonalisable
mistakes.fix: A matrix is diagonalisable iff the sum of geometric multiplicities equals n. Repeated eigenvalues can break this — check before claiming a full eigenbasis.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Find the eigenvalues of A = [[3, 1], [0, 2]] and explain why A is diagonalisable.
payload.answer: Upper triangular: eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 3 and 2. Distinct eigenvalues imply two independent eigenvectors, so A is diagonalisable: A = PDP^(-1) with D = diag(3, 2).
payload.source: Common 6-mark question across branches

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: A x = lambda x; solve det(A - lambda I) = 0 for eigenvalues.
Eigenvectors: null space of (A - lambda I) for each lambda.
2x2 check: sum of eigenvalues = trace; product = det.
Distinct eigenvalues guarantee diagonalisability; repeated ones need a multiplicity check.

questions.prompt: Eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are:
questions.explanation: For diagonal D, D x = lambda x holds for each coordinate axis with lambda equal to that diagonal entry.

questions.prompt: Sum of eigenvalues of A equals:
questions.explanation: The coefficient of lambda^(n-1) in the characteristic polynomial is -trace, so the roots sum to trace.

questions.prompt: A matrix with eigenvalues 2 and 5 has determinant:
questions.explanation: det = product of eigenvalues = 2 * 5 = 10.

courses.title: SQL & Databases Mastery
courses.subtitle: Query, join, aggregate, design and tune the database every placement test and production service depends on
courses.description:
Every software role — backend, data analyst, full-stack, even ML engineering — screens with SQL. This course takes you from writing a first SELECT to designing normalised schemas, choosing indexes that actually get used, reasoning about transactions, and using window functions for the analytics queries that appear in real take-home tests.

Eight lessons across four modules. Every lesson follows the nine-step structure: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, the exam angle, a server-graded quiz and a one-screen summary. A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final exam; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** any student or working developer who wants SQL to be a strength rather than something to google under deadline pressure. Campus OA database rounds, analyst interviews and backend screens all draw from the same pool of patterns taught here.

**What you need:** basic programming familiarity helps but is not required. A free PostgreSQL or MySQL instance to practise on is recommended — these are not spectator topics.
outcomes: Write SELECT queries with filtering, sorting and limits using the correct evaluation order
Combine tables with INNER, LEFT and anti-joins without multiplying or dropping rows
Summarise data with GROUP BY, HAVING and NULL-aware aggregates
Nest subqueries and rewrite them as readable CTEs
Design schemas in 3NF with proper keys and constraints
Choose composite indexes that match the leftmost-prefix rule and verify with EXPLAIN
Explain ACID and isolation levels in plain language
Compute running totals, ranks and shares with window functions
courses.about_course:
SQL is unusual in the curriculum: it is the one skill that appears in first-year courses, placement tests, internships and every backend job — and it is still taught badly in most colleges as a list of keywords rather than a mental model.

This course builds the mental model first. Query evaluation order explains why aliases fail in WHERE and why HAVING exists. Join cardinality explains why reports suddenly show ten times the expected rows. The leftmost-prefix rule explains why an index you added is never used. Each concept has a geometric or procedural picture, and the exam questions become applications of that picture rather than puzzles.

Normalization and transactions close the loop: you will be able to design a small schema that does not corrupt itself under concurrent writes, and defend those design choices in an interview. Window functions finish the course with the analytics pattern that modern take-home tests assume.

Every lesson ends with a quiz graded on the server, and the course finishes with a 15-question timed exam drawn from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.
prerequisites: Basic computer literacy
Willingness to run practice queries on a free PostgreSQL or MySQL instance
audience: Students preparing for campus placements and OA database rounds
Aspiring backend and full-stack developers
Anyone targeting data analyst or data engineer roles
Working developers who want to systematise SQL knowledge
