units.title: SELECT, Filtering & JOINs
units.summary: Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT. NULL uses IS NULL. LEFT + COUNT(right.key) for zero-safe counts; LEFT + WHERE right IS NULL for anti-joins.
questions: Why can you not use a SELECT alias in WHERE?
INNER vs LEFT: how do you decide?
Write the anti-join for customers with no orders.

units.title: Aggregation & Subqueries
units.summary: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col); aggregates ignore NULLs. WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups. Scalar subqueries for comparisons; NOT EXISTS over NOT IN when NULLs are possible; CTEs for readability.
questions: Difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(col)?
When do you use HAVING instead of WHERE?
Why avoid NOT IN with a subquery that may return NULL?

units.title: Schema, Constraints & Indexes
units.summary: PRIMARY KEY = unique + NOT NULL. CHECK passes on NULL — pair with NOT NULL. NUMERIC for money. Composite index: equality columns first (most selective), range/sort last; FKs need explicit indexes in PG.
questions: Why is FLOAT unsafe for monetary values?
State the leftmost-prefix rule for composite indexes.
Are foreign key columns auto-indexed in PostgreSQL?

units.title: Normalization, Transactions & Windows
units.summary: 1NF atomic; 2NF no partial dependency; 3NF no transitive non-key dependency. ACID; isolation levels trade anomalies for concurrency. Window functions run after WHERE/GROUP BY; filter window results in an outer query.
questions: Define 3NF and one anomaly it prevents.
What does READ COMMITTED allow and forbid?
How do you write a running total per customer?

important_questions: Write a query for top 10 customers by revenue in a date range.
Explain why COUNT(*) after LEFT JOIN inflates counts.
Find employees earning above their department average (two ways).
Design indexes for a multi-tenant orders table filtered by tenant_id and status.
Normalise a denormalised order table to 3NF.
Explain the difference between RANK and ROW_NUMBER.
When would you choose SERIALIZABLE over REPEATABLE READ?

previous_year_questions.question: TCS NQT: Write SQL to find the second highest salary from an Employee table.
previous_year_questions.solution: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee); or use DENSE_RANK() = 2.

previous_year_questions.question: Infosys: Difference between WHERE and HAVING with an example.
previous_year_questions.solution: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Example: WHERE salary > 10000 HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.

previous_year_questions.question: Capgemini: What is a composite index and what is the column order rule?
previous_year_questions.solution: Index on multiple columns; the leftmost-prefix rule means queries must constrain the leading column(s) to use it. Equality columns first.

bank.prompt: Which clause filters rows BEFORE grouping?
bank.explanation: WHERE runs before GROUP BY; HAVING runs after aggregation.

bank.prompt: To find NULL values you write:
bank.explanation: Equality with NULL is UNKNOWN; IS NULL is the correct predicate.

bank.prompt: Logical evaluation order starts with:
bank.explanation: Source rows are identified first, then filtered, grouped, projected, sorted.

bank.prompt: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col):
options: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs
bank.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row; COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values.

bank.prompt: AVG(salary) when some salaries are NULL:
options: Ignores NULLs and averages the rest
bank.explanation: AVG, SUM, MIN, MAX all ignore NULLs.

bank.prompt: LEFT JOIN from customers to orders with COUNT(*) for a customer with 0 orders gives:
bank.explanation: The NULL-filled order row is still a row; COUNT(*) counts it as 1. Use COUNT(o.id) for the correct 0.

bank.prompt: Customers with no orders are found with:
options: LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.key IS NULL
bank.explanation: The anti-join pattern: keep all left rows, filter to those with no match.

bank.prompt: NOT IN returns no rows when the subquery has:
bank.explanation: One NULL makes the whole NOT IN UNKNOWN; prefer NOT EXISTS.

bank.prompt: A correlated subquery:
options: References outer columns and re-executes per outer row
bank.explanation: Correlation means dependence on the current outer row.

bank.prompt: PRIMARY KEY implies:
bank.explanation: Primary keys are both unique and non-NULL.

bank.prompt: CHECK (amount > 0) when amount is NULL:
bank.explanation: UNKNOWN does not fail CHECK; pair with NOT NULL.

bank.prompt: FLOAT is unsafe for money because:
options: It cannot represent many decimals exactly
bank.explanation: Binary floating point drifts on decimal fractions; use NUMERIC or integer paise.

bank.prompt: An index on (a, b) can serve:
options: WHERE a = 1 or a = 1 AND b = 2
Any WHERE on a or b
bank.explanation: Leftmost prefix rule: the leading column a must be constrained.

bank.prompt: PostgreSQL foreign key columns are:
bank.explanation: You must index FKs yourself or parent deletes scan the child table.

bank.prompt: WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x' ignores a plain index on email because:
options: A function is applied to the column
bank.explanation: Create an expression index on LOWER(email) or rewrite the predicate.

bank.prompt: 2NF eliminates:
options: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
bank.explanation: 2NF requires full dependency on the whole composite key.

bank.prompt: 3NF eliminates:
bank.explanation: Non-key columns must not determine other non-key columns.

bank.prompt: READ COMMITTED prevents:
bank.explanation: Uncommitted data is invisible; committed changes between reads can still differ.

bank.prompt: Running total per customer uses:
bank.explanation: Window SUM with an ordered frame keeps rows and adds a cumulative column.

bank.prompt: Window functions are evaluated:
options: After WHERE and GROUP BY, before ORDER BY/LIMIT
bank.explanation: Logical order places windows after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and before DISTINCT/ORDER BY/LIMIT.

bank.prompt: ON DELETE CASCADE on order_items means:
options: Delete items when the order is deleted
bank.explanation: Deleting the parent order removes its line items automatically.

bank.prompt: A derived table is:
options: A subquery in the FROM clause
bank.explanation: FROM (SELECT ...) AS t is a derived table; WITH is a CTE.

bank.prompt: ORDER BY in a subquery without LIMIT is:
options: Not guaranteed to affect outer query order
bank.explanation: To guarantee order, sort in the outermost query (or use a window function).

bank.prompt: Which aggregate counts distinct non-NULL values?
bank.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT col) removes duplicates and skips NULLs.

bank.prompt: Durable in ACID means:
bank.explanation: Durability: once commit returns, the data is on stable storage.

bank.prompt: Atomicity guarantees:
options: All statements commit or none do
bank.explanation: All-or-nothing: partial failures roll back the whole transaction.

bank.prompt: ROW_NUMBER() differs from RANK() in that:
options: ROW_NUMBER gaps on ties; RANK does not
bank.explanation: ROW_NUMBER always gives sequential unique numbers; RANK gives equal numbers on ties then skips ahead.

bank.prompt: To find employees above the company average salary:
bank.explanation: A scalar subquery supplies the average; aggregates cannot appear directly in WHERE.

bank.prompt: Composite index column order rule for WHERE a = ? AND b = ?:
bank.explanation: Leftmost prefix: put the column that filters more rows first among equality columns.

bank.prompt: Soft delete typically means:
options: A deleted_at timestamp instead of DELETE
bank.explanation: Rows remain with deleted_at set; queries filter WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

project.title: Build and query a small schema end to end
project.brief: Design a 3NF schema for a mini e-commerce system (customers, products, orders, order_items) with proper keys and constraints. Populate with at least 20 rows of realistic sample data. Then write and run: (1) a LEFT JOIN report of customers with order counts including zero-order customers, (2) a GROUP BY + HAVING revenue report, (3) a subquery or CTE finding above-average spenders, (4) a window-function running total per customer, and (5) one EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an indexed vs unindexed query with a short note on what changed. Submit the SQL script and a short write-up.

modules.title: Module 1 — SELECT, Filtering & JOINs
modules.summary: Query shape, WHERE clauses, and the join types every interview asks about.

lessons.title: SELECT, WHERE and the query lifecycle
lessons.summary: Read a query the way the engine reads it, and filter rows without guessing.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write a SELECT with column projections, aliases and computed expressions
Filter rows with WHERE using comparison operators, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and NULL checks
Order and limit results with ORDER BY and LIMIT/OFFSET
Explain the logical order in which a SQL query is evaluated

payload.text: A product manager asks you for "top 10 customers by revenue in the last quarter who have not returned an order". That is one SELECT with a join, a GROUP BY, a HAVING, an ORDER BY and a LIMIT. Every clause has a fixed position in the query and a fixed position in the engine's evaluation order. Learn that order once, and multi-clause questions stop being intimidating.

A SELECT statement answers: which rows, which columns, in what order, how many.

**The logical evaluation order** (not the written order):

1. FROM / JOIN — identify the source rows.
2. WHERE — filter rows (before grouping).
3. GROUP BY — collapse rows into groups.
4. HAVING — filter groups (after grouping).
5. SELECT — choose columns and compute expressions.
6. DISTINCT — remove duplicate rows.
7. ORDER BY — sort the result.
8. LIMIT / OFFSET — cut the result.

This is why you cannot use a column alias inside WHERE (the alias is only resolved at step 5) and why WHERE filters rows while HAVING filters groups.

**NULL is three-valued logic.** NULL means "unknown", not zero or empty string. Comparisons with NULL return NULL (treated as false), so `WHERE col = NULL` never matches. Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` instead. Similarly, aggregates ignore NULLs: COUNT(col) skips NULLs, COUNT(*) counts rows.

payload.title: NULL in WHERE
payload.text: `WHERE salary = NULL` returns zero rows even when NULLs exist, because NULL = NULL is not true. Always write `IS NULL`.

payload.title: Select explicit columns, never SELECT *
payload.text: Explicit columns make queries readable, use indexes, and stop schema changes upstream from breaking your code. In interviews, always name the columns.

payload.title: Filter, compute and order in one query
payload.problem: From an orders table (id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at), list the order id and amount for paid orders above 1000 placed in 2025, newest first, limited to 10 rows.

steps.title: Identify source and filters
steps.desc: Source: orders. Filters: status = paid, amount > 1000, created_at in 2025.
steps.code_snippet:
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND amount > 1000
  AND created_at >= '2025-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-01-01'

steps.title: Project only the needed columns
steps.desc: Select id and amount. Add a computed column for amount with GST if wanted.
steps.code_snippet: SELECT id, amount

steps.title: Order and limit
steps.desc: Newest first: created_at DESC. Top 10: LIMIT 10.
steps.code_snippet:
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10

payload.solution: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount > 1000 AND created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

payload.title: Write these queries
payload.prompt:
1. List names of employees in department 3 earning more than 50000.
2. Find products whose name starts with "Pro" and price is between 100 and 500.
3. List all users with a NULL phone number, ordered alphabetically by name.
payload.hint: 1: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id = 3 AND salary > 50000. 2: WHERE name LIKE 'Pro%' AND price BETWEEN 100 AND 500. 3: WHERE phone IS NULL ORDER BY name.

mistakes.mistake: Using = with NULL
mistakes.fix: NULL = NULL is not true. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

mistakes.mistake: Putting aggregates in WHERE
mistakes.fix: WHERE filters rows before grouping. Aggregate conditions belong in HAVING.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that LIKE is case-sensitive in some engines
mistakes.fix: PostgreSQL LIKE is case-sensitive; use ILIKE or LOWER() for case-insensitive matching. MySQL default collation is usually case-insensitive.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why does `SELECT * FROM t WHERE col <> NULL` return no rows even when col has NULLs?
payload.answer: Any comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not true or false. WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are dropped. Use IS NOT NULL instead.
payload.source: Standard interview warmup

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
NULL is unknown; use IS NULL, never = NULL.
SELECT explicit columns; never SELECT * in production code.
WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows BEFORE grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE runs before GROUP BY; HAVING runs after.

questions.prompt: To find NULL values you write:
questions.explanation: Equality with NULL is always UNKNOWN; IS NULL is the correct test.

questions.prompt: Logical order of evaluation starts with:
questions.explanation: The engine first identifies source rows (FROM/JOIN), then filters, groups, projects, sorts.

lessons.title: JOINs — inner, left, and the ones that matter
lessons.summary: Combine tables without multiplying rows or silently dropping them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN and predict row counts
Distinguish a missing match from a NULL-filled match
Join a table to itself with aliases for hierarchical data
Diagnose accidental row multiplication from non-unique join keys

payload.text: You run a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders to list every customer with their order count. The report says a customer with 50 orders appears 50 times. The join is correct; the aggregation is missing. Row multiplication from joins is the single most common production bug in reporting SQL, and this lesson teaches you to see it before the stakeholder does.

A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column.

**The four joins that matter:**

| Join | Kept rows | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| INNER | Only matching pairs | Both sides must have data |
| LEFT | All left rows; NULL-fill right where no match | Keep every left entity, with optional detail |
| RIGHT | All right rows; NULL-fill left | Mirror of LEFT |
| FULL OUTER | All rows from both sides | Find orphans on either side |

**The row-multiplication rule:** if the join key is not unique on one side, each left row matches multiple right rows and the result has more rows than either input. COUNT(*) after a join is therefore not "count of customers" unless you aggregate per customer first.

**Self-join:** join a table to itself using aliases, e.g. employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id to pair each employee with their manager.

**Anti-join (find orphans):** LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.key IS NULL returns left rows with no match — the classic "customers who never ordered" query.

payload.title: INNER vs LEFT is a product decision
payload.text: Ask: should a customer with zero orders still appear in the report? If yes, LEFT JOIN. If only customers with orders matter, INNER JOIN. This is a requirements question, not a syntax question.

payload.code:
-- Anti-join: customers with no orders
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

payload.title: LEFT JOIN with a count, done correctly
payload.problem: List every customer and their order count, including customers with zero orders.

steps.title: Decide the join direction
steps.desc: Every customer must appear even with zero orders: LEFT JOIN from customers to orders.
steps.code_snippet:
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id

steps.title: Aggregate per customer, not per row
steps.desc: COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL order ids, so customers with no orders get 0. COUNT(*) would count the NULL-filled row as 1 — wrong.
steps.code_snippet: COUNT(o.id) AS order_count

steps.title: Complete the query
steps.desc: GROUP BY the customer columns, then order by count descending.
steps.code_snippet:
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY order_count DESC;

payload.solution: SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY order_count DESC;

payload.title: Write these
payload.prompt:
1. List all products and their category name (products LEFT JOIN categories).
2. Find employees who have never been assigned a task (anti-join).
3. Pair each employee with their manager (self-join).
payload.hint: 1: SELECT p.name, c.name FROM products p LEFT JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.id. 2: LEFT JOIN tasks, filter WHERE t.id IS NULL. 3: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id.

mistakes.mistake: Using COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN and getting inflated numbers
mistakes.fix: COUNT(*) counts NULL-filled rows as 1. Use COUNT(right.key) which skips NULLs, or aggregate in a subquery first.

mistakes.mistake: Joining on a non-unique key without aggregating
mistakes.fix: If the right side has duplicate keys, each left row multiplies. Deduplicate the right side or aggregate before joining.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing LEFT and RIGHT when the tables are written in a different order
mistakes.fix: LEFT keeps all rows from the table written immediately after FROM/LEFT JOIN. Rewrite RIGHT as LEFT by swapping table order — it is clearer.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Write a query to find customers who have never placed an order.
payload.answer: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL; — the anti-join pattern: keep all customers, filter to those whose order match is NULL.
payload.source: Classic interview question

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: INNER keeps matches only; LEFT keeps all left rows with NULL-fill.
COUNT(*) counts NULL-filled rows; COUNT(right.key) does not.
Non-unique join keys multiply rows — always check cardinality.
Anti-join: LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.key IS NULL finds orphans.

questions.prompt: A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders, with COUNT(*), gives a customer with 5 orders a count of:
questions.explanation: The customer row joins to 5 order rows; COUNT(*) counts all 6 rows including any NULL-fill only if zero orders. With 5 matching orders there is no NULL row, but if the customer had 0 orders COUNT(*) still returns 1. The safe count is COUNT(o.id).

questions.prompt: To find customers with no orders you use:
options: LEFT JOIN + WHERE right IS NULL
questions.explanation: The anti-join pattern keeps all left rows, then filters to those with no match on the right.

questions.prompt: Joining employees to themselves to get managers is called:
questions.explanation: A self-join uses aliases to treat one table as two logical relations.

modules.title: Module 2 — Aggregation, GROUP BY & Subqueries
modules.summary: Group rows into summaries, filter groups with HAVING, and nest queries without losing readability.

lessons.title: GROUP BY, HAVING and aggregate functions
lessons.summary: Summarise data correctly, and know exactly which aggregate ignores NULLs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX with correct NULL behaviour
Group rows with GROUP BY and filter groups with HAVING
Use COUNT(DISTINCT col) to count unique values
Explain why every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY

payload.text: The finance team wants "average order value per city, only for cities with more than 100 orders last year". Two filters: one on rows (last year) and one on the summary (more than 100 orders). WHERE handles the first; HAVING handles the second. Mixing them up is the most common aggregate error in take-home tests.

Aggregates collapse many rows into one summary value.

| Function | NULL handling | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| COUNT(*) | Counts all rows | Includes rows where every column is NULL |
| COUNT(col) | Skips NULLs in col | Use this for "how many have a value" |
| COUNT(DISTINCT col) | Skips NULLs, counts unique | For unique customer ids etc. |
| SUM / AVG | Ignore NULLs | AVG = SUM / count of non-NULL |
| MIN / MAX | Ignore NULLs | Work on strings and dates too |

**GROUP BY** partitions the result set into groups; each group produces one output row. Every column in the SELECT list must either be an aggregate or appear in GROUP BY — otherwise the value within the group is ambiguous.

**HAVING** filters groups after aggregation, like WHERE filters rows before it. A query can have WHERE without HAVING, HAVING without WHERE, or both.

Typical shape:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

payload.title: Filter rows in WHERE, groups in HAVING
payload.text: Push every predicate that does not involve an aggregate into WHERE. It reduces the rows before grouping and is faster and clearer.

payload.title: SELECT list vs GROUP BY mismatch
payload.text: PostgreSQL and standard SQL reject `SELECT city, customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY city` because customer_id is not determined by city. Either add it to GROUP BY or aggregate it.

payload.title: Two-level filter: rows then groups
payload.problem: From orders (id, customer_id, city, amount, created_at), report each city's order count and total revenue for 2025, only for cities with more than 50 orders.

steps.title: Filter rows first with WHERE
steps.desc: Restrict to 2025 before any aggregation so the group statistics only see that year.
steps.code_snippet:
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-01-01'

steps.title: Group by city and aggregate
steps.desc: COUNT(*) for order count; SUM(amount) for revenue.
steps.code_snippet:
GROUP BY city
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue

steps.title: Filter groups with HAVING
steps.desc: Only keep groups where the count exceeds 50. HAVING can reference the aggregate directly.
steps.code_snippet: HAVING COUNT(*) > 50

steps.title: Order the summary
steps.desc: Sort by revenue descending for the report.
steps.code_snippet: ORDER BY revenue DESC;

payload.solution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01' GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 50 ORDER BY revenue DESC;

payload.title: Write these aggregates
payload.prompt:
1. Average salary per department, only departments with avg > 40000.
2. Count distinct customers who ordered in 2025.
3. Max and min order amount per status.
payload.hint: 1: GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 40000. 2: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) with WHERE on date. 3: GROUP BY status with MIN(amount), MAX(amount).

mistakes.mistake: Using COUNT(*) when you mean COUNT(col)
mistakes.fix: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values. For "how many customers left a review", use COUNT(review_col).

mistakes.mistake: Putting an aggregate predicate in WHERE
mistakes.fix: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 10` is invalid — WHERE runs before grouping. Use HAVING.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that AVG ignores NULLs
mistakes.fix: AVG(salary) divides by the number of non-NULL salaries. If you need NULLs as zero, use AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0)).

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(customer_id)?
payload.answer: COUNT(*) counts every row in the group. COUNT(customer_id) counts only rows where customer_id is not NULL. For a LEFT JOINed orders table, COUNT(*) includes the NULL-filled order rows of customers with no orders; COUNT(order_id) correctly reports 0 for them.
payload.source: Frequent HR-screen question

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Aggregates ignore NULLs except COUNT(*).
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
Every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY.
COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values.

questions.prompt: COUNT(*) differs from COUNT(col) in that:
options: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row; COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values in that column.

questions.prompt: To filter groups after aggregation you use:
questions.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results; WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

questions.prompt: AVG(salary) when some salaries are NULL:
options: Ignores NULLs and averages the rest
questions.explanation: AVG (like SUM, MIN, MAX) ignores NULLs; only COUNT(*) includes them.

lessons.title: Subqueries and CTEs
lessons.summary: Nest a query inside another, and rewrite it as a CTE when the nesting gets unreadable.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write a scalar subquery in SELECT, WHERE or FROM
Use IN / EXISTS / ANY with subqueries for semi- and anti-joins
Rewrite a nested subquery as a Common Table Expression for readability
Decide when a correlated subquery is necessary versus a join

payload.text: The classic interview prompt: "find employees earning more than the average salary of their department". You cannot put AVG in WHERE, and a plain JOIN cannot reference the same table's group average without a subquery. The answer is either a correlated subquery in WHERE or a join against a pre-aggregated derived table — both patterns appear in every SQL screening test.

A subquery is a query nested inside another. Placement determines its type:

| Placement | Type | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SELECT list | Scalar subquery | Exactly one value |
| WHERE with IN / EXISTS | Semi-join | Filters rows by membership |
| FROM | Derived table | A temporary result set to join |
| HAVING | Group filter subquery | A single value per group comparison |

**Correlated subquery** references the outer query's row; it re-executes per outer row. Useful but often slower than an equivalent join.

**EXISTS vs IN:** EXISTS checks for any matching row (semi-join semantics); IN checks membership in a set. For NULL handling, NOT IN is dangerous: if the subquery returns any NULL, the whole NOT IN evaluates to unknown and returns zero rows. Prefer NOT EXISTS.

**CTE (WITH clause):** names a subquery so the main query reads top-to-bottom.

WITH dept_avg AS (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
  FROM employees GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN dept_avg d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal;

payload.code:
-- Correlated subquery in WHERE
SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id = e.department_id
);

payload.title: NOT IN with NULLs
payload.text: If the subquery for NOT IN can return NULL, the result is empty. Use NOT EXISTS instead — it is NULL-safe and usually clearer.

payload.title: Employees above their department average, two ways
payload.problem: List employees earning more than the average salary of their own department.

steps.title: Correlated subquery form
steps.desc: For each employee, re-compute the department average in a nested SELECT that references the outer department_id.
steps.code_snippet: WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department_id = e.department_id)

steps.title: CTE + join form
steps.desc: Pre-aggregate department averages into a CTE, then join employees to it and filter. Same result, usually faster and easier to read.
steps.code_snippet:
WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM employees GROUP BY department_id)
SELECT e.name, e.salary FROM employees e JOIN dept_avg d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal;

payload.solution: Both forms are correct. Prefer the CTE + join: the aggregation happens once, not once per employee, and the query reads top-to-bottom.

payload.title: Write these
payload.prompt:
1. Products that have never been ordered (NOT EXISTS).
2. Customers whose total spending exceeds 10000 (subquery in HAVING or CTE).
3. Rewrite #1 as a LEFT JOIN anti-join.
payload.hint: 1: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.product_id = p.id). 2: GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000. 3: LEFT JOIN orders, WHERE o.id IS NULL.

mistakes.mistake: Using NOT IN when the subquery can return NULL
mistakes.fix: Any NULL in the NOT IN list makes the whole predicate unknown. Rewrite as NOT EXISTS.

mistakes.mistake: Writing a correlated subquery when a join is cheaper
mistakes.fix: The correlated form re-executes per outer row. A CTE or derived table aggregates once. Use correlated only when the logic truly needs per-row context.

mistakes.mistake: Selecting extra columns in an IN subquery
mistakes.fix: IN compares against a single column. Multi-column membership needs row constructors or EXISTS.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Find all employees who earn more than the average salary of the whole company.
payload.answer: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees); — the subquery is uncorrelated (no outer reference), so it executes once and returns a scalar.
payload.source: Standard first-round screening

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Scalar subquery returns one value; IN/EXISTS filter rows; FROM subquery is a derived table.
Correlated subqueries reference the outer row and re-execute per row.
NOT IN breaks on NULLs; prefer NOT EXISTS.
CTEs (WITH) name subqueries for readability and single-pass aggregation.

questions.prompt: A subquery in the FROM clause is called:
questions.explanation: A derived table is a subquery in FROM that produces a temporary result set to join against.

questions.prompt: NOT IN returns no rows when the subquery contains:
questions.explanation: One NULL in the NOT IN list makes the comparison unknown for every row; use NOT EXISTS instead.

questions.prompt: A correlated subquery:
options: References outer query columns and re-executes per outer row
questions.explanation: Correlation means the inner query depends on the current outer row, so the engine evaluates it repeatedly.

modules.title: Module 3 — Schema Design, Constraints & Indexes
modules.summary: Create tables that enforce rules at the database level, and index them so reads stay fast.

lessons.title: CREATE TABLE, keys and constraints
lessons.summary: Declare primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness and defaults so bad data never enters.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write a CREATE TABLE with appropriate column types and NOT NULL constraints
Declare primary keys and understand their role as unique non-NULL identifiers
Add foreign keys that enforce referential integrity with sensible ON DELETE behaviour
Use UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT to push validation into the schema

payload.text: A startup ships an orders table without a primary key, then discovers duplicate rows after a retry bug in the API. There is no way to identify "the" order to refund. An hour of schema design in the beginning saves a week of data cleanup later. Constraints are not bureaucracy — they are the database refusing to store lies.

DDL (Data Definition Language) creates and alters structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.

**Column types (PostgreSQL-flavoured, common across engines):**

| Need | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Whole numbers | INTEGER / BIGINT | BIGINT for counts that may exceed 2B |
| Decimals / money | NUMERIC(12,2) | Exact; never FLOAT for money |
| Text | TEXT / VARCHAR(n) | TEXT when length is unbounded |
| Point in time | TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ | TIMESTAMPTZ stores UTC |
| True/false | BOOLEAN | With DEFAULT false |
| JSON document | JSONB | Queryable, indexed (PostgreSQL) |

**Constraints** are rules the DBMS enforces on every write:

| Constraint | Enforces | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PRIMARY KEY | Unique + NOT NULL identifier | id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY |
| FOREIGN KEY | Value exists in parent table | REFERENCES customers(id) |
| UNIQUE | No duplicates (NULLs allowed multiple in PG) | email UNIQUE |
| NOT NULL | Column must have a value | name TEXT NOT NULL |
| CHECK | Boolean expression holds | CHECK (amount > 0) |
| DEFAULT | Fallback when column omitted | status TEXT DEFAULT 'new' |

**ON DELETE behaviour** for foreign keys:
- RESTRICT / NO ACTION: block the parent delete.
- CASCADE: delete children too.
- SET NULL: null out the child FK.
- SET DEFAULT: set to the default value.

Choose based on ownership: line items should CASCADE with the order; a customer's address history might SET NULL or be soft-deleted instead.

payload.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status      TEXT   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'
              CHECK (status IN ('new','paid','shipped','cancelled')),
  amount      NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (customer_id, id)
);

payload.title: Soft delete beats hard delete for user data
payload.text: Add a deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ column instead of DELETE. History stays intact for audits and un-deletes are trivial. Reserve hard deletes for GDPR erase requests.

payload.title: Design a two-table schema with integrity
payload.problem: Write CREATE TABLE statements for customers and orders such that: every order belongs to a real customer, amounts are positive, and order status is one of four values.

steps.title: Customers first (parent)
steps.desc: Primary key id, unique email, NOT NULL name.

steps.title: Orders second (child)
steps.desc: FK to customers with RESTRICT (block deleting a customer who has orders). CHECK constraints for status and amount.
steps.code_snippet:
customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
amount NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN (...))

steps.title: Verify the rules hold
steps.desc: Insert a negative amount: rejected by CHECK. Delete a customer with orders: rejected by RESTRICT. Insert status "foo": rejected by CHECK.

payload.solution: The schema itself now rejects the three classic bad writes. Application validation is still useful for UX, but the database is the last line of defence and must not trust the app.

payload.title: Design these
payload.prompt:
1. A products table with SKU unique, price >= 0, and a category FK.
2. An order_items table that CASCADEs when its order is deleted.
3. Add a CHECK that an order's delivery date is after its order date.
payload.hint: 1: sku TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE; price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0); category_id REFERENCES categories(id). 2: order_id REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. 3: CHECK (delivery_date > ordered_at) — careful with NULLs: CHECK passes if the expression is NULL, so add NOT NULL if required.

mistakes.mistake: Using FLOAT or DOUBLE for money
mistakes.fix: Floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly. Use NUMERIC(12,2) or store integer paise.

mistakes.mistake: FORGETTING that CHECK passes on NULL
mistakes.fix: CHECK (amount > 0) is UNKNOWN when amount is NULL, and UNKNOWN passes. Add NOT NULL alongside every CHECK that must always hold.

mistakes.mistake: ON DELETE CASCADE on a parent that owns irreplaceable history
mistakes.fix: Cascading deletes from customers to orders destroys financial history. Prefer RESTRICT + soft delete for anything audited.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why is FLOAT unsafe for monetary amounts?
payload.answer: IEEE-754 binary floating point cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly (0.1 becomes 0.1000000000000000055...). Summing millions of such values drifts; banks notice. Use NUMERIC(p,s) for exact decimal arithmetic or BIGINT paise.
payload.source: Backend engineering screening

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: DDL: CREATE / ALTER / DROP / TRUNCATE.
PRIMARY KEY = unique + NOT NULL; FOREIGN KEY enforces parent existence.
CHECK expressions pass on NULL — pair with NOT NULL.
NUMERIC for money; never FLOAT. Choose ON DELETE deliberately.

questions.prompt: PRIMARY KEY implies:
questions.explanation: A primary key column cannot be NULL and must uniquely identify each row.

questions.prompt: CHECK (amount > 0) when amount is NULL:
questions.explanation: UNKNOWN does not fail CHECK. Add NOT NULL if a value is mandatory.

questions.prompt: ON DELETE CASCADE means:
options: Delete child rows when parent is deleted
questions.explanation: CASCADE propagates the parent delete to all referencing child rows.

lessons.title: Indexes — when they help and when they hurt
lessons.summary: Pick the right index for the query, and know the write cost you are paying.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain how a B-tree index speeds up equality and range predicates
Create a composite index that matches the query column order rule
Recognise when an index is unused (leading-column rule, functions on the column)
Weigh index write cost and choose indexes that match real query patterns

payload.text: An orders table with 10 million rows takes 8 seconds to answer WHERE customer_id = 42. One CREATE INDEX later it takes 2 milliseconds. The same table starts rejecting writes at 30 ms instead of 1 ms, because every insert now maintains four indexes. Indexes are a read-speed / write-speed trade, and choosing them blindly is how databases get slow in production.

An index is an auxiliary structure (usually a B-tree) that maps key values to row locations, turning a full table scan into a tree search.

**What an index speeds up:**
- Equality: WHERE customer_id = 42
- Range: WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
- ORDER BY / GROUP BY on the indexed columns (avoids a sort)
- JOIN on the indexed key

**Composite index column order (the leftmost-prefix rule):**
An index on (a, b, c) can serve queries filtering on a, or a+b, or a+b+c — but NOT on b alone or b+c without a. Put the most selective, most frequently filtered column first.

**When an index is NOT used:**
- The column is wrapped in a function: WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x' ignores an index on email. Use an expression index on LOWER(email) instead.
- The leading column of a composite index is not in the query.
- The query returns most of the table (the planner prefers a scan).
- The column has very low cardinality (e.g. boolean) unless combined with other columns.

**Write cost:** every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update every index on the table. Four indexes can double or triple write latency. Index only columns that real queries filter, join or sort on.

payload.title: Index decision cheat-sheet
rows: Index them (FKs are not auto-indexed in PG)
Column used only in ORDER BY
Composite index can avoid a sort
Skip; combine into a composite if needed
Expression index, or rewrite the query

payload.title: Check with EXPLAIN before adding indexes
payload.text: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the slow query. If it shows a sequential scan on a large table with a selective predicate, an index is likely the fix. If it already uses an index, the problem is elsewhere.

payload.title: Choose a composite index for a reporting query
payload.problem: The query WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND status = 'active' AND created_at >= '2025-01-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC is slow. Design the index.

steps.title: List the filtered columns
steps.desc: Equality columns: tenant_id, status. Range column: created_at. Sort: created_at DESC.
steps.code_snippet:
Equality: tenant_id, status
Range/sort: created_at

steps.title: Apply the column order rule
steps.desc: Equality columns first (most selective first among them), then the range/sort column last. tenant_id is usually more selective than status.
steps.code_snippet:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_status_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);

steps.title: Verify with EXPLAIN
steps.desc: The plan should show an index scan using the new index, with a filter on created_at (range conditions cannot use a bitmap AND after equality in older planners, but the leading equality columns are used).

payload.solution: CREATE INDEX on (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC). Equality columns lead; the range and sort column trails. Always confirm with EXPLAIN — theory predicts, the planner decides.

payload.title: Design indexes for these queries
payload.prompt:
1. WHERE email = 'x@y.z' (login path).
2. WHERE order_id = 5 AND line_no = 2 (order item lookup).
3. WHERE LOWER(slug) = 'intro-to-sql' (URL routing).
payload.hint: 1: single-column index on email (or UNIQUE at design time). 2: composite (order_id, line_no) matching the query order. 3: expression index on LOWER(slug); a plain index on slug is unused by the LOWER() predicate.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming foreign keys are auto-indexed
mistakes.fix: PostgreSQL does NOT index FK columns. A child table with millions of rows and an unindexed FK makes every parent delete a full child scan. Index every FK.

mistakes.mistake: Building indexes on every column "just in case"
mistakes.fix: Each index costs write throughput and disk. Start from the actual slow queries; add indexes that EXPLAIN shows are needed.

mistakes.mistake: Composite index with the wrong leading column
mistakes.fix: Index (status, tenant_id) does not help WHERE tenant_id = 7 (leading column status is not constrained). Order matters: equality columns first.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: An index on (a, b) can serve which WHERE clauses?
payload.answer: WHERE a = ..., WHERE a = ... AND b = ..., and range on a with optional b — i.e. any query that constrains the leading column a. It cannot serve WHERE b = ... alone, because the B-tree is sorted primarily by a.
payload.source: DBA / backend interview staple

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: B-tree indexes speed equality, range, ORDER BY and JOIN on their columns.
Composite order: equality columns first (most selective), range/sort last.
Function on the column disables a plain index; use an expression index.
Every index slows writes; FKs need explicit indexes in PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: An index on (a, b) can accelerate:
options: WHERE a = 1 or WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2
Any WHERE on a or b
questions.explanation: Leftmost prefix: a must be constrained for the index to apply; b alone cannot use it.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL foreign key columns are:
questions.explanation: You must create the index yourself, or every parent delete scans the child table.

questions.prompt: WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x' ignores an index on email because:
options: the predicate applies a function to the column
questions.explanation: The B-tree stores email, not LOWER(email). Create an expression index on LOWER(email) or rewrite the predicate.

modules.title: Module 4 — Normalization, Transactions & Advanced Queries
modules.summary: Design tables in 3NF, reason about ACID, and use window functions for running totals and rankings.

lessons.title: Normalization up to 3NF
lessons.summary: Remove repeating data without making queries impossible to write.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in plain language with a concrete example
Normalise a denormalised table into 3NF step by step
Recognise when deliberate denormalisation is the right trade-off
Spot update, insert and delete anomalies in a bad schema

payload.text: An orders table stores customer_name and customer_email on every order row. When a customer changes their email, you must UPDATE thousands of rows — miss one and the data is inconsistent forever. That is an update anomaly, and normalization is the systematic fix. Every design interview eventually asks "is this schema normalised?"; this lesson gives the answer structure.

Normalization splits tables so each fact is stored once. The anomalies it prevents:

| Anomaly | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- |
| Insert | Cannot record a customer who has no orders yet (if customer data is only on orders) |
| Update | Changing one fact requires updating many rows |
| Delete | Deleting the last order deletes the customer record too |

**1NF — atomic values.** No repeating groups or arrays in a cell. A phone_numbers column with "98765,98766" violates 1NF; split into a separate table.

**2NF — 1NF + no partial dependency.** Every non-key column depends on the WHOLE primary key, not just part of it. This matters for composite keys: if key is (order_id, product_id), a column "product_name" depends only on product_id — partial dependency, violates 2NF. Fix: move product_name to a products table.

**3NF — 2NF + no transitive dependency.** Non-key columns do not depend on each other. If employees.department_id determines department_name, then department_name is transitively dependent on employee_id via department_id. Fix: move department_name to a departments table.

**Practical target for most applications: 3NF.** Enough to eliminate the classic anomalies, not so fragmented that every read needs five joins.

**When to denormalise deliberately:** read-heavy reporting tables, materialised views, and hot paths where a join costs too much. Denormalise with eyes open: add triggers or jobs to keep the copies consistent.

payload.title: Normal forms, quickly
rows: 1NF + no partial dependency on part of a composite key

payload.title: Normalise first, denormalise later with evidence
payload.text: Get the 3NF design correct. If profiling shows a join is hot, denormalise that one path — not the whole schema preemptively.

payload.title: Normalise a denormalised orders table
payload.problem: You have a single table Orders(order_id, product_id, product_name, product_price, customer_id, customer_name, customer_email, qty). Bring it to 3NF.

steps.title: 1NF check
steps.desc: Each cell holds one value; (order_id, product_id) as composite key means one row per line item. Already 1NF if no multi-value cells.

steps.title: 2NF fix — remove partial dependencies
steps.desc: product_name and product_price depend only on product_id, not on the full composite key. Move them to a products table keyed by product_id.
steps.code_snippet: Products(product_id PK, product_name, product_price)

steps.title: 3NF fix — remove transitive dependencies
steps.desc: customer_name and customer_email depend only on customer_id. Move them to customers. Remaining Orders columns depend fully on the composite key and not on each other.
steps.code_snippet:
Customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, customer_email)
OrderLines(order_id, product_id, qty, PK(order_id, product_id))
Orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK)

payload.solution: Four tables: Customers, Products, Orders (header), OrderLines (composite key). Customer email changes in one row. New products can exist before any order. Deleting an order line does not erase the product.

payload.title: Normalise these
payload.prompt:
1. Student(student_id, name, course1, course2, course3) — bring to 1NF/2NF.
2. Invoice(invoice_id, client_id, client_city, item, price) — bring to 3NF.
3. Identify the anomaly in a schema that stores employee.department_name directly.
payload.hint: 1: one row per (student, course): Enrolments(student_id, course_code). 2: Clients(client_id, client_city); InvoiceItems(invoice_id, item, price). 3: update anomaly — changing the department city requires updating every employee row.

mistakes.mistake: Normalising to BCNF/4NF for a simple CRUD app
mistakes.fix: 3NF is the practical target. Higher normal forms add joins for diminishing anomaly protection; only pursue them when the data model truly demands it.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing 2NF and 3NF
mistakes.fix: 2NF is about composite keys and partial dependencies. 3NF is about transitive dependencies between non-key columns. Both require 1NF first.

mistakes.mistake: Denormalising without a consistency story
mistakes.fix: A copied column that can drift is worse than a join. If you denormalise, add a trigger, constraint or job that keeps the copy truthful.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define 3NF and give one anomaly a 3NF schema prevents.
payload.answer: A schema is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and no non-key column transitively depends on the primary key through another non-key column. Example prevention: storing department_name on every employee row would force an update across all employees when the department is renamed; a separate departments table updates one row.
payload.source: DB design interview standard

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: 1NF atomic; 2NF no partial dependency; 3NF no transitive non-key dependency.
Anomalies: insert, update, delete — normalization eliminates them.
Practical target: 3NF; denormalise only with evidence and a consistency plan.
Composite keys make 2NF violations common — check partial dependencies carefully.

questions.prompt: 2NF eliminates:
options: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
questions.explanation: 2NF requires every non-key column to depend on the whole key, not a subset of a composite key.

questions.prompt: 3NF eliminates:
questions.explanation: Transitive: non-key A determines non-key B, so B should live with A, not with the main entity.

questions.prompt: Updating customer email stored on every order row risks:
options: An update anomaly (inconsistent data if one row is missed)
questions.explanation: Update anomaly: one logical fact is stored many times; partial updates create inconsistency.

lessons.title: Transactions, isolation and window functions
lessons.summary: Guarantee all-or-nothing writes, understand dirty reads, and compute running totals without self-joins.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: State the ACID properties and what each one guarantees
Distinguish READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE isolation levels
Use window functions for running totals, ranks and row-to-row comparisons
Decide when a window function replaces a correlated subquery

payload.text: A bank transfer debits one account and credits another. If the process crashes after the debit and before the credit, money vanishes. Transactions exist so the database commits both or neither. Separately, a product dashboard needs "each sale as a percent of its category total" — a window function computes that in one pass; a correlated subquery does it in N passes.

**ACID:**

| Property | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Atomicity | All statements in the transaction commit, or none do |
| Consistency | Constraints and rules hold after commit |
| Isolation | Concurrent transactions do not see each other's uncommitted work (level-dependent) |
| Durability | Committed data survives crashes |

**Isolation levels and their anomalies:**

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| READ UNCOMMITTED | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| READ COMMITTED | No | Yes | Yes |
| REPEATABLE READ | No | No | Yes (PG: mostly no, uses snapshot) |
| SERIALIZABLE | No | No | No |

Most web apps run at READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL default). Financial ledgers often need REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE plus explicit locking.

**Window functions** compute across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them (unlike GROUP BY):

- Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
- Rank within group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY price DESC)
- Share of total: SUM(amount) OVER () for a grand total to divide by
- Row-to-row compare: LAG(col) OVER (ORDER BY id) for the previous row's value

Syntax shape: function() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame).

Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY, so you cannot filter on a window result in the same query's WHERE — wrap it in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.

payload.code:
-- Running total per customer
SELECT customer_id, created_at, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY customer_id
         ORDER BY created_at
         ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
       ) AS running_total
FROM orders;

payload.title: FOR UPDATE to prevent lost updates
payload.text: Two concurrent transfers reading the same balance and writing new balances can lose one update (read-modify-write race). SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the rows for the duration of the transaction.

payload.title: Rank products within each category and share of category revenue
payload.problem: From order_items (product_id, category_id, revenue), rank products by revenue within each category and compute each product's share of its category total.

steps.title: Rank within partition
steps.desc: PARTITION BY category_id creates one ranking per category; ORDER BY revenue DESC puts the top seller first.
steps.code_snippet: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS cat_rank

steps.title: Category total as a window
steps.desc: SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category_id) repeats the category total on every row of that category.
steps.code_snippet: SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category_id) AS cat_total

steps.title: Divide for share
steps.desc: Share = revenue / cat_total. Cast to avoid integer division in some engines.
steps.code_snippet: revenue * 1.0 / cat_total AS cat_share

payload.solution: SELECT product_id, category_id, revenue, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS cat_rank, revenue * 1.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category_id) AS cat_share FROM order_items;

payload.title: Write these
payload.prompt:
1. Running balance per account using SUM OVER ordered by transaction time.
2. LAG to find each row delta from the previous row.
3. Transactions at SERIALIZABLE: when would you choose it over REPEATABLE READ?
payload.hint: 1: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY posted_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING). 2: amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id). 3: when write skew between concurrent transactions must be impossible (e.g. transfer + balance check across accounts).

mistakes.mistake: Using GROUP BY when you meant a window function
mistakes.fix: GROUP BY collapses rows; OVER () keeps them. "Each row plus its category total" is a window, not a group.

mistakes.mistake: Filtering a window result in the same WHERE
mistakes.fix: Windows are computed after WHERE. Wrap the window query in a CTE or subquery, then filter the outer query.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming REPEATABLE READ prevents phantoms in every engine
mistakes.fix: SQL standard says phantoms are possible; PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ uses a snapshot and does prevent them in practice. Check your engine docs.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Write a query for each order showing amount and the running total per customer.
payload.answer: SELECT customer_id, created_at, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total FROM orders;
payload.source: Analytics SQL screening

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
Isolation levels trade anomalies for concurrency; READ COMMITTED is the common default.
Window functions keep row detail while computing across related rows.
PARTITION BY splits windows; ORDER BY + frame defines the running set.
Cannot filter window results in the same WHERE — use a subquery/CTE.

questions.prompt: READ COMMITTED prevents:
questions.explanation: You never see other transactions uncommitted data, but another commit between your reads can change values you re-read.

questions.prompt: Running total per customer uses:
options: SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at)
questions.explanation: Window SUM with an ordered frame keeps each row and adds a cumulative column.

questions.prompt: Window functions are evaluated:
options: After WHERE and GROUP BY, before DISTINCT/ORDER BY/LIMIT
questions.explanation: Logical order: WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> window functions -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.

courses.title: Web Development Bootcamp
courses.subtitle: HTML, modern CSS, JavaScript, forms, APIs and performance — the frontend stack every product team hires for
courses.description:
Every product has a web interface, and every product team needs people who can build one properly. This bootcamp covers the foundation the frameworks assume you already know: semantic HTML, the CSS box model, flexbox and grid, modern JavaScript with the DOM, accessible forms, REST API integration and a performance workflow with the browser DevTools.

Eight lessons across four modules. Every lesson follows the nine-step structure: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, the exam angle, a server-graded quiz and a one-screen summary. A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final exam; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** students who have copied tutorial code but cannot yet build a page from scratch, and anyone preparing for a junior frontend interview. The course deliberately teaches the platform (HTML/CSS/JS) before any framework, so React or Vue later becomes an acceleration rather than a crutch.

**What you need:** a browser and a text editor. A free hosting account (GitHub Pages, Netlify or similar) is recommended for the project so you finish with a live URL, not just local files.
outcomes: Write semantic, accessible HTML with correct landmarks and form controls
Predict box-model sizing and fix overflowing layouts with border-box
Build responsive layouts with flexbox, grid and mobile-first media queries
Write modern JavaScript: const/let, arrow functions, array methods, async/await
Manipulate the DOM safely with delegation and textContent
Validate and submit accessible forms with inline errors
Consume REST APIs with a central fetch client and a loading/error/data state machine
Use Network and Performance panels to diagnose load time and interaction jank
courses.about_course:
Most "learn web development" content jumps straight into a framework. That works for demos and fails for careers: when something breaks, you need to read HTML and CSS, understand the event loop, and reason about the network. This course teaches the platform first.

HTML is taught as meaning, not tags — landmarks, heading order, and why a button is not a div. CSS is taught through the box model and cascade so layout stops being guesswork; flex and grid then become tools with clear jobs. JavaScript covers the modern subset actually used in production: immutable bindings, pure array transforms, the practical event loop, and fetch with real error handling. Forms and performance close the loop with the accessibility and measurement habits that separate professionals from tutorial-followers.

Every lesson ends with a quiz graded on the server, and the course finishes with a 15-question timed exam drawn from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

A browser and text editor (VS Code recommended)

Anyone who can follow a tutorial but cannot yet build independently

modules.title: Module 1 — HTML Structure & CSS Fundamentals
modules.summary: Semantic markup and the box model — the two ideas every frontend job interview assumes.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML: structure that means something
lessons.summary: Write markup that browsers, screen readers and search engines can actually understand.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain why semantic tags matter for accessibility and SEO
Build a page skeleton with header, nav, main, section, article, aside and footer
Choose the correct heading level and form control type
Know when a div is appropriate and when a semantic element is required

payload.text: A recruiter's screen reader opens your portfolio site. Every region is announced as "group" because the page is sixty divs. The same site rebuilt with header, nav, main and section announces landmarks the tool can jump between. Nothing about the visual design changed — only the meaning. That difference is why "just use divs" is a career-limiting habit.

HTML describes meaning and structure; CSS describes appearance; JavaScript describes behaviour. Mixing those jobs produces pages that are fragile and inaccessible.

**Semantic elements and what they announce:**

| Element | Meaning | Landmark? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| header | Introductory content or nav for a section | Yes (banner when top-level) |
| nav | Major navigation links | Yes |
| main | Dominant content of the document | Yes |
| section | Thematic grouping of content | No |
| article | Self-contained composition (post, card) | No |
| aside | Tangentially related content | Yes (complementary) |
| footer | Closing content for a section or page | Yes (contentinfo when bottom) |

**Headings form an outline.** Do not skip levels (h1 then h3). One h1 per page typically names the page. Screen readers build a heading tree users navigate; skipped levels break that tree.

**Forms:** always use the right input type. type=email, type=tel, type=number, type=date give mobile keyboards, native validation, and autofill hints. A type=text input for an email address costs real usability.

**Images need alt text.** Decorative images get alt="" (empty string, not omitted); informative images get a description. Screen readers skip empty alt; missing alt often gets the file name read aloud.

payload.title: One h1, then descend
payload.text: h1 names the page; h2 are major sections; h3 subsections. Never use a heading for visual size — that is CSS's job.

payload.title: onclick on a non-button
payload.text: A div with onclick is invisible to keyboard users and screen readers. Use <button> for actions and <a> for navigation; style them to look like whatever you want.

payload.title: Rebuild a div soup as semantic landmarks
payload.problem:
Convert this markup to semantic HTML without changing the visual order:
...
...
...

steps.title: Identify roles
steps.desc: top = page header + primary nav; content = main with an article; bottom = footer with secondary info.
steps.code_snippet:
header > nav
main > article
footer

steps.title: Rewrite with landmarks
steps.desc: Replace each structural div with the matching semantic element. Keep classes for styling hooks if needed.
steps.code_snippet:
<header><nav>...</nav></header>
<main><article>...</article></main>
<footer>...</footer>

steps.title: Fix headings and links inside
steps.desc: Site title becomes h1 inside header (or main, depending on layout). Post title becomes h2 inside article. Nav links stay <a href>.

payload.solution: Same pixels, different meaning. The accessibility tree now exposes banner, navigation, main, article and contentinfo landmarks; the outline has a coherent heading tree; crawlers attribute the content correctly.

2. A contact form with name, email, phone and message fields — correct types and labels.
3. A page with a sidebar of related links (semantic element for the sidebar?).

mistakes.mistake: Using heading tags purely for font size
mistakes.fix: Headings define outline order, not appearance. Style with CSS; choose the level that matches document structure.

mistakes.fix: Missing alt often reads the file name aloud. Informative images get a description; decorative ones get alt="".

mistakes.fix: div/span with onclick exclude keyboard users. Use button or a with proper roles when you must.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: HTML = meaning; CSS = appearance; JS = behaviour.
Landmarks: header, nav, main, aside, footer — screen reader jump points.
One h1; never skip heading levels.
Correct input types; labels for every control; alt on every img.

questions.prompt: Which element is a screen-reader landmark?
questions.explanation: header (banner when top-level), nav, main, aside and footer are landmarks.

questions.prompt: A decorative image should have:
questions.explanation: Empty alt tells assistive tech to skip it; omitting alt may cause the file name to be read.

questions.explanation: button is focusable, keyboard-activatable and announced as a button by default.

lessons.title: CSS box model, selectors and cascade
lessons.summary: Predict exactly how much space an element occupies, and control which rules win.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute total element width from content, padding, border and margin
Use box-sizing: border-box and explain why frameworks default to it
Write class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors with correct specificity
Trace the cascade: origin, specificity and source order

payload.text: A two-column layout keeps overflowing by 16 pixels. The content is exactly 50% wide, so it should fit. It does not, because each column also has 8px padding and a 1px border that the browser adds outside the declared 50%. box-sizing: border-box makes the declared width include padding and border — one line that prevents an entire family of layout bugs.

**The box model:** every element is content + padding + border + margin.

| Part | Inside the border? | Affects layout? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| content | — | Yes (defines intrinsic size) |
| padding | Inside border, outside content | Yes, adds to visual size |
| border | Edge of the box | Yes, adds to visual size |
| margin | Outside the border | Yes, collapses between siblings (vertical) |

Default box-sizing is content-box: width applies to content only. border-box: width includes content + padding + border. Frameworks set * { box-sizing: border-box } because it makes "width: 50%" mean what a human expects.

**Specificity** ranks selectors as (inline, id, class/attribute/pseudo-class, type/pseudo-element). Higher tuple wins. !important overrides the cascade entirely — avoid it; fix specificity or cascade order instead.

**Cascade order when specificity ties:** later rule wins. Import order and stylesheet order matter.

payload.title: Prefer classes over ids for styling
payload.text: Ids win specificity wars and cannot be reused. Style with classes; reserve ids for JS hooks and form labels.

payload.title: Fix the overflowing two-column layout
payload.problem: .col { width: 50%; padding: 8px; border: 1px solid #ccc; } — two .col siblings overflow their container.

steps.title: Compute the default total width
steps.desc: content 50% + padding 16px + border 2px per column. Two columns exceed 100% by 36px.

steps.title: Switch to border-box
steps.desc: Declared width now includes padding and border, so two 50% columns fit exactly.
steps.code_snippet: .col { box-sizing: border-box; width: 50%; padding: 8px; border: 1px solid #ccc; }

steps.title: Or use a modern layout instead
steps.desc: display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr handles gaps and sizing without manual width math.
steps.code_snippet: .row { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }

payload.solution: box-sizing: border-box on both columns fixes the overflow. Prefer grid or flex for multi-column layouts so you rarely compute widths by hand.

payload.title: Answer these
payload.prompt:
1. An element has width: 200px, padding: 10px, border: 2px. Total outer width with content-box? With border-box?
2. Which wins: .btn.primary or #submit?
3. Why do vertical margins collapse but horizontal ones do not?
payload.hint: 1: content-box 224px; border-box 200px. 2: #submit (id beats class). 3: Adjacent in-flow block siblings share one margin = max of the two; horizontal margins never collapse because boxes are side by side.

mistakes.mistake: Fighting the cascade with !important everywhere
mistakes.fix: One !important arms race leads to ten. Restructure selectors or reorder sheets instead.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing content-box and border-box in one project
mistakes.fix: Set * { box-sizing: border-box } at the top of the stylesheet and keep it consistent.

mistakes.mistake: Using ids for reusable component styles
mistakes.fix: Ids have high specificity and cannot repeat. Classes are the correct styling hook.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What does box-sizing: border-box change?
payload.answer: The declared width/height includes content, padding and border, instead of applying to content alone. Prevents layouts from overflowing when padding and border are added to a percentage width.
payload.source: Every CSS screening question

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Box model: content, padding, border, margin — know which parts add size.
border-box makes width include padding+border; frameworks default to it.
Specificity tuple: inline > id > class > type; ties broken by source order.
Style with classes; avoid !important.

questions.prompt: box-sizing: border-box means the declared width includes:
questions.explanation: border-box folds padding and border into the declared width/height.

questions.explanation: Both #title .card and .card #title score (0,1,1,0) — equal specificity; source order breaks ties. In interview framing, remember: any id component beats pure class selectors like .card .title.
