questions.explanation: Margin collapsing: adjacent vertical margins merge to the max value.

modules.title: Module 2 — JavaScript Fundamentals & the DOM
modules.summary: Variables, functions, events and querying the page — the runtime half of frontend.

lessons.title: Variables, functions and control flow in modern JS
lessons.summary: let/const, arrow functions, array methods and the async model that frameworks build on.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Choose between const, let and avoid var for variable declaration
Write and compose arrow functions and pure array methods (map, filter, reduce)
Explain the event loop at a practical level: call stack, microtasks, macrotasks
Use fetch with async/await and handle errors without silent failures

payload.text: A dashboard fetches three APIs in sequence, each waiting for the previous one, taking 900 ms total. The APIs are independent; they should take 300 ms. The fix is one line of modern JS: Promise.all. Understanding that the browser can do independent I/O concurrently — and that await only pauses your function — separates junior from mid-level frontend code.

**Declarations:** const by default; let when reassignment is needed; never var (function-scoped, hoisted, confusing).

**Functions:** prefer arrow functions for callbacks (lexical this, concise). Named function declarations still suit hoisted utility functions.

**Array methods replace loops for transforms:**

| Method | Use |
| --- | --- |
| map | Transform each element, return new array |
| filter | Keep elements matching a predicate |
| reduce | Collapse array to a single value |
| find / some / every | Search / membership checks |
| forEach | Side effects only; returns undefined |

**The event loop (practical model):** JavaScript runs single-threaded. Synchronous code occupies the call stack. Resolved promises queue as microtasks (run first); setTimeout callbacks queue as macrotasks (run after microtasks drain). await yields to the event loop, letting the page stay responsive.

**fetch + async/await:** fetch does not reject on HTTP 4xx/5xx — you must check response.ok. Wrap in try/catch for network errors; check status for HTTP errors.

payload.title: const first, let when rebinding
payload.text: Most variables never need reassignment. const documents intent and catches accidental reassignment at development time.

payload.title: fetch does not throw on 404
payload.text: A 404 response is a successful network fetch of an error page. Always check response.ok before calling .json() and treating the body as data.

payload.title: Parallelise independent requests
payload.problem: Rewrite sequential fetches so total latency is the max of the three, not the sum.

steps.title: See the sequential mistake
steps.desc: await a, then await b, then await c stacks latencies: 300+300+300 = 900ms.
steps.code_snippet:
const a = await fetch(A); // 300ms
const b = await fetch(B); // +300ms
const c = await fetch(C); // +300ms

steps.title: Start all three, then await
steps.desc: Promise.all takes an array of promises and resolves when all settle. Start all three fetches before awaiting.
steps.code_snippet: const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([fetch(A), fetch(B), fetch(C)]);

steps.title: Handle partial failure if needed
steps.desc: Promise.all rejects on the first failure. For independent best-effort loads, use Promise.allSettled and inspect each result status.
steps.code_snippet: const results = await Promise.allSettled([fetch(A), fetch(B)]);

payload.solution: Promise.all for all-or-nothing parallelism; Promise.allSettled when partial results are acceptable. The key insight: create the promises first (they start running), then await them together.

payload.title: Write these
payload.prompt:
1. Filter an array of products to in-stock items over 1000, then map to their names.
2. Reduce an array of orders to total revenue.
3. Fetch a URL, handle both network errors and non-ok HTTP status.
payload.hint: 1: products.filter(p => p.stock > 0 && p.price > 1000).map(p => p.name). 2: orders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.amount, 0). 3: try/catch around fetch; if (!res.ok) throw.

mistakes.mistake: Using await inside a forEach
mistakes.fix: forEach ignores the returned promise; iterations still run concurrently without waiting. Use for...of with await, or map + Promise.all.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that fetch resolves on 404/500
mistakes.fix: Check response.ok. A 500 with an HTML error body will make .json() throw a confusing parse error.

mistakes.mistake: var in modern code
mistakes.fix: var is function-scoped and hoisted; let/const are block-scoped and TDZ-protected. Use const/let only.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why does `const [a,b] = await Promise.all([fetch(x), fetch(y)])` finish faster than two sequential awaits?
payload.answer: Both fetches are initiated before either await runs, so the network requests proceed concurrently. Each await only pauses its own function; the browser continues both transfers in parallel. Latency becomes max(t1, t2), not t1+t2.
payload.source: Mid-level frontend interview

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: const default; let for reassignment; no var.
map/filter/replace transform loops; reduce collapses to a value.
Promise.all for parallel all-or-nothing; allSettled for partial.
fetch resolves on HTTP errors — check response.ok.

questions.prompt: const vs let: choose const when:
questions.explanation: const prevents reassignment; the object/array contents can still mutate.

questions.prompt: fetch("/missing") with a 404 response:
questions.explanation: HTTP error statuses still resolve the fetch promise; check .ok before parsing.

questions.prompt: Promise.all rejects when:
questions.explanation: One rejection fails the whole Promise.all; use allSettled for tolerance.

lessons.title: DOM manipulation and events
lessons.summary: Query elements, react to user actions, and update the page without a framework.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Query and update elements with querySelector, textContent and classList
Attach event listeners, understand bubbling, and use event delegation
Create and remove elements safely without innerHTML for user data
Prevent default behaviour for forms and links when needed

payload.text: A todo list attaches a click listener to every delete button when the list renders. After adding 100 items, removing one re-binds listeners for the other 99. Event delegation solves it: one listener on the parent, checking event.target.closest. It is the pattern every DOM-heavy codebase uses, and it is one concept to learn.

**Querying:** document.querySelector for the first match; querySelectorAll for a NodeList (convert with spread or Array.from for array methods).

**Updating:** textContent for text (safe from HTML injection); classList.add/remove/toggle for classes; setAttribute for attributes; style properties for inline styles (prefer classes for anything non-trivial).

**Events and bubbling:** a click on a child bubbles up through ancestors. You can listen on an ancestor and use event.target to find the original element.

**Delegation:** put one listener on a stable parent; on each event, check event.target.closest('selector') for the element you care about. Works for elements added later without re-binding.

**Creating nodes:** createElement + append is safe for user data. Avoid innerHTML with interpolated user content — it is an XSS vector. If you must set HTML from trusted strings, at least understand the risk.

**preventDefault:** form submit reloads the page by default; link navigation follows href. Call event.preventDefault() when you want to handle the action in JS.

payload.title: Never innerHTML user content
payload.text: Pasting user-supplied strings into innerHTML executes any HTML/JS they contain. Use textContent or createElement.

payload.title: Delegated delete for a dynamic list
payload.problem: A list re-renders on every change. Attach delete handling without re-binding listeners each render.

steps.title: Listen once on the stable parent
steps.desc: The ul (or container) exists for the page lifetime. Attach the click listener once at init.
steps.code_snippet: container.addEventListener('click', onClick);

steps.title: Find the button inside the target
steps.desc: Clicks may land on the button's icon child. closest walks up to the element with your selector.
steps.code_snippet: const btn = event.target.closest('button[data-delete]');

steps.title: Act and let render rebuild the list
steps.desc: Remove the item from your data array, re-render the list. No listener re-binding required.

payload.solution: One listener survives infinite re-renders. This is why frameworks can re-render wholesale without leaking listeners — delegation is the native equivalent.

payload.title: Build these
payload.prompt:
1. A counter with + and - buttons that update a display via delegation.
2. A form that prevents default and appends the typed name to a list (no page reload).
3. Toggle a "dark" class on body when a button is clicked.
payload.hint: 1: click on parent; closest('[data-step]'). 2: submit listener + preventDefault; textContent for the name. 3: document.body.classList.toggle('dark').

mistakes.mistake: Re-attaching listeners after every render
mistakes.fix: Use event delegation on a stable ancestor. Or remove old listeners before adding new ones (leak-prone and error-prone).

mistakes.mistake: innerHTML with user or API data
mistakes.fix: XSS risk. Use textContent or build nodes with createElement.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that events bubble
mistakes.fix: A listener on a child may fire for intended grandchild clicks — or a listener on document may catch everything. Know the path; stopPropagation sparingly.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is event delegation and why is it useful?
payload.answer: Attaching one listener to a common ancestor and using event.target / closest to handle events from descendant elements (including ones not yet in the DOM). Saves listeners, survives re-renders, and is the standard pattern for dynamic lists.
payload.source: Frontend DOM interview standard

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: querySelector(All) to find; textContent/classList to update.
Events bubble; delegation listens on a stable parent + closest().
createElement/textContent for user data; never innerHTML it.
preventDefault stops form submit reloads and default link navigation.

questions.prompt: Event delegation relies on:
options: Event bubbling to a stable ancestor
questions.explanation: The event bubbles up; closest() on the target finds the actionable element.

questions.prompt: Safely setting user-supplied text uses:
questions.explanation: textContent sets plain text and does not parse HTML, avoiding XSS.

questions.prompt: Form submit reloads the page unless you:
questions.explanation: preventDefault cancels the browser default action (navigation/reload).

modules.title: Module 3 — Responsive Layouts & Forms
modules.summary: Flexbox, grid and media queries for mobile-first pages; accessible forms that actually validate.

lessons.title: Flexbox, Grid and media queries
lessons.summary: Build layouts that collapse cleanly from desktop to phone without float hacks.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use flexbox for one-dimensional rows or columns with gap, alignment and wrapping
Use grid for two-dimensional layouts with fr units and template areas
Apply mobile-first media queries with a min-width breakpoint strategy
Know when flex, grid or plain block flow is the right tool

payload.text: Before flexbox, every layout tutorial began with "clear: both" and negative margins. A navigation bar that used to take forty lines of float CSS is now display: flex; justify-content: space-between; gap: 1rem. Grid handles the page skeleton in three more lines. This lesson is the toolkit that makes those two paragraphs true for you.

**Flexbox** — one axis (row or column):

| Property | Values you will use |
| --- | --- |
| display | flex |
| flex-direction | row (default) / column |
| justify-content | flex-start / center / space-between / space-around (main axis) |
| align-items | stretch / center / flex-start (cross axis) |
| gap | 1rem — replaces margin hacks between items |
| flex-wrap | wrap — items flow to new lines when needed |

**Grid** — two axes:

| Property | Values you will use |
| --- | --- |
| display | grid |
| grid-template-columns | 1fr 2fr / repeat(3, 1fr) / minmax(200px, 1fr) |
| gap | row-gap / column-gap or gap |
| grid-template-areas | named regions for complex layouts |

fr is a fraction of free space. minmax(200px, 1fr) ensures a floor while still filling.

**Mobile-first media queries:** write the base CSS for small screens, then add min-width queries for larger ones. This keeps the default payload small and avoids the "desktop styles then try to undo them on mobile" trap.

    .card { width: 100%; }
    @media (min-width: 640px) { .card { width: 50%; } }
    @media (min-width: 1024px) { .card { width: 25%; } }

payload.title: Flex for toolbars and rows; grid for page skeletons
payload.text: Navigation bars, button groups, card footers: flex. Overall page layout, image galleries, dashboards: grid. Both together is normal — grid for the shell, flex inside each cell.

payload.title: Do not set fixed pixel widths for columns
payload.text: Fixed widths break on small screens. Prefer fr, percentage, or minmax so the layout adapts without a media query for every possible width.

payload.title: A responsive card grid, mobile-first
payload.problem: Cards should be full width on phones, two-up on tablets, three-up on desktop, with consistent gaps.

steps.title: Base: single column
steps.desc: Grid with one column is the mobile default; gap handles spacing between cards.
steps.code_snippet: .grid { display: grid; gap: 1rem; grid-template-columns: 1fr; }

steps.title: Tablet: two columns
steps.desc: A min-width query overrides the template for wider viewports.
steps.code_snippet: @media (min-width: 640px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }

steps.title: Desktop: three columns with minmax
steps.desc: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)) avoids overflow from long content inside flexible tracks.
steps.code_snippet: @media (min-width: 1024px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)); } }

payload.solution: Three breakpoints, one grid container, zero float clearing. Adding a fourth card needs no layout change — grid reflows automatically.

payload.title: Build these
payload.prompt:
1. A navbar: logo left, links right on desktop; stacked on mobile.
2. A two-column article + sidebar that becomes one column below 768px.
3. A footer with three equal columns using grid.
payload.hint: 1: flex row with justify-content space-between; flex-direction column on mobile. 2: grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr with min-width query. 3: grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr).

mistakes.mistake: Desktop-first with max-width queries
mistakes.fix: Mobile-first min-width is simpler: one base style, progressive enhancement. Undoing desktop styles on small screens gets messy fast.

mistakes.mistake: Using float for layout
mistakes.fix: Floats are for wrapping text around images. Flex and grid exist for layout; use them.

mistakes.mistake: Fixed pixel widths that break on narrow screens
mistakes.fix: Percentage, fr and minmax keep layouts fluid. Fixed widths are for intentional design constraints (e.g. a max-width reading column).

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: When would you choose CSS Grid over Flexbox?
payload.answer: When you need to control both rows and columns simultaneously — page shells, galleries, dashboards with defined regions. Flex is ideal for one-dimensional distribution (nav bars, button rows, stacked panels).
payload.source: Frontend layout interview

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Flex = one axis; grid = two axes; use both in one page happily.
gap replaces margin hacks; fr for fractional widths; minmax for floors.
Mobile-first: base styles for small screens, min-width queries upward.
Avoid fixed pixel widths and float-based layouts.

questions.prompt: Mobile-first CSS means:
options: Write desktop then use max-width to shrink
Base styles for small screens, min-width queries upward
questions.explanation: Start small, enhance upward — simpler cascade, smaller base payload.

questions.prompt: Best tool for a page shell with header, sidebar, main and footer regions:
questions.explanation: Grid can name and place regions on both axes in one rule.

questions.prompt: flex: 1 on a flex child means:
options: Grow to fill free space with basis 0%
questions.explanation: flex: 1 is shorthand for flex-grow: 1, flex-shrink: 1, flex-basis: 0% — equal share of free space.

lessons.title: Forms: validation, accessibility and submission
lessons.summary: Build forms that work with keyboards, screen readers, and real validation — not just a submit button.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Associate every input with a label using for/id or wrapping
Use required, pattern, type and custom JS validation together
Show inline, accessible error messages tied to their fields
Submit forms via fetch without a full page reload, handling success and failure

payload.text: A signup form looks fine but loses half its mobile conversions. The email field uses type=text, the phone field uses type=text, error messages appear as red text with no aria-live, and the submit button is 20px from the screen edge. None of these are "bugs" in the crash sense; all of them are form design failures that a checklist prevents. This lesson is that checklist.
**Every control needs a label.** Either

payload.title: novalidate + your own messages, or rely on native
payload.text: If you keep native validation, do not set novalidate — let the browser show its bubbles. If you want custom styled messages, add novalidate and implement checks yourself, preserving the same accessibility wiring.

payload.title: Accessible inline validation on submit
payload.problem: Validate an email field on submit; show an error below the input and set aria-invalid.

steps.title: Listen to submit with preventDefault
steps.desc: Stop the page reload; read the value with FormData or input.value.
steps.code_snippet: form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); ... });

steps.title: Validate and paint the error
steps.desc: Check with a simple pattern or validity API; unhide the error element, set its text, and mark the input aria-invalid.
steps.code_snippet: err.textContent = 'Enter a valid email'; err.hidden = false; input.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');

steps.title: Clear the error on input
steps.desc: As soon as the user types, remove aria-invalid and hide the message so the form feels responsive, not punitive.

payload.solution: Errors are tied to fields, announced (role=alert / aria-live), and cleared on input. The same wiring works whether you use native validation or custom JS.

payload.title: Build these
payload.prompt:
1. A login form: email + password, both labelled, with autocomplete attributes.
2. A password + confirm-password pair with a cross-field JS check.
3. Submit a form via fetch to a mock endpoint; show a success toast or an error message.
payload.hint: 1: autocomplete=email / current-password. 2: compare on submit; aria-describedby the confirm error. 3: FormData + fetch POST; check response.ok; disable button while pending.

mistakes.mistake: Using placeholder as the only label
mistakes.fix: Placeholders vanish on input and are not reliably announced. Always use a real label.

mistakes.mistake: Red text errors with no programmatic association
mistakes.fix: aria-describedby and aria-invalid (or role=alert) let assistive tech connect the message to the field.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to re-enable the submit button after a failed fetch
mistakes.fix: A stuck disabled button looks broken. Use finally or explicit success/failure paths to re-enable.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why is a placeholder not a replacement for a label?
payload.answer: Placeholders disappear once the user types, have low contrast by default, and are not consistently announced as the field name. Labels remain visible and are programmatically associated via for/id.
payload.source: Accessibility interview question

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Label every input; placeholder is not a label.
Native attributes (required, type, pattern) give free accessible validation.
Errors: aria-describedby + aria-invalid; clear on input.
fetch + FormData for AJAX submit; guard against double-submit.

questions.prompt: The correct way to associate a label with an input:
questions.explanation: for/id association is the accessible, clickable-label pattern.

questions.prompt: aria-invalid="true" on an input means:
questions.explanation: It programmatically marks the control as invalid for assistive tech.

questions.prompt: To submit a form without a page reload you:
questions.explanation: Cancel the default submit, then send the data with fetch (or XHR).

modules.title: Module 4 — APIs, Performance & Dev Tools
modules.summary: Consume REST APIs, measure real performance, and debug with the browser like a professional.

lessons.title: Consuming REST APIs from the browser
lessons.summary: GET, POST, headers, auth and error handling — the contract every frontend job assumes.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Call a REST API with fetch: method, headers, body and credentials
Handle JSON responses and non-2xx status codes explicitly
Send authenticated requests with a bearer token or cookie session
Design a small loading / error / data UI state machine around a request

payload.text: An intern's page shows "undefined" whenever the API is slow, and silently drops errors when the token expires. The API is fine; the client treats every response as success. REST has a simple contract: request in, status code out, JSON body. Honour that contract and half of production frontend bugs disappear.

**Anatomy of a fetch request:**

| Part | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| URL | Resource location |
| method | GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE |
| headers | Content-Type, Authorization, Accept |
| body | Payload for POST/PUT (JSON.stringify); GET must not have one |
| credentials | 'include' to send cookies cross-origin; 'same-origin' default |

**Response handling checklist:**
1. Check response.ok — network success is not application success.
2. Branch on status: 401 means re-auth, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 422 validation, 500 server.
3. Parse JSON once; handle empty bodies on 204.

**Auth patterns:**
- Cookie session: fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }); server sets HttpOnly cookie.
- Bearer token: fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token } }).

**UI state machine:** every request-driven view has at least three states — loading, error, data. Render each distinctly; never leave a spinner stuck forever. Add a timeout or abort with AbortController for hung requests.

payload.title: One API client, many call sites
payload.text: Centralise fetch: status handling, auth headers and JSON parsing live in one place. Feature code calls api() and only cares about data or a typed error.

payload.title: Three-state data view with AbortController
payload.problem: A list view should show spinner, error retry, or data — and cancel stale requests when the filter changes.

steps.title: Model the states
steps.desc: state = { status: "idle" | "loading" | "error" | "data", data, error }. Render switch on status.
steps.code_snippet:
loading -> spinner
error -> message + retry
data -> list

steps.title: Abort the previous request
steps.desc: Keep an AbortController per fetch; abort it before starting a new one so slow responses do not overwrite newer results.

steps.title: Handle abort as silence, not error
steps.desc: catch (err) { if (err.name === "AbortError") return; setError(err); } — aborted requests should not paint an error UI.

payload.solution: Explicit state machine + AbortController. The user sees a spinner while loading, a retry button on failure, and never a stale result from an older filter.

payload.title: Implement these
payload.prompt:
1. GET a list endpoint; render items; show error + retry on failure.
2. POST a form as JSON with a bearer token header.
3. Add a 10-second timeout using AbortController.
payload.hint: 1: three-state switch; check response.ok. 2: method POST, headers Authorization + Content-Type, body JSON.stringify(data). 3: setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 10000).

mistakes.mistake: Assuming res.json() always works
mistakes.fix: 204 No Content and some error bodies are not JSON. Guard with a catch or check content-type.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring 401/expiry and leaving a broken UI
mistakes.fix: Central client should detect 401 and route to re-auth (redirect or silent refresh) instead of rendering empty data.

mistakes.mistake: Letting a slow response overwrite a newer one
mistakes.fix: Abort the previous request when a new one starts, or track a request id and discard stale results.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What does response.ok cover?
payload.answer: true when status is in 200–299. A resolved fetch with status 404 or 500 still has ok=false — you must check it before treating the body as valid data.
payload.source: Frontend API interview

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: fetch resolves on HTTP errors — always check response.ok.
Centralise fetch in one client: headers, auth, JSON, error types.
Model loading / error / data explicitly; never leave spinners stuck.
AbortController cancels stale or timed-out requests.

questions.prompt: response.ok is true for status:
questions.explanation: ok covers the whole 2xx success range.

questions.prompt: To send JSON with fetch you:
options: Pass an object as body directly
stringify the body and set Content-Type: application/json
questions.explanation: Body must be a string; the header tells the server how to parse it.

questions.prompt: AbortController is used to:
questions.explanation: abort() rejects the fetch promise with AbortError; useful for stale filters and timeouts.

lessons.title: Performance budgets and the DevTools workflow
lessons.summary: Measure before you optimise; use the Performance and Network panels like a professional.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Interpret Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP (or FID) and CLS
Use the Network panel to find the slowest request and understand waterfall order
Use the Performance panel to find long tasks and layout thrash
Apply three practical optimisations: image sizing, code splitting awareness, and caching headers

payload.text: A site "feels slow" but the DOMContentLoaded event fires in 400 ms. The Performance panel shows a 1.2-second long task on the main thread after load — a chart re-render blocking every click. Feeling slow and loading slow are different problems with different tools. This lesson teaches you to tell them apart in five minutes.

**Core Web Vitals (what Google ranks and users feel):**

| Metric | What it measures | Good |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) | When the main content paints | <= 2.5s |
| INP (Interaction to Next Paint) | Latency of interactions across the visit | <= 200ms |
| CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) | Unexpected layout movement | <= 0.1 |

**Network panel essentials:**
- Waterfall: DNS, TCP, TLS, request, response — see where time goes.
- Status codes and size at a glance; filter by type.
- Disable cache to measure cold loads; leave it on for repeat-view realism.

**Performance panel essentials:**
- Record a session, look for long tasks (>50ms) blocking the main thread.
- Purple (layout) and green (recording) in the flame chart reveal forced synchronous layout ("layout thrash") from reading offsetHeight in a loop after writing styles.

**Three practical optimisations:**
1. Images: correct dimensions, modern formats, lazy-load below the fold.
2. Scripts: defer non-critical JS; split large bundles so first paint is not blocked.
3. Caching: immutable assets get long max-age + hashed filenames; HTML stays no-cache or short.

payload.title: Quick wins by symptom
rows: Hero image size / LCP element; render-blocking CSS/JS
Long tasks in Performance panel; heavy event handlers
Images/slots without reserved dimensions; late-loading ads/fonts

payload.title: Measure on a throttled 3G/Moto G profile
payload.text: Desktop broadband hides problems real users hit. Throttle CPU and network in DevTools before concluding "it is fast".

payload.title: Diagnose a janky list re-render
payload.problem: Clicking "Sort" freezes the UI for ~600 ms on a 5,000-row table. Find and fix the cause.

steps.title: Record with the Performance panel
steps.desc: Reproduce the click while recording. Look for a long task spanning the sort handler.
steps.code_snippet: Long task ~600ms in click handler

steps.title: Identify layout thrash or unbatched work
steps.desc: Reading offsetWidth inside a loop after writing style forces synchronous layout each iteration. Or sorting + re-creating 5,000 DOM nodes per click.

steps.title: Fix: batch DOM writes, or virtualise
steps.desc: Sort in JS once, then one re-render. For very large lists, only render visible rows (virtualisation).
steps.code_snippet:
sort once -> single innerHTML/textContent update
or windowed list rendering

payload.solution: The bottleneck was main-thread work, not the network. One sort pass + one DOM update, or virtualisation for huge lists, drops the handler to single-digit milliseconds.

payload.title: Do these in DevTools
payload.prompt:
1. Open Network, reload with cache disabled, identify the largest and slowest request.
2. Record Performance while scrolling a long page; find any long task.
3. Check a hero image: are width/height (or aspect-ratio) set to prevent CLS?
payload.hint: 1: sort the waterfall by time or size columns. 2: look for yellow/red bars in the main thread track. 3: missing dimensions are a common CLS cause.

mistakes.mistake: Optimising without measuring
mistakes.fix: A guess optimisation may do nothing or regress performance. Capture a baseline in Network/Performance first, then compare after.

mistakes.mistake: Compressing images forever while ignoring a 2 MB JS bundle
mistakes.fix: The largest bytes on the critical path win. Check the waterfall: if JS dominates LCP, split or defer the bundle.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving browser cache disabled and calling the site slow
mistakes.fix: Real users get cached assets on repeat visits. Measure both cold and warm loads.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What does CLS measure and what usually causes high CLS?
payload.answer: Cumulative Layout Shift scores unexpected movement of visible content. Common causes: images or embeds without reserved dimensions, late-loading fonts swapping metrics, and ads or banners injected above existing content.
payload.source: Frontend performance interview

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: LCP <= 2.5s, INP <= 200ms, CLS <= 0.1 are the Core Web Vitals.
Network waterfall for load time; Performance panel for main-thread jank.
Layout thrash: reads after writes in a loop force sync layout.
Measure first (throttled), then optimise the actual bottleneck.

questions.prompt: CLS stands for:
questions.explanation: CLS measures unexpected layout movement during the visit.

questions.prompt: A long task on the main thread typically causes:
questions.explanation: Blocking the main thread delays processing of clicks and input — INP suffers.

questions.prompt: To measure a cold load fairly you should:
options: Disable cache in the Network panel
questions.explanation: Network > Disable cache (with DevTools open) simulates a first-time visitor.

courses.title: Digital Electronics
courses.subtitle: Number systems, Boolean algebra, K-maps, combinational and sequential circuits — the ECE exam and Viva foundation
courses.description:
Digital Electronics is the first serious ECE/EEE course in most university syllabi, and the one every Viva and written exam tests hardest. This course covers the full foundation in eight compact lessons: binary, octal, hex, BCD and Gray codes; Boolean algebra with De Morgan and K-map minimization; adders, multiplexers, decoders and encoders; and sequential logic from flip-flops through counters and finite state machines.

Every lesson follows the nine-step structure: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, the exam angle, a server-graded quiz and a one-screen summary. A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** first- and second-year ECE/EEE students, and any CS student who wants the hardware fundamentals that interviews still ask. The course is exam-oriented without being shallow — every worked example is the kind of problem that appears on mid-terms and in placement screening.

**What you need:** pen and paper for the maps and truth tables; a browser for the quizzes. No simulator or lab kit is required, though anyone with one should re-verify the worked circuits on it.
outcomes: Convert between binary, octal, hexadecimal and decimal accurately
Encode and decode BCD, Gray and ASCII, and compute parity bits
Apply De Morgan's laws and absorption to simplify Boolean expressions
Minimize functions on 2-, 3- and 4-variable K-maps
Design and cascade adders, and build two’s-complement subtractors
Use MUX, decoders and priority encoders as standard building blocks
Work with D, JK and T flip-flops via characteristic and excitation tables
Design mod-N counters and sketch Moore/Mealy FSMs with state tables
courses.about_course:
University digital electronics courses often move too fast through number systems before landing students in K-maps and flip-flops they do not fully own. This course slows the foundation down to eight focused lessons, then accelerates once the basics are solid.

Codes and conversions come first because every later topic assumes them. Boolean algebra and K-maps are taught as a single minimization workflow — not as isolated tricks. Combinational circuits are presented as a fixed vocabulary (adders, MUX, decoders) that you recombine rather than re-derive. Sequential circuits close the course with the design recipe that answers "design a mod-6 counter" or "draw a traffic-light FSM" — the two questions that appear most often in exams and interviews.

Each lesson ends with a quiz graded on the server, and the course finishes with a 15-question timed exam from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

Comfort with binary numbers (helpful but re-taught in Module 1)

lessons.title: Binary, Octal and Hexadecimal
lessons.summary: Positional bases, weight expansion and fast base-16/base-8 conversions.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Expand a binary number using positional weights
Convert between binary, octal and hexadecimal in both directions
Convert decimal to binary by repeated division

payload.text: Every processor stores numbers as bits. Hex is just a compact way humans read four bits at a time — 0x3F is the byte 00111111.

**Positional notation:** a digit's value is digit x base^position, counting positions from 0 at the right. The decimal 345 = 3x100 + 4x10 + 5x1.

**Binary (base 2):** only 0 and 1. 1011_2 = 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1x1 = 11_10.

**Octal (base 8) and Hex (base 16):** one octal digit = three binary bits; one hex digit = four bits. Convert by regrouping bits from the LSB, padding with leading zeros — never by going through decimal twice.

**Decimal to any base:** repeated division by the base; read remainders bottom-to-top (LSB first).

payload.title: Hex grouping is four bits, not three
payload.text: Octal groups of 3 and hex groups of 4 both start from the binary LSB. Pad the leftmost group with zeros.

payload.title: Leading-zero padding mistakes
payload.text: When converting 11011 to octal you must pad: 010 111 — not 11 011.

payload.title: Convert 255 decimal to binary and hex

mistakes.fix: The first remainder is the least significant bit. Reading MSB-first gives a bit-reversed number.

mistakes.fix: 1001 converted as octal without padding becomes 11 instead of 012.

lessons.title: BCD, Gray and Character Codes
lessons.summary: How decimal digits, error-resistant counters and text are encoded as bits.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Encode a decimal number in BCD and decode it back
Explain why Gray code changes only one bit between consecutive values
State the ASCII code for a character and compute a simple parity bit

payload.text: Cash registers, seven-segment displays and instrument panels do not store "42" as binary 101010 — they store BCD 0100 0010 so each digit lights its own seven-segment group.

**BCD (Binary Coded Decimal):** each decimal digit gets its own 4-bit nibble. 42 -> 0100 0010. Sixteen of the 32 nibble patterns are unused — arithmetic on BCD needs correction after sums that exceed 9.

**Gray code:** a reflected binary code where successive values differ by exactly one bit. That property prevents multi-bit glitches in mechanical encoders (e.g. a rotary shaft encoder) during transitions.

**ASCII / text codes:** ASCII maps characters to 7 bits (extended 8-bit variants exist). Unicode/UTF-8 is the modern superset — but exam questions still test ASCII positions: 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, '0' = 48.

**Parity:** a single extra bit that makes the total number of 1s even (even parity) or odd (odd parity) — the cheapest error detector.

payload.title: BCD vs plain binary
payload.text: BCD wastes range but keeps each decimal digit independently addressable — ideal for display hardware.

payload.title: Gray code construction
payload.text: Reflect the existing list and prefix 0 on the first half, 1 on the reflected half. Start: 00, 01 -> reflect -> 11, 10.

payload.title: BCD for 389 and Gray for 5

steps.title: Split into decimal digits
steps.desc: 389 into digits: 3, 8, 9.

payload.hint: Two decimal digits, two nibbles.

mistakes.mistake: Treating BCD as plain binary
mistakes.fix: BCD(23) is 0010 0011, not the binary 0001 0111.

mistakes.mistake: XOR direction in Gray conversion
mistakes.fix: Gray bit i = binary bit i XOR binary bit i+1 (higher bit). Reversing the pairing flips the code.

lessons.title: Boolean Algebra & De Morgan's Laws
lessons.summary: Simplify expressions with identities, duality and De Morgan — the language of every digital circuit diagram.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply De Morgan's theorems to push negations through AND/OR
Simplify Boolean expressions with absorption and consensus
Convert between SOP and POS forms

payload.text: A designer writes F = A·B + A·B̄ + 0. The simplify step A·(B + B̄) = A collapses two gates into one wire — and that is how chip area shrinks in real products.

**Basic laws:** identity (A+0=A, A·1=A), idempotent (A+A=A), complement (A+Ā=1, A·Ā=0), distributive, and absorption (A + A·B = A).

**De Morgan's theorems:**
- (A · B)‾ = A̅ + B̅
- (A + B)‾ = A̅ · B̅

A bubble on a NAND equals AND-with-inverted-inputs. Every circuit can be redrawn with only NAND or only NOR gates.

**SOP / POS:** sum-of-products (OR of ANDs) and product-of-sums (AND of ORs). Canonical forms list every minterm or maxterm — useful before K-maps.

**Duality:** swap AND↔OR and 0↔1 to get a dual theorem for free.

payload.title: Push bubbles instead of expanding
payload.text: For (A+B+C)‾, push the bubble: A̅·B̅·C̅. Faster and less error-prone than minterm expansion.

payload.title: Simplify F = A·B + A·B̄ + A̅·B̄
payload.problem: Reduce to minimal SOP.

steps.title: Rewrite
steps.desc: Expression becomes A + A̅·B̄.

steps.title: Apply X + X̄·Y = X + Y
steps.desc: A + B̄.

payload.solution: F = A + B̄

payload.hint: Distribute A out first.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing XOR with OR
mistakes.fix: XOR is true for exactly one high input; OR is true for at least one.

lessons.title: Karnaugh Maps & Minimization
lessons.summary: Map truth tables onto K-maps, group 1s in powers of two, and write minimal SOP.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Plot a truth table onto a 2-, 3- or 4-variable K-map
Form largest possible groups of 1s including wrap-around
Write the minimal SOP expression from the map

payload.text: Exams hand you a 4-variable truth table and ask for the "minimum SOP". The K-map is the two-minute method that beats algebraic trial every time.

**K-map layout:** cells are numbered in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ by one bit. 3-variable maps are 2x4; 4-variable maps are 4x4.

**Grouping rules:**
1. Groups must contain 1, 2, 4, 8... cells (powers of two).
2. Groups may wrap around edges.
3. Take the largest groups first; overlapping is allowed and encouraged.
4. Every 1 must be covered by at least one group.

**Reading a group:** a group of size 2^k eliminates k variables. Write the literals that stay constant across the group.

**Don't-cares (X):** treat as 1 or 0, whichever makes a larger group.

payload.title: Start with the largest group
payload.text: Find any octet, then quads, then pairs, then singles. Singles cost more gates.

payload.title: Groups of 3 or 5 are illegal
payload.text: Only power-of-two group sizes correspond to eliminating whole variables.

payload.title: Minimize a 3-variable function

steps.title: Minimal cover
steps.desc: A̅·B̅ covers 0,1; A·C covers 5,7; A̅·C̅ covers 0,2 (m2).

payload.solution: F = A̅·B̅ + A·C + A̅·C̅

lessons.title: Adders and Subtractors
lessons.summary: Half adder, full adder, ripple-carry and the borrow-based subtractor.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Design half and full adders from truth tables
Cascade full adders into an n-bit ripple-carry adder
Build a subtractor using two’s complement and a control bit

payload.text: A CPU ALU starts exactly here: one full adder, then eight of them, then thirty-two. Every multi-bit adder in silicon is a cascade of the same one-bit cell.

**Half adder:** two inputs (A, B); outputs Sum = A⊕B, Carry = A·B. No carry-in.

**Full adder:** three inputs (A, B, Cin); Sum = A⊕B⊕Cin, Cout = A·B + Cin·(A⊕B). This is the cell you cascade.

**Ripple-carry adder:** chain full adders; Cout of bit i feeds Cin of bit i+1. Simple, but carry ripples — O(n) delay. Faster designs (carry-lookahead) precompute group generates/propagates.

**Subtractor:** A − B = A + B̄ + 1 (two’s complement). One adder with B inverted and Cin=1 when subtracting, Cin=0 when adding — the classic adder/subtractor with a mode bit.

payload.title: Mode bit M on the adder/subtractor
payload.text: M=0: B passes through, Cin=0 → add. M=1: B is inverted, Cin=1 → subtract. Same hardware, two operations.

payload.title: 2-bit ripple-carry addition
payload.problem: Add 10_2 + 11_2 using two full adders.

steps.title: Assemble result
steps.desc: Final carry-out is the MSB of the result.

mistakes.fix: If Cin=0 is guaranteed for the LSB, a half adder works; otherwise use a full adder.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the +1 when subtracting

lessons.title: MUX, Demux, Encoder & Decoder
lessons.summary: The data-routing family: select lines choose paths; decoders expand addresses into one-hot lines.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Realize any Boolean function with a multiplexer plus inverters
Explain encoder vs priority encoder
Expand a decoder into minterm lines and enable logic

payload.text: A 2:1 MUX with select S implements Y = S̄·D0 + S·D1 — one gate-level expression, one chip. FPGAs are largely giant mux fabrics.

**Multiplexer (MUX):** n select lines choose among 2^n data inputs. 2:1: Y = S̄·D0 + S·D1. Any n-variable function can be realized with a 2^(n−1):1 MUX using one variable as the select and the rest as data functions.

**Demux:** one input, n select lines route it to one of 2^n outputs — the inverse of a MUX.

**Encoder:** many inputs → few outputs representing the active input index. **Priority encoder:** if multiple inputs are high, the highest-index one wins (critical for interrupt controllers).

**Decoder:** n select lines → 2^n one-hot outputs. A decoder plus OR gates implements any SOP directly (each output line is a minterm).

payload.title: Encoder vs priority encoder
payload.text: A plain encoder gives garbage if two inputs are high; always prefer the priority version in real designs.

payload.hint: Each output is a minterm of A and B.

mistakes.fix: Select lines control which data input reaches the output; data lines carry the function values.

mistakes.mistake: Decoder outputs as ORed minterms
mistakes.fix: Each decoder output IS one minterm; OR the needed lines to build SOP.

lessons.title: Flip-Flops and Latches
lessons.summary: SR, D, JK and T flip-flops: characteristic tables, excitation and the clock edge.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Distinguish a level-sensitive latch from an edge-triggered flip-flop
Use the characteristic and excitation tables of D, JK and T
Convert one flip-flop type into another via excitation mapping

payload.text: A CPU register file is thousands of identical D flip-flops clocked on the same edge. One cell, cloned — this lesson is that cell.

**Latch vs flip-flop:** a latch is level-sensitive (transparent while enable is high). A flip-flop samples on a clock edge (rising or falling) — the edge is what makes synchronous design predictable.

**SR latch:** S=1,R=1 is forbidden (race / invalid state). **D flip-flop:** Q follows D at the edge — the universal storage cell. **JK flip-flop:** J=K=1 toggles — solves the SR forbidden case. **T flip-flop:** T=1 toggles, T=0 holds — built from D with feedback.

**Characteristic table:** next state Q(t+1) from current inputs.
**Excitation table:** which inputs produce a desired Q→Q(t+1) — used when designing counters and FSMs.

**Asynchronous inputs:** preset (force 1) and clear (force 0) override the clock — used for initialization, not for logic.

payload.title: Excitation table workflow for counters
payload.text: Write the state sequence, fill the required Q→Q(t+1) per bit, read the needed T or JK inputs from the table, then K-map the input logic.

payload.title: Toggle with a D flip-flop
payload.problem: Design a toggle stage using one D flip-flop.

steps.title: Desired behavior
steps.desc: Q(t+1) = Q(t) when T=0, Q̅(t) when T=1.

steps.title: Map to D
steps.desc: D flip-flop: Q(t+1) = D, so D must equal the desired next state.

steps.title: Feedback equation
steps.desc: D = T̅·Q + T·Q̅ = T⊕Q.

payload.solution: D = T⊕Q — XOR the current Q with the toggle input.

payload.title: JK excitation for Q→Q̅
payload.prompt: What J, K values force a toggle from any state?
payload.hint: Look at the excitation table row for 0→1 and 1→0.

mistakes.fix: Forbidden — outputs race. Use JK or D instead.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing async preset with sync logic
mistakes.fix: Preset/clear ignore the clock; only use them for power-on reset.

lessons.title: Counters, Registers and FSMs
lessons.summary: Ripple and synchronous counters, shift registers, and the two-process FSM template.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify counters as ripple (async) or synchronous and state the trade-off
Design a mod-N counter with proper wrap-around

payload.text: Every protocol parser, traffic light and UART bit-timer is an FSM plus a counter. Interviewers love "design a mod-6 counter" because it tests the whole sequential toolkit in one question.

**Ripple (async) counter:** each stage clocks from the previous Q — simple, but cumulative delay makes high-speed designs unsafe. **Synchronous counter:** all flip-flops share the clock; next-state logic is combinational — faster, slightly more gates.

**Mod-N counter:** counts 0..N−1 then wraps. For non-power-of-two N, detect the terminal count and force the reset/next-state.

**Shift registers:** serial-in/serial-out, serial-in/parallel-out — the basis of UART and delay lines. Johnson and ring counters are cyclic shift variants.

**Finite state machines:**
- **Moore:** outputs depend only on state — safer timing.
- **Mealy:** outputs depend on state AND inputs — often fewer states, glitch-prone at transitions.

**Design recipe:** states → state table → state assignment → excitation K-maps → circuit. Two-process VHDL/Verilog: sequential state register + combinational next-state/output.

courses.title: Basic Electrical Engineering (BEE)
courses.subtitle: DC circuits, network theorems, AC fundamentals and machines — the universal first-year subject, exam-ready
courses.description:
Basic Electrical Engineering is the first-year subject shared by EEE, ECE, Mechanical and Civil cohorts — and the one that sets the tone for every machines and power course that follows. This course covers the full foundation in eight compact lessons: Ohm's law and power, series-parallel networks with KVL/KCL, superposition and Thevenin/Norton equivalents, maximum power transfer, AC phasors and RLC impedance, real/reactive/apparent power with power-factor correction, and a machines/transformer primer with the EMF and turns-ratio equations.

Every lesson follows the nine-step structure: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, the exam angle, a server-graded quiz and a one-screen summary. A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** first-year engineering students facing their BEE mid-terms and finals, and anyone who wants the electrical fundamentals that electronics and power courses assume. The course is exam-oriented — every worked example is the type of problem that appears on university papers.

**What you need:** a scientific calculator. No lab kit is required, though re-verified calculations on a breadboard or simulator deepen the intuition.
outcomes: Apply Ohm's law and compute power in all four common forms
Reduce series-parallel resistor networks and solve two-loop circuits with KVL/KCL
Use superposition, Thevenin and Norton theorems to simplify multi-source networks
Apply maximum power transfer and interpret its 50% efficiency
Represent sinusoids as phasors and compute RLC impedance
Compute real, reactive and apparent power; design basic power-factor correction
Write the DC machine EMF and torque equations; explain back EMF and starting
Apply ideal transformer ratios and compute efficiency and regulation
courses.about_course:
Most first-year electrical courses race through DC theory before landing students in AC phasors and machine equations they do not own. This course slows the foundation to eight focused lessons, then accelerates once the basics are solid.

DC circuits and network theorems come first because every later topic assumes KVL/KCL fluency and Thevenin thinking. AC fundamentals teach phasors as the tool that converts calculus into the DC methods already learned. Power and power factor close the "why industries care" loop. The machines module is deliberately a primer — enough EMF, torque and transformer theory to pass BEE exams and to understand the courses that come next, without pretending to be a full machines course.

Each lesson ends with a quiz graded on the server, and the course finishes with a 15-question timed exam from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply Ohm's law to find V, I or R in simple branches

payload.text: Your hostel electricity bill is energy in kWh; the geyser rating plate is power in kW. Confusing the two is the most common first-year mistake — and it costs marks every exam season.

**Ohm's law (linear, passive sign convention):** V = I·R when temperature and material properties are constant. Applies to resistors, not to diodes or non-linear devices.

**Passive sign convention:** current enters the + terminal of a passive element. Power P = V·I > 0 means the element absorbs power; P < 0 means it supplies.

**Power forms:** P = VI = I²R = V²/R — pick the form that has the known quantities. Maximum power transfer and heating problems almost always want I²R.

**Energy:** W = P·t. In utility billing, W is in kilowatt-hours: a 2 kW geyser running 1.5 h consumes 3 kWh.

payload.text: KVL is conservation of energy around a loop; KCL is conservation of charge at a node. Every mesh and nodal analysis method on top of them is just bookkeeping.

**Series:** same current; R_eq = R1 + R2 + ... Voltage divides in proportion to resistance.

**Parallel:** same voltage; 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... Current divides inversely to resistance. Two-resistor shortcut: R1||R2 = (R1·R2)/(R1+R2).

**KVL:** the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero.

**KCL:** the algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero.

**Solution recipe for a two-loop circuit:** assign branch currents with directions, write one KCL per essential node, one KVL per independent loop, solve the linear system. Direction is a guess — a negative answer just means the true direction is opposite.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: A three-source bridge looks impossible until you kill two sources and solve three easy circuits. Superposition is not a trick — it is linearity made usable.

**Superposition:** in a linear network with multiple independent sources, the response in any branch is the sum of the responses caused by each source acting alone. Kill other voltage sources (short) and current sources (open). Dependent sources are NOT killed.

**Thevenin:** any two-terminal linear network equals V_th in series with R_th. V_th = open-circuit voltage at the terminals; R_th = V_oc / I_sc, or turn off independent sources and combine resistances looking into the terminals (with a test source if needed).

**Norton:** I_N in parallel with R_N, with R_N = R_th and I_N = V_th / R_th. Source transformation converts freely between the two.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: State and apply the maximum power transfer theorem

payload.text: Antenna matching, speaker amplifiers and sensor front-ends all design for maximum power transfer. The theorem is one line; the efficiency surprise around it is where marks are won.

**Maximum power transfer:** a load R_L drawn from a network with Thevenin resistance R_th receives maximum power when R_L = R_th. Then P_max = V_th² / (4·R_th).

**Efficiency at match:** only 50% of the developed power reaches the load — the other half is lost in R_th. Power systems deliberately do NOT match (they want efficiency, not max load power); communication and audio stages do match.

**Reciprocity:** in a linear network with a single independent source, if a current I in branch A produces voltage V in branch B, then the same current I in branch B produces V in branch A. Valid only for single-source, linear, bilateral networks without dependent sources breaking it.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: AC analysis by differential equations is painful; by phasors it is algebra. One transform turns calculus into the DC methods you already know.

**Sinusoid:** v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ). Phasor: V = V_m ∠φ (rms phasors use V_rms). Frequency ω = 2πf.

**Impedance:** Z_R = R; Z_L = jωL; Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC). Impedances add in series and combine in parallel exactly like resistors, but with complex arithmetic.

**Series RLC:** Z = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC)). Resonance when ωL = 1/(ωC), i.e. ω₀ = 1/√(LC). At resonance the impedance is purely resistive and current is maximum for a voltage source.

**Admittance:** Y = 1/Z = G + jB, convenient for parallel branches.

lessons.title: AC Power and Power Factor
lessons.summary: Real, reactive and apparent power; the power triangle; why factories install capacitor banks.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute real (P), reactive (Q) and apparent (S) power
Determine power factor and the phase angle from impedance
Explain power-factor correction with a parallel capacitor

payload.text: An industrial consumer with pf = 0.6 draws more current for the same real power and pays penalties. Sizing a capacitor bank is a standard BEE problem — and a real job task.

**Apparent power:** S = V_rms · I_rms (VA). **Real power:** P = S · cosφ = VI cosφ (W) — the useful work. **Reactive power:** Q = S · sinφ (VAR) — energy shuttled between source and reactive elements. **Power factor:** cosφ = P/S, lagging if current lags (inductive), leading if current leads (capacitive).

**Power triangle:** S² = P² + Q². Raise pf by adding capacitive Q (cancels inductive Q).

**Correction sizing:** Q_c = P (tanφ₁ − tanφ₂), C = Q_c / (ω V²).

**Three-phase:** P = √3 V_L I_L cosφ for balanced loads.

payload.title: Lagging pf means inductive load
payload.text: Motors lag; capacitor banks bring pf back toward unity.

payload.title: Power-factor correction
payload.problem: A 10 kW load at pf 0.6 lagging (50 Hz, 230 V) is corrected to 0.95 lagging. Find the required capacitor kVAR and µF.
payload.solution: Q_c ≈ 10 kVAR; C ≈ 600 µF at 230 V, 50 Hz.

payload.title: Apparent power from P and pf
payload.prompt: P = 8 kW, pf = 0.8 lagging. Find S and Q.
payload.hint: S = P/cosφ; Q = √(S²−P²).

mistakes.mistake: Using peak voltage in S = VI
mistakes.fix: Always RMS for apparent and real power.

mistakes.mistake: Wrong sign on corrected Q
mistakes.fix: Capacitors supply VARs — they subtract from inductive Q.

payload.answer: cosφ = P/S. Correction reduces current (I²R losses, tariff penalties) for the same real power.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: S = VI (VA); P = VI cosφ; Q = VI sinφ.
Power factor correction adds capacitive VARs to cancel inductive VARs.
Three-phase balanced: P = √3 V_L I_L cosφ.

modules.title: Module 4 — DC Machines & Transformers
modules.summary: EMF equation, torque-speed basics and the ideal transformer ratio — the machines primer every branch needs.

lessons.title: DC Machines: EMF and Torque
lessons.summary: Construction, back EMF, the two universal equations and speed control intuition.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write the DC machine EMF and torque equations with correct symbols
Explain back EMF and why a stalled motor draws dangerous current
Relate armature resistance, supply and speed in shunt motors

payload.text: A DC motor started direct-on-line without a starter can burn its armature in seconds — because back EMF has not yet developed to limit the current. That single fact is half the machines viva.

**Construction:** stator field (permanent magnet or field winding), rotor armature with commutator and brushes. Commutator rectifies so torque stays unidirectional.

**EMF equation:** E = (φ Z N P) / (60 A) — φ flux per pole, Z conductors, N rpm, P poles, A parallel paths (A = P for lap, A = 2 for wave).

**Torque:** T = (φ Z P I_a) / (2π A) — electromagnetic torque proportional to flux and armature current.

**Motor equation:** V = E + I_a R_a. At start, N=0 so E=0 and I_a = V/R_a (huge) — hence starters with series resistance. Running: E ≈ V, so I_a adjusts to load.

**Speed:** N ∝ (V − I_a R_a)/φ. Shunt speed control: vary field flux (above base) or armature voltage (below base).

payload.title: Back EMF is the self-regulator
payload.text: As speed rises, E rises, I_a falls — the machine settles. Stall and that protection vanishes.

payload.title: No starter, no motor
payload.text: Never DOL-start a large DC shunt motor; always insert starting resistance.

payload.title: Back EMF and armature current
payload.problem: A 220 V DC motor has R_a = 0.5 ohm. Running, I_a = 20 A. Find E and the starting current if started DOL.

steps.title: Compare
steps.desc: 440 A is 22× the running current — a starter is mandatory.

payload.solution: E_running = 210 V; I_start(DOL) = 440 A.

payload.title: Compute EMF
payload.prompt: 4-pole lap-wound DC machine, φ = 0.02 Wb, Z = 1000, N = 1500 rpm. Find E.
payload.hint: A = P for lap winding.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting A in the EMF equation
mistakes.fix: Lap: A=P; wave: A=2. Wrong A scales E incorrectly.

mistakes.mistake: Treating starting current as abnormal
mistakes.fix: It is expected physics (E=0); the starter is how machines survive it.

payload.question: Why must a DC shunt motor be started with a starter?
payload.answer: At standstill back EMF is zero, so I_a = V/R_a is dangerously high; the starter limits initial current.
payload.source: The most common machines short-answer.

points: E = φZNP/(60A); T = φZP I_a/(2πA).
Motor: V = E + I_a R_a; stall ⇒ no back EMF ⇒ huge current.
Speed ∝ (V − I_a R_a)/φ — flux and voltage control.

lessons.title: Transformers: Ratios, Losses and Regulation
lessons.summary: Ideal transformer equations, real losses, efficiency and voltage regulation.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply turns, voltage and current ratios of an ideal transformer
Separate core (iron) and copper losses and compute efficiency
Define voltage regulation and its dependence on winding impedance

payload.text: Every appliance charger is a transformer. Grid transmission at hundreds of kV exists purely because transformers make I²R losses tiny for the same power.

**Ideal transformer:** V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂ = a; I₁/I₂ = 1/a; power in = power out. Primary and secondary MMFs balance: N₁I₁ = N₂I₂ (no-load I₀ neglected).

**Real losses:** copper loss = I²R in each winding (load dependent); iron/core loss = hysteresis + eddy, roughly constant with load (depends on V and f).

**Efficiency:** η = P_out / (P_out + P_core + P_cu). Max efficiency when copper loss = iron loss.

**Voltage regulation:** %reg = (V₂,nl − V₂,fl) / V₂,fl × 100 — drop under load due to winding impedance.

**Auto-transformer:** shared winding; lighter/cheaper for small ratio changes but no galvanic isolation.

payload.title: Efficiency peak at loss crossover
payload.text: Design sets core loss ≈ full-load copper loss so peak efficiency sits near typical loading.

payload.title: Turns ratio and efficiency
payload.problem: A 230/2300 V step-up transformer delivers 10 kW at pf 0.8 with P_core = 100 W and P_cu = 150 W at that load. Find a, I₁, I₂ and η.

steps.title: Primary current
steps.desc: I₁ = a·I₂ = 54.3 A (ideal ratio).

payload.title: Find copper loss at peak efficiency
payload.prompt: For the transformer above, what copper loss maximizes η and what is that η?
payload.hint: Peak when P_cu = P_core.

mistakes.mistake: Applying current ratio directly to impedances
mistakes.fix: Z₁/Z₂ = a² — impedance transforms with the square of the turns ratio.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting pf in current calculation
mistakes.fix: I = S/V = P/(V pf) for real-power-specified loads.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the ideal transformer voltage and current ratios.
payload.answer: V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂ and I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁ (power conserved).
payload.source: Opens almost every transformer unit.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Ideal: V∝N, I∝1/N, P_in = P_out.
Copper loss ∝ I²; core loss roughly constant.
Peak efficiency at P_cu = P_core; regulation measures voltage drop under load.

questions.explanation: Primary over secondary equals turns ratio.

questions.explanation: Standard transformer result.

courses.title: Generative AI for Students
courses.subtitle: LLM fundamentals, prompting, RAG and applied workflows — the AI literacy every placement and product role expects
courses.description:
Generative AI stopped being a novelty and became a baseline skill on job descriptions. This course gives you the mental model and the working habits: how language models actually predict text, why they hallucinate, how to write prompts that behave like briefs, how retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in real documents, and how to evaluate, cost and secure a GenAI feature.

Four modules, eight lessons on the nine-step standard: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, server-graded quiz and revision summary. A 30-question bank feeds the timed final exam; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** students and early-career engineers who use chatbots daily but cannot yet explain tokens, context windows or RAG — and who need repeatable workflows for research, writing, coding and placement prep without getting burned by fabricated citations.

**What you need:** access to any mainstream chat assistant for the practice prompts. No coding is required, though Module 3 shows how engineers wire models into products.
courses.thumbnail_alt: Generative AI for Students course cover
outcomes: Explain next-token prediction, tokens, context windows and temperature
Diagnose hallucination and apply grounding, RAG and verification mitigations
Write prompts using the role/task/constraints/format skeleton with few-shot examples
Chain prompts and add critic passes for complex tasks
Describe a RAG pipeline and choose sensible chunking and retrieval strategies
Build a golden eval set and track token cost for a GenAI feature
Defend against prompt injection and handle PII with practical controls
Run safe workflows for research, writing, coding and placement preparation
courses.about_course:
Most "intro to AI" content either oversells the magic or drowns you in math you do not need yet. This course sits in the applied middle: enough mechanism to predict how the tool will behave, and enough engineering to build or evaluate real features.

Module 1 builds the probability-machine mental model — tokens, windows, sampling, hallucination and retrieval — so every later trick has an explanation. Module 2 turns prompting from incantation into brief-writing with a reusable skeleton and chain patterns. Module 3 covers what happens when you ship: chunking, hybrid retrieval, structured outputs, evaluation, cost tiers and safety. Module 4 applies all of it to study, writing, coding and career workflows, with verification treated as part of the workflow rather than an afterthought.

Each lesson ends with a server-graded quiz; the course closes with a 15-question timed exam from a 30-question bank. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

Basic computer literacy; no programming required
audience: Students preparing for AI-forward internships and placements
Junior engineers adding GenAI literacy to their profile
Project builders wiring chat features into apps
Anyone tired of unreliable AI outputs and fake citations

modules.title: Module 1 — How Language Models Actually Work
modules.summary: Tokens, next-token prediction, context windows and why models hallucinate — the mental model that makes every tool usable.

lessons.title: Tokens, Prediction and Context
lessons.summary: What a language model computes, how far it can "see", and what temperature really changes.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain next-token prediction in plain language
Estimate tokens from text and understand context-window limits
Describe what temperature and top-p sampling control

payload.text: A chatbot does not "know" facts the way a database does. It predicts likely next tokens from patterns in training data. Once you see it as a probability machine, hallucinations and prompt tricks stop being mysterious.

**Training objective:** a language model is trained to predict the next token given all previous tokens. "Large" refers to parameter count; the capability emerges from scale, not from a separate reasoning engine.

**Tokenization:** text is split into subword tokens (roughly 4 characters or ~0.75 English words per token). "unbelievable" might be un-believ-able — three tokens. Token count matters because it drives cost and the context limit.

**Context window:** the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once (8k, 32k, 128k, 200k+ depending on the model). Text beyond the window is invisible to that request — the model is not "forgetting", it never saw it.

**Temperature:** scales logits before sampling. Low (0–0.3) → more deterministic, good for extraction and code. High (0.7–1.2) → more varied, good for brainstorming. Temperature 0 is not strictly greedy across implementations, but behaves near-deterministic.

**Top-p (nucleus) sampling:** keep the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p (e.g. 0.9). Temperature and top-p both shape randomness; you rarely need to change both.

payload.title: Why "large"

lessons.title: Hallucination, Knowledge Cutoffs and Guardrails
lessons.summary: Why models invent citations, how knowledge cutoffs work, and practical mitigations.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain why hallucinations are a natural side effect of generation
Describe knowledge cutoff and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
Apply concrete mitigations: grounding, citations requests, and verification

payload.text: A lawyer submitted a brief with six case citations invented by a model. The cases did not exist. The model was not lying — it was completing legal-looking text patterns. The fix is process, not scolding the model.

**Hallucination:** fluent, confident text that is not supported by facts or by the provided context. Causes: the objective rewards plausibility, not truth; sparse or ambiguous training signal on niche topics; pressure from the prompt to always answer.

**Knowledge cutoff:** training data ends at a fixed date. Events after that date are unknown unless the product has live search, tools, or user-provided context.

**RAG (retrieval-augmented generation):** retrieve relevant documents at request time and place them in the context. The model then answers "according to these documents" — grounding claims in sources you control.

**Mitigations that work:**
1. Provide the source material (RAG or paste-in).
2. Ask for citations to the provided text, not to invented URLs.
3. Instruct: "If the answer is not in the context, say you do not know."
4. Verify high-stakes claims (medical, legal, financial, code APIs) independently.
5. Prefer models/products with browsing or tool-use when freshness matters.

lessons.title: Structure: Role, Task, Constraints, Format
lessons.summary: A four-part prompt skeleton that turns vague requests into reliable outputs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Assemble prompts with role, task, constraints and output format
Use few-shot examples to pin style and schema
Iterate with targeted revisions instead of restarting

payload.text: Two people ask for "a good email". One gets a generic paragraph; the other gets a subject line, three bullets, and a CTA — because the second prompt specified the job. Prompting is brief-writing, not spell-casting.

**The four-part skeleton:**
1. **Role** — who the model should act as ("You are a placement mentor for final-year CSE students.").
2. **Task** — the single concrete objective.
3. **Constraints** — length, tone, audience, what to avoid, what is out of scope.
4. **Format** — markdown sections, JSON schema, bullet count, subject line + body, etc.

**Few-shot examples:** show 1–3 input→output pairs. Examples beat adjectives ("be concise") because they demonstrate the exact style and structure.

**Delimiters:** wrap provided material in clear fences (### or XML-like tags) so the model does not confuse source text with instructions.

**Iteration:** if the output is 80% right, do not rewrite from scratch — say what to keep and what to change ("Keep the structure; make the tone less formal and cut the second paragraph").

payload.text: Ask one prompt to "research, outline, write and fact-check" and quality collapses in the middle. Separate the steps and each one becomes reliable — the same reason factories use assembly lines.

**Chaining:** step 1 produces structured intermediate output that step 2 consumes. Example: extract facts → outline → draft → critique → revise. Each step has its own format and success criteria.

**Critic / reflection:** after a draft, run a second pass: "List any unsupported claims and vague sentences; then rewrite." Critic models or even the same model with a different prompt often catch real issues.

**Self-consistency (lightweight):** sample a few answers at moderate temperature and take the majority or merge — useful for classification and math-ish tasks.

**Tools over prompt stuffing:** arithmetic, current facts, file contents, database queries and code execution belong to tools. A 5k-word prompt that tries to hard-code a calculator is worse than one tool call.

**Router pattern:** first call classifies the request (support vs sales vs bug) with a tiny structured output; then a specialized prompt handles it.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe the RAG pipeline: ingest, chunk, embed, retrieve, generate
Choose a chunking strategy and why it matters for recall

payload.text: A support bot that answers from your helpdesk docs needs retrieval, not fine-tuning. Wrong chunk size is the single most common reason "the answer exists but the model never sees it".

**RAG pipeline:**
1. **Ingest** — load PDFs, HTML, tickets.
2. **Chunk** — split into passages (commonly 300–800 tokens with 10–20% overlap).
3. **Embed** — map each chunk to a vector; store in a vector DB with metadata.
4. **Retrieve** — embed the query, fetch top-k similar chunks (optionally re-rank).
5. **Generate** — put chunks in context with instructions to cite.

**Why chunk?** Embeddings represent a passage as one point; oversized chunks blur topics, tiny chunks lose context. Overlap prevents answers from being split across a boundary.

**Hybrid retrieval:** combine vector similarity with keyword/BM25 search — exact identifiers (error codes, part numbers) often fail pure vector search.

**Structured outputs:** ask for JSON with a schema (or use constrained decoding / tool calls where available). Validate with a schema library; retry with the validation error on failure. Products consume JSON, not essays.

**Function calling:** the model selects a tool and arguments; your code executes and returns results. Keep tool descriptions short, non-overlapping, and name actions precisely.

lessons.summary: Golden sets, regression tests, token economics and abuse resistance for GenAI features.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Build a small golden eval set and score retrieval + generation separately
Estimate cost and latency from tokens and model tier

payload.text: Teams ship GenAI features with vibes: "seems good on my examples". One weekend of golden-set evals catches more regressions than another week of prompt fiddling.

**Eval layers:**
1. **Retrieval metrics** — recall@k: did the right chunk appear?
2. **Generation quality** — faithfulness (supported by context), correctness, tone; LLM-as-judge with rubrics plus a human spot-check.
3. **Task success** — did the user finish their job (deflection rate, edit distance of accepted outputs)?

**Golden set:** 30–100 real examples with expected behavior; run on every prompt/model/chunking change. Cheap insurance.

**Cost:** price = input tokens × rate_in + output tokens × rate_out. Long contexts make re-generation expensive; cache stable system prompts where supported. Right-size: small models for routing/ extraction, larger for hard synthesis.

**Latency:** time-to-first-token vs total; streaming UX hides total.

**Prompt injection:** untrusted text (web pages, user uploads) that contains instructions like "ignore previous rules". Defenses: separate data from instructions in the prompt, minimize tool permissions, require confirmation for side effects, scan outputs.

**PII and abuse:** redact or block personal data in logs; rate-limit; content filters for disallowed use.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: The difference between students who get value from GenAI and those who get burned is verification. Same tools, opposite outcomes — the workflow is the product.

**Research playbook:**
1. Ask for an outline and key questions first (not the final text).
2. Gather sources yourself (library, Google Scholar, docs) or use a product with citations.
3. Paste sources and ask for synthesis strictly from them, with quote-level citations.
4. Ask for a "gaps and caveats" section; verify every number and citation manually.

**Writing playbook:** outline → draft in sections → critique pass (structure, tone, redundancy) → final edit yourself. You own the voice; the model owns the heavy first pass. Never submit raw generation — admission/HR tools and readers detect the flatness quickly.

**Coding playbook:**
1. Describe the contract: inputs, outputs, edge cases, language and constraints.
2. Ask for a plan first for non-trivial changes; then code.
3. Run tests — generated code that "looks right" is untested code.
4. Paste errors back verbatim; iterate with the failing test visible.
5. Review for security: injection, secrets, unsafe deserialization, missing authz.

**What not to outsource:** final fact-checks, understanding your own thesis, anything requiring accountability for the output.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: One generic resume gets ignored; one tailored, truthful resume gets callbacks. GenAI is great at the tailoring — and catastrophic at inventing projects you cannot defend in the interview.

**Resume tailoring (safe):**
1. Paste JD; extract required skills and keywords.
2. Map them to your real projects; reorder bullets to surface matches.
3. Rewrite bullets with action verbs and metrics you can defend ("cut API latency 30%" only if true).
4. Never add skills, titles or dates you do not have — the interview is the truth test.

**Mock interview:** give the role, level and topic; ask the model to ask one question at a time, wait for your answer, then critique (structure via STAR, correctness, missing points) and continue. Do rounds: behavioral, technical fundamentals, problem-solving.

**Case / OA practice:** ask for problems of increasing difficulty; request hints only after a real attempt; ask for a post-mortem review of your solution.

**Assessment reality:** many companies use AI-detection heuristics and, more importantly, live interviews. Formulas written by AI that you cannot explain are a net negative. Use AI to learn and rehearse, not to fabricate.

**Ethics:** disclose where policy requires it; respect tool rules in exams; your portfolio should contain work you can narrate end-to-end.
