courses.title: DSA Mastery for Interviews
courses.subtitle: Complexity, arrays, trees, graphs and DP — the patterns that clear OAs and technical rounds
courses.description:
Data structures and algorithms remain the single highest-leverage filter in engineering hiring. This course teaches the patterns interviewers actually use, not a tour of every exotic structure: Big-O fluency and constraint budgets, two pointers and sliding windows, hashing and monotonic stacks, linked-list surgery, trees and BSTs, heaps and greedy proofs, graph templates (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, topological sort), and a dynamic-programming recipe that turns "hard" problems into state-recurrence work. A final lesson covers the 45-minute interview conversation itself — clarify, example, brute force, optimize, code, test.

Four modules, eight lessons on the nine-step standard: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, server-graded quiz and revision summary. A 30-question bank feeds the timed final; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** students preparing for campus placements, off-campus OAs and interviews at product and service companies. Assumes you can write basic code in any language; every pattern is shown with complexity and edge cases called out.

**What you need:** a language you can code in during practice. No prior competitive programming is required.
courses.thumbnail_alt: DSA Mastery for Interviews course cover
outcomes: Read constraints and pick the right complexity tier before coding
Apply two pointers and sliding windows to linear scan problems
Solve frequency, complement and grouping problems with hash maps
Use stacks and the monotonic-stack template for next-greater families
Perform linked-list reversal, cycle detection and merge with O(1) extra space
Traverse and validate trees; answer LCA and BST-order questions
Use heaps for top-k, merge-k and running median; justify simple greedy proofs
Implement BFS, DFS, Kahn topological sort and Dijkstra correctly
Design DP states and recurrences; code memo and tabulation forms
Run a structured interview conversation end-to-end
courses.about_course:
Most DSA courses either dump theory with no interview focus or chase contest problems that never appear in campus rounds. This course is built around the patterns that show up repeatedly in service and product company interviews: the constraint-budget rule, sliding window, hash complements, monotonic stack, pointer surgery on lists, BST bounds, heap top-k, three graph templates and a DP recipe.

Each lesson is a compact nine-block unit: why the pattern matters, the mental model, a fully worked example, practice with hints, the traps that cost offers, and the exact question an interviewer will ask next. The closing playbook turns technical communication into a skill you can rehearse — not just algorithm recognition.

A 15-question timed exam from a 30-question bank gates the verifiable TieEdu certificate.
prerequisites: Comfort writing basic programs (loops, functions, arrays) in any language

Anyone facing product-company OA and technical rounds

payload.text: An interviewer asks for O(n log n). You write O(n²) and pass the sample tests. The real test fails at n = 10⁵. Complexity is not decoration — it is the pass/fail gate before your code runs.

**Big-O** describes how runtime or memory grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. O(n²) with a small constant can beat O(n log n) for tiny n, but interview constraints (n up to 10⁵–10⁶) almost always mean O(n²) will TLE.

**Common tiers and what they allow:**
- O(1), O(log n) — any n
- O(n), O(n log n) — n up to ~10⁵–10⁶
- O(n²) — n up to ~5000–10⁴
- O(2ⁿ), O(n!) — n only up to ~20–25

**Amortized analysis:** average cost per operation over a sequence, not the worst single op. Dynamic-array push is O(1) amortized even though a single resize is O(n).

**Space:** count auxiliary memory, not the input (unless you modify it in place). Recursion depth counts toward space.

payload.title: Check constraints first

lessons.title: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
lessons.summary: The two array patterns that turn O(n²) scans into O(n) passes.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Recognize when a sorted array or pair-sum problem wants two pointers
Implement fixed and variable sliding windows
Convert a brute-force nested loop into a linear window update

payload.text: Longest substring without repeating characters looks O(n²) with a set per position. One moving window makes it O(n). Interviewers plant these problems specifically to see if you know the pattern.

**Two pointers:** indices L and R move toward each other or in the same direction with purpose. Classic uses: pair-sum in a sorted array (move the pointer whose value is too small/large), palindrome checks, merging, in-place partitioning.

**Sliding window:** a window [L, R] over the array that grows by advancing R and shrinks by advancing L when a constraint breaks. Maintain a running aggregate (sum, count, map) and update it in O(1) per move.

**Fixed window:** size k; add element entering, remove element leaving.

**Variable window:** expand R until the window is invalid or complete; then move L to restore validity; record best answer.

**When not to use:** unsorted pair-sum (use a hash set instead); non-monotonic constraints that force full resets — sometimes a hash map "last index" approach is cleaner.

payload.title: Window invariant
payload.text: Write in one sentence what is always true inside [L,R]. If you cannot, the window is wrong.

payload.title: Off-by-one on removal
payload.text: When shrinking, remove the element AT L before incrementing L, not after.

steps.desc: Window [L,R] with a char→count map. Expand R; update counts.

steps.title: Shrink when invalid
steps.desc: While map size > k: decrement s[L], drop if zero, L++.

steps.title: Track answer
steps.desc: Max width after each valid window.

payload.solution: O(n) time, O(k) space for the map.

payload.hint: Initial sum of first k, then add s[i] and subtract s[i−k].

mistakes.fix: Update incrementally — that is what makes the pattern O(n).

mistakes.fix: Sorting is O(n log n); for unsorted, use a hash set of complements in one pass.

lessons.title: Hash Maps, Stacks and Monotonic Patterns
lessons.summary: O(1) lookups and the LIFO stack as a tool for matching, next-greater and expression problems.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use hash maps/sets to trade space for O(n) lookups
Solve bracket-matching and expression problems with a stack
Apply the monotonic stack template to next-greater and histogram problems

payload.text: Two-sum goes from O(n²) brute force to O(n) the moment you store complements in a map. The "next greater element" array is the same idea in stack clothing — one template, dozens of OA questions.

**Hashing:** average O(1) insert/lookup/delete. Use for frequency counts, seen-sets, complement lookups and grouping anagrams. Worst case is O(n) per op (collisions) but irrelevant in interviews.

**Stack (LIFO):** push/pop/peek. Natural for: matching brackets, undo, DFS by hand, expression evaluation and any "last unfinished thing" state.

**Monotonic stack:** keep stack elements in increasing (or decreasing) order. For each new element, pop while the top is on the wrong side; the popped element's "next greater/smaller" is the current element. O(n) total because each element is pushed and popped once.

**Template (next greater to the right):**
for i in 0..n-1:
  while stack not empty and a[stack.top] < a[i]:
    ans[stack.pop] = a[i]
  stack.push(i)
remaining indices in stack have no next greater (answer 0 or −1).

payload.title: Store indices, not just values, in monotonic stacks
payload.text: You often need the position to compute distances and widths.

payload.title: Next greater element
payload.problem: Array [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]. For each element, find the next greater element to the right (or −1).

steps.desc: Stack empty, push 0.

steps.title: i=1 (1)
steps.desc: 2 > 1, push 1. stack=[0,1].

steps.title: i=2 (2)
steps.desc: Pop 1 (ans[1]=2); top 2 is not < 2; push 2.

steps.title: i=3 (4)
steps.desc: Pop 2 (ans[2]=4), pop 0 (ans[0]=4); push 3.

steps.title: i=4 (3)
steps.desc: 4 > 3, push 4. End: ans[3]=ans[4]=−1.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to drain the stack at the end
mistakes.fix: Leftover indices have no next-greater — set the default explicitly.

lessons.summary: Cycle detection, middle node, reversal and merge — pointer work without extra arrays.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Detect a cycle and find the cycle start with Floyd’s algorithm
Reverse a linked list iteratively and understand the recursive form
Merge two sorted lists and delete nodes in O(1) extra space

payload.text: Interviewers watch linked-list questions for how you track prev/current/next — not for the final pointer. Rushing the surgery is how candidates lose the offer on an "easy" problem.

**Dummy head:** a temporary node before the real head. Avoids special-casing empty lists and head deletion/insertion.

**Floyd cycle:** slow = one step, fast = two steps. If they meet, a cycle exists. To find the start: reset one pointer to head; move both one step — the meeting point is the start.

**Reverse (iterative):** prev = null; while curr: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. Return prev.

**Merge two sorted lists:** walk both with a dummy tail; always attach the smaller node. O(n+m) time, O(1) extra space.

**Fast/slow for middle:** when fast reaches end, slow is at the middle (useful for palindrome checks and "reorder list").

payload.title: Always draw three arrows
payload.text: Before writing reversal or delete code, sketch prev, curr, next on paper.

payload.title: Losing the rest of the list
payload.text: Save curr.next before rewiring curr.next, or the remainder of the list is unreachable.

payload.title: Find cycle start

steps.title: Detect
steps.desc: Floyd: slow 1 step, fast 2 steps until they meet.

steps.title: No meeting
steps.desc: If no meeting, no cycle.

steps.title: Locate start
steps.desc: Reset p = head; move p and slow one step each; first meeting node is the start.

payload.solution: O(n) time, O(1) space — no hash set of visited nodes.

lessons.title: Binary Trees and BSTs
lessons.summary: Traversals, height, LCA and the sorted-order property interviewers probe constantly.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write inorder, preorder and postorder recursively and iteratively
Compute height and depth; validate a BST with range bounds
Find lowest common ancestor in a binary tree and in a BST

payload.text: Inorder on a BST prints keys in sorted order — that single property converts tree questions into "what order do I visit nodes". If you can recurse on left/right and combine, you can solve most tree problems.

**Traversals:**
- Preorder (node, left, right) — copy/serialize, prefix expressions.
- Inorder (left, node, right) — sorted order on BSTs.
- Postorder (left, right, node) — delete/evaluate postfix.

**Height:** max depth of any leaf + 1 (or 0 for null — pick a convention and state it). Recurrence: h = 1 + max(h(left), h(right)). O(n).

**BST validation:** pass an open interval (min, max) down the tree; each node must lie strictly inside. Comparing only with the parent is wrong (a deep descendant can violate order).

**LCA (general binary tree):** if left and right searches both return non-null, current node is the LCA; otherwise return whichever side was non-null. O(n).

**LCA (BST):** walk from the root: both smaller → go left; both larger → go right; else current is the split point. O(h).

payload.title: Iterative inorder with a stack
payload.text: Push left spine; pop, visit, go right once. Expect to be asked for the iterative version.

payload.title: Validate a BST with bounds

steps.title: Why bounds matter
steps.desc: Parent-only checks accept a deep left descendant larger than the root.

lessons.title: Heaps and Greedy Correctness
lessons.summary: Priority queues for top-k and scheduling; greedy strategies you can actually defend.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use a min/max heap for top-k, running median and merge-k problems
State the exchange argument idea when justifying a greedy choice
Solve interval scheduling and Huffman-style problems with heaps

payload.text: Top-k of a stream in O(n log k) with a size-k min-heap is one of the most repeated OA snippets. Greedy without a correctness argument is just hope — interviewers will ask why it works.

**Heap / priority queue:** binary heap gives O(1) peek and O(log n) push/pop. Min-heap for "smallest first"; max-heap via negation or a max-heap type.

**Top-k pattern:** maintain a min-heap of size k; for each element push then pop if size > k. At the end the heap holds the k largest. O(n log k).

**Running median:** two heaps — max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half; rebalance so sizes differ by at most 1. Median is the top of the larger heap (or average of both tops).

**Merge k sorted lists:** min-heap of the current head of each list; pop smallest, push its next. O(N log k) for N total elements.

**Greedy correctness:** the exchange argument — show any optimal solution can be swapped, step by step, to match the greedy choice without getting worse. Classic correct cases: activity selection by end time, fractional knapsack by value/weight, Huffman coding, earliest deadline first.

**When greedy fails:** 0/1 knapsack (use DP), graph shortest path with negative edges (Bellman-Ford), some coin systems (greedy coin change is not always optimal).

payload.title: Greedy is a proof obligation
payload.text: Always be ready with one sentence of exchange argument or a counterexample family.

lessons.title: Graph Traversal and Shortest Paths
lessons.summary: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra — three templates that cover most graph OAs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Implement BFS for unweighted shortest path and connected components
Use DFS for cycles, topological order and flood fills
Run Dijkstra with a min-heap and state when it is valid

payload.text: Maze shortest path is BFS. Course schedule is topological sort. Network delay is Dijkstra. Three templates, a whole category of OA problems.

**Graph representation:** adjacency list — map/list of node → neighbors. O(V+E) space. Prefer list over matrix unless dense (E ≈ V²) or you need O(1) edge queries.

**BFS:** queue, visit level by level. First time you reach a node in an unweighted graph is the shortest path length. Marks visited when enqueued, not when dequeued (avoids duplicates in queue).

**DFS:** stack or recursion. Use for components, cycle detection, topo sort (postorder reverse), bipartite check, flood fill. Watch recursion depth on large V — iterative DFS if V > ~10⁴.

**Topological sort:** only on a DAG. Kahn’s algorithm: compute in-degrees, enqueue zeros, peel nodes, reduce neighbors. If you cannot peel all nodes, a cycle exists.

**Dijkstra:** non-negative edge weights only. Min-heap of (dist, node); skip stale heap entries (dist > best known). O((V+E) log V). Invalid with negative weights — use Bellman-Ford instead.

payload.title: Mark visited on enqueue for BFS

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define a DP state and recurrence for 1-D problems (climb stairs, house robber, coin change)
Convert recursion + memo to bottom-up tabulation and space-optimize when possible
Run a structured interview conversation: clarify → examples → brute → optimize → code → test

payload.text: DP feels like magic until you realize every solution is the same three questions: what is the state, what is the recurrence, and in what order do states depend? Ask those in order and most "hard" DPs become mechanical.

**DP recipe:**
1. **State** — the smallest subproblem signature (i, remaining, mask...).
2. **Recurrence** — how state S depends on smaller states.
3. **Base cases** — and the direction of evaluation (top-down memo or bottom-up).
4. **Answer** — which state is the goal.

**Climbing stairs:** dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]; dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1.

**House robber:** dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]+a[i]) — skip or take.

**Coin change (min coins):** dp[x] = min over coins c of dp[x-c] + 1; dp[0]=0, else ∞.

**Space optimization:** if dp[i] only needs a constant window of previous states, keep just those variables (O(1) space).

**Interview playbook (45 min):**
1. Clarify inputs/outputs and constraints (2–3 min). Restate the goal.
2. Work a tiny example on the board (3 min).
3. State the brute force and its complexity (2 min) — even if you cannot code it.
4. Optimize: patterns (two pointers, heap, DP, graph) (5–10 min).
5. Agree on the approach, then code cleanly (15–20 min).
6. Dry-run with the example; test edge cases (empty, n=1, duplicates, negatives).
7. Discuss complexity and one follow-up. Ask if they want the optimal space version.

courses.title: AutoCAD Fundamentals
courses.subtitle: Precision 2D drafting, layers and blocks, plotting and collaboration — skills architecture, civil and mechanical juniors are hired for
courses.description:
AutoCAD remains the common language of 2D engineering documentation. This course takes you from a blank sheet to issued PDFs: units and coordinates, object snap, the draw/modify commands that dominate daily work, layer standards, blocks with attributes, dimensions, floor-plan and section workflows, paper-space viewports at true scale, plotting with CTB, xrefs and file hygiene, and a portfolio checklist aimed at junior drafting roles.

Four modules, eight lessons on the nine-step standard: objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, server-graded quiz and revision summary. A 30-question bank feeds the timed final; passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** students in architecture, civil, mechanical, interior design and related fields who need employable CAD habits — not just command trivia. Anyone who has "played with AutoCAD" but has never issued a correctly scaled sheet will find the missing pieces here.

**What you need:** AutoCAD, BricsCAD or a compatible 2D CAD package with a free trial or lab license. Exercises use real-unit drafting (mm).
outcomes: Set units, coordinates and object snap for accurate production drawing
Use core draw and modify commands including offset, trim, fillet and array
Organize drawings with disciplined layers and ByLayer properties
Create reusable blocks with attributes for symbols and title blocks
Draft plans and sections with correct hatch and annotation habits
Compose paper-space layouts with scaled, locked viewports
Plot correct PDFs with CTB and manage multi-sheet output
Clean, xref and hand off files with professional hygiene practices
courses.about_course:
Most AutoCAD "crash courses" list commands and stop. Employers notice the difference between someone who can OFFSET a wall and someone who keeps layers, attributes, viewport scales and plot settings in order. This course teaches the production path from the first lesson: snap to geometry, modify with intent, annotate on layers, compose in paper space, and clean before you issue.

Architectural and civil examples drive Modules 1–3; Module 4 covers the collaboration habits (xrefs, audit, purge, eTransmit) and a portfolio structure junior drafters can finish in a weekend. The closing exam verifies both command knowledge and process judgment.
prerequisites: A computer that can run AutoCAD, BricsCAD or similar
Basic spatial drawing comfort (hand sketches help)
audience: Architecture, civil, mechanical and interior design students
Junior drafters refreshing professional standards
Site engineers who need to read and edit consultant DWGs
Anyone preparing for a CAD-based internship or job test

lessons.title: Workspace, Units and Object Snap
lessons.summary: Set a drawing up correctly before the first line — units, snap, grid and coordinates.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Configure drawing units, limits and grid for a civil or mechanical sheet

Enable and interpret object snap modes (endpoint, midpoint, center, intersection)

payload.text: A drawing made in the wrong units is scrap. A line drawn near an endpoint but not on it breaks fillets, hatches and dimensions later. Setup discipline is what separates production drawings from sketches.

**Units:** UNITS command sets length type (decimal, architectural, engineering) and precision. For Indian civil work often mm or m; mechanical often mm. INSUNITS controls insert scale for blocks/xrefs.

**Coordinates:**
- Absolute: 100,50 (from origin 0,0)
- Relative: @50,0 (from last point)
- Polar relative: @100<45 (length 100 at 45°)

**Grid and snap:** GRID displays a reference lattice; SNAP constrains cursor movement. Ortho (F8) limits to horizontal/vertical; Polar (F10) guides at set angles.

**Object snap (OSNAP):** locks the cursor to exact geometry points — endpoint, midpoint, center, quadrant, node, intersection, perpendicular, tangent, extension. Run-time OSNAP vs one-time osnap overrides (shift+right-click). Always draw to real snaps, not eyeballed proximity.

**Dynamic Input (F12):** shows lengths/angles at the cursor — useful once you trust the numbers.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use LINE, CIRCLE, ARC, RECTANG, POLYLINE and PLINE correctly

Choose polyline vs exploded lines for editing and hatching

payload.text: A senior draftsman once said the job is 20% draw and 80% modify. Learning OFFSET+TRIM and ARRAY turns a 2-hour elevation into a 15-minute job.

**Draw essentials:**
- LINE — segments; C to close; U undo last segment.
- CIRCLE — center-radius (default), 2P, 3P, TTR (tangent-tangent-radius).
- ARC — 3-point default; start-center-end variants for precision.
- RECTANG — two corners; fillet/chamfer options before drawing.
- PLINE — polyline with width; one object, easier trim/fillet as a whole.
- POLYLINE vs LINE: a polyline is a single entity (one layer/color, closed area for hatch/area).

**Modify essentials:**
- TRIM (TR) — trim to cutting edges; select all = fence mode in newer releases.
- EXTEND (EX) — the dual of trim.
- OFFSET (O) — parallel copy at distance; workhorse for walls, ribs, stairs.
- FILLET (F) — round corner (radius R); CHAMFER — bevel.
- MIRROR (MI) — reflect; keep or delete source.
- ARRAY (AR) — rectangular, polar, path arrays with counts/spacing.
- MOVE (M) / COPY (CO) / SCALE (SC) / ROTATE (RO).

**Selection:** window (L→R) selects fully inside; crossing (R→L) selects touched. Fence for messy areas.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create and manage layers with color, linetype and lineweight

Control visibility with freeze/thaw, on/off and lock appropriately

payload.text: A drawing where every line is red BYCOMMAND is unmaintainable. Layers let you hide dimensions while editing structure, print walls thicker than furniture, and hand off a sheet without a 30-minute explanation.

**Layers** are the primary organization tool: name by discipline and role (A-WALL, A-DOOR, A-DIMS, E-POWER, S-COL).

**Object properties:** Color, Linetype, Lineweight, Plot style. Best practice: set objects to BYLAYER and control appearance on the layer itself.

**Linetype:** Continuous, Dashed, Center, Hidden — load via LINETYPE before assigning. LTSCALE scales dash patterns to the drawing.

**Visibility:**
- On/Off — hides objects; still regenerates.
- Freeze/Thaw — hides and unloads from memory; better for xrefs and large sheets.
- Lock — visible but not editable; good for background underlays.

**Layer states / filters:** save sets of on/off/frozen for different deliverables (plan vs furniture plan).

**VPSCALE / plot:** lineweight display is paper-dependent; rely on plot style tables (CTB/STB) for final print control.

payload.title: One property rule
payload.text: Objects BYLAYER always; change the layer to change the look of many objects at once.

payload.title: Do not freeze the layer you are drawing on
payload.text: New objects on a frozen layer are invisible — a classic "where did my line go" bug.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create, insert and edit blocks with a sensible base point

payload.text: The same door appears 40 times on a floor plan. As a block, one update edits all. As 40 exploded line-sets, you redraw the office. Blocks are the single biggest productivity lever in 2D CAD.

**Blocks:** a named collection of entities stored once, inserted many times. Base point matters — it is the insertion handle. Use WBLOCK to save blocks to external files for reuse across projects.

**Attributes:** text placeholders inside a block (tag, prompt, default). Title blocks use ATTRIB for project, sheet, date, scale. Edit values with ATTEDIT / EATTEDIT or by double-click.

**Dynamic blocks (advanced):** visibility states, stretch actions, lookup tables — one block with many configurations. Worth knowing for libraries.

**Dimensions:** linear (DLI), aligned (DAL), angular (DAN), radial (DRA/DRE), diameter (DDI), ordinate (DOR).

**Dimension style (DIMSTYLE):** unit precision, arrowheads, text height, gaps, alternate units. Set once per office standard; annotative scaling keeps text readable across view scales.

**Association:** dimensions stay linked to geometry; moving an endpoint updates the dimension if association is on.

lessons.title: Plans, Sections and Hatching

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Draft a simple floor plan with walls, openings and room labels
Create a section with correct cut-line convention and hatch (poche)
Use associative HATCH that updates when boundaries change

payload.text: Employers hire draftspeople who can produce a clean plan-section-elevation set — not just operate the mouse. This lesson mirrors how real architectural sheets are built in 2D CAD.

**Plan discipline:** draw walls as closed polylines or double-line offsets; openings by TRIM with door/window blocks inserted; rooms labeled on A-ANNO-TEXT with room name + area if required.

**Section basics:** the cut plane location is shown on the plan with a section line (heavy line + arrows + label A-A). The section view shows what is cut (poché/hatch) and what is beyond (elevation lines).

**Poché:** the material cut through is filled — diagonal hatch for masonry, solid for RC, specific patterns per material legend.

**HATCH (H):** pick internal point or select boundary; associative hatch re-fires when the boundary edits. Patterns: ANSI31 (general), AR-CONC (concrete), SAND, STEEL. Scale (HPSCALE / pattern scale) must suit the drawing scale — too dense becomes solid on plot.

**Elevation markers and levels:** level datums (±0.000) with finished floor levels; section level callouts.

**Workflow order:** grid → structural/wall lines → openings → furniture/equipment → annotation → hatch → plot.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create paper-space layouts with titled title blocks

payload.text: Model space is infinite; the plotter sheet is not. Candidates who only print from model space at "fit to page" never show a true 1:100 elevation. Paper space is the professional path.

**Model space vs paper space:**
- Model: draw 1:1 in real units, forever.
- Paper (Layout): the sheet; floating viewports are windows onto model at defined scales.

**Viewport scale:** select viewport → Properties → Standard scale (1:100, 1:50) or set with ZOOM 1/100xp while the viewport is active (MSLIDE/CHSPACE workflow). Then Lock viewport so pans do not destroy scale.

**Annotative objects:** text/dimensions that auto-scale per viewport — keeps notes readable in 1:100 plan and 1:20 detail without style forks.

**Plot (PLOT / Ctrl+P):**
- Printer: DWG to PDF (or your office PDF driver).
- Paper size: A1/A2/A3 as required.
- Plot area: Layout (paper space).
- Plot style table: office CTB (color→lineweight).
- Center the plot; scale 1:1 for layouts.

**Publish / batch plot:** PUBLISH for multi-sheet PDF sets.

**Export for consultants:** eTransmit packages DWG + xrefs + fonts + CTB.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Attach and manage external references with correct paths

payload.text: A 40 MB DWG that takes two minutes to open is usually 38 MB of orphaned junk and unreferenced blocks. Cleanup is not glamorous; it is the difference between a usable deliverable and a complaint email.

**Xrefs (external references):** link another DWG into the current drawing without exploding it. Benefits: shared background (architectural plan under structural), parallel work, single source of truth, smaller host files.

**Attach vs Overlay:** overlay does not nest-attach into hosts that reference this file — use overlay in circular team structures.

**Path types:** absolute, relative, and eTransmit-friendly relative paths. Broken xref paths after moving folders are the #1 xref problem — use PROJECT SEARCH PATHS or relative paths.

**Cleanup toolkit:**
- AUDIT — fix errors.
- PURGE / -PURGE all — remove unused named objects (layers, blocks, styles). Run -PURGE with All for deep clean.
- OVERKILL — delete duplicate/overlapping entities.
- -DWGUNITS / -UNITS script — normalize units on import.
- RECOVER / RECOVERALL — emergency open of damaged files.

**DWG formats:** save as current DWG for work; issue older versions (e.g. 2018) when consultants run older AutoCAD.

**Naming:** Project_Number_SheetTitle_Rev.dwg — boring and searchable beats clever.

payload.text: Portfolios full of tutorial copies get skipped. A hiring manager wants to see: correct scale, layer discipline, clean annotation, one complete sheet set. This lesson tells you exactly what to put in.

**Templates (DWT):** locked layers, text styles, dimstyles, layouts, title block. Start every job from the office template.

**DesignCenter (ADC):** browse other DWGs and drag layers, blocks, dimstyles into the current drawing — fast library reuse without xref clutter.

**Sheet sets (SHEETSET):** manage a multi-sheet project as one set — sequential sheet numbers, unified publish, model references per sheet. Offices with large drawing sets live in sheet sets.

**Role map:**
- Architecture / interiors: plans, elevations, sections, furniture layouts.
- Civil: site plans, layouts, road/section drawings, levels.
- Mechanical: part drawings, assemblies, GD&T annotations, BOM views.
- MEP consultants: clash-aware backgrounds via xref.

**Portfolio rules (6–10 sheets):**
1. Cover + role statement.
2. One complete mini sheet set (plan + section + elevation) at correct scales.
3. One mechanical/detail set if applicable.
4. Sheet showing layers/standards (cleanliness proof).
5. Short write-up: tools, units, what you did vs template.
6. Optional: before/after cleanup case.

**Tools adjacency:** AutoCAD + basic Excel for schedules; PDF markup; familiarity with Revit/BricsCAD is a plus — say what you actually know.

courses.title: Git & GitHub Mastery
courses.subtitle: From first commit to confident collaboration — snapshots, branching, PRs, hooks and disaster recovery
courses.description:
Every engineering team runs on Git, yet most students meet it as a pile of half-remembered commands. This course builds the three-area mental model (working tree, staging area, repository) and then layers the skills you will actually use daily: clean commits, branching and merging, pull requests, remotes and forks, stash and cherry-pick, bisect, hooks and reflog recovery.

Short lessons, real command sequences, and a final exam with certificate eligibility. Free forever — Git is infrastructure for your whole career.

**Who this is for:** first-years through final-years in every branch, and anyone about to join a team that uses GitHub.

**What you need:** a machine with Git installed (or a GitHub account to follow along in the browser).
courses.thumbnail_alt: Git and GitHub Mastery course cover
outcomes: Explain working tree, staging area and repository without hand-waving
Create focused commits and read history with log, show and diff
Branch, merge and rebase with a clear sense of when each is safe
Run a fork + PR workflow and write PRs reviewers actually merge
Use stash, cherry-pick, bisect and worktree as daily tools
Recover "lost" commits with reflog and ship hotfixes with revert
courses.about_course:
University lab manuals often teach Git as a list of commands to memorize. This course teaches the model those commands sit on: three places for your files, branches as cheap pointers, and remotes as other people's copies of the same history.

Once the model is solid, the daily skills follow naturally: staging only what belongs in a commit, reviewing history before undoing, opening pull requests that get merged, and recovering from resets and bad merges without panic. The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a real repository with a feature branch, a tag and a demonstrated recovery.

Each lesson is short, written for phones, and ends with a server-graded quiz.
prerequisites: Comfort using a terminal or Git Bash (helpful; commands are spelled out)
A free GitHub account if you want to follow along online
audience: First- through final-year students in every branch joining team projects
Anyone about to contribute to an open-source repository

modules.title: Module 1 — Snapshots, Commits, History
modules.summary: Working tree, staging area and commits — the three-area mental model that makes every other command obvious.

lessons.title: Repository, Staging and Commits
lessons.summary: init, status, add, commit — and why Git has a staging area at all.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain the working tree, staging area and repository as three places
Initialize a repo, stage changes selectively and create clear commits
Read git status and git log and interpret what they tell you

payload.text: Git is not a backup button. It is a snapshot machine: you choose what goes into the next snapshot (staging), then freeze it with a message (commit). Once that model clicks, add/commit/status stop feeling random.

**Three places:**
1. **Working tree** — the files you edit on disk.
2. **Staging area (index)** — the shortlist of changes for the next commit.
3. **Repository (.git)** — permanent history of committed snapshots.

**Daily loop:** edit → git status → git add (stage) → git commit → (optionally) git push later.

**Why staging?** You can commit only the related half of a messy working session. Stage file A, leave file B unstaged, commit a clean unit of work.

**Commit messages:** subject line under ~72 characters, imperative mood ("Add login form", not "Added"). Body explains why when the why is not obvious.

**git status** answers: what changed, what is staged, what is untracked. Learn to read the three sections.

**History:** git log --oneline --graph for a compact view; git show for one commit's diff.

payload.title: Commit often, push deliberately
payload.text: Small commits are reviewable; history is free. Pushing is a separate social/sync decision.

payload.title: Never commit secrets
payload.text: API keys, .env files and tokens must stay out of history — once pushed, treat them as leaked and rotate.

lessons.title: Inspecting History and Undoing Safely
lessons.summary: log, show, diff, restore and reset — travel through history without losing work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use log, show and diff to understand what changed and when
Discard unstaged edits with restore and unstage with restore --staged
Choose the right reset mode (--soft, --mixed, --hard) and use reflog after mistakes

payload.text: The fear of Git is almost always the fear of losing work. History is append-only; almost everything destructive has a recovery path if you know the command. This lesson buys that confidence.

**Reading history:**
- git log --oneline --graph --decorate
- git show <commit> — full patch of that commit
- git diff — unstaged changes; git diff --staged — staged vs last commit

**Safer undos:**
- git restore file — throw away unstaged edits to that file (working tree only).
- git restore --staged file — unstage; keep edits in the working tree.
- git commit --amend — rewrite the last commit message or fold a tiny fix (never amend a commit you already pushed to a shared branch without coordination).

**reset (moves the branch pointer):**
- --soft HEAD~1 — undo last commit, keep changes staged.
- --mixed HEAD~1 (default) — undo last commit, keep changes in working tree, unstaged.
- --hard HEAD~1 — destroy staged and working-tree changes to match the previous commit. Use only when you are sure; prefer stash or branch first.

**reflog:** "where have I been" for HEAD and branches. If you reset --hard by accident, git reflog often saves you within the default 90 days.

payload.title: Prefer restore over reset for single files
payload.text: restore is scoped; reset moves history pointers — different jobs.

payload.title: Avoid amend/rebase on shared branches
payload.text: Rewriting published history forces teammates to repair their clones.

payload.title: Undo a bad last commit without losing files

steps.title: Step 2 - mixed reset

steps.title: Step 3 - verify
steps.desc: git status: previous commit content is now unstaged edits.

steps.title: Step 4 - recommit cleanly
steps.desc: Fix the work; git add; git commit with a better message.

payload.solution: History rewound one step; files preserved in the working tree.

lessons.title: Branches, Merge and Rebase
lessons.summary: Create, switch and merge branches; understand fast-forward, true merge commits and rebase.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create and switch branches; explain what a branch pointer actually is
Perform a fast-forward vs three-way merge and read the result
Rebase a feature branch onto main and state when rebase is unsafe

payload.text: A branch in Git is a 41-byte pointer, not a copy of the repo. That is why branching is instant and why "merge" is just pointer arithmetic plus a possible merge commit. Interviews ask this constantly.

**Branch = movable pointer** to a commit. HEAD names the current branch. git switch -c feature makes a new pointer at HEAD and moves HEAD there.

**Fast-forward merge:** if main has not diverged, the branch pointer simply moves forward — no merge commit.

**Three-way merge:** when both sides advanced, Git finds a common ancestor and creates a merge commit with two parents. Conflicts appear when the same lines changed on both sides.

**Rebase:** replays your commits on top of another base as new commits (new hashes). History looks linear. Golden rule: do not rebase commits that are already public on a shared branch.

**merge vs rebase:** merge preserves true history including the branch shape; rebase gives linear history for local cleanup. Team policy wins — follow the repo.

payload.title: switch vs checkout
payload.text: git switch is for branches; git restore is for files. Newer Git prefers this split.

payload.title: Do not rebase pushed work without team agreement
payload.text: It rewrites hashes and will require force-push, breaking others.

payload.title: Feature branch then merge

steps.desc: git switch main && git switch -c feature/login.

steps.title: Step 2 - commit on feature

steps.title: Step 3 - merge
steps.desc: git switch main; git merge feature/login (fast-forward if main idle).

steps.title: Step 4 - inspect
steps.desc: git log --oneline --graph shows the line of work.

steps.title: Step 5 - cleanup
steps.desc: Optionally git branch -d feature/login after merge.

payload.solution: Feature integrated; branch pointer deleted locally.

payload.hint: Commit on both sides before merging.

mistakes.mistake: Committing on main when a feature branch was intended
mistakes.fix: Check git branch and HEAD before the first edit.

mistakes.mistake: Resolving conflicts by taking "all theirs" blindly

lessons.title: Team Workflow: PR, Review and Hotfix

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe a GitHub-flow branch/PR/main cycle for a small team
Push a branch, open a PR and respond to review comments productively
Ship a hotfix and keep main releasable

payload.text: The PR is where careers are made or delayed. Clean commits, a useful description and small diffs get you merged; mystery force-pushes get you ignored.

**GitHub flow (small teams):**
1. main always releasable.
2. Branch from main for each change.
3. Commit in small reviewable units; push to the fork or origin branch.
4. Open a PR: what, why, how to test, screenshots if UI.
5. Review; address comments with new commits (not silent force-pushes unless agreed).
6. Merge (squash, merge commit, or rebase — team policy).
7. Delete the merged branch.

**Push:** git push origin feature/login — updates the remote branch. First push: -u to set upstream.

**Review etiquette:** keep diffs small; separate mechanical reformat from logic changes; reply to every comment (done / question / push-back with reason).

**Hotfix:** branch from the released main (or a release tag), minimal fix, PR, deploy, cherry-pick or merge back to develop if you use one.

**Tags:** lightweight markers for releases: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First release"; git push origin v1.0.0.

lessons.title: Remotes: clone, fork, fetch, pull, push
lessons.summary: How origin and upstream map onto GitHub; what pull really runs; keeping branches in sync.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain origin, upstream and the fork workflow
Use clone, remote -v, fetch, pull and push correctly
Distinguish fetch (safe) from pull (fetch + merge/rebase)

payload.text: Interviews love asking: "What is the difference between git pull and git fetch?" If you can only say "one is safe", you are halfway there. This lesson finishes the map.

**clone** — full local copy of a remote repo including history and a default remote named origin.

**remote -v** — lists URLs; origin is the default name for "your" remote. In a fork workflow, origin may be your fork and upstream the official repo.

**fetch** — downloads new commits/refs; does NOT change your working tree or current branch. Safe anytime.

**pull** — fetch + integrate (merge by default, or rebase with --rebase). It can create a merge commit or conflicts in your working tree.

**push** — uploads commits to a remote branch. Fails if remote is ahead (non-fast-forward); pull first, or force-push only on personal branches you own.

**Fork flow:** fork on GitHub → clone your fork → add upstream → push to origin → PR from your fork to upstream.

**Tags:** git push origin v1.0.0 ships release markers.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: A repo without a README is a locked drawer with no label. Most open-source maintainers reject PRs that ignore issue templates — not out of meanness, but because unclear work costs them hours.

**Issue hygiene:** bug template (steps, expected, actual, environment); feature template (problem, proposal, alternatives). Label with area + kind. Link PRs with "Fixes #12".

**README:** what it is, who it is for, install in three commands, minimal usage example, link to docs/contributing. Update in the same PR that changes behavior.

**LICENSE:** without one, default copyright applies — people cannot legally reuse. Pick intentionally (MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL...).

**Releases:** tag vX.Y.Z (semver: breaking/feature/fix), GitHub Release notes from the tag, attach artifacts if needed.

**CODEOWNERS:** auto-request reviewers for paths. CONTRIBUTING.md: how to run tests and the PR bar.

**Security:** never commit secrets; SECURITY.md for private vulnerability reports; rotate if leaked.

lessons.title: Stash, Cherry-pick, Bisect, Worktree
lessons.summary: Park work, move single commits, binary-search history, and run two branches without switching chaos.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use stash to park dirty work and restore it safely
Cherry-pick a single good commit onto another branch
Binary-search a regression with bisect; parallelize with worktree

payload.text: Production is on fire on Friday. You need one commit from last month, not the whole feature branch. Stash, cherry-pick and bisect are the emergency tools — and they show up in senior interviews.

**stash:** git stash push -m "wip" saves tracked changes and reverts the tree; git stash list / pop / apply restores. Prefer push -m over bare stash. Untracked files need -u.

**cherry-pick:** git cherry-pick <sha> applies one commit's diff as a new commit on HEAD (new hash). Good for hotfixing a release branch.

**bisect:** git bisect start; git bisect bad HEAD; git bisect good v1.0; checkout middle commits; Git halves the search. Automate with git bisect run ./test.sh.

**worktree:** git worktree add ../fix-branch hotfix — second directory, same repo, different branch. No more stashing mid-review to jump branches.

**range-diff / log -S:** find when a string appeared: git log -S "functionName" --oneline.

lessons.title: Hooks, .gitignore & Disaster Recovery
lessons.summary: Client hooks that block bad commits, ignore rules that keep secrets out, and reflog playbooks when everything seemed lost.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Configure pre-commit and commit-msg hooks for quality gates
Write a correct .gitignore (and avoid ignoring files that should be tracked)
Recover from reset --hard, bad merges and orphaned commits with reflog

payload.text: Hooks are the seatbelt that stops a secret or a red test from entering history. Recovery is the knowledge that even after panic-clicks, Git usually still has your bytes — for a while.

**Hooks:** scripts in .git/hooks (or configured via core.hooksPath). Common:
- pre-commit — lint/tests; non-zero exit blocks the commit.
- commit-msg — validate message format (conventional commits).
- pre-push — last gate before remote.
Hooks are local by default; teams share them via a tracked hooks/ dir or a tool (Husky, pre-commit framework).

**.gitignore:** patterns for build output, IDE files, .env. Tracked files are not ignored until untracked — git rm --cached path. Never rely on ignore for secrets you already committed; rotate keys.

**.gitattributes:** force LF, mark binary files, export-ignore.

**Recovery playbook:**
1. Stop committing.
2. git reflog — find the last good SHA.
3. git switch -c rescue <sha> or git reset --hard <sha> once sure.
4. For pushed mistakes: revert commits on public branches instead of rewriting history.
5. fsck / dangling objects if reflog was expired — last resort.

payload.title: Recovery scenario

courses.description:
Linux shows up everywhere: lab machines, cloud VMs, CI runners and almost every backend interview. This course teaches the shell you actually use — navigation and permissions, the grep/sed/awk pipeline that beats any GUI for logs, processes with kill and systemd, packages, SSH and network checks, then enough bash to automate the boring half of your day.

Eight compact lessons, each with a worked example you can type along, a practice prompt and a server-graded quiz. Finish with the timed final exam and a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** first-years who have only used Windows, placement candidates facing Linux rounds, and anyone deploying a project to a cloud box for the first time.

**What you need:** any Linux sandbox, WSL, or a free cloud VM. Commands are written so you can also follow along on a school lab machine.
courses.thumbnail_alt: Linux and Shell Basics course cover
outcomes: Move around the filesystem with absolute and relative paths confidently

courses.about_course:
Most students meet Linux as a list of commands to memorize for a lab exam. This course teaches the model underneath: a single filesystem tree, permissions as three triples, text as the universal interface, and processes as things you can name and signal.

By Module 2 you can answer "what failed in this log last hour" without a GUI. By Module 4 you have a cron'd backup script with set -euo pipefail — the kind of artifact interviewers actually ask about. The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a small automation you can show in a resume bullet.

Optional: WSL on Windows, or access to any Linux shell for practice

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use pwd, ls, cd and interpret absolute vs relative paths
Create and remove directories safely (mkdir -p, rmdir, rm -r care)
Read ls flags and predict what a command will touch before running it

payload.text: Every server, CI runner and cloud VM assumes you can drive a shell. The filesystem tree is the same shape on your laptop, a lab Linux box and a production container — once navigation is muscle memory, everything else is vocabulary.

**Where you are:** pwd prints the working directory. Everything relative resolves from there.

**Absolute vs relative:**
- Absolute starts at / (root): /home/you/notes.txt
- Relative starts from cwd: notes.txt or ../shared/todo.md
- ~ expands to your home directory; . is here; .. is parent.

**Listing:** ls, ls -l (long), ls -a (hidden), ls -lah (human sizes). Colour output means: blue directory, green executable, cyan symlink.

**Changing directory:** cd /var/log, cd .., cd - (previous), cd (home).

**Create / remove:**
- mkdir -p a/b/c — parents as needed, no error if exists.
- rmdir empty_dir — only if empty.
- rm -r dir — recursive; rm -rf is powerful and irreversible. Prefer trash or explicit paths. Never rm -rf / or unquoted variables that might be empty.

**Read before you destroy:** ls the target; echo "$VAR" before rm -rf "$VAR".

payload.title: Tab completion is mandatory

lessons.title: Files, Copy, Move and Permissions Intro
lessons.summary: cp, mv, rm, touch, and the first honest look at chmod and who owns a file.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Copy, move and rename files and directories with correct flags
Explain file ownership (user, group, other) and read ls -l mode strings

payload.text: Interviewers ask: "How do you give execute permission only to the owner?" If you can decode -rwxr-xr-- and answer with chmod u+x, you already sound like someone who has administered a box.

**Core file commands:**
- cp src dest, cp -r dir dest (directories)
- mv old new — rename or move; same filesystem is atomic rename
- rm file; rm -r dir
- touch file — create empty or update mtime
- file path — detect type when the extension lies

**ls -l anatomy:** -rwxr-xr-- user group size date name
- First char: type (- file, d directory, l symlink)
- Next nine: three triples user / group / other: r=4 w=2 x=1

**chmod:**
- Symbolic: chmod u+x script.sh, chmod go-w file (remove write from group/other)
- Numeric: chmod 755 dir-or-script (rwxr-xr-x), chmod 644 conf (rw-r--r--)
- Directories need x to enter (cd) and w to create children.

**Ownership:** chown user:group file (usually root). chgrp group file.

**umask** controls default create modes; do not memorize edge cases, know that it subtracts from 666/777.

payload.title: Common modes
rows: rwxr-xr-x — scripts, dirs you want others to enter

payload.text: A production log is 2 GB. You need every 500 error from last hour. GUI editors choke; grep and tail do it in seconds. This is the highest-ROI Linux skill for placement and on-call.

**Reading:**
- cat whole file (bad for huge files)
- less file — scroll; G end; /pattern search; q quit
- head -n 20 / tail -n 50; tail -f live-follow
- wc -l lines; file path type detection

**Pipes and redirects:**
- cmd | next — stdout of left becomes stdin of right
- > overwrite file; >> append; 2> errors; 2>&1 merge errors into stdout
- cmd | tee out.txt — print and save

**grep:**
- grep "ERROR" app.log
- grep -i case-insensitive; -n line numbers; -r recursive; -v invert; -E extended regex
- grep -c count matches
- Combined: grep -in 'timeout' /var/log/*.log

**Other filters:** sort, uniq -c (sort first), cut -d: -f1, tr, paste.

**Composition:** grep ERROR app.log | tail -n 20 | cut -d' ' -f1-4

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: You have a 50k-line CSV of student emails with a typo domain. sed fixes it in one command. awk can print every user who failed a threshold. These are not ancient curiosities — they are daily ops tools.

**sed:**
- sed 's/old/new/' file — first match per line
- sed 's/old/new/g' — all matches
- sed -i 's/…/…/' file — in-place (GNU); backup with sed -i.bak
- sed -n '10,20p' file — print a range
- sed '5d' — delete line 5

**awk:**
- Fields default split on whitespace: $1 first column, $0 whole line
- awk '{print $1, $3}' file
- awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd — custom field separator
- awk '/ERROR/ {print $0}' — pattern-action
- awk '{sum+=$2} END {print sum}' — aggregate

**sort / uniq:**
- sort file; sort -n numeric; sort -k2 sort by column 2
- sort file | uniq -c — counts; sort -nr for top offenders
- cut -d, -f1-3 csv — cut fields

**tr** for character translate/delete: tr -d '\r' (strip CR).

lessons.title: Processes and Services
lessons.summary: What is running, who owns it, how to stop it cleanly, and reading systemd status.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: List and filter processes with ps and understand PID/PPID
Stop processes with kill signals SIGTERM vs SIGKILL correctly
Read systemctl status and journalctl for a failing service

payload.text: Your Node app "hangs". Ctrl+C does nothing over SSH. You need kill -9 with a PID — and the sense to try SIGTERM first so the process can flush state.

**Seeing processes:**
- ps aux — all processes, classic columns (USER PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND)
- ps aux | grep node
- pidof name; pgrep pattern
- top / htop — live; sort by CPU/MEM; q quit
- /proc/PID/status, /proc/PID/cwd for the brave

**Signals:**
- kill PID — default SIGTERM (15): polite, lets the app clean up
- kill -9 PID — SIGKILL: cannot be caught; last resort; may leave locks/tmp files
- kill -HUP often reloads config for daemons that support it

**systemd:**
- systemctl start|stop|restart|status name
- systemctl enable name — start on boot
- journalctl -u name -n 50 --no-pager — recent logs
- journalctl -u name -f — follow

**Zombie / defunct:** dead child not reaped; usually parent bug; kill the parent carefully.

**Load vs CPU:** load average includes runnable + uninterruptible; a high load with low CPU often means I/O wait or stuck D-state.

payload.title: pgrep -af pattern

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: Campus cloud VMs are Linux. You will apt install, ssh in, open a port for a demo, and wonder why curl fails until you check the firewall. These three skills cover 90% of early cloud friction.

**Packages:**
- Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt update && sudo apt install pkg; apt search; apt remove
- RHEL/Fedora: sudo dnf install pkg
- snap/flatpak exist; prefer distro packages when unsure
- Never blindly curl | sudo bash from unknown sources

**SSH:**
- ssh user@host; ssh -p 2222 user@host
- ssh-keygen -t ed25519; ssh-copy-id user@host; then key auth
- ~/.ssh/config host aliases; StrictHostKeyChecking is a security feature — understand before disabling
- scp file user@host:/path ; rsync -avz dir/ host:dir/

**Network checks:**
- ip a or hostname -I — your addresses
- ss -tulpn — listening TCP/UDP with process
- curl -v https://example.com — verbose HTTP
- curl -I — headers only; curl -o file — download
- ping, dig / nslookup for DNS
- wget as alternative downloader

**Firewall awareness:** ufw on Ubuntu (ufw allow 8080); cloud security groups are a second gate — both must allow traffic.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Structure a bash script with shebang, strict mode and functions

payload.text: Twenty times a day you run the same three commands. A 15-line script with set -euo pipefail is the difference between a junior and someone whose work multiplies.

**Skeleton:**
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# -e exit on error; -u unset vars are errors; -o pipefail: any pipe stage fails

**Variables:** NAME=value (no spaces). Use "$NAME" always. Read input: read -r name. Positionals: $1 $2, $@ all args. Special: $? last exit code.

**Conditionals:**
if [[ -f file ]]; then ...; elif [[ "$x" == "y" ]]; then ...; else ...; fi
Tests: -f file, -d dir, -e exists, -z empty, -n nonempty, [[ a == b ]], [[ a -lt b ]]

**Loops:**
for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done
while read -r line; do ...; done < file
for ((i=0; i<3; i++))

**Functions:** name() { ...; } — call with name arg1.

**Exit codes:** exit 0 success; non-zero failure. if command; then uses the code. Keep scripts honest: nonzero on real failure so cron/email alerts work.

**chmod +x script.sh** then ./script.sh.

lessons.title: Automation: Cron, Chmod and Real Habit
lessons.summary: Schedule work, make scripts safe to share, and build a personal ops checklist.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Install a user crontab and read system cron layout

payload.text: Cron is the oldest "cloud function" in the industry. Nightly backups, log rotation and report emails still run there on fleets that also run Kubernetes — the mental model transfers.

**User crontab:**
- crontab -e — edit; crontab -l — list; crontab -r — remove (careful)
- Format: minute hour day month weekday command
- Example daily 02:15: 15 2 * * * /home/you/backup.sh >> /home/you/backup.log 2>&1
- % in the command is special in cron — avoid or escape

**System layout:** /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.daily/ — root-managed; know they exist.

**Logs:** cron mail or your own >> logfile. Silent cron is how backups "have always been fine" until they were not.

**Hardening before you share a script:**
- set -euo pipefail; quote vars; no secrets hard-coded (use env or a 600 config)
- chmod 755 scripts; chmod 600 secrets
- Prefer absolute paths inside cron jobs (PATH is minimal in cron)

**Pre-flight checklist for destructive ops:**
1. pwd and echo the target path
2. Dry-run if the tool supports it
3. Backup or snapshot
4. Then run
5. Verify with a read-only command

**Where to go next:** man 7 bash for signals/job control; shellcheck for linting your scripts.

courses.title: Operating Systems
courses.subtitle: Processes, scheduling, concurrency, deadlock, memory, paging, virtual memory and file systems — exam + interview core
courses.description:
Operating Systems is the course every CSE/IT syllabus shares and every product interview still asks about. This course covers the full university core in eight compact lessons: process models and PCBs, FCFS through Round Robin with Gantt-chart arithmetic, critical sections with mutexes and semaphores, the classic producer-consumer and deadlock conditions, paging with TLB math, page replacement including Belady and thrashing, file inodes and allocation, and disk scheduling with RAID.

Every lesson uses the nine-block structure (objectives, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, graded quiz, summary). A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** second- and third-year CSE/IT students preparing for university exams, GATE fundamentals, and placement interviews that ask OS questions.

**What you need:** pen and paper for Gantt charts and fault counts; a browser for the quizzes.
outcomes: Explain processes, PCBs and the five-state model without hand-waving
Compute waiting/turnaround times for FCFS, SJF, SRTF and Round Robin
Apply mutex/semaphore patterns and state the critical-section criteria
List Coffman conditions and distinguish prevention vs Banker avoidance
Translate virtual addresses with paging and solve TLB effective-time problems
Count page faults for FIFO/LRU/Optimal and explain thrashing
Compare file allocation methods and solve basic disk-scheduling and RAID questions
courses.about_course:
University OS courses often split into two painful halves: process/CPU theory and memory/file systems. This course keeps one continuous thread — how the kernel multiplexes the machine — and drills the arithmetic examiners actually grade: Gantt charts, effective access time, page-fault tables and head-movement sums.

Concurrency is taught with runnable mental models (producer-consumer wait order, lock ordering for deadlock) rather than only pseudocode. Virtual memory is taught as the reason your laptop survives 30 tabs, so thrashing and working sets stick. The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a short written OS design note you can revise from before finals.
prerequisites: Comfort with basic data structures
Any programming language (pseudocode is explained line by line)
audience: CSE/IT students in semester 3–5 facing university OS exams
Placement candidates preparing for OS interview rounds
GATE aspirants building core CS fundamentals
Anyone who wants a correct mental model of processes, memory and disks

lessons.title: Processes, States and Threads
lessons.summary: What a process is, the PCB, the five-state model, and how threads share address space.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: Interview opener: "What is the difference between a process and a thread?" If you say "thread is lighter" without naming the shared address space, you lose half the marks. This lesson builds the model examiners actually want.

**Program vs process:** A program is passive text on disk. A process is a program in execution with its own address space, registers and kernel resources. One program → many concurrent processes.

**PCB (Process Control Block):** the kernel's identity card for a process — PID, process state, program counter, CPU registers, memory-management info, accounting, I/O status.

**Five-state model:**
1. **New** — admitted, not yet admitted to ready queue
2. **Ready** — waiting for CPU
3. **Running** — instructions executing on a CPU
4. **Waiting/Blocked** — waiting for I/O or an event
5. **Terminated** — finished; PCB reclaimed

Transitions: admit → ready; dispatch → running; I/O wait → waiting; I/O done → ready; exit → terminated. Preemption: running → ready (time slice over).

**Context switch:** save state of current process, load state of next. Pure overhead — no useful work. Cost grows with address-space size (more to swap) and with TLB flushes on some architectures.

**Threads:** a thread is a unit of schedulability inside a process.
- Shared: code, data, heap, open files, signal handlers
- Private: thread ID, program counter, registers, stack, errno

User-level threads are invisible to the kernel (one blocking call blocks all). Kernel-level threads are scheduled independently. Java's default model is 1:1 kernel threads on modern JVMs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute average waiting and turnaround time for FCFS, SJF, SRTF and RR

payload.text: Campus OS papers open with a Gantt chart question. Four processes, four arrival times, one waiting-time average. The students who win marks have a fixed procedure — not vibes. This lesson is that procedure.

**Metrics (memorize the formulas):**
- Turnaround time = completion − arrival
- Waiting time = turnaround − burst
- Response time = first run − arrival (RR cares about this)

**FCFS (non-preemptive):** order of arrival. Simple; convoy effect — one long job blocks short ones behind it.

**SJF (non-preemptive):** shortest burst next. Optimal average waiting if bursts known. Needs future knowledge (estimates via exponential average).

**SRTF (preemptive SJF):** if a new job arrives with shorter remaining burst, preempt. Best average waiting in theory; can starve long jobs.

**Round Robin:** time quantum q. Circular ready queue; each runs at most q then goes to the back (if not finished). Response time bounded. Small q → many switches (overhead); large q → degrades to FCFS. Typical q = 10–100ms, larger than context-switch cost by an order of magnitude.

**Priority:** highest priority first. Preemptive or not. Starvation risk → aging (gradually boost waiting jobs).

**Multilevel feedback queues:** several ready queues by priority; a job that uses too much CPU is demoted; I/O-heavy jobs stay high. Adaptive without perfect burst knowledge.

**How to draw a Gantt chart:** timeline bar; at each decision point list arrivals that just joined; apply the algorithm rule; record completion times; fill the table.

lessons.title: Critical Sections, Mutex & Semaphores
lessons.summary: Why races happen, the three requirements, and how locks and counting semaphores enforce them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain race conditions with a concrete interleaving
State the three critical-section requirements (mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting)
Use binary mutexes and counting semaphores; distinguish wait/signal semantics

payload.text: Two threads increment the same counter and you lose updates. No compiler warning, no crash — just a wrong answer at 2 a.m. Concurrency bugs are silent. Exams test whether you can name the fix and prove the properties.

**Race condition:** result depends on uncontrolled interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data.

**Critical-section problem — three requirements:**
1. **Mutual exclusion** — at most one process in its CS at a time
2. **Progress** — if no one is in CS and some want in, those not in remainder must not block selection
3. **Bounded waiting** — after a request, a bound on how long before entry

**Peterson's solution:** two-process software solution using turn[] and flag[]; satisfies all three on classical hardware (needs memory barriers on modern weak models).

**Mutex lock:** acquire() blocks until the lock is held; release() frees it.忙-waiting = spinlock (bad on single core, ok on short critical sections on multi-core).

**Semaphore S:** integer + wait(S)/signal(S).
- wait (P): if S>0 then S-- else block
- signal (V): S++ ; if waiters, wake one
- Binary semaphore: S ∈ {0,1} ≈ mutex (but mutex may have ownership/recursive semantics OS-specific)
- Counting semaphore: capacity for N concurrent entrants

**Implementation note:** wait/signal must be atomic (disable interrupts, or hardware CAS).

**Deadlock risk:** a missing wait before signal can invert order and hang forever — always pair acquire/release on all paths (including early returns).

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Solve producer-consumer with semaphore pairs (full, empty, mutex)
Explain readers-writers preference trade-offs

payload.text: Deadlock questions are cheap marks if you can recite the four conditions and one avoidance algorithm. The real value: every distributed systems outage postmortem eventually mentions a lock cycle.

**Producer-consumer (bounded buffer):**
- empty = N (slots free), full = 0 (items), mutex = 1
- Producer: wait(empty); wait(mutex); produce; signal(mutex); signal(full)
- Consumer: wait(full); wait(mutex); consume; signal(mutex); signal(empty)
- Order matters: wait(empty) before mutex (else deadlock); signal(mutex) before signal(full).

**Readers-writers:**
- First readers-writers: readers preferred — writers can starve
- Second: writers preferred — readers can starve after a writer queues
- Fair/FCFS variants balance both
- Classic: read_count with its own mutex; write_mutex for writers

**Dining philosophers:** classic deadlock if everyone picks left fork first. Fixes: resource hierarchy (always lower fork id first), limit N−1 at table, arbiter/ticket.

**Deadlock — four Coffman conditions (all must hold):**
1. Mutual exclusion
2. Hold and wait
3. No preemption
4. Circular wait

**Handling strategies:**
- Prevention: break one condition by design (e.g. force lock ordering ⇒ break circular wait)
- Avoidance: Banker's algorithm — only grant if resulting state is safe
- Detection + recovery: allow, detect with resource-allocation graph cycle, then kill/preempt
- Ignorance: most general-purpose OSes "ignore" and rely on programmer care

**Banker's sketch:** Need matrix, Max, Allocation; Available. Safe sequence exists ⇒ grant. Unsafe ⇒ refuse even if currently available looks enough.

lessons.title: Paging & Address Translation
lessons.summary: Logical vs physical addresses, page tables, TLB, and how a two-level table halves memory waste.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Translate logical to physical addresses with page number + offset
Explain page-table size problems and multi-level / hashed schemes
Compute effective access time with a given TLB hit ratio

payload.text: Every laptop runs paging. When an interviewer asks "how does virtual memory work?", they are testing whether you can walk an address from CPU to RAM without hand-waving.

**Address types:** Logical (virtual) address generated by CPU; physical address seen by memory unit. MMU performs the mapping.

**Fixed-size paging:**
- Memory split into equal **frames**; process into equal **pages** (same size)
- Page table maps page# → frame#
- Address = page number p (high bits) + offset d (low bits)
- Physical = frame f for p, same offset d
- No external fragmentation; internal fragmentation up to one page per process

**Page table entry (PTE):** frame number + bits: valid/present, protection, dirty/modified, reference, caching disabled, etc.

**Page-table size:** one entry per page. 32-bit, 4KB pages ⇒ 2^20 entries. At 4 bytes each ⇒ 4MB per process — too much. Fixes:
- Two-level (hierarchical) tables — page directory + page tables; only allocate used regions
- Inverted page table — one entry per frame
- Hashed page tables for sparse 64-bit spaces

**TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer):** small fast associative cache of recent p→f. Hit: one memory cycle for the TLB + one for data. Miss: walk page table(s) then fill TLB.
Effective access time = h × (TLB + mem) + (1−h) × (TLB + 2×mem + … page-walk cost)

**Thrashing preview:** too many processes ⇒ working sets don't fit ⇒ constant page faults (Module 3 lesson 2).

payload.title: Term
rows: Fixed-size logical unit in the process
Byte within the page/frame; identical before/after map

payload.title: Offset never changes

lessons.title: Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
lessons.summary: Demand paging, FIFO/LRU/Optimal/Clock, Belady anomaly, working-set model and thrashing.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute page-fault counts for FIFO, LRU and Optimal on a reference string
Explain Belady anomaly and why stack algorithms avoid it
Describe working set and thrashing; connect to degree of multiprogramming

payload.text: Give a reference string and 3 frames; count faults for FIFO vs LRU. If you can do that cleanly under exam pressure, you have earned the virtual-memory unit. Then the same intuition explains why your laptop freezes when 30 Chrome tabs fight for RAM.

**Demand paging:** pages loaded only on fault. Valid/invalid bit; invalid ⇒ page fault trap → OS fetches from disk → update PTE → restart instruction.

**Page fault cost:** disk latency dominates (ms vs ns). Optimize with prepaging, clean-page (no write-back) free lists.

**Replacement algorithms (string of page references, F frames):**
- **FIFO:** replace oldest arrival. Suffers **Belady's anomaly** — more frames can mean more faults.
- **LRU:** replace least recently used. Stack algorithm (no Belady). Expensive to implement exactly (timestamps / counter); approximations: second-chance / Clock uses reference bit.
- **Optimal (OPT/MIN):** replace page not used for the longest future. Best bound; needs future — offline benchmark only.
- **Clock:** circular buffer; reference bit R; hand sweeps; if R=0 replace else clear R and continue (second chance).

**Counting rule for exams:** walk the string; at each reference if page not in any frame → fault (count it) and apply the algorithm to pick victim; update reference bits/ages.

**Thrashing:** process working set (active pages) doesn't fit in RAM ⇒ every instruction faults ⇒ CPU utilization collapses. Working-set model tracks Δ recent references. Degree of multiprogramming must satisfy Σ working sets ≤ frames. OS response: swap out processes (reduce multiprogramming), not allocate more frames to everyone.

**Allocation:** per-process frames proportional to program size / priority; global vs local replacement trade-offs.

payload.title: Draw a frame table per step
payload.text: Exams award method marks even when arithmetic slips.

payload.title: Belady is FIFO-specific among the classics
payload.text: Saying "more frames always help" is wrong for FIFO.

payload.title: FIFO vs LRU on a short string
payload.problem: String: 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2. F=3. Count faults for FIFO and LRU.

steps.title: FIFO frames
steps.desc: Fault at 7,0,1,2 (evict 7),0 hit,3 (evict 0),0 fault (evict 1),4 (evict 2),2 fault (evict 3),3 fault (evict 0),0 fault (evict 4),3 hit,2 fault (evict 3). Total FIFO faults = 10.

steps.title: LRU
steps.desc: Track last use; faults at 7,0,1,2,0 hit,3,0 hit,4,2,3,0,3 hit,2 hit. Total LRU faults = 9.

steps.title: Compare
steps.desc: LRU ≤ FIFO here as expected on many textbook strings.

steps.title: Re-check
steps.desc: Each miss: was the page already resident?

steps.title: Method
steps.desc: Write the frame table in the answer sheet — method matters.

payload.solution: FIFO ≈ 10 faults, LRU ≈ 9 faults (verify with your table; small strings can tie).

payload.hint: Count carefully; anomaly is F=3 worse than F=4 for FIFO on some strings.

mistakes.fix: Needs future references; use as lower bound only.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing thrashing with a single page fault
mistakes.fix: Thrashing is sustained fault storms when working sets exceed RAM.

payload.source: Replacement unit one-liner.

payload.title: Lesson summary

modules.title: Module 4 — File Systems & I/O
modules.summary: Inodes, directory structure, allocation methods, disk scheduling (FCFS/SSTF/SCAN/C-SCAN) and RAID basics.

lessons.title: Files, Inodes & Disk Allocation
lessons.summary: File attributes, inodes vs directory entries, contiguous/indexed allocation and free-space management.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe file attributes and the role of the inode/directory split
Compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation (fragmentation + speed)
Explain free-space bitmaps and linked free lists at a high level

payload.text: Unix asked "why can I delete a file that is still open by another process?" The answer is the inode vs name split. Exams love this; production debugging loves it more.

**File attributes:** name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, time/creator. The name is user-facing; the identity is internal.

**Directory:** mapping names → file control blocks / inodes. Operations: create, delete, search, list, rename, traverse. Directory itself is a file of entries.

**Inode model (Unix):** inode holds metadata + block pointers; directory entries map names → inode numbers. Unlink removes the name; data lives until last hard-link and open fds drop (nlink / refcount). Explains open-file-deleted semantics.

**Allocation methods:**
1. **Contiguous:** start block + length. Fast random access; external fragmentation; file growth hard.
2. **Linked:** each block points to next. No external frag; poor random access; pointer overhead; reliability of links.
3. **FAT:** links collected in a table on disk — compromise.
4. **Indexed:** inode holds array of block pointers (plus indirect for large files). Good random access; index block is a single point of failure/size limit.

**Free-space tracking:**
- Bit map / bitmap: one bit per block; find n contiguous bits = allocation search cost
- Linked list of free blocks; group/count methods
- Coalescing free extents reduces external fragmentation for contiguous allocators

**Cluster / extent:** allocate groups of blocks to cut metadata and improve sequential throughput.

payload.title: Inode ≠ directory entry
payload.text: Hard links = multiple names, one inode; soft link = another name file pointing at a path.

payload.title: Growth cost of contiguous files
payload.text: Appending may need a new region and a copy if the next blocks are taken.

payload.title: Hard link vs unlink while open
payload.problem: Process A opens /data/report.txt; process B runs rm; A keeps reading.

steps.title: open()
steps.desc: Increments file refcount; path resolves via directory → inode.

steps.title: rm
steps.desc: Removes directory entry (name); nlink drops; refcount still > 0 because of A.

steps.title: Inode stays
steps.desc: Inode + data blocks remain until last close.

steps.title: Read continues
steps.desc: A continues to read correctly; new opens by name fail (ENOENT).

steps.title: Last close
steps.desc: OS frees data and inode.

payload.solution: Unix open-file deletion semantics via name vs object split.

payload.title: Inode pointer math
payload.prompt: An inode has 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect and one double-indirect (block size 4KB, 4-byte pointers). Max file size?
payload.hint: Direct + (blocks per indirect) + (blocks per double).

mistakes.mistake: Saying linked allocation supports fast seek to block k
mistakes.fix: You must walk k pointers — O(k).

mistakes.mistake: Confusing hard and soft links
mistakes.fix: Hard link shares the inode; soft link is a path shortcut and breaks if target path changes.

payload.question: Why does deleting an open file not crash the reader on Unix?
payload.answer: Directory entry is removed but the inode stays until nlink and open refcounts hit zero.
payload.source: File-system concept question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Name and object are separate (inode model).
Contiguous = fast + fragile; linked/indexed trade speed for flexibility.
Bitmaps and free lists manage free space.
