lessons.title: Disk Scheduling & RAID
lessons.summary: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN/C-SCAN/LOOK, elevator cost, and RAID 0/1/5 trade-offs for exams and interviews.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute total head movement for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN and C-SCAN given a queue
Explain why SSTF can starve edge requests
Map RAID levels 0, 1, 5 to redundancy, capacity and write cost

payload.text: Disk exams are arithmetic with a story: the head is an elevator. Cloud interviews then jump to RAID: "how many disks can fail in RAID 5?" If you can do both, you cover the storage unit completely.

**Disk geometry (logical view for exams):** cylinder/track/block numbers; queue of requests; head starts at some cylinder; goal = minimize total seek distance (and sometimes total time).

**Schedulers:**
- **FCFS:** fair; long detours possible.
- **SSTF:** nearest request next; good average; can starve far requests.
- **SCAN (elevator):** head sweeps to end, reverse; services along the way.
- **C-SCAN:** one direction only; jump to other end and continue (fairer variance).
- **LOOK / C-LOOK:** reverse/jump at last request instead of physical end (practical variants).

**Cost metric in exams:** total head movement in cylinders (sum of |next − current|). Draw the path; sum segments.

**RAID (cheap disks, big logical volume):**
- **RAID 0 — striping:** no parity; capacity all disks; speed up; zero redundancy.
- **RAID 1 — mirroring:** full copy; best read (either side) and simple rebuild; 50% capacity cost.
- **RAID 5 — distributed parity:** stripe + rotating parity; survives one disk failure; write penalty on parity updates; usable = (n−1)/n.
- **RAID 6:** dual parity; survives two failures.

**Failure math:** RAID 5 tolerates 1 failed disk; RAID 6 tolerates 2; RAID 1 tolerates 1 (per mirror pair).

**Related terms:** hot spare, rebuild time, URE risk (why large RAID 5 rebuilds scare operators — mention in viva for depth).

payload.title: SCAN vs C-SCAN vs LOOK in one line each
payload.text: SCAN both ends; C-SCAN one-way reset; LOOK stops at last request.

payload.title: SSTF starvation
payload.text: Edge cylinders can wait forever under heavy center load — aging variants exist.

payload.title: SSTF head movement
payload.problem: Queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Head starts at 53. Total movement for SSTF?

steps.title: Re-check
steps.desc: Always pick the unvisited nearest to current head.

steps.title: Contrast
steps.desc: With FCFS path if asked (often worse).

payload.solution: SSTF total head movement = 236 cylinders (from this start).

payload.title: SCAN path
payload.prompt: Same queue, head 53, SCAN toward higher end then reverse. Total movement?
payload.hint: Go to the high end first (e.g. 199 if disk ends there), then sweep down.

mistakes.mistake: Saying RAID 5 survives two disk failures
mistakes.fix: One only; use RAID 6 for two.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the starting head position in sums
mistakes.fix: First segment is from the initial head, not from the first request.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: How many disk failures can RAID 5 tolerate?
payload.answer: One distributed-parity failure.
payload.source: Storage interview staple.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Disk schedulers trade fairness vs total seek.
SSTF can starve; SCAN/C-SCAN are elevator families.
RAID 0 speed, 1 mirror, 5 single parity, 6 dual parity.

questions.prompt: RAID 5 usable capacity for 4×1TB disks is approximately:
questions.explanation: (n−1)/n with distributed parity.

questions.prompt: C-SCAN differs from SCAN by:
options: Returning to the other end without servicing on the reverse trip
questions.explanation: One-way service sweep.

questions.prompt: SSTF’s main weakness is:
questions.explanation: Edge requests can wait indefinitely.

courses.title: Computer Networks
courses.subtitle: OSI to TCP/IP, subnetting, TCP internals, DNS/HTTP/DHCP, TLS security and modern delivery — exam + interview core
courses.description:
Computer Networks is the CSE subject that shows up in university exams, GATE and every infrastructure or backend interview. This course covers the full core in eight compact lessons: layered models and encapsulation, MAC/IP/port addressing with ARP, framing and CRC, switches and routers, IPv4 subnetting arithmetic, distance-vector vs link-state routing, the TCP handshake with flow and congestion control, DNS/HTTP/DHCP, TLS with firewalls, and wireless/SDN/CDN for modern context.

Every lesson uses the nine-block structure (objectives, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, graded quiz, summary). A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** second- and third-year CSE/IT students preparing for university exams, GATE fundamentals, and placement interviews that ask networking questions.

**What you need:** pen and paper for subnetting and handshake diagrams; a browser for the quizzes.
outcomes: Map every OSI layer to its job, PDU and representative protocols
Trace a packet through addressing: MAC, IP, port and ARP resolution
Solve subnetting problems: prefix, ranges, broadcast and usable counts
Compare RIP vs OSPF and explain longest-prefix matching
Explain TCP handshake, teardown, flow control and congestion control
Outline DNS resolution, HTTP status classes and DHCP DORA
Describe TLS goals, firewall tiers and CDN/SDN value in modern delivery
courses.about_course:
Networking courses often fail in one of two ways: pure theory with no packets, or protocol trivia without the why. This course keeps the causal chain visible — every layer exists because the layer below could not do that job — and spends its arithmetic where examiners do: subnetting tables and TCP window math.

The security module is deliberately practical: you will be able to say exactly what the padlock in the address bar proves, why a packet filter cannot see HTTPS paths, and what WPA3 fixes over WPA2. The modern module (Wi-Fi, SDN, CDNs) gives you interview-ready language for how content actually reaches a phone in another city.

The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a short subnet design note you can revise from before finals.
prerequisites: Basic digital logic and binary arithmetic
Comfort with any programming language (pseudocode is explained)
audience: CSE/IT students in semester 3–5 facing university networking exams
Placement candidates preparing for networking and backend rounds
GATE aspirants building core CS fundamentals
Anyone who wants to understand what happens between a URL and a response
courses.branch_label: CSE / IT core (also useful for AI-DS)

exam_prep.target: University mid-terms and finals; GATE CS core; placement networking rounds

units.title: Layers & Addressing
units.summary: OSI 7 layers; TCP/IP merges 5–7. PDUs: segment/packet/frame/bits. Encapsulation adds headers down, strips up. MAC (per-link), IP (end-to-end), port (per-process). ARP maps IP→MAC on the LAN. NAT multiplexes private IPs onto one public IP.
questions: Name the OSI layers and one protocol each.

units.title: Data Link, Subnetting & Routing
units.summary: Switch learns source MAC, forwards on destination, floods unknowns and broadcasts. CRC detects corruption. Subnet: usable = 2^h − 2; increment = 256 − interesting octet. RIP = distance vector + hops (max 15); OSPF = link state + Dijkstra. Longest prefix match wins.
questions: Collision vs broadcast domain for hub/switch/router.

Compare RIP and OSPF in a table.
What problem does CIDR aggregation solve?

units.title: Transport & Applications
units.summary: TCP: handshake SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK, seq/ACK arithmetic, cumulative ACKs, retransmission. Flow control = rwnd; congestion control = cwnd (slow start → avoidance, halve on loss). UDP = connectionless, used by DNS/DHCP/VoIP. DNS A/AAAA records; HTTP 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx; DHCP DORA.
questions: Draw the three-way handshake.
Flow control vs congestion control.
Trace a recursive DNS lookup.
Steps of DHCP with ports 67/68.

units.title: Security & Modern Networks
units.summary: Symmetric (AES) for bulk; asymmetric (RSA/ECC) for identity and key exchange; hashes for integrity. TLS: certificate chain auth + key exchange + AEAD records. Firewalls: packet filter → stateful → L7. WEP broken, WPA3 preferred. SDN centralises control plane. CDN = edge cache + DNS steering.
questions: Why does HTTPS need certificates if it also encrypts?
Can a packet filter block a specific HTTPS URL? Why/why not?
What did WPA3 fix over WPA2?
State the main idea of SDN and one benefit of a CDN.

important_questions: OSI vs TCP/IP with a mapping table.
How a switch learns and forwards, with an example trace.
Full subnetting worked example: ranges, broadcast, usable counts.
Distance-vector vs link-state comparison (RIP vs OSPF).
TCP three-way handshake and why three messages are needed.
Flow control vs congestion control with rwnd and cwnd.
Recursive DNS lookup step by step.
Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption with usage in TLS.

previous_year_questions.question: Subnet 200.10.0.0/24 into 4 equal subnets. Give each subnet ID, broadcast and usable range.
previous_year_questions.solution: Borrow 2 bits → /26, increment 64. Subnets .0, .64, .128, .192 (host octet of third byte as applicable); each 64 addresses, 62 usable; broadcasts at block end (.63, .127, .191, .255 in the split octet).

previous_year_questions.question: Explain the TCP three-way handshake. Why not a two-way handshake?
previous_year_questions.solution: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK synchronises both sequence numbers and confirms both directions. Two ways cannot confirm the server received the client ISN and that the server can reach the client.

previous_year_questions.question: Compare distance-vector and link-state routing with one protocol each and note a weakness of distance vector.
previous_year_questions.solution: Distance vector (RIP): Bellman-Ford, hop metric, simple but count-to-infinity and slow convergence. Link state (OSPF): full topology + Dijkstra, fast convergence, more CPU/memory and flooding overhead.

project.title: Small-office subnet & service design note
project.brief: Design a small office network on paper (4–6 pages or equivalent markdown): (1) a public /29 or /28 split into VLAN subnets for staff, guests and servers with usable ranges and gateways; (2) which device cuts each broadcast domain and why; (3) the TCP/UDP ports each service needs (web, mail, DNS, SSH) and where TLS terminates; (4) one firewall policy sketch (allow/deny rules) and one CDN recommendation for a public site. modules.title: Module 1 — Foundations: Layers, Models & Encapsulation
modules.summary: Why networks are layered, the OSI vs TCP/IP models, encapsulation/decapsulation, and the addressing types every exam asks about.

lessons.title: Layered Models: OSI vs TCP/IP
lessons.summary: The seven OSI layers, the four/five-layer TCP/IP model, and what each layer actually does for a packet in flight.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Name the OSI and TCP/IP layers in order and state the job of each
Map OSI layers to their TCP/IP counterparts
Explain why layering exists (independence, replaceability, clear contracts)

payload.text: Interviewer: "You type a URL and press Enter — which layers are involved, and in what order?" If you can narrate that story top-to-bottom, every layer-definition question in the syllabus is already answered.

**Why layers?** Each layer offers a service to the one above and hides how it is implemented. You can swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet without touching TCP or the browser. Protocols on the same layer on two machines "talk past each other" — horizontal protocols, vertical services.

**OSI (7 layers, top → bottom):**
7. **Application** — user services (HTTP, DNS, SMTP)
6. **Presentation** — encoding, encryption, compression
5. **Session** — dialogs, checkpointing, session setup
4. **Transport** — end-to-end delivery, segmentation, reliability (TCP/UDP)
3. **Network** — logical addressing and routing (IP, ICMP)
2. **Data Link** — framing, MAC addressing, error detection (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
1. **Physical** — bits on the medium (voltage, light, radio)

**TCP/IP model (what the internet actually uses):**
- Application (merges OSI 5–7)
- Transport (OSI 4)
- Internet (OSI 3)
- Network Access / Link (OSI 1–2)

**Units each layer moves:**
| Layer | PDU |
|---|---|
| Transport | Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) |
| Network | Packet |
| Data Link | Frame |
| Physical | Bits |

**Encapsulation:** each layer adds its own header (and the data link layer adds a trailer) as the data travels down; the receiver strips them on the way up (decapsulation).

steps.title: Data Link

steps.title: Physical
steps.desc: Bits modulated onto 2.4/5 GHz radio; AP forwards toward the internet.

steps.desc: Reverse: strip headers layer by layer; HTTP handler reads GET.

mistakes.mistake: Saying TCP/IP and OSI are the same model
mistakes.fix: OSI is the 7-layer teaching model; TCP/IP is the 4/5-layer implementation the internet uses.

mistakes.mistake: Placing IP at layer 2 or TCP at layer 3
mistakes.fix: IP = network (3), TCP = transport (4).

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Which OSI layer is responsible for end-to-end error recovery and flow control?
payload.answer: Layer 4, Transport (TCP).
payload.source: Classic university short question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Layering = service up, protocol across, independence between.
OSI 7 layers; TCP/IP merges 5–7 into Application.
PDUs: segment (L4), packet (L3), frame (L2), bits (L1).

questions.prompt: The TCP/IP "Internet" layer corresponds to which OSI layer?
questions.explanation: Both handle logical addressing and routing.

questions.prompt: Encapsulation means:
options: Each lower layer adding a header (and trailer) to the data above
Splitting TCP streams at the router

lessons.title: Addressing & Encapsulation in Detail
lessons.summary: MAC vs IP vs port addresses, ARP resolution, NAT at a glance, and how a URL becomes bits on the wire.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Distinguish MAC, IP and port addresses and the layer/scope of each
Describe ARP resolution between two hosts on a LAN
Trace a URL lookup: DNS then TCP handshake then HTTP

payload.text: Two laptops on the same café Wi-Fi both talk to youtube.com — same destination IP at the router, but different MACs at every hop. Exams love to catch you conflating the three addressing types.

**Three addressing types:**
- **MAC (layer 2):** burned-in hardware address (48-bit, e.g. 3C:22:FB:...), local to the LAN segment, changed at every router hop (per link).
- **IP (layer 3):** logical address of the host, globally routable, stable across links (until DHCP/NAT changes it).
- **Port (layer 4):** identifies the application/process on the host (0–65535; well-known 0–1023: 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH, 53 DNS).

Together a connection is identified by the 5-tuple: (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port, protocol).

**ARP (Address Resolution Protocol):** host knows the destination IP on its LAN, not the MAC → broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.7?" → owner replies unicast with its MAC → sender caches it. Routers do not forward ARP broadcasts (that is why broadcast domains stop at the router).

**DNS before HTTP:** browser asks resolver for example.com → A/AAAA record → cached IP. Only then can IP packets start.

**NAT (Network Address Translation):** home router rewrites private LAN IPs (192.168.x.x) to one public IP, tracking mappings by (IP, port) so replies come back to the right device. Why it exists: IPv4 address scarcity.

**One packet, many hops:** at each router: L2 frame received → CRC checked → decapsulated to L3 → TTL decremented (if 0, ICMP Time Exceeded) → new L2 header for the next link → retransmitted.

payload.title: ARP cache is why the first packet is slow
payload.text: Miss → broadcast round-trip before data flows; hits come from cache.

payload.title: Private IPs are not routable on the internet
payload.text: 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x — routers drop them without NAT.

payload.title: First packet from A to B on a LAN
payload.problem: Host A (192.168.1.10) pings host B (192.168.1.20) for the first time. What messages go out?

steps.title: ARP cache miss
steps.desc: A broadcasts: "Who has 192.168.1.20? Tell 192.168.1.10".

steps.title: ARP reply
steps.desc: B unicasts its MAC to A; A caches IP→MAC.

steps.title: ICMP echo
steps.desc: A builds ICMP Echo Request; ICMP payload wrapped in IP (src .10, dst .20).

steps.title: Frame
steps.desc: L2 header: src MAC = A, dst MAC = B; FCS appended.

steps.title: Reply
steps.desc: B sends Echo Reply reversed; both cache entries reused later.

payload.solution: ARP first (broadcast + unicast reply), then ICMP in IP in Ethernet frame.

payload.title: Five-tuple
payload.prompt: Write the five-tuple for your SSH session to 203.0.113.5 from port 51000.
payload.hint: Two IPs, two ports, protocol name.

mistakes.mistake: Saying the MAC address stays the same end-to-end
mistakes.fix: MACs change at every router hop; only IP is end-to-end.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking DNS is part of HTTP
mistakes.fix: DNS is a separate application-layer service that usually runs first.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is the purpose of ARP?
payload.answer: Resolve a known IPv4 address on the local network to the destination MAC address.
payload.source: Networking viva staple.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: MAC = per-link hardware, IP = end-to-end logical, port = per-process.
ARP broadcasts on the LAN to find the MAC for an IP.
NAT maps many private IPs to one public IP using port mappings.

questions.prompt: A router changes which header(s) when forwarding between two links?
options: L2 header (and FCS) only; IP stays
questions.explanation: Link-local headers rewritten; end-to-end IP preserved (NAT at the edge is the exception).

questions.prompt: Well-known port 443 is used by:
questions.explanation: HTTP=80, HTTPS=443.

questions.prompt: Which address does NOT change as a packet crosses routers?
questions.explanation: IP is the end-to-end identifier.

modules.title: Module 2 — Data Link & Network Layers
modules.summary: Framing, error detection (CRC), switching vs broadcasting, IPv4 addressing and subnetting, and the core routing algorithms.

lessons.title: Framing, Error Detection & Switching
lessons.summary: How bits become frames, how CRC catches corruption, and how switches and routers move frames differently.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe framing and its three problem areas (size, noise, synchronisation)
Explain how CRC detects errors and what the sender/receiver do
Differentiate hub vs switch vs router behaviour for broadcast and MAC learning

payload.text: A single flipped bit in a 1500-byte frame is invisible to your eyes and fatal to a file. The data-link layer is the layer that notices — before IP ever sees it.

**Framing:** the physical layer delivers a raw bit stream with no boundaries. The data-link layer adds delimiters so the receiver can find where a frame starts and ends.

Framing problems the syllabus names:
1. **Framing** — where does the frame begin/end? (byte stuffing, bit stuffing, length field)
2. **Noise** — a burst of noise can destroy a frame; frames must be small enough that errors are detected (and retransmitted), not silently merged.
3. **Synchronisation** — sender and receiver clocks must agree on bit timing.

**Error detection:**
- **Parity:** 1 extra bit; detects odd bit errors only. Weak.
- **Checksum:** one's-complement sum over the data; used at IP/UDP/TCP levels.
- **CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check):** treat frame as polynomial, divide by a generator polynomial, append the remainder as FCS. Receiver recomputes; mismatch → discard frame. Detects all burst errors up to the generator degree. The workhorse of Ethernet (CRC-32).

CRC flow: sender computes remainder over (data × x^n) mod G, appends it; receiver divides received bits by G — remainder 0 means likely intact.

**Switching:**
- **Hub (layer 1):** repeats every bit to all ports — one collision domain.
- **Switch (layer 2):** reads destination MAC, forwards only to that port, builds a **MAC address table** by learning source MACs per port. Isolates collision domains (one per port).
- **Router (layer 3):** forwards on IP between different networks; broadcasts do not cross it.

Broadcast domain: all devices that hear each other's broadcasts — cut by routers (and VLANs).

**Ethernet frame (simplified):** dst MAC | src MAC | type/length | payload (46–1500 bytes) | FCS. Minimum payload forces padding (runt frames are discarded).

payload.title: Switch learning rule
payload.text: Learn source MAC → port; forward/lookup by destination MAC; flood if unknown.

payload.title: CRC detects, it does not fix
payload.text: Detection at L2 = discard; recovery is a higher-layer (TCP) or link-level retransmission concern.

payload.title: Switch learns then forwards
payload.problem: Empty switch; host A (MAC A) on port 1 sends to unknown host B (MAC B) on port 3.

steps.title: Frame arrives
steps.desc: Switch sees src = A on port 1 → learns A↔port 1 in MAC table.

steps.title: Lookup
steps.desc: Dst = B not in table → flood out every port except 1 (split horizon on the port it came in).

steps.title: B replies
steps.desc: Frame src = B on port 3 → learned; dst = A found → forwarded only to port 1.

steps.title: Table now
steps.desc: A→1, B→3. Future frames A→B go straight across, no flooding.

steps.title: Broadcast
steps.desc: ARP request dst FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF still floods everywhere — switches do not stop broadcasts.

payload.solution: Learn sources, look up destinations, flood unknowns; broadcasts always flood.

payload.title: Collision vs broadcast domain
payload.prompt: 5 hosts on a hub vs 5 hosts on a switch: how many collision domains each? How many broadcast domains?
payload.hint: Hub = shared; switch ports isolate collisions but share broadcasts.

mistakes.mistake: Saying a switch stops broadcast traffic
mistakes.fix: Switches flood broadcasts (broadcast domain unchanged); routers and VLANs cut them.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing CRC with error correction
mistakes.fix: CRC only detects; the frame is dropped and retransmitted by a higher layer.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: How does a switch build its forwarding table?
payload.answer: It learns by inspecting the source MAC address of incoming frames and the port they arrive on.
payload.source: Common exam question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Framing solves boundaries, noise and synchronisation.
CRC-32 detects corruption at L2; receiver discards bad frames.
Switch = MAC learning, one collision domain per port; router = IP + cuts broadcasts.

questions.prompt: Which device forwards traffic based on MAC address?
questions.explanation: Layer-2 device.

questions.prompt: CRC is best described as:
options: Error detection using polynomial division remainder
questions.explanation: Remainder appended as FCS; mismatch → discard.

questions.prompt: A hub creates:
questions.explanation: Shared medium — all ports one domain.

lessons.title: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting & Routing
lessons.summary: Classes (legacy), CIDR/subnet masks, VLSM thinking, and how routers choose the next hop (static vs RIP vs OSPF vs flooding).

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute network and broadcast addresses from an IP/mask
Subnet a /24 into smaller networks and size each
Compare distance-vector (RIP) and link-state (OSPF) routing at exam depth

payload.text: Subnetting is the arithmetic exam of networking: 5 marks, 8 minutes, no calculator mercy. The rest of the course cannot save you here — only worked reps can.

**IPv4 structure:** 32 bits = network portion + host portion, split by the subnet mask (/prefix).

- /24 = 255.255.255.0 → 256 addresses, 254 usable hosts
- /25 = 255.255.255.128 → 128 addresses, 126 hosts
- /26 = .192 → 64 addresses, 62 hosts
- /27 = .224 → 32 addresses, 30 hosts
- /28 = .240 → 16 addresses, 14 hosts

**Reserved:** network address (all host bits 0) and broadcast (all host bits 1) are never assigned to hosts. Usable = 2^(32−prefix) − 2.

**Classes (legacy, still asked):** A 1–126 (mask /8), B 128–191 (/16), C 192–223 (/24), D 224–239 multicast, E 240–255 experimental. 127 = loopback. Private ranges: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16.

**CIDR:** "192.168.1.0/26" notation; route aggregation summarises many prefixes into one (reduces routing-table size).

**VLSM:** give subnets different sizes to fit needs (point-to-point /30 = 4 addresses, 2 usable — routers waste fewer IPs).

**Routing algorithms:**
- **Static:** manually configured; fine for small networks.
- **Distance vector (RIP):** each router shares its distance vector (hop counts) with neighbours; Bellman-Ford; max 15 hops; suffers count-to-infinity; simple but slow convergence.
- **Link state (OSPF):** each router floods its link-state advertisements, builds a full topology map, runs Dijkstra (SPF); fast convergence, no hop-count limit; scales better.
- **Flooding:** send every packet out all interfaces except incoming — used in early networks (and inside link-state flooding itself).

**Next-hop decision:** longest prefix match wins when multiple routes cover the destination.

payload.title: Subnet math shortcut
payload.text: Increment = 256 − interesting octet (e.g. mask .192 → increment 64 → networks at 0, 64, 128, 192).

payload.title: RIP is a distance-vector protocol limited to 15 hops
payload.text: Hop 16 = unreachable; OSPF is the link-state answer.

payload.title: Subnet 192.168.1.0/24 into four equal LANs
payload.problem: Four departments need equal subnets. Find the new prefix and each subnet range.

steps.title: Need
steps.desc: 4 subnets → need 2 extra network bits (2^2 = 4) → new prefix /26.

steps.title: Subnet 1
steps.desc: 192.168.1.0/26 — network .0, hosts .1–.62, broadcast .63.

payload.solution: Four /26 subnets; each has 64 addresses (62 usable).

payload.title: Network address
payload.prompt: Host IP 172.20.5.77/27 — network address, broadcast, and usable range?
payload.hint: Increment = 256 − 224 = 32; find the block containing .77.

mistakes.mistake: Including network and broadcast addresses in the usable count
mistakes.fix: Usable hosts = 2^h − 2.

mistakes.mistake: Saying OSPF uses hop count
mistakes.fix: OSPF uses cost (bandwidth-based); hop count is RIP.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Which routing algorithm builds a complete map of the network and runs Dijkstra?
payload.answer: Link-state routing (OSPF).
payload.source: Standard 8-mark comparison question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Prefix splits network vs host bits; usable = 2^h − 2.
Equal subnetting: borrow bits until 2^borrowed ≥ required subnets.
RIP = distance vector + hops; OSPF = link state + Dijkstra.

questions.prompt: /26 gives usable hosts:
Broadcast address of 10.0.0.0/30 is:
questions.explanation: Block of 4: .0 network, .1–.2 hosts, .3 broadcast.

questions.prompt: The maximum hop count in RIP is:
questions.explanation: Classic RIP limit.

modules.title: Module 3 — Transport & Application Layers
modules.summary: TCP vs UDP, the three-way handshake, reliability and flow/congestion control, then DNS, HTTP and DHCP at exam depth.

lessons.title: TCP: Connection, Reliability & Control
lessons.summary: Segment structure, the three-way handshake and teardown, ACK/retransmission, sliding-window flow control and congestion control.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: State what TCP guarantees and what it explicitly does not
Draw the three-way handshake and four-step teardown with flags
Separate flow control (receiver window) from congestion control (cwnd)

payload.text: The internet carries both your bank transfer and your cat video — one demands zero loss, the other demands speed. TCP and UDP are two different answers to that question, and interviewers check whether you know why.

**TCP (Transmission Control Protocol):** connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, byte-stream service.
- **Connection:** 3-way handshake SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK (both sides agree initial sequence numbers).
- **Reliability:** each byte has a sequence number; cumulative ACKs; missing data retransmitted after RTO (retransmission timeout); duplicate/out-of-order segments handled.
- **Ordering:** receiver reassembles by sequence number.
- **Flow control:** receiver advertises a **window (rwnd)** in every ACK — sender never overruns the receiver buffer.
- **Congestion control:** sender maintains **cwnd** (congestion window); effective send size = min(rwnd, cwnd). Phases: slow start (exponential growth until threshold), congestion avoidance (linear), on loss: multiplicative decrease (halve/threshold), fast recovery.
- **Full-duplex:** data flows both ways simultaneously; teardown uses FIN/ACK pairs (4-way) since each direction closes independently.

**Common TCP flags:** SYN (open), ACK, FIN (close), RST (reset), PSH, URG.

**TCP header essentials:** src/dst port, sequence + ack numbers, window size, checksum, flags. (UDP is 8 bytes: ports, length, checksum.)

**UDP:** connectionless, no ordering, no retransmission — best-effort but minimal delay. Used by DNS, DHCP, VoIP, streaming, video calls, games. Multicast/broadcast come only with UDP.

**Choosing:** reliability + ordering (web, file, email, SSH) → TCP; latency sensitivity where a lost frame is acceptable (voice, live video, DNS queries) → UDP.

**Handshake vs HTTP request:** the TCP connection is reusable (keep-alive); one connection can carry many HTTP request/response pairs.

payload.title: Flow vs congestion control in one line each
payload.text: Flow control protects the receiver (rwnd); congestion control protects the network (cwnd).

payload.title: Handshake count questions
payload.text: Opening = 3 messages; closing = 4 messages (FIN each way) unless combined.

payload.title: Sequence and ACK arithmetic
payload.problem: Client sends 1000 bytes from seq 5000; server ACKs. What does the ACK carry, and what if the second segment is lost?

steps.title: Segment 1
steps.desc: seq = 5000, carries bytes 5000–5999 (1000 bytes).

steps.title: ACK
steps.desc: Server ACK = 5000 + 1000 = 6000 (next expected byte).

steps.title: Segment 2
steps.desc: Client sends seq = 6000, 500 bytes; it is lost in the network.

steps.title: Timeout
steps.desc: RTO expires at the sender; segment 2 retransmitted with seq 6000 unchanged.

steps.title: Recovery
steps.desc: Server ACK 6500 arrives; dup ACKs / fast retransmit may trigger even earlier.

payload.solution: ACK 6000 after first segment; lost segment retransmitted with same seq; final ACK 6500.

payload.title: Window math
payload.prompt: Receiver window = 8000 bytes, cwnd = 6000 bytes, MSS = 1000. How many bytes may the sender put on the wire right now?
payload.hint: Effective window = min(rwnd, cwnd).

mistakes.mistake: Saying TCP guarantees delivery of messages (not a byte stream)
mistakes.fix: TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery of a byte stream — message boundaries are not preserved.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing rwnd and cwnd
mistakes.fix: rwnd = receiver buffer room (flow control); cwnd = sender guess of network capacity (congestion control).

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why does TCP use a three-way handshake?
payload.answer: To synchronise both sides initial sequence numbers and confirm both can send and receive before data flows.
payload.source: Evergreen university question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-oriented; UDP: minimal and connectionless.
Handshake SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK synchronises sequence numbers.
Flow control = rwnd; congestion control = cwnd (slow start → avoidance).

questions.prompt: Which flag starts a TCP connection?
questions.explanation: SYN opens; SYN-ACK acknowledges.

questions.prompt: A receiver advertises its buffer room via:
questions.explanation: rwnd is the flow-control window.

questions.prompt: Which protocol is connectionless and unacknowledged?
questions.explanation: UDP headers are just ports, length, checksum.

lessons.title: DNS, HTTP & DHCP
lessons.summary: Recursive DNS resolution, HTTP request/response and status codes, cookies/keep-alive, and how DHCP hands out an address.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Trace a recursive DNS lookup from stub resolver to authoritative server
Identify the parts of an HTTP request/response and key status codes
Explain the four DHCP steps (DORA) and what each returns

payload.text: Opening tieedu.com runs two applications you never see: DNS (find the address) and DHCP (you already had one when you joined the Wi-Fi). Both are "boring" until they are down — then everything is broken.

**DNS (Domain Name System) — application layer, port 53 (UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers):**
- Hierarchical tree: root → TLD (.com, .in) → authoritative (example.com) servers.
- **Iterative vs recursive:** client asks resolver recursively ("answer me fully"); resolver walks the tree iteratively, caching as it goes.
- Record types: **A** (name → IPv4), **AAAA** (→ IPv6), **CNAME** (alias), **MX** (mail), **NS** (name server), **PTR** (reverse).
- Caching with **TTL** — why a DNS change is not instant everywhere.

**HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) — application layer, TCP 80 (443 for HTTPS/TLS):**
- Request: method (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE), path, version, headers, optional body.
- Response: status line (version, code, phrase), headers, body.
- Status classes: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx redirect (301 permanent, 302 found, 304 not modified), 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 unauthorised, 403 forbidden, 404 not found), 5xx server error (500 internal, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable).
- **Statelessness:** each request is independent; state carried by cookies (Set-Cookie header) or tokens.
- **Keep-alive:** reuse one TCP connection for many requests (faster than handshake per request).
- HTTP/1.1 pipelining, HTTP/2 multiplexing — mention for depth.

**DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — UDP ports 67/68, DORA:**
1. **Discover** — client broadcasts "any DHCP server?"
2. **Offer** — server(s) offer an IP + lease parameters.
3. **Request** — client accepts one offer (broadcast, so all servers know).
4. **Ack** — server confirms; lease timer starts.
Delivers: IP, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server(s), lease time. DHCP relay agents let one server serve many subnets.

payload.title: DHCP = DORA
payload.text: Discover → Offer → Request → Ack, all broadcast until the lease is confirmed.

payload.title: DNS default port
payload.text: 53 UDP for queries — mixing it with HTTP 80 is an easy lost mark.

payload.title: Recursive DNS lookup for www.example.com
payload.problem: Your stub resolver has a cold cache. List the steps to get the A record.

steps.title: Stub → resolver
steps.desc: Your OS asks the configured recursive resolver (e.g. ISP or 8.8.8.8).

steps.title: Root
steps.desc: Resolver asks a root server: "who handles .com?" → referral to .com TLD servers.

steps.title: TLD
steps.desc: Resolver asks a .com TLD server → referral to example.com authoritative NS.

steps.title: Authoritative
steps.desc: Resolver asks example.com NS → answer: A record 93.184.216.34 (TTL 3600).

steps.title: Cache + reply
steps.desc: Resolver caches per TTL and returns the IP to the stub resolver; browser connects.

payload.solution: Stub → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative → cached answer; each hop cached for TTL.

payload.title: Status code choice
payload.prompt: A logged-in user POSTs a form missing a required field. Which status code family, and one specific code?
payload.hint: The server understood but refuses due to the client sending bad data.

mistakes.mistake: Saying HTTP is stateful by itself
mistakes.fix: HTTP is stateless; cookies/tokens add state at the application level.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting DHCP is UDP, not TCP
mistakes.fix: Client has no address yet — connection setup is impossible; broadcast UDP is used.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the four steps of DHCP with the mnemonic.
payload.answer: DORA: Discover (client broadcast), Offer (server), Request (client accepts), Ack (server confirms lease).
payload.source: Frequent 4–6 mark question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: DNS: hierarchical name → address with A/AAAA/MX records and TTL caching.
HTTP: request/response, 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx status classes, cookie-based state.
DHCP DORA configures IP, mask, gateway and DNS over UDP broadcasts.

questions.prompt: DNS queries usually default to:
questions.explanation: UDP for single queries; TCP for zone transfers.

questions.prompt: Status 404 means:
options: Resource not found on the server
questions.explanation: Client error — server understood, no such resource.

questions.prompt: In DORA, the step where the client broadcasts which offer it accepts is:
questions.explanation: Request — broadcast so other servers retract their offers.

modules.title: Module 4 — Security, Wireless & Modern Networks
modules.summary: Symmetric vs asymmetric crypto, TLS in one page, firewalls and NAT, Wi-Fi basics, and how CDNs and cloud networking changed delivery.

lessons.title: Network Security: TLS, Firewalls & Threats
lessons.summary: Encryption basics, the TLS handshake at exam depth, firewall types, and the attacks every syllabus names.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Differentiate symmetric and asymmetric encryption and where each is used
Outline what the TLS handshake achieves (auth, key exchange, integrity)
Classify packet-filtering vs application-layer firewalls and name core attack types

payload.text: The padlock in the address bar is three ideas stacked: asymmetric crypto to prove identity and share a secret, symmetric crypto to encrypt the bulk fast, and a firewall somewhere in the middle deciding what may pass. Interviewers pull on any one thread.

**Crypto foundations:**
- **Symmetric** (AES, ChaCha20, DES/3DES legacy): one shared key encrypts and decrypts. Fast — used for the data itself. Problem: how do two strangers share the key?
- **Asymmetric** (RSA, ECC, Ed25519): key pair — public key encrypts (or verifies), private key decrypts (or signs). Slower; solves key exchange and signatures.
- **Hashing** (SHA-256): one-way fixed digest — integrity, not confidentiality.
- **Hybrid in practice:** asymmetric protects a pre-master secret; both sides derive symmetric session keys.

**TLS 1.3 handshake (simplified, exam-friendly):**
1. ClientHello (supported ciphers, key share) → ServerHello + certificate.
2. Client verifies certificate chain against a trusted CA, authenticates the server (and optionally mutual TLS).
3. Key exchange derives shared session keys; Finished messages verify integrity of the handshake.
4. Application data flows encrypted with symmetric keys (integrity via AEAD — encryption + MAC together).

**HTTPS = HTTP over TLS.** Certificate binds domain name to public key — that binding is what stops trivial MITM.

**Firewalls:**
- **Packet filtering (layer 3/4):** rules on src/dst IP, port, protocol; fast, blind to payload.
- **Stateful:** tracks connections (knows SYN/ACK belongs to an established flow).
- **Application/NGFW (layer 7):** inspects actual HTTP/TLS SNI content; can block URLs/apps.
- **DMZ:** semi-trusted zone between internet and internal network for public servers.

**Attack taxonomy:**
- **MITM:** attacker relays and can alter traffic (defeated by TLS authentication).
- **Sniffing:** promiscuous capture on shared media (Wi-Fi legacy WEP broken; use WPA3).
- **DoS/DDoS:** exhaust resources; distributed botnets; mitigated by scrubbing/CDN/anycast.
- **Injection/spoofing:** IP spoofing, DNS spoofing/cache poisoning (Kaminsky-style randomness matters).
- **Password attacks:** brute force vs credential stuffing; countermeasures = rate limits + MFA.

payload.title: TLS authenticates via certificates, not encryption itself
payload.text: Encryption hides data; the certificate chain is what proves who you are talking to.

payload.title: DoS vs DDoS
payload.text: DoS = one source; DDoS = distributed botnet — mitigation differs (scale matters).

payload.title: Where does each crypto type run in HTTPS?
payload.problem: Map certificate verification, session-key exchange and page data encryption to symmetric/asymmetric.

steps.title: Certificate check
steps.desc: Server RSA/ECDSA signature over its cert verified with the CA public key — asymmetric.

steps.title: Key exchange
steps.desc: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (in TLS 1.3 key share) derives the pre-master secret — asymmetric family, forward secrecy.

steps.title: Session keys
steps.desc: Both sides derive identical symmetric keys from the shared secret.

steps.title: Page data
steps.desc: HTTP body encrypted with AES-GCM (symmetric AEAD) — fast enough for video.

steps.title: Integrity
steps.desc: AEAD tag detects tampering on every record.

payload.solution: Asymmetric for identity and key agreement; symmetric for the actual traffic.

payload.title: Firewall choice
payload.prompt: You must block a specific malware URL path inside HTTPS traffic. Packet filtering or layer-7 firewall — and what else do you need?
payload.hint: Deep inspection of application content implies terminating or proxying TLS.

mistakes.mistake: Saying encryption alone proves the server identity
mistakes.fix: Anyone can encrypt; certificates + chain validation prove identity.

mistakes.mistake: Calling hashing encryption
mistakes.fix: Hashes are one-way and not reversible — integrity, not confidentiality.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Differentiate symmetric and asymmetric encryption with one example of each.
payload.answer: Symmetric: one shared key (AES) — fast bulk data. Asymmetric: public/private pair (RSA) — key exchange and signatures.
payload.source: Standard 6-mark question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Symmetric = speed, asymmetric = trust bootstrap and signatures.
TLS: certificate auth + key exchange + AEAD-encrypted application data.
Firewalls progress: packet filter → stateful → layer-7; TLS + MFA defeat most classics.

lessons.title: Wireless, SDN & Modern Delivery
lessons.summary: Wi-Fi generations at a glance, 4G/5G concepts, software-defined networking, load balancing, and how CDNs put content near you.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Summarise Wi-Fi evolution (WEP→WPA3) and why each generation existed
Explain what SDN separates (control vs data plane) and why it matters
Describe how a CDN and load balancer reduce latency and add resilience

payload.text: A user in Chennai watches a lecture served from an edge node 10 km away while the origin server sits in Virginia — that is a CDN. The exam version and the interview version are the same answer: put bits close to the consumer.

**Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11):**
- Standards: 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ax (Wi-Fi 4/5/6/6E) — more channels, MIMO, OFDMA, higher modulation.
- Security evolution: **WEP** (broken, static keys) → **WPA** (TKIP, temporary fix) → **WPA2** (CCMP/AES, the long-time standard) → **WPA3** (SAE handshake, resistant to offline dictionary attacks).
- CSMA/CA: wireless cannot sense collisions reliably (hidden node), so senders avoid collisions instead of detecting them (RTS/CTS optional).

**Cellular (4G/5G) concepts:** cell towers, handover between cells, spectrum bands; 4G = all-IP packet core; 5G = eMBB (speed), URLLC (ultra-reliable low latency), mMTC (massive IoT); network slicing gives virtual networks with different guarantees on shared infrastructure.

**SDN (Software-Defined Networking):**
- Separates **control plane** (routing decisions) from **data plane** (packet forwarding) from centralised controllers with programmable flow tables.
- Network becomes software: central view, fast reconfiguration, easier automation; traditional routers bundle both planes per device.

**Load balancing:** distribute requests across servers (round robin, least connections, consistent hashing); health checks; horizontal scale. L4 (TCP connections) vs L7 (HTTP routing, cookies, paths).

**CDN (Content Delivery Network):**
- Cache static content at edge PoPs near users; DNS steers you to the nearest edge.
- Reduces latency (shorter RTT), absorbs traffic spikes, origin stays protected.
- Dynamic content: edge compute / cache-busting; cache headers (max-age, ETag) control reuse.

**Cloud networking ideas:** VPC, subnets, security groups (stateful firewall rules), gateways, anycast routing — same primitives, different branding.

payload.text: Cache at the edge + DNS steering = content delivered from near the user.

payload.title: 5G is not only "faster"

courses.title: DBMS
courses.subtitle: ER models, SQL, normalization, transactions, concurrency control and crash recovery — exam + interview core
courses.description:
DBMS is one of the highest-weight subjects in every CSE university paper and a favourite of placement interviewers. This course covers the full core in eight compact lessons: ER diagrams and their relational mapping, keys and relational algebra including division, SQL core with joins and aggregation, subqueries/views/indexes, functional dependencies with attribute closure, normalization from 1NF through BCNF with lossless-join checks, transactions with ACID and serializability, and concurrency control with 2PL plus write-ahead-logging recovery.

Every lesson uses the nine-block structure (objectives, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, graded quiz, summary). A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** second- and third-year CSE/IT students preparing for university exams, GATE fundamentals, and placement interviews that ask database questions.

**What you need:** pen and paper for closures, normal forms and precedence graphs; a browser for the quizzes.
outcomes: Draw ER diagrams and map them to tables with correct FK placement
Use relational algebra including select, project, join and division
Write SQL with joins, aggregation, subqueries and views correctly
Explain B+ tree vs hash indexes and when each is used
Compute attribute closures and normalize relations to 3NF/BCNF
State ACID and test conflict serializability with precedence graphs
Explain 2PL, deadlock policies and write-ahead logging recovery
courses.about_course:
University DBMS papers reward a repeatable method: identify the FDs, compute closures, detect the violated normal form, split, verify. This course drills exactly that method, then does the same for the two big theory units — serializability graphs and recovery logs — so exam answers follow a fixed, checkable sequence instead of hope.

The SQL lessons are written for people who will use SQL daily: clause evaluation order, the WHERE vs HAVING distinction, NULL behaviour in NOT IN, and indexes explained as "why did my query get fast". The concurrency and recovery lessons close with the industry-standard answers (Strict 2PL, WAL, checkpoints) that interviewers expect to hear.

The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a small schema design you can show as proof of skill.
prerequisites: Basic set theory and logical reasoning
Any programming language (SQL syntax is taught from scratch)
audience: CSE/IT students in semester 3–5 facing university DBMS exams
Placement candidates preparing for SQL and database rounds
GATE aspirants building normalization and transaction fundamentals
Backend/developer beginners who want relational design to click

Subqueries: correlated + NOT EXISTS over NOT IN. Views: saved queries, aggregated views not updatable. units.summary: FD X → Y = Y determined by X; test via X⁺ ⊇ Y. Armstrong: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity. Anomalies: insert/update/delete. Forms: 1NF atomic; 2NF no partial on composite key; 3NF no non-key→non-key; BCNF every determinant a superkey. Decomposition: lossless join (shared key) + dependency preservation; BCNF may lose preservation.

Conflict serializability ⇔ acyclic precedence graph (same item, different txns, ≥1 write = conflict). 2PL grow-then-shrink; Strict 2PL holds X locks to commit; deadlock: wait-for detection, wait-die/wound-wait prevention, timeouts. WAL: log before page; recovery redoes committed, undoes losers from the last checkpoint; commit in log = durable.

previous_year_questions.question: Given R(A,B,C,D) with FDs AB → C, C → D: find all candidate keys and state the highest normal form of R (justify).
previous_year_questions.solution: Key = (A,B): (AB)⁺ = {A,B,C,D}. D is prime? No — C → D with C non-key... check prime status: candidate AB only; C→D is non-key→non-key → not 3NF if C not prime; C is not in key AB → violates 3NF (and BCNF since C is not a superkey). Highest form: 2NF (partial? AB is composite, nothing depends on part alone given FDs) — so 2NF, not 3NF.

previous_year_questions.question: Explain two-phase locking. Is every 2PL schedule recoverable? What does Strict 2PL add?
previous_year_questions.solution: 2PL: locks acquired only in growing phase, released only in shrinking → conflict serializable. Basic 2PL alone can allow dirty reads/cascading aborts (not necessarily recoverable); Strict 2PL holds X locks until commit/abort → recoverable and cascadeless.

previous_year_questions.question: Describe the write-ahead logging protocol and the actions taken during recovery after a system crash.
previous_year_questions.solution: Before a modified page is written to disk, the corresponding log records must be on stable storage. After crash, start from last checkpoint: redo all transactions with commit records (repeat history), undo uncommitted transactions using undo information in reverse order, writing compensation records.

modules.title: Module 1 — ER Model & Relational Model
modules.summary: Entities, attributes, relationships and cardinalities; ER to relational mapping; keys; and the relational algebra every exam starts with.

lessons.title: ER Diagrams to Tables
lessons.summary: Drawing and reading ER diagrams: entities, relationship sets, cardinality and participation, generalisation, and how an ER model becomes tables.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Identify entities, attributes, relationship sets and keys in an ER diagram
Distinguish cardinality ratios (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and total vs partial participation
Map an ER diagram to relational tables including FK placement rules

payload.text: Every DBMS exam paper opens with "Draw the ER diagram for X" — and every software design interview closes with "how would you model this?" The skill is identical: decide what is a thing, what is a fact about a thing, and where the relationship lives.

**ER building blocks:**
- **Entity set:** a noun (Student, Course). Weak entity set: no key of its own, identified via an owner entity (Dependent of Employee) — double rectangle, partial key with dashed underline.
- **Attributes:** simple/derived (age from DOB)/multivalued (ovals double)/composite. Key attribute underlined.
- **Relationship set:** a verb (Enrolls, Works_For). Degree = number of participating entity sets.

**Cardinality:**
- 1:1 — one A relates to at most one B (Head manages Department)
- 1:N — one A relates to many B (Department has Employees)
- M:N — many A relate to many B (Student Enrolls Course)

**Participation:** total (every A must participate — double line) vs partial (optional — single line).

**Keys in relationships:** for 1:1 the relationship can borrow a key from either side; for 1:N the key of the N-side entity moves into the 1-side table as FK; for M:N a new junction table with PK = (keyA, keyB).

**ER → relational mapping rules:**
1. Each strong entity set → one table; attributes become columns; key = primary key.
2. 1:1 relationship → merge tables or add FK + UNIQUE on the participating side.
3. 1:N → add FK on the N-side.
4. M:N → new relation with composite PK of both participant keys (plus relationship attributes).
5. Multivalued attribute → separate table.
6. Weak entity → table with owner FK; PK = (owner PK, partial key).
7. Generalisation (ISA) → single table with type discriminator, or one table per subclass (design trade-off).

**Relational model vocabulary:** relation = table, tuple = row, attribute = column, domain = allowed values, degree = columns, cardinality = rows.

lessons.title: Keys & Relational Algebra
lessons.summary: Superkey, candidate key, primary key, foreign key; then select, project, join, set ops and division — the operators exams drill.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify superkey vs candidate key vs primary key vs composite key
Apply select/project/rename and Cartesian product correctly
Perform natural join and division on small relations by hand

payload.text: Relational algebra looks useless until you realise every SQL query the optimiser runs is algebra. Then division — "find customers who bought every product" — becomes a party trick instead of a panic.

**Keys:**
- **Superkey:** any attribute set that uniquely identifies tuples (possibly oversized: (roll, name)).
- **Candidate key:** minimal superkey — no attribute can be removed and still be unique. A relation can have several; one becomes **primary key**; the rest are alternates.
- **Composite key:** key made of multiple attributes (junction tables).
- **Foreign key:** column(s) in table A referencing the candidate key of table B — integrity constraint, values must exist (or be NULL if allowed).

**Relational algebra operators:**
- **σ (select):** filter rows by predicate — like WHERE. σ_{grade>6}(Enrolls)
- **π (project):** pick columns — like SELECT list. π_{name}(Student)
- **ρ (rename):** rename relations/attributes for self-joins.
- **× (Cartesian product):** all pairs — expensive; joins are its filtered versions.
- **⋈ natural join:** product + equality on all common attributes, common columns appear once.
- **θ-join:** join with an arbitrary condition (e.g. ⋈_{A.x > B.y}).
- **∪, ∩, −:** set ops — need union-compatible relations (same attributes, compatible domains).
- **÷ (division):** R ÷ S = tuples of R whose A-parts are paired with **all** B-parts in S. The "for all / every" operator.

**Equivalences optimisers use:** σ commutes with × (push selections down), π prunes columns early — this is why query order in SQL (FROM→WHERE→SELECT) is free to reorder.

rows: FROM a JOIN b (on shared columns)
NOT EXISTS / correlated NOT IN pattern

modules.title: Module 2 — SQL: Core, Advanced & Indexes
modules.summary: DDL and DML, joins and aggregation, subqueries and views, then B+ tree and hash indexes — what they are and why queries get faster.

lessons.title: SQL Core: DDL, Joins & Aggregation
lessons.summary: CREATE/ALTER/DROP, WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING, inner/outer joins, and the query-clause execution order examiners love to ask.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write CREATE TABLE with PK, FK and NOT NULL constraints
Use inner vs left/right/full outer joins correctly on small datasets
Apply GROUP BY with HAVING and know clause evaluation order

payload.text: Interviewer: "Why does WHERE filter before GROUP BY but HAVING filters after?" If you can answer that by narrating how rows flow through the pipeline, you will never write a broken aggregate query again.

**DDL (structure):** CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE (ADD/DROP/MODIFY columns and constraints), DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE (removes all rows, keeps structure; no WHERE).
**DML (data):** INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (all support WHERE — never run an unfiltered UPDATE in production).

**Clause order (evaluation, not writing):**
1. FROM/JOIN — where rows come from
2. WHERE — row-level filter (before grouping)
3. GROUP BY — bucket rows
4. HAVING — bucket-level filter (after grouping)
5. SELECT — compute columns / aliases
6. ORDER BY — sort (last, aliases allowed)
7. LIMIT/OFFSET — cut the result

**Joins:**
- INNER — only matching pairs.
- LEFT OUTER — all left rows + matches (NULLs on the right where missing).
- RIGHT OUTER — mirror of left.
- FULL OUTER — all rows from both sides.
- SELF JOIN — same table twice with aliases (employee and manager).
- CROSS JOIN — Cartesian product.

**Aggregation:** COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX with GROUP BY. Rules: every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY. NULLs are skipped by aggregates except COUNT(*).

**Constraint toolkit:** PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES ..., UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK (condition), DEFAULT value. PRIMARY KEY implies NOT NULL + UNIQUE (single-column).

payload.title: Clause
headers: Filters rows or groups, before/after GROUP BY

payload.title: LEFT vs RIGHT is from the FROM order
payload.text: FROM a LEFT JOIN b = keep every row of a, regardless of b.

payload.title: UPDATE without WHERE
payload.text: Changes every row — the classic production incident. Always filter.

lessons.title: Subqueries, Views & Indexes
lessons.summary: Correlated subqueries, views as saved queries, then B+ tree and hash indexes — structure, uniqueness and when the optimiser uses them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write scalar, IN-list and correlated subqueries and say when each runs
Create views and state their update limitations
Explain B+ tree properties and why point/range queries get faster with indexes

payload.text: A 10-million-row table answers a lookup in milliseconds because of a B+ tree — or crawls because someone forgot an index. "Explain EXPLAIN" is a top-5 database interview question.

**Subqueries:**
- **Scalar:** one value — used in comparisons/SELECT (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM ...).
- **IN list:** column IN (subquery results) — often rewritten as semi-join.
- **Correlated:** references the outer row; executed per outer row (use with care; NOT EXISTS is the classic "for all" pattern).
- **EXISTS / NOT EXISTS:** existence test — better than IN when NULLs are involved (IN with NULL in the subquery result can behave surprisingly).

**Views:** V AS (SELECT ...) — a named saved query.
- Simplify complex joins, restrict columns (security), stabilise reporting.
- Simple views over one table are often updatable (INSERT/UPDATE through the view); views with aggregates, GROUP BY, DISTINCT or joins generally are not.

**Indexes (speed structures beyond the heap file):**
- **B+ tree:** balanced tree, all leaves linked; internal nodes = separators; every key appears in a leaf. Properties exams want: balanced (same depth), high fan-out (few disk I/Os), leaves linked → excellent **range scans** (B-trees do not link leaves as well).
- **Hash index:** hash(key) → bucket — O(1) point lookup; poor for range queries.
- **Clustered vs non-clustered:** clustered = rows physically in key order (one per table); non-clustered = index with row pointers (many per table).
- **Primary key index:** usually implicit unique index.
- **Write cost:** every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE may touch the index → slower writes, faster reads.
- **Covering index:** query satisfied entirely from index leaves — no table lookup.

**EXPLAIN / query plan:** shows join order and index usage — the practical follow-up to any index question.

payload.title: Index
rows: Range on the sort key (one per table)

payload.title: Index rule of thumb
payload.text: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY — especially selective ones; skip low-cardinality columns like gender.

payload.title: Views are not tables
payload.text: They store a query definition; a heavy view can be slow unless the engine materialises it.

payload.title: Correlated EXISTS vs IN
payload.problem: Customers (cid, name) and Orders (cid, ...). Find customers who have placed at least one order.

steps.title: IN form

steps.desc: NOT IN breaks on NULLs (any NULL → result empty/unknown); NOT EXISTS handles it correctly — prefer NOT EXISTS.

payload.answer: Balanced (equal depth to root), high fan-out, all records/pointers in linked leaves, internal nodes hold separator keys only — giving efficient point and range access.
payload.source: Classic DBMS exam question.

payload.title: Lesson summary

Views = saved queries with column restriction and partial updatability.
B+ tree = balanced + linked leaves (ranges); hash = O(1) equality only.

modules.title: Module 3 — Functional Dependencies & Normalization
modules.summary: Functional dependencies and closure, Armstrong axioms, update anomalies, and 1NF → 2NF → 3NF → BCNF with decomposition steps.

lessons.title: Functional Dependencies & Anomalies
lessons.summary: What an FD states, computing attribute closure, candidate keys via closure, and the insert/update/delete anomalies FDs expose.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Interpret X → Y and compute the attribute closure X⁺
Derive candidate keys from closures of available attributes
Name the three update anomalies and connect them to bad design

payload.text: "Student takes Course; Course has Instructor; Instructor lives in Building" — a single flat table seems fine until you delete the last course an instructor teaches and lose their office too. That is a deletion anomaly, and normalization is the fix.

**Functional dependency X → Y:** given a value of X, the value of Y is uniquely determined. Read: "X functionally determines Y".

Examples: roll → name (each roll has one name); roll, cid → grade (one grade per student per course).

**Armstrong's axioms (basis for closure rules):**
1. **Reflexivity:** Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y
2. **Augmentation:** X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ
3. **Transitivity:** X → Y, Y → Z ⇒ X → Z
Derived: union (X→Y, X→Z ⇒ X→YZ), decomposition (X→YZ ⇒ X→Y, X→Z), pseudo-transitivity.

**Attribute closure X⁺:** start with X, repeatedly apply FDs until no growth. Uses:
- Test if X → Y holds: Y ⊆ X⁺?
- Find candidate keys: for relation R, take Z = all attributes; a superkey S has S⁺ = all attributes. Candidate keys are minimal such sets — often closure of (all attributes minus any single determinant) = candidate key when the remainder has empty closure.

**Anomalies of a denormalised (bad) table:**
- **Insertion anomaly:** cannot record an instructor with no course until a course exists (attributes jammed together).
- **Update anomaly:** change instructor's building in one row but not another → inconsistency.
- **Deletion anomaly:** delete the last course of an instructor → also lose instructor's details.

Fix = decompose into relations each describing ONE fact — which is exactly normalization.

payload.title: Axiom
rows: X → Y, Y → Z ⇒ X → Z

payload.title: Closure practice
payload.text: Closure is the single highest-value algorithm in the normalization unit — drill it on paper.

payload.title: Partial vs transitive dependency (the 2NF/3NF trigger words)
payload.text: Partial = part of a composite key determines non-key; transitive = non-key determines another non-key.

payload.title: Candidate key via closure
payload.problem: R(A, B, C, D) with FDs: A → B, B → C, C → D. Find candidate keys.

steps.title: Only determinant
steps.desc: A is the only left-hand side that determines others.

steps.title: Closure of A
steps.desc: A⁺ = {A} → +B → +C → +D = {A,B,C,D} — covers all attributes.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.desc: No proper subset of {A} exists — so A is minimal.

steps.title: Result
steps.desc: Candidate key = {A}; B⁺ = {B,C,D} ≠ all, C⁺, D⁺ similar — not keys.

steps.title: Non-key columns
steps.desc: B, C, D are prime? No — only A is prime; everything else is non-key attribute.

payload.solution: Candidate key = A; closure confirms it determines every attribute.

payload.title: Anomaly hunt
payload.prompt: Table EmpProj(eid, ename, pid, pname, hours). Give one deletion anomaly scenario.
payload.hint: What disappears when the last row containing some entity is removed?

mistakes.mistake: Saying X → Y means X and Y are the same
mistakes.fix: It means Y is uniquely determined by X — Y may be functionally trivial but the FD still holds.

mistakes.mistake: Computing closure only once and guessing
mistakes.fix: Iterate until no attribute is added — two rounds are often needed.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define functional dependency and state Armstrong axioms.
payload.answer: X → Y: identical X values imply identical Y values. Axioms: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity.
payload.source: Standard 6-mark opener.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: X → Y = Y determined by X; test with attribute closure X⁺.
Closure gives superkeys/candidate keys and implication tests.
Insert/update/delete anomalies motivate decomposition.

questions.prompt: Armstrong axiom "transitivity" states:
options: X → Y and Y → Z implies X → Z
questions.explanation: Chain of dependency.

questions.prompt: To check whether X → Y holds you compute:
questions.explanation: Closure of the left side.
