questions.explanation: Loss of unrelated entity data.

lessons.title: Normal Forms 1NF to BCNF
lessons.summary: Step-by-step normalization: 1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependency, 3NF no transitive dependency, BCNF strict determinants — with decomposition checks.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Test a relation against 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF in order
Decompose a violated relation and verify lossless join (and dependency preservation)
Explain why BCNF can force a trade-off with dependency preservation

payload.text: Normalization questions are algorithm questions with marks attached: detect the violation, name the normal form, split, verify. Learn the checklist and the same four steps answer almost any question.

**1NF — atomic values:** no repeating groups/multi-valued cells/arrays. Fix: split multi-values into rows or a separate table. (Also keys must exist.)

**2NF — 1NF + no partial dependency:** for composite candidate keys, no non-key attribute may depend on only PART of the key. Fix: move partial dependents into their own table keyed by the key part.

**3NF — 2NF + no transitive dependency:** no non-key → non-key dependency (equivalently: every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key). Fix: move X → Y (both non-key) into a table keyed by X.

**BCNF — strict:** for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X must be a superkey. Stricter than 3NF: any determinant must be a key. Situations 3NF keeps but BCNF splits (overlapping candidate keys).

**Decomposition checks:**
- **Lossless join:** decomposing then re-joining gives no extra (spurious) tuples — guaranteed if every split shares a common attribute that is a key of one side (common-attribute rule).
- **Dependency preservation:** every original FD can be checked using just one of the resulting tables (possibly with unions). BCNF guarantees lossless join but may NOT preserve dependencies — that is the classic BCNF trade-off exam.

**Practical order:** 1NF → 2NF (partial) → 3NF (transitive) → BCNF (superkey determinants). Most production schemas aim for 3NF/BCNF.

payload.title: Form
rows: Non-key depends on part of a composite key
Determinant that is not a superkey

payload.title: The slogan
payload.text: Every non-key attribute depends on: the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key (so help me Codd).

payload.title: BCNF vs dependency preservation
payload.text: BCNF always allows lossless reconstruction; it can break easy dependency checking — 3NF is sometimes preferred in practice.

payload.title: Normalize a student-course-instructor table
payload.problem: R(roll, cid, sem, grade, instructor, building) with FDs: (roll, cid) → grade; cid → instructor; instructor → building. Key = (roll, cid).

steps.title: 1NF
steps.desc: All cells atomic — pass.

steps.title: 2NF check
steps.desc: grade depends on the whole (roll, cid) key — fine. But cid → instructor means part of key determines non-key → VIOLATES 2NF.

steps.title: First split
steps.desc: Course(cid PK, instructor, building) and Enrolls(roll, cid PK/FK, grade). Lossless: shares cid, a key of Course.

steps.title: 3NF check on Course
steps.desc: instructor → building with both non-key → transitive dependency → violates 3NF.

steps.title: Final split
steps.desc: Course(cid, instructor) and Instructor(instructor PK, building). All relations now in BCNF (each determinant is a key).

payload.solution: Three tables: Enrolls, Course, Instructor — 3NF/BCNF, lossless at each split.

payload.title: BCNF case
payload.prompt: R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B. Is it 3NF? BCNF? What splits?
payload.hint: Is C a superkey? Is B a superkey?

mistakes.mistake: Applying 2NF before confirming a composite key
mistakes.fix: Single-attribute keys cannot violate partial dependency — 2NF is automatic there.

mistakes.mistake: Splitting without a shared key
mistakes.fix: Arbitrary splits can be lossy — always keep a common attribute that is a key of one part.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Differentiate 3NF and BCNF with an example statement.
payload.answer: 3NF allows a non-superkey determinant only when the dependent attribute is prime; BCNF requires EVERY determinant to be a superkey — stricter.
payload.source: Frequent comparison question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: 1NF atomic; 2NF no partial; 3NF no transitive; BCNF determinants are keys.
Decompose on violated FD; check lossless join + dependency preservation.
BCNF = lossless but may lose dependency preservation.

questions.prompt: 2NF eliminates:
options: Partial dependency on a composite key
questions.explanation: Non-key depends on part of key.

questions.prompt: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial FD X → Y:
options: X is part of a key
questions.explanation: Determinant must be a key.

questions.prompt: A decomposition is lossless when:
options: Natural join of parts returns exactly the original tuples
questions.explanation: No spurious tuples on re-join.

modules.title: Module 4 — Transactions, Concurrency & Recovery
modules.summary: ACID, schedules and serializability, two-phase locking, deadlock handling, timestamp ordering, write-ahead logging and crash recovery.

lessons.title: Transactions & Serializability
lessons.summary: Transaction states, ACID at exam depth, conflict vs view serializability, and recovering a schedule you are given on paper.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: State ACID with one-sentence definitions and map each to a mechanism
Draw a schedule and test conflict serializability via precedence graph
Explain the transaction lifecycle states (active, partially committed, committed, aborted)

payload.text: A bank transfer that debits but never credits is a textbook lost update — and a real outage. ACID is the industry's answer to "what does correct mean when two things break at once".

**Transaction:** logical unit of work; either ALL statements take effect or NONE (atomicity).

**ACID:**
- **Atomicity (A):** all-or-nothing — enforced via undo logging / rollback (DBMS component: recovery manager).
- **Consistency (C):** execution takes the DB from one valid state to another; integrity constraints, triggers, FDs hold — responsibility shared with the application.
- **Isolation (I):** concurrent transactions do not interfere — locking, MVCC, serializability.
- **Durability (D):** committed changes survive crashes — WAL, checkpoints, backups.

**Transaction states:** Active → (all ops done) Partially Committed → Committed; Active → Aborted (failure or ROLLBACK); from aborted → new Active after restart. Only committed data is durable/visible to others under strict isolation.

**Schedule:** interleaving of operations of multiple transactions. Sequential = one at a time. A schedule is **serializable** if its effect equals SOME serial order.

**Conflict serializability:** two operations conflict if same data item, different transactions, and at least one is a write.
- Build a **precedence graph**: edge Ti → Tj if an op of Ti conflicts before an op of Tj.
- **Acyclic graph ⇔ conflict serializable**; topological order gives the equivalent serial schedule.

**View serializability:** same final state AND same reads-from relations as some serial schedule — strictly broader (blind writes can qualify); conflict-serializable ⇒ view-serializable, not vice versa.

**Recoverable schedules (bonus depth):** Tj should not commit before a transaction whose writes it read — otherwise cascading aborts. **Cascadless** = no dirty reads at all.

payload.title: ACID
rows: All or nothing — undo log / rollback
Rules hold across the txn — app + constraints

payload.title: Precedence graph in three steps
payload.text: 1) Skip reads-then-reads; 2) edge for every conflict pair (earlier → later); 3) cycles mean NOT conflict-serializable.

payload.title: Serializable ≠ sequential execution
payload.text: Interleaving is allowed — the RESULT must match some serial order.

payload.title: Conflict serializability test
payload.problem: Schedule S: T1:R(A), T2:R(A), T2:W(A), T1:W(A). Serializable?

steps.title: List conflicts
steps.desc: T1:R(A) vs T2:W(A) — conflict, T1 before T2 → edge T1→T2.

steps.title: Second conflict
steps.desc: T2:W(A) vs T1:W(A) — conflict, T2 before T1 → edge T2→T1.

steps.title: Graph
steps.desc: Edges T1→T2 and T2→T1 form a cycle.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.desc: Cycle present → NOT conflict serializable.

steps.title: Fix idea
steps.desc: Reorder so both writes come from one transaction first (2PL would have prevented this interleaving).

payload.solution: Cycle in precedence graph → not conflict serializable.

payload.title: Graph without a cycle
payload.prompt: S: T1:R(X), T1:W(X), T2:R(X), T2:W(X). Build the graph — is it serializable, and to which order?
payload.hint: One edge only, if any.

mistakes.mistake: Calling any interleaved schedule serializable
mistakes.fix: Only those equivalent to a serial order — check the graph.

mistakes.mistake: Saying ACID is provided only by the DBMS engine
mistakes.fix: Consistency in particular depends on application logic plus DB constraints.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define conflict serializability and the test for it.
payload.answer: A schedule is conflict serializable if swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations can transform it into a serial schedule; tested by building a precedence graph — acyclic iff conflict serializable.
payload.source: Standard 8-mark question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: ACID = atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability (with mechanisms).
Serializability = same effect as some serial order.
Precedence graph: cycles ⇒ not conflict-serializable.

questions.prompt: A committed transaction's updates surviving a crash is:
questions.explanation: WAL + stable storage.

questions.prompt: Conflict serializability is decided by:
options: Whether the precedence graph is acyclic
questions.explanation: Acyclic ⇔ conflict serializable.

questions.prompt: Two operations conflict when they:
options: Involve different transactions on the same item with at least one write
questions.explanation: Same item, different txns, ≥1 write.

lessons.title: Concurrency Control & Recovery
lessons.summary: Two-phase locking, deadlock policies, timestamp ordering, write-ahead logging, checkpoints and ARIES-style recovery at syllabus depth.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain strict 2PL and how it guarantees conflict serializability
Compare deadlock handling: detection, prevention and timeouts
Walk a write-ahead logging recovery: redo committed, undo losers, use checkpoints

payload.text: Two exam questions carry the most marks in most DBMS papers: "Explain two-phase locking" and "How does the DBMS recover after a crash?" This lesson is those two answers, worked through.

**Two-Phase Locking (2PL):**
- **Growing phase:** may acquire locks, never release.
- **Shrinking phase:** may release locks, never acquire.
- Two phases ⇒ conflict-serializable (the theorem examiners want stated).
- **Strict 2PL (what real engines use):** hold all exclusive locks until COMMIT/ABORT — avoids cascading aborts and dirty reads. **Rigorous 2PL** also holds shared locks to the end.

**Lock types:** shared (S) for reads — multiple holders; exclusive (X) for writes — single holder. Compatibility: S-S yes, S-X no, X-X no.

**Deadlock:** cycle of transactions waiting for each other's locks.
- **Detection:** build wait-for graph, look for cycles, choose a victim to roll back.
- **Prevention:** wait-die / wound-wait (timestamps decide who waits or aborts — no cycles possible).
- **Avoidance:** timeouts (simple, used in practice).
- **Victim choice:** youngest/least-progressed transaction.

**Timestamp ordering:** each txn gets a unique timestamp; operations must appear in timestamp order (T-S overlapping rules); too-old reads abort.

**Recovery — write-ahead logging (WAL):**
- Log record BEFORE modifying the DB page: <Ti, X, old, new> (undo/redo info).
- Rule: **log must reach stable storage before the data page does.**
- **Recovery after crash:** scan log from last checkpoint — redo committed transactions (their changes may be on disk or not), undo uncommitted (loser) transactions using undo records (in reverse).
- **Checkpoint:** flush dirty pages + log a checkpoint so recovery does not scan the entire log.
- Commit point: <Ti, commit> durable in log = the transaction is durably committed even if pages are dirty in buffer.

ARIES buzzwords for interviews: analysis phase → redo phase (repeat history) → undo phase; compensation log records (CLR) make undo idempotent.

payload.title: Why Strict 2PL rules production
payload.text: Holding X locks to commit gives recoverable + cascadeless schedules in one stroke.

payload.title: WAL direction matters
payload.text: Log before page — the reverse breaks durability: a page could hit disk with no log record to redo/undo.

payload.title: Crash recovery walk-through
payload.problem: Checkpoint taken; then T1 commits, T2 (large, uncommitted) is mid-work; power fails. What does recovery do?

steps.title: Start point
steps.desc: Recovery reads log backward/forward from the last checkpoint — not from time zero.

steps.title: T1
steps.desc: Commit record in log → T1 is a winner; REDO its updates (repeat history) even if some pages were flushed.

steps.title: T2
steps.desc: No commit record → loser; UNDO its logged changes in reverse using old-values; write compensation log records.

steps.title: Durability proof
steps.desc: Because commit preceded page flush (WAL), any T1 change on disk had a log record — nothing committed is lost.

steps.title: Aftermath
steps.desc: Database returns to state: T1 fully applied, T2 fully rolled back — consistent state.

payload.solution: Checkpoint narrows the log; redo winners, undo losers; WAL guarantees the log had what pages needed.

payload.title: 2PL phase naming
payload.prompt: Txn takes S(A), X(B), releases S(A), then requests X(C). Does this violate 2PL? Why?
payload.hint: Releasing then acquiring crosses the shrinking boundary.

mistakes.mistake: Saying 2PL alone prevents deadlocks
mistakes.fix: 2PL guarantees serializability; deadlocks need detection/prevention on top.

mistakes.mistake: Recovering by scanning the whole log always
mistakes.fix: Checkpoints exist precisely to bound recovery time.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the write-ahead logging rule and explain its role in durability.
payload.answer: A log record for a change must reach stable storage before the changed data page does — so committed data on disk always has log support for redo/undo after a crash.
payload.source: Top recovery question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: 2PL: grow then shrink; Strict 2PL holds X locks to commit.
Deadlocks: detect via wait-for graph, prevent via timestamps, or time out.
WAL: log first; recovery redoes committed, undoes losers from the last checkpoint.

questions.prompt: In 2PL, after releasing the first lock the transaction enters:
questions.explanation: No new locks allowed afterwards.

questions.prompt: The WAL rule states that:
options: Data pages must be written before log records
Log records must reach stable storage before their data pages
Redo runs before undo always on live systems
questions.explanation: Log-before-data.

questions.prompt: Strict 2PL differs from basic 2PL by:
questions.explanation: Gives cascadeless, recoverable schedules.

courses.title: Signals & Systems
courses.subtitle: Convolution, Fourier series & transform, sampling theorem, Laplace & Z-transforms, Bode plots and modulation — ECE exam + interview core
courses.description:
Signals & Systems is the language every ECE, EE and AI-DS student is expected to speak in university exams, GATE and core interviews. This course covers the full standard syllabus in eight compact lessons: signal classification and the four system properties (linearity, TI, causality, BIBO stability), the convolution integral/sum with the graphical method, Fourier series with symmetry shortcuts, the Fourier transform and its properties, the sampling theorem with Nyquist rate and aliasing, Laplace transforms with ROC-based stability reading, the Z-transform as the discrete twin, Bode plots and filter prototypes, and amplitude modulation as the flagship application of frequency shifting.

Every lesson uses the nine-block structure (objectives, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, graded quiz, summary). A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** ECE/EE/CS students in semester 3–6 preparing for university exams, GATE EC/EE fundamentals, and interviews that ask signals-and-systems questions.

**What you need:** pen and paper for transforms, pole-zero plots and Bode sketches; a calculator for magnitude arithmetic.
outcomes: Classify signals and test systems for linearity, TI, causality and BIBO stability
Compute convolutions graphically and analytically (CT and DT)
Use Fourier series symmetry rules and compute standard Fourier transform pairs
Apply the sampling theorem: Nyquist rate, aliasing diagnosis and reconstruction
Compute Laplace and Z-transforms with correct ROCs and read stability off poles
Sketch Bode magnitude plots and identify cutoff, Q and filter type
Explain AM as frequency shifting and state the envelope-detection condition
courses.about_course:
University Signals & Systems papers reward a fixed method: classify first, test the four properties, choose the transform that kills the hard part, apply the algebraic property, invert, and interpret stability or bandwidth in the original domain. This course drills exactly that method across convolution, Fourier, Laplace and Z, so exam answers follow a checkable sequence instead of guesswork.

The sampling and modulation lessons are written for people who will build real systems: Nyquist is not a mnemonic, it is the reason your phone microphone is digital; AM is not a formula to memorise, it is the frequency-shift property in a trench coat. The Bode lesson closes with the straight-line sketch method interviewers expect you to draw live on a whiteboard.

The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a small analysis note you can show as proof of skill.
prerequisites: Basic calculus (integration) and complex numbers
Comfort with exponentials and trigonometry
audience: ECE/EE students in semester 3–5 facing university Signals & Systems exams
GATE EC/EE aspirants building transform fundamentals
Placement candidates preparing for core ECE interview rounds
CS/AI students who want signal processing foundations for audio/ML

units.summary: CT/DT, energy/power, periodicity (rational ratio for sums), even/odd. Four tests: linearity (weighted sums), TI (delay input ⇒ delayed output), causality (no future input), BIBO (∫|h| < ∞ for LTI). LTI ⇒ convolution; graphical flip–shift–multiply–integrate; commutative, widths add, δ identity; rect*rect = triangle.

units.title: Fourier Series, Transform & Sampling
units.summary: Trig/exponential FS with symmetry shortcuts (even ⇒ cosine, odd ⇒ sine, half-wave ⇒ odd harmonics). FT pairs: δ↔1, e^{−at}u ↔ 1/(a+jω), rect ↔ sinc, cos ↔ impulses. Properties: time shift (phase), frequency shift (modulation), convolution ↔ multiplication, Parseval. Sampling: x_s spectrum = copies spaced fs; Nyquist fs > 2B; anti-alias LPF before ADC; reconstruction LPF.

State the convolution property and its LTI significance.

units.title: Laplace & Z-Transforms
units.summary: Bilateral Laplace with ROC strip; causal ⇒ right of rightmost pole; stable ⇔ ROC includes jω ⇔ all poles LHP. Unilateral derivative rule turns ODEs into algebra. H(s) = Y/X; poles = natural modes. Z-transform: unit circle = DTFT slice; pairs for u[n], aⁿu[n]; causal stable ⇔ all poles inside |z| < 1; difference equations via z-algebra.

units.title: Bode Plots & Modulation

Filters: LPF/HPF/BPF/notch; Butterworth flat, Chebyshev steep. AM: m(t)cos(ωc t) ⇒ copies at ±ωc; conventional AM with μ ≤ 1 for envelope detection; DSB-SC coherent; SSB half-bandwidth.

important_questions: Four system properties with standard test procedures and counterexample signals.
Convolution integral graphical method with all overlap stages labelled.
Fourier series with symmetry analysis before integration.
Sampling theorem statement, Nyquist rate and reconstruction filter conditions.
Laplace ROC rules mapping to causality and BIBO stability.
Z-transform difference-equation solving with partial fractions.
Bode straight-line sketch from a pole/zero description.
AM as frequency-shift property with envelope-detection condition.

previous_year_questions.question: A continuous-time LTI system has impulse response h(t) = e^{−2t}u(t). Is the system causal and stable? Justify using the ROC of H(s).
previous_year_questions.solution: h(t) = 0 for t < 0 ⇒ causal. H(s) = 1/(s+2) with ROC Re(s) > −2, which includes the jω axis (σ = 0) and has its only pole at s = −2 (LHP) ⇒ BIBO stable. ∫|h| dt = 1/2 < ∞ confirms independently.

previous_year_questions.question: State the sampling theorem. A signal x(t) = 2cos(100πt) + sin(2000πt) is sampled at 700 Hz. Identify any aliased components and state the minimum correct sampling rate.
previous_year_questions.solution: Theorem: band-limited B ⇒ perfect reconstruction from fs > 2B via ideal LPF. Components: 50 Hz and 1000 Hz; B = 1000 Hz ⇒ Nyquist rate 2000 Hz. At fs = 700 Hz the 1000 Hz tone folds to |1000 − 700| = 300 Hz (alias); the 50 Hz component does not alias (700 > 100) but the composite is corrupted. Fix: fs ≥ 2000 Hz or pre-LPF at 1000 Hz then sample ≥ 2000.

previous_year_questions.question: Explain how amplitude modulation illustrates the Fourier frequency-shift property. What condition must hold for envelope detection of conventional AM, and why?
previous_year_questions.solution: Multiplication by cos(ωc t) shifts M(ω) to ±ωc scaled by ½ — the frequency-shift property. Envelope detection (diode + LPF) recovers the message only when modulation index μ = max|m(t)|/A ≤ 1, so the envelope A + m(t) never becomes negative; otherwise overmodulation clips the envelope and distorts the recovered audio.

project.title: Signals analysis notebook
project.brief: Pick one real signal (voice clip, sensor CSV, or generated square wave + channel model) and analyse it end-to-end in a markdown/PDF notebook (or Jupyter export): (1) classify it (energy/power, periodicity, bandwidth estimate); (2) compute or sketch its spectrum (Fourier series or transform) with symmetry notes; (3) if sampling, state the Nyquist rate, choose fs, and show one aliased vs non-aliased scenario; (4) design a simple first- or second-order filter (write H(s), mark cutoff on a Bode sketch) and state what it removes; (5) if using modulation, draw the before/after spectrum. Include any code or hand calculations as an appendix.

modules.title: Module 1 — Foundations: Signals, Systems & Convolution
modules.summary: Signal classifications, system properties (linearity, time-invariance, causality, stability), LTI systems and the convolution integral/sum.

lessons.title: Signals & System Properties
lessons.summary: Continuous vs discrete, energy vs power, periodicity; then the four properties every exam asks: linearity, time-invariance, causality, BIBO stability.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify signals: CT/DT, energy/power, periodic/aperiodic, even/odd
Test a system for linearity and time-invariance with standard inputs
State causality and BIBO stability and test each on given systems

payload.text: Every ECE exam paper in signals starts the same way: "Check whether the system y(t) = x(t)cos(t0) is linear, causal and stable." Four tests, ten minutes, full marks — if you know the tests by heart.

**Signal vocabulary:**
- **CT vs DT:** x(t) continuous argument vs x[n] integer index.
- **Energy vs power:** E = ∫|x(t)|²dt (finite energy ⇒ energy signal, zero average power); P = lim(1/T)∫|x|² over T. Power signals have infinite energy (e.g. periodic). A zero signal is both (trivially).
- **Periodic:** x(t) = x(t+T0), fundamental T0 = smallest such T. DT: x[n] = x[n+N], fundamental N smallest positive integer. Sum of two periodic signals is periodic only if T1/T2 is rational.
- **Even/odd:** x(t)=x(−t) even; x(t)=−x(−t) odd; any signal = even part + odd part.

**System properties (the four exam tests):**
1. **Linearity:** T{a·x1 + b·x2} = a·T{x1} + b·T{x2}. Test with weighted sum of two inputs. Breaks on: amplitude nonlinearity (x²), offsets (x + 1), modulations by t·x(t).
2. **Time-invariance (TI):** input delayed by t0 ⇒ output delayed by t0. Test: y(t,t0) = T{x(t−t0)} equals y(t−t0). Breaks on: coefficients that vary with t (t·x(t), cos(t)x(t)).
3. **Causality:** output at time t depends only on present/past inputs, never future. Test: x1 = x2 on (−∞, t0] ⇒ outputs equal there. Any system writing y(t) = x(t+1) is noncausal.
4. **BIBO stability:** every bounded input (|x| ≤ Mx < ∞) gives bounded output (|y| ≤ My < ∞). For LTI: stable iff impulse response absolutely integrable, ∫|h(t)|dt < ∞ (DT: Σ|h[n]| < ∞).

**LTI = Linear + Time-Invariant.** Only for LTI systems do convolution, transfer functions, frequency response and the whole transform toolkit apply. That is why the first two tests come first in every question.

lessons.title: Convolution: The LTI Workhorse
lessons.summary: Convolution integral for CT and sum for DT: intuition, graphical method steps, commutativity, and the identity with the impulse response.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute the convolution of two simple signals graphically and analytically
Explain flip-shift-multiply-integrate as the operational recipe
Use convolution properties: commutativity, associativity, identity with δ

payload.text: One integral answers every LTI question: give me any input and I will give you the output — because I know h(t). Convolution is not an arbitrary formula; it is the mathematical statement of "the present is a weighted sum of the recent past".

**Convolution integral (CT LTI):**
y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ

**Convolution sum (DT LTI):**
y[n] = x[n] * h[n] = Σ_k x[k] h[n − k]

**Why it works (impulse decomposition):** any signal = superposition of shifted impulses: x(t) = ∫ x(τ) δ(t−τ) dτ. LTI system responds to each δ with shifted scaled h; superposition assembles the integral.

**Graphical recipe (flip–shift–multiply–integrate):**
1. Replace t by τ: x(τ), h(τ).
2. Flip one function: h(−τ).
3. Shift by the observation time t: h(t−τ).
4. Multiply overlap region; integrate (CT) / sum (DT).
5. Repeat across t or n — the overlapping interval changes in stages; results are piecewise.

**Properties:**
- Commutative: x*h = h*x (choose the easier flip).
- Associative & distributive over +.
- y(t) = x(t)*δ(t) = x(t) (identity).
- Widths add: duration(y) = duration(x) + duration(h) (finite-length signals).
- LTI system fully characterised by h(t): H(s) or H(jω) is the transform of h.

**Examples to know cold:** rect * rect = triangle; rect * exp(−at)u(t) = exponential rise; u(t) * u(t) = t·u(t) (ramp).

payload.title: Flip the shorter/rectangular one
payload.text: Commutativity lets you flip whichever function makes the overlap stages simplest.

payload.title: Limits of integration follow the overlap
payload.text: Do not blindly integrate −∞..∞; the product is nonzero only where both windows overlap.

payload.title: rect * rect by stages
payload.problem: x(t) = u(t) − u(t−1) (unit rect on [0,1]), h(t) same. Find y(t).

steps.title: Stage 1 (t < 0)
steps.desc: Shifted h(t−τ) sits left of x — no overlap ⇒ y = 0.

steps.title: Stage 2 (0 ≤ t ≤ 1)
steps.desc: Partial overlap: integral = ∫₀^t 1 dτ = t — linear rise.

steps.title: Stage 3 (1 ≤ t ≤ 2)
steps.desc: Overlap shrinks: ∫_{t−1}^1 dτ = 2 − t — linear fall.

steps.title: Stage 4 (t > 2)
steps.desc: No overlap ⇒ 0. Result: triangle from 0 to 2, peak 1 at t=1.

payload.solution: y(t) = triangle: t for 0≤t≤1, 2−t for 1<t≤2, 0 elsewhere — width 2 = 1+1.

modules.title: Module 2 — Fourier Analysis & Sampling
modules.summary: Fourier series (trig/exponential), Fourier transform pairs and properties, frequency response of LTI systems, and the sampling theorem.

lessons.title: Fourier Series & Transform
lessons.summary: Decomposing periodic signals into harmonics, the transform for aperiodic signals, key pairs and the linearity/time/frequency-shift properties.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write trigonometric and exponential Fourier series for standard waveforms
State the Fourier transform pair and compute it for rect and exp decays
Apply linearity, time-shift and frequency-shift (modulation) properties

payload.text: Fourier turned one hard problem (solving differential equations for arbitrary inputs) into easy ones (scale the response at each pure tone). Every filter, codec and modulation scheme you will ever meet is that idea in hardware.

**Fourier series (periodic, period T0, ω0 = 2π/T0):**
- Trig form: x(t) = a0/2 + Σ [aₙcos(nω0t) + bₙsin(nω0t)]
  - aₙ = (2/T0)∫ x(t)cos(nω0t)dt, bₙ similarly with sin.
- Exponential form (preferred): x(t) = Σ cₙ e^{jnω0t}
  - cₙ = (1/T0)∫_T x(t)e^{−jnω0t}dt; c₋ₙ = cₙ* for real x.
- Even signal ⇒ only cosine (bₙ=0); odd ⇒ only sine (aₙ=0); half-wave symmetry ⇒ only odd harmonics.

**Fourier transform (aperiodic, limit of series as T0→∞):**
X(jω) = ∫ x(t) e^{−jωt} dt;  x(t) = (1/2π)∫ X(jω)e^{jωt} dω

Key pairs to memorise:
- δ(t) ↔ 1
- 1 ↔ 2π δ(ω)
- e^{−at}u(t), a>0 ↔ 1/(a + jω)
- rect(t/T) ↔ T·sinc(ωT/2) (sampling form varies with sinc definition — be consistent)
- triangular pulse ↔ T·sinc²( )
- cos(ω0t) ↔ π[δ(ω−ω0) + δ(ω+ω0)]

**Properties:**
- Linearity; time shift e^{−jωt0} (phase only); frequency shift (multiplication by e^{jω0t}) ↔ X(ω−ω0) — **modulation**.
- Differentiation: d/dt ↔ jω; integration ↔ X/(jω) + πX(0)δ(ω).
- Convolution: x*h ↔ X·H — the LTI frequency-response theorem.
- Parseval: energy in time = energy in frequency.

**LTI frequency response:** H(jω) = F{h(t)}; steady-state output to e^{jω0t} is H(jω0)e^{jω0t} — filter = shaping magnitude and phase per frequency.

lessons.title: Sampling & Reconstruction
lessons.summary: Ideal sampling as multiplication by an impulse train, the spectrum as periodic repetition, Nyquist rate, aliasing and practical reconstruction.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Derive the sampled-spectrum (periodic repetition) formula
Compute the Nyquist rate for a signal with given bandwidth
Diagnose aliasing and state conditions for perfect reconstruction

payload.text: Your phone records voice at 8 kHz — not because voices stop at 4 kHz by law, but because Nyquist said so. And the reconstructed voice is perfect only because of that one theorem. Sampling is where continuous math meets digital everything.

**Ideal sampling:** multiply by impulse train s(t) = Σ δ(t − nTs):
x_s(t) = x(t)·s(t) = Σ x(nTs) δ(t − nTs)

Multiplication in time ⇒ convolution in frequency (with the train's spectrum: impulses at ωs = 2π/Ts, scaled by 1/Ts):
X_s(ω) = (1/Ts) Σ X(ω − nωs) — the baseband spectrum repeated every ωs.

**Nyquist–Shannon theorem:** if the highest frequency in X(ω) is B (bandwidth), the copies do not overlap iff ωs > 2B, i.e. sampling rate **fs > 2B (Nyquist rate = 2B)**. Then an ideal low-pass filter (cutoff between B and fs−B) reconstructs x(t) exactly.

**Aliasing:** fs < 2B ⇒ spectral copies overlap; high frequencies masquerade as low ones — irreversible in post-processing. Symptom: wagon-wheel effect, beat frequencies in audio.

**Practical pipeline:** anti-alias LPF (analog, before ADC) → sample & hold → ADC (quantisation is a separate, lossy step) → digital processing → DAC → reconstruction LPF.

**DT frequency view:** sampling maps analog frequency ω to normalized digital frequency Ω = ωTs ∈ [−π, π]; ωs corresponds to Ω = 2π (one full turn of the DTFT circle) — why DT spectra are periodic with period 2π.

**Undersampling trick (exam depth):** bandpass signals can be sampled below 2B_high if chosen so spectral copies land in disjoint bands — 2× bandwidth can suffice with correct placement.

rows: Ideal LPF, gain Ts, cutoff ∈ (B, fs − B)

payload.title: Alias diagnosis
payload.text: If fs < 2B the copies overlap; increase fs or pre-filter (anti-alias LPF) first.

payload.title: Nyquist rate vs Nyquist frequency
payload.text: Nyquist rate = 2B (minimum fs); Nyquist frequency = fs/2 (highest representable). Exams swap these — read carefully.

payload.title: Nyquist rate of a composite signal

steps.title: Frequencies
steps.desc: cos term: f1 = 50 Hz; sin term: f2 = 1000 Hz. B = max = 1000 Hz.

steps.title: Nyquist rate
steps.desc: fs ≥ 2B = 2000 Hz — choose ≥ 2000 samples/s for perfect recovery.

steps.title: At fs = 700
steps.desc: The 1000 Hz component aliases to |1000 − 700| = 300 Hz (mod fs folding) — a phantom 300 Hz tone appears.

steps.title: Also
steps.desc: 50 Hz component: 700 > 100 — no alias for it, but the composite still fails.

steps.title: Fix
steps.desc: Sample ≥ 2000 Hz, or LPF at 1000 Hz before sampling below 2000.

payload.solution: Nyquist rate 2000 Hz; at 700 Hz the 1 kHz tone folds to 300 Hz (aliasing).

modules.title: Module 3 — Laplace & Z-Transforms
modules.summary: Bilateral/unilateral Laplace with ROC, pole-zero plots and stability reading, transfer functions, then the Z-transform as the DT twin.

lessons.title: Laplace Transform, ROC & Transfer Functions
lessons.summary: Region of convergence as the "where does the sum converge" answer, pole-zero reading of stability/causality, and H(s) for LTI systems.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute unilateral Laplace transforms of standard signals with their ROCs
Read causality and stability off the ROC / pole locations
Form H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) and identify poles as natural-response frequencies

payload.text: The Fourier transform fails on signals that blow up (e^{3t}u(t) has no FT). Laplace adds a convergence exponent σ to tame them — and the ROC it forces on you turns out to encode causality and stability. The "extra" variable carries the answers.

**Bilateral Laplace:** X(s) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t)e^{−st}dt, s = σ + jω.
Along the imaginary axis (σ=0) it reduces to the Fourier transform — FT is a slice of Laplace.

**Why ROC exists:** the integral may converge only for a strip of σ values — the Region Of Convergence. Poles (where X(s) = ∞) bound the ROC; the ROC never contains a pole.

**Pairs (unilateral, t≥0):**
- u(t) ↔ 1/s, Re(s) > 0
- e^{−at}u(t) ↔ 1/(s+a), Re(s) > −a
- cos(ω0t)u(t) ↔ s/(s²+ω0²)
- t^n e^{−at}u(t) ↔ n!/(s+a)^{n+1}
- δ(t) ↔ 1
- derivative: x′(t) ↔ sX(s) − x(0⁻) (unilateral — turns ODEs into algebra)

**ROC rules → system reading:**
- Right-sided signal ⇒ ROC = right of rightmost pole ⇒ causal system.
- Left-sided ⇒ ROC left of leftmost pole ⇒ anticausal.
- Two-sided ⇒ strip between poles.
- **Stability of causal LTI ⇔ ROC includes the jω axis ⇔ all poles in the LEFT half-plane (Re(s) < 0).**
- Marginally stable: poles ON jω axis (e^{jω0t} persists); unstable: any RHP pole.

**Transfer function:** H(s) = L{h(t)} = Y(s)/X(s) with zero initial conditions.
- Poles = natural (transient) modes e^{pᵢt}; zeros shape amplitude/phase.
- Region of convergence of H(s) = ROC of h(t) — same causal/stable reading.
- Frequency response = H(jω) — evaluate H(s) on the jω axis where the ROC includes it.

**Pole placement:** LHP ⇒ decaying exponentials (stable); RHP ⇒ growing (unstable); jω ⇒ sustained oscillation. Multi-pole repeated roots ⇒ t·e^{at} envelopes.

payload.title: ROC one-liner
payload.text: Causal ⇒ right of rightmost pole; stable ⇒ ROC touches jω; for causal systems, both ⇔ all poles LHP.

lessons.title: Z-Transform: The DT Twin
lessons.summary: Z-transform definition, ROC as annuli, inverse and difference-equation solving, poles/zeros on the z-plane reading stability for causal DT systems.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute z-transforms of standard DT signals with correct ROCs
Solve a linear constant-coefficient difference equation via z-transforms
Read DT stability/causality from pole locations relative to the unit circle

payload.text: Every digital filter you will ever write — in a phone, a car, a radio — is a difference equation, and the z-transform is how engineers prove it will behave. If Laplace is the analog toolkit, z is the same toolkit rotated into discrete time.

**Definition (one-sided, common in courses):** X(z) = Σ_{n≥0} x[n] z^{−n}, z ∈ ℂ.
Related to DTFT by z = e^{jΩ} — the unit circle is the DTFT slice, just as the jω axis is the FT slice of Laplace.

**Pairs (causal, n ≥ 0):**
- δ[n] ↔ 1
- u[n] ↔ z/(z−1) = 1/(1−z^{−1}), |z| > 1
- a^n u[n] ↔ z/(z−a) = 1/(1−az^{−1}), |z| > |a|
- n a^n u[n] ↔ az/(z−a)², |z| > |a|
- cos(Ω0 n)u[n] ↔ z(z−cos Ω0)/(z²−2z cos Ω0 + 1), |z| > 1

**Properties:** linearity; time shift z^{−1} (with initial-condition terms unilaterally); multiplication by a^n ↔ X(z/a) (DT analog of s-shift); convolution ⇒ multiplication (Y = H·X) — the filter theorem.

**ROC as annulus/circle regions:** right-sided ⇒ outside circle |z| > R; left-sided ⇒ inside; two-sided ⇒ ring R1 < |z| < R2. ROC never contains a pole.

**Stability reading (causal DT LTI):** stable ⇔ ROC includes the unit circle ⇔ **all poles inside the unit circle |z| < 1**. Outside ⇒ unstable; on the circle ⇒ marginally stable (persistent oscillation/DC).

**Difference equations:** take z-transform of both sides term-by-term (shifts become powers of z with zero ICs), solve H(z) = Y/X, then invert via partial fractions + tables. Coefficients of the DE appear directly in the denominator — feedback poles live there.

**System function:** H(z) = Z{h[n]}; poles = natural modes pᵢ^n; frequency response = H(e^{jΩ}) = H(z)|_{z=e^{jΩ}}.

payload.title: Unit circle ⇔ stability

lessons.title: Bode Plots & Filter Design Basics
lessons.summary: Magnitude/phase response, straight-line Bode asymptotes for poles/zeros, cutoff and bandwidth, and first/second-order filter prototypes.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Sketch magnitude Bode plots for first-order and second-order systems from pole/zero locations
Read −3 dB cutoff, bandwidth and Q from a transfer function
Match prototype filters (LPF/HPF/BPF) to passband/stopband specs

payload.text: A Bode plot turns H(jω) from a wall of complex algebra into two pencil-and-paper lines. EE interviews love asking you to sketch one live — with poles at −2 and zeros at origin you should see the shape before you calculate anything.

**Frequency response:** H(jω) = |H(jω)|∠H(jω). Bode plots: log-frequency x-axis; magnitude in dB (20log10|H|); phase in degrees.

**Straight-line rules (single real pole/zero at ω = ωp):**
- Zero at origin (jω): +20 dB/decade slope, phase +90°.
- Pole at origin (1/jω): −20 dB/decade, phase −90°.
- Real zero (1 + jω/ωz): slope +20 dB/decade starting at ωz; phase 0 → +90°.
- Real pole (1/(1 + jω/ωp)): slope −20 dB/decade from ωp; phase 0 → −90°.
- Corner frequency = pole/zero location; actual curve is −3 dB at corner (asymptote meets here).

**Second-order (complex poles) — resonant shape:**
H(s) = ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²) (LPF prototype)
- ωn = natural frequency; ζ = damping.
- ζ < 1/√2 ⇒ peak (resonance) near ωn; peak height ~ 1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²)).
- Higher Q = 1/(2ζ) ⇒ sharper peak, longer ringing in time.
- Slope beyond ωn: −40 dB/decade (two poles).

**Filter prototypes:**
- LPF: pass |ω| < ωc; HPF: pass |ω| > ωc; BPF: pass ω1..ω2; BS/ notch: reject one band.
- Specs: passband ripple, stopband attenuation, transition width → order n (higher n = steeper, more components/group delay).
- Butterworth: maximally flat passband; Chebyshev: steeper transition with ripples; both all-pole classics.

**Decibels to remember:** −3 dB = half power (×0.707 voltage); −6 dB ≈ ×0.5 voltage; −20 dB/decade = one pole; −40 = two.

lessons.title: Modulation & System Applications
lessons.summary: Amplitude modulation as multiplication in time = frequency shift, DSB/SSB/envelope detection, and where LTI/transform thinking appears in comms, audio and control.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain AM as multiplication by a carrier and sketch the spectrum before/after
Distinguish DSB-SC, AM with carrier, and SSB; state the envelope-detection condition
Map real products (radio, audio EQ, PID control) onto the course toolkit

payload.text: AM radio is 100 years old and still one-line Fourier: multiply the message by cos(ωc t) and every station owns a different spectral real-estate band. Learn this and "how does the radio know which song is theirs" becomes a five-second answer.

**Amplitude modulation = multiplication in time:**
s(t) = m(t)·cos(ωc t) ⇒ S(jω) = ½[M(ω − ωc) + M(ω + ωc)] — spectrum COPIED to ±ωc (frequency-shift property).

**Variants:**
- **DSB-SC** (double sideband, suppressed carrier): s = m·cos(ωc t). Compact power, needs coherent (synchronous) detection.
- **Conventional AM** (with carrier): s = [A + m(t)]cos(ωc t), A large enough that A + m(t) ≥ 0. Envelope = A + m(t) — detectable by a simple diode + LPF (envelope detector). Wasteful (carrier power) but cheap receivers — classic broadcast trade.
- **SSB** (single sideband): transmit only one sideband (filter method or phase method). Half bandwidth, harder to generate — telephony/fax heritage.
- **Vestigial / FM** — beyond this course's core; FM is angle modulation (constant envelope, noise-robust).

**Envelope detection condition:** modulation index μ = max|m|/A < 1 (no overmodulation); otherwise envelope clips and audio distorts. RC time constant: 1/ωc ≪ RC ≪ 1/Wm (carrier passes, message follows).

**Coherent detection:** multiply by local cos(ωc t) and LPF — recovers m(t)/2 (plus a DC/IF offset term if frequencies mismatch).

**Where the whole course shows up in products:**
- **Audio EQ / crossovers:** banks of biquad filters = H(s) prototypes; Bode plot tuning in DAWs.
- **Digital audio/OFDM:** sampling theorem + FFT; guard intervals combat ISI (channel impulse response spread).
- **PID control:** Laplace transfer functions of plant + controller; pole placement = closed-loop stability (LHP again).
- **Medical/telemetry sensors:** anti-alias filtering before ADC; envelope detectors in amplitude-based sensing.
- **JPEG/MPEG:** 2D frequency transforms — "which frequencies carry the picture" is still spectral thinking.

**Exam angle:** problems usually chain transforms: model → transform (Laplace/z/FT) → algebraic solve (multiply/divide) → inverse → interpret (stability, bandwidth, aliasing).

courses.title: Thermodynamics
courses.subtitle: Laws, entropy & availability, gas and vapour power cycles, refrigeration, combustion and psychrometrics — ME exam + interview core
courses.description:
Thermodynamics is a gatekeeper subject in every mechanical engineering programme and a staple of core placement interviews. This course compresses the full standard syllabus into eight compact lessons: systems, the state postulate and the four laws with Clausius inequality; boundary work and pure-substance property evaluation with steam tables; entropy, isentropic efficiencies and availability (exergy) analysis; Otto, Diesel and Dual air-standard cycles with MEP; the Rankine cycle with reheat and regeneration; vapour-compression refrigeration with COP; combustion equations, excess air and adiabatic flame temperature; and psychrometrics for HVAC.

Every lesson uses the nine-block structure (objectives, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, graded quiz, summary). A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** ME/PI/automotive students in semester 3–5 preparing for university exams, GATE ME fundamentals, and placement interviews that ask thermo questions.

**What you need:** pen and paper, a scientific calculator, and access to steam tables (a compact table is fine).
outcomes: Classify systems and apply the state postulate and four laws correctly
Compute boundary work for polytropic and other standard processes
Evaluate pure-substance properties with quality and steam-table lookups
Calculate entropy changes, isentropic efficiencies and exergy destruction
Analyze Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles with efficiency and MEP
Solve Rankine-cycle problems including reheat and regeneration effects
Compute COP for refrigeration and heat-pump vapour-compression cycles
Balance combustion equations and use psychrometric properties for HVAC
courses.about_course:
University thermodynamics papers reward a disciplined sequence: fix the state, choose the property model (ideal gas vs steam table), pick the correct law or cycle form, balance the energy, then check feasibility with the Second Law. This course trains exactly that sequence across power and refrigeration cycles so answers follow a checkable method rather than formula roulette.

The availability and combustion lessons go beyond plug-and-chug: they teach you to ask "where is the useful work potential destroyed?" and "is this mixture rich or lean?" — the two questions that separate an engineer from a calculator operator in interviews.

The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a small cycle or HVAC analysis you can show as proof of skill.
prerequisites: Basic calculus and algebra
Introductory physics (energy, temperature, pressure)
audience: ME/PI/automotive students facing university thermodynamics exams
GATE ME aspirants building cycle-analysis fundamentals
Placement candidates preparing for core mechanical interview rounds
HVAC and energy-sector beginners who want the math to click

units.title: Laws, Systems & Properties
units.summary: Open/closed/isolated systems; state postulate (two independent intensive properties). Zeroth defines temperature; First: ΔU = Q − W (closed) or SFEE for control volumes; Second: Clausius ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, Kelvin–Planck, entropy; Third: S = 0 at 0 K. Boundary work: isobaric PΔV, isochoric 0, polytropic (P₂V₂−P₁V₁)/(1−n). Quality x only inside the dome; ideal gas u = u(T).

units.title: Entropy, Availability & Gas Cycles
units.summary: ΔS ideal gas = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁); two-phase ΔS via quality. Isentropic efficiency: turbine actual/isen; compressor in isen/actual. Availability Ψ/Helmholtz forms; I = T₀S_gen; η_II = W/W_rev. Otto η = 1 − 1/r^(k−1); Diesel adds cutoff correction; Dual between them; MEP = W_net/displacement. Same r: Otto ≥ Dual ≥ Diesel (air-standard).
questions: Derive Otto efficiency and compare with Diesel at same r.

Worked turbine isentropic efficiency problem.

units.title: Vapour Power & Refrigeration

Reheat raises mean addition T and outlet quality; regeneration preheats feedwater via bleed. Refrigeration: COP_R = q_L/w; COP_HP = COP_R + 1; Carnot COP with Kelvin. Vapour-compression: isen compression, condensation, isenthalpic throttle, evaporation; superheat and subcooling improve COP and protect compressor.

units.title: Combustion & Psychrometrics
units.summary: Stoichiometric CₓHᵧ + (x+y/4)O₂ → xCO₂ + (y/2)H₂O; carry 3.76 N₂ per O₂ for air. φ = AFR_act/AFR_stoich (>1 rich); % theoretical air; lean → leftover O₂; rich → CO. AFT rises with preheat/fuel value, falls with dilution. Psychrometrics: ω = 0.622 P_v/(P−P_v); φ = P_v/P_g(T); dew point = saturation of current P_v; HVAC processes on the chart; dry-air basis for balances.

Isentropic efficiency definitions for turbine vs compressor (ratio flip).
Otto/Diesel efficiency derivations and MEP calculation.

previous_year_questions.question: An ideal Rankine cycle operates between 3 MPa/350°C and 10 kPa. Given h₃ = 3116 kJ/kg, s₃ = 6.745 kJ/kg·K, and at 10 kPa s_f = 0.649, s_g = 8.150, h_f = 192, h_fg = 2392 kJ/kg. Neglecting pump work, determine the thermal efficiency and comment on turbine outlet quality.
previous_year_questions.solution: Isentropic expansion: s₄ = s₃ = 6.745 ⇒ x₄ = (6.745−0.649)/(8.150−0.649) ≈ 0.813. h₄ = 192 + 0.813×2392 ≈ 2137 kJ/kg. w_t = 3116−2137 = 979; q_in ≈ 3116−192 = 2924 (pump neglected). η ≈ 979/2924 ≈ 33.5%. Outlet quality ≈ 0.81 — about 19% moisture; practical designs would add reheat to reduce blade erosion.

previous_year_questions.question: A vapour-compression refrigerator has h₁ = 400, h₂ = 430, h₃ = h₄ = 250 kJ/kg. Find COP_R, COP_HP, and discuss the effect of 5 K subcooling.
previous_year_questions.solution: q_L = h₁ − h₄ = 150; w = h₂ − h₁ = 30; q_H = h₂ − h₃ = 180. COP_R = 150/30 = 5; COP_HP = 180/30 = 6 = COP_R + 1. Subcooling lowers h₃ further, increasing q_L per kg (since h₄ = h₃ after the isenthalpic throttle) and raising COP, at the cost of a slightly longer condenser.

previous_year_questions.question: Balance the stoichiometric combustion of propane (C₃H₈) in air and compute the mass-based stoichiometric air-fuel ratio. M_air ≈ 29 kg/kmol.
previous_year_questions.solution: C₃H₈ + 5(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O + 18.8 N₂. Moles of air per mole fuel = 5 + 18.8 = 23.8. Mass air = 23.8 × 29 ≈ 690; mass fuel = 3×12 + 8 = 44. AFR_stoich ≈ 690/44 ≈ 15.7 kg air per kg propane.

project.title: Cycle or HVAC analysis note
project.brief: Pick one real system (a small Rankine or vapour-compression design, an IC-engine cycle study, or an HVAC coil/room calculation) and analyze it in a markdown/PDF notebook: (1) define the cycle or process and list assumptions; (2) fix each state point using tables or ideal-gas relations (show the property model chosen and why); (3) compute work, heat and efficiency/COP for each component and the overall cycle; (4) perform one Second-Law check (isentropic efficiency, irreversibility, or Carnot bound comparison); (5) suggest one practical improvement (reheat, regeneration, subcooling, excess-air tuning, etc.) and quantify its benefit if possible. Include any software output or hand calculations as an appendix.
project.submission_hint: PDF, public markdown, or a GitHub link — state tables or EES/MATLAB snippets are welcome; the reasoning and state-by-state bookkeeping matter more than polish.

modules.title: Module 1 — Foundations: Laws, States & Properties
modules.summary: Thermodynamic systems and state postulate, zeroth/first/second laws, work and heat sign conventions, and pure-substance property lookup.

lessons.title: Systems, State & the Four Laws
lessons.summary: Control mass vs control volume, the state postulate, zeroth through second laws with the Clausius inequality, and theKelvin–Planck statement.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify systems (open/closed/isolated) and apply the state postulate
State the zeroth, first, second and third laws and what each forbids
Use Clausius inequality to decide if a cycle is possible, reversible or impossible

payload.text: A heat engine that converted all heat to work would end civilization's energy crisis overnight — the Second Law says it is not just hard, it is mathematically forbidden. Every power plant, refrigerator and living cell obeys the same boundary.

**System vocabulary:**
- **Open (control volume):** mass crosses boundary — turbines, nozzles, compressors.
- **Closed (control mass):** fixed mass, energy crosses as heat/work — piston-cylinder.
- **Isolated:** neither mass nor energy — universe as a whole (theoretical).
- **State postulate:** two independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible system — the foundation of every property table.

**Zeroth law:** if A equilibrates with B and B with C, then A with C — defines temperature and makes thermometers possible.

**First law (energy conservation):** for a closed system, δQ − δW = dU; path-independent U, path-dependent Q and W. Rate form: Q̇ − Ẇ = dU/dt. For a control volume use the SFEE (steady-flow energy equation): Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ(h₂ − h₁ + Δke + Δpe).

**Second law (directionality):** heat does not spontaneously flow cold→hot; work does not convert to heat with 100% efficiency in a cycle. Equivalent statements:
- **Clausius:** ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 (equality reversible).
- **Kelvin–Planck:** no cycle can convert heat entirely to work; some must reject to a low-T sink.
- **Entropy (Clausius definition):** dS = δQ_rev/T; for any process ΔS ≥ ∫δQ/T.

**Third law:** entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero — absolute zero is unreachable in finite steps.

payload.title: Law
rows: Thermal equilibrium is transitive — temperature exists
Energy is conserved: ΔU = Q − W (closed)
Entropy of an isolated system never decreases
S = 0 at 0 K for a perfect crystal; absolute 0 unattainable

payload.title: Sign convention lock-in
payload.text: Q > 0 into system, W > 0 done BY system — pick this everywhere and never flip mid-problem.

payload.title: First law cannot reject perpetual motion of the first kind
payload.text: Energy bookkeeping alone; the Second Law rejects the second kind (100%-efficient cycle).

payload.title: Clausius inequality test
payload.problem: A cycle receives 1000 kJ at 800 K and rejects 600 kJ at 300 K. Is it possible? Reversible?

steps.title: Compare to zero
steps.desc: Negative, so Clausius inequality is satisfied — the cycle is possible.

steps.title: Reversible?
steps.desc: Equality holds only for reversible cycles. Here ∮δQ/T = −0.75 ≠ 0, so irreversible.

steps.title: Cross-check efficiency
steps.desc: η = 1 − 600/1000 = 0.40. Carnot bound at same temps: 1 − 300/800 = 0.625. 0.40 < 0.625 — consistent with irreversibility.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.desc: Possible and irreversible; if ∮δQ/T > 0 it would be impossible.

payload.solution: ∮δQ/T = −0.75 kJ/K < 0 → possible but irreversible (not a Carnot cycle).

payload.title: Inequality flip
payload.prompt: A proposed cycle has ∮δQ/T = +0.2 kJ/K. What is the verdict, and why is the sign decisive?
payload.hint: Clausius allows ≤ 0 only.

mistakes.mistake: Treating Q and W as state functions
mistakes.fix: Only U, H, S, T, P are state functions; Q and W are path-dependent — never write dQ, write δQ.

mistakes.mistake: Applying the closed-system First law to a turbine
mistakes.fix: Turbines are control volumes — use SFEE with enthalpy h, not internal energy U.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the Kelvin–Planck statement of the Second Law and its equivalence to Clausius.
payload.answer: No cycle can have as its sole result the conversion of heat from a single reservoir entirely into work. Equivalence proof: assume a Clausius violator (net heat cold→hot with no work) and couple it to a Kelvin–Planck engine to build a forbidden engine.
payload.source: Standard proof question in ME exams.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: State postulate: two independent intensive properties fix a simple compressible state.
Zeroth defines T; First conserves energy; Second sets direction; Third anchors S.
Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 is the universal cycle feasibility test.

lessons.title: Work, Heat & Pure-Substance Properties
lessons.summary: Boundary work under polytropic processes, heat transfer modes, ideal-gas vs real-gas treatment, and steam-table / T–s diagram reading.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute boundary work for polytropic, isobaric and isochoric processes
Choose ideal-gas vs steam-table property evaluation correctly
Read quality, saturation values and superheat from a T–s or steam table

payload.text: The difference between "PV = mRT is fine here" and "you needed the steam tables" is the difference between a correct rankine-cycle efficiency and a wrong one that still looks plausible. Choosing the property model is half the marks.

**Boundary work (closed system):** W_b = ∫P dV.
- Constant P: W = P(V₂ − V₁)
- Isochoric (V = const): W = 0
- Polytropic (PVⁿ = const): W = (P₂V₂ − P₁V₁)/(1 − n) = mR(T₂ − T₁)/(1 − n) for ideal gas, n ≠ 1
- Isothermal ideal gas: W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁)

**Heat transfer modes:** conduction (Fourier, q = −k∇T), convection (Newton cooling, q̇ = hAΔT), radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann, q̇ = εσAT⁴).

**Ideal gas:** PV = mRT (or Pv = RT). Valid at high T, low P (far from saturation). u = u(T), h = h(T) only — composition of P,V does not affect them for ideal gases.

**Pure substance & phase:** at a given T, P_sat pairs. Quality x = m_vap/m_total in the wet region:
- v = v_f + x·v_fg; u = u_f + x·u_fg; h = h_f + x·h_fg; s similarly.
- x is undefined outside the dome (subcooled liquid, superheated vapor).
- Critical point: T_c, P_c — above it, no distinct liquid/vapor.

**Steam table use:**
1. Given (T, P): if P = P_sat(T) → two-phase; if P > P_sat → subcooled liquid (often use compressed liquid ≈ sat liquid at T); if P < P_sat → superheated vapor → use superheat tables.
2. Find quality if two-phase: x = (h − h_f)/h_fg.

**T–s diagram:** dome, constant-P lines (flat in two-phase, rise in single phase), Carnot rectangle as the reference cycle.

payload.title: x undefined outside the dome
payload.text: Never compute quality for superheated or subcooled states — go straight to the correct table.

payload.title: Ideal gas near saturation
payload.text: Steam at 100°C, 1 atm is NOT ideal-gas territory for property work — use steam tables; ideal gas is for hot, low-pressure gases.

payload.title: Polytropic compression work
payload.problem: Air (ideal gas) in a piston-cylinder: 300 K, 100 kPa compressed polytropically (n = 1.3) to 500 kPa. Find work per kg. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.

steps.title: Compute
steps.desc: 0.287 × 132 / (−0.3) ≈ −126.3 kJ/kg — negative: work done ON the gas (compression).

steps.title: Sanity
steps.desc: Compression ⇒ W < 0 by our sign convention (W > 0 out). ✓

steps.title: If asked heat
steps.desc: q = Δu + w; need c_v for Δu — energy balance closes it.

payload.solution: w ≈ −126 kJ/kg (work input to compress 1 kg of air).

payload.title: Two-phase quality
payload.prompt: Saturated mixture at 200 kPa with h = 2500 kJ/kg. Find quality using h_f = 504.7, h_fg = 2201.6 kJ/kg.
payload.hint: x = (h − h_f)/h_fg.

mistakes.mistake: Computing quality for superheated states
mistakes.fix: x only exists inside the vapor dome — outside, use the appropriate single-phase table.

mistakes.mistake: Using PV = mRT for steam near saturation
mistakes.fix: Real-gas effects dominate near the dome — steam tables (or correlations) are required.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define quality and state the conditions under which it exists.
payload.answer: Quality x = m_vapour/m_total for a saturated liquid–vapour mixture; it exists only inside the vapour dome where liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. Undefined for subcooled liquid or superheated vapour.
payload.source: Frequent short-answer question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Boundary work = ∫P dV; polytropic closed form (P₂V₂−P₁V₁)/(1−n).
Ideal gas: u, h depend on T only; real substances need tables.
Quality x applies only in the two-phase region; use h = h_f + x·h_fg.

questions.explanation: No volume change, no boundary work.

questions.prompt: Quality x is meaningful when the state is:
questions.explanation: Only inside the dome.

questions.explanation: Joule's law: u = u(T).

modules.title: Module 2 — Entropy, Availability & Gas Cycles
modules.summary: Entropy as property and direction-finder, T–s analysis, exergy/availability and irreversibility, Otto/Diesel/Dual air-standard cycles.

lessons.title: Entropy & Availability (Exergy)
lessons.summary: Entropy change calculations for ideal gases and pure substances, isentropic efficiencies, availability and second-law efficiency.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute ΔS for ideal gases and across heat-transfer processes
Use isentropic efficiencies of turbines and compressors correctly
Calculate availability, irreversibility and second-law efficiency

payload.text: Two turbines produce the same shaft work; one destroys more exergy than the other. First-law efficiency cannot tell them apart — second-law (availability) analysis can, and that is why power-plant audits use it.

**Entropy as a property:**
- Clausius: dS = δQ_rev/T; inequality: ΔS ≥ ∫δQ/T (equality reversible).
- Isolated system: ΔS ≥ 0 — entropy is the direction clock.
- ΔS for heat transfer at constant T: ΔS = Q/T.
- Ideal gas: Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁) = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁).
- Two-phase: Δs = s_f + x·s_fg at the state; across a constant-T phase change, ΔS = Q/T_sat.

**Isentropic efficiency (steady-flow devices):**
- Turbine: η_turb = actual w / isentropic w = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s)
- Compressor/pump: η_comp = isentropic w / actual w = (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁) — inverted so η ≤ 1.
- Nozzle: η_nozzle = actual Δke / isentropic Δke.

**Availability (exergy) — useful work potential:**
- Closed system: Φ = (U − U₀) + P₀(V − V₀) − T₀(S − S₀)
- Steady-flow stream: ψ = (H − H₀) − T₀(S − S₀)
- Irreversibility: I = T₀·S_gen = ΔΨ_total (lost work potential)
- Second-law efficiency: η_II = (actual work)/(maximum possible work) = W/W_rev or exergy recovered/exergy supplied.

**Where exergy dies:** throttling (ΔH ≈ 0 but S_gen > 0), finite-ΔT heat transfer, friction, unrestrained expansion.

payload.title: Second law always wins the tie-break
payload.text: Equal First-law outputs? Compare S_gen or exergy destruction — lower destruction = better design.

payload.title: Compressor efficiency is inverted on purpose
payload.text: For "work-consuming" devices η = isen/actual so it stays ≤ 1; using the turbine formula gives η ≥ 1.

payload.title: Turbine isentropic efficiency
payload.problem: Steam turbine: inlet h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.9 kJ/kg·K; condenser P₂ = 10 kPa with h₂s = 2100 kJ/kg; actual outlet h₂ = 2300 kJ/kg. Find η_turb.

steps.title: Entropy check
steps.desc: s₂ > s₂s (= s₁) since s₁ = 6.9 at isentropic exit — irreversibility raised outlet entropy and enthalpy.

steps.title: Exergy read
steps.desc: Lost work = T₀·S_gen; part of the 200 kJ/kg gap is that destruction.

payload.solution: η_turb ≈ 82% — the missing 18% of ideal work became irreversibility (plus any kinetic effects neglected).

payload.title: Throttling exergy
payload.prompt: A valve drops pressure with h_in = h_out. Where did the exergy go, and what is S_gen sign?
payload.hint: Throttling is isenthalpic, never isentropic for real gases/liquids with ΔP.

mistakes.mistake: Using the turbine efficiency formula for a compressor
mistakes.fix: Flip the ratio for work-input devices so η stays ≤ 1.

mistakes.mistake: Calling high First-law efficiency "good" without exergy context
mistakes.fix: A 90% turbine can still destroy huge exergy if the stream had high availability — check η_II.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define second-law (exergetic) efficiency and contrast it with First-law efficiency for a heat engine.
payload.answer: η_II = W_actual/W_rev_max (or exergy recovered/supplied). First-law η = W/Q_H ignores the quality of energy and the environment state; η_II accounts for how much of the available work potential was actually captured.
payload.source: Common conceptual question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: ΔS ≥ ∮δQ/T; isentropic process is the reversible adiabatic reference.
Turbine η = actual/isen; compressor η = isen/actual (both ≤ 1).
Availability Ψ/Helmholtz-Gibbs forms; irreversibility I = T₀S_gen.

questions.prompt: For a compressor, isentropic efficiency is:
questions.explanation: Inverted so η ≤ 1 for work-consuming devices.

questions.prompt: Irreversibility equals:
questions.explanation: Gouy–Stodola theorem.

questions.prompt: Throttling a real fluid through a valve results in:
questions.explanation: Irreversible pressure drop increases entropy.

lessons.title: Air-Standard Cycles: Otto, Diesel & Dual
lessons.summary: Mean effective pressure, compression ratio effects, efficiency formulas for Otto/Diesel/Dual, and how real IC engines deviate.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Derive and apply Otto and Diesel efficiency formulas from compression/expansion ratios
Compute MEP and compare cycles at equal displacement
Explain Dual cycle as the realistic spark/compression-ignition blend

payload.text: Raise the compression ratio of a petrol engine and efficiency climbs — until knock destroys the pistons. Diesel engines run higher ratios because they compress only air. The Otto/Diesel formulas are the mathematical version of that trade-off.

**Air-standard assumptions:** fixed air mass, closed cycle, combustion replaced by heat addition, exhaust by heat rejection, constant properties (often cold-air-standard with constant c_p, c_v, k).

**Otto cycle (spark ignition):** 1-2 isentropic compression (r = V₁/V₂), 2-3 constant-V heat addition, 3-4 isentropic expansion, 4-1 constant-V heat rejection.
η_Otto = 1 − 1/r^(k−1)

**Diesel cycle (compression ignition):** 1-2 isentropic compression, 2-3 constant-P heat addition (cutoff ratio r_c = V₃/V₂), 3-4 isentropic expansion, 4-1 constant-V rejection.
η_Diesel = 1 − (1/r^(k−1)) · (r_c^k − 1)/(k(r_c − 1))

**Dual (mixed) cycle:** constant-V then constant-P heat addition — closer to modern high-speed CI engines; efficiency between Otto and Diesel for same r.

**Mean effective pressure:** MEP = W_net / V_displaced (V₁ − V₂) — the "average push" on the piston; good for comparing engines of different size.

**Comparisons (same r, same heat addition):**
- Otto has the highest efficiency of the three (heat added at highest average T).
- Diesel at same r is slightly lower but real CI engines run higher r (no knock limit), so real Diesel often beats real Otto.
- Higher k (cooler gases) raises all efficiencies.

**Real deviations:** finite-time heat transfer, friction (FMEP), heat loss, incomplete combustion, blowdown losses — real η is well below air-standard.

payload.title: Cycle
rows: Between Otto and Diesel at same r

payload.title: Same r, compare instantly
payload.text: Otto ≥ Dual ≥ Diesel at identical compression ratio; remember Diesel recovers in practice via higher allowable r.

payload.title: Do not plug r_c into Otto
payload.text: Only Diesel/Dual use cutoff ratio — Otto's efficiency depends on r alone (air-standard).

payload.title: Otto efficiency and MEP
payload.problem: Petrol engine, r = 9, k = 1.4. Find η_Otto. If q_in = 800 kJ/kg, find w_net and MEP with v₁ = 0.8 m³/kg.

steps.title: MEP
steps.desc: MEP = w_net/Δv = 468/0.711 ≈ 658 kPa (≈ 6.6 bar) — a realistic petrol MEP order of magnitude.

steps.title: Reality check
steps.desc: Real engines land lower (30–40% net) due to friction, finite-time losses, real gas effects.

payload.solution: η ≈ 58.5%, w_net ≈ 468 kJ/kg, MEP ≈ 6.6 bar.

payload.title: Diesel cutoff effect
payload.prompt: At fixed r and k, what happens to η_Diesel as r_c → 1, and what does that limit become?
payload.hint: r_c → 1 collapses heat addition to a point — limit approaches Otto-like expression at constant P?

mistakes.mistake: Using compression ratio interchangeably with cutoff ratio
mistakes.fix: r = V_max/V_min over the full stroke; r_c = V₃/V₂ only spans the heat-addition leg.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting air-standard efficiencies as achievable engine efficiency
mistakes.fix: They are upper bounds on the idealized cycle — real engines subtract friction, heat loss, and finite-time effects.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Show that for the same compression ratio the Otto cycle is more efficient than the Diesel cycle, and explain why real Diesels still win at the pump.
payload.answer: At fixed r and heat input, Otto adds heat at the highest average temperature, maximizing η per Carnot-like reasoning; Diesel's constant-P leg spreads addition to lower T. In practice CI engines tolerate far higher r (no knock), which more than offsets the per-cycle penalty.
payload.source: Classic derivation + discussion question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Otto η = 1 − 1/r^(k−1); Diesel adds cutoff-ratio correction ≤ Otto at same r.
MEP normalizes work output across engine sizes.
Dual blends V+P heat addition; real engines fall short of all air-standard limits.

At the same compression ratio, which cycle is most efficient (air-standard)?
questions.explanation: Constant-V addition at highest T.

questions.explanation: Average effective pressure over the stroke.

lessons.title: Rankine Cycle & Improvements
lessons.summary: The steam power cycle: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser; why reheat and regeneration raise efficiency; dryness fraction limits.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Analyze the ideal Rankine cycle with steam-table enthalpies
Explain reheat and regeneration and compute cycle efficiency changes
Relate turbine outlet quality to blade erosion and design fixes

payload.text: Every thermal power plant on Earth — coal, nuclear, solar-thermal — runs a Rankine-family cycle. The boiler makes steam, the turbine extracts work, the condenser dumps heat, the pump sends water back. Understanding its four states is understanding the grid.

**Ideal Rankine cycle states:**
1 → 2: isentropic pump (subcooled liquid compressed)
2 → 3: constant-P heat addition in boiler (to superheated vapour)
3 → 4: isentropic turbine (work out; may end in wet region)
4 → 1: constant-P/constant-T heat rejection in condenser

**Energy balances (per kg):**
- w_turb = h₃ − h₄
- w_pump = v₁(P₂ − P₁) ≈ h₂ − h₁ (incompressible liquid approximation)
- q_in = h₃ − h₂
- q_out = h₄ − h₁
- η_Rankine = w_net/q_in = 1 − q_out/q_in

**Why Rankine beats a gas cycle at the same T limits:** phase change lets large q transfer nearly isothermally in the boiler/condenser, better matching the Carnot rectangle on T–s.

**Reheat:** expand in turbine to intermediate P, reheat to T_max, expand again. Raises mean temperature of heat addition AND outlet quality (less moisture erosion).

**Regeneration (feedwater heaters):** bleed steam at intermediate pressure to preheat feedwater before the boiler — raises average T of heat addition (closer to Carnot) at the cost of some turbine work. Open vs closed FWHs.

**Efficiency levers:** higher boiler P and T (until material limits), lower condenser P (better vacuum), reheat stages, more regeneration stages (with diminishing returns).

payload.title: Pump work is tiny — but not zero
payload.text: Liquid v is small so w_p is often < 2% of w_turb, yet skipping it breaks the energy balance.

payload.title: Outlet quality below ~0.88 hurts blades
payload.text: Wet droplets erode turbine blades — that is why reheat exists in real plants.

payload.title: Ideal Rankine efficiency
payload.problem: Boiler 3 MPa, 350°C; condenser 10 kPa. Using h values: h₃ = 3116 kJ/kg, s₃ = 6.745; at 10 kPa, s_f = 0.649, s_g = 8.150, h_f = 192, h_fg = 2392. Find η. (Ignore pump work for the first cut.)

steps.title: Efficiency
steps.desc: η ≈ 979/2924 ≈ 0.335 (33.5%) — typical ideal Rankine scale.

steps.title: Quality flag
steps.desc: x₄ ≈ 0.81 — below the comfort zone; real design would reheat.

payload.solution: η ≈ 33–34% ideal; outlet moisture ~19% motivates reheat.

payload.title: Reheat reasoning
payload.prompt: Explain two distinct benefits of reheat (one thermodynamic, one mechanical/reliability).
payload.hint: Think mean addition temperature AND droplet damage.

mistakes.mistake: Treating pump work as zero in exacting problems
mistakes.fix: Even if small, include w_p = v(P_boiler − P_cond) for complete bookkeeping and correct q_in.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing reheat with regeneration
mistakes.fix: Reheat = re-expand after reheating; regeneration = bleed to preheat feedwater. Different mechanisms.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: How do reheat and regeneration improve the Rankine cycle? State the primary mechanism of each.
payload.answer: Reheat raises the average temperature of heat addition and increases turbine outlet quality (reduces moisture). Regeneration preheats feedwater with bled steam, raising the mean heat-addition temperature closer to Carnot, improving efficiency at some turbine-work cost.
payload.source: Evergreen 6–8 mark question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Rankine four-state energy balance: w_t, w_p, q_in, q_out from enthalpies.
η = 1 − q_out/q_in; limited by mean addition/rejection temperatures.
Reheat fixes moisture + mean T; regeneration lifts mean T via bleed preheat.

questions.prompt: The Rankine cycle is preferred over a gas cycle at the same temperature limits mainly because:
options: Phase change allows large isothermal heat transfer
questions.explanation: Better T-s "rectangle" match.

questions.prompt: Primary mechanical reason for reheat is:
questions.explanation: Wetness damages blades.

questions.prompt: Regeneration improves efficiency by:
options: Raising mean temperature of heat addition via feedwater preheat
questions.explanation: Bled steam preheats feedwater.

lessons.title: Vapour-Compression Refrigeration & COP
lessons.summary: COP definitions, ideal and practical vapour-compression cycle, effect of superheat/subcooling, and refrigerant selection trade-offs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute COP_ref and COP_HP from cycle enthalpies and relate them
Analyze a practical vapour-compression cycle with superheat and subcooling
Explain why throttling dominates irreversibility in refrigeration

payload.text: Your fridge moves heat from 4°C to a 30°C kitchen every second it runs — "downhill" in temperature is exactly what the Second Law forbids without work. COP tells you how cheaply you buy that violation of intuition.

**COP definitions:**
- Refrigeration: COP_R = desired effect (Q_L) / work in = q_L/w_net
- Heat pump: COP_HP = Q_H/w_net = COP_R + 1 (same cycle, different accounting)
- Carnot bounds: COP_R,C = T_L/(T_H − T_L); COP_HP,C = T_H/(T_H − T_L) — use Kelvin.

**Ideal vapour-compression (4 devices):**
1 → 2: isentropic compression of saturated vapour (to superheated)
2 → 3: constant-P condensation to saturated liquid
3 → 4: isenthalpic throttling to low P (two-phase)
4 → 1: constant-P evaporation (absorb q_L)

**Practical refinements:**
- **Superheat at compressor inlet:** ensures dry compression (protects compressor); slight q_L increase.
- **Subcooling before throttle:** lowers h₃, increases q_L per kg, raises COP.
- **Throttling loss:** the big irreversibility — replacing the expansion valve with an expander/turbine recovers work and pre-cools the liquid (used in large systems).

**Why not a heat engine running backward "reversed Carnot"?** Real compressors cannot handle wet vapor (slugging) and finite-rate heat transfer forbids pure Carnot — hence the standard four-device layout.

**Refrigerants:** ammonia (high latent heat, toxic), R-134a (HFC, mobile/AC), CO₂ (transcritical, low-GWP trend). Ozone (CFC/HCFC) and GWP (HFC) regulations shape the modern list — HFOs and blends are the replacement wave.

payload.title: Term
rows: Vapor heated past sat. before/after compression
Liquid cooled below sat. before throttle

payload.title: Add 1, do not memorize twice
payload.text: If you have COP_R, COP_HP is just +1 for the same cycle — verify from enthalpies when in doubt.

payload.title: Kelvin in Carnot COP
payload.text: Using Celsius in T_L/(T_H−T_L) gives nonsense — always convert to absolute temperature.

payload.title: Vapor-compression COP
payload.problem: Refrigerant: h₁ = 400 (evap exit, sat vap), h₂ = 430 (compressor exit), h₃ = 250 (cond exit, sat liq), h₄ = h₃ after throttle. Find COP_R and COP_HP.

steps.title: First-law check
steps.desc: q_L + w = 150 + 30 = 180 = q_H ✓ (closed accounting).

steps.title: COP_R
steps.desc: COP_R = 150/30 = 5.0 — a strong domestic/commercial figure.

steps.title: Takeaway
steps.desc: Moving 150 units of heat costs only 30 units of work — heat pumps "create" useful heat from the environment at leveraged cost.

payload.solution: COP_R = 5, COP_HP = 6.

payload.title: Subcooling gain
payload.prompt: Explain why 5 K of liquid subcooling before the throttle increases q_L per kg, using the h–T diagram mentally.
payload.hint: Throttle is isenthalpic from a lower h₃.

mistakes.mistake: Using Celsius in Carnot COP
mistakes.fix: Convert to Kelvin — otherwise COP bounds are meaningless.

mistakes.mistake: Calling COP "efficiency" with a percentage mindset
mistakes.fix: COP routinely exceeds 1 (even 5–6) because it is a ratio of heat moved to work, not heat-to-heat.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Derive the relationship COP_HP = COP_R + 1 for a vapour-compression system and comment on typical COP magnitudes.
payload.answer: q_H = q_L + w by energy balance, so COP_HP = q_H/w = (q_L + w)/w = COP_R + 1. Typical COP_R ≈ 2–6 for practical systems — far above 1 because the environment supplies most of the moved heat.
payload.source: Standard derivation + discussion.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: COP_R = q_L/w; COP_HP = COP_R + 1; Carnot bounds need Kelvin.
Four-device vapour-compression; throttling is the dominant irreversibility.
Superheat protects compressors; subcooling boosts q_L and COP.

questions.explanation: COP_HP = COP_R + 1.

questions.explanation: Valve/expansion device: h constant, S increases.
