modules.title: Module 4 — Combustion, Mixtures & Psychrometrics
modules.summary: Air-fuel ratios, stoichiometric/actual combustion analysis, adiabatic flame temperature, and psychrometric properties for HVAC.

lessons.title: Combustion & Air-Fuel Analysis
lessons.summary: Theoretical vs actual air, excess air, combustion equation balancing, and adiabatic flame temperature reasoning.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Balance hydrocarbon combustion equations and find stoichiometric AFR
Interpret excess air and leftover O₂/N₂ in product gas analysis
Reason about adiabatic flame temperature and its engineering limits

payload.text: A gas turbine that runs lean (excess air) stays cooler and makes fewer NOx; run too lean and it flames out. Every combustor designer lives on the air-fuel ratio line — and that line starts with balancing one combustion equation.

**Stoichiometric combustion (general hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ):**
CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4) O₂ → x CO₂ + (y/2) H₂O

**Fuel-specific anchors:**
- Methane CH₄: CH₄ + 2(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 7.52 N₂
- Propane C₃H₈: C₃H₈ + 5(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O + 18.8 N₂
- Octane C₈H₁₈ (gasoline surrogate): 2C₈H₁₈ + 25(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O + 94 N₂

**Air-fuel ratio:**
- Stoichiometric AFR_stoich = m_air/m_fuel at exactly enough O₂.
- Actual AFR; equivalence ratio φ = (A/F)_actual/(A/F)_stoich. φ > 1 rich, φ < 1 lean.
- Percent theoretical air = 100% × (moles O₂ actual)/(moles O₂ stoich); excess air = that − 100%.

**Rich vs lean products:**
- Lean: leftover O₂ in products, CO₂ and H₂O as calculated, plus extra N₂.
- Stoichiometric: only CO₂, H₂O, N₂ (complete combustion idealization).
- Rich: incomplete — CO, unburned H₂/hydrocarbons appear; less O₂ available than demanded.

**Adiabatic flame temperature (AFT):** temperature if combustion ran with Q = 0 (no heat loss) starting from reactants at 25°C. Higher AFT with:
- Higher initial T (preheat/turbocharging effect)
- Higher calorific value fuel
- Less inert dilution (less excess air/N₂) — pure O₂ flames run hottest
- Dissociation at extreme T lowers the theoretical ceiling (energy goes into breaking CO₂/H₂O)

**Heating values:** HHV includes latent heat of water vaporization in products; LHV excludes it (common in gas-turbine work).

payload.title: Term
rows: Air/fuel mass ratio at exact O₂ demand
With vs without water condensation latent heat

payload.title: N₂ rides along everywhere
payload.text: Air is ~21% O₂, 79% N₂ by mole — include 3.76 N₂ per O₂ in every balanced equation or product masses will be wrong.

payload.title: Rich combustion is not "more power only"
payload.text: It wastes fuel and emits CO/HC — modern engines target stoichiometric or lean with aftertreatment.

payload.title: Stoichiometric methane AFR
payload.problem: CH₄ combustion in air. Find mole-based AFR and mass-based AFR_stoich. M_CH₄ ≈ 16, M_air ≈ 29 kg/kmol.

steps.title: Balanced equation
steps.desc: CH₄ + 2(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 7.52 N₂.

steps.title: Moles of air
steps.desc: Per mol fuel: 2 O₂ + 7.52 N₂ = 9.52 mol air.

steps.title: Mole AFR
steps.desc: AFR_mol = 9.52/1 = 9.52 mol air per mol CH₄.

steps.title: Mass AFR
steps.desc: m_air = 9.52 × 29 ≈ 276; m_fuel = 16 ⇒ AFR_stoich ≈ 276/16 ≈ 17.2 (≈ 17.2 kg air/kg methane).

steps.title: Sanity
steps.desc: Matches the known ~17:1 for methane — good memory check for exams.

payload.solution: AFR_stoich ≈ 17.2 kg air per kg CH₄ (9.52 mol basis).

payload.title: Excess air products
payload.prompt: Combustion with 150% theoretical air: where does the extra O₂ end up, and what happens to N₂ moles vs stoichiometric?
payload.hint: 50% extra O₂ plus proportional extra N₂ dilutes products.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting N₂ from air in product calculations
mistakes.fix: N₂ is inert but massive — it dominates product mass and lowers flame temperature.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up φ > 1 with lean
mistakes.fix: φ > 1 means MORE fuel than stoich (rich); lean is φ < 1 or % theoretical air > 100.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define excess air and explain its effect on combustion product composition and flame temperature.
payload.answer: Excess air = percent oxygen supplied above stoichiometric. It adds leftover O₂ and extra N₂ to products, dilutes the flame, lowers adiabatic flame temperature (good for NOx control and turbine inlet limits) but can reduce combustion efficiency if excessive.
payload.source: Common short/long question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Balance CₓHᵧ with (x + y/4) O₂; carry 3.76 N₂ per O₂ for air.
φ and % theoretical air describe rich/lean; rich → CO, lean → leftover O₂.
AFT rises with preheat and fuel heating value, falls with dilution and dissociation.

questions.prompt: For lean combustion (excess air), products contain:
options: Leftover O₂ plus CO₂, H₂O, N₂
questions.explanation: Extra oxygen remains after reaction.

questions.prompt: Equivalence ratio φ > 1 indicates:
questions.explanation: More fuel than stoichiometric demand.

questions.prompt: Adiabatic flame temperature is highest with:
questions.explanation: Less inert dilution + higher initial enthalpy.

lessons.title: Psychrometrics: Moist Air & HVAC
lessons.summary: Humidity ratio, relative humidity, dew point, dry- and wet-bulb temperatures, and simple heating/cooling/dehumidification processes on the psychrometric chart.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute humidity ratio and relative humidity from partial pressures
Identify standard HVAC processes (sensible heating, cooling, dehumidify, humidify) on a psych chart
Apply the moist-air energy balance (ṁ_a·Δh) for coil and room calculations

payload.text: Every air conditioner is a psychrometric problem in a metal box: know the room's humidity ratio, know the coil's exit state, and the tonnage follows from one enthalpy difference. Comfort engineering is applied thermodynamics with a chart.

**Moist air = dry air + water vapor (treated as ideal-gas mixture):**
- Total P = P_a (dry air) + P_v (vapor); P_v = φ·P_g(T), where P_g = P_sat(T).
- **Humidity ratio (absolute humidity):** ω = m_v/m_a = 0.622·P_v/(P − P_v) kg vapor/kg dry air.
- **Relative humidity:** φ = P_v/P_g (0–100%) — how "full" the air is vs saturation at that T.
- **Dew point:** temperature at which current P_v becomes P_sat — cooling below it causes condensation.
- **Dry-bulb:** thermometer reading; **wet-bulb:** cooled by evaporation — depression indicates dryness.
- **Humid volume, enthalpy:** h ≈ c_pa·T + ω·(h_g° + c_pv·T) — charts tabulate h and ω.

**Chart processes (slope intuition):**
- Sensible heating: right along constant ω (T up, φ down).
- Sensible cooling: left along constant ω until dew point, then follow saturation + condensation.
- Dehumidification: cool below dew point (coil) — ω and T both drop; may reheat for comfort.
- humidification: add vapor (up on chart).

**Coil/room energy balance (steady):**
ṁ_a(h_out − h_in) = q̇ ( sensible-only approx: ṁ_a c_p ΔT ).
Moisture balance: ṁ_a(ω_out − ω_in) = ṁ_v added/removed.

**Comfort & design:** summer AC ~ 24°C, 50% RH; ASHRAE charts drive coil selection; latent vs sensible split determines if you need a bigger coil or a dehumidifier.

payload.title: Dry-air basis keeps balances clean
payload.text: All ω, ṁ_a bookkeeping is per kg of DRY air — moisture is the passenger, not the base.

payload.title: RH is temperature-dependent
payload.text: Same ω at higher T = lower RH — do not treat RH as an absolute moisture measure; use ω for mass balances.

payload.title: Humidity ratio from partial pressure
payload.problem: At 30°C, P_sat ≈ 4.24 kPa, P = 101.3 kPa, φ = 60%. Find P_v, ω, and dew point.

steps.title: Dew point
steps.desc: Find T where P_sat(T) = 2.55 kPa — between ~20–22°C (from steam table: ~21.5°C). Cool below this and condensation starts.

steps.title: Comfort read
steps.desc: ω ≈ 16 g/kg is a typical summer outdoor value; cooling coil must condense down to ~10 g/kg for comfort.

steps.title: Balance use
steps.desc: Room load: ṁ_a·Δh sets coil capacity; ω drop sets dehumidification duty.

payload.solution: P_v ≈ 2.55 kPa, ω ≈ 0.0161, dew point ≈ 21.5°C.

payload.title: Chart sketch
payload.prompt: Sketch (describe) the path for: (a) sensible heating, (b) cooling with dehumidification on a summer coil.
payload.hint: Constant ω right; saturation line then left-down for (b).

mistakes.mistake: Using relative humidity in mass/energy balances
mistakes.fix: Convert to ω (humidity ratio) — balances are per kg dry air with absolute moisture content.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting latent load in AC sizing
mistakes.fix: Total coil load = sensible + latent; humid climates are latent-dominated.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define humidity ratio and relative humidity, and explain why humidity ratio is used in energy/mass balances.
payload.answer: Humidity ratio ω = m_v/m_a (kg vapor per kg dry air); relative humidity φ = P_v/P_g(T). Balances use ω because dry air mass is conserved through coils/processes and moisture transfer is proportional to absolute, not relative, content.
payload.source: Core psychrometrics question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Moist air as ideal-gas mixture; ω and φ from P_v and P_g(T).
Dew point = saturation of current vapor pressure; crossing it condenses water.
HVAC processes read as paths on the psych chart; balances use dry-air basis.

questions.prompt: Humidity ratio ω is defined as:
options: Mass of vapor per mass of dry air
Mass of vapor per total mass
questions.explanation: Dry-air denominator.

questions.prompt: Cooling air below its dew point causes:
questions.explanation: Vapor crosses saturation and condenses.

questions.prompt: In psychrometric energy balances, the base mass is:
questions.explanation: ṁ_a·Δh with dry-air flow.

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics
courses.subtitle: Fluid statics, Bernoulli, flow measurement, momentum forces, pipe losses, dimensional analysis and open-channel flow — ME exam + interview core
courses.description:
Fluid Mechanics underpins civil, mechanical and ocean engineering, and it is a favourite of core placement interviews. This course compresses the standard syllabus into eight compact lessons: the hydrostatic law with manometers, hydrostatic force and centre of pressure, buoyancy with metacentre stability, flow kinematics and the Bernoulli equation, venturi/orifice flow measurement, the momentum equation with jet and pipe-bend forces, Darcy–Weisbach pipe losses with the Moody diagram, and dimensional analysis plus open-channel flow with hydraulic jumps.

Every lesson uses the nine-block structure (objectives, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam angle, graded quiz, summary). A 30-question bank feeds a 15-question timed final. Passing earns a verifiable TieEdu certificate.

**Who this is for:** ME/CE students in semester 3–5 preparing for university exams, GATE ME/CE fundamentals, and placement interviews that ask fluid-mechanics questions.

**What you need:** pen and paper, a scientific calculator, and the ability to sketch control volumes and free-body diagrams.
outcomes: Apply the hydrostatic law and compute forces/centres of pressure on submerged surfaces
Analyze floating-body stability with metacentre height and rigid-body acceleration
Use Bernoulli and continuity for Pitot, venturi and orifice problems
Apply the momentum equation to jets, vanes and pipe-bend reaction forces
Compute Darcy–Weisbach major and minor losses and read the Moody diagram
Derive Pi groups with the Buckingham theorem and state similitude rules
Classify open-channel flow and size hydraulic jumps with conjugate depths
courses.about_course:
University fluid-mechanics papers reward a disciplined method: fix the control volume or fluid column, choose the governing equation (hydrostatics, Bernoulli, momentum, or Darcy), apply continuity where velocities couple, and check the dimensionless regime (Re, Fr) before trusting an idealized formula. This course drills that method across statics, measurement, forces, pipe flow and open channels.

The momentum and open-channel lessons are written for people who will design real systems: jet forces size Pelton buckets, Darcy losses size pumps, and hydraulic jumps size stilling basins at the foot of every spillway. The dimensional-analysis lesson closes with the model-testing logic interviewers expect when they ask "how would you test this at 1:50 scale?".

The final exam draws from a 30-question bank; the certificate project is a small flow-system analysis you can show as proof of skill.
prerequisites: Basic calculus and algebra
Introductory physics (forces, pressure, energy)
audience: ME/CE students facing university fluid-mechanics exams
GATE ME/CE aspirants building flow-analysis fundamentals
Placement candidates preparing for core mechanical/civil interview rounds
Hydraulics and piping beginners who want the method to click
courses.branch_label: Mechanical / Civil / Ocean core (also useful for Production)

exam_prep.target: University mid-terms and finals; GATE ME/CE core; placement fluid-mechanics rounds

units.title: Fluid Statics & Buoyancy
units.summary: Hydrostatic law dp/dz = −ρg; p = p₀ + ρgh; absolute/gauge/vacuum; manometer column walking. Plane-surface force F = p_c A; centre of pressure y_cp = y_c + I/(y_c A); vertical rectangle 2h/3. Archimedes F_B = ρ_f g V_disp; floating equilibrium; metacentre M, BM = I/V, GM > 0 stability. Rigid-body acceleration: surface slope a_x/g, g_eff = g ± a_z.
questions: Force + centre of pressure on a submerged rectangular gate.
Stability check with GM for a floating box.
Manometer pressure balance.
Effect of vertical acceleration on fluid pressure.

units.title: Kinematics, Bernoulli & Measurement
units.summary: Material derivative a = ∂V/∂t + (V·∇)V; streamlines/pathlines/streaklines coincide only in steady flow. Bernoulli p/ρg + V²/2g + z along a streamline (steady, inviscid, incompressible); add H_p, H_t, h_L. Pitot: V = √(2Δp/ρ). Venturi/orifice/nozzle: Q = C_d A₂ V₂,th with V₂ from Bernoulli + continuity; manometer Δp/ρg = h(SG − 1).
questions: Pitot airspeed from stagnation pressure.
Venturi discharge with mercury manometer reading.
When Bernoulli fails (jumps, machines, rotational flow).
Convective acceleration in a nozzle.

units.title: Momentum & Pipe Flow
units.summary: ΣF = ṁ(V_out − V_in); jet on flat plate F = ρAV²; moving vane uses V − u; Pelton max power at u = V/2. Pipe bend anchoring forces via CV + gauge pressure. Re = VD/ν; laminar f = 64/Re; Darcy–Weisbach h_f = f(L/D)V²/2g; Colebrook/Moody for turbulent; minor h_m = K V²/2g; hydraulic diameter 4A/P.
questions: Jet force on plate / moving bucket.
Pipe bend reaction force.
Moody-based head loss for a steel line.
Series vs parallel pipe reasoning.

units.title: Dimensional Analysis & Open Channel
units.summary: Buckingham Pi: (n − k) groups; Re, Fr, We, Ma, Eu. Similitude: geometric, kinematic, dynamic; ships match Fr, correct Re. Open channel: Fr = V/√(gD) with D = A/T; specific energy E = y + V²/(2g); critical depth y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}; hydraulic jump conjugate depths y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1); ΔE = (y₂−y₁)³/(4y₁y₂).
questions: Derive C_D = f(Re) via Buckingham Pi.
Jump sizing: y₂, energy loss from given y₁, V₁.
Critical depth and regime classification.
Model-law choice (Re vs Fr) for a spillway vs a ship.

important_questions: Hydrostatic force and centre-of-pressure derivation for a plane surface.
Metacentre and GM stability criterion with a numerical floating-body example.
Bernoulli assumptions and a complete venturi/orifice discharge derivation.
Momentum-equation jet-force derivation and Pelton moving-vane extension.
Darcy–Weisbach + Colebrook/Moody for turbulent pipe friction.
Buckingham Pi worked example (drag or open-channel wave speed).
Hydraulic-jump conjugate-depth derivation and energy-loss formula.
Re vs Fr model-law selection for different hydraulic structures.

previous_year_questions.question: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge 1 m below the free surface of water. Determine the hydrostatic force on the gate and the position of the centre of pressure from the free surface.
previous_year_questions.solution: Centroid at y_c = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 m; A = 6 m²; F = ρg y_c A = 1000×9.81×2.5×6 ≈ 147.2 kN. I_xx,c = bh³/12 = 2×27/12 = 4.5 m⁴; y_cp = y_c + I/(y_c A) = 2.5 + 4.5/(2.5×6) = 2.8 m below the free surface (0.3 m below the centroid).

previous_year_questions.question: Water flows in a 100 mm commercial-steel pipe (ε = 0.045 mm) at 2 m/s for 50 m. ν = 1×10⁻⁶ m²/s. Find the Darcy friction factor and major head loss.
A rectangular channel carries water with y₁ = 0.3 m and V₁ = 6 m/s. If a hydraulic jump forms, find the downstream depth y₂ and the energy lost across the jump. g = 9.81 m/s².

project.title: Flow-system analysis note
project.brief: Pick one real or well-specified flow system (a pump-fed pipe line, a tank-orifice or venturi measurement, a jet-driven impulse turbine stage, or an open-channel section with a jump) and analyze it in a markdown/PDF notebook: (1) define the system, draw/list the control volume or fluid column and list assumptions; (2) identify the dominant dimensionless regime (Re, Fr) and justify the equations you choose (hydrostatics, Bernoulli, momentum, Darcy–Weisbach); (3) compute pressures, velocities, forces, head losses or conjugate depths step-by-step with units; (4) perform one sanity check (e.g. energy grade line trend, GM stability, or Fr classification before/after a jump); (5) suggest one design improvement (diameter change, meter choice, roughness reduction, jump dissipator sizing) and quantify its effect if possible. Include diagrams or calculator output as an appendix.
project.submission_hint: PDF, public markdown, or a GitHub link — hand sketches photographed are fine; the control-volume choice and unit discipline matter more than production polish.

modules.title: Module 1 — Fluid Statics
modules.summary: Pressure variation with depth, manometers, Pascal's law, buoyancy (Archimedes), and hydrostatic forces on plane and curved surfaces.

lessons.title: Pressure, Manometers & Hydrostatic Force
lessons.summary: The hydrostatic law, absolute vs gauge pressure, piezometric head, and computing resultant force + centre of pressure on submerged plane surfaces.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply the hydrostatic law to find pressure at any depth in a static fluid
Distinguish absolute, gauge and vacuum pressure; compute with manometers
Locate the centre of pressure and resultant hydrostatic force on a plane surface

payload.text: A dam wall two metres thick at the base and a submarine hull a few centimetres thick obey the same pressure-versus-depth law. Get the hydrostatic integral wrong and the structure fails; get it right and you can design tanks, manometers and hydraulic presses with the same three lines of algebra.

**Hydrostatic law:** dp/dz = −ρg (z measured upward). For constant ρ:
- p = p₀ + ρgh (pressure increases with depth)
- Two points at the same elevation in a connected static fluid of the same density have the same pressure (Pascal / hydrostatic paradox).

**Pressure measures:**
- Absolute: p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge
- Vacuum: p_vac = p_atm − p_abs when p_abs < p_atm (quoted as positive)
- Piezometric head: p/(ρg) + z = constant along a vertical in a static fluid — the workhorse of groundwater and manometer problems.

**Manometers:** balance pressure columns. U-tube with a gauge fluid of density ρ_m: walk from one leg to the other adding ρgh when descending, subtracting when ascending, set equal at the end.

**Hydrostatic force on a plane submerged surface:**
- Resultant magnitude: F = p_c × A, where p_c is pressure at the centroid of the submerged area A (works even if the surface is not horizontal, for constant Ϸ).
- Centre of pressure (where the resultant effectively acts): for a rectangular gate of width b hinged along the top edge submerged to depth h₁ with height h₂ below the hinge:
  y_cp = y_c + I_xx,c/(y_c × A)
  where y is measured along the surface from the free surface, y_c is centroid distance, I_xx,c is second moment about the centroidal axis parallel to the free surface.
- For a vertical rectangle from the surface: y_cp = (2/3)×height — always below the centroid, because pressure grows with depth.

**Curved surfaces:** resolve into horizontal component (force on the vertical projection, acting at its centroid-pressure point) and vertical component (weight of the fluid column above the curved surface, real or imaginary).

payload.title: Centroid shortcut for symmetric gates
payload.text: For a full-width rectangle whose top edge is at the free surface, y_c = h/2 and y_cp = 2h/3 — memorise the 2/3 result; the integral derivation is the proof.

payload.title: Never use surface-average pressure on a tilted gate
payload.text: F = p_c × A is exact for constant ρ, but the centre of pressure is NOT the centroid unless the surface is horizontal.

payload.title: Rectangular gate force and centre of pressure
payload.problem: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide × 3 m high has its top edge 1 m below the free surface of water. Find F and y_cp (from the surface).

steps.title: Centroid depth
steps.desc: Gate spans depth 1 m to 4 m; centroid at y_c = 1 + 3/2 = 2.5 m.

steps.title: Second moment
steps.desc: I_xx,c = b h³/12 = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴ (about centroidal axis parallel to surface).

steps.title: Centre of pressure
steps.desc: y_cp = y_c + I_xx,c/(y_c A) = 2.5 + 4.5/(2.5 × 6) = 2.5 + 0.3 = 2.8 m below the surface.

steps.title: Sanity
steps.desc: y_cp > y_c as expected (always below centroid for pressure growing with depth).

payload.solution: F ≈ 147 kN; centre of pressure at 2.8 m below the free surface (0.3 m below the centroid).

payload.title: Inverted gate
payload.prompt: Same gate but with its BOTTOM edge at the free surface (extending upward is impossible — so flip: bottom edge just below surface, extending downward 3 m). Where is y_cp relative to the centroid now vs the previous case?
payload.hint: Top edge at 0, bottom at 3 m — compute y_c and compare.

mistakes.mistake: Using p = ρgh with h measured from the bottom of the tank
mistakes.fix: h is always depth below the FREE SURFACE (or the piezometric reference) — fix the datum first.

mistakes.mistake: Setting y_cp = y_c for a vertical or tilted gate
mistakes.fix: Only a horizontal surface has y_cp = y_c; everywhere else the deeper, higher-pressure part pulls the resultant down.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define centre of pressure and state why it does not coincide with the centroid of a vertical submerged plane.
payload.answer: Centre of pressure is the point where the resultant hydrostatic force effectively acts. For a vertical surface, pressure increases linearly with depth, so the lower half contributes more force than the upper half, shifting the resultant below the centroid (y_cp = y_c + I_xx,c/(y_c A) > y_c).
payload.source: Standard definition + reasoning question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: dp/dz = −ρg; p = p₀ + ρgh with h from the free surface.
F on a plane = p_c × A; y_cp always ≥ y_c for non-horizontal surfaces.
Curved surfaces decompose into horizontal (projected vertical area) + vertical (fluid weight) components.

questions.explanation: Classic 2/3 result — below the centroid.

lessons.title: Buoyancy, Stability & Fluid Acceleration
lessons.summary: Archimedes' principle, metacentre height and floating-body stability, and fluid acceleration (rigid-body motion) including the horizontal barometer effect.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply Archimedes' principle to find buoyant force and equilibrium draft
Explain metacentre, GM and the stability criterion for floating bodies
Compute pressure variation in a fluid accelerating horizontally or vertically

payload.text: Why does a steel ship float while a steel cube sinks? Archimedes answers "why it floats"; the metacentre answers "why it does not capsize". Every naval architecture and offshore engineering problem starts with these two ideas.

**Archimedes' principle:** the buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced, acting upward through the centre of buoyancy (centroid of the displaced volume).
- Floating equilibrium: Weight of body = weight of displaced fluid; solve for draft/displaced volume.
- Submerged completely: if ρ_body > ρ_fluid, it sinks (needs external force or a hollow hull to reduce average density).

**Floating stability — metacentre:**
- Centre of buoyancy B; as the body heels by a small angle θ, B moves to B′.
- Metacentre M: the point where the new vertical through B′ intersects the original centreline.
- BM = I/V_displaced, where I is the second moment of the waterplane area about the tilt axis.
- GM = MB (distance from M to the centre of gravity G, measured positive upward from G).
- **Stable if GM > 0** (M above G); neutral if GM = 0; unstable (capsizes) if GM < 0.
- Large BM (wide waterplane) or low G (ballast low, tall structures top-heavy) — the design levers.

**Rigid-body fluid acceleration:**
- Horizontal acceleration a_x: free surface tilts, dp/dx = −ρa_x, dp/dz = −ρ(g). Resultant surface slope: tan α = a_x/g (surface normal leans opposite the acceleration).
- Vertical acceleration a_z: effective gravity g_eff = g ± a_z; p = ρ(g ± a_z)h — a lift accelerating upward increases apparent weight/pressure; free fall (a_z = −g) makes the fluid weightless (p = 0 inside).

**Relative equilibrium:** fluid at rest relative to an accelerating container — use a coordinate system attached to the container and replace g with g_eff = g − a (vector subtraction).

payload.title: Ballast low, structures high
payload.text: Lowering G (heavy keel) or widening the waterplane (raising I, hence BM) both increase GM and improve stability.

payload.title: GM > 0 is necessary but not the whole story
payload.text: Large-angle stability (GZ curves) matters in real ships; GM is the small-angle (initial) stability measure exam problems test.

payload.title: Floating box draft and metacentre
payload.problem: A rectangular box 3 m × 2 m × 1 m high (horizontal base 3×2) floats in water (ρ = 1000), total mass 4000 kg, G at 0.4 m above the base. Find draft and GM.

steps.title: Displaced volume
steps.desc: V = 6 × 0.667 ≈ 4 m³; B is at d/2 = 0.333 m above the base (centroid of displaced prism).

steps.title: Metacentric radius
steps.desc: I about the tilt axis (through centroid of waterplane 3×2, tilting about the 2-m-wide axis): I = (2 × 3³)/12 = 4.5 m⁴. BM = I/V = 4.5/4 = 1.125 m.

steps.title: M height
steps.desc: M is 1.125 m above B: height of M above base = 0.333 + 1.125 = 1.458 m.

steps.title: GM
steps.desc: G at 0.4 m above base: GM = 1.458 − 0.4 = +1.058 m > 0 — stable.

payload.solution: Draft ≈ 0.67 m; BM ≈ 1.13 m; GM ≈ +1.06 m — initially stable floating body.

payload.title: Top-heavy check
payload.prompt: If the same box's centre of gravity rises to 1.5 m above the base, what happens to GM and the stability verdict?
payload.hint: M height unchanged (depends on B and I only); compare to new G.

mistakes.mistake: Measuring GM from the waterline instead of from G
mistakes.fix: GM = (height of M) − (height of G) — both measured from a common datum such as the keel/base.

mistakes.mistake: Using g in a vertically accelerating lift problem
mistakes.fix: Replace with g_eff = g ± a_z; upward acceleration increases apparent fluid density/pressure effects.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define metacentre and state the small-angle stability criterion for a floating body.
payload.answer: The metacentre M is the point where the vertical through the shifted buoyancy centre B′ (after a small heel angle) intersects the original centreline. For small angles, the body is stable if M lies above G, i.e. GM > 0; it returns to upright. If GM < 0 the couple after a small tilt capsizes the body.
payload.source: Evergreen naval-architecture / FM short question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: F_B = ρ_fluid g V_disp; floating bodies displace their own weight.
BM = I/V_disp; stable ⇔ GM = (height of M) − (height of G) > 0.
Accelerating fluids: tilt the surface (a_x/g) or scale g with a_z.

questions.prompt: A body floats in equilibrium when:
options: Buoyant force equals the weight of the body
Buoyant force equals the weight of the body's material only
Density of body equals density of fluid always
questions.explanation: Weight of displaced fluid = total weight of body.

questions.prompt: A floating body is (initially) stable when:
questions.explanation: Small-angle stability criterion.

questions.prompt: In rigid-body horizontal acceleration a_x, the free surface slope satisfies:
questions.explanation: Surface normal leans opposite the acceleration vector.

modules.title: Module 2 — Kinematics & Bernoulli
modules.summary: Velocity and acceleration fields, streamlines/pathlines, flow nets, and the Bernoulli equation with applications to orifices, venturimeters and Pitot tubes.

lessons.title: Flow Kinematics & the Bernoulli Equation
lessons.summary: Eulerian description, material acceleration, streamline vs pathline, irrotational flow, and deriving/using Bernoulli along a streamline with losses.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute convective and local acceleration from a velocity field
Distinguish streamline, pathline and streakline; state when they coincide
Apply Bernoulli between two points with head-loss terms correctly

payload.text: Bernoulli's equation is the fluid-mechanics analogue of energy conservation — but it only holds along a streamline in steady, inviscid, incompressible flow. Interviewers love asking where it breaks (across a shock, through a pump, with friction), and that is exactly where the marks are.

**Eulerian vs Lagrangian:** Eulerian watches a fixed control volume (velocity field V(x,y,z,t)); Lagrangian follows fluid particles. Most engineering analysis is Eulerian.

**Velocity field and acceleration (material derivative):**
a = dV/dt = ∂V/∂t + (V·∇)V
- Local (unsteady) term: ∂V/∂t
- Convective term: (V·∇)V — nonzero even in steady flow if the path is not a straight line of uniform velocity (e.g. flow through a nozzle).

**Streamlines:** curves tangent to V at an instant; dx/u = dy/v = dz/w. Pathlines: actual particle histories. Streaklines: loci of particles that passed through a fixed point (dye/smoke injection).
- Steady flow ⇒ all three coincide. Unsteady ⇒ they diverge.

**Rotational vs irrotational:** fluid particle spinning about its own axis. Irrotational (vorticity = 0) is the assumption that unlocks velocity potentials — ideal for external flow around bodies.

**Bernoulli (steady, incompressible, inviscid, along a streamline):**
p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = constant = total (Bernoulli) head
- p/ρg = pressure head; V²/2g = velocity head; z = elevation head.
- Between two points with a pump (head added H_p), turbine (removed H_t) and losses (h_L):
  p₁/(ρg) + V₁²/(2g) + z₁ + H_p − H_t − h_L = p₂/(ρg) + V₂²/(2g) + z₂

**When Bernoulli breaks:** across a hydraulic jump or normal shock (finite losses), through regions with viscosity boundary layers (total head drops), between different streamlines in rotational flow (each streamline has its own constant).

**Applications:**
- Orifice/venturi: derive velocity from a pressure drop (Q = C_d A √(2Δh) style).
- Pitot-static tube: stagnation point V = 0 gives V = √(2(p₀ − p)/(ρ)) = √(2gh).
- Free jet from a tank: Torricelli V = √(2gh).

payload.title: Head term
rows: sum of the three (constant on a streamline)

payload.title: Always pick a datum for z
payload.text: Set z = 0 at the most convenient point (usually the lower port or free surface) so the elevation term disappears cleanly.

payload.title: Bernoulli ≠ energy equation for machines
payload.text: Across pumps/turbines include H_p/H_t explicitly or use the full steady-flow energy equation with shaft work.

payload.title: Pitot tube airspeed
payload.problem: A Pitot-static probe in air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) measures (p₀ − p) = 300 Pa. Find the flow velocity.

steps.title: Stagnation point
steps.desc: At the probe nose, V₂ = 0; Bernoulli along the streamline: p₁/(ρ) + V₁²/2 = p₂/(ρ) + 0.

steps.title: Compressibility check
steps.desc: Mach ≈ 22.36/340 ≈ 0.066 « 0.3 — incompressible assumption valid.

steps.title: Practical note
steps.desc: Real probes need a calibration factor C_d near 1; formula above is ideal.

payload.solution: V ≈ 22.4 m/s from the stagnation-pressure difference.

payload.title: Nozzle convective acceleration
payload.prompt: Steady 1-D flow through a shrinking nozzle: does the material acceleration have a nonzero convective term? Explain without numbers.
payload.hint: V changes along the path even though ∂V/∂t = 0.

mistakes.mistake: Applying one Bernoulli constant across different streamlines in rotational flow
mistakes.fix: Each streamline has its own constant in rotational flow; only irrotational flow gives a domain-wide constant.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting h_L when the problem mentions pipe friction or a long duct
mistakes.fix: Real pipes always lose head; only "negligible friction" exam setups drop h_L.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the assumptions behind Bernoulli's equation and one engineering application.
payload.answer: Steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, valid along a streamline (or across the whole field if additionally irrotational). Application examples: Pitot-static airspeed (stagnation pressure), venturi flow measurement, orifice/tank efflux (Torricelli).
payload.source: Standard assumptions + application question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Acceleration = local ∂V/∂t + convective (V·∇)V.
Streamline = pathline = streakline only in steady flow.
Bernoulli: p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant along a streamline (with H_p/H_t/h_L as needed).

questions.explanation: Time-independence collapses all three.

lessons.title: Flow Measurement: Venturi, Orifice & Nozzles
lessons.summary: Differential-pressure flow meters, discharge coefficients, and sizing orifice/venturi problems with manometer readings.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Derive the theoretical discharge through a venturi or orifice from Bernoulli + continuity
Use the discharge coefficient C_d correctly in practice problems
Compare venturi (low loss) vs orifice (cheap, high loss) meter trade-offs

payload.text: A venturi meter in a water main can meter municipal supply to ±1% while wasting almost no pressure; an orifice plate costs a fraction of that but eats head for breakfast. Choosing between them is a pure engineering-economics decision anchored in two applications of Bernoulli.

**Differential pressure meters — the common thread:**
1. Bernoulli between the upstream (1) and throat/vena-contracta (2) along a horizontal streamline: p₁ + ½ρV₁² = p₂ + ½ρV₂².
2. Continuity: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ ⇒ V₁ = (A₂/A₁)V₂.
3. Solve for V₂: V₂ = √[2(p₁ − p₂)/(ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²))]
4. Actual discharge: Q_actual = C_d A₂ V₂,th where C_d accounts for real losses and contraction.

**Venturi meter:** gradual convergence then slow diffuser — C_d ≈ 0.95–0.98, very low permanent head loss (most pressure recovered in the diffuser). Used when downstream head matters (water distribution).

**Orifice meter:** thin plate with a sharp-edged hole; vena contracta forms downstream. C_d ≈ 0.6–0.65 (area ratio dependent). Cheap, easy to install, but large permanent pressure loss (~60–80% of Δp is not recovered).

**Nozzle meter:** between the two — C_d ≈ 0.96, moderate loss, robust for dirty fluids.

**Manometer reading:** for a U-tube with gauge fluid ρ_m between the two taps:
(p₁ − p₂)/(ρg) = h(ρ_m/ρ − 1) — the classic (SG − 1)h form. Substitute into the discharge formula for Q in terms of manometer deflection h.

**Pitot-static (already seen):** velocity at a point, not a full-line discharge — V = √(2Δp/ρ).

payload.title: Always square-root the pressure term
payload.text: Discharge goes as √Δp — doubling the flow roughly quadruples the manometer reading; exam questions test this scaling constantly.

payload.title: Do not forget the (1 − β⁴) contraction term
payload.text: β = d₂/d₁; omitting (1 − β⁴) under the radical is only valid for d₂ « d₁ (e.g. large tank drain).

payload.title: Venturi discharge from manometer reading
payload.problem: Horizontal water venturi: d₁ = 100 mm, d₂ = 50 mm, mercury manometer reads 150 mm. C_d = 0.98, ρ_Hg = 13600, ρ_w = 1000. Find Q.
payload.solution: Q ≈ 0.012 m³/s (12 L/s) with the venturi contraction and discharge coefficient applied.

payload.title: Orifice vs venturi loss
payload.prompt: Same Δp and throat size: which passes more flow (before permanent loss), and which wastes more downstream pressure? Explain.
payload.hint: C_d differences vs permanent recovery.

mistakes.mistake: Using throat AREA without the discharge coefficient for real flow
mistakes.fix: Q_actual = C_d × A × V_theoretical; skipping C_d is only OK for ideal-theory questions.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing mm and m in the manometer term
mistakes.fix: Convert h to metres (or consistent units) before multiplying by (ρ_m/ρ − 1) — a silent 1000× error otherwise.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Derive the theoretical velocity at a venturi throat and explain the role of the discharge coefficient.
payload.answer: Bernoulli + continuity: V₂ = √[2(p₁−p₂)/(ρ(1 − β⁴))], β = d₂/d₁. C_d multiplies this to give actual flow, accounting for viscous losses and (for orifices) vena-contracta contraction; hence Q_actual = C_d A₂ V₂,th with C_d < 1.
payload.source: Classic derivation question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Differential meters combine Bernoulli + continuity; Q ~ √Δp.
Venturi: high C_d, low loss; orifice: low C_d, cheap, high loss.
Manometer: Δp/ρg = h(SG_m − 1); always apply C_d for actual discharge.

questions.explanation: Efficient diffusion recovers most pressure.

questions.explanation: Square-root relationship from Bernoulli.

Lower C_d and higher permanent loss

modules.title: Module 3 — Momentum & Pipe Flow
modules.summary: The linear momentum equation for control volumes, force of jets on plates and vanes, Darcy–Weisbach losses, and pipe-flow problem solving.

lessons.title: Momentum Equation & Jet Forces
lessons.summary: Reynolds transport theorem intuition, applying ΣF = ṁ(V_out − V_in) to jets hitting plates/vanes, and reaction forces on pipe bends.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply the linear momentum equation to a steady control volume with one inlet/outlet
Compute jet impact force on stationary flat plates, inclined plates and moving vanes
Find anchoring/reaction forces on pipe bends and nozzles

payload.text: Pelton-wheel turbines and fire-hose recoil are the same equation with opposite signs: the fluid's change of momentum is the force the structure must supply. Momentum is how fluids push things — and every rotating machine in a power plant is a momentum-transfer device.

**Linear momentum equation (steady, CV):**
ΣF_ext = ṁ(V_out − V_in)
- ΣF includes pressure forces on the control surface, gravity on the fluid, and reaction forces from solid boundaries (what you solve for).
- Vectors matter: resolve into components; the force of the jet on the plate is opposite to the force of the plate on the fluid (Newton III).

**Jet on a stationary flat plate (normal impact):**
- Assume jet fully deflects parallel to the plate (or stops): V_out along the plate ≈ same magnitude, normal component destroyed.
- F_plate_on_fluid = ṁ(0 − (−V)) normal to plate = ρAV²; force ON plate = ρAV² in the jet direction.
- Inclined plate at angle θ to the jet: normal component only — F = ρAV² sin θ (for perfect normal-only deflection models).

**Moving vane (e.g. Pelton bucket):**
- Relative velocity at inlet: V_r = V − u (u = vane speed).
- Force on vane: F = ṁ_rel × (V_r,in − V_r,out)_normal. For a smooth vane turning flow by angle β (deflection angle from the incoming relative direction): specific work per mass = u(V − u)(1 + cos β); maximum power when u = V/2.

**Pipe bend / nozzle reaction:**
- Draw a CV around the bend; include inlet/outlet momentum fluxes and pressure forces (use gauge pressure for convenience since p_atm cancels in a CV open to atmosphere elsewhere).
- Solve for the flange/bolting force needed to hold the bend in place — the number a piping engineer actually orders from.

**Impulse–momentum reality checks:** viscous shear and gravity are often small compared with momentum change in high-speed jets; neglected terms must be justified, not silently dropped.

payload.title: Situation
rows: ΣF = ṁ(V_out − V_in) with pressure terms

payload.title: Newton III on every jet problem
payload.text: Compute the force on the FLUID first via the momentum equation; the force on the plate/bend is the negative of that — fewer sign errors.

payload.title: Do not mix absolute and relative velocity in moving-vane problems
payload.text: Momentum flux through the CV uses absolute velocities; the vane's work interaction uses relative velocities — keep both straight or the Pelton formula comes out wrong.

payload.title: Jet force on a fixed plate
payload.problem: Water jet (ρ = 1000) hits a large stationary flat plate normally: V = 15 m/s, d = 40 mm. Find the force on the plate.

steps.title: Momentum change (fluid)
steps.desc: Normal component goes from V to ~0 (spreads parallel): ΔV_normal = 0 − 15 = −15 m/s.

steps.title: Force on fluid
steps.desc: F_fluid = ṁ ΔV = 18.85 × (−15) ≈ −283 N (in −jet direction).

steps.title: Force on plate
steps.desc: Newton III: F_plate = +283 N in the jet direction ≈ 0.28 kN.

payload.solution: F ≈ 283 N (≈ 0.28 kN) pushing the plate in the jet direction.

payload.title: Pelton bucket force

Normal flat plate: F = ρAV²; moving vane uses relative velocity.

lessons.title: Pipe Flow: Darcy–Weisbach & Losses
lessons.summary: Major friction losses, minor losses, Moody diagram reading, and solving single-pipe systems with the energy equation.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply Darcy–Weisbach for major head loss with the correct friction factor
Compute minor losses with loss coefficients and combine with major losses
Read the Moody diagram (laminar vs turbulent, rough vs smooth) and solve for unknown diameter or length

payload.text: A 100 mm water main and a 90 mm one can differ in pump power by more than 40% — head loss scales roughly with V² and strongly with diameter. Pipe sizing is the everyday application of viscous-flow theory, and Darcy–Weisbach is the equation behind every pump datasheet.

**Laminar vs turbulent (Reynolds number):**
Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν
- Pipe flow: Re < ~2300 laminar; > ~4000 turbulent; in between — transitional (unstable).
- Laminar friction factor: f = 64/Re (Darcy) — exact for circular pipes.

**Darcy–Weisbach major loss:**
h_f = f (L/D) (V²/2g)
- f from Moody/Colebrook for turbulent flow: 1/√f = −2 log₁₀( (ε/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re√f) ) — implicit; Swamee–Jain explicit approximation is fine for exams.
- ε = absolute roughness (commercial steel ~0.045 mm, drawn copper ~0.0015 mm, concrete ~0.3–3 mm — memorise the steel value for exams).
- Fully rough (high Re): f depends on ε/D only; smooth-pipe (low Re turbulent): f depends on Re only.

**Minor losses (fittings, entrances, exits, bends, valves):**
h_m = K V²/2g, sum over all fittings — each K is empirical (sharp entrance ~0.5, well-rounded ~0.05, exit to reservoir ~1.0, 90° regular elbow ~0.3–0.9, gate valve wide open ~0.2 — order-of-magnitude values).

**Total system head (energy equation between two reservoirs):**
Δz = h_pump = h_f + Σh_m (for pump-driven flow between large tanks; static lift Δz plus all losses).

**Non-circular ducts:** use hydraulic diameter D_h = 4A/P (perimeter); apply Darcy with D_h — works for annuli, square ducts, etc.

**Series/parallel pipes:** series: same Q, add h_f; parallel: same h_f, split Q. Solve with continuity + loss equations.

payload.title: Check the flow regime before grabbing Moody
payload.text: Re < 2300 ⇒ f = 64/Re exactly — no diagram needed; only turbulent flow requires the Moody/Colebrook route.

payload.title: Darcy f is 4× the Fanning f used in some chemistry texts
payload.text: ME/CE exams use Darcy (Moody, h_f = f L/D V²/2g). If a question quotes Fanning, multiply by 4 — read carefully.

payload.title: Steel pipe major loss
payload.problem: Water (ν = 1×10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows at 2 m/s in a 100 mm ID commercial-steel pipe, L = 50 m. Find h_f.

steps.title: Reynolds number
steps.desc: Re = VD/ν = 2 × 0.1 / 1e-6 = 2×10⁵ — turbulent.

steps.title: Friction factor
steps.desc: Colebrook/Swamee–Jain with Re = 2e5, ε/D = 0.00045 gives f ≈ 0.016–0.017 (read Moody: slightly rough regime).

steps.title: Pump implication
steps.desc: A pump serving this line needs ≥ 1.68 m of friction head plus static lift and minor losses.

payload.solution: h_f ≈ 1.7 m of water for the 50 m steel line at 2 m/s.

payload.title: Diameter sensitivity
payload.prompt: Halve the diameter at the same volumetric flow rate (so V quadruples). How does h_f scale? Roughly what factor?
payload.hint: h_f ~ V²/D ~ Q²/D⁵ at constant Q.

mistakes.mistake: Using the smooth-pipe formula for old rusty concrete
mistakes.fix: Fully rough flow ignores Re — use the rough-zone f(ε/D) from Moody, not the Blasius smooth correlation.

mistakes.mistake: Adding minor-loss K values without converting to a common velocity head
mistakes.fix: Each K multiplies the LOCAL V²/2g at that fitting — different pipe sizes need local velocities or an equivalent-length conversion.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the Darcy–Weisbach equation and define each term. How is f obtained for laminar vs turbulent flow?
payload.answer: h_f = f (L/D) (V²/2g): f = Darcy friction factor (dimensionless), L length, D internal diameter, V mean velocity, g gravity. Laminar (Re < 2300): f = 64/Re exactly. Turbulent: from Moody diagram or Colebrook equation using Re and relative roughness ε/D.
payload.source: Evergreen pipe-flow question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Re decides laminar (f = 64/Re) vs turbulent (Moody/Colebrook).
h_f = f(L/D)V²/2g major; h_m = K V²/2g minor; hydraulic diameter for non-circular.
Series: add losses at common Q; parallel: split Q at common h_f.

questions.explanation: Exact Hagen–Poiseuille result.

questions.explanation: Same formula written with D/L or L/D grouping — check the given form.

questions.explanation: Well-rounded entrances drop to ~0.05; exit to a reservoir is ~1.0.

modules.title: Module 4 — Dimensional Analysis & Open Channel Flow
modules.summary: Buckingham Pi theorem, model scaling laws, specific energy, Froude-number regimes, and hydraulic jumps in open channels.

lessons.title: Dimensional Analysis & Similitude
lessons.summary: Rayleigh/Buckingham Pi methods, common dimensionless groups in fluid mechanics, and the three similitude conditions (geometric, kinematic, dynamic).

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Derive dimensionless Pi groups via the Buckingham Pi theorem
Identify and interpret Re, Fr, We, Ma and Ca in appropriate problems
State geometric, kinematic and dynamic similarity requirements for model tests

payload.text: A 1:50 scale model of a ship in a towing tank predicts the full-size vessel's resistance only because both share the same Reynolds and Froude numbers — which is often impossible to satisfy simultaneously. Model testing is the art of choosing which dimensionless group dominates, and that choice starts with dimensional analysis.

**Base dimensions in mechanics:** M (mass), L (length), T (time) — three independent dimensions (force F is MLT⁻², not a fourth base in MLT systems).

**Rayleigh method:** assume the dependent variable is a product of powers of the influencing variables; equate exponents of M, L, T and solve.

**Buckingham Pi theorem:** n variables with k independent dimensions → (n − k) dimensionless Pi groups. Steps: pick k repeating variables covering all dimensions (but not the dependent variable); combine each remaining variable with the repeating set; solve exponent systems so each Pi is dimensionless.

**Key dimensionless groups:**
- Reynolds Re = ρVL/μ = VL/ν — inertia/viscous (dominates pipe/boundary-layer/airfoil drag at high speed).
- Froude Fr = V/√(gL) — inertia/gravity (dominates free-surface flows, ship waves, open channels).
- Weber We = ρV²L/σ — inertia/surface tension (droplets, capillary, spray).
- Mach Ma = V/c — compressibility (gas dynamics).
- Euler Eu = Δp/(ρV²) — pressure/inertia (fully submerged, no free surface).
- Cauchy/elastic — inertia/elasticity (water hammer, structural-fluid coupling).

**Similitude (model → prototype):**
- Geometric: all lengths scale by the same ratio L_r.
- Kinematic: velocity/time ratios consistent with the length scale and chosen time scale.
- Dynamic: all relevant force (dimensionless group) ratios equal — Re equality for viscous-dominated flow, Fr equality for free-surface flow, both (impossible without a second fluid) for ships — hence wave-makers or CFD corrections.

**Model laws:** if Re-dominated, match Re (viscous similitude); if Fr-dominated, match Fr (gravity similitude); if both matter (ship resistance), split the force budget (frictional by Re-correction, wave-making by Fr).

payload.title: Repeating-variable checklist
payload.text: Choose variables that between them contain M, L and T exactly (e.g. ρ, V, L), and never pick the dependent variable itself.

payload.title: Cannot match Re and Fr simultaneously with water at geometric scale
payload.text: Ship-model law: match Fr for wave pattern; correct friction via ITTC-style Re extrapolation — do not claim true dynamic similarity.

payload.title: Buckingham Pi on drag force
payload.problem: Drag F on a submerged body depends on ρ, V, L, μ. Find the Pi relation.

steps.title: Count
steps.desc: n = 5 variables (F, ρ, V, L, μ); k = 3 dimensions (M, L, T) ⇒ 2 Pi groups.

steps.title: Repeating set
steps.desc: Choose ρ, V, L — they span M, L, T.

steps.title: First Pi (with F)
steps.desc: Π₁ = F/(ρV²L²) — the drag coefficient C_D.

steps.title: Second Pi (with μ)
steps.desc: Π₂ = μ/(ρVL) = 1/Re.

steps.title: Result
steps.desc: C_D = φ(Re) — drag coefficient is a function of Reynolds number only (for incompressible, fully submerged flow) — the classic experimental drag-curve form.

payload.solution: C_D = F/(½ρV²A) (or ρV²L² form) = function of Re — dimensional analysis predicts the structure of every drag experiment.

payload.title: Open-channel Pi
payload.prompt: Wave speed c in shallow water depends on g and depth h only. Derive the dimensionless group (should reduce to c/√(gh) = constant).
payload.hint: n = 3, k = 2 (L, T) ⇒ one Pi.

mistakes.mistake: Including force F as a base dimension alongside M, L, T in MLT systems
mistakes.fix: Force is derived (MLT⁻²); using both F and M as bases creates dependency and breaks the Pi count.

mistakes.mistake: Applying Re-similitude to a spillway model
mistakes.fix: Free-surface gravity flows are Fr-dominated — match Froude number, not Reynolds.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the Buckingham Pi theorem and apply it to show drag on a submerged body is C_D = f(Re).
payload.answer: n variables with k independent dimensions yield (n − k) dimensionless groups. For F = f(ρ, V, L, μ): 5 − 3 = 2 groups; C_D = F/(ρV²L²) and Re = ρVL/μ; hence C_D = φ(Re).
payload.source: Standard dimensional-analysis derivation.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Buckingham Pi: (n − k) dimensionless groups from M, L, T analysis.
Re (viscous), Fr (free surface), We (surface tension), Ma (compressibility).
Similitude: geometric + kinematic + dynamic; ships match Fr, correct Re.

questions.explanation: Buckingham Pi theorem.

questions.explanation: Gravity dominates over viscosity for wave patterns.

questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis result for submerged flow.

lessons.title: Open Channel Flow: Specific Energy & Hydraulic Jumps
lessons.summary: Critical depth, subcritical/supercritical regimes, specific-energy diagrams, and the hydraulic-jump momentum relation.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute critical depth and classify flow as subcritical or supercritical via Froude number
Use the specific-energy diagram to analyze channel transitions (steps, sluices)
Apply continuity + momentum to size a hydraulic jump and its energy loss

payload.text: Below every big dam spillway there is a violent whitewater roller — a hydraulic jump — deliberately engineered to dissipate energy before it erodes the riverbed. The jump is not a bug; it is a momentum-balance machine that civil engineers design on purpose, and its size is fixed by two equations you already know.

**Open channel basics:** flow driven by gravity along a slope; the free surface adjusts so pressure is hydrostatic across any vertical (normal to the bed for mild slopes).

**Froude number (open channel):** Fr = V/√(gD), where D = hydraulic depth = A/T (flow area / top width); for a wide rectangular channel D ≈ depth y.
- Fr < 1 subcritical (deep, slow — disturbances travel upstream).
- Fr = 1 critical.
- Fr > 1 supercritical (shallow, fast — disturbances cannot travel upstream).

**Specific energy:** E = y + V²/(2g) (energy per unit weight above the channel bottom).
- For a given rectangular-channel discharge per width q: E = y + q²/(2gy²).
- Minimum E at critical depth y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}; at critical flow V = √(gD) (wide channel: V = √(gy_c)).
- Two alternate depths share the same E (one sub, one super) except at E_min.

**Channel transitions:**
- Smooth step up (h): E₂ = E₁ − h; may choke if the step is too high.
- Sluice gate / sluice: forces supercritical under the gate from a subcritical reservoir; use specific energy + continuity (and sometimes momentum if there is a jump).

**Hydraulic jump:** abrupt transition from supercritical to subcritical with large turbulence and energy loss (but momentum conserved horizontally if bed friction neglected).
- For a rectangular channel: y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1) — the classic conjugate-depth relation.
- Energy loss: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂).
- Froude at the upstream side must be > 1; the jump length is a few times the jump height (empirical ~5–7 y₂ for design).

**Where jumps appear:** spillway bases (energy dissipators), abrupt changes in slope, sluice-gate exits.

payload.title: Fr before touching E diagrams
payload.text: One line of Fr classification prevents half the specific-energy sign errors — always compute Fr first.

payload.title: Hydraulic jumps lose energy but conserve horizontal momentum (neglecting friction)
payload.text: Do not try to use the energy equation across the jump — it is highly dissipative; use momentum + continuity for conjugate depths.

payload.title: Hydraulic jump sizing
payload.problem: Rectangular channel, y₁ = 0.3 m, V₁ = 6 m/s. Find y₂, Fr₁, and energy loss. g = 9.81.

steps.title: Froude upstream
steps.desc: Fr₁ = V₁/√(gy₁) = 6/√(9.81×0.3) = 6/√2.943 ≈ 6/1.716 ≈ 3.50 — supercritical, a jump can form.

steps.title: Velocity downstream
steps.desc: Continuity (wide channel, same width): V₂ = V₁ y₁/y₂ = 6 × 0.3/1.35 ≈ 1.33 m/s.

steps.title: Fr check downstream
steps.desc: Fr₂ ≈ 1.33/√(9.81×1.35) ≈ 1.33/3.64 ≈ 0.37 < 1 ✓ (subcritical after the jump).

steps.title: Energy loss
steps.desc: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂) = (1.05)³/(4×0.3×1.35) ≈ 1.158/1.62 ≈ 0.715 m — substantial dissipation.

payload.solution: Fr₁ ≈ 3.5; y₂ ≈ 1.35 m; ΔE ≈ 0.72 m dissipated in the jump.

payload.title: Choking on a step
payload.prompt: Flow approaches critical over a raised bed step. If the step is raised further, what happens to the upstream depth? Explain with the E-diagram.
payload.hint: E available above the step shrinks; upstream must back up to raise E₁.

mistakes.mistake: Using Bernoulli (energy) across a hydraulic jump
mistakes.fix: The jump is dissipative — energy is NOT conserved; use momentum (conjugate-depth relation) + continuity.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to use hydraulic depth A/T for non-rectangular sections in Fr
mistakes.fix: Fr = V/√(gD) with D = A/T; the √(gy) shortcut is wide-rectangle only.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define critical flow in an open channel and derive the conjugate-depth relation for a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel.
payload.answer: Critical flow: Fr = 1, specific energy minimum for the given discharge; y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3} for a wide rectangular channel. Jump: apply continuity (V₁y₁ = V₂y₂) and horizontal momentum balance (pressure + momentum flux equal across the jump, friction neglected) to obtain y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1).
payload.source: Standard open-channel derivation.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Fr = V/√(gD) classifies subcritical (Fr < 1) vs supercritical (Fr > 1).
E = y + V²/(2g); minimum at critical depth; two alternate depths per E > E_min.
Hydraulic jump: conjugate depths via Fr₁; large ΔE = (y₂−y₁)³/(4y₁y₂) — engineered energy dissipation.

questions.prompt: Critical flow in a wide rectangular channel occurs when:
questions.explanation: Minimum specific energy for the discharge.

questions.prompt: A hydraulic jump transforms flow from:
questions.explanation: Abrupt deceleration with energy loss.

questions.prompt: Specific energy E in an open channel is defined as:
options: Energy per unit weight above the channel bottom: y + V²/(2g)
questions.explanation: E = y + V²/(2g).

courses.title: Excel for Students
courses.subtitle: Three hours from pasted data to a defensible tracker — formulas, charts and the clean-up pass that fixes other people's exports
courses.description:
Every internship report, placement spreadsheet and lab record eventually lands in Excel — and almost nobody was actually taught it. This is the three-hour version: the grid and the data types that silently break totals, the formulas that cover most real work, tables and charts that answer questions honestly, and the five-step clean-up pass for any CSV you did not create.

It ends with a capstone you can defend in an interview: a two-sheet attendance-and-fees tracker with live SUMIFS, an IF status column inside a real Excel Table, and one honest chart. The certificate is issued for that file, not for notes about it.

**Who this is for:** any student, any branch, who has ever pasted data into Excel, squinted at a total that was slightly wrong, or been handed a "report template" with no idea which formulas to trust.

**What you need:** Excel, LibreOffice Calc or Google Sheets (the formulas and shortcuts are identical). No prior spreadsheet knowledge.
outcomes: Spot and fix numbers stored as text before they corrupt a total
Write formulas with correct relative and absolute references
Use SUM/COUNT/AVERAGE and audit them with COUNT vs COUNTA
Build IF conditionals and decode #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #REF! and #NAME?
Turn a raw range into a Ctrl+T Table with safe sorting and filtering
Build honest charts — and recognise a misleading one
Run the five-step clean-up pass on any pasted or CSV data
Ship a two-sheet SUMIFS tracker you can defend line by line
courses.about_course:
This course is built around one idea: Excel is not taught anywhere properly, and everybody is assumed to already know it. Four modules, eight lessons, three hours — each lesson the same nine steps (objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice task, common mistakes, interview angle, quiz, summary), every worked example a real spreadsheet problem rather than a synthetic one.

Module 1 fixes the foundation most people never got: what Excel actually stores in a cell, and why a total can be wrong while looking right. Module 2 is the formula toolkit — references, the four aggregates, IF logic and error decoding. Module 3 covers tables, sorting safely and charts that do not lie. Module 4 is the cleanup pass for other people's data, ending in the capstone tracker.

The interview angle runs through every lesson: "why is my SUM wrong", "what is wrong with this chart", "relative vs absolute" — these are the Excel questions placement tests actually ask, and by the end you will have answered all of them on your own file.
prerequisites: Excel, LibreOffice Calc or Google Sheets installed (any version from the last eight years)
No prior spreadsheet formulas required
audience: First- and second-year students who were never taught Excel properly
Anyone who has pasted data and distrusted the total
Internship and placement prep — Excel tests are common in aptitude rounds
Any branch: lab records, fee sheets and project reports all land in Excel

units.title: Cells, types & references
units.summary: A1 notation; ranges first:last; numbers vs text vs dates (dates are serial numbers). Apostrophe forces text; left-alignment is the tell. $ locks: $C$1 fixed, C$1 row, $C1 column; F4 cycles.
questions: Why does a number typed with a leading apostrophe never sum?
What is the difference between C$1 and $C1 when copied down?
How are dates stored underneath the display format?

units.title: Aggregates & auditing
units.summary: SUM/AVERAGE/COUNT use numeric cells only; COUNTA counts anything non-empty. COUNT < COUNTA = text hiding in a numeric column. AVERAGE silently divides by the numeric count — audit before trusting.
questions: COUNT is 8, COUNTA is 10 — what is wrong and how do you fix it?
Why can AVERAGE return a plausible-looking wrong number?
Which function counts cells containing text?

units.title: IF logic & errors
units.summary: IF(test, true, false); test tiers highest-first so a 92 is not caught by >=40. IFS replaces deep nesting. Errors: #DIV/0! zero divisor, #VALUE! text-as-number, #REF! deleted cells, #NAME? typo, #N/A lookup miss, circular = self-dependent.
questions: Why must the highest tier be tested first in nested IFs?
What does #REF! tell you that #NAME? does not?
Blank cells compare as what in a numeric test?

units.title: Tables, sort & filter
units.summary: Ctrl+T: auto-expansion, filter dropdowns, optional totals. Sort moves rows; filter hides rows. One cell inside the block = safe sort; one highlighted column = scrambled data. Multi-key: Add Level, top level is primary.
questions: Why does sorting a single selected column corrupt the dataset?
What does the Totals Row show when a filter is applied?
What is the safe first click before any sort?

units.title: Honest charts
units.summary: Column/bar = categories; line = time; pie = few positive parts of one whole. Columns start at zero — truncated axes are the classic lie. Titles state the finding; label both axes; data labels only when exact values matter.
questions: Why must a column chart's y-axis start at zero?
Which chart type suits a six-month attendance trend?
What is wrong with a 9-slice pie of negative and positive values?

units.title: Cleanup & capstone
units.summary: Five-step pass: TRIM/CLEAN (+SUBSTITUTE for CHAR(160)) → Text to Columns → Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) → Remove Duplicates (read the report) → Data Validation (preventive only). Capstone: Records table + Summary with SUMIFS structured refs, IF status column, one honest chart.
questions: Why does TRIM miss a pasted space that looks normal?
Why are structured references (Table[Column]) safer than B2:B500?
Data Validation on existing bad rows — does it fix them?

important_questions: Your SUM is slightly under the hand-added total. Diagnose it in three steps.
Explain relative vs absolute references and give a formula that needs the $ lock.
What is wrong with a column chart whose y-axis runs 380–420?
Walk through your five-step clean-up pass on a pasted CSV.
Why does COUNTA exceed COUNT in a column that "looks like all numbers"?
Build a three-tier grading formula and defend the order of the tests.

previous_year_questions.question: A colleague's dashboard shows marks pasted from a portal. The average is visibly too high. What do you check first, and which two functions prove the diagnosis?
previous_year_questions.solution: Check alignment and run COUNT vs COUNTA on the column — COUNTA > COUNT proves some cells are text. AVERAGE silently skips them (dividing by fewer cells), which shifts the mean. Fix with Text to Columns or VALUE(), then re-average.

previous_year_questions.question: =VLOOKUP is not needed here — explain why =IF(A2>=60,"Pass","Fail") returns Fail for a visible 75, and how to repair the sheet.
previous_year_questions.solution: The cell holds text (e.g. "75" with a leading apostrophe), so >=60 is false. Prove with =ISNUMBER(A2) → FALSE. Repair via Data → Text to Columns → Finish (converts text-numbers in place), or a =VALUE(A2) helper pasted as values.

previous_year_questions.question: You must show monthly expense trends to a supervisor in one chart. Which type, and what two labelling rules make it honest?
previous_year_questions.solution: A line chart — months are a time sequence, and trends read as shape. Label both axes (month, amount) and title the chart with the finding, not the topic. A trend line may zoom the y-range for shape; a column comparison of the same data must start at zero.

bank.prompt: In A1 notation, what does the range C3:C10 represent?
bank.explanation: C3:C10 is one column (C) spanning rows 3 to 10 — eight cells.

bank.prompt: A cell displaying 45% is left-aligned. What does SUM do with it?
bank.explanation: Left-alignment indicates text storage. SUM silently ignores text even when it looks numeric.

bank.prompt: How are dates stored inside Excel?
options: As serial numbers with a date format
bank.explanation: 1 Jan 1900 is serial 1; every date is that number wearing a date display format.

bank.prompt: Which shortcut fills every cell in the current selection with what you just typed?
bank.explanation: Ctrl+Enter commits the entry into all selected cells at once.

bank.prompt: A number typed with a leading apostrophe ('92) is stored as:
bank.explanation: The apostrophe forces text storage; the cell displays 92 but SUM ignores it.

bank.prompt: The Name Box (top-left, beside the formula bar) shows:
bank.explanation: It always names the active cell or range; typing a reference there jumps to it.

bank.prompt: Which feature keeps the header row visible while scrolling a long table?
bank.explanation: View → Freeze Panes pins the chosen rows/columns in the viewport.

bank.prompt: A cell with Currency format shows ₹1,250. What do formulas see?
bank.explanation: Currency is a display lens; the stored value the formulas use is the number 1250.

bank.prompt: Which of these survives a save-as-CSV round-trip?
bank.explanation: CSV stores raw values only — every visual format is stripped on export.

bank.prompt: To flag cells below 75% in a percent-formatted column, the Less Than rule threshold is:
bank.explanation: Stored percent values are decimals (82% = 0.82), so the rule compares against 0.75.

bank.prompt: =B2*$C$1 is filled from row 2 to row 6. The row-5 formula is:
bank.explanation: B2 is relative and advances to B5; $C$1 is fully absolute and stays put.

bank.prompt: COUNT returns 8 and COUNTA returns 10 on the same range. This means:
options: Two cells hold text, not numbers
bank.explanation: COUNT counts numbers only; COUNTA counts non-empty. The gap of 2 is text cells.

bank.prompt: AVERAGE over ten cells where two hold text returns a mean based on:
bank.explanation: Text and blanks are skipped entirely — the divisor is the numeric count, 8.

bank.prompt: Which key cycles absolute/relative reference styles while editing a formula?
bank.explanation: F4 cycles B1 → $B$1 → B$1 → $B1 on the reference under the cursor.

bank.explanation: C$1 locks the row number (1) while the column stays relative; $C1 locks the column instead.

bank.prompt: Which function returns the count of non-empty cells including text?
bank.explanation: COUNTA counts any non-empty cell; COUNT counts numeric-typed cells only.

bank.prompt: =IF(A2>=85,"D",IF(A2>=40,"P","F")) with A2=92 returns:
bank.explanation: The first TRUE branch wins — 92 matches the >=85 test first.

bank.prompt: A formula ultimately depending on itself produces:
bank.explanation: Excel cannot resolve a self-dependent calculation and raises the circular-reference warning.

bank.prompt: #VALUE! inside a SUM formula most likely indicates:
options: Text is present where numbers are expected
bank.explanation: Text (including apostrophe-forced numbers) in a numeric operation is the classic #VALUE! cause.

bank.prompt: Blank cells in a numeric test like =IF(A2>0,"yes","no") are treated as:
bank.explanation: Blank compares as 0, so an empty A2 fails >0 and returns the false branch.

bank.prompt: Which error code means a formula name was misspelled?
bank.explanation: #NAME? signals an unrecognised function or defined name — usually a typo.

bank.prompt: IFERROR(A2/B2,0) is best described as:
options: Hiding every problem in the sheet
Returning a fallback when the main expression errors
bank.explanation: It substitutes the fallback (0) only when the inner expression raises an error — useful for display cells, dangerous when overused.

bank.prompt: Safest way to sort a column inside a data block?
options: Select one cell inside the column
bank.explanation: One cell inside the block lets Excel expand to the contiguous range and move whole rows.

bank.prompt: In a two-level Sort dialog, the top level is:
bank.explanation: Levels apply top-down; the first listed level is the primary sort key.

bank.prompt: A Ctrl+T Table automatically adds:
bank.explanation: Tables ship with header dropdowns; totals rows and styles are optional toggles.

bank.prompt: Which chart best shows one student's attendance across six months?
bank.explanation: A time series reads as shape — a line chart is the honest choice.

bank.prompt: A column chart's y-axis should normally:
options: Start just below the minimum value
bank.explanation: Truncated axes exaggerate bar differences; columns and bars must start at zero.

bank.prompt: A pie chart is honest only when its slices are:
bank.explanation: Pie represents parts of a single whole — all positive, few enough to read.

bank.prompt: TRIM does not remove a pasted gap that looks like a space. The gap is most likely:
options: A full-width space from a formula
bank.explanation: Non-breaking spaces (CHAR(160)) survive TRIM; remove them with SUBSTITUTE(x,CHAR(160),"") before TRIM.

bank.prompt: Outstanding SUMIFS (31,000) + Paid-side SUMIFS (45,000) = 76,000, but SUM total = 84,000. Most likely cause?
options: Some Paid cells are neither exactly Y nor N
bank.explanation: Rows whose Paid cell has trailing spaces, wrong case or blanks match neither criterion — the arithmetic gap is the audit signal; clean the column and re-validate.

project.title: Build your attendance & fees tracker
