modules.title: Module 1 — Cells, Ranges & Formatting
modules.summary: The grid, cell types that actually matter, ranges, and the formatting that survives a CSV export.

lessons.title: The Grid: Cells, References & Data Types
lessons.summary: Rows, columns, A1 references, ranges, and the three data types Excel treats differently — numbers, text and dates.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Navigate the grid and name any cell or range with A1 notation
Tell apart numbers, text and dates — and why Excel treats them differently
Enter and edit data with the keyboard shortcuts that save real time

payload.text: A marks sheet where 92 is stored as text sorts below 8. A budget where "1,200" is text never sums. Half of every "Excel bug" in a college submission is a data-type problem in a cell that looks fine on screen.

**The grid:** columns are lettered A, B, C…; rows are numbered 1, 2, 3…. A cell is its column letter + row number — B3 is column B, row 3. The Name Box (top-left, left of the formula bar) always shows the active cell's name; click it and type a reference to jump there.

**Ranges:** a rectangle of cells written first-cell:last-cell — A1:A10 is a column of ten cells, B2:D5 is a 3×4 block, 2:2 is all of row 2. Every function in this course takes ranges as input.

**Three data types Excel treats differently:**
- **Numbers** — right-aligned by default, sum in SUM(), compare numerically.
- **Text** — left-aligned, IGNORED by SUM(). A number typed with a leading apostrophe ('92) is forced to text.
- **Dates** — secretly numbers. 1 Jan 1900 is serial 1; today is a five-digit number with a date format on top. This is why date arithmetic works and why a "date" stored as text never sorts chronologically.

**Entry shortcuts worth muscle memory:** Enter moves down, Tab moves right, Enter on the last row wraps to the top of the range you were typing into. F2 edits the active cell in place. Ctrl+Enter fills the whole selection with what you typed. Escape cancels an entry mid-way.

payload.title: Reference
rows: Absolute cell — never shifts when copied

payload.title: Name Box as a calculator
payload.text: Select any range and the Name Box area shows Count and Sum instantly — no formula needed. Select cells and look bottom-left of the status bar; right-click the status bar to add Average too.

payload.title: The apostrophe trap
payload.text: Typing '92 stores TEXT that looks like a number. It will not sum, it sorts after every real number, and SUM() silently skips it. Watch the alignment: left means text.

payload.title: Spot the text-numbers in a marks column
payload.problem: A column C2:C11 should hold ten marks. SUM(C2:C11) returns 340 but adding the visible values by hand gives 428. Why?

steps.title: Count the cells
steps.desc: COUNT(C2:C11) returns 8, not 10 — two cells are not numbers.

steps.title: Find them
steps.desc: ISNUMBER(C2) filled down (Ctrl+D) returns FALSE on the two text cells.

steps.title: See why
steps.desc: Those two were pasted from a portal export with a leading apostrophe — they are left-aligned.

steps.title: Fix
steps.desc: Select the column: Data → Text to Columns → Finish converts text-numbers in place. Or multiply a helper column by 1.

payload.solution: Two marks were stored as text (left-aligned). Text-to-Columns or a 1× helper converts them; SUM then returns the true 428.

payload.title: Audit a pasted column
payload.prompt: Paste any ten numbers into A1:A10, then force two of them to text with a leading apostrophe. Run COUNT, SUM and AVERAGE — record how each treats the text cells, then convert them and re-run.
payload.hint: COUNT counts numbers only; COUNTA counts everything; SUM and AVERAGE ignore text.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming SUM ignores text silently — the total is just "a bit low"
mistakes.fix: A skipped cell is not a rounding error; it is missing data. Cross-check COUNT against the expected row count every time a total surprises you.

mistakes.mistake: Editing a cell when you meant to select a range
mistakes.fix: F2 edits in place; Enter commits and moves. If you typed into a cell by accident, Esc cancels with no change.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why does SUM ignore a cell containing a number that was typed with a leading apostrophe?
payload.answer: The apostrophe forces text storage. Text is never included in SUM/AVERAGE/MIN/MAX even when it looks like a number; Excel only includes numeric-typed cells.
payload.source: Data types — the single most examined Excel concept in placement tests.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: A1 notation: column letter + row number; ranges use first:last.
Numbers, text and dates are three different types — dates are secretly numbers.
A leading apostrophe forces text; left-alignment is the visual tell.
Ctrl+Enter fills a whole selection; F2 edits in place; Esc cancels.

questions.prompt: In A1 notation, the range B2:D5 covers:
questions.explanation: B to D is 3 columns; rows 2 to 5 is 4 rows; 3 × 4 = 12 cells.

questions.prompt: A cell shows 92 but is left-aligned. What does SUM do with it?
questions.explanation: Left-alignment signals text storage; SUM only adds numeric-typed cells.

questions.prompt: Dates in Excel are stored as:
questions.explanation: 1 Jan 1900 is serial 1; every date is that serial number wearing a format.

questions.prompt: Which shortcut fills the entire current selection with what you just typed?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Enter commits into every selected cell; Ctrl+D fills down only.

lessons.title: Formatting That Survives Export
lessons.summary: Number formats, conditional formatting, freeze panes, and the formats that vanish when the file becomes a CSV.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply number formats (currency, percent, date) without changing the underlying value
Use conditional formatting to make outliers visible at a glance
Freeze panes and size a sheet so it stays readable at 200 rows

payload.text: Formatting is not decoration — it is how a reader finds the three cells that matter in two hundred. But half of it is paint that a CSV export strips away: know which half is structure and which half is costume.

**Number formats are a lens, not a rewrite.** A cell holding 0.125 with Percent format shows 12.5% — the value underneath is still 0.125, and formulas use 0.125. Currency format adds ₹ and thousands separators; Date format displays a serial as 15/10/2026. Change the format and the value never moves.

**Conditional formatting** colours or flags cells by rule: Home → Conditional Formatting. The three rules worth knowing:
- Highlight Cell Rules → Greater Than / Between — numeric thresholds.
- Top/Bottom Rules → Top 10% — relative standout.
- Color Scales — a heatmap; good for a 200-row table, noise for a 5-row one.

**Structure that survives export:** column widths, row heights, freeze panes, number formats and cell borders are all presentation stored in the file. A CSV keeps NONE of it — CSV is raw values, comma-separated, one row per line. What survives a CSV round-trip is only the data itself and the display text of each cell. Never hand someone a formatted xlsx when they asked for CSV, and never re-import a CSV expecting your formats back.

**Freeze panes:** View → Freeze Panes locks the header row (and optionally the first column) so they stay visible while you scroll. For any table longer than one screen, this is not optional.

payload.title: Feature
rows: Yes — that is all CSV is

payload.title: Freeze before you scroll
payload.text: Ctrl+Home jumps to A1 from anywhere. Freeze the header row the moment a table passes one screen — re-finding your place in 400 rows costs more time than the freeze ever will.

payload.title: Percent format is not multiplication
payload.text: Percent format DISPLAYS 0.125 as 12.5%; it does not multiply by 100. If a formula needs the percentage as a number, use the 0.125 value directly or multiply explicitly.

payload.title: Flag the attendance outliers
payload.problem: Column B holds attendance percentages (0.82, 0.91, 0.55…) for 120 students. Make sub-75% cells red without touching the values.

steps.title: Select the data
steps.desc: Click the column-B header to select the whole column.

steps.title: New rule
steps.desc: Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cell Rules → Less Than…

steps.title: Threshold
steps.desc: Type 0.75 (the stored value is a decimal, not 75) and pick the red-fill style.

steps.title: Verify
steps.desc: The 0.55 row lights up; 0.82 does not. The underlying values are unchanged — check with a formula on one cell.

payload.solution: A Less-Than-0.75 conditional rule on column B flags every student under 75%. Values untouched; the rule is metadata that a CSV would drop.

payload.title: Heatmap a marks block
payload.prompt: Take a 10×5 block of marks. Apply a 3-colour scale conditional format, then save as CSV, re-open the CSV and note exactly what came back.
payload.hint: Compare side by side: the xlsx keeps colours and widths; the CSV keeps only values.

mistakes.mistake: Typing 75 instead of 0.75 in a percent-formatted column
mistakes.fix: The stored value is the decimal. A cell showing 82% holds 0.82 — your rule threshold must be 0.75, not 75.

mistakes.mistake: Sending a formatted xlsx when the receiver asked for CSV
mistakes.fix: CSV cannot carry formats. If the receiver needs the ₹ symbol or colour flags, send the xlsx (or a screenshot) alongside the CSV.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A cell displays "₹1,250" with currency format. What value do formulas see, and what does a CSV export contain?
payload.answer: Formulas see the raw number 1250 — the ₹ and separators are display format only. A CSV export contains the displayed text as typed/stored (1250 or the formatted string depending on export settings), but never the currency formatting itself.
payload.source: Format-vs-value, the classic "my SUM broke after export" interview question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Number formats change display, never the stored value formulas use.
Conditional formatting flags outliers by rule; thresholds use stored values (0.75, not 75).
Freeze panes before scrolling any table longer than a screen.
CSV keeps values only — every visual format is stripped on export.

questions.prompt: A cell with Percent format displays 12.5%. What value does =A1*2 return?
questions.explanation: The stored value is 0.125; ×2 = 0.25, which Percent format would display as 25%.

questions.prompt: Which of these survives a save-as-CSV round-trip?
questions.explanation: CSV is raw values only — every visual feature is file-format metadata that CSV does not carry.

questions.prompt: To flag cells below 75% in a percent-formatted column, the Less Than rule threshold is:
questions.explanation: Stored values are decimals — the rule compares against 0.75.

questions.prompt: Freeze Panes is used to:
options: Keep header rows visible while scrolling
questions.explanation: It pins header rows/columns in view; it is presentation, not protection.

modules.title: Module 2 — Formulas & Core Functions
modules.summary: Relative vs absolute references, the SUM/AVERAGE/COUNT family, IF logic, and the error codes every formula reader must decode.

lessons.title: References, SUM/COUNT/AVERAGE & Absolute Locks
lessons.summary: Writing your first formula, relative copying, $ locks, and the four aggregate functions that cover most real work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write formulas with = and copy them correctly across rows and columns
Use $ absolute references so a copied formula keeps pointing at one cell
Apply SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT and COUNTA to the right kind of data

payload.text: Every Excel formula starts with = and almost every broken Excel formula is a copy that moved. One missing $ on a tax-rate cell turns a correct budget into a confidently wrong one — and the total still looks plausible.

**Writing a formula:** select a cell, type =, then a calculation — =B2+C2, =B2*0.1, =SUM(B2:B10). The result appears in the cell; the formula shows in the formula bar. Ctrl+` (grave accent) toggles between showing all formulas and all results.

**Relative references shift when copied.** =B2*C$1 copied down one row becomes =B3*C$2 — the row number moves with you. That is usually what you want (each row multiplies its own B value) — and exactly wrong when one input cell must stay fixed.

**The $ lock:** place $ before the part that must not move. $C$1 never shifts; C$1 keeps the column but lets the row move; $C1 locks the column only. The classic rate-cell layout: put the tax rate once in $C$1, then fill =B2*$C$1 down the column — every row multiplies by the same single rate cell.

**The four aggregates:**
- SUM(range) — adds numeric cells only.
- AVERAGE(range) — sum ÷ count of numeric cells; empty and text cells are skipped, not counted as zero.
- COUNT(range) — counts numeric cells only.
- COUNTA(range) — counts non-empty cells (numbers AND text).

The COUNT vs COUNTA pair is the audit tool: if COUNTA is 10 but COUNT is 8, two cells are text — exactly the type bug from Module 1.

payload.title: F4 cycles lock types
payload.text: With the cursor on a reference inside the formula, F4 cycles B1 → $B$1 → B$1 → $B1 → B1. Faster and safer than typing dollars by hand.

payload.title: AVERAGE silently skips text
payload.text: If two of ten marks are stored as text, AVERAGE divides by 8 — the average looks normal and is wrong. Audit with COUNT vs COUNTA before trusting any average.

payload.title: Line-item budget with a locked rate cell
payload.problem: B2:B6 holds five item costs; $C$1 holds GST at 0.18. Column C must show 18% of each item cost.

steps.title: Formula in C2
steps.desc: =B2*$C$1 — B2 relative (moves per row), $C$1 absolute (stays the rate).

steps.title: Fill down
steps.desc: Double-click the fill handle (or drag) to C6 — each row now points at its own B row and the same $C$1.

steps.title: Total row
steps.desc: =SUM(B2:B6) in B7 and =SUM(C2:C6) in C7.

steps.title: Check
steps.desc: Click C4: formula should read =B4*$C$1. If it reads =B4*C3 the lock is missing.

payload.solution: =B2*$C$1 filled down gives each row the same 18% rate; the SUM row totals cost and GST separately.

payload.title: Audit a broken fill
payload.prompt: Build the budget above, then rebuild column C WITHOUT the $ on $C$1 and fill down. Click each cell and observe which rate cell each row grabs. Fix it with F4.
payload.hint: Without the lock, C3 grabs C2, C4 grabs C3 — the rate drifts into the results column.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting $ on the rate cell when filling down
mistakes.fix: Every formula that shares one input cell must lock it: $C$1. Verify by clicking a mid-column cell and reading the formula bar.

mistakes.mistake: Using AVERAGE on a column with text-numbers and trusting the result
mistakes.fix: Run COUNT and COUNTA first. If they differ, convert the text cells before averaging — the average divided by the wrong count is silently wrong.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: In =B2*$C$1 filled from row 2 to row 6, what does the row-5 formula reference, and why?
payload.answer: =B5*$C$1. B2 is relative so it advances to B5; $C$1 is fully absolute so it stays pointing at the single rate cell in every row.
payload.source: Relative vs absolute — the most frequently tested Excel reference concept.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Formulas start with =; relative references shift when copied.
$ locks: $C$1 fixed entirely, C$1 row-relative, $C1 column-relative; F4 cycles.
SUM/AVERAGE/COUNT use numeric cells only; COUNTA counts any non-empty.
COUNT < COUNTA means text is hiding in a numeric column.

questions.prompt: With =B2*$C$1 in C2 filled down to C6, the row-5 formula is:
questions.explanation: B2 advances per row; $C$1 is locked to the one rate cell.

questions.prompt: COUNT and COUNTA differ on a column. What does that indicate?
options: Some cells hold text, not numbers
questions.explanation: COUNT counts numbers; COUNTA counts everything non-empty — the gap is text cells.

questions.prompt: AVERAGE over ten cells where two are text returns a mean based on:
questions.explanation: Text and blanks are skipped entirely — the divisor is the numeric count (8).

questions.prompt: Which key cycles absolute/relative reference styles while editing a formula?
questions.explanation: F4 cycles B1 → $B$1 → B$1 → $B1 on the reference under the cursor.

lessons.title: IF Logic & Decoding Errors
lessons.summary: IF conditionals, nested IFs, the IFS upgrade, and what #REF!, #VALUE!, #DIV/0! and circular references actually mean.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Build IF formulas that return one of two outcomes from a test
Read and repair the four most common formula errors
Recognise when a nested IF should become IFS or a lookup instead

payload.text: A results sheet that prints PASS/FAIL from a mark, a fee column that charges concession rates only for eligible students — branching is where a spreadsheet stops being a list and starts being a decision. And every branch you write is one more chance to meet #VALUE! at 2 a.m.

**IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false):** the test is any comparison — >, <, >=, <=, <>, =. =IF(A2>=40,"PASS","FAIL") returns the word PASS when A2 is 40 or more, else FAIL. Numbers and text both work; text literals always take double quotes.

**Comparisons Excel accepts:** A2>40, A2=B3, A2<>"", ISBLANK(A2), A2>=40. Note <> means "not equal". A blank cell in a numeric comparison is treated as 0, which is why =IF(A2>0,...) on a blank cell returns the false branch — usually what you want, but know it.

**Nested IF** handles tiers: =IF(A2>=85,"Dist",IF(A2>=60,"Pass",IF(A2>=40,"Comp","Fail"))). Excel allows 64 levels deep; anything past three or four becomes unreadable — use IFS(A2>=85,"Dist",A2>=60,"Pass",A2>=40,"Comp",TRUE,"Fail") which tests in order and needs no closing parentheses stack.

**The error codes, decoded:**
- #DIV/0! — you divided by zero or by an empty cell.
- #VALUE! — a formula got text where it needed a number (the apostrophe bug, arriving late).
- #REF! — a reference points at deleted cells; the address is gone. Undo or rebuild the reference.
- #NAME? — a misspelled function name, or a name Excel does not recognise.
- #N/A — a lookup failed to find its key (Module 3's VLOOKUP home).
- Circular reference warning — a formula ultimately depends on itself (C1 = A1 + C1). Excel cannot resolve it; find it via Formulas → Error Checking, or enable Iterative Calculation only if you truly mean a self-referencing model.

Trace precedents (Formulas → Trace Precedents) draws arrows to every cell a formula reads — the fastest way to find which input is producing the error.

payload.title: Error
rows: Divided by zero or an empty cell
Text where a number was required

payload.title: IFERROR wraps the ugly away
payload.text: =IFERROR(A2/B2,0) returns 0 instead of #DIV/0! when B2 is empty. Use it for dashboard cells a viewer should never see broken — but do not wrap everything: an error you hide is an error you never fix.

payload.title: Blank cells compare as zero
payload.text: =IF(A2>0,"yes","no") on an empty A2 returns "no" because blank is treated as 0. If "not yet entered" is a third state you care about, test ISBLANK(A2) first.

payload.title: Grades with a three-tier IF
payload.problem: A2 holds a percentage. Return Distinction for ≥85, Pass for ≥40, otherwise Fail.

steps.title: Order matters
steps.desc: Test from the top: =IF(A2>=85,"Distinction",IF(A2>=40,"Pass","Fail")).

steps.title: Why top-down
steps.desc: A 92 satisfies both >=85 and >=40 — the first TRUE branch wins, so the highest tier must be tested first.

steps.title: Edge case
steps.desc: A2 = 40 returns Pass (>= is inclusive). A2 blank returns Fail (blank = 0).

steps.title: IFS variant
steps.desc: =IFS(A2>=85,"Distinction",A2>=40,"Pass",TRUE,"Fail") — same logic, no nested parentheses.

payload.solution: =IF(A2>=85,"Distinction",IF(A2>=40,"Pass","Fail")) — highest tier tested first so a 92 is not caught by the >=40 branch.

payload.title: Fee concession formula
payload.prompt: B2 is annual family income. Charge fee 5000 if income < 300000, 8000 if < 600000, else 12000. Write it as a nested IF, then as IFS.
payload.hint: Order: test the smallest threshold first with <, or the largest first with >= — pick one convention and stay consistent.

mistakes.mistake: Testing tiers in the wrong order
mistakes.fix: If A2=92 hits the >=40 branch first, it returns Pass. Always test the highest threshold first (or use IFS top-down, which enforces order visually).

mistakes.mistake: Spreading a lookup across 6 nested IFs
mistakes.fix: Three tiers is IF territory; more belongs to IFS or — better still — a VLOOKUP/lookup table (Module 3), where changing a band is editing a cell, not surgery on a formula.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: =IF(A2>=60,"Pass","Fail") returns Fail for A2=75. Give the most likely cause and the check.
payload.answer: Most likely A2 holds text (e.g. "75" typed with a leading apostrophe), so the numeric comparison >=60 fails. Check with =ISNUMBER(A2) — FALSE confirms text storage; convert via Text to Columns or VALUE().
payload.source: IF + the data-type bug — the two course themes combined, a favourite of placement tests.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: IF(test, true_value, false_value); text values need double quotes.
Test tiers highest-first so a value cannot fall into a lower band it also satisfies.
IFS replaces deep nesting; TRUE as the last test is the default branch.
#DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #REF!, #NAME?, #N/A each name a specific defect — read them, do not blanket-hide them.

questions.prompt: =IF(A2>=85,"D",IF(A2>=40,"P","F")) with A2=92 returns:
questions.explanation: The first TRUE branch wins — 92 matches >=85 first.

questions.prompt: #VALUE! in a SUM formula most likely means:
options: Text is present where numbers are expected
questions.explanation: Text (including apostrophe-forced numbers) inside a numeric operation raises #VALUE! — or is silently skipped by SUM.

questions.prompt: A formula that ultimately depends on itself produces:
questions.explanation: Excel cannot resolve a self-dependent calculation and warns at entry.

questions.prompt: Blank cells in a numeric comparison like A2>0 are treated as:
questions.explanation: Blank is 0 for comparison purposes — so an empty cell fails >0 and returns the IF false branch.

modules.title: Module 3 — Tables, Sorting, Filtering & Charts
modules.summary: Excel Tables, sort vs filter, and the two chart types that answer the two questions data usually asks.

lessons.title: Tables, Sort & Filter
lessons.summary: Ctrl+T tables, structured references, single vs multi-key sort, and filter without destroying neighbouring data.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Convert a range into an Excel Table and use its auto-expanding totals
Sort by one and two keys without scrambling the rows
Filter to a subset and know when SORT/FILTER formulas beat the buttons

payload.text: Sort a names column without selecting the whole table and you have just detached every student from their marks — silently, with no warning dialog. Data integrity in Excel is mostly about selecting the right rectangle before you press the button.

**Ctrl+T makes a Table.** A Table is a structured object, not just bold headers: it auto-expands when you type in the row below, its headers get filter dropdowns, and a Totals Row (Table Design → Totals Row) can show SUM/AVERAGE per column that updates as rows are added. Formulas inside a table can use structured references — =[@Cost]*$C$1 reads as "this row's Cost column times the rate cell" and is far more readable than =B4*$C$1.

**Sort vs filter:**
- Sort rearranges ROWS. Select any single cell in the column, Data → Sort A to Z / Z to A — Excel auto-expands to the contiguous block. NEVER select just the one column: that is the scramble.
- Multi-key sort: Data → Sort, Add Level — e.g. Class ascending, then Marks descending. Order of levels is priority, top to bottom.
- Filter hides rows. Data → Filter (or Ctrl+T gives it free) — dropdown per column: text filters, number filters, colour filters. Hidden ≠ deleted; Clear Filter restores.

**Sort-safe rules:** every column of the table must be selected (or use a Table object, which sorts correctly from one cell). No blank header cells. No merged cells inside the data range — merged cells make "the row" ambiguous and are the fastest route to scrambled data.

**FILTER (365/2021) vs the buttons:** =FILTER(A2:D100,C2:C100="CSE","none") spills a live view of matching rows — it updates when source data changes, which a static filtered copy does not. Use buttons for a one-off look; use FILTER for a view someone else will refresh.

payload.title: Action
rows: One cell INSIDE the column (Excel expands)
One cell inside; set levels in the dialog
One cell inside; Ctrl+T adds dropdowns free
Select the FULL block including headers

payload.title: Sort by a helper, not the display text
payload.text: Sorting a "10th, 9th, 12th" class label alphabetically gives nonsense. Add a numeric helper column (10, 9, 12) and sort on that instead.

payload.title: One column selected = scrambled table
payload.text: If you select ONLY the marks column and sort, the marks detach from their names permanently (Ctrl+Z immediately if caught). Select a single cell inside the column, or the whole table.

payload.title: Top 3 scorers per class, two-key sort
payload.problem: A1:D100 holds Name, Class, Marks, Result. Rank the sheet by Class A→Z, then Marks highest-first within each class.

steps.title: Enter the dialog
steps.desc: Click one cell inside the data; Data → Sort.

steps.title: Level 1
steps.desc: Sort by Class, A to Z.

steps.title: Level 2
steps.desc: Add Level — then by Marks, Largest to Smallest. Level order = priority.

steps.title: Verify
steps.desc: Within each class block the marks now descend; names still match their marks (headers travelled with their rows).

payload.solution: Two-level sort: Class ascending, Marks descending. Every row moved whole, so Name/Result stayed attached.

payload.title: Filter and total a fee sheet
payload.prompt: Build a 30-row Name/Class/Fee table, Ctrl+T it, enable the Totals Row showing SUM of Fee. Filter Class = "CSE" and watch the total change. Clear the filter and confirm it restores.
payload.hint: The Totals Row recalculates against visible (filtered) rows — that is the point.

mistakes.mistake: Sorting one column while the rest of the row stays put
mistakes.fix: Select a single cell inside the column (Excel expands) or the whole table. Never highlight just the one column.

mistakes.mistake: Merged cells inside a data range
mistakes.fix: Unmerge first (Home → Merge & Center → Unmerge). Merged cells make row boundaries ambiguous; sort and filter become unsafe.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why can sorting a single selected column corrupt a dataset, and how do you sort safely?
payload.answer: Excel moves only the selected cells, so values detach from their row's other columns — names no longer match marks. Sort safely by selecting one cell inside the column (Excel auto-expands to the contiguous block) or by using a Ctrl+T Table, which always moves whole rows.
payload.source: Data-integrity classic — almost every Excel aptitude test includes it.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Ctrl+T: auto-expanding Table with filter dropdowns and optional totals row.
Sort moves rows; filter hides rows; both start from one cell inside the data.
Multi-key sort: Add Level; the top level is the primary key.
Never sort a single highlighted column; never merge cells inside data.

questions.prompt: Safest way to sort a column of a data block?
options: Select the whole column in the grid
Select one cell inside the column
questions.explanation: One cell inside the block lets Excel expand to the contiguous range and move whole rows.

questions.prompt: In a two-level Sort dialog, the top level is:
questions.explanation: Levels apply top-down; the first listed level is the primary sort key.

questions.prompt: A Ctrl+T Table automatically adds:
questions.explanation: Tables ship with header dropdowns; totals and styles are optional toggles.

questions.prompt: Filtering a table with the Totals Row enabled changes the total to show:
questions.explanation: Subtotals/totals respond to visibility — that is how per-class views are produced without copying data.

lessons.title: Charts That Answer a Question
lessons.summary: Column vs line vs pie (when each is honest), chart essentials, and the anti-chart-lie checklist.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Pick the chart type that matches the question being asked
Build a clean chart: right data orientation, titled axes, honest scale
Recognise the misleading-chart tricks every interviewer tests for

payload.text: A column chart with a truncated y-axis can make a 2% dip look like a collapse. Interviewers know this — "what is wrong with this chart?" is a standard question — and so should you, whether you are building the slide or auditing someone else's.

**Match chart to question:**
- Column (bar) — compare categories at one moment: marks per class, fee per branch. Discrete items.
- Line — change over TIME: attendance across months, XP over a semester. The x-axis must be a continuous time or ordered sequence.
- Pie — parts of ONE whole, ≤ 5 slices, all positive. If your pie has nine slices or negative values, it is a column chart wearing a costume.
- Bar (horizontal) — same as column but for long category names (company names, role titles) that would collide on a horizontal axis.

**Build it right:** select the data WITH headers (labels travel with values), Insert → recommended chart or pick the type. Then fix the defaults:
- Chart title states the finding ("CSE attendance trails ECE by 9 points"), not just the topic ("Attendance").
- Axis titles on both axes. A bare number axis is a puzzle, not a chart.
- Data labels only when the reader needs exact values — otherwise they are ink.
- Legend only when there are ≥ 2 series.

**The honesty checklist (interview bait):**
- Y-axis starts at zero for columns and bars. A column chart from 380 to 420 exaggerates a small gap.
- Line charts MAY zoom the y-range — time trends are read as shape — but say so if the range is truncated.
- Pie slices sum to 100% of ONE thing; "other" beyond ~15% should be investigated, not swept up.
- Same data, same scale, when comparing two charts side by side.

**Switching type later:** right-click the chart → Change Chart Type. Data selection stays; only the rendering changes — safe to experiment.

payload.title: Select with headers, always
payload.text: Include the header row and first column in your selection before Insert → Chart: Excel then auto-names the series and axis labels correctly. Chart without labels is a puzzle you force the reader to solve.

payload.title: The truncated-axis lie
payload.text: A column chart whose y-axis starts at 380 turns a 5% gap into a visual chasm. Columns and bars must start at zero; only line charts may zoom, and even then state the range.

payload.title: Attendance trend across six months
payload.problem: Monthly attendance percentages for one student, Jan–Jun. Show the trend honestly.

steps.title: Orientation
steps.desc: Time on the x-axis — months in a column, percentages beside them; select both with headers.

steps.title: Chart type
steps.desc: Insert → Line Chart (with markers). One series, one question: is attendance rising or falling?

steps.title: Label it
steps.desc: Title: "Attendance dips each March and recovers by June". Y-axis title "Attendance %", x-axis "Month".

steps.title: Scale check
steps.desc: A percentage line may zoom (e.g. 70–100%) for shape — acceptable for a trend line; never do this for columns.

payload.solution: A labelled line chart with month axis and % axis; the title states the finding, and the zoomed y-range is legitimate for a single trend line.

payload.title: Fix a lying chart
payload.prompt: Chart five branch averages as columns with the y-axis manually set to 60–85. Observe the exaggerated gaps. Reset the axis to start at 0 and compare the visual story.
payload.hint: Right-click the y-axis → Format Axis → Bounds → Minimum = 0.

mistakes.mistake: Pie chart with 8+ slices or negative values
mistakes.fix: Pie needs a small set of positive parts of one whole. Use a bar chart for many categories; negatives cannot be a "slice" at all.

mistakes.mistake: Column chart with a truncated y-axis
mistakes.fix: Set the axis minimum to 0. If the differences then look small, that is because they ARE small — report the number, not a manufactured visual gap.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A colleague shows a column chart of two department budgets, y-axis from ₹9.5L to ₹10.5L, claiming a "massive" gap. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
payload.answer: Column charts must start the y-axis at zero; a truncated axis visually amplifies a small difference. Reset the axis minimum to 0 — the real gap is around 5%, which the honest chart will show as modest. Report the numeric difference alongside.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Column/bar compare categories; line shows time; pie is a small set of positive parts.
Select data WITH headers; title the chart with the finding, label both axes.
Columns and bars start at zero; only trend lines may zoom the y-range.
"What is wrong with this chart?" = check axis start, labels, slice count, scale consistency.

questions.prompt: Which chart best shows one student's attendance across six months?
questions.explanation: Time series reads as shape — line is the honest choice.

questions.prompt: A column chart's y-axis should normally:
options: Start just below the minimum value
Use a log scale by default
questions.explanation: Truncated axes exaggerate bar differences — columns must start at zero.

questions.prompt: A pie chart is honest only when slices are:
questions.explanation: Parts of a single whole, all positive, few enough to read — otherwise use bars.

questions.prompt: The best chart title states:
questions.explanation: A title that names the insight ("X leads by 9 points") beats a topic label ("Attendance").

modules.title: Module 4 — Data Cleanup & Real Workflows
modules.summary: The repeatable clean-up sequence for pasted data, Flash Fill, and a capstone attendance tracker you can defend line by line.

lessons.title: The Clean-Up Sequence for Pasted Data
lessons.summary: A repeatable five-step pass — TRIM/CLEAN, Text to Columns, Flash Fill, remove duplicates, validation — for any CSV you did not create.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply the standard clean-up pass to a pasted dataset in a fixed order
Use TRIM, CLEAN and SUBSTITUTE to kill invisible whitespace and control characters
Use Flash Fill to split or join patterns without writing formulas

payload.text: Every real Excel session starts the same way: paste something someone else exported, then spend twenty minutes finding out what is wrong with it. Learn the pass once and that twenty minutes becomes four.

**The five-step pass, in this order:**
1. **TRIM + CLEAN the text columns.** TRIM removes leading/trailing spaces and collapses doubles (the most common invisible defect). CLEAN removes non-printing control characters pasted from web pages. =TRIM(CLEAN(A2)) is the standard combo. Fill down, paste-values over the original.
2. **Text to Columns where a column holds two things.** "Ananya Rao" → Name + Surname, or "12-10-2026" split on the hyphen. Data → Text to Columns, Delimited or Fixed width.
3. **Flash Fill for patterned joins/splits.** Type the first result you want in the adjacent column (e.g. first name from full name, or 10-digit mobile from "91 98765 43210"), then Ctrl+E — Excel detects the pattern and fills the rest. Works for case changes, id extraction, and reformatting dates into one shape.
4. **Remove duplicates.** Data → Remove Duplicates, tick the key columns. ALWAYS read the dialog's report: "12 duplicates removed, 88 unique remain" — if it says 80 removed from 100 you selected the wrong keys.
5. **Data validation to keep it clean.** Data → Data Validation: whole numbers between bounds, list dropdowns for branch/year, date ranges. An invalid entry is stopped (or warned) at typing time instead of discovered at analysis time.

**Invisible defects worth naming:** non-breaking spaces (Alt+160 / CHAR(160)) look like spaces but TRIM does not remove them — =SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160),"") does. Numbers stored as text (Module 1). Dates in two formats in one column (12/10/2026 vs 12-Oct-26) — Flash Fill or TEXT() normalises them.

payload.title: Clean on a helper column first
payload.text: Run TRIM/CLEAN into a NEW column, verify with COUNTA, then paste-values over the original. Cleaning in place with no undo trail is how a dataset gets destroyed mid-cleanup.

payload.title: Read the Remove Duplicates report
payload.text: The dialog tells you exactly how many rows it deleted. Read it. If the number is far larger than the repeats you expected, Ctrl+Z immediately — you probably keyed on the wrong column.

payload.title: Clean a pasted attendance export
payload.problem: A pasted column has full names with trailing spaces and non-breaking spaces, plus a few exact-duplicate rows. Produce a clean unique name list with a first-name helper.

steps.title: Whitespace pass
steps.desc: =TRIM(CLEAN(SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160),""))) in B2, fill down — handles regular, control and non-breaking spaces in one shot.

steps.title: Verify the pass
steps.desc: COUNTA(A) vs COUNTA(B) should match (no rows lost); spot-check a name that had a trailing space.

steps.title: Flash Fill first names
steps.desc: Type the first name of row 1 in C2, then Ctrl+E — Excel fills the pattern down the column.

steps.title: De-duplicate
steps.desc: Select B (or A:C), Data → Remove Duplicates on the name column; read the removed/remaining report.

payload.solution: TRIM+CLEAN+SUBSTITUTE normalises whitespace, Flash Fill extracts first names, Remove Duplicates leaves a unique list — each step verified before the next destructive one.

payload.title: Clean your own export
payload.prompt: Export any 30-row list you have (contacts, marks, fees) to CSV, re-import it, run the five-step pass, and write down which defects each step actually found. Note anything the pass missed.
payload.hint: Common surprises: non-breaking spaces from web pastes, numbers stored as text, dates in two shapes.

mistakes.mistake: Running Remove Duplicates before checking which column is the key
mistakes.fix: Duplicates are relative to the selected key columns. Tick only the true identity columns; read the removed-count report before moving on.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming TRIM removes all whitespace
mistakes.fix: TRIM handles spaces only — non-breaking spaces (CHAR(160)) survive it. Wrap with SUBSTITUTE(x,CHAR(160),"") for web-pasted data.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A pasted name column still shows "double spaces" after TRIM. Explain and give the full fix.
payload.answer: The gaps are non-breaking spaces (CHAR(160)), commonly pasted from web pages; TRIM only collapses regular spaces. Fix: =TRIM(CLEAN(SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160),""))) — SUBSTITUTE removes the non-breaking characters, CLEAN strips control characters, TRIM normalises the regular spaces.
payload.source: The invisible-character question — a recurring favourite because it looks like a TRIM bug and is not.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Clean-up order: TRIM/CLEAN → Text to Columns → Flash Fill → Remove Duplicates → Validation.
TRIM misses CHAR(160); pair it with SUBSTITUTE for web-pasted data.
Ctrl+E Flash Fill learns a pattern you demonstrate in the first row.
Always read the Remove Duplicates report; validate inputs to keep data clean permanently.

questions.prompt: Which function removes non-breaking spaces that TRIM leaves behind?
questions.explanation: CHAR(160) is the non-breaking space; SUBSTITUTE removes it before TRIM normalises the rest.

questions.prompt: Flash Fill is triggered with:
questions.explanation: Type one example of the pattern in the adjacent cell, then Ctrl+E fills the column.

questions.prompt: Before clicking OK in Remove Duplicates you should:
options: Tick only the true key columns and plan to read the report
questions.explanation: Duplicates are relative to the selected keys; the report then tells you exactly how many rows were deleted.

questions.prompt: The safest way to apply a cleanup formula over a raw column is:
options: Fill a helper column, verify, then paste-values over
questions.explanation: Helper column first keeps an undo trail and a verification step before the raw data is replaced.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build a Attendance & Fees Tracker
lessons.summary: Apply the full course — types, formulas, IF, tables, charts, clean-up — to one small tracker you can defend in an interview.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Assemble a two-sheet tracker (records + summary) using every tool from Modules 1–3
Wire summary formulas (SUM/COUNTIF/AVERAGE, IF status, a chart) that stay correct as rows are added
Present the tracker: what each sheet answers, and why the formulas are trustworthy

payload.text: This is the artefact the certificate is issued for. Not notes about Excel — a working file with live formulas, a chart that answers a real question, and a clean-up pass you can narrate. If you can defend every formula in it, you can defend yourself in the interview.

**The tracker, two sheets:**
- **Records** — one row per student per month: ID, Name, Class, Month, Attendance %, Fees Paid (Y/N), Fees Amount. Built as a Ctrl+T Table so it expands safely and the filter dropdowns come free.
- **Summary** — the questions anyone actually asks: total fees collected, count pending, average attendance per class, a pass/fail or dues-status column via IF, and one chart.

**Formulas that stay correct when rows are added:**
- =SUMIFS(Fees[Amount],Fees[Paid],"N") — outstanding fees (structured references follow the table as it grows).
- =COUNTIF(Fees[Class],"CSE") — headcount per class.
- =AVERAGEIFS(Fees[Attendance],Fees[Class],"C2") — average attendance per class.
- Status column inside the table: =IF([@Paid]="Y","Clear","Dues") — row-relative, copies itself on expansion.
- Chart: column chart of average attendance per class, y-axis from zero, titled with the finding.

**The clean-up pass you will narrate:** the Records sheet starts as a pasted export — you apply TRIM/CLEAN, Flash Fill a first-name column if asked, Remove Duplicates on ID+Month, and add Data Validation (Class from a list; Attendance 0–1). Say this out loud in the interview; it is the whole course in sixty seconds.

**Defence questions to rehearse:** Why SUMIFS not SUM? (Conditional — matches Paid=N.) Why a Table? (Auto-expansion + structured refs keep formulas valid as data grows.) Why does the chart y-axis start at zero? (Columns must — honest comparison.) What if attendance is pasted as text? (COUNTA>COUNT audit catches it; Text to Columns fixes.)

payload.title: Sheet
rows: What happened — one row per student-month
What to do — totals, dues, per-class averages, chart

payload.title: Structured references are the interview answer
payload.text: Fees[Amount] names the column inside the table — the formula keeps working when the table grows, unlike a fixed B2:B500. Use them in the Summary sheet and mention why.

payload.title: Validation is not retroactive
payload.text: Data Validation stops NEW bad entries; it does not fix rows already pasted. Run the clean-up pass first, then add validation to keep the sheet clean from now on.

payload.title: The outstanding-fees formula, end to end
payload.problem: Fees table has columns Paid (Y/N) and Amount. Summary must show total outstanding.

steps.title: Conditional sum
steps.desc: =SUMIFS(Fees[Amount],Fees[Paid],"N") — adds Amount only where Paid is N.

steps.title: Cross-check
steps.desc: =SUM(Fees[Amount])-SUMIFS(Fees[Amount],Fees[Paid],"Y") must equal the same number; if not, some Paid cell is neither Y nor N.

steps.title: Count the cases
steps.desc: =COUNTIF(Fees[Paid],"N") — the number of students with dues; pair it with the total for the summary tile.

steps.title: Chart it
steps.desc: A small column chart: outstanding by Class (SUMIFS with class criteria per class row). Y-axis zero-based, titled with the largest-dues finding.

payload.solution: SUMIFS on the table columns gives outstanding fees; the subtraction cross-check validates every Paid cell is exactly Y or N; COUNTIF gives the headcount behind the rupee figure.

payload.title: Ship the tracker
payload.prompt: Build the full two-sheet tracker from scratch with at least 12 Records rows across two classes. Include: SUMIFS outstanding, per-class AVERAGEIFS, an IF status column inside the table, and one honest chart. Save it as YourName-Excel-Capstone.xlsx.
payload.hint: Build Records as a Table FIRST; write Summary formulas with structured references after.

mistakes.mistake: Fixed ranges (B2:B500) in Summary formulas
mistakes.fix: New rows fall outside the range and silently drop out of totals. Use Table structured references (Fees[Amount]) so the range follows the data.

mistakes.mistake: Adding Data Validation before cleaning pasted rows
mistakes.fix: Validation does not touch existing values. Clean first (the five-step pass), then validate to keep future entries honest.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Your Summary shows SUM(Fees[Amount]) = 84,000 but outstanding SUMIFS(...,"N") = 31,000 while adding the Paid="Y" side gives 45,000. What is wrong?
payload.answer: 31,000 + 45,000 = 76,000 ≠ 84,000 — some Paid cells are neither exactly "Y" nor exactly "N" (trailing spaces, lowercase, or blanks). Audit with =COUNTA(Fees[Paid]) vs COUNTIF Y + COUNTIF N; TRIM/clean the Paid column and re-validate with a Y/N dropdown.
payload.source: Cross-check reasoning — the capstone defence question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Two sheets: Records (raw rows, a Table) and Summary (SUMIFS/COUNTIF/AVERAGEIFS + one chart).
Table structured references keep formulas valid as rows are added.
Cross-check conditional totals against the unconditional total; the gap exposes dirty keys.
Narrate the clean-up pass in the interview — it proves the whole course in one minute.

questions.prompt: Why use Fees[Amount] instead of B2:B500 in the Summary?
options: It follows the table as rows are added
questions.explanation: Structured references auto-expand with the table; fixed ranges silently miss new rows.

questions.prompt: SUMIFS(Fees[Amount],Fees[Paid],"N") computes:
questions.explanation: SUMIFS adds the sum range only where every criteria range matches — here, unpaid rows.

questions.prompt: Data Validation on a column:
questions.explanation: Validation is preventive, not retroactive — clean existing data first, then validate.

questions.prompt: Outstanding (31,000) + Paid-side (45,000) does not equal the SUM total (84,000). Most likely cause:
options: Some Paid cells are not exactly Y or N
questions.explanation: Trailing spaces, case or blanks make rows match neither criteria; the arithmetic gap is the audit signal.

courses.title: AI Literacy for Everyone
courses.subtitle: From "what is AI" to a toolkit you actually run — how the models work, how to prompt them, how to verify what comes back, and how to keep your name on work you can defend
courses.description:
Everyone is now expected to work alongside AI, almost nobody was taught what it actually is, and the gap between the two is where bad grades, bad hires and bad decisions happen. This course closes that gap in ten modules and forty lessons: first the honest technical foundation — what AI, machine learning and deep learning really mean, how a neural network learns, how a large language model reads text and predicts tokens, and how a frontier model is built from internet-scale pretraining through supervised fine-tuning to RLHF. Then the practical half: prompting that works (structure, system instructions, few-shot examples, step-by-step reasoning, iteration like debugging), the tools landscape (chat vs coding vs search, media generation, free vs paid vs local), and the everyday uses that matter — research, learning code, drafts, exam prep and resumes — each welded to a verification routine rather than a leap of faith.

The last stretch is the part most courses skip: limits and safety (hallucination, bias, privacy, academic integrity, deepfakes, the honest jobs picture) and then your own practice — workflows with humans placed where the stakes are, a prompt library you reuse, rubrics for judging output, and a short ethics code you wrote yourself. It ends with a capstone that is a real artifact, not a quiz: five AI use-cases you actually ran, ten prompts with before/after evidence, your verification checklist, one hallucination you caught, and the rules you will keep. The certificate is issued for that document, not for notes about it.

**Who this is for:** any student — any branch, technical or not — who uses (or is expected to use) AI tools and wants to know what they are doing when they do; placement-prep students who need AI literacy for aptitude rounds and interviews; working professionals who must supervise AI output rather than be supervised by it.

**What you need:** no mathematics, no programming, no prior AI course. A browser, and — for the practice lessons — access to any free AI chat tool. Everything else is taught here from first principles.
courses.thumbnail_alt: AI Literacy for Everyone course cover
outcomes: Explain AI, machine learning, deep learning and data science precisely — and place LLMs inside that map
Describe how a neural network learns and how a frontier model is made (pretraining, SFT, RLHF)
Use tokens, context window, temperature and knowledge cutoff to predict what a model can and cannot do
Write prompts with role, task, constraints and format — plus system rules, few-shot examples and step-by-step reasoning
Iterate on prompts with a diagnose-first loop and a small fixed test set
Choose correctly between chat assistants, coding assistants, AI search, media tools, free/paid tiers and local models
Use AI for research, code learning, writing drafts, exam prep and resumes — with verification built into every workflow
Detect hallucination, recognise bias, protect your data, and follow academic-integrity rules
Build personal workflows with human-in-the-loop gates and maintain a prompt library you actually reuse
Judge output with rubrics, apply honesty/attribution/harm ethics, and ship a capstone toolkit backed by evidence
courses.about_course:
This course is built around one claim: using AI well is a skill with two halves — understanding the machine and disciplining the output — and almost everyone is flying with neither. Forty lessons, each the same nine steps (objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice task, common mistakes, exam/interview angle, quiz, summary), every worked example real rather than decorative.

Modules 1 to 5 build the foundation without mathematics. Module 1 defines AI, machine learning, deep learning and data science — and walks the history from expert systems through the statistical turn to the generative wave. Module 2 covers how machines learn: features and labels, the three learning paradigms, why you never test on training data, and overfitting. Module 3 demystifies neural networks with real numbers — a neuron's arithmetic, what layers add, what training actually changes, and what a loss function measures. Module 4 goes inside a large language model: tokens, next-token prediction, embeddings and attention intuition, the context window, temperature, top-p and the knowledge cutoff. Module 5 completes the picture with how frontier models are made — corpus and pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF and alignment, then model families, open vs closed weights and the token arithmetic that governs cost.

Module 6 begins the practical half: the role/task/constraints/format skeleton, system prompts as soft contracts, few-shot examples that teach boundaries, chain-of-thought reasoning with its rationalisation caveat, and prompt iteration treated as debugging. Module 7 maps the tools — chat assistants, coding assistants and AI search as three species with different failure modes; image, video and voice tools with their structural limits; free vs paid vs API vs self-hosted; and a selection procedure that puts data sensitivity first. Module 8 applies all of it to study and work — research and summarisation with a verification routine, code explained until you understand it, drafts you edit before shipping, and exam/resume/placement work under the evidence test. Module 9 confronts the limits honestly: hallucination mechanisms and checks, bias and where it enters the pipeline, privacy of whatever you paste, academic integrity, deepfakes and misinformation, and the jobs question without hype. Module 10 turns knowledge into practice — workflows with human-in-the-loop gates, a maintained prompt library, rubrics for judging quality, an ethics recap (honesty, attribution, harm), and the capstone: your personal AI toolkit with real evidence of use.

The interview and exam angle runs through every lesson — "why is this prompt generic", "what does temperature actually change", "where does bias enter", "why can't detectors settle deepfakes" — the AI-literacy questions aptitude rounds and panel interviews increasingly ask, and that you will be able to answer from first principles rather than from headlines.
prerequisites: Nothing — no mathematics, no programming, no prior AI courses
A browser on a phone or computer; for the practice lessons, access to any free AI chat tool
audience: Students of any branch who use — or are expected to use — AI tools and want to understand them
Non-technical students who need a first-principles introduction without maths or code
Placement-prep students: AI literacy is now common in aptitude rounds and panel interviews
Working professionals who must verify and supervise AI output in their daily work

exam_prep.target: AI literacy / digital-skills assessments — all branches

units.title: What AI is (M1)
units.summary: AI = machines performing intelligent tasks; ML = learning from data inside that goal; DL = neural-network methods inside ML; data science = the broader practice of extracting value from data (overlapping, not nested the same way). History: expert systems (hand-written rules) hit a ceiling on ambiguity and maintenance; the statistical turn learned patterns from data; deep learning scaled it; transformers + scale produced the generative wave. Narrow vs general AI: today's systems are narrow — superhuman in one box, brittle outside; AGI is hypothetical. Daily AI: recommendation, spam filter, maps ETA — each predicts something specific; literacy is noticing what.
questions: Draw the AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL nesting and place data science relative to it.
Why could expert systems not scale, and what replaced them and why?
Give one example of narrow AI and state exactly what it cannot do outside its box.

units.title: How machines learn (M2)
units.summary: Dataset anatomy: features (inputs), label (target), and why data quality dominates model cleverness. Paradigms by feedback: supervised (labelled examples — classify/regress), unsupervised (structure without labels — clustering), reinforcement (rewards from actions). Splits: train/validation/test; test stays untouched or it leaks; cross-validation when data is scarce; leakage produces secretly useless models. Overfitting = high variance (memorises training specifics; fix with more data, simplification, regularisation, early stopping); underfitting = high bias (too simple; increase capacity). Diagnosis via the gap between train and validation curves — never via training accuracy alone.
questions: Why is testing on training data worse than useless — what does it estimate?
Distinguish overfitting from underfitting using train/validation numbers, and give the fix for each.
What is data leakage, and how does it survive until production?

units.title: Neural networks (M3)
units.summary: Neuron = weighted sum + bias + activation. Depth helps because layers compose features hierarchically (edges → shapes → objects); in practice depth beats width. Training changes the weights: random initialisation (symmetry must break), forward pass, loss, backpropagation of error, small steps along the gradient (gradient descent), repeat. Learning rate controls step size: too high = oscillation/divergence, too low = glacial. Loss = one number measuring wrongness; the choice of loss encodes what you care about; loss and accuracy are different views (smooth optimisable signal vs discrete correctness). None of this requires calculus to operate — only the mechanism.
questions: Walk the training loop: forward pass, loss, weight update — what changes between epochs?
Why must initial weights differ across neurons in a layer?
Symptoms of a learning rate that is too high vs too low?

units.title: Inside a large language model (M4)
units.summary: Text → tokens (subword units; long/rare words cost more tokens; token counts drive price and limits). The one task: next-token prediction — every essay, chat and code block is that objective at scale. Embeddings: meaning as nearby points; attention: dynamic relevance weighting so each token looks at the right others; together they connect distant words. Context window: everything visible per pass — a hard capacity limit, not a style setting. Temperature/top-p: sampling dials — low = most likely, deterministic-ish (extraction); high = diverse, riskier (brainstorming). Knowledge cutoff: when training data stopped — hence live facts need retrieval or sources, never recall.
questions: Why do models count tokens instead of words, and what does that drive?
What does temperature change — and what does it NOT change?
A question needs a post-cutoff fact. What are the two honest options, and what is the trap?

units.title: How frontier models are made (M5)
units.summary: Pretraining: curated corpus (quality filtering, dedup, licensing) + next-token objective at trillion-token scale → a base model: a continuator, not a chatbot. Parameters = trained numbers = capacity; counts inform, never decide (data, tokens, MoE, post-training all mediate). SFT: curated prompt→response demonstrations install format, manners, refusals — thousands to millions of examples, quality over quantity; can add behaviour, not knowledge. RLHF: pairwise preferences → reward model → policy optimisation (or DPO-style direct preference tuning) — buys taste; risks: over-refusal, reward hacking, proxy over-optimisation. Deployment: open weights (control, ops burden) vs closed API (capability, dependency); token economics: bill = input×rate + output×rate; output is costlier and sequential, so it drives cost and latency.
questions: Why is a base model not yet a chat assistant — what does post-training add?
Explain the RLHF pipeline and one risk it introduces.
Compute the monthly cost of a workload given per-million input/output rates — and name the biggest lever.

units.title: Prompting that works (M6)
units.summary: Underspecified prompts get statistically average answers — supply the missing dimensions. Skeleton: role (register), task (one verb), constraints (audience, length, facts, exclusions), format (shape); fence pasted data with delimiters; permit clarifying questions. System prompts: standing policy in the system seat — testable behaviour rules, output contract, uncertainty policy, injection clause; soft constraints, not guarantees. Few-shot: in-context examples teach mappings and boundaries; keep them correct, consistent, covering the hard branch; changes behaviour, never knowledge. Chain of thought: intermediate tokens act as working memory — strong on multi-step work, but chains can rationalise wrong answers. Iterate like an engineer: run → inspect → diagnose (missing spec / conflicting spec / capability / input) → one change → retest on a mini test set.
questions: Name the four prompt components and say what each one controls.
Why do examples usually beat prose when they disagree?
Describe the diagnosis-first iteration loop and why only one change per round.

units.title: Tools and everyday uses (M7–M8)
units.summary: Three text species: chat (parametric recall + pasted context), coding assistants (executable output — the strongest verification loop), AI search (live retrieval + citations that still need opening). Media shelf: image/video/voice with structural fails (rendered text, counting, identity drift, consent); generation for mood, real tools for facts and typography. Free vs paid: money buys limits, model tier, features and data terms — never accuracy; find training/retention settings yourself. Local models: privacy, offline, zero token cost, hardware-capped capability; constraints (data path) decide category before capability. Study/work uses with verification: research (classify claims, trace citations), code (run, read, test edges), drafts (fact/tone/specificity/responsibility passes), resumes (evidence test: every claim defensible) — the sender always owns the message.
questions: Rank the three text species by output checkability and justify your routing for a live-fact question.
What does a paid subscription actually buy — and what can it never buy?
Walk the four-pass check over an AI-drafted email, with an example of what each pass catches.

units.title: Risks, ethics and your practice (M9–M10)
units.summary: Hallucination = plausible-shaped tokens where knowledge is absent (no truth-check in generation); risk tracks specificity — citations, numbers, dates, post-cutoff facts; fix by grounding + claim classification + tracing; temperature never fixes facts. Bias enters via data (history), objective (typicality), raters (taste) — mitigate with rubrics, counter-examples, diverse tests; people-affecting decisions stay with humans. Privacy: pasted text travels (retention, possible training, review) — green/amber/red bins, redact, minimise, never paste credentials; third-party data needs rights. Integrity: institution policy + the principle of work you can defend; detectors unreliable — process evidence is the fair proof. Deepfakes: verify origin and corroboration, not the artefact; forwarding is publication. Jobs: tasks change before jobs do — specification, verification and accountability rise in value. Practice: workflows with gates placed by error cost × reversibility × checkability; a prompt library with slots, checks and test dates; rubrics over vibes; ethics = honesty, attribution, harm, and the comfort test. Capstone: your toolkit with real evidence.
questions: Why is hallucination structural, and what two mitigations reduce it without eliminating it?
Place a human gate in a weekly workflow and justify the position with cost and reversibility.
What does honesty require when submitting AI-assisted work, and what does attribution require?

important_questions: Explain why an underspecified prompt produces a generic answer, using the next-token objective — and name the four components that fix it.
Walk through the RLHF pipeline and explain one failure mode (over-refusal or reward hacking) with its mitigation.
Why does asking a model to show step-by-step reasoning often improve accuracy? Give the mechanism and one caveat.
Design a five-step verification routine for AI-supplied facts and citations, and explain why mismatched citations are the most dangerous failure class.
Trace three stages where bias enters an LLM pipeline and give one mitigation at each.
Compare a cloud API and a local model on privacy, cost and capability — and give two situations where local wins.
A weekly workflow auto-sends AI-drafted messages. Redesign it with human-in-the-loop gates and justify each gate's position.
What distinguishes a reusable prompt-library entry from a saved transcript? Specify five fields and the purpose of each.

previous_year_questions.question: An AI assistant supplies five "sources" for an essay. Walk through your verification routine, and explain why one of the five — a citation that opens to a real paper that does not contain the claimed finding — is worse than a source that does not exist.
previous_year_questions.solution: Routine: (1) extract all checkable claims; (2) classify each (citation, number, date, interpretation); (3) search title + author for every citation and read the supporting passage; (4) cross-check load-bearing numbers against primary sources and dates against official pages; (5) stamp each claim verified/unverified/contradicted before use. The mismatched citation is the worst class because it passes casual inspection — the link works, the paper is real, and the reader's trust in the source transfers to a claim the source does not make. A fabricated source at least fails in one click; a mismatch survives until someone reads the passage — which is exactly why you read the passage.

previous_year_questions.question: A model's answers on a company's internal benchmark improved sharply after an alignment run, but human reviewers report the answers are "more polished and less accurate". What happened, and how would you fix it?
previous_year_questions.solution: Classic reward hacking: the policy optimised surface correlates of the reward model (structure, confident framing, thorough-looking lists) rather than true quality — the proxy diverged under pressure, and over-optimisation pushed the metric up while real quality fell. Fixes: (1) retrain/augment the reward signal with fresh preferences where factual accuracy is the tiebreaker, including hard negatives that are well-structured but wrong, so structure alone stops paying; (2) gate the optimisation loop on held-out human evaluation and factual probes — stop when human scores fall regardless of the reward-model score — and strengthen the constraint anchoring the model to its pre-optimisation behaviour. The Module 2 principle, recurring at scale: you get the metric you choose.

previous_year_questions.question: Your team wants to use a chat assistant for summarising client documents that cannot leave the company network. Outline the decision process and the workflow you would insist on.
previous_year_questions.solution: Decision process, in order: (1) the hard constraint — data egress is forbidden, so consumer chat is out regardless of quality; the category is set before benchmarks are discussed. (2) Category-appropriate options: self-hosted open-weight model on company infrastructure, or a provider offering a contractual zero-retention/private tier if policy permits egress under DPA — capability validation on real documents comes next (Module 5's checklist). (3) Workflow: paste only the minimum necessary (redaction of identifiers even inside the boundary), summarisation prompts that demand quotes and preserved caveats, and a human verification pass against the source document before any summary leaves the team. (4) Governance: retention and training settings documented, access logged, and the rule written down — the human gate sits at approval, because a wrong client summary is an irreversible credibility event.

bank.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning?
options: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
AI and machine learning are two names for the same field
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning
Data science is a subset of deep learning
bank.explanation: The terms nest: AI is the broad goal of machines performing intelligent tasks; machine learning is the data-driven approach inside it; deep learning is the neural-network-based family inside machine learning.

bank.prompt: Why did the expert-systems era of AI (roughly the 1970s–80s) hit a ceiling?
options: Computers were too slow to evaluate the rules
Hand-written rules could not scale to ambiguity, exceptions and learning from new data — and maintaining them became impossible
Expert systems used the wrong programming language
Researchers were forbidden from deploying rule engines
bank.explanation: Rule engines worked inside narrow, well-defined boxes; every edge case needed a new hand-written rule, so coverage and maintenance collapsed. The statistical/learning turn was the field's answer to exactly that limit.

bank.prompt: A system beats world champions at chess but cannot plan a simple trip. It is best described as:
options: Narrow AI — superhuman inside one defined task, with no transfer beyond it
A reinforcement-learning system that never trained
bank.explanation: Today's AI is narrow: brilliance in a single box, brittleness outside it. AGI — general, transferable competence — remains hypothetical.

bank.prompt: In a model that predicts house sale prices from size, location and age, the label is:
options: The sale price — the quantity being predicted
bank.explanation: Features (size, location, age) are the inputs; the label is the target the model learns to predict — here, the sale price.

bank.prompt: Why must the test set stay untouched until the end of model development?
options: Models become slower as training continues
It provides an unbiased estimate of performance on unseen data; peeking leaks information and inflates scores
The test set is too small to train on
Training on test data crashes the program
bank.explanation: The test set stands in for the future data the model will meet in production. Any decision made while looking at it (feature choice, tuning, early stopping) leaks information, so the final score flatters the model.

bank.prompt: A model scores 99% on training data and 61% on validation data. Which sequence of moves is most defensible?
options: Add more layers and train longer until training accuracy rises further
Collect more representative data, simplify or regularise the model, and stop training at the validation-optimal point
Lower the evaluation threshold so 61% counts as passing
Delete the validation set and evaluate on training data
bank.explanation: The gap is classic overfitting (high variance): the model memorised training specifics that do not generalise. More/better data, reduced complexity, regularisation and early stopping attack the real problem; the other options either worsen it or simply hide it.

bank.prompt: An artificial neuron computes:
options: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function
A database lookup keyed by the input
The average of every weight in the network
A random label for the input
bank.explanation: Multiply each input by a weight, add the results and a bias, then apply a non-linear activation. Stacking and training billions of these units is the whole of a deep network.

bank.prompt: During training the loss oscillates wildly and often diverges instead of settling. Most likely cause and fix?
options: Learning rate too high — lower it (and check batch size)
Learning rate too low — raise it
The test set was used for training — restart the model
bank.explanation: Oversized weight updates step past minima instead of into them — the signature of a learning rate set too high. Smaller steps (and sometimes larger batches) restore a descending loss curve.

bank.prompt: Why does initialising every weight in a hidden layer to exactly the same value stop the layer learning useful features?
options: It makes the model too large for the GPU memory
Symmetric neurons receive identical gradients and stay identical, so the layer learns one repeated feature instead of a diverse hierarchy
It forces every activation to exactly zero forever
It deletes the loss function from the computation
bank.explanation: Identical units compute identical outputs and receive identical gradients, so they never diverge — the layer collapses to a single duplicated detector. Random initialisation breaks this symmetry so different units can specialise.

bank.prompt: Why does the word "internationalization" usually consume several tokens?
options: The model charges extra for long words
Tokenizers split text into subword units, so long or rare words decompose into multiple tokens
Punctuation inside words is counted separately
The context window limits characters per word
bank.explanation: BPE-style tokenizers build a vocabulary of frequent subword pieces; a long, unusual word is covered by several of them. This is why token counts — not word counts — drive cost and limits.

bank.prompt: You are extracting structured fields from a form and need consistent, repeatable output. Which approach is right, and why?
options: High temperature, so the model explores more possibilities
Low (near-zero) temperature — sampling concentrates on the most likely tokens, favouring determinism suited to extraction
Temperature only affects the context window
bank.explanation: Temperature reshapes the sampling distribution: low values favour the argmax-ish, most probable tokens — stable, fact-style output for extraction; high values diversify creative work and also raise error risk.

bank.prompt: A task needs details from page 1 of a 180,000-token document, but the model's context window is 128,000 tokens. Best approach?
options: Raise the temperature so the model compresses it in
Extract or summarise the relevant section (or chunk and retrieve) and place only that material in the prompt
Split the document into 180 separate chats and average the answers
Ask the model to recall page 1 from memory
bank.explanation: The window is a hard limit, not a style setting. Chunking plus retrieval (or targeted extraction) puts the needed material inside the window; temperature does not affect capacity, averaging invites inconsistency, and "memory" of a specific pasted document is not a feature.

bank.prompt: In RLHF, human raters typically provide supervision by:
options: Writing a perfect response for every prompt from scratch
Comparing two sampled responses and choosing which is better
Labelling every token as good or bad
Coding a rule database of preferences
bank.explanation: Pairwise comparison is what humans do reliably and cheaply; those judgements train a reward model (or drive DPO-style updates) rather than serving as a per-token signal.

bank.prompt: A freshly pretrained base model asked "what is photosynthesis?" replies with three more questions about photosynthesis. Best explanation?
options: It is a text-continuation engine not yet post-trained (SFT and alignment) to follow instructions and hold a chat format
The question exceeded the context window
Temperature was set to exactly zero
bank.explanation: Pretraining produces a powerful continuator, not an assistant. Instruction-following, answer format and refusal behaviour are installed in supervised fine-tuning and alignment — the post-training stages.

bank.prompt: After an alignment run, reward-model scores rise while human reviewers judge the answers less accurate but more structured. Diagnosis and response?
options: Reward hacking / proxy over-optimisation — harden the reward signal with accuracy-focused preferences and gate the loop on held-out human evaluation
Context-window overflow — increase the window size
bank.explanation: The optimiser exploited surface correlates of the reward (structure, confident framing) instead of quality — the classic proxy-metric divergence. Fixes: accuracy-focused preference data with hard negatives, plus stopping power from held-out human evals, not bigger windows.

bank.prompt: Why does the prompt "write about internships" typically produce a generic paragraph?
options: The model refuses to engage with vague requests
Unspecified dimensions (audience, length, purpose) carry no conditioning, so output converges on the statistically typical treatment
The model has never seen internship content
The context window is too small for detail
bank.explanation: Next-token prediction conditions on what is present; absent specifications default to the corpus average, which reads as generic. Role, task, constraints and format supply the missing signal.

bank.prompt: Your few-shot classifier's examples route every ambiguous ticket to "Other", while your prose says "use Bug when a defect is plausible". Outputs follow the examples. The fix:
options: Add ten more examples of any kind
Align prose and demonstrations — change the examples to show a plausible defect routed to Bug (or change the prose to match the examples)
bank.explanation: Demonstrated behaviour usually outweighs described behaviour. The example set is teaching a policy your instruction contradicts; make both say the same thing.

bank.prompt: Why can requiring step-by-step reasoning improve answers on multi-step problems — and what is the key caveat?
options: It increases the model's parameter count; the caveat is cost only
Intermediate reasoning tokens act as working memory that later tokens condition on; the caveat is that a fluent chain can rationalise a wrong answer, so independent verification is still required
It triggers a live web search; the caveat is connectivity
It lowers the temperature; the caveat is latency
bank.explanation: Autoregressive generation has no scratchpad but its own output — required intermediate steps put sub-results into the context. But those steps are generated for plausibility too, which is why reasoning aids, and never replaces, verification.

bank.prompt: What most distinguishes AI search from a plain chat assistant?
options: It retrieves live indexed material and generates answers conditioned on it, usually with citations
bank.explanation: Retrieval in front of generation breaks the training-cutoff ceiling and anchors answers in real passages — while citations, being generated text, still require opening and reading the source.

bank.prompt: Which statement about upgrading from a free AI tier to a paid subscription is TRUE?
options: It buys higher limits, the flagship model, gated features and stronger data controls — not truthfulness
It updates the knowledge cutoff to today
bank.explanation: Money moves the instrument (limits, model tier, features, privacy terms); it never moves the verification problem. Accuracy comes from grounding and checks, not from the billing plan.

bank.prompt: Which pair is CORRECT about local / on-device models?
options: Pro: data stays on the device and there is no per-token cost; Con: capability is capped by hardware, so hard reasoning suffers
Pro: always more capable than cloud APIs; Con: they require internet access
Pro: includes live web knowledge by default; Con: expensive per token
Pro: zero setup; Con: conversations always upload to the vendor
bank.explanation: Local models buy privacy, offline use and fixed cost, and charge a capability ceiling plus setup/ops. They are the right choice for sensitive material and simple transformations — not for frontier reasoning.

bank.prompt: Before submitting research that used an AI assistant, the single most important verification step is:
options: Opening every cited source to confirm it exists and actually supports the claim
Asking the same model to confirm its citations
Paraphrasing the citations in your own words
bank.explanation: Citations are generated text: they can be fabricated or attached to the wrong claim (mismatch). Only opening the source and reading the supporting passage verifies it.

bank.prompt: Which resume edit is legitimate use of AI?
options: Adding a leadership metric you cannot source
Rewriting your true responsibilities with stronger action verbs and honest job-description vocabulary
