Inventing a certification to clear ATS filters
Claiming you led a team you merely assisted
bank.explanation: Presentation of true claims is fair game; invented scope or metrics are soft fabrication that interviews systematically expose (the evidence test: source, names, process, measurement).

bank.prompt: Why should an AI summary of a contract or policy never replace reading the original?
options: Compression silently drops conditions, exceptions and scope — precisely the parts that determine your obligations
Models cannot process long documents at all
bank.explanation: Summaries are an index into high-stakes text: use them to find where to read, then read those passages yourself — the qualifiers are the first casualties of compression.

bank.prompt: A model confidently invents a citation that looks perfectly formatted. The root cause is:
options: A virus in the model weights
Generation optimises plausibility, not truth — when knowledge is absent, the slot is filled with citation-shaped tokens
The temperature was set too low
bank.explanation: Nothing in generation verifies claims; next-token prediction completes patterns. Precise, checkable objects like citations are therefore the highest-risk outputs and must be traced externally.

bank.prompt: Stereotypical defaults in model output mainly originate from:
options: The random seed used at initialisation
Training data that encodes historical patterns, reinforced by an objective that rewards statistically typical continuations
bank.explanation: Data carries the skew; the objective makes "common" equal to "expected". Post-training rater preferences can add taste on top, which is why rubrics, counter-examples and human review are the practical controls.

bank.prompt: A student pastes their entire unpublished thesis draft — including a co-authored chapter — into a free chatbot. Which option best states three risks AND a better workflow?
options: Risks: retention/training use compromising novelty, third-party rights over co-authored material, and loss of custody via review processes or sub-processors; better: disable training for the session, paste only redacted single sections, or use a local model for full-draft passes
Risk: slow answers; better: switch to a paid plan
Risk: an AI detector flags the thesis later; better: rewrite the text before pasting
Risk: the model will publish the thesis; better: delete the chat afterwards
bank.explanation: Unpublished work faces novelty and confidentiality exposure under default retention/training practices; co-authored material belongs partly to others; custody widens beyond the app. Minimising, redacting and using private/local channels addresses the actual risks — deletion afterwards does not.

bank.prompt: "Human-in-the-loop" most accurately means:
options: A person is a required gate at a defined step — specification, approval or verification — in the pipeline
A human types every prompt character by character
A human personally trains the model
A human watches the tokens stream in real time
bank.explanation: It names a control placement: humans own the steps where judgement and consequences live, positioned by error cost, reversibility and checkability — not by the tool's recent track record.

bank.prompt: Which combination of fields turns a saved prompt into a reusable library entry?
options: The surrounding chat history and the number of times you used it
Named slots for inputs, a verification checklist, known failure modes, and a model + last-tested date
The prompt's word count and formatting
The vendor's marketing description of the model
bank.explanation: Slots generalise one instance into a template; checks and failure modes make reuse safe; model/date make re-testing and retirement honest. Transcripts without these remain one-off artefacts.

bank.prompt: You grade two fluent candidate outputs with a precommitted rubric and pick the one that scores higher even though it is less elegant. Best justification?
options: Rubrics are required by every AI vendor
Quality for a task is defined by precommitted, checkable criteria — which separate fitness for purpose from fluency, and fluency correlates poorly with truth
Longer rubrics automatically produce better results
Elegant prose is prohibited in academic work
bank.explanation: The rubric operationalises "good" before the outputs are seen, so the decision rests on task fit rather than style. This is the evaluation discipline that keeps fluency from masquerading as correctness.

project.title: Build your personal AI toolkit and prompt library
project.brief: Produce one document (doc, notes file or small repo — your choice) containing five sections, all backed by evidence from real sessions. (1) Five AI use-cases you actually ran across different domains (e.g. research summary, code explanation, email draft, resume-bullet improvement, study drill): for each, the task, the tool chosen with a one-line justification, the workflow with its human gate, the verification you performed, and the honest outcome including failures. (2) Your ten best prompts with before/after outputs: the naive first attempt and its unedited output, the improved prompt (role/task/constraints/format, system rules, few-shot or step-by-step where they apply), its unedited output, and a one-line note on which single change mattered. (3) Your verification checklist: the repeatable checks you now run (claim classification, citation tracing, fact pass, edge-case runs — whichever apply to your tasks), written as steps with evidence they executed. (4) One hallucination you caught: the claim, the check that detected it, what you did, and what it taught you about your risk profile — or, if you have not caught one, a deliberate test (five checkable claims, all verified) with the real result reported honestly. (5) Your ethics rules: three to five lines you follow (disclosure, no secrets pasted, verify before submit, attribution, harm) plus your comfort-test sentence. Close with a short reflection: what improved, what still fails, what you will not use AI for, and how the library will be maintained.
project.submission_hint: Link to the document on a public drive (anyone-with-link can view) or a public repository.

modules.title: Module 1 — What AI Actually Is
modules.summary: Clear definitions separating AI, machine learning, deep learning and data science; the history from expert systems to the generative wave; narrow vs general AI; and the AI already running in your pocket.

lessons.title: Four Words People Mix Up: AI, ML, Deep Learning, Data Science
lessons.summary: What each term actually means, how the four relate as nested ideas and overlapping practices, and why getting the vocabulary right is the first real AI skill.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and data science in one sentence each
Explain how ML is a subset of AI and deep learning a subset of ML
Classify a given real-world system as rule-based AI, machine learning, or neither
Tell apart a data-science project from a machine-learning project

payload.text: Job postings list "AI/ML/Data Science" as if it were one skill. Interviewers ask "what is the difference between AI and deep learning?" and watch your face. In one common version of that question, candidates who cannot draw the boundary between the terms stall — not because the answer is hard, but because they never made the distinctions concrete. This lesson makes them concrete.

**Artificial intelligence** is the broad goal: machines that perform tasks that normally require human intelligence — understanding language, recognising faces, making decisions, planning routes. AI as a field is decades older than the machine-learning boom. Early AI systems were hand-written rules: chess programs with opening books typed in by experts, spam filters with hundreds of if-then conditions. The important thing about the definition is that it is about the *task*, not the *method*. If a system does something smart-looking, it is doing an AI task — no matter how it was built.

**Machine learning** is a *way of building* AI systems: instead of writing the rules, you show the system thousands or millions of examples and let it discover the rules itself. A hand-written spam filter says "if the email contains 'viagra', mark it spam". A machine-learned spam filter is shown 100,000 emails labelled spam and not-spam and learns the patterns that separate them — including patterns no human would have thought to write down, like combinations of words, sender reputation and timing. Arthur Samuel coined the term in 1959; the modern usage is precise: a machine-learning system improves its performance at a task as it sees more data, without being explicitly programmed rule-by-rule.

**Deep learning** is machine learning built from **neural networks** with many layers — hence "deep". A neural network is a stack of small, adjustable units loosely inspired by brain cells; each layer transforms its input into a slightly more useful representation. Early neural networks had two or three layers and could barely recognise a handwritten digit. Modern ones have hundreds of layers and power image recognition, speech assistants and every large language model. The "deep" in deep learning refers exactly and only to this layer stacking. All deep learning is machine learning; not all machine learning is deep.

**Data science** is the odd one out — it is a *practice*, not a subset. A data scientist analyses data to answer questions: how did sales change after the festival discount? Which students are at risk of dropping out? That work uses statistics, SQL, charts and sometimes machine learning, but a data-science project can be entirely prediction-free. Machine learning builds a system that makes predictions on new data; data science produces insights and decisions from data. They overlap heavily — most ML people do some data analysis, many data scientists use ML — but they are not the same job or the same thing.

Think of it as nested circles with one circle offset: AI is the largest goal; ML is the dominant modern technique inside it; deep learning is the dominant family of ML techniques inside that. Data science sits partly inside and partly outside — it shares the data work but aims at understanding rather than at building an autonomous system. When someone says "we use AI", the useful follow-up question is always: "hand-written rules, learned from data, or deep learning?" — because the answer changes everything about reliability, cost and what the system can be trusted with.

payload.title: The four terms at a glance
rows: The goal: machines doing intelligent tasks
A method: learn rules from data
Did it learn from examples rather than hand-written rules?
A family of ML using multi-layer neural nets
Is a neural network with many layers involved?
A practice: extracting insights from data
Is the deliverable an analysis or a deployed predictor?

payload.title: Interview soundbite
payload.text: A clean, honest answer: "AI is the goal — intelligent behaviour in machines. Machine learning is how most of it is built today: learn from data instead of hand-written rules. Deep learning is ML with multi-layer neural networks, and it is what powers modern vision and language models. Data science overlaps all of it but aims at insights, not autonomous systems."

payload.title: Do not equate AI with robots
payload.text: Most AI is invisible software — ranking your feed, transcribing your voice, flagging fraud. Anthromorphising AI as a robot or a brain leads to both over-trusting and under-trusting systems. Judge the mechanism, not the metaphor.

payload.title: Classify five systems correctly
payload.problem: Classify each as classic (rule-based) AI, machine learning, deep learning, data science, or none of these: (a) a spreadsheet SUM formula, (b) an email spam filter trained on labelled emails with a shallow model, (c) ChatGPT answering a question, (d) a dashboard showing monthly churn by city, (e) a 1990s chess engine with expert-written opening rules.

steps.title: (a) SUM formula
steps.desc: It computes correctly but performs no task requiring intelligence — no learning, no rules approximating judgement. None of the four.

steps.title: (b) Spam filter, shallow model
steps.desc: It learned from labelled emails — machine learning. No deep neural network involved, so not deep learning.

steps.title: (c) ChatGPT
steps.desc: A large language model: a deep neural network trained on vast text. Deep learning, which is also ML, which is also an AI system. All three labels apply.

steps.title: (d) Churn dashboard
steps.desc: Analysis of data to produce insight — data science. If it instead predicted which users will churn next month, machine learning would enter the picture too.

steps.title: (e) 1990s chess engine
steps.desc: Intelligent behaviour from hand-written expert rules, not from data. Classic AI — the expert-systems lineage. AI without ML.

payload.solution: A: none. B: machine learning. C: deep learning (and ML and AI). D: data science. E: classic rule-based AI. The key discriminator every time: were the smarts hand-written or learned from data?

payload.title: Audit the "AI" in your apps
payload.prompt: List five apps you used today that claim some form of AI. For each, write one line: rule-based, learned from data (ML), deep learning, or just statistics — and say what evidence makes you think so. You will not always know; note your confidence.
payload.hint: Personalised feeds, voice assistants, photo search, autocorrect and fraud alerts are almost always learned; calendar reminders usually are not.

mistakes.mistake: Using "AI" and "machine learning" interchangeably in every sentence
mistakes.fix: Reserve AI for the goal or system and ML for the learn-from-data method. If a system runs on hand-written rules, "AI" is fair but "ML" is wrong.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking deep learning means "the AI understands like a human"
mistakes.fix: "Deep" only describes architecture — many stacked layers. It says nothing about understanding, consciousness or general intelligence.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming every data-science project builds an ML model
mistakes.fix: Many deliverables are analyses, dashboards or reports. Prediction is one tool in the data-science kit, not the definition of the field.

mistakes.mistake: Believing AI must involve a neural network
mistakes.fix: Rule-based systems, decision trees, nearest-neighbour search and classic search algorithms are all legitimate AI. Neural networks are just the technique that won the recent decade.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: "Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI." True or false, and justify with one example of AI that is not machine learning.
payload.answer: True — nesting holds. Example of AI that is not ML: a chess engine driven by hand-written opening books and evaluation rules, or a 1980s medical expert system whose knowledge physicians typed in. The system performs an intelligent task, but its knowledge was programmed, not learned.
payload.source: Standard opening question in AI/DS placement interviews and university viva exams.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: AI = the goal (intelligent task performance); ML = learn rules from data; deep learning = ML with multi-layer neural nets.
All deep learning is ML; all ML is a way of building AI; AI itself predates ML by decades.
Data science is a practice aimed at insight, overlapping ML but not contained in it.
The one diagnostic question: were the smarts hand-written, or learned from examples?

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between deep learning and machine learning?
options: They are independent fields that occasionally cooperate
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning
They are two names for the same technique
questions.explanation: Deep learning is the branch of ML built on multi-layer neural networks — a subset, not a sibling or a superset.

questions.prompt: A hospital scores patient readmission risk with a logistic regression trained on past records. This is primarily:
questions.explanation: A model learned from labelled historical data is machine learning. (A data scientist may have built it, but the system itself is ML.)

questions.prompt: A 1980s expert system diagnoses plant diseases from 500 if-then rules written by agronomists. The correct label is:
questions.explanation: It performs an intelligent task via hand-written rules — AI, but nothing was learned from data, so not ML.

questions.prompt: Which task is LEAST likely to be a machine-learning system?
options: Sorting emails into spam and inbox
Adding two numbers in a spreadsheet cell
Ranking search results for a query
questions.explanation: Spreadsheet arithmetic is deterministic computation — no learning, no inference approximating judgement. The other three are classic learned systems.

lessons.title: From Expert Systems to the Generative Wave: A Short History of AI
lessons.summary: The three AI winters, why rules hit a ceiling, the statistical turn, the deep-learning breakthrough, and how we arrived at large language models.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Name at least four eras of AI history in order and describe what defined each
Explain why expert systems succeeded in narrow domains but failed as general intelligence
Describe what changed in the 2010s that made deep learning dominate
Trace the line from word statistics to today's generative models

payload.text: In 1966, MIT's ELIZA fooled some users into thinking a crude chatbot understood them — the first recorded "AI hype cycle". Governments then cut funding, and the field entered its first winter. Since then AI has been declared both the future and a dead end at least four times. Knowing the pattern protects you from both the hype and the despair: every wave since has been driven by one genuine capability jump, not magic.

**The founding vision (1950s).** Alan Turing asked "can machines think?" and proposed his imitation test in 1950. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop, organised by John McCarthy, coined "artificial intelligence" and set the agenda: build general reasoning systems. Early optimism was enormous — researchers predicted human-level machine intelligence within a generation. They were wrong about the timeline by about seventy years and counting, but right that the problem was worth working on.

**Symbolic AI and expert systems (1960s–1980s).** The first dominant approach, sometimes called "good old-fashioned AI", represented knowledge as symbols and reasoning as manipulation of those symbols: facts plus rules. PROLOG reasoned over logical rules. In the 1970s and 1980s, **expert systems** commercialised the idea — MYCIN diagnosed blood infections, XCON configured computer orders at DEC, and companies sold "knowledge engineering" as a service: sit with a domain expert, write down their rules, ship the rules engine. It worked beautifully inside narrow, well-structured domains. It collapsed at the edges: the rules were brittle (no rule for the novel case), acquiring rules from experts did not scale, and real-world knowledge — the vast implicit common sense humans have — could not be written down. Funding collapsed. The 1970s and late 1980s were AI winters.

**The statistical turn (1990s–2000s).** AI quietly rebranded around probability. Instead of asking "what are the rules?", practitioners asked "what patterns are in the data?". Speech recognition switched to hidden Markov models; mail filters to Naive Bayes; search engines to statistical ranking. Speech recognition went from a research curiosity to a shipped product during this era. Machine learning — systems that estimate their parameters from data — became the practical default. Meanwhile AI largely left the term "AI" behind on résumés; the work was called machine learning, data mining, or NLP, and funding was steadier because the systems produced measurable value.

**The deep-learning breakthrough (2012–2017).** Three ingredients converged: GPUs that could train huge networks, datasets like ImageNet with millions of labelled images, and algorithmic tricks (ReLU activations, dropout, better optimisation) that made deep networks trainable. In 2012, AlexNet cut the ImageNet error rate dramatically versus the best hand-engineered pipelines — the moment the field pivoted. Suddenly deep learning beat decades of feature engineering in vision, then speech, then language. The recipe generalised: more data, more compute, more layers.

**Attention and the generative wave (2017–now).** The 2017 "Attention Is All You Need" paper introduced the Transformer. GPT models applied it at scale: trained on internet-scale text to predict the next token, larger models kept getting better in a smooth, predictable way (scaling laws). ChatGPT (late 2022) put the result in front of billions of people. The jump from prior chatbots was not a new kind of knowledge — it was fluency, instruction-following and breadth, produced by next-token prediction plus alignment training. Diffusion models drove a parallel revolution in images. We are now in the generative era: the same transformer recipe extends to code, video, audio and multi-modal systems.

The honest reading of this history: each era solved one hard sub-problem (search, knowledge representation, statistical pattern learning, representation learning, sequence modelling and alignment) and over-promised on the rest. The systems are real; the general intelligence is not here yet.

payload.title: AI eras at a glance
rows: General reasoning by search and logic
Brittle; knowledge acquisition did not scale
HMM speech, Naive Bayes spam, Google ranking
GPT family, Claude, Gemini, diffusion images
Hallucination, cost, narrowness of real understanding

payload.title: Why "AI winter" keeps happening
payload.text: A winter starts when capability demos outrun what the technology can actually ship, funders notice, and money dries up. The antidote has always been the same: a measurable commercial win (expert-system configuration savings, web search ranking, AlexNet accuracy, LLM assistants). Track the shipped product, not the press release.

payload.title: Use history to read today's news
payload.text: When a headline says "AI now does X", ask which era's pattern this is: a genuine capability jump (like ImageNet 2012) or a demo that hides brittleness (like many expert-system claims of the 1980s). The tell is whether independent people can reproduce the result on their own data.

payload.title: Place five milestones on the timeline
payload.problem: Put these in order and say what each unlocked: (a) ChatGPT launch, (b) MYCIN, (c) AlexNet wins ImageNet, (d) Dartmouth workshop, (e) "Attention Is All You Need".

steps.title: 1956 — Dartmouth
steps.desc: Names the field; frames AI as general reasoning. Unlocks: research identity and funding narrative.

steps.title: 1970s — MYCIN
steps.desc: Expert system diagnosing infections at ~competent-level accuracy in its narrow domain. Unlocks: commercial hope; later exposes the rule-brittleness ceiling.

steps.title: 2012 — AlexNet
steps.desc: Deep CNN crushes ImageNet benchmark with GPU training. Unlocks: industry-wide pivot to deep learning.

steps.title: 2017 — Transformer paper
steps.desc: Attention-based architecture scales cleanly for language. Unlocks: the recipe behind every modern LLM.

steps.title: Late 2022 — ChatGPT
steps.desc: Instruction-tuned, RLHF-aligned LLM exposed to the public. Unlocks: generative AI as a mass-market product category.

payload.solution: Order: Dartmouth (1956) → MYCIN (1970s) → AlexNet (2012) → Attention paper (2017) → ChatGPT (2022). Each unlocked one thing the previous era could not do; none of them delivered the 1956 promise of general intelligence.

payload.title: Read an AI headline like a historian
payload.prompt: Find one recent AI news article. Write half a page: which era's pattern does it resemble (expert-system overclaim, statistical quiet win, deep-learning breakthrough, or generative hype)? What evidence would confirm or refute that reading?
payload.hint: Look for: independent reproduction, measurable benchmarks, real users shipping real work — or vague demos, vendor-only data, and "coming soon".

mistakes.mistake: Believing AI started with ChatGPT
mistakes.fix: The field is seventy years old. ChatGPT is the most recent of at least five major waves, and its core ideas (Transformers, scaling) date to 2017 and before.

mistakes.mistake: Concluding "expert systems failed, therefore rules are useless"
mistakes.fix: Rules remain ideal for compliance, determinism and narrow well-specified domains. Modern systems mix learned components with rules and checks deliberately.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking each era replaced the previous one entirely
mistakes.fix: They layer. Search engines still use classical statistics; production systems still use decision trees and rules; deep learning sits on top of that stack.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the 2012 deep-learning pivot as sudden luck
mistakes.fix: It needed three simultaneous prerequisites — large labelled datasets, GPU compute, and training tricks. Understanding the prerequisites tells you where the next jump could come from.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What were the main reasons expert systems failed to deliver general intelligence, and how did the machine-learning approach address (or sidestep) each failure?
payload.answer: Failures: (1) brittleness — no rule for novel cases; (2) knowledge acquisition bottleneck — experts' tacit knowledge could not all be written down; (3) no common sense — millions of trivial facts humans know implicitly were missing; (4) maintenance cost — rule bases grew unmanageably. ML sidesteps (1) and (2) by learning statistical regularities directly from data, including patterns experts never articulated. It does not truly solve (3) — modern models approximate common sense from data, which is why they still fail in odd edge cases — and it trades the rule-maintenance problem for a data-and-compute problem.
payload.source: Classic graduate AI exam essay; also common in senior ML interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: AI began in 1956 as a quest for general reasoning; expert systems (1970s–80s) shipped narrow value on hand-written rules.
Two AI winters followed overpromised capability; the field survived by pivoting to measurable, narrow wins.
The 1990s–2000s statistical turn made "learn from data" the default and quietly built today's search and speech systems.
2012 AlexNet and the 2017 Transformer set up the generative wave; ChatGPT (2022) was alignment plus scale meeting the public.
History's lesson: genuine capability jumps are narrow and reproducible; hype is neither.

questions.prompt: What was the "knowledge acquisition bottleneck" of expert systems?
options: Lacking compute to run the rules
The difficulty of writing down all expert knowledge, including tacit common sense
Rules were too slow to evaluate
Experts refused to cooperate with researchers
questions.explanation: Experts know far more than they can articulate; rule bases covered only the sliver that could be written down, leaving the system brittle outside it.

questions.prompt: What three ingredients converged around 2012 to make deep learning dominant?
options: GPUs, large labelled datasets, and better training techniques
More rules, better experts, faster CPUs
questions.explanation: Compute (GPUs), data (ImageNet-scale datasets) and algorithms (ReLU, dropout, improved optimisation) arrived together; AlexNet proved the combination.

questions.prompt: The Transformer architecture ("Attention Is All You Need") was published in:
questions.explanation: 2017. GPT-style pretraining built on it starting 2018; ChatGPT reached the public in late 2022.

questions.prompt: Which era best matches this description: systems that learned probability distributions from data and powered speech recognition and spam filtering before deep learning?
questions.explanation: The 1990s–2000s statistical turn: hidden Markov models, Naive Bayes, empirical risk minimisation — learning from data but without deep representation learning.

lessons.title: Narrow AI vs General AI: Why Today's AI Is Brilliant and Brittle
lessons.summary: The spectrum from narrow tools to the hypothetical general intelligence, why narrow systems can be superhuman in one box and clueless outside it, and what that means for how you should trust them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define artificial general intelligence (AGI) and place it correctly as a research goal, not a product
Give at least three concrete examples of narrow AI exceeding human performance
Explain the "brittleness" of narrow AI with an out-of-distribution example
Apply an appropriate trust level to a narrow AI system in a real scenario

payload.text: In 2016, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's strongest Go players, including the legendary "Move 37" no human would have played. The same general wave of technology still misreads a rotated traffic sign, invents a lawyer's citations, or confidently tells you a book summary for a book that does not exist. Superhuman and clueless are not contradictions once you understand what narrow means.

**What "narrow" means.** Every AI system shipping today is **artificial narrow intelligence (ANI)**: built for a specific task or family of tasks, in a specific context, with a specific distribution of inputs. A chess engine, a spam filter, a face unlock, a coding assistant, a medical-imaging tool — all narrow. "Narrow" is not an insult; it is the reason these systems work at all. A narrow system can be trained on the exact problem until it is better than any human at that problem: Go, protein-structure prediction, real-time traffic routing, board-game tactics. The capability is real and deep — inside the box.

**What AGI is — and is not.** Artificial general intelligence is the hypothetical system with human-like breadth: able to learn and transfer competence across virtually any intellectual task, including tasks it was never trained for, with flexible common sense and planning. No such system exists as of this writing. Debates about "have we reached AGI?" are usually debates about definitions, not demonstrations. For practical purposes, treat AGI as a research horizon, not a product you can buy, deploy, or blame.

**Why narrow AI is brittle.** A narrow system learns the *distribution* of its training data — the statistical patterns of the situations it has seen. Change the distribution and performance can collapse without warning. A stop-sign classifier trained mostly on upright signs in daylight fails on a graffiti-stickered or rotated sign. A medical model trained on scans from one hospital's machine degrades on another hospital's machine. In machine-learning language this is an **out-of-distribution** failure; in plain language, the system never learned "stop signs", it learned "the visual patterns that co-occurred with stop signs in my data". Humans generalise from thin evidence; current AI generalises only as far as its data covers.

**The capability/brittleness map.** The practical skill is to place a task on two axes: how narrow is the task, and how costly is a mistake? Low-cost, well-covered tasks (drafting an email, suggesting a route) are great uses — errors are cheap to catch. High-cost, edge-case-heavy tasks (autonomous medical dosing, unreviewed legal filings) are dangerous uses — the tail cases are exactly where narrow systems fail and where the cost lands. Notice that modern LLMs *look* general — one system writes code, poetry and recipes — but each is a pattern-completion behaviour learned from text, still brittle in exactly the narrow-AI way: confident in-distribution, unreliable when the question is odd, factual, or outside its training patterns.

**Narrow AI is also uneven.** Even inside its box, a system's skill is lumpy: superhuman on average cases, weaker on adversarial or rare ones. This is why the right posture toward narrow AI is neither awe nor dismissal but *supervised collaboration*: let it do the heavy generative or predictive work, keep a human on the verification and the edge cases, and never let it silently make the final call in a high-stakes domain you do not understand.

payload.title: Two-axis trust check
rows: Safety, legal, financial or reputational harm
Not enough to audit the output
Human-in-the-loop, or do not use yet

payload.title: "Human-level at X" does not mean "general intelligence at X"
payload.text: A model that passes a medical exam is matching exam-question patterns; it has not demonstrated bedside judgement on rare presentations. Benchmarks measure the benchmark's distribution — always ask what the benchmark left out.

payload.title: The brittleness checklist
payload.text: Before trusting a narrow system on a new job, ask: is this input like its training situations? what happens at the weird edge? who verifies? If you cannot answer, treat the output as a draft, not a decision.

payload.title: Place a task and set the trust level
payload.problem: A campus startup wants to auto-reject rental applications using an ML model trained on historical approvals. Classify the system on the narrowness/cost axes and decide the right deployment posture.

steps.title: Narrowness check
steps.desc: The model predicts one thing (approve/reject) from structured features — genuinely narrow. But the training data reflects past decisions, including any past discrimination; new applicant profiles may differ from training.

steps.title: Cost check
steps.desc: A wrong rejection denies someone housing — high human cost, hard to appeal if the reason is opaque.

steps.title: Distribution check
steps.desc: Applicants whose profiles shifted (gig income, new visa categories) are out-of-distribution; the model will still output a confident score.

steps.title: Posture decision
steps.desc: Not suitable for autonomous rejection. Suitable as a triage assistant: rank applications for human review, require stated reasons, audit approval rates across groups, keep appeal paths.

payload.solution: Narrow + high-cost + opaque = assist, do not automate. Use the model to prioritise human review, never to issue final rejections; require human sign-off and fairness audits. The system's narrowness is fine — the unattended high-stakes call is the problem.

payload.title: Map your own AI uses
payload.prompt: List six ways AI touched your day (feed ranking, navigation, autocomplete, spam filtering, voice assistant, homework help…). For each: name the narrow task, estimate the cost of a wrong output (low/medium/high), and rate your current trust. Flag any where trust is high but cost is also high — that gap is where trouble lives.
payload.hint: Trust should roughly track verification you actually do, not the average quality of past outputs.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a system good at task A is reliable at nearby task B
mistakes.fix: Competence does not transfer implicitly. A code assistant's fluency says nothing about its grasp of your company's security rules; test the specific task.

mistakes.mistake: Reading fluent language from an LLM as understanding
mistakes.fix: Fluency is the trained behaviour; accuracy is a separate axis. Judge outputs by evidence (citations you check, code you run), never by confidence of tone.

mistakes.mistake: Dismissing narrow AI because it is "not AGI"
mistakes.fix: Narrow beats human by wide margins in many boxes, and those boxes are where the economic value is. The goal is fit-for-purpose reliability, not general intelligence.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming past performance guarantees edge-case performance
mistakes.fix: Averages hide tails. Ask explicitly: what does this system do on rare, adversarial, or shifted inputs? That is where narrow systems fail.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why a self-driving system can outperform humans on highways yet still fail at unusual road configurations, using the concept of training distribution.
payload.answer: Highway driving is a heavily covered, structured distribution — millions of similar lane-following, car-following situations in training (real and simulated). Unusual configurations (hand-drawn temporary signs, missing markings, emergency vehicles in odd positions) are rare or absent from that distribution. The system's competence is pattern coverage, not road comprehension; outside covered patterns, behaviour degrades unpredictably. This is classic narrow-AI brittleness: superhuman in-distribution, unreliable out-of-distribution — hence the engineering emphasis on geofencing, fallbacks and continued human supervision.
payload.source: Common AI-safety and autonomous-systems interview question; also appears in ethics-of-AI course exams.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Every deployed AI today is narrow: superhuman inside its trained box, unreliable outside it.
AGI remains a research hypothesis, not a product — treat "AGI reached?" claims with suspicion.
Brittleness = out-of-distribution failure: the system learned training-data patterns, not the underlying concept.
Trust decisions need two axes: narrowness of the task and cost of a wrong output.
High-stakes narrow tasks need a human in the loop, stated reasons, and audits — not full automation.

questions.prompt: As of today, commercial AI systems like GPT-class models, AlphaFold and face unlock are best classified as:
questions.explanation: Each performs a specific family of tasks learned from data — narrow intelligence. None demonstrates flexible general competence.

questions.prompt: A stop-sign classifier trained mostly on clean daylight photos fails on a sticker-defaced sign. This failure is best explained as:
options: Out-of-distribution input — the test case differs from training patterns
questions.explanation: The model learned patterns of its training distribution; the defaced, rotated sign falls outside it, and performance collapses without warning.

questions.prompt: Which deployment is the WISEST use of a narrow AI system?
options: Fully automated loan rejections with no appeal
AI triage ranking applications for human reviewers who make final decisions
AI diagnosing patients with no doctor in the loop
AI grading exams with no human audit of its rubric
questions.explanation: Keeping the high-stakes final call with a human uses the AI's ranking strength while containing its brittleness on unusual cases.

questions.prompt: "Move 37" in AlphaGo vs Lee Sedol illustrates that narrow AI can:
options: Outperform humans with genuinely novel creative strategies within its domain
Achieve general intelligence in board games
Transfer its Go skill to other life domains
Understand the game the way a human master does
questions.explanation: The move was surprising to experts yet effective — deep pattern search within the narrow domain. It does not imply general intelligence or transferable understanding.

lessons.title: The AI Already in Your Pocket: Recommendations, Spam Filters, Maps and More
lessons.summary: A guided tour of the machine-learning systems you use daily, what each one actually predicts, and how to start noticing AI in ordinary software.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Identify at least six everyday systems powered by machine learning and state what each predicts
Distinguish learned ranking from hand-written business rules in a product you use
Explain how a spam filter and a maps ETA each combine ML with non-ML components
Describe one feedback loop where user behaviour retrains a model

payload.text: Every morning your phone quietly runs dozens of learned models before you finish unlocking it: spam filtered overnight, feed ranked while you slept, keyboard autocomplete suggesting your next word, face unlock firing, maps predicting traffic before you asked. If you cannot name what each one predicts, you are using systems you do not understand with your data and your attention. Ten minutes of anatomy fixes that.

**The pattern behind all of them.** Every everyday ML system is the same shape: **input features → learned model → prediction → some action → new data**. The features are numbers derived from the situation (your past clicks, an email's words, road segments and time of day). The model converts features to a prediction (probability of enjoyment, probability of spam, minutes to destination). The product acts on the prediction (rank items, move mail, draw an ETA), and your reaction becomes new training data. Once you can recite that loop for a system, you understand its level — and its failure modes.

**Recommendation systems.** Netflix, YouTube, Instagram and Spotify all rank a huge inventory against *your* history. The classic recipe mixes three signals: **collaborative filtering** ("users like you also liked this"), **content-based filtering** (items like the ones you watched — same artist, same topic embeddings) and a **business/rule layer** (promote new releases, down-rank watched items). The prediction target is some proxy for enjoyment: click, watch time, completion, thumbs-up. Two consequences you have felt: the filter bubble (your rankings narrow to your habits) and popularity bias (big items get shown to gather more data). The "For You" page is not an editor's choice list — it is a live prediction of what keeps you watching, updated by every second you stay or leave.

**Spam filters.** Gmail's filter is a learned classifier over features like word frequencies, sender reputation, bulk-sender signals, and your own past marks ("not spam" / "report"). ML handles the fuzzy patterns no human rule list would cover; explicit rules still catch hard policies (blocked attachments, org-level blocks); and everything you mark retrains the system. False positives are the famous cost — a legitimate email in spam — which is why providers keep the bar asymmetric and why "why was this filtered?" is a genuinely answerable question in most mail apps.

**Maps and ETAs.** Your navigation app fuses three layers: a **graph model** of roads (classical algorithms, not ML), **live traffic** from probe data — phones moving at measured speeds, which is itself a crowd-sourced sensor network — and a **learned ETA model** that predicts travel time per road segment by time of day, day of week, weather and events, then combines segments. Traffic accidents, jams and reroutes all emerge from that fusion. The "AI" here is the prediction layer; the routing algorithm on top is a decades-old shortest-path family (A*, contraction hierarchies). Knowing which layer does what tells you why ETAs are eerily good in dense cities and poor where few phones travel.

**The quieter ones.** Voice assistants: speech-to-text models plus an intent classifier plus often an LLM for answers. Autocorrect/autocomplete: essentially tiny next-token predictors running on-device — the same core idea as a large language model, shrunk to your keyboard. Face unlock: a face-embedding model comparing your face to a stored vector, with a spoof-detection layer. Fraud alerts on your card: anomaly-scoring models over transaction features. Email autocomplete subject lines, photo search ("beach"), YouTube's "up next", Uber's up-front price, UPI's fraud check — same loop, different features and targets.

**The feedback loop trap.** Because your reactions are training data, these systems optimise for engagement-shaped targets. A news feed that learned "outrage keeps thumbs scrolling" will show more outrage — not because anyone programmed outrage, but because the proxy said so. This is why understanding the predicted target ("what number is this model trying to raise?") is the single most useful literacy skill: it explains the product's behaviour better than its mission statement.

payload.title: Everyday systems: what each one actually predicts
rows: Your history, item embeddings, co-behaviour of similar users
Words, sender reputation, bulk signals, your past marks
Road segments, time of day, live probe speeds, weather

payload.title: How to see the model's target
payload.text: Ask: "what behaviour increases when this feature improves?" If watch-time suggestions increase watch time, the target is watch time. If a shopping feed surfaces clickbait, engagement is the likely proxy — and quality is only as good as the proxy.

payload.title: Hybrid by design
payload.text: Few production systems are pure ML. Expect a learned component, a rules layer (policies, business logic) and a fallback path. When something goes wrong, find out which layer produced the decision — the fix is different in each.

payload.title: Reverse-engineer the feed you are reading right now
payload.problem: Take any short-form video feed. Using the input→model→action loop, explain why the third video appeared, what the system was optimising, and what you can do to steer it.

steps.title: Inputs
steps.desc: Your recent watch time and skips per video, likes and shares, the current video's embedding, and what similar users engaged with. Session context (time of day) is also in play.

steps.title: Model
steps.desc: A ranker scoring candidate videos by predicted engagement — often expected watch time or a weighted mix of watch, like and share probabilities.

steps.title: Action
steps.desc: The app shows the highest-scoring candidate it believes you have not seen; autoplay starts before you decide, biasing the data toward watching.

steps.title: Steering
steps.desc: Deliberate signals beat passive ones: long-press and "not interested" on topics you want less; search and fully watch videos you want more; periodic history clears reduce legacy bias. The model reads every one of these actions as a label.

payload.solution: The third video was the highest predicted-engagement candidate given your recent behaviour and cohort signals. You are not choosing from the library — you are being ranked against it. Steering works because your deliberate actions are the cleanest labels in the training stream.

payload.title: Trace one system end to end
payload.prompt: Pick one system from the table (or another you use). For a single recent interaction, write the loop in concrete terms: what exact features probably fed the model, what it predicted, what action the app took, and what your reaction taught it. Keep it under 150 words.
payload.hint: If you are unsure of a feature, list two candidates and mark which you are confident about — reasoning about uncertainty is part of the skill.

mistakes.mistake: Calling every automated feature "AI"
mistakes.fix: Autoplay timers, static top-10 lists and deterministic pricing rules are not ML. The test from Lesson 1.1 applies: did it learn patterns from data, or was it programmed rule-by-rule?

mistakes.mistake: Believing the recommendation is "what you would like" rather than "what a proxy predicts you will engage with"
mistakes.fix: Engagement proxies (watch time, clicks) correlate with but differ from satisfaction. Knowing the proxy explains clickbait, rabbit holes and why "watch later" lists grow.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming maps ETAs come from GPS alone
mistakes.fix: GPS gives current positions; the ETA is a learned per-segment time prediction blended with historical patterns. Rural roads fail because probe data is thin, not because GPS is broken.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking you cannot influence these systems
mistakes.fix: Explicit signals (not-interested, complete watches, searches, muting channels) are among the strongest labels you can send. Passive scrolling is also a signal — usually the weakest and least intentional one.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe how collaborative filtering differs from content-based recommendation, and give one limitation of each.
payload.answer: Collaborative filtering recommends from behavioural co-occurrence: users who interacted with item A also liked item B — no understanding of content required. Limitation: cold start (new users/items with no interaction history get poor recommendations) and popularity bias. Content-based filtering matches item features to the user's past item features (same genre, topic, artist, embedding similarity). Limitation: it stays inside the user's demonstrated taste — limited serendipity and reinforcement of existing preferences. Production systems blend both plus a rules layer.
payload.source: Standard recommender-systems question in DS interviews; also common in product-analytics case rounds.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Everyday ML follows one loop: features → learned prediction → product action → your reaction as new data.
Feeds rank by predicted engagement; spam filters classify with learned patterns plus rules; maps fuse classical routing with learned ETAs.
Autocorrect is a tiny next-token predictor — the same idea as an LLM, at keyboard scale.
Proxies drive products: find the number the model is trained to raise and you can predict the product's behaviour.
Your deliberate signals (not-interested, full watches, searches) are the strongest steering inputs you send.

questions.prompt: What does a short-form video feed's ranking model primarily predict?
options: Which videos are objectively the highest quality
A proxy for engagement — e.g. probability or amount of watch time
Which videos the uploader paid to promote only
The factual accuracy of each video
questions.explanation: The ranker is trained on engagement outcomes (watch time, likes, shares). Quality and accuracy are only as good as that proxy.

questions.prompt: A Gmail spam filter combines:
options: Learned classifiers plus policy rules and user feedback signals
questions.explanation: Production filters blend learned models, hard policy rules, and retraining signals from user actions like "not spam" or "report".

questions.prompt: Maps ETAs are unusually good in dense cities but weaker on remote mountain roads mainly because:
options: Remote roads have thin probe data, so the learned segment predictions are less informed
Mountain roads are illegal for routing apps
City drivers drive more predictably by law
questions.explanation: The learned per-segment models depend on crowd-sourced speed data; sparse traffic on remote roads means weaker predictions, not worse GPS.

questions.prompt: Which action sends the CLEANEST intentional training signal to your feed?
options: Long-pressing "not interested" on an unwanted topic
Leaving the app open in the background
Watching an ad to the end
questions.explanation: Explicit negative feedback is a direct labelled example. Passive behaviour is weak, noisy signal; background time is not a preference at all.

modules.title: Module 2 — How Machines Learn
modules.summary: Learning from examples — features, labels, training data; the three learning paradigms with real examples; the train/validation/test discipline; and the overfitting/underfitting intuition that explains most bad models.

lessons.title: Learning From Examples: Features, Labels and Training Data
lessons.summary: What a machine-learning dataset actually contains, how features and labels are chosen, and why data quality beats model cleverness in almost every real project.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define features, labels and training examples using a concrete dataset
Turn a raw table into a features-plus-label description of a prediction task
Explain at least three ways real training data goes wrong (leakage, bias, drift)
Argue why a better dataset often beats a better model

payload.text: A widely cited industry rule of thumb says data scientists spend most of their time cleaning and preparing data, not building models. Learners find that disappointing — they signed up to build AI, not to fix spreadsheets. Then their first project ships a model that scores brilliantly offline and fails in production, and they discover the rule of thumb was generous: data is not part of the job, it is the job.

**The anatomy of an example.** Machine learning means learning a function from examples, and every example has the same anatomy: a set of **features** (the inputs — numbers or categories describing the situation) and a **label** (the output you want the model to predict). Predict whether an email is spam? Features: word counts, sender domain, time sent, number of links. Label: 1 for spam, 0 for not. Predict tomorrow's delivery time? Features: route, hour, day, weather, historical segment speeds. Label: actual minutes. The model's whole job at prediction time is: take new features, output a prediction — learn the arrow features → label from thousands of labelled arrows.

**Features are a design decision, not a given.** Raw data rarely arrives as ready features. A "customer" row becomes features like recency of last purchase, purchase frequency, average order value. A photo becomes a grid of pixel values (or, in modern systems, embeddings a neural net computed). Choosing features is choosing what the model is allowed to see — and what it can possibly learn. Miss a predictive feature and no model can recover it; include a leaky one and every model will cheat (more below). Feature engineering used to be the core craft of classical ML; deep learning partially automated it by learning representations from raw pixels and characters, but the human still chooses *which* raw data enters the pipe and how the task is framed.

**Labels: where the money goes.** Labels are expensive — someone or something must produce the truth. Options each carry tradeoffs: human annotation (accurate-ish, slow, costly, annotator disagreement is real), user behaviour as implicit labels (cheap, abundant, biased toward engagement), existing databases (fast, inherits historical errors), or heuristics/rules (cheap but circular — the model can at best learn to imitate your rules). A famous cautionary tale pattern: a hospital built a model to predict which patients need extra care; the labels came from "who cost the most last year", which is a cost proxy, not a need proxy — the model learned to find expensive patients, not sick ones. The label choice *is* the task definition.

**Why data quality beats model cleverness.** Two teams on the same task: one tries three standard algorithms with clean, well-chosen features and trustworthy labels; the other uses a cutting-edge model on messy, leaky, biased data. Team one wins, usually by a wide margin, usually every time. Models are commodity components; data is specific to your problem. The failure modes are all data-shaped: **label errors** teach the model wrong associations; **selection bias** means training data does not represent deployment (training on desktop clicks, deploying to phones); **leakage** means a feature secretly contains the answer (a "churn prediction" feature that records whether the customer already cancelled); and **drift** means yesterday's data no longer matches today's world (a fraud model trained before a new payment method exists). None of these show up as a crash — they show up as a model that works and quietly lies.

**The practical mindset.** Before choosing a model, interrogate the dataset: Where did the rows come from? Who labelled them and how? Could any feature encode the future or the answer? Does the training population match the deployment population? What will change in six months? This is not bureaucracy — it is the actual leverage in a machine-learning project.

payload.title: One dataset, named properly
rows: Categorical; high-cardinality — needs encoding or hashing
Numeric; cheap and surprisingly informative for spam
The target; came from user "report spam" clicks — biased but cheap
Must be excluded at prediction time — leakage if used as a feature

payload.title: Leakage is the silent killer
payload.text: A feature that would not exist (or would be knowable) at real prediction time will make your offline metrics spectacular and your production model useless. Whenever a model scores "too good", your first suspect is leakage.

payload.title: Data-first project order
payload.text: 1) Write the prediction in one sentence (features in, label out). 2) Build a tiny dataset by hand and inspect 50 rows. 3) Establish a dumb baseline (majority class, simple average). 4) Only then try models. This order prevents weeks of elegant work on an unsound task.

payload.title: Design the dataset before the model
payload.problem: A college wants to predict which students will fail a course so advisors can intervene. Sketch the features, the label, and name two leakage risks.

steps.title: Write the task
steps.desc: Predict at week 4 of the semester: P(student fails final course grade) using only information available by week 4.

steps.title: Features (available by week 4)
steps.desc: Attendance count so far, assignment submission counts and scores, LMS login frequency, prior-semester GPA, credits carried, distance from home (optional, sensitive).

steps.title: Label
steps.desc: End-of-semester outcome: fail (D/F/withdraw) vs pass — from the registrar, defined before modelling.

steps.title: Leakage risks
steps.desc: (1) Any feature recorded after week 4 (final attendance, later assignment scores) leaks the future. (2) A feature like "advisor already flagged this student" leaks prior human decisions the model should replace, creating a self-fulfilling loop.

steps.title: Bias check
steps.desc: Training on past cohorts embeds past intervention effects and demographic patterns. Define the intervention, audit subgroup false-positive rates, and treat predictions as triage for human advisors, not automatic judgements.

payload.solution: A week-4 features snapshot, a registrar-defined fail label, and an explicit ban on post-cutoff and prior-decision features. The dataset design — cut-off date, label definition, leakage audit — determines whether the model can be trusted at all; the algorithm is the easy part.

payload.title: Spec a dataset for something you care about
payload.prompt: Choose one prediction you could plausibly make in your own life or campus (bus delay, exam readiness, club event turnout). Write: one-sentence task, 5–8 features with their sources, the label and how you would obtain it, and two things that could poison the data. Do not build a model.
payload.hint: If you cannot get even 50 honest labelled examples by hand, the project is not ready for ML — pick a simpler task or a cheaper label source.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the model first and bending the data to fit it
mistakes.fix: The task (features → label) comes first. Model choice is a late, boring, benchmarkable decision — not the creative core of the project.

mistakes.mistake: Using features computed after the prediction moment
mistakes.fix: Define the prediction time explicitly, then audit every feature against it. Anything knowable only later is leakage — delete it.

mistakes.mistake: Treating any available column as a label
mistakes.fix: Labels must match the decision you actually want to make. "High cost" is not "high need"; "clicked" is not "satisfied". Name the target like a product decision.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring who is missing from the data
mistakes.fix: Selection bias hides in collection: only survey responders, only paying users, only scanned documents. If deployment adds a population the data lacks, expect silent failure there.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A bank builds a loan-default model; among the columns is `recovered_amount`, populated only after a default occurs and collection succeeds. Why is this a problem, and what is the general principle?
payload.answer: `recovered_amount` is unknown at application time — it exists only in the label's future. As a feature it leaks information downstream of the outcome, inflating offline metrics and collapsing in production where the column does not yet exist. General principle: every feature must be knowable at the exact moment the prediction will be made; anything derived from the outcome or from post-decision data must be quarantined to the label side of the split.
payload.source: Classic leakage interview question in banking and fintech ML rounds.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: ML learns the arrow features → label from thousands of labelled examples.
Features are designed; labels are chosen; both are the real creative decisions.
Bad labels teach bad models — the label defines the task as much as your prompt does.
Leakage, selection bias and drift are the three data poisons; none crash, all lie.
Clean, representative, well-specified data beats model cleverness in nearly every real project.

questions.prompt: In a spam-detection dataset, "number of links in the email" is an example of a:
questions.explanation: It is an input describing the example; the label would be spam / not-spam.

questions.prompt: A churn model uses a feature "cancellation_confirmed_date". The customer is being scored BEFORE they cancel. This is:
options: Data leakage — the feature is unknowable at prediction time
questions.explanation: The column only exists downstream of the outcome; including it inflates offline metrics and cannot exist in production scoring.

questions.prompt: Why is the choice of label especially consequential?
options: Labels determine which algorithm you may use
The label literally defines what the model is optimised to predict
Labels only matter for unsupervised learning
questions.explanation: Predicting "high cost" instead of "high need" produces a different system entirely — the model will faithfully chase whatever target you supply.

questions.prompt: Which is MOST likely to improve a stuck ML project?
options: Switching to a larger neural network
Auditing and fixing label errors and training/deployment mismatch
Rewriting the code in a faster language
questions.explanation: When metrics stall, data problems (labels, leakage, population mismatch) usually dominate algorithm tweaks.

lessons.title: The Three Ways Machines Learn: Supervised, Unsupervised, Reinforcement
lessons.summary: The learning paradigms distinguished by what feedback the learner gets, with concrete examples of each and guidance on which question each answers.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify a learning problem as supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement based on its feedback signal
Give a real-world example of each paradigm and state what the feedback is
Explain semi-supervised and self-supervised learning as practical blends
Match a business question to the correct paradigm and output type

payload.text: Three identical-looking projects can be three different species. "Predict tomorrow's stock price", "group our customers into segments", and "teach a robot to walk" all look like "AI work" on a slide. But the first has labels, the second has none, and the third has neither labels nor a teacher — only a score that arrives after a lifetime of trying. Which species you are in determines your data, your metrics, and your chances.

**Supervised learning — learning with a teacher.** You have a dataset of examples where someone has already provided the correct answer: the **label**. Learn the function features → label so you can predict labels for unseen examples. Two classic shapes: **classification** (discrete answers — spam/not-spam, disease/no-disease, which digit is this?) and **regression** (continuous answers — price in rupees, delivery minutes, temperature). Roughly the commercially dominant form of ML, because most business questions are supervised: will this user churn, is this transaction fraud, how long will this take. The catch is always labels: supervised learning trades annotation cost for a clear target and clear metrics.

**Unsupervised learning — learning without a teacher.** You have examples but no labels, and the goal is to find structure in the data itself. The flagship task is **clustering**: group customers by purchase behaviour without telling the algorithm what the segments should be (k-means and its relatives); the groups are yours to interpret and name. Other unsupervised jobs: **dimensionality reduction** for visualising high-dimensional data in 2-D (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP); **anomaly detection** — find the transactions that do not fit any cluster (fraud, machine failure, network intrusion); **topic modelling** over documents. The eternal difficulty of unsupervised learning: there is no ground-truth score for "correct clusters". Two algorithms can both be right with different granularities. Unsupervised output is a lens for a human, not an answer to grade.

**Reinforcement learning — learning by doing and scoring.** No teacher labels each action. Instead, an **agent** takes **actions** in an **environment**, receives **rewards** (or penalties), and learns a **policy** — a strategy for choosing actions that maximises cumulative reward. Classic examples: AlphaGo (reward = winning the game); robotics locomotion (reward = forward progress minus falling); recommendation systems framed as bandits (reward = engagement); RLHF in chatbots (reward = human preference ratings of answers). RL's signature features: **delayed reward** (the good opening move in Go pays off 50 moves later), **exploration vs exploitation** (try something new vs repeat what worked), and often enormous sample needs — simulated environments or massive parallel training are usually required. It is the paradigm that matches how you actually teach a skill: not by labelling every step, but by grading outcomes.

**The blends that run the world.** Pure paradigms are textbook-clean; production is blended. **Self-supervised learning** manufactures labels from the data itself — predict the next word in a sentence (the label is the word that follows: supervision without human annotation). This is how every large language model is pretrained, and it blurs supervised and unsupervised more than any other idea in modern ML. **Semi-supervised learning** labels a little, propagates structure to the rest. **Active learning** asks a human to label only the examples the model is least sure about — cutting annotation cost dramatically. When someone says "we use AI", asking "which paradigm?" is a shortcut to understanding what they built, what data they needed, and what they can claim about it.

payload.title: Self-supervised: the modern workhorse
payload.text: LLMs are trained by hiding part of the data and predicting it — next word, missing span, next image patch. The labels come free from the data itself. This is why internet-scale corpora became trainable: no human had to label a trillion sentences.

payload.title: Classify by feedback, not by buzzword
payload.text: Ignore what the deck calls the project. Ask: "what signal teaches the system?" Labels → supervised. No signal, structure-hunting → unsupervised. Sequential actions + delayed score → reinforcement. This single question resolves almost every classification argument.

payload.title: Classify three project proposals
payload.problem: Classify each and name the output: (a) "Score each UPI transaction 0–100 for fraud using five years of labelled cases", (b) "Group our 40,000 retail customers into behaviourally distinct segments for a marketing test", (c) "Get a chatbot's answers ranked closer to human raters' preferences".

steps.title: (a) Fraud scoring
steps.desc: Supervised, regression-flavoured (or classification if thresholded). Feedback: historical labelled fraud/legit cases. Output: a per-transaction score.

steps.title: (b) Customer segments
steps.desc: Unsupervised clustering. Feedback: none — no one labelled segments. Output: group assignments that humans must interpret and validate against business reality.

steps.title: (c) Chatbot preferences
steps.desc: Reinforcement learning (specifically RLHF). Human raters compare answers; that preference data trains a reward signal; the model is updated to maximise it. Output: a tuned model/policy. Note the pipeline also contains supervised steps — more in Module 5.

payload.solution: (a) Supervised — labels exist, output is a score. (b) Unsupervised — no labels, output is groups for humans to judge. (c) Reinforcement — action = answer, reward = human preference, output = an improved response policy. The feedback signal, not the topic, decides the paradigm.

payload.title: Paradigm-hunt in job posts
payload.prompt: Find three real "AI/ML intern" or junior job descriptions. For each, infer the paradigm from the described work (data, tasks, metrics), write one sentence justifying your call, and note any signal that suggests the posting itself confuses paradigms.
payload.hint: Phrases like "labelled dataset", "accuracy/F1" suggest supervised; "segment", "cluster", "explore structure" suggest unsupervised; "reward", "preference", "agent", "trial and error" suggest RL.

mistakes.mistake: Calling every group-finding task "classification"
mistakes.fix: Classification needs labels to learn from. Grouping unlabelled customers is clustering — the segments are discovered, not predicted from a supervised target.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking reinforcement learning means "the model reinforces good answers in a chat"
mistakes.fix: RL has a precise meaning: sequential actions, delayed reward, policy learning. "Reinforcement" in casual speech is not the paradigm; RLHF is.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming unsupervised learning needs less care because "there are no labels"
mistakes.fix: Evaluation is harder, not easier. Garbage-in still produces clusters — of the garbage. Feature choice and validation by domain inspection become the whole game.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring blends (self-supervised, semi-supervised, RLHF) when forced to pick one label
mistakes.fix: Real pipelines are staged: self-supervised pretrain, supervised fine-tune, reinforcement preference-tune. Name the stage you mean; do not force the whole system into one box.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Classify and justify: a delivery company (i) predicts courier delivery time per order, (ii) discovers regional demand clusters for warehouse planning, (iii) learns courier-assignment rules online from customer ratings and late-delivery penalties.
payload.answer: (i) Supervised regression — labelled historical deliveries provide features → minutes. Output: a per-order time prediction. (ii) Unsupervised clustering — no labels; the algorithm groups regions by demand patterns and humans interpret the clusters. (iii) Reinforcement learning — assignment decisions (actions) followed by delayed rewards/penalties (ratings, lateness); the system learns an assignment policy to maximise cumulative reward. If forced to pick the paradigm of the whole company: it is a supervised-first ML shop with one RL-flavoured optimisation layer.
payload.source: Typical multi-part classification question in operations-analytics interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Supervised = labels; shapes into classification and regression; the commercial default.
Unsupervised = structure without labels (clustering, anomaly detection, visualisation); humans judge success.
Reinforcement = actions plus delayed reward, learning a policy; the paradigm of games, control, and RLHF.
Self-supervised training (predict the hidden part) is how LLMs learn at internet scale with no human labels.
Diagnose any project by its feedback signal, not its buzzword.

questions.prompt: Predicting a house price in rupees from its features is best described as:
questions.explanation: Continuous numeric target from labelled examples = supervised regression.

questions.prompt: Grouping unlabeled customers into behavioural segments is an example of:
questions.explanation: No labels exist; the algorithm discovers groups, and humans interpret them.

questions.prompt: In reinforcement learning, the learner receives:
options: A correct label after every action
A delayed reward or penalty signal
questions.explanation: RL feedback is evaluative (good/bad outcome), often delayed across a sequence of actions, not instructional labels.

questions.prompt: How do large language models obtain supervision for pretraining?
options: Self-supervised learning — predict text hidden in the data itself (e.g. the next token)
They are not trained on data
questions.explanation: Labels are manufactured from the corpus: the model predicts the next token, and the actual next token supervises it — no human annotation needed.

lessons.title: Train, Validation, Test: Why You Never Test on Training Data
lessons.summary: The three-way split, cross-validation, the honest-metrics mindset, and how leakage through the split produces models that are secretly useless.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Split a dataset into train/validation/test sets and state the purpose of each
Explain why training accuracy is not evidence of real-world performance
Use a validation set correctly for model selection without contaminating the test set
Describe k-fold cross-validation and when it earns its cost

payload.text: A classic interview trap: "Your model scores 99% accuracy on the data it trained on. What have you learned?" The right answer is: almost nothing. A sufficiently large model can memorise its training data — including the labels of noise — and still fail on every new example. The question is not whether you scored well on the data you studied; it is whether you scored well on data you deliberately kept hidden from yourself.

**The core idea: hide data from yourself.** A model's job is to perform on examples it has never seen. So the evaluation ritual mirrors that: hold out data the model is not allowed to train on, then measure on the held-out part. The standard three-way split: **training set** (the model learns parameters from this — usually the largest slice, commonly 60–80%); **validation set** (used during development to compare models, choose settings, and decide when to stop — the model never trains on it, but *you* tune against it repeatedly); **test set** (untouched until the very end — a single, honest report card for the final chosen model, and ideally used once).

**Why training accuracy lies.** Training metrics measure how well the model fit the data it saw — including its noise. A model complex enough can nearly memorise the training set: perfect scores, zero real skill. The gap between training performance and held-out performance is the first health indicator you should look at. If training is 99% and validation is 72%, you are not "nearly done" — you have a generalisation problem (more in the next lesson).

**The validation set is not a free lunch either.** Every time you check validation performance and change something, information about the validation set leaks into your decisions. Check it fifty times across fifty architectures and your "validation" score becomes optimistic — you have overfit *to the validation set* through your own iteration. This is why the test set must stay sealed: it measures the whole pipeline (model + your tuning process) on data that influenced nothing. When people "iterate on the test set" (peek, tweak, peek), test scores decay into validation scores and the final number stops meaning anything.

**Cross-validation: when data is scarce.** With limited data, a single split is noisy — unlucky splits make good models look bad. **k-fold cross-validation** splits the data into k parts (commonly 5 or 10), trains k times, each time holding out one part, and averages the scores. You get a stabler estimate and use every example for both training and evaluation across folds. Costs k times the compute, so on huge datasets a single split (or a time-based split) is preferred. One special case matters in practice: **time-series and event data must be split by time, not randomly** — train on months 1–9, validate on month 10, test on month 11. Random splits let the future leak into the past and inflate every metric.

**Data leakage through the split.** Leakage is not only bad features (Lesson 2.1); it is also bad splitting. Two classic forms: **group leakage** — near-duplicate rows (same patient's multiple scans, same user's many transactions, same article in train and test) let the model recognise rather than generalise; fix by splitting by group (patient, user, document). **Preprocessing leakage** — computing scaling, encoding or feature transforms on the full dataset before splitting; fix by fitting preprocessing on training only, then applying it to validation and test. Both produce beautiful offline numbers and ugly production numbers.

**The discipline in one sentence:** train on train, choose on validation, report on test, split by time or group when the data demands it, and touch the test set like it is a sealed exam envelope — once.

payload.title: What each split is for (and forbidden from)
rows: Final honest estimate of the whole process

payload.title: Preprocessing must happen inside the split
payload.text: Normalising with the mean of the whole dataset (before splitting) leaks test information into training. Fit scalers, encoders and feature transforms on train only; apply the fitted transform to val/test.

payload.title: Sanity check: shuffle the labels
payload.text: Train with labels randomly shuffled. If your pipeline still gets well above chance accuracy, you have leakage somewhere — the model is reading the answer through a side channel. This 10-minute test has caught million-rupee mistakes in industry.

payload.title: Set up an honest evaluation for a course-failure predictor
payload.problem: You have 8,000 historical student records spanning five academic years and want to predict course failure for next year. Design the split, the tuning process, and the final report.

steps.title: Split by time, not randomly
steps.desc: Train: years 1–3 (≈4,800 rows). Validation: year 4 (≈1,600). Test: year 5 (≈1,600). Next year's students are the future — the split should mimic that.

steps.title: Group check
steps.desc: If a student appears in multiple courses/years, keep each student entirely within one split (group by student id) so the model cannot recognise individuals across sets.

steps.title: Tune on validation only
steps.desc: Try three model families and a handful of settings; compare validation scores; pick the best and freeze it. Do not touch test yet.

steps.title: Final evaluation
steps.desc: Run the frozen pipeline once on the year-5 test set. Report that number, plus subgroup metrics (by department, by prior GPA band) — overall accuracy can hide concentrated failures.

payload.solution: Chronological split (years 1–3 train, year 4 validation, year 5 sealed test), group-by-student integrity, tuning confined to validation, one final test evaluation. The test score is your best available estimate of next year's performance — because nothing in the pipeline ever saw year 5.

payload.title: Run the label-shuffle test mentally, then for real if you can
payload.prompt: Take any small labelled dataset (the classic Iris dataset ships with most ML libraries). Describe exactly how you would split it 60/20/20. Then, if you can run code: train a simple model on shuffled labels and record the training vs held-out accuracy. If you cannot run code, write what you predict would happen and why.
payload.hint: With shuffled labels, training accuracy can climb toward 100% via memorisation while held-out accuracy collapses to chance (~33% on a 3-class problem).

mistakes.mistake: Reporting training accuracy as the model's accuracy
mistakes.fix: Training scores measure fit, not skill. Quote held-out (validation or test) numbers only — and say which split they came from.

mistakes.mistake: Iterating on the test set ("just one more peek")
