Hence the pairing rule: **reasoning improves odds; verification owns correctness.** For anything that matters, require an independent check — a different method, a substitution, a recount — or perform the check yourself.

**Iteration as engineering.** A prompt is a program whose test suite is a handful of real inputs. The loop: (1) **Run** the prompt on three to five representative inputs, including one nasty edge case. (2) **Inspect** against criteria — not vibes: content correct? all constraints met? format exact? (3) **Diagnose** into a failure class: *missing specification* (you never said it), *conflicting specification* (you said two things), *capability* (the model cannot do this well regardless), or *input problem* (bad/noisy context). (4) **Change one thing** — one added constraint, one changed example, one reformatted request. (5) **Retest** on the same inputs, and confirm nothing previously passing broke. Change two things at once and you learn nothing when it improves — or when it doesn't.

Keep a **mini test set**: five inputs that represent your real usage plus your known edge case, stored beside the prompt. It costs ten minutes to assemble and saves you from the classic regression — a prompt that fixed the last complaint and broke the three jobs it used to do right. Log versions with dates; models update silently, and a prompt that worked last month may behave differently now (Module 10 turns this habit into a library). And know when to stop: when three iterations do not fix a failure class, the problem is probably capability or context, not wording — supply better material, split the task, change tools, or accept a smaller scope. Prompting has diminishing returns, and recognising that boundary is part of the skill.

payload.title: Diagnose first, then edit
rows: Model never mentions the length limit
Add a word cap; cut contradictory detail requests
Specify the exact shape, add one example
Require an independent check; simplify or decompose
Right for simple inputs, fails hard ones
Supply more context, decompose, or change task scope

payload.title: One change per iteration
payload.text: Prompt debugging is controlled experimentation. Batch edits destroy the signal: a fix that works cannot be attributed, and a regression cannot be traced. Version your prompts and change them one line at a time.

payload.title: Reasoning-shaped text is not proof
payload.text: A fluent chain of steps can be post-hoc justification for an answer the model already leaned toward. Treat visible reasoning as a window into plausibility — then verify with a method the model did not just narrate.

payload.title: The token bill of thinking
payload.text: Long visible reasoning inflates output tokens — the expensive, slow kind (Module 5). For trivial tasks ask for the answer only; for hard tasks, ask for brief structured working. Reserve full reasoning for work that justifies the cost.

payload.title: Iterate a job-screening prompt through three rounds
payload.problem: Task: turn a job description into a screening checklist for a student. Round 1 prompt: "Make a checklist from this job description." Output: fluffy, includes nice-to-haves as requirements, inconsistent bullet format. Run the iteration loop until the output is usable.

steps.title: Round 1 — run and diagnose
steps.desc: Test on two different job descriptions. Failure class: *missing specification* — no distinction between required and preferred, no format, no audience. Not a capability problem: the model summarised fine, it just guessed what "checklist" meant.

steps.title: Round 2 — one change: structure the spec
steps.desc: New prompt: "Extract from the description: (a) hard requirements the candidate must have, (b) preferred skills, (c) role purpose in one line. Format: three headed sections, hard requirements as checkboxes. Do not invent requirements not present in the text."
steps.code_snippet:
R2: roles split + checkbox format + "do not invent"
Result: structure fixed; still mixes implied skills
       ("communication") into hard requirements.

steps.title: Round 3 — diagnose again: conflicting evidence
steps.desc: The model promotes widely-implied skills to requirements. Change one thing: add an evidence rule — "hard requirements must be verbatim-anchored in the text; move anything inferred to preferred" — plus one example pair showing an inferred skill placed in preferred.

steps.title: Retest and freeze
steps.desc: Re-run all three job descriptions (the mini test set): every hard requirement now traces to a line in the source; format stable; nothing that passed in round 2 broke. Record prompt version + date; note the residual failure (rarely: dense PDFs misread) as a context problem, not a wording problem.

payload.solution: Three iterations, one change each: missing specification → structure and evidence rule → example demonstrating inference placement. The loop worked because diagnosis came before editing: round 2 fixed format, round 3 fixed content, and each round was validated against the same three inputs so improvement was measured rather than felt.

payload.title: Run two real iterations
payload.prompt: Take your worst-performing prompt from Lesson 1. Run it, classify the failure (missing spec / conflicting spec / capability / input problem), make exactly one change, retest on the original input plus one new edge case, and write two lines: what you changed, what actually moved. Repeat once more.
payload.hint: If round one changed nothing, you probably edited the wrong class — capability failures need better context or a smaller task, not more adjectives.

mistakes.mistake: Changing five things after one bad output
mistakes.fix: You cannot attribute the next result. One change, one retest — the same discipline as any debugging session.

mistakes.mistake: Treating visible reasoning as verification
mistakes.fix: Steps can rationalise a wrong answer. Require a different method, substitution, or your own check for anything with consequences.

mistakes.mistake: Never testing the prompt on an edge case
mistakes.fix: A prompt validated only on happy paths fails exactly when it matters. Keep one nasty input permanently in your test set.

mistakes.mistake: Iterating forever on a capability ceiling
mistakes.fix: Three failed rounds on the same failure class means wording is not the bottleneck. Add context, decompose, change tools — or narrow the ask.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain, using autoregressive generation, why requiring step-by-step reasoning can improve answers on multi-step problems. Then name one way visible reasoning can mislead.
payload.answer: Generation is sequential: each token conditions on everything before it, and the model has no internal scratchpad beyond its own output. For a dependent multi-step problem answered immediately, the final answer tokens have no intermediate results to condition on. Requiring intermediate steps puts those results into the context — arithmetic states, premises, sub-conclusions — so later tokens compute from completed work instead of doing everything in one leap; empirically this raises accuracy and makes errors localisable. The failure mode: reasoning tokens are also sampled for plausibility, so a model can generate a fluent, confident chain that post-hoc justifies an already-wrong answer — reasoning is an aid, not proof; independent verification remains necessary.
payload.source: Standard chain-of-thought question in LLM interviews and evaluation discussions.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Step-by-step text becomes working memory in the context window — strong on dependent multi-step tasks.
Elicit it with structure (restate → operate → compute), decomposition, and self-check instructions.
Reasoning tokens are generated, not guaranteed: fluency can rationalise a wrong answer.
Iterate like an engineer: run → inspect → diagnose into a class → one change → retest on a fixed mini test set.
After three failed rounds, stop editing words — fix context, decompose, or change tools.

questions.prompt: Asking a model to "think step by step" often helps because:
options: Intermediate tokens give later tokens concrete results to condition on, acting as working memory
questions.explanation: Autoregressive generation has no scratchpad but its own output; required intermediate steps become context for the answer tokens.

questions.prompt: A model produces an elegant four-step solution that ends in a wrong answer. This is best described as:
options: Rationalisation — reasoning-shaped tokens are generated for plausibility, not guaranteed correctness
Proof the model cannot do arithmetic at all
questions.explanation: The chain is sampled like any other text; a fluent derivation can smuggle an unjustified leap. Verify with a separate method.

questions.prompt: Your prompt returns perfect structure but wrong content. Which failure class fits, and what is the first move?
options: Specification: format is set, content requirements are not — add explicit content constraints and evidence rules
No failure: structure is what was asked
questions.explanation: Diagnose before editing: satisfied format with failed substance means the content rules were never specified.

questions.prompt: During iteration, the safest experimental discipline is to:
options: Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch each round
Change one thing and retest against a fixed set of inputs
Test only on new inputs each time
Let the model suggest its own replacement prompt and accept it
questions.explanation: One change plus a fixed test set is what makes improvement attributable instead of anecdotal.

modules.title: Module 7 — The AI Tools Landscape
modules.summary: What the different species of AI tool actually are — chat assistants, coding assistants, AI search, image/video/voice generators — what free and paid tiers really buy you, how to choose a tool for a job, and when running a model on your own device beats the cloud.

lessons.title: Chat Assistants, Coding Assistants and AI Search: Three Species of Tool
lessons.summary: How the three most-used text tools differ in grounding, feedback loops and failure modes — and why the difference decides how much you must verify.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Distinguish chat assistants, coding assistants and AI search by how they produce answers
Rank tasks by how verifiable their outputs are, and match tools accordingly
Identify the characteristic failure mode of each tool species
Choose correctly among the three for a concrete task

payload.text: A student uses three AI tools in one afternoon: a chat assistant to explain recursion, an IDE assistant to fix a broken script, and an AI search to find last week's policy change. All three answered fluently. Only one of them was running the code before replying, and only one was pointing at pages published after the model was trained. "AI tool" is not one category — three different machines wore the same label, and trusting them identically is how people get burned.

**Chat assistants: parametric conversationalists.** The general-purpose chat product is a language model (Modules 4 and 5) plus an interface: it conditions on your conversation and generates text from what its weights absorbed during training. Strengths: drafting, explanation, transformation, brainstorming, working with material you paste in. Structural limits: its knowledge has a training cutoff (Module 4), it has no automatic access to live facts, and nothing in the loop checks its claims — fluency and accuracy are uncorrelated enough that you must treat it as a fast, well-read collaborator whose citations are provisional. When chat answers a current-affairs question, it is either recalling stale training material or confabulating; either way the answer needs an outside check.

**Coding assistants: the verifiable species.** An IDE assistant or agent works on code, and code has a property prose lacks — *it can be executed*. Autocomplete suggests the next lines; chat-in-the-editor explains and rewrites; agentic tools edit files, run tests and iterate on their own errors. This creates the healthiest loop in consumer AI: generate → run → fail → fix → pass, where the machine's output carries its own feedback signal. The characteristic trap is subtler than people expect: code that *looks* canonical can still be wrong — hallucinated library functions that do not exist in any version, logic that passes the happy path and breaks on empty inputs, security holes, imports from packages that are not installed. The rule that makes coding assistants genuinely useful: **run everything, read everything you run, and test the edges** — the loop only pays off when you actually close it.

**AI search: retrieval in front of the model.** AI search (and the "deep research" modes of assistants) does something structurally different: it queries an index of live pages, pulls back passages, and generates an answer *conditioned on those passages*, usually with citations. That breaks the parametric knowledge ceiling — it can discuss events after any training cutoff — and grounding in retrieved text measurably reduces the freest-form confabulation, because there is material in the window to anchor to. The characteristic trap: **citations are generated text too**. Links can be fabricated, mismatched to the claim, or point to a page that does not say what the summary claims; the format "answer with footnote numbers" is exactly the kind of shape a next-token model reproduces fluently regardless of truth. Verify by opening the source and checking the sentence, not by admiring the presence of a link.

**Matching tool to task.** Three questions decide it. (1) *Does the answer depend on facts that change or postdate training?* → AI search (or a chat assistant given the sources). (2) *Is the output executable or otherwise checkable by a machine?* → coding assistant, and close the loop. (3) *Is the output a judgement or a draft?* → chat assistant, plus a human pass. Note also that the species are converging — chat products add search and code execution, search products add chat — so ask what *this* answer was grounded in, not what the product is called. A single product can give you a grounded, cited answer in one turn and a free-willed confabulation in the next.

payload.title: The three species at a glance
rows: Plausible code that fails on edges

payload.title: Grounding is a spectrum, not a switch
payload.text: Pasting a document into a chat assistant is a mini form of grounding: the answer can condition on material in the window. Anything the model was NOT given — live facts, your database, this morning's email — is either retrieved, recalled from training, or invented. Ask which of the three happened.

payload.title: Verifiability outranks brand in tool choice
payload.text: For a bug, the tool whose output you can execute beats the tool with the best reputation. For a live fact, the tool that retrieves beats the tool that recalls. Choose by how checkable the output is.

payload.title: A citation is not a verification
payload.text: AI-search citations can be fabricated or attached to the wrong claim. Opening the link and reading the relevant line is the verification; the link itself is only a lead.

payload.title: Route three real requests to the right species
payload.problem: Same afternoon, three jobs: (A) the app crashes with a TypeError when saving settings; (B) what changed in the university's hostel policy this month; (C) a 300-word announcement for the coding club. Choose tools and specify the verification each one needs.

steps.title: Job A — code that fails
steps.desc: Coding assistant, with the stack trace and the offending file. Its output is executable: run the fix, reproduce the original steps, then test an edge (empty input, double-save). Verification is built in — the app either saves or it does not.

steps.title: Job B — a fact that changes
steps.desc: AI search (or chat with search enabled). Training cutoff makes chat-only recall useless for "this month's" changes; retrieval brings back candidate pages. Verification: open the official hostel/notice-board page and confirm the date and wording — the generated summary is only an index into the real source.

steps.title: Job C — a draft with taste
steps.desc: Chat assistant. Nothing to retrieve and nothing to execute — you need structure, tone and a working call-to-action. Supply the facts (date, venue, fee) as context, then verify the human way: does every name, date and link match reality? Would you sign it?

steps.title: Cross-check the species boundaries
steps.desc: Each job failed when handed to the wrong tool: chat would have invented the policy update; search would have mangled the stack trace into a blog-style answer; the coding assistant would have written a competent announcement with two invented event details. Match the grounding model to the fact pattern first.

payload.solution: Code → coding assistant (verify by running); changing facts → AI search (verify by opening official sources); drafts → chat (verify against supplied facts and your judgement). The routing logic is: what kind of claim is this, and what evidence would falsify it? Pick the tool whose output carries that evidence with it.

payload.title: Run one task through two species
payload.prompt: Take one question you actually have. Ask it in a plain chat assistant and in an AI search (or a search-enabled mode), then compare: which cited sources, which answered from memory, where did they disagree? Open one citation from each and score whether the source supports the claim.
payload.hint: The disagreement is the lesson — note which answer you would have trusted if you had only asked one tool.

mistakes.mistake: Using a chat assistant for events after its training cutoff
mistakes.fix: Use AI search or give it the sources in context. Chat-only answers to "what happened last week" are recall or confabulation at best.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting coding-assistant output without running it
mistakes.fix: Hallucinated APIs and happy-path logic look perfect in review. Execute, then test one edge case — the loop is the point of the tool.

mistakes.mistake: Treating any citation as proof
mistakes.fix: Open the link and read the supporting sentence. Fabricated and mismatched citations are the characteristic AI-search failure.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a tool by product name instead of grounding
mistakes.fix: Features converge; grounding does not. Ask what THIS answer was built from — weights, retrieved pages, or your files.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What structurally distinguishes AI search from a plain chat assistant, and why does that reduce — but not eliminate — the need for verification?
payload.answer: A chat assistant generates from parametric memory (training weights plus conversation context); AI search first retrieves live material from an index and generates conditioned on those passages, attaching citations. Because the answer window contains actual source text, claims are anchored and freshness no longer depends on a training cutoff — so the freest forms of confabulation drop. It does not eliminate verification because synthesis is still generated token by token: citations can be fabricated or mismatched, passages can be over-generalised, and the model can add uncited claims around grounded ones. Hence: retrieve better, then still open the source and check the sentence.
payload.source: Common product-and-trust question in AI literacy and research-skills assessments.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Chat = parametric recall plus your pasted context; no built-in truth check, cutoff-bound.
Coding assistants have the strongest loop because code executes — close the loop or lose the benefit.
AI search retrieves live text and cites it, breaking the cutoff ceiling; citations are still generated.
Route by claim type: checkable output → executor; changing facts → retrieval; judgement/draft → chat + human.
Products converge; the grounding behind an individual answer is what you actually verify.

questions.prompt: A plain chat assistant answers a question about an event from last week. The main risk is:
options: Its knowledge comes from training and pasted context — the answer may be stale or invented
Its context window is too small
questions.explanation: No retrieval means the model recalls from training (cutoff-bound) or confabulates plausibly; use search or supply sources.

questions.prompt: What makes coding assistants the most verifiable of the three species?
options: Their output can be executed — running and testing gives an independent feedback signal
They are connected to live search
questions.explanation: Compilation, tests and runtime turn output quality into something checkable by machine rather than by taste.

questions.prompt: An AI-search answer links to a real-looking article. Why must you still open it?
options: Citations are generated too — they can be fabricated or fail to support the claim made
Opening links increases your quota use
questions.explanation: The citation is part of the generated text; only reading the source establishes that it says what the summary claims.

questions.prompt: Which request should go to an AI search rather than a plain chat assistant?
options: Explain how a hash map works
Rewrite my email in a formal tone
Summarise what changed in a policy this month
questions.explanation: Anything whose facts postdate training or change over time needs retrieval; the others are transformations chat handles well.

lessons.title: Image, Video and Voice: The Generative Media Shelf
lessons.summary: What text-to-image, video and speech tools actually produce, how prompting differs across modalities, their structural failure patterns, and the verification and rights questions that come with them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe what image, video and voice generation tools do well and where they structurally fail
Prompt a media model with subject, style, composition and technical language
Recognise synthetic media artefacts and the limits of detection
State the consent, rights and verification issues attaching to generated media

payload.text: A student needs a poster for a tech fest by evening. Twenty minutes later they have a striking image — and three subtle disasters: the event name is misspelled in a decorative font, the "building" in the background has windows that dissolve into stairs, and nobody involved consented to the very real-looking face on the flyer. The tools are fast and genuinely good; they fail in characteristic, predictable ways, and the poster went out anyway. This lesson is about knowing those failure modes before the deadline, not after the complaint.

**Text-to-image: what it is doing.** Modern image generators (diffusion models and relatives — Module 5's "generative" family tree in one line) turn a text description into an image by learning what images look like and denoising toward your description. Prompting here is not the four-part essay of Lesson 1; it is a compact stack of **subject + context + style/lighting + composition + technical terms**: "a cluttered study desk at night, warm lamp light, shot at 35mm, shallow depth of field, top-down composition". Natural language works, but camera and art vocabulary gives you precise, well-represented levers because that vocabulary is abundant in training data. Editing tools (inpainting, erasing, background replace, image-to-image) are often more useful than regenerating: change one region, keep the rest.

Structural failures worth memorising: **rendered text** (signs, posters, logos come out misspelled or ornamental — the model generates letter-like shapes, not typography), **fine detail and counting** (hands, fingers, repeated objects, stairs and railings), **identity consistency** (the same character across multiple images drifts), and **real entities** (real logos, brands and faces are approximations). These are not fixed by better adjectives — they are properties of how the models learned. That is why designers use generators for concepts, backgrounds and variants, then set real text in a real type tool.

**Video and voice, honestly described.** Video generation currently produces short clips: strong for abstract visuals, transitions, mood b-roll; weak at long coherent scenes, physics that survives scrutiny, dialogue sync and anything resembling a documentary claim. Cost and review time are high — a usable minute can take many generations and a human pass — so the practical uses are concept pitches, social formats and illustrative motion, not factual record. Voice tools split in two: **speech synthesis** (text-to-speech for narration, accessibility read-alouds, drafts of voiceovers — now good enough that pacing and emphasis are controllable) and **speech recognition** (transcription of lectures and meetings — genuinely useful, with error rates that rise on accents, jargon and noise, so transcripts of anything important need a proofread). **Voice cloning** deserves its own warning: a convincing clone can be made from seconds of captured audio, which makes consent the deciding question — cloning your own voice is a feature, cloning someone else's without permission is a harm, and the same applies to faces.

**Understanding media, not just making it.** Vision-language models accept images and answer about them: read this chart, extract this form's fields, transcribe this board photo. This is the verification-friendly half of the media shelf — OCR-style extraction can be checked field by field against the original — but it inherits the text model's habits: it can misread a digit, invent a plausible field, or describe an image generically when asked something specific. Always compare extraction against the source image.

**Trust and provenance.** Synthetic media defeats naive heuristics ("video is real, text is fake"). Detection tools exist but are unreliable as a primary defence: accuracy varies by format, generated content keeps improving, and edited-real media confuses everything. Some generators embed watermarks and some producers attach content-credentials metadata (cryptographically signed origin records), but adoption is partial and metadata is easily stripped by re-uploading. The durable habit is journalistic: trace the origin, check the account and its history, look for corroboration from independent sources, and treat emotionally perfect, perfectly provoking media as suspect by default. (Module 9 takes this to its conclusion with deepfakes and misinformation.)

payload.title: Media tools by job
rows: Rendered text, counting, real logos, identity drift
Inspect details; set real text afterwards
Complex scene changes, consistency across edits
Short motion clips, pitches, social formats
Long scenes, physics, dialogue sync, factual claims
Fine print, rare handwriting, edge digits

payload.title: Prompt media the way a director briefs
payload.text: Subject, setting, light, lens, composition, mood — in that order — beats a paragraph of adjectives. Specific physical vocabulary (lens, angle, lighting) maps onto abundant training patterns and gives you control.

payload.title: Consent travels with a face or a voice
payload.text: Real-looking faces and cloned voices of real people need permission. Also check licence terms: some free tiers claim training rights over uploads or restrict commercial use of outputs — the terms page, not the demo, decides.

payload.title: Plan the media kit for a college tech fest
payload.problem: Budget: zero. One week. Deliverables: a poster image, a 30-second teaser clip, a voiceover for a 2-minute explainer, and a chart slide showing registration numbers. Decide tools, prompt directions, and the verification and rights pass for each.

steps.title: Poster — generate the visual, not the typography
steps.desc: Image model for the background/hero visual with a director-style prompt (subject, lighting, composition, mood). Leave the event name, dates and QR code OUT of the generated image; composite them in a design tool with real text. Prevents the misspelled-title failure entirely.

steps.title: Teaser — accept what the tool can honestly do
steps.desc: Short generated motion clips (abstract tech visuals, transitions) cut together — not a storyline with actors. Budget frames: generate several, keep the two that survive inspection. If a person must appear on camera, use real footage you have rights to.

steps.title: Voiceover — synthesis vs recognition
steps.desc: Synthesised narration if no one wants to record (test pronunciation of names and terms — synthesize, listen, edit). Captions come from transcription, then a human proofread — never publish auto-captions unreviewed, they mis-transcribe exactly the names and numbers people check.

steps.title: Chart — extraction is not creation
steps.desc: Registration numbers come from your actual sheet. If you use vision tools to pull numbers out of a scanned form, verify each field against the source image — one misread digit in a public chart is a credibility event. Render the chart in a spreadsheet, not a generated picture.
steps.code_snippet:
Poster:  image model -> visual only -> real text on top
Teaser:   3-5 short generated clips -> human edit -> cut
Voice:    TTS draft -> listen -> fix names -> export
Chart:    real data -> verify any OCR extraction -> render

payload.solution: Generate where generation is strong (visual mood, short motion, narration) and keep everything factual or textual in tools you control (real type, real data, real sources). Each deliverable ends with its own check: inspect fine detail, proofread captions, verify extracted numbers, and confirm you hold the rights to every face, voice and clip you ship.

payload.title: Generate, then audit
payload.prompt: Generate one image with a structured prompt (subject, setting, light, lens, composition). Then list three things you checked before you would show it to anyone — text, hands/edges, real-world logic. Finally, ask a vision-enabled assistant "what is wrong with this image?" and compare its list with yours.
payload.hint: If you cannot name the artefacts you are looking for, you will not catch them in a hurry — that is the whole exercise.

mistakes.mistake: Asking an image model to render your event title, price or logo
mistakes.fix: Generated letterforms are approximations and usually wrong. Generate the visual; set the type yourself in a design tool.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a generated image or clip as evidence
mistakes.fix: Synthetic media depicts nothing that happened. For anything factual — news, events, people — only original, corroborated sources count.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping licence and consent checks
mistakes.fix: Free tiers differ on commercial rights and on whether uploads may train models; faces and voices need consent. Read the terms for the tier you are on.

mistakes.mistake: Publishing auto-transcripts and captions unreviewed
mistakes.fix: Speech recognition degrades on names, numbers, accents and noise — precisely what matters. Proofread against the audio before publishing.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Name two structural limitations of current text-to-image models and give the practical workflow each one implies.
payload.answer: (1) Rendered text: the model produces letter-like shapes rather than typography, so titles, prices and logos come out misspelled or ornamental — implication: generate the visual only, and set all real text in a design tool as a compositing step. (2) Fine detail and counting (hands, repeated objects, structural logic like stairs): implication: inspect at full size and expect to regenerate or inpaint rather than trust the first result; for anything that must be exact (charts, forms, products), render with deterministic tools instead. Both limitations are properties of the generative approach, not of prompting effort — the workflow routes around them rather than arguing with them.
payload.source: Standard applied question on generative-media limits in design and marketing interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Image prompting = subject + setting + light + lens + composition; real text is set outside the generator.
Memorise the structural fails: rendered text, counting/detail, identity drift, real entities.
Video = short illustrative motion, not factual record; voice synthesis and transcription both need human passes.
Consent and licences attach to faces, voices and uploads — check the terms for your tier.
Detection is unreliable as a first line: trace origin, corroborate, and distrust perfect provocation.

questions.prompt: Why should an event title be added AFTER generating a poster image?
options: Generated images are always low resolution
Image models render letterforms as approximations — text usually comes out misspelled or ornamental
Image models refuse all text prompts
questions.explanation: Text rendering remains structurally weak; generate the visual and composite real typography on top.

questions.prompt: Which task is best served by speech-to-text transcription?
options: Publishing unreviewed captions for a lecture with student names
Converting a meeting recording into a draft that is then proofread against the audio
Generating a news report from scratch
Creating a cloned voice of a colleague
questions.explanation: Transcription shines as a first draft; names, numbers and accents are exactly where it errs, so a proofread pass is mandatory.

questions.prompt: You need a picture of a real event that happened yesterday. The right move is:
options: Generate it — it will look convincing
Use original photography or verifiable footage with a traceable source
Ask a vision model to recall it
Enhance an old photo and relabel it
questions.explanation: Synthetic media depicts nothing that happened; factual imagery needs a real, traceable origin.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to clone their voice for a project. The deciding consideration is:
options: Whether they have given consent and the licence permits the use
questions.explanation: Consent and licence terms govern faces and voices — permission converts a risk into a feature.

lessons.title: Free Tiers, Subscriptions and API Credits: What You Actually Pay
lessons.summary: The four ways to consume AI, what money genuinely buys (and what it never does), the data terms hidden in "free", and a decision frame for students and teams.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compare free tiers, paid subscriptions, per-token APIs and self-hosted open models
Identify what a paid plan actually changes: limits, model tier, features and data terms
Locate training-use and retention settings hidden in free consumer products
Choose a consumption mode for a concrete usage pattern

payload.text: Two students use "the same AI" for a semester. One stays on a free tier and quietly hits daily caps mid-revision-week, gets the smaller model, and never notices that her pastes may be used to improve the product. The other pays a modest subscription, gets the stronger model, longer files and an opt-out toggle she found in settings — and still gets hallucinations. Money changed her limits and her data terms. It did not change the truthfulness of anything, and confusing those two facts is expensive in both directions.

**The four consumption modes.** (1) **Free consumer tier**: a funded sample — generous enough to hook you, throttled with rate limits (messages per day, slower access at peak), often the provider's smaller or older model, shorter context, fewer file features, and the most permissive default data terms. (2) **Subscription**: you rent the full product — higher or no practical caps, the current flagship model, longer context, file projects, research modes, image/video minutes, priority speed, and usually the privacy controls (training opt-outs, longer retention windows). (3) **API credits**: raw model access priced per million tokens (Module 5, Lesson 4), input and output separately — no chat interface, you build the workflow, you own integration, error handling and evaluation, and you can mix models by task. (4) **Self-hosted open weights**: free to download, costly to run (hardware, ops, time — Module 5), decisive when data must not leave your boundary. Students live in (1) and (2); builders need (3); institutions with sensitivity rules eventually need (4).

**What money genuinely buys.** Five things, in order of practical impact: **limits** (the cap you hit is the feature you use least when you need it most); **model tier** (free tiers often route to smaller models — same brand, different engine, visibly different quality on hard tasks); **features** (file uploads, long documents, deep-research modes, canvas/projects, image minutes — frequently gated entirely); **data terms** (training opt-outs, retention windows, zero-retention enterprise options, and contractual terms for organisations); **support and guarantees** (SLA, uptime commitments, business terms). Note what is absent from that list: **truthfulness**. No tier buys accuracy. A paid plan gives you a better instrument, not a verified answer — verification (Modules 8 and 9) is not upsold because it cannot be.

**The part "free" hides.** Consumer free products are frequently funded by exactly two things: your rate-limited attention (upsell path) and your data (improvement path). Defaults differ by provider and change over time, so the durable skill is *locating the settings*: look for "improve the model for everyone", "data controls", "memory", "chat history" — and understand what each toggle actually does (training inclusion vs short-term retention for abuse prevention are different switches). Turning off training on a free tier is usually possible and always worth doing for personal material. Also read what the tier says about human review of conversations — providers describe sampling for safety and quality differently, so read your provider's wording rather than assuming the best or the worst.

**When free is genuinely enough.** Occasional drafting, explanation, brainstorming and light study — under the daily cap, with the smaller model — free is fine, and pretending otherwise would be hype. Pay when usage is daily and cap-bound, when you need the flagship model for hard reasoning, when you work with long documents, or when you need the data terms. Build an API integration when you are automating something with real volume (per-token arithmetic from Module 5 applies directly — often cheaper than a subscription at scale, and far more expensive if you mis-estimate). Self-host when compliance forbids egress or volume makes APIs uneconomic. The mistakes at each level are symmetrical: paying for a plan you underuse, staying free while hitting caps every day, and reaching for an API when a subscription would do.

payload.title: What each mode gives and costs
rows: Rate limits, smaller model, permissive data defaults
Flagship model, no practical caps, files, privacy toggles
Raw model access, model mixing, automation
No UI; you build evals, errors, cost control
Data never leaves, no per-token bill

payload.code:
# When the subscription stops paying for itself
sub_price_month = 700        # hypothetical INR/month
api_input_rate  = 0.10        # INR per 1K input tokens (hypothetical)
api_output_rate = 0.40        # INR per 1K output tokens (hypothetical)

calls_per_month = 6000
in_tok, out_tok = 800, 300    # per call

api_bill = calls_per_month*(in_tok/1000*api_input_rate
                          + out_tok/1000*api_output_rate)
print(api_bill)               # compare with sub_price_month
# Then subtract: UI time, evals you must build, error handling.

payload.title: Find the data settings today, not after
payload.text: Five minutes in Settings → Data/Privacy on every tool you use: switch off training on your chats where offered, decide on memory, and note what the tier promises about retention. It is the cheapest privacy action available to you.

payload.title: "Free" does not mean "no cost" — and not only because of data
payload.text: Daily caps bind at the worst moment, smaller models fail harder tasks quietly, and commercial-use rights differ across free tiers (especially for image tools). Check limits, model routing and licence before building a habit on any free tier.

payload.title: Pick a mode for three real usage patterns
payload.problem: (A) A second-year who uses AI twice a week for explanation and light drafting. (B) A placement-prep student using it daily for mock interviews, resume iteration and aptitude explanations, hitting the free cap most evenings. (C) A final-year team automating resume-tailoring for 200 submissions a month inside their own web app. Recommend modes and name what each must check before committing.

steps.title: A — occasional, low stakes → free tier
steps.desc: Usage sits under caps; a subscription would rent an instrument that stays in the case. Must check: data settings (training opt-out) and the current model routing, so quality surprises are understood rather than blamed.

steps.title: B — daily and cap-bound → subscription
steps.desc: The cap is now the binding constraint, and the harder tasks (mock interview feedback, reasoning questions) benefit from the flagship model. Check: the actual monthly price against usage, the privacy toggles, and cancel-ability — subscriptions should be justified monthly, not by identity.

steps.title: C — volume + product → API
steps.desc: 200 submissions/month with programmatic formatting is automation, not conversation: APIs price per token, let each submission route (small model for tailoring, large for review), and integrate with validation. Check the arithmetic first — tokens/month × rates vs subscription plans — plus budget alerts and error handling.
steps.code_snippet:
200 subs * (2500 in + 700 out) tokens
= 500K in + 140K out tokens/month
* rates  -> compare with team subscription cost

steps.title: Decision summary
steps.desc: Mode follows pattern: frequency × task hardness × programmatic need × data sensitivity. Also state the non-purchase: none of the three modes buys verification — all three still require the checklists from Modules 8 and 9.

payload.solution: A stays free (with data settings tightened), B subscribes (caps and model tier are now binding), C uses the API (volume plus integration plus per-model routing). Each decision is justified by usage pattern rather than brand, and each includes the data-terms check — while remembering that no tier upgrades truthfulness, only the instrument.

payload.title: Audit the tiers you are on
payload.prompt: For each AI tool you used this week: note your current mode (free/subscription/API), the daily or monthly limits, which model you believe you are getting, and the state of its training/retention settings. Write two lines: what you would gain by paying, and whether you would actually use it.
payload.hint: Look in Settings → Data/Privacy and the plan/limits page — not in the marketing copy.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming free means the data path is protected
mistakes.fix: Free tiers often carry the most permissive defaults. Locate the training opt-out and retention description yourself — defaults differ by provider and change over time.

mistakes.mistake: Paying for a plan because of brand rather than bottleneck
mistakes.fix: If you never hit caps and your tasks are simple, a subscription buys you little. Pay when a specific limit, model tier or feature is actually binding.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting any tier to fix accuracy
mistakes.fix: Paid plans buy capability, limits and terms — not truth. Verification habits are tier-independent and remain yours.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing between API and subscription without arithmetic
mistakes.fix: Compute tokens × rates for your real volume (Module 5 formula), then add the engineering time APIs demand. Both directions of this mistake are common and measurable.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A student asks whether the free tier is "good enough". Give a four-question decision frame, and explain why upgrading never solves one specific problem.
payload.answer: Four questions: (1) Does usage sit under the daily/monthly caps — including your worst week, not your average? (2) Do your tasks need the flagship model (hard reasoning, long documents), or is the routed smaller model sufficient? (3) Are the free tier's data terms acceptable for what you paste — training opt-out present, retention understood? (4) Do you need gated features (file projects, research modes, image minutes, commercial-use rights)? The problem upgrading never solves: truthfulness — higher tiers buy capability, limits, features and terms, so hallucination-prone outputs still require the verification discipline regardless of plan.
payload.source: Everyday product-choice question in digital literacy and AI-tool onboarding interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Four modes: free tier, subscription, API credits, self-hosted open weights — matched to usage patterns.
Money buys limits, model tier, features, data terms and support — never accuracy.
Free tiers are funded by attention and often by data: find training/retention settings yourself.
Decide from frequency × hardness × programmatic need × sensitivity, with token arithmetic when automating.
Whatever you pay, the verification checklist from Modules 8 and 9 still applies in full.

questions.prompt: Which does a paid subscription MOST reliably buy over a free tier?
options: Higher limits, the flagship model, gated features and stronger data controls
questions.explanation: Subscriptions change limits, model tier, features and terms — truthfulness is not on the price list.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to stop your chats being used for model training?
options: Settings → data/privacy controls, and the tier's retention description
questions.explanation: Training inclusion and retention are configured in data controls and described in the terms — defaults vary and change, so check yours.

questions.prompt: When is the API (pay-per-token) mode the right choice?
options: When you want a chat interface
When you are automating volume programmatically and can do the cost arithmetic
When you want the free tier
questions.explanation: APIs suit machine-driven volume with routing and integration needs — priced per token, no UI, engineering is on you.

questions.prompt: Your subscription gives you the flagship model but you still receive a confident wrong answer. This shows that:
options: Paid tiers improve capability and limits, not verification — checking remains your job
questions.explanation: Accuracy is a property of grounding and verification practice, not of the billing plan.

lessons.title: Choosing a Tool for the Job — and Running Models on Your Own Device
lessons.summary: A repeatable selection procedure for the whole landscape, plus what local and on-device models actually offer: privacy, offline use, zero per-token cost — and their real capability ceiling.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply a five-question selection procedure to choose an AI tool for a task
Explain what running a local or on-device model means in practice
State when local models beat cloud APIs and when they cannot compete
Assemble a personal toolkit mapped to tasks rather than brands

payload.text: The fastest way to feel the trade-off: summarise a personal diary entry with a cloud assistant — instant, excellent, and now sitting on someone else's servers — then do the same with a model running on your own laptop, offline. Slower, visibly less polished, and nothing left the machine. Neither run was the "right answer". They were answers to different questions, and tool selection is the skill of asking the right question first.

**A selection procedure you can reuse.** Five questions, in order: (1) **What is the claim pattern?** Live/changing facts → a retrieval-grounded tool; executable output → a coding assistant with a run loop; drafts and judgement → chat. (2) **How checkable is the output?** The less checkable, the more you want a tool that shows its sources or reasoning, and the more human review you budget. (3) **Can the data leave?** Personal, medical, client or unpublished material narrows the field before quality is discussed — hard constraints decide categories (Module 5, Lesson 4). (4) **What is the volume and hardness?** High volume favors cheap/fast routing; hard reasoning favors frontier models; low frequency favors free tiers. (5) **What is actually available to you?** Account, budget, device, offline need, organisation policy. Run the questions in order — when (3) says "no", the answer to (1) barely matters.

**Local and on-device: what it means.** A **local model** is downloadable open weights running on your own hardware — a laptop GPU or CPU, a workstation, a home server — through a chat app or runtime designed for it. An **on-device model** is a small model baked into your phone, laptop OS or browser, often on a dedicated neural accelerator, sometimes running entirely offline. Both invert the cloud bargain: no per-token bill, no rate caps, no network dependency, and — the decisive property — **input text never leaves the device**. The costs are equally concrete: capability is capped at what fits your hardware (today: small models — competent at summarising, rewriting, extraction, simple code and casual conversation; visibly weaker at long-context synthesis and hard multi-step reasoning), memory and battery are consumed while running, setup and updates are on you, and the model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff with no retrieval unless you add one.

**Where local genuinely wins.** Three situations, all variations on one theme — *the material should not travel*: personal notes, journals, medical or legal documents you would not paste into a web form; work with sensitive code or client data under policy that forbids external processing; and offline or connectivity-poor use (trains, fieldwork, low bandwidth) where zero latency-to-network and no usage caps matter. Add a fourth: very high-frequency, simple tasks where an API bill or subscription caps are the binding constraint and a small local model is good enough. **Where local cannot compete:** frontier-level reasoning, very long contexts, up-to-the-minute knowledge without your own retrieval, multimodal heavy lifting, and anything where the quality gap between a 3B-on-laptop model and a frontier API is the difference between usable and not. A middle path exists and is underrated: cloud tools *with* the right settings — training off, minimal pasted context, redaction — handle most personal material acceptably once you have done the Lesson 3 data-terms audit.

**Assemble the toolkit, not the fan collection.** The goal of this module is a small, boring, reliable set: one chat assistant you know the limits of, one search-grounded path for current facts, one coding assistant with a run habit, one local model for material that should not travel, and a standing rule for when each is used — that mapping is exactly what the Module 10 capstone asks you to document and keep. Judge tools by your own tests on your own tasks for a week, not by launch videos: the tool that survives a week of your real work is the tool you have chosen.

Small model — solid basics, weak hard reasoning

# A personal-toolkit routing rule (conceptual)
def route(task, data_sensitivity, needs_live_facts, hard_reasoning):
    if data_sensitivity == "high":      return "local model"
    if needs_live_facts:                return "AI search / grounded chat"
    if task == "code":                  return "coding assistant (run it)"
    if hard_reasoning:                  return "frontier chat model"
    return "fast/cheap model or free tier"

# Sensitivity is checked BEFORE capability - constraints pick the category.

payload.title: Test candidate tools on your real week

payload.title: A local app is not automatically private

payload.title: Build and route a student's personal AI toolkit
payload.problem: A student's weekly AI needs: (1) daily study Q&A and difficult-concept explanations; (2) Python debugging for lab work; (3) summarising a private personal journal; (4) current affair and policy questions for a debate club; (5) occasional poster images for events. Choose a tool for each, justify with the five questions, and flag what must be verified.

steps.title: Apply question 3 first for journal summaries
steps.desc: Private personal material: the data path decides — a local model (or a cloud tool with training off, minimal paste and redaction) is the category-appropriate answer. Capability needed is basic summarisation, squarely inside small-model competence.

steps.title: Route by claim pattern for the rest
steps.desc: Study Q&A → chat assistant (drafts/explanation, verify against textbook); Python debugging → coding assistant with the run habit (execute, read the diff); current affairs → AI search (open the sources); posters → image model with text composited outside (Lesson 2).

journal      -> local (data path decides)
study Q&A    -> chat + verify vs textbook
debug lab    -> coding assistant + run
policy Qs    -> AI search + open sources
posters      -> image model + real text

steps.title: Check availability and cost against reality
steps.desc: Budget zero, laptop with modest specs: local model = a small quantised model via a desktop runtime (fits memory, slower but private); everything else on free tiers with data settings tightened. Caps will bite study Q&A in exam week — that is the known failure, noted rather than denied.

steps.title: Write the standing rules and the verification layer
steps.desc: Rules: nothing sensitive goes to cloud; every factual claim gets an external check; every code change gets run; every citation gets opened. Then run the toolkit for a week and revise — the selection procedure is a loop, not a ceremony.

payload.solution: Sensitivity-first routing (journal → local), then claim-pattern routing (facts → search, code → coding assistant, explanation → chat, media → image model with real typography), constrained by availability (free tiers + one local install) and closed by written verification rules. The toolkit is small on purpose: five tasks, four tools, four rules — which is exactly the structure the capstone asks you to maintain.

payload.title: Run one task locally
payload.prompt: Install or locate a local/on-device model (desktop runtime, phone built-in feature, browser option) and give it the same task you recently gave a cloud assistant — something low-stakes like summarising a public paragraph. Compare: quality, speed, convenience, and the data-path difference. Write three lines on which tasks you would now move local permanently.
payload.hint: You are not benchmarking for the internet — you are discovering which of YOUR tasks fit inside your device's capability ceiling.

mistakes.mistake: Ranking tools before checking the data constraint
mistakes.fix: If the material cannot leave, capability comparisons are irrelevant — the constraint selects the category first. Question 3 runs before questions 1, 2 and 4.

mistakes.mistake: Judging local models by frontier expectations
mistakes.fix: A small on-device model is a different instrument: excellent at basic transformations, weak at hard reasoning. Assign it the tasks its ceiling covers and it will beat nothing gracefully.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a local app never talks to the internet
mistakes.fix: Inference may be local while history sync, telemetry and model downloads are not. Verify what the wrapper uploads, not just where the model runs.

mistakes.mistake: Accumulating tools instead of a toolkit
mistakes.fix: More apps without routing rules means inconsistent quality and duplicated data exposure. Fewer tools, explicit rules, one scorecard — that is the selection procedure's output.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Give two situations where a local model beats a cloud API, and two where it cannot compete. Explain the underlying principle.
payload.answer: Local wins when: (1) the material must not leave the device — journals, medical or client documents, sensitive code — because the data path is the hard constraint; and (2) offline or capped-frequency simple work — summarising, rewriting, extraction — where zero per-token cost and no network dependency dominate. Local loses when: (1) frontier-level multi-step reasoning or very long context is required, because capability is bounded by what fits the hardware; and (2) up-to-date knowledge or heavy multimodal work is needed without your own retrieval layer, since the model is frozen at its cutoff. Principle: tool selection runs constraints (privacy, connectivity, cost) before capability, then matches the task's hardness to the model class — the same ordering as every build-vs-buy decision in Module 5.
payload.source: Standard edge-vs-cloud deployment reasoning, simplified for AI literacy.

Local/on-device buys privacy, offline use and zero token cost — and charges a capability ceiling and ops burden.
Sensitive material decides the category before capability is even discussed.
A toolkit is a small set of tools plus written routing rules — not a folder full of apps.

Solving a hard multi-constraint optimisation problem
questions.explanation: Sensitive material plus basic transformation plus no network need — exactly the local win condition.

modules.title: Module 8 — AI for Study and Work
modules.summary: The daily uses, taught with the verification habit welded on: research and summarising you can trust, code explained until you understand it, drafts you edit before shipping, and exam, resume and placement work where being wrong is expensive.

lessons.title: Research and Summarising: Fast First Passes, Then Verification
lessons.summary: Where AI genuinely accelerates reading and sense-making, where it quietly fails, and a concrete routine for checking what comes back before it enters your work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Identify research and summarisation tasks where AI adds real speed
Classify AI-supplied claims by checkability and verify them against primary sources
Design a summarisation prompt that preserves caveats and provenance
Run a citation-tracing check that catches fabricated and mismatched sources

payload.text: An essay built entirely from AI-generated "sources" collapsed in ten minutes when the supervisor opened the first link: the paper did not exist, the author was invented, and the date belonged to a different decade. The student had done everything else right — structure, argument, prose. What was missing took one minute per source to fix and should have taken ten minutes total: open the link, read the line. Research with AI is fast; research without verification is a countdown.

**What AI is genuinely good at in research.** Compression and organisation: turning a 40-page report into a two-paragraph brief (when you give it the report), structuring scattered notes into an outline, generating the *questions* a topic raises, translating or rephrasing dense passages to your level, comparing two documents you paste, and screening whether an abstract is worth a full read. All of these are transformations of material you supply or well-bounded general knowledge — tasks where errors are visible on inspection. What it is structurally bad at: facts that change (deadlines, policies, prices), precise citations (author-year-journal details), obscure or recent claims, and numbers of any kind. Those live in the model's parametric memory or nowhere (Module 7, Lesson 1) — which is exactly where confabulation hides.

**The verification routine.** Adopt one, and run it every time research leaves the chat window: (1) **List the claims.** Extract every checkable assertion — names, dates, numbers, citations, "studies show" statements. (2) **Classify.** Anchor fact (settleable by a document), live fact (changes over time), interpretation (arguable). Anchor facts get source checks; live facts get official pages with dates; interpretations get treated as arguments to weigh, not findings to quote. (3) **Trace citations.** Search the title + author: does the paper exist, does it say that, is your quote actually in it? Mismatched citations — real source, wrong claim — are more dangerous than fabricated ones because the link opens. (4) **Cross-check the load-bearing numbers** against a second independent source, and note the date relative to the model's cutoff (Module 4). (5) **Record status**: verified / unverified / contradicted, before anything propagates into your notes. Ten seconds of annotation per claim now beats an hour of recovery later.

**Summarising honestly.** A summary prompt should specify audience, length, and — critically — **what must be preserved**: "keep all numbers, conditions and caveats; flag any sentence where the original hedges". Summaries silently drop the conditions attached to findings ("in a 12-week trial, n=40" becomes "studies show"). For high-stakes documents — contracts, policies, safety instructions, graded readings — the summary is an *index into* the document, never a replacement for it: use it to find where to read, then read those passages. Ask for provenance as you go: "quote the sentence each point comes from", which both improves faithfulness and gives you a fast checking handle (Module 4's context window means it can quote exactly what you pasted).

**One structural habit: ask what is missing.** After a research summary, request the counter-considerations: "what would a sceptic of this summary say?" and "what could not be checked from these documents?" This is cheap, and it compensates for the model's tendency toward tidy narrative — real bodies of evidence are messier than any synthesis sounds. Keep the outputs in two columns in your notes: what the AI said, and what you verified. The columns converge only through your work.

payload.title: Claim type → check
rows: Find the paper; read the record
Official page with a visible date, today
Original source; note sample and conditions
Search title+author; confirm the claim is in it
Treat as argument — compare other readings

Research prompt with verification built in:
"Using ONLY the two documents below, produce:
 1. a 150-word summary for a first-year reader,
 2. every factual claim as a bullet with the exact
    sentence it came from,
