Do not add facts from memory; write (not in docs) instead."

<doc1> ... </doc1>   <doc2> ... </doc2>

payload.title: Ask for the hedge, not just the finding
payload.text: "What conditions, sample sizes or caveats accompany this result?" forces the qualifiers back into view — they are the first thing a fluent summary trims and the first thing a supervisor asks for.

payload.title: Unverified citations are the highest-risk research output
payload.text: Fabricated references and mismatched real references both survive spellcheck and plagiarism checks only until someone opens the link. Trace every citation before it enters a bibliography.

payload.title: Verify an AI research summary before it enters an essay
payload.problem: You asked for background on a topic and received a five-bullet summary: two citations, a statistic, a policy date and a causal claim. Walk the routine, decide what is usable today, and write the notes you would actually keep.

steps.title: List and classify the five claims
steps.desc: Citations ×2 = anchor facts; statistic = anchor/numeric; policy date = live fact; causal claim = interpretation. Each class gets a different check — this classification step prevents the classic error of treating all five as equally supported.

steps.title: Trace the citations
steps.desc: Search title + author for each. Possible outcomes: source exists and supports the claim (keep, quote the line); source exists but does not say that (mismatch — rewrite or drop); nothing found (fabricated — drop and tell the model citations must be verifiable).
steps.code_snippet:
claim 1: search "Exact Title Author 2021"
-> found + passage matches  : verified
-> found, different claim   : mismatch - rewrite
-> not found                : fabricated - drop

steps.title: Check the number and the date
steps.desc: Statistic: locate the original study; note conditions (sample, period, population) — otherwise your essay overstates it. Policy date: open the official page today; live facts carry their own expiry, and a deadline quoted from training data is usually wrong by now.

steps.title: Handle the interpretation and record status
steps.desc: The causal claim is an argument: ask for the opposing reading and check whether your sources support causation or only correlation. Write the ledger: two verified bullets with quotes, one number with conditions, one date checked today, one interpretation marked as argued — only the verified items go in the essay.

payload.solution: Classify, trace, cross-check, record — citation tracing catches the fabrication, original-source reading catches the overstated number, an official dated page catches the stale policy, and marking the causal claim as interpretation keeps an argument from masquerading as a finding. The essay now rests on a five-line verification ledger instead of a fluent paragraph.

payload.title: Run the full routine once, for real
payload.prompt: Ask an assistant for five factual claims on a topic you half-know. Classify each claim, verify each one against an independent source, and keep a three-column record (claim / status / source). Report the honest tally: verified, unverified, contradicted — and what failure type each failure was.
payload.hint: Do not pick an obscure topic to make the model look good — the point is measuring your own verification routine on ordinary material.

mistakes.mistake: Submitting AI-generated references unopened
mistakes.fix: Trace title + author + supporting line for every citation. Fabricated and mismatched references are the most common way AI-assisted research fails under review.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a summary as the document
mistakes.fix: Summaries drop conditions, caveats and scope. For high-stakes readings, use the summary as an index and read the passages that carry the conclusions yourself.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting a confident tone as evidence of checking
mistakes.fix: Fluency is orthogonal to verification. Confidence should change nothing about your routine — only a traceable source should.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring dates on live facts
mistakes.fix: Deadlines, policies and prices drift after any training cutoff. Always re-check them on the official, dated page before acting or citing.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Design a five-step verification routine for factual claims and citations obtained from an AI assistant, and explain why mismatched citations are especially dangerous.
payload.answer: Steps: (1) extract every checkable claim from the output; (2) classify each as anchor fact, live fact, numeric claim, citation or interpretation; (3) trace citations by searching title and author, then confirm the cited passage actually supports the claim; (4) cross-check load-bearing numbers and dates against primary or official sources, noting currency relative to the model's cutoff; (5) annotate each claim verified/unverified/contradicted before it enters notes or drafts. Mismatched citations are the worst failure class because they pass casual inspection — the link opens, the source is real, so the reader's trust transfers to a claim the source does not make; fabrication is at least detectable in one click.
payload.source: Standard research-integrity question for AI-assisted coursework and journalism workflows.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: AI accelerates compression and organisation of material you supply — not live facts, precise citations or numbers.
Verify by classifying claims, tracing citations, cross-checking numbers, and stamping status.
Summaries must preserve caveats; for high-stakes documents they index, never replace, the original.
Mismatched citations (real source, wrong claim) are more dangerous than fabricated ones.
Keep two columns — AI-said and you-verified — and let only your work move items across.

questions.prompt: Which research task suits an AI assistant WITHOUT needing external verification?
options: Structuring your pasted notes into an outline
Stating how many citations a 2023 paper has
Naming the exact volume and page of a journal article
questions.explanation: Organising material you supplied is a transformation; the others are checkable facts that must come from live sources.

questions.prompt: An AI citation opens to a real paper that does not contain the claimed finding. This is:
options: A mismatched citation — more dangerous than fabrication because the source looks verified
questions.explanation: Real source plus unsupported claim transfers unearned trust — always read the cited passage, not just the link.

questions.prompt: Why must a policy deadline from an AI answer be re-checked even if the answer feels authoritative?
options: Deadlines change over time and the model's knowledge has a training cutoff
AI is banned from knowing policies
Deadlines are always wrong in training data
The model refuses to answer about dates
questions.explanation: Live facts drift after cutoff; only the official dated page settles them.

questions.prompt: The safest use of an AI summary of a contract clause is to:
options: Rely on it entirely instead of reading the clause
Use it to locate the relevant passage, then read that passage yourself
Post it publicly for a second opinion
Ask the model to sign off on it
questions.explanation: Summaries are an index into high-stakes text; conditions and exceptions are exactly what compression drops.

lessons.title: Learning and Explaining Code With AI
lessons.summary: Using coding assistants to understand, debug and practise — with the run-everything discipline that turns plausible code into code you actually know.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Formulate code-learning prompts that produce explanations you can absorb and test
Use AI for debugging without outsourcing the understanding
Recognise hallucinated APIs and happy-path-only logic in generated code
Apply the academic-integrity boundary to AI-assisted programming work

payload.text: Two students get the same fix from the same assistant. One pastes it in, it runs, the lab is submitted, and the viva question "what does this line do?" ends the story. The other asks the assistant to explain the change on a small example, runs her own test on an empty input, and can defend every line. The tool was identical; one of them bought an answer, the other bought an explanation. Code is the one domain where the difference is provable in public — in thirty seconds, at the viva.

**Why code is the best subject to learn with AI.** Code is executable and precise: an explanation can be checked by running it, a claim about behaviour can be tested with one input, and errors surface in exact messages rather than in taste. That makes it the ideal pairing — an assistant that can explain at *your* level, endlessly patient, available at 2am — plus a machine that instantly tells you whether the result holds. The uses, in ascending order of value: explaining unfamiliar code line by line; tracing execution with a concrete input ("walk through this with list = [3,1,2]"); translating between languages; debugging with the actual error message and the actual snippet; generating small exercises at your level; suggesting tests; and documenting what you wrote.

**Prompts that produce learning, not just answers.** State your level and the gap: "I know Python loops but not recursion — explain this function with one concrete call stack, then give me a similar exercise without the solution." Ask for misconceptions: "what do students most often get wrong about this?" Ask for the minimal runnable version stripped of your project's noise. Ask for a check: "what input would distinguish a correct from a near-correct implementation?" These prompts push the assistant into a teaching mode with testable outputs — and the follow-up habit matters: **retype the core of it yourself and run it**. Reading code you did not execute produces the illusion of understanding; typing and running converts it to the real thing.

**Debugging without outsourcing the diagnosis.** The efficient loop: paste the error verbatim, the smallest reproducing snippet, and what you expected. Then, before accepting the fix, ask *why* the bug happened — a fix you cannot explain is a fix you cannot reuse. Test the fix against the original failing case and one edge case (empty input, zero, duplicate, boundary value) — generated fixes routinely repair the reported symptom while breaking a neighbour. And keep the scope small: assistants debug a function far better than a whole application at once, because you can verify the first and only admire the second.

**The failure modes to expect.** (1) **Hallucinated APIs** — plausible methods that exist in some library, some version, or nowhere: verify any unfamiliar function against official docs before trusting it. (2) **Happy-path logic** — code that passes your example and fails on empty, null, negative or duplicate inputs; that is what tests are for, and it is why "it ran" is not "it works". (3) **Silent environment assumptions** — imports not installed, a newer language feature than your interpreter, a different default. The verification stack that defeats all three: run it, read every line you run, add one edge-case test, check unfamiliar APIs in the docs.

**The integrity boundary.** Learning with AI and submitting with AI are governed by one rule: **you must be able to defend every line you submit.** If your course prohibits AI-assisted code on graded work, the rule is the rule regardless of the tool's usefulness. Where AI help is permitted, understand and be ready to explain the whole submission — the viva is not a formality, it is the enforcement mechanism, and "the assistant wrote it" is an admission, not a defence. Keep evidence of your process (versions, commits, test runs) — it protects you as much as it incriminates shortcuts.

payload.title: Code-learning prompts that work
rows: "Explain this function for someone who knows loops but not recursion; use input X; then give one exercise."
"Walk through execution with this exact input; show variable values at each step as a table."
"Here is the error, the snippet and expected vs actual. What is the root cause — then the fix."
"Give three edge cases this code does not handle, with inputs that prove it."
"Generate a similar problem at this difficulty, without the solution; check my attempt after."

payload.code:
# The verification stack for any AI-provided code
code = ai_answer
run(code)                      # 1. does it execute at all?
read_every_line(code)          # 2. do you know what each line does?
test_edge_cases(code)          # 3. empty / zero / duplicate / max
check_unfamiliar_apis(code)    # 4. docs: does it exist in this version?
# "It ran" passes only step 1.

payload.title: Ask for the why before you accept the fix
payload.text: "Why was it broken and why does this fix it?" turns a patch into a pattern you keep. A fix you cannot explain will silently fail the next variant of the same bug.

payload.title: Generated code is optimised for plausibility, not for your edge cases
payload.text: Models reproduce common, canonical solutions — including APIs that do not exist and logic that ignores empty inputs. Run, read, and test the boundary before anything reaches a submission or a repository.

payload.title: Understand a recursive function you must present in class
payload.problem: You must explain a recursive binary-search implementation to your class next week. You understand loops but recursion still feels like magic. Use an assistant to build real understanding, and verify each step.

steps.title: Get a concrete trace, not an abstraction
steps.desc: Prompt: "Explain binary search recursion to someone who knows loops. Trace it with list [1,3,5,7,9] and target 7: show the call stack, arguments and return values at each level." A table of states beats any paragraph — and you can verify it by hand in one minute.

steps.title: Convert to the loop you trust, then compare
steps.desc: Ask for the iterative version side by side: "show both and list what maps to what (mid calculation, base case ↔ loop condition)." Anchoring the unfamiliar in the familiar exposes whether you actually understand or merely recognise.
steps.code_snippet:
recursive base case  <->  loop termination
argument shrinking    <->  lo/hi moving
return on found       <->  break with index

steps.title: Test your understanding adversarially
steps.desc: Ask: "give me three edge cases this implementation mishandles" (empty list, single element, duplicates) and predict the behaviour yourself before running. Then actually run it on those inputs — prediction-then-check is what converts watching into knowing.

steps.title: Build the presentation and the defence
steps.desc: Write your own three-slide explanation (no copy-paste), rehearse the walkthrough with target 7, and prepare two viva questions: "why O(log n)?" and "what happens with duplicates?" Every claim in your presentation has been run — you are now defending your own work, with AI as the tutor you hired.

payload.solution: A concrete traced example you verified by hand, a translation into the paradigm you already trust, adversarial edge-case prediction followed by execution, and finally your own original write-up — the assistant produced explanations and exercises, but every claim you will present was checked by you. Understanding you can defend, which is exactly what the viva measures.

payload.title: Explain, run, and be quizzed
payload.prompt: Take a small function you did not write (yours from a teammate, an open-source snippet, or your lab's starter code). Get a line-by-line explanation with a concrete trace, then run it on one input yourself and verify the trace matches. Finally ask for two quiz questions about it and answer before revealing.
payload.hint: If the trace you ran disagrees with the trace you were given, the explanation is suspect — trust the machine that executes.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting code without running it
mistakes.fix: Execution is the free verifier code gets. Run it, then probe one edge case — unrun code is unverified prose.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for an entire application in one shot
mistakes.fix: You cannot verify what you cannot hold in your head. Build and verify in small pieces; assistants are strongest at function-scale tasks with clear boundaries.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting a library function because the name looks right
mistakes.fix: Hallucinated APIs are the signature failure of code generation. Confirm unfamiliar functions and their version-specific behaviour in official documentation.

mistakes.mistake: Submitting AI-assisted code you cannot explain
mistakes.fix: Vivas and code reviews ask what you did and why. Work only within what you can defend — it is both the integrity rule and the learning rule.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why is code unusually verifiable compared with written prose, and how should that change how you use AI for it?
payload.answer: Code carries its own feedback loop: it compiles or does not, runs or throws, passes tests or fails — correctness can be established mechanically rather than by judgement, and failures report exact locations. Prose has no equivalent oracle; its errors surface only when a knowledgeable reader checks. This asymmetry should shape usage: for code, lean hard on generation (explanations, fixes, tests, refactors) because every claim can be closed by running it — always execute, read every line, and add an edge-case test; and for prose, lean less and check more, because fluency there has no runtime to catch it. The same tool deserves different trust in the two domains: verified collaborator for code, unverified drafter for text.
payload.source: Frequently used to teach evaluation asymmetry between code and natural-language AI outputs.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Code is the best AI-learning domain: every explanation can be executed and checked.
Prompt for level, trace, misconceptions and edge cases — then retype and run the core yourself.
Debug with root-cause questions and edge tests; "it ran" is only step one.
Expect hallucinated APIs, happy-path logic and environment assumptions — verify in docs and tests.
Integrity boundary: submit only code you can defend line by line.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest verification available for AI-generated code?
options: Running it and testing edge cases
Asking the same model if it is correct
Checking that it looks like documentation examples
questions.explanation: Execution plus boundary tests is an independent, mechanical check — prose has no equivalent oracle.

questions.prompt: AI-generated code works for your sample but crashes on empty input. This failure mode is called:
questions.explanation: Generated code targets the common case; empty/zero/duplicate inputs are where it breaks — hence edge-case tests.

questions.prompt: An unfamiliar method call compiles in the AI's answer. Before relying on it you should:
options: Trust it — the model knows the standard library
Confirm the method exists in your library version via official documentation
questions.explanation: Hallucinated APIs are a signature failure — plausible names, wrong versions, or libraries that never had the method.

options: Use it anyway and rewrite slightly
Use it for practice and submit only work you produced and can defend under the stated rule

questions.explanation: Institutional rules define the boundary; learning uses are legitimate, graded submissions follow the stated policy — and you must defend your work regardless.

lessons.title: Writing Drafts You Don't Ship Blind
lessons.summary: AI as a first-draft engine for emails, reports and documentation — and the human passes that make the difference between a draft and a liability.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Structure a drafting prompt with real facts, audience and constraints
Run fact, tone, specificity and responsibility passes over AI-generated drafts
Recognise and remove generic filler that betrays unedited generation
State why authorship keeps accountability with the human who sends

payload.text: A project-update email went out last semester with a deadline that had quietly slipped two weeks earlier — inherited from the AI draft, unchecked, because the draft read so smoothly that checking felt unnecessary. Smoothness is not accuracy. The fix took thirty seconds in a calendar; the credibility cost of a wrong date to your supervisor did not have a thirty-second fix. Drafting with AI is a genuine time-saver — once you accept that the clock you save comes out of the checking budget, never out of it.

**The draft workflow.** Treat AI as a first-draft engine and yourself as the editor of record: you supply the material, the model compresses it into structure and prose, you verify and own every claim before it leaves your outbox. The prompt side: give **audience** (who reads it, what they already know), **purpose** (what you want them to do or understand), **the real facts** (dates, numbers, names, decisions — pasted, not remembered by the model), **constraints** (length, tone, format, what must be included) and optionally **your voice sample** (a previous message of yours, for style). The rule underneath: **outputs are only as specific as your inputs** — a prompt with no facts gets a draft full of placeholders and plausible filler, which is precisely the draft people ship by accident.

**The four passes.** (1) **Fact pass** — highlight every number, date, name, link and commitment; verify each against your calendar, records or source. This is where AI drafts cause real damage: the model will generate a *plausible* date and a *typical* figure because unspecified slots get filled. (2) **Tone pass** — would you say it this way? Does it sound like you, your team, your culture? AI defaults to a bland mid-effort corporate register that reads oddly from a student or a small team. (3) **Specificity pass** — cut the generic: "in today's fast-paced environment", "I hope this email finds you well" repeated at scale, empty adjectives, conclusions that restate the ask. Generic filler is the visible fingerprint of unedited generation, and readers notice it faster than they notice typos. (4) **Responsibility pass** — read the final version as the person who will be asked about it: "if this is wrong, who is blamed, and have I checked the parts that could be wrong?" If you would not sign it, do not send it.

**What must never come from the model.** Facts you did not supply: statistics, quotations, citations, commitments ("we will deliver by Friday"), legal or HR statements, apologies on behalf of others, and any praise or criticism of a named person. Ask for those slots to be left marked — "write [DATE] where the deadline goes" is a good prompt precisely because it prevents invention. For professional contexts, keep a standing note in your prompt library (Module 10) with your organisation's conventions: sign-off style, formal/informal line, mandated disclosures.

**Voice, attribution and the accountability rule.** Using AI to sharpen your writing is ordinary professional practice — like a spellchecker with opinions — provided the substance is yours and your organisation's rules permit it. What is not ordinary: presenting generated content as fully your own where disclosure is required, or letting it make claims you have not verified. The principle to carry: **the sender owns the message.** No mail client has a "the model wrote it" button that redirects consequences; the recipient will hold you to every sentence. That single fact — accountability does not transfer — is the whole argument for the four passes.

payload.title: Draft type → what AI does → what you must check
rows: Facts, requests, and whether you agree

payload.code:
Drafting prompt skeleton:
"You are drafting [type] for [audience] so that they [purpose].
Facts you must use exactly (do not invent others):
  - deadline: [DATE]
  - attendance: 120 students, 4 venues
  - decision: schedule shifts to Wednesdays
Tone: direct, warm, no corporate filler.
Length: under 150 words. Mark anything missing as [..]."

# Then run the four passes: fact / tone / specificity / responsibility.

payload.title: Paste your real facts into the prompt
payload.text: The single biggest quality jump in drafting comes from supplying the actual data. Placeholders and invented specifics are what a fact-less prompt buys — and what a fact-pass catches only if you notice.

payload.title: Never let a model commit, quantify or characterise on your behalf
payload.text: Deadlines, statistics, quotations, legal wording, performance judgements about people — all must originate from you or a source you checked. A confident invented figure is the most expensive sentence in an email.

payload.title: Draft and defend a project update to a supervisor
payload.problem: Your team's demo slipped from Friday to Tuesday; two of five modules are done; a dependency (the API key) is pending. You need a 150-word update email. Draft it with AI, then run all four passes and produce the final version.

steps.title: Prompt with facts, not vibes
steps.desc: Supply: audience (supervisor who knows the project), purpose (inform of slip, state plan, request the key), facts (slip Friday → Tuesday, 2/5 modules done, blocker = API key), tone (direct, no apology theatre), format (≤150 words). Instruct: use only these facts, mark anything else [..].

steps.title: Fact pass
steps.desc: Verify against reality: is Tuesday correct in the shared plan? Is 2/5 right as of today? Is the API key still the actual blocker? Fix any drift — the model may have written "by early next week" because you did not pin it.

steps.title: Tone and specificity passes
steps.desc: Cut whatever you would not say aloud: "I hope this email finds you well", "unforeseen circumstances", "moving forward". Ensure the ask (key by Monday) is explicit rather than buried — specificity is what makes an update actionable.
steps.code_snippet:
cut:  "in light of unforeseen challenges..."
keep: "Demo moves Fri -> Tue. 2/5 modules done.
       Blocker: API key. Could you approve it by Mon?"

steps.title: Responsibility pass and send
steps.desc: Read as the recipient: does the update make a commitment you can keep (Tuesday demo with 3/5 modules?), does it blame anyone, is the ask unambiguous? Sign only after you can defend every line — which you now can, because every fact was supplied and checked by you.

payload.solution: Facts-first prompt → four passes → a 150-word email where every number and date has been reconciled with reality, the register sounds like a person, the filler is gone, and the commitment is one you intend to keep. The AI produced the structure in seconds; the passes are what make sending it safe.

payload.title: Edit your own AI draft and account for every change
payload.prompt: Take one real message you need to send this week. Draft it with AI using supplied facts, then edit it yourself. Record each change you made under one of the four pass names (fact / tone / specificity / responsibility) and note why. The change log is your evidence of real editing rather than rubber-stamping.
payload.hint: If your log is empty, either the prompt was unusually perfect or you did not really read it. It is almost always the second.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model fill in numbers, dates or names
mistakes.fix: Supply them in the prompt or mark slots explicitly ([DATE]). Then run the fact pass anyway — invented specifics arrive wearing confident prose.

mistakes.mistake: Sending after reading only for flow
mistakes.fix: Flow is the easiest quality to fake. Read once for facts, once for tone, once for what you are committing to — in that order, before anyone else sees it.

mistakes.mistake: Prompting with no facts and blaming the generic output
mistakes.fix: A fact-less prompt buys a template. Paste the actual material — audience, purpose, data — and genericness collapses immediately.

mistakes.mistake: Believing "the AI wrote it" redistributes blame
mistakes.fix: Accountability sits with the sender on every channel. Recipients, rules and consequences follow you, not the tool.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why "the AI wrote it" is not a defence for a factual error in a submitted report, and describe the four passes that would have caught it.
payload.answer: Authorship does not transfer accountability: you chose to submit the document, the reader relies on you, and institutional and professional rules attach consequences to the submitter — the tool is an instrument, like a calculator or a spellchecker, not a co-signatory. The four passes: (1) fact pass — verify every number, date, name and citation against sources; (2) tone pass — confirm the register is genuinely yours and appropriate; (3) specificity pass — remove generic filler and confirm the content makes concrete, checkable statements; (4) responsibility pass — read the final version as the person who will be questioned about it and confirm you can defend each line. Any report that passed the fact pass cannot contain an unchecked AI-invented figure.
payload.source: Standard accountability question in professional-ethics and AI-policy assessments.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: AI drafts from what you supply; audience, purpose and real facts are the prompt's fuel.
Four passes before sending: fact, tone, specificity, responsibility.
Never let generation commit, quantify, quote or judge — mark the slots instead.
Generic filler is the fingerprint of an unedited draft; readers spot it fast.
The sender owns the message: accountability never moves to the tool.

questions.prompt: The most reliable way to stop an AI draft inventing a deadline is to:
options: Supply the exact date in the prompt or mark a [DATE] slot it must not fill
questions.explanation: Unspecified slots get filled with plausible content; explicit facts or marked placeholders prevent invention at the source.

questions.prompt: Which pass catches "I hope this email finds you well" repeated across every message you send?
questions.explanation: The specificity pass removes generic filler — the visible fingerprint of unedited generation.

questions.prompt: Why does accountability stay with the person who sends AI-assisted writing?
options: AI has no legal personality — the sender chose to submit it, and readers and rules attach consequences to the submitter
questions.explanation: Tools do not carry responsibility; the human who selects and submits the text does — in every professional and academic setting.

questions.prompt: The responsibility pass asks you to:
options: Read the final version as the person who will be questioned about it, and confirm each line is defensible
Ask the model to rate its own draft
questions.explanation: It converts "would I sign this?" into a deliberate step — the last gate before anything leaves your outbox.

lessons.title: Exam Prep, Resumes and Cover Letters: High-Stakes Documents, Verified
lessons.summary: Where AI legitimately accelerates placement preparation — and the truth rule that keeps an improved resume from becoming a self-inflicted rejection.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Generate practice material from your own verified syllabus and notes
Improve resume bullets using only claims you can evidence
Tailor cover letters to a real job description without fabricating fit
Use AI for mock interviews and identify claims that fail under questioning

payload.text: A resume gained one polished line under AI editing: "Led a team of 10 to deliver projects 30% ahead of schedule." The interview had four questions queued behind that line — who were the ten, which projects, which schedule, which measurement. The candidate could answer none of them. The line did not beat the ATS; it built a trap and walked the candidate into it. The same tool that strengthens a true sentence will happily manufacture a false one with better grammar.

**Exam and placement prep — the honest uses.** (1) **Practice generation**: give the assistant your actual syllabus, notes or textbook chapter and ask for questions *at your level* — objective, short-answer, and application questions — then attempt them and ask for evaluation against your material. The rule that makes this safe: questions come from *your provided source*, and every answer is checked against it, because a model inventing a syllabus question teaches you the wrong syllabus. (2) **Weak-topic explanation**: ask for a second explanation when the lecture did not land, at a stated level, with a worked example you then solve yourself — the Module 8.2 learning loop applied to theory. (3) **Interactive drilling**: "quiz me one question at a time on thermodynamics, increasing difficulty, tell me why each answer is wrong" — an actual tutor pattern, and one of the best uses in this course. (4) **Gap mapping**: paste a syllabus and your notes, ask what is uncovered — then verify coverage yourself against the official syllabus. What AI prep must never become: a source of memorised answers presented as fact without checking, or a substitute for actually attempting problems with a pen.

**Resumes: improve the truth, never the facts.** The legitimate moves are mechanical and valuable: tighten wording ("responsible for" → "built", "worked on" → concrete verbs), restructure bullets to action → task → result, align *terminology* with the job description (if the JD says "stakeholder coordination" and you did exactly that, use their words — ATS keyword matching rewards honest lexical overlap), fix formatting and length, and surface what is missing (no quantification? no outcomes?). Every claim must pass the **evidence test**: can you state the source of this number, name the team, walk through the process, and discuss it for two minutes under questioning? If not, it does not belong — soft fabrication (rounding 3 to 10, "led" for "participated in") is the most common way candidates sabotage themselves, because interviews are precisely an evidence-taking process. Quantify only from real records; when a real number exists, AI helps you present it cleanly, which is the whole fair use.

**Cover letters: fit, not flattery.** Provide the actual job description and your actual background; ask for a draft that argues *fit* with specific examples from your record — then rewrite the opening yourself, because generic admiration of the company is detectable instantly. Verify every company fact you assert (products, recent work) against their site — models generalise companies into clichés.

**Mock interviews, done properly.** Ask the assistant to interview you for a specific role: questions first, no answers; then your answers; then blunt feedback — which answer lacked structure, which claim sounded inflated, what follow-up would expose thin knowledge. STAR-format stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result) built from your real experiences become rehearsable this way. Then the golden rule of this whole lesson, stated once: **anything you cannot defend in person must not be on the page.** Resume, cover letter, interview answers — AI optimises presentation; your evidence is the only thing that survives contact with an actual panel.

payload.title: High-stakes document → AI assist → mandatory check
rows: Answer key vs textbook; coverage vs official syllabus
Verb choice, structure, JD keyword alignment
Every claim evidenced; every number sourced
Company facts on their site; voice is yours
Stories are real; numbers match your resume
Cross-check with course material before memorising

payload.code:
The evidence test for any resume line:
claim  = "Led a team of 10 ... 30% ahead of schedule"
Q1 source of "10"?      -> 4 people incl. you  (rewrite: "of 4")
Q2 which projects?      -> two, name them      (specific)
Q3 which schedule?      -> the lab deadline    (context)
Q4 how measured?        -> no measurement      (CUT or state fact)
# Every surviving word must answer all four.

payload.title: Feed the assistant the real job description
payload.text: Fit comes from comparison, not composition: paste the JD and your background, and ask for the three strongest truthful matches plus the two weakest areas. Honest gap lists are more useful than flattering drafts.

payload.title: Interviewers audit exactly what polish invented
payload.text: A decorated metric turns one weak line into four failing answers — a worse outcome than an honest line. Panels do not check every bullet; they check the impressive ones.

payload.title: Turn a real internship record into defensible resume bullets
payload.problem: Internship record: "worked on the company dashboard, helped with data cleaning, made some charts, attended client calls." Job description asks for "data analysis, stakeholder communication, dashboard reporting". Produce three improved bullets that survive the evidence test.

steps.title: Extract the true inventory first
steps.desc: Before prompting, list facts from your own records: dashboard = a Tableau dashboard refreshed weekly; cleaning = a 12k-row sales CSV with duplicate removal; charts = three trend charts for a monthly review; client calls = attended four review calls and took notes. Now the raw material exists and cannot be invented.

steps.title: Map to JD vocabulary honestly
steps.desc: JD terms with truthful matches: "data analysis" ← cleaning + trends; "dashboard reporting" ← the Tableau dashboard; "stakeholder communication" ← review calls and the notes you circulated. Alignment here is lexical, not factual — you are using your real work in the employer's words.

steps.title: Draft bullets, then apply the evidence test
steps.desc: Ask for action-verb bullets using only the inventory. Then audit each: can you defend the row count, the cadence, your specific contribution? Cut or reword anything beyond the record — "led" becomes "built", "increased accuracy 40%" (invented) disappears entirely.
steps.code_snippet:
OK:  "Cleaned a 12k-row sales dataset (dedup + fixes) used
      in weekly dashboards"
CUT: "Improved data accuracy by 40%"  <- no measurement

steps.title: Tailor the cover letter with the same discipline
steps.desc: Draft from JD + inventory: one paragraph on the fit (dashboard + review calls), one specific example, one line on why the company — verified on their site. Rewrite the opener yourself. Two-minute rehearsal per bullet, then ship.

payload.solution: Inventory → honest JD mapping → bullets constrained to the inventory → evidence-test audit → tailored letter with verified company facts. Every surviving claim has a source (your records) and a defence (two-minute rehearsal). The polish went into presentation of true work, which is exactly the limit AI should operate under for anything a panel will read.

payload.title: Run the evidence test on your own resume
payload.prompt: Take your three most important resume bullets. For each, write the four evidence answers (source of each number, names, process, measurement). Then ask an assistant to "stress-test this bullet for a panel: give the five follow-up questions an interviewer would ask". Mark any bullet that cannot survive — and rewrite it to what you can actually defend.
payload.hint: The bullets you can defend are already good; the exercise is finding the ones you cannot before an interviewer does.

mistakes.mistake: Letting AI strengthen a claim beyond what you did
mistakes.fix: "Helped" becoming "led" is soft fabrication with better grammar. Constrain the prompt to your inventory and apply the evidence test to every line.

mistakes.mistake: Practising on questions the model invented about your syllabus
mistakes.fix: Generate from your actual materials and check answers against the textbook — invented exam questions teach wrong content with full confidence.

mistakes.mistake: Sending a cover letter with stock praise and no specifics
mistakes.fix: Generic flattery signals a template. One verified company fact plus one real example of your fit outweighs three adjectives.

mistakes.mistake: Memorising model interview answers verbatim
mistakes.fix: Panels detect recitation and follow-up questions expose it. Rehearse stories from your real experience in STAR form; keep the structure, never the script.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A candidate lets AI add an impressive but unverifiable metric to their resume. Trace the likely consequences across screening and interview, and state the rule that prevents this.
payload.answer: Screening: the metric may indeed attract attention and advance the candidate — the temptation is that it sometimes "works" at this stage. Interview: panels probe impressive claims first; the candidate cannot name the measurement, baseline or period, producing four consecutive failures that discredit the rest of the (true) resume as well — the classic asymmetric loss, where one inflated line poisons trustworthy ones. Post-hire it becomes a conduct issue on record. Prevention rule: anything you cannot defend in person must not be on the page — every number traceable to a source, every "led" backed by what you actually led. AI may reword true claims; it must never originate them.
payload.source: Standard resume-integrity question in placement-preparation and HR interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Best exam-prep uses: generate from your own materials, drill interactively, map gaps — then verify.
Resume work = presentation of true claims: wording, structure, honest JD vocabulary.
Evidence test: source, names, process, measurement — every line must answer all four.
Cover letters argue fit with specifics; company facts come from the company.
The rule: nothing on the page that you cannot defend in the room.

questions.prompt: Where should practice exam questions come from?
options: The model's general knowledge of what exams ask
Your actual syllabus, notes and textbook — with answers checked against them
Last year's paper from an unrelated university
Whatever the model finds most interesting
questions.explanation: Generation from your provided materials keeps practice aligned with the real exam; unchecked questions teach wrong content confidently.

questions.prompt: Your job description says "stakeholder coordination" and you did attend client review calls. The right move is:
options: Use the employer's honest vocabulary for the work you actually did
Avoid the phrase so nothing can be questioned
questions.explanation: Lexical alignment with the JD for truthful work is legitimate (and helps keyword matching); fabricating scope is not.

questions.prompt: What is the evidence test for a resume bullet?
options: Whether an AI rates it highly
Whether you can state the source of every number, name the people, explain the process and discuss it at length
Whether it contains an action verb
questions.explanation: An interview is an evidence audit; every claim on the page must have a defence attached before it ships.

questions.prompt: The best use of an assistant in interview preparation is to:
options: Generate perfect answers to memorise verbatim
Act as a questioner: ask role-specific questions, then give blunt feedback on your real answers
Write your entire STAR stories for you
Predict the exact questions that will be asked
questions.explanation: Questioning plus feedback rehearses performance; memorised scripts collapse the moment a follow-up question arrives.

modules.title: Module 9 — Limits, Risks and Safety
modules.summary: The failure modes that matter in daily life: why models hallucinate and how to catch them, where bias comes from, what happens to whatever you paste, where academic integrity sits, and how to think about deepfakes, misinformation and the jobs question without panic or hype.

lessons.title: Hallucination: Why Models Invent Facts and How You Catch Them
lessons.summary: The structural cause of confident falsehoods, the claim types that hallucinate most, and a checking routine sized to everyday use rather than paranoia.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain hallucination as a consequence of plausible-next-token generation
Rank claim types by hallucination risk and verification cost
Apply targeted checks: citation tracing, cross-examination and independent sources
State what temperature can and cannot do about factual errors

payload.text: A lawyer filed a brief containing court cases that did not exist — invented wholecloth by an assistant, complete with citations formatted well enough to pass a first read. The error was not exotic; it was the ordinary behaviour of a system that produces whatever looks most like a citation, asked by someone who trusted fluency as a proxy for truth. Every hallucination story you have heard is a variant of that one: a plausible-shaped token sequence, delivered with the confidence of a machine that has no concept of not knowing.

**The mechanism, plainly.** A language model generates the next token that is *most plausible given everything so far* (Module 4). Plausible is not true: the training process never distinguishes "this sentence is factual" from "this sentence follows the pattern of factual sentences". Nothing in the architecture marks a claim as verified, retrieves a record to confirm it, or raises an error when the underlying knowledge is absent. When the prompt presses for a specific shape — five citations, a statistic, a date, a quote — and the weights do not contain a clean answer, the model fills the slot with the most citation-shaped, statistic-shaped, date-shaped content it can produce. Instructed helpfulness amplifies this: models are trained (Module 5) to answer rather than stall, so the failure mode is silent substitution of plausible content for absent knowledge, not an apology.

**Where hallucination concentrates.** Risk is not uniform — it tracks *specificity* and *obscurity*: (1) **citations and references** — maximum risk; a bibliographic record is a precise, verifiable object and models routinely synthesise plausible author-year-journal combinations; (2) **numbers and statistics** — precise values are rarely absorbed intact; (3) **names, dates and quantities of specific things** (versions, page numbers, event details); (4) **anything after the knowledge cutoff** (Module 4) — retrieval-less answers about recent events are recall-or-invent; (5) **long-tail entities** — obscure papers, small companies, regional facts: the less training signal, the more completion pressure matters. Low-risk by contrast: transformations of what you pasted, well-known concepts explained in your own words, code you can run, and math you can recompute. Notice the pattern: **risk falls as checkability rises** — that asymmetry is the whole strategy.

**The checks, sized to the claim.** (1) **Flag-checkable nouns**: every name, number, date and citation in an output gets flagged mentally as "verify before use". (2) **Trace citations** exactly as in Module 8: search title + author, open it, read the line. (3) **Cross-examine the model**: "what are you least sure about?" and "which parts of this answer would you not rely on?" — imperfect (the model's self-report is itself generated), but it reliably surfaces hedging that prompts the right second look. (4) **Independent confirmation**: any load-bearing fact gets a second source that does not come from the same conversation. (5) **Known-answer probes**: when evaluating a tool for ongoing use, ask questions you already know the answer to — if it is confidently wrong about things you know, calibrate downward for things you don't. And for high-stakes domains (medical, legal, financial, safety), the rule is simple: AI input is *search and drafting*, never the decision.

**Two beliefs to kill.** First, "temperature 0 fixes hallucination": temperature only narrows sampling toward the most likely tokens — it makes output *consistent*, and a consistent falsehood is still false; factual grounding comes from context, retrieval and verification, not from dial settings. Second, "the model says it doesn't know, so it doesn't": self-reported uncertainty is generated text too — useful as a signal, never as a certificate. Hallucination cannot be prompted away entirely; it can be *budgeted*: keep claims checkable, keep checks proportionate to consequences, and let the Module 8 verification routine do its work every time output matters.

payload.title: Hallucination risk by claim type
rows: Search title + author; open and read

payload.title: Why confident tone proves nothing
payload.text: Calibration — matching confidence to evidence — is not trained directly; helpfulness and fluency are. A sentence's certainty level is a style property, statistically uncorrelated with its truth in exactly the cases that hurt you.

payload.title: Ask "what would you not rely on here?"
payload.text: A cheap second pass: models often flag their weakest points when asked directly. Treat the answers as a to-do list for verification, not as absolution.

payload.title: Hallucinations scale with instruction pressure
payload.text: "Give exactly five sources" when three exist guarantees two inventions. Ask for what the material supports and explicitly permit "only two found" — you get an honest count instead of a padded one.

payload.title: Audit a research answer containing six claims
payload.problem: Prompt: "Give me six key facts about the history of the UPI payment system with sources." Output: six confident bullets — two dates, two statistics, one person attribution, one "first of its kind" claim, each with a citation-looking source. Triage and verify before any of it touches your notes.

steps.title: Classify all six by risk
steps.desc: Dates ×2 = high (specific); statistics ×2 = high (precise numbers); person = high (entity); "first of its kind" = medium (comparative claim); citations across all six = highest risk as a class. Note that the claim types most likely to be checked by a reader are exactly the ones most likely to be wrong.

steps.title: Trace the citations first
steps.desc: Search each title and author. This is the fastest filter: fabricated sources collapse immediately, mismatches collapse when you read the passage, survivors get promoted to "candidate-verified". Expect at least one non-existent entry in a six-citation batch from an unretrieved chat.
steps.code_snippet:
6 citations -> search each
found + supports claim : candidate
found, other content   : mismatch -> cut
no result              : fabricated -> cut

steps.title: Verify numbers and dates independently
steps.desc: Each statistic gets its original source (or gets cut); each date gets an official timeline page. Check internal consistency too — statistics that contradict the dates ("launched 2016, adopted by 2010") expose synthesis errors without any search at all.

steps.title: Handle the comparative claim and write the ledger
steps.desc: "First of its kind" needs a defined comparison class — ask the model what it means, then check with an independent source; these sweeping framings are often wrong in a way that changes meaning. Ledger each claim verified/unverified/cut before anything enters your notes; keep the citations that survived as your working bibliography.

payload.solution: Risk classification routes each claim to the right check: citations traced first (fastest kill), numbers and dates to independent sources, comparative claims interrogated and confirmed — with a status ledger as the deliverable. The output that survives is smaller than six bullets and is now usable; the process takes minutes, which is the correct price of the routine.

payload.title: Measure your own hallucination exposure
payload.prompt: Ask for five specific, checkable facts on a niche topic (a regional policy, an obscure historical event, a minor library version). Verify all five with independent sources. Record the honest tally and the failure type of each miss — fabricated, stale, conflated, or wrong number. Then re-ask permitting uncertainty ("say when you do not know") and compare.
payload.hint: Compare the two runs: you are measuring how much of the first run's confidence was style rather than knowledge.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent, detailed answers are accurate
mistakes.fix: Fluency is a style property trained directly; truth is not. Details are as easy to invent as generalities — arguably easier.

mistakes.mistake: Believing temperature 0 prevents fabrication
mistakes.fix: It narrows sampling to the most likely tokens — consistent output, possibly consistently wrong. Grounding requires context, retrieval or checks.

mistakes.mistake: Reading "I'm not certain, but…" as a safety signal
mistakes.fix: Hedging is generated like everything else and is not calibrated to actual reliability. It is a prompt to verify, not a certificate of doubt.

mistakes.mistake: Pressuring exact counts the material cannot support
mistakes.fix: "Give ten sources" when four exist manufactures six. Ask for what is supported and explicitly allow a shortfall.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why hallucination is a structural consequence of next-token prediction rather than a simple bug, and give two mitigations that reduce it without eliminating it.
payload.answer: The objective trains plausibility, not truth: nothing in pretraining, SFT or alignment marks a token sequence as fact-checked, and there is no lookup step that fails loudly when knowledge is absent — so when a prompt demands a citation-shaped or number-shaped slot the weights cannot fill, the model completes with the most plausible content of that shape. It is structural because the same mechanism that produces all useful text produces the fabrications; removing it would remove generation. Mitigations: (1) grounding — supply documents or retrieval so answers condition on provided evidence rather than parametric recall; (2) verification workflows — claim classification, citation tracing and independent sources (Module 8), plus instruction that permits "I don't know" and asks for supported counts only. Both reduce harm; neither guarantees truth, which is why consequential decisions keep a human in the loop.
payload.source: Core safety-and-reliability question in LLM literacy and applied AI interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Hallucination = plausible-shaped tokens standing in for absent knowledge; nothing marks truth during generation.
Risk tracks specificity and obscurity: citations, numbers, dates, recent and niche facts are hot zones.
Checks scale with stakes: flag checkable nouns, trace citations, cross-examine, confirm independently.
Temperature controls consistency, not truth; self-reported uncertainty is also generated text.
Grounding and verification reduce hallucination — only humans and sources close the gap.

questions.prompt: Hallucination happens primarily because the model is trained to:
options: Generate the most plausible continuation, not a verified one
questions.explanation: The objective rewards plausibility; no fact-checking step exists in generation, so absent knowledge gets plausible-shaped substitutes.

questions.prompt: Which claim type carries the HIGHEST hallucination risk?
options: Explaining a paragraph you just pasted
A specific bibliographic citation with author, year and journal
Code you are about to run
questions.explanation: Precise, checkable records are easy to synthesise plausibly and hard to ground — the classic high-risk object.

questions.prompt: Setting temperature to 0 will:
options: Make output consistent and more deterministic — consistency with the truth is a separate question
Force the model to cite sources
questions.explanation: Temperature narrows the sampling distribution; a stable answer can still be wrong, and grounding is what fixes facts.

questions.prompt: A prompt demands exactly eight sources for a thin topic. The expected failure is:
options: Invented citations to satisfy the count
questions.explanation: Instruction pressure on a count the material cannot support guarantees padding — permit shortfall instead.

lessons.title: Bias, Stereotypes and Where They Come From
lessons.summary: How the data, the objective and the alignment pipeline each inject bias into model output — what it looks like in practice — and how to work with (and around) it responsibly.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Trace three sources of bias through the training pipeline
Identify stereotypical defaults in generated text and images
Apply prompt-level and process-level mitigations without over-trusting them
Recognise when a biased output must go to humans, not back into the loop

payload.text: Ask a model to picture "a CEO" and then "a nurse", in two different cultural settings — and count how often the generated defaults track the old stereotype regardless of the culture you named. Now ask the same model to "help screen these résumés". The gap between a charming party trick and a hiring shortlist is exactly one step, and that step is where stereotype stops being amusing.

**Bias is inherited, not conjured.** Nothing in a model invents prejudice from nothing; it learns distributions from data, and the world's text carries history. Three entry points matter. (1) **Training data**: the open web over-represents some groups as authors and subjects, encodes occupational and cultural stereotypes in billions of examples, under-represents some languages and dialects, and contains slanted reporting and outdated norms — the model averages what it read (Module 5, Lesson 1). (2) **The objective and the data pipeline**: next-token prediction optimises *typical* continuation, so the statistically common association (doctor → he, nurse → she) is, precisely, what the model learned to produce; filtering and quality scoring also embed choices about what counts as good data. (3) **Post-training and raters**: alignment learns from human preferences (Module 5, Lesson 3) — raters have their own cultural positions and guidelines, so the model's "helpful" defaults encode a particular taste, including its blind spots.

**What it looks like in output.** *Default personas*: generated names, genders, roles and family structures that reflect narrow defaults unless counter-instructed. *Uneven quality*: better grammar, nuance and idiomatic range in high-resource languages; worse comprehension and refusal behaviour in low-resource ones — an equity problem, not just a style one. *Judgement skew*: sentiment, tone and "professionalism" assessments that penalise dialect, culture or non-dominant communication styles. *Refusal asymmetry: stricter handling of some topics and identities than others. *Homogenised culture*: local nuance flattened toward the dominant cultural centre. None of this requires malice — it is what averaging unbalanced data produces, and it resurfaces in generated images (Lesson 2), search-adjacent products, moderation systems, and any downstream system that inherits model judgements.

**Mitigations — two levels, with honest limits.** *Prompt level*, for your own outputs: specify counter-examples ("give three candidate profiles with varied backgrounds"), replace vague person-requests with explicit rubrics ("evaluate against these four stated criteria"), rephrase and compare (if two phrasings of the same request yield different judgements about a person, you have found the model's hidden weighting), and generate multiple variants instead of accepting the first default. *Process level*, for anything that affects people: never let a model be the judge of a person without a written rubric supplied by a responsible human; require diverse test cases before adopting a tool for screening, moderation or grading; keep the decision, and the accountability, with a person — the placement of the human from Module 10. Honest limits: prompt fixes shape *your* outputs, not the weights; bias can be reduced but not deleted, because "neutral" itself encodes a norm and trade-offs between competing fairness definitions are genuine engineering dilemmas. The durable skills are noticing, testing, and refusing to launder biased output into decisions.

payload.title: Source → mechanism → symptom
rows: Web text carries history and skew
Whatever the model reaches for first

payload.title: Make criteria explicit to shrink default-driven skew
payload.text: "Assess this application against these four stated criteria, quoting evidence for each" replaces a vague judgement with a rubric — the highest-leverage prompt-level bias control there is.

payload.title: Biased output about people must not re-enter the pipeline
payload.text: A shortlist, moderation flag or grade generated from stereotyped output becomes institutional bias with a machine's confidence attached. People-affecting judgements need rubrics, diverse testing and human decision-makers.

payload.title: "Neutral" is also a position
payload.text: Removing one stereotype does not produce objectivity — model defaults encode whichever norms dominated the data. This is why diverse evaluation and explicit criteria beat assertions that a tool is unbiased.

payload.title: Diagnose and rework a biased screening prompt
payload.problem: A club uses an assistant to shortlist 40 applications for a technical role: prompt = "pick the five strongest candidates and explain why." Output: a shortlist clustered around one communication style and one profile type, with vague praise ("looks confident"). Diagnose the sources at work and rebuild the process.

steps.title: Name what happened
steps.desc: An unanchored "strongest" request (your prompt, ambiguous) let the model substitute its learned association for a criterion (objective + data); vague evaluative language in the feedback ("confident", "professional") shows style-based judgement rather than evidence.

steps.title: Supply a rubric and require evidence
steps.desc: Rewrite: "Score each application 1–4 on: relevant skills, concrete project evidence, clarity of stated goals. Quote the supporting text for every score. Do not infer traits from writing style." Criteria in, defaults out — and quoted evidence makes each score auditable.
steps.code_snippet:
before: "pick the 5 strongest, explain why"
after:  score 4 criteria x 40 apps,
        quote evidence, no trait inference,
        flag missing info as "not stated"

steps.title: Test for residual skew
steps.desc: Run counterfactual checks: does the ranking change if irrelevant surface features change? Are scores explained by quotes or by adjectives? Inspect for under-represented names/styles appearing with systematically lower clarity scores — the concrete symptom to look for.

steps.title: Put the human back where the stakes are
steps.desc: Final selection stays with people reading the rubric outputs, checking the evidence quotes, and owning the decision. Record the rubric and the checks — that documentation is what turns "we used AI" into "we used a documented, auditable screen".

payload.solution: The failure was ambiguity meeting learned defaults; the fix is an explicit rubric with quoted evidence, counterfactual testing for residual skew, and human decision-making over the machine's scored summary. Note what the fix did NOT do: change the model. It changed the task you gave it — which is all any prompt-level mitigation can do.

payload.title: Find a default, then break it
payload.prompt: Ask an assistant to "describe a typical day" for three occupations in two cultural settings. List the assumptions it made unprompted (gender, family, status, setting). Then re-ask with explicit counter-instructions and compare. Write down which changes stuck and which defaults survived.
payload.hint: Defaults that survive explicit counter-instructions show you what is deepest in the distribution — that residue is what process-level controls exist for.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a model is objective because it is mathematical
mistakes.fix: The arithmetic optimises typical continuation of skewed data. Mathematical machinery does not confer neutrality — it executes the bias efficiently.

mistakes.mistake: Believing one clever prompt removes bias
mistakes.fix: Prompting shapes outputs you generate; it does not change weights or other users' outputs. For people-affecting work, rubrics, tests and humans are the control.

mistakes.mistake: Treating "the model said" as evidence about a person
mistakes.fix: A model judgement is an opinion generated from distributions — cite criteria and observed facts instead, or leave people out of model-mediated assessment entirely.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring bias in your own wording
mistakes.fix: Ambiguous or loaded requests pull defaults forward. Request criteria explicitly; if your prompt smuggles assumptions, no mitigation downstream will undo them.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Name three stages of the LLM pipeline where bias enters, and give one mitigation at each stage.
payload.answer: (1) Pretraining data: web text encodes historical and cultural skew and unequal representation — mitigate with curation, filtering, rebalancing and multilingual inclusion by the provider; at your level, by counter-examples and diverse test cases in your own use. (2) The training objective: next-token prediction rewards statistically typical continuations, hardwiring "common" as "expected" — mitigate by instruction and rubrics that redefine what should be typical for your task. (3) Post-training/rater preferences: alignment encodes rater demographics and guidelines — mitigate with diverse rater pools and held-out fairness evaluations (provider side), and by never letting aligned taste stand as a judge of people in your workflows (user side). Cross-cutting mitigation: keep human decision-makers with explicit criteria wherever output affects people.
payload.source: Standard responsible-AI question on bias sources across the ML lifecycle.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Bias enters via data (history), objective (typicality) and alignment (rater taste).
Symptoms: default personas, uneven language quality, judgement skew, refusal asymmetry, cultural flattening.
Prompt-level: counter-examples, explicit rubrics, rephrase-and-compare, multiple variants.
Process level: rubrics, diverse tests, human decisions for anything affecting people.
Mitigation reduces skew; it never certifies neutrality — keep evidence, not adjectives.

questions.prompt: Model bias toward stereotypes primarily originates in:
options: The random seed used at initialisation
Training data that encodes historical patterns, amplified by an objective that rewards typical continuations
questions.explanation: Data carries the skew; the next-token objective makes the statistically common association the expected output.

questions.prompt: Which prompt change most reduces default-driven judgement about applicants?
options: Providing explicit criteria with required quoted evidence for each score
questions.explanation: Ambiguity is what defaults fill; a rubric with evidence requirements replaces them with auditable criteria.

questions.prompt: A model produces lower "professionalism" scores for a regional dialect in screening output. The correct response is:
options: Accept it — dialect correlates with quality
Treat it as a signal to inspect the criteria, test for skew, and keep humans on the decision
questions.explanation: Style-based judgement of people is exactly the failure class to catch with testing and human review, not to launder into a decision.

questions.prompt: Which statement about prompt-level bias mitigation is accurate?
options: It shapes the outputs you generate but cannot change the model itself or other users' outputs
It only works on paid tiers
questions.explanation: Prompting is conditioning, not training — the durable controls for people-affecting uses are process-level.

lessons.title: Privacy and Academic Integrity: What You Share and What Counts as Work
lessons.summary: Where pasted text actually goes, the categories you should think twice about, the settings worth finding — and the rules that keep AI help from becoming a misconduct finding.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe the data path of a pasted message in a cloud AI product
Categorise material by sensitivity and choose a safer alternative workflow
Locate and set training, retention and memory controls
Apply institutional AI rules to decide permitted and prohibited uses of AI in coursework

payload.text: A student pasted her full medical certificate, her entire group project (including a teammate's code) and three lines of her password reset email into a chatbot "just to check the wording". Nothing bad was published — and that is exactly the trap: the absence of a visible incident is not the absence of exposure. The question is never "did anything happen" but "what does the product's terms allow to happen", and almost nobody reads those terms at the moment they paste.

**The data path.** When you send a message to a cloud assistant, it travels over HTTPS to the provider's servers, joins your conversation history (retention policies vary — hours, weeks, or until you delete, depending on product and settings), and is processed by the provider and its sub-processors (hosting, monitoring, safety tooling). Depending on product, tier and settings, conversations may be **retained for abuse detection and quality**, **used to improve models** (often a toggle you can find — Lesson 3), and **occasionally reviewed by humans** in sampling processes the provider describes in its terms (typically for safety and quality, typically redacted — but "typically" is doing real work in that sentence: read your provider's actual wording). Two further facts worth internalising: retention and training defaults differ by product and tier and *change over time*, so the durable habit is locating the settings rather than memorising them; and anything routed through plugins, shared links or team workspaces widens the audience beyond "the model".

**Sort your material into three bins.** *Green*: public information, your own drafts you would post anyway, published course material — paste freely. *Amber*: personal but non-identifying (anonymised records, generalised questions, excerpts with names stripped), internal-but-ordinary material — paste with redaction and with training controls off. *Red*: passwords, API keys and tokens (never — not even a "test" key); government identifiers, financial and health records; unpublished research; client, employer or third-party confidential documents (you likely lack the right to share someone else's data at all); others' personal messages and images. The red bin gets alternatives: a local model (Module 7), an enterprise tier with contractual data terms, or no AI at all. The practical middle path for most daily work: **paste the smallest sufficient excerpt, redact identifiers, keep training off, and never paste secrets.** Data-protection law (in India, the DPDP Act and its rules; equivalents elsewhere) increasingly defines these obligations for organisations — but your personal hygiene is what protects your own material today.

**Academic integrity in the AI era.** Institutions are still converging, so *your institution's written policy is the authority* — read it before you use AI on graded work, and re-read it when it updates. Beneath the policy sits the stable principle: **submit work you can authorise and defend.** From it follow the norms most policies encode: undisclosed ghostwriting of graded submissions is the core violation (the work must be substantially yours, with AI help disclosed where required or permitted); using AI to *understand* material, brainstorm, get feedback, explain code (Module 8) and draft-and-you-rewrite is generally the permitted zone — but permitted zones are defined by your syllabus, not by this course; disguising someone else's work (including pasting and lightly rewriting) compounds the original problem. Two honest notes about enforcement: AI detectors are unreliable — error-prone in both directions — so neither panicking at a low "AI score" nor trusting a high one is rational; and process evidence (versions, drafts, notes, chat history) is the practical way to demonstrate your authorship when asked. When in doubt, ask your instructor — a two-minute question beats a misconduct case.

payload.title: The three bins
rows: Public info, your own publishable drafts
Anonymised data, generalised questions, work excerpts
Redact + training off + smallest sufficient excerpt
Passwords/keys, IDs, health/finance, unpublished work, others' data
Local model, contractual enterprise tier, or no AI

payload.title: Third-party data is a rights problem, not just a privacy one
payload.text: Pasting a teammate's code, a patient record or a client document shares data you may have no right to share. Confidentiality duties travel with the material — permission from you is not permission from everyone it concerns.

payload.title: Find the data settings once per tool
payload.text: Settings → Data/Privacy: turn off training on your chats where offered, decide about memory/history, and read the retention sentence in the terms. Ten minutes total across your tools, renewed whenever settings change.

payload.title: Never paste credentials — even as a test
payload.text: Keys pasted into a chat are logged somewhere, may be retained, and may surface in later contexts. Rotate any key you have ever pasted; treat paste boxes like public boards.

payload.title: Triage a messy paste-queue and an AI-assisted report
payload.problem: Two situations. (A) A student is about to paste into a free chatbot: her full medical leave certificate (with ID number), the group's entire shared folder of notes including a teammate's code, and a client-style brief from her internship. (B) An AI-assisted lab report: she used an assistant to explain the theory and structure the write-up, and her own words for everything submitted. Triage both.

steps.title: Bin (A) item by item
steps.desc: Medical certificate = Red (health + identifier) → summarise to a redacted text you actually need ("what are the dates and tone for a leave note?") with identifiers stripped, or handle offline. Group notes with teammate code = Red/Amber boundary → paste only your own subsection, redacted; you lack rights to your teammate's material. Internship brief = Red → employer confidentiality; ask a general question without the document, or use nothing at all.

steps.title: Choose the alternative workflow
steps.desc: What does she actually need? For the leave note: a template from public material + her facts. For the notes: her own excerpt only, training off. For the internship: a generic structure question with no client content. Pattern: extract the *need* from the *material* and share only the need.
steps.code_snippet:
need:  "tone + structure of a leave application"
paste: dates + redacted facts (no ID, no diagnosis)
never: the certificate itself

steps.title: Check (B) against policy and principle
steps.desc: Read the institution's written rule: does it require disclosure? Is AI-assisted explanation/structuring within the permitted zone? Regardless: every submitted word must be hers, every claim verified against the source material, and she must be able to explain the whole report — the Module 8.2 defence standard.

steps.title: Record the process
steps.desc: Keep drafts, the chat history of her questions (not the output paste), and her own edits — process evidence that demonstrates authorship if ever questioned, and the honest mirror of what she actually did.

payload.solution: (A) All three pastes were wrong: bin them Red, then share only the underlying need in redacted, minimal form — the general question survives, the sensitive document never travels. (B) Is defensible if the institution permits the help, the substance is hers and verified, and she can explain every part — with process evidence kept. Privacy and integrity reduce to the same reflex: share and submit only what you can stand behind.

payload.title: Audit your last ten conversations
payload.prompt: Open your recent AI conversation history. For each: did it contain anything in the Amber or Red bin — names, numbers, identifiers, others' data, credentials? Note which settings (training, memory, retention) were on at the time. Write one process change you will apply from now on, and rotate anything that should never have been pasted.
payload.hint: Look for the boring violations — "harmless" internal documents and casually pasted personal details are where real exposure accumulates.

mistakes.mistake: Pasting whole confidential documents to get a small output
mistakes.fix: Extract the need, redact identifiers, paste the smallest sufficient excerpt — or use a local/contractual channel when the material must not travel at all.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming free-tier chats are private because nothing bad happened
mistakes.fix: Absence of incident ≠ absence of exposure. The terms, retention and review practices define the risk; locate and set them per tool.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting AI-detector scores as verdicts
mistakes.fix: Detectors error in both directions and are not a fair adjudication mechanism. Authorship is demonstrated by process — drafts, versions, notes — not by a percentage.

mistakes.mistake: Using AI to disguise rather than to help
mistakes.fix: Pasting another person's work and rewriting it compounds the original violation with deception. Work within the permitted zone: understanding, feedback, drafting you then make your own.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A student pastes their entire unpublished thesis draft into a free chatbot. Identify three risks and describe one better workflow for the same need.
payload.answer: Risks: (1) confidentiality and future-publication integrity — the draft may be retained under the product's logging terms and potentially used for training by default settings, compromising novelty claims and any journal expectations of unpublished work; (2) third-party rights — co-authored passages, supervisor comments and quoted-unpublished material belong partly to others, whom the student cannot consent for; (3) loss of control — shared links, sub-processors and staff-review processes (as described in terms) put the text outside the student's custody, with no reliable way to confirm downstream handling. Better workflow: turn off training/history for the session, paste only the specific section being edited (smallest sufficient excerpt) with citations and names redacted, or use a local model for full-draft passes, and keep a versioned copy so any change remains traceable to her own edits.
payload.source: Privacy-and-research-integrity scenario common in AI-policy assessments.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Pasted text travels: transport → history/retention → possible training and review — settings define the rest.
Three bins: green paste, amber redact and minimise, red never (keys, IDs, health, others' data).
Find training/memory/retention controls per tool; defaults change, so habits beat memorised settings.
Institutional policy is the authority on graded work; the principle is work you can authorise and defend.
Detectors are unreliable both ways — process evidence is the fair proof of authorship.

questions.prompt: Before pasting an internal document into a free AI chatbot, the best first question is:
options: May this data leave my organisation or my control under its terms and settings?
Is the model the newest one?
questions.explanation: Data path and terms decide before capability — this is the Module 7 constraint-first rule applied to privacy.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs firmly in the "never paste" bin?
options: A redacted draft of your own essay
