questions.explanation: Credentials pasted anywhere should be considered exposed and rotated; no redaction level makes a key safe to share.

questions.prompt: The most reliable way to demonstrate authorship of AI-assisted coursework when questioned is:
options: An AI-detector score in your favour
Process evidence: drafts, versions, notes and your ability to explain every part of the submission
A written note from the assistant
questions.explanation: Detectors are error-prone; versions plus defence of the work are what institutions can actually evaluate.

questions.prompt: Under most institutional policies, which use of AI on a graded assignment is most likely to be permitted?
options: Submitting an assistant's full answer with a light rewrite
Using it to understand the material and get feedback, then producing and defending your own submission per the stated policy
Using it covertly after a ban, undetected
questions.explanation: Understanding, feedback and drafting-you-own are the normal permitted zone — but your institution's written rule is the authority.

lessons.title: Deepfakes, Misinformation and the Jobs Question
lessons.summary: Synthetic media as an everyday hazard, a verification routine that does not depend on detectors, and an honest, non-hyped frame for what AI does to work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Recognise common synthetic-media patterns and their practical red flags
Apply a source-and-corroboration routine instead of relying on detectors
Distinguish task automation from job elimination in the employment discussion
Describe skills that gain value as generation becomes cheap

payload.text: During a tense week, a voice note circulates on a student group: the dean, apparently, changing a rule in a specific, infuriating way. The voice is his. The words were never spoken. It took one call to the actual office to deflate it — but the note had already been forwarded forty times, and the correction travelled a fraction as far. The economics of that sentence — fabrication cheap, verification costly, correction slow — is the whole misinformation problem in miniature.

**Synthetic media, without the mystery.** Voice cloning needs seconds of captured audio; face-swap and lip-sync video are commodity tools; generated images and fake "news-style" pages are a prompt away (Module 7, Lesson 2). What has changed is not that fakery is new — photo editing and actor re-recordings are old — but that the cost of convincing fabrication collapsed toward zero while distribution keeps rewarding provocation. Detection tools exist and are not worthless, but they cannot be your first line: accuracy varies with format and quality, real-but-selectively-edited media confuses classifiers, generated quality keeps improving, and you rarely have the original to compare against. Watermarks and signed content-credentials metadata help where producers and platforms adopt them — adoption is partial and metadata strips on re-upload. **Therefore: verify the source, not the artefact.**

**A routine that works without forensics.** (1) **Trace origin** — who first published it, on what account, with what history? Screenshots and forwarded clips are already orphans; find the original. (2) **Lateral reading** — open new tabs: is any independent, reputable outlet reporting the same event? One source alone is a lead, not a fact. (3) **Check date and context** — real footage from another event, mislabelled, is the oldest trick; confirm when and where. (4) **Mind the affect** — content engineered to provoke instantly (outrage, fear, glee) deserves *more* skepticism, not less; virality is a distribution property, not an evidence property. (5) **Proportion the response** — decide what you would do on the strength of this alone; if the answer is "change a belief, a vote, a bank transfer, a public accusation", verification is mandatory and forwarding is not neutral: sharing amplifies. (6) **After major events, slow down** — the first hours are when fabrication peaks. This routine scales down to a ten-second check for trivial content and up to full research for anything consequential.

**The jobs question, handled honestly.** Two failure modes to avoid: techno-panic ("all white-collar jobs are ending") and dismissal ("it never really changes anything"). The accurate frame: **tasks change before jobs do.** Roles are bundles of tasks; automation takes the task-shaped pieces that are cheap to generate — first drafts, boilerplate code, summaries, routine correspondence — and leaves specification, verification, judgement, relationships and accountability. Historically, technology has redistributed work as much as eliminated it, while genuinely killing specific *tasks* (that is not comfort — specific occupations have been hit hard; the honest statement is that prediction at the individual level is unreliable). What rises in value when generation is cheap: **choosing and specifying well** (Module 6 skills), **verifying** (Modules 8–9), **domain depth** that lets you judge output, **responsibility-bearing roles** where someone must sign, and **human-facing work** where trust and presence are the product. What falls first: work that is mostly undifferentiated text production with no verification step. The strategic response is not fear; it is becoming the person who directs and checks the tools better than the person who only consumes their output.

payload.title: Deepfake / misinfo red flags
rows: No original source, only a clip or screenshot
Provenance has been cut — find the first publication
Sole account, new or locked history
Independent corroboration is the real test
Real media, wrong event — check when/where
Request for urgency, secrecy or money
Pressure exists to bypass your checking

payload.title: Detectors are a tool, not a verdict
payload.text: Detection accuracy varies by format and improves/decays as models evolve. Treat a detector result as one weak signal beside origin-tracing and corroboration — never as the thing that settles it.

payload.title: Forwarding is a decision
payload.text: Every share is a small publication under your name. For anything consequential, the verification routine runs before the share button, not after the damage.

payload.title: The correction never travels as far
payload.text: Fabrications spread on emotion; corrections spread on diligence. Your personal rule should be: check before amplifying — you cannot rely on a later retraction to undo your share.

payload.title: Handle a viral clip and a headline about jobs
payload.problem: Part 1: a 20-second clip shows a faculty member apparently endorsing a paid certificate scheme, circulating with angry comments. Part 2: an article claims "AI will eliminate 40% of jobs by 2030, says study". Work both through the routines from this lesson.

steps.title: Clip — trace before reacting
steps.desc: Find the original poster and account history; search the claim text and the faculty member's name across reputable outlets; check whether the institution has issued anything; note the clip's cut points (a 20-second excerpt is context-free by construction).

steps.title: Clip — decide proportionally
steps.desc: If origin and corroboration are absent, the correct status is unverified — no comment, no share, no forwarding to other groups. If the concern is real, the verified path exists: contact the office directly. Either way the emotional charge never substitutes for provenance.

steps.title: Headline — interrogate the claim shape
steps.desc: "40% of jobs" has the structure of an AI-generated or heavily distorted summary: find the study, check what it actually measured (task exposure ≠ job elimination), who funded it, what "by 2030" and "eliminate" mean in it. Specific percentages with vague referents are a classic confabulation signature.
steps.code_snippet:
headline -> find the study -> what was measured?
tasks exposed? occupations modelled? assumptions?
"exposure" != "elimination" != "unemployment"

steps.title: Headline — replace with the frame
steps.desc: Keep the task-versus-job distinction from the concept: which tasks get automated, which roles absorb verification and accountability, what skills gain value. That frame survives whatever the specific study said — which is why the frame, not the percentage, is what you should carry.

payload.solution: Clip: origin → corroboration → proportionate response, defaulting to unverified-and-unshared when provenance is missing. Headline: find the primary study, distinguish exposure from elimination, and fall back on the task-bundle frame that is robust to bad statistics. Both exercises end the same way: the feeling the content produced has zero weight in the verdict.

payload.title: Run the routine on something you nearly shared
payload.prompt: Find a piece of media or a headline from this week that made you want to react. Run the six-step routine: origin, independent coverage, date/context, affect check, proportion, share decision. Write five lines: status (verified/unverified), what you would have assumed without checking, and what you did.
payload.hint: Pick something you actually reacted to emotionally — the routine only teaches anything when the stakes are real.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a detector result as proof
mistakes.fix: Detectors are format-sensitive and imperfect in both directions. Origin and corroboration are the durable tests; the detector is one weak signal.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming video and audio are inherently real
mistakes.fix: Cloning and swapping are commodity operations now. Any clip without provenance starts as unverified — that is not cynicism, it is the current baseline.

mistakes.mistake: Reading "jobs" headlines at face value
mistakes.fix: Separate task exposure from occupational elimination from unemployment; check what the study measured. Most headlines collapse three different claims into one.

mistakes.mistake: Forwarding first, verifying later
mistakes.fix: Sharing is publication and corrections travel slower. For anything with consequence, the routine runs before the share — every time.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why can deepfake detection tools not serve as a user's primary defence, and what should a user do instead?
payload.answer: Detection is an arms race on the artefact itself: accuracy varies by media type and quality, generated content keeps improving, edited-real media confuses classifiers, watermarks and metadata are optional and easily stripped, and users rarely possess a clean original for comparison. A verdict from such a tool is one imperfect signal, not proof. Users should verify the source instead: trace the original publication and account history, read laterally across independent reputable outlets, check date and context for reused media, notice engineered provocation, and gate any consequential belief or action on corroboration — while treating detectors as a secondary hint. The core shift: from "is this image synthetic?" to "who says this happened, and who else confirms it?"
payload.source: Media-literacy and platform-safety question; mirrors election/crisis guidance from news organisations.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Fabrication cost collapsed while distribution rewards provocation — the core misinformation dynamic.
Detection cannot be first line; verify origin, corroboration, date/context, and your own affect.
Forwarding is publication: check before amplifying, because corrections travel slower.
Jobs frame: tasks change before jobs do; bundles get re-specified, not simply deleted.
Value rises in specification, verification, domain depth and accountable, human-facing work.

questions.prompt: The most reliable first check on a viral clip is:
options: Running it through a deepfake detector
Tracing the original source and checking independent reputable coverage
Reading the comments for expert opinion
questions.explanation: Provenance and corroboration are artefact-independent; detectors are imperfect secondary signals at best.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest red flag that a circulating "news" item is unverified?
options: It exists only as a screenshot or forwarded clip with no traceable original publication
It was posted in the evening
questions.explanation: Missing provenance means nobody can weigh the original context — every other signal is weaker than that one.

questions.prompt: The healthiest frame on "AI will eliminate jobs" claims is:
options: Ignore them entirely — technology always creates jobs
Treat them as panic — nothing really changes
Separate task exposure from role elimination: tasks are automated first, roles get re-specified, and the individual predictions are unreliable
Take the headline percentage as a plan of record
questions.explanation: Tasks change before jobs do; bundles of tasks are re-specified with verification and accountability retained — and precise forecasts deserve scrutiny.

questions.prompt: When generation is cheap, which skill rises most in value?
options: Specifying work well and verifying output against evidence
questions.explanation: When anyone can generate, the scarce abilities are deciding what is needed and judging what is true — Modules 6 and 9's core skills.

modules.title: Module 10 — Your AI Practice
modules.summary: Turning nine modules of knowledge into a personal system: workflows with humans placed where the stakes are, a prompt library you actually reuse, a rubric for judging output quality, an ethics recap — and the capstone: a real AI toolkit with evidence of use.

lessons.title: Personal Workflows and Human-in-the-Loop: Where AI Fits, Where You Do
lessons.summary: Decomposing recurring tasks, assigning steps to model or human by risk and checkability, and measuring honestly whether the workflow actually saved time.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decompose a recurring task into steps and assign each to AI or human
Place human checkpoints by error cost, reversibility and checkability
Recognise automation bias and other drift risks in repeated workflows
Measure net time saved including verification effort

payload.text: A student automated her weekly club-update routine: AI summarised the chat log, drafted the announcement, and — one lazy Sunday — she posted it unchecked. It was accurate about everything except the venue, which had moved. The failure was not the model; it was a workflow with no checkpoint at the one step where being wrong actually costs something. Workflows are where individual prompt skills become systems — and systems fail at their seams.

**From prompt to workflow.** A workflow is a recurring task written down as steps. Take something you do weekly — an update email, a study-notes pass, a bug-fix routine — and decompose it: (1) *gather inputs* (chat log, notes, error trace), (2) *specify the ask* (what the output must do), (3) *AI steps* (summarise, draft, restructure, explain, generate candidates), (4) *verification* (facts, code, links, edge cases — Modules 8 and 9), (5) *decision* (approve, adapt, discard), (6) *publish or submit*. The division of labour follows a simple principle: **AI takes steps where generation is cheap and errors are visible; you take steps where judgement, rights and consequences live.** Most failed AI adoptions are really unexamined workflows — someone automated step 3 and forgot step 4 exists.

**Human-in-the-loop (HITL), placed by risk.** "Human in the loop" means a person is a required gate at some position in the pipeline — not a spectator. Three placements: *before* (you write the spec and supply verified context — the cheapest control), *during* (approval gates: nothing sends, commits or submits without a human click — the strongest control), and *after* (verification pass on output — the most common one, and the one people skip). Choose by three properties of the step: **error cost** (what breaks if this is wrong — a subject line and a court filing are not the same), **reversibility** (can the error be undone in a minute, or is it permanent — sent messages, commits, public posts), and **checkability** (how cheaply output can be checked — code checks itself; persuasive prose does not). Low cost + reversible + checkable → automate with light review. High cost or irreversible → human decision, always, regardless of how good the model has been lately. That last clause is the point: your HITL placement is set by consequences, not by recent experience of the tool.

**Drift risks.** Two patterns corrode workflows over time. *Automation bias*: as outputs stay good for weeks, checking quietly shortens, then disappears — right up until the distribution of inputs shifts (new data, new template, a model update — Module 7) and errors return unnoticed. Countermeasures: keep the check a fixed, named step in your written workflow; sample-audit even when confident; re-run your mini test set (Module 6) after any model or prompt change. *Scope creep*: a workflow built for summaries grows an auto-send feature, then an auto-reply — each step shaves seconds and moves the gate. Watch where the human gate migrates; if it drifts toward the end of higher-stakes steps, pull it back deliberately.

**Measure honestly.** The net saving is *time saved including verification*, minus the time spent building and maintaining the workflow. Count honestly for two weeks: generation is fast, but the checks you must do are not optional — they are the price of the workflow being safe. A routine that saves 30 minutes but needs 25 minutes of checking is a modest win, not a transformation; a routine where checking also catches your own errors is a better one than it looks. Write the workflow down — one page, steps, gates, checks — because a workflow that exists only in your head cannot be audited, taught or fixed.

payload.title: Placing the human gate
rows: Draft emails; summaries of your own notes

payload.code:
# A written workflow, one page
weekly_update:
  1 gather:   chat log + calendar        (you)
  2 specify:  template + facts           (you, from library)
  3 generate: summary + draft            (AI)
  4 verify:   dates/venue/links/names    (you - FIXED step)
  5 approve:  nothing sends without you  (you - gate)
  6 publish:  send                       (you)
net_time = t(before) - t(after) - t(maintain)

payload.title: Write the workflow before you automate it
payload.text: One page of steps and gates exposes the missing verification step while it is still cheap to add. The page is also what you audit when results drift.

payload.title: Automation bias is silent
payload.text: Long streaks of good output are exactly when checking erodes — and inputs change without notice. Keep verification a fixed named step, not a habit that fades with confidence.

payload.title: Redesign a weekly routine with gates
payload.problem: Ravi's routine: every Sunday he reads 40+ club chat messages, writes action items, drafts a status email to the faculty advisor, and sends it. It takes about 90 minutes and he skips it half the time. Redesign it as a workflow with explicit AI steps and human gates, then estimate net time.

steps.title: Decompose and assign
steps.desc: Gather (export chat log + his own notes) → you; specify (from template: audience = advisor, must include decisions, pending items, next meeting date) → you; generate (summary + action items + draft) → AI; verify → fixed human step; approve → gate; send → you. Decisions remain his: which items escalate, what tone with the advisor.

steps.title: Design the verification around what breaks
steps.desc: Error cost analysis: wrong date/venue = credibility hit with faculty (irreversible once sent); missed action item = a project stalls. So the check list is exactly: every date against the calendar, every name against the roster, every commitment matches what was agreed in chat.
steps.code_snippet:
check: dates -> calendar | names -> roster
       commitments -> quoted chat lines
strip: anything the log does not support

steps.title: Place the gates
steps.desc: During-gate at send (nothing goes without his click, because the email is irreversible and high-trust); after-gate at verification (fixed step before it). No auto-send, ever, for this workflow — regardless of how good the drafts get.

steps.title: Measure net effect over two weeks
steps.desc: Expected: 90 → ~35 minutes (generation + checking) plus occasional template maintenance. Track actuals: if checking creeps past 30 minutes the prompt/template needs work, not the check. Re-audit after any model update — and keep one weekly item deliberately hand-written as a control sample.

payload.solution: A six-step workflow with AI confined to generation, verification as a fixed named step, an approval gate before sending, and an honest measurement including checking time. The design question was never "can AI write this" — it was "which step, if wrong, costs Ravi credibility" — and the gate sits there.

payload.title: Map your own workflow
payload.prompt: Take one recurring task and write it as 5–7 steps. Mark each AI / human, place one human gate by error cost, and name the verification check for each AI step. Run it once for real and time both halves. Report: net minutes saved, and what the verification actually caught.
payload.hint: If the verification step caught nothing on the first run, you are either very good or not really checking — the second run usually settles it.

mistakes.mistake: Handing over the decision, not just the drafting
mistakes.fix: AI may prepare options; the approve/send/submit step stays yours wherever consequences are real. Gates sit where errors become permanent.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping checks because the tool has been reliable
mistakes.fix: Reliability streaks end when inputs or models change. Verification is a fixed step in the written workflow, not a mood that depends on recent experience.

mistakes.mistake: Counting generation time only
mistakes.fix: Net saving includes verification and maintenance. Measure the whole loop for two weeks before calling anything a time-saver.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping the workflow in your head
mistakes.fix: Unwritten workflows cannot be audited when they drift, taught to a teammate, or repaired after an incident. One page: steps, gates, checks.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define human-in-the-loop and explain how you decide where to place the human gate for a given step.
payload.answer: Human-in-the-loop means a person is a required, non-skippable gate at a defined position in an AI pipeline — specification before, approval during, or verification after — rather than a passive observer of automated output. Placement is decided by three properties of the step: error cost (how much damage a wrong output causes), reversibility (whether the error can be undone — sent messages and public posts cannot), and checkability (how cheaply and reliably output can be verified). Low-cost, reversible, machine-checkable steps tolerate light after-the-fact review; high-cost or irreversible steps require an in-loop approval gate regardless of the model's recent track record — because the gate exists for the day the model, the inputs or the settings change.
payload.source: Core applied-AI governance question; standard in product and ML-practice interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Decompose recurring tasks; AI generates, humans specify, verify, decide and publish.
Place gates by error cost × reversibility × checkability — not by how reliable the tool feels today.
Human-in-the-loop: before (spec), during (approval), after (verification) — pick deliberately.
Fight automation bias with fixed named checks, sample audits and mini test sets after changes.
Measure net time honestly: generation minus verification minus maintenance; write the workflow down.

questions.prompt: Human-in-the-loop most accurately means:
options: A human writes every prompt character by character
A person is a required gate at a defined step — spec, approval or verification — in the pipeline
The model is trained on human data
A human watches the model generate tokens in real time
questions.explanation: It describes a control placement in the process, not typing habits or training provenance.

questions.prompt: Which step most needs an in-loop approval gate?
options: Generating bullet variants for a slide
Auto-sending a message that corrects a public record (irreversible, high trust)
questions.explanation: High cost plus irreversibility decides: gates follow consequences, not the tool's recent accuracy streak.

questions.prompt: Automation bias is best described as:
options: Bias introduced by automated data collection
Checking that quietly erodes as outputs stay good — until inputs or models shift and errors return unnoticed
A model refusing to act without approval
questions.explanation: The trust-decay failure mode: the workflow's check shortens exactly when a silent distribution change makes it necessary again.

questions.prompt: When measuring whether an AI workflow "saved time", you must include:
options: Verification time and maintenance time alongside generation
questions.explanation: Net saving is whole-loop: generation + checks + upkeep. Omitting checks is how unsafe workflows get called efficient.

lessons.title: Building a Prompt Library You Actually Reuse
lessons.summary: Turning one-off prompts into versioned, tested assets — the entry format, the generalisation step, and the maintenance habits that keep a library alive.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Convert a successful ad-hoc conversation into a reusable template with slots
Design a library entry with the fields that make reuse possible
Apply versioning, test-date and verification discipline to stored prompts
Curate a small library from your own highest-frequency tasks

payload.text: Six weeks into heavy AI use, most people have re-written the same prompt four times, cannot find the version that worked, and have no idea which model it worked on. Meanwhile the small number who kept a page of prompts copy-paste, adjust two slots, and ship. The difference is not cleverness — it is treating prompts the way programmers treat code: stored, versioned, tested, reused. You do not need an engineer's tooling; you need a page and some discipline.

**A prompt is an asset — once it is generalised.** The conversation that produced a great output is raw material: it contains your task description, the constraints that mattered, the example that pinned the format, and — buried in it — the two specifics that only apply to that one request. The library step is *extraction*: pull the general structure out of the particular instance, replace the particulars with **slots** ({audience}, {document}, {job_description}, {word_limit}), and store the result as a template you can fire at any input. Without slots, you are storing transcripts; with slots, you are storing capability.

**The entry format.** One entry, one task. Fields that earn their place: **name** (what job it does, in your words — "JD-to-resume-bullet matcher"); **use case** and *when to reach for it*; **slots** (the inputs it expects, with a note on what good input looks like); **the prompt** (with slots inline, verbatim as tested); **constraints/format** (what the output contract is); **verification checklist** (the 2–4 checks this specific output needs — citation tracing for research entries, edge-case run for code entries, fact pass for emails — this is the field people skip and the one that makes the library worth having); **known failure modes** (what went wrong before: "invents dates if {deadline} is empty"); **model + last tested date** (prompts are written against a specific model's behaviour, and models change silently); and one **example pair** (sample input → good output, so future-you can see the target without re-running history). A notes app with a template per page, or a spreadsheet with a row per entry, both work — the tool matters far less than the fields.

**How to build it in a week.** Collect from evidence, not ambition: go through your last month of chats and star the outputs you actually used. Take the top three tasks by frequency (for most students: summarising, drafting messages, explaining/reformatting material — your list will differ). Generalise each: identify slots, write the template, test it on **three fresh inputs** (the real test — a prompt that only works on its original input is not generalised yet), record failures honestly in the field. Total effort: an hour or two. That is the entire MVP of your library.

**Maintenance is the whole game.** Libraries die in three ways: never used (because the collection step never happened or entries are hard to find — keep names job-shaped and search-friendly); stale (because models update and entries carry no test dates — re-test quarterly or after a notice about model changes, and update the date or retire the entry); and unchecked (because someone stripped the verification field during tidying — never ship an entry without its checks; a library without checklists is a library of traps). Add an entry only after its second successful use; prune entries you have not touched in months; keep private data out of examples before sharing a page with teammates. A library of fifteen honest entries beats a graveyard of two hundred aspirational ones.

payload.title: Library entry fields
rows: Job-shaped so you can find it under pressure
What input it expects — and what "good input" means
The 2–4 checks this output type requires
What broke before, so it does not again
Sample input → good output as the target

payload.code:
# Entry: resume-bullet-from-worklog (tested 2026-10, model X)
slots: {worklog} {job_description} {max_bullets=4}
prompt: |
  "Turn this worklog into resume bullets for the JD below.
   Rules: only facts present in the worklog; action verbs;
   quantify ONLY numbers that appear; map honest terminology
   to JD keywords. Output: {max_bullets} bullets, <=25 words each.
   Mark anything unsupported as [verify]."
checks:  evidence test per bullet | JD keyword match | no invented numbers
fails:   inflates scope verbs ("helped" -> "led") when log is vague

payload.title: Store the checks inside the entry
payload.text: A prompt without its verification checklist is half an asset — future-you will reuse the prompt and skip the check. The checklist travels with the template or it does not happen.

payload.title: Undated entries rot silently
payload.text: Model updates change prompt behaviour without telling you. Record model + date on every entry, re-test after updates, and retire rather than trust stale pages.

payload.title: Turn one great conversation into an entry
payload.problem: Last week you got an excellent output: a messy paragraph of meeting notes converted into a clean decision log (decisions / action items with owners / open questions). The prompt was assembled ad hoc across three messages, including a sample. Convert it into a library entry.

steps.title: Reconstruct and separate
steps.desc: Pull from the transcript: the instruction ("convert meeting notes into three sections…"), the constraint that mattered ("owners only when explicitly stated, else unassigned"), the format rules, and the sample you supplied. Separate general structure from this-meeting specifics (the actual notes become a slot).

steps.title: Generalise with slots and write the entry fields
steps.desc: Slots: {notes}, {meeting_date}, {sections}. Name: "notes → decision log". Add the checklist (owners real? every decision traceable to a line? no invented dates?) and failure modes ("invents action items when notes are ambiguous — added clarification clause").
steps.code_snippet:
slots: {notes} {meeting_date}
check: decision | trace to source line
       owner only if named else "unassigned"
       no date not present in notes

steps.title: Test on three fresh inputs
steps.desc: A standup log, a long messy thread, a sparse five-line note. Three inputs because generalisation fails on the distribution, not the original: sparse notes are where action items get invented. Fix what breaks — one change per iteration, Module 6 discipline — then finalise.

steps.title: Record model, date and example pair
steps.desc: Save with model name and test date, plus one sample input → good output for future reference. Note the second-use rule: the entry graduates from "candidate" to "library" after one more real successful use — entries are added on evidence, not enthusiasm.

payload.solution: Transcript → separation of structure from specifics → slots, checks and failure modes → three-input test → dated entry with example pair. The reusable asset is not the prompt text alone: it is prompt + slots + checks + known failures + test date — which is exactly the difference between a page you reuse and a scroll you never open again.

payload.title: Start your library with three entries
payload.prompt: Pick your three most repeated AI tasks from real usage. For each: write an entry with name, slots, verbatim prompt, verification checklist, known failure mode, and last-tested date. Test each on one fresh input today. One page per entry, in whatever tool you will actually open.
payload.hint: Start from conversations you already had — collecting from evidence beats inventing entries for tasks you rarely do.

mistakes.mistake: Storing raw transcripts instead of templates
mistakes.fix: Transcripts are clutter with one-off specifics buried in them. Extract the structure, name the slots, keep one example pair — the rest goes.

mistakes.mistake: Entries without test dates or model names
mistakes.fix: Prompt behaviour is version-specific and models change silently. Undated entries cannot be trusted or re-validated.

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the verification checklist during tidying
mistakes.fix: The checklist is the field that makes reuse safe. An entry without checks invites the exact shortcut that produced your past failures.

mistakes.mistake: Building a giant library you never fire
mistakes.fix: Reuse is the success metric. Add on second use, prune what you never touch, and name entries by the job so you can find them fast.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What distinguishes a reusable prompt-library entry from a saved successful prompt? Specify five fields and explain the purpose of each.
payload.answer: A saved prompt is a frozen transcript tied to one input; a library entry is a generalised, tested, maintained asset. Five fields: (1) slots — named placeholders for the inputs, converting one instance into a family of uses; (2) the verbatim prompt as tested — copy-paste ready with slots inline, avoiding reconstruction errors; (3) verification checklist — the specific checks this output type demands, so reuse carries its safety with it; (4) known failure modes — prior breakage (e.g. invented dates when a slot is empty) so traps are not re-walked; (5) model + last tested date — because prompts are written against particular model behaviour that changes silently, making re-testing possible and retirement honest. An example pair of input → good output completes the entry by showing the target without a rerun.
payload.source: Prompt-operations question; reflects professional prompt-management practice.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Generalise conversations into templates: extract structure, name the slots, keep one example.
Entry = name + slots + verbatim prompt + checks + failure modes + model/date + example pair.
Test on three fresh inputs — a prompt that only works on its original input is not generalised.
Maintenance decides value: re-test after model changes, prune dead entries, add on second use.
A prompt without its checklist is a trap stored for future-you.

questions.prompt: The step that turns a successful conversation into a reusable asset is:
options: Copying the whole transcript to a notes file
Generalising specifics into named slots while keeping the structure and checks
Uploading it to a prompt marketplace
questions.explanation: Slots convert one instance into a template for a family of inputs; transcripts remain tied to their original request.

questions.prompt: Which field prevents a stored prompt from silently breaking after a model update?
questions.explanation: Only a dated, model-tagged entry can be re-tested and retired honestly when behaviour drifts.

questions.prompt: Why must the verification checklist be stored inside the entry?
options: To increase the prompt's accuracy automatically
So reuse carries its own safety — future firing of the prompt fires its checks too
questions.explanation: Checks separated from prompts get skipped; embedding them makes verification part of the copy-paste act.

questions.prompt: A library of 200 entries where you use 4 is best described as:
options: A graveyard — value comes from reuse, not count
questions.explanation: The success metric is fired prompts with their checks; entries added on ambition and never used are dead weight.

lessons.title: Is This Good and Is This Right: Evaluating Output and Your Ethics Rules
lessons.summary: A rubric-based way to judge AI output instead of vibing at it, and the honesty, attribution and harm principles that keep your name on work you can stand behind.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define task-specific quality criteria and grade output against a short rubric
Apply checks that raise verifiability for uncheckable claims
State personal ethics rules covering honesty, attribution and harm
Connect evaluation failures to prompt improvements in your library

payload.text: Two outputs sit side by side: both fluent, both well structured, both confident — one is right. If your judging method is "reads well", you cannot tell them apart, and fluency is exactly what language models optimise. Evaluation is the skill underneath every other skill in this course: prompting gets you output, workflows place it, but only judging turns output into work you are willing to sign.

**"Good" is a specification, not a feeling.** Start by writing what good means *for this task* — three to five criteria, checkable where possible. Research summary: faithful to source, caveats preserved, claims traceable, right length. Resume bullet: true claim, evidence available, action verb, JD vocabulary honoured. Code fix: solves the original bug, passes edge cases, no new dependencies, readable. Email: every fact correct, ask explicit, tone yours, filler removed (the Module 8 passes are a rubric; you have been building one all along). Grade each candidate output against the rubric — quickly, with marks — and pick or edit accordingly. Teams should write theirs down; individuals can keep four lines in the library entry (Module 10, Lesson 2). The transformation is real: once criteria are explicit, disagreements become specific ("fails caveat preservation") instead of vague ("something feels off"), and — critically — you can notice *regressions* after you change a prompt.

**Checks sized to the output.** For claims: spot-check the load-bearing ones against sources (Module 8 routine — you do not need to verify a tone-only draft the way you verify statistics). For structure: diff against the requested format — if you asked for three bullets with a constraint each and got five without them, that is a rubric failure regardless of eloquence. For anything uncheckable in itself, *raise verifiability by construction*: ask for the source sentence, the derivation, the test run, the quoted line — formats you can verify beat formats you must trust. And the tempting shortcut — **asking another model "is this good?"** — is a weak signal at best: same family of heuristics, same blind spots, correlated failures; a second opinion from a machine that shares the first machine's training distribution is a coin flip with extra steps. Use it, if at all, as a generator of *checks*, never as the check.

**Ethics recap — three rules, one test.** Everything in this course converges into how you behave when nobody is grading the tool: **Honesty** — do not misrepresent how work was made or what it contains; disclose where rules or norms require it; never let an AI-assisted artefact claim certainty you did not establish; do not use synthetic media to deceive (Module 9). **Attribution** — cite the human sources your work draws on (verified citations, not generated ones); respect licences and terms for both the inputs you paste and the outputs you use; where AI assistance is acknowledged in your field or institution, acknowledge it; do not pass off others' work — human or model — as solely yours. **Harm** — consider who is affected before you generate: personalised deception, harassment, biased screening and mass-produced falsehood cause real damage, and "the tool made it easy" is not a mitigation (Module 9). Underneath all three sits the principle the course has repeated from different angles: **accountability does not transfer**. The name on the submission, the send button, the commit — that person carries it.

The final test to keep in your pocket, applied before shipping anything that matters: *Would I be comfortable explaining exactly how this was made — every prompt, every source, every check — to the person it affects?* If yes, proceed. If the explanation would embarrass you, the problem is not the tool.

payload.title: Rubric sketches by task
rows: Faithful to source · caveats kept · claims traceable · right length
True claim · evidenced number · action verb · JD vocabulary
Fixes bug · passes edge tests · no new deps · readable
Facts correct · ask explicit · tone yours · no filler
Accurate vs textbook · right level · worked example · self-check

payload.title: Rubrics beat vibes — and they compound
payload.text: Criteria you wrote once get reused in every library entry, every iteration and every regression check. Ten minutes of rubric-writing pays out across months of use.

payload.title: "Another model says it's fine" is not verification
payload.text: A second model shares the first one's blind spots; agreement between them is weak evidence. Convert second opinions into checks you run yourself — sources, tests, arithmetic.

payload.title: Ethics rules should be personal and written
payload.text: Three to five rules you actually follow ("no secrets pasted", "verify before submit", "disclose when required") outperform abstract principles you cannot recall. Write them at the end of this module and keep them in the library.

payload.title: Grade two candidate outputs and sign one
payload.problem: Task: a 200-word study note explaining convolution to a classmate, from your course material. Two candidates arrive — A and B. Write the rubric, grade both, choose or edit, and run the ethics check before "submitting".

steps.title: Define the rubric (before looking)
steps.desc: Four criteria: (1) accurate against your course material — no mechanism invented; (2) correct level — classmate knows arrays, not calculus; (3) one concrete worked detail (kernel size × image size → output size); (4) ends with a self-check question. Precommitting prevents the fluent one from winning by vibes.

steps.title: Grade both against the rubric
steps.desc: A: elegant, mentions stride/padding/history — fails (2) and (3): calculus crept in, no concrete arithmetic. B: plain, has the worked multiplication, ends with a check — passes 1–4 after you verify the arithmetic and one mechanism claim against your notes. Marks: A fails on fit despite superior prose.

steps.title: Edit and verify the load-bearing bits
steps.desc: Take B, fix one imprecise sentence, and verify the two checkable items: the size arithmetic (recompute it) and the mechanism statement (point at the lecture note line). Only verified items survive — fluency earned nothing.
steps.code_snippet:
rubric: acc | level | worked detail | self-check
A:  P  F  F  P   (fluent, wrong fit)
B:  P  P  P  P   (after 2 verifications)

steps.title: Run the ethics test
steps.desc: Honesty: you will state it as your note, drawn from course material — is that true? Yes. Attribution: the definition traces to your lecturer's material — cited in your study notes. Harm: none plausible. Comfort test: could you defend every line to your instructor? Submit.

payload.solution: A precommitted four-criterion rubric separated quality from fluency, verification settled the checkable claims, the edit fixed the single weak sentence, and the ethics pass (honesty / attribution / harm / comfort) closed the loop. The output you submit is now both good *by your specification* and right *by your principles* — the two halves of the lesson.

payload.title: Write and use a four-line rubric
payload.prompt: For your single most common AI task, write four criteria as checkable statements. Grade today's real output against it, note which criterion failed, and make the one prompt change in your library entry that addresses it. Report: rubric, score, prompt diff.
payload.hint: If a criterion cannot be answered yes/no after a quick look, rewrite it until it can — vague criteria produce vague scores.

mistakes.mistake: Judging by fluency
mistakes.fix: Fluency is the model's home ground and is uncorrelated with truth in exactly the cases that matter. Grade against precommitted criteria, not prose quality.

mistakes.mistake: No criteria, so no improvement possible
mistakes.fix: You cannot iterate on "felt wrong". Write 3–5 checkable criteria; failures then name their fix ("caveat preservation" → add a constraint).

mistakes.mistake: Treating evaluation as only for code
mistakes.fix: Code has a runtime; prose and research have rubrics and sources. Every output type needs its judge — the judge is just manual.

mistakes.mistake: Ethics as an afterthought at submission time
mistakes.fix: Honesty, attribution and harm decide what you generate in the first place. Run the comfort test before the work exists, not while you are clicking submit.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: You must submit an AI-assisted essay under your institution's policy. What does honesty require, and what does attribution require?
payload.answer: Honesty: represent the work truthfully — follow the written policy exactly (if disclosure of AI assistance is required or the use exceeds the permitted zone, disclose; do not present generated analysis as verified when you have not checked it); every factual claim must be one you have verified, because submitting an unverified AI-invented fact is a false statement regardless of who typed it; and be prepared to explain and defend the whole essay, since authorship includes understanding. Attribution: cite the human sources the essay draws on — with references you traced and confirmed, not model-generated lists — credit ideas and quotations properly, and acknowledge AI assistance in the manner the institution or field specifies. Where policy is silent, apply the comfort test: submit only what you could explain, prompt by prompt and source by source, to your instructor.
payload.source: Standard academic-integrity question for AI-era coursework policy assessments.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Good = precommitted, checkable criteria for the task — write 3–5 before you look at output.
Raise verifiability by asking for sources, derivations and runs; second models are weak signals.
Iteration feeds back: each rubric failure becomes a constraint in your library entry.
Ethics: honesty (how it was made and what it claims), attribution (sources and licences), harm (who is affected).
Accountability never transfers — keep the comfort test: could you explain every step to the person affected?

questions.prompt: The main advantage of grading AI output with a written rubric is:
options: It replaces vague impressions with checkable criteria, enabling consistent judgement and targeted prompt fixes
It is required by all providers
questions.explanation: Explicit criteria make quality comparable across outputs and failures actionable in your next iteration.

questions.prompt: A research summary is fluent and well structured but drops the sample-size caveat from the source. Against a rubric that requires "caveats preserved", it:
options: Fails on a named criterion, so the fix is a specific prompt constraint, not a rewrite from scratch
Passes if the tone is confident
questions.explanation: That is the rubric working: a specific failure naming its own remedy.

questions.prompt: Asking a second model to confirm your output is best treated as:
options: A weak signal that may suggest checks you then run yourself
questions.explanation: Models share training distributions and blind spots; agreement is not independent evidence.

questions.prompt: The ethics "comfort test" asks:
options: Whether you could explain every prompt, source and check behind the work to the person it affects

lessons.title: CAPSTONE — Build Your Personal AI Toolkit and Prompt Library
lessons.summary: The course's final deliverable: five real use-cases, ten tested prompts with before/after evidence, your verification checklist, a caught hallucination, and the ethics rules you will keep — plan it, run it, reflect.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Plan five real AI use-cases across study, work and personal tasks
Produce before/after prompt evidence demonstrating the Module 6 iteration loop
Document a verification checklist and one genuinely caught hallucination
Write personal ethics rules and a maintenance plan for the toolkit

payload.text: Everything so far has been exercises. This lesson is different: the deliverable is a document that proves you can run the whole loop — choose a tool, write and iterate a prompt, verify what came back, catch the model lying once, and state the rules you will not break. Not a certificate quiz: a working file, your name on it, evidence inside. The course claimed you would finish with a practice. Now you build it.

**What you are building.** One document (a doc, a note, a small repo — your choice) titled as your personal AI toolkit and prompt library, containing five sections. (1) **Five use-cases you actually ran** — across different domains (for example: research summary for a subject, code explanation, an email draft, resume bullet improvement, study drill). Each entry: the task, the tool chosen and *why* (Module 7's selection procedure in one line), the workflow with its human gate (Module 10.1), what verification you performed, and the honest outcome — including anything that failed. (2) **Your ten best prompts, before and after** — for each: the naive first attempt and its output (the "before"), the improved prompt built from Modules 6 and 10.2, and its output (the "after"), with a one-line note on *which change mattered*. This is the section that proves iteration rather than asserting it — keep the real outputs, unedited. (3) **Your verification checklist** — the general checks you now run (claim classification, citation tracing, fact pass, edge-case run — whichever apply), tailored to your tasks, written as steps you can execute. (4) **One hallucination you caught** — what the model claimed, how you detected it (which check fired), what you did, and what it taught you about where your own risk concentrates; if you have not caught one, manufacture the conditions: ask five checkable questions on a niche topic, verify all five, and report what you find honestly. (5) **Your ethics rules** — three to five lines you will actually follow (from Lesson 3: disclosure, no secrets pasted, verify before submit, attribution, harm check), plus your comfort-test sentence.

**How to run it.** Plan first: pick the five use-cases from tasks you genuinely have this week — the capstone fails when people invent tasks to sound impressive. Work over a week if possible; a single session works but produces thinner evidence. For every use-case, *save the conversation*: before-prompt, before-output, after-prompt, after-output, checks run. Maintain your library in parallel (Lesson 2 fields), because entries and evidence come from the same sessions. When a check catches something — a wrong date, a fabricated source — you have found your hallucination case study; document it the day it happens.

**Reflect — the part people skip, the part that matters.** Write four honest paragraphs: what improved in your outputs over the week (with one concrete before/after as proof); what still fails and where you now expect failure (specific: "citations in long research answers", "dates when I don't supply them"); what you deliberately will *not* use AI for (a real list — graded material if your policy says so, personal judgement calls, anything you cannot verify); and how the library gets maintained (re-test dates, quarterly prune, what triggers an update). The reflection is what converts a week of activity into a practice — because the toolkit will drift without it.

**Common ways this goes wrong.** Describing instead of running (a capstone about *what you would do* has no evidence — the before/after outputs are the evidence); importing prompts from the internet without testing them on your inputs (they are someone else's evidence); claiming verification you did not perform (the checklist must have check marks, not aspirations); and building a tool *list* instead of a toolkit — five apps you opened once is not a system; five tasks with routing rules, prompts and checks is. The standard, plainly: every claim in the document backed by an artifact from a real session.

# Evidence template for one use-case entry
use_case: "summarise chapter 4 notes into revision cards"
tool:     chat assistant (cloud, training off) - why: pasted notes,
          transformation task, verification by re-reading chapter
workflow: paste -> prompt -> generate -> CHECK (cards vs chapter)
          -> gate: I approve each card -> keep

payload.title: Collect evidence as you go, not at the end
payload.text: Save each before/after and each caught error the day it happens. Reconstruction from memory produces polished fiction — the exact failure mode this course spent ten modules teaching you to avoid.

payload.title: Do not manufacture a fake hallucination story
payload.text: If you have not caught one, run the honest test (five verifiable questions, verify all five) and report the real result — including "none of these failed". Fabricating the evidence would fail the ethics rules in section 5 of your own document.

payload.title: Assemble one complete use-case entry, end to end
payload.problem: Neha's real task: "read my rough project notes and produce a two-paragraph progress update for my supervisor." Walk the full capstone loop for this single entry and show exactly what gets pasted into the document.

steps.title: Run it for real with routing and a gate
steps.desc: Tool: chat assistant — transformation of supplied material, no live facts; data: her own project notes (green bin, no confidential third-party data). Workflow: notes pasted → prompt from library → generate → fact pass (dates, percentages vs her records) → gate: she approves before sending. She runs it and saves the session.

steps.title: Capture before and after honestly
steps.desc: Before-prompt: "write a progress update from these notes" → generic, invented a completion percentage. After-prompt: slots ({notes}, {audience}), constraint "use only numbers present in the notes; mark gaps as [ ]", format "two paragraphs, ≤120 words". Save both outputs unedited — the invented percentage is the interesting artefact, not an embarrassment.
steps.code_snippet:
before: "write update from these notes"
        -> invented "70% complete"
after:  "only numbers present; mark gaps [..]"
        -> "[..] modules done (3 of 5 listed)"

steps.title: Run the checks and log the result
steps.desc: Fact pass: one date was wrong in her own notes (she fixed the source, not the output); the invented percentage is caught by the evidence rule before sending. Checklist update: "for progress updates — every number traceable to notes or marked [..]". Entry filed with model, date, failure modes.

steps.title: Write the reflection fragment
steps.desc: From this entry alone: improved (no invented numbers after the evidence rule); still fails (dates when her notes are sloppy — supply them explicitly); will not use AI for (the decision about what to tell the supervisor — generation only, judgement hers); maintenance (re-test entry monthly, prune unused). Four honest lines, and the entry is complete.

payload.solution: One real task, fully instrumented: routing decision, workflow with a gate, unedited before/after evidence showing the exact iteration, a check that fired, a library entry with date and failure mode, and four lines of reflection. Repeat four more times across different domains — with your ten prompts distributed among them — and the capstone document is built from artifacts instead of intentions.

payload.title: Start the document today — use-case one
payload.prompt: Create the capstone document with its five section headings. Complete use-case #1 from a task you actually have today: tool choice line, workflow with gate, before/after prompts and outputs saved verbatim, checks run, outcome. Do not wait for five — one evidenced entry beats five planned ones, and momentum compounds.
payload.hint: Pick a task with a verification handle (something you can check against a source) so your first entry ends with a check that genuinely ran.

mistakes.mistake: Describing the practice instead of running it
mistakes.fix: The document lives or dies on artifacts: real prompts, real outputs, real check marks. A capstone of intentions fails the evidence standard the course taught.

mistakes.mistake: Importing impressive prompts you never tested
mistakes.fix: Unverified internet prompts are someone else's evidence on someone else's inputs. Every entry needs a successful run on YOUR task before it enters the ten.

mistakes.mistake: Claiming verification that did not happen
mistakes.fix: Checklists with aspirational ticks are the exact dishonesty section 5 forbids. Either the check ran (log it) or it did not (say so, then run it).

mistakes.mistake: Submitting a tool list rather than a toolkit
mistakes.fix: Apps opened once are consumption. A toolkit is tasks + routing rules + prompts + checks + maintenance — five tasks with evidence, not five logos.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why does the capstone require before/after outputs from actual runs rather than a list of prompts you have collected?
payload.answer: Because the course's central claim is behavioural, not informational: that you can run an iteration loop (specify → run → diagnose → change one thing → retest) and judge the result with checks. A list demonstrates exposure; before/after artifacts demonstrate the loop working — the naive output shows the failure that motivated the change, the improved output shows its effect, and the one-line change note shows causal attribution rather than coincidence. Evidence from your own runs also proves the prompts fit your tasks (generalisation with slots, tested on real inputs) and that verification actually executed (check marks against saved outputs). In short: prompts are cheap, and collection is easy; a documented, verifiable practice is the thing worth certifying.
payload.source: Capstone-defence question; mirrors portfolio-assessment logic in skills-based courses.
