courses.title: Python for AI
courses.subtitle: Forty lessons from your first print() to a shipped end-to-end notebook — Python, NumPy, pandas, honest charts, core statistics and your first scikit-learn models
courses.description:
Every AI course starts by assuming you already speak Python. This one does not. It is the complete zero-to-first-model path in ten modules: the language itself (variables, strings, structures, functions, control flow, errors), the two libraries AI work actually runs on (NumPy at array speed, pandas on real tables), how to look at data without lying to yourself (honest charts, file and API workflows, a re-runnable cleaning pipeline), the statistics every model sits on (mean, variance, distributions, correlation versus causation), and finally scikit-learn — where you split honestly, beat a baseline, and read your first LinearRegression and DecisionTree with the numbers they deserve.

Every lesson follows the same nine steps (objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice task, common mistakes, exam/interview angle, four-question quiz, summary), so the format never becomes another thing to learn. The course ends with a capstone: one notebook, a stranger can run it top to bottom, and it goes from raw data to a defensible model verdict — the artifact you show, not the notes you took.

**Who this is for:** any student — any branch — who was told to "learn Python for AI" and wants one honest course that finishes with a real pipeline, not a certificate for watching videos.

**What you need:** a browser (Google Colab needs zero install) or any machine that can install Python 3.9+. No prior programming assumed.
outcomes: Set up Python and run code confidently in scripts, the REPL and Jupyter/Colab notebooks
Use variables, f-strings and the four basic types without type-confusion bugs
Choose and manipulate lists, tuples, dicts and sets — including comprehensions — with the right mutation semantics
Write small functions with clean parameters, returns, scope and docstrings; install packages with pip inside a venv
Drive confident branches and loops, and read a traceback to fix the actual error
Use NumPy arrays, vectorized operations, slicing, broadcasting and seeded randomness on real numeric data
Load, inspect, select, filter, join and group pandas DataFrames — and handle missing data with a reported strategy
Build honest matplotlib/seaborn charts matched to the question, and save figures and outputs reproducibly
Read CSV/JSON files and APIs safely, and package cleaning into a re-runnable pipeline with a defect report
Compute core statistics and train/evaluate a first scikit-learn model against a baseline with an honest train/test split
courses.about_course:
This course is built around one gap: every AI syllabus starts at "import pandas", and everyone who falls behind fell behind in week one — in Python itself. Ten modules close that gap in order, each one earning the next.

Module 1 gets code running three ways (interpreter, script, notebook) and fixes the mental model: names point at values, input() is always text, and the four basic types behave differently in arithmetic. Module 2 is the container toolkit — lists, tuples, dicts and sets — chosen by mutability and lookup needs rather than habit. Module 3 turns scripts into functions: parameters, defaults done right (the mutable-default trap included), scope, imports, pip and virtual environments. Module 4 is control flow and the error skills that separate people who ship from people who stall: honest branches, loops that finish, tracebacks read bottom-up, and a debug loop you can repeat. Module 5 crosses into NumPy — dtype and shape, vectorization that beats Python loops, fancy indexing, broadcasting and seeded randomness — the array literacy every model assumes.

Part II is the applied half. Module 6 is pandas: Series and DataFrame, the six-readout inspection ritual, loc versus iloc, merges, groupby and missing-data strategies that report what they did. Module 7 is seeing data without lying — matplotlib's object interface, matching chart type to question, subplots and seaborn, and the honesty rules (zero-based bars, disclosed log scales, takeaways in titles). Module 8 is real data work: CSV and JSON safely, APIs with timeouts and courtesy, a cleaning pipeline that returns (data, report), and saving figures and outputs so someone else can rerun you. Module 9 is the statistics every model sits on — mean, median, variance with the n − 1 correction, sampling intuition, correlation versus causation with real confounders, and outliers. Module 10 assembles everything into scikit-learn: the X/y contract, honest held-out evaluation, baselines you must beat, LinearRegression and a DecisionTree read against those baselines — and the capstone notebook that proves the whole chain end to end.

The exam/interview angle is threaded through every lesson, and the final exam draws fifteen questions from a thirty-question bank spanning all ten modules. The certificate is issued for the capstone notebook — a thing you can open, run and defend — not for attendance.
prerequisites: A browser (Google Colab needs zero install) or any computer that can install Python 3.9+
No prior programming experience assumed — Module 1 starts from zero
High-school algebra is enough for the statistics and NumPy sections
audience: Engineering students of any branch who need Python for labs, projects or placements
Aspiring AI/ML/data-science learners told to "first learn Python" without a roadmap
Students preparing for placement Python rounds and aptitude-style coding questions
Anyone who knows a little Python but has never touched NumPy, pandas or scikit-learn
courses.branch_label: AI/DS primary — open to all branches

exam_prep.target: University Python / Data Science semester exams & placement Python rounds — AI/DS primary, all branches

units.title: Foundations: setup, variables, strings, types
units.summary: Three runtimes: interpreter, script, notebook (cells share one kernel). Names bind to objects — dynamic typing; reassignment rebinds, never converts. Strings immutable; f"{x:.2f}" is a display spec; slicing start:stop excludes stop. input() always returns str; int/float/bool/None arithmetic (True == 1, None only equals None).
questions: Why does input() * 2 concatenate instead of doubling, and how do you fix it?
What does f"{value:.2f}" change — the number or its printed form?
After x = 5; x = "hi", what happened to the integer 5?

units.title: Data structures: list, tuple, dict, set
units.summary: List: mutable, ordered, indexed/sliced; mutation methods change in place. Tuple: immutable and hashable — dict keys and set elements. Dict: O(1) lookup; d["k"] raises on miss, d.get("k") returns None/default. Set: uniqueness + union/intersection/difference. Comprehensions build lists/dicts/sets declaratively. Choose by mutability need and lookup pattern.
questions: Why can a tuple be a dict key but a list cannot?
What is the difference between d["k"] and d.get("k") on a missing key?
When is a set the right container instead of a list?

units.title: Functions, imports & readable code
units.summary: Positional then keyword arguments; defaults bind once at def — the [] trap persists state across calls. return sends values back; assignment inside a function makes a name local (UnboundLocalError even when a global exists). import finds modules; pip installs; venv isolates. Docstrings document contracts; PEP 8 naming keeps code readable.
questions: Why does def f(item, bucket=[]) silently accumulate state across calls?
What raises UnboundLocalError even when a global of the same name exists?
What must a function docstring document beyond what the name says?

units.title: Control flow, errors & debugging
units.summary: if/elif/else: order boundary tests highest-first. for + range(stop) excludes stop; while needs a guard that eventually fails. break exits, continue skips; loop-else runs only when no break happened. try/except catches specific exceptions; else is the success path; finally always runs. Tracebacks read bottom-up: the last frame is where it died.
questions: What does the else block on a for loop mean?
Which try/except clause runs only when no exception occurred?
Which traceback line tells you where the failure actually is?

units.title: NumPy: arrays, vectorization, broadcasting
units.summary: ndarray: homogeneous typed block — shape + dtype; beats list-of-objects on memory and speed. Whole-array arithmetic is element-wise (list * 2 concatenates; array * 2 doubles). Boolean masks filter and count. Fancy indexing selects by position lists. Broadcasting stretches compatible shapes. sum/mean/std collapse along axis. np.random.default_rng(seed) makes sampling reproducible.
questions: Why is a * 2 different for a Python list and a NumPy array?
What does arr.sum(axis=0) return for a (rows × cols) array?
Why does df[["col"]] stay 2-D when a single-feature X must?

units.title: pandas: Series, DataFrame & groupby
units.summary: Series = labeled 1-D; DataFrame = labeled 2-D table. read_csv then the six-readout ritual: head, shape, dtypes, info, describe, missing counts. df["col"] → Series; df[["col"]] → DataFrame. loc = label, iloc = position; boolean masks filter rows. merge joins on keys; groupby = split-apply-combine. isna().sum() per column decides the fill/drop strategy — always reported.
questions: df["x"] and df[["x"]] — what makes them different objects?
What three steps does a groupby aggregation always perform?
Why inspect dtypes and missing counts BEFORE any maths?

units.title: Visualization & data workflows
units.summary: fig, ax = plt.subplots() — the object interface every chart should use. Histogram = distribution; scatter = relationship; line = time; bar = category. Subplots grids iterate axes arrays; seaborn reads column names. Honesty: bars start at zero; log scales disclosed; titles state the finding. Files: with open + UTF-8; json module; to_csv(index=False); pathlib paths; requests with timeout + raise_for_status; cleaning functions return (df, report); savefig + output/ bundle.
questions: Why must a bar chart's value axis start at zero?
Why does to_csv(..., index=False) matter on read-back?
What does the (clean_df, report) tuple from a cleaning function buy you?

units.title: Statistics & first ML models
units.summary: Mean vs median under skew; variance = mean squared deviation; sample variance uses n − 1 (degrees of freedom). Sampling distributions: means of many samples concentrate — the intuition behind CLT. Correlation r measures linear association, never causation — confounders drive both variables. Outliers via IQR fences. ML: split train/test with random_state (+ stratify) BEFORE learned preprocessing; beat the dummy baseline; LinearRegression coef_ are associations; DecisionTree + confusion matrix locate errors; verdicts in domain units on held-out data only.
questions: Why split BEFORE imputing or scaling with statistics learned from data?
What bar must a model beat before its accuracy means anything?
A feature with a large coef_ — can you call it a cause? Why not?

important_questions: Explain dynamic typing: why does x = 5; x = "hi" work, and what class of bugs does it cause?
List three differences between a Python list and a NumPy array, and say which wins for 10^6 numeric operations.
Walk through the six-readout inspection ritual on a fresh CSV and say what each readout can catch.
Why does sample variance divide by n − 1, and what goes wrong if you divide by n?
Two variables correlate at r = 0.95 — can you claim causation? Give the confounder counterexample.
State the train/test discipline: where the split happens relative to cleaning/imputation, and why random_state appears everywhere.
Your classifier scores 92% on a 2%-fraud dataset by always predicting "safe". Diagnose the number and name the metric family you would use instead.

previous_year_questions.question: A function is defined as def greet(name, msg="Hi"): return f"{msg}, {name}!". Explain the argument-binding rules and show one call that raises TypeError even though both parameters have values available.
previous_year_questions.solution: Positional arguments bind left to right; keyword arguments bind by name; a default fills any parameter left out (defaults must follow parameters they can fill). greet("Ada", "Hello", "extra") raises TypeError: greet() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given — the third positional has nothing to bind to. Greeting("Ada", msg="Hey") is valid: one positional, one keyword, no conflict.

previous_year_questions.question: A CSV marks column mixes numbers with the text "Absent". Write the pandas steps to count the non-numeric entries, convert safely, and decide a fill strategy — without silently averaging garbage.
previous_year_questions.solution: df = pd.read_csv(path); df["marks"].value_counts(dropna=False).head() shows how many Absent; pd.to_numeric(df["marks"], errors="coerce") turns them into NaN instead of raising; missing = df["marks"].isna().sum() quantifies the damage. Decide with evidence: drop rows if few and MCAR, or fill with a stated value (median) and record the count in a report dict. Never let read_csv guess silently — check dtypes after load, because a mixed column arrives as object dtype and mean() would either fail or lie.

previous_year_questions.question: Explain why evaluating a model on its own training data gives an inflated score, and demonstrate the correct evaluation protocol using train_test_split with random_state and stratify.
previous_year_questions.solution: A model can memorise training rows (especially flexible ones like deep trees) and score near-perfectly there while failing on new cases — training accuracy measures capacity to memorise, not to generalise. Protocol: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y); fit ONLY on train; score ONLY on test. random_state pins the shuffle so results reproduce; stratify keeps class proportions equal in both halves so metrics on imbalanced data stay comparable. Fit a most_frequent/mean dummy on the same train split first — the real model only earns its score by beating that bar.

bank.prompt: Which environment keeps variables alive between executed cells until the kernel is restarted?
options: A .py script run once with python script.py
A text editor with Python syntax highlighting
bank.explanation: Notebook cells share one live kernel: every executed cell sees the same namespace. A script starts fresh on each run.

bank.prompt: After x = 5 followed by x = "hi", what is true?
options: x holds both values at once
The integer 5 was converted into a string
The name x now points at a str object; the 5 may be garbage-collected
A TypeError is raised because names are typed
bank.explanation: Names are labels bound to objects. Rebinding x points it at a new str object; the integer is untouched and unreferenced.

bank.prompt: user types 4 and the code runs name = input(); print(name * 2). The output is:
bank.explanation: input() always returns str. "4" * 2 is string repetition → "44". Wrap with int(input()) to compute numerically.

bank.prompt: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]. What does nums[1:3] evaluate to?
bank.explanation: Slicing is start:stop with the stop excluded — indices 1 and 2 only → [2, 3].

bank.prompt: d = {"a": 1}. What is the difference between d["b"] and d.get("b")?
options: d["b"] raises KeyError; d.get("b") returns None (or a supplied default)
d.get("b") raises KeyError; d["b"] returns None
bank.explanation: Bracket access assumes the key exists and raises when it does not; get() is the safe lookup with an optional default.

bank.prompt: What is the length of s = {(1, 2), (1, 2), (3,)}?
options: 2 — equal tuples collapse to one element
1 — tuples are unhashable, so this fails
bank.explanation: Tuples of numbers are hashable; the two identical (1, 2) tuples are equal, so the set keeps one copy → length 2.

bank.prompt: def f(a, b=2): return a + b. What does f(3) return?
options: A TypeError — defaults must come first
bank.explanation: The default fills the omitted parameter: f(3) binds a=3, b=2 → 5.

bank.prompt:
x = 10
def f():
    x = x + 1
    return x
f()  # what happens?
bank.explanation: Assigning to x inside f makes it local for the whole function, so the right-hand x + 1 reads the local name before it exists.

bank.prompt:
def append_to(el, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(el)
    return bucket
append_to(1); append_to(2)  # returns?
options: [1, 2] then [1, 2] — the default list persists between calls
A TypeError — default lists are forbidden
bank.explanation: The default [] is created once at def time and reused. Use bucket=None and bucket = bucket or [] inside instead.

bank.prompt: What does list(range(2, 7)) produce?
bank.explanation: range is start:stop with stop excluded — five values from 2 up to (not including) 7.

bank.prompt: When does the else block attached to a for loop run?
options: Only when the loop finished without hitting break
Only when the loop body ran zero times
bank.explanation: loop-else means "no break": the else runs when the iterable is exhausted normally; any break skips it.

bank.prompt: In try / except / else / finally, which clause runs ONLY when no exception was raised in try?
bank.explanation: except handles the failure, finally always runs, and else is the success path — it runs only when try completed cleanly.

bank.prompt: a = np.array([1, 2, 3]). What is a * 2?
bank.explanation: NumPy arithmetic is element-wise vectorization. A Python list * 2 would concatenate the list twice — different semantics.

bank.prompt: a = np.array([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]). What does (a > 2).sum() return?
bank.explanation: a > 2 is a boolean mask; True counts as 1, so summing the mask counts matching elements — three of them.

bank.prompt: For a 2-D array of shape (rows, cols), what does arr.sum(axis=0) return?
options: One value per column — the rows are collapsed
One value per row — the columns are collapsed
bank.explanation: axis=0 is the row axis: the reduction walks down the rows, leaving a 1-D result with one sum per column.

bank.prompt: On a DataFrame df, df["marks"] and df[["marks"]] differ in that:
options: They are identical views of the same object
df["marks"] is a Series (1-D); df[["marks"]] is a DataFrame (2-D)
df["marks"] only works when marks is the index
bank.explanation: One bracket selects a column as a Series; a list of columns keeps the DataFrame shape — the distinction every sklearn pipeline relies on.

bank.prompt: df.loc[3] and df.iloc[3] differ because:
options: loc uses the index LABEL 3; iloc uses the 4th row by POSITION
iloc includes the row named 3 only if it exists
bank.explanation: loc is label-based (the row whose index equals 3); iloc is integer-position-based (offset 3, the fourth row).

bank.prompt: df.groupby("city")["sales"].mean() computes:
options: The mean of all sales, ignoring city
One mean sales value per distinct city — split, apply, combine
The median of the first city only
bank.explanation: groupby splits rows by city, applies mean to each group's sales, and combines the results into one row per city.

bank.prompt: Which chart best answers "how are student marks distributed across the class?"
options: Scatter plot of marks vs marks
bank.explanation: A distribution question takes a histogram — bins of one numeric variable. Lines are for time; scatter for two variables.

bank.prompt: A column chart comparing department budgets must start its value axis at zero because:
options: Truncated baselines exaggerate the bar-length differences, which encode the values
Zero is always the minimum budget
It makes the chart load faster
bank.explanation: Bar length is the visual quantity; clipping the axis lets tiny differences look like multiples. Only lines may zoom for shape.

bank.prompt: A report plots monthly revenue on an undisclosed log-scaled y-axis and claims "explosive growth". What is dishonest?
options: Log scales are always illegal in charts
The axis transformation is hidden, so readers misread the rate of change the linear data actually shows
The chart should have been a pie
bank.explanation: Log scales are legitimate for wide-range data — when disclosed. Hiding the scale lets the shape imply growth the raw numbers do not support.

bank.prompt: Why does df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False) pass index=False?
options: To stop pandas writing the DataFrame index as a phantom first column
It is required — to_csv fails without it
bank.explanation: The default index=True writes row labels into the CSV, which read back as a junk Unnamed: 0 column. Drop it unless you need it.

bank.prompt: The point of with open(path) as f: instead of open(path) alone is that:
options: It reads the file twice for safety
The file is guaranteed to be closed when the block exits, even if an exception is raised
It opens the file in binary mode
bank.explanation: The context manager closes on every exit path — success or crash — so handles and buffers never leak.

bank.prompt: requests.get(url) without a timeout is a defect because:
options: The call can hang forever — a polite client always bounds its wait and checks status_code
JSON cannot be parsed without a timeout
bank.explanation: No timeout means a stuck server freezes your script indefinitely. Pass timeout=… and handle r.raise_for_status() before parsing JSON.

bank.prompt: Ten salaries average ₹50,000; one ₹10,00,000 salary is added. Which statistic moves more?
bank.explanation: The mean divides by n and absorbs every value; the median only reorders — one extreme value barely shifts it.

bank.prompt: Sample variance divides by n − 1 (ddof=1) because:
options: Each squared deviation uses a mean estimated from the same data, losing one degree of freedom; dividing by n would underestimate the population variance
Variance is always negative without the correction
bank.explanation: The estimated mean fits the data slightly too well. The n − 1 (Bessel) correction unbiases the estimate of the population variance.

bank.prompt: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths correlate at r = 0.9. The correct conclusion is:
options: Correlation is not causation — hot weather is a confounder driving both
bank.explanation: A third variable (temperature/season) raises both. Only controlled designs — not observational r — support causal claims.

bank.prompt: In scikit-learn, a feature matrix with 500 samples and 6 features has shape:
bank.explanation: The contract is (n_samples, n_features): rows are observations, columns are features.

bank.prompt: On a dataset that is 98% class "safe", a model predicting "safe" always scores 98% accuracy. The correct reading is:
options: The model is excellent — ship it
Accuracy is misleading under imbalance — the model adds nothing over the most_frequent baseline; use precision/recall or F1
Accuracy should be computed on training data instead
bank.explanation: The dummy already scores 98%. Honest evaluation compares against that bar and uses metrics that see the minority class.

bank.prompt: You impute missing values and select features using the FULL dataset, and only then split train/test. Why is the test score inflated?
options: Leakage: statistics computed from test rows influenced training, so the test set is no longer unseen
bank.explanation: Any learned preprocessing must be fitted on train only (fit on X_train, transform both). Full-data fitting lets test information leak into the model.

project.title: Ship an end-to-end Python-for-AI notebook
project.brief: Produce one Jupyter/Colab notebook on a dataset of your choice (a built-in sklearn dataset such as iris or diabetes, or any CSV you cleaned yourself) that a stranger can run top to bottom on a fresh kernel. The eight sections are fixed: (1) the question — one sentence naming the decision, target and features; (2) load + inspect — the six-readout ritual; (3) clean + report — every fill, coercion and drop counted in a printed report dict; (4) EDA — at least three charts (distribution, relationship, category), each with a one-line takeaway and honest axes; (5) split FIRST — train_test_split with random_state=42, plus stratify for classification, before any learned preprocessing; (6) baseline — DummyRegressor/DummyClassifier scored and recorded; (7) the real model — LinearRegression for a regression target or DecisionTreeClassifier for classification, fit on train only; (8) compare + confess + save — baseline vs model metrics side by side in domain units, the confusion matrix or a residual summary, a limitations paragraph naming test size, single-split uncertainty, suspected confounds and one concrete forbidden use, and an output/ bundle (cleaned CSV, metrics.json, figures). No cell may depend on manual state.
project.submission_hint: Link to a public Colab or GitHub notebook (anyone-with-link can view) that runs top to bottom without errors.

modules.title: Module 1 — Python Foundations: Setup, Variables, Strings & Basic Types
modules.summary: Getting Python running (interpreter, scripts, Jupyter/Colab), how variables and dynamic typing actually work, strings and f-strings for real output, and input/print with int, float, bool and None.

lessons.title: Getting Python Running: Interpreter, Scripts, Jupyter & Colab
lessons.summary: What Python is, the three ways to run code, how to verify your install, and how notebook state differs from a script.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Verify a Python 3 installation and start and exit the interactive interpreter
Write, save and run a .py script from the terminal
Run multi-cell code in Google Colab or Jupyter and explain how kernel state works
Choose the right runner (interpreter, script or notebook) for a given task

payload.text: Day one of every Python class splits into two groups: the students who spend the evening fighting an installer, and the one who opens colab.research.google.com and runs their first line in forty seconds. Nothing in this course is learned by reading alone — you learn Python by running Python. Ten minutes to a working runner removes the only real barrier between you and every lesson after this one.

**What Python actually is.** Python is a high-level programming language. When you run a .py file, Python first translates your source into an intermediate form called **bytecode**, and then a Python runtime executes that bytecode. You never see or manage that translation — there is no separate "compile" step to remember. Edit, run, read the result, edit again. That fast iteration loop is a large part of why Python won data science and AI: when your work is exploration, the speed of the edit-run cycle often matters more than the raw speed of the executed code.

**Three ways to run code — and they behave differently:**
1. **The interpreter (REPL).** Type `python3` at a terminal (often just `python` on Windows) and you get a `>>>` prompt. Every line you type is evaluated immediately and its result printed. `exit()` returns you to the shell. Perfect for checking what one line does — terrible for anything longer than a screen, because the session ends when you close it.
2. **A script.** A plain text file ending in `.py` holding a sequence of statements. You run it with `python3 myfile.py`, it executes **top to bottom exactly once**, prints whatever you print, and exits. State does not survive: every run starts fresh. This is how real programs are delivered.
3. **A notebook (Jupyter or Google Colab).** Code is split into **cells** you run one at a time, in any order you like, in a **kernel** — a long-lived process that keeps every variable alive between cells. Cell 1 can load a dataset; cells 2–50 can explore it without reloading. Notebooks are the native format of AI work: almost every ML tutorial, Kaggle analysis and research result you meet is a notebook. Their power (experiment interactively) is also their trap (state can go stale — see below).

**Which one when.** Interpreter: a one-line question ("does this sort work?"). Script: anything you will keep, re-run, or hand to someone else. Notebook: data analysis, charts, teaching, and learning — which is why this course shows notebook cells alongside runnable scripts.

**Installing, honestly.** Only Python 3 matters — Python 2 reached end of life in 2020 and any `python2` you find is a museum piece. Current versions are 3.11 through 3.13; any of them runs every example in this course. On Windows, install from python.org and tick **"Add python.exe to PATH"** during setup — skipping that box is the single most common reason the `python` command mysteriously does not exist later. macOS and most Linux distributions already ship `python3`. Google Colab needs no installation at all: a free Linux machine in your browser with NumPy, pandas, matplotlib and much of the AI stack preloaded. The catch is ownership: a Colab machine is rented RAM tied to your session, so anything you want to keep must be saved to Google Drive or downloaded before you disconnect.

payload.title: Three runners, three behaviours
rows: All variables live in the kernel

payload.title: Zero-install first hour
payload.text: If anything about installing fails, open incognito chrome and go to colab.research.google.com → File → New notebook. You get a working Python 3 session with the AI stack in under a minute. Come back to local installs after Lesson 3.

payload.title: python versus python3
payload.text: On macOS and Linux the bare command python is either missing or points at Python 2, which will reject modern syntax with confusing errors. Get in the habit of typing python3 (and verifying python3 --version). On Windows the installed command is python.

payload.title: From a blank machine to a running program
payload.problem: You have never run Python on this computer. Reach the point where you can (a) check the version, (b) run a one-liner, (c) run a saved script, and (d) run a notebook cell — and know which output belongs to which method.

steps.title: 1. Check what is installed
steps.desc: In a terminal, ask Python for its version. Any 3.x answer means you are ready; a "command not found" means install first (or just use Colab).
steps.code_snippet:
python3 --version
# Windows: python --version
# Expected: Python 3.12.7

steps.title: 2. Talk to the interpreter
steps.desc: Start the interpreter, evaluate two lines, then leave. The >>> prompt means Python is waiting for one statement at a time.
steps.code_snippet:
python3
>>> print(3 * 14)
42
>>> exit()

steps.title: 3. Run a saved script
steps.desc: Put this in a file named hello.py in a folder you know, then run it by path. Output is plain — no prompts, no In/Out numbers.
steps.code_snippet:
# hello.py
name = "Ada"
print("Hello,", name)

# then in the terminal:
python3 hello.py

steps.title: 4. Run a notebook cell
steps.desc: Open colab.research.google.com → New notebook. Paste into the first cell and press the play button (or Shift+Enter). A second cell can print(x) — the kernel kept x alive. Close the tab and both are gone.
steps.code_snippet:
x = 6 * 7
print(x)   # 42

payload.solution: Version check gives Python 3.x; the interpreter answered 42 for one line; hello.py printed "Hello, Ada" as a one-shot script; the notebook kept x across cells. Recognise each output style — prompt-led (interpreter), plain (script), numbered cells (notebook) — because confusing them is how people misread where a result came from.

payload.title: Set up and record your runner
payload.prompt: Open Colab (or your local install) and run three cells in order: (1) print your Python version with import sys; print(sys.version), (2) create a variable student = "your name" and print it, (3) print the variable again after re-running cell 1. Note exactly what persists and what does not.
payload.hint: Re-running cell 1 does not touch student, because cells share one kernel — but restarting the runtime (Runtime → Restart runtime) wipes everything.

mistakes.mistake: Typing python and getting "command not found" or an ancient Python 2 banner
mistakes.fix: Use python3 explicitly and confirm with python3 --version. On Windows, reinstall from python.org with the "Add to PATH" checkbox ticked.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting notebook variables to survive closing the browser
mistakes.fix: The kernel is rented memory tied to your session. Save code cells (they are safe in the file); re-run them after a restart to rebuild state.

mistakes.mistake: Running python myfile.py from a folder that does not contain the file
mistakes.fix: The error "can't open file ... myfile.py" is a path problem, not a Python problem. cd to the folder first, or pass the real path: python3 scripts/hello.py.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming everything you run shares one environment
mistakes.fix: Your terminal, your local Jupyter kernel and a Colab session are three separate Pythons with separate packages. This is exactly why Module 3 covers virtual environments.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is the difference between a compiled and an interpreted language, and where does Python actually sit?
payload.answer: A compiled language (C, C++, Rust) translates the whole source into machine code ahead of time, producing a separate executable you then run. An interpreted language executes the source (or an intermediate form of it) statement by statement at run time. Python is a hybrid: it compiles source to bytecode — cached in a __pycache__ folder — and executes that bytecode on a virtual machine, so there is no separate build step but also no direct machine-code translation. The trade-off is rapid edit-run iteration and portability across platforms versus lower raw execution speed, which is precisely the gap libraries like NumPy close later in this course.
payload.source: Standard opening question in Python placement rounds and university unit tests.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Python runs three ways: interpreter (one line at a time), script (top to bottom once), notebook (cells with live kernel state).
Running Python compiles to bytecode behind the scenes — no separate compile step, fast edit-run loop.
Only Python 3 matters; verify with python3 --version and beware the python versus python3 naming trap.
Colab gives you a free, preloaded environment in the browser — but its state and files are session-bound.
Notebook state lives in the kernel: persistent until you restart, unreliable if you run cells out of order.

questions.prompt: Which command correctly checks your Python version on macOS or Linux?
questions.explanation: python3 is the Python 3 command on macOS/Linux; the bare python is often missing or is Python 2.

questions.prompt: A notebook cell runs x = 6 * 7 and a later cell prints x successfully. This works because:
options: Notebooks save variables into the .py file automatically
Cells share variables held alive by the kernel process
Colab uploads the variable to Google Drive
print() searches all previous cells for the name
questions.explanation: The kernel is a long-lived process holding every variable until the session restarts; nothing is saved to disk by running a cell.

questions.prompt: Why can re-running notebook cells out of order produce wrong results or errors?
options: Python forbids running cells more than once
The kernel recompiles the notebook each run
Kernel state may no longer match what later cells expect
questions.explanation: Cells mutate shared kernel state; after reordering or partial re-runs, names may hold older or missing values than the cell assumes.

questions.prompt: The key behavioural difference between a script and a notebook is:
options: Scripts can use variables, notebooks cannot
Notebooks run code once; scripts keep it alive between cells
Scripts run top-to-bottom once with fresh state; notebooks keep live state between cells
There is no difference — both just print output
questions.explanation: A script is executed from top to bottom and exits; a notebook keeps a kernel alive so cells build on each other.

lessons.title: Variables and Dynamic Typing: Names Point at Values
lessons.summary: Assignment as naming, why variables have no type of their own, reassignment, aliasing, and naming rules that keep code readable.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create variables with valid names and read assignment right-to-left
Explain dynamic typing: the name is a label, the object carries the type
Predict the result of reassignment and of aliasing a list with b = a
Inspect any value's type at the interpreter with type() and isinstance()

payload.text: In Java you write int age = 21 and the compiler refuses age = "twenty-one". Python says nothing at write time — it will happily run for minutes and then crash on the line where the string finally meets arithmetic. Worse: b = a on a list does not copy anything, so one line quietly changes two "different" variables. Both surprises vanish the moment you understand one idea: a variable is a name stuck on a value, not a box holding it.

**Assignment is naming.** The line `age = 21` does three things: it creates the object 21 in memory, it binds the name `age` to that object, and it does nothing else — no declaration, no reserved box, no type slot. Read `=` right to left: *age gets bound to 21*. When you later write `age = age + 1`, Python evaluates the right side (21 + 1 = 22), creates a **new** integer object 22, and rebinds the name `age` to it. The old object 21 is not modified — integers cannot be modified at all (they are **immutable**); it simply stops being referenced.

**Dynamic typing: the name has no type — the value does.** `age` can point at 21 on one line and at `"twenty-one"` on the next. Nothing converts; the label just moves to a different object. This is what "dynamically typed" means: types are attached to objects and checked **while the program runs**, not before it runs. Consequences, in order of how they bite beginners:
- Type errors appear at execution time, and only on the line that actually runs — a branch you never tested can hide a type bug indefinitely.
- `type(x)` tells you what class of object `x` currently refers to: `type(5)` → `<class 'int'>`, `type("5")` → `<class 'str'>`. The strings `"5"` and the number `5` are entirely different objects that merely print similarly.
- Python 3.5+ supports **type hints** (`def total(marks: list[int]) -> float:`) which document intent and let tools like mypy check your code — but the Python interpreter itself ignores them at run time. Hints are notes to humans and linters, not enforcement.

**Naming rules and conventions.** Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, may not start with a digit, and are case-sensitive — `Age` and `age` are two unrelated names. Keywords (`if`, `for`, `class`, `import`, `def`...) are reserved; assigning to one is a SyntaxError. Conventions are not enforced but are universal: `snake_case` for variables and functions, `CamelCase` for classes, `ALL_CAPS` for constants, and descriptive over short — `total_marks` beats `tm` every time your code is read again in three months (including by you).

**Aliasing: the sharpest early edge.** `b = a` never copies. For immutable values (int, str, float, tuple) that is harmless — nothing can change under you. For **mutable** objects like lists, both names point at **one** object, so `b.append(9)` is visible through `a` too. If you wanted a copy, you had to ask for one explicitly (`b = a.copy()`). You will live inside this behaviour for the rest of the course — pandas DataFrames, NumPy arrays and every dataset you load behave the same way — so it pays to see it once, deliberately, in five lines of pure Python.

payload.title: Reading the common lines
rows: Create int 5, bind name x to it
Evaluate old x, create a new int, rebind x — no mutation
Legal: x now points at a str; 5 is untouched elsewhere
y points at the SAME object as x — not a copy
Returns the class of x's current object

payload.title: Prove aliasing to yourself in ten seconds
payload.text: At the interpreter: a = [1, 2, 3] then b = a then b.append(4) then print(a). Seeing [1, 2, 3, 4] teaches more than any paragraph — including this one.

payload.title: "=" is not equality
payload.text: Assignment binds a name (a = b). Comparison asks a question and yields True or False (a == b). Python will not stop you writing if x = 5 by accident in modern versions only because it is a SyntaxError — but mixing them up in prose and interviews still costs marks.

payload.title: Predict the output before running it
payload.problem:
Without running anything, state the exact output of this script, then verify by running it:

a = 10
b = a
a = 20
c = [1, 2]
d = c
d.append(3)
print(a, b, c, d)

steps.title: Lines 1–2: bind two names to one int
steps.desc: a = 10 creates int 10; b = a points b at the same 10. Harmless so far — integers are immutable, so there is nothing to change.

steps.title: Line 3: rebind, not modify
steps.desc: a = 20 creates a NEW int 20 and moves the name a. b still points at 10, because rebinding a never touches whatever b points to.

steps.title: Lines 4–6: bind two names to one list
steps.desc: d = c makes both names refer to the same list object. Lists are mutable, so d.append(3) modifies that single shared object.

steps.title: Line 7: read it all off
steps.desc: a is 20, b is 10, and c and d both show the same mutated list [1, 2, 3] — because they were never two lists.

payload.solution: Output: 20 10 [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3]. Reassignment moves a name (integers are replaced wholesale); aliasing shares one mutable object. If line 5 had been d = c.copy(), the last two items would read [1, 2] and [1, 2, 3].

payload.title: Alias, rebind, copy
payload.prompt: Write one script that demonstrates all three behaviours and prints labelled results: (1) rebind an int and show an old name keeping its value, (2) alias a list with b = a and mutate it so both names show the change, (3) make an independent copy so mutating it leaves the original alone. Add a comment on each line saying whether it rebinds or mutates.
payload.hint: Use a = a.copy() or b = list(a) for the independent copy; print(type(x)) for at least two values.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting a type error the moment you write a suspicious line
mistakes.fix: Python checks types while running, not while you type. Exercise every branch you wrote — an untested if-branch is where type bugs hide.

mistakes.mistake: Reusing one name for totally different things (total = 0, later total = "many")
mistakes.fix: It is legal and it breaks every later arithmetic line on that name. One job per name; when the job changes, pick a new name.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking b = a copies a list
mistakes.fix: It creates a second name for one object. Ask explicitly: a.copy(), list(a), or slicing a[:] for a shallow copy.

mistakes.mistake: Writing variable names that collide with keywords or start with digits (2nd_place, class_name is fine, class is not)
mistakes.fix: Keywords like class, if, import are reserved — assigning to them is a SyntaxError. Start with a letter and use snake_case.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the difference between these two lines and give the value of y in each case: (a) a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); y = a  (b) a = [1, 2]; b = a.copy(); b.append(3); y = a
payload.answer: Both use =, which binds a name to an object — it never copies. In (a), b and a name the SAME list, so append(3) is visible through both: y = [1, 2, 3]. In (b), .copy() creates a second list object, b points at the new one and mutates it, while a keeps the original: y = [1, 2]. The assignment operator never copies; only an explicit copy method does. This aliasing distinction is the classic first Python interview question because it predicts how bugs spread through real code.
payload.source: Frequent warm-up question in Python interviews; also a university viva favourite.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Assignment binds a name to an object; read = as "gets bound to", right to left.
Variables have no type — the object they currently name does; type(x) reveals it.
Rebinding creates a new object; immutable values (int, str) are never changed in place.
b = a shares one object — with lists, mutation through either name is visible in both.
Names: letters/digits/underscore, no leading digit, case-sensitive, snake_case by convention.
Dynamic typing moves errors to run time — test every branch you write.

questions.prompt: After x = 5; x = "five"; type(x) the result is:
questions.explanation: The name was rebound to a string object; type() reports the class of whatever the name points at now.

questions.prompt: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3). What is a?
questions.explanation: b = a shares one list object; appending through b mutates the same list a names.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a valid Python variable name?
questions.explanation: Names may not begin with a digit; the rest are all legal (and snake_case, snake_case, camelCase respectively).

questions.prompt: In Python, a variable's type is determined by:
options: The object the name currently refers to
The file it was defined in
questions.explanation: Python is dynamically typed: types belong to objects, and names can be rebound to objects of any type.

lessons.title: Strings and f-strings: Text You Can Shape
lessons.summary: String literals, indexing and slicing, immutability, f-string expressions and format specs, and the methods that transform text.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create strings with single, double and triple quotes and escape characters correctly
Index and slice strings, including negative indices and reverse steps
Build dynamic output with f-strings, expressions and format specs like .2f
Transform strings with common methods (strip, lower, split, join, replace)

payload.text: Before any language model reads a single word, a human has already built the string it sees: cleaned, trimmed, cased, labelled. Text work is the quiet majority of real data pipelines. It is also where beginners produce their most memorable bugs — a "marks" column that will not add because of one hidden space, or output that reads total is {n} because someone forgot the f.

**Strings are sequences of characters — and they are text, not numbers.** Python 3 strings are Unicode, so "₹450", a Devanagari word like "नमस्ते", and plain ASCII all behave identically: one string, one sequence of characters, indexable position by position. Quote choice is cosmetic: `'he said "hi"'` and `"it's fine"` are the same kind of object; pick whichever avoids escaping. A backslash introduces special characters — `\n` newline, `\t` tab, `\\` a literal backslash, `\'` a quote inside a single-quoted string. Triple quotes (`"""like this"""`) hold multi-line text, which is why docstrings and prompt templates use them.

**Indexing and slicing — learn it once, use it on every sequence.** Characters are numbered from 0: for `s = "Python"`, `s[0]` is `"P"` and `s[5]` is `"n"`. Negative indices count from the end: `s[-1]` is `"n"`. A slice `s[start:stop:step]` includes `start` and excludes `stop` — `s[0:3]` is `"Pyt"`, so `s[:3]` is the same and `s[3:]` is `"hon"`. `s[::2]` takes every second character (`"Pto"`), and `s[::-1]` reverses the string (`"nohtyP"`). `len(s)` gives the length. Out-of-range access raises IndexError — Python never silently returns nothing.

**Strings are immutable.** `s[0] = "p"` raises TypeError: strings do not support item assignment. Every "change" is actually the creation of a new string: `s = s.lower()` rebinds `s` to a new object; `s.lower()` alone, discarded, does nothing. This is the string version of the aliasing lesson: methods return **new** strings and never modify the receiver.

**f-strings: the default way to build text (Python 3.6+).** Prefix the literal with `f` and put expressions inside braces: `f"Hello, {name}!"`. The brace content is real Python — arithmetic, function calls, indexing all work: `f"{len(name)} chars"`, `f"{scores[0]:.1f}"`. A colon introduces a **format spec** applied to the rendered value:

| Spec | Example | Output | Meaning |
| `:.2f` | `f"{3.14159:.2f}"` | `3.14` | fixed-point, 2 decimals |
| `:>8` | `f"{42:>8}"` | `      42` | right-align in 8 columns |
| `:<15` | `f"{'Ada':<15}"` | `Ada             ` | left-align in 15 columns |
| `:,` | `f"{1234567:,}"` | `1,234,567` | thousands separators |
| `:.1%` | `f"{0.856:.1%}"` | `85.6%` | percent, 1 decimal |

Double braces (`{{` and `}}`) print a literal brace. Older styles — the `%` operator and `"{}".format(x)` — still appear in legacy code; you must be able to read them, but you should write f-strings.

**The methods you will use daily.** `s.strip()` removes leading/trailing whitespace (including newlines), `s.lower()`/`s.upper()` case-fold, `s.replace("old", "new")` substitutes, `s.split(",")` returns a **list** of pieces, `s.startswith("http")` tests, and `",".join(parts)` glues a list into one string — note the call sits on the **separator**, not the list. Together, strip → lower → split is the "ingest raw text" handshake you will repeat in every data lesson of this course.

payload.title: Braces evaluate anything
payload.text: f"{sum(scores) / len(scores):.1f}" is one line: compute, then format. If you find yourself concatenating with + across several conversions, an f-string almost always does it more clearly.

payload.title: Forgotten f, or a discarded method
payload.text: "Total: {n}" prints the braces literally — the f is not optional. And s.strip() on its own line changes nothing: strings are immutable, so rebind it with s = s.strip().

payload.title: Turn raw text into a clean report line
payload.problem: A data export gave you "  ada lovelace  \n" (messy spaces, trailing newline, lowercase) and a score of 87.4567. Produce clean, aligned output without printing stray spaces.

steps.title: 1. Clean the text
steps.desc: strip() removes the surrounding whitespace and newline; title() upper-cases the first letter of each word. Both return NEW strings, so rebind.
steps.code_snippet:
raw = "  ada lovelace  \n"
name = raw.strip().title()
print(name)   # Ada Lovelace

steps.title: 2. Format the numbers inside an f-string
steps.desc: The format spec .1f rounds the display to one decimal; the underlying float is unchanged.
steps.code_snippet:
score = 87.4567
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f} points")

steps.title: 3. Align a tiny table
steps.desc: The < and > specs pad each field to a fixed width so the columns line up — the same trick used for fixed-width log and report output.
steps.code_snippet:
print(f"{'NAME':<15}{'SCORE':>7}")

lessons.title: input(), print() and the Four Basic Types: int, float, bool, None
lessons.summary: Reading user input safely (it is always text), printing with sep/end, and how int, float, bool and None behave in arithmetic.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Read a value with input() and convert it to the correct type explicitly

payload.text: A student builds a marks calculator. The user types 10 and then 4, and the program confidently prints 104 — or crashes with "can only concatenate str not int to str". The bug is one line old and completely invisible: input() returned text, and text plus a number is either string glue or a TypeError. Every beginner meets this; every professional recognises it instantly.

**input() always returns a string — without exception.** `name = input("Name: ")` displays the prompt, waits for a line, and binds whatever was typed as a **str**. It does not care that you typed `42`: you get `"42"`. Consequences:
- `age = input("Age: ")` then `age + 1` either raises TypeError (str + int) or, if the other operand were a string, silently produces concatenation ("42" + "1" = "421") — the nastier outcome, because no error fires.
- The fix is explicit conversion at the point of reading: `age = int(input("Age: "))`, `marks = float(input("Marks: "))`.
- Conversion can fail. `int("abc")` raises **ValueError**, and a subtle trap: `int("3.14")` also raises ValueError — you must go through float first (`int(float("3.14"))` → 3). Handling bad input gracefully with try/except is Lesson 4.3's job; today, know that the failure exists and where it comes from.

**The four types you will use constantly.**
- **int** — whole numbers with unlimited size: `42`, `-7`, even `10 ** 100` (a 101-digit integer, exact — no overflow).
- **float** — binary floating-point decimals: `3.14`, `1e-3` (0.001). Floats are approximations: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` in IEEE 754 — a fact that will matter in every statistics lesson later. A whole number written with a dot (`2.0`) is a float.
- **bool** — `True` and `False`, capitalised (lowercase `true` is a NameError borrowed from JavaScript). Booleans are secretly integers: `True + True == 2`, and `int(True) == 1`. Truth testing: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}` and `None` are falsy; almost everything else is truthy. `bool(x)` shows you the answer.
- **None** — the explicit "nothing here" value. A function with no return statement hands back None; an optional field with no value is None. Its type is `NoneType` and `None` is its only member. Always compare with `is None` /`is not None` rather than `== None`, because identity is the question you actually mean.

**Arithmetic decides its own output types.** On two ints, `+ - * **` give int (`2 ** 10` → `1024`). `/` **always** gives float (`7 / 2` → `3.5`, even `6 / 3` → `2.0`). `//` floor-divides to an int-ish result (`7 // 2` → `3`), `%` takes the remainder (`7 % 2` → `1`), and mixing int with float promotes to float. Comparisons (`== != < > <= >=`) always produce bool. `round(x, 2)` and `abs(x)` round out the toolkit.

**print() is more configurable than it looks.** `print(a, b, c)` joins with a space (`sep=" "`) and ends with a newline (`end="\n"`) — both are parameters you can override: `print("Loading", end="")` keeps the cursor put for progress output; `print(a, b, sep=" — ")` changes the joiner. `print()` alone prints a blank line. In notebooks, a bare expression at the end of a cell shows a numbered `Out[ ]` repr, while print() shows exactly what you asked for — knowing which is which stops you misreading results.

lessons.title: Lists: Indexing, Slicing and Mutation
lessons.summary: Ordered, growable collections: reading and writing positions, slicing with start:stop:step, and which methods change a list in place.

payload.title: What you will learn

payload.text: Two bugs open almost every beginner data project. One: "list index out of range" because the model returned 99 predictions for 100 rows. Two: a marks list that silently lost its order because someone wrote scores = scores.sort() and stored None. Lists are the first container you learn and the one you will still be writing in every module of this course — so the index arithmetic and the in-place methods are worth twenty focused minutes now.

**What a list is.** A list is an **ordered, mutable** sequence that can hold any number of values, of any types: `scores = [91, 88, 95]`, `mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, True, None]`. You write it with square brackets and commas; `len(scores)` is its length. "Ordered" means positions are stable and meaningful — the first element stays first until you move it. "Mutable" means you can change it after creation, which is the entire difference between lists and tuples (Lesson 2.2).

**Indexing — positions count from zero.** `scores[0]` is 91, `scores[2]` is 95, and `scores[-1]` counts from the end (95 again, `scores[-3]` is 91). Reading past the end raises `IndexError: list index out of range` — Python never invents a value for you. Writing by index overwrites in place: `scores[1] = 99` changes one slot without touching the others. Membership tests read naturally: `91 in scores` is `True`.

**Slicing — a copy of a window.** `scores[start:stop:step]` includes `start`, excludes `stop`, and by default steps by 1:
- `scores[:2]` → first two elements,
- `scores[2:]` → everything from index 2 on,
- `scores[::2]` → every second element,
- `scores[::-1]` → the whole list reversed.
A slice is always a **new list** (a shallow copy of that window), so `copy = scores[:]` is one way to duplicate. Slice assignment is mutation: `scores[0:2] = [100, 101]` replaces two elements — and because slices are windows rather than single slots, you can even change the list's length with them (`scores[1:1] = [7, 8]` inserts).

**Mutation methods — know what each returns.**
- `append(x)` adds one element at the end; `extend(iterable)` adds every element of another iterable.
- `insert(i, x)` puts x at position i (shifting the rest right).
- `pop(i)` removes and **returns** element i (default: last) — this is the method that gives a value back.
- `remove(x)` deletes the **first** occurrence of x (ValueError if absent); `del scores[i]` deletes by position.
- `sort()` sorts **in place** and returns `None`; `sorted(scores)` returns a **new** sorted list. `reverse()` flips in place and also returns `None`; `scores[::-1]` builds a reversed copy.
- `index(x)` gives the position of x; `count(x)` how often it appears; `clear()` empties.

**Building lists.** `list(range(5))` → `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]`; `list("abc")` → `['a', 'b', 'c']`; `[0] * 5` repeats; `a + b` concatenates into a **new** list. And the aliasing rule from Lesson 1.2 still stands: `b = a` shares one list — copy with `a.copy()`, `list(a)` or `a[:]` when you need independence.

lessons.title: Tuples vs Lists: When Immutability Is a Feature
lessons.summary: Immutable sequences, unpacking, enumerate and zip, hashable keys — and the decision rule for tuple versus list.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create tuples correctly, including single-element and nested cases
Index, slice and unpack tuples, and explain why they cannot be mutated
Use enumerate() and zip() to iterate over positions and parallel sequences
Decide whether a given requirement calls for a list or a tuple, with a reason

payload.text: Try this at the interpreter: {[28.6, 77.2]: "Delhi"}. Python replies TypeError: unhashable type: list. Change the brackets to parentheses and it works. That one error explains why coordinates, records and returns are written as tuples everywhere in Python: some structures must be frozen before Python will trust them as keys.

**A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence.** You write it with parentheses and commas: `point = (28.6, 77.2)`, `student = ("Ada", 91.5, "CSE")`. Two syntax facts that trip everyone once: `t = (1)` is just the integer 1 (parentheses around one expression), and a true one-element tuple needs a trailing comma — `t = (1,)` or `t = 1,`. An empty tuple is `()`. With those in hand, everything you know from lists applies: `t[0]`, `t[-1]`, `t[1:3]`, `len(t)`, `x in t` all work. What does **not** work is assignment: `point[0] = 99` raises `TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment`. Immutability is total — no append, no sort, no slice assignment.

**Why anyone would choose the weaker option:**
1. **Fixed records.** `name, marks, dept = student` unpacks by position. Because the tuple cannot change shape, that unpacking can never break — the third field will always exist. A list could be shortened by some other line and your `a, b, c = record` then dies with "not enough values to unpack".
2. **A promise not to modify.** Passing a tuple into a function tells it: this data is read-only. It is documentation with teeth, unlike a comment.
3. **Hashability.** Hashability means an object can be turned into a stable integer fingerprint for dict/set lookup, which requires that its contents can never change. Tuples of hashable items qualify; lists do not. Hence `{(28.6, 77.2): "Delhi"}` is a legal dict key and `{[28.6, 77.2]: "Delhi"}` is not. This is why coordinates, timestamp pairs and (row, column) indices show up as tuples in real code.
4. **Cost.** Tuples are slightly smaller and marginally faster to create than lists — real at scale inside huge loops, irrelevant otherwise.

**Unpacking.** Assignment distributes by position: `x, y = 1, 2`; too many or too few values raise ValueError; `first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]` captures the tail as a list. The one-line swap `a, b = b, a` works because the right side is packed into a tuple before anything is reassigned.

**enumerate and zip — the two iteration builtins you will use daily.** `for i, value in enumerate(items):` walks with positions (`enumerate(items, start=1)` for 1-based numbering). `for name, m in zip(names, marks):` walks two sequences in lockstep, producing a tuple per step — and it **stops at the shorter sequence**, which can hide missing data unless you check lengths first. Both return tuples per iteration precisely because a position-and-value pair is a fixed record.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why can a tuple be used as a dictionary key while a list cannot, even when both hold the same values?
payload.answer: Dictionary keys must be hashable: Python stores the key's hash to jump straight to the right bucket, and that hash must stay valid for the key's lifetime. A tuple's contents cannot change, so its hash never changes — lookup stays correct. A list is mutable: if it were allowed as a key, appending to it after insertion would change its hash and the entry would become unreachable. Python therefore rejects it at once with TypeError: unhashable type: list. The same rule governs set membership, and it is why structured identifiers (coordinates, timestamps, keys of a composite field) are tuples in real code.

lessons.title: Dictionaries: Lookup Instead of Search
lessons.summary: Key-value mappings, safe access with get(), iteration with items(), and why hash-table lookup beats scanning a list.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create dictionaries and read, write and delete values by key
Iterate with keys(), values() and items() in the idiomatic forms
Handle missing keys safely with get(), in and setdefault
Build a frequency table from a list of values in a single loop

payload.text: Ask a list of ten thousand names "is Zara here?" and Python may compare every one. Ask a dict holding the same names and it computes where Zara lives and answers in about one step. That gap — linear scan versus near-constant jump — is why every mapping in software is a hash table: Python kwargs, JSON objects, a model's configuration, the vocabulary in a tokenizer. Learn one container, recognise it everywhere.

**What a dict is.** A dict is an **unordered mapping** from keys to values — in Python 3.7+ it also remembers **insertion order**, which you can rely on for display. Written with curly braces and `key: value` pairs: `marks = {"ada": 91, "alan": 88}`. Keys must be **hashable** (str, int, float, bool, tuple — not list or dict); values can be anything, including lists, dicts, even other dicts of dicts. The dict is the single most used structure in real Python: function keyword arguments are dicts, JSON objects parse into dicts, `os.environ` is a dict, and pandas wraps column names and metadata in dicts before you ever see them.

**Reading and writing.** `marks["ada"]` → 91. A missing key raises **KeyError** — dicts never guess. `marks["grace"] = 95` inserts or overwrites (assignment is upsert). `del marks["alan"]` removes a pair. `"ada" in marks` tests **keys** (never values — `91 in marks` is False even though 91 is stored). `len(marks)` counts pairs. Rebuild or merge: `dict(marks)` / `marks.copy()`, `marks.update({"grace": 96, "lin": 78})`.

**Safe access.** `marks.get("zed")` returns `None` instead of raising; `marks.get("zed", 0)` returns a stated default. This distinction has a sharp edge: `if marks.get("count"):` is False both when the key is missing **and** when its value is 0, 0.0, "" or None. If presence matters, ask about presence: `if "count" in marks:` (or `marks.get("count") is not None`).

**Why lookup is fast.** A list search is a conversation: "is it this one? this one? this one?" — up to N comparisons (O(n)). A hash table computes a fingerprint of the key, jumps directly to a bucket, and confirms in about one step — O(1) on average for get, set and delete. Ten thousand entries: thousands of comparisons versus a couple of memory hops. The costs are memory overhead and the fact that you must have a *key*; if your access pattern is "position 437 in insertion order", a list is still right.

**The idiomatic loop.** `marks.items()` yields (key, value) pairs: `for name, m in marks.items():`. Values alone: `marks.values()`; keys are the default iteration: `for k in marks:`. Building counts in a loop is the canonical dict recipe:

`counts = {}` → `for w in words: counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1`

You will write that shape hundreds of times — word frequencies, label counts, per-user totals, bucketing predictions. Dict comprehensions do the same in one line: `{w: len(w) for w in words}`. Convert two lists with `dict(zip(names, marks))`.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Compare the average time complexity of looking up a value in a list by key-like scan versus a dict lookup, and state one situation where the list is still the better choice.
payload.answer: A list search must compare elements one by one until it finds a match or reaches the end — O(n) average, O(1) only if you are lucky with position 0. A dict stores each key's hash and jumps to the right bucket, so get/set/delete are O(1) on average (hash collisions can degrade this, hence "average"). A list is still preferable when: order and position are the access pattern (queue, stack, sorted scan), you iterate over all elements more often than you look any up, memory per element matters (dicts carry overhead), or you need to store positions and there is no natural key.

lessons.title: Sets, Comprehensions & Choosing the Right Structure
lessons.summary: Unique values and set algebra (union, intersection, difference), list/dict/set comprehensions, and a decision rule for picking a container.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create sets and use add, remove, discard, in and len safely
Apply union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference to real problems
Write list, dict and set comprehensions with filtering conditions
Choose list, tuple, dict or set for a requirement and justify the choice

payload.text: A placement portal holds 50,000 applications in a list and asks "has this email already applied?" for each new one. Written naively — scan the list for every check — that is roughly 1.25 billion comparisons. Written with a set of seen emails it is 50,000 near-instant checks. Same question, four orders of magnitude apart, and the fix is one line of vocabulary you will learn in the next twenty minutes.

**Sets: uniqueness as a data type.** A set is an **unordered collection of unique, hashable values**: `{1, 2, 3}`. Duplicates disappear the moment you build one — `set([1, 1, 2, 2, 3])` → `{1, 2, 3}`. Two syntax traps: the empty set must be written `set()` because `{}` is an empty **dict**, and elements must be hashable (same rule as dict keys — `set([[1, 2]])` raises TypeError). Core methods: `add(x)` (no effect if present), `remove(x)` (KeyError if absent), `discard(x)` (silently skips), `pop()` (removes and returns some element), plus `len` and `in` — and membership is near-constant time, which is the whole point.

**Set algebra — four operators worth their ink:**
- `a | b` **union**: everything in either,
- `a & b` **intersection**: only what is in both,
- `a - b` **difference**: in a but not in b,
- `a ^ b` **symmetric difference**: in exactly one of them.
Each also has an in-place form (`a.update(b)`, `a.intersection_update(b)`, ...). These turn questions like "who is in the new list but not the old?" into one expression instead of a nested loop — and because the operands are sets, each question is answered in roughly O(len) rather than O(len²).

**Dedup without losing order.** `list(set(xs))` is the fast one-liner, but sets are unordered, so your original sequence order is gone. When order matters (it usually does — "first occurrence" often carries meaning), keep a `seen` set as a companion:

`seen, out = set(), []` → for each x: if x not in seen → seen.add(x); out.append(x)

One pass, O(n) total, order preserved. This is the pattern interviewers ask you to write from memory.

**Comprehensions: build a whole collection in one expression.** The shape is `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`:

`[w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 4]`

Read it left to right: *for each w in words, take those longer than four characters, and yield w.upper()*. There are three flavours — list `[...]`, dict `{k: v ...}`, set `{...}` — all sharing the same grammar, and all faster and more idiomatic than building the same collection with an empty list plus append. Conditions can filter (an `if` **after** the for) or transform (an `if ... else` **before** the for). Nested loops work: `[f"{r}-{c}" for r in range(3) for c in range(3)]`. The discipline: one or two clauses, readable in a line or two — three chained conditions or any try/except means a plain for-loop is the clearer choice. Python 3 comprehension variables also do not leak into the surrounding scope, so they do not clobber your names.

**Choosing the structure — the rule to memorise:**
| Requirement | Structure |
| Ordered sequence you index/append/sort | **list** |
| Fixed record, never changes, maybe a key | **tuple** |
| Look values up by an identifier | **dict** |
| Uniqueness tests or set algebra | **set** |
If you cannot decide, ask: do I need positions, a lookup, uniqueness, or a frozen record? — in that order of frequency in data code.

lessons.title: def, Parameters, Defaults and *args
lessons.summary: Defining and calling functions, positional versus keyword arguments, default values done right, and collecting extra arguments with *args and **kwargs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define a function with def, call it, and capture the value it evaluates to
Pass arguments positionally and by keyword and use default values correctly
Collect arbitrary extra arguments with *args and **kwargs
Write a correct default for a list parameter (and explain why [] is wrong)

payload.text: A student pasted the same five-line average calculation into eight places across a lab file. When the rule changed (weight the last test double), they fixed six of the eight copies — and spent the evening hunting the other two. Functions are not a syntax topic; they are how one bug gets fixed once instead of eight times. And there is a famous trap hiding in default values that has broken code at companies worth billions — you will meet it in the next ten minutes.

**What a function is.** A function is a named block of statements you can run on demand, with optional inputs (**parameters**) and an optional output (**return value**). You define it once with `def`, then call it any number of times:

```
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

message = greet("Ada")     # the call evaluates to "Hello, Ada!"
```

The `def` line ends with a colon; the body is indented four spaces (Python requires consistent indentation — mixing tabs and spaces raises TabError). Calling evaluates the arguments, runs the body, and the whole call expression becomes the return value — or `None` if the function returns nothing. The payoff of factoring logic into functions: you write it once, test it once, fix it once, and give it a name that documents its purpose.

**Three ways to pass arguments.**
- **Positional** — `greet("Ada")`: matched to parameters by order. The everyday form.
- **Keyword** — `greet(name="Ada")`: matched by name, order-free, and self-documenting at the call site. `sorted(xs, reverse=True)` is readable precisely because the keyword names the switch.
- **Defaults** — `def greet(name, punctuation="!"):`: if the caller omits a parameter, its default is used. Two rules: parameters **with** defaults must come **after** required ones (`def f(a=1, b)` is a SyntaxError — non-default argument follows default argument), and any caller can override a default by passing that keyword.

**The mutable-default trap — memorise this one.** Default values are evaluated **once**, at the moment the `def` line runs, not per call. For immutable defaults (numbers, strings, None) that is invisible. For a list it is a bug factory:

```
def add_item(item, bucket=[]):      # WRONG — one list, shared by every call
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add_item("a")     # ['a']
add_item("b")     # ['a', 'b']  — the "empty" default remembered
```

Every call that omits `bucket` appends to the **same** list object created at definition time. The correct pattern is the universal fix — default to None and create the fresh object inside:

```
def add_item(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

**Collecting extra arguments.** A single star packs any number of **positional** extras into a tuple; a double star packs **keyword** extras into a dict:

```
def mean(*numbers):        # numbers is a tuple
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

def profile(**fields):     # fields is a dict
    print(fields)

mean(1, 2, 3)                  # 2.0
profile(name="Ada", year=2)    # {'name': 'Ada', 'year': 2}
```

`*args` and `**kwargs` are only naming conventions — the star is the mechanism, so `*nums` and `**config` work identically. The reverse works too: `mean(*[1, 2, 3])` unpacks a list into positional arguments. Once arguments are packed, all your Module 2 knowledge applies: iterate the tuple, key into the dict.

payload.title: Defaults: None, then build
payload.text: The safe shape for any mutable default is always the same: def f(x, bucket=None), then if bucket is None: bucket = []. Once you can type it from muscle memory, the trap can never bite you again.

payload.title: Default expressions run once
payload.text: Python evaluates default values when the function is DEFINED, not when it is called. That is the mechanism behind the shared-list bug — and behind time.time() defaults that freeze at startup. Immutable defaults are fine; mutable ones are not.

payload.title: A small grading toolkit built from functions
payload.problem: Write mean(*numbers) to average any number of scores, and report(name, marks, subject="Maths", pass_mark=40) that prints one line per student. Call report for two students, one using defaults and one overriding them with keywords.

steps.title: 1. The variadic helper
steps.desc: *numbers collects every positional argument into a tuple — so mean(91, 88) and mean(91, 88, 95) both work with no signature change. Inside, tuple skills (len, iteration) do the rest.
steps.code_snippet:
def mean(*numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

steps.title: 2. The caller with defaults
steps.desc: Required parameters come first; the two optional ones carry defaults. The body composes the helper — one job per function.
steps.code_snippet:
def report(name, marks, subject="Maths", pass_mark=40):
    average = mean(*marks)
    verdict = "PASS" if average >= pass_mark else "FAIL"
    print(f"{name} ({subject}): avg {average:.1f} -> {verdict}")

steps.title: 3. Call with positional and keyword arguments
steps.desc: The first call leans on both defaults; the second overrides them by name. Nothing about the function changes between the two.
steps.code_snippet:
report("Ada", [91, 88, 95])
# Ada (Maths): avg 91.3 -> PASS

report("Alan", [35, 42], subject="Science", pass_mark=50)
# Alan (Science): avg 38.5 -> FAIL

steps.title: 4. Notice the unpacking
steps.desc: marks arrives as a list; mean(*marks) unpacks it back into positional arguments. Packing (*args) and unpacking (*list) are the same star, used in two places.
steps.code_snippet:
scores = [70, 80]
print(mean(*scores))   # 75.0 — identical to mean(70, 80)

payload.solution: Two small functions, each with one job, compose into a grading toolkit. mean() accepts any number of scores via *numbers; report() carries sensible defaults it can override per call. Output: "Ada (Maths): avg 91.3 -> PASS" and "Alan (Science): avg 38.5 -> FAIL". One average bug fixed inside mean() would fix every caller at once.

payload.prompt: Write two functions and test them: (1) add_item(item, bucket=None) that appends to a freshly created list when bucket is omitted — call it twice with no bucket and prove the two results are separate lists; (2) format_line(label, value, width=12) that prints label left-aligned and value right-aligned using f-string specs. Then call format_line with the width overridden by keyword.

mistakes.mistake: def add(item, bucket=[]) — the default list that remembers
mistakes.fix: Default to None and build the list inside the body. Default values are created once at def time, so any mutable default is shared across all calls that omit it.

mistakes.mistake: Putting a required parameter after one with a default
mistakes.fix: def f(a=1, b) is a SyntaxError. Order parameters: required first, optional last — or give everything defaults deliberately.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing a function that prints with one that returns
mistakes.fix: print() ends the call and the expression evaluates to None. If you need the result later, return it: result = f(x) only works when f actually returns.

mistakes.mistake: Mutating the caller's list inside a function without saying so
mistakes.fix: Parameters reference the same objects (aliasing from Module 1), so append inside is visible outside. Either document the mutation loudly or return a new value instead.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What does this code print across three calls, and why?  def add(item, bucket=[]): bucket.append(item); return bucket  —  add("a"), add("b"), add("c")
payload.answer: The default list is created ONCE, when the def line executes, so every call that omits bucket shares that same list object. Results: first call ['a'], second ['a', 'b'], third ['a', 'b', 'c'] — the 'empty' default has been accumulating. The fix is the standard None pattern: def add(item, bucket=None): if bucket is None: bucket = [] — a new list is then created per call. This trap is a fixture of Python interviews precisely because it looks harmless and only misbehaves at run time.
payload.source: The most frequently recycled mutable-default question in Python interviews and exam papers.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: def names a block; the call expression evaluates to the return value, or None if there is no return.
Arguments are positional or keyword; defaults must trail required parameters.
Default values are evaluated once at definition time — never use a mutable ([] , {}) default; use None.
*args packs positionals into a tuple; **kwargs packs keywords into a dict; *mylist unpacks at the call site.
One function, one job — compose small functions instead of growing one big one.

questions.prompt: Which call is ILLEGAL for def f(a, b=2, c=3)?

questions.prompt: def f(*nums): return len(nums). The call f(1, 2, 3) returns:
questions.explanation: *nums collects all positionals into a tuple, whose length is 3.

questions.prompt: The correct pattern for a function that needs a fresh list default is:
options: def f(x, bucket=None) with creation inside
Any of the first two are fine
questions.explanation: Only None avoids the shared-mutable-default bug; the body then builds a new list per call.
