questions.explanation: Missing return means the call expression is None — a common source of "it worked when I printed it" bugs.

lessons.title: return, Scope & Why Your Variable Forgot Its Value
lessons.summary: Returning values (including pairs), the three channels a function can affect the caller through, local versus global scope, and the UnboundLocalError explained.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Return single and multiple values and unpack them at the call site
Distinguish return from print and from mutating an argument
Explain local scope and why assignment inside a function makes a name local
Fix an UnboundLocalError without resorting to careless global statements

payload.text: count = 0 at the top level; a function that does count = count + 1; one call. Python answers: UnboundLocalError: local variable 'count' referenced before assignment — even though count exists, right there, globally. Beginners stare at this for hours because the English reading ("just add one to the existing count") is perfectly reasonable. The Python reading is different, and once you have it, whole categories of "my variable forgot its value" bugs vanish.

**return hands a value back; print only talks to the screen.** A function body can end with `return <value>`, which immediately ends the function and makes the **call expression** evaluate to that value: `result = double(5)`. Without a return, the result is `None`. Functions may return several values at once by returning a tuple — `return min(xs), max(xs)` — which callers unpack: `lo, hi = stats(xs)`. An early `return` on its own (a guard clause) exits without a value, which is the clean way to refuse bad input:

```
def safe_div(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return None          # refuse early, cleanly
    return a / b
```

**Three channels from a function to the outside world.** Know which one you are using:
1. **return** — the preferred channel. The caller decides what happens next (`total = sum(xs)`).
2. **Print** — a side effect aimed at humans. Fine in scripts and during debugging; useless if you wanted the value (`y = print("hi")` leaves y as None).
3. **Mutation** — changing a passed object in place (`xs.append(1)` inside a function changes the caller's list, because both names reference one object — Module 1 aliasing again). Real code uses this (every list method does), but a function that mutates silently is a function callers must be warned about. Mixed "sometimes I return, sometimes I print, sometimes I mutate" functions are the hardest to test; keep each function on one channel.

**Scope: where names live.** A name created by assignment **inside** a function is **local** to that call: it exists while the function runs and disappears afterwards. You may freely **read** names defined outside (global scope, plus built-ins like `print` and `len`). But here is the rule that produces the famous error: **if a name is assigned anywhere inside a function, Python treats it as local everywhere inside that function.** So:

```
count = 0
def bump():
    count = count + 1     # UnboundLocalError
bump()
```

Because `count = ...` appears inside `bump`, the compiler marks `count` local for the entire body; the right-hand side then tries to read the local before it exists. The error message is accurate — it is not about your global at all.

**The clean fixes, in order of preference:**
1. **Pass the value in and return the new one:** `count = bump(count)` — no hidden state, trivially testable.
2. **Work on a local:** `def bump(): local = 1; return local` when the value starts inside.
3. **`global count`** at the top of the function opts into the global explicitly and makes the error go away — but it couples the function to distant state; use rarely, and only with a clear reason. (`nonlocal` is the same idea for an enclosing *function's* variable, which you will meet with nested closures later.)

**Name lookup, simplified.** When you use a name, Python checks: the function's **local** scope, then any **enclosing** function scopes, then the **global** module scope, then the **built-ins**. First hit wins. This also explains why naming a variable `list` or `sum` "works" until some line in the same scope needs the real builtin — do not shadow built-ins.

payload.title: A function's three outward channels
headers: When it is the right one
rows: Computing a value — the default choice
Reporting to a human; returns None
In-place update of data you own — document it

payload.code:
count = 0

def bump():
    count = count + 1   # local by rule -> UnboundLocalError

# Fix 1: pass in, return out
def bump(n):
    return n + 1

count = bump(count)      # count is now 1
print(count)

payload.title: Do not name variables after built-ins
payload.text: list = [1, 2] or sum = 0 shadows the built-in for the rest of the scope; later sum(xs) raises TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. Python will not stop you — style rules exist to stop you.

payload.title: Repair a function that mixes all three channels
payload.problem:
This crashes:  total = 0
def add_all(xs):
    for x in xs:
        total = total + x
        print("running total:", total)
    print("done")
print(add_all([1, 2, 3]))

Diagnose every problem, rewrite it, and state what the fixed version prints.

steps.title: 1. Diagnose the crash
steps.desc: The assignment total = total + x inside the function makes total local for the whole body, so the very first read raises UnboundLocalError — the global 0 is never consulted.

steps.title: 2. Give the function its own local
steps.desc: Start an accumulator inside, do the work, and RETURN the value instead of printing it. Now the function has one job: compute.

steps.title: 3. Let the caller decide what to do
steps.desc: Capture the return value at the top level and print there. The same function now works for summing, storing or feeding another calculation.
steps.code_snippet:
total = add_all([1, 2, 3])
print(total)   # 6

steps.title: 4. Verify the other paths
steps.desc: Empty list gives 0 (the loop simply never runs). Try add_all([]) — no crash, sensible answer. A function that returns a value on every path is a function callers can trust.
steps.code_snippet: print(add_all([]))   # 0

payload.solution: The original raised UnboundLocalError on the first iteration. The rewrite keeps the accumulator local, returns it, and lets the caller print: printing 6 for [1, 2, 3] and 0 for []. One channel per function — return here, print at the top level.

payload.title: Convert side effects into returns
payload.prompt: Take any function you wrote earlier that printed its answer. Rewrite it to RETURN the value instead, then write two new lines at the top level: one that stores the result in a variable and prints it later, and one that uses the result directly inside an f-string. Also reproduce the UnboundLocalError from the concept with your own variable name, read the exact error text, and fix it with the pass-in-return-out pattern.
payload.hint: If the error says "referenced before assignment", an assignment in the function made the name local — that is the clue, not a bug in your global.

mistakes.mistake: Reading a global inside a function and assigning to the same name
mistakes.fix: Assignment makes the name local throughout the function → UnboundLocalError. Pass the value as a parameter and return the new one; reach for global only with strong justification.

mistakes.mistake: y = print("something") and then using y
mistakes.fix: print returns None, so y is None and the next operation on it fails. Print for humans; return for values.

mistakes.mistake: A function that returns a value on some paths and falls off the end on others
mistakes.fix: Callers get None on those paths and crash three frames later. Make every path return, or return an explicit None as a documented sentinel.

mistakes.mistake: Naming a variable sum, list, input or type
mistakes.fix: You shadow the built-in for the rest of the scope and break later calls. Rename (total, items, raw, kind) — a rule formatters and linters will also flag.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Given a global count = 0 and a function containing count = count + 1, explain exactly why Python raises UnboundLocalError, and give the cleanest fix.
payload.answer: Python decides a name's scope at compile time, by scanning the function body: any assignment to a name makes that name LOCAL for the entire function, not just from that line onward. So inside bump(), count is local everywhere; the right-hand side count + 1 tries to read the local before it has been assigned, and Python raises UnboundLocalError at that moment — the global count is irrelevant to the lookup. Cleanest fix: count = bump(count) where bump takes the current value as a parameter and returns the incremented one. Alternatives are a local accumulator returned at the end, or an explicit global count declaration (works, but hides coupling and is discouraged).
payload.source: Standard scope question in Python exams and screening tests; the exact error text is practically an interview meme.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: return ends the function and makes the call expression yield the value; several values return as a tuple.
Functions reach outside via return, print or mutation — pick one per function and be explicit.
Names assigned inside a function are local everywhere inside it, even before the assignment line.
UnboundLocalError means the name was local by rule, not missing — fix by passing values in and returning them.
Do not shadow built-ins (list, sum, type, input); name lookup is local → enclosing → global → built-in.

bump()

lessons.title: Imports, pip, Virtual Environments & Notebooks
lessons.summary: How Python finds modules, installing packages with pip, isolating projects with venv, and the notebook workflow AI work actually uses.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use the four common import forms and explain how Python locates a module
Install and pin packages with pip, including python -m pip
Create, activate and use a virtual environment for one project
Set up a notebook or Colab workflow with installs and recorded requirements

payload.text: Your script imports pandas perfectly in the terminal. You paste the same line into Jupyter and get ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'. Neither program is broken — they are two different Pythons with two different package collections, and nobody told you. This lesson is the map of that hidden landscape; without it, half of every AI course you take is spent fighting the environment instead of learning.

**import: how Python finds other code.** A **module** is a .py file; a **package** is a folder of modules (often with an __init__.py). The forms you will use daily:
- `import math` then `math.sqrt(25)` — the whole module under a prefix. Clear provenance; the default style.
- `from math import sqrt` then `sqrt(25)` — pull specific names. Handy, but two modules with the same name (two different `plot` functions) then collide.
- `import numpy as np` — an alias. `np.` is such a strong convention in data science that code without it reads oddly.
- `from math import *` — imports everything. Avoid it outside quick experiments: it pollutes the namespace and hides where names came from.

When you import, Python looks in a fixed order: built-in modules first, then the folder of your script, then the entries of **sys.path** (which includes the environment's **site-packages** — where pip installs things). A `ModuleNotFoundError` means nothing on that path matched: usually, the package is not installed in the environment you are currently running.

**pip: installing from PyPI.** The Python Package Index hosts hundreds of thousands of open-source packages; `pip install pandas` fetches the latest compatible build and drops it into the current environment's site-packages. Daily commands: `pip list` (what is installed), `pip show pandas` (version and location), `pip install pandas==2.2.2` (pin an exact version — reproducibility), `pip install -r requirements.txt` (install everything a project lists). When several Pythons exist on one machine, prefer the unambiguous form `python3 -m pip install pandas`: that guarantees you are installing into the same interpreter that will run the code.

**Virtual environments: one package shelf per project.** Without isolation, every project shares one global site-packages, so installing "pandas 2.x" for project B silently upgrades project A — which needed 1.x — and both break. A **venv** is a folder containing a private interpreter plus its own empty site-packages:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv              # create (folder .venv/)
source .venv/bin/activate          # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate             # Windows
python -m pip install pandas       # installs INTO the venv
deactivate                         # leave the venv
```

While activated, your shell shows a (.venv) prefix and `python` and `pip` point inside the folder. Two clarifications that save confusion later: a venv does **not** copy the standard library (math, json, csv are shared — only third-party packages are isolated), and the venv folder should never be committed to git (add .venv to .gitignore).

**Recording and reusing.** `python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt` writes the exact installed versions. Anyone — including future you on a new laptop — rebuilds the whole environment in three commands: create venv, activate, `pip install -r requirements.txt`. For AI work this is the professional default: one venv per project, a requirements file in the repo, and a notebook or script per experiment. In **Colab**, installs are per-session: run `%pip install package` in a cell (prefer `%pip` over `!pip` — it targets the running kernel's interpreter), and remember the session is wiped when it ends. Locally in Jupyter, select the venv's interpreter as the notebook kernel so the notebook and the environment are the same Python.

rows: Pinned list to rebuild an environment

payload.title: One venv per project, always
payload.text: Name it .venv in the project root, activate before any pip or python work in that folder, and treat "did you activate the venv?" as the first question whenever something imports wrongly.

payload.title: pip installed it — but into which Python?
payload.text: If your terminal imports fine and Jupyter does not (or vice versa), you installed into one environment and are running in another. Check with python -m pip --version and align the notebook kernel with the environment.

payload.title: Set up a clean project from zero
payload.problem: Create a project folder marks-analysis that needs pandas only. End with: an isolated environment, pandas installed and importable, a requirements file, and confidence that a classmate can rebuild it.

steps.title: 1. Create and enter the environment
steps.desc: The venv lives inside the project folder as .venv — after activation, every python and pip in this shell points at it.
steps.code_snippet:
mkdir marks-analysis
cd marks-analysis
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

steps.title: 2. Install into it, then verify the import
steps.desc: python -m pip ties the install to the interpreter you will run. The python -c one-liner imports without creating a file — the fastest existence check there is.
steps.code_snippet:
python -m pip install pandas
python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
# e.g. 2.2.2

steps.title: 3. Record the exact versions
steps.desc: Freeze writes a pinned list. Commit this file to version control with your code — it is the recipe for the whole environment.
steps.code_snippet:
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
# requirements.txt now contains a line like: pandas==2.2.2

steps.title: 4. Prove it rebuilds anywhere
steps.desc: A classmate (or you, next month) needs only these three commands to reproduce your exact environment — no guessing which packages, no version roulette.
steps.code_snippet:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

payload.solution: A .venv holds pandas alone; requirements.txt pins it; the import check confirms the running interpreter sees it. Notebooks in this project should select this venv as their kernel (or run %pip install pandas in Colab, understanding the session is temporary). Environment trouble shrinks to one question: which Python am I in right now?

payload.title: Build and rebuild an environment
payload.prompt: In a new folder: create a venv, activate it, install the requests package, verify with python -c "import requests; print(requests.__version__)", write requirements.txt, deactivate, then delete the venv and rebuild it from the requirements file alone. Time how long the rebuild takes.
payload.hint: If import fails after activation, check you used python -m pip (not a pip bound to another interpreter) and that the activation ran in this shell.

mistakes.mistake: pip install into the system Python "because it is quicker"
mistakes.fix: You pollute a shared environment and create future version conflicts. Thirty seconds of venv setup saves the afternoon later — always.

mistakes.mistake: Installing a package in the terminal and expecting Jupyter to see it
mistakes.fix: Different interpreters, different site-packages. Point the notebook kernel at the venv, or install inside the notebook with %pip install.

mistakes.mistake: Using !pip install in a notebook by habit
mistakes.fix: !pip runs whatever pip is first on the shell PATH; %pip targets the running kernel's environment. Prefer %pip — it removes the whole class of mismatch.

mistakes.mistake: Never recording dependencies
mistakes.fix: Without requirements.txt, nobody — including future you — can rebuild the project. Freeze after every meaningful install; commit the file.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is a virtual environment, why do Python projects use one, and what does it NOT contain?
payload.answer: A virtual environment is a self-contained directory (created by python -m venv .venv) holding a copy (symlink or launcher) of a Python interpreter plus its own private site-packages folder. Projects use one because pip installs into the *current* environment: sharing a single global site-packages means project B's upgrades can break project A's pinned versions — the classic dependency conflict. With a venv, each project gets exactly the packages it needs, activated via a shell script, and pinned in requirements.txt for reproducibility. Crucially, a venv does NOT contain a copy of the standard library (math, json, os and friends are shared with the base interpreter); it isolates only third-party packages.
payload.source: Evergreen interview question for any data/ML tooling round; also common in university practical exams.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: import pulls in modules; prefer import x / import x as np over from-imports and never wildcard in real code.
pip installs from PyPI into the CURRENT environment; python -m pip removes the multi-interpreter ambiguity.
A venv is a per-project interpreter plus empty site-packages — activate it before installing or running.
The standard library is shared; only third-party packages are isolated.
requirements.txt (pip freeze) makes an environment rebuildable anywhere — the backbone of reproducible AI work.
Colab sessions are rented: %pip installs work until the session ends.

lessons.title: Docstrings, Naming & Code Others Can Read
lessons.summary: Writing docstrings that document contracts, PEP 8 naming conventions, comments versus names, and refactoring unreadable code into small named functions.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write one-line and multi-line docstrings and retrieve them with help()
Apply PEP 8 naming conventions to variables, functions, classes and constants
Refactor a dense script into small functions with meaningful names
Explain the difference between a comment, a docstring and a good name

payload.text: A recruiter once let candidates debug a function on a whiteboard. The code was correct; the names were x, t, a2 and temp. Nobody finished — not because the logic was hard, but because reading consumed all the time. Code is read far more often than it is written, and in AI especially your future self reading a six-month-old notebook is the most important reader you will ever write for.

**Readability is a functional requirement.** Python's own design documents treat style as part of the language: the Zen of Python (type `import this` at a REPL) says "Readability counts" and "Namespaces are one honking great idea — let's do more of those!". In practice readability comes from three sources, in order of impact: **good names**, **docstrings**, and **comments** — with linters and formatters enforcing the mechanical parts so you can spend attention on the semantic ones.

**Docstrings: the contract of a function.** A string literal placed as the first statement of a function (module or class) is its docstring — documentation that lives inside the code, travels with it, and is readable at any REPL:

```
def mean(*numbers):
    """Return the arithmetic mean of the given numbers."""
```

That one-liner style is the everyday standard: state WHAT the callable delivers, and any sharp edges — never HOW the body works (the body already shows how). Richer callables get multi-line docstrings:

```
def grade(name, marks, pass_mark=40):
    """Print a pass/fail line for one student.

    Args:
        name: student identifier
        marks: list of numeric marks
        pass_mark: threshold for a PASS (default 40)
    """
```

Docstrings are stored in the callable's `__doc__` attribute: `help(grade)` prints it at the REPL, `grade?` shows it in Jupyter, and every editor surfaces it as a tooltip. Try writing the docstring **before** the body — if you cannot state the contract in a line, the function is probably doing too much.

**Comments, and what they are for.** A comment explains **why** a non-obvious choice exists: a workaround for a library bug, a business rule, a constraint. It does not restate the line (`i = i + 1  # increment i` adds noise, not meaning). Dead code should be deleted, not commented out — version control remembers it. Docstrings say **what**; comments say **why**; names carry the rest.

**PEP 8 naming — the conventions that make Python look like Python:**

| Entity | Convention | Example |
| Variables, parameters, functions | snake_case | total_marks, is_valid, grade_report() |
| Classes | CamelCase | StudentRecord, GradeBook |
| Modules, packages | short lowercase | student_tools.py |
| Constants | ALL_CAPS | MAX_RETRIES = 5, PASS_MARK = 40 |
| Internal helpers | leading underscore | _parse_row() |
| Booleans | is_ / has_ / can_ | is_empty, has_marks |

These are not enforced by the interpreter — `Total Marks` would run — but they are enforced by every reviewer, linter and codebase you will ever join. Shadowing built-ins (`list`, `sum`, `type`, `input`) is a related sin: it works until a line needs the real built-in.

**Structure habits that compound.** One function, one job — if a function needs a comment explaining "mode 2", it wants to be two functions. Prefer early guard-clause returns over deep nesting. Keep lines under roughly 88–100 characters; four-space indents; blank line between functions. Auto-formatters (black is the standard) apply all of this mechanically, which is exactly why Python teams argue about logic, not spacing.

payload.title: Three documentation tools, three jobs
rows: Why was this written this way?

payload.code:
def percent_at_or_above(marks, threshold):
    """Return the percentage of marks that are >= threshold."""
    passed = sum(1 for m in marks if m >= threshold)
    return passed / len(marks) * 100

print(percent_at_or_above([70, 90, 40, 60], 50))   # 75.0
help(percent_at_or_above)

payload.title: Read your diff aloud
payload.text: If a colleague could not guess what a changed line does from its name and the surrounding docstring, rename before you commit. The rename costs thirty seconds; the confused review costs an hour.

payload.title: Refactor an unreadable function
payload.problem:
Improve this without changing its behaviour:  def f(a, b):
    t = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        if a[i] >= b:
            t = t + 1
    return t / len(a) * 100

print(f([70, 90, 40, 60], 50))

Say what it computes, rename it, document it, and remove the indexing loop.

steps.title: 1. Reverse-engineer the behaviour
steps.desc: It counts how many entries of a are at least b, divides by the total, and scales to a percentage — "what percentage of marks cleared the threshold?". The call therefore prints 75.0 (three of four).

steps.title: 2. Name everything for the domain
steps.desc: f → percent_at_or_above, a → marks, b → threshold, t → passed. Add a one-line docstring stating the contract. Instantly readable — no comment needed.
steps.code_snippet:
def percent_at_or_above(marks, threshold):
    """Return the percentage of marks that are >= threshold."""

steps.title: 3. Replace index-walking with iteration
steps.desc: range(len(a)) with a[i] is a C habit, not a Python one. Iterate values directly, and count with a generator expression inside sum(). A guard clause handles the empty list — the original divided by zero here.
steps.code_snippet:
if not marks:
        return 0.0
    passed = sum(1 for m in marks if m >= threshold)
    return passed / len(marks) * 100

steps.title: 4. Verify identical behaviour on the old and new paths
steps.desc: Same call, same answer — plus the new empty-list path returns 0.0 instead of raising ZeroDivisionError. Refactoring improves structure; checking outputs proves it changed nothing else.
steps.code_snippet:
print(percent_at_or_above([70, 90, 40, 60], 50))   # 75.0
print(percent_at_or_above([], 50))                  # 0.0

payload.solution: The opaque f() became percent_at_or_above(marks, threshold) — same 75.0 result, a documented contract, readable iteration, and a safe empty-list path. Every name now answers "what does this mean in the gradebook?" without a single explanatory comment.

mistakes.fix: Document the contract: inputs, output, side effects, sharp edges. The body already shows the how; readers need the what and the why.

mistakes.mistake: Names like x1, temp, data_final_v2 for domain concepts
mistakes.fix: Rename to what they mean: marks, raw_line, active_students. If you struggle to name it, that is a signal the thing is doing two jobs.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Distinguish a comment, a docstring and a well-chosen identifier as forms of documentation, giving a good example of each.
payload.answer: A comment (`# API throttles to 1 req/s — retry above that`) explains WHY and lives only in the source; the interpreter ignores it. A docstring is a string literal as the first statement of a function/class/module, stored in __doc__, surfaced by help() and editors, and documents WHAT the callable promises ("""Return the mean of numbers, or None if empty.""" ). A good identifier (`pass_mark`, `active_students`) documents meaning at every use site and costs nothing at run time. Priority: get the name right, add the docstring for the contract, and use comments only for the non-obvious why — everything else is noise reviewers will ask you to remove.
payload.source: Common code-quality discussion question in interviews; also standard in Python style (PEP 257/8) exam units.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Docstrings document the contract of a function; help() and __doc__ display them at any time.
Write what a callable promises, not how its body works; the one-liner style is the daily standard.
Names do most of the documentation work: snake_case variables/functions, CamelCase classes, ALL_CAPS constants.
Comments explain why; docstrings explain what; delete dead code rather than commenting it out.
Refactor in steps: rename, extract small functions, replace index loops with iteration — then verify identical output.

Immediately before the def line, as a comment

options: The signature only, never the docstring
An error if the function has no arguments

questions.prompt: Which naming is correct for a class, a function and a constant respectively?
questions.explanation: PEP 8: CamelCase for classes, snake_case for functions and variables, ALL_CAPS for constants.

questions.explanation: Modes usually mean two jobs; separate functions with clear names remove the need for the explanatory comment entirely.

modules.title: Module 4 — Control Flow, Errors & Debugging
modules.summary: Conditional logic with if/elif/else, loops with for/while and break/continue, exceptions and try/except/finally with real traceback reading, and a repeatable method for debugging and testing small functions.

lessons.title: if / elif / else: Decisions That Do Not Lie
lessons.summary: Boolean conditions, comparison and logical operators, truthiness done deliberately, and branch chains whose boundaries are actually right.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write conditions using comparison operators, and/or/not and membership tests
Structure multi-way branches with if/elif/else so exactly one path runs
Apply truthiness rules on purpose (falsy values) instead of by accident
Order threshold branches from strictest to loosest so boundaries fall correctly

payload.text: An attendance script asked "is there a reason for the absence?" with if reason_text: — and since input() always returns a string, typing nothing was the only way to fail the check. Every typed excuse, including "x", counted. The branch logic was syntactically perfect and semantically wrong. Conditions are where programs first learn to lie to you, so this lesson treats them as the precision instrument they are.

**What an if statement does.** An `if` evaluates a condition and runs its indented block **only** when that condition is True. Syntax is fixed: the header ends with a colon, the block is indented (four spaces, consistently — mixing indents is a TabError), and one or more statements live in the block:

```
if marks >= 75:
    eligible = True
    print("Eligible")
```

The condition is any expression that produces a bool. Comparisons: `==` (equal), `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Logical operators are written as words: `and`, `or`, `not`. Python also allows the mathematical chaining you cannot write in most languages: `60 <= marks < 75` is one normal condition, and `a == b == c` compares all three.

**elif and else: one chain, one winner.** `elif` (never "else if") adds further conditions; `else` catches everything left and must come last. At most **one** branch of the chain runs — Python tests in order and stops at the first True condition:

```
if marks >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif marks >= 75:
    grade = "B"
elif marks >= 60:
    grade = "C"
else:
    grade = "F"
```

Order matters when thresholds overlap: put the **strictest** condition first. If you tested `marks >= 60` first, every score of 95 would match C and stop the chain — the classic off-by-branch bug. An `else` is optional; leaving it out means nothing forces a default, which is a deliberate choice in guard-heavy code.

**Short-circuit evaluation.** `and` stops at the first False operand; `or` stops at the first True. That is not trivia — it is a safety tool: `if xs and xs[0] > 0:` never evaluates `xs[0]` when the list is empty, because `xs` is already False. You will use that guard pattern permanently.

**Truthiness: every value already has a boolean answer.** Conditions do not require `== True`. Python calls these **falsy**: `False`, `None`, `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()`. Nearly everything else is truthy — including `"False"`, `[0]` and any non-empty container. So `if items:` means "the list has at least one element" and `if name:` means "a non-empty string". The sharp edge: `0` and `""` are perfectly valid **data** that also happen to be falsy. When "was anything provided?" matters more than "is it non-empty?", ask precisely: `if marks is not None:`. And membership reads like English: `if "ada" in roster:`, `if key not in counts:` — on a dict or set this is the fast O(1) test from Module 2.

payload.title: Falsy and truthy — the values that surprise people
rows: Any non-empty string, including one with spaces

payload.title: Float equality is a trap
payload.text: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False in floating point. Compare with tolerance instead: abs(total - expected) < 1e-9, or the library helper math.isclose(a, b). Exact == on computed floats is a bug waiting for a different machine.

payload.title: A grading function with honest boundaries
payload.problem: Write grade(marks) returning "A" for >= 90, "B" for >= 75, "C" for >= 60, "F" below, and "INVALID" for marks that are None or outside 0–100. Test every boundary: 90, 89.9, 75, 60, 59.9, None, 101.

steps.title: 1. Guard the invalid cases first
steps.desc: A guard clause at the top refuses bad data immediately and keeps the rest of the function free of nested ifs. Note "is None" — not "== None" — for the missing-value check.

steps.title: 2. Chain the thresholds, strictest first
steps.desc: Each valid branch returns at once, so exactly one decision runs per call. Order 90 → 75 → 60 guarantees a 95 can never be caught by a looser threshold.

steps.title: 3. Test the boundaries, not just the middles
steps.desc: Boundary values are where branch logic breaks. 89.9 must be B, not A; 60 must be C, not F. Testing 75 alone would prove almost nothing.

steps.title: 4. Expected output — read the edges closely
steps.desc: Every boundary lands one side of the line exactly as specified, and both invalid inputs come back as text instead of an exception.

payload.solution: Guard clause first, then a strict-to-loose chain of early returns. The same logic as a full if/elif/else would nest one level deeper for no benefit. Boundary tests confirm each edge: 89.9 is B, 60 is C, 59.9 is F, and invalid inputs return "INVALID" instead of raising — a function whose behaviour you can trust at every threshold.

payload.title: Ticket pricing with real guards
payload.prompt: Write ticket_price(age) returning "INVALID" for None or ages outside 0–120, "child" (< 12), "adult" (12–59) and "senior" (>= 60). Then add a second function that multiplies the price (300 / 700 / 400) by quantity, refusing non-positive quantities with "INVALID". Test ages 11, 12, 59, 60 and the boundary of the quantity rule.
payload.hint: Guard clause, then thresholds from strictest to loosest — same shape as the worked example, different domain words.

mistakes.mistake: Writing if marks = 75: in a condition
mistakes.fix: Assignment inside a condition is a SyntaxError in modern Python — the language is protecting you. Compare with ==.

mistakes.mistake: Loose threshold before strict threshold in the same chain
mistakes.fix: The first True branch wins, so marks >= 60 before marks >= 90 steals every A student. Order conditions from strictest to loosest.

mistakes.mistake: Treating if x: as "the user provided a value"
mistakes.fix: 0, 0.0, "" and [] are falsy but perfectly valid. When absence matters, ask about absence: if x is None: — not if x:.

mistakes.mistake: Exact equality on computed floats
mistakes.fix: Binary floating point makes 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. Compare with a tolerance (abs(a - b) < 1e-9) or math.isclose().

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain short-circuit evaluation of and and/or, and give one defensive use of it.
payload.answer: With and, Python evaluates operands left to right and returns False as soon as one is falsy — later operands are never evaluated. With or, it returns True at the first truthy operand. Defensive use: if xs and xs[0] > 0 avoids IndexError on an empty list, because xs being [] already makes the and False and Python skips xs[0] entirely. Similarly if value is not None and value.strip(): tests presence before calling a method. Short-circuiting is not an optimisation detail — it is how Python expresses safe guards in a single condition.
payload.source: Common theory question in university exams; also used as a live whiteboard probe in interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: if runs its indented block only for a True condition; elif adds tested alternatives; else catches the rest.
Exactly one branch of a chain runs; order overlapping thresholds from strictest to loosest.
and/or/not are the logical operators; and/or short-circuit, which powers safe guards like xs and xs[0].
Falsy: None, 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, set() — everything else truthy; use is None when absence is the real question.
Membership (in / not in) reads like English and is O(1) on dicts and sets.

questions.prompt: What happens with if marks = 75: in Python 3?
questions.explanation: Assignment is banned inside conditions by the compiler; comparisons use ==.

questions.prompt: With the chain >= 90 A, >= 75 B, >= 60 C, what does grade(89.9) return?
questions.explanation: 89.9 fails the >= 90 test and matches the next strictest branch: B.

questions.prompt: Which value evaluates to False inside an if?
questions.explanation: Empty containers are falsy; the others are non-empty and therefore truthy.

questions.prompt: and and or are said to short-circuit because:
options: They run faster than bitwise operators
They stop evaluating operands once the result is determined
They convert operands to int first
They only work on bool objects
questions.explanation: and returns False at the first falsy operand; or returns True at the first truthy one — later operands are skipped entirely.

lessons.title: for and while: Loops That Finish
lessons.summary: Iterating with for and range, condition-driven while loops, break and continue, and the two off-by-one traps that cause most loop bugs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Iterate lists, strings, dicts and ranges with for, using enumerate when positions matter
Use range(start, stop, step) and predict its exact contents
Write a while loop with an explicit update and kill infinite loops deliberately
Control flow with break and continue, and explain the loop-else clause

payload.text: range(1, 10) was meant to print 1 to 10. It printed 1 to 9 — every single time, for an entire cohort. The stop value is excluded in Python, and that one half-open convention also explains list slices and why for i in range(len(xs)) so often ends in IndexError. One convention, learned once, kills an entire family of off-by-one bugs.

**for walks an iterable, element by element.** `for item in collection:` binds `item` to each element in turn and runs the block. Lists, strings (one character at a time), dicts (keys by default), sets, ranges — and later, pandas columns and NumPy arrays — are all iterable:

```
for name in ["Ada", "Alan"]:
    print(name)

for ch in "Hi":
    print(ch)          # H, then i
```

When you need positions too, use `enumerate` rather than indexing: `for i, name in enumerate(names, start=1):`. Index-walking (`for i in range(len(xs)):`) is occasionally necessary, but enumerate says the same thing without the noise.

**range(start, stop, step) — always half-open.** `range(5)` is 0,1,2,3,4 — the stop value is **never included**. `range(2, 7)` is 2,3,4,5,6. `range(1, 11, 2)` is 1,3,5,7,9. Steps can be negative: `range(10, 0, -2)` is 10,8,6,4,2. The trap to memorise: wanting "1 to 10" means `range(1, 11)`. The same exclusive-stop convention governs slices (`xs[:10]` takes indices 0–9), so it is one rule applied everywhere.

**while: loop while a condition holds.** Use `while` when you do not know the count in advance — waiting for valid input, retrying a request, converging towards a tolerance:

```
attempts = 0
while attempts < 3:
    # ... do something ...
    attempts += 1
```

Every while loop needs a **guaranteed path to False**: a counter that grows, a flag that flips, or a sentinel value. Forget that update and the loop never ends. If one does spin, Ctrl+C in the terminal (or Interrupt kernel in Jupyter) stops it — learn that shortcut before you need it at 1 a.m.

**break and continue.** `break` leaves the **innermost** loop immediately; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and tests the condition again. Typical pairs: search-then-stop (break once found) and skip-noise (continue past rows you do not want). Use them sparingly — a loop stuffed with breaks is a function that needs splitting.

**The loop-else clause.** A loop may carry an `else` block that runs **only if the loop finished normally — i.e. break was never hit**. It reads oddly until you see the use case: a search that reports failure only when the search actually failed:

```
for x in xs:
    if is_prime(x):
        print("found", x)
        break
else:
    print("no prime found")
```

The else belongs to the for, not to the if — a confusion so common it is a fixture of exams.

**Do not mutate the thing you are iterating.** Appending to or removing from the list inside its own loop skips elements (Python walks by position, not by content). Iterate a copy (`for x in xs[:]`) or build a new list with a comprehension instead.

payload.title: for or while — which loop, when
rows: Stop when the change is small enough

payload.title: Ask what makes the while False
payload.text: Before running any while loop, name the line that will end it. If you cannot point at it, the loop is infinite by construction.

payload.title: A validated retry loop that always terminates
payload.problem: Ask the user for a whole number between 1 and 10, up to three attempts. On a valid entry, print it and stop; on invalid text or out-of-range values, warn and retry; after three failures, report failure. The loop must end no matter what the user does.

steps.title: 1. The skeleton with a guaranteed exit
steps.desc: A counter that increases every attempt makes the condition (attempts < 3) False after three passes — termination guaranteed even if every input is junk.
steps.code_snippet:
attempts = 0
while attempts < 3:
    raw = input("Number 1-10: ")
    attempts += 1
    # validation goes here

steps.title: 2. Validate with continue, succeed with break
steps.desc: The isdigit check short-circuits: if the text is not numeric, int(raw) never runs, so no ValueError can escape. continue retries; break exits on success.
steps.code_snippet:
if not raw.isdigit() or not (1 <= int(raw) <= 10):
        print("Invalid — try again.")
        continue
    print(f"You entered {raw}")
    break

steps.title: 3. Report failure with loop-else
steps.desc: The else runs only when the loop ended WITHOUT break — exactly the "all attempts failed" case, with no extra flag variable.
steps.code_snippet:
else:
    print("Three failed attempts.")

steps.title: 4. Walk both paths
steps.desc: Valid input on the first try: one prompt, success message, else skipped. Three junk inputs: three prompts, then the else prints. There is no fourth path.
steps.code_snippet:
# Path A: "7"     -> "You entered 7"
# Path B: x,x,x   -> three warnings, then "Three failed attempts."

payload.solution: A while loop bounded by an attempts counter, continue for bad input, break for success, and loop-else for the failure report. Termination is structural, not hopeful: no matter what is typed, this program ends within three prompts.

payload.title: Sentinel total and a filtered walk
payload.prompt: Write two loops: (1) a while loop that repeatedly asks for a number, adding each to a running total, and stops when the user types "done" — print the total at the end; (2) a for loop over words = ["cat", "", "dog", "  ", "bird"] that prints only non-empty words after stripping, using continue to skip the blanks. Then rewrite loop (2) with a list comprehension.
payload.hint: Compare raw == "done" before converting; in the comprehension, put the strip in the expression and the filter after the for.

mistakes.mistake: Writing range(1, 10) expecting it to include 10
mistakes.fix: Stop is exclusive: range(1, 11) gives 1..10. The same half-open rule governs every slice in Python.

mistakes.mistake: A while loop whose condition variable never changes
mistakes.fix: Infinite loop. Make the update unavoidable: increment a counter at the top of the body, or break on a sentinel the user can actually type.

mistakes.mistake: Appending to or removing from the list being iterated
mistakes.fix: Python walks by position, so shifting elements skips or repeats items. Iterate a copy (xs[:]) or build a fresh list with a comprehension.

mistakes.mistake: Reading the loop-else as an else for the nearest if
mistakes.fix: The else belongs to the for/while and runs only when the loop ended without break. Rename it mentally to "if the loop never broke".

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What does the else clause attached to a for loop do, and when is it useful? Give one example.
payload.answer: A for...else runs its else block ONLY when the loop completed its iterations without executing break — that is, nothing in the loop early-exited it. If break ran, the else is skipped. Useful for search: scan the collection, break on the first match, and let the else handle the 'not found' case without a found-flag variable. Example: for x in xs: if x > 100: print('found', x); break / else: print('no value above 100'). The pitfall is that readers pair else with the nearest if; the language pairs it with the loop.
payload.source: A favourite short-answer question in Python exams precisely because the pairing confuses people.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: for walks any iterable; use enumerate when you need positions, not manual indices.
range is half-open: range(1, 11) is 1..10 — the same exclusive-stop rule as slices.
while fits unknown iteration counts; every while needs a guaranteed route to False.
break exits the innermost loop; continue skips to the next iteration; both sparingly.
loop-else runs only when no break happened — the built-in "not found" handler.
Never mutate a collection while iterating it; iterate a copy or rebuild with a comprehension.

questions.prompt: How many values does list(range(2, 10, 2)) contain, and what are they?
questions.explanation: Start at 2, step 2, stop before 10 → [2, 4, 6, 8].

questions.prompt: Inside a loop, continue causes:
options: The rest of the current iteration to be skipped
questions.explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration; break is the one that ends the loop.

questions.prompt: A for...else block runs when:
options: The loop body raises an exception
The loop finished without executing break
The else belongs to the last if inside the loop
questions.explanation: else signals "no break happened" — the natural place for not-found handling.

questions.prompt: A while loop is the right choice when:
options: The number of iterations is not known in advance
You want a for-loop with fewer lines
The loop body runs exactly once
questions.explanation: while re-tests its condition each pass — ideal for input validation, retries and convergence.

lessons.title: Errors & try/except: Reading Tracebacks Like a Pro
lessons.summary: Exception types, traceback anatomy, try/except/else/finally, and recovering from bad input without hiding real bugs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Name the common exception types and predict which one a snippet raises
Read a traceback bottom-up to locate the failing line and the cause
Write try/except/else/finally that catches only the expected failure
Build a validated-input loop that recovers from bad user entries

payload.text: A wall of red text ends with one line that contains the entire diagnosis: ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc'. Most beginners scroll to the top in panic and read the traceback like a novel, top to bottom. Professionals read it like a verdict: last line first, then the nearest frame in their own file. Same text, ten times the speed — this lesson teaches the reading order.

**Exceptions are objects that signal trouble.** When something goes wrong, Python **raises** an exception; if no handler exists, the program stops and prints a traceback. The types you will meet in this course, and what each actually means:

| Exception | Raised when | Example |
| TypeError | Right type of operation, wrong type of value | "a" + 1, len(5) |
| ValueError | Right type, bad value | int("abc"), float("12x") |
| IndexError | Position does not exist | xs[99] on a 3-item list |
| KeyError | Dict key does not exist | counts["missing"] |
| ZeroDivisionError | Division by zero | 10 / 0 |
| AttributeError | Object has no such method/attr | s.lenght (typo) |
| FileNotFoundError | open() on a missing path | open("nope.txt") |
| ModuleNotFoundError | An import cannot be resolved | pandas not installed |
| UnboundLocalError | Local name read before assignment | the count = count + 1 trap |

Note the division of labour that trips people: `int("abc")` is a **ValueError** (the type is right — string — but the contents are not a number), while `"a" + 1` is a **TypeError** (string plus int is meaningless at all).

**Anatomy of a traceback — read it bottom-up.** The final line is the verdict: exception type, then a human message naming the specifics. Above it, frames list the call chain, most recent call last, each with file, line number and the source line that was executing:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "marks.py", line 2, in <module>
    total = total + float(raw)
ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc'
```

Reading order: (1) the last line — type and message; (2) the **last frame whose file is your code** — that is the failing line; (3) the values that fed that line. The message here even quotes the offending text. You do not need to understand every frame; the top frames are usually library plumbing.

**try/except: handle what you expect.**

```
raw = input("Marks: ")
try:
    marks = float(raw)
except ValueError:
    print("Please type a number like 87.5")
else:
    print(f"Got {marks}")          # runs ONLY if try succeeded
finally:
    print("Input step complete")   # ALWAYS runs
```

The professional rules:
1. **Catch the narrowest useful type.** `except ValueError:` documents your expectation. A bare `except:` swallows everything — including KeyboardInterrupt and your own bugs — and turns a loud failure into a silent wrong answer.
2. **Handle or re-raise.** If you cannot meaningfully recover, let the exception propagate. `except: pass` is a code smell that has shipped production outages.
3. **else runs on success, finally runs always** — finally is for cleanup (closing a file, printing a summary), never for the main logic.
4. **Bind the details:** `except ValueError as e:` lets you print the message (e) or log it.

**Validated input — the pattern you will reuse forever.** Combine the retry loop (4.2) with try/except (here). Keep the `try` **inside** the loop, around the single conversion statement:

```
while True:
    raw = input("Marks (0-100): ")
    try:
        marks = float(raw)
    except ValueError:
        print("Type a number, please.")
        continue
    if 0 <= marks <= 100:
        break
    print("Out of range — try again.")
```

Scope the try tightly: the smaller the try block, the clearer which statement failed and the less real bug gets accidentally caught.

payload.title: Traceback reading order
payload.text: Last line (verdict) → last frame in YOUR file (failing line) → values on that line. Only then scroll up. If the traceback ends inside library code, your bug is usually in the data or arguments you handed it.

payload.title: Never catch what you cannot handle
payload.text: except: pass hides crashes until a user finds them. Catch specific types, and if recovery is impossible, re-raise or let it propagate — a loud failure beats a silent wrong number.

payload.title: Parse a messy CSV line without crashing
payload.problem: A line from a broken export reads "87,92,abc,76". Convert every field to a float, report the total of the valid ones and list the rejected fields — one bad value must not abort the rest.

steps.title: 1. Split into fields
steps.desc: str.split(",") turns the line into a list of four candidate numbers, including the poison pill "abc".
steps.code_snippet:
line = "87,92,abc,76"
fields = line.split(",")

steps.title: 2. Convert field by field, with try INSIDE the loop
steps.desc: The narrow try wraps only the risky conversion. A ValueError from one field is caught, recorded, and the loop moves on — other exception types still crash loudly, which is exactly what we want.

steps.title: 3. Report honestly
steps.desc: State both the partial success and the rejects — never silently drop data. The counts should add up: 3 valid + 1 rejected = 4 fields.
steps.code_snippet:
print(f"Total of {len(fields) - len(bad)} values: {total}")
print(f"Rejected: {bad}")

steps.title: 4. Expected output
steps.desc: 87 + 92 + 76 = 255.0 across three values; "abc" is named rather than hidden. Delete the bad row upstream later — but the parser survived to tell you about it.
steps.code_snippet:
# Total of 3 values: 255.0
# Rejected: ['abc']

payload.solution: A per-field try/except ValueError caught exactly the expected failure and continued: total 255.0 over three values, rejected ["abc"]. Compare with one big try around the whole loop — a single bad field would have aborted everything, and the except could not have said which field failed. Narrow scope is what makes exception handling honest.

payload.title: Recover, then file-check
payload.prompt: Write two programs: (1) the validated-input loop from the concept, run it with "abc", "150", then "87.5" and observe all three messages; (2) a snippet that tries to open "notes.txt" and catches FileNotFoundError as e, printing a friendly message including the missing filename from e. Create the file and re-run to prove the success path still works.
payload.hint: In program (2), the filename is inside the exception: print(f"Could not open: {e.filename}").

mistakes.mistake: Catching bare except (or except Exception: pass)
mistakes.fix: It hides every failure, including KeyboardInterrupt and your own bugs. Catch the specific type you expect — ValueError for conversions, KeyError for lookups, FileNotFoundError for paths.

mistakes.mistake: Wrapping an entire program in one try block
mistakes.fix: The except cannot tell you which line failed and may catch unrelated bugs. Wrap only the risky statement — usually one conversion, one open, one lookup.

mistakes.mistake: Reading the traceback top-down in a panic
mistakes.fix: Read the last line first (type + message), then the last frame in your own file. That is the failing line; everything above it is context.

mistakes.mistake: Continuing after an except with a variable never assigned
mistakes.fix: If float(raw) fails, marks never exists — the next line raises NameError. Assign a sentinel (marks = None) and re-check it, or re-loop until the value is valid.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain exactly when the try, except, else and finally blocks execute, using an example that converts user input to a float.
payload.answer: try: the code you consider risky runs first; if it completes without an exception, the rest of the try is skipped as finished. except ValueError: runs only when a ValueError is raised inside the try — other exception types propagate. else: runs only when the try completed successfully (no exception) — a natural place for code that needs the converted value. finally: runs no matter what — success, exception, or even a return/break leaving the block — which makes it the right home for cleanup (closing files, printing progress), never for main logic. In the input example: bad text → except; good text → else; every run → finally.
payload.source: A near-guaranteed question in Python unit tests and interview screens.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Exceptions distinguish wrong TYPE (TypeError) from right-type-wrong-value (ValueError) and missing access (IndexError/KeyError).
Read tracebacks bottom-up: verdict line, then the last frame in your own file.
try holds the risky statement; except names the expected failure; else runs on success; finally always runs.
Catch narrow, handle or re-raise — bare except and pass hide real bugs as silent wrong answers.
Validated input = retry loop with try around the single conversion inside it.

lessons.title: Debugging Methodically & Testing Small Functions
lessons.summary: A repeatable debug loop (reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, fix, prevent), print-based debugging done properly, and asserts that stop bugs from coming back.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply the reproduce–isolate–hypothesise–fix–prevent loop to a real bug
Use targeted debug prints (type, length, repr) to expose assumptions
Write assert-based tests for a small pure function including boundary cases
Distinguish crash bugs from silent wrong-answer bugs and pick the right tool

payload.text: A function returns 50.0 where everyone expects 75.0. No crash, no traceback — just a quietly wrong number that passed review and showed up in a submission. Crashing bugs are loud; wrong-answer bugs are silent, and they are the ones that matter. The difference between a two-hour panic and a ten-minute fix is not intelligence — it is a method, which this lesson hands you in full.

**Debugging is a process, not a talent.** The professional loop, in order:
1. **Reproduce.** Find the smallest input that shows the failure. Three numbers you can check by hand beat three thousand you cannot. If you cannot reproduce it, you have not found the bug yet — "it happens sometimes" is an unsolved reproduction, not a bug report.
2. **Read what the program says.** Traceback (4.3) if it crashed. If it did not crash, the program is not talking — so you make it talk (step 3).
3. **Isolate.** Shrink inputs, cut unrelated code, and interrogate the values: `print(type(x), len(x))`, `print(repr(x))` (repr shows quotes around strings and makes None or an empty string obvious). The bug lives in the gap between what you assume the value is and what it actually is.
4. **Hypothesise, then test one belief.** "I bet the list is empty on the last pass" is a hypothesis; one print proves or kills it. Changing three things at once and re-running proves nothing — you are not running an experiment, you are rolling dice.
5. **Fix minimally and verify both ways.** Make the smallest change that addresses the hypothesis; re-run the reproduction, then re-run your earlier working cases to confirm nothing else broke.
6. **Prevent recurrence.** Ask how the bug got in (no test at that boundary? misleading name?) and leave a test behind. A bug found twice is a process failure.

**Print debugging, done properly.** Vague prints (`print("here")`) waste time. Useful debug prints answer questions: what is the type, how long is it, what is the exact value?
`print(f"DEBUG rows={len(rows)} first={rows[0]!r}")` — the `!r` conversion shows the repr, so strings display with quotes, None is unmistakable, and trailing spaces become visible. Keep prints labelled (DEBUG prefix), and delete or gate them before you commit. When prints proliferate, Python's built-in debugger arrives with one keyword: `breakpoint()` (3.7+) drops you into a `(Pdb)` prompt where `p name` prints a variable, `n` executes the next line, `c` continues, `q` quits. For code the size of this course, disciplined prints are usually faster — but know the next tool exists.

**Testing: the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.** A **pure function** (same inputs → same output, no side effects) is trivially testable: write down input/output pairs you can compute by hand and assert them:

```
def percent_at_or_above(marks, threshold):
    """Return the percentage of marks that are >= threshold."""
    if not marks:
        return 0.0
    return sum(1 for m in marks if m >= threshold) / len(marks) * 100

def test_percent():
    assert percent_at_or_above([70, 90, 40, 60], 50) == 75.0
    assert percent_at_or_above([], 50) == 0.0
    assert percent_at_or_above([50], 50) == 100.0
    print("all tests passed")
```

`assert condition, "message"` raises AssertionError when the condition is false and does nothing otherwise. Test **boundaries**: empty input, one element, values exactly at the threshold, duplicates, negatives. Boundaries find more bugs per line than any random big input — branch logic almost always breaks at its edges. Later, the pytest framework collects functions named `test_*` and runs them all; the habit of naming test functions from day one costs nothing and scales to any project.

**Bug taxonomy — match the symptom to the tool.** A crash gives a traceback (read it). A silent wrong answer needs intermediate-value prints (no exception will ever point at the bug). "Works here, fails there" is usually environment (Module 3: which Python, which packages). Slowness is usually algorithm (Module 2: a list scan inside a loop). Naming the class of bug in the first ten minutes saves the next fifty.

payload.title: Debug at toy scale
payload.text: Shrink the dataset until the wrong answer still appears with values you can compute on paper. The bug that survives toy scale is the real bug; the one that vanishes was an environment or data-volume issue.

payload.title: A fix without a reproduction is a guess
payload.text: You cannot verify a fix for something you cannot repeat. And if the fix holds, add the reproduction as an assert — otherwise the bug will be back in three refactors, and it will deny everything.

payload.title: Hunt a silent wrong-answer bug, step by step
payload.problem: average([70, 80, 50]) returns 50.0, but the mean of the passing marks (those above 60) is 75.0. There is no exception — just a wrong number. Find and fix it, then leave a test behind.

steps.title: 1. Reproduce small and compute the answer by hand
steps.desc: Three numbers you can add on paper. Passing marks are 70 and 80; their mean is 150/2 = 75.0. The program says 50.0 — a silent wrong answer, no traceback to lean on.

steps.title: 2. Interrogate the intermediates
steps.desc: One targeted print inside the loop shows the mechanism immediately: 50 is excluded from the total, yet len(xs) still counts it. The numerator and denominator disagree about what is being averaged.

steps.title: 3. Form one hypothesis and fix it minimally
steps.desc: Hypothesis: the denominator counts rejected values. Fix: filter FIRST, then average the filtered list — numerator and denominator now describe the same set.

steps.title: 4. Verify, then leave a guard behind
steps.desc: The reproduction now gives 75.0. Two asserts — including the empty-passing case — make this bug unable to return quietly.
steps.code_snippet:
assert average([70, 80, 50]) == 75.0
assert average([50, 55]) == 0.0
print("all tests passed")

payload.solution: The loop added only passing marks to the total but divided by every mark. Filtering first (kept = [x for x in xs if x > 60]) aligns both sides: average([70, 80, 50]) is now 75.0, and the two asserts lock the behaviour — including the zero-passing edge — so a future edit that reintroduces the mismatch fails loudly instead of quietly.

mistakes.mistake: Changing code before you can reproduce the failure
mistakes.fix: You cannot confirm a fix for an unreproducible bug. Freeze a failing input first — it becomes your regression test the moment the fix lands.

mistakes.mistake: Editing three things between runs
mistakes.fix: One hypothesis, one change, one run. Otherwise a green result tells you nothing about which change did it.

mistakes.mistake: Adding except: pass while debugging
mistakes.fix: Hiding the exception hides the evidence. Let errors be loud until the very end of the session; only then decide how to handle them properly.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting one successful run as "it works"
mistakes.fix: Test boundaries: empty input, a single element, values exactly at a threshold, duplicates, negatives. Almost every real bug hides at an edge, not in the middle.

payload.question: Describe, in order, the steps you would take when a Python function returns a plausible but incorrect value with no exception raised.
payload.answer: 1) Reproduce with the smallest input you can verify by hand — silent bugs are invisible at scale. 2) Since no traceback exists, print the intermediates (values, types, lengths, repr) around the suspect logic; wrong-answer bugs are found by inspection, not by the interpreter. 3) Isolate: shrink the input and the code path until the gap between expected and actual is on one line. 4) State a specific hypothesis about that line, change one thing, and re-run. 5) Verify both the original reproduction and the previously working cases. 6) Convert the reproduction into an assert (regression test) so the class of bug cannot return silently. Emphasise that for silent bugs, intermediate-value prints and hand-computed expectations replace the traceback as the diagnostic instrument.

assert locks behaviour: test boundaries (empty, single, exact-threshold, negative) — they find the most bugs.

lessons.title: NumPy Arrays vs Python Lists: dtype, Shape & Memory
lessons.summary: What an ndarray actually stores, how it is created, and why one block of typed memory beats a list of Python objects for AI work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Import NumPy and create arrays with array, zeros, ones, full, arange and linspace
Read an array's shape, dtype, size and ndim and explain what each means
Explain why a homogeneous numeric array is smaller and faster than a list of numbers
Convert between lists and arrays and predict which operations copy and which mutate

payload.text: Two lines, both legal, both completely different: [1, 2, 3] + [4, 5, 6] glues two lists into [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], while np.array([1, 2, 3]) + np.array([4, 5, 6]) adds element-wise and answers [5, 7, 9]. The same operator, two different worlds. Every AI library you meet — pandas, PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn — lives in the second world, and this lesson is the border crossing.

**What NumPy is.** NumPy (Numerical Python) is the foundation of the entire Python data stack: `import numpy as np` is the first line of nearly every data notebook ever written. Its core object is the **ndarray** — a fixed-size, multidimensional array of *homogeneous* raw data. pandas DataFrames are column-stacks of ndarrays under the hood; deep-learning tensors copy its shape-and-dtype design; when code "goes numeric" in Python, it goes through something shaped like this.

**A list of numbers versus an array of numbers.** A Python list is an array of **references** to full Python objects: every element is a tagged, reference-counted object that could live anywhere in memory — and could be a different type from its neighbours. A NumPy array is one **contiguous block of raw memory** of a single fixed type (dtype), plus a small header recording shape and strides. Four consequences, all of which you will feel:
1. **Memory.** A float64 in an array is 8 raw bytes. The same number in a list is a Python object costing several times that, plus the pointer in the list. A million numbers: ~8 MB as an array versus tens of MB as a list.
2. **Speed.** Array arithmetic runs as a compiled C loop over raw memory — no per-element type checks, no object creation. This is why Python, despite being a slow interpreter, is the language of AI: the heavy loops never run in Python.
3. **Homogeneity.** One dtype per array. `np.array([1, "two"])` coerces everything to text (`<U21` — unicode strings) — usually a signal that something upstream went wrong, not a feature.
4. **Element-wise operators.** Lists concatenate with +; arrays add with +. Array comparison (`>`, `==`) yields a boolean **mask array**, not a single bool — the seed of the filtering you will do in every ML pipeline.

**Creating arrays.**
```
a = np.array([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])      # from a list
np.zeros((2, 3))                   # 2×3 of 0.0 (float by default)
np.ones(4)                         # four 1.0s
np.full((2, 2), 7)                 # fill with a constant
np.arange(0, 10, 2)                # [0 2 4 6 8] — the range() of arrays
np.linspace(0, 1, 5)               # five evenly spaced points from 0 to 1
np.eye(3)                          # identity matrix
```
Note the default: `zeros` and `ones` produce **float64** arrays, because floating point is the default currency of numeric work.

**The four attributes you check on every array:**
- `a.shape` — tuple of sizes per dimension: `(3, 4)` is 3 rows × 4 columns.
- `a.dtype` — element type: int64, float64, bool, <U21 (text).
- `a.size` — total element count (the product of shape).
- `a.ndim` — number of dimensions.

**Reshape, convert, and who owns the memory.** `a.reshape(2, 3)` reinterprets the same elements with a new shape (a **view** when the layout allows — writes can be visible to the original; covered properly in Lesson 5.3). `a.astype(np.float32)` makes a converted **copy** with a new dtype. `a.tolist()` returns a plain Python list copy; `np.array(some_list)` copies list data into a fresh buffer — mutating one afterwards never touches the other.

import numpy as np

Every step was deliberate about copies versus views — the discipline that Module 5 is built to install.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why a NumPy array of a million float64 values is both smaller and faster to process than a Python list of the same million numbers.
payload.answer: Storage: the array holds one contiguous block of 8-byte raw float64 values plus one small header (shape, dtype, strides) — about 8 MB total. The list holds a million pointers, each pointing to a separate Python float OBJECT that carries a type tag, reference count and value (tens of bytes apiece, allocated wherever the allocator found room) — tens of MB, scattered in memory. Speed: array arithmetic executes as a compiled C loop over that contiguous buffer, with none of Python's per-element dispatch, type checks or object creation; list arithmetic must fetch, type-check and construct a new Python object per element through the interpreter. Contiguous storage also fits cache lines far better. That combination — C-loop execution over raw memory, orchestrated by Python one call at a time — is why Python became the language of numerical AI despite the interpreter itself being slow.
payload.source: The standard "why NumPy?" question in data-science interviews; also a favourite in university DS exams.

lessons.title: Vectorization: Why NumPy Is Fast
lessons.summary: Whole-array arithmetic, boolean masks for filtering and counting, and the measured difference between a Python loop and one vectorised call.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define vectorisation and explain where the time saved actually goes
Apply arithmetic, comparison and logical operations to whole arrays
Filter, count and summarise data with boolean masks
Convert a per-element Python loop into its vectorised equivalent

payload.text: Square a million numbers with a list comprehension, then with one array expression. The stopwatch shows the array call finishing tens of times faster — and that is a deliberately boring example. Real models perform this kind of arithmetic billions of times per training run; without vectorised kernels underneath, modern AI in Python would not exist. Vectorisation is not a micro-optimisation. It is the reason the stack works at all.

**What vectorisation is.** A **vectorised operation** is one call that applies an operation to every element of an array, executed as a compiled loop inside NumPy rather than a Python-level loop. `a * 2`, `a + b`, `np.sqrt(a)`, `a ** 2`, `a > 60` — each is a single Python-level dispatch that hands the whole array to a C kernel. The interpreter runs once; the per-element work never touches a Python object. Measured on a million elements, vectorised arithmetic typically runs **10× to 100×** faster than the equivalent list loop — plus it allocates one result array instead of a million temporary objects.

**Where the list loop spends its life.** For each element: dereference the pointer, read the type tag, decide which C function implements the operation for those types, execute it, build a *new* Python object for the result, store a reference. That per-element dispatch is roughly a hundred times the cost of the raw arithmetic itself. NumPy's kernels skip all of it: one loop over a pointer, multiply, store — a loop so tight the compiler vectorises it with CPU SIMD instructions. Python orchestrates; C computes. That is the whole architecture of numerical Python.

**The operations you now have:**
- **Arithmetic** — `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b`, `a / b`, `a ** 2`, scalar mixing (`a * 0.01`): all element-wise, all one call.
- **Comparison → boolean mask** — `passed = scores >= 60` yields an array of True/False the same shape as scores. Masks are questions you ask of the whole dataset at once:
  `scores[passed]` (the passing scores), `passed.sum()` (how many — True counts as 1), `passed.mean()` (the fraction passing, since mean of booleans is their rate).
- **Mask algebra** — combine questions with `&` (and), `|` (or), `~` (not): `senior_pass = (marks >= 60) & (ages >= 60)`. Parentheses are mandatory because `&` binds *tighter* than comparisons: `marks > 60 & ages > 60` means something else entirely, and nothing stops you writing it.
- **Reductions (preview)** — `a.sum()`, `a.mean()`, `a.min()`, `a.max()`, `a.std()` collapse an array to a scalar; the axis versions arrive in Lesson 5.4.
- **Conditional slices** — `a[a < 0].mean()` averages only the negatives (check `a.any()` first — an empty selection gives nan and a RuntimeWarning).

**When a loop is still the right tool.** Vectorise *numeric, element-wise* work over large data. Keep the Python loop when the per-item work is heavy and irregular: opening files, parsing text, branching on complex logic, a few thousand iterations. Real AI code is layered exactly this way — a Python loop over epochs and batches, inside which every numeric step is a vectorised call. Knowing which layer a piece of logic belongs to is half of writing fast numerical Python.

**Measure honestly.** In notebooks, `%timeit expression` reports a robust timing; in scripts, the `timeit` module. Benchmark at realistic sizes (a thousand elements measure interpreter noise; a million measure the algorithm), and compare like with like — including import costs and any data conversion.

payload.title: One million elements: where the time goes
rows: One raw operation in a C loop

payload.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([55, 72, 90, 41, 88, 63, 95, 70, 38, 84])
passed = scores >= 60

print(passed)                 # [False  True  True False  True  True  True  True False  True]
print(passed.sum())           # 7 — number of True
print(f"{passed.mean():.0%}") # 70% — fraction of True
print(scores[passed])         # [72 90 88 63 95 70 84]

payload.title: and/or/not versus &/|/~
payload.text: Python's and/or/not demand single boolean values and raise "ambiguous truth value" on arrays. Arrays use the element-wise operators & | ~ — always with parentheses: (a > 0) & (a < 1).

payload.title: Filter and scale a million scores the vectorised way
payload.problem: scores = np.array([55, 72, 90, 41, 88, 63, 95, 70, 38, 84]). Report (a) how many scores passed (>= 60) and the pass rate, (b) the mean of the passers, (c) every score min-max scaled to the 0–1 range — all without writing a single for loop.

steps.title: 1. Ask the question once, as a mask
steps.desc: One comparison produces a boolean array. sum() counts the Trues; mean() of booleans is their rate — True is 1, False is 0.
steps.code_snippet:
passed = scores >= 60
print(passed.sum())                 # 7
print(f"{passed.mean():.0%}")       # 70%

steps.title: 2. Select with the mask, then reduce
steps.desc: scores[passed] is a new 1-D array of the seven passing scores; calling .mean() on it is one more vectorised reduction. 562 / 7 is about 80.3.
steps.code_snippet: print(f"{scores[passed].mean():.1f}")   # 80.3

steps.title: 3. Scale with array arithmetic
steps.desc: Min-max scaling is three vectorised steps: subtract the minimum, divide by the range. Scalars broadcast against the whole array (Lesson 5.4) — no loop anywhere.
steps.code_snippet:
scaled = (scores - scores.min()) / (scores.max() - scores.min())
print(np.round(scaled[:3], 3))     # [0.298 0.596 0.912]

steps.title: 4. Watch the loop version lose
steps.desc: The list version must do per-element Python arithmetic on a million items; on typical hardware it is an order of magnitude slower than the array expression — same maths, different execution model.
steps.code_snippet:
big = np.random.randn(1_000_000)
xs = big.tolist()
# %timeit [(x - big.min()) / (big.max() - big.min()) for x in xs]   # ~10x slower than the vector form
# %timeit (big - big.min()) / (big.max() - big.min())

payload.solution: Mask once (7 of 10 passed — 70%), reduce the selection (mean 80.3), scale everything with three array expressions (first values ≈ 0.298, 0.596, 0.912). One Python-level dispatch per operation; all per-element work in C. The list-comprehension version computes identical numbers roughly ten times slower — and that gap only widens with size.

mistakes.mistake: Using Python's and / or / not on arrays
mistakes.fix: They raise ValueError: truth value of an array is ambiguous. Use & | ~ with parentheses — (a > 0) & (a < 1).

mistakes.mistake: Writing a > 60 & b < 30 without parentheses
mistakes.fix: & binds tighter than comparison operators, so this parses as a > (60 & b) < 30 — nonsense or an error. Always bracket the comparisons first.

mistakes.mistake: Hand-looping a vectorisable operation over a large array
mistakes.fix: If the per-item work is element-wise arithmetic or comparison, express it as one array operation. Keep loops for heavy per-item logic (I/O, parsing, branching).

mistakes.fix: a[a > limit].mean() on an empty selection returns nan with a RuntimeWarning. Guard with if a[mask].size: (or mask.any()) before reporting.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is vectorisation, and why can Python — a slow interpreted language — be the leading language for numerical AI work?
payload.answer: Vectorisation means expressing an operation once so that it is applied to an entire array by a compiled kernel, rather than element-by-element through the Python interpreter. NumPy stores data as contiguous typed buffers and implements each operation as a tight C loop (often using CPU SIMD instructions), so the per-element work has none of Python's type-checking, object-creation or interpreter-dispatch overhead — typically 10–100× faster than an equivalent list loop. The Python layer only orchestrates: one interpreter call dispatches a whole-array operation. Every higher library (pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow) follows the same architecture — slow, flexible Python on the outside; fast, fixed kernels on the inside. That division of labour is precisely why Python is viable for training and serving models despite the interpreter itself being slow.
payload.source: The architecture question behind almost every "Python performance" discussion in ML interviews.
