lessons.title: Indexing, Fancy Indexing & Slicing in NumPy
lessons.summary: 2-D indexing with [row, col], slices and steps, boolean and integer-array indexing — and the view-versus-copy rules that cause silent data bugs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Index and slice 1-D and 2-D arrays with start:stop:step on each axis
Select arbitrary elements with boolean masks and integer-array (fancy) indexing
State which operations return views and which return copies, and verify with shares_memory
Extract single rows, columns and submatrices idiomatically

payload.text: sub = grades[:3]; sub[0, 0] = 99 — and three rows of the original dataset changed with it. No warning, no error, correct-looking code. NumPy slices are **views**: they share the same memory. This is the single most common silent bug in numerical Python, it has caused wrong results in published research, and it takes one paragraph to understand plus one habit (.copy()) to never be bitten by again.

**The half-open rule carries over — the memory semantics do not.** Indexing and slicing follow everything you know: `a[0]`, `a[-1]`, `a[1:4]`, `a[::2]`, `a[::-1]` — start included, stop excluded, optional step. But NumPy's basic slicing returns a **view**: a window onto the **same underlying buffer**. `sub = a[:3]` does not copy nine values; it creates a lightweight array object with its own shape/strides pointing at the same memory. Writing through the view writes to the original. `np.shares_memory(a, sub)` returns True — use it whenever unsure; `sub = a[:3].copy()` buys independence when you need it. Views exist because copying a 4 GB dataset to look at part of it would be absurd; the price is vigilance.

**2-D indexing: the comma is the axis separator.** For `m` of shape (4, 3):
- `m[i, j]` — the single element at row i, column j (idiomatic; `m[i][j]` also works but builds a temporary).
- `m[i]` — row i, as a 1-D **view**.
- `m[:, j]` — column j (the colon means "everything on this axis"), also a view.
- `m[0:2, 1:3]` — a submatrix window (rows 0–1, columns 1–2), a view.
Three dimensions show up immediately in images (height × width × channels): `img[r, c, :` is one pixel's channels.

**Boolean mask indexing — always a copy.** The mask must have the same shape as the array (or match the indexed axis):
- `a[a > 60]` — the selected values, flattened into a new 1-D array.
- `a[a < 0] = 0` — assignment through a mask **does** modify the original in place (the selection is a copy; the *write* targets the matching positions).
- `m[m > 90]` works on a 2-D array and returns a 1-D result — selections flatten; shapes do not survive.

**Fancy (integer-array) indexing — also a copy.** Pass arrays of indices to collect arbitrary positions, honouring order and repeats:
```
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
idx = np.array([3, 0, 0, 1])
a[idx]          # array([40, 10, 10, 20])
```
On 2-D data, index rows and columns separately: `m[[0, 2], :` takes rows 0 and 2; `m[:, [1, 3]]` takes columns 1 and 3. One nuance worth knowing before it surprises you: `m[[0, 2], [1, 3]]` **pairs** the indices — it returns elements (0,1) and (2,3), a 1-D result of length 2 — not the 2×2 submatrix. The submatrix needs `m[np.ix_([0, 2], [1, 3])]`. When fancy shapes look wrong, print the result's .shape and re-read this rule.

**The view/copy cheat sheet — pin this to your notes:**

| Operation | Returns |
| Basic slicing a[1:3] | view (shared memory) |
| m[i], m[:, j] row/column picks | view |
| Boolean mask a[mask] (read) | copy |
| Fancy index a[[0, 2]] | copy |
| a.astype(dtype) | copy |
| a.reshape(...) | view when possible |
| a.copy() | copy |

The asymmetry is deliberate: *slices* are cheap windows; *selections* must gather scattered elements into new memory anyway, so they hand you independence for free.

payload.question: Contrast basic slicing with boolean-mask and fancy indexing in NumPy with respect to memory sharing, and give the danger each behaviour creates.
payload.answer: Basic slicing (a[1:4], m[0], m[:, 1]) returns a VIEW: a lightweight array over the SAME buffer, so np.shares_memory(a, view) is True and writes through the view silently modify the original — the danger is unintended data corruption (or, conversely, 'fixing' a slice and wondering why the source changed). Boolean masks and integer-array (fancy) indexing return COPIES: gathered into fresh memory, independent of the source — the danger is the mirror image: edits to the selection do NOT propagate where a developer expected them to, and memory doubles for large selections. astype and tolist also copy; reshape usually views. The professional habit is to decide deliberately: slice to look, slice.copy() to own.

lessons.title: Broadcasting, Reductions by Axis & Random Numbers
lessons.summary: Arithmetic between different shapes, sum/mean/std along an axis, and seeded random sampling — the three habits behind every normalisation pipeline.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply the broadcasting shape rules and fix a non-broadcastable shape error
Use sum, mean, min and max with axis=0 and axis=1 on 2-D arrays
Standardise a dataset column-wise using keepdims broadcasting
Generate reproducible random numbers with a seeded default_rng

payload.text: One line of machine learning hygiene — z = (data - data.mean(axis=0)) / data.std(axis=0, keepdims=True) — standardises every feature of a dataset with no loops anywhere. It works because of two quiet superpowers: reductions that collapse an axis, and broadcasting that stretches a result back across the data. Add seeded randomness and you have the three habits behind every normalisation, split and sampling step you will ever run.

**Broadcasting: arithmetic between shapes that are not equal.** NumPy stretches the smaller array along missing or length-1 dimensions instead of refusing the operation. The rules, precisely:
1. Align shapes **right-to-left**.
2. Each pair of dimensions must be **equal, or one of them must be 1**.
3. The result shape is the element-wise maximum of the two.

```
m = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])       # (2, 3)
v = np.array([10, 20, 30])      # (3,)
m - v                           # (2, 3) — each row gets v applied
```

v is treated as (1, 3), then stretched to (2, 3) — *conceptually*: the kernel loops with tiny strides rather than materialising a full copy, so broadcasting is both convenient and cheap. Scalars (shape ()) broadcast against everything: `m * 2`, `m - m.mean()`. When the rule breaks — `(2, 3) + (2,)` — NumPy raises "operands could not be broadcast together", because 3 and 2 match with neither equal nor 1. The famous near-miss: you meant to add a per-**row** vector to a (2, 3) matrix, but wrote a (2,) array; the fix is `v.reshape(2, 1)`, a (2, **1**) column that broadcasts across columns.

**Reductions along an axis.** Aggregates collapse data:
- `m.sum()` — everything → scalar.
- `m.sum(axis=0)` — collapse the **row** axis → per-column totals, shape (3,).
- `m.sum(axis=1)` — collapse the **columns** → per-row totals, shape (2,).
The mnemonic that never fails: **axis=k is the axis that disappears.** `mean`, `min`, `max`, `std`, `any`, `all` all take axis the same way — `m.mean(axis=1)` is each student's average when rows are students and columns are tests. `keepdims=True` keeps the collapsed axis as a length-1 dimension, which is exactly what you need so the result broadcasts cleanly against the original: `m.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)` is shape (1, 3) — one mean per column, ready to subtract from every row.

**Standardising — the ML ritual.** Column-standardise: subtract each column's mean, divide by each column's standard deviation:
```
z = (data - data.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)) / data.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
```
After this, every feature has mean ≈ 0 and std ≈ 1 — the precondition of gradient descent, distance-based models and most normalisation advice you will hear. One expression, two axis-reductions, one broadcast — the whole module in a single line.

**Random numbers, reproducibly.** Modern NumPy builds a generator object; the seed makes "random" repeatable:
```
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
rng.random(3)                 # three uniforms in [0, 1)
rng.normal(0, 1, 100)         # 100 draws from a standard normal
rng.integers(1, 7, 5)         # five dice rolls, 1..6 inclusive of start, exclusive of stop
rng.choice(["cat", "dog"], size=4)   # sample labels
```
Reproducibility is not a nicety: every train/test split, initial weight and shuffle in a real project must be regenerable, or nobody — including you next month — can reproduce a result. Seed for anything you report; leave unseeded for pure exploration. Note the same half-open habit as range: integers(1, 7) gives 1–6.

payload.problem: data = np.array([[5.0, 10.0, 15.0], [6.0, 12.0, 18.0], [4.0, 8.0, 12.0]]) — three samples × three features. Column-standardise it: each feature should end with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, computed without a single loop.

steps.title: 1. Inspect, then reduce along rows
steps.desc: axis=0 collapses the row axis, leaving one statistic per column. The means come out as [5, 10, 15] — one clean reduction call.

steps.title: 2. Same for the standard deviations, keeping dims
steps.desc: keepdims=True leaves the result as (1, 3) instead of (3,) — the same numbers, but shaped to broadcast down every row without any reshape call.

col_std = data.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
print(col_std.shape)   # (1, 3)

steps.title: 3. One broadcasting expression does the rest

steps.code_snippet: z = (data - col_mean) / col_std

steps.desc: Round away floating-point dust (means land at ~1e-16, not exactly 0) and check: every column now averages 0 with standard deviation 1.

print(np.round(z.std(axis=0), 10))    # [1. 1. 1.]

payload.solution: Two axis-0 reductions with keepdims=True produced per-column statistics shaped (1, 3); broadcasting stretched them across the rows in one arithmetic expression; verification shows column means of 0 and standard deviations of 1 (after rounding floating-point dust). Three concepts from this lesson — axis, keepdims, broadcasting — combined into the standardisation ritual used in every ML pipeline you will ever run.

payload.answer: Rules: align shapes right-to-left; each dimension pair must be equal or contain a 1; the result takes the element-wise maximum shape. (2, 3) + (3,): the 3s match, and the missing leading dimension of the vector is treated as 1, which broadcasts against the 2 — conceptually (1, 3) stretched to (2, 3), so each row receives the vector. (2, 3) + (2,): aligning right gives 3 vs 2 — neither equal nor 1 — and there is nothing on the left of the vector to balance the remaining 2, so NumPy raises a broadcast error. Fix depends on intent: per-column application keeps the (3,) vector as-is; per-row application reshapes it to (2, 1), a column that broadcasts across the three columns.

lessons.title: Series & DataFrame: The Two Objects Everything Rests On
lessons.summary: What a Series and a DataFrame actually store, how the index works, the attributes you read on every table, and the column-selection idioms.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create Series and DataFrames from dictionaries and lists
Explain the index as labels and read shape, dtypes, columns and index on any table
Select a single column as a Series and a column subset as a DataFrame
Describe how pandas columns rest on NumPy arrays under the hood

payload.text: Every data job on Earth starts the same way: pd.read_csv(...), then df.head(). Two lines, one object — the DataFrame — and most people never learn what is actually inside it. Understanding the anatomy (labels, columns, dtypes, index) is the difference between using pandas and being used by its surprises.

**pandas in one sentence.** pandas (from "panel data", imported as `import pandas as pd`) is the Python library for labelled tables. Its two objects are all you need for the next five modules: the **Series** (one labelled column) and the **DataFrame** (a table of aligned Series).

**The Series: 1-D labels + values.** A Series is a NumPy array with an **index** attached — an array of labels, one per value:
```
cities = pd.Series(
    ["Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi"],
    index=["c1", "c2", "c3"],
    name="city",
)
cities["c2"]    # "Pune" — label lookup, not position 2
```
The default index is 0..n-1 (a RangeIndex), but any labels work: ids, dates, strings. Values carry one dtype (NumPy heritage); the index is itself a pandas object with its own dtype.

**The DataFrame: a table of aligned Series.** A DataFrame is a set of Series that **share one index** — rows line up by label, columns may each have their own dtype:
```
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":  ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"],   # object (text)
    "marks": [85, 92, 78],                # int64
    "passed": [True, True, False],        # bool
})
```
A dict of equal-length lists is the most common constructor; a list of row-dicts and a 2-D array plus columns= also work. Internally each column is typically one contiguous ndarray — which is why column-wise operations stay vectorised at C speed (Module 5 all the way down).

**The attributes you read on every table, every time:**
- `df.shape` — (rows, columns).
- `df.columns` — the column-label Index.
- `df.index` — the row-label Index.
- `df.dtypes` — one dtype per column.
- `len(df)` — row count; `df.size` — total cells.
- `df.head(n)` — first n rows (default 5) — the sanity glance.

**Column selection — two shapes, one meaning.** `df["marks"]` (or `df.marks`, with caveats) returns a **Series** — one column. `df[["marks"]]` — a list, even of one — returns a **DataFrame** — a table. Same data, different contract: a DataFrame keeps column names and dtypes for the next chained call. Row selection is label-based (`df.loc`) or position-based (`df.iloc`) — both arrive properly in Lesson 6.3.

**Adding columns.** `df["pct"] = df["marks"] / 100` assigns a whole Series aligned on the index — the vectorised NumPy expression becomes a new column. Assignment by label is how every feature in an ML pipeline is born.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the relationship between a DataFrame, its columns and NumPy arrays. Why can pandas load a million-row CSV quickly and compute a column mean at near-C speed?
payload.answer: A DataFrame is a collection of Series that share one row index. Each Series wraps one-dimensional labelled data whose values are, in the common case, a single contiguous NumPy ndarray of one dtype — so a DataFrame is heterogeneous across columns but homogeneous within each. That design lets pandas load a CSV by allocating one typed column buffer per column (no per-cell Python objects) and lets column operations like df["marks"].mean() dispatch straight into NumPy's compiled reduction kernels. Python orchestrates the table logic (labels, alignment, joins); C computes the numbers — the same division of labour that made NumPy fast, now applied column-wise.

lessons.title: read_csv & the Inspection Ritual
lessons.summary: Loading CSVs correctly and the six-readout inspection (head, shape, dtypes, info, describe, missing counts) that finds dirty data before it finds you.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Load a CSV from a path or URL with pd.read_csv and its key parameters
Run head, shape, dtypes, info, describe and value_counts and interpret each output
Count missing values per column with isna().sum()
Spot a numeric column stored as text and plan its repair

payload.text: A model trained on data nobody inspected is a confident machine for producing garbage. Ninety percent of real data work is the inspection you do in the first ten minutes after loading — and this lesson turns that ten minutes into a ritual you never skip.

**pd.read_csv — the front door.** The simplest call loads a comma-separated file (or URL) into a DataFrame, guessing dtypes from the first rows:
```
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df = pd.read_csv("https://example.com/data.csv", nrows=1000)  # preview big files
```
Parameters you will actually use: `sep` for other delimiters (a tab-separated file needs the two-character string backslash-t), `usecols` to load a subset, `parse_dates=["date"]` to build real datetimes, `na_values=["NA", "-", ""]` to teach pandas what "missing" looks like in this file, and `nrows` to preview a file too big for RAM. read_csv infers types by sampling values — an inference, not a guarantee. That is why the next step is never analysis. It is inspection.

**The inspection ritual — six readouts, in order:**
1. `df.head()` — does the data match the schema? Wrong header rows, shifted columns and mojibake show up here.
2. `df.shape` — (rows, columns). Remember this number; filters and drops must be reconciled against it.
3. `df.dtypes` — one type per column. "Looks numeric, stored as object" lives here.
4. `df.info()` — dtypes plus non-null counts plus memory. Count < rows means missing values, and it prints them per column in one screen.
5. `df.describe()` — count/mean/std/min/25%/50%/75%/max for numeric columns. The 50% row is the median; count below shape[0] is the missing-value signal again.
6. `df["col"].value_counts()` — for any category-like column: which levels exist, how rare is the rare one.

**Reading the red flags.** An object-dtype column of "prices" means pandas met a non-numeric character (₹, commas, stray spaces) and kept everything as text — `pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")` converts, turning the junk into NaN you can count and fix consciously (Lesson 8.3 makes this a pipeline step). A float column where you expected ints usually means NaNs (float is the only numeric type that holds NaN). Duplicate-looking categories ("delhi" vs "Delhi ") reveal themselves in value_counts. The ritual does not fix anything — it tells you what to fix, in order of damage.

payload.title: The inspection menu
rows: Does it look like the schema?
Rows lost or gained during load

payload.code:
from io import StringIO
import pandas as pd

csv_text = "city,revenue\nDelhi,120\nPune,90\nKochi,\nDelhi,130\n"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv_text))

print(df.head())
print(df.shape)              # (4, 2)
print(df.info())              # revenue: 3 non-null -> 1 missing
print(df.describe())
print(df.isna().sum())        # city 0, revenue 1

payload.title: Naive dtype guessing is how bad data reaches models
payload.text: read_csv reads a sample of values to pick dtypes. One dirty cell can flip a whole column to text — or a column of codes like 007, 012 can lose leading zeros to int64. Keep na_values, dtype and parse_dates in your mental toolkit; verify with dtypes after every load.

mistakes.mistake: Loading a huge CSV in full to "just look at it"
mistakes.fix: Use nrows=1000 for the first look, confirm the schema, then decide whether the full load belongs in memory or should move to chunked reading.

mistakes.mistake: Treating describe() as a full data audit
mistakes.fix: describe() covers numeric columns only and hides missing-value semantics beyond count. Pair it with info() and isna().sum() — different readouts, different blind spots.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that count in describe() is the non-null count

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: You load a CSV of employee data. Outline the inspection ritual, naming each readout and the specific defect class it is designed to reveal.
payload.answer: In order: (1) head() — schema sanity: headers in the right place, no shifted columns, no encoding garbage. (2) shape — the row/column count you will reconcile every later drop against. (3) dtypes — type errors, especially numeric-looking columns stored as object because of symbols or spaces. (4) info() — non-null counts per column, the fastest missing-value census, plus memory usage. (5) describe() — numeric distributions: impossible min/max values, median (50%) versus mean (skew hint), count below the row total. (6) value_counts() on category-like columns — rare levels, case and whitespace duplicates, unintended classes. Only after the ritual do you plan repairs, because every repair (coerce, fill, drop) is chosen in response to what these six readouts exposed.

lessons.title: Select, Filter, loc & iloc
lessons.summary: Column subsets, boolean-mask filtering, label-based loc versus position-based iloc, safe assignment, and readable method chains.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Select single and multiple columns and filter rows with boolean masks
Use loc (labels, inclusive) and iloc (positions, half-open) to reach any cell
Assign new values safely through .loc instead of chained indexing
Chain query/sort/head operations into one readable expression

payload.text: df.loc[3, "marks"] and df.iloc[3, 2] return the same number today — and different numbers the moment someone sorts the table. One means "label 3", the other means "position 3". Knowing which contract you signed is the difference between an analysis and an anecdote.

**Two axes, two addressing schemes.** A DataFrame is rows × columns; selection picks from both. Columns first: `df["marks"]`, `df[["name", "marks"]]`. Rows come in three flavours:

**1. Boolean masks — filter by question.** The Module 5 skill, now with labels:
```
df[df["marks"] >= 80]
df[(df["marks"] >= 60) & (df["city"] == "Delhi")]   # parentheses mandatory
```
The mask must be the same length as the frame; the result keeps matching rows (a copy in the common case).

**2. loc — label-based, inclusive.** `df.loc[rows, cols]` where each side is a label, list of labels, slice of labels or mask. Label slices include BOTH ends (unlike NumPy):
```
df.loc[1:3, "name":"marks"]     # rows labelled 1..3 inclusive, columns name..marks
df.loc[df["marks"] > 80, ["name", "marks"]]
```
**3. iloc — position-based, half-open.** Integers only, NumPy rules: `df.iloc[0]` first row, `df.iloc[0:2, 0:2]` a 2×2 block, `df.iloc[[0, 2]]` rows zero and two. The mental model: **loc speaks the index, iloc speaks the ruler.**

**Assignment that sticks.** The safe form writes through .loc in one statement:
```
df["grade"] = "C"                                     # new column, every row
df.loc[df["marks"] >= 90, "grade"] = "A"             # conditional fill
```
The chained form `df[df["marks"] > 80]["grade"] = "A"` operates on a temporary selection — pandas may refuse to write back (SettingWithCopyWarning) and the change silently fails. One .loc statement, both axes specified, no warning.

**Chains and query.** Readable pipelines put filters next to their data:
```
top = (df[df["marks"] >= 60]
         .sort_values("marks", ascending=False)
         .head(3))
df.query("marks >= 60 and city == 'Delhi'")
```
query() moves conditions into a string — convenient for many conditions; remember its world is expressions, so column names with spaces need backticks and Python variables use @name.

payload.title: loc vs iloc — the contract table
Chained assignment is the silent no-op
payload.text: df[mask]["col"] = value may do nothing at all with only a warning. Always assign through a single .loc[row_mask, "col"] = value statement — both axes in one shot.

payload.title: Sort-proof your code with loc
payload.text: If an analysis must survive someone re-sorting or re-indexing the source table, address by label (loc) or by condition — never by "row 7". Position is a snapshot; labels and questions are contracts.

payload.title: Query a grade table four ways and assign safely
payload.problem: grades DataFrame: students indexed s1..s4 with marks [85, 92, 78, 61] and city [Delhi, Pune, Delhi, Kochi]. Report (a) every pass mark (>= 60) with name and marks; (b) s2's marks; (c) the third row by position; then (d) add a grade column: "A" for marks >= 90, else "B" — without chained assignment.

steps.title: 1. Mask filter with a column subset
steps.desc: The question "who passed" becomes a mask; .loc with a column list returns a tidy two-column result.
steps.code_snippet:
import pandas as pd

grades = pd.DataFrame(
    {"marks": [85, 92, 78, 61],
     "city": ["Delhi", "Pune", "Delhi", "Kochi"]},
    index=["s1", "s2", "s3", "s4"],
)
print(grades.loc[grades["marks"] >= 60, ["marks"]])

steps.title: 2. Label vs position, side by side
steps.desc: loc['s2'] is the label s2; iloc[2] is the third row regardless of labels — here s3, marks 78. Same table, two contracts.
steps.code_snippet:
print(grades.loc["s2", "marks"])   # 92 (label s2)
print(grades.iloc[2]["marks"])    # 78 (position 2 = s3)

steps.title: 3. Seed the column, then fill by mask
steps.desc: Give every row a default with plain assignment, then upgrade the high scorers through .loc[row_mask, "col"] — the write-back that reliably sticks.
steps.code_snippet:
grades["grade"] = "B"
grades.loc[grades["marks"] >= 90, "grade"] = "A"
print(grades["grade"].tolist())   # ["B", "A", "B", "B"]

steps.title: 4. Chain for readability
steps.desc: One parenthesised expression: filter, order, take three. Chains keep the logic in the order you think it — provided every step returns a frame.
steps.code_snippet:
top3 = (grades.reset_index()
          .sort_values("marks", ascending=False)
          .head(3))
print(top3[["index", "marks"]].to_string(index=False))

payload.solution: Mask-plus-loc produced the passing subset; loc by label and iloc by position returned different rows on purpose (92 vs 78), demonstrating the two contracts; the grade column was seeded with "B" then upgraded to "A" for s2 through a single .loc write; and a three-step chain delivered the top three rows. Every access said explicitly whether it meant labels or positions.

payload.title: Address everything, twice
payload.prompt: With sales = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Delhi", "Pune", "Delhi", "Kochi", "Pune"], "revenue": [120, 90, 130, 75, 95]}, index=[10, 11, 12, 13, 14]): (1) iloc the first two rows and both columns; (2) loc the rows labelled 12 and 14; (3) Delhi revenues only, via mask; (4) label-slice 11:13 and explain why 14 is not included; (5) add bonus = revenue * 0.1, then set revenue >= 120 rows bonus to 0.2 of revenue via .loc; (6) chain: cities with revenue over 90, sorted descending, top 2.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting loc slices to stop before the end label
mistakes.fix: loc slices INCLUDE the stop label (11:13 → 11, 12, 13). iloc keeps NumPy's half-open rule. Mixing the two conventions is the classic off-by-one in pandas.

mistakes.mistake: df[mask]["col"] = value — the chained write
mistakes.fix: Write df.loc[mask, "col"] = value. One statement, both axes, and pandas can return the SettingWithCopyWarning telling you the chained form may have done nothing.

mistakes.mistake: Passing a boolean mask to iloc
mistakes.fix: iloc speaks positions, not questions. Translate the mask with .loc[mask] or with mask.to_numpy().nonzero()[0] positions when you truly need iloc.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting parentheses around combined conditions
mistakes.fix: df[df.revenue > 90 & df.city == "Pune"] parses wrongly because & binds tighter. Wrap each comparison: (df.revenue > 90) & (df.city == "Pune").

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Contrast df.loc and df.iloc on indexing basis, slice semantics and mask support. When would you deliberately choose iloc even though loc exists?
payload.answer: loc indexes by LABEL — it reads the frame's index and column names, its slices include both endpoints, and it accepts boolean masks for row/column selection. iloc indexes by integer POSITION — 0..n-1, half-open NumPy slice semantics, no mask support (positions only). You choose iloc deliberately when the operation is genuinely positional: taking the first k rows after a sort (the head rows' labels are arbitrary), slicing a block by machine offset, or indexing into frames whose labels are not meaningful (default RangeIndex after reset_index). You choose loc when labels carry meaning — dates, ids — or when the selection is a condition, because a condition survives re-sorting while a position does not.

loc speaks the index; iloc speaks the ruler — same table, different contracts.

lessons.title: merge, groupby, Missing Data & Tidy Workflows
lessons.summary: Joining tables, the split-apply-combine pattern, honest missing-value strategies, and the tidy-data shape that makes every later step easier.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Join two tables with pd.merge and choose how= deliberately
Aggregate with groupby using sum/mean and multi-function agg
Detect missing values and choose dropna versus a justified fillna
Reshape wide data to tidy long form with melt

payload.text: The question is "which city earns the most?" — and the answers live half in an orders table and half in a customers table. merge to connect, groupby to summarise, fillna to stop one blank cell from erasing a whole row. Three calls, one sentence of insight: this is where pandas stops being a spreadsheet and starts being analysis.

**merge — tables that belong together.** `pd.merge(left, right, on="city", how="inner")` matches rows by key. The `how` argument is the relationship decision:
- `"inner"` — only keys present in both.
- `"left"` — every left row; right side filled with NaN where no match.
- `"right"` / `"outer"` — right rows only / all keys from both.
Two traps: keys repeating on BOTH sides multiply rows (a 3×2 key match yields 6 rows — always compare shape before and after); and unmatched left rows arrive with NaNs in every right column, which is silent information loss unless you count them. The habit `validate="many_to_one"` makes pandas check the relationship and raise instead of multiplying.

**groupby — split, apply, combine.** `df.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum()` splits rows into per-city groups, applies the sum per group, combines into one Series indexed by city. Multiple aggregates at once name the outputs:
```
df.groupby("city").agg(
    total=("revenue", "sum"),
    orders=("revenue", "count"),
    avg=("revenue", "mean"),
)
```
This one pattern — group by a question's category, apply numeric summaries, get a tidy result — produces most of the numbers in every business report you will ever read.

**Missing data — three honest moves.** First count: `df.isna().sum()`. Then choose, and say which you chose: `dropna()` (loses rows — report how many), a constant/median/mode `fillna` (state the value and why), or keep NaN for pandas to skip in aggregations (sum and mean ignore NaN by default — convenient, but the denominator changed, so say so). Filling the median of a column is defensible for a quick numeric repair; doing it BEFORE splitting train/test leaks future information (Module 9 returns to close that door properly).

**Tidy data.** The shape every tool expects: **one variable per column, one observation per row, one table per observational unit.** Wide data (`month`s as columns: Jan, Feb, Mar) violates it — each month is an observation of a revenue variable. `pd.melt(df, id_vars=["city"], var_name="month", value_name="revenue")` turns wide into tidy long form: three rows per city instead of three columns. Tidy frames group, merge and plot without contortions; untidy frames spend their life being reshaped.

payload.title: Row explosion after merge is always a key problem
payload.text: If merge triples your rows, the key repeats on both sides. Check nunique on each key, pick the true grain, or aggregate one side first — never "fix" it with drop_duplicates and hope.

payload.title: From two messy tables to one tidy summary
payload.problem: orders (city, revenue) contains one missing revenue; a wide monthly frame holds Jan/Feb/Mar revenue per city. (1) Fill the missing revenue with the column median and report what you filled. (2) Summarise total revenue per city with groupby. (3) Melt the wide monthly frame to tidy long form.

steps.title: 1. Count holes, then fill with a reported value
steps.desc: isna().sum() proves one missing cell; the median fill is one line — and the fill value is stated, not hidden.
steps.code_snippet:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Delhi", "Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi", "Pune"],
    "revenue": [120.0, 130.0, 90.0, None, 95.0],
})
print(orders.isna().sum())          # revenue 1
median_rev = orders["revenue"].median()   # 95.0
orders["revenue"] = orders["revenue"].fillna(median_rev)

steps.title: 2. Split-apply-combine per city
steps.desc: groupby("city") splits five rows into three groups; sum() applies per group; combine gives one row per city — the report table.
steps.code_snippet:
summary = orders.groupby("city").agg(
    total=("revenue", "sum"),
    orders=("revenue", "count"),
)
print(summary)

steps.title: 3. Melt wide months into tidy rows
steps.desc: id_vars stay as columns; month columns become values of a new month column; the numbers land in revenue. One observation per row from here on.
steps.code_snippet:
monthly = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Delhi", "Pune"],
    "Jan": [120, 90],
    "Feb": [130, 95],
})
tidy = pd.melt(monthly, id_vars=["city"],
               var_name="month", value_name="revenue")
print(tidy.shape)   # (4, 3) — two cities x two months

payload.solution: The single hole was found (isna), filled with the stated median 95.0, and the per-city agg table (total, count) came from one split-apply-combine. The wide month columns melted into a tidy (city, month, revenue) frame with 4 rows — the shape groupby, merge and seaborn all expect. Every number is traceable to a declared operation.

payload.title: Join, summarise, reshape, defend
payload.prompt: students: id, city, marks (with marks missing in one row); cities: city, region. (1) Left-merge cities onto students and count how many rows gained a region; (2) inner-merge and explain which students disappeared and why; (3) groupby region: mean marks with named agg, using skipna defaults — then state what the missing mark did to the mean; (4) fill the missing mark with the city-group median via transform (df["marks"].fillna(df.groupby("city")["marks"].transform("median"))) and re-run the agg; (5) build a 3-column wide frame and melt it.
payload.hint: transform returns one value per original row — that is what makes group-aware filling align correctly.

mistakes.mistake: merge that multiplies rows, then deduplicating blindly
mistakes.fix: Diagnose with nunique on the key in both tables; aggregate the many side to the correct grain first, or validate="many_to_one". drop_duplicates hides the grain error instead of fixing it.

mistakes.mistake: dropna() without counting what was dropped
mistakes.fix: Always report rows before and after. Silent row loss invalidates every percentage downstream — "we analysed 84% of the data" must be a stated fact, not a surprise.

mistakes.mistake: Filling with statistics computed from data you should not see yet
mistakes.fix: A median fill computed on the full table leaks test-set information into training (Module 9.4). Compute fill values on the training split only — the pipeline version arrives in Module 8.3.

mistakes.mistake: Concatenating misaligned frames instead of merging on keys
mistakes.fix: pd.concat stacks by position or index labels; it does not match semantics. When rows correspond by an id, merge on that id or align explicitly.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the split-apply-combine pattern with a concrete groupby example, and state the three tidy-data rules.
payload.answer: split: groupby("city") partitions the rows into one group per city value; apply: an aggregation such as sum() (or a named .agg with several functions) computes one or more statistics within each group; combine: pandas reassembles the per-group results into one Series/DataFrame indexed by the group keys — e.g. total revenue per city in one row each. The tidy-data rules: (1) each variable is a column (not a month encoded as three column names); (2) each observation is a row; (3) each type of observational unit gets its own table. Tidy frames feed groupby, merge and plotting directly; wide frames require melt (or pivot) before any of those tools behave.
payload.source: The classic "explain groupby" + "what is tidy data" pair, common in DS university papers and analyst interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: merge(on, how) joins by key: inner/left/right/outer — check shape for row explosion.
groupby = split-apply-combine; .agg(name=(col, "func")) builds named summary tables.
Missing data: count with isna().sum(), then drop (report losses), fill (state the value), or let NaN skip (state the changed denominator).
Never compute fill statistics on data you should not see yet — train-only fills come in M8/M9.
Tidy data: one variable per column, one observation per row, one table per unit.
pd.melt(id_vars=..., var_name=..., value_name=...) converts wide to tidy long form.

questions.prompt: pd.merge(a, b, on="city", how="left") keeps:
options: Every row of a; unmatched b columns become NaN
questions.explanation: Left join preserves the left frame's rows and pads unmatched keys with NaN from the right.

questions.prompt: df.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum() implements which pattern?
questions.explanation: Rows split by city key, sum applied per group, results combined into one Series indexed by city.

questions.prompt: df.isna().sum() reports:
questions.explanation: One count per column — the fastest way to size the damage before choosing dropna or fillna.

questions.prompt: Wide monthly columns (Jan, Feb, Mar) become tidy long form with:
questions.explanation: melt unpivots the month columns into (month, revenue) rows while id_vars stay as columns.

modules.title: Module 7 — Visualization: Seeing Data Without Lying
modules.summary: The matplotlib figure/axes anatomy, choosing between histogram, scatter, line and bar by the question being asked, multi-panel subplots, seaborn for DataFrame-native EDA, and the rules of honest visualization.

lessons.title: matplotlib Anatomy: Figure, Axes & the Object Interface
lessons.summary: How a matplotlib figure is built from a Figure, Axes and artists — and why every chart should start with fig, ax = plt.subplots().

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create a figure and axes with plt.subplots and size them deliberately
Draw a scatter plot and label axes, title and legend on the Axes
Explain the Figure / Axes / artist hierarchy in plain language
Save a chart to PNG with savefig and the settings that matter

payload.text: Nearly every chart you have ever seen in a paper, dashboard or AI blog post began as a few lines of matplotlib. Ten minutes on its anatomy buys you a lifetime of charts: the same figure, axes and labels machinery scales from a two-line scatter to a forty-panel research figure.

**matplotlib's object tree.** Three layers, always the same:
- The **Figure** — the whole image (canvas, background, all panels).
- One or more **Axes** — a single plot area with its own x/y axes, ticks and scales. "Ax" is singular; the plural is still "axes", which confuses everyone once.
- **Artists** — everything drawn inside: lines, markers, bars, text, legends. An Axes owns its artists; the Figure owns its Axes.

**The object interface, once.** Modern matplotlib practice is the object interface — never the older stateful `plt.plot(...)` calls that draw onto some hidden "current" axes:
```
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.scatter([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
ax.set_xlabel("x")
```
`plt.subplots()` returns the Figure and one Axes (nrows=1, ncols=1 by default). Everything else is a method ON that axes: `ax.plot`, `ax.scatter`, `ax.hist`, `ax.bar`, `ax.set_title`, `ax.set_xlabel`, `ax.set_ylabel`, `ax.legend`. The payoff is control: with several Axes (Lesson 7.3) the stateful interface loses track of "where am I drawing", while ax-based code names its target every time.

**Labelling is not decoration — it is the chart.** An unlabelled plot is a rumour. Every chart gets: axis labels WITH units ("Study hours (per week)"), a title that says what the chart shows, a legend whenever more than one series shares the panel, and honest scales (Lesson 7.4). `ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)` adds light reference lines; `fig.tight_layout()` stops labels from colliding with the frame.

**Saving before showing.** In scripts, `fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")` writes the file — `dpi` sets resolution (100–150 for screen, 300 for print), `bbox_inches="tight"` crops the white margins that otherwise eat labelling space. In notebooks the final expression `plt.show()` displays the figure; in scripts savefig is what makes the chart exist at all.

payload.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
marks = [55, 62, 71, 83, 88]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(hours, marks, color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Study hours per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Marks")
ax.set_title("More study hours, higher marks")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("study_vs_marks.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

payload.title: One figure, one Axes — until you need more
payload.text: plt.subplots() with no arguments is the correct default. Reach for multiple panels only when the question needs them; a second Axes that repeats the first is clutter.

payload.title: Build and save a labelled scatter figure from scratch
payload.problem: Plot study hours against marks for five students as a scatter, label everything, add a light grid, save as a 150-dpi PNG and display. Then answer: what object owns the scatter points?

steps.title: 1. Create figure and axes with an explicit size
steps.desc: figsize is inches — (6, 4) suits a notebook column and a report side panel. Creating the axes object first means every later call has a named target.
steps.code_snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
marks = [55, 62, 71, 83, 88]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

steps.title: 2. Draw the data on the axes
steps.desc: ax.scatter takes two equal-length sequences and places one marker per pair. Everything drawn after this belongs to this Axes.
steps.code_snippet: ax.scatter(hours, marks, color="steelblue", label="Students")

steps.title: 3. Label, title, legend, grid
steps.desc: Labels carry meaning; the legend appears only because we passed label= and called ax.legend(). Grid lines are reference, not decoration.
steps.code_snippet:
ax.set_xlabel("Study hours per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Marks (out of 100)")
ax.set_title("More study hours, higher marks")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

steps.title: 4. Layout, save, show
steps.desc: tight_layout reserves room for the labels; savefig writes the PNG before the window opens; show displays it. In scripts, dropping show and keeping savefig is enough.
steps.code_snippet:
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("study_vs_marks.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

payload.solution: One Figure, one Axes; the markers are artists owned by that Axes. Labels and units on both axes, a finding-style title, a legend, a soft grid — then tight_layout, a 150-dpi PNG on disk, and the on-screen display. The same eight lines, retargeted to plot/hist/bar, produce every other chart in this course.

payload.title: Your first three figures
payload.prompt: Using the object interface only: (1) a line chart of daily downloads [120, 145, 132, 168, 190] over days 1–5, labelled and titled; (2) a bar chart of revenue per city (Delhi 120, Pune 90, Kochi 75) with city names on the x-axis — use ax.bar(["Delhi","Pune","Kochi"], [120, 90, 75]); (3) a histogram of marks = [45, 55, 62, 71, 74, 78, 83, 88, 91, 95] with bins=5 and an edge colour so the bins are visible. Save each with a distinct filename.
payload.hint: Every chart follows the same skeleton: subdraw via subplots, draw on ax, label, tight_layout, savefig.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing stateful plt.plot(...) with object-interface calls
mistakes.fix: Pick the object interface and stay there. plt.plot draws on an implicit "current axes" that may not be the one you think once figures multiply.

mistakes.mistake: Saving after show() in a script and getting a blank PNG
mistakes.fix: Some backends clear or detach the figure at show. Save first, show second — or skip show entirely in non-interactive scripts.

mistakes.mistake: Untitled, unlabelled charts "just for me"
mistakes.fix: Tomorrow's "just for me" becomes next week's screenshot in someone's slide. Label from the first draft; tight_layout fixes the collisions.

mistakes.mistake: Tiny default figsize with big data
mistakes.fix: Overplotting and clipped labels come from the default 6.4 x 4.8 inches. Set figsize for the target medium and re-render until every label is readable.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the matplotlib Figure / Axes / artist hierarchy, and justify the "always use fig, ax = plt.subplots()" convention.
payload.answer: A Figure is the top-level image container owning one or more Axes; each Axes is a single plotting panel with its own x/y coordinate system, ticks and limits; every drawn element — lines, markers, patches, text — is an Artist owned by an Axes (or the Figure). The object interface is preferred because it makes the target explicit: ax.scatter() cannot accidentally draw on the wrong panel, whereas the stateful plt.scatter() draws on whatever axes matplotlib currently considers "current", which silently breaks once a program creates several figures or panels. Explicit Axes also enable programmatic control — loops over axes, shared scales, per-panel titles — that the stateful interface cannot express cleanly.
payload.source: The standard matplotlib theory question in data-science practicals and interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Hierarchy: Figure (image) → Axes (panel) → artists (drawn elements).
Always build with fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=...) and draw ON ax.
Label axes with units, title the finding, legend multi-series panels, grid lightly.
fig.tight_layout() prevents label collisions; savefig(dpi, bbox_inches="tight") before show.
The object interface scales to multi-panel figures; the stateful interface does not.

questions.prompt: In fig, ax = plt.subplots(), ax represents:
options: One plotting panel with its own x/y axes
questions.explanation: subplots returns (Figure, Axes); the Axes is the panel you draw data and labels on.

questions.prompt: Which call adds the entry shown in ax.legend()?
options: A label= argument on the draw call plus ax.legend()
questions.explanation: Legend entries come from label= (or explicit handles); ax.legend() only places them on the chart.

questions.prompt: The recommended way to prevent x/y labels being clipped at the figure edge is:
questions.explanation: tight_layout adjusts subplot padding so titles, labels and ticks fit inside the saved figure.

questions.prompt: fig.savefig("c.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") — bbox_inches="tight" does:
options: Crops the figure to the bounding box of the artists, removing dead margin
questions.explanation: Without it, saved charts carry large white margins; tight cropping keeps the labels and drops the emptiness.

lessons.title: Choosing the Chart: Histogram, Scatter, Line or Bar
lessons.summary: Match the chart to the question — distribution, relationship, trend or category comparison — and stop decorating start communicating.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Map a data question to histogram, scatter, line or bar and justify the choice
Draw a histogram with sensible bins and read the shape it reveals
Draw line and bar charts without letting either lie about the data
Write a one-line takeaway under every chart you produce

payload.text: Two analysts get the same marks data. One draws a pie of "grades"; the other draws a histogram and finds the distribution is bimodal — two study cohorts hiding in one average. The chart is not a picture of the data; it is an argument about the data. Choosing the chart is choosing the argument.

**The question chooses the chart — never the reverse.** Four workhorse questions, four honest answers:

**1. How is ONE numeric variable distributed? → histogram.** `ax.hist(values, bins=10)` cuts the range into bins and bars the counts. Read: centre (typical value), spread (range/width), shape (symmetric? skewed left/right? two humps?). Bins are a lens, not a fact — try 5, 10 and 30 bins on the same data; if the "story" changes wildly, say so rather than picking the flattering one.

**2. Do TWO numerics move together? → scatter.** `ax.scatter(x, y)` plots one marker per pair. Read: direction (up/down), strength (tight cloud vs scattered), form (linear? curved? clusters?), and outliers (points far off the cloud). This is also where correlation lives — and where causation does NOT automatically live (Module 9.3).

**3. What happens over an ORDERED sequence — usually time? → line.** `ax.plot(x, y)` connects values in order. Lines imply continuity between points: legitimate for daily temperatures, dishonest for unrelated categories. A line chart of "revenue per customer-id" is noise with a pen.

**4. How do CATEGORIES compare on one number? → bar.** `ax.bar(names, heights)` compares aggregates (mean revenue per city, count per department). Bar lengths are read from the baseline — so bars must start at zero (Lesson 7.4 shows the damage when they do not). Aggregation first: groupby, then bar.

**The chart-lying families to avoid.** Pie charts: only honest for a few positive parts of one whole (slices summing to something meaningful); six slices of alphabet soup is a bar chart's job. 3D anything: perspective distorts lengths — bar values become unreadable. Dual axes: two scales invites fake correlation; prefer two panels (Lesson 7.3). The discipline: after every chart, write ONE sentence stating the finding — "Marks concentrate around 70–85 with a left tail" — and check the chart actually supports that sentence.

payload.title: Question → chart, the decision table
rows: How does a measure change over time/order?

payload.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

marks = [45, 55, 62, 71, 74, 78, 83, 88, 91, 95]
hours = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].hist(marks, bins=5, edgecolor="black")
axes[0].set_title("Distribution of marks")
axes[1].scatter(hours, marks)
axes[1].set_title("Hours vs marks")
axes[2].bar(["Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi"], [120, 90, 75])
axes[2].set_title("Revenue by city")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

payload.title: Bins, ranges and sorts are editorial choices
payload.text: The same histogram with 5 versus 40 bins can look flat or spiky; the same bar chart sorted or unsorted looks decisive or chaotic. Choose defaults that serve the question, and disclose when a choice was load-bearing.

payload.title: Answer four questions about one small dataset, four charts
payload.problem: Data: marks of 10 students [45, 55, 62, 71, 74, 78, 83, 88, 91, 95] with study hours [2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14]; city revenue Delhi 120, Pune 90, Kochi 75; daily downloads [120, 145, 132, 168, 190] over days 1–5. Answer: (a) how are marks distributed? (b) do hours and marks move together? (c) which city earns most? (d) what is the downloads trend?

steps.title: 1. Distribution → histogram
steps.desc: One variable, one axis of bins. Left-skewed shape: most marks cluster high, a tail pulls down-left. That is the answer to "how are marks distributed".
steps.code_snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

marks = [45, 55, 62, 71, 74, 78, 83, 88, 91, 95]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.hist(marks, bins=5, edgecolor="black")
ax.set_xlabel("Marks")
ax.set_ylabel("Students")
ax.set_title("Most marks cluster high; a few drag the tail down")

steps.title: 2. Relationship → scatter
steps.desc: Two numerics per student, one marker each. Tight upward cloud = strong positive association; the takeaway sentence names it without claiming cause.
steps.code_snippet:
hours = [2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(hours, marks)
ax.set_xlabel("Study hours per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Marks")
ax.set_title("Study hours and marks rise together")

steps.title: 3. Categories → bar (aggregated first)
steps.desc: Three cities, one revenue each — no aggregation needed beyond the groupby habit. Zero baseline preserves honest length comparison.
steps.code_snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.bar(["Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi"], [120, 90, 75])
ax.set_ylabel("Revenue (lakh)")
ax.set_title("Delhi leads revenue; Kochi trails by 45 lakh")

steps.title: 4. Time order → line
steps.desc: Days 1 to 5 are ordered; connecting them shows the shape of the trend. The one non-monotonic dip (day 3) stays visible — lines keep the warts.
steps.code_snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [120, 145, 132, 168, 190], marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.set_ylabel("Downloads")
ax.set_title("Downloads trend up with a day-3 dip")

payload.solution: Four questions, four charts, four one-line takeaways: histogram → left-skewed high cluster; scatter → strong positive hours–marks association (not causation!); bar → Delhi top, zero-based lengths; line → rising trend with a visible day-3 dip. Each chart was selected by its question, each carries units and a finding-style title, and no chart was asked to answer a question it distorts.

payload.title: Choose, draw, take away
payload.prompt: For each, name the chart type BEFORE coding, then draw it with the object interface and write the one-line takeaway: (1) monthly rainfall for 12 months; (2) age versus blood-pressure for 200 patients; (3) pass percentage across four sections of one class; (4) the distribution of sleep hours of 50 students. Then deliberately draw (1) as a pie and list two reasons the pie is worse.
payload.hint: Ordered sequence → line; two numerics → scatter; one numeric → histogram; few categories → bar.

mistakes.mistake: Using a line chart across unordered categories
mistakes.fix: Lines imply continuity and order. If the x-axis has no natural sequence (customer ids, unordered names), use bars — sorted bars if ranking matters.

mistakes.mistake: Pie charts with many slices, negatives or non-whole totals
mistakes.fix: Pie is for a handful of positive parts summing to one whole. Beyond that use bars — angles are far harder to compare than lengths.

mistakes.mistake: One histogram, one bin count, one confident story
mistakes.fix: Bin choice is a free parameter. Try at least two bin settings; if the apparent shape moves, report the sensitivity instead of the flattering version.

mistakes.mistake: Charts without the takeaway sentence
mistakes.fix: A chart you cannot summarise in one honest sentence has not answered a question yet. Write the sentence — if it will not write, redraw.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State which chart type answers each: (a) spread and skew of one numeric variable; (b) association between two numeric variables; (c) revenue comparison across four cities; (d) weekly trend over a quarter. Justify each choice by what the eye compares.
payload.answer: (a) Histogram — bars over value bins let the eye compare frequencies across the range, revealing centre, spread, skew and multimodality. (b) Scatter — one marker per (x, y) pair shows direction, strength, form and outliers of the association directly. (c) Bar chart of the aggregated revenue — length from a common baseline is the most accurate visual comparison of magnitude across categories; start at zero. (d) Line chart — connecting ordered time points makes trend and breaks visible as shape, which bars would obscure by treating each week as unrelated. The organising principle: distribution → histogram, relationship → scatter, categories → bar, ordered sequence → line.
payload.source: The "which chart and why" question — universal in analyst interviews and DS exam practicals.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: The question picks the chart: distribution → hist, relationship → scatter, order → line, categories → bar.
Histograms depend on bins — test more than one setting before claiming a shape.
Lines require a natural order; bars compare categories and must start at zero.
Pie charts only for few positive parts of one whole; avoid 3D and dual axes.
Every chart earns its place with a one-sentence takeaway that the chart supports.

questions.prompt: The honest chart for "how are exam marks distributed across 300 students" is:
questions.explanation: One numeric variable, many observations — the histogram of value bins answers it directly.

questions.prompt: A line chart across x-axis categories with no natural order:
options: Is fine if the line is straight
Implies continuity the data does not have — use bars instead
questions.explanation: Lines read as sequence and continuity; unordered categories break that contract.

questions.prompt: When histogram shapes keep changing as you vary bins=, the honest response is:
options: Freeze the most attractive bin count and publish
Report that the shape is sensitive to binning, and show the sensitivity
questions.explanation: Binning is a free parameter; a story that depends on it is a story about the bins, not the data.

questions.prompt: A bar chart comparing city revenues must start its value axis at zero because:
options: Bar length encodes value from the baseline — truncating it exaggerates differences
Zero is always the minimum of revenue data
questions.explanation: Length from a shared baseline IS the encoding; move the baseline and the ratio between bars becomes a lie (Lesson 7.4 quantifies it).

lessons.title: Subplots & seaborn: Multi-panel EDA Dashboards
lessons.summary: Building 2x2 grids with plt.subplots, iterating axes arrays, and using seaborn for statistical charts that read column names straight from DataFrames.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Create a grid of axes with plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) and address each panel
Compose a multi-panel EDA figure with shared context and per-panel titles
Use seaborn histplot, scatterplot and boxplot with data= and x=/y= arguments
Explain what seaborn adds over raw matplotlib for DataFrame work

payload.text: Exploratory data analysis is never one chart — it is the same dataset seen six ways in one glance. A 2x2 dashboard of distribution, relationship, category and correlation panels is what "getting to know a dataset" actually looks like, and both matplotlib subplots and seaborn make it a ten-line job.

**Subplots: many Axes, one Figure.** `plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)` returns a NumPy array of Axes:
```
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))
axes[0, 0].hist(marks, bins=10)
axes[0, 1].scatter(hours, marks)
axes[1, 0].bar(cities, revenue)
axes[1, 1].plot(days, downloads)
fig.suptitle("EDA dashboard")
fig.tight_layout()
```
Index it like a matrix: `axes[0, 1]` is row 0, column 1. Useful arguments: `sharex=True` / `sharey=True` to align scales across panels that compare the same variable, and `constrained_layout=True` as a modern alternative to tight_layout for complex grids. Per-panel `ax.set_title("...")` keeps each question labelled; `fig.suptitle` titles the whole figure.

**seaborn: statistical charts that speak DataFrame.** seaborn (`import seaborn as sns`) sits on top of matplotlib — same Figure and Axes objects, richer statistical defaults, and its functions accept `data=`, `x=`, `y=` as column NAMES so charts stay reproducible from the table itself:
```
sns.set_theme()   # once per session — styles everything
sns.histplot(data=df, x="marks", hue="passed", kde=True)
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="hours", y="marks", hue="city")
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="city", y="revenue")
sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
```
What each buys you: `hue=` adds honest colour-grouping with a legend built in; `kde=True` overlays a smoothed density on a histogram (a model of the shape — treat it as commentary, not data); boxplot shows median, quartiles and outlier points per category (Module 9 defines them properly); heatmap paints a correlation matrix with annotations. Because seaborn draws on matplotlib Axes, you can pass `ax=` to place any seaborn chart INSIDE a subplot panel — `sns.boxplot(..., ax=axes[1, 0])` — which is how dashboards mix both libraries panel by panel.

payload.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

sns.set_theme()
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "hours": [2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14],
    "marks": [45, 55, 62, 71, 74, 78, 83, 88, 91, 95],
    "city": ["Delhi"] * 5 + ["Pune"] * 5,
})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))
sns.histplot(data=df, x="marks", bins=5, ax=axes[0, 0])
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="hours", y="marks", hue="city", ax=axes[0, 1])
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="city", y="marks", ax=axes[1, 0])
sns.heatmap(df[["hours", "marks"]].corr(), annot=True,
            cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=axes[1, 1])
fig.suptitle("EDA dashboard — marks dataset")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

payload.title: seaborn and matplotlib share the same Axes
payload.text: Every seaborn function accepts ax=. Draw matplotlib panels and seaborn panels in the same grid without switching libraries mid-thought.

payload.title: Assemble a 2x2 EDA dashboard for the marks dataset
payload.problem: Build one figure with four panels for the 10-student marks/hours/city data: (0,0) marks histogram, (0,1) hours-vs-marks scatter coloured by city, (1,0) marks boxplot per city, (1,1) annotated hours-marks correlation heatmap. Title the figure and keep the panels aligned.

steps.title: 1. Frame the data and theme once
steps.desc: A tidy DataFrame is the input both libraries want. sns.set_theme() applies readable defaults for the whole session.
steps.code_snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

sns.set_theme()
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "hours": [2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14],
    "marks": [45, 55, 62, 71, 74, 78, 83, 88, 91, 95],
    "city": ["Delhi"] * 5 + ["Pune"] * 5,
})

steps.title: 2. Create the grid
steps.desc: 2x2 panels at (10, 8) inches — room enough for four readable charts. axes is a 2-D array; address panels by [row, col].
steps.code_snippet: fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))

steps.title: 3. Fill each panel with the chart its question demands
steps.desc: Distribution, relationship, category comparison, correlation — one question per panel, each passed the same ax= target so nothing lands on a ghost axes.
steps.code_snippet:
sns.histplot(data=df, x="marks", bins=5, ax=axes[0, 0])
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="hours", y="marks", hue="city", ax=axes[0, 1])
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="city", y="marks", ax=axes[1, 0])
sns.heatmap(df[["hours", "marks"]].corr(), annot=True,
            cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=axes[1, 1])

steps.title: 4. Suptitle, layout, show
steps.desc: One figure-level title, tight_layout for spacing, plt.show() to render. The whole EDA first pass lives on one screen.
steps.code_snippet:
fig.suptitle("EDA dashboard - marks dataset")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

payload.solution: One Figure, four Axes, four questions answered: marks distribution (histogram), hours–marks relationship with city colours (scatter + hue), per-city spread (boxplot), and the numeric correlation (annotated heatmap with fixed vmin/vmax so the colour scale cannot flatter the number). Every seaborn call named its ax= target; suptitle and tight_layout closed the layout. That is a complete first-pass EDA in a dozen lines.

mistakes.mistake: Addressing axes[0] when the grid is 2-D
mistakes.fix: With 2x2, axes[0] is the first ROW (an array of two Axes), not a panel. Use axes[0, 0]. For 1-D grids, plt.subplots(2, squeeze=False) avoids the one-panel-squeeze surprise.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting ax= and drawing a seaborn chart outside the grid
mistakes.fix: seaborn defaults to creating its own current figure. In a dashboard every call must carry ax= so the panel lands where you think it does.

mistakes.mistake: Heatmap over a DataFrame with text columns
mistakes.fix: df.corr() errors or silently misbehaves on non-numerics — pass numeric_only=True or select numeric columns explicitly before corr().

mistakes.mistake: Rainbow hue with a dozen levels
mistakes.fix: Cap categorical hue levels at a handful; bin continuous variables into meaningful groups or facet into small multiples instead of colouring everything.

payload.answer: fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8)) returns a Figure and a 2x2 NumPy array of Axes; each panel is addressed as axes[row, col], e.g. axes[0, 0] top-left and axes[1, 0] bottom-left. seaborn functions draw on matplotlib Axes and accept ax=, so the boxplot is placed with sns.boxplot(data=df, x="city", y="revenue", ax=axes[1, 0]).
