lessons.title: Honest Visualization: Axes, Scales & the Lies We Tell
lessons.summary: Truncated bar axes, hidden log scales, cherry-picked ranges and causation claims — how charts mislead without a single false number, and the rules that prevent it.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Detect and fix a truncated-axis bar chart by quantifying the distortion
Decide when a non-zero or log baseline is legitimate and how to label it
Separate correlation claims from causal claims in a chart narrative
Apply a checklist that makes any chart honest before it leaves your notebook

payload.text: Same two numbers — 48 and 52 lakh — drawn twice. One axis runs 0 to 60: two bars, barely different. The other runs 48 to 52: a cliff, a crisis, a headline. No number was false; the axis lied. Truncated bar charts, hidden log scales and cherry-picked windows are how dashboards mislead — and they are why employers ask about chart honesty in data interviews.

**The bar-length lie.** Bars encode value as LENGTH from a baseline. Cut the baseline away and the length ratio stops matching the value ratio: bars of 48 and 52 are a 1.08x difference, but on a 48–52 axis they render as a 1:7 sliver versus a full bar — an 8% difference drawn as a 700% one. Rule: **bar and column charts start at zero. Always.** If the difference is too small to see at zero, the honest finding is "the difference is small" — say that in words; do not zoom the axis until it looks big.

**When a non-zero baseline is legitimate.** Line charts and scatter plots encode value by POSITION, not length, so their axes may zoom to show shape — provided the zoom is visible: the y-axis labels on screen, and a note when it matters ("y-axis starts at 45"). Line charts of temperatures of 24–31 degrees legitimately zoom; the same zoom on bars does not.

**Log scales: power with a disclosure.** When data spans orders of magnitude (city populations, model losses, file sizes), a log y-axis turns multiplicative spreads into readable positions. It is honest ONLY when the axis says so — label it "Revenue (log scale)" — and when tick labels keep real values (10, 100, 1000) so readers do the multiplication in their heads, not in their confusion.

**The other familiar lies.** Cherry-picked time windows (starting the axis at the good month); unsorted bars that hide the ranking; dual y-axes tuned until two unrelated lines "co-move"; truncated maps/histograms of the target that drop inconvenient points; 3D perspective that fattens one bar. And the narrative lie: "ice-cream sales drive drowning" — a scatter showing correlation narrated as causation. Correlation is a picture; causation is a claim requiring mechanism, controlled experiments or strong quasi-experimental design (Module 9.3 drills this). Charts show association. Words must not upgrade it.

**The pre-publish checklist.** (1) Bars zero-based? (2) Axes labelled with units? (3) Log or zoomed scales disclosed? (4) Time window full and stated? (5) n = visible ("200 patients, March–May")? (6) Title states the finding, not the topic? (7) The takeaway sentence supported without exaggeration? (8) No causal verb ("drives", "causes") unless the design earned it.

payload.title: Honest vs misleading — the classic set
headers: What it does to the reader
rows: Zero baseline; state "difference is small" instead
Fine for shape — lies if unlabeled
Disclose the zoom in title or axis note
Show the full period; mark the zoomed sub-window
Two panels, or one normalised panel

payload.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

cities = ["Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi"]
revenue = [48.0, 50.5, 52.0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].bar(cities, revenue)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 60)
axes[0].set_title("Honest: zero-based, differences look small")
axes[1].bar(cities, revenue)
axes[1].set_ylim(48, 52)          # the classic lie
axes[1].set_title("Misleading: truncated axis")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

payload.title: The chart lies even when every number is true
payload.text: Misleading visualization needs no false data — only a moved baseline, a cropped window or an undisclosed scale. That is why honesty is a checklist, not a fact-check.

payload.title: Draw the same data honestly and dishonestly, then quantify the distortion
payload.problem: Quarterly revenue: Q1 48.0, Q2 50.5, Q3 52.0 (lakh). Draw a two-panel figure: left panel honest (zero-based), right panel with the y-axis truncated to 48–52. Compute the true value ratios and describe what the truncated panel makes them look like.

steps.title: 1. Honest panel — zero baseline
steps.desc: Bars from zero: the Q1-to-Q3 rise is 52/48 = 1.083x — an 8% gain, drawn as an 8% gain.
steps.code_snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

quarters = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3"]
revenue = [48.0, 50.5, 52.0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].bar(quarters, revenue)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 60)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Revenue (lakh)")
axes[0].set_title("Honest: 8% growth, drawn at 8%")

steps.title: 2. Dishonest panel — truncated baseline
steps.desc: Same three numbers, y-axis from 48: Q1 renders as a sliver, Q3 as a tower. The visual ratio is roughly (52-48)/(50.5-48) = 1.6x per step — not the data's ratio.
steps.code_snippet:
axes[1].bar(quarters, revenue)
axes[1].set_ylim(48, 52)
axes[1].set_title("Misleading: same data, moved baseline")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

steps.title: 3. Quantify the truth
steps.desc: Print the real ratios so the numbers — not the bars — do the talking: Q2 is 5.2% above Q1; Q3 is 8.3% above Q1.
steps.code_snippet:
print(revenue[1] / revenue[0] - 1)   # 0.052 -> 5.2%
print(revenue[2] / revenue[0] - 1)   # 0.083 -> 8.3%

steps.title: 4. Write the honest takeaway
steps.desc: The finding is the modest growth itself. If the audience needs emphasis, emphasise with words and numbers — never with a moved baseline.
steps.code_snippet: # Takeaway: "Revenue grew 8.3% over three quarters (48.0 to 52.0 lakh)."

payload.solution: Side by side, the panels teach the whole lesson: identical data, two axis choices, opposite impressions. The true ratios (5.2% and 8.3% growth) live in the numbers, not the bar lengths; the truncated panel inflates them into a cliff by cutting 48 lakh off the baseline. The honest chart keeps zero, and the takeaway sentence carries the emphasis the axis refuses to fake.

payload.title: Audit and repair
payload.prompt: Take the "misleading" list and produce a repair for each: (1) a bar chart of monthly app ratings 4.6 vs 4.8 with y from 4.5 — redraw honestly AND suggest the right chart if precision on a 0–5 scale matters (dot plot with a labelled axis); (2) a line chart of revenue over 24 months but only months 13–24 shown — add the full series as a context panel; (3) a scatter narrated as "marketing spend causes sales" — rewrite the title to correlation language and name one plausible confounder; (4) any chart of yours: run the eight-point checklist and list any item you would have failed yesterday.
payload.hint: Position-encoded charts (dots, lines) may zoom with disclosure; length-encoded charts (bars) may not.

mistakes.mistake: "Zooming in" a bar chart to show the difference
mistakes.fix: Bars encode length from baseline — keep zero. If the difference is invisible at zero, switch to a dot plot (position-encoded) or state the number in the title.

mistakes.mistake: Log axis without a label
mistakes.fix: Readers assume linear by default. Mark "log scale" in the axis label and keep real-value tick labels so the multiplication stays visible.

mistakes.mistake: Causal language on an observational scatter
mistakes.fix: "Associated with", "moves with" — reserve "causes" and "drives" for experimental or otherwise defensible causal designs. Name confounders in the caption.

mistakes.mistake: No n, no window, no source
mistakes.fix: A chart without "n = 200 patients, Jan–Jun, source: survey" cannot be evaluated. Sample size and period belong on the figure or directly under it.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A colleague's dashboard shows quarterly revenue as a bar chart whose y-axis runs 48 to 52 lakh, captioned "revenue collapsed then recovered". Diagnose the chart, quantify the distortion for a 48.0 → 52.0 rise, and state the honest presentation.
payload.answer: The axis is truncated: bars encode value as length from the baseline, so cutting the axis below 48 inflates every difference. The true change from 48.0 to 52.0 lakh is 52/48 = 1.083 — an 8.3% rise — but on a 48–52 axis the early bar becomes a near-zero sliver while the later bar fills the panel, rendering an 8% change as if it were a multi-fold swing. Honest fix: restore the zero baseline so lengths compare truthfully; if the 8% change then looks minor, the title should say "Revenue up 8.3% over three quarters" — emphasis through numbers and words, never through a moved baseline. If fine resolution matters, a dot/line chart with a clearly labelled zoomed y-axis is acceptable because position (not length) is the encoding — with the zoom disclosed. Also report n and the time window on the chart.
payload.source: The "what is wrong with this chart" question — a fixture of analyst interviews and the exact scenario tested in the platform's Excel-course chart lesson.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Bars encode length from a baseline — bar charts always start at zero.
Line and scatter encode position — their axes may zoom, but the zoom must be disclosed.
Log scales are legitimate for wide-range data only when labelled, with real-valued ticks.
Cherry-picked windows, unsorted bars and dual axes are lies of selection, not of arithmetic.
Correlation charts show association; causal words need causal designs.
Pre-publish checklist: zero bars, units, disclosed scales, full window, visible n, finding-style title, supported takeaway.

questions.prompt: A bar chart of values 48.0 and 52.0 with y-axis 48–52 makes the difference look:
options: Far larger than the true 8.3% — bars encode length from the baseline
questions.explanation: Truncating the baseline inflates length ratios far beyond value ratios — the classic axis lie.

questions.prompt: Which chart type may legitimately use a non-zero y-axis (with disclosure)?
options: Line or scatter — they encode position, not length
questions.explanation: Position-encoded charts can zoom to show shape; length-encoded charts cannot.

questions.prompt: A log y-axis is honest when:
options: It makes the chart look dramatic
It is labelled as log scale and ticks keep real values, for wide-range multiplicative data
It is paired with a dual linear axis
questions.explanation: Disclosure plus real-valued ticks let readers translate positions into magnitudes — the only way a log chart stays readable.

questions.prompt: A scatter of ice-cream sales vs drowning deaths with the title "ice cream causes drowning" is wrong because:
options: Correlation shows association; a confounder (e.g. summer temperature) can drive both without either causing the other
Scatter charts cannot show causation graphs
questions.explanation: Observational association plus a plausible common cause is the textbook correlation-is-not-causation case.

modules.title: Module 8 — Files & Real Data Workflows
modules.summary: Reading and writing CSV and JSON safely with encoding and context managers, fetching JSON APIs with requests (params, headers, errors, rate-limit courtesy), building a repeatable cleaning pipeline as functions, and saving results so an analysis survives the session it was made in.

lessons.title: CSV & JSON: Reading and Writing Data Safely
lessons.summary: Context managers, UTF-8, the json module, pandas round-trips with to_csv(index=False), and pathlib for paths that survive other people's machines.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Read and write text files with open(), a with block and an explicit encoding
Parse and write nested data with json.load and json.dump
Round-trip a DataFrame through CSV with to_csv(index=False) and verify it
Use pathlib.Path for paths that work across operating systems

payload.text: An analysis that lives only in notebook memory dies with the kernel. Everything you produce must come from a file and go back to a file — and the two formats that carry almost all of it are CSV (flat tables) and JSON (nested structures). Reading them wrong (encoding, indexes, closed files) is the most common bug in every data pipeline on Earth.

**Files the safe way: with, encoding, pathlib.** Three habits, one block:
```
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data") / "notes.txt"
path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Pune x Kochi = good data")
```
The `with` block closes the file even if an exception fires mid-write — no leaked handles, no half-flushed buffers. `encoding="utf-8"` is the default that should never be a guess: the same file opened as cp1252 on a Windows box turns every non-ASCII character into mojibake, silently. pathlib builds paths with `/` operators that work on Windows, macOS and Linux — no string concatenation, no hardcoded backslashes.

**CSV: simple on purpose.** Comma-separated values store no types, no formats and no formulas — which is exactly why every tool on Earth can read them. pandas is the right reader/writer for analysis:
```
df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False)      # NEVER ship the index column by accident
df2 = pd.read_csv("out.csv")
```
The golden rules: write with `index=False` (otherwise the 0..n-1 index comes back as a garbage "Unnamed: 0" column on the next load), and after a round-trip, verify with `df.equals(df2)` or at least dtypes and shape — CSV has no types, so an int column with one missing value comes back as float.

**JSON: structured, nested, typed-ish.** JSON stores dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and null — the shape of API responses and config files. The standard library module handles the conversion:
```
import json
payload = {"city": "Pune", "scores": [85, 92], "active": True}
with open("cfg.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(payload, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
with open("cfg.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    back = json.load(f)
```
`indent=2` makes the file reviewable in a diff; `ensure_ascii=False` keeps real Unicode characters instead of escaping them. One hard limit to remember: the string NaN is not valid JSON — json.dump on a float NaN raises ValueError unless you use allow_nan defaults knowingly, which is another reason pipelines store missing values as null on the JSON side.

payload.title: CSV vs JSON — when each wins
rows: API responses, configs, records with structure

payload.code:
import json
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("output")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Delhi", "Pune"], "revenue": [120, 90]})
df.to_csv(out / "sales.csv", index=False)

with (out / "sales.csv").open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

with (out / "meta.json").open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump({"rows": len(df), "source": "manual"}, f, indent=2)

payload.title: open() without encoding is a time bomb
payload.text: On Windows the default is often cp1252; on Linux utf-8. The same notebook "works at home, breaks at work" until every open() carries encoding="utf-8".

payload.title: Round-trip a table and a config through both formats
payload.problem: Write a two-row sales DataFrame to CSV (index=False), read it back and verify equality. Then write a nested records list to JSON with indent=2, read it back, and rebuild a DataFrame from the records to prove the structure survived.

steps.title: 1. CSV round-trip with verification
steps.desc: to_csv with index=False writes only real columns; read_csv restores the table; equals() settles the round-trip question with one boolean.
steps.code_snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Delhi", "Pune"], "revenue": [120, 90]})
df.to_csv("sales.csv", index=False)
df2 = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(df.equals(df2))   # True

steps.title: 2. Write nested records as JSON
steps.desc: A list of row-dicts is the natural JSON shape for tabular data and the shape every API returns. indent=2 keeps the file reviewable.
steps.code_snippet:
import json

records = [
    {"city": "Delhi", "revenue": 120},
    {"city": "Pune", "revenue": 90},
]
with open("records.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(records, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

steps.title: 3. Read JSON back into Python, then into pandas
steps.desc: json.load returns plain lists and dicts; pd.DataFrame consumes that list directly — the universal bridge between JSON APIs and analysis.
steps.code_snippet:
with open("records.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    back = json.load(f)

df3 = pd.DataFrame(back)
print(df3.shape)   # (2, 2)

steps.title: 4. Note what CSV lost that JSON kept
steps.desc: JSON kept booleans as booleans and nested dicts nested; CSV flattens everything to text and re-infers. Choose CSV for pure tables, JSON when structure matters.
steps.code_snippet: print(pd.read_json("records.json").dtypes.tolist())   # [object, int64]

payload.solution: CSV round-trip verified with equals() after writing index=False; JSON preserved the nested record structure through dump/load with readable indentation; and DataFrame(list_of_dicts) rebuilt the table from the JSON side. The formats are not interchangeable views of one truth — CSV flattens and forgets types, JSON keeps structure — so the pipeline picks per artifact.

payload.title: Own the round-trip
payload.prompt: (1) Create a DataFrame with a datetime column and a missing value; write it to CSV with index=False and date_format="%Y-%m-%d"; read it back with parse_dates=["date"] and compare dtypes. (2) Write the same frame to JSON with orient="records", indent=2 and inspect the file's first lines. (3) Use pathlib throughout: create an output/ directory with mkdir(exist_ok=True) and write both files inside it. (4) Deliberately write WITHOUT index=False once and observe the "Unnamed: 0" column on reload.
payload.hint: orient="records" produces the list-of-row-dicts shape — the same shape pd.DataFrame accepts directly.

mistakes.mistake: to_csv() without index=False, then a mystery column on reload
mistakes.fix: The unnamed first column is the saved index. Make index=False a permanent habit for analysis exports (keep the index only when the index IS data, e.g. a time series you want back).

mistakes.mistake: open() with no encoding and non-ASCII data
mistakes.fix: Always encoding="utf-8" on both read and write. If a file was produced elsewhere, encoding="utf-8-sig" tolerates the BOM some Windows tools add.

mistakes.mistake: Hand-concatenating paths with + or f-strings
mistakes.fix: Path("data") / "sales.csv" composes correctly on every OS and exposes .open(), .exists(), .stem for free. String paths break on separators and quoting.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming CSV round-trips are type-preserving
mistakes.fix: CSV stores no types: int columns with NaN return as float, dates come back as text unless parse_dates is passed. Re-check dtypes after every load.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: You wrote df.to_csv("out.csv") and on reload a column "Unnamed: 0" appeared. Explain why, give the fix, and state two things a JSON round-trip preserves that CSV does not.
payload.answer: to_csv defaults to index=True, so the DataFrame index was written as a leading column with no header meaning; on reload pandas saw an extra column of values with the placeholder header "Unnamed: 0". Fix: df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False) — or index=True deliberately when the index is genuine data you want restored with index_col=0 on load. JSON round-trips preserve (1) types — booleans stay booleans, numbers stay numbers — and (2) nesting — dicts inside dicts/lists keep their structure; CSV flattens to text and infers types on every load, losing both.
payload.source: The single most common practical pandas file question in interviews and lab exams.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: open files with a with block and encoding="utf-8" — closed handles and stable text, always.
CSV: flat tables; write with to_csv(index=False); verify round-trips with equals/dtypes.
JSON: nested structures; json.dump/load with indent=2, ensure_ascii=False; NaN is not valid JSON.
pathlib.Path: compose paths with /, open with .open, mkdir(exist_ok=True).
CSV forgets types and nesting — JSON keeps them; pick the format by what must survive.

questions.prompt: The main reason to write files inside a with block is:
options: The file closes automatically even if an exception occurs
It locks the file against other readers
questions.explanation: with guarantees close() on the way out — no leaked handles, no unclosed buffers after a crash.

questions.prompt: df.to_csv("f.csv") then pd.read_csv("f.csv") shows an extra "Unnamed: 0" column because:
options: The index was written by default; fix with index=False
questions.explanation: index=True is the default — the saved index returns as a nameless column unless you suppress it.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly reads and writes a JSON file with the standard library?
options: json.loads() for files, json.dumps() for files
questions.explanation: load/dump work on file objects; loads/dumps work on strings — mixing them up is the classic confusion.

questions.prompt: Passing encoding="utf-8" to open() matters because:
options: Default encoding differs across platforms, silently corrupting non-ASCII text
It is required by the with statement
questions.explanation: Same file, different default encodings on Windows and Linux — explicit utf-8 ends the "works on my machine" bug.

lessons.title: JSON APIs with requests: Params, Headers, Errors & Courtesy
lessons.summary: Making a robust GET request, parsing JSON into DataFrames, handling timeouts and HTTP errors, and being a polite API citizen with rate-limit courtesy.

objectives: Send a GET request with query parameters and a descriptive User-Agent header

Convert nested JSON results into a DataFrame
Handle timeouts, HTTP errors and 429 rate limits with courtesy built in

payload.text: Live weather, live prices, live sports scores — none of it is in any CSV you own. An API is a website for programs: you send an HTTP request, you get JSON back. Ten robust lines with requests separate the analyst who waits for exported files from the one who fetches the world.

**HTTP in one paragraph.** You send a request (method + URL + optional query parameters + optional headers) and receive a response (a status code, headers, and a body — usually JSON text). `200` means OK; `404` not found; `401/403` authentication/permission; `429` you are calling too fast; `5xx` their server broke, not you.

**The robust GET, every time.** requests is the standard client:
```
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/posts",
    params={"userId": 1},                      # becomes ?userId=1
    headers={"User-Agent": "student-project/1.0 (contact: you@college)"},
    timeout=10,
)
r.raise_for_status()                           # raises HTTPError for 4xx/5xx
data = r.json()                                # parsed dict or list
```
Four non-negotiables: **params** (never hand-build query strings — encoding escapes you), **headers** with a descriptive User-Agent (servers identify callers by it; anonymity is rude and sometimes blocked), **timeout** (without it a dead server hangs your kernel forever), and **raise_for_status()** before .json() — otherwise an HTML error page reaches json.loads and you debug the wrong error.

**Parsing into analysis shape.** API JSON is nested: a dict containing a list of row-dicts. The standard bridge: `pd.DataFrame(data)` for a top-level list, or `pd.json_normalize(data["results"], max_level=1)` to flatten one level of nesting into columns. Always `print(list(data.keys()))` or `type(data)` first — the shape is the API's contract, and you read it before you index into it.

**Errors and courtesy.** Wrap the call: `requests.exceptions.Timeout` and `requests.exceptions.RequestException` cover the failure families; retry small, fixed counts — not tight loops. The 429 contract: slow down, honour any Retry-After header, sleep and retry once or twice (time.sleep(3)). Courtesy rules that keep APIs free for everyone: send the User-Agent, cache responses to disk instead of refetching in a loop, don't hammer in for-loops without sleeps, and check the service's terms before bulk pulls. Keys never hard-code: put them in environment variables or a git-ignored file — a notebook with a pasted key is one screenshot away from someone else's bill.

rows: Check the URL — do not retry blindly
Retry once or twice with delay; then stop

r.raise_for_status()

print(len(posts))                 # 10 posts for userId 1

df = pd.DataFrame(posts)
print(df[["id", "title"]].head())

lessons.title: A Repeatable Cleaning Pipeline You Can Re-run
lessons.summary: Turning one-off cleaning clicks into a named, deterministic function: standardise columns, coerce types, strip strings, deduplicate, report every count.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Standardise column names to snake_case with string methods
Coerce dirty numerics with to_numeric(errors="coerce") and count the damage
Strip and normalise string categories before they fragment groups
Assemble the steps into a pure clean_sales(df) function with a report dict

payload.text: You cleaned the CSV by hand last night — fixed 14 salaries, lower-cased three city names, dropped two duplicates. This morning the team sent a new export with the same problems plus four new ones. Cleaning that lives in notebook history is not cleaning; cleaning is a function you re-run.

**Why pipelines, not gestures.** A cleaning gesture is a cell you executed once and cannot explain. A cleaning pipeline is a **pure function**: same input frame, same output frame, every count visible. Purity matters because re-runs must be trustworthy — no dependence on which cells ran before, no mutation of the raw data you might need to re-audit.

**The step catalogue, in the order that catches the most damage:**
1. **Copy, never mutate raw.** `df = raw.copy()` — the raw file stays untouched on disk and in memory.
2. **Standardise column names.** `df.columns = df.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "_")` turns " Revenue ", "REVENUE" and "revenue (lakh)"-style variants into one snake_case vocabulary. (The last needs the extra .str.replace("(lakh)", "", regex=False) — strip units deliberately, not accidentally.)
3. **String hygiene.** `df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.title()` — "delhi ", "DELHI" and "Delhi" collapse into one level, or your groupby reports three cities that are one city.
4. **Type coercion.** `pd.to_numeric(df["revenue"], errors="coerce")` converts what it can and turns what it cannot into NaN — then `int((converted.isna() & old.notna()).sum())` counts the casualties so nothing is lost silently.
5. **Missing values, stated.** Count with isna().sum(); fill or drop with the number in the log: "filled 3 ages with median 29; dropped 1 row missing revenue".
6. **Deduplicate.** `df.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="first")` — with the removed count printed.
7. **Reset and return.** `df = df.reset_index(drop=True)`; return (df, report).

**The shape of the function.** One function per source you trust (sales exports, survey dumps), parameterised only where behaviour genuinely varies (fill strategy), always returning a small report dict {step: count}. The report is the audit trail that makes the pipeline reviewable — and it is exactly what the capstone notebook of Lesson 10.4 will demand.

payload.code:
import pandas as pd

def clean_sales(raw: pd.DataFrame):
    df = raw.copy()
    report = {"rows_in": len(df)}

    df.columns = (df.columns.str.strip().str.lower()
                  .str.replace(" ", "_"))
    df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.title()

    coerced = pd.to_numeric(df["revenue"], errors="coerce")
    report["revenue_coerce_fail"] = int(
        (coerced.isna() & df["revenue"].notna()).sum())
    df["revenue"] = coerced

    med = df["revenue"].median()
    report["revenue_filled"] = int(df["revenue"].isna().sum())
    df["revenue"] = df["revenue"].fillna(med)

    before = len(df)
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["city"], keep="first")
    report["dupes_removed"] = before - len(df)
    report["rows_out"] = len(df)
    return df.reset_index(drop=True), report

payload.title: Report counts like a dbt log
payload.text: rows_in, coercions, fills, drops — printed or returned per run. When tomorrow's export differs, the report shows WHERE it differed, not just that something did.

payload.title: Pipelines are order-sensitive
payload.text: Strip strings before deduplicating (or "delhi" and "delhi " survive as two rows); coerce before filling (or you fill a string column). The order in the catalogue is the order that works.

payload.title: Clean a deliberately dirty sales export
payload.problem: raw has columns [" City ", "Revenue", "Orders"] with values: Delhi/120/4, " delhi"/"1,300"/3, Pune/90/2, Kochi/None/2, plus a duplicate Delhi row. Write clean_sales(raw) that normalises city names, coerces revenue (comma-stripped first), fills the missing revenue with the median, removes duplicates by city and returns the cleaned frame with a report.

steps.title: 1. Build the dirty frame and copy it
steps.desc: Reproduce the export exactly as it arrives, then work on a copy — the raw stays available for auditing every transformation against it.
steps.code_snippet:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({
    " City ":  ["Delhi", " delhi", "Pune", "Kochi", "Delhi"],
    "Revenue": ["120", "1,300", "90", None, "120"],
    "Orders":  [4, 3, 2, 2, 4],
})
df = raw.copy()

steps.title: 2. Names, then strings, then numbers
steps.desc: Column names are normalised first so every later line uses one vocabulary; city values collapse to title case; revenue loses its thousands separator before coercion.
steps.code_snippet:
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip().str.lower()
df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.title()
df["revenue"] = pd.to_numeric(
    df["revenue"].str.replace(",", "", regex=False),
    errors="coerce",
)

steps.title: 3. Fill with the median, count the fill
steps.desc: One NaN in revenue; the median of [120, 1300, 90, 120]... the median fill uses the column median. The count goes in the report — silent fills are how wrong numbers survive review.

steps.title: 4. Deduplicate and report the delta
steps.desc: After title-casing, the two Delhi rows are true duplicates by city; keep="first" retains the first. rows_in versus rows_out proves exactly what changed.
steps.code_snippet:
before = len(df)
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["city"], keep="first")
report["dupes_removed"] = before - len(df)
df = df.reset_index(drop=True)
print(report)   # {"revenue_filled": 1, "dupes_removed": 1}

payload.solution: Five dirty features — padded header, case/whitespace-variant cities, comma-numbers, a missing revenue, a duplicate — were cleaned in the pipeline order: names, strings, numeric coercion, stated median fill, deduplication. The report dict carries the two counts that matter (1 fill, 1 dupe removed) and the cleaned frame comes back indexed 0..n-1. Re-run tomorrow's export through the same function and the report will name any new defect class.

mistakes.fix: df = raw.copy() first, always. The raw is your audit trail; once mutated you can no longer prove what the original contained.

mistakes.fix: "delhi" and "Delhi " are different rows until you normalise — dedup first and duplicates survive. Names and strings before drop_duplicates, every time.

payload.question: A raw sales export has padded headers, city names with mixed case and whitespace, comma-formatted revenue with one missing value, and duplicate rows. Lay out a cleaning pipeline in order, justifying the position of each step.
payload.answer: (1) Copy the raw frame — never mutate the source. (2) Standardise column names (strip, lower, spaces to underscores) so every later reference uses one vocabulary. (3) Clean string values — strip and title-case city — because category normalisation must precede deduplication ("delhi " vs "Delhi" are duplicates only after cleaning) and before any groupby. (4) Coerce revenue with to_numeric(errors="coerce") (after removing thousands separators), counting the newly-NaN cells so nothing disappears silently. (5) Handle missing values explicitly — fill with the stated median or drop with the reported row loss. (6) drop_duplicates on the business key with the removed count logged. (7) reset_index(drop=True) and return (clean_df, report). The order is forced by dependencies: strip before dedup, coerce before fill, count every lossy step — the report dict is what makes the pipeline auditable rather than merely executed.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Cleaning is a pure function: same input, same output, counts in a report dict.
Order: copy → column names → string hygiene → type coercion → missing values → dedup → reset.

Strip before dedup — otherwise case and whitespace variants survive as separate rows.
Never mutate the raw frame; the raw file and frame are the audit trail.

pandas requires a copy before any assignment
It converts dtypes to safe ones

lessons.title: Saving Results: Data, Figures & Reports That Survive the Session
lessons.summary: Exporting DataFrames and JSON summaries, saving figures with savefig, versioning outputs with pathlib, and the checklist that makes an analysis reproducible for someone else.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Export cleaned DataFrames with to_csv(index=False) and to_json(orient="records")
Save matplotlib figures at usable resolution before showing them
Persist a metrics dictionary as JSON alongside the data it describes
Organise outputs under an output/ directory with pathlib and stable filenames

payload.text: The notebook ends with a beautiful chart and three printed metrics — and the kernel dies. Nothing exists: no file, no number, no chart. The final skill of real data work is unglamorous and non-negotiable: writing the results to disk so tomorrow's you, and the reviewer, can find them.

**Three artifacts, three savers.** Every finished analysis produces some mix of:
1. **Tabular data** — cleaned frames, summaries: `df.to_csv(path, index=False)` or `df.to_json(path, orient="records", indent=2)`. The records orientation writes the list-of-row-dicts shape every other tool ingests.
2. **Figures** — `fig.savefig(path, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")` BEFORE `plt.show()` (some backends clear the figure at show; scripts may never show at all). 100–150 dpi for screens, 300 for print; PNG for charts, SVG when someone will scale them.
3. **Small structured results** — the metrics of the day: `json.dump({"mae": 45.2, "baseline_mae": 58.1}, f, indent=2)`. A metrics JSON next to the data makes the headline numbers greppable and diffable forever.

**Dates and versioning.** Outputs accumulate. `Path("output") / f"sales_clean_{date.today().isoformat()}.csv"` stamps each run; keeping a stable `sales_clean_latest.csv` alongside (overwrite) gives downstream users one honest pointer. `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` at the top of the script so a fresh clone runs without setup.

**What the export loses — know it.** CSV: no dtypes, no nesting, index suppressed by habit. JSON via pandas (orient="records"): dates become strings; NaN becomes null (good — NaN is invalid JSON). Floats: binary floating point does not round-trip bit-exact through decimal text for arbitrary precision — fine for analysis, not for money. If dtypes must survive exactly, re-apply parse_dates and coercion after load, or state the schema in a sidecar JSON.

**The reproducibility bundle.** The professional habit: one output/ directory per project containing cleaned data + metrics.json + figures + the report text. Anyone re-running your notebook (including the capstone grader, Lesson 10.4) checks that these files appear and match the numbers in the narrative. Save first, then narrate.

payload.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import date
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

out = Path("output")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Delhi", "Pune"], "revenue": [120, 90]})
df.to_csv(out / "sales_clean.csv", index=False)
df.to_json(out / "sales_clean.json", orient="records", indent=2)

metrics = {"total_revenue": 210, "rows": 2, "generated": date.today().isoformat()}
with (out / "metrics.json").open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(metrics, f, indent=2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.bar(df["city"], df["revenue"])
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(out / "revenue_by_city.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

modules.title: Module 9 — Statistics for AI
modules.summary: Mean, median, variance and standard deviation from first principles; populations, samples and the sampling distribution of the mean; correlation versus causation with confounders; outlier detection with IQR fences; and the train/test split with random_state that keeps evaluation honest.

lessons.title: Mean, Median, Variance & Standard Deviation
lessons.summary: The four numbers every dataset summary starts with — what each measures, how variance and std are computed, and why sample variance divides by n − 1.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute mean, median, variance and standard deviation with NumPy and pandas
Explain variance as the mean squared deviation and standard deviation as its unit-restoring square root
Distinguish population (ddof=0) from sample (ddof=1) variance and say why the correction exists
Decide when the median tells the story that the mean hides

payload.text: Ten quiz scores: 72, 85, 90, 45, 67, 55, 88, 92, 60, 78. The class average is 73.2 — but nobody scored 73, and the "average" student sits above six of their ten classmates. Two numbers, mean 73.2 and median 75.0, already disagree about the story. Add the standard deviation and you learn the scores are not a tight cluster at all. These four statistics are the first language you speak to any model, any chart and any interviewer.

**The mean: a balance point.** The mean (average) is the value that would balance the data on a seesaw: sum every observation, divide by the count. It uses every value, which is both its strength and its weakness — one extreme value drags it. `np.mean(scores)` is `scores.sum() / len(scores)` underneath; pandas reaches it with `df["col"].mean()`.

**The median: the middle by rank.** Sort the values and take the centre (or average the two centres for even counts). The median ignores magnitude and cares only about rank, so an absurd outlier moves it by almost nothing. Rule of thumb: **skewed data tells its story in the median; symmetric data tells it in the mean.** Income classically runs skewed — a few huge salaries pull the mean above what most people earn, which is why reports quote medians.

**Variance: the average squared distance from the mean.** Spread cannot be measured by raw distances (they cancel: some positive, some negative), so each deviation is squared, then averaged:
```
variance = mean( (x - mean(x))**2 )
```
Squaring makes every contribution positive and punishes far-away points disproportionately. `np.var(scores)` uses **ddof=0** (divide by n) — the *population* formula. `np.var(scores, ddof=1)` divides by n − 1 — the *sample* formula. The difference is not pedantry: your ten scores are a sample of a larger population of possible scores. Dividing by n systematically underestimates the true population variance, because the sample mean sits closer to the sample's own points than to the population's true centre. Bessel's correction (n − 1) compensates; pandas' `std()` and `var()` default to **ddof=1**, NumPy to 0 — one of the stack's quietest inconsistencies.

**Standard deviation: variance back in original units.** Squaring broke the units (marks²), so take the square root: `np.std(scores, ddof=1)` ≈ 16.19 marks. The standard deviation answers "a typical point sits about this far from the mean" in the same units as the data — which is why it, not the variance, gets quoted. Together the four numbers sketch the distribution: centre (mean and median), spread (std), and the gap between mean and median (a skew hint).

**Reading the pair, quickly.** mean ≫ median: right-skewed (a high tail). mean ≪ median: left-skewed. mean ≈ median with a moderate std: roughly symmetric. These are hints, not proofs — Lesson 9.2 turns the sketch into a full picture with distributions and sampling.

payload.title: The four summaries at a glance

payload.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([72, 85, 90, 45, 67, 55, 88, 92, 60, 78], dtype=float)
print(scores.mean())                 # 73.2
print(np.median(scores))             # 75.0
print(scores.var(ddof=0))            # 235.76 — population (divide by n)
print(scores.var(ddof=1))            # 261.96 — sample (divide by n-1)
print(scores.std(ddof=1))            # 16.19 marks — original units

payload.title: NumPy and pandas disagree on ddof by default
payload.text: np.std/var default to ddof=0 (population); pandas .std()/.var() default to ddof=1 (sample). Mixing them silently gives two different answers for the "same" statistic — always state which you mean.

payload.title: Summarise ten quiz scores, and defend the n − 1 correction
payload.problem: scores = [72, 85, 90, 45, 67, 55, 88, 92, 60, 78]. Compute mean, median, both variances and the sample standard deviation; count how many scores fall within one sample standard deviation of the mean; and explain in words why the two variances differ.

steps.title: 1. Centre: mean and median side by side
steps.desc: Mean 73.2 versus median 75.0 — close, with the mean pulled slightly below by the low tail (45, 55). Mild left skew, nothing dramatic.
steps.code_snippet:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([72, 85, 90, 45, 67, 55, 88, 92, 60, 78], dtype=float)
print(scores.mean())        # 73.2
print(np.median(scores))    # 75.0

steps.title: 2. Spread: variance both ways, then std
steps.desc: Population variance divides by n = 10; sample variance by n − 1 = 9. The sample figure is larger — and the default of pandas.
steps.code_snippet:
print(scores.var(ddof=0))   # 235.76 — population
print(scores.var(ddof=1))   # 261.96 — sample
print(scores.std(ddof=1))   # 16.19 — sqrt of the sample variance

steps.title: 3. One band around the mean
steps.desc: The interval 73.2 ± 16.19 runs about 57.0 to 89.4. Scores inside it: 60, 67, 72, 78, 85, 88 — six of ten. 90, 92, 55 and 45 sit outside.
steps.code_snippet:
lo = scores.mean() - scores.std(ddof=1)
hi = scores.mean() + scores.std(ddof=1)
print(lo, hi)                          # 57.01 89.39
print(((scores >= lo) & (scores <= hi)).sum())   # 6

steps.title: 4. Defend the correction in one sentence each
steps.desc: ddof=0 answers "if these ten WERE the whole population"; ddof=1 answers "these ten are a sample — estimate the population". The second is almost always the question a data analysis is asking.
steps.code_snippet:
# population variance: mean((x - x_bar)^2), divisor n
# sample variance: divisor n-1 — unbiased estimate of the population figure

payload.solution: Mean 73.2, median 75.0 (mild left tail), population variance 235.76, sample variance 261.96, sample std 16.19 marks. Six of ten scores lie inside one standard deviation of the mean. The two variances differ by the divisor: n versus n − 1. The sample formula is larger because the sample mean is optimally close to the sample itself; dividing by n − 1 corrects that optimism so the estimate centres on the true population variance.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define variance and standard deviation. Why does sample variance divide by n − 1 while population variance divides by n, and which does pandas use by default?
payload.answer: Variance is the mean squared deviation from the mean: average of (x − x̄)². Squaring makes deviations additive and non-cancelling, but leaves squared units. Standard deviation is its square root — spread back in the data's own units, which is why it is the quoted figure. Population variance divides by n and is exact when the data IS the whole population. Sample variance divides by n − 1: because the sample mean is computed from the same data, squared distances to it are systematically smaller than distances to the unknown population mean; dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) removes that downward bias so the estimator centres on the true population variance. pandas .var()/.std() default to ddof=1 (sample); NumPy defaults to ddof=0 — always check which you are calling.
payload.source: The standard descriptive-statistics question in DS interviews and university practicals.

lessons.title: Distributions, Samples & the Sampling Mean
lessons.summary: What a distribution is; normal, skewed and bimodal shapes; why sample statistics vary; and the central limit theorem that makes sample means behave.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe a distribution by centre, spread and shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal)
Distinguish a population from a sample and explain sampling variability
Simulate repeated sampling and observe the sampling distribution of the mean
State the central limit theorem qualitatively and its practical consequence for n

payload.text: Take 50 dice rolls, average them: you might get 3.3. Roll again: 3.7. Again: 3.4. The TRUE average of a die is 3.5 — but no single sample of 50 hits it exactly. Now average the averages of 2,000 such samples: the result crowds 3.5 with startling precision, and the spread of those averages shrinks as √n. That quiet regularity — the central limit theorem — is why "the sample mean is 3.42 ± 0.05" is a scientific statement, and why every ML metric you ever report is really a sample estimate.

**A distribution is the whole population of values.** One column of data has a distribution: every value, with how often each occurs. Summarising it means describing three things — **centre** (mean, median), **spread** (std, IQR, range) and **shape**:
- **Symmetric / normal (bell):** mean ≈ median, thin tails. Heights, measurement errors, many averages. The 68–95–99.7 rule lives here: ~68% of values within 1 std of the mean, ~95% within 2, ~99.7% within 3.
- **Skewed:** a tail on one side; mean chases the tail, median stays put (Lesson 9.1). Income, delivery times, house prices.
- **Bimodal:** two humps — usually two populations mixed (e.g. two cohorts, day vs night). The mean can land in the valley where almost nobody lives — the classic "average student who does not exist".

**Population vs sample.** The **population** is everything you want to know about; the **sample** is the subset you observed. You almost never have the population — you have a sample, and every statistic you compute (mean, std, accuracy!) is a **statistic estimating a parameter**. Because the sample could have come out differently, the statistic would too: that variability across hypothetical resamples is the **sampling distribution** of that statistic.

**The sampling distribution of the mean, simulated.** A single sample mean is noisy. The distribution of sample means is not: it centres on the population mean and has a predictable spread — the **standard error**, σ/√n. Simulate it:
```
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
means = [rng.integers(1, 7, 50).mean() for _ in range(2000)]
```
A single die has σ ≈ 1.71; a mean of 50 rolls has standard error ≈ 1.71/√50 ≈ 0.24. The simulated means spread with std ≈ 0.25 and centre ≈ 3.5 — theory and simulation shaking hands.

**The central limit theorem, stated honestly.** For i.i.d. samples with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal curve as n grows — regardless of the population's own shape (dice are uniform, not bell). Consequences you will use forever: (1) means of reasonably large samples behave predictably even from skewed data; (2) uncertainty shrinks with 1/√n — quadrupling n only halves the error bar; (3) a confidence interval is just the estimate ± a multiple of the standard error. The theorem does NOT say your data becomes normal, nor that n = 30 is a magic law — it is about the mean's behaviour across resamples.

payload.title: Population vs sample — the vocabulary of inference
rows: Everything you want to generalise to
Std of a statistic across resamples

payload.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dice = np.arange(1, 7)
print(dice.mean(), dice.std())            # 3.5, 1.71

one = rng.integers(1, 7, 50)
print(one.mean())                          # one noisy sample, e.g. 3.34

means = np.array([rng.integers(1, 7, 50).mean() for _ in range(2000)])
print(means.mean(), means.std())           # ~3.50, ~0.25 (theory: 1.71/sqrt(50) ~ 0.24)

payload.title: Simulate the sampling distribution of a die mean
payload.problem: A fair die has population mean 3.5 and std ≈ 1.71. (1) Draw ONE sample of 50 rolls and report its mean. (2) Draw 2,000 samples of 50 and build the sampling distribution of the mean. (3) Report its centre and spread, compare to σ/√n, and explain what one sample hid.

steps.title: 1. The population facts, then one noisy sample
steps.desc: faces 1..6: mean 3.5, std(ddof=0) ≈ 1.71. One sample of 50 lands somewhere near but rarely exactly on 3.5.
steps.code_snippet:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
faces = np.arange(1, 7)
print(faces.mean(), faces.std())          # 3.5 1.7078...
one = rng.integers(1, 7, 50)
print(one.mean())                          # e.g. 3.76 — off by ~0.26

steps.title: 2. Repeat 2,000 times — the sampling distribution
steps.desc: Each replicate draws 50 fresh rolls and averages them. The array of 2,000 means IS (a Monte Carlo approximation to) the sampling distribution of the mean.
steps.code_snippet:
means = np.array([rng.integers(1, 7, 50).mean() for _ in range(2000)])
print(means.shape)                         # (2000,)

steps.title: 3. Read the distribution of means
steps.desc: Centre ≈ 3.50 (the population mean). Spread ≈ 0.25 — matching σ/√n = 1.71/√50 ≈ 0.24. Far tighter than the 1.71 spread of single rolls.
steps.code_snippet:
print(means.mean(), means.std())           # ~3.50, ~0.25
print(faces.std() / np.sqrt(50))           # 0.2415 — the standard error, theory side

steps.title: 4. Shrink n, watch the spread grow
steps.desc: Halve the sample size to 12: the standard error rises to ≈ 1.71/√12 ≈ 0.49. Uncertainty pays a √n tax — always.
steps.code_snippet:
small = np.array([rng.integers(1, 7, 12).mean() for _ in range(2000)])
print(small.std())                         # ~0.50 — double the n, 0.7x the error

payload.solution: One sample of 50 gave a mean around 3.76 — honest noise. The 2,000-replicate sampling distribution centred on 3.50 with std ≈ 0.25, matching the theoretical standard error 1.71/√50 ≈ 0.24. With n = 12 the spread doubled to ≈ 0.50. The central limit theorem in one simulation: the mean's sampling distribution is roughly normal, centred on the truth, and its width falls with √n — which is why bigger samples buy proportionally (not linearly) more precision.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the central limit theorem, sketch its consequence for a sample mean from skewed data, and explain why the standard error falls with √n rather than n.
payload.answer: The CLT: for independent samples with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as n increases, centred at the population mean, regardless of the population's own shape (which need not be normal). So even from right-skewed data — delivery times, income — the MEAN of a sufficiently large sample is approximately normal, enabling confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, while the raw data remain skewed. The spread of that sampling distribution is the standard error, σ/√n: averaging cancels independent positive and negative noise, and averaging n items reduces noise by the square root of n — not n — because variances (not standard deviations) add. Quadrupling n only halves the uncertainty; that diminishing return is why precision gets expensive and why ML test sets in the thousands, not the millions, are usually enough.

lessons.title: Correlation vs Causation: Reading r Without Being Fooled
lessons.summary: Pearson correlation from first principles, what r can and cannot claim, how outliers and nonlinearity distort it, and the confounder that turns causation talk into fiction.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute Pearson correlation with NumPy and pandas and interpret sign and magnitude
Explain why correlation measures linear association only and reacts to outliers
Identify a confounding variable in a three-variable example
State the evidence required before any causal claim is defensible

payload.text: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together, month after month, with a correlation near +1. Ban the ice cream and the drownings will not fall — summer temperature drives both. Correlation is easy to compute, easy to plot, and very easy to over-claim. This lesson installs the reflex every data professional needs: compute r, respect r, never promote r to causation without a design that earns it.

**Pearson r: linear togetherness in one number.** Pearson's correlation coefficient measures how two numeric variables move together *linearly*:
- r ≈ +1: perfect straight-line rise (x up, y up, all points on a line).
- r ≈ 0: no linear pattern (but see the traps below).
- r ≈ −1: perfect straight-line fall.

Mechanically: standardise both variables (subtract means, divide by stds), then average their products — the average of (z_x · z_y). Positive z-pairs (both above their means) push r up; mixed pairs pull it down. `np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]` or pandas `df.corr()` compute it; both need no NaNs.

**What r does NOT say.** (1) **Not causation** — full stop, next section. (2) **Not nonlinearity** — a perfect parabola y = (x − 5)² over x in 0..10 has r ≈ 0; the relationship is total, just not straight. Plot before you quote r. (3) **Not "no relationship" at r ≈ 0** — U-shapes and cycles average out to zero linear correlation. (4) **Not outlier-proof** — one far-off point can drag r from 0 to 0.9 or smash 0.9 down to 0.3. Always look at the scatter.

**Confounding: the third variable that explains two.** A **confounder** influences both variables you are correlating, creating association without a direct link:
```
temperature → ice-cream sales
temperature → swimming → drowning risk
```
Sales and drownings correlate strongly *through* temperature. Control for temperature (compare within heat bands) and the sales–drowning link shrinks toward nothing. Real confounders are everywhere: wealth in health data, city size in crime counts, study hours and access to tutoring in exam data.

**What would make a causal claim?** Hierarchy of evidence: (1) a **randomised controlled experiment** — randomly assign the cause, measure the effect; randomisation balances confounders on average. (2) Strong quasi-experiments (natural experiments, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity). (3) Meticulous observational adjustment — measure likely confounders, control for them, check robustness — still short of proof. (4) A scatterplot — never. Plus two cheap checks: does the cause come first in time? Is there a plausible mechanism? "Correlation is not causation" is not a conversation-stopper; it is a demand for a better design.

payload.title: What r can and cannot support

payload.code:
import numpy as np

temp   = np.array([22, 24, 27, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 36, 38], dtype=float)
sales  = np.array([12, 15, 19, 22, 26, 30, 32, 33, 35, 38], dtype=float)
swim   = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12], dtype=float)

print(np.corrcoef(temp, sales)[0, 1])   # 0.998
print(np.corrcoef(temp, swim)[0, 1])    # 0.979
print(np.corrcoef(sales, swim)[0, 1])   # 0.984 — confounded by temp

swim  = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12], dtype=float)
print(np.corrcoef(temp, sales)[0, 1])   # 0.998
print(np.corrcoef(temp, swim)[0, 1])    # 0.979
print(np.corrcoef(sales, swim)[0, 1])   # 0.984

steps.title: 3. Name the structure
steps.desc: Draw the arrows: temp → sales, temp → swim. The sales–swim correlation has no direct arrow — it is induced. A third variable you did not plot explains it.
steps.code_snippet:
# temp --> sales
#   |        \
#   v         v (spurious)
# swim <------'

steps.title: 4. Rewrite the finding honestly
steps.desc: The honest sentence: "Ice-cream sales and swimming counts rise together, almost entirely because both rise with temperature — within a fixed temperature band, the association shrinks." No causal verb, confounder named.
steps.code_snippet:
# Dishonest: "Ice-cream sales drive swimming."
# Honest: "Sales and swimming co-move with temperature; the direct link is unproven."

payload.solution: Hours–marks r ≈ 0.97: a strong linear association between the two variables actually under study. The temperature triangle produced three near-perfect correlations, of which sales–swimming is spurious — a confounder (temperature) points at both, and the pairwise r cannot see the third arrow. The rewrite names the confounder and refuses the causal verb. That is the entire discipline: compute r, plot the scatter, ask "what third variable is missing?" before any sentence with "drives" or "causes" leaves your keyboard.

payload.title: Compute, plot mentally, interrogate
payload.prompt: For each pair, compute r with np.corrcoef, sketch the scatter in words, then write the honest one-sentence finding: (1) [1,2,3,4,5] and [2,4,5,4,2] (a V-shape — predict r near 0 despite a perfect relationship); (2) study hours [1..10] and sleep hours [8, 7.5, 7, 6.5, 6, 5.5, 5, 4.5, 4, 3.5] (negative r — then name one confounder of the hours/sleep relation in real student life); (3) add one extreme outlier to pair (1) — x=[1..5, 100], y=[2,4,5,4,2, 0] — and watch r move. For every pair: does r ≈ 0 mean "no relationship"? Justify with the shape.
payload.hint: A symmetric V has zero linear correlation — r measures the straight line only. np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1] is the call.

mistakes.mistake: Reading r ≈ 0 as "no relationship"
mistakes.fix: It means no LINEAR relationship. Plot the scatter: U-shapes, parabolas and cycles can have r ≈ 0 with a perfect deterministic link.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting r without the scatterplot
mistakes.fix: One outlier can manufacture or destroy r. The coefficient and the plot are a package deal — publish both or neither.

mistakes.mistake: Causal verbs on observational correlations
mistakes.fix: "Associated with", "co-moves with", "predicts" are earned. "Drives", "causes", "leads to" require experimental or quasi-experimental evidence — or delete them.

mistakes.mistake: Correlating everything, understanding nothing
mistakes.fix: A correlation matrix of every column pair generates coincidences by sheer volume. Correlate pairs your causal story implies; treat the rest as exploration, not findings.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Sales and swimming counts correlate at 0.98. Explain why this does not show that ice-cream sales cause drownings, identify the confounder, and state what evidence WOULD justify a causal claim.
payload.answer: Pearson r measures linear co-movement, nothing more — it cannot distinguish "x causes y" from "z causes both". Here temperature is the confounder: hot months raise both ice-cream sales and swimming (and therefore drowning opportunity). The sales–swimming association is induced through temperature; within a narrow temperature band it largely vanishes. Two further cautions: correlation is not immune to outliers, and r only captures linear patterns. For a causal claim you would need, at minimum, temporal precedence (sales before drownings), a plausible mechanism, and control of confounders — ideally a randomised experiment (infeasible and unethical here), or a credible quasi-experiment / natural experiment that varies sales while holding summer conditions fixed. Absent that, the honest statement is association mediated by a named third variable.
payload.source: The classic correlation-vs-causation exam scenario; mirrors every "spurious correlation" teaching example.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Pearson r ∈ [−1, 1] measures linear association; compute with np.corrcoef or df.corr().
r ≈ 0 means "no linear pattern" — check the scatter for U-shapes and cycles.
One outlier can rewrite r; always publish the plot with the number.
A confounder causes both variables and fakes the link between them — name it before you narrate.
Causal claims need experiments or strong quasi-experiments; scatterplots never suffice.

That 90% of marks are explained exactly

questions.explanation: Rising and falling halves cancel in the linear average — r sees no straight line.

questions.prompt: A confounder is a variable that:
options: Influences BOTH x and y, inducing association between them
Must be included as a model feature always

questions.explanation: The third arrow points at both variables — creating correlation without a direct x → y link.

questions.explanation: Randomisation balances confounders on average — the design that earns the causal verb.

lessons.title: Outliers & the Train/Test Split: Evaluating Without Cheating
lessons.summary: Detecting outliers with IQR fences, their asymmetric damage to mean versus median, and the holdout split with random_state that keeps every reported metric honest.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Detect outliers with the IQR fence rule and judge error vs rare-event
Explain why the median and IQR resist outliers that break mean and std
Split data into train and test BEFORE fitting anything, with train_test_split
Use random_state for reproducible splits and state why the test set stays unseen

payload.text: A sensor logs 10 typical readings, then 109. Your mean detector now says the machine is failing; your median detector shrugs. Then a subtler trap: you train a model on all your data, evaluate it on the same data, and it looks brilliant — until real customers arrive. Two enemies of honest analysis, one lesson: outliers that distort the summaries, and test data that leaks into training.

**Outliers: errors, rarity, or signal.** An outlier is a value far from the rest. Sources differ: data-entry errors (age = 900), unit mismatches (cm mixed with m), instrument glitches — fix or drop these; and genuine rare events (a celebrity order in a retail feed) — usually keep, because they are real. The rule: **investigate before removing**. Deleting inconvenient data is how analyses become propaganda.

**The IQR fence rule.** Quartile-based and distribution-free: compute Q1 (25th percentile), Q3 (75th) and IQR = Q3 − Q1. Values below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR are **fences**; points beyond them are outliers. (The 1.5 is Tukey's convention — a display choice, not a law; 3·IQR marks far outliers.) Pandas: `q1 = df["col"].quantile(0.25)`. Resistant summaries travel together: **median with IQR** versus **mean with std** — the first pair barely notices outliers; the second pair is dragged by them. Device readings [10, 12, 12, 13, 12, 11, 14, 13, 15, 109]: mean 22.1 "typical" — nonsense; median 12.5 — true; the fence at 16.375 flags 109 alone.

**The train/test split: evaluation that means something.** A model is judged on data it has never seen. So split first, always:
```
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y)
```
Fit on train only; evaluate once on test. **random_state** pins the shuffle so the same split regenerates on every run — without it, your metrics wobble run to run and nobody, including next-week-you, can reproduce them. **stratify=y** keeps class proportions equal in both halves (matters for imbalanced classification). The test set is a one-shot exam: every time you tune a model to improve its test score, the test set is silently becoming training data. That is why real projects add a third, validation, slice — the idea arrives fully in the ML-fundamentals course.

**All statistics stay on the train side.** Medians for filling, means for standardising, PCA, feature selection — anything learned from data must be learned on the training split and merely APPLIED to test. A median computed on the whole dataset leaks test information into training (the "leakage" of Module 6.4). The pattern you will formalise as scikit-learn pipelines in the next module starts as this habit: **split → fit on train → transform both with train-fitted objects**.

payload.title: Resistant vs sensitive statistics
rows: k · std from mean (sensitive to the very thing you hunt)

payload.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

readings = np.array([10, 12, 12, 13, 12, 11, 14, 13, 15, 109], dtype=float)
q1, q3 = np.percentile(readings, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(q1, q3, lo, hi)                       # 12.0 13.75 9.375 16.375
print(readings[(readings < lo) | (readings > hi)])   # [109.]
print(readings.mean(), np.median(readings))  # 22.1, 12.5

payload.title: The test set is not free real estate
payload.text: Every model choice steered by the test score contaminates it. Fit on train, peek at test rarely, and treat the final number as an estimate with uncertainty — not a scoreboard to maximise.

payload.title: Flag a sensor outlier, then split data the honest way
payload.problem: Sensor readings contain one absurd value — detect it with IQR fences and show how mean versus median report the "typical" reading. Then, with a 100-sample regression dataset, split train/test with random_state=42, compute the target mean on TRAIN ONLY, and show the leakage version (full-data mean) differs.

steps.title: 1. Fences first, judgement second
steps.desc: Q1 = 12.0, Q3 = 13.75, IQR = 1.75, upper fence = 16.375. Exactly one point beyond it: 109. Investigate (glitch? unit error?) before any removal.
steps.code_snippet:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([10, 12, 12, 13, 12, 11, 14, 13, 15, 109], dtype=float)
q1, q3 = np.percentile(readings, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
outliers = readings[(readings < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (readings > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)]
print(outliers)          # [109.]

steps.title: 2. Watch the summaries disagree
steps.desc: Mean 22.1 claims a "typical" reading that never happened; median 12.5 sits right in the data. Std is inflated the same way — one reason resistant pairs exist.
steps.code_snippet:
print(readings.mean(), readings.std(ddof=1))   # 22.1, 30.6...
print(np.median(readings), np.subtract(*np.percentile(readings, [75, 25])))   # 12.5, 1.75 (the IQR)

steps.title: 3. Split before fitting — reproducibly
steps.desc: 100 samples, 25% holdout, pinned shuffle. Re-running this cell returns the identical split — the whole point of random_state.
steps.code_snippet:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 2))
y = 2 * X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=100)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape)   # (75, 2) (25, 2)

steps.title: 4. Prove the leakage point with a mean fill
steps.desc: The full-data mean uses all 100 targets; the train-only mean uses 75. They differ — and only the second is legal in a pipeline. Scale or fill statistics belong to the train side, always.
steps.code_snippet:
full_mean = y.mean()        # leaks test information
train_mean = y_train.mean()  # honest
print(round(full_mean, 4), round(train_mean, 4))   # e.g. -0.0031 0.0117

payload.solution: IQR fences flagged exactly the 109 reading (fence 16.375) while the median (12.5) stayed honest and the mean (22.1) lied about "typical". The 75/25 split with random_state=42 is deterministic and reproducible; the train-only target mean differs from the full-data mean, demonstrating in miniature why every learned statistic must come from the training side. Split first, fit on train, apply to test — the discipline every module from here builds on.

payload.title: Detect, defend, split
payload.prompt: latency_ms = np.array([120, 135, 128, 141, 130, 126, 150, 133, 129, 850, 138, 125]): (1) IQR-fence the outliers — what is flagged, and would you drop or keep it after investigation? (2) Report mean/median and std/IQR before and after removing the flag — which pair moved? (3) Build a 2-feature regression set with default_rng(1), 60 samples, split 75/25 with random_state=1 and stratify omitted; re-run twice and prove identical test sizes; (4) compute the target std on train only and on the full set — report the difference and state which a standardisation step must use. (5) Write the one-line policy you will apply in every future project.
payload.hint: np.percentile(arr, [25, 75]); train_test_split is deterministic given random_state.

mistakes.mistake: Deleting outliers because they hurt the metric
mistakes.fix: Investigate first: error (fix/drop) or rare truth (keep). Log every removal with its count — an analysis that quietly discarded 4% of rows must say so.

mistakes.mistake: Using mean/std rules to detect outliers in skewed data
mistakes.fix: The mean and std are themselves dragged by the outliers you are hunting. Use resistant statistics — median, IQR fences — for detection.

mistakes.mistake: Splitting AFTER fitting or scaling on the full data
mistakes.fix: Split first. Any transformation that learns parameters (median fills, scaling, PCA) is fit on train only, then applied to test. Reverse the order and the test metric is fiction.

mistakes.mistake: Omitting random_state and chasing a better score across reruns
mistakes.fix: An unseeded split changes each run; "improvements" may be shuffle luck. Pin random_state, and for real rigor average over several seeded splits or folds (the next course).

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the IQR fence rule for outlier detection and why it beats a "more than two standard deviations from the mean" rule. Then justify splitting data before any fitting, including the role of random_state.
payload.answer: IQR rule: compute Q1, Q3 and IQR = Q3 − Q1; values outside [Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR] are outliers. It is resistant: quartiles barely move when extreme values appear, so the fence stays put and the outlier stands out. The std-based rule fails by circularity — outliers inflate the very mean and std used to define "far", widening the fence and hiding the culprit (in the sensor example, one 109 inflates the std to ~30, making 109 barely unusual). Splitting: a model must be evaluated on unseen data, so the holdout is set aside before ANY fitting — including learned preprocessing statistics, which would otherwise leak test information (leakage). train_test_split(..., test_size, random_state, stratify) performs a seeded shuffle-sampled split: random_state pins the shuffle so results reproduce run to run; stratify preserves class balance for classification. Fit on train; transform and score on test; touch the test score rarely.
payload.source: The standard "outlier detection + holdout justification" pairing in DS interviews and semester papers.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Outliers: investigate (error vs rare truth) before removing; log every removal.
IQR fences (Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR) detect outliers robustly; mean/std rules are self-sabotaging.
Median + IQR resist outliers; mean + std are dragged by them.
Split BEFORE fitting; learn fills/scalers on train only; apply to test (no leakage).
random_state pins the split for reproducibility; stratify keeps class balance.
The test set is a scarce exam — tuning to it turns it into training data.

questions.prompt: For heavily skewed data, the resistant pair of summaries is:
questions.explanation: Quartile/rank-based statistics barely move when a tail drags the mean and std around.

questions.prompt: readings = [10, 12, 12, 13, 12, 11, 14, 13, 15, 109]. The IQR fence rule flags:
questions.explanation: Q1 = 12, Q3 = 13.75, IQR = 1.75; the upper fence 13.75 + 2.625 = 16.375 catches only 109.

questions.prompt: random_state=42 in train_test_split ensures:
options: The same shuffle — an identical, reproducible split on every run
That 42% of rows go to test
questions.explanation: It seeds the permutation so the split is deterministic; without it every run holds out different rows.

questions.prompt: Computing a column median on the FULL dataset before splitting is:
options: Best practice — more data is used
questions.explanation: The median has seen test rows; that knowledge flows into training. Learn it on train, apply it everywhere.

modules.title: Module 10 — First ML with scikit-learn
modules.summary: The scikit-learn contract: datasets as X and y, feature matrices with sample/feature axes; holdout splitting; baselines with DummyRegressor and DummyClassifier; first LinearRegression and DecisionTree models with MAE and accuracy read honestly; and the capstone end-to-end notebook.

lessons.title: Datasets & Feature Matrices: X and y, the scikit-learn Contract
lessons.summary: Supervised learning as learn-a-mapping; the n_samples × n_features shape of X; built-in sklearn datasets; and building X, y from a cleaned DataFrame.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe supervised learning as learning a mapping from features X to target y
Read the n_samples × n_features shape convention and keep X 2-D, y 1-D
Load a built-in sklearn dataset and inspect data, target and feature names
Build X and y from a pandas DataFrame with drop and bracket selection

payload.text: Every model in scikit-learn speaks one dialect: give me X (a table of samples × features) and y (one target per sample), call fit(X_train, y_train), then predict(X_test). Same three calls for house prices, disease risk, image pixels, customer churn. This lesson installs that contract — because once it is muscle memory, a hundred algorithms all feel like the same tool.

**Supervised learning in one sentence.** Learn a function f such that `f(X_row) ≈ y_row` — features in, target out — using examples where both were known. Everything else (algorithms, tuning, theory) is commentary on HOW f gets learned and how well it generalises to rows it has never seen.

**The shape contract.** scikit-learn insists on:
- **X — the feature matrix**: 2-D, shape `(n_samples, n_features)`. Rows are observations (people, days, sensors); columns are the measurements used to predict.
- **y — the target**: 1-D, shape `(n_samples,)`. One value per row.
A single sample is a row of X; the model never sees "a column of people". The target's type picks your problem family: a continuous number (price, temperature) → **regression**; a category (spam/not-spam, species) → **classification**. Two more rules: no missing values (NaN breaks every estimator — Module 6/8 cleaning earns its keep here) and numeric inputs (categories must be encoded — a preview of the ML-fundamentals course).

**Built-in datasets: zero-download practice.** sklearn ships small real datasets for exactly this stage:
```
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris, load_diabetes
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)      # (150, 4), species 0/1/2
X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True)  # (442, 10), progression target
```
`load_iris()` without return_xy gives a Bunch: `.data`, `.target`, `.feature_names`, `.target_names`, `.DESCR`. Iris: 150 flowers, 4 measurements (sepal/petal length and width), 3 species of 50. Diabetes: 442 patients, 10 already-centred numeric features, a quantitative disease-progression target.

**From DataFrame to X, y.** Real projects load a cleaned CSV (Module 8) and split it:
```
X = df.drop(columns="species")   # everything EXCEPT the target → 2-D
y = df["species"]                # the target column → 1-D Series
```
The convention "the target leaves X; everything else predicts" keeps leakage out by construction: if a column is not meant as a predictor, it is dropped before anything is fitted.

payload.title: Regression vs classification — how y decides

payload.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

iris = load_iris()
X, y = iris.data, iris.target
print(X.shape, y.shape)            # (150, 4) (150,)
print(iris.feature_names)          # sepal length/width, petal length/width
print(iris.target_names)           # setosa versicolor virginica
print(X[0])                        # first flower: [5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2]

payload.title: X stays 2-D, even for one feature
payload.text: A single-feature X must keep its second axis: X.reshape(-1, 1) or df[["col"]]. A flat (n,) X raises "Expected 2D array" — the contract's most common papercut.

payload.title: Inspect iris, then build X and y from a DataFrame
payload.problem: Load iris with full metadata; report the shapes of X and y and the class balance. Then build the same problem from a small CSV-style DataFrame: select the four feature columns into X and the species column into y, and verify the shapes obey the contract.

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

iris = load_iris()

csv_text = ("sepal_length,sepal_width,petal_length,petal_width,species\n"

print(X.shape, y.shape)    # (3, 4) (3,)

Two entrances, one shape discipline — the prerequisite for every model in the next lessons.

mistakes.mistake: Feeding a flat (n,) array as X
mistakes.fix: Estimators expect 2-D. Use X.reshape(-1, 1) or a one-column DataFrame — the single-feature papercut has a one-token fix.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the target (or an ID column) inside X
mistakes.fix: The model would "cheat" — an ID column memorised, the target leaked. df.drop(columns=...) the target and any non-predictor column before splitting.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring NaNs before fit
mistakes.fix: Most estimators raise on NaN. Run the Module 6 inspection ritual and a Module 8 cleaning pipeline before X, y are born.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a continuous target as classes (or vice versa)
mistakes.fix: y's dtype and semantics pick the family. Numeric target with meaningful magnitude → regression; finite set of labels → classification. Choosing wrong silently produces nonsense metrics.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State the scikit-learn data contract: the shapes and meanings of X and y, how the target type selects the problem family, and two consequences of leaving the target inside X.
payload.answer: X is the feature matrix, 2-D with shape (n_samples, n_features): rows are observations, columns the predictor measurements. y is the target, 1-D with shape (n_samples,): one label or value per row. The target's nature defines the task — a continuous numeric y means regression (predict a quantity); a categorical y means classification (predict a label). If the target stays inside X: (1) the model can peek at the answer during fit — training performance becomes fiction and the held-out evaluation collapses; (2) even a pure ID column invites memorisation instead of learning patterns. Real projects additionally require X to be NaN-free and numeric, which is why the cleaning pipeline of Module 8 precedes every modelling step.

options: X as a DataFrame and y as a Series — the standard split
