modules.title: Module 6 — Evaluation: Choosing the Metric from the Cost of Errors
modules.summary: Evaluation as an economics problem rather than a scoreboard: reading the cost of a false alarm against the cost of a miss; the confusion matrix with precision, recall and F1 computed by hand; ROC-AUC versus PR-AUC when the positive class is rare; regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE) and which one the business actually feels; and the two disciplines that make any number worth reporting — cross-validation and baselines.

lessons.title: The Cost of Errors: Confusion Matrices, Precision, Recall, and F1
lessons.summary: Every classification metric is arithmetic on four cells — and the right metric is the one whose denominators match the mistake that costs you money.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Build a 2x2 confusion matrix from raw predictions and compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 by hand
Derive the primary metric from an explicit cost of false positives versus false negatives
Decide between precision, recall and F1 given a stated business cost, and defend the choice
Explain why accuracy collapses on a 1%-positive dataset and compute the majority-class baseline that proves it

payload.text: A bank ships a fraud model that is 99.4% accurate. It also misses 60% of actual fraud, because the model learned that almost nothing is fraud. Meanwhile a screening model that catches nearly every case gets fired for being "only 70% accurate" — because its false alarms annoyed the operations team. Both verdicts came from the same number, accuracy, and both were wrong. The metric is not a formality you pick after training; it is the contract that says which mistake you are willing to make. Get it wrong and you will optimise the model into the opposite of what anyone wanted.

**Four cells, one matrix.** Take every prediction and sort it by two questions: what did the model say, and what was actually true. Predicted positive/negative crossed with actual positive/negative gives four counts: **TP** (predicted yes, truly yes), **FP** (predicted yes, actually no — a false alarm), **FN** (predicted no, actually yes — a miss), **TN** (predicted no, truly no). This is the confusion matrix, and — this is the part interviewers probe — *every* classification metric you will ever meet is arithmetic on those four numbers. Accuracy = (TP+TN)/all. Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of everything the model flagged, how much was real — a statement about the quality of your alarms. Recall (sensitivity, TPR) = TP/(TP+FN): of everything that was real, how much did you catch — a statement about your coverage. F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R): the harmonic mean of the two, a single number that punishes any model that is strong on one side and useless on the other (P = 0.90, R = 0.10 gives F1 = 0.18, not 0.50 — the harmonic mean drags toward the smaller operand). Keep the denominators straight: precision's denominator is *predictions*; recall's denominator is *actual positives*. Nearly every confusion in an interview is a denominator confusion.

**The cost matrix decides the metric.** Before choosing a metric, price the mistakes. A false positive on a fraud alert costs an operations review (minutes, salary); a false negative costs the stolen amount, perhaps multiplied by reputational loss. A missed cancer screening costs a life trajectory; a false alarm costs a follow-up test. Write it as a cost: total cost = C_FN·FN + C_FP·FP. That single line resolves every "which metric?" debate. If C_FP dominates (you may not accuse a loyal customer of fraud), you are buying **precision** — few alarms, all of them defensible. If C_FN dominates (you may not let threats through), you are buying **recall** — catch everything, tolerate noise. If you genuinely cannot price the two, F1 is the honest compromise, because it refuses to let one side do all the talking. Note what F1 assumes: implicitly equal weight on precision and recall, and it ignores TN entirely — correct for a rare-positive problem, wrong when true negatives are the bulk of your value (spam filtering still cares that 99% of mail passes untouched; that is a specificity story).

**Accuracy, and its well-known lie.** Accuracy is the right metric exactly when classes are balanced *and* the two error types cost roughly the same. Break either condition and it misleads. On a dataset with 1% positives, a model that always answers "not positive" scores 99% while catching nothing — accuracy measured the model's laziness, not its skill. So the first number you compute alongside accuracy is the **baseline**: majority-class accuracy, or stratified-random predictions. A model that scores 0.96 against a 0.96 baseline has added nothing, no matter what the leaderboard says. This is the baseline discipline from Module 1 meeting the arithmetic of Module 6: report (metric, baseline, confusion matrix) together, always.

**From counts to practice.** In scikit-learn: confusion_matrix(y, pred) prints the grid (careful with row/column orientation — sklearn puts *actual* in rows by convention: [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]] for binary labels), precision_recall_fscore_support gives all three, classification_report wraps them with support counts, and f1_score(y, pred, pos_label=...) picks which class is "positive". For multiclass you must state the averaging: **macro** gives every class equal weight (the honest view of rare classes), **weighted** scales by support (flatters the majority), **micro** pools all counts (in single-label problems it equals accuracy — usually the least informative choice). Thresholding matters too: these numbers are computed at whatever decision boundary you used, usually 0.5 by default. The threshold is a dial, not a constant — you will move it in Lesson 6.2, and every move trades FP against FN exactly as the cost line demands.

payload.code:
# Confusion matrix, P/R/F1, and the baseline — in the order you should run them
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (confusion_matrix, precision_recall_fscore_support,
                             accuracy_score, classification_report)

# 0. The baseline first — everything else is judged against it
base = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(X_train, y_train)
y_base = base.predict(X_test)
print("baseline accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, y_base))

# 1. Your model
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))          # [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]
p, r, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_test, y_pred, average="binary")
print(f"precision={p:.3f} recall={r:.3f} f1={f1:.3f}")

# 2. The honest report, with the positive class named explicitly
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, digits=3, zero_division=0))

# 3. A cost line: choose the threshold that minimises C_FN*FN + C_FP*FP
import numpy as np
proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
is_pos, is_neg = (y_test == 1), (y_test == 0)
C_FN, C_FP = 10000, 500            # business prices, not guesses
costs = [(t, C_FN * (is_pos & (proba < t)).sum() + C_FP * (is_neg & (proba >= t)).sum())
         for t in np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 18)]
best_t, best_cost = min(costs, key=lambda x: x[1])
print("threshold", round(best_t, 2), "min cost", best_cost)

payload.title: Accuracy without a baseline is not a result
payload.text: On 1%-positive data, always-negative scores 99%. Print majority-class (or dummy) accuracy in the same cell as your model number, or the number means nothing.

payload.title: Report the matrix, not just the scalar
payload.text: One F1 hides two different failures. The confusion matrix plus a per-class report lets you say exactly which mistake grew when a number moved — and that is what an interviewer or a stakeholder actually wants to hear.

payload.title: A fraud model by hand: matrix, metrics, baseline, and the cost line
payload.problem: 1,000 transactions; 40 are truly fraudulent. Your model flags 60 transactions as fraud; 30 of them are real fraud. (a) Fill the confusion matrix. (b) Compute precision, recall, F1 and accuracy. (c) Compare accuracy with the always-not-fraud baseline. (d) With each missed fraud costing Rs 10,000 and each false flag costing Rs 500 of analyst time, which strategy is cheaper?

steps.title: (a) The four cells
steps.desc: TP = 30 (flagged and real). FN = 40 - 30 = 10 (real fraud never flagged). FP = 60 - 30 = 30 (flagged, not fraud). TN = 960 - 30 = 930 (correctly passed; 960 non-fraud rows minus the 30 false alarms). Totals check: 30 + 30 + 10 + 930 = 1,000.

steps.title: (b) The four metrics
steps.desc: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 30/60 = 0.50 — half the alerts are real. Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 30/40 = 0.75 — three quarters of fraud caught. F1 = 2PR/(P+R) = 2(0.50)(0.75)/(1.25) = 0.75/1.25 = 0.60. Accuracy = (30+930)/1000 = 960/1000 = 0.96.

steps.title: (c) The baseline that embarrasses the accuracy
steps.desc: A model that never flags anything gets TN = 960, FN = 40, and accuracy = 960/1000 = 0.96 — identical to your model. By accuracy, the two are indistinguishable; by recall, yours catches 30 frauds the baseline never will. Accuracy was measuring the class balance, not the model.

steps.title: (d) The cost line decides
steps.desc: Your model: 10 misses x Rs 10,000 + 30 false flags x Rs 500 = Rs 1,00,000 + Rs 15,000 = Rs 1,15,000. Never-flag baseline: 40 misses x Rs 10,000 + 0 = Rs 4,00,000. The model saves Rs 2,85,000 per 1,000 transactions while posting the same accuracy. That sentence — not the 96% — is the business case.

payload.solution: Matrix: TP 30, FP 30, FN 10, TN 930. Precision 0.50, recall 0.75, F1 0.60, accuracy 0.96 — exactly the baseline accuracy of 0.96. Cost: model Rs 1,15,000 vs baseline Rs 4,00,000, so the model wins by Rs 2,85,000. The lesson in one line: pick the metric whose denominator maps to your cost, prove it beats a baseline, and show the matrix so nobody can hide behind one number.

lessons.title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC: Ranking Quality When the Positive Class Is Rare
lessons.summary: What threshold-free metrics really measure, why a beautiful ROC curve can hide a useless precision number on 1%-positive data, and how to pick the operating threshold from cost.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Interpret ROC-AUC as the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative
Compute precision from an FPR/recall pair on an imbalanced dataset and explain why the ROC plot flatters it
State the random baseline for ROC-AUC and for PR-AUC under a given class prevalence
Select a deployment threshold from an explicit cost or capacity constraint rather than defaulting to 0.5

payload.text: The demo curve is gorgeous: hugs the top-left corner, area under the curve 0.97. The stakeholder deploys it, then discovers that at the recall the business needs, three of every four fraud alerts are false. Nothing lied — the ROC curve simply answered a different question than the one being asked. ROC-AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds while weighting the false-positive rate against the whole negative class, and on a 1:100 problem the whole negative class is a very forgiving audience. This lesson teaches you to read both curves, know which one your class balance makes honest, and to never confuse a good curve with a good operating point.

**Scores, thresholds, labels.** A classifier usually emits a *score* (probability or margin), not a final label. The threshold converts one to the other, and every threshold produces one pair of rates: true positive rate (recall) and false positive rate, FPR = FP/(FP+TN). Sweep the threshold from "flag everything" to "flag nothing" and you trace the **ROC curve**: TPR against FPR. Start at (0,0) (threshold so high nothing is flagged) and end at (1,1) (everything flagged). The **ROC-AUC** is the area under that curve, and its cleanest interpretation is probabilistic: *the chance that a randomly chosen positive example receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one*. Random guessing gives 0.50 (the diagonal), perfect ranking gives 1.0, and — a favourite interview line — an AUC of 0.90 means: pick one fraud and one legitimate transaction at random; the model ranks the fraud higher 90% of the time. Because it is built from ranking, ROC-AUC ignores the threshold entirely: it measures the model's ordering ability, and only the ordering.

**Why ROC flatters imbalance.** The FPR denominator is the *actual negatives*. With 10,000 negatives and 100 positives, a 1% FPR is 100 false alarms — a queue that will drown any team — yet on the ROC plane that operating point sits at (0.01, 0.80), visually indistinguishable from perfection. Translate it into precision (the question the business asks): catching 80 of 100 positives with 99 false alarms gives precision = 80/(80+99) ≈ 0.45. Good-looking curve, barely half the alerts real. The **precision-recall curve** plots precision against recall across thresholds and refuses to hide this, because precision's denominator includes the false alarms themselves. Its baseline is the *prevalence*: a random ranker achieves average precision ≈ 100/10,100 ≈ 0.01 on that data — so an AUPRC of 0.30 is 30x random, while the same model might show ROC-AUC 0.92 that looks merely "very good" against a 0.50 baseline. The rule of thumb: **balanced problems → ROC-AUC is fine; rare positives (say under ~10%) → PR-AUC (average precision) is the metric of record, and ROC-AUC becomes a secondary sanity number.** One caveat that cuts the other way: PR-AUC changes when prevalence changes, so you may compare models on the same test set but never compare AUPRC numbers across datasets with different positive rates. In sklearn: roc_curve, auc, roc_auc_score; precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score (prefer average precision over the trapezoid on discretised PR curves — it interpolates properly).

**The operating point is a decision, not a default.** AUC summarises the whole curve, but production runs at exactly one threshold. Choose it from constraints: (1) **cost** — sweep thresholds, compute C_FN·FN + C_FP·FP at each, deploy the minimum (Lesson 6.1's arithmetic, now continuous); (2) **capacity** — "the fraud team can review 200 alerts a day" → pick the threshold whose flag count equals the budget, then report the precision and recall you get there; (3) **constraint** — "precision at least 0.60" or "recall at least 0.90" → find the threshold that satisfies the constraint with margin. All three need *calibrated* probabilities if you read the threshold as a probability; a well-ranked but miscalibrated model can be thresholded by score, but not reasoned about as risk. Calibration tools (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) and calibration curves exist for exactly this; naive Bayes and uncalibrated SVM margins are the classic offenders from Module 5. Final discipline: after choosing the threshold on validation data, freeze it, evaluate once on the test set, and report the confusion matrix *at that threshold* beside both AUCs. Curves are for comparing models; matrices are for running a business.

payload.code:
# Both curves, both AUCs, and a cost-chosen threshold
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_curve, roc_auc_score, precision_recall_curve,
                             average_precision_score, confusion_matrix)
import numpy as np

proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
print("ROC-AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3))
print("AP (PR-AUC):", round(average_precision_score(y_test, proba), 3))
print("prevalence (random PR baseline):", round(y_test.mean(), 4))

fpr, tpr, thr_roc = roc_curve(y_test, proba)
prec, rec, thr_pr = precision_recall_curve(y_test, proba)

# Operating point from cost: same sweep as Lesson 6.1, on the score axis
C_FN, C_FP = 10000, 500
best = min(
    ((t, C_FN * ((y_test == 1) & (proba < t)).sum() +
            C_FP * ((y_test == 0) & (proba >= t)).sum())
     for t in np.unique(proba)),
    key=lambda x: x[1],
)
thr = best[0]
y_at_thr = (proba >= thr).astype(int)
print("threshold", round(float(thr), 3), "cost", best[1])
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_at_thr))   # the matrix you actually ship with

payload.title: A high AUC does not bless the deployed operating point
payload.text: AUC-ROC is an average over thresholds you will never run. Always report the confusion matrix at the chosen threshold — that is the only place the business lives.

payload.title: Report AUPRC next to the prevalence
payload.text: "AP = 0.31 on 1.8% positives" is interpretable (17x random); "AP = 0.31" alone is not. The baseline travels with the number.

payload.title: The same model, read through both curves
payload.problem: A fraud test set has 100 positives and 9,900 negatives (9,900 + 100 = 10,000). At one threshold the model catches 80 positives (recall 0.80) with an FPR of 1%. (a) Compute precision at that point. (b) Describe where the point sits on the ROC plane. (c) What are the random baselines for ROC-AUC and for average precision here? (d) The fraud team can review 150 alerts a day on this volume — is this threshold deployable?

steps.title: (a) Precision from the FPR
steps.desc: FP = FPR x negatives = 0.01 x 9,900 = 99. TP = 80. Precision = 80/(80 + 99) = 80/179 ≈ 0.45. Fewer than half the alerts are real fraud — an analyst rejecting 99 wasted cases a day on this slice.

steps.title: (b) The ROC view of the identical fact
steps.desc: The point is (FPR = 0.01, TPR = 0.80) — in the top-left corner, visually "excellent". The ROC plane did not lie; it simply normalised the false alarms by 9,900 negatives, which makes 99 false alarms look like almost nothing.

steps.title: (c) Baselines
steps.desc: ROC-AUC baseline = 0.50 (random ranking), always. Average precision baseline = prevalence = 100/10,000 = 0.01. So AP should be read as a multiple of 0.01, while ROC-AUC is read against 0.50 — two different rulers for the same model.

steps.title: (d) Capacity check
steps.desc: Alerts = TP + FP = 80 + 99 = 179 per 10,000 transactions. Scale to daily volume: if 10,000 transactions arrive per day, 179 alerts exceeds a 150/day budget. Raise the threshold until alerts ≤ 150, then recompute precision and recall at that exact point and report them — capacity is a legitimate tiebreaker when cost is unknown.

payload.solution: (a) Precision ≈ 0.45 (80/179). (b) ROC point (0.01, 0.80) — flattering by construction on rare positives. (c) Random ROC-AUC = 0.50; random AP = prevalence = 0.01. (d) 179 alerts breaches a 150/day budget — raise the threshold to fit capacity, then report P/R and the confusion matrix at that threshold. One model, two curves, one operating decision: PR for honesty under imbalance, ROC for ranking shape, cost/capacity for the threshold.

payload.title: Find the operating point yourself
payload.prompt: On any imbalanced binary dataset: fit a probabilistic model, compute ROC-AUC and average precision, and print the prevalence. Plot (or tabulate) both curves. Pick the threshold that meets precision >= 0.50 (or minimises a cost you define), and print the confusion matrix there. Note the gap between "best AUC" and "usable operating point".
payload.hint: If AP is a large multiple of prevalence while ROC-AUC is a modest distance above 0.5, you are on imbalanced data — lead with PR.

mistakes.mistake: Leading with ROC-AUC on a 1:100 problem
mistakes.fix: Report average precision with prevalence as the baseline; keep ROC-AUC as a secondary ranking check only.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing AUPRC numbers across datasets with different positive rates
mistakes.fix: AP moves with prevalence by construction. Compare models on the same test set, or normalise against the baseline explicitly (AP / prevalence as a lift multiple).

mistakes.mistake: Passing hard 0/1 labels instead of scores into roc_auc_score
mistakes.fix: AUC on binary labels uses a single operating point and reports tie-heavy garbage (effectively one point on the curve). Feed probabilities or decision scores.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the threshold on the test set
mistakes.fix: The threshold is a hyperparameter: choose it on validation/CV (by cost or capacity), freeze it, and touch the test set exactly once with the frozen pipeline.

mistakes.mistake: Reading threshold 0.5 as optimal by default
mistakes.fix: 0.5 is optimal only under calibrated probabilities and symmetric costs. With asymmetric costs or a capacity limit, the optimal threshold is almost never 0.5.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define ROC-AUC probabilistically. A test set is 1% positive; the model achieves TPR 0.80 at FPR 0.01. Compute the precision at that point (assume 10,000 rows), give the random baselines for both AUCs, and state which curve you would lead with and why.
payload.answer: ROC-AUC = P(score(positive) > score(negative)) — the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative; 0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect ordering; it is threshold-free and ignores calibration. Rows: 100 positives, 9,900 negatives. TP = 80; FP = 0.01 x 9,900 = 99; precision = 80/179 ≈ 0.45. Baselines: ROC-AUC random = 0.50; PR-AUC random = prevalence = 0.01 (so AP 0.30 would be 30x random). Lead with the precision-recall curve / average precision: at this prevalence the ROC plane normalises false alarms by 9,900 negatives and makes 99 wasted reviews look negligible, while precision exposes that fewer than half the alerts are real. ROC-AUC stays useful as a threshold-free ranking sanity check; the deployed threshold is then chosen by cost or alert-queue capacity, and the shipped confusion matrix is reported at that threshold.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: ROC-AUC = the probability a random positive outranks a random negative; it measures ranking, not the deployed decision.
FPR is normalised by the negative class, so ROC curves flatter rare-positive problems; precision includes false alarms and does not.
Random baselines: ROC-AUC 0.50 always; PR-AUC equals prevalence — always quote it with the positive rate.
Lead with PR-AUC under heavy imbalance; compare AUPRC only within one dataset.

options: The fraction of predictions that are correct at threshold 0.5
The probability that a randomly chosen positive example scores higher than a randomly chosen negative one
The area of the confusion matrix that is correct
questions.explanation: It is a ranking probability over all thresholds: 0.5 is random ordering, 1.0 is perfect ordering.

questions.prompt: On data with 1% positives, a random ranker achieves an average precision of approximately:
questions.explanation: The PR baseline equals prevalence: with 1% positives, a random ordering averages about 0.01 precision across recall levels.

questions.prompt: Your model shows ROC-AUC 0.97 but, at the recall you need, only 35% of alerts are real. The best explanation is:
options: ROC normalises false positives by the huge negative class, so rare-positive problems flatter ROC while precision exposes the false-alarm load
The model is miscalibrated, so the curve is invalid
questions.explanation: FPR = FP/(FP+TN): with thousands of negatives, dozens of false alarms still look tiny on the ROC plane. The PR curve shows the same operating point honestly.

options: Always at 0.5, because that is the default
On validation data by minimising expected cost or meeting a capacity/constraint target, then frozen before the test set is touched
On the test set, to maximise test F1
At the threshold where the ROC curve is closest to the corner
questions.explanation: The threshold is a tuned decision variable tied to cost or capacity; tuning it on test data leaks the test set.

lessons.title: Regression Metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE and MAPE (and When Each One Lies)
lessons.summary: Four numbers for continuous predictions — their arithmetic, their units, their tolerance for outliers, and the honest reason a business prefers one over another.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute MAE, MSE, RMSE and MAPE by hand from four predictions and interpret each in plain English
Explain why RMSE is always at least MAE and what a large gap between them signals
Identify the failure modes of MAPE (zeros, near-zeros, asymmetry) and propose a guarded alternative
Choose the primary regression metric from the stakeholder loss function and compare against a mean baseline

payload.text: Two teams report their demand-forecasting model. Team A: "MAE 42 units — we are off by 42 boxes on average." Team B: "RMSE 61 units." Same model? Neither can say until they agree on what an error costs. If every missed box costs the same, the average absolute error is the price. If a single huge miss shuts a factory line, the squared error — which charges quadratically for disasters — is the price. And if the CFO asks "what error percentage are we talking about?", someone is about to say MAPE and quietly divide by a near-zero target. Regression metrics look like four ways of computing "how wrong"; they are four different opinions about which wrongness matters.

**Four formulas, four opinions about what an error is.** Let eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ be the residuals on your test set. **MAE** = mean|eᵢ| — the average mistake, in the target's own units; every error counts linearly, so a 10-unit miss costs exactly ten times a 1-unit miss and one catastrophe cannot drown out the rest. **MSE** = mean eᵢ² — units are *squared* (rupees squared, kilograms squared), which makes it a great optimisation target (smooth and differentiable everywhere) and a terrible slide statistic; its real message is that it charges quadratically, so a single 100-unit miss outweighs a hundred 10-unit misses. **RMSE** = √MSE — the same verdict with the units restored, which is why it is the default headline number; it always satisfies RMSE ≥ MAE (the root-mean of |e| is never below the mean of |e|), it sits between MAE and the largest error, and for roughly Gaussian errors it lands near 1.25 × MAE. That ratio is a diagnostic: **RMSE far above MAE means a small number of huge errors is driving your score** — go look at those rows before you trust either number. **MAPE** = mean(|eᵢ|/|yᵢ|) × 100 — unitless and instantly readable ("we are off by 5% on average"), which is exactly why finance teams ask for it, and exactly why it needs guards.

**Where MAPE lies.** Three failure modes, each worth a sentence in any report that uses it. (1) **Zeros and near-zeros**: y = 0 makes the term undefined; y = 12 makes an ordinary 30-unit error a 250% error — MAPE is dominated by whichever targets happen to be small, not by whichever predictions are worst. (2) **Asymmetry**: with non-negative predictions, under-prediction can never exceed 100% (ŷ ≥ 0 caps |e|/y at 1) while over-prediction is unbounded — so optimising MAPE systematically pushes forecasts *low*. (3) **Equal weight on unequal targets**: a 2-unit error on a target of 4 scores the same as a 200-unit error on a target of 400, which is rarely the economics. Guardrails: exclude or floor near-zero targets explicitly; use **WAPE** = Σ|eᵢ| / Σ|yᵢ| (aggregate error over aggregate volume — stable, weights big targets as the business does); or use a **symmetric MAPE** variant with its own caveats. And when the two directions genuinely cost differently (an unsold coat versus a stockout, in retail), no symmetric metric is right: use **quantile (pinball) loss** — pinball(y, ŷ_q, q) penalises under- and over-shoot by q and 1−q — and pick q from the cost ratio. Under asymmetric cost, the *model* changes too: you are now fitting the cost-optimal quantile, not the mean.

**Choosing from the stakeholder's loss, and the baseline that anchors it.** The decision procedure: (1) write the cost of an error as a function of its size and direction; (2) pick the metric whose sensitivity curve matches it — roughly linear → MAE; quadratic/disaster-averse → RMSE; proportional/percentage → WAPE or guarded MAPE; directional → pinball; (3) always report a second view (MAE + RMSE together; MAPE + WAPE together) so outliers and target-mix effects are visible; (4) compare against **DummyRegressor(strategy="mean" or "median")** on the same split — a model that does not beat the mean predictor has learned nothing, whatever R² says; (5) state R² only as "variance explained relative to the mean baseline on this dataset" — it can be negative, and it is meaningless to compare across datasets with different y-spread, because the denominator (variance of y) changed. Numbers on a slide should be in units the stakeholder owns: "RMSE ₹1.4 lakh" beats "MSE 1.96e10".

payload.title: Regression metrics at a glance
rows: Blind to which rows are catastrophic
Symmetric cost; noisy labels; report the honest average
Unreadable units; dominated by worst row
Looks like MAE but punishes tails
Targets strictly positive and well away from zero
When a few wild rows wreck the mean

payload.code:
# All four metrics, the baseline, and the outlier share of MSE
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
import numpy as np

y_true = np.array([100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0])
y_pred = np.array([110.0, 180.0, 330.0, 520.0])

mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
rmse = float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)))
wape = np.abs(y_true - y_pred).sum() / np.abs(y_true).sum() * 100
# guarded MAPE: skip (or floor) targets near zero instead of dividing by them
mask = np.abs(y_true) > 1e-9
mape = np.mean(np.abs((y_true[mask] - y_pred[mask]) / y_true[mask])) * 100
print(f"MAE={mae:.1f} RMSE={rmse:.2f} MAPE={mape:.1f}% WAPE={wape:.1f}%")

# Baseline on the SAME split — the number your model must beat
dummy = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(y_true.reshape(-1, 1), y_true)
y_base = dummy.predict(y_true.reshape(-1, 1))
print("mean-baseline MAE:", mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_base))

# Which row is driving MSE?
sq = (y_true - y_pred) ** 2
print("share of MSE from worst row:", round(float(sq.max() / sq.sum()) * 100, 1), "%")

# Asymmetric cost -> quantile (pinball) loss at q = cost-implied quantile
from sklearn.metrics import mean_pinball_loss
print("pinball@0.7:", mean_pinball_loss(y_true, y_pred, alpha=0.7))

payload.title: MAPE on targets containing zero (or near-zero) values is not a metric, it is a division error
payload.text: One y = 0 makes it infinite; small y values dominate the average. Report WAPE (or MAE in units) and state the exclusion rule if you must use a percentage.

payload.title: Always report one robust and one tail-sensitive metric together
payload.text: MAE + RMSE tells the reader the typical miss and whether a few rows are exploding; MAPE + WAPE does the same for percentages. Two numbers, one paragraph of honest diagnosis.

payload.title: Four metrics by hand, plus the mean baseline and the MSE hog
payload.problem: Actual demand [100, 200, 300, 400]; predictions [110, 180, 330, 520]. Compute MAE, MSE, RMSE and MAPE. Then compute the mean baseline MAE, and report what share of MSE the single worst error contributes.

steps.title: MAE, MSE, RMSE
steps.desc: MAE = (10 + 20 + 30 + 120)/4 = 180/4 = 45. MSE = (100 + 400 + 900 + 14,400)/4 = 15,800/4 = 3,950. RMSE = √3,950 ≈ 62.8 — in target units, and about 1.4x the MAE (a healthy-but-visible outlier pull).

steps.title: MAPE
steps.desc: Per-row: 10/100 = 10%, 20/200 = 10%, 30/300 = 10%, 120/400 = 30%. MAPE = (10 + 10 + 10 + 30)/4 = 15%. Note the pattern: MAPE is happy here only because no target is near zero — move the last actual to 4 and the same error becomes 3,000%.

steps.title: Baseline and the MSE hog
steps.desc: Mean baseline: predicted 250 on every row → |errors| = 150, 50, 50, 150 → baseline MAE = 400/4 = 100. The model (45) beats it by 55 — real skill, not target luck. MSE share from the worst row: 14,400/15,800 = 91%. One prediction out of four explains 91% of RMSE — if you fix or explain that row, the headline moves; that is exactly what "RMSE ≫ MAE" was telling you.

payload.solution: MAE = 45, MSE = 3,950, RMSE ≈ 62.8, MAPE = 15%. Mean baseline MAE = 100, so the model has genuine skill (45 vs 100). The worst row contributes 91% of MSE — report MAE and RMSE together and inspect that row, because the tail, not the typical case, is currently writing your headline number.

payload.title: Compute, compare, diagnose
payload.prompt: On any regression dataset (boston-style, housing, or demand data): split once, fit a linear model and a tree model, and report MAE, RMSE, MAPE (guarded for zeros) and WAPE for both — plus DummyRegressor mean/median baselines on the same split. Write two sentences: which model wins on MAE vs RMSE, and what the RMSE/MAE ratio implies about outliers in this dataset.
payload.hint: If the tree wins RMSE but ties MAE, it is cleaning up tail errors; if MAPE and WAPE disagree wildly, small targets are distorting MAPE.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting MSE (or a squared-unit number) to a stakeholder
mistakes.fix: Report RMSE or MAE in target units — "off by 45 boxes", not "MSE 3,950 boxes squared". Keep MSE where it belongs: inside the loss.

mistakes.mistake: Using MAPE on data with zeros, near-zeros, or heavy small-value rows
mistakes.fix: Switch to WAPE or MAE, or state and enforce an exclusion/floor rule. Never let one y ≈ 0 row write the report.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting R² as if it were accuracy, or comparing it across datasets
mistakes.fix: R² is improvement over the mean baseline on THIS dataset (can be negative; denominator is that dataset's variance). Quote it with the baseline metric, never alone or across different y-spreads.

mistakes.mistake: Picking RMSE because it is the default, without checking the cost shape
mistakes.fix: RMSE encodes "big errors are quadratically worse". If the business feels errors linearly, MAE is the true number; if directionally, pinball at the cost-implied quantile. State the loss you are optimising.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing models without a mean/median baseline on the same split
mistakes.fix: DummyRegressor takes one line. If your model does not beat it by more than split noise, the problem is the target or the features — not the algorithm.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Compute MAE, RMSE and MAPE for actual [100, 200, 300, 400] and predicted [110, 180, 330, 520]. State what a large RMSE/MAE gap signals, two reasons MAPE is dangerous here, and which metric you would choose if over-forecasting cost half as much as under-forecasting.
payload.answer: Errors: +10, −20, +30, +120. MAE = 180/4 = 45. MSE = 15,800/4 = 3,950 → RMSE ≈ 62.8. MAPE = (10% + 10% + 10% + 30%)/4 = 15%. RMSE/MAE ≈ 1.4 — a large gap means the squared-error tail dominates: the worst row alone is 14,400/15,800 = 91% of MSE, so a few catastrophic predictions drive the headline. MAPE dangers: (1) division by zero/near-zero targets makes it undefined or dominated by tiny rows (here every target happens to be large, which is luck, not safety); (2) it is asymmetric — under-prediction is capped at 100% while over-prediction is unbounded, so minimising MAPE biases forecasts low. With under-forecasting costing twice as much as over-forecasting, neither symmetric metric fits: use quantile (pinball) loss at the quantile implied by the cost ratio (q = C_under/(C_under + C_over) in the standard formulation), or equivalently a cost-weighted absolute error — and report MAE alongside it for comparability. Anchor everything to a mean-baseline DummyRegressor on the same split.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: MAE = typical miss in target units (linear cost); MSE = squared units, quadratic cost, training-loss territory; RMSE = MSE in readable units.

lessons.title: Cross-Validation and Baselines: Earning the Right to Report a Number
lessons.summary: k-fold, stratified, grouped and time-ordered splits; why every learned preprocessing step belongs inside the fold; and the trivial models your number is judged against.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain why a single holdout score is a noisy estimate and compute mean and spread across k folds by hand
Choose between plain k-fold, stratified, grouped and time-ordered splits given a dataset's structure
Prevent cross-validation leakage by placing all fitted preprocessing inside a Pipeline within the folds
Compare a model against a dummy baseline and decide whether the gain exceeds fold noise

payload.text: The dataset has 1,200 rows. You split 80/20 once and get 0.87. Your classmate splits the same data differently and gets 0.81. Both of you are about to argue about algorithms. Neither has established that 0.87 and 0.81 are even different numbers — with one holdout, the score depends on which rows happened to land where, and the difference could be pure luck. Worse, the winner who never measured a baseline cannot tell you whether 0.87 means anything: if always predicting the majority class scores 0.86, the entire exercise added one point. Evaluation has exactly two jobs — estimate performance with a spread, and compare against the obvious alternative — and this lesson is the discipline that does both.

**Why one holdout is not an estimate.** A single 20% test split answers "how did this particular model do on these particular 240 rows?" — and that answer moves when rows move. With small data the sampling noise of one split is routinely several accuracy points, which is larger than most of the improvements you will fight for. **k-fold cross-validation** replaces luck with structure: shuffle (when legitimate), cut the data into k equal folds; for each of k rounds, train on k−1 folds and score the held-out fold; report the mean across folds — and, just as important, the spread. Every row serves as test data exactly once; each round still trains on (k−1)/k of the data, so the estimate slightly *understates* the final model (trained on all data) — a small, known bias you accept in exchange for much lower variance. k = 5 or 10 are the standards: smaller k (2–3) trains on less data per round (more bias, cheaper); very large k (leave-one-out) trains n times, correlates the folds badly, and has famously high variance for little gain. Cross-validation creates no new information — it is a better *measurement instrument*, not more data. And it has a price: with P hyperparameter configurations and k folds, the search costs k·P fits — budget it before you start (Lesson 7.3 makes this arithmetic central).

**Match the split to the structure of the data.** Plain KFold with shuffling assumes rows are independent and identically distributed. Three violations, three different splitters. (1) **Rare classes**: with 1% positives, unstratified folds can contain zero or a handful of positives — recall becomes undefined or wild. StratifiedKFold keeps each fold's class proportions aligned with the dataset's (in classification, the default you should reach for). (2) **Groups**: if a patient contributes 20 records, a user leaves 50 sessions, or near-duplicate documents from one source are scattered across rows, random folds put the *same entity* in train and test. The model half-recognises the entity, scores soar, and the number describes memorisation, not generalisation. GroupKFold (and StratifiedGroupKFold when you also need class balance) keeps every member of a group on one side. (3) **Time**: future rows in training to predict the past is time travel. Use TimeSeriesSplit or an explicit cut date, always training on the past and testing on what follows. Random k-fold on time-ordered data mixes market regimes together and routinely overstates future performance by points — the same data-mixing instinct that will hide drift in Module 9. Rule of thumb: shuffle only for genuinely i.i.d. data; everything else has a splitter that respects its dependence structure.

**Leakage lives or dies inside the pipeline.** Any preprocessing that *learns from data* — imputation statistics, scalers, PCA, feature selection, target encoding, oversampling like SMOTE — must be fit on the training folds only. The classic leak: StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) on the whole dataset *before* cross-validation, so every fold's held-out rows already influenced the mean and variance the model trained with. The leak is small for a scaler on clean data and enormous for feature selection or target encoding, but the principle is identical: evaluation must mimic deployment, where you will never have statistics computed from the future. The fix is mechanical: put every step in a Pipeline and cross_validate the pipeline, so scikit-learn refits each step on each training fold and applies it untouched to that fold's test rows. The same rule settles the oversampling debate — SMOTE before splitting leaks synthetic examples of test rows; SMOTE inside an imblearn Pipeline inside the folds is correct. Finally, if you *tune* hyperparameters on cross-validation and then report that same cross-validated score as your result, you have selected your number the way you selected your model: optimistically. The honest options are nested CV (inner loop tunes, outer loop estimates) or a fixed validation for tuning plus a sealed test set touched exactly once.

**Baselines: the other half of the report.** Every reported metric needs a comparison point: **DummyClassifier** (most_frequent, stratified, or prior-proportional) and **DummyRegressor** (mean or median) establish what the algorithm must beat; a *domain* baseline is often harder still — persistence ("tomorrow equals today" for time series), last year's value, the current rules engine, or simple heuristics your operations team already trusts. A useful framing is the skill score: skill = (model − baseline) / (perfect − baseline) — it says what fraction of the available improvement you captured, on the metric's own scale. The reporting discipline, in one line: metric with mean ± spread across folds, split scheme (k, shuffle?, stratify?, group column?), pipeline statement, and the baseline — *together*. If the model's edge over baseline is smaller than the fold spread, you do not have a result; you have noise with a model attached, and the honest next move is better features or better labels, not a bigger algorithm. That sentence is the spine of every honest evaluation you will ever write.

rows: KFold (shuffled) or train/test with a fixed seed
Score depending on one lucky holdout
Folds with zero (or a handful of) positives — undefined or wild metrics
Repeated entities (patients, users, devices, duplicate docs)
Entity recognition across the split — memorisation scored as generalisation

Nested CV, or validation for tuning + sealed test
Reporting the best-of-many CV score as the result

payload.code:
# Leakage-safe CV against a dummy baseline, mean +/- spread
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier, DummyClassifier as Dummy
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),  # fit INSIDE each fold
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),                   # same — inside the pipeline
    ("model", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)),
])

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
res = cross_validate(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring=["accuracy", "average_precision"],
                     return_train_score=True)
print("val acc: %.3f +/- %.3f" % (res["test_accuracy"].mean(),
                                  res["test_accuracy"].std()))
print("val AP : %.3f +/- %.3f" % (res["test_average_precision"].mean(),
                                  res["test_average_precision"].std()))

# Baseline on the SAME folds — the bar to clear
dummy = Dummy(strategy="stratified", random_state=0)
base = cross_validate(dummy, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="accuracy")
print("dummy  : %.3f +/- %.3f" % (base["test_score"].mean(), base["test_score"].std()))

# Grouped data: same entity never on both sides
# groups = df["patient_id"].values
# gcv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
# cross_validate(pipe, X, y, groups=groups, cv=gcv, scoring="accuracy")

payload.title: Fitting scaler/selector/SMOTE before CV is leakage
payload.text: Held-out rows must be invisible to anything that learns. Only transformations that touch training-fold rows may run — which means everything learned lives inside the Pipeline.

payload.title: One line, four facts: metric, spread, scheme, baseline
payload.text: "Accuracy 0.85 +/- 0.03, 5-fold stratified CV, preprocessing inside folds, dummy 0.62." That sentence is a defensible result; "accuracy 0.87" is not.

payload.title: Mean and spread by hand, a group leak in the wild, and the budget of a search
payload.problem: (a) Five stratified folds give accuracies [0.86, 0.83, 0.88, 0.81, 0.87] with a majority-class baseline of 0.62. Compute mean and standard deviation and judge the result. (b) The data is 1,000 rows from 50 patients (20 records each). Random 5-fold CV scores 0.95; GroupKFold by patient scores 0.71. Explain. (c) You plan to grid-search 20 hyperparameter configurations with 5 folds — how many fits, and what must you not report?

steps.title: (a) Mean and spread
steps.desc: Mean = (0.86 + 0.83 + 0.88 + 0.81 + 0.87)/5 = 4.25/5 = 0.85. Deviations: +0.01, −0.02, +0.03, −0.04, +0.02; variance ≈ 0.0034/5 = 0.00068 → sd ≈ 0.026, so report 0.85 ± 0.03. Against the 0.62 baseline the gap is +0.23 — nearly eight times the spread. Verdict: real skill, confidently reported.

steps.title: (b) The group leak
steps.desc: With random folds, each patient's 20 records are spread across train and test — the model can key off patient-specific fingerprints (stable vitals, device quirks, phrasing) and effectively recognise the person. 0.95 measures recall of identities. GroupKFold holds all 20 records of each patient on one side, forcing the model to generalise to unseen people: 0.71 is the deployment number. The 24-point difference was entirely memorisation dressed as evaluation.

steps.title: (c) The search budget and the forbidden report
steps.desc: Fits = 20 configs x 5 folds = 100 training runs (plus the final refit on all data). What you must not do: pick the best config and quote its mean CV score as your final result — that number was maximised over 20 candidates and is optimistic (best-of-N selection; Lesson 7.4 quantifies the inflation). Use inner CV for selection and an outer loop or a sealed holdout for the number you publish.

payload.solution: (a) 0.85 ± 0.03 vs baseline 0.62 — gain of 0.23, far beyond fold noise: report it as such. (b) 0.95 was entity memorisation; GroupKFold by patient gives the honest 0.71. (c) 100 fits, and never report the winning config's selection CV score as the result — nest it or confirm on a sealed holdout. Evaluation is a protocol, not a number: structure-aware splits, learned steps inside the folds, spread reported, baseline attached.

payload.title: Run the defensible evaluation
payload.prompt: On one dataset: (1) build a Pipeline with imputation + scaling + model; (2) run 5-fold StratifiedKFold cross_validate printing mean and std; (3) run the same folds with a dummy baseline; (4) if your data has any grouping or time structure, redo it with GroupKFold or a date split and compare. Write the one-line result statement for each — scheme, spread, baseline included.
payload.hint: If grouped/time CV scores much lower than random CV, your original number was measuring structure in the rows, not generalisation — that gap is the most valuable number you produced.

mistakes.mistake: Fitting preprocessing (scaler, selector, encoder, SMOTE) on the full dataset before CV
mistakes.fix: Pipeline everything and cross_validate the pipeline — each fold's held-out rows then stay unseen by every learned step.

mistakes.mistake: Random k-fold on grouped or time-ordered data
mistakes.fix: GroupKFold for repeated entities, TimeSeriesSplit/date cuts for time. Match the splitter to the dependence structure, or the score describes memorisation or time travel.

mistakes.mistake: Tuning on cross-validation and reporting that same CV score as the result
mistakes.fix: Nested CV, or tune on a validation split and evaluate once on a sealed test set. A score maximised over many candidates is a biased estimate by construction.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting the mean without the spread, or the best fold
mistakes.fix: mean ± std across folds, every time; best-fold is selection noise. The spread is what tells your reader whether two models differ at all.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the baseline because the number "looks good"
mistakes.fix: DummyClassifier/DummyRegressor on identical folds is one line. No baseline, no claim — 0.87 means nothing next to an unknown 0.86.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: You must evaluate a classifier on 2,000 rows with 3% positives, repeated records for 60 users, and hyperparameters to tune. Specify your evaluation protocol: splitter, k, pipeline discipline, baseline, tuning strategy, and exactly what single number you would report.
payload.answer: Splitter: StratifiedGroupKFold (5 folds) with the user id as group — stratification keeps ~3% positives present in every fold; grouping stops the model recognising a user's own records across the split. Pipeline: imputation/encoding/scaling (and any resampling — SMOTE only inside an imblearn Pipeline) fit inside each training fold, so fold test rows stay unseen. Baseline: DummyClassifier(strategy="stratified") (and most_frequent for accuracy context) evaluated on the identical folds. Tuning: inner cross-validation inside each outer training fold (nested CV), or a dedicated validation split — never the outer score used for selection. Report: outer-CV mean ± std for the primary metric with its baseline beside it, e.g. "AP 0.31 ± 0.04 (5-fold stratified-group CV), prevalence 0.03, dummy AP 0.03"; refit the chosen configuration on all available training data, and only if a sealed test split exists, quote its single frozen-threshold confusion matrix once. In one sentence: structure-aware splits, learned steps inside folds, spread and baseline attached, selection separated from estimation.
payload.source: Classic evaluation-protocol design question (splitter choice + leakage + baseline) in ML interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: One holdout is noisy; k-fold gives a mean and a spread by rotating the held-out fold — every row tested exactly once.
Match the splitter: stratified for rare classes, grouped for repeated entities, time-ordered for temporal data; shuffle only i.i.d. data.
Everything that learns (imputer, scaler, selector, encoder, SMOTE) lives inside a Pipeline fitted within the folds — otherwise CV leaks.
Tuning on CV and reporting the same CV score is selection bias; nest the loops or seal a holdout.
No baseline, no claim: DummyClassifier/DummyRegressor on identical folds, plus any domain baseline worth beating.
The report format: metric ± spread, split scheme, pipeline statement, baseline — all four together or the number is not defensible.

questions.prompt: StratifiedKFold is preferred over plain KFold when:
options: Class proportions differ strongly between classes, so every fold must preserve the class balance
questions.explanation: Without stratification, rare classes can vanish from a fold entirely, making the metric undefined or wildly unstable.

questions.prompt: 20 records exist for each of 50 patients. Random k-fold yields 0.95 while GroupKFold by patient yields 0.71. The best interpretation is:
options: Random folds let the model recognise each patient's own records across train/test — 0.95 measured memorisation; 0.71 is the honest estimate
questions.explanation: Entity overlap across the split inflates scores; groups must stay on one side for the number to describe generalisation to new patients.

questions.prompt: You run StandardScaler().fit_transform on the whole dataset before cross-validation. The consequence is:
options: Fold test rows leak into the training statistics through the global mean/variance, so CV is optimistic; fit the scaler inside a Pipeline per fold
questions.explanation: Any learned statistic must come from the training fold only; the pipeline refits each step per fold automatically.

questions.prompt: Model CV accuracy is 0.84 ± 0.03; the stratified dummy baseline is 0.83 ± 0.02. The honest conclusion is:
options: The model has essentially no skill over the trivial baseline; improve features/labels or reframe the target before adding complexity
questions.explanation: The 0.01 gain sits inside the noise band. A model must beat its baseline by more than the spread to justify existing.

modules.title: Module 7 — Overfitting, Regularisation & Hyperparameter Tuning
modules.summary: The two failure modes of learning, named and quantified: bias and variance as a decomposition you can compute, learning curves as the diagnosis instrument, every regularisation lever across model families, the three species of hyperparameter search (grid, random, Bayesian/Optuna) with their budget arithmetic, feature importance done honestly (impurity vs permutation and their caveats), and a leakage re-audit from the vantage point of tuning pressure.

lessons.title: Bias–Variance and Learning Curves: Diagnosing the Gap Before You Fix It
lessons.summary: Why the same error has two very different causes, the decomposition that separates them numerically, and the curve plot that tells you whether more data will ever help.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decompose an expected prediction error into bias², variance and noise using given summary statistics
Diagnose underfitting vs overfitting from train and validation scores alone
Read a learning curve and predict whether collecting more data will improve the model
Apply the correct lever set for each regime and justify why the wrong lever makes things worse

payload.text: Two models land on your desk. Model A scores 0.71 on train and 0.69 on validation: barely a gap, and both numbers are mediocre. Model B scores 0.99 on train and 0.74 on validation: a gaping chasm. The instinct of every junior practitioner is to treat both as "overfitting" and reach for regularisation. Applied to Model A, that advice is malice — you cannot regularise a model that is already too simple; you will only push both scores down together. Diagnosis before prescription is the whole lesson: two failures with identical-looking symptoms of "bad validation score" have opposite treatments, and the bias–variance picture plus one plot tells you which one you have.

**The decomposition: one error, three sources.** For squared-error prediction, the expected error at a point splits exactly into three parts: E[(y − f̂(x))²] = **bias²** + **variance** + **irreducible noise**. **Bias²** is the systematic miss — the average of your predictions across many retrainings, compared with the truth; a model that always predicts 7 when the truth is 10 has bias −3 and bias² 9, regardless of how stable it is. **Variance** is the instability — how much your fitted model swings when the training set changes: a model that fits 7.2 on one sample and 11.8 on another has high variance even if its average is perfect. **Noise** is the part no model can reach — label error, unmeasured variables, randomness in the world; it sets the floor that even a perfect model cannot cross. The engineering consequence is the classic trade-off: add capacity (deeper trees, higher-degree features, weaker regularisation) and bias falls while variance rises; remove capacity and the reverse. The optimal model sits where bias² + variance is minimised — *not* where training error is minimised, and *not* where bias alone is smallest. In classification the same picture holds qualitatively (the decomposition has extra terms under 0-1 loss, but the regimes and the levers are identical), which is why you can reason about a classifier with a regression diagram and still be right.

**The symptoms table, memorised.** **High bias (underfitting)**: training error is *high* and validation error is *similarly high* — the gap is small because the model fails on both. The model cannot capture the pattern even with all the data it has. **High variance (overfitting)**: training error is *low* (often near zero) and validation error is much worse — the gap is the signature; the model learned the training set's particulars, including its noise. The remedies are mirror images: for high bias — a more expressive model, more/better features, weaker regularisation, longer training (up to the point where it can fit); for high variance — more training data, stronger regularisation, a simpler model, early stopping, augmentation, ensembling. Applying a variance remedy to a bias problem actively harms you: stronger regularisation on an already-underfit model drives both scores down toward the baseline. Note the sneaky third case: *both* scores near the baseline with a small gap is not "stable" — it is a model that has learned nothing, which is a bias diagnosis plus a feature/target problem.

**Learning curves: the experiment that decides whether to buy data.** Plot training-set score (or error) and validation score against the *size of the training set* (learning_curve in sklearn does the subsampling for you). The two archetypal shapes answer the most expensive question in ML — "will more data help?" — before you spend a rupee on it. **High-bias curve**: both curves rise quickly then *plateau together* at a poor level; the gap was never big and the validation curve is flat — more rows will not help, because the model class cannot express the pattern. Buy capacity or features, not data. **High-variance curve**: the training curve stays high and the validation curve is still *climbing* with a wide, narrowing gap — more data is exactly the right purchase, because each new row constrains the memorisation further. **Both curves still rising**: you are data-limited and capacity-adeate — collect more (and consider a slightly bigger model once they flatten). Reading these curves turns arguments into plots: "should we label 50,000 more rows?" becomes a visual answer rather than an opinion. One caveat to carry into the deep-learning era: very large models can drive training error nearly to zero *and still* generalize well at scale (the modern "double descent" picture), so treat the classical decomposition as the reliable diagnostic for the tabular, small-to-medium-n world this course works in — and remember that even in that world, the curve tells you the *regime*, while fresh experiments tell you the *fix*.

**The workflow, end to end.** (1) Establish baseline (Module 6). (2) Plot train/validation scores and the learning curve. (3) Label the regime: high bias, high variance, or data-limited. (4) Apply only the levers for that regime — one at a time. (5) Re-plot; regimes shift as you fix things (a variance-fixed model often reveals new bias). The two numbers to keep on screen are the **gap** (validation − training, in metric units) and the **distance to baseline** (validation − baseline). Overfitting is a big gap; uselessness is a small distance to baseline; the worst place to be is both.

payload.title: Two failures, opposite treatments
rows: More capacity, better features, weaker regularisation — never stronger regularisation
More data, stronger regularisation, simpler model, early stopping — never more capacity
Collect/label more data; revisit only after curves flatten
Stop tuning the algorithm — fix the target, features or labels

payload.code:
# Learning curves: the buy-data-or-not experiment
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

estimator = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)
sizes, train_s, val_s = learning_curve(
    estimator, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc",
    train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 8), n_jobs=-1, random_state=0,
)
print("train:", np.round(train_s.mean(axis=1), 3))
print("valid:", np.round(val_s.mean(axis=1), 3))

# Baseline line for AUC is 0.5 — draw it so the gap has two reference points
plt.plot(sizes, train_s.mean(axis=1), label="train")
plt.plot(sizes, val_s.mean(axis=1), label="validation")
plt.axhline(0.5, ls="--", label="random baseline")
plt.xlabel("training rows"); plt.ylabel("ROC-AUC"); plt.legend(); plt.show()

# Regime check in words: gap = train - val at full size; plateau = last delta
print("gap:", round(float(train_s.mean(axis=1)[-1] - val_s.mean(axis=1)[-1]), 3),
      "val still rising:", round(float(val_s.mean(axis=1)[-1] - val_s.mean(axis=1)[-2]), 3))

payload.title: Regularising an underfit model makes both scores worse
payload.text: A small gap with low scores is high bias. Stronger penalties, fewer features or shallower trees will lower train and validation together — diagnose the regime first, always.

payload.title: Put the baseline on every train/validation plot
payload.text: The gap tells you the regime; the distance to baseline tells you whether the regime even matters. A perfect fit of a useless target still sits on the baseline.

payload.title: The decomposition by hand — and why the lowest-bias model loses
payload.problem: Three candidate models are retrained on 20 different samples of the same dataset. At the point of interest the truth is 10. Model A averages predictions of 7.4 (spread sd 1.0); Model B averages 9.6 (sd 2.5); Model C averages 8.5 (sd 1.4). Irreducible noise sd = 2. Compute expected MSE for each (bias² + variance + noise²) and choose the model to deploy.

steps.title: Bias² per model
steps.desc: Bias = mean prediction − truth. A: 7.4 − 10 = −2.6 → 6.76. B: 9.6 − 10 = −0.4 → 0.16. C: 8.5 − 10 = −1.5 → 2.25. B is by far the least biased — and that will not save it.

steps.title: Variance and noise
steps.desc: Variance = sd² of the predictions across retrains: A: 1.0² = 1.00; B: 2.5² = 6.25; C: 1.4² = 1.96. Noise = 2² = 4.00 for all three — it is the floor no model removes.

steps.title: Total expected error
steps.desc: A: 6.76 + 1.00 + 4.00 = 11.76. B: 0.16 + 6.25 + 4.00 = 10.41. C: 2.25 + 1.96 + 4.00 = 8.21. Model C wins despite B's near-perfect average — B pays for its accuracy with swings of ±2.5 per retrain, and the swings cost more than C's steady −1.5 miss.

steps.title: Reading it as a decision
steps.desc: A is the underfit model (huge bias, tiny variance — its lever is more capacity). B is the overfit model (tiny bias, huge variance — its lever is regularisation or more data). C is the tuned middle. Note also: with noise² = 4, even the theoretical best floor is 4 — no amount of modelling beats the label quality. If noise dominates for everyone, collect better labels.

payload.solution: Expected MSE: A 11.76, B 10.41, C 8.21 → deploy C. The least-biased model (B) is not the best model: tuning minimises bias² + variance, not bias alone — and both A and B are one lever away from C (A: more capacity; B: more regularisation or more data). The irreducible 4.00 shows the ceiling set by label quality.

payload.title: Run the diagnosis on your own model
payload.prompt: Take any classifier or regressor you trained in this course: print training and validation scores for a shallow/simple and a deep/complex configuration, compute the gap for each, and plot a learning_curve (5-fold) for the better one. Write three sentences: the regime, whether the validation curve is still climbing at full data size, and whether you would spend next month collecting data or adding features.
payload.hint: Plateaued curves with a small gap = buy capacity/features; a wide gap with the validation curve still rising = buy data; validation flat near baseline = fix target/features before touching the algorithm.

mistakes.mistake: Treating every gap as overfitting and reaching for regularisation
mistakes.fix: Check the train score first. High train + low val = variance; low train ≈ low val = bias. The levers are opposites.

mistakes.mistake: Judging generalisation from training accuracy
mistakes.fix: Training score only proves fit. Quote validation/CV with spread and baseline; a 0.99 train number is diagnostic input (it says variance), never a result.

mistakes.mistake: Buying more data for a high-bias model
mistakes.fix: Learning curves decide this: a plateaued validation curve will not lift with rows. Capacity or features move bias; data moves variance.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing models at different training-set sizes or noise levels
mistakes.fix: The decomposition only compares fairly on the same data; and remember the noise floor — if label error dominates, no architecture discussion matters.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define bias and variance in one sentence each. Given bias = −2.6, prediction sd across retrains = 1.0 and noise sd = 2, compute the expected MSE. A second model has bias = −0.4 and sd = 2.5. Which do you deploy, and what lever would fix the loser in each case?
payload.answer: Bias = the systematic offset of the average prediction from the truth (how wrong the model is on average across retrains); variance = how much the fitted model changes when the training set changes (instability). Model 1: expected MSE = (−2.6)² + 1.0² + 2² = 6.76 + 1.0 + 4 = 11.76. Model 2: (−0.4)² + 2.5² + 4 = 0.16 + 6.25 + 4 = 10.41. If a third model offers bias −1.5 and sd 1.4 (8.21) it wins outright; between these two, Model 2 wins despite near-zero bias because its variance costs more. Levers: the high-bias loser (Model 1) needs more capacity, better features or weaker penalties; the high-variance loser (Model 2) needs more data, stronger regularisation, simpler structure or early stopping. The deploy rule is minimum bias² + variance, both measured on the same data — and note the noise floor of 4 that bounds every model.
payload.source: Evergreen bias–variance exam question (decomposition arithmetic + remedy mapping).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Expected error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise; tuning minimises the sum, never bias alone.
High bias: train low and val similarly low — needs capacity/features; high variance: train high, val much lower — needs data or regularisation.
The remedies are opposites; applying the wrong one moves both scores in the wrong direction.
Learning curves answer "will more data help?": plateau = no, validation still climbing = yes.
Track two numbers: the train/val gap (regime) and the distance to baseline (whether it matters).
Label noise sets a floor — when noise² dominates, better labels beat better algorithms.

questions.prompt: A model scores 0.72 on training data and 0.70 on validation data, both near the baseline. The diagnosis is:
options: High bias (underfitting) — the model cannot capture the pattern; more regularisation would make it worse
questions.explanation: Low scores with almost no gap means both sets defeat the model equally — the lever is capacity, features or target framing, not regularisation.

questions.prompt: The bias–variance decomposition of expected squared error is:
questions.explanation: Squared bias plus variance plus irreducible noise variance — the standard decomposition under squared loss.

questions.prompt: Your learning curve shows training score flat and high, validation score still rising with a wide gap as rows increase. The right next move is:
options: Collect more training data (and/or simplify) — the gap is variance and data is the proven lever
questions.explanation: A climbing validation curve with a persistent gap means the model is still memorising what data has not yet constrained: buy data.

questions.prompt: Across many retrains, a model's predictions average 9.6 where the truth is 10, with sd 1.5, and noise sd = 2. Its expected MSE contribution from bias is:
questions.explanation: Bias = 9.6 − 10 = −0.4; bias² = 0.16. (Variance would be 2.25 and noise 4, for a total of 6.41.)

lessons.title: Regularisation Levers: Every Knob That Trades Fit for Generalisation
lessons.summary: One idea expressed in a dozen settings — alpha in linear models, depth and leaf size in trees, shrinkage in boosting, k in kNN — plus early stopping and the one-standard-error rule for choosing among them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: State what regularisation does to the bias–variance balance and predict the effect of increasing any family's penalty knob
List the principal regularisation levers for linear, tree, forest, boosting, kNN and SVM models and what each controls
Apply the one-standard-error rule to pick a regularised configuration from a cross-validation table
Explain why penalties require standardised features and how early stopping acts as free regularisation

payload.text: Every model family in this course has a knob that says "be simpler". Ridge has alpha; a decision tree has max_depth; a random forest has min_samples_leaf; gradient boosting has learning_rate; kNN has k; an SVM has C. They are taught in separate chapters, wired through different code, and named as if they were unrelated features of unrelated algorithms. They are not: each one is the same dial seen from a different angle — the price you charge the model for complexity, paid in training fit, refunded in generalisation. Learn it as one idea with a family of names and you will never again guess a hyperparameter's direction in an interview.

**What the penalty actually buys.** Regularisation adds a cost for complexity to the training objective: minimise (fit error) + λ · (model complexity), where λ is the strength and "complexity" is measured in whatever currency the family uses — squared coefficient size for Ridge, absolute coefficient size for Lasso, tree size for cost-complexity pruning, path length for isolation, distance span for kNN. Raising λ pushes the solution toward simpler functions: predictions shrink, boundaries smooth, fewer splits, smaller neighbourhoods. In bias–variance terms you are *buying bias to shed variance* — which is exactly why the direction of every one of these knobs is the same, and why over-regularising underfits (the far end of every curve: all coefficients at zero means the model predicts the mean, all tree depth at one means majority votes).

**The levers, by family.** **Linear models**: alpha (λ) is the strength dial — Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero without zeroing any, which tames correlated features by shrinking them together; Lasso (L1) drives some coefficients to *exactly* zero, performing feature selection; ElasticNet mixes both (l1_ratio), useful when features come in correlated groups. Critical detail: the penalty compares coefficients to each other, so features must be standardised first — a coefficient on a feature measured in rupees is not commensurable with one on a ratio, and an unscaled penalty distorts which feature gets cut. (Module 3 did this arithmetic; this lesson makes it a rule: scale, then regularise.) **Decision trees**: max_depth and max_leaf_nodes cap structure; min_samples_leaf forces every leaf to carry enough rows that its prediction is an average rather than a memorised singleton (often the single most effective smoothing knob); ccp_alpha is the explicit cost-complexity pruning parameter — train fully, then prune the branch whose removal buys enough impurity reduction to pay for its leaf count. **Random forests**: n_estimators lowers variance through averaging (gains flatten after a few hundred; almost never the overfitting knob), while max_depth/min_samples_leaf/max_features keep individual trees weak so their errors stay uncorrelated — remember Module 4: the forest's regularisation is *decorrelation plus averaging*, not any single tree's fit. **Gradient boosting**: learning_rate (shrinkage) and n_estimators form one joint lever — small learning rates need more trees but usually generalise better; max_depth of 2–4 keeps each learner a weak contributor; subsample < 1 adds stochastic noise that regularises like bagging; **early stopping** watches validation error during training and halts when it stops improving (patience in iterations) — a regulariser that picks the effective iteration count for you, and the default defence for boosted trees. **kNN**: k itself — larger k smooths the boundary (more bias, less variance); weight by distance to let near neighbours dominate. **SVM**: C is the soft-margin price of errors and gamma the RBF influence radius (Module 5) — jointly, they are this family's λ. **Neural nets** (a preview for the DL course): weight decay (L2), dropout, batch size, augmentation and early stopping play the identical roles. One family's table is another family's vocabulary: the interview answer is the mapping, not the memorisation.

**Choosing strength: the curve and the one-standard-error rule.** Sweep λ on a log grid (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100 — regularisation strength is a scale, not a step) and plot CV error against λ: the classic U-shape — falling as variance is shed, rising again as bias takes over. Two selection rules: **pick the minimum** (maximises the CV mean), or the more conservative **one-standard-error rule**: find the best mean and its standard error, then choose the most regularised (simplest) configuration whose mean lies within one standard error of the best. The one-SE rule exists because CV differences under one SE are indistinguishable from noise — and when two candidates are statistically tied, the simpler one is the better bet for data you have not seen. Report the chosen λ, the CV curve shape and the final untouched test number; never tune λ on the test set. Also worth knowing: **regularisation and data volume substitute for each other** — with abundant data, strong penalties matter less (there is enough signal to estimate many parameters); with scarce data, λ does much of the stabilising work.

payload.title: The regularisation levers, one row per family
rows: Unscaled features distort the penalty; log-scale the grid
Too deep a prune collapses to the majority class
n_estimators mainly costs time, it rarely overfits
Each learner contributes less, more slowly
Small lr without more trees simply underfits
k=1 memorises; k=n predicts the global mean
Must be tuned jointly with gamma, on scaled features
Patience tuned on the same validation set you report

payload.code:
# Regularisation path + the one-standard-error rule
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate, KFold

# alpha is a SCALE parameter: always search it on a log grid
alphas = np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)

cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

# RidgeCV does the inner CV over the log grid; cross_validate wraps the outer loop
inner = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
ridge_cv = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()),
                     ("ridge", RidgeCV(alphas=alphas, cv=inner))])
out = cross_validate(ridge_cv, X_train, y_train, cv=cv,
                     scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", return_estimator=True)

best_alphas = [e.named_steps["ridge"].alpha_ for e in out["estimator"]]
print("alpha chosen per outer fold:", np.round(best_alphas, 3))

# One-standard-error rule, computed on an explicit CV table:
# means = np.array([...])  # CV error per alpha (ascending grid)
# ses   = np.array([...])  # standard error per alpha
# i_best = means.argmin()
