payload.code:
# Dendrogram as the granularity dial: cut where the business says so
import numpy as np
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Z = linkage(X, method="ward")   # merge adding the least within-cluster variance

dendrogram(Z, color_threshold=5, truncate_mode="lastp", p=30)
plt.axhline(5, ls="--")        # the cut = the argument you can defend
plt.ylabel("merge height (variance units for ward)")
plt.show()

labels = fcluster(Z, t=5, criterion="distance")   # groups formed by merges <= 5
print("clusters:", labels.max(), "sizes:", np.bincount(labels)[1:])

# same data, four linkages - compare STRUCTURE, not raw heights
for m in ("single", "complete", "average", "ward"):
    Zm = linkage(X, method=m)
    print(m, "->", fcluster(Zm, t=5, criterion="distance").max(), "clusters at h=5")

payload.title: Single linkage chaining and ward height scales
payload.text: Single linkage will weld two clusters together through one bridge row of noise; check the cut under complete linkage too. Ward heights are variance increases (scipy uses squared distances) - never compare them numerically with single/complete heights.

payload.title: Stability before shipping a taxonomy
payload.text: Re-run on 80% of rows and match clusters (adjusted Rand index against the full run). High agreement means structure; low agreement means your categories are a property of the sample, not the customers.

payload.title: Merge sequence under three linkages, and what a cut means
payload.problem: Four points on a line: A = 1, B = 2, C = 10, D = 11. Pairwise distances: d(A,B) = 1, d(C,D) = 1, d(A,C) = 9, d(A,D) = 10, d(B,C) = 8, d(B,D) = 9. (a) What merges first? (b) After forming X = {A, B} and Y = {C, D}, compute the distance between X and Y under single, complete and average linkage. (c) At what final height does the tree close under each? (d) Cutting at height 5 gives how many clusters; cutting at height 9 under complete linkage? (e) Why is a ward dendrogram not directly comparable?

steps.title: (a) First merges
steps.desc: The two smallest distances are d(A,B) = 1 and d(C,D) = 1, so A and B merge into X at height 1, and C and D merge into Y at height 1. Two clusters remain: X and Y.

steps.title: (b) X to Y under three rules
steps.desc: The four cross distances are 9, 10, 8, 9. Single = min = 8. Complete = max = 10. Average = (9 + 10 + 8 + 9) / 4 = 9. Same data, three different numbers - the rule, not the data, chose them.

steps.title: (c) Closing heights
steps.desc: Under single the tree closes at 8, under average at 9, under complete at 10. The ordering (single <= average <= complete) always holds because min <= mean <= max of the same set.

steps.title: (d) Reading the cuts
steps.desc: Cut at 5: nothing above height 1 has merged, so every method gives two clusters, {A, B} and {C, D}. Cut at 9 under complete: the merge needs height 10, so still two clusters; under single it would already be one cluster (closed at 8). The cut height is a granularity dial whose meaning depends on the linkage that produced the tree.

steps.title: (e) Ward is on another scale
steps.desc: Ward merges by the increase in total within-cluster variance (scipy computes it from squared distances), so its heights are variance additions, not row-to-row distances. Two ward heights cannot be compared with single/complete heights, and a cut value of 5 in one method means nothing in another - choose cuts per method, from structure or domain, never by copying the number.

payload.solution: Merges: AB and CD at height 1; X-to-Y distance = 8 (single), 10 (complete), 9 (average); tree closes at 8 / 10 / 9 respectively. Cut at 5 yields {A, B} and {C, D} under every rule; cut at 9 yields one cluster under single but two under complete. Ward heights are variance increases (squared-distance based) and live on a different scale - compare structure across methods, never raw heights.

payload.title: Cut the same tree at two heights and defend both
payload.prompt: Build an agglomerative clustering (ward and complete) on a real table with 500 to 5,000 rows. Cut each at two heights that give roughly 3 and 8 clusters. Write the cluster sizes for both cuts, compute a stability score (re-run on a random 80% and match with adjusted Rand index), and produce a two-sentence description of each segment in business language. Which cut would you ship and what evidence supports it?
payload.hint: Sizes tell you if one segment is a dumping ground; stability tells you if the taxonomy survives resampling; the business sentence is the real acceptance test - if you cannot write it, the cut is arbitrary.

mistakes.mistake: Cutting the dendrogram wherever the picture looks tidy
mistakes.fix: Record a rule before looking: domain granularity, a stability threshold, or downstream lift. A cut chosen after seeing the plot is a result manufactured to fit the eye.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing merge heights across linkage methods (especially ward)
mistakes.fix: Heights are defined by the method: pairwise distances for single/complete/average, variance increases for ward. Compare which rows group together, not the y-values.

mistakes.mistake: Running hierarchical clustering on tens of thousands of rows and wondering where the memory went
mistakes.fix: The full distance matrix is O(n squared) memory. Sample, pre-aggregate, or switch to k-means/BIRCH; use hierarchical on the sample to inform k, then assign the rest.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the dendrogram leaf order as an ordering of the rows
mistakes.fix: Siblings can be drawn in either order without changing the clustering; only merge structure and heights carry meaning, not left-to-right sequence.

mistakes.mistake: Fitting clusters on all rows and then feeding cluster id to a supervised model evaluated on a holdout
mistakes.fix: The cluster feature must be fitted on training rows only (scaler + linkage + cut on train, assignment rule for validation) or the segment id leaks test information.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Compare single, complete, average and ward linkage, including one failure mode each. A dendrogram must be cut to produce segments for a marketing team: describe how the cut replaces k, what two things you must not do when reading heights, and one test that tells you whether the taxonomy is stable.
payload.answer: Single: minimum pairwise distance between clusters - follows elongated shapes but chains groups through bridge rows of noise. Complete: maximum distance - compact groups, but one outlier can dominate the distance. Average: mean of pairwise distances - a robust compromise. Ward: merges the pair that adds least to total within-cluster variance - balanced, k-means-like, but its heights are variance increases (scipy uses squared distances), not distances. The cut: cutting at height h keeps every merge formed at or below h, so the cut chooses the number of clusters after seeing the structure - the post-hoc replacement for choosing k up front; pick it from domain meaning, stability or downstream lift, never from visual tidiness. Two reading rules: never compare heights across linkage methods (different units), and never read the leaf order as an ordering of observations. Stability test: re-run on a random 80% subsample, match the clusters to the full run with adjusted Rand index (or per-cluster Jaccard overlap); high agreement indicates structure that survives resampling, low agreement means the taxonomy is a property of the sample and should not be shipped as fact.
payload.source: Interview-grade synthesis (linkage comparison + dendrogram interpretation).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Agglomerative clustering merges nearest groups until one remains; the full history is a dendrogram, and a cut at height h replaces the choice of k.
Linkage decides the answer: single chains, complete is compact but outlier-sensitive, average is a compromise, ward minimises added within-cluster variance.
Ward heights are variance increases, not distances - never compare them with single/complete heights, and never read leaf order as meaning.
Cost is O(n squared) memory for the distance matrix: sample first, or switch to k-means/BIRCH at scale.
Clustering pays when it summarises for humans, features a downstream model (fit on train), samples intelligently, or grounds anomaly detection - it decorates when a label could have been measured.
Stability under resampling is the cheapest honesty test before a taxonomy ships.

questions.prompt: Four points with d(A,B) = 1, d(C,D) = 1, and cross distances 9, 10, 8, 9 between {A,B} and {C,D}. The distance between the two clusters under single and complete linkage is:
questions.explanation: Single takes the minimum cross distance (8), complete takes the maximum (10); average would give (9 + 10 + 8 + 9) / 4 = 9.

questions.prompt: Ward linkage is defined by:
options: The minimum pairwise distance between clusters
The merge that increases total within-cluster variance the least
The maximum pairwise distance between clusters
The cosine angle between cluster centroids
questions.explanation: Ward optimises the same variance-addition criterion family as k-means, which is why its dendrogram heights are variance increases (scipy uses squared distances) rather than row distances.

questions.prompt: You cut a dendrogram at height h. The resulting clusters are:
options: The h clusters closest to the root
The groups formed by every merge whose height is at most h
The leaves within h positions of each other in the drawing
Always exactly the same as k-means with k = h
questions.explanation: The cut keeps the tree below a height threshold: merges at or below h define the groups. The count of resulting clusters depends on the merge heights, so cluster count is not equal to h.

questions.prompt: Hierarchical clustering with the full distance matrix becomes impractical mainly because:
options: The algorithm needs labels for each merge
Memory and time grow with the square of the number of rows (O(n squared) storage), so tens of thousands of rows exhaust memory
It can only handle one feature
Dendrograms cannot be drawn for more than 10 clusters
questions.explanation: Every pair must be stored (and naively re-compared), so cost grows quadratically: sample or pre-aggregate for large n, or use k-means/BIRCH and keep hierarchical clustering for structure discovery on samples.

lessons.title: Anomaly Detection: Robust Statistics, Isolation, and Alert Budgets
lessons.summary: Three kinds of anomalies, why mean and standard deviation hide the very outlier you are hunting, how isolation forests separate rarity from normality, and how to set a threshold from cost instead of folklore.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify an anomaly as point, contextual or collective and say what evidence would confirm it
Compute median-MAD robust z-scores and contrast them with mean-sigma z-scores on the same sample
Explain isolation-forest logic and set contamination from an alert budget
Choose an alarm threshold from a cost matrix and an alert rate the team can actually absorb

payload.text: A payments service alarms at mean + 3 sigma on checkout latency. Traffic is calm for days, then one request takes 95 ms while nobody is watching. The morning review finds no alert: that single 95 ms reading joined the sample, pushed the mean to 48.5 and sigma to 17.6, and the spike itself measured only 2.6 sigma - inside the band. The outlier rewrote the ruler used to measure it. The next week a real degradation sat at 72 ms, comfortably under the fattened threshold, and cost an hour of incident time. The monitor was never bad at arithmetic; it was measuring location and spread with statistics that one weird value is allowed to vandalise.

**Three species of weird.** A **point anomaly** is a single row that is far from the rest: one transaction of Rs 9,00,000 in an account of small spenders. A **contextual anomaly** is normal in one context and strange in another: 70 ms latency at 3 am is alarming, 70 ms during a flash sale is Tuesday - the row is only anomalous relative to time, season or segment. A **collective anomaly** is a *sequence or pattern* that is odd even though every individual row looks fine: five logins from five countries in four minutes, where each login alone is ordinary. The species decides the tool: point anomalies suit distance or density methods, contextual ones need a seasonal baseline or features of the context, and collective ones need sequence models or window statistics. Calling everything a point anomaly is the most common design error in monitoring.

**Rulers that cannot be vandalised: median and MAD.** The mean and standard deviation have a breakdown point near zero - a single sufficiently large value can move them arbitrarily, and (worse) inflate sigma enough to hide itself: the **masking** effect. The robust pair resists this: the **median** is the middle value and ignores how extreme the tails are (it can absorb up to half the data before breaking), and the **MAD** (median absolute deviation) is the median of |x - median|. The standard robust z-score is 0.6745 x (x - median) / MAD - the 0.6745 rescales MAD to be comparable with sigma for Gaussian data - and the conventional flag threshold is 3.5 (Iglewicz and Hoaglin). Two caveats to carry: MAD of 0 (more than half the values identical) makes the score undefined - fall back to mean absolute deviation or a business floor; and robust does not mean contextual - a robust score still does not know it is Sunday.

**Isolation forest: rarity as a short path.** Instead of density or distance, this method exploits the defining property of anomalies: they are **few and different**. Build trees that recursively pick a random feature and a random threshold between min and max; every row walks down until isolated in a leaf. Points that are rare and far out get cut off in a handful of splits; normal points in the dense core need many. The anomaly score comes from the average path length - shorter is more anomalous (normalised against a random-sample baseline). Practical knobs: n_estimators (a few hundred for stability), **contamination** (the fraction of the training set you expect to be anomalous - it sets the decision threshold, so set it from your alert budget or known incident rate, not to make the output look right), and feature hygiene (irrelevant columns dilute splits and bury the signal). Isolation forests are fast, scale to large n, need no labels, and handle mixed numeric features well; they are *novelty-or-outlier* detectors - if the world drifts, yesterday's scores drift with it. **Local Outlier Factor** is the density alternative: it compares each point's local density with its k neighbours, catching anomalies that are normal-looking globally but strange within their neighbourhood - at O(n squared) cost.

**Evaluation and thresholds: there are no labels, so design the loop.** With no ground truth you cannot compute accuracy - so (1) hold back a few *confirmed* incidents from the past as a labelled sanity set and report recall on them plus alert volume on clean periods; (2) judge by **precision at the alert budget**: if the team can investigate 20 alerts a day, is the top-20-by-score list useful?; (3) set the threshold from the **cost matrix** - false alarm cost (analyst time, alarm fatigue) versus miss cost (the incident) - not from folklore like 3 sigma; (4) remember every flag is a *hypothesis for a human*, not a verdict, because the domain cost of a wrong accusation can dwarf the detection gain. Finally, drift is the meta-trap: after a release, the new normal looks anomalous until the detector adapts, and retraining on unreviewed flags teaches it that the incident was normal. Review before retrain, always.

payload.title: Detectors: what each one is actually measuring
rows: Robust location and spread, thresholded at 3.5
MAD = 0; seasonality and context not modelled
Anomalies isolate in fewer random splits
Dense anomaly clumps; irrelevant features dilute splits
Local density vs k nearest neighbours
n large (O(n squared)); regimes with different densities
You hold labels from past incidents
Labels are scarce or drift makes them stale

payload.code:
# Robust z-scores plus an isolation forest under an alert budget
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

med = np.median(x)
mad = np.median(np.abs(x - med))
if mad > 0:
    robust_z = 0.6745 * (x - med) / mad          # Iglewicz-Hoaglin
else:
    robust_z = 0.7979 * np.abs(x - med) / np.mean(np.abs(x - med))
print("median/MAD flags:", np.where(np.abs(robust_z) > 3.5)[0])

print("mean/sigma z of worst:", np.round(np.max(np.abs(x - x.mean()) / x.std()), 2))

# isolation forest: score first, threshold from the alert budget
clf = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, contamination=0.01, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X)
scores = -clf.score_samples(X)                   # higher = more anomalous
budget = int(0.01 * len(X))                      # 1 percent of rows may be alerted
top = np.argsort(scores)[-budget:]
print("alerting on", budget, "rows; top score:", round(float(scores[top[-1]]), 3))

payload.title: The mean-and-sigma ruler masks the very outlier you hunt
payload.text: One extreme value inflates sigma and drags the mean, so the value that caused the problem measures as normal (masking), and borderline rows get swept in (swamping). Use median/MAD for thresholds and keep seasonal baselines per context.

payload.title: Set the threshold from the alert budget, then let the cost matrix argue
payload.text: Ask how many alerts a day the team can actually investigate, take the top of the ranked scores, and check miss-cost against false-alarm cost. An unactionable detector is worse than none: every false alarm spends trust.

payload.title: The masking effect: 95 ms hides inside 3 sigma
payload.problem: Checkout latencies for eight requests (ms): 40, 42, 41, 43, 44, 42, 41, 95. (a) Compute the mean and population sigma, then the z-score of 95 - does a 3-sigma rule fire? (b) Compute the median, MAD and the robust z-score of 95 at the 3.5 threshold - does it fire? (c) Explain the disagreement quantitatively. (d) The team can investigate 1 alert per 100 requests; how would you turn either detector into a defensible alerting rule?

steps.title: (a) Mean and sigma
steps.desc: Sum = 388, mean = 48.5. Squared deviations: 72.25, 42.25, 56.25, 30.25, 20.25, 42.25, 56.25, 2162.25 - total 2482. Population variance = 2482 / 8 = 310.25, sigma = 17.61. z(95) = (95 - 48.5) / 17.61 = 2.64 - below 3, so the 3-sigma alarm NEVER FIRES on the most extreme value in the sample.

steps.title: (b) Median, MAD and robust z
steps.desc: Sorted: 40, 41, 41, 42, 42, 43, 44, 95 - median = (42 + 42) / 2 = 42. Absolute deviations: 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 53 - sorted: 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 53 - MAD = (1 + 1) / 2 = 1. Robust z = 0.6745 x (95 - 42) / 1 = 35.7, far beyond 3.5: flagged instantly. The 44 ms row scores 0.6745 x 2 / 1 = 1.35, comfortably clean.

steps.title: (c) Why they disagree
steps.desc: The outlier itself inflated sigma from a typical 1-2 ms to 17.61 and dragged the mean up by 5.8: the statistic used as the ruler was rewritten by the thing being measured (masking - breakdown point of mean/sigma is near 0 percent). The median ignored the tail entirely (it can resist up to 50 percent contamination) and MAD measured the body of the distribution, so the 95 stands out by 53 MADs instead of hiding inside 2.6 sigmas.

steps.title: (d) From score to rule
steps.desc: Budget = 1 alert per 100 requests = top 1 percent. Rank every request by |robust z| (or by -score from an isolation forest, which also uses the other features) and alert on the top 1 percent; equivalently set the threshold at the 99th percentile of scores. Then add the context layer: suppress or re-baseline during known windows (backups, flash sales), require two consecutive flags for paging, and log every false alarm to re-price miss cost vs false-alarm cost at the next review.

payload.solution: Mean 48.5, sigma 17.61, z(95) = 2.64 - the 3-sigma rule misses the anomaly that broke its own ruler. Median 42, MAD 1, robust z(95) = 35.7 - flagged at the 3.5 threshold while normal rows stay below 1.4. The disagreement is masking: mean/sigma have near-zero breakdown, median/MAD resist half the sample. Operational rule: rank by robust score, alert on the top 1 percent (the budget), gate by context windows, and keep re-pricing the threshold from the false-alarm vs miss cost matrix.

payload.title: Inject anomalies and count what each detector catches
payload.prompt: Take a clean metric (latency, daily sales, sensor readings) and inject three synthetic anomalies: one spike, one drift to a new level, and five consecutive mildly high readings. Run a mean/sigma z-detector, a median/MAD detector and IsolationForest (contamination 0.01). Tabulate: which detector caught which anomaly, how many false alarms each raised on the clean days, and which anomaly type needs a window or context rule rather than a per-row score.
payload.hint: Point spikes should fall to all three; level shifts break per-row detectors until the window moves (that is contextual drift); collective mild runs are caught by sequences, not single-row scores - that gap tells you what monitor to add.

mistakes.mistake: Thresholding with mean and sigma on skewed, spike-prone data
mistakes.fix: Use median and MAD (robust z at 3.5) for point anomalies; the mean/sigma pair has near-zero breakdown and masks the very value you are hunting.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring context: alarming on values that are normal in their window
mistakes.fix: Model the context - per-hour or per-day baselines, holiday and campaign flags - or explicitly suppress known windows. Contextual anomalies are defined by context, not by the row.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a detector flag as proof and acting on it directly
mistakes.fix: A flag is a hypothesis for a human. Route to review, capture the verdict, and only feed reviewed labels back - otherwise you automate accusations and poison your own training data.

mistakes.mistake: Tuning contamination until the output matches expectations
mistakes.fix: contamination is a budget statement about expected anomaly share (or a cost-derived threshold). Setting it to force a desired conclusion makes the detector a mirror of your prior, not a measurement.

mistakes.mistake: Retraining on unreviewed flags
mistakes.fix: If an incident was flagged and then retrained as normal, the next model learns the incident was normal. Review first, then retrain; keep confirmed incidents in a held-back sanity set for recall checks.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: For the latencies 40, 42, 41, 43, 44, 42, 41, 95 compute (i) mean, sigma and the 3-sigma verdict for 95; (ii) median, MAD and the robust z verdict at 3.5. Explain the disagreement in one term and justify why the robust pair is the default for thresholding. Finish by describing how an alert threshold should be chosen in production.
payload.answer: (i) mean = 48.5; sum of squared deviations = 2482, variance = 310.25, sigma = 17.61; z(95) = 46.5 / 17.61 = 2.64 < 3 - the rule does not fire, even on the most extreme value. (ii) median = 42; absolute deviations are 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 53, which sort to 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 53, so MAD = (1 + 1) / 2 = 1; robust z = 0.6745 x 53 / 1 = 35.7 > 3.5 - flagged, while 44 scores 1.35. Disagreement: masking - the outlier inflated sigma (and pulled the mean), so the ruler was vandalised by the value it was measuring; mean/sigma have a breakdown point near zero while median/MAD tolerate up to half contamination, which is why the robust pair is the default for thresholds. Production threshold: rank by robust (or model-based) score, alert on the volume the team can investigate (alert budget), derive the cut from the cost matrix of false alarm versus miss, gate by context windows and consecutive-hit rules, and re-price the threshold when the reviewed outcomes change - never from folklore constants alone.
payload.source: Evergreen robust-statistics exam question (masking arithmetic + threshold design).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Point, contextual and collective anomalies need different tools - per-row scores only catch the first species.
Mean and sigma are vandalisable: one extreme value inflates sigma and hides itself (masking), so use median/MAD robust z with the 3.5 threshold.
Isolation forests score rarity as a short path through random splits; contamination is a budget statement, not a discovered truth.
There are no labels: evaluate with held-back incidents, precision at the alert budget, and alert volume on clean periods.
Set thresholds from the cost matrix and the team capacity - every false alarm spends trust, and every unactionable alert is worse than no detector.
Review verdicts before retraining, or the model learns that incidents are normal.

questions.prompt: The robust z-score used with median and MAD is 0.6745 x (x - median) / MAD. The constant 0.6745 is there to:
options: Rescale MAD so the statistic is comparable with a sigma-based z-score for Gaussian data
Convert MAD into a mean absolute deviation
questions.explanation: MAD measures the 50th percentile of deviations, which is smaller than sigma for a Gaussian; 0.6745 maps it onto a sigma-equivalent scale so familiar thresholds transfer.

questions.prompt: An isolation forest flags a row as anomalous when:
options: Its distance to the global centroid is largest
Random feature-threshold splits isolate it in fewer steps (shorter average path length), because it is few and different
Its feature values exceed 3 standard deviations
It forms a cluster of size one after k-means
questions.explanation: The method encodes rarity directly: rare, outlying rows are cut off quickly by random splits, while dense-core rows need many splits - short path equals high anomaly score.

questions.prompt: Checkout latency of 70 ms during a midnight backup window, where 70 ms is routine, but alarming at noon: this is best classified as:
options: A contextual anomaly - normal in one context, strange in another
Not an anomaly at all, since the value is ordinary
questions.explanation: The row is only odd relative to its context (time of day, season, segment). Detecting it needs a contextual baseline or context features, not a global threshold.

questions.prompt: Why does a mean-and-sigma (3-sigma) alarm sometimes fail to fire on the most extreme value in a sample?
options: The extreme value itself inflates sigma and pulls the mean toward it (masking), so its own z-score shrinks below the threshold
The alarm compares against the median instead
3-sigma alarms only work for negative values
questions.explanation: Both statistics are computed from the same sample: the outlier widens the band it is judged against. Median/MAD resist this because they ignore how extreme the tails are.

lessons.title: PCA, t-SNE and UMAP: What a 2-D Plot Is Allowed to Claim
lessons.summary: PCA as variance accounting with a component budget you compute yourself, the scaling decision that makes or breaks it, and the strict list of sentences a non-linear embedding plot can and cannot support.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute explained-variance ratios and cumulative variance, and choose a component count at a stated threshold
Decide when to standardise before PCA and explain the unit-domination failure it prevents
Use PCA honestly for compression, denoising and leakage-safe features in a pipeline
State which claims a t-SNE or UMAP plot supports, and which claims it fabricates

payload.text: An intern runs t-SNE on 3,000 customer rows, gets a picture with seven crisp islands, and writes in the slide: "Our customers fall into seven distinct groups." A senior engineer changes one argument - perplexity from 30 to 5, new random seed - and the islands rearrange: three of them split, two fused, one vanished. Same data, different painting. Nothing about the customers changed between the two runs, so the difference between the pictures cannot be evidence about customers. The 2-D plot is a hypothesis generator you follow up with numbers; treating it as the finding is the most common way beautiful visualisation becomes bad science.

**PCA: spend a variance budget.** Principal component analysis finds the orthogonal directions along which the data varies most. Procedure: centre every column (subtract the mean - this is not optional), then either diagonalise the covariance matrix or, equivalently and more stably, take the singular value decomposition of the centred matrix. The eigenvectors are the **components** (linear combinations of the original features, ordered by importance) and the eigenvalues are the **variance captured** by each. The working number is the **explained-variance ratio**: eigenvalue divided by total variance, per component, and its cumulative sum - which answers the only question that matters: how many components buy 95% of the variance? The dropped components carry the remainder, and reconstruction error measured on standardised data is exactly that dropped fraction. Three properties define what PCA is: it is **linear** (rotations and projections only - it cannot unfold a spiral), **unsupervised** (it maximises variance, which is not the same as preserving the label), and **scale-sensitive** (the covariance matrix is computed in your units, so the widest column dominates component 1).

**The scaling decision, stated as a rule.** If your columns are in different units or ranges (MB and counts, rupees and ratings), run PCA on standardised data: the correlation-matrix PCA, whose eigenvalues sum to the number of features - a free sanity check, because trace-invariance tells you immediately whether the matrix you diagonalised was standardised or not. If all columns genuinely share units and you want structure in raw magnitude, covariance PCA is defensible - but say so in the report. Skipping the decision means PCA quietly becomes a unit converter: with one feature at variance 10,000 and another at variance 4, component 1 is the first feature wearing a disguise, and the second feature's signal about the target is discarded as noise. Two more usage rules: fit the scaler and PCA **on training rows only** (a PCA fitted on all data leaks test-distribution information into the features), and remember the sign of a component is arbitrary - component 1 pointing "up" in one run points "down" in an otherwise identical run, so never interpret a sign, only loadings and magnitudes.

**What PCA is for.** Compression (store 40 components instead of 500 columns), denoising (low-variance directions are often noise - often, not always, since a rare class can live in a low-variance direction), decorrelation (feed uncorrelated components to a model that assumes it), speed, mitigating the curse of dimensionality, and honest 2-D visualisation: the top two components are the two largest-variance directions, plotted with real axis units, so distances are *linear-globally* meaningful up to the projection loss. What it is not: a feature selector with a target in mind (use supervised methods for that), a guarantee that 95% variance means 95% accuracy, or a clusterer by itself - though clustering in PCA space is a perfectly good practice.

**t-SNE and UMAP: local neighbourhood painters.** Both are non-linear optimisers that place points in 2-D (or low-D) so that *neighbourhoods* stay neighbours: t-SNE converts distances to conditional probabilities and matches them between high-D and low-D; UMAP builds a fuzzy neighbourhood graph and lays it out preserving local connectivity. The consequence is the whole lesson: **local structure is approximately preserved; global geometry is not guaranteed.** Between-cluster distances, relative cluster sizes, densities and empty space in the picture are all shaped by parameters (t-SNE perplexity, UMAP n_neighbors and min_dist) and by the seed - two runs of the same data routinely disagree on everything except which points are tight neighbours. Therefore the rule set: cluster and score in the original or PCA space, never in the embedding; use the picture to *notice* candidate structure and then verify it numerically (silhouette in the real space, stability across seeds, downstream lift); treat a t-SNE picture as a hypothesis with a run-to-run stability check attached; and when a reviewer demands "just show the clusters", show the PCA plot with axis values *and* the embedding side by side, labelled by what each may claim. t-SNE and UMAP are excellent at surfacing rare subgroups that linear PCA hides, and useless as evidence that seven groups exist.

# PCA budget, then embed only for looking
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)      # never let units choose your components
pca = PCA().fit(Xs)                          # fit on TRAIN rows in a real pipeline
ratios = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
print("per component:", np.round(ratios, 3))
print("cumulative:  ", np.round(np.cumsum(ratios), 3))
print("trace check (should equal n features):", round(pca.explained_variance_.sum(), 3))

n95 = int(np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(ratios), 0.95) + 1)
print("components for 95% variance:", n95)
Z = PCA(n_components=n95, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xs)   # Z goes to the model

plt.scatter(Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1], s=8)           # top two PCs: real linear geometry
plt.xlabel("PC1"); plt.ylabel("PC2"); plt.show()

# t-SNE / UMAP: look, then VERIFY in Xs or Z - never cluster inside the embedding

payload.title: Computing clusters or metrics inside a t-SNE/UMAP picture
payload.text: The embedding optimises neighbourhood probabilities, not distances you can compare. Run k-means and silhouette in Xs or in PCA space; use the picture only to generate the hypothesis you then test.

payload.title: Report the cumulative curve with the component count
payload.text: One line - components kept, variance retained, dropped variance as reconstruction error - turns a dimensionality decision from a default into a defensible number. Add the trace check to prove you standardised.

payload.title: Reading an eigenvalue budget, and the unit-domination trap
payload.problem: Five features were standardised; the eigenvalues of their correlation matrix are 2.5, 1.4, 0.7, 0.3 and 0.1. (a) Compute the explained-variance ratio of each component and the cumulative series. (b) How many components reach at least 95%? (c) If only three are kept, what fraction of variance is lost, and what is the reconstruction error on standardised data? (d) What does the sum of the eigenvalues confirm? (e) Now two raw features: MB with variance 10,000 and count with variance 4, PCA on unscaled data - what does component 1 become, and what is the fix?

steps.title: (b) The component budget
steps.desc: Three components stop at 92% - short of the 95% target. Four reach 98%, so the answer is 4 components. State it as a decision: "4 of 5 components, 98% variance retained, 2% dropped".

steps.title: (c) Cost of keeping three
steps.desc: Dropped variance = 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4 of 5.0 = 8%. On standardised data, mean squared reconstruction error per feature equals the dropped fraction, 0.08 - the reconstruction is off by roughly 0.28 standard deviations per feature on average (square root of 0.08).

steps.title: (d) The sanity check
steps.desc: The eigenvalues sum to 5.0 - exactly the number of features. For standardised data the correlation matrix has trace equal to the feature count (trace invariance: standardisation pins every variance at 1), so this confirms correlation PCA. A sum of 14,007 instead would tell you the matrix was a raw covariance matrix and the widest column was voting unopposed.

steps.title: (e) Unit domination
steps.desc: On unscaled data the total variance is about 10,000 + 4 = 10,004, so the MB feature holds 99.96% of it: component 1 aligns with MB (the count feature contributes a rounding error), and PCA becomes a rescaling of one column while the count signal is discarded as noise. Fix: standardise (or convert to comparable units) before PCA, or make the correlation-matrix choice explicitly - then re-check the trace equals 5.

payload.solution: Ratios 0.50 / 0.28 / 0.14 / 0.06 / 0.02; cumulative 0.50 / 0.78 / 0.92 / 0.98 / 1.00; 4 components for >= 95%. Keeping 3 loses 8% of variance = 0.08 mean squared reconstruction error on standardised data. The eigenvalue sum of 5.0 confirms correlation (standardised) PCA. With raw MB (variance 10,000) vs count (variance 4), unscaled PCA makes PC1 the MB column - standardise first, then the trace check proves you did.

payload.title: Build the evidence pack before anyone shows a t-SNE
payload.prompt: On one dataset: standardise, fit PCA, and report the explained-variance table with the component count at 95%. Then produce three pictures of the same data - top two PCs, t-SNE at perplexity 5, t-SNE at perplexity 30 - each with a different random seed on a second run. List which visual claims (number of groups, relative sizes, spacing between groups) stayed the same across all four pictures and which changed. Conclude in two sentences what you would tell a stakeholder the plots show.
payload.hint: Anything that survives every run and parameter is a candidate fact to verify numerically; anything that moves is a property of the layout algorithm - report it as "structure to investigate", never as a finding.

mistakes.mistake: Running k-means or computing silhouette inside a t-SNE/UMAP embedding
mistakes.fix: Cluster and score in the original or PCA space; the embedding is for eyes. Metrics computed there measure the layout algorithm, not the data.

mistakes.mistake: Interpreting PC axis values or sign as real-world quantities
mistakes.fix: A component is a weighted mix of features with arbitrary sign; interpret via loadings (which features dominate and their relative weight), not the axis number, and never read direction as cause.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping standardisation because the data "looks fine"
mistakes.fix: Covariance PCA is unit-sensitive: the widest column wins by construction. Standardise when units or ranges differ, and confirm with the trace check (eigenvalues sum to the feature count).

mistakes.mistake: Fitting the scaler and PCA on all rows before splitting
mistakes.fix: PCA is learned structure: fit on training rows inside the pipeline, transform validation and test with the fitted object - otherwise test-distribution information leaks into the features.

mistakes.mistake: Equating 95% explained variance with 95% of the predictive signal
mistakes.fix: Variance is unsupervised; the label can live in a low-variance direction. Retain components by variance for compression, but validate the downstream metric after the reduction.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Eigenvalues of a standardised 5-feature correlation matrix: 2.5, 1.4, 0.7, 0.3, 0.1. Give the cumulative explained variance, the number of components for 95%, and the reconstruction error of a 3-component model. Then: a colleague shows a t-SNE plot and claims the distances between clusters and their relative sizes are real - state three claims the plot cannot support and one workflow that would test the claim properly.
payload.answer: Total = 5.0; cumulative explained variance = 50%, 78%, 92%, 98%, 100% - so 4 components are required for at least 95% (3 gives only 92%). Keeping 3 drops 0.4 of 5.0 = 8% of variance, i.e. mean squared reconstruction error of 0.08 per standardised feature. The eigenvalue sum equal to 5 confirms correlation PCA on standardised data. Claims the t-SNE picture cannot support: (1) the distance between two far clusters - the non-linear layout distorts global geometry; (2) the area of a cluster - size follows local density and parameters, not population; (3) that the group count is a property of the data - perplexity and seed routinely split, merge or delete islands on identical rows. Legitimate workflow: generate candidate groups from the picture, then verify numerically in the original or PCA space - fit the clustering there, report silhouette and stability across resamples and seeds, check downstream lift on a held-out metric, and only then present the groups, with the picture as illustration rather than evidence.
payload.source: Interview-grade synthesis (PCA arithmetic + embedding interpretation discipline).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: PCA = centre, then rotate onto directions of decreasing variance; explained-variance ratios and their cumulative sum set the component budget.
Correlation (standardised) PCA has eigenvalues summing to the feature count - the trace check that proves you scaled.
Scale-sensitive, linear and unsupervised: PCA can neither unfold non-linear structure nor promise that retained variance equals retained signal.
Fit scaler and PCA on training rows only; component sign is arbitrary, interpret loadings instead.
t-SNE and UMAP preserve local neighbourhoods, not global geometry - distances, sizes and even cluster counts move with seed and parameters.
Cluster and score in real space, embed for eyes, and verify every picture with stability, silhouette or downstream lift before it becomes a claim.

questions.prompt: Explained-variance ratios of the first three components are 0.50, 0.28 and 0.14. To retain at least 95% of variance you need:
options: Four components - three reach only 92%, the fourth crosses 95%
All five components, since nothing below 95% can be dropped
questions.explanation: Cumulative: 0.50, 0.78, 0.92 - three components are short of the threshold, so you go to four (0.98 with the fourth). Thresholds are crossed by adding components, never reached by rounding.

questions.prompt: You run PCA on columns measured in MB (variance 10,000) and counts (variance 4) without standardising. What happens?
options: Both features contribute equally to the components
PC1 aligns with the MB column (it holds about 99.9% of total variance) and the count feature is discarded as noise - PCA becomes a unit converter
PCA refuses to run until columns are scaled
The components are automatically normalised to unit variance
questions.explanation: PCA maximises variance in your units: the widest-scale feature wins outright. Standardise (correlation PCA) or convert units first - otherwise component 1 is the MB column wearing a disguise.

questions.prompt: A t-SNE plot shows two islands with a large gap. The justified interpretation is:
options: The gap size proves how different the groups are, and each island size reflects its population

Only that those points were close neighbours in the high-dimensional data - the gap distance, cluster areas and island count are shaped by perplexity and seed, so verify structure in original/PCA space
The plot is invalid and should be discarded entirely
The islands are exactly the clusters you should deploy
questions.explanation: t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, not global geometry: inter-cluster distance, cluster area and even the number of islands move with perplexity and seed. Treat the picture as a hypothesis and verify clustering in original/PCA space.

questions.prompt: Principal component analysis finds directions that:
options: Maximise variance of the (centred) data, subject to being orthogonal to earlier components
Minimise reconstruction error of the labels
Separate classes by the largest margin
questions.explanation: PCA is unsupervised variance maximisation with orthogonality constraints - no labels involved (maximising target correlation is PLS/ supervised methods; max-margin separation is SVM).

modules.title: Module 9 — ML in Production: Drift, Monitoring, Fairness and Restraint
modules.summary: What happens after deployment: telling covariate shift, prior shift and concept drift apart with PSI arithmetic and a root-cause-first playbook; monitoring the layers labels cannot answer daily (data quality, score distributions, training-serving skew, slices); fairness as competing harm definitions that cannot all hold when base rates differ; and the judgement call of choosing rules over models with human review designed and measured instead of assumed.

lessons.title: Drift: Detecting When the World Changed Under Your Model
lessons.summary: Three different things called drift, the PSI computation that quantifies a distribution shift on four bins, and a root-cause-first playbook that stops you retraining on a bug.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify a given shift as covariate, prior/label or concept drift and name what stays unchanged in each
Compute PSI by hand from binned training and current percentages and interpret it against the 0.10 and 0.25 thresholds
Diagnose the cause of a performance drop before choosing between rebaselining, retraining and rebuilding
Design monitoring for delayed labels using input and score distributions as interim signals

payload.text: A credit-risk model held 0.84 AUC for two years. In March it slid to 0.76. The team's instinct was to retrain that evening. One engineer asked a different question first: which features moved, and when did they start moving? The answer: a partner app changed its income field from monthly to yearly figures on 2 March - every income feature suddenly multiplied by about twelve, and no amount of retraining on that feed would have helped, because the data was wrong, not the relationship. The fix was one line in the ingestion pipeline and a validation rule. Drift monitoring that skips root cause is a machine for retraining on garbage faster.

**Three shifts, three different repairs.** Drift is not one phenomenon, and each type demands a different response. **Covariate shift:** the input distribution P(X) changes while the relationship P(Y|X) stays the same - a new device mix, a marketing channel that brings different customers, income fields multiplied by twelve. The model is still correct in principle; the data it sees moved. **Prior (label) shift:** P(Y) changes while P(X|Y) is stable - the fraud rate doubles overnight because a new attack campaign starts; features of fraud still look like fraud, but fraud is now commoner, so every probability the model outputs needs recalibration (the posterior must be adjusted for the new base rate, not relearned). **Concept drift:** P(Y|X) itself changes - the same features now lead to a different outcome. Customers learn the routing rules, sensors age, competitors respond; yesterday's mapping is genuinely obsolete and only new training data repairs it. A fourth, benign category is **recurring/seasonal change** - the same pattern every December - which calls for seasonality-aware baselines, not a retrain that half-learns last Christmas. The type determines the fix: wrong data means fix the pipeline, prior shift means recalibrate, concept drift means retrain, seasonality means model the calendar.

**PSI: the cheap numeric alarm.** Population Stability Index compares a binned distribution now against the training distribution: PSI = sum over bins of (actual share - expected share) x ln(actual share / expected share). Procedure: take the training sample of a feature or the model's training-time scores, cut it into 10 equal-frequency bins (deciles), apply those same edges to the current window, compute each bin's share in both, and sum. Read it against the working thresholds: below 0.10 = stable; 0.10 to 0.25 = moderate, investigate; above 0.25 = significant shift, act. PSI is one number per feature or for the score vector, so you can watch hundreds cheaply, and the bin-by-bin table tells you *where* the mass moved (which is the first clue to cause). Its limits: it needs enough rows per bin (clip tiny shares to avoid division blow-ups), it says nothing about whether the shift *matters* to performance, and it fires on both real drift and pipeline bugs - which is exactly why it is a trigger for diagnosis, never a trigger for blind retraining. Companion tests: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic for a single continuous feature (statistically sharp - so sharp that with a million rows it flags trivial differences; pair every p-value with an effect size), and simple null-rate or category-share alarms for categorical columns.

**The playbook: confirm, localise, classify, then act.** (1) **Confirm it is real** - is the shift in the data or in the *data pipeline*? Check schema, null rates, units, timezones, joins; a surprising PSI on one feature almost always localises there. (2) **Localise** - which features moved, since when, correlated with which release, region or campaign? Plot PSI or means over time to find the change point. (3) **Classify** using the three-shift table above: P(X) moved with stable relationship = covariate (fix source or retrain with the corrected feed); only the base rate moved = recalibrate thresholds and expected volumes; relationship broke = concept drift, retrain; calendar-driven = seasonality. (4) **Act and validate** - retrain on a time-ordered window (never random-shuffle splits across time), evaluate on the most recent sealed period, deploy behind a canary or shadow mode against the incumbent, and keep the old model ready to roll back. (5) **Close the loop** - add the failed check to monitoring so the same cause alarms within days next time.

**Monitoring while labels are late.** Many outcomes arrive weeks or months after the prediction (defaults, churn, clinical results), so accuracy cannot be your daily alarm. Use the cheap proxies: PSI or KS on the features and on the **score distribution** (if scores shift, either X moved or the world moved - either way look), data-quality rates (nulls, unseen categories, range violations), and volume anomalies. Beware **early-label bias**: retraining on only the labels that have arrived so far trains on outcomes that were easier or faster to resolve (approved loans default later than rejected ones are never observed), which quietly distorts the target - wait for matured labels or model the censoring explicitly. The daily dashboard is therefore mostly *input* health; the *performance* panels light up on label cadence, and the gap between them is where the playbook runs.

payload.title: The three shifts - what moves, what stays, what fixes it
rows: Fix the source if wrong; otherwise retrain on current data
Recalibrate probabilities and thresholds; retrain only if prolonged
Retrain on recent, time-ordered data; revalidate features
Seasonal baselines and calendar features - not repeated retraining

payload.code:
# PSI: score distribution now vs at training, plus the verdict band
def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    edges = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))  # TRAINING edges
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected, edges)[0] / len(expected)
    a = np.histogram(actual, edges)[0] / len(actual)
    e, a = np.clip(e, 1e-4, None), np.clip(a, 1e-4, None)       # no divide by zero
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))

for window, name in zip(weekly_scores, ["w4", "w8", "w12"]):
    s = psi(train_scores, window)
    verdict = "stable" if s < 0.10 else ("investigate" if s < 0.25 else "major shift")
    print(name, round(s, 3), verdict)

# A high PSI on ONE feature is a localisation clue, not a retraining order.
# Confirm the pipeline, find the change point, classify the shift, THEN act.

payload.title: Retraining without a root cause entrenches the bug
payload.text: Most sudden "drift" incidents are ingestion faults - units, timezones, joins, schema changes. Confirm the data is valid first; retraining on a broken feed teaches the model the breakage is correct.

payload.title: Watch the score distribution daily, performance on label cadence
payload.text: Scores are available the moment predictions are made: PSI on scores is your interim alarm while labels are weeks away. Performance panels then confirm or clear the alarm when outcomes mature.

payload.title: PSI by hand: a window that fails the 0.25 test
payload.problem: A model was trained when its score distribution was uniform across four quartile bins: 25%, 25%, 25%, 25%. In the current window the same bins hold 7%, 15%, 28% and 50%. (a) Compute PSI with the standard formula. (b) Give the verdict against the 0.10 / 0.25 thresholds. (c) Name two very different real-world causes consistent with this number and the first check for each. (d) State what you would NOT do purely because of this PSI value.

steps.title: (b) Sum and verdict
steps.desc: PSI = 0.2291 + 0.0511 + 0.0034 + 0.1733 = 0.4569, about 0.46. That is above 0.25, so the shift is significant: the monitoring rule says act - diagnose now, not "watch and wait". Note where the mass went: the top bin nearly doubled while the bottom bin shrank, so scores moved upward as a whole.

steps.title: (c) Two causes, two first checks
steps.desc: Cause 1: pipeline fault - a unit change, a broken join dropping a predictive column, or leakage entering the feed. First check: null rates, schema, value ranges, and per-feature PSI to see if one feature drives the score move. Cause 2: real world - a seasonal campaign, a new customer segment from a marketing push, or genuine concept change. First check: correlate the change point with releases and campaign calendars, and compare input PSI against performance once labels mature.

steps.title: (d) What not to do
steps.desc: Do not retrain tonight on this evidence alone. PSI says a distribution moved, nothing about why or whether accuracy suffered; retraining on a broken feed legitimises the breakage, and retraining on a seasonal spike teaches the model that December is the new normal. Confirm, localise, classify - then apply the matching repair (fix source, recalibrate, retrain on time-ordered data, or add seasonality).

payload.solution: PSI = 0.2291 + 0.0511 + 0.0034 + 0.1733 = 0.4569 (about 0.46) - well above the 0.25 significance threshold, driven by the top bin doubling and the bottom bin collapsing. Possible causes: ingestion fault (check schema, nulls, per-feature PSI first) or genuine shift (correlate the change point with releases and campaigns, then confirm with matured performance). The wrong response is blind retraining: PSI triggers diagnosis, and the repair follows the shift classification - fix the source, recalibrate, retrain on time-ordered data, or model the season.

payload.title: Localise a shift with per-feature PSI
payload.prompt: Take two windows of your own data (or a synthetic time split) and compute PSI per feature plus PSI on the model scores. Rank features by PSI. For the top two, write the change point you observe (the first window where it jumps), one plausible pipeline cause and one plausible real-world cause. Only if you cannot find a pipeline cause, define the retraining window you would use and the time-ordered validation split you would evaluate on.
payload.hint: One feature dominating score PSI points at that feature's feed; a synchronized jump across many features points at a pipeline-wide event (schema, timezone, join) or a genuine regime change - the breadth of the jump is the diagnostic.

mistakes.mistake: Retraining the moment any PSI crosses 0.25
mistakes.fix: PSI is a diagnosis trigger: confirm the feed is valid, localise the feature and change point, classify the shift, then choose the matching repair (fix / recalibrate / retrain / seasonality).

mistakes.mistake: Calling every performance drop concept drift
mistakes.fix: Check the three-shift table first: covariate shift and pipeline faults look identical to concept drift in a headline metric but need no retraining at all - they need the source corrected.

mistakes.mistake: Shuffling time into the train/validation split when retraining after drift
mistakes.fix: Random splits mix the future into the past and score the model on a world it had already seen. Split by time and seal the most recent period as the evaluation.

mistakes.mistake: Retraining on partially matured labels
mistakes.fix: Early labels are biased (fast-resolving outcomes over-represented). Wait for maturity or model the censoring; otherwise the new model learns a distorted target.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a tiny p-value from a KS test as proof of material drift
mistakes.fix: With large n, KS flags negligible differences. Always pair statistical tests with an effect size (PSI, mean shift) and with whether performance or the decision boundary actually moved.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Distinguish covariate shift, prior shift and concept drift, stating for each what changes, what stays stable and the appropriate first repair. Then compute PSI for bin shares (training 25/25/25/25 vs current 7/15/28/50) and give the verdict, plus the first three steps of your incident playbook.
payload.answer: Covariate shift: P(X) changes while P(Y|X) is stable - inputs moved but the relationship still holds; first repair is fixing the source if the data is wrong, otherwise retraining on current data (probabilities usually remain calibrated). Prior/label shift: P(Y) (the base rate) changes while P(X|Y) is stable - first repair is recalibrating probabilities and re-tuning thresholds for the new base rate. Concept drift: P(Y|X) changes - the relationship itself is obsolete; repair is retraining on recent time-ordered data with feature re-examination. PSI: (0.07-0.25)ln(0.28) + (0.15-0.25)ln(0.60) + (0.28-0.25)ln(1.12) + (0.50-0.25)ln(2) = 0.2291 + 0.0511 + 0.0034 + 0.1733 = 0.4569 (about 0.46) - above 0.25, significant shift. Playbook: (1) confirm the data is valid (schema, nulls, units, joins - pipeline faults mimic drift), (2) localise which features moved and find the change point in time, (3) classify the shift with the table and apply only that repair, validating on a sealed time-ordered holdout with the incumbent kept for rollback.
payload.source: Evergreen MLOps exam question (drift taxonomy + PSI arithmetic).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Covariate shift moves P(X); prior shift moves P(Y); concept drift moves P(Y|X) - the repair is different for each (fix source, recalibrate, retrain).
PSI = sum (actual share - expected share) x ln(actual/expected) over training-defined bins; below 0.10 stable, 0.10-0.25 investigate, above 0.25 act.
PSI fires on bugs as easily as on real drift - confirm the feed, localise the feature, find the change point, then classify before repairing.
Retrain on time-ordered windows with a sealed recent holdout; never shuffle time, never retrain on immature labels.
While labels are late, monitor features and score distributions daily - performance panels confirm on the label cadence.

questions.prompt: P(X) is unchanged, P(X|Y) is unchanged, but P(Y) has doubled after a fraud campaign. This is:
options: Prior (label) shift - repair by recalibrating probabilities and thresholds for the new base rate
questions.explanation: Only the base rate moved; class-conditional feature distributions are stable, so Bayes-conditional probabilities shift by a constant factor - recalibration is the repair, not full retraining.

questions.prompt: PSI for a feature comes out at 0.46 against training-defined bins. The correct action is:
options: Treat it as a significant shift (> 0.25): diagnose the cause (pipeline vs real world), classify the shift, then apply the matching repair
Retrain on the current window before investigating
questions.explanation: 0.46 exceeds the 0.25 significance threshold, so act - but "act" means diagnose and classify first; retraining before root-causing risks entrenching an ingestion bug.

questions.prompt: PSI is computed by:
options: Comparing model accuracy this month with accuracy last month
Binning the training sample (e.g. deciles), applying those same edges to the current window, and summing (actual share - expected share) x ln(actual/expected) across bins
Measuring the correlation between features and the target in both windows
Counting the number of categories that disappeared
questions.explanation: PSI compares binned distributions using training-defined edges: the sum over bins of (a - e) x ln(a/e). Bins must come from training so the comparison has a fixed reference.

questions.prompt: A seasonal business repeats the same December pattern every year and the model alerts every December. Best response:
options: Retrain every December on the latest data
Treat it as recurring drift: add calendar/season features and seasonal baselines so the pattern is expected rather than relearned
Raise the PSI threshold above 0.25 permanently
questions.explanation: Recurring change is structure, not deterioration: a seasonal baseline or calendar feature makes December predictable, whereas repeated retraining spends cycles half-learning the same cycle and risks forgetting the rest of the year.

lessons.title: Monitoring in Production: Slices, Skew and the Metrics You Can Actually See
lessons.summary: The layered monitoring stack that works when labels are weeks late, the slice arithmetic that proves one overall number can hide a collapse, and the training-serving skew check that catches silent feature bugs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Lay out the monitoring layers (data quality, distributions, scores, ops, performance, slices) and state what each can and cannot tell you
Reproduce the slice-collapse arithmetic showing how an overall metric hides a failing subgroup
Define training-serving skew and design a backfill test that detects it
Design an alerting setup with thresholds, owners and runbooks that survives contact with the on-call team

payload.text: A fraud model reported 0.90 accuracy all quarter while it was quietly failing one segment: 98% of traffic came from a healthy slice scoring 0.91, and 2% of traffic - a new merchant category - scored 0.55. The overall number never moved, because a weighted average of 0.98 x 0.91 and 0.02 x 0.55 is 0.90, close enough to last quarter to pass every review. The failure was visible for months in a table nobody plotted. Monitoring a model with one global number is monitoring the average of your success and your failure, and hoping the success is bigger.

**A stack of layers, because no single metric can see everything.** Production monitoring is not one graph; it is layers that fail independently. **Layer 1 - data quality:** schema changes, null rates, range violations, unseen categories, value frequencies (cheapest, catches the ingestion bugs that cause most incidents). **Layer 2 - input distributions:** PSI or KS per feature against training - did the world of inputs move? **Layer 3 - score/output distribution:** the model's own predictions over time; a shift here with stable inputs means the model is amplifying small input moves, and a shift with unstable inputs localises the cause. **Layer 4 - operations:** latency percentiles (p95, p99 - averages hide the tail users feel), error rates, throughput, timeouts, dependency health. **Layer 5 - performance:** accuracy, AUC, calibration, business metrics - *once labels arrive*, on their cadence, always with a baseline period. **Layer 6 - slices:** the same performance metrics cut by the segments that matter. Layers 1-4 run continuously on every prediction; layer 5 runs when truth matures; layer 6 runs forever, because that is where failures hide.

**Slice monitoring: the arithmetic of hiding.** An overall metric is a weighted average over slices: 0.98 x 0.91 + 0.02 x 0.55 = 0.8918 + 0.0110 = 0.9028, reported as 0.90 - indistinguishable from a healthy 0.90 while a slice sat at 0.55. The fix is procedural, not clever: (1) choose slices **in advance** - region, device, plan, channel, language, price band, new-vs-existing, any group with a different harm story - because slices discovered after a failure are always the wrong ones for the next failure; (2) set a **floor** (minimum acceptable metric per slice) and a **gap rule** (slice more than, say, 10 points below overall triggers an incident); (3) respect **sample size** - a slice with 40 rows cannot support a claim (use confidence intervals or pool until n is meaningful; a 55% on n = 40 has a wide interval), and state n next to every slice number; (4) monitor the **volume** of each slice too - a slice disappearing is itself an alarm (an upstream partner stopped sending that traffic). Slice metrics are also where fairness (next lesson), region outages and season effects surface - one panel, many alarms.

**Training-serving skew: the silent one.** The model validates at 0.92 offline and scores badly online, with identical inputs "in spirit". Skew means the features the model sees at serving differ from the features it learned from - different code paths (offline SQL vs online feature service), timezones or window boundaries computed differently, aggregations that include the future offline but only the past online (point-in-time violation), preprocessing fitted separately, or the training table joining a table that the online system cannot reach. It produces no data-quality alarm, because every value is plausible. Two tests catch it: **backfill** - take training rows with known features, re-compute them through the *serving* pipeline, and diff column by column (any mismatch is skew), and **canary comparison** - run the new model in shadow, compare its scores with the old model's on identical traffic and investigate systematic divergence. Prevention: one shared feature definition used by both paths (feature store or generated code), point-in-time joins by construction, and a freshness SLA per feature.

**Alerts that do not train people to ignore them.** Every alert needs a threshold with rationale, an owner, and a runbook saying what to check in the first ten minutes; otherwise alerts are noise with a siren. Separate **pages** (wake someone: error rate, score collapse, data quality hard-fail) from **tickets** (business hours: PSI drift, slice gap, volume dip). Use hysteresis and multi-window rules (two consecutive bad windows) so a single noisy hour does not wake anyone, and review alert precision monthly: if the team cannot remember the last alert that mattered, the thresholds have already failed. Also monitor the monitor: dead dashboards, stale pipelines and unsent alerts are the most common outage of monitoring itself - a weekly synthetic alarm tests the whole chain.

payload.code:
# Slice panel + the arithmetic that hides failures
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# overall accuracy is a weighted average - the weights hide the tail
sl = df.groupby("segment").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({"n": len(g), "acc": (g.pred == g.y).mean()}))
overall = float((sl["n"] * sl["acc"]).sum() / sl["n"].sum())
sl["gap"] = overall - sl["acc"]
print("overall:", round(overall, 3))
print(sl.sort_values("acc").head())

FLOOR, GAP = 0.75, 0.10                       # set BEFORE the failure
bad = sl[(sl["acc"] < FLOOR) | (sl["gap"] > GAP)]
for seg, row in bad.iterrows():
    acc, n = row["acc"], int(row["n"])
    if n >= 100:                           # n too small = no claim
        page(f"slice {seg}: acc {acc:.2f} n {n}")

# volume disappearing is an alarm too
if sl["n"].min() < 0.5 * sl["n"].median():
    ticket("a segment lost more than half its traffic - check upstream")

payload.title: Backfill-test your features before trusting a live score
payload.text: Offline and online feature code drifts apart silently: different SQL, windows, timezones, preprocessing. Recompute training rows through the serving path and diff - any mismatch is skew that no data-quality alarm will ever catch.

payload.title: Set slice floors and gap rules before the first incident
payload.text: Slices discovered after a failure never cover the next one. Pre-register segments, floors, gap rules and minimum sample sizes, then let the panel fire without a meeting about what to look at.

payload.title: The slice that the headline number ate
payload.problem: A classifier serves 100,000 predictions: 98,000 from segment A with 0.91 accuracy, 2,000 from segment B with 0.55 accuracy. (a) Compute the overall accuracy. (b) Explain why no weekly review would have flagged it. (c) With floors of 0.75 and a gap rule of 10 points, what should the panel have fired, and on which signals - with the sample-size caveat? (d) Segment B is a new merchant category that appeared 6 weeks ago: name the two additional panels (not accuracy) that would have caught the problem earlier, and the fix sequence.

steps.title: (a) Overall arithmetic
steps.desc: Overall = 0.98 x 0.91 + 0.02 x 0.55 = 0.8918 + 0.0110 = 0.9028, reported as 0.90. The 0.35 collapse in B contributes only 0.007 of the total - below the noise of any weekly comparison.

steps.title: (b) Why reviews missed it
steps.desc: Reviews tracked one global number against last week: 0.90 versus 0.90, a pass. The weighted average moves by slice_size x slice_change, so a 2% slice can lose 36 points before the headline moves half a point. Averages are designed to be insensitive to exactly the thing you need to notice.

steps.title: (c) What the pre-registered panel fires
steps.desc: Segment B: accuracy 0.55 < floor 0.75 (fire) and gap 0.90 - 0.55 = 0.35 > 0.10 (fire). n = 2,000 is large enough that the estimate is trustworthy - state n beside the number so nobody waves it off as noise. Segment A passes both. The panel should have paged on the floor breach and opened an incident ticket citing the gap.

steps.title: (d) Earlier signals and the fix sequence
steps.desc: Panel 1: slice VOLUME over time - a new category arriving as 0 to 2% then growing is visible before any label exists. Panel 2: slice-level score distribution or input PSI (is the model confidently wrong on unseen categories? low confidence or extreme scores both localise it). Fix sequence: confirm the label quality for B (new categories often have broken labels), check training coverage (was B represented in training?), then either retrain with B, add a fallback path (route low-coverage categories to human review), or ship a category-aware feature - and add B to the pre-registered slice list permanently.

payload.solution: Overall = 0.98 x 0.91 + 0.02 x 0.55 = 0.9028 (0.90) - a 36-point slice collapse moved the headline by 0.7 points, so weekly global reviews were blind by construction. Pre-registered panel: B breaches both the 0.75 floor (0.55) and the 10-point gap (0.35), on n = 2,000, which is solid evidence. Earlier catches without labels: slice volume trend (new category arriving) and slice score/input distributions. Then: verify labels for the new category, check training coverage, and retrain, route to human review, or add a category-aware feature - with the slice added to the permanent panel.

mistakes.mistake: Watching one overall metric and calling the model healthy
mistakes.fix: Pre-register slices with floors and gap rules: a 2% slice at 0.55 leaves the headline at 0.90. Overall numbers are for trends; slices are for failure.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing slices after the incident
mistakes.fix: Post-hoc slices cover yesterday's failure. Fix the list from the harm map (regions, devices, plans, channels, new categories) and revisit it each quarter.

mistakes.mistake: Judging a slice of 40 rows as a collapse (or as proof of health)
mistakes.fix: Show n with every slice metric and apply a minimum-n or confidence-interval gate before firing; pool or extend the window until the estimate is meaningful.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming offline validation proves online behaviour
mistakes.fix: Training-serving skew is invisible to offline metrics: backfill training rows through the serving feature path and diff, and shadow-run models to compare score distributions on identical traffic.

mistakes.mistake: Firing alerts with no owner, threshold rationale or runbook
mistakes.fix: Pages for user-facing breakage, tickets for drift and dips, multi-window rules against noise, and a monthly precision review - unactionable alerts train the team to ignore monitoring.

payload.question: A model reports overall accuracy 0.90: segment A is 98% of traffic at 0.91, segment B is 2% at 0.55. payload.answer: Overall = 0.98 x 0.91 + 0.02 x 0.55 = 0.8918 + 0.0110 = 0.9028 (0.90): the slice collapse contributed about 0.007, below week-to-week noise, so a global trend line never moved. Detection: backfill - recompute training rows through the serving pipeline and diff every column - plus shadow/canary comparison of new-model vs incumbent scores on identical traffic; prevention is a single shared feature definition for both paths.
