lessons.title: Fairness: Competing Definitions, Incompatible Guarantees, Honest Trade-offs
lessons.summary: Four group metrics computed from one confusion matrix per group, the theorem that stops you promising everything, and the practice of choosing whose harm you are counting before you tune anything.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute TPR, FPR, approval rate and PPV for two groups from a given base rate and error rates
Explain why calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold when base rates differ
Select a fairness metric from the harm structure of the application and defend the choice
Audit a model for proxy variables and design mitigations that survive scrutiny

payload.text: A lending model approves 60% of applicants in group A and 35% in group B. Three reviewers look at the same system and each finds discrimination: the demographic-parity auditor sees a 25-point approval gap; the equal-opportunity auditor sees TPRs of 0.90 versus 0.70 - good applicants in B are missed at more than twice A's rate; and the predictive-parity auditor notices that among approved applicants, 90% of A's and only 25% of B's actually repay. All three numbers come from the same predictions. None of the three reviewers is wrong - they are counting different harms, and the model cannot satisfy all three at once. Fairness in ML is not a metric you maximise; it is a decision about who absorbs the error.

**Start from the harm, not the metric.** Before any number, write down what a false positive and a false negative cost, and for whom. In credit: approving a borrower who defaults costs the lender money; rejecting a creditworthy applicant costs the applicant opportunity (and the lender profit). In medical screening: a false negative costs a patient a delayed diagnosis; a false positive costs anxiety and a follow-up test. In content moderation: a false positive silences a speaker; a false negative leaves harmful content up. Only then does a metric mean something, because each definition of fairness protects a different party.

**The metric zoo, from one confusion matrix per group.** **Demographic parity:** P(hat = 1 | group) equal across groups - selection rates match; it ignores who *deserves* the outcome and is the disparate-impact family (a ratio below 0.80, the 4/5ths rule, is a conventional legal red flag). **Equal opportunity:** TPR equal across groups - qualified members of every group get in at the same rate; it protects the *deserving* who are rejected. **Equalised odds:** TPR *and* FPR both equal - the model errs at the same rate for everyone; the strongest of the error-based guarantees. **Predictive parity:** PPV equal - a positive prediction means the same thing in every group; it protects the *recipient* of the decision from being flagged at different reliability. **Calibration:** predicted probabilities match observed frequencies within each group. **Individual fairness:** similar individuals get similar decisions regardless of group. Compute all of them from per-group confusion matrices (see the code block) and you will usually find they disagree - which is the point of the next paragraph.

**The incompatibility theorem - why you must choose.** When base rates (the true positive prevalence) differ between groups, calibration within groups and equal false-positive/false-negative rates **cannot hold simultaneously** except in degenerate cases (Chouldechova 2017; Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan 2016). Intuition: predictive parity says the score has the same meaning in both groups; equal error rates say the same threshold cuts both groups at the same operating point - with different prevalences, those two statements cannot both be true, because the same score implies different posterior risks. The practical consequence is liberating: there is no "fair setting" waiting to be found by testing more metrics. You are choosing - explicitly, in writing, with stakeholders - which error you are willing to concentrate and in whose ledger. Note the seductive non-solutions: **removing the protected attribute does not remove the effect** (proxies - postcode, occupation, device, purchase patterns - reconstruct it, and you lose the ability to measure group metrics at all, which is worse); **equal thresholds with unequal calibration** silently concentrate harm wherever the score is systematically shifted.

**Practice: measure, document, mitigate, then verify.** (1) **Measure** per-group confusion matrices, all candidate metrics, gaps with sample sizes, and intersectional cuts (group x region - single-axis audits hide within-group disparity). (2) **Document** the chosen metric and why, in the model card, including metrics deliberately not chosen. (3) **Mitigate** at the right stage: better and more representative labels (the most honest lever), rebalanced sampling, threshold selection per group (legally sensitive in many jurisdictions - involve counsel; some jurisdictions treat group-specific thresholds as discriminatory by construction), abstention or human review for low-confidence or high-stakes cases, and feature work to break proxies (remove or transform reconstructed attributes and check what remains). (4) **Verify** post-mitigation that the utility did not collapse and the gap moved as predicted - and remember the upstream question: if the *policy* (who may even apply, what counts as qualified) is discriminatory, the model merely automates it accurately; fix eligibility and label definitions first. Finally, fairness metrics are group statistics - they say nothing about any individual. Individual review, appeals and explanation are not optional extras; they are where the residual harm of every group-level guarantee gets caught.

payload.title: One model, four fairness questions
rows: What a positive flag means to the recipient
Who gets flagged in absolute numbers

payload.code:
# Per-group confusion metrics: compute them all, then choose consciously
def group_report(y, pred, group):
    out = {}
    for g in sorted(set(group)):
        m = group == g
        tp = int(((pred == 1) & (y == 1) & m).sum())
        fn = int(((pred == 0) & (y == 1) & m).sum())
        fp = int(((pred == 1) & (y == 0) & m).sum())
        tn = int(((pred == 0) & (y == 0) & m).sum())
        out[g] = {
            "n": int(m.sum()),
            "tpr": tp / (tp + fn),
            "fpr": fp / (fp + tn),
            "approval": (tp + fp) / max(tp + fp + fn + tn, 1),
            "ppv": tp / max(tp + fp, 1),
        }
    return out

rep = group_report(y_test.values, preds, group.values)
for g, r in rep.items():
    print(g, {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in r.items()})

rates = [r["approval"] for r in rep.values()]
di = min(rates) / max(rates)          # 4/5ths rule: below 0.80 = red flag
print("disparate impact ratio:", round(di, 3))
# Every number here is a DIFFERENT harm. Write down whose harm you count.

payload.title: Dropping the protected column does not make the model blind
payload.text: Postcode, occupation, device and browsing patterns reconstruct it; you just lose the ability to measure group metrics. Keep the attribute for AUDITING (with governance), fix proxies and labels, and choose the error you accept - in writing.

payload.title: Write the harm statement before picking the metric
payload.text: One paragraph: who is hurt by a false positive, who is hurt by a false negative, and which group-level guarantee you are buying with which sacrifice. That paragraph is the fairness requirement; the metric is its translation.

payload.title: Two groups, one model, four incompatible verdicts
payload.problem: A loan model: group A approval 0.60 with TPR 0.90 and FPR 0.15; group B approval 0.35 with TPR 0.70 and FPR 0.30. (a) Recover each group's true base rate (share who actually repay). (b) Compute PPV among approved applicants in each group. (c) Compute the demographic-parity gap and the disparate-impact ratio, with the 4/5ths verdict. (d) Show that TPR, FPR and PPV disagree in direction across groups and explain what the incompatibility theorem says about trying to equalise all of them. (e) Which single metric would you choose for a lender, and what must the model card say?

steps.title: (a) Base rates from the approval identity
steps.desc: approval = TPR x p + FPR x (1 - p). Group A: 0.60 = 0.90p + 0.15(1 - p) = 0.15 + 0.75p, so p = 0.45/0.75 = 0.60. Group B: 0.35 = 0.70p + 0.30(1 - p) = 0.30 + 0.40p, so p = 0.05/0.40 = 0.125. Base rates: A = 0.60, B = 0.125 - already very different, which drives everything below.

steps.title: (b) Predictive value of an approval
steps.desc: Group A: TP share = 0.90 x 0.60 = 0.54 of the group; approvals = 0.60; PPV = 0.54/0.60 = 0.90 (FP share = 0.15 x 0.40 = 0.06, checks: 0.54 + 0.06 = 0.60). Group B: TP share = 0.70 x 0.125 = 0.0875; approvals = 0.35; PPV = 0.0875/0.35 = 0.25 (FP share = 0.30 x 0.875 = 0.2625; 0.0875 + 0.2625 = 0.35, checks). An approval in group A means "90% will repay"; in group B it means "25% will repay".

steps.title: (c) Disparate impact
steps.desc: Demographic-parity gap = 0.60 - 0.35 = 0.25. Disparate-impact ratio = 0.35/0.60 = 0.583, below the 0.80 (4/5ths) threshold: a red flag under US-style disparate-impact analysis regardless of intent.

steps.title: (d) The directions and the theorem
steps.desc: TPR favours A (0.90 vs 0.70): B's good applicants are missed more. FPR favours A too (0.15 vs 0.30): B's bad applicants are approved at double the rate. PPV favours A overwhelmingly (0.90 vs 0.25): B's approvals are far less reliable. So B is worse off on every error-based measure while the approval-gap narrative suggests A is "favoured" - the metrics point in different directions because base rates (0.60 vs 0.125) differ. The incompatibility theorem says calibration/predictive parity and equal error rates cannot both hold across groups with unequal base rates, so no threshold setting can make all four numbers match; equalising TPR and FPR necessarily breaks PPV parity, and vice versa.

steps.title: (e) Choosing and documenting
steps.desc: For a lender the binding harms are: creditworthy applicants wrongly rejected (FN - the fairness-of-opportunity harm) and defaults approved (FP - the prudential harm). Choose equal opportunity as the primary guarantee (equal TPR), accept that FPR and PPV will differ, and set the operating threshold from the cost of default vs lost margin. The model card must state: base rates per group, all four metrics with n, the chosen metric and the harm rationale, the metrics knowingly not equalised and why, intersectional cuts examined, mitigation applied (label quality, sampling, human review for borderline cases), and the appeal path for individual rejections.

payload.solution: Base rates: A = 0.60, B = 0.125 (from approval = TPR x p + FPR x (1-p)). PPV: A = 0.54/0.60 = 0.90, B = 0.0875/0.35 = 0.25. Demographic gap 0.25; disparate-impact ratio 0.583 < 0.80 (flagged). TPR (0.90 vs 0.70), FPR (0.15 vs 0.30) and PPV (0.90 vs 0.25) all differ across groups and cannot all be equalised with unequal base rates - the incompatibility theorem makes that a proof, not a tuning failure. Choose by harm (equal opportunity for a lender: protect the wrongly rejected), state the sacrifice (FPR/PPV parity not achieved), and document everything in the model card with sample sizes and an appeal path.

payload.title: Audit a real or public dataset with the full metric set
payload.prompt: Using a public dataset with a sensitive attribute (e.g. Adult income, COMPAS-style, or a credit set), train a simple model and produce the per-group confusion table: TPR, FPR, approval rate, PPV, base rate, with n. Compute the demographic-parity gap and disparate-impact ratio. Then write the harm paragraph: which error hurts whom, which metric you adopt as primary, and which guarantee you are explicitly sacrificing. Check one proxy: remove the sensitive column, retrain, and show the group gap barely moved.
payload.hint: Removing the attribute while the gap persists is the demonstration that proxies carry it - the fix lives in labels, features and thresholds, not in hiding the column you need for measurement.

mistakes.mistake: Picking a fairness metric because it gives the smallest gap
mistakes.fix: Choose the metric from the harm structure first (who is hurt by FP, who by FN), then report the gap. Metric-shopping until the number looks good is selecting on the outcome you want to defend.

mistakes.mistake: Deleting the protected attribute and declaring the model blind
mistakes.fix: Proxies reconstruct it; you have only destroyed your ability to measure group metrics. Keep the attribute under governance for auditing, and fix proxies and labels instead.

mistakes.mistake: Promising demographic parity and calibration at the same time under unequal base rates
mistakes.fix: It is provably impossible: equal error rates and within-group calibration cannot coexist when prevalences differ. Choose which guarantee you buy and record the sacrifice.

mistakes.mistake: Auditing only one axis (gender OR region, never both)
mistakes.fix: Intersectional cuts (group x region x device) expose disparities that vanish in single-axis averages. Report cells with n and pool or flag small samples.

mistakes.mistake: Treating group metrics as sufficient justice for individuals
mistakes.fix: Group guarantees say nothing about any single applicant: keep human review, reason codes and an appeal path, and feed appeal outcomes back into the audit.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Group A: approval 0.60, TPR 0.90, FPR 0.15. Group B: approval 0.35, TPR 0.70, FPR 0.30. Recover both base rates, compute PPV per group and the disparate-impact ratio, and use the results to explain why demographic parity, equal opportunity and predictive parity cannot all be satisfied here. What should the model card record?
payload.answer: Base rates: A: 0.60 = 0.15 + 0.75p gives p = 0.60; B: 0.35 = 0.30 + 0.40p gives p = 0.125. PPV: A = (0.90 x 0.60)/0.60 = 0.90; B = (0.70 x 0.125)/0.35 = 0.25 (check: B false approvals = 0.30 x 0.875 = 0.2625, and 0.0875 + 0.2625 = 0.35). Disparate-impact ratio = 0.35/0.60 = 0.583, below 0.80 - a red flag on demographic parity alone. The metrics conflict because base rates differ by 0.475: demographic parity demands equal selection rates (0.60 vs 0.35 today); equal opportunity demands equal TPR (0.90 vs 0.70 today); predictive parity demands equal PPV (0.90 vs 0.25 today). The incompatibility theorem (Chouldechova; Kleinberg et al.) proves that with unequal prevalence, calibration within groups and equal FPR/FNR cannot hold simultaneously - so equalising TPR/FPR will break PPV parity and vice versa; no threshold setting resolves it. The model card must record: per-group base rates, n, and all four metrics with gaps; the chosen primary metric and the harm rationale; the guarantees knowingly not met and why; mitigation steps (label quality, sampling, thresholds with legal review, human review of borderline cases); intersectional results; monitoring cadence; and the individual appeal path.

Calibration (predictive parity) and equal TPR/FPR cannot hold simultaneously - the incompatibility result makes that a theorem, not a tuning failure
The model is fair if you drop the group column
questions.explanation: Unequal prevalence makes equal error rates and within-group calibration mutually exclusive; you must choose which guarantee to buy and document the sacrifice.

questions.prompt: In lending, the primary harm of a false negative is:
options: A creditworthy applicant is rejected - equal opportunity (equal TPR) is the metric that protects them
The lender loses money on a default
questions.explanation: FN = qualified applicant turned away: the fairness-of-opportunity harm, guarded by equal TPR (equal opportunity). The lender's money harm is the false positive, guarded by FPR control.

questions.prompt: You delete the protected attribute from training data. The likely result is:
options: The group gap disappears because the model cannot see the group
The gap largely persists via proxies (postcode, occupation, device), and you have also lost the ability to measure group metrics
Calibration becomes equal across groups automatically
questions.explanation: Proxies reconstruct the attribute, so the effect survives; worse, without the column (held separately for audit) you cannot compute any group metric at all - the audit blindfold, not fairness.

lessons.title: When Not to Use ML - and How to Keep a Human in the Loop on Purpose
lessons.summary: The decision table that favours three lines of rules over a model when the arithmetic says so, the payback and capacity calculation behind that decision, and human review as a designed, measured component rather than a comfort blanket.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decide between rules and ML for a given problem using data, label, scale and cost criteria
Compute daily operating cost, capacity feasibility and payback period for both options
Design a human-in-the-loop workflow with an abstention band, escalation path and measured combined performance
Detect and measure automation bias before it turns review into rubber-stamping

payload.text: A logistics team spent four months and Rs 6,00,000 building a classifier to decide which parcels get opened for inspection. The prior rule was three lines: sender never inspected before, weight over 2 kg, cross-border - open. When the model finally shipped, its precision was 0.87 against the rule's 0.85, inside the noise. The four months, the monitoring burden and the drift risk had been spent rediscovering logic the operations manager had written in 2019. The question "can we build a model?" had never been paired with the question "is there anything to learn that we do not already know?", and that question - not accuracy - is the real gate.

**The gate questions, in order.** Ask them before any modelling, because each one can end the project honestly. (1) **Is there a label?** If the outcome cannot be defined, recorded and trusted - "good service", "risky customer" with no realized outcome - there is nothing to learn from, and the project becomes opinion laundering with a probability attached. (2) **Is there signal beyond what we already encode?** If the decision is three stable rules and someone can write them, rules win: they are free to run, perfectly explainable, auditable, and they never drift. Build ML where the mapping is genuinely complex (vision, language, high-dimensional behaviour) or where the world changes too fast for hand-written logic. (3) **Is there enough data of acceptable quality?** Small n plus noisy labels plus rare positives is a guaranteed way to spend a quarter measuring noise. (4) **Is the error cost compatible with model behaviour?** Models fail softly and mysteriously; if a wrong output triggers irreversible harm with no review (autonomous dosing, irreversible financial transfers, life-safety), you need deterministic bounds or a human gate by design. (5) **Can we operate it?** Monitoring, retraining, alert response and on-call are recurring costs that exist forever - if the team has no capacity to watch it, deployment is negligence with a delay. (6) **Do we have the right to use the inputs?** Privacy, consent, regulation and reciprocity are gates too, not paperwork.

**The arithmetic that settles it: cost, capacity, payback.** Compare options on *operating* numbers, not demos. Rules cost what review costs at their flag rate; ML costs its review volume plus compute plus the recurring monitoring tax; both must fit inside the review team's daily capacity, because a detector that flags more than the team can investigate does not fail loudly - it fails by queue. Add the build cost and divide: payback = build cost / daily saving. Then stress-test the conclusion: if volume halves, if the review rate doubles, if monitoring costs more than modelled - does the choice still hold? The honest answer is often hybrid: ML to *rank and triage* (the model sorts the queue, humans decide) captures most of the value while keeping the human in the consequential position. And include what rules give you for free: reason codes for every decision, deterministic test coverage, and zero drift risk.

**Human-in-the-loop as a designed component.** Three deployment modes, each needing its own metrics: **model decides** (only for low-stakes, well-monitored, calibrated cases), **model proposes, human disposes** (the default for consequential decisions), and **human decides with model assist** (model ranks, explains or retrieves; human owns the call). Design the boundary explicitly with an **abstention band**: scores above 0.8 auto-decide, below 0.2 auto-decide the other way, and the middle - where the model is uncertain and the stakes are highest - routes to review. Choose the band width from review capacity (band = what the team can actually process daily), and set escalation rules (high-value cases always human regardless of score). Then **measure the combination, not the model**: run a design where you can compare human-alone, model-alone and human+model on the same held-out cases - the combined system must beat both, otherwise the human is decoration. Watch for **automation bias**: reviewers who see the model's verdict first tend to agree with it (overrides fall to a trickle and accuracy tracks the model exactly). Countermeasures: blind-first reviews on a random sample (verdict recorded before revealing the score), forced reason capture on overrides, periodic gold-standard cases injected to score the reviewer, and dashboards of override rate by reviewer - an override rate near zero is an alarm, not a compliment. Close the loop: every overturned decision becomes a labelled case, every review a training signal, and every model update re-tested against the human baseline before it takes more autonomy.

**Restraint is a deliverable.** The mature outcome of a scoping exercise can be "keep the rules", "ship assist-mode only", or "fix the label and re-measure in a quarter" - and shipping that recommendation with the arithmetic behind it is senior practice. The model that does not get built cannot drift, cannot discriminate, cannot wake anyone at 3 am, and cannot be wrong at Rs 4,00,000 a mistake.

payload.title: Rules, model, or hybrid - the gate table
rows: No one to monitor drift or alerts

payload.code:
# The decision arithmetic before any model gets built
reviews_ml, rate, run = 480, 12.50, 500   # reviews/day, Rs per review, daily run cost
reviews_rules = 660
build = 105000                            # build + validation, one-off

rules_cost = reviews_rules * rate
ml_cost = reviews_ml * rate + run
saving = rules_cost - ml_cost
print("rules/day:", rules_cost, " ml/day:", ml_cost, " saved/day:", saving)
print("payback days:", build / saving)              # 105000 / 1750 = 60
print("fits capacity?", reviews_ml <= 500, "rules fit?", reviews_rules <= 500)

# Human-in-the-loop: the model may abstain exactly where it is weakest
p = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
decision = np.where(p > 0.80, "auto-approve",
            np.where(p < 0.20, "auto-reject", "human-review"))
print("auto share:", round(float(np.mean(decision != "human-review")), 3),
      "queue:", int(np.sum(decision == "human-review")))   # must be <= capacity

payload.title: An override rate near zero means reviewers have stopped reviewing
payload.text: Show the score first and humans converge on it within weeks (automation bias). Blind-first sample reviews, forced override reasons and gold-standard injections keep the combined system honest - and keep measuring human+model against both alone.

payload.title: Band the abstention by capacity, escalate by stakes
payload.text: The width of the human-review band is a staffing number, not a modelling vanity: queue = band share x volume must fit daily capacity. High-value or irreversible cases go to a human regardless of score.

payload.title: Rules vs ML: cost, capacity and payback in one pass
payload.problem: A claims desk processes 10,000 claims/day. The rules engine flags 660/day for review; a proposed ML system would flag 480/day. Each review costs Rs 12.50 of analyst time; the ML system also costs Rs 500/day to run and monitor. The review team can absorb at most 500 reviews/day. Building and validating the ML system costs Rs 1,05,000 one-off. (a) Daily cost of each option and daily saving. (b) Which option fits capacity, and what actually happens to the one that does not? (c) Payback period for ML. (d) List two findings that would flip the decision back to rules, and one architecture that hedges the bet.

steps.title: (b) Capacity feasibility
steps.desc: Capacity is 500/day. ML needs 480 - it fits with 20 reviews of headroom. Rules need 660 - they exceed capacity by 160/day, so 160 reviews pile up every day: roughly 1,120 per week sit unreviewed, claims age past SLA, and the flag rate quietly becomes fiction (the desk starts auto-closing flags). The "cheaper" option was already failing a constraint the cost line did not show.

steps.title: (c) Payback
steps.desc: Payback = build cost / daily saving = 1,05,000 / 1,750 = 60 days. Two months to recover the build, after which the ML path is Rs 1,750/day cheaper - about Rs 6.4 lakh a year at constant volume - provided monitoring does not eat the saving.

steps.title: (d) What flips it back, and the hedge
steps.desc: Flip 1: no stable, trusted label for what the model is meant to predict (a disputed or unrecorded outcome means the model learns annotation habits, not truth). Flip 2: monitoring and retraining capacity does not exist, so drift would run unwatched for months - the Rs 500/day run cost becomes a person who was never hired. Flip 3 (bonus): the decision requires per-claim reason codes the model cannot produce reliably. Hedge architecture: keep the rules as the floor, use the ML score to RANK the queue (triage mode) so humans still decide every flagged case, and measure the combined system against rules-alone on a holdout; graduate to auto-decide only the band where the model demonstrably beats the review baseline.

payload.solution: (a) Rules Rs 8,250/day; ML Rs 6,500/day (480 x 12.50 + 500); saving Rs 1,750/day. (b) ML fits 500/day capacity; rules at 660 overflow by 160/day - a queue that silently becomes SLA breach and auto-closed flags. (c) Payback = 1,05,000/1,750 = 60 days. (d) Rules win again if the label is untrustworthy, if monitoring capacity does not exist, or if reason codes are mandatory; the hedged design is ML-as-triage with humans deciding, measured against rules-alone, graduating to automation only where the evidence supports it.

payload.title: Run the gate on an idea you have
payload.prompt: Take a project idea (yours or imaginary) and answer the six gate questions in writing: label, learnable signal beyond rules, data volume, error-cost structure, operating capacity, right to use inputs. Then do the arithmetic: expected flag volume, cost per review, daily cost of rules vs ML, build cost, payback, and capacity fit at your expected volume. Finish with the deployment mode you would choose (auto / model-proposes-human-disposes / human-with-assist) and the one metric you would use to prove the combined system beats both parts alone.
payload.hint: If any gate question fails, the deliverable is the recommendation itself - "keep the rules, fix the label, come back in a quarter" is a successful scoping outcome, not a dead project.

mistakes.mistake: Building a model to rediscover a rule that is already written and correct
mistakes.fix: Ask what the model can learn that you do not already know. If the logic fits in three lines and never changes, run the rules and spend the engineering budget elsewhere.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing options on accuracy demos and ignoring operating cost and capacity
mistakes.fix: Count review volume x cost, run cost, monitoring tax and capacity fit daily - a detector that flags more than the team can handle fails quietly through the queue.

mistakes.mistake: Deploying irreversible, high-stakes decisions with no review path
mistakes.fix: Set an abstention band and escalation rules so uncertain or high-value cases reach a human; require deterministic bounds for anything unreviewable.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming human review adds accuracy without measuring it
mistakes.fix: Measure human-alone, model-alone and human+model on the same cases; if the combination does not beat both, the reviewer is decoration (or worse, a liability).

mistakes.mistake: Treating a near-zero override rate as reviewer quality
mistakes.fix: It is automation bias: show scores blind-first on a sample, force reason codes on overrides, inject gold-standard cases and track override rates per reviewer.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: State six gate questions to answer before building any model, marking which answer favours rules. Then for a desk with 660 rule-flags/day at Rs 12.50 per review versus an ML system flagging 480/day plus Rs 500/day run cost, capacity 500/day and build cost Rs 1,05,000: compute daily costs, payback and the capacity verdict. How would you hedge?
payload.answer: Gates: (1) Is there a trusted label? (no = stop, rules or fix labels). (2) Is there signal beyond what we can write as rules? (no = rules). (3) Enough quality data? (no = stop or collect). (4) Is the error cost compatible with model failure - reviewable or requiring deterministic bounds? (irreversible unreviewable harm = rules/human gate). (5) Is there staffed capacity to monitor, alert and retrain? (no = do not deploy). (6) Right and consent to use the inputs? (no = stop). Arithmetic: rules = 660 x 12.50 = Rs 8,250/day; ML = 480 x 12.50 + 500 = Rs 6,500/day; saving = Rs 1,750/day; payback = 1,05,000/1,750 = 60 days. Capacity: ML 480 <= 500 fits; rules 660 > 500 overflow by 160/day - the queue silently becomes SLA breach and auto-closed flags, so rules are actually infeasible at this volume. Hedge: keep rules as the floor, use the ML score to rank the human queue (triage), measure human+model against rules-alone on a holdout, and only graduate bounded score bands to auto-decision once the combined evidence supports it.
payload.source: Interview-grade synthesis (build-vs-buy gates + operating arithmetic).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Gate before building: trusted label, signal beyond rules, sufficient data, compatible error costs, staffed monitoring, right to use inputs.
Rules win for stable three-line logic, mandatory reason codes and unreviewable harm; ML wins for complex mappings with volume and monitoring capacity.
Compare on operating numbers: daily review cost, run cost, capacity fit and payback - capacity overflow fails silently through the queue.
Human-in-the-loop needs design: abstention band sized to capacity, escalation by stakes, and measured human+model vs each alone.
Watch automation bias with blind-first samples, override reasons and gold-standard injections; an override rate near zero is an alarm.
Not building (or shipping triage-only) is a legitimate, senior deliverable - the model that does not exist cannot drift or discriminate.

questions.prompt: Which finding most strongly favours keeping a rules engine instead of building ML?
options: The dataset has 2 million labelled examples
The decision is three stable, auditable conditions with mandatory reason codes and no learnable residual signal
The team has on-call staff for monitoring
The error cost is asymmetric but reviewable
questions.explanation: If the logic is writable, stable and must be explained per decision, a model only re-learns what you already know while adding drift, monitoring and audit burden.

questions.prompt: Rules flag 660 reviews/day, ML flags 480/day, each review costs Rs 12.50, ML adds Rs 500/day run cost. Daily saving of ML is:
questions.explanation: Rules: 660 x 12.50 = 8,250. ML: 480 x 12.50 + 500 = 6,500. Saving = 1,750/day (and payback on a Rs 1,05,000 build = 60 days).

questions.prompt: The human-review band in a score-based workflow should be set by:
options: Review capacity and stakes: the queue (band share x volume) must fit daily capacity, and irreversible cases escalate to humans regardless of score
questions.explanation: The band is a staffing and risk decision: too wide and the queue overflows (silent failure), too narrow and consequential cases auto-decide. Escalation by stakes is independent of the score.

questions.prompt: Reviewers override the model in fewer than 1 percent of cases and their accuracy exactly tracks the model. Best interpretation:
options: The model is perfect and the team is excellent
Automation bias - reviewers are rubber-stamping; verify with blind-first sample reviews, forced override reasons and injected gold-standard cases
The thresholds are set too wide
Nothing - this is the ideal operating point
questions.explanation: Independence has collapsed: measure human-alone, model-alone and human+model; blind-first reviews and gold cases restore a genuine second opinion instead of an echo chamber.

modules.title: Module 10 — The ML Lifecycle, Experimentation and Defending Your Work
modules.summary: The capstone layer: the end-to-end lifecycle from framing to retirement with a worked churn specification, experimentation hygiene (pre-registration, SRM checks, guardrails and the selection-inflation arithmetic that kills most reported lifts), the model card as a structured accountability document, and the capstone defence - a lifecycle walkthrough plus the ten classic interview questions every graduate should be able to answer from memory.

lessons.title: The ML Lifecycle: From Business Goal to Monitored System
lessons.summary: The eight stages that separate a demo from a system, and a full worked specification turning "reduce churn by 20%" into a buildable, launchable, monitored ML project.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Name the lifecycle stages and the artifact each stage must produce before the next begins
Convert a vague business goal into a prediction problem with unit, prediction time and a timing-safe label
Write baselines, offline metrics and online success criteria before any model is trained
Define release strategy, monitoring and retirement triggers for a deployed model

payload.text: Two teams start on the same day. Team A opens a notebook, tries four algorithms, reaches 0.93 AUC in two weeks, demos triumphantly - and then stalls for three months: nobody can say what the model replaces, which decisions it changes, what happens when the label arrives late, or who gets paged when it degrades. Team B spends the first week writing one page: the decision, the prediction moment, the label timing rule, the baseline, the capacity constraint, the ship criteria and the rollback plan. Their model reaches only 0.88 - and ships in week four, because every question a reviewer could ask already had an answer on that page. The difference was never modelling skill; it was that Team B treated the lifecycle as the deliverable and the model as one stage of it.

**Eight stages, each with an artifact.** (1) **Problem framing** - what decision changes, for whom, and how often; artifact: a one-page decision spec. (2) **Success metrics** - the business metric, the offline proxy, guardrails and baselines; artifact: written ship criteria *before* training. (3) **Data** - sources, labels, privacy and rights, timelines; artifact: a data card and an availability audit (every column must exist at prediction time). (4) **Features and baseline** - feature definitions shared between training and serving, plus the dumb baselines (mean, majority, current rule); artifact: the baseline table your model must clear. (5) **Modelling and validation** - right split (time/group aware), CV protocol, tuning budget; artifact: an evaluation report with error analysis, not just a score. (6) **Release** - shadow, canary, ramp, rollback; artifact: a launch plan with gates. (7) **Monitoring** - the six layers from Module 9 plus ownership; artifact: dashboards, thresholds, runbooks. (8) **Retirement and retraining** - triggers, cadence, model registry; artifact: a decision log. Skipping a stage does not delete it - it reappears later as an incident, a rework or a compliance question.

**Framing: the goal is not the target.** Leadership asks for "20% less churn". That is a business outcome influenced by pricing, product and support - a model alone cannot deliver it, and predicting churn is not the same as reducing it. The translation keeps three things separate: the **decision** (who gets a retention call this week?), the **prediction** (probability this customer does not renew in the next 30 days, given what is known at a fixed moment), and the **intervention** (the offer, which has its own effect that must be measured against a holdback). Freeze the **prediction time** first (for churn: say, 7 days before cycle end) and enforce a timing rule on the **label**: it may only use events strictly after prediction time, and every feature must be computable strictly before it. That single rule kills the leakage family: cancellation flags, refund records and anything the retention team wrote after contacting the customer are banned from X even though they predict beautifully.

**Metrics and baselines, written before training.** Offline: choose the metric from the harm and the rarity (PR-AUC for rare events, calibration if probabilities drive thresholds, precision at k when only k actions fit per day) and report it against three baselines - always-the-base-rate, the current production rule, and a simple linear model. Online: the metric that pays (retention rate among treated vs a no-contact **holdback**, revenue per customer, cost per save), plus **guardrails** (opt-out rate, complaint rate, margin) that veto the launch if they move the wrong way. Then the ship criteria as numbers: offline improvement over baseline by X, calibration error below Y, canary healthy for Z days, no guardrail breach - all frozen before the first training run, because criteria written after seeing results are not criteria.

**Release, monitor, retire.** Release is a ladder: **shadow** (model scores alongside production, no effect - compare distributions and catches), **canary** (5-10% of traffic, watch alerts and guardrails), **ramp** (25, 50, 100% with automatic rollback on threshold breach), always with the incumbent still deployable in one command. Monitoring is the Module 9 stack with named owners: data quality and score PSI daily, slice metrics on label cadence, ops continuously, a retraining trigger when PSI or performance crosses its line, and a **retirement** trigger too - every model has an expiry: a stale champion that nobody revalidates is a liability with a dashboard. The lifecycle closes where it started: re-ask the framing question each quarter - is the decision still being made this way? - because the fastest way to a useless model is a perfect answer to a question the business has already stopped asking.

payload.title: The lifecycle gates - artifact required before moving on
rows: One-page decision spec (unit, prediction time, label timing)
A model nobody uses; leakage baked in
Baselines + offline/online metrics + guardrails + ship criteria
What legally exists at prediction time?
Data card + availability audit + shared feature definitions
How does it reach users safely?
Is it still true, and when does it die?

payload.code:
# Ship gate: baselines first, capacity-aware metrics, criteria frozen
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score

base_rate = float(np.mean(y_test))
rule_ap = average_precision_score(y_test, rule_scores)     # current production rule
model_ap = average_precision_score(y_test, model_scores)

K = 500                                     # outreach capacity: calls per day
order = np.argsort(-model_scores)[:K]
precision_at_k = float(np.mean(y_test[order]))
rule_order = np.argsort(-rule_scores)[:K]
rule_at_k = float(np.mean(y_test[rule_order]))

print("base rate:", round(base_rate, 4))
print("rule AP:", round(rule_ap, 4), " model AP:", round(model_ap, 4))
print("precision@500 rule:", round(rule_at_k, 4),
      "model:", round(precision_at_k, 4))

# Criteria written BEFORE training - the gate decides, not the demo
gates = {
    "beats_rule_ap": model_ap > rule_ap + 0.02,
    "beats_rule_at_k": precision_at_k > rule_at_k,
    "calibration_ok": True,                 # fill from reliability diagram
}
print(gates, "SHIP" if all(gates.values()) else "HOLD")

payload.title: Writing ship criteria after looking at results
payload.text: Post-hoc criteria are press releases. Freeze baselines, thresholds, guardrails and ramp rules before the first training run, and record the date - reviewers will ask for exactly that.

payload.title: The one-page decision spec is the cheapest artefact in the course
payload.text: Decision, unit, prediction time, label timing rule, capacity, baselines, guardrails, ship and rollback criteria - one page that turns every later argument into a checklist item.

payload.title: Turning "reduce churn by 20%" into a buildable specification
payload.problem: A subscription business asks ML to cut churn by 20%. Write the full specification: (a) the ML question with unit and prediction time; (b) the label with its timing rule; (c) three candidate features and two banned ones with reasons; (d) the offline metric and three baselines; (e) the online experiment design with holdback and guardrails, given an outreach capacity of 500 calls/day; (f) the ship criteria you freeze before training.

steps.title: (a) Decision, unit, prediction time
steps.desc: Decision: which customers get a retention outreach this week (the model ranks; humans call). Unit: one customer-cycle. Prediction time: fixed at 7 days before cycle end - all features frozen as of that instant. ML question: P(no renewal within 30 days past cycle end | state at day D - 7). The 20% business goal stays OUT of the model definition; it is the outcome the intervention must move, measured against a holdback.

steps.title: (b) Label with timing rule
steps.desc: Label = 1 if the subscription is cancelled or payment fails within 30 days after cycle end, computed strictly from events after prediction time. Timing rule stated in one line: the label may reference only events later than day D - 7; anything at or before D is a feature, anything after is either the label or banned. Churn definitions must also decide whether planned cancellations and non-payments both count - write it down, because the label is the project.

steps.title: (c) Features: two banned
steps.desc: Valid (computable before D): 8-week usage trend (sessions last 4 weeks vs prior 4); support contacts raised before D; payment failures and dunning status before D; tenure and plan tier. BANNED: cancellation-initiated flag (it is the label arriving early) and retention-offer-sent status (written by the intervention team after contact - the feature encodes the treatment and a previous process, a textbook process-leak). Also audit: does any feature get computed with full-month data when only 7 days exist? That is point-in-time leakage.

steps.title: (d) Offline metric and baselines
steps.desc: Primary: PR-AUC (churn is rare; ROC-AUC and accuracy flatter). Secondary: calibration by decile (thresholds are set on probabilities) and precision@500 (only 500 calls fit per day - the metric is the capacity). Baselines: (1) always predict base rate - AP equals prevalence; (2) current rule (no login in 14 days) scored the same way; (3) logistic regression on the same features - the complexity floor.

steps.title: (e) Online experiment
steps.desc: Randomise customer-cycles into treatment (ranked model list, agents work top-down) and a 5% no-contact holdout that keeps receiving business-as-usual. Primary online metric: 30-day renewal rate on at-risk customers (treatment vs holdback). Guardrails: opt-out/complaint rate, margin after offer cost, calls per save, agent handle time. Run long enough to cover a full renewal cycle, check sample ratio daily (SRM = broken randomisation), and analyse intention-to-treat.

steps.title: (f) Ship criteria, frozen
steps.desc: Offline: PR-AUC beats the current rule by at least +0.02 and precision@500 beats it outright; calibration error within tolerance on the top decile; no subgroup (tenure band, plan, region) below floor with n >= 100. Release: shadow 1 week (score distributions match, no feature errors), canary 5% with auto-rollback on PSI > 0.25 or guardrail breach, ramp 25/50/100%. Retire/retrain trigger: PSI > 0.25 on two consecutive days or PR-AUC (on matured labels) below baseline.

payload.solution: Spec: decision = outreach ranking; unit = customer-cycle; prediction = renewal failure probability 7 days out; label = non-renewal within 30 days (post-prediction events only); features frozen at D with cancellation/retention flags banned; offline = PR-AUC + precision@500 vs three baselines; online = 5% holdout with renewal-rate primary and complaint/margin guardrails; ship criteria frozen in advance (offline margins, subgroup floors, shadow-canal-ramp gates) with PSI and matured-performance retraining triggers. The 20% goal is then tested as an intervention outcome against the holdback, not claimed by the model.

payload.title: Write your own one-page decision spec
payload.prompt: Pick a problem you care about and fill every line of the spec: decision and decision-maker; unit; prediction time; label with timing rule; three features with their availability timestamps and two deliberately banned ones; three baselines; offline metric plus one capacity or cost metric; online design with holdback and guardrails; ship criteria; monitoring triggers; retirement trigger. Then give it to a friend and let them attack it - every question they raise that the page already answers is a defect the project will never pay for.
payload.hint: If you cannot state the prediction time in one sentence, you cannot audit a single feature - fix that first. If there is no baseline, there is no project: a score without a floor is an unverifiable number.

mistakes.mistake: Equating the business goal with the prediction target
mistakes.fix: Predict the observable outcome (non-renewal), decide the intervention separately, and measure the business goal against a holdback - the model alone never delivers a percentage goal.

mistakes.mistake: Training before baselines, metrics and ship criteria exist
mistakes.fix: Freeze the ladder (base rate, current rule, simple model) and the gate numbers first; criteria written after results are press releases.

mistakes.mistake: Letting post-prediction events into features
mistakes.fix: State prediction time, then audit every feature: computable strictly before it, or banned. Cancellation flags, retention-offer status and outcome-derived aggregates are the classic leaks.

mistakes.mistake: Shipping without shadow, canary, ramp and a one-command rollback
mistakes.fix: Every release stage catches a different failure class (feature errors, distribution shift, guardrail breaches); deploy is a ladder with automatic rollback, not an event.

mistakes.mistake: No retrain or retirement trigger after launch
mistakes.fix: A model with no expiry is a zombie: define PSI and performance triggers, retraining cadence, ownership and a documented retirement path in the launch plan.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: List the eight lifecycle stages with the artifact each must produce. Then for a churn model, define the prediction time and explain why a retention-offer-sent feature must be banned even though it predicts churn strongly.
payload.answer: Stages and artifacts: (1) problem framing - one-page decision spec (decision, unit, prediction time, label timing rule); (2) success metrics - baselines, offline/online metrics, guardrails, ship criteria frozen pre-training; (3) data - data card, rights/privacy, availability audit; (4) features and baseline - shared train/serve feature definitions plus the dumb baselines to clear; (5) modelling and validation - time/group-aware evaluation report with error analysis; (6) release - shadow/canary/ramp plan with rollback gates; (7) monitoring - the layered dashboards, thresholds and runbooks with named owners; (8) retirement/retraining - triggers, cadence and decision log. For churn: prediction time = a fixed instant (e.g. 7 days before cycle end) at which all features are frozen and from which the label window runs forward. Retention-offer-sent must be banned because it is written by the intervention team AFTER the risk was recognised (and often after contact): it encodes the business process and a previous selection into X, it is unavailable when the model must make the ranking that triggers the offer (circular), and on deployment the feature distribution collapses because the model itself changes who gets offers - a leakage that guarantees train-serve skew. Features must exist, in meaning and in code, strictly before prediction time.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Lifecycle: framing, metrics, data, features/baseline, validation, release, monitoring, retirement - each stage ships an artifact, and skipped stages return as incidents.
Separate the decision, the prediction and the intervention; freeze prediction time first and audit every feature against it.
Baselines (base rate, current rule, simple model) and ship criteria are written before training - post-hoc criteria are not criteria.
Labels use only post-prediction events; process features written after contact are leaks that also guarantee serving skew.
Release is a ladder (shadow, canary, ramp, rollback); monitoring has owners and thresholds; every model carries a retrain and a retirement trigger.

questions.prompt: The correct FIRST stage of an ML project is:
options: Problem framing: the decision, unit, prediction time and label timing rule, then the metrics and baselines
Collecting as many features as possible
questions.explanation: Nothing downstream can be audited without the framing page: it fixes what the label means, which features are legal and what success pays as. Algorithms come after baselines.

questions.prompt: Why is a "retention offer sent" column banned as a feature for churn prediction?
options: It is written by the intervention process after risk was recognised - it encodes the business process, is unavailable at ranking time, and collapses in distribution once the model changes who gets offers
questions.explanation: The feature is post-decision, circular (the model triggers it) and self-destroying under deployment - the three signatures of process leakage, regardless of how predictive it looks offline.

questions.prompt: Baselines for a churn model should include:
options: Only the previous version of the same model
Always-predict-the-base-rate, the current production rule, and a simple linear model - the floor your model must clear to be worth operating
A large language model for comparison
No baseline; PR-AUC speaks for itself
questions.explanation: A score without a floor is unverifiable: base rate shows what prevalence alone gives, the rule shows what the business already achieves, and the linear model prices the complexity you are adding.

questions.prompt: A launched model with no retraining or retirement trigger is best described as:
options: A zombie - it will silently degrade, and without documented triggers, ownership and a rollback path nobody will notice until a review does
questions.explanation: Drift is normal; the lifecycle closes with explicit PSI/performance retrain triggers and an expiry decision. An immortal model without owners is unmanaged risk with a dashboard.

lessons.title: Experimentation Hygiene: Pre-Registration, Power and the Arithmetic of False Wins
lessons.summary: Why the best-of-50 A/B result is usually noise, the four checks that keep an experiment honest, and the protocol you write before the traffic starts flowing.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute expected best-of-N selection inflation and judge a reported lift against it
Run a two-proportion z-test and a power calculation for a target minimum detectable effect
Detect sample ratio mismatch and name what it invalidates
Write a pre-registered experiment plan with primary metric, guardrails and ship criteria

payload.text: A growth team tests 50 button variants over four weeks, finds the winner at +0.6 points, and announces a win at the all-hands. Nobody asks the question that ends the meeting: with day-to-day noise of half a point, how much lift would the LUCKIEST of 50 identical variants show by pure chance? The answer, from one line of statistics, is about 1.4 points - more than double what they found. Their +0.6 does not beat randomness; it loses to it. The team did not lie, and they did not learn anything either: they ran a search over noise and reported the maximum. Experimentation hygiene is the discipline that makes sure a number means something.

**Pre-registration: decide before you look.** An experiment is a promise made in advance: one **primary metric**, the **minimum detectable effect (MDE)** you care about, the **sample size** required to see it, the **duration**, the **guardrails** that veto a win, and the **ship criteria** - all written down before the first assignment is served. Change any of them after seeing data and you are shopping for significance: with enough peeks and enough metric variants, everything reaches p < 0.05 eventually. Companion rules: **no peeking** (repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon test inflates false positives - either commit to the horizon, use always-valid confidence sequences, or pre-plan interim looks with error spending), and **one primary metric** (secondary metrics are diagnostics, not alternatives to promote from).

**Power: the sample size arithmetic.** For a two-proportion comparison, the standard error of the difference is approximately sqrt(p(1-p)(1/n1 + 1/n2)); at p = 0.5 with n = 10,000 per arm that is sqrt(0.25 x 2/10000) = 0.707 percentage points. A detected +0.6-point lift against SE 0.707 is z = 0.85 - not significant (p about 0.20) even as a single pre-registered test. Power for a target delta: n per arm = 2 x (z for 95% + z for 80%) squared x p(1-p) / delta squared = 2 x (1.96 + 0.84) squared x 0.25 / delta squared, which for delta = 0.6 points is about 109,000 per arm. Read that as a business statement: either run a six-figure-per-arm test, chase a larger effect, or use variance reduction (CUPED - covariates from the pre-period as control variates, commonly cutting variance 10-50% and thus the required n) to make a small MDE affordable. An underpowered experiment does not find "no effect"; it finds nothing, at full cost.

**Selection inflation: why best-of-N never wins on its own.** If N variants each produce a noisy estimate with standard deviation sigma, the expected maximum of the N estimates exceeds the truth by roughly sigma x sqrt(2 ln N) even when all N are identical. With sigma = 0.5 points and N = 50: 0.5 x sqrt(2 x ln 50) = 0.5 x sqrt(7.82) = 0.5 x 2.80 = 1.4 points of expected lift from pure selection. The same arithmetic (Module 7) applies to hyperparameter sweeps, and to trying many metrics or segments until one glows. The defence is structural: pre-register the winner count (usually one variant versus one control), correct for multiple comparisons when you genuinely test many (Bonferroni, or false-discovery control), and confirm the frozen winner once on untouched traffic.

**The four hygiene checks.** (1) **Sample ratio mismatch (SRM):** did the arms receive the traffic split you assigned? Compare assigned vs observed with a chi-square goodness-of-fit; any significant mismatch (most orgs alarm at p < 0.001) means randomisation, redirects, bot filtering or logging is broken, and EVERY metric in the test is suspect - stop, do not interpret. (2) **Guardrails:** metrics that must not regress (latency, error rate, opt-out, revenue-per-user, complaint rate) with veto power. (3) **Novelty and novelty-plus:** new UIs get a novelty spike and an early-adopter skew - run long enough to cover a full usage cycle (weekly seasonality included) and look at the time series of the effect, not just the aggregate; an effect that decays from day 1 is usually novelty. (4) **Interference:** when units affect each other (marketplace auctions, social feeds, pricing), SUTVA breaks and per-user randomisation lies - randomise at the cluster (market, region, seller) or switch design. Then close the loop: log the result including negatives (the pre-registered plan, the SRM check, the verdict, the ship decision), because a culture that only remembers wins re-runs the same experiments forever.

payload.title: Experiment failures and their signature
rows: p-value dips below 0.05 on some check, then drifts up
Pre-register one primary metric and horizon; always-valid intervals if you must watch daily
Observed split differs from assigned split (chi-square alarm)
Stop and debug assignment, redirects and logging - all metrics are invalid until it clears
Winner among many variants beats noise by sigma x sqrt(2 ln N)
Few arms, multiple-comparison correction, confirm on untouched traffic
Effect size decays over days or varies by exposure share
Run full cycles, plot effect over time, hold a long-run holdback
Randomise at cluster level or use switchback designs

payload.code:
# Is the lift real? Inflation, z-test, power - three lines each
import numpy as np
from math import log, sqrt

# 1) best-of-N selection inflation (all 50 variants may be identical)
sigma, N = 0.5, 50                       # daily noise (points), variants tried
inflation = sigma * sqrt(2 * log(N))
print("expected best-of-50 noise lift:", round(inflation, 2), "points")
# 0.5 * sqrt(2 * ln 50) = 1.40 points - a +0.6 win LOSES to randomness

# 2) two-proportion z-test at n = 10,000 per arm
n, p1 = 10000, 0.50
p2 = 0.506                                    # observed +0.6 points
se = sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) * (2 / n))
z = (p2 - p1) / se
print("SE (points):", round(se * 100, 2), " z:", round(z, 2), "-> not significant")

# 3) sample size for a 0.6-point MDE at 80% power, 5% significance
delta = 0.006
n_per_arm = 2 * (1.96 + 0.84) ** 2 * 0.25 / delta ** 2
print("n per arm needed:", int(n_per_arm))   # about 109,000

# SRM: assigned 50/50 but observed different? chi-square - if it fires, STOP
from scipy.stats import chisquare
counts = [50210, 49790]
print("SRM p-value:", chisquare(counts).pvalue)  # alarm below 0.001

payload.title: A significant SRM invalidates every metric in the test
payload.text: Broken assignment (redirect bugs, bot filters, logging gaps) contaminates arms non-randomly: no p-value downstream is trustworthy. Alarm on chi-square p < 0.001 and debug before reading any result.

payload.title: Pre-register the plan and log the negatives
payload.text: One page: primary metric, MDE, n, duration, guardrails, ship criteria - timestamped before traffic flows. Logging failed experiments is the only thing that stops the org from re-running them forever.

payload.title: Judging the +0.6 point "win" from 50 variants
payload.problem: A team tested 50 variants; the best beat control by +0.6 points. Daily/segment noise sigma = 0.5 points. At n = 10,000 per arm with control rate 50%, the treatment showed 50.6%. (a) Compute the expected best-of-50 lift from pure selection and give a verdict. (b) Compute the standard error and z for the observed lift as a SINGLE pre-registered test. (c) Compute the per-arm sample size needed to detect 0.6 points at 80% power and 5% significance. (d) Rewrite the experiment so a real 0.6-point effect would be believable.

steps.title: (a) Selection inflation
steps.desc: Expected max of 50 noise estimates above truth ~ sigma x sqrt(2 ln N) = 0.5 x sqrt(2 x ln 50) = 0.5 x sqrt(7.824) = 0.5 x 2.80 = 1.40 points. The reported +0.6 is LESS than half of what pure luck over 50 variants produces. Verdict: indistinguishable from searching noise - the experiment as run supports no claim.

steps.title: (b) Even as one test, it fails
steps.desc: SE = sqrt(0.5 x 0.5 x 2/10000) = sqrt(0.00005) = 0.00707 = 0.707 points. z = 0.6 / 0.707 = 0.85. For a two-sided 5% test the critical value is 1.96 - we are far below it (p about 0.20). So the lift is not significant even before accounting for the 50-way search, which makes it strictly worse.

steps.title: (c) Power for a 0.6-point MDE
steps.desc: n per arm = 2 x (1.96 + 0.84) squared x 0.5 x 0.5 / 0.006 squared = 2 x 7.84 x 0.25 / 0.000036 = 3.92 / 0.000036 = about 108,900 per arm (round to 109k). At 10,000 per arm the test is roughly 10x underpowered for the effect the team hopes to see.

steps.title: (d) The protocol that makes a 0.6-point win believable
steps.desc: Pre-register ONE primary metric and ONE treatment (or correct for N arms); power at the MDE first - 109k per arm, or apply CUPED using pre-period covariates to cut variance and n; check SRM before reading metrics; no peeking (fixed horizon or always-valid intervals); guardrails with veto; run through full weekly cycles to rule out novelty; then confirm the frozen winner on a fresh holdout. Only a lift that survives that gauntlet ships with a number attached.

payload.solution: (a) 0.5 x sqrt(2 ln 50) = 1.40 points of expected pure-selection lift; the +0.6 win is inside the noise floor of the search - verdict: no effect demonstrated. (b) SE = 0.707 points, z = 0.85, p about 0.20: not significant even as a single pre-registered test. (c) n about 109,000 per arm for 80% power at 5% significance. (d) Pre-register one comparison at the right power (or CUPED-reduce variance), SRM check, no peeking, guardrails, full-cycle duration, holdback confirmation - then the number means something.

payload.title: Pre-register a real experiment
payload.prompt: Take a product change you would like to test and write the full plan before anything runs: primary metric with baseline value, MDE, power calculation for n, duration in usage cycles, assignment unit (user/session/cluster - justify), SRM check and alarm threshold, two guardrails with veto rules, ship criteria, and the analysis you will run exactly once. Then compute the selection inflation you would face if you instead tried 10 metrics and 5 segments looking for a win (sigma = 0.4 points) and state what that number forbids.
payload.hint: Inflation = sigma x sqrt(2 ln N) with N = the number of opportunities you gave yourself to be lucky (metrics x segments x variants) - if it exceeds your MDE, your MDE was theatre.

mistakes.mistake: Peeking daily at a fixed-horizon test and stopping when significant
mistakes.fix: Each look is another chance to cross the line: commit to the horizon, use always-valid confidence sequences, or pre-plan interim looks with error spending.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting the best of many variants, metrics or segments
mistakes.fix: Expected best-of-N lift is sigma x sqrt(2 ln N); keep arms few, correct for multiplicity, and confirm the frozen winner on untouched traffic.

mistakes.mistake: Reading results while the sample ratio mismatch alarm is lit
mistakes.fix: SRM means assignment or logging is broken and every downstream metric is contaminated: stop, debug, restart. A beautiful p-value on broken randomisation is fiction.

mistakes.mistake: Launching underpowered tests and concluding no effect
mistakes.fix: Power at the MDE before launch: n = 2 (1.96 + 0.84) squared p(1-p)/delta squared, or shrink variance with CUPED; otherwise the test buys nothing at full cost.

mistakes.mistake: Shipping a win with no holdback left behind
mistakes.fix: Keep a persistent holdout to measure the long-run effect (novelty decay, equilibrium shifts); a win measured only in week one is a novelty artifact more often than not.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define pre-registration and sample ratio mismatch. For sigma = 0.5 points and 50 variants, compute the expected pure-selection lift and judge a reported +0.6-point win. Then compute the SE and z at n = 10,000 per arm (control 50%) and the per-arm n for a 0.6-point MDE at 80% power, 5% significance.
payload.answer: Pre-registration: fixing the primary metric, MDE, sample size, duration, guardrails, analysis and ship criteria in writing before traffic flows - so no element can be revised after seeing data (which would turn the test into metric shopping). SRM: a mismatch between assigned and observed arm sizes (chi-square on the split, alarm at p < 0.001), which indicates broken assignment or logging and invalidates every metric in the test until debugged. Selection: sigma x sqrt(2 ln 50) = 0.5 x sqrt(7.824) = 0.5 x 2.80 = 1.40 points expected from pure luck - a +0.6 lift is well inside that, so it demonstrates nothing. Single-test arithmetic: SE = sqrt(0.5 x 0.5 x 2/10000) = 0.707 points; z = 0.6/0.707 = 0.85 versus the 1.96 critical value - not significant (p about 0.20) even before the multiplicity penalty. Power: n per arm = 2 x (1.96 + 0.84) squared x 0.25 / 0.006 squared = about 109,000. Conclusion: pre-register, power properly (or CUPED), check SRM, never peek, keep guardrails and a holdback - only then does a 0.6-point effect carry meaning.
payload.source: Evergreen experimentation exam question (inflation + power arithmetic).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Pre-register: one primary metric, MDE, n, duration, guardrails, ship criteria - written before traffic; after-the-fact plans are metric shopping.
Best-of-N expected lift ~ sigma x sqrt(2 ln N): sigma 0.5 and 50 variants = 1.40 points of pure noise - a 0.6-point win loses to it.
SE of a difference ~ sqrt(p(1-p) x 2/n): 0.707 points at 10k/arm makes +0.6 insignificant (z = 0.85); a 0.6-point MDE needs about 109k per arm.
SRM invalidates everything in the test; guardrails veto; novelty needs full cycles; interference needs cluster or switchback designs.
No peeking without always-valid intervals, and always keep a long-run holdback plus a log of negative results.

questions.prompt: Fifty variants are tested; sigma of daily noise is 0.5 points. The expected lift of the BEST variant from pure selection alone is approximately:
questions.explanation: sigma x sqrt(2 ln 50) = 0.5 x 2.80 = 1.40 points. Any reported best-of-50 lift below that is inside the noise floor of the search itself.

questions.prompt: A chi-square check shows observed arm sizes of 50,210 and 49,790 against a 50/50 assignment with p = 0.0004 (alarm threshold 0.001). You should:
options: Proceed - the split looks close to 50/50
Stop and debug assignment, redirects and logging before reading any metric: SRM means randomisation is broken and all downstream results are contaminated
Switch to the secondary metric instead
Increase the sample size until it clears
questions.explanation: A significant sample ratio mismatch says the arms did not receive their assigned traffic non-randomly - every comparison downstream inherits that bias, however small the size difference looks.

questions.prompt: With p = 0.5 and n = 10,000 per arm, a +0.6-point difference has z about 0.85. This means:
options: The effect is real but small
Even as a single pre-registered test it is not significant at 5% (critical z = 1.96) - and the team then compounded this by searching 50 variants
The control rate must be wrong
questions.explanation: z = 0.6 / 0.707 = 0.85 < 1.96, so p about 0.20: no evidence in one look; the best-of-50 search makes the claim strictly weaker, not stronger.

questions.prompt: To detect a 0.6-point lift with 80% power at 5% significance (baseline 50%) you need roughly:
questions.explanation: n = 2 x (1.96 + 0.84) squared x 0.25 / 0.006 squared is about 109,000 per arm - or a variance-reduction method like CUPED to make a smaller n honest.

lessons.title: Model Cards: Writing the Accountability Document
lessons.summary: The nine sections every deployed model needs, what each one protects against, and a worked card that a reviewer, a lawyer and a new engineer can all interrogate.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Produce a model card with all nine standard sections filled with real content, not placeholders
Write an out-of-scope section that prevents specific foreseeable misuses
Specify disaggregated evaluation (factors, metrics, subgroups, sample sizes) in a table skeleton
Version the card with the model so documentation and artefact never drift apart

payload.text: Six months after a hiring-screening model shipped, three people ask it three questions. The engineer asks: which training window and features produced this version? The compliance officer asks: which groups was it evaluated on, and what were the error rates? The customer asks: can we use it to rank freelance candidates too? Nobody can answer the first two from documentation - the third was being done already, by a team that assumed "it worked for employees". The model itself is fine; the system around it is unaccountable. A model card is the cheapest fix: one document, nine sections, versioned with the artefact, that answers those questions before they are asked - and the out-of-scope section is the one that stops the freelance ranking before a lawyer does.

**What a model card is (and is not).** A model card (Mitchell et al., 2019) is a structured, versioned document attached to a deployed model - not a marketing page, not a paper, not the README. Its nine sections each exist to close a specific failure of memory or imagination. (1) **Model details**: owner, version, date, architecture, hyperparameters, training code commit, registry path - provenance so anyone can reconstruct what is running. (2) **Intended use**: the decision, the users, the context, the input distribution the model expects. (3) **Out-of-scope use**: the foreseeable misuses you are forbidding explicitly - different population, different decision, automated action without review - because "we never imagined that use" is not a defence when the use was obvious. (4) **Factors and metrics**: which factors (subgroups) the model was evaluated on, which metrics were chosen and why (the harm-driven choice from Module 9). (5) **Evaluation data**: datasets, time windows, sizes, sampling method - was it time-ordered, was it representative, how old is it. (6) **Quantitative analyses**: the disaggregated results table - overall AND per factor, with n and intervals; a single aggregate number is exactly what the card exists to prevent. (7) **Training data and procedure**: sources, labelling process and its known issues, features with availability times, preprocessing, split strategy, tuning budget, seeds. (8) **Ethical considerations**: privacy exposure, consent and rights, potential harms by group, feedback loops (the model changing the world it measures), appeal paths. (9) **Caveats and recommendations**: known failure modes, distribution assumptions, monitoring hooks, retrain triggers, who to contact.

**The out-of-scope section is the teeth.** Weak out-of-scope text says "not intended for other purposes" - unenforceable and uninformative. Strong text enumerates: populations not covered (tenure below two cycles, traffic from partner apps), decisions not covered (pricing, termination, any irreversible action without human review), coupling not covered (using scores as labels for a downstream model, combining with other systems into a composite decision you never tested), and temporal limits (valid only while PSI stays below its threshold; expires at the next retraining). Each line is a sentence a reviewer can check against reality - which is the point.

**Disaggregated evaluation is the heart.** The quantitative section is a table: rows = overall plus every factor worth protecting (tenure band, plan tier, region, language, device, protected attributes under governance), columns = n, the primary metric, the operational metric (precision at k), calibration error, each with confidence intervals where n allows; small-n cells get flagged rather than averaged away. Beside the table sit qualitative analyses: a hand-reviewed error sample per subgroup (what does the model get wrong, in sentences), and the decision taken on the results (which floors were set, which trade-offs accepted - the fairness work of Module 9 recorded as a decision, not an aspiration).

**Versioning: the doc must travel with the artefact.** The card carries the model version, training-data window and code commit; the registry refuses promotion without one; any retraining, feature change or threshold move creates a new card version (changelogs beat dissertations). Distribution matters too: the card lives where decisions get made - beside the deploy button, in the incident channel, attached to the API docs - because documentation nobody can find is documentation nobody has. The test for adequacy is a simple drill: give the card to a colleague who has never seen the project and ask them five questions (what does it predict, for whom, what breaks it, how was it measured, what must never be done with it). If they cannot answer, the card is written for its author, not its readers.

payload.title: The nine sections and the failure each one prevents
rows: Owner, version, date, code commit, registry path
Nobody knows what is actually running
Silent scope creep into new decisions
Named populations, decisions and couplings forbidden
Subgroups evaluated, metrics chosen and why
Metric choice presented as objective fact
Stale or unrepresentative test sets passing as truth

One aggregate number hiding a collapsed slice

Privacy, harms by group, feedback loops, appeal path

from datetime import date

card = {
    "model_version": "churn-gbm-2.3.1",

    ],

    "operational_metric": "precision@500/day",

    },

}

# Registry gate: promotion blocked unless the card version matches the model version.

payload.title: A card written once and never versioned rots faster than no card
payload.text: Retraining, feature changes and threshold moves all require a card update; a registry that accepts a model without a matching card version manufactures exactly the stale-documentation problem it was meant to solve.

payload.title: Run the five-question drill on every card
payload.text: A colleague who never saw the project must answer: what does it predict, for whom, what breaks it, how was it measured, what must never be done? Failing readers, not failing sections, is the test.

payload.title: Filling the two hardest sections for a churn model
payload.problem: Draft the Intended use, Out-of-scope use, and the Quantitative analyses skeleton for the churn model of Lesson 10.1 (ranked outreach, 500 calls/day, PR-AUC primary). Include at least three out-of-scope lines with the reason each protects you, and design the evaluation table so a slice collapse cannot hide. Then say how the card is versioned and where it lives.

steps.title: Intended use
steps.desc: Predicts P(non-renewal within 30 days) at 7 days before cycle end; output is a RANK for human outreach agents (top 500/day), in the consumer subscription product, for customers with 2+ completed cycles on the current pricing page. Users: retention agents and the ranking service. The score informs prioritisation only; offers, messaging and pricing remain human decisions.

steps.title: Out-of-scope use (three with reasons)
steps.desc: (1) Customers with under 2 cycles - not represented in training; early-tenure behaviour differs and the model would fail silently on them. (2) Any automated cancellation, downgrade or collection action - the model is a probability from observational data, not a verdict; irreversible actions need human review and reason codes. (3) Re-scoring partner-app or post-pricing-change traffic without revalidation - feature distributions shift (the Module 9 PSI problem), so scores outside the audited distribution are unvalidated. Bonus line: do not use churn scores as labels to train downstream models - that compounds errors and hides the original metric.

steps.title: Quantitative analyses skeleton
steps.desc: Rows: overall, then each factor - tenure bands (2-4, 5-12, 13+ cycles), plan tier, region, language - including the protected-attribute audit cuts held under governance. Columns: n, PR-AUC, precision@500, calibration error (top decile), all with 95% intervals where n permits; cells with n < 100 flagged as insufficient rather than reported bare. A slice at 0.55 under an overall 0.90 cannot hide because the floor rule (Module 9) lives in the table: any cell below floor or more than 10 points under overall triggers review before release. Beside the table: qualitative error review (30 hand-checked cases per major subgroup) and the decisions taken from both.

steps.title: Versioning and placement
steps.desc: Header fields: model version, code commit, training window, evaluation window, owner, date - and every retrain, feature change or threshold move bumps a card version with a changelog entry. The registry blocks promotion without a matching card version. Placement: next to the deploy button, in the API documentation, linked from the runbook and the incident channel - findable at the moment of decision, not in a wiki nobody opens. Expiry date and retrain triggers are fields, so the card expires loudly alongside the model.

payload.solution: Intended use: rank 2+ cycle subscribers for human outreach 7 days pre-renewal, top 500/day, PR-AUC primary. Out-of-scope: under-2-cycle customers (unrepresented), automated cancellation/collection (needs human review), unvalidated partner or post-pricing traffic (distribution shift), and feeding scores back as labels (error compounding). Evaluation table: overall + subgroup rows (tenure, plan, region, language), columns n / PR-AUC / precision@500 / calibration with intervals, floor rules enforced in-table, small-n flagged, qualitative error review beside it. Versioned with model version and commit, registry-gated, placed beside deploy and in the runbook, with expiry and retrain triggers as mandatory fields.

payload.title: Write a card for a model you already built
payload.prompt: Take any model from this course and write its full nine-section card with real content: provenance fields, intended use, five out-of-scope lines, factors and metrics with rationale, evaluation data windows and sizes, a disaggregated quantitative table with n, training procedure including features and split, ethical considerations, caveats with monitoring hooks and expiry. Then hand it to someone who has never seen the project and take notes on every question they ask that the card fails to answer - those are the revisions.
payload.hint: If you cannot fill a section with specifics, that section is documenting a gap in the project, not a gap in your writing - which is exactly the information the card exists to surface.

mistakes.mistake: Writing a vague out-of-scope section ("not intended for other uses")
mistakes.fix: Name the populations, decisions and couplings you forbid, each with a reason - specific lines are checkable; generalities are unenforceable.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting only the aggregate evaluation number
mistakes.fix: The card exists to prevent this: disaggregated table with n and intervals, floor rules per cell, small-n cells flagged instead of averaged into comfort.

mistakes.mistake: Documentation that is not versioned with the model
mistakes.fix: Card version = model version; retrain, feature or threshold changes bump it; registry promotion blocked without a matching card. Changelog, not rewrite.

mistakes.mistake: Listing metrics without saying why they were chosen
