mistakes.mistake: Calling degradation "overfitting"
mistakes.fix: Overfitting: train error down, test error up. Degradation: train error itself rises with depth — an optimization problem, not a statistical one. The distinction is exactly what motivated residual learning and earns marks in exams.

mistakes.mistake: Believing skip connections magically add information
mistakes.fix: They add nothing to representational content — elementwise addition changes the FUNCTION CLASS only in how easily identity/near-identity maps are expressed and how gradients route. The insight is optimization geometry, not new data or new capacity.

mistakes.mistake: Applying residual addition across mismatched tensor shapes
mistakes.fix: Elementwise add requires identical shapes; dimension changes go through the projection shortcut (strided 1x1 conv + BN). Broadcasting or reshaping to force an add silently breaks the residual algebra.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming ResNet's contribution was confined to vision
mistakes.fix: The transformer block (x + Sublayer(norm(x))) IS the residual idea transplanted: pre-norm residual stacks are why 100-layer language models train. Architecture lineage cuts across domains — this one is genuinely universal.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the degradation problem in plain deep CNNs and show algebraically why identity shortcuts fix gradient flow. Why are projections (1x1 convs) used in shortcuts at downsampling stages?
payload.answer: Degradation: increasing plain-CNN depth beyond ~20 layers raised BOTH training and test error — optimisation failure (not overfitting), caused by difficulty learning identity-like transforms and by vanishing/exploding products of layer Jacobians. Fix, algebraically: a residual unit computes y = x + F(x). Backpropagating, dL/dx = dL/dy * (I + dF/dx): the identity term contributes an UNATTENUATED +I component to the gradient, so signal reaches early layers through a path that no settings of F can eliminate (F can at most modify it) — versus a plain unit where the gradient is purely the product dF_L/dx * ... * dF_1/dx, which shrinks or explodes multiplicatively with depth. Additionally, forward: y = x + F(x) makes identity trivially reachable by driving F to zero, so a deeper residual net can in principle represent the shallower net's function, easing optimisation. At stages where spatial size or channel count changes, the shortcut cannot add x directly (shapes mismatch); a projection shortcut — strided 1x1 convolution with matching channels, usually followed by normalization — maps x into the output space so the residual addition remains structurally valid while the highway property persists through the projected path.
payload.source: Core GATE/advanced-DL question on ResNets; the algebraic gradient argument is the expected centre of a full-marks answer.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Degradation: plain nets past ~20 layers train WORSE — optimization failure, not overfitting.
Residual learning: learn F(x) where H(x) = x + F(x); identity becomes an easy target (drive F to zero).
Gradient highway: dL/dx = dL/dy * (1 + dF/dx) — the +1 term cannot vanish, unlike multiplicative plain chains.
Bottleneck (1x1 reduce -> 3x3 -> 1x1 restore) buys depth cheaply; [3,4,6,3] notation specifies ResNet-50.
The residual+pre-norm pattern migrated into transformer blocks — ResNet's deepest influence is outside vision.

questions.prompt: The degradation problem refers to the observation that very deep plain CNNs:
options: Overfit badly while training error keeps falling
Show HIGHER training error than shallower counterparts — an optimisation failure
Run out of GPU memory before training
Have too many parameters for the dataset
questions.explanation: Both training AND test error rise with depth in plain nets — if it were overfitting, training error would be falling. The problem is difficulty training, addressed by residual connections.

questions.prompt: In a residual unit y = x + F(x), the backpropagated gradient satisfies:
options: dL/dx = dL/dy * dF/dx (the shortcut contributes nothing)
dL/dx = dL/dy * (I + dF/dx) — an identity term that cannot vanish
Gradients do not pass through skip connections
questions.explanation: Differentiating the sum gives the identity plus the learned branch: the +I highway guarantees gradient flow regardless of F's weights — the core fix for vanishing gradients at depth.

questions.prompt: The purpose of the 1x1 conv layers in a bottleneck block is to:
options: Reduce channel dimensionality before the expensive 3x3 (and restore it after), cutting FLOPs/params substantially
questions.explanation: Reduce-operate-restore: 1x1 cuts C -> C/4, the 3x3 runs at reduced width, 1x1 expands back — ~17x cheaper at C=256 than full-width stacks, enabling 50-152 layer variants at practical cost.

questions.prompt: Why must a projection shortcut (1x1 conv with stride) be used when a block downsamples?
options: Elementwise addition requires matching shapes; the projection maps the shortcut input to the output's stride and channel count
To reduce the learning rate internally
Skip connections must always include a convolution
questions.explanation: x and F(x) are added elementwise — different spatial size or channel count makes this impossible. The strided 1x1 conv transforms x into the output space so the residual sum stays valid.

lessons.title: Transfer Learning: Freeze, Fine-Tune, and When Features Transfer
lessons.summary: The feature-hierarchy argument for why ImageNet features generalize, the freeze-vs-fine-tune decision ladder, layer-wise learning-rate decay, and a working fine-tune recipe for small-data regimes.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain which layers of a pretrained CNN learn generic vs task-specific features and why unfreezing order matters
Choose between linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning for a described dataset/task
Execute layer-wise unfreezing with per-layer learning rates and state what signs tell you to stop
Identify domain-gap conditions under which ImageNet features transfer poorly and ImageNet pretraining fails

payload.text: You have 400 labelled medical images and a 12-million-parameter vision problem. Training from scratch: hopeless — the network will memorize your 400 images and memorize them badly. Fine-tuning a ResNet pretrained on ImageNet: state-of-the-art within an afternoon. Same architecture, same 400 images — the difference is inheriting a feature extractor that already knows edges, textures, shapes, and object parts from 1.2 million images someone else paid to learn. Transfer learning is not a trick; it is the economic foundation of applied deep learning, and knowing its boundaries — when it FAILS — separates practitioners from cargo-culters.

**Why transfer works: the hierarchy argument.** CNN features organize by specificity: earliest layers (edges, gradients, colors), middle layers (textures, parts, motifs), late layers (object-category-adjacent patterns strongly tuned to the pretraining label space). Crucially, the EARLY AND MIDDLE layers are largely DOMAIN-AGNOSTIC — a Gabor-like edge detector is as useful for X-rays as for cats — while the last layers are the most pretraining-task-specific. Transfer exploits exactly this asymmetry: reuse the general feature extractor, retrain only the task-specific head. The ImageNet prior carries further than intuition suggests: natural-image statistics (scale invariances, texture/shape regularities) provide useful inductive bias for medical imaging, satellite imagery, art, and even some non-visual domains — but the transfer DEGRADES smoothly as the domain gap widens (more on failure conditions below).

**The freeze/fine-tune ladder (three rungs).** (1) LINEAR PROBING / HEAD-ONLY TRAINING: freeze ALL backbone parameters, train only a new classifier head on frozen features. Cheap (only head params train), stable, the correct FIRST step: it measures how linearly separable your classes are in the pretrained feature space. If linear probing already gives good accuracy, your task is close to the pretraining domain. (2) PARTIAL FINE-TUNING: unfreeze the LAST stage(s) of the backbone (the most task-specific) while keeping early stages frozen; train with a small lr. Standard when classes are visually novel (medical textures, satellite, industrial defects). (3) FULL FINE-TUNUNING: all layers train with SMALL learning rates (1e-5 to 1e-4 range for CNN backbones; ~10-100x smaller than the head lr). Needed for large domain gaps or when you have enough data to justify moving every weight without destroying generic features.

**Discriminative learning rates and unfreezing discipline.** One global lr treats edge detectors (should barely move) and the classifier head (should learn a lot) identically — wrong. Discriminative fine-tuning: head lr = 1e-3, final stage = 1e-4, earlier stages = 1e-5 or lower — each layer moves proportionally to how task-specific it is. Unfreezing one stage per K epochs (bottom-up discipline reversed: unfreeze from the TOP) lets you watch val loss after each addition; if it degrades when you unfreeze stage N, revert — stage N's features were fine as-is or the lr there is too high. Companion warning: NORM LAYERS. When fine-tuning with small batches, keep BN layers frozen in eval mode (their running statistics would otherwise be corrupted by tiny batches — the Module 2.3 trap recurs here in the most common applied setting). Linear probing + BN frozen is the industry-standard safe baseline.

**When ImageNet features transfer (and when they don't).** TRANSFER WELL: same modality (natural photos), similar granularity (objects/scenes), target data scarce (dozens to thousands per class). The 2019 "does ImageNet transfer?" (Kornblith et al.) result: across 12 vision datasets, ImageNet pretraining beats training from scratch on almost all — and better ImageNet accuracy correlates with better transfer, with dataset RESOLUTION and DIVERSITY mattering more than the specific label taxonomy. TRANSFER POORLY OR NOT AT ALL: (a) modality shift — medical grayscale, spectrograms, remote sensing with very different statistics (RGB natural-image priors can even mislead early); (b) new fine-grained distinctions that confuse generic features (species/severity grades where the head lacks separable signal); (c) very high resolution than pretraining (models input-size transfers via interpolation of conv weights — works but imperfect); (d) tasks where the shortcut features learned on ImageNet are actively adversarial (texture-biased decisions failing on shape-defined data). Remedies: domain-appropriate self-supervised pretraining (the 2020s increasingly prefers MAE/contrastive pretraining on YOUR domain's unlabelled data over ImageNet supervision), medical foundation models, longer full fine-tuning with augmentation.

**The 2026 practical default.** 1) Pick a modern pretrained backbone (torchvision/timm: ConvNeXt, EfficientNet, ViT — all ship pretrained weights). 2) Replace the head, linear probe, measure. 3) Unfreeze last stage with discriminative lrs; keep BN frozen for small batches; early-stop on val. 4) Only then full fine-tune at 1e-5-ish if val still says capacity-bound. 5) If the domain gap is large, consider self-supervised in-domain pretraining first. Data augmentation (and label-preserving crops) remains the highest-leverage addition at every rung. This ladder — probe, partial, full — is the entire applied playbook, and its discipline (never unfreeze more than the val evidence supports) saves models that a single-step "unfreeze everything, lr 1e-3" run destroys.

payload.title: Fine-tune decision ladder
rows: Measuring feature quality; classes close to pretraining domain
Moderate gap; limited data; safest accuracy gains
Large domain gap AND enough data to move everything safely
Pretrain on in-domain unlabelled, then above
Big modality gap (medical/satellite) with plentiful unlabelled data

payload.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import models

model = models.resnet50(weights=models.ResNet50_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V2)

# Rung 1: linear probe — freeze everything
for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False
model.fc = nn.Linear(2048, 10)              # new head; only these train
probe_params = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
print("training params:", sum(p.numel() for p in probe_params))   # 20,490

# Rung 2: partial — unfreeze layer4 with a discriminative lr
for p in model.layer4.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = True
head_params  = list(model.fc.parameters())
late_params  = list(model.layer4.parameters())
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([
    {"params": head_params, "lr": 1e-3},
    {"params": late_params, "lr": 1e-4},      # 10x smaller deeper in
], weight_decay=0.01)

# Keep BN statistics frozen while doing this (small batches!)
for m in model.modules():
    if isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm2d):
        m.eval()                              # running stats protected

# Rung 3: full — add early layers at ~1e-5, keep BN eval or use larger batches
for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = True
# ... then re-group parameter groups with per-stage lrs (1e-5 early -> 1e-3 head)

payload.title: Linear probing is your cheap diagnostic before any fine-tuning
payload.text: Frozen features + logistic head = a fast answer to "how separable are my classes in pretrained space?" If probe accuracy is already 85% of your target, partial fine-tuning will close it cheaply. If probe is near chance, the domain gap is real — budget for heavy fine-tuning or in-domain pretraining.

payload.title: One learning rate across a whole pretrained network is the most common fine-tune disaster
payload.text: Head at 1e-3 while edge detectors share that rate destroys generic features in the first epochs (catastrophic forgetting of the prior you paid for). Discriminative lrs (10-100x smaller deeper in) are not optional tuning — they are the safe default.

payload.title: Plan a fine-tune for a 600-image medical dataset
payload.problem: Task: classify 5 skin-lesion types; 600 labelled 512x512 colour images total (120/class); pretrained ResNet-50 (224x224 input) available; you have one GPU for a day. Design the full plan: preprocessing, rung choice with justification, per-group learning rates, BN handling, augmentation, and the metric + decision rule for advancing to the next rung.

steps.title: Preprocessing and split
steps.desc: Resize/crop to 224x224 with ImageNet normalization (match pretraining statistics — wrong normalization silently ruins features). Stratified split: ~480 train / 120 val (per class preserved). With only 120/class, val noise is real: report mean over 3 seeds or use 5-fold for final numbers.

steps.title: Rung 1: linear probe
steps.desc: Freeze all; train head at lr 1e-3, AdamW, ~20 epochs, class-balanced loss (5 balanced classes but small N — weight anyway if counts differ). Metric: macro-F1 (lesion classes matter equally). Rule: advance if probe macro-F1 < 0.75 (head must relearn — domain gap exists) but note the level for comparison.
steps.code_snippet: frozen backbone;  head lr=1e-3;  20 epochs;  track val macro-F1

steps.title: Rung 2: unfreeze layer4, discriminative lrs
steps.desc: layer4 lr 1e-4, head lr 1e-3, BN frozen (eval mode — batches of 16 corrupt running stats). Strong augmentation: flips, rotations, mild colour jitter, random resized crops. ~30 epochs with patience 8. Advance rule: val macro-F1 improves by >1 point over probe — keep; if it DROPS below probe after 10 epochs, revert and lower layer4 lr to 3e-5.
steps.code_snippet: lr groups: head 1e-3, layer4 1e-4;  BN.eval();  patience 8

steps.title: Rung 3: full fine-tune (only if still capacity-bound)
steps.desc: Unfreeze all: stage lrs [1e-5, 3e-5, 1e-4, 1e-3] (earliest lowest), BN still frozen OR train with batch 32+, 15-20 epochs. Sign to STOP and keep rung 2: val F1 flat or down while train F1 soars — you are overfitting 480 images; regularization cannot fix insufficient data, and the probe+partial result stands. Report final on the held-out test once.
steps.code_snippet: stage lrs: 1e-5, 3e-5, 1e-4, head 1e-3;  stop if train/val diverge

payload.solution: Plan: ImageNet-normalized 224 crops, stratified 480/120, then probe (head 1e-3, frozen, macro-F1 baseline) -> partial (layer4 at 1e-4, head 1e-3, BN frozen, heavy augmentation) -> full (stage-wise 1e-5..1e-3) ONLY if validation proves capacity is the binding constraint. Each rung gated by a stated metric rule, each with an explicit revert condition. With 600 images, expect rung 2 to be the sweet spot — and expect the whole pipeline to beat from-scratch training by a wide margin, which is the entire point of the transfer stack.

payload.title: Run the three-rung ladder on a real dataset
payload.prompt: On any small dataset (CIFAR-10 subset of 100/class works, or a Kaggle set): fine-tune a pretrained ResNet-18 through all three rungs — linear probe, last-stage partial, full fine-tune — holding augmentation, epochs, and metric constant (only lrs/groups differ). Record macro-F1 per rung. Write the curve of rung vs accuracy and explain the observed shape: monotonic? Diminishing? Divergent? What would make you stop at rung 2?
payload.hint: If full fine-tuning beats partial only marginally (or loses), rung 2 is your production choice — extra risk and compute must buy real accuracy to justify themselves.

mistakes.mistake: Fine-tuning at the same lr you would use to train from scratch
mistakes.fix: Pretrained weights are valuable prior knowledge; lr 1e-3 across a full backbone destroys it within epochs (catastrophic forgetting). Use 10-100x smaller lrs for backbone groups, and always apply discriminative scaling.

mistakes.mistake: Letting BatchNorm running stats update on small fine-tune batches
mistakes.fix: Put the backbone in eval() mode (or keep requires_grad False on BN params AND eval mode) during head/partial training; tiny-batch statistics corrupt a well-trained feature extractor. Standard practice — the Module 2.3 warning at its most consequential.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming ImageNet pretraining always helps
mistakes.fix: For grayscale medical, spectrogram, or heavily out-of-distribution inputs, natural-image features can underperform random init or in-domain self-supervised pretraining. Always keep from-scratch and in-domain-pretrained baselines in the comparison table.

mistakes.mistake: Starting with full unfreezing because "more training = better"
mistakes.fix: Full unfreezing on 600 images overfits and forgets generic features fast. The ladder exists to find the minimum unfreezing that meets your target: probe first, then add freedom only where validation demands it.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why early CNN layers transfer across domains while late layers are task-specific, and describe a safe fine-tuning procedure for a small dataset, including norm-layer handling.
payload.answer: Early convolutional filters learn generic local primitives (edges, gradients, colour contrasts, simple textures) that recur across virtually all image domains — their statistics are dictated by natural-image regularities rather than by the pretraining label set. Deeper layers compose these primitives into class-adjacent patterns increasingly entangled with the pretraining task's categories, so their features are less reusable without adaptation. Hence the asymmetry: keep early layers frozen, retrain late layers/head. Safe procedure for a small dataset: (1) replace the head and LINEAR PROBE with the whole backbone frozen — establishes the feature-quality baseline cheaply; (2) unfreeze only the last stage, using discriminative learning rates (e.g., head 1e-3, last stage 1e-4) with early stopping on validation; (3) expand unfreezing stage-by-stage only while validation improves, never full-unfreeze blindly; (4) keep BatchNorm layers in evaluation mode (frozen running statistics) throughout unless batches are large — small fine-tune batches otherwise overwrite good statistics with noisy ones; (5) apply strong label-preserving augmentation and class-balanced sampling/loss. Stop at the rung where validation stops benefiting — extra unfreezing beyond that point buys overfitting and forgetting, not accuracy.
payload.source: The canonical transfer-learning question in advanced DL courses and a staple of CV engineering interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Transfer exploits feature hierarchy: early layers are generic, late layers task-specific — reuse the general, retrain the specific.
The ladder: linear probe -> partial (top stage) fine-tune -> full fine-tune, each rung gated by validation evidence.
Discriminative learning rates (10-100x smaller deeper in) protect pretrained features; head trains fastest, edges barely move.
Freeze BatchNorm stats when fine-tuning with small batches — a silent-corruption trap with a one-line fix.
ImageNet transfer is strong but bounded: modality/texture gaps and label-structure mismatch are where it degrades — test, never assume.

questions.prompt: In a pretrained CNN, which layers are generally MOST reusable across unrelated domains?
options: The earliest convolutional layers (edges, textures, colour gradients)
questions.explanation: Early filters capture generic local primitives dictated by image statistics, not the pretraining label set; later layers entangle with task-specific categories and need more adaptation.

questions.prompt: Linear probing (training a head on a fully frozen backbone) is valuable first because it:
options: Trains the model faster than any alternative
Cheaply measures how linearly separable the new classes are in the pretrained feature space before risking the backbone
Removes the need for a loss function
questions.explanation: It isolates feature quality: strong probe = features already fit the task; weak probe = real domain gap. It is a diagnostic AND a safe baseline before any risky unfreezing.

questions.prompt: When fine-tuning on 600 images with batch size 16, BatchNorm layers should be:
options: Kept in eval mode with frozen running statistics (or replaced) to avoid corruption by noisy small-batch statistics
Trained with a 100x higher learning rate
questions.explanation: Small batches produce unreliable BN statistics that overwrite good pretrained running stats — the standard fix is eval-mode freezing for the backbone during fine-tuning.

questions.prompt: Discriminative fine-tuning refers to:
options: Using progressively smaller learning rates for earlier (more generic) layers and larger rates for the head/late layers
Applying different dropout rates per stage
Training on a curated hard-negative set
questions.explanation: Generic early features should barely move (small lr), while the task-specific head learns quickly (large lr) — per-group learning rates that respect layer specificity.

modules.title: Module 4 — Sequence Models Before Transformers
modules.summary: RNNs as unrolled computation graphs with persistent hidden state and truncated BPTT, the vanishing/exploding gradient pathology of long chains, LSTM and GRU gate mechanics with hand-computed cell updates, bidirectional and stacked variants, an honest account of where RNNs still fit, and the sequential bottleneck that motivated attention.

lessons.title: The RNN: Unrolling, Hidden State, and Backpropagation Through Time
lessons.summary: One recurrence written once and unrolled into a deep feedforward graph, what the hidden state carries, BPTT as ordinary backprop on the unrolled copy, and truncated BPTT as the practical compromise.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write the RNN recurrence and unroll it for a 4-step sequence into an equivalent feedforward graph
Explain what the hidden state encodes and why it is a learned, fixed-size memory
Compute forward outputs of a simple RNN cell step by step with real numbers
Distinguish full BPTT from truncated BPTT and state the memory/gradient-horizon tradeoff

payload.text: A language model must predict the next word knowing everything before it — but also must forget. Reading "the trophy would not fit in the suitcase because it was too big", the word "it" refers to the trophy, not the suitcase; two sentences earlier, the pronoun sense flips. An RNN faces this with one brutally simple weapon: a single vector of numbers, rewritten at every step, that must carry whatever matters forward and discard the rest. No attention, no retrieval, no growing context window — one fixed-width summary, endlessly rewritten. Understanding what that design can and cannot do explains both the RNN era's achievements and why attention was invented.

**The recurrence, written once.** At each time step t, the RNN receives input x_t and its previous hidden state h_{t-1}, and computes:

h_t = tanh(W_hh * h_{t-1} + W_xh * x_t + b)
y_t = W_hy * h_t + b_y

Same weights W_hh, W_xh, W_hy at EVERY step — weight sharing across time, exactly like convolution shares across space. h_0 is usually initialized to zeros. The hidden state is the model's working memory: a fixed-width vector (say 256 or 1024 floats) summarizing everything relevant from steps 1..t-1 that survives into step t. "Everything relevant" is learned from data — the network is TRAINED to write useful information into h and erase stale information, a genuinely hard optimization target (which is precisely why gates — next lesson — were invented).

**Unrolling: the identity that makes it all click.** Draw the recurrence for a length-4 sequence and you get EXACTLY a 4-layer feedforward network with SHARED weights across the layers: x_1 -> h_1 -> h_2 -> h_3 -> h_4, inputs entering at each step. Unrolling reveals three truths at once. (1) An RNN IS a deep network — depth equals sequence length. (2) Backprop through an RNN is ordinary backprop on the unrolled graph — no new calculus needed; the algorithm applied to this graph is called BPTT (backpropagation through time). (3) The vanishing/exploding gradient problem is now obvious in advance: gradients from y_4 back to h_1 multiply through FOUR weight/Jacobian factors — for a length-1000 sentence, ~1000 factors. Chain rule does the rest (Module 1.3's pathologies, now multiplied through TIME).

**BPTT concretely.** To train on the sequence (x_1..x_T, labels at each step), you unroll, compute all outputs, sum per-step losses L = sum_t L_t, and backpropagate across the unrolled graph — accumulating gradients into the SHARED weights (each weight gets contributions from every step's path; PyTorch's backward on an RNN loop does this transparently). Two complications that bite: (1) MEMORY — storing all T hidden states and activations for backward is O(T * batch * hidden); a 1000-step sequence with large hidden states exhausts GPU memory fast. (2) GRADIENT HORIZON — true sequence dependencies can span thousands of steps, but gradients flowing that far both blow up memory and vanish/explode mathematically. 

**Truncated BPTT: the standard compromise.** Process the sequence in segments of, say, 128-512 steps: run forward THROUGH segments (carrying hidden state and its value detached between segments — the state keeps flowing as data), but backpropagate only within each segment (detaching h between chunks stops gradients crossing the boundary). Result: gradients span ~segment length; long-range learning happens only INDIRECTLY as state-carrying statistics; memory is bounded. TensorFlow/PyTorch "stateful" RNN training and language-model training of the pre-transformer era (LSTMs on word-level corpora) all ran this way. Its honest limitation: an LSTM trained with 128-step truncation learns dependencies up to a few hundred steps RELIABLY; beyond that, you are hoping the hidden state organizes itself — which gradients never directly verify.

**Design variants, briefly.** GRU/LSTM (next lesson) replace the tanh cell with gated ones. Stacking: h_t^l from h_t^{l-1} gives depth ACROSS time-steps. Bidirectional: two recurrent passes (forward and backward), concatenated per step — powerful for tagging/translation encoders, but REQUIRES the whole sequence in advance (no online generation). Many-to-one (classification: last/averaged state), many-to-many (per-step outputs), sequence-to-sequence (encoder consumes input, decoder emits output — the 2014-2017 architecture that made neural machine translation work; attention's debut stage). Next lesson: the gradient wall this design hits, and the gates that patched it.

payload.title: Unrolled RNN: shared weights across time
RNN output modes
rows: POS tagging, per-frame labelling, language modelling

payload.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn

# The recurrence, explicit — one step of an RNN cell by hand-equivalent math
torch.manual_seed(0)
rnn = nn.RNN(input_size=3, hidden_size=4, batch_first=True)   # tanh cell, shared over time
x = torch.randn(1, 5, 3)                 # (batch=1, seq_len=5, features=3)
y, h_n = rnn(x)                          # y: all step outputs; h_n: final state
print(y.shape, h_n.shape)                # [1, 5, 4]  [1, 1, 4]

# Manual one-step computation (what the cell does internally):
def rnn_step(x_t, h_prev, W_xh, W_hh, b):
    h_t = torch.tanh(W_xh @ x_t + W_hh @ h_prev + b)   # shared weights every step
    return h_t

# Truncated BPTT pattern: carry state, stop gradients at segment boundaries
segs = torch.split(x, 2, dim=1)          # 5 steps -> segments of 2
h = None
for seg in segs:
    out, h = rnn(seg, h if h is not None else None)
    loss = (out ** 2).mean()
    loss.backward()                      # grads span ONLY this segment
    h = h.detach()                       # <-- truncate: state flows, gradient stops
    rnn.zero_grad()

payload.title: Hidden state is a learned cache — inspect it
payload.text: Plot h_t norms over a sequence: healthy models show structure (state builds, resets at boundaries like sentence ends). A state whose norm explodes toward the end of sequences means unstable dynamics; a state pinned near zero means the model is ignoring history — both diagnosable before any accuracy metric moves.

payload.title: Do not claim BPTT is a different algorithm from backprop
payload.text: BPTT is backprop applied to the UNROLLED graph, with gradient accumulation into shared weights. Exam answer precision matters: "the same chain rule, applied through time" is correct; "a special temporal algorithm" is not.

payload.title: Unroll and forward a 3-step RNN with tiny numbers
payload.problem: Scalar input x, scalar hidden state h, single units for hand-traceability. W_xh = 0.5, W_hh = 0.8, b = 0, activation tanh (use values: tanh(0.4)=0.38, tanh(0.66)=0.58, tanh(1.4)=0.89 — compute as needed). Sequence: x_1 = 0.8, x_2 = -0.4, x_3 = 1.2; h_0 = 0. (a) Compute h_1, h_2, h_3. (b) Which weight path would a gradient from loss at step 3 travel to reach W_xh's step-1 contribution? (c) What does the multiplication across steps imply for length-50 sequences?

steps.title: Step 2
steps.desc: z_2 = 0.5*(-0.4) + 0.8*0.38 = -0.2 + 0.304 = 0.104. h_2 = tanh(0.104) ≈ 0.104 (small input, near-linear region). Note the negative input barely dents the state — history dominates this step.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.desc: z_3 = 0.5*1.2 + 0.8*0.104 = 0.6 + 0.083 = 0.683. h_3 = tanh(0.683) ≈ 0.593. Final state mixes all three inputs, weighted by decaying powers of W_hh — an exponential memory kernel (0.8^n) of the past.

steps.title: Gradient path and its consequence
steps.desc: Loss at step 3 to W_xh's step-1 effect: chain = d h3/d h2 * d h2/d h1 * d h1/d W_xh — three Jacobian factors, each bounded by W_hh * tanh' (<= 0.8 here) times downstream terms. At length 50: ~0.8^49-ish factor if tanh' averages ~0.5, giving ~1e-5 or worse — vanishing. Magnitudes >1 across factors explode instead. This multiplicative-through-time behaviour IS the RNN gradient pathology.
steps.code_snippet: path: dL/dh3 -> dh3/dh2 -> dh2/dh1 -> dh1/dWxh  (product of ~0.4 factors)

payload.solution: h_1 = 0.38, h_2 ≈ 0.104, h_3 ≈ 0.593: each state is a recency-weighted blend of inputs with geometric decay 0.8^n. The step-3 loss reaches step-1's weights only through a PRODUCT of per-step Jacobians — over 50 steps that product collapses toward zero (or explodes above 1), which is exactly the vanishing/exploding problem and the reason plain tanh RNNs learn only short-range dependencies. Gates (LSTM/GRU) and, ultimately, attention are the two historical answers.

payload.title: Unroll an RNN in a diagram and in PyTorch
payload.prompt: Take the 5-step sequence ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat"] (map each word to a random 8-dim vector). (a) Draw the unrolled graph with shared weights, marking where one loss per step would attach for language modelling. (b) Run nn.RNN(8, 16) over it in PyTorch, print output shapes, and verify y[:, t] depends on x_0..x_t but not x_{t+1} by perturbing a future input and comparing earlier outputs. (c) State in one sentence what this non-causality direction implies for decoder design.
payload.hint: Perturb x_4, assert y_0..y_3 unchanged, y_4 changed — causality flows forward only. Decoders need outputs at t to depend only on inputs <= t (masking — foreshadowing masked attention).

mistakes.mistake: Assuming each step's output depends on FUTURE inputs
mistakes.fix: A vanilla RNN is causal: h_t sees only x_1..x_t. Bidirectional RNNs deliberately break this for offline encoders (the backward pass sees the future) — fine for tagging, impossible for autoregressive generation.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing hidden-state flow with gradient flow under truncation
mistakes.fix: In truncated BPTT the state VALUE carries across segments (the model can still USE old information), but gradients stop at boundaries (learning to WRITE that old information far back is not directly trained). Detach controls gradients, not data.

mistakes.mistake: Claiming RNNs have no parameter growth with sequence length
mistakes.fix: Correct: parameters are fixed (shared W's across time) — that is the point. MEMORY during training, however, grows with unrolled length — fixed parameters, growing activation storage. Keep the two bookkeeping systems straight.

mistakes.mistake: Treating tanh's bounded output as sufficient to keep states stable forever
mistakes.fix: h_t is bounded, but the JACOBIAN products through time still vanish/explode (tanh' shrinks, W_hh multiplies). Bounded activations do not imply healthy gradients — the pathology lives in derivatives, not values.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define backpropagation through time and explain why an RNN's gradient with respect to early-step weights involves products of many Jacobian terms. What practical compromise is used for long sequences?
payload.answer: BPTT is backpropagation applied to the unrolled (in-time) computation graph of an RNN: the recurrence is replicated once per time step, producing a deep feedforward graph with shared weights; gradients of the total (summed) loss are computed across all steps and accumulated into the shared parameters. Differentiating a loss at step T with respect to parameters influencing step t requires the chain rule across every intermediate step: the gradient is a product of per-step Jacobian factors (d h_{k+1} / d h_k = diag(f'(W_hh h_k + ...)) * W_hh ...), one factor per time step from t to T. With T large, this product shrinks geometrically toward zero when the average factor's norm is below one (vanishing gradients — early steps get no learning signal) or grows without bound when above one (exploding gradients — unstable updates). Hence plain RNNs cannot learn long-range dependencies directly. Practical compromise: TRUNCATED BPTT — process long sequences in segments, carrying the hidden-state value across segment boundaries (detached from the graph) while backpropagating only within each segment; this bounds memory and gradient products at the cost of limiting the directly learned dependency horizon to the segment length (gated cells — LSTM/GRU — extend the effective horizon further).
payload.source: Standard advanced-DL/GATE question; the BPTT definition plus vanishing-product argument is the expected core.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: An RNN rewrites one hidden state per step with shared weights — unrolling reveals a deep feedforward net, one layer per time step.
BPTT is ordinary backprop on the unrolled graph, with gradients accumulated into shared weights.
Gradient products through time cause vanishing/exploding signals — early steps starve or updates blow up at long sequence lengths.
Truncated BPTT detaches state between segments: values flow forever, gradients only across the segment — the memory/learning-horizon tradeoff.
The hidden state is a fixed-width, learned summary — its capacity ceiling is what attention later bypassed.

questions.prompt: An RNN unrolled for T time steps is equivalent to a feedforward network with:
options: T layers sharing the same parameters
One layer applied repeatedly without backpropagation
questions.explanation: The recurrence replicated across time forms a T-layer deep net whose weights are tied — the same W_hh/W_xh at every step; BPTT is then backprop on that unrolled graph.

questions.prompt: In truncated BPTT, detaching the hidden state between segments means:
options: The state VALUE stops being passed forward
The state value still flows as data, but gradients do not propagate across the segment boundary
The hidden state is reinitialised each segment
Weights are frozen after the first segment
questions.explanation: detach() blocks only the gradient path; the state itself carries forward so the model can still USE long history — it just cannot directly TRAIN the writing of that history across the boundary.

questions.prompt: The gradient of a late-step loss with respect to early-step parameters passes through:
options: One Jacobian factor regardless of sequence length
A product of per-step Jacobian factors — one per intervening time step
questions.explanation: The chain rule through T steps multiplies T-1 Jacobians (each involving W_hh and the activation derivative); the product vanishes below unit norm and explodes above — the temporal version of the deep-net gradient problem.

questions.prompt: A vanilla (tanh) RNN's hidden state can be best described as:
options: A lookup table of seen tokens
A fixed-width vector rewritten at each step, intended to summarize all relevant history
A copy of the entire input sequence
questions.explanation: Fixed-capacity learned summary — bounded in width no matter the sequence length, which is both its elegance (fixed parameters) and its eventual bottleneck (what attention replaced).

lessons.title: Vanishing Gradients, and the Gate Surgery of LSTM and GRU
lessons.summary: Why tanh RNNs lose long-range dependencies mathematically, then the LSTM's three gates with hand-computed cell updates, GRU's merged two-gate economy, and what gates actually buy.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain the vanishing-gradient mechanism in a plain RNN in terms of the tanh-derivative and W_hh product
Compute an LSTM cell's forget/input/output gates and cell state for one step with given numbers
Contrast GRU against LSTM: gate count, candidate computation, and when the difference matters little
State what gates enable (selective persistence) that a plain tanh recurrence cannot express

payload.text: Here is a sentence an LSTM was built for: "The employees of the company, who had worked there for decades before the merger was announced, were shocked when THEY were laid off." The pronoun sits 24 words from its referents — and every word between them is noise a naive recurrent net must preserve through a chain of matrix multiplications that erases it. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber saw this coming in 1997: gradients through long chains decay exponentially, so the network literally cannot learn to connect distant events. Their fix was surgical — give the cell a highway of its own, and put learned gates on the ramps.

**The vanishing gradient, precisely.** In a plain RNN, h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + ...). The gradient from step t+k back to step t is a product of k factors, each containing diag(tanh'(z)) * W_hh. Two multiplicative killers: (1) tanh' <= 1 and typically << 1 (average ~0.5, shrinking toward 0 in the saturating tails); (2) if the spectral norm of W_hh is below 1 (common under stable training), each factor is < 1 — k factors give an ~0.4^k decay: at k = 50, 1e-20 — learning signal from distant past is numerically zero. Exploding is the mirror (norms > 1), historically patched by global gradient clipping. The deep-net answer from Module 2 (residual highways) had no RNN analogue until LSTM's cell state — a path where gradients multiply by ~1 instead of ~tanh' * W_hh.

**LSTM: three gates and one highway.** The LSTM cell maintains TWO states: hidden h_t (output, filtered) and cell state c_t (the highway — internal memory flowing through time with minimal interference). Four computed quantities per step, all sigmoids/candidates:

f_t = sigmoid(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f)          FORGET gate: how much of c_{t-1} to keep
i_t = sigmoid(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i)           INPUT gate: how much candidate to admit
c~_t = tanh(W_c [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c)             candidate memory
c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * c~_t                  cell update (the multiplication-addition!)
o_t = sigmoid(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o)           OUTPUT gate: how much cell state to expose
h_t = o_t * tanh(c_t)

Read the cell update carefully: c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + (stuff). Along the gradient path d c_t / d c_{t-1} = f_t — a SOFT value in (0,1), not a matrix-Jacobian-tanh product. If the forget gate sits near 1 (its common trained state), gradients flow backward through time nearly UNATTENUATED — the same trick as ResNet's +1, in multiplicative-sigmoid clothing. Crucially the gate values are LEARNED PER STEP AND PER DIMENSION from the current context: the network learns WHEN to remember (carry the pronoun's referent for 24 words) and WHEN to clear (reset at sentence boundaries) — selective persistence, which a plain tanh cell cannot express because it always overwrites h_t = tanh(everything).

**The forget-gate bias trick.** Initialize forget-gate bias positively (say +1 or +2): at start of training, sigmoid(b_f) ≈ 0.73-0.88 — the cell begins by PASSING information, not erasing it. Forgetting to do this (bias 0 -> gate 0.5, halving the cell each step) measurably hurts sequence tasks. This is one of the most replicated small tricks in recurrent modelling.

**GRU: the two-gate economy.** Cho et al. (2014) merged LSTM's forget and input gates into ONE update gate z_t, dropped the separate output gate (exposes h_t = (1-z_t)*h~_t + z_t*h_{t-1}-ish, precisely: h_t = (1 - z_t) * h~_t + z_t * h_{t-1} where h~ is the tanh candidate), and let a reset gate r_t control how much past enters the candidate. Fewer parameters (~25% less), often matching LSTM quality on moderate tasks; LSTM retains the edge on some very-long-range or memory-heavy tasks (its separate cell state is a purer highway). Practical verdict: try GRU first for speed; use LSTM where every point matters and budget allows; the two are close enough that the CHOICE matters far less than gates-versus-no-gates.

**What gates bought — and their limits.** They bought: gradient flow over hundreds of steps (empirically 100-1000 with BPTT tricks), selective memory (the actual mechanism for long-dependency tasks: copying, memorisation, language modelling with long contexts), and the workhorse of speech, MT, and time-series from ~2013-2017 (LSTM machines translated Google Translate's 2016 neural MT; still live in parts of speech synthesis and on-device sequence tasks where latency budgets forbid attention's quadratic cost). They did NOT buy: true random access (still one rewriting stream — to USE a fact you must have preserved it all along the chain), parallel training (h_t depends on h_{t-1}: T sequential steps per forward = T sequential gradient steps — the wall Transformers shot through), or open-ended context (fixed-width states, same as vanilla RNN). Gates fixed the gradient AND kept the bottleneck — the last gap attention closed.

payload.title: LSTM vs GRU vs plain RNN

payload.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn

# One LSTM cell computation, made explicit (hidden=1 for hand-traceability)
def lstm_step(x_t, h_prev, c_prev, W, b):
    gates = torch.sigmoid(W['f'] @ x_t + W['fh'] @ h_prev + b['f'])   # forget
    i    = torch.sigmoid(W['i'] @ x_t + W['ih'] @ h_prev + b['i'])    # input
    c_tilde = torch.tanh(W['c'] @ x_t + W['ch'] @ h_prev + b['c'])    # candidate
    c_t = gates * c_prev + i * c_tilde                                # <-- highway update
    o    = torch.sigmoid(W['o'] @ x_t + W['oh'] @ h_prev + b['o'])    # output
    h_t = o * torch.tanh(c_t)
    return h_t, c_t

lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size=8, hidden_size=16, num_layers=2, batch_first=True)
x = torch.randn(3, 10, 8)             # batch 3, seq 10, feat 8
out, (h_n, c_n) = lstm(x)
print(out.shape, h_n.shape, c_n.shape) # [3,10,16] [2,3,16] [2,3,16]  (2 stacked layers)

gru = nn.GRU(input_size=8, hidden_size=16, num_layers=2, batch_first=True)
out_g, h_g = gru(x)
print(out_g.shape, h_g.shape)          # same shapes; fewer parameters inside

payload.title: Forget-gate bias: check it when long tasks fail
payload.text: If your LSTM's memory tasks (copy, long-range language) train poorly early, inspect forget-gate biases: all near 0? Set them to +1..+2 and retrain. Gate-activation histograms over training tell the memory story directly — forget sitting at 0.5 forever means the cell never learned selective persistence.

payload.title: Do not say LSTM "solves" the vanishing gradient problem
payload.text: It MITIGATES it: gradients can flow far through the c-highway when forget gates stay high, but gates driven to saturation still clip paths, BPTT truncation still limits horizon, and exploding gradients still need clipping. Accurate exam language: "gates create an approximately identity-preserving cell-state path".

payload.title: Compute one LSTM step by hand
payload.problem: Scalar cell, one unit throughout. h_0 = 0.2, c_0 = 1.0, x_1 = 0.5. Given pre-activation values (already including weights): forget pre-act = 0.5, input pre-act = -1.0, candidate pre-act = 0.4, output pre-act = 0.0. Use sigmoid(0.5) = 0.62, sigmoid(-1.0) = 0.27, tanh(0.4) = 0.38, sigmoid(0) = 0.5. (a) Compute f_1, i_1, c~_1, c_1, o_1, h_1. (b) Now compute c after 50 more IDENTICAL steps (forget gate each step) — compare against a plain tanh RNN's ~0.4^50 gradient factor. (c) What does gate f = 0.62 imply for gradient retention per step?

steps.title: Gates and candidate
steps.desc: f_1 = sigmoid(0.5) = 0.62. i_1 = sigmoid(-1.0) = 0.27 (input mostly closed — this step writes little). c~_1 = tanh(0.4) = 0.38. o_1 = sigmoid(0) = 0.5.

steps.title: Cell update
steps.desc: c_1 = f * c_0 + i * c~ = 0.62*1.0 + 0.27*0.38 = 0.62 + 0.103 = 0.723. The old memory mostly survived (62%) and a little new content arrived (10%).

steps.title: Hidden output
steps.desc: h_1 = o * tanh(c_1) = 0.5 * tanh(0.723) = 0.5 * 0.619 = 0.310. The output gate throttles how much of the (protected) memory is EXPOSED — c keeps full history, h is the filtered view.

steps.title: Fifty identical steps and the gradient comparison
steps.desc: With f = 0.62 constant and no new input (i*c~ = 0): c decays as 0.62^n. After 50 steps: 0.62^50 ≈ 4e-11 — memory itself fades unless the gate rises toward 1 (in trained models, forget on kept information sits near 0.95+, giving 0.95^50 ≈ 0.08 — 9 orders of magnitude better retention). Gradient path: d c_t/d c_{t-k} = product of f's — pure sigmoid values, no tanh-derivative matrix sandwich. Compare plain RNN: ~0.4^50 = 1e-20. At f = 0.98: 0.98^50 = 0.36 — a PRACTICAL learning signal at 50 steps.

payload.solution: c_1 = 0.723, h_1 = 0.310: memory preserved, candidate mostly rejected, exposure throttled. Gradient retention equals the product of forget gates — at f = 0.98, 50-step gradients retain 36% of signal versus the plain RNN's 1e-20; that four-orders-plus difference at moderate lengths (and far more at 100+) is the whole justification for gate surgery. Train your forget gates to stay high on retained content and long-range learning becomes numerically possible.

payload.title: Train the long-dependency benchmark
payload.prompt: Implement the copy task: input = K random tokens, delimiter, then T steps of padding; target = reproduce the K tokens after the delimiter. Train (a) a vanilla tanh RNN, (b) an LSTM, same hidden size, T = 50. Plot test accuracy vs T for T in [10, 20, 40, 50] for both. Report where each collapses and explain the vanilla RNN's failure using gradient-norm-per-timestep logs you capture during training.
payload.hint: Log mean |gradient| entering the cell at each time step (register hooks on the recurrent weights per time). Vanilla: gradient decays geometrically toward early steps; LSTM: flatter profile — the numbers will match the theory directly.

mistakes.mistake: Saying LSTM has "no vanishing gradient problem"
mistakes.fix: Mitigation, not elimination: the c-highway with high forget gates greatly extends the horizon, but saturated gates, truncation, and exploding norms remain. Precision on this distinction is exactly what advanced exams probe.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing the cell state c_t with the hidden state h_t
mistakes.fix: c_t is the full internal memory flowing through time (the highway); h_t = o_t * tanh(c_t) is the output-facing, gated view. Memory can persist in c while h shows something filtered — dual-state design is the point.

mistakes.mistake: Believing LSTM/GRU solved long contexts, so transformers were unnecessary
mistakes.fix: Gates extended usable ranges to hundreds of steps, but still through a SEQUENTIAL single stream — no parallel-across-time training, no random access to arbitrary positions. Long-context LLMs (10k+) are infeasible as RNN chains; attention was a different kind of fix.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming GRU is always worse because it has fewer gates
mistakes.fix: GRU matches or beats LSTM on many tasks while training faster with fewer parameters — merged gates often suffice. The gate-count difference matters only on specific long-memory tasks; treat it as an empirical, budget-based choice.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the LSTM cell update equations, explain how the forget gate enables long-range gradient flow, and state the advantage of the GRU's design.
payload.answer: At step t: forget f_t = sigmoid(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f); input i_t = sigmoid(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i); candidate c~_t = tanh(W_c [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c); cell c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c~_t; output o_t = sigmoid(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o); hidden h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t). Long-range flow: the gradient of a late loss w.r.t. c_{t-1} through the cell update is d c_t/d c_{t-1} = diag(f_t) — elementwise sigmoid values rather than a product of matrix Jacobians and tanh derivatives; when f_t is near 1 (the typical trained state for retained information, often aided by positive forget-bias initialisation), gradients propagate across many steps with near-unity retention, whereas a plain tanh RNN multiplies by diag(tanh')W each step and decays geometrically. The gates are learned per step per dimension, giving SELECTIVE persistence: write, hold, or erase according to context. GRU advantage: merges forget+input into a single update gate z_t and drops the separate output gate (h_t = (1-z_t) ⊙ c~_t + z_t ⊙ h_{t-1} with a reset gate shaping c~_t), reducing parameters by ~25% and computation per step while delivering near-LSTM quality on most tasks — a simpler, faster cell when the full LSTM memory machinery is not measurably needed.
payload.source: High-frequency advanced-DL exam question; gate equations plus the diag(f_t) gradient argument constitute a full-marks answer.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Plain RNN gradients multiply through tanh-derivatives and W_hh — geometric decay erases long-range signal (exploding needs clipping).
LSTM: f/i/o gates + tanh candidate maintain a cell-state highway where gradients multiply by f_t (~1 when remembering), enabling selective persistence.
c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * c~_t is the key line: near-identity gradient path, unlike any tanh-stack recurrence.
GRU merges gates into update+reset — fewer parameters, near-LSTM results; the gate choice matters less than having gates.
Gates fixed the gradient but kept sequential training and fixed-width memory — attention addresses both.

questions.prompt: The LSTM cell state's gradient with respect to the previous cell state passes through:
options: The full W_hh matrix times tanh'
Elementwise forget-gate values (diag(f_t)) — approximately identity when the gate is near 1
questions.explanation: c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * c~_t differentiates to f_t elementwise — sigmoid values in (0,1), near 1 when remembering — instead of a shrinking matrix-tanh Jacobian product.

questions.prompt: The role of the forget gate f_t is to:
options: Control how much of the previous cell state c_{t-1} is retained into c_t
Select which input features to read
questions.explanation: f_t elementwise-multiplies the old cell state before the input gate adds new content — "how much of my memory do I keep this step", learned per step and per dimension.

questions.prompt: A practical, well-replicated LSTM trick is to initialise forget-gate bias to a POSITIVE value (e.g. +1) because it:
options: Starts the cell passing (remembering) rather than erasing, improving early long-range learning
questions.explanation: sigmoid(0) = 0.5 would halve memory each early step; sigmoid(1) ≈ 0.73 biases the initial cell toward retention — a small init detail with measurable task-level effects.

questions.prompt: The GRU differs from the LSTM by:
options: Merging forget and input into a single update gate and dropping the separate output gate, giving fewer parameters
questions.explanation: GRU: update gate z_t replaces (forget, input); reset gate r_t shapes the candidate; h alone suffices — ~25% fewer parameters with near-LSTM empirical performance.

lessons.title: Bidirectional Models, Stacks, and Where RNNs Still Fit
lessons.summary: Going both directions at once for encoders, stacking for depth, seq2seq with encoder-decoder state handoff, an honest scorecard of RNNs in the 2020s, and the design constraints that still favour them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain what a bidirectional RNN computes and identify tasks where it is invalid (autoregressive decoding)
Design a stacked encoder-decoder seq2seq configuration for a translation-style task
List three 2020s application areas where recurrent components remain the right tool, with reasons
Compare an RNN-based sequence model against a transformer on the axes of parallelism, context, and inductive bias

payload.text: Every large language model you talk to today still contains recurrence's descendants — but the raw bidirectional RNN has a strange modern life. It sits inside speech recognition front-ends (you can listen to a whole utterance before deciding its first phoneme), inside some on-device time-series controllers where milliseconds and milliwatts are the entire budget, and inside the token-mixing half of a few 2020s architectures (Mamba, RWKV) that re-emerged because linear-time sequential models DO something attention cannot: constant memory over infinite streams. The RNN's story did not end in 2017 — it narrowed into niches where its constraints are features.

**Bidirectional RNNs: two passes, concatenated memory.** A standard RNN only sees the past. A bidirectional RNN runs TWO recurrent passes over the SAME sequence: forward (h->_t from x_1..x_t) and backward (h<-_t from x_T..x_t), then concatenates h_t = [h->_t ; h<-_t] as the representation at each position. Each position's encoding now summarizes BOTH directions' context — the classic example: "bank" in "river bank" is disambiguated by the word AFTER it; a forward-only encoder encoding "bank" at position 3 never sees "river". For offline tagging, chunking, NER, and encoder-side representation learning, bidirectionality is a big, cheap win (parameters double, quality often jumps).

**Why bidirectionality is FORBIDDEN in decoders.** At generation time step t, the model must predict x_{t+1} knowing only x_1..x_t — a backward pass would need the future tokens that do not exist yet. Worse: teacher-forced training with a backward pass LEAKS the target into every representation (the backward state at t literally contains x_T..x_{t+1}), so the model learns to cheat, and inference collapses. The rule: bidirectional for encoders over complete inputs; unidirectional (causal) for decoders/generators. (This causal/non-causal split reappears exactly in transformer design: BERT-style bidirectional encoders vs GPT-style causal decoders — next module makes this precise with attention masks.)

**Stacking: depth across representations.** Run an RNN layer, take ALL its outputs as the input to ANOTHER RNN layer (h^l_t = RNN_layer_l(h^{l-1}_t)). Stacking adds abstraction levels: layer 1 might encode phonetic/acoustic patterns, layer 2 word-ish patterns, layer 3 phrase patterns — the hierarchy argument from Module 1 applied over sequences. Typical: 2-4 layers (deeper stacks hit diminishing returns AND multiply sequential cost); hidden widths often equal across layers for clean state handoffs. Bidirectional + stacked is the classic encoder: 2-layer bidirectional LSTM was the default NMT/speech encoder of 2015-2017.

**Seq2seq: the state-handoff pattern.** Sequence-to-sequence (Sutskever, Vinyals, Le 2014): a bidirectional/unidirectional LSTM ENCODER consumes the whole input; its final states (every layer's h_T and c_T) initialise the DECODER; the decoder then generates the output autoregressively, feeding its own previous output as next input (teacher forcing during training, scheduled sampling debates notwithstanding). Information for translation must squeeze through that finite state vector — the "information bottleneck" problem. Bahdanau et al. (2014) noticed the fix: let the decoder LOOK BACK at all encoder states at every step instead of through one vector — that is attention, born inside the RNN era to fix the RNN's own bottleneck (Module 4.4 details).

**The 2020s RNN scorecard — honest version.** LOSING: language modelling and machine translation at scale (transformers dominate on quality, parallelism, and long-range access); anything wanting trillions of tokens of pretraining (sequential training is too slow); retrieval-style tasks needing random access to context (attention does it natively). STILL WINNING or competing: (a) STREAMING / ONLINE inference with constant state — keyword spotting, wake-word detection, on-device anomaly detection where you must process forever-length streams in O(1) memory; (b) TIGHT LATENCY/POWER edge controllers — small GRUs in sensor fusion, robotics control loops, where 1-10k-parameter cells run in microseconds without attention's KV buffers; (c) certain time-series and control tasks where strong sequential inductive bias + tiny data beats attention's flexibility; (d) the hybrid frontier: MAMBA/state-space models (2023-2026) are recurrent-linear-time models with learned selection — proving recurrence's efficiency argument survived while fixing its content-bottleneck; RWKV blends RNN inference with transformer training. Speech pipelines still use BiLSTM/GRU layers in production ASR. The lesson: architecture choice is about CONSTRAINTS — if you need random access and massive parallel pretraining, attention; if you need constant-memory streaming at microsecond latency, recurrence wins and always has.

**The comparison table you should be able to produce from memory.** Parallelism: RNN O(1) parallel-across-time (must step sequentially); transformer full (all positions). Context: RNN fixed state; transformer attends to all in window (KV cache grows linearly with length at inference). Inductive bias: RNN strong locality/recency bias (helps on small data, hurts when distant info matters); transformer weak prior, learns positions via encoding. Training length handling: RNN truncated BPTT; transformer fixed/positional windows with quadratic-in-length attention cost (next module).

payload.title: RNN vs transformer (the axes that decide designs)
rows: Attention over all positions in window
Direct — any position attends to any other
Attention matrix / KV grows with T (O(T^2) compute)
