import torch, torch.nn as nn

# Bidirectional encoder: two directions, concatenated per step
bi = nn.LSTM(input_size=64, hidden_size=128, bidirectional=True, batch_first=True)
x = torch.randn(8, 30, 64)              # 8 sequences of length 30
out, (h_n, c_n) = bi(x)
print(out.shape)                        # [8, 30, 256]  (128 forward + 128 backward)
print(h_n.shape)                        # [2, 8, 256] -> layer 0 fwd+h_bwd stacked

# NOTE the leak: a backward pass at position t contains x_T..x_{t+1}.
# For GENERATION this is illegal — decoders must stay unidirectional (causal).

# Stacked encoder-decoder seq2seq skeleton
enc = nn.LSTM(64, 128, num_layers=2, batch_first=True)          # takes full input
dec = nn.LSTM(128, 128, num_layers=2, batch_first=True)         # generates output
_, (h_n, c_n) = enc(src)                                        # final states...
_, _ = dec(tgt_in, (h_n, c_n))                                  # ...seed the decoder
# (Bahdanau attention would additionally let each dec step see ALL enc outputs)

payload.title: The encoder/decoder question to ask before any architecture choice
payload.text: Does this task need the WHOLE input before any output (classify/tag/encode: bidirectional fine) or must each output depend only on previous outputs (generate: causal only)? This single question rules out half the design space immediately — and it is exactly the BERT-vs-GPT question next module formalizes.

payload.title: Teacher forcing with a bidirectional decoder leaks labels
payload.text: If the backward direction during training can see future target tokens, the model learns to copy the future and fails at inference. Auditing whether any bidirectional component touches TARGET tokens is a mandatory review step in seq2seq implementations.

payload.title: Design the RNN for three different tasks
payload.problem: Specify architecture choices (direction, layers, output mode, state handoff) for: (A) part-of-speech tagging a complete sentence; (B) streaming next-word prediction on a live microphone feed; (C) English-to-French translation. For each justify direction, and state whether teacher forcing applies. Then count parameters qualitatively: which configuration is largest and why?

steps.title: Task A: POS tagging (offline, per-token labels)
steps.desc: Input is complete, every tag may use both-sided context: 2-layer BIDIRECTIONAL LSTM, many-to-many output (a classifier on each concatenated h_t). No teacher forcing (labels are per-position, not autoregressive). Parameter count: 4 gates * (directions=2) * (layers=2) * per-layer weights — bidirectional doubles the recurrent params.
steps.code_snippet: BiLSTM, 2 layers, many-to-many;  no teacher forcing

steps.title: Task B: streaming next-word (online, causal)
steps.desc: Future unavailable AND the stream may be endless: single-direction (forward-only) GRU/LSTM, state carried indefinitely, many-to-one output at each step (word distribution), truncated BPTT for training segments. Bidirectional strictly illegal (future tokens do not exist; also leaks). Teacher forcing applies during training (condition on true previous words), with state carried across training segments via detach.
steps.code_snippet: unidirectional GRU, stateful;  causal;  truncated BPTT

steps.title: Task C: translation (encoder-decoder)
steps.desc: Encoder over the FULL source sentence may be bidirectional (source is complete when encoding — 2-layer BiLSTM). Decoder over the TARGET must be unidirectional/causal, initialised with encoder final states, trained with teacher forcing (feed true previous target tokens), decoded greedily/beam at inference. No backward pass ever touches target-side states.
steps.code_snippet: enc: BiLSTM (full source);  dec: uni LSTM + teacher forcing

steps.title: Parameter comparison
steps.desc: Largest: Task C — it contains BOTH a full bidirectional encoder AND an autoregressive decoder, roughly twice Task A's recurrent machinery plus output projections over the target vocabulary (often the single biggest tensor: hidden x vocab). Task B is smallest (one unidirectional layer, small vocab head). This mirrors real systems: generation stacks are encoder+decoder; streaming edge models stay tiny and recurrent.
steps.code_snippet: C (enc+dec+vocab head) > A (Bi) > B (uni single)

payload.solution: A: 2-layer bidirectional LSTM, per-position outputs, no forcing — both-sided context is legal and helpful. B: forward-only GRU with carried state, causal by necessity, teacher-forced training on truncated segments. C: bidirectional encoder + unidirectional decoder, teacher forcing on targets, autoregressive decoding. Parameter ranking C > A > B, dominated in C by vocab-sized output projections. Direction legality — not accuracy fashion — drives these choices.

payload.title: Audit an RNN system design
payload.prompt: You inherit a speech-pipeline design: "Bidirectional LSTM encoder over audio, autoregressive LSTM decoder for streaming TTS output tokens, teacher-forced training." Find every flaw (there are at least two serious ones), state WHY each fails at inference, and write the corrected architecture — including whether any component may legitimately stay bidirectional.
payload.hint: The decoder sees live requests — bidirectional decoder leaks future target tokens and is impossible online. Also consider: is the audio complete before decoding (yes — encoder may stay Bi), and how does state handoff work?

mistakes.mistake: Using a bidirectional RNN anywhere in an autoregressive generator
mistakes.fix: The backward pass reads tokens that will not exist at inference (or leaks them during training). Causal-only on the target side, always — the direct ancestor of masked attention in decoders.

mistakes.mistake: Stacking 8 RNN layers because transformer blocks stack 12
mistakes.fix: Each added RNN layer multiplies SEQUENTIAL depth (time steps x layers per step) and historically yields diminishing returns past ~3-4 layers without careful tricks. Depth budgets are architecture-specific, not transferable across paradigms.

mistakes.mistake: Concluding "RNNs are dead" from transformer dominance in language
mistakes.fix: RNN/GRU components remain standard in streaming detection, edge control, parts of speech pipelines, and re-emerge in modern state-space hybrids. The correct claim: for parallel-pretrained, random-access language models, attention won — a narrower statement.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to detach hidden state across segments in stateful training
mistakes.fix: Without detaching, BPTT graphs grow unboundedly across the stream and OOM; with full reinit, the model loses long memory. Detach-between-segments is the standard pattern — value flows, gradient stops.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why are bidirectional RNNs appropriate as encoders but invalid in autoregressive decoders? Illustrate with a leakage argument and connect it to a named transformer-era counterpart.
payload.answer: An encoder processes a COMPLETE input (a sentence to tag, audio to transcribe) before/while producing representations; running a backward pass lets each position's representation incorporate right-side context, which is legitimate because that context exists at encoding time and never has to be "generated". An autoregressive decoder must produce output token y_t conditioned only on y_<t (and the encoded input): at inference the future y_>t does not exist, so a backward recurrent pass cannot even be computed. Worse, during teacher-forced TRAINING, a backward pass over target tokens would place future ground-truth tokens inside every state from which predictions are made — the model can trivially copy the future, achieving low training loss while collapsing at inference (label leakage). Hence decoders are strictly unidirectional/causal. The transformer-era counterpart is exactly the BERT-vs-GPT split: BERT-style bidirectional masked models suit understanding/encoding over complete text, while GPT-style models use CAUSAL attention masks (position t attends only to positions <= t) for generation — the attention mask is the transformer formalisation of this same encoder/decoder directionality rule.
payload.source: Classic seq2seq/interview question; the leakage argument and the BERT/GPT causal-mask connection are what distinguish top answers.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Bidirectional RNNs concatenate forward and backward states for both-sided context — legal only when the full input exists (encoders).
Autoregressive decoders must be causal: backward passes are impossible at inference and leak targets during training.
Stacking adds representational depth across time; seq2seq hands encoder final states to the decoder — the birthplace of attention.
RNNs still fit streaming O(1)-memory inference, edge latency/power budgets, small-data time series, and modern state-space hybrids.
The RNN-vs-transformer axes: across-time parallelism, random access, context limits, and inductive bias — choose by constraints.

questions.prompt: A bidirectional RNN's output at position t concatenates:
options: The forward state summarizing x_1..x_t and the backward state summarizing x_T..x_t
The hidden and cell states of one LSTM
questions.explanation: Forward pass sees the past through t; backward pass runs from the end toward t — each position's representation summarizes both directions of context.

questions.prompt: Bidirectional RNNs cannot be used in an autoregressive decoder because:
options: The backward pass needs future tokens that do not exist at inference, and would leak ground-truth targets during teacher-forced training
questions.explanation: Both failure modes stem from causality: unavailable future at generation time; label leakage at training time. The model would cheat during training and collapse in deployment.

questions.prompt: In a seq2seq model, the decoder is typically initialised from:
options: The encoder's final (per-layer) hidden and cell states for the complete source sequence
questions.explanation: The encoder's final states are the compressed source representation handed to the decoder as its starting memory — the design whose bottleneck motivated Bahdanau attention.

questions.prompt: In the 2020s, recurrent components still commonly appear in:
options: Frontier LLM pretraining at trillion-token scale
Streaming/edge tasks needing O(1) state, constant-memory inference and microsecond latency (plus modern state-space hybrids)
questions.explanation: Transformer dominance applies to parallel-pretrained, random-access language workloads; streaming detection, tight-latency control, and Mamba/RWKV-style hybrids are where recurrence's constant-state efficiency remains the right constraint match.

lessons.title: The Bottleneck That Motivated Attention
lessons.summary: Why squeezing a sentence into one vector must lose information, Bahdanau's additive attention as differentiable look-back, the encoder-decoder alignment it learned, and the logical step from attending over RNN states to attending directly over tokens.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe the seq2seq fixed-vector bottleneck and why it degrades with sequence length
Explain Bahdanau attention as a differentiable, learned lookup over encoder states with softmax weights
Compute attention weights from a toy alignment score matrix by hand
Trace the design evolution from attention-over-RNN-states to full self-attention (transformer)

payload.text: The 2014 neural translation model had one job and one weakness: compress an entire French sentence into a single vector, then unpack it into English. Researchers noticed the translation quality collapsed as sentences lengthened past ~20 words — and for a German sentence beginning "Ich reiste nach Berlin, wo ich drei Jahre..." the model would translate the opening beautifully only if it was SHORT, because by the end of the encoding, the details of the beginning had been smeared into statistical mush. The fix proposed was almost impertinently simple: at every generation step, let the decoder look back at ALL encoder positions and pick, by a learned softmax, which ones matter. That single idea — attention — is the seed of every large language model in existence.

**The fixed-vector bottleneck, stated formally.** The encoder maps a source sequence of length T_s to a finite state: either a single vector or a small set of layer-direction summaries (for a 2-layer BiLSTM: 4 x hidden floats total, say 1024 numbers). The decoder must generate from that alone. Information-theoretically, an arbitrary source sequence has unbounded entropy; a fixed-width vector cannot losslessly encode it, so SOMETHING must be discarded — and gradient descent discards whatever hurts the training objective least, which empirically is the low-frequency detail: names, numbers, long-distance agreements, word order in the middle. Empirical signature of the bottleneck: BLEU/accuracy vs sentence length curves drooping steadily after ~15-25 tokens; copy-style tasks (named entities) failing disproportionately. The same signature reappears, at far larger scale, as "lost in the middle" in long-context LLMs decades later — the bottleneck relocated, not eliminated, by naive pooling.

**Bahdanau attention: differentiable look-back.** Keep ALL encoder hidden states (h_1..h_{T_s}) — not just the last. At decoder step s, with its current state z_s, compute a compatibility score e_{s,t} = score(z_s, h_t) for every source position t (originally: a small feedforward net v^T tanh(W_1 z_s + W_2 h_t) — "additive" attention; later simplifications use dot products). Turn scores into weights with SOFTMAX: alpha_{s,t} = exp(e_{s,t}) / sum_k exp(e_{s,k}) — a learned, differentiable DISTRIBUTION over source positions (weights sum to 1; interpretable!). The context vector: c_s = sum_t alpha_{s,t} * h_t — a weighted average of encoder states, dominated by the positions the scorer found relevant. Decoder then computes its step from [z_s, c_s] instead of z_s alone. Crucially EVERYTHING is differentiable: the alpha weights are learned end-to-end by the same backprop that trains everything else — no external alignment tooling, no hard rules. Training implicitly learns ALIGNMENT: visualizing alpha over (source, target) positions reveals the model's soft word correspondences — "le" attending to "the", articles drifting under reordering — alignment discovered as a by-product of translation loss.

**What this fixed, quantitatively.** Translation quality stopped collapsing with length; the model could copy rare words by attending directly to them (name translation improved markedly); and the alpha matrix gave the field its first widely-used attention visualization (widely MISused too — attention weights are not causal explanations; correlation, not proof of use — a caution worth carrying into the LLM era's attention-map lore). The mechanism's conceptual jump: replace "remember everything through a chain" with "retrieve what you need, when you need it". Memory went from lossy sequential to indexed random access — scored by a learned query.

**From attention-over-states to self-attention to transformers — the three logical steps.** (1) ADDITIVE ATTENTION in seq2seq (Bahdanau 2014): decoder queries encoder states; positions in a chain of RNN outputs. (2) Luong/other score variants + multi-step refinements (2015-2016): dot-product scoring, better scoring functions; attention becomes standard inside NMT stacks. (3) THE OBSERVATION (Vaswani et al. 2017): if attending over RNN-generated states works well, why generate the states with an RNN at all? Every RNN-state already summarizes its prefix — but the summary is expensive and lossy. Compute CONTEXTUALIZED representations directly: let every position attend to every position of a raw embedding sequence — SELF-ATTENTION (queries, keys, values all from the same sequence) — stack it with feed-forwards, add positional information (positions have no recurrence to imply order), and you have the transformer. The RNN provided the sequence-modelling scaffolding attention was born inside; attention then replaced it entirely, because direct all-to-all interaction (a) removes the lossy sequential summary, (b) parallelizes across positions, (c) gives O(1) path length between ANY two positions instead of O(T) — long dependencies become one dot product away.

**The economic framing (why this matters for your course trajectory).** RNN era: each new long dependency paid a chain-tax (gradients and information both degrade over distance). Attention: dependency cost is flat in distance — position 1 reaches position 4096 as cheaply as position 4097. Everything in Part II of this course — multi-head attention, positional encodings, BERT/GPT, LLM training — is the direct maturation of the mechanism introduced in this lesson: a softmax-weighted retrieval of values guided by query-key compatibility. Learn it here as "learned, differentiable, content-based lookup" and the next module is expansion, not revelation.

payload.title: The bottleneck lineage
rows: All encoder states kept; softmax lookup per step
O(1) path to any source position

payload.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Bahdanau-style additive attention by hand on a toy step
# Decoder state at step s, encoder states h_1..h_3 (dim 4)
torch.manual_seed(0)
z_s = torch.randn(4)                       # current decoder state
H = torch.randn(3, 4)                      # three encoder states

W1, W2, v = torch.randn(4, 4), torch.randn(4, 4), torch.randn(4)

# Compatibility: e_t = v . tanh(W1 z + W2 h_t)
e = torch.stack([v @ torch.tanh(W1 @ z_s + W2 @ H[t]) for t in range(3)])
alpha = F.softmax(e, dim=0)                # learned distribution over source positions
print("scores:", e.round(decimals=2))
print("attention weights:", alpha.round(decimals=3), "sum =", alpha.sum().item())

context = alpha @ H                        # c = sum_t alpha_t * h_t  -> weighted average
print("context shape:", context.shape)     # [4] — the retrieval the decoder conditions on

# Note: alpha is fully differentiable; training the translation loss trains the
# alignment itself. Visualize alpha over (source, target) = classic alignment plots.

payload.title: Attention weights are a debugging tool, not proof
payload.text: High weight on token X does not prove the output DEPENDS on X (attention can be non-causal; value vectors and later layers may ignore it). For dependency claims, use ablation/causal tracing. Attention maps are great for spotting alignment failures (the model looking at the wrong source region) — exactly how they were first used in NMT.

payload.title: Do not "just average" encoder states as a modern substitute for attention
payload.text: Mean/last-state pooling recreates the 2014 bottleneck in miniature: fixed vector, position-blurred, detail-destroying. Pooling is fine for broad classification (where the head wants one summary), catastrophic for generation or precise extraction — anything that must RETIE specific content to specific positions.

payload.title: Compute additive attention over three encoder states
payload.problem: Decoder state z = [1.0, 0.0]. Encoder states: h_1 = [1.0, 1.0], h_2 = [0.0, 1.0], h_3 = [-1.0, 1.0]. Score function (given): e_t = 0.8 * (z · h_t) + 0.3. (a) Compute e_1, e_2, e_3. (b) Softmax them into alpha (use exp values e^1.1 = 3.00, e^0.3 = 1.35, e^-0.5 = 0.61). (c) Compute context c = sum alpha_t h_t. (d) Interpret: which source positions does this decoder step retrieve, and how would you expect c to change if z flipped to [-1.0, 0.0]?

steps.title: Softmax to attention weights
steps.desc: Denominator = 3.00 + 1.35 + 0.61 = 4.96. alpha = [3.00, 1.35, 0.61]/4.96 = [0.605, 0.272, 0.123]. Sums to 1 — a proper distribution: 60% of retrieval focused on position 1.

steps.title: Context vector
steps.desc: c = 0.605*[1,1] + 0.272*[0,1] + 0.123*[-1,1] = [0.605 + 0 - 0.123, 0.605 + 0.272 + 0.123] = [0.482, 1.0]. A weighted blend pulled toward h_1 (the state aligned with z's positive first coordinate).

steps.title: Flip z and predict the shift
steps.desc: z = [-1, 0]: scores become e_t = 0.8*(-h_t[0]) + 0.3 -> e_1 = -0.5, e_2 = 0.3, e_3 = 1.1 — EXACTLY reversed. Softmax: [0.123, 0.272, 0.605] — retrieval mass swings to h_3. The mechanism is content-addressed: matching query-key sign patterns select different memories. This query-dependent re-weighting per step IS the look-back that fixed seq2seq.
steps.code_snippet: z flipped: alpha -> [0.123, 0.272, 0.605]  (mass on h3)

payload.solution: Scores [1.1, 0.3, -0.5] -> weights [0.605, 0.272, 0.123] -> context [0.482, 1.0], dominated by h_1. Flipping the query z reverses the ranking entirely ([0.123, 0.272, 0.605], dominated by h_3): attention is a query-conditioned, softmax-normalized, differentiable retrieval — content-based addressing. From this mechanism to self-attention (query = key = value source: the sequence itself) is one conceptual substitution, which the next module executes.

payload.title: Visualize what attention learned
payload.prompt: Train a small seq2seq model (single-layer LSTM encoder/decoder with Bahdanau attention) on character-level reverse-copy or a tiny translation corpus. Plot the alpha matrix for a few sequences as a heatmap. Describe the structure you see for reverse-copy (expect a clear anti-diagonal) and for any real pairs (rough word alignment). Then state one failure case: a sequence where the heatmap is diffuse, and what that predicts about output quality.
payload.hint: Reverse-copy: position t in output attends to position T-t of input — diagonal stripe. Diffuse alpha everywhere = the model did not learn alignment = expect hallucinated or dropped content.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking attention replaced the encoder's need to represent context
mistakes.fix: Attention SELECTS among position representations; those representations still must be contextualized (RNN states did this, transformers do it via self-attention layers). Retrieval over uncontextualized embeddings is far weaker — representation and selection are complementary.

mistakes.mistake: Reading alpha heatmaps as causal explanations of model behaviour
mistakes.fix: Attention weights show where a head LOOKS, not what the output DEPENDS ON; values can be overwritten downstream and attention can be redundant. Use them for alignment debugging; use ablation for causal claims.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming the fixed-vector bottleneck disappeared with attention
mistakes.fix: It moved: attention gives random access within the attended window, but pooling-based embeddings (sentence vectors), truncated contexts, and KV-cache limits recreate fixed/limited-width summaries elsewhere. "Lost in the middle" results are the bottleneck's long-context echo.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping positional information once recurrence is removed
mistakes.fix: RNNs implied order through step sequence; self-attention is permutation-equivariant over positions — without positional encodings, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are identical input sets. Position must be re-injected explicitly (next module).

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the seq2seq fixed-vector bottleneck, describe Bahdanau attention's computation (scoring, softmax, context), and explain how it differs conceptually from full self-attention in transformers.
payload.answer: Bottleneck: a standard encoder-decoder compresses the entire source into the encoder's final finite state(s); since a fixed-width vector cannot losslessly encode an unbounded sequence, details are discarded, with translation quality degrading as length grows (empirically past ~15-25 tokens) — long-range specifics like names and middle-of-sentence structure are smeared out. Bahdanau attention: at each decoder step s, score every encoder state against the current decoder state — e_{s,t} = v^T tanh(W_1 z_s + W_2 h_t); normalize across source positions with softmax to get attention weights alpha_{s,t} (a learned distribution summing to 1); form the context c_s = sum_t alpha_{s,t} h_t, a differentiable weighted average emphasizing relevant positions; condition the decoder's next step on [z_s, c_s]. All components are trained end-to-end by the same loss, and the alpha matrix implicitly learns word alignment. Conceptual difference from self-attention: Bahdanau attention is CROSS-attention where the query comes from the decoder's recurrent state and keys/values are encoder outputs — a look-back into another sequence's RNN-computed states. Transformer self-attention instead computes queries, keys, AND values from the SAME sequence directly (no RNN states anywhere), lets every position interact with every position in one parallel step, and is stacked into the whole encoder/decoder — removing both the lossy recurrent chain and the sequential dependency across positions. Attention was born as an RNN accessory; self-attention promoted it to the primary sequence operator.
payload.source: The canonical "pre-transformer history" question in advanced DL courses; a favourite for testing whether attention's origin is understood, not just its equations.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Fixed-vector seq2seq loses information with length — details smear; quality droops past ~20 tokens.
Bahdanau attention: score (z, h_t), softmax to weights, weighted-sum context — differentiable, learned, interpretable alignment.
Attention converts lossy sequential memory into content-addressed retrieval: O(1) path to any source position.
Self-attention is the final substitution: Q, K, V all from the sequence itself — no RNN states, full parallelism, the transformer's core.
Attention weights debug alignment but do not prove causation; pooling recreates the bottleneck wherever it is used for precise tasks.

questions.prompt: The primary defect of fixed-vector seq2seq encoding is that:
options: It is too slow to train
A finite vector cannot losslessly hold an unbounded sequence, so details are discarded and quality degrades with length
questions.explanation: Information must be squeezed through a fixed-width state; gradient descent keeps what the loss needs most and discards the rest — showing up as length-dependent quality droop and name/copy failures.

questions.prompt: In Bahdanau attention, the context vector c_s at decoder step s is:
options: A softmax-weighted average of ALL encoder states, with weights from scoring compatibility with the current decoder state
questions.explanation: c_s = sum_t alpha_{s,t} h_t with alpha from softmax over e_{s,t} = score(z_s, h_t) — the differentiable retrieval that replaced reliance on the last state alone.

questions.prompt: Attention weights alpha_{s,t} are produced by a softmax over compatibility scores, which means they:
options: Sum to 1 across source positions and form a differentiable distribution trained end-to-end
questions.explanation: Softmax normalizes scores into a probability distribution (sum 1, positive, differentiable) — trainable with everything else, and interpretable as a soft alignment view.

questions.prompt: The conceptual step from Bahdanau attention to the transformer's self-attention was to:
options: Compute queries, keys, and values directly from the sequence itself instead of attending over RNN-generated encoder states — eliminating the recurrent chain and enabling full parallelism
Apply attention only to the final layer
questions.explanation: If attending over contextual states works, generate those states by attention itself: all positions interact with all positions in one parallel operation — the RNN, the sequential dependency, and the lossy prefix summary all removed at once.

modules.summary: Scaled dot-product attention computed with real matrices, queries/keys/values with plain-English glosses, multi-head attention as parallel subspaces, positional encoding and why permutation-equivariant attention needs it, encoder versus decoder stacks with masked attention, the BERT-vs-GPT objective split, the parallelism argument that killed recurrence, and FLOPs/parameter arithmetic for a transformer block.

lessons.title: Self-Attention Step by Step: Queries, Keys, Values, and the Scaling Factor
lessons.summary: The attention equation derived from content-based retrieval intuition, a full matrix computation with hand-computable numbers, why softmax and the sqrt(d_k) divisor are both load-bearing, and what one attention layer actually does to a sequence.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute Q, K, V projections and the full softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V product on a 3-token toy example
Explain each of Q, K, V using the database/retrieval analogy and map the analogy back to matrices
Justify the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling factor from the variance argument and predict what happens without it
State two properties of self-attention (permutation equivariance, all-to-all path length) and their consequences

payload.text: Here is the entire idea of self-attention in one sentence: for every position in a sequence, produce a QUESTION (query), match it against every position's LABEL (key) by dot product, softmax the matches into weights, and read out a weighted AVERAGE of the CONTENTS (values). That is it — a learned, differentiable dictionary lookup, executed for all positions in parallel, with all projections learned from data. Every large language model on earth is built from millions of copies of this one operation. This lesson computes it by hand until it is boring, which is the goal.

**The retrieval analogy, made exact.** You are at a library desk. Your request slip (QUERY) describes what you want. Every shelf carries a catalogue card (KEY) describing what it holds. You compute a match score between your request and every card (dot product: aligned vectors score high), convert scores into attention weights via softmax (a distribution over shelves: total budget 1, most-relevant shelf gets most weight), then read the weighted average of the shelf CONTENTS (VALUES — what you actually take away). The weights are query-dependent: a different request re-ranks the same shelves (this is exactly the z-flip demo from the last lesson). In transformers, the sequence itself plays all three roles: each position's embedding produces its own Q (via W_Q), K (via W_K), V (via W_V) — three learned linear projections of the SAME input. Hence SELF-attention: the sequence queries, labels, and serves itself.

**The equation, one line.** Given input X (sequence length T, model dimension d_model):

Q = X W_Q,  K = X W_K,  V = X W_V       (three linear maps, learned)
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) ) V

Read the shapes like a machine: Q is (T x d_k), K is (T x d_k), so QK^T is (T x T) — the ALL-PAIRS score matrix, where entry (i, j) scores how much position i's query matches position j's key. Row-wise softmax turns each row into a distribution over position j (over what position i attends to). Multiplying by V (T x d_v) mixes values: output row i = weighted average of all value vectors, weights = row i of the attention matrix. Output is (T x d_v): every position gets a contextualized representation in ONE step. Note the ingredients from earlier modules, all present: a linear projection (Module 1), softmax (Module 1.3/3.4), a weighted sum (the Bahdanau move), and parallelism across the T axis (where RNNs could not).

**Why the / sqrt(d_k) — the variance argument.** Suppose Q and K entries are i.i.d. with mean 0, variance 1, dimension d_k. Each dot product q·k = sum of d_k products: variance = d_k. So as d_k grows (64 -> 128), scores spread wider — with, say, d_k = 64, typical |score| ~ 8, and softmax of a vector with spread ±8 saturates: outputs become near-one-hot, gradients vanish (softmax's tail gradient dies — the saturation pathology from Module 1.2, now inside attention). Dividing by sqrt(d_k) rescales score variance back to ~1 for ANY d_k, keeping softmax in its informative gradient-rich region. Remove the scaling at large d_k and you train an attention layer that behaves like hard argmax with dead gradients. This is one of the paper's one-line details that carry real engineering weight.

**What softmax does here (and its inductive bias).** Row-softmax makes attention COMPETITIVE: positions bid for a fixed budget of 1 — increasing one weight necessarily decreases others (contrast with, e.g., sigmoid gating where each is independent). Consequences: context mixtures are always normalized averages (values can't all dominate); extreme competition can create attention-collapse (one position takes everything) — related to attention entropy discussions and to why some modern variants (e.g., sparse/max variants in research) tinker here. The zero-sum competition also makes attention patterns interpretable as distributions — the alignment plots of Module 4.4, now self-generated.

**Properties you must be able to derive.** (1) PERMUTATION EQUIVARIANCE without positions: self-attention treats input as a SET — permute rows of X and outputs permute identically (scores depend on content pairs, not indices). "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce identical per-position results absent position signals — hence positional encoding (next lesson) is MANDATORY, not decorative. (2) PATH LENGTH O(1): any position directly reaches any other in a single attention step — gradients and information do not traverse a chain (contrast Module 4's O(T) chain). This flat path length is why transformers learn long-range dependencies RNNs could not. (3) COMPUTE O(T^2 * d): the T x T score matrix is quadratic in sequence length — the famous quadratic-cost shadow of the architecture (memory/latency implications examined in lesson 5.4).

**What one layer does, practically.** For each token, output = its old embedding + (attention-weighted mix of contextual info from relevant positions) — attention LAYER 1 empirically tracks syntax (previous-token/next-token heads), deeper layers track coreference, semantic roles, and task-relevant relations (the mechanistic-interpretability head catalogue). Stack the operation with per-position feed-forward blocks (the "mixing across positions" then "processing each position" alternation) and you have the transformer block — lesson 5.3 assembles the full stack.

payload.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

torch.manual_seed(0)
T, d_model, d_k = 3, 4, 4                   # toy: 3 tokens, model dim 4

X = torch.randn(T, d_model)                 # embeddings of 3 tokens
W_Q, W_K, W_V = (torch.randn(d_model, d_k) for _ in range(3))

Q, K, V = X @ W_Q, X @ W_K, X @ W_V         # (3 x 4) each

scores = Q @ K.T                            # (3 x 3) all-pairs compatibility
scaled = scores / math.sqrt(d_k)            # <-- variance control: var(scores) ~ d_k
alpha = F.softmax(scaled, dim=-1)           # each ROW sums to 1: a distribution over positions
out = alpha @ V                             # (3 x 4): weighted mixture of values per position

print("scores\n", scores.round(2))
print("attention weights (rows sum to 1)\n", alpha.round(3))
print("output shape:", tuple(out.shape))    # (3, 4) — every position contextualized at once

# One-line functional form, exactly as in the paper:
def attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, mask=None):
    q, k, v = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    s = q @ k.T / math.sqrt(q.size(-1))
    if mask is not None:                    # future-masking arrives in lesson 5.3
        s = s.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf'))
    return F.softmax(s, dim=-1) @ v

payload.title: Read the attention matrix as a map of the model's moment
payload.text: Row i (position i's weights over positions j) answers "who is i consulting?". Diagonal-dominant rows = token mostly self-focused (identity-ish); previous-token rows = local syntax heads; a row pointing across a long gap = long-range dependency (coreference etc.). This matrix is the most human-readable activation in any transformer.

payload.title: Forgetting the sqrt(d_k) at larger dimensions silently kills training
payload.text: At small toy dimensions softmax still trains without scaling; at d_k = 64+ with typical init, scores saturate early and gradients die — a debugging mystery that looks like "the model is not learning attention". Always keep the scaling term; it is part of the definition, not an optional tweak.

payload.title: Compute scaled attention on 3 tokens by hand
payload.problem: After projections (already applied), for a 2-dimensional toy: d_k = 2, so sqrt(d_k) = 1.414. Queries/keys/values: q_1 = [2, 0], q_2 = [1, 1], q_3 = [0, 2]; k_1 = [2, 0], k_2 = [1, 1], k_3 = [0, 2]; v_1 = [1, 0], v_2 = [0, 1], v_3 = [1, 1]. (a) Compute the raw score matrix QK^T. (b) Scale by 1/1.414. (c) Row 1: softmax it (use scaled scores -? compute exp values), get alpha_1. (d) Compute position 1's output = alpha_1 · V. (e) Without scaling, what does row 1 look like, and why is that worse for gradients?

steps.title: Scale by 1/sqrt(2)
steps.desc: S/1.414 = [[2.83, 1.41, 0], [1.41, 1.41, 1.41], [0, 1.41, 2.83]]. Variance of scores back near 1 instead of 2; softmax will spread more evenly (softer weights, healthier gradients).

steps.title: Row 1 softmax (scaled)
steps.desc: exp: e^2.83 = 16.95, e^1.41 = 4.10, e^0 = 1. Sum = 22.05. alpha_1 = [16.95, 4.10, 1]/22.05 = [0.769, 0.186, 0.045]. Position 1 attends mostly to ITSELF (highest match), some to position 2, little to 3 — a plausible "previous-token/self" pattern.

steps.title: Output at position 1
steps.desc: out_1 = 0.769*[1,0] + 0.186*[0,1] + 0.045*[1,1] = [0.769 + 0.045, 0.186 + 0.045] = [0.814, 0.231]. A value mixture dominated by v_1 but contaminated with context from v_2, v_3 — the token's representation now knows its neighbors.

steps.title: The no-scaling contrast
steps.desc: Row 1 unscaled: scores [4, 2, 0] -> exp [54.6, 7.39, 1] / 63 = [0.867, 0.117, 0.016]. Sharper, but at d_k = 64 typical score spread is ±8: weights become ~one-hot (0.9999...), softmax gradient ~alpha*(1-alpha) ~ 1e-4 or smaller — the layer stops learning to attend. Scaling keeps scores in softmax's responsive band for any width.
steps.code_snippet: unscaled row1 = [0.867, 0.117, 0.016]  (and worse at d_k=64)

payload.solution: Scores [[4,2,0],[2,2,2],[0,2,4]] -> scaled by 1/1.414 -> row-1 weights [0.769, 0.186, 0.045] -> output [0.814, 0.231]: a contextually mixed representation for position 1, computed in ONE matrix operation with no recurrence. The scaling factor kept softmax out of saturation — remove it at realistic widths and attention degenerates into near-argmax with dead gradients. This 5-line computation, tiled across layers and heads, is the transformer.

payload.title: Build and probe attention on a real sentence
payload.prompt: Using PyTorch nn.MultiheadAttention (one head, batch_first), run attention over "the animal didnt cross the street because it was too tired" (tokenize simply, embed with random vectors of dim 64). Extract and print the attention matrix. Then: (a) identify which position attends most to which; (b) REPLACE the embedding of "tired" with a random vector and observe how row for "it" changes; (c) explain in two sentences whether this constitutes evidence that the model resolves coreference.
payload.hint: Random weights mean patterns reflect initialization, not learned structure — use this to learn the plumbing first; (c) should be an honest "no": one forward pass on random weights proves nothing about learned coreference (the attention-vs-causation caution).

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the sqrt(d_k) scaling because "softmax already normalizes"
mistakes.fix: Softmax normalizes WEIGHTS, not score magnitude — large raw scores still saturate softmax into hard argmax with vanishing gradients. Scaling controls the pre-softmax variance, a separate job.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming attention outputs are already position-aware
mistakes.fix: Pure self-attention is permutation-equivariant: content pairs determine scores, not indices. Without positional encoding, word-order information never enters — reordering the input merely reorders outputs identically.

mistakes.mistake: Reading QK^T scores as probabilities
mistakes.fix: Scores are unbounded compatibility logits; only after row-softmax do they become a distribution. Score matrices are asymmetric (row i's match to j differs from row j's to i) — attention is directed, not symmetric similarity.

mistakes.mistake: Believing one attention layer "understands" relationships
mistakes.fix: Early heads track local/syntactic patterns; semantic/coreference relations emerge across many layers and heads with residual paths. Judging capability from a single layer's weights misreads how depth composes the mechanism.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Write the scaled dot-product attention formula, explain the role of each component (Q, K, V, transpose, softmax, sqrt(d_k)), and derive why scores must be divided by sqrt(d_k).
payload.answer: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. Q, K, V are learned linear projections of the input sequence (Q = XW_Q etc.), each T x d_k (or d_v): Q holds per-position queries ("what am I seeking"), K per-position keys ("what do I offer"), V per-position values ("what content is available to read"). QK^T computes the T x T matrix of all query-key dot-product compatibility scores — position i versus position j — so the transpose aligns keys as columns for row-wise scoring. Row-wise softmax converts each row of raw scores into a probability distribution over positions (weights nonnegative, summing to 1) — the retrieval weights for that query. Multiplying by V yields, at each row, the weighted average of value vectors — the retrieved representation. Scaling derivation: assume query/key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1; then each dot product q·k = sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i has variance d_k (sum of d_k unit-variance terms). For d_k = 64, the standard deviation of raw scores is 8, pushing softmax into saturated regions where its derivative alpha(1-alpha) approaches zero and gradients vanish. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) rescales the score variance to approximately 1 independent of dimension, keeping softmax in the high-gradient regime — empirically essential at the widths real transformers use.
payload.source: The standard transformer question in every advanced DL exam and ML interview since 2018 — expect the variance derivation for full marks.

/sqrt(d_k) holds score variance at ~1 for any width — without it, softmax saturates and attention gradients die.
Attention is permutation-equivariant without positions (hence positional encoding) and gives O(1) path length between any pair of positions.

questions.prompt: In scaled dot-product attention, the matrix QK^T has shape:
questions.explanation: Q is T x d_k and K^T is d_k x T, so the product is T x T: entry (i, j) is position i's query matched against position j's key.

questions.prompt: The attention weights entering the weighted sum over V are obtained by:
options: Applying a linear layer to scores
Row-wise softmax over scaled scores, giving each row a distribution summing to 1
Taking the absolute value of scores
questions.explanation: softmax per query-row converts raw compatibility logits into a nonnegatve, sum-1 distribution over positions — the retrieval weights for that query.

questions.prompt: Dividing scores by sqrt(d_k) is necessary because:
options: It reduces memory usage by half

questions.explanation: With unit-variance components, q·k has variance d_k; sqrt(d_k) scaling returns variance to ~1, keeping softmax in its responsive gradient region for any dimension.

questions.prompt: Without any positional encoding, a stack of self-attention layers computes:
options: Permutation-equivariant results: reordering input tokens merely reorders outputs — no order information exists to learn

questions.explanation: Scores depend only on content pairs; the operation has no index awareness. "dog bites man" vs "man bites dog" yield identical per-position outputs — order must be injected explicitly.

lessons.title: Multi-Head Attention and Positional Encoding
lessons.summary: Why one attention distribution per position is too little, how h parallel heads in low-dimensional subspaces fix it, and the positional signals (sinusoidal, learned, relative) that make an order-blind operator sequence-aware.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute multi-head split/concat/projection shapes for a given model dim and head count
Explain why multiple heads in lower dimensions beat one full-width head, with the subspace/relationship-type argument
Compare sinusoidal vs learned absolute vs relative positional encodings on extrapolation and cost
Diagnose a position-handling bug (shuffled tokens, interpolation of positions) from symptoms

payload.text: Ask a single question about "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big" and you will find at most ONE relationship: who attends to whom with one set of weights. But the sentence contains several simultaneous relationships: syntactic attachment (did-not-fit -> suitcase), coreference (it -> trophy), semantic role (too big -> trophy). One attention distribution per token must choose ONE winner. The transformer's answer: run 8 or 64 attention computations side by side, each with its own learned projections — each free to specialize in a different relationship TYPE. Multi-head attention, plus the positional signals this lesson also covers, are the two structural upgrades that turn the raw mechanism from a demo into a language model.

**The single-head limitation.** One head outputs, at each position, ONE weighted mixture of values with ONE weight vector. Softmax rows are competitive (budget of 1): if "it" puts 0.7 on "trophy", the remaining 0.3 must cover everything else — attachment relations, local syntax, negation scope all compete for the same budget. Empirically single-head attention learns an averaged, blurry compromise across relationship types: good at none. (This is also why attention visualizations from single heads mislead — the model's actual computation is distributed.)

**Multi-head, mechanically.** With model dim d_model = 512 and h = 8 heads: split each projection bank into h groups of d_k = d_v = 64. Head i computes softmax(Q_i K_i^T / sqrt(64)) V_i independently (in PyTorch: one nn.MultiheadAttention does this as batched matmuls). Outputs CONCATENATED back to (T x 512), then a final output projection W_O: MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1..head_h) W_O. Total parameters: h heads x (d_model x d_k x 3) + final d_model x d_model — roughly the SAME as one full-width head doing 4 matmuls of 512x512 (because 8 x 512x64 = 512x512 per projection set: the splitting is a reshape, not a capacity change). So multi-head buys DIVERSITY (h independent softmax distributions in h learned subspaces) at constant parameter cost — the classic "spend compute on parallel perspectives" trade.

**Why low dimensions per head actually help.** Two arguments, both standard. (1) SUBSPACE SPECIALIZATION: each head's W_Q/W_K projections choose a 64-dim slice of the 512-dim content space — attention patterns operate on RELATIONSHIPS as seen through that slice. One head can encode one relation pattern; h heads can encode h simultaneously (empirically: heads specialize to previous-token, next-token, delimiter-matching, coreference, positional-bias patterns — the interpretability head catalogue). (2) SOFTMAX REITS: each head has its own competitive budget — head 3 can put 0.9 on "trophy" for coreference while head 5 spends 0.9 on the local previous token for syntax. With one head, these would fight; with h heads, they coexist. Dimension-per-head also keeps score variances tame (the sqrt(64) scaling), echoing lesson 5.1's argument. (Practical nuance: heads are NOT guaranteed distinct — redundancy is measurable, and "attention head pruning" research shows many heads are removable or mergeable.)

**Positional encoding: giving order to an order-blind operator.** Self-attention is permutation-equivariant (5.1); sequence tasks are not. Fix: add a positional signal to the embeddings (or, in later designs, inject relative position information inside attention). Two families:

ABSOLUTE (Vaswani's original): PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d}), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(same) — a fixed sinusoidal code where each dimension oscillates at a different frequency, so any offset produces a LINEAR transform of the pattern (allowing the model to learn relative offsets: PE(pos + k) relates to PE(pos) by a fixed rotation-like mixing), and positions are bounded in [-1, 1], enabling modest extrapolation beyond training length (original paper: unseen lengths generalized OK because sinusoids are smooth functions of position — though modern evidence shows this advantage is weaker in practice than hoped). LEARNED absolute: nn.Embedding(max_len, d_model) trained like everything else — simple, dominant in practice (GPT-2/3 style), but hard-capped at max position index (GPT-2: 1024 — extend by interpolating weights, imperfectly). RELATIVE/ROPE: Rotary Position Embeddings rotate Q and K by position-dependent angles so attention SCORES depend only on (i - j) — relative distance, exactly. RoPE is the 2023-2026 LLM standard (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek): it extrapolates better than learned absolutes, respects translation structure of language, and interacts cleanly with long-context extensions (NTK/YaRN interpolation methods all manipulate RoPE's frequency bands). ALiBi (press et al.): linear distance penalties on scores — another strong extrapoloation option.

**Selection guide.** New vision/classic transformers: learned absolute or sinusoidal, both fine. Modern LLMs: RoPE, essentially universally. Long-context work: RoPE with frequency scaling — the engineering surface of context extension (lesson 5.4's compute story is its other half). Key exam point: ANY of these must accomplish the same thing — make the model distinguish "position 2 then 3" from "3 then 2"; permutation equivariance is a property of the attention OPERATION, and position must be injected somewhere (embeddings, attention scores, or both).

payload.title: Positional encoding options
rows: Hard cap at max_len (interpolate to extend)
Rotates Q and K inside attention
Best of family — extend via frequency scaling (YaRN/NTK)
Added as score bias by distance

payload.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, math

# Multi-head: the split, done transparently
d_model, h, T = 512, 8, 10
x = torch.randn(T, d_model)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (nn.Linear(d_model, d_model) for _ in range(3))   # ONE big projection...
q, k, v = Wq(x), Wk(x), Wv(x)

def heads(t):                                    # ...then split into h subspaces
    return t.view(T, h, d_model // h).transpose(0, 1)   # (h, T, d_k)
Q, K, V = heads(q), heads(k), heads(v)

scale = math.sqrt(d_model // h)                  # sqrt(d_k) PER HEAD (64 -> 8)
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-1, -2) / scale         # (h, T, T): one score matrix PER head
alpha = scores.softmax(-1)
head_out = alpha @ V                             # (h, T, d_k)
concat = head_out.transpose(0, 1).reshape(T, d_model)   # back to (T, 512)
out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)(concat)        # output projection W_O
print(out.shape)                                 # [10, 512] — same width, 8 perspectives

# Sinusoidal positional encoding (original transformer)
def sinusoidal_pe(max_len, d_model):
    pos = torch.arange(max_len).unsqueeze(1).float()
    i = torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float()
    angle = pos / (10000 ** (i / d_model))
    pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model)
    pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(angle)
    pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(angle)
    return pe
print(sinusoidal_pe(100, 512).shape)             # [100, 512]

# Rotary (RoPE) intuition — rotate q,k by position: score(q_i, k_j) depends on (i - j)
def rope(angle, vec):                            # 2D block rotation
    c, s = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle)
    return torch.stack([vec[..., 0::2] * c - vec[..., 1::2] * s,
                        vec[..., 0::2] * s + vec[..., 1::2] * c], -1)

payload.title: Head count vs head dim: keep d_k ~ 64
payload.text: Common configs: 8 heads x 64 (d_model 512), 16 x 64 (1024), 32 x 64-128 (4096+). The pattern: d_model grows, heads grow, d_k stays in the 64-128 band where scaling and specialization work well. When reading a model card, d_model / heads gives you d_k instantly.

payload.title: Extrapolating learned absolute positions past max_len is a silent failure
payload.text: Ask a GPT-2-style model (learned PE, max 1024) for 2000 positions and the embedding lookup either errors or forces ad-hoc index remapping — quality drops with no crash. RoPE's frequency-scaling tools (YaRN etc.) exist precisely because position extrapolation is an engineering surface, not an automatic property.

steps.title: Per-head shapes
steps.desc: Per head: Q, K are (T x d_k) = (128 x 64); V is (128 x 64). All 8 heads together: (8, 128, 64) as a batched tensor; scores per head: (8, 128, 128). Concat after: (128, 512).

steps.title: Attention parameter parity
steps.desc: Multi-head: W_Q = 512 x 512, W_K = 512 x 512, W_V = 512 x 512, W_O = 512 x 512 — total 4 x 512 x 512 = 1,048,576. Splitting into heads is a reshape of the SAME projection matrix (8 x [512 x 64] = 512 x 512 per projection). "One 512-wide head": identical 4 matrices — IDENTICAL parameter count. Multi-head = free diversity.

steps.title: Full block parameters
steps.desc: Attention: 1,048,576 (+ biases negligible). FFN: 512 x 2048 + 2048 x 512 = 1,048,576 + 1,048,576 = 2,097,152 (often no bias in modern LLMs). Block total ≈ 3,145,728 (+ norms ~1k). FFN share: 2.10M / 3.15M ≈ 66.7% — two-thirds of block parameters live in the per-token FFN, not attention (despite attention's fame).

steps.title: Distributions per position per layer
steps.desc: 8 heads = 8 independent softmax rows per position per layer (each a full distribution over T positions). Across L layers: 8L retrievals per token. The model's "who consults whom" computation per layer per token is genuinely multi-perspective — the reason single-head visualizations never told the whole story.
steps.code_snippet: 8 softmax distributions per position per layer

payload.solution: (a) Per head Q/K/V: 128 x 64; per-head score matrix 128 x 128. (b) Multi-head and full-width variants use the SAME four 512x512 projections — parameter parity (1.05M); heads are free parallel perspectives via reshaping. (c) Block ≈ 3.15M params, FFN holding ~67%. (d) 8 independent attention distributions per position per layer. The economics: attention buys diversity at no parameter cost, and the FFN — not attention — carries most block capacity.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking each head computes attention over different TOKENS
mistakes.fix: Every head sees the same sequence; heads differ in their PROJECTIONS (which subspace of content they compare) and their learned scoring behaviour — not in which positions exist. Heads = different questions asked of the same text.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming multi-head costs quadratic extra parameters
mistakes.fix: Splitting d_model into h heads of d_k = d_model/h keeps total projection parameters constant (h * 3 * d_model * d_k = 3 * d_model^2). Diversity comes from h separate softmax operations and subspaces, not from added weights.

mistakes.mistake: Believing sinusoidal encodings are what modern LLMs use
mistakes.fix: The 2017 paper's sinusoids were largely displaced by learned absolute embeddings (GPT/BERT era), and those by RoPE (LLaMA era). If your exam/interview answer says "all transformers use sine waves", it is two generations stale.

mistakes.mistake: Adding positional encoding twice or forgetting it entirely in a custom model
mistakes.fix: Typical design: add absolute PE to embeddings exactly once at input (or use RoPE inside attention INSTEAD) — doing both or neither are both real implementation bugs; symptoms: shuffled-token sensitivity vanishing, or double-counted position priors.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain multi-head attention: how it is computed, why parameters do not increase relative to a single full-width head, and what it buys. Then compare sinusoidal and learned positional encodings, naming the modern default for LLMs and why.
payload.answer: Computation: the input is projected to Q, K, V of full width d_model, reshaped into h heads of dimension d_k = d_model/h; each head independently computes softmax(Q_i K_i^T / sqrt(d_k)) V_i over the same sequence; the h outputs (T x d_v each) are concatenated to (T x d_model) and passed through an output projection W_O. Parameter parity: projections are h separate d_model x d_k maps per Q/K/V — which sum to d_model x d_model each (h * d_k = d_model), identical to a single full-width projection; splitting is a reshape of the same learned capacity. Benefit: h independent softmax distributions in h learned low-dimensional subspaces — heads can specialise in different relationship types (local syntax, coreference, delimiter matching, positional biases) simultaneously, instead of competing for one softmax budget of 1 per position; empirically this multi-perspective capacity improves quality at constant parameter cost (redundancy across heads notwithstanding). Positional encodings: sinusoidal — fixed sin/cos functions at geometric frequencies, added to embeddings; no training parameters, modest extrapolation by smoothness. Learned — a trainable embedding table indexed by absolute position; simple, matches training distribution, but hard-limited to max position and retraining/interpolation needed to extend. Modern LLMs overwhelmingly use ROTARY (RoPE) — a relative scheme rotating Q and K so scores depend on position DIFFERENCES, with frequency scaling for long-context extension — as the de facto default (LLaMA/Mistral/Qwen/DeepSeek); learned absolute remains common in vision transformers.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Multi-head: h independent attention computations in h subspaces, concatenated + output-projected — diversity at constant parameters.
Each head gets its own softmax budget: multiple relationship types coexist instead of competing for one weight distribution.
Keep d_k around 64-128; heads scale with model width, not the other way around.
Positional information is mandatory (permutation equivariance otherwise): sinusoidal or learned absolute added to embeddings; RoPE (relative) is the modern LLM default.
Position extrapolation beyond training length is an engineering problem — learned absolute fails silently, RoPE needs frequency scaling.

questions.prompt: Multi-head attention with d_model = 512 and 8 heads uses d_k = 64 per head. Total projection parameters versus a single full-width head are:

questions.explanation: h separate d_model x d_k projections sum to d_model x d_model each for Q, K, V — exactly a full-width projection; the split is a reshape, not added capacity.

questions.prompt: The main functional benefit of multiple heads is that:
options: Each head processes a different sentence in the batch
Each head computes an independent attention distribution in its own learned subspace, letting different relationship types be captured simultaneously
Heads reduce the quadratic cost of attention
questions.explanation: One head must spend a single softmax budget across all relations; h heads each get their own — specialization (syntax, coreference, positional patterns) coexists rather than averaging into a blur.

questions.prompt: Rotary position embeddings (RoPE), now standard in LLMs, work by:
options: Adding a learned vector to each embedding
Rotating queries and keys by position-dependent angles so attention scores depend on relative position (i - j)
Concatenating position indices to the input
questions.explanation: RoPE encodes position as rotation of Q/K; the inner product after rotation depends on the angular difference — relative distance — which extrapolates and scales for long context better than absolute lookup embeddings.

questions.prompt: A model with learned absolute positional embeddings of max_len = 512 asked to process 800 tokens will:
options: Automatically learn positions 513-800 on the fly
Fail or require out-of-range handling — the embedding table has no rows beyond 511, and any ad-hoc extension degrades quality silently
questions.explanation: A finite learned table ends at max_len; running past it forces truncation, index remapping, or interpolation — all degrade without a hard crash. This extrapolation gap is a key reason RoPE displaced learned absolutes.

Distinguish encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder models by objective, mask, and use case
State what cross-attention queries/keys/values come from in a seq2seq transformer

payload.text: Two models, identical attention mechanism, opposite world-views. BERT reads a sentence with BOTH sides visible, hides 15% of tokens, and must guess them from context — a reader's skill: cloze, comprehension, classification. GPT sees only the left context and must produce the very next token — a writer's skill: continuation, generation. Same blocks, one difference — the MASK — and from that fork grew the entire modern model taxonomy: understanding models vs generation models vs the seq2seq middle path that translation built. This lesson assembles the architecture, then explains the fork.

**The encoder stack (BERT's body).** N identical blocks (12 in BERT-base, 12-96 in modern encoders). Each block: (1) multi-head SELF-attention over the whole sequence — every position attends to every position (bidirectional, NO mask); (2) position-wise feed-forward network: FFN(x) = W_2 · gelu(W_1 x) applied independently at each position with expansion (d_model -> d_ff = 4 x d_model -> d_model) — the "think about the gathered info" step; (3) residuals + layer norms around each sublayer, PRE-norm in modern variants (x + Sublayer(LN(x)) — ResNet's lesson, applied everywhere) with post-norm in the original 2017 formulation (LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))). Input: token embeddings + positional encodings. Output at each position: a contextualized representation used for classification, tagging, or as keys/values for a decoder.

**The decoder stack (GPT's body, and translation's second half).** Same skeleton with two differences: (1) MASKED (causal) self-attention — position i may attend only to positions <= i, enforced by setting all score entries where j > i to negative infinity BEFORE softmax (they become weight 0 exactly). Masked attention makes each output depend only on left context — the legal foundation for autoregressive generation and the direct formal descendant of Module 4's "decoders must be causal" rule. (2) In encoder-decoder transformers, an additional CROSS-ATTENTION sublayer between masked self-attn and FFN: queries from the decoder's current states, keys and values from the ENCODER's outputs — Bahdanau attention with dot-product scoring and multiple heads, unchanged in spirit. A decoder-only LLM (GPT/LLaMA) simply omits the cross-attention (no encoder) — full-length causal self-attention over the prompt+generation.

**Causal masking, computed.** For T = 4, the mask is a lower-triangular 0/1 matrix: row i allows columns 0..i. Implementation: scores.masked_fill(upper_triangle, -inf), then softmax — rows become distributions over the visible prefix only (row 3 sums weights over all 4; row 0 only over itself: a position can always attend to itself). The causal property is what makes training massively parallel DESPITE generation being sequential: during teacher-forced training, ALL next-token predictions are computed in ONE forward pass (each position's output already only saw its prefix — no leakage), while INFERENCE must still generate one token per step (feed back the last token, recompute attention with the growing KV cache — lesson 5.4's efficiency story).

**The three model families, and the fork's cause.** ENCODER-ONLY (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT): bidirectional self-attention, no mask, pretrained with MASKED LANGUAGE MODELLING (hide 15% of tokens, predict them — plus NSP in original BERT) and typically fine-tuned for classification, QA extraction, tagging — understanding tasks where the whole input exists. DECODER-ONLY (GPT family, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek): causal masked self-attention, NEXT-TOKEN PREDICTION objective, pretrained autoregressively and used for generation, chat, reasoning — anything you prompt. ENCODER-DECODER (original transformer, T5, BART, mBART, NMT systems): bidirectional encoder + masked decoder + cross-attention, pretrained with span corruption (T5) or denoising; traditional strength: translation, summarization, tasks with distinct input/output modalities. The 2018-2020 history: BERT dominated understanding benchmarks, GPT-1/2 showed scaling of generative pretraining, and by GPT-3 (2020) the "one causal model for everything via prompting" view began winning the market — today's LLM landscape is overwhelmingly decoder-only, with encoder-decoder persisting in translation/summarization products and encoder-only in classification-as-a-service. The masks differ; the blocks do not.

**Reading a spec sheet, finally.** "12-layer, 768-dim encoder with 12 heads" = BERT-base: 12 blocks, d_model 768, d_k 64, bidirectional. "32-layer decoder, 4096-dim, 32 heads, d_ff 11008" = a LLaMA-7B-class model: 32 masked blocks, d_k 128, SwiGLU FFN expansion ~2.7x with gate — decode it all from Module 5's vocabulary: blocks = layers, dims = d_model, heads -> d_k, FFN dims, and the mask tells you which family. (For the parameter counting that makes "7B" mean something, the next lesson does the arithmetic.)

payload.title: Three families, one mechanism
rows: Generation, chat, code, reasoning — modern LLM default

payload.code:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
import math

# Causal mask: the one line that makes generation legal
T = 4
scores = torch.randn(T, T)
causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T))               # lower triangle = 1
scores_masked = scores.masked_fill(causal == 0, float('-inf'))
alpha = F.softmax(scores_masked, dim=-1)
print(alpha.round(3))
# row 0: [w, 0, 0, 0]      <- attends only to itself
# row 1: [w, w, 0, 0]      <- prefix of length 2
# row 3: [w, w, w, w]      <- full visibility (all are "past" of position 3)
assert torch.allclose(alpha.triu(diagonal=1), torch.zeros(T, T))  # strict future = 0

# Transformer block (pre-norm, modern ordering)
class Block(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=512, h=8, ffn=2048):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = torch.nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.attn = torch.nn.MultiheadAttention(d, h, batch_first=True)
        self.ln2 = torch.nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.ffn = torch.nn.Sequential(
            torch.nn.Linear(d, ffn), torch.nn.GELU(), torch.nn.Linear(ffn, d))
        self.register_buffer('mask', torch.triu(torch.ones(999, 999), 1) == 0)

    def forward(self, x):
        a, _ = self.attn(self.ln1(x), self.ln1(x), self.ln1(x), attn_mask=self.mask)
        x = x + a                                  # residual around sublayer 1
        x = x + self.ffn(self.ln2(x))               # residual around sublayer 2
        return x

# Cross-attention (seq2seq decoder sublayer): Q from decoder, K/V from encoder
# cross_attn(query=dec_x, key=enc_out, value=enc_out)

payload.title: The mask tells you the family before the name does
payload.text: Reading a new model's code: attention with no mask -> encoder; lower-triangular mask -> decoder-only; both a triangular mask AND a cross-attention call to encoder outputs -> encoder-decoder seq2seq. One grep for triu/masked_fill classifies any architecture.

payload.title: Post-norm vs pre-norm changes training stability, not capacity
payload.text: Original 2017 post-norm (LN after residual) needed warmup care and capped practical depth; pre-norm (x + Sublayer(LN(x))) trains deeper stacks stably with less warmup sensitivity — modern default. If a deep model diverges early in training, LN placement is one of the first suspects.

payload.problem: Decoder-only model, d_model = 8, 2 heads, T = 4 tokens. (a) State the sublayer order in one block and what each sublayer does at position 2 specifically (which positions can masked self-attn at position 2 see?). (b) A cross-attention in an encoder-decoder variant at position 2: what do Q, K, V come from, and what is K/V's length? (c) Compute the number of score entries zeroed by the causal mask at T = 4, and the general formula. (d) Given per-head d_k = 4, verify the scaling divisor for this model.

steps.title: Block order and position 2 visibility
steps.desc: Pre-norm order: LN -> masked MHA -> residual add -> LN -> FFN -> residual add. At position 2 (0-indexed), masked self-attention may attend to positions 0, 1, 2 — row 2 of the attention matrix has exactly 3 nonzero weights (columns 3 forced to 0 by the mask), each summing to 1 across those 3. Position 2's output depends only on tokens 0-2 — causal by construction.
steps.code_snippet: pos 2 sees cols {0,1,2};  col 3 masked -> weight = 0

steps.title: Cross-attention sources
steps.desc: Q = projections of the DECODER's current hidden states (length T_dec: at step s, the positions generated so far); K, V = projections of the ENCODER's outputs (length T_enc: the complete source). So the decoder's question is answered from the full input — this is Bahdanau's c_s = sum alpha h_t, now with learned Q/K/V projections and h heads. Score matrix shape: (T_dec x T_enc), unlike square self-attention.
steps.code_snippet: Q: [T_dec, d];  K,V: [T_enc, d];  scores: [T_dec, T_enc]

steps.title: Mask arithmetic
steps.desc: Full score matrix: T^2 = 16 entries. Masked (strict upper triangle, j > i): T(T-1)/2 = 4*3/2 = 6 entries set to -inf -> exactly 0 after softmax. General: for length T, T(T-1)/2 of T^2 entries are zeroed — about half the matrix at large T, i.e., causal models still compute (and store) the full square matrix in naive implementations, only relying on the mask for correctness (which is where FlashAttention-style skipping earns its memory savings).
steps.code_snippet: T=4: 6 of 16 entries masked;  general: T(T-1)/2

steps.title: Scaling check
steps.desc: d_model = 8, h = 2 -> d_k = 8/2 = 4. sqrt(d_k) = 2. Scores = QK^T / 2. The divisor uses PER-HEAD d_k, not d_model — using d_model (sqrt(8) = 2.83) would under-scale by 41%, a subtle but real mismatch.
steps.code_snippet: d_k = 8/2 = 4;  scale = sqrt(4) = 2

payload.solution: (a) LN -> masked self-attn -> residual -> LN -> FFN -> residual; position 2 sees only positions 0-2. (b) Cross-attn: Q from decoder, K/V from encoder outputs — scores are (T_dec x T_enc), the sequentiel look-back upgraded to multi-head. (c) 6 of 16 entries masked at T=4; T(T-1)/2 generally. (d) scale = sqrt(d_k) = sqrt(4) = 2 — the per-head dimension, never d_model. Four details, each a place implementations go subtly wrong; each a favourite exam check.

payload.hint: Full document + label = encoder (bidirectional); generation = decoder-only (causal); two-language transformation with distinct input/output = encoder-decoder with cross-attention.

mistakes.mistake: Applying cross-attention between two decoder sequences in a decoder-only LLM
mistakes.fix: Decoder-only models have NO encoder and NO cross-attention — everything is causal self-attention over one stream (prompt + generation). Cross-attention exists only in encoder-decoder architectures (T5, NMT). Mislabeling sublayers confuses audits of any new model.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the mask during training but using it at inference (or vice versa)
mistakes.fix: Training without the mask lets each position see the answer (future tokens) and produces a model that fails at generation; inference without it is impossible anyway. Teacher forcing + mask is the consistent pair — check any custom loop for this exact inconsistency.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming BERT can generate text naturally
mistakes.fix: BERT's bidirectional masked objective never trains left-to-right continuation; text generation with BERT-style models requires awkward fill-in schemes (and is generally abandoned). Objective + mask define capability — architecture alone does not.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up where LayerNorm sits between pre-norm and post-norm when reading papers
mistakes.fix: Post-norm: LN(x + Sublayer(x)) — original transformer, harder to train at depth. Pre-norm: x + Sublayer(LN(x)) — modern default (GPT-2+ transition), stabilizes deep training. Schematics differ; code diffs are one line; exam answers get marked on the distinction.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the transformer decoder's masked self-attention: its purpose, mechanics (how masking is implemented), and its gradient/behavioural consequences. What does it make possible during training that sequential RNN generation could not do?
payload.answer: Purpose: enable autoregressive generation while keeping training parallel — each output position may depend ONLY on positions at or before it, mirroring the requirement that a generative model at inference sees no future tokens. Mechanics: before softmax, all score entries with key-position j > query-position i are set to -infinity (implementation: add a lower-triangular boolean/float mask, or masked_fill with -inf); softmax maps -inf to exactly zero weight, so row i of the attention matrix distributes its unit mass over positions 0..i only. (Formally the mask keeps the causal factorization p(x_1..x_T) = prod p(x_t | x_<t) consistent with training.) Consequences: the representation at position t is a function of the prefix only — legal at inference; row lengths differ per position so early positions have softmax over fewer entries; about half the score matrix is structurally zero. What it makes possible: with teacher forcing, the ENTIRE training sequence computes next-token logits at all T positions in ONE forward pass (all rows already satisfy causality), so training parallelizes across time — something the RNN's mandatory step-by-step recurrence could never do (Module 4's sequential wall). Inference remains sequential by nature (each new token depends on previous ones), optimized with KV caching rather than recomputation.
payload.source: Standard transformer-mechanics exam/interview question; the training-parallelism point is what links it back to the RNN comparison.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Encoder = bidirectional self-attn + FFN per block (BERT): whole input visible, understanding tasks.
Decoder = masked causal self-attn + FFN (GPT), plus cross-attention (Q from decoder, K/V from encoder) when a source exists.
Causal masking = lower-triangular -inf before softmax: rows distribute weight over the prefix only — generation-legal, training-parallel.
Objectives fork the lineage: masked prediction (BERT, encoder) vs next-token (GPT, decoder) vs denoising (T5, enc-dec).
Pre-norm residuals + per-head d_k scaling + correct mask placement: the implementation details where architectures silently break.
