lessons.title: Compression: Quantization, Distillation, and Pruning
lessons.summary: Post-training int8/int4 with a per-weight error bound you can compute, distillation as temperature-scaled KL, and pruning from magnitude sparsity to hardware N:M — plus the bandwidth arithmetic that makes compression change latency.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Quantize and dequantize a tensor symmetrically and bound the per-weight error at s/2
Compute memory and decode-bandwidth effects of fp32/fp16/int8/int4 representations
Formulate temperature-scaled distillation loss with the T^2 gradient-scale correction
Choose between unstructured, structured, and N:M pruning by the hardware that will run it

payload.text: A 1.7B-parameter assistant needed 3.4 GB in fp16 — the phone target was under 1 GB. The winning recipe was not one trick: int4 weights (0.79 GiB), a distilled student trained from the original, and 2:4 structured sparsity on the accelerator that supported it. Compression is a stack of techniques, each with a number attached — and every number in this lesson is small enough to compute by hand before you run anything.

**Quantization: integers with a scale.** Symmetric per-tensor int8: pick s = max|w| / 127, map w -> q = clamp(round(w/s), -127, 127), dequantize with q x s. Rounding error per weight is at most s/2 — the whole accuracy question is how big s gets: per-OUTPUT-CHANNEL scales shrink s for outlier channels (a channel with max|w| = 2.0 no longer drags the whole tensor's s upward); per-group scales (groups of 128, GPTQ/AWQ style) shrink it further at the cost of one scale per group (fp16 scale per 128 weights = 1.56% storage overhead — 26.6 MB for 1.7B weights, negligible). ACTIVATIONS are harder: they have dynamic range and token outliers, so W8A8 schemes calibrate activation ranges (SmoothQuant migrates activation outliers into weights), while WEIGHT-ONLY formats (W4A16) keep activations fp16 and dequantize weights into fp16 GEMMs — the practical default for open models. Quality cliff: ~8-bit is usually lossless; ~4-bit with group scales + a little fine-tuning (or QAT — fake-quant in the training graph) stays within noise; below 4 bits expect visible degradation without QAT. Accuracy validation is ALWAYS task metrics (perplexity/accuracy delta vs fp16 baseline), never weight MSE.

**Distillation: transfer the distribution, not the labels.** Softmax at temperature T: p_i = exp(z_i/T) / sum — higher T flattens the distribution, exposing RELATIVE logits (the dark knowledge: "this image is 60% t-shirt, 30% pullover, 5% coat"). Loss: L = (1 - alpha) x CE(hard labels) + alpha x T^2 x KL(p_teacher^T || p_student^T). The T^2 factor compensates: softmax gradients scale as 1/T^2 at temperature T, so without it the soft term's gradients vanish as T grows and T becomes a noise knob instead of a sharpening knob. Why it works: the teacher's soft targets are a richer, lower-variance signal than one-hot labels — a small student trained on them beats the same student trained on labels alone (extra data need not be labeled — self-distillation from a bigger sibling).

**Pruning: remove weights, carefully.** Unstructured magnitude pruning: zero the smallest |w| (global or per-layer threshold) to a target sparsity (e.g., 90%); on dense kernels this buys NOTHING in wall-clock — memory only shrinks with sparse formats, and many stacks do not exploit them. STRUCTURED pruning removes whole channels/filters/attention heads → dense-but-narrower models that any kernel speeds up (measured speedup < theoretical because of fixed overheads and uneven layer sensitivity — prune iteratively: prune -> fine-tune -> re-evaluate, per layer). HARDWARE sparsity: N:M (2:4 = 2 nonzeros per 4-element group, 50%) is supported natively by Ampere+ tensor cores → ~2x math throughput with a post-training mask + brief fine-tune. The lottery-ticket finding: dense networks contain sparse subnetworks that, re-initialized, train to full accuracy alone — the theory behind why masks survive fine-tuning. Compose the stack: distill to a student, quantize the student, prune structured — each layer of the stack re-validated on the task metric.

payload.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# ---- symmetric int8: quantize, dequantize, bound ----
def quant_symmetric(w, axis=None):
    if axis is None:                                   # per-tensor
        s = w.abs().max() / 127
    else:                                              # per-output-channel
        s = w.abs().amax(dim=axis, keepdim=True) / 127
    q = (w / s).round().clamp(-127, 127).to(torch.int8)
    return q, s

q, s = quant_symmetric(torch.randn(1024, 512))
w_hat = q.float() * s
print("s:", s.item(), "| error bound s/2:", (s / 2).item())
print("int8 bytes:", q.numel(), "vs fp32:", q.numel() * 4)

# ---- temperature-scaled distillation loss ----
def distill_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T=4.0, alpha=0.7):
    soft = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1),
                    F.log_softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1),
                    reduction="batchmean") * (T * T)
    hard = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)
    return (1 - alpha) * hard + alpha * soft

# ---- magnitude pruning to target sparsity ----
def prune_(model, sparsity=0.9):
    for name, p in model.named_parameters():
        if p.dim() >= 2 and "weight" in name:
            k = int(p.numel() * sparsity)
            thresh = torch.kthvalue(p.abs().flatten(), k).values
            p.masked_fill_(p.abs() < thresh, 0.0)      # fine-tune after this!

payload.title: Validate compression on the task, not on weights
payload.text: Weight-space MSE says nothing about decision boundaries: a 4-bit tensor can look "close" and still flip the top-1 logit that matters. Always report task deltas vs the fp16 baseline — perplexity/accuracy/F1 — for every compression point you ship.

payload.title: Unstructured sparsity is a storage feature, not a speed feature
payload.text: 90% zeros on dense kernels runs at dense speed; memory saves only appear with sparse formats that many runtimes do not use. If latency is the goal, prune STRUCTURED (channels/heads) or use hardware-supported 2:4 — and measure end-to-end at the serving batch size, not a FLOPs calculator.

payload.title: Bound an int8 quantizer, size an int4 model, and compute a distillation term
payload.problem: Weights with max|w| = 0.08 quantized symmetric int8. (a) Scale s, the per-weight error bound, and the dequantized value/error for w = 0.0313. (b) A 1.7B model in fp32/fp16/int8/int4 (GiB) plus per-128-group fp16 scale overhead for int4. (c) Distillation: teacher probs [0.9, 0.1], student probs [0.6, 0.4] — KL(teacher || student) in nats, and the scaled soft term at T = 4. (d) Compare the hard-label CE for the same student prediction. (e) Bandwidth: on 1,555 GB/s HBM, theoretical decode ceiling for 1.7B fp16 weights vs int4 — tokens/sec per stream (weights-only model), and the ratio.

steps.title: (a) Scale and error bound
steps.desc: s = 0.08/127 = 6.299e-4; rounding puts every weight within s/2 = 3.15e-4 of its true value. For w = 0.0313: q = round(0.0313/6.299e-4) = round(49.69) = 50; dequantized = 50 x 6.299e-4 = 0.031496; error = 0.031496 - 0.0313 = 1.96e-4 — comfortably inside the 3.15e-4 bound. Per-channel scales would only shrink s further for this layer by removing cross-channel outlier influence.

steps.title: (b) Memory ladder
steps.desc: fp32: 6.33 GiB; fp16: 3.17 GiB; int8: 1.58 GiB; int4: 0.79 GiB (weights only). Scales at group 128 in fp16: (1.7e9/128) x 2 B = 26.6 MB ≈ 0.025 GiB — 3% of the int4 payload, acceptable. int4 hits the under-1-GB phone budget that fp16 (3.17 GiB) missed; activations/KV remain fp16 — the budget that decides context length (module 10.3).

steps.title: (c) KL and temperature scaling
steps.desc: KL(p||q) = 0.9 ln(0.9/0.6) + 0.1 ln(0.1/0.4) = 0.9 ln 1.5 + 0.1 ln 0.25 = 0.9(0.40546) + 0.1(-1.38629) = 0.36492 - 0.13863 = 0.22629 nats. Scaled at T = 4: T^2 x KL = 16 x 0.22629 = 3.62 nats — the soft term dominates when alpha = 0.7, as intended: it is the richer signal (full distribution vs one hot).

steps.title: (d) Hard label for comparison
steps.desc: CE = -ln(0.6) = 0.5108 nats for the one-hot truth. The teacher term carries the same target plus the runner-up structure (0.9 vs 0.6 margin AND the 0.1 vs 0.4 tail) — strictly more information per example at the cost of teacher inference. Note the asymmetry: KL is computed teacher-to-student (KL(p||q)), so the student is penalized for putting mass where the teacher puts none — never reverse the arguments.
steps.code_snippet: hard CE = -ln 0.6 = 0.5108 nats (soft carries more)

steps.title: (e) Bandwidth ceiling
steps.desc: Decode is weight-streaming bound: ceiling = HBM bandwidth / bytes-per-token-of-weights. fp16: 1.7e9 x 2 B = 3.4e9 B -> 1555/3.4 = 457 tok/s. int4: 1.7e9 x 0.5 B = 8.5e8 B -> 1555/0.85 = 1,829 tok/s. Ratio = 4.0x theoretical — real serving lands around 2.5-3.5x because KV reads, kernel launches, and sampling overheads occupy part of each step. The whole point of weight-only int4: decode is bandwidth-bound, so bytes/param IS tokens/sec.
steps.code_snippet: fp16 457 tok/s ; int4 1829 tok/s ; 4.0x ceiling

payload.solution: (a) s = 6.299e-4, bound 3.15e-4; w = 0.0313 -> q = 50 -> 0.031496 (error 1.96e-4). (b) 6.33/3.17/1.58/0.79 GiB; group scales +0.025 GiB. (c) KL = 0.2263 nats; T^2 KL = 3.62 at T = 4. (d) Hard CE = 0.5108 — the teacher distribution carries strictly more per-example information. (e) 457 vs 1,829 tok/s = 4.0x ceiling (2.5-3.5x in practice).

payload.title: Build the compression frontier for one model
payload.prompt: Take a fine-tuned classifier or small LM: (1) PTQ int8 (per-tensor vs per-channel) and int4 (group 128) — report task metric deltas vs fp16 and the exact memory table; (2) distill into a 4x-smaller student: sweep T in {1,2,4,8} and alpha in {0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9} — show why T=8 without enough alpha underperforms; (3) prune unstructured 50/80/90% and structured (channels) 25/50% — measure REAL latency at your serving batch size for each, and explain any zero speedup; (4) try 2:4 masking if hardware supports it; (5) compose two techniques (e.g., distilled student + int4) and verify the combined delta is not additive-worse; (6) present the frontier: quality vs memory vs latency with one recommended point per deployment target.
payload.hint: For (3), unstructured pruning latency staying FLAT on dense kernels is the expected lesson, not a bug. For (2), watch the soft loss magnitude: T^2 matters — check gradient scales at T=8 with and without it.

mistakes.mistake: Deriving scales from the whole tensor when channels differ wildly
mistakes.fix: One outlier channel inflates per-tensor s and wastes int8 levels on every other channel. Use per-output-channel (int8) or per-group-128 (int4) scales; the storage overhead (~1.5% at group 128) buys most of the accuracy you were about to lose.

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the T^2 factor in distillation
mistakes.fix: Softmax gradients shrink ~1/T^2 as T rises; without T^2 the soft term fades toward zero at high temperatures and T acts like a mute. Keep L = (1-a) CE + a T^2 KL so temperature controls SHARPNESS, not magnitude.

mistakes.mistake: Shipping unstructured sparsity as a latency win
mistakes.fix: Dense kernels process zeros like any number — no speedup; memory savings need sparse formats most runtimes lack. For latency, prune channels/heads (structurally narrower) or use hardware N:M (2:4) — and benchmark end-to-end at serving batch sizes.

mistakes.mistake: Compressing without a task-metric gate
mistakes.fix: Weight MSE or even a single forward-pass smoke test hides boundary flips. Gate every compression point on the full eval set (perplexity/accuracy/F1 vs fp16), plus a regression golden set — compression bugs ship silently otherwise.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe post-training quantization: give the symmetric int8 procedure, derive the per-weight error bound in terms of the scale s, and explain per-channel and per-group scaling. Then formulate the distillation objective with temperature and justify the T^2 factor, and contrast unstructured, structured, and N:M pruning by the speedups each can actually deliver.
payload.answer: Symmetric int8: s = max|w|/127 (per tensor) — or per output channel / per group of 128; q = clamp(round(w/s), -127, 127); dequantize q x s. Error analysis: round() places q within 0.5 of w/s, so |w - q s| <= s/2 per weight — e.g., max|w| = 0.08 gives s = 6.30e-4 and bound 3.15e-4. Larger s (driven by outliers) means larger absolute error across the tensor, which is why per-channel/group scales localize the max and shrink effective s at the cost of storing scales (fp16 per 128 weights = 1.56% overhead). Activations need calibration (W8A8) or stay fp16 (weight-only W4A16, the common open-model recipe). Distillation: L = (1-alpha) CE(hard) + alpha T^2 KL(p_t^T || p_s^T) with softmax at temperature T; higher T flattens distributions and exposes relative logits (dark knowledge); gradients of the T-softmax scale as 1/T^2, so the T^2 multiplier keeps the soft-term magnitude constant — T becomes a sharpness control instead of a volume control. Validate on task metrics vs the fp16 baseline, never weight MSE. Pruning: unstructured magnitude sparsity saves memory only with sparse formats and runs at dense speed on normal kernels (~no latency gain); structured channel/head pruning produces genuinely smaller dense models → real (if sub-linear) speedups on any hardware; N:M (2:4) is hardware-supported on Ampere+ tensor cores → ~2x math throughput at 50% sparsity with brief fine-tuning after masking — prune iteratively, re-validating the task metric each round.
payload.source: Deployment-heavy interview: "how would you get this model on a phone?" — numbers expected.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Symmetric int8: s = max|w|/127, error <= s/2; per-channel/group scales fight outliers cheaply.
Memory ladder: 6.33 / 3.17 / 1.58 / 0.79 GiB for fp32/fp16/int8/int4 at 1.7B.
Distillation: (1-a) CE + a T^2 KL(teacher||student); T^2 neutralizes the 1/T^2 gradient shrink.
Pruning: unstructured = storage only; structured = real speedup; 2:4 = hardware 2x — measure end-to-end.
Decode is bandwidth-bound: bytes/param IS tokens/sec — int4 gives a 4.0x theoretical ceiling.

questions.prompt: Symmetric int8 quantization with max|w| = 0.08 gives a per-weight error bound of:
questions.explanation: s = 0.08/127 = 6.299e-4; rounding guarantees error <= s/2 = 3.15e-4 for every weight in the tensor.

questions.prompt: In L = (1-alpha) CE + alpha T^2 KL(p_t || p_s), the T^2 factor is needed because:
options: Softmax gradients shrink approximately as 1/T^2 at temperature T — T^2 restores their magnitude
Cross-entropy is undefined at high T
questions.explanation: Without T^2 the soft term silently fades as T rises; with it, temperature controls distribution sharpness rather than loss scale.

questions.prompt: 90% unstructured magnitude pruning typically delivers on a dense GPU kernel:
options: About 1x — zeros still cost dense compute; memory saves need sparse formats
questions.explanation: Dense kernels waste the sparsity: latency stays ~flat unless the stack exploits sparse storage — for speed, prune structured or use hardware 2:4.

questions.prompt: Weight-only int4 improves decode speed mainly because decode is:
options: Memory-bandwidth-bound — streaming fewer weight bytes per token raises tokens/sec
questions.explanation: Each decode step streams the weights: ceiling = HBM bandwidth / bytes-per-token — 4.0x fewer bytes (fp16 -> int4) approaches 4.0x ceiling before overheads.

lessons.title: Serving and Evaluation in Practice
lessons.summary: TTFT versus TPOT and who is bound by what, the KV-cache budget formula, perplexity done comparably, contamination and judge bias in evaluation, and cost per million tokens with utilization honestly included.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decompose request latency into prefill and decode and classify each by its bottleneck
Compute KV-cache memory for GQA and MHA configurations from first principles
Design an evaluation suite resistant to contamination, batching artifacts, and judge bias
Convert GPU economics into cost per million tokens at stated utilization

payload.text: A team benchmarked their endpoint at "90 ms average latency" and shipped — then p99 hit 4 seconds under load and the product review went badly. The average hid queueing; the queueing hid batching; and their eval suite, it turned out, contained 5% of its test items in the training corpus. Evaluation and serving are where honest numbers are made or destroyed, and both fields run on arithmetic you already know.

**Latency has two regimes.** Every request = PREFILL (prompt processing: all prompt tokens in parallel — compute-bound, FLOPs dominated by attention's T^2 term; time-to-first-token TTFT is essentially prefill time plus queueing) and DECODE (one new token per step: sequential, memory-bandwidth-bound — stream weights + KV cache each step; tokens/second/sequence is the inverse of TPOT, time-per-output-token). End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + (n-1) x TPOT (n = new tokens): interactive products optimize TTFT and TPOT p99; offline batch jobs optimize aggregate throughput (bigger batches amortize weight streaming: throughput rises with batch until memory/KV limits — but interactive latency pays queueing for it). SCHEDULING: static batching waits for the longest sequence (wasted slots); CONTINUOUS (in-flight) batching admits/retires sequences per step — near-full utilization at chat latencies — plus prefix caching (shared system prompts skip re-prefill), chunked prefill (mix long prompts into decode without stalling), and speculative decoding (module 8.3) for TPOT. Report p50/p95/p99 AND throughput at a stated concurrency — never a single mean.

**KV-cache budget (the constraint behind every context-length claim).** Bytes = B x L x T x n_kv_heads x d_head x 2 (K and V) x bytes_per_elem. Llama-class example: L = 32 layers, d_head = 128, n_kv = 8 (GQA — recall module 5.4), T = 4096, fp16: ONE sequence = 2 x 32 x 4096 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 536,870,912 B = 0.5 GiB; B = 8 concurrent → 4.0 GiB (4.29 GB). Full MHA (n_kv = 32) → 4x that: 16.0 GiB (17.2 GB) — GQA's 4x saving, paid in a modest quality cost. KV grows LINEARLY in T and B: 32k context = 8x the T=4096 figure — which is why GQA, KV quantization (fp8/int8 KV), sliding-window attention, and paged KV (vLLM-style block management that kills fragmentation) are the serving stack's core, and why "supports 128k context" is a memory statement as much as a quality statement.

**Evaluation that survives contact with reality.** Layers: (1) OFFLINE held-out metrics — task metrics (accuracy/F1/PR-AUC), perplexity = exp(mean NLL) — but ppl is TOKENIZER-DEPENDENT (byte-BPE vs character models are not comparable — module 7.2's tokenizer is part of the metric); compare only within a tokenizer, or move to bits-per-byte/character for cross-model claims. (2) CONTAMINATION defense: measure n-gram overlap between train and test; with 5% contaminated items all memorized, a 70%-true model reports 0.95 x 70 + 0.05 x 100 = 71.5% — a free +1.5 points; decontaminate or switch test sets. (3) HUMAN/JUDGE preference — MT-Bench-style pairwise or rubric judging: LLM judges carry position bias (prefer the first/second answer — randomize order and average both), length bias (longer looks better — control or penalize), and self-preference (models favor their own style); calibrate the judge against a human-labeled subset (agreement %) before trusting it. (4) ONLINE A/B with guardrails (latency, safety, cost as non-inferiority gates) and rollback criteria. (5) PRODUCTION monitoring: golden-set regression in CI (a fine-tune may not move the suite), drift (input/embedding distribution), feedback loops (user edits become training data — filter them), safety/refusal suites re-run per release.

**Cost arithmetic.** Cost per 1M tokens = GPU $/hour x 3600 / (tokens/hour at stated utilization). Ideal: 2,000 tok/s → 7.2M tok/h → at $2.00/GPU-h: $0.278/M. At 70% utilization (batching reality, long prompts eating prefill): effective 1,400 tok/s → 5.04M/h → $0.397/M. Long prompts shift cost into prefill (compute) while long generations stream decode (bandwidth) — both billed in tokens, but they stress different bottlenecks; quote cost WITH the utilization assumption or the number is marketing.

payload.title: Latency and eval vocabulary
rows: Hides behind the mean; dominated by long prompts
Time per output token after the first
Batching raises throughput while worsening it
Shipping "average latency" alone conceals tail explosions
Plain accuracy lies on imbalanced sets

payload.code:
import time, statistics, math
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# ---- offline eval: perplexity from TOTAL NLL (not batch averages) ----
@torch.no_grad()
def perplexity(model, dl, pad_id=0):
    nll, tokens = 0.0, 0
    for input_ids, labels in dl:
        logits = model(input_ids.to("cuda"))
        nll += F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1).float(),
                               labels.to("cuda").flatten(),
                               ignore_index=pad_id, reduction="sum").item()
        tokens += (labels != pad_id).sum().item()
    return math.exp(nll / tokens)          # tokenizer-dependent: compare like for like

# ---- latency percentiles at a stated concurrency ----
def bench(send_request, prompts, concurrency=8, n=500):
    ttfts, tpots = [], []
    for i in range(n):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        r = send_request(prompts[i % len(prompts)])
        first = time.perf_counter() - t0
        ttfts.append(first)
        tpots.append((time.perf_counter() - t0 - first) / max(r.n_new - 1, 1))
    pct = lambda xs, p: sorted(xs)[int(p * len(xs))]
    return dict(ttft_p50=pct(ttfts, 0.5), ttft_p99=pct(ttfts, 0.99),
                tpot_p50=pct(tpots, 0.5), tpot_p99=pct(tpots, 0.99),
                concurrency=concurrency)      # always report the load too

# ---- judge calibration: swap order, both directions ----
def judge_pair(prompt, ans_a, ans_b, judge):
    s1 = judge(prompt, ans_a, ans_b)      # A first
    s2 = judge(prompt, ans_b, ans_a)      # B first
    return s1, s2                          # disagreement -> position bias in action

payload.title: One tokenizer, one perplexity
payload.text: Perplexity = exp(mean NLL) is meaningful only for models sharing the tokenizer — a character model can "beat" a BPE model by tokenizing differently. For cross-model claims use bits-per-byte (cross-entropy / ln 2 per byte), the tokenizer-invariant metric from module 7.

payload.title: Uncalibrated LLM judges are biased measuring instruments
payload.text: Position, length, and self-preference biases move win-rates by several points — enough to pick the wrong model in an A/B. Randomize order (score both directions), control length, and publish judge-human agreement on a labeled subset before any "model X beats Y" claim.

GPU: 1,555 GB/s HBM, $2.00/hour, sustained 2,000 tok/s at stated load. (a) TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end latency for the request. (b) KV-cache bytes per sequence and for the batch; same batch with full MHA (n_kv = 32). (c) Mean NLL 2.3026 — perplexity; why it cannot be compared to a character-level model. steps.title: (b) KV-cache budget
steps.desc: Per sequence: 2 (K,V) x 32 layers x 4096 T x 8 heads x 128 dim x 2 B(fp16) = 536,870,912 B = 0.5 GiB. Batch 8: 4.0 GiB (4.29 GB) — before weights and activations. Full MHA (n_kv = 32, 4x): 16.0 GiB (17.2 GB) for the same batch — GQA saved 12 GiB here, and at T = 32,768 every figure multiplies by 8 (GQA batch = 32 GiB). This is the arithmetic behind "context length x concurrency" capacity planning.
steps.code_snippet: GQA: 0.5 GiB/seq, 4.0 GiB x8 ; MHA: 16.0 GiB x8

steps.title: (c) Perplexity
steps.desc: PPL = exp(mean NLL) = exp(2.3026) = 10.00 — a model whose average next-token distribution gives the true token probability 1/10 behaves like a uniform 10-way guess on average. Comparability: PPL is per-TOKEN, and tokens differ across tokenizers (BPE merges vary; one model might get an easier segmentation) — report within-tokenizer only, or use bits-per-byte = mean NLL (nats) / ln 2 per byte for cross-family claims (module 7.2).
steps.code_snippet: exp(2.3026) = 10.00 ; cross-tokenizer -> bits-per-byte

steps.title: (d) Cost per million tokens
steps.desc: Ideal: 2,000 tok/s x 3600 = 7.2M tok/h → $2.00 / 7.2 = $0.278 per 1M tokens. At 70% utilization (queueing, prefill overhead, imperfect batching): effective 1,400 tok/s → 5.04M tok/h → $2.00/5.04 = $0.397/M. Quote the second number in capacity planning: utilization assumptions are the difference between a 43% cost error and an honest budget.
steps.code_snippet: ideal $0.278/M ; at 70% util $0.397/M

steps.title: (e) Contamination inflation
steps.desc: Measured = 0.95 x 70% + 0.05 x 100% = 66.5 + 5.0 = 71.5% — a free +1.5 points for nothing, and that is the OPTIMISTIC case (memorized items score perfectly; partially leaked sets inflate less but still move leaderboard positions). Defense: n-gram overlap scan between train and test, decontamination before splitting, sealed fresh test sets, and live A/B where contamination cannot help.

payload.solution: (a) TTFT 40 ms, TPOT 25 ms, total 2,515 ms. (b) GQA 0.5 GiB/seq, 4.0 GiB for batch 8; MHA 16.0 GiB — linear in B and T. (c) PPL = 10.00; tokenizer-dependent — use bits-per-byte across families. (d) $0.278/M ideal, $0.397/M at 70% utilization. (e) 71.5% measured (+1.5 inflated) — decontaminate and A/B.

payload.title: Benchmark and evaluate like a serving team
payload.prompt: Against any local or hosted model: (1) measure TTFT and TPOT p50/p95/p99 across 3 prompt lengths and concurrency 1/4/16 — show the throughput-vs-latency curve and where queueing starts; (2) compute the KV-cache table for your model/config at T = 1k/8k/32k and batch 1/8/32 — verify one cell with torch (allocate and measure); (3) report perplexity for two models WITH the same tokenizer, and bits-per-byte if tokenizers differ; (4) contamination audit: n-gram overlap your eval set against a public corpus (or your train split) and recompute a score after removing hits; (5) run a judge pairwise eval with order swapped — quantify position bias (disagreement rate) and calibrate against 20 human-labeled pairs; (6) write the cost model: tokens/hour at measured utilization, $/M, with the assumption sheet attached.
payload.hint: For (1) expect TPOT to worsen with concurrency while aggregate tokens/s rises — that crossing IS the interactive/offline trade. For (5), disagreement above ~10% means the judge is measuring order, not quality.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting mean latency without percentiles or load
mistakes.fix: Means hide queueing tails; p99 at concurrency 8 is the user experience. Always publish p50/p95/p99 with the stated concurrency, prompt-length mix, and batch settings — otherwise the number is not reproducible and the tail is invisible.

mistakes.mistake: Static batching for an interactive product
mistakes.fix: Waiting for the slowest sequence in the batch inflates everyone's TPOT; continuous/in-flight batching retires finished sequences per step and keeps slots full. Interactive = continuous batching; offline throughput jobs = big static batches.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing perplexities across tokenizers
mistakes.fix: PPL is per-model-token: a tokenizer that merges more aggressively gets an easier denominator. Compare within one tokenizer, or convert to bits-per-byte (nats/byte / ln 2) — the only honest cross-family language-model comparison.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting an LLM judge without order-swaps and calibration
mistakes.fix: Position and length biases shift win-rates enough to reverse conclusions. Score both answer orders, control length, and report agreement with human labels on a subset — an uncalibrated judge is an instrument with unknown bias.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define TTFT and TPOT, classify each by its computational bottleneck, and derive the end-to-end latency for a 100-token completion given prefill and decode rates. Give the KV-cache memory formula, compute it for a GQA configuration, and contrast with MHA. Finally, lay out an evaluation plan covering perplexity comparability, contamination, judge calibration, and cost per million tokens.
payload.answer: TTFT = time to first token = queueing + prefill; prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel — compute-bound (attention T^2 grows quadratically with prompt length). TPOT = inter-token latency after the first = one decode step: sequential, memory-bandwidth-bound (stream weights + KV per token; batching amortizes weights but adds queueing). E2E = TTFT + (n-1) x TPOT: prefill 2,048 @ 51,200 tok/s = 40 ms; decode 40 tok/s → TPOT 25 ms; 100 tokens → 40 + 99 x 25 = 2,515 ms. KV cache bytes = B x L x T x n_kv x d_head x 2 x bytes/elem: L=32, T=4096, n_kv=8, d=128, fp16, B=1 → 2x32x4096x8x128x2 = 0.5 GiB; B=8 → 4.0 GiB; MHA (n_kv=32) → 4x = 16 GiB — linear in B and T, which is why GQA, KV quantization, sliding windows, and paged KV exist. Evaluation: (1) perplexity = exp(mean NLL) computed from total NLL/token counts (never batch-average) and only within a tokenizer (bits-per-byte across families); (2) contamination — n-gram overlap scan; 5% leaked + memorized turns 70% into 71.5%; (3) LLM judges — order both ways, control length, calibrate against human labels; (4) online A/B with latency/safety/cost guardrails and rollback rules; (5) cost = $/GPU-h x 3600 / tokens-at-stated-utilization: 2,000 tok/s → 7.2M tok/h → $0.278/M ideal, $0.397/M at 70% — quote the utilization or the price is fiction.
payload.source: The systems-interview pairing: "explain your latency and defend your eval" — asked together at serving teams.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: TTFT = compute-bound prefill (+ queueing); TPOT = bandwidth-bound decode; E2E = TTFT + (n-1) x TPOT.
KV bytes = B x L x T x n_kv x d x 2 x bytes — linear in batch and context; GQA-8 example: 0.5 GiB/seq vs 4x for MHA.
PPL = exp(mean NLL) from totals; tokenizer-dependent — cross-family claims use bits-per-byte.
Contamination (5% leak = +1.5 pts) and judge bias (position/length/self) are measurable — measure them.
Cost/M tokens = GPU$/h x 3600 / (tok/s x 3600 x utilization) — always state utilization.

questions.prompt: Decode (token-by-token generation) is primarily bound by:
options: Memory bandwidth — streaming weights and KV cache per token
questions.explanation: Each step reads the weights (and KV) to produce one token: bytes-per-token divided by HBM bandwidth is the throughput ceiling — exactly what int4/quantized KV attack.

questions.prompt: A GQA model with L=32, T=4096, n_kv=8, d_head=128, batch 8, fp16 needs for the KV cache:
questions.explanation: 2x32x4096x8x128 = 2^28 elements x2 B = 0.5 GiB per sequence; x8 batch = 4.0 GiB (MHA with 32 KV heads would be 16 GiB).

questions.prompt: Perplexity values are directly comparable between models only when:
options: Both have the same parameter count
Both use the same tokenizer (otherwise use bits-per-byte)
questions.explanation: PPL = exp(mean NLL) is per model-token; tokenizers segment differently — cross-family comparison needs the tokenizer-invariant bits-per-byte.

questions.prompt: The cost of 2,000 tok/s on a $2.00/GPU-hour device at 70% utilization is about:
questions.explanation: Effective 1,400 tok/s → 5.04M tok/h → 2.00/5.04 = $0.397/M — utilization assumptions belong in every price you quote.

lessons.title: CAPSTONE: Design an End-to-End Deep Learning System
lessons.summary: The full design doc — requirements to monitoring with every number attached — plus the frontier it must face: mixture-of-experts memory versus compute, RoPE and long-context KV growth, multimodal token spaces, and on-device int4 economics.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Produce a complete system design: requirements, data, model, training, evaluation, serving, monitoring
Compute serving budgets: tokens/day to GPU-hours to dollars with headroom
Reason about MoE, long-context, and on-device trade-offs with concrete arithmetic
Define quality/safety gates and rollback criteria before shipping anything

payload.text: Every module of this course has been a section of one document. A design that says "fine-tune an LLM, evaluate with a judge, deploy on GPUs" is not a design — it is a wish. The capstone asks for the other kind: constraints with numbers (p99, $/M tokens, safety gate), data with provenance, an evaluation suite that has survived contamination checks, and monitoring that tells you when to roll back. The frontier architectures later in this lesson are new entries in the same document — same questions, different arithmetic.

**The design doc, in seven sections.** (1) REQUIREMENTS: task definition, quality bar vs a baseline (metric + minimum improvement + confidence), p99 latency, cost ceiling per 1M tokens or per request, safety/privacy constraints, and the rollback criteria you will accept BEFORE training. (2) DATA: sources with consent/licensing, dedup and quality filters (module 7.1 at your scale), labeling plan and agreement stats, split hygiene (time/entity, sealed test), PII handling. (3) MODEL: build vs fine-tune vs distill — the capacity-vs-data evidence from 10.1, parameter count against your D ≈ 20N compute view (7.3), quantization target chosen with 10.2 numbers, and a documented reason the frontier option (MoE, long context) was or was not chosen. (4) TRAINING: objective, schedule with LR/accumulation arithmetic (9.4), instrumentation from step 0 (grad-norm/LR/scale traces), checkpoint/resume policy, and budget (GPU-hours from the C = 6ND view). (5) EVALUATION: golden set (contamination-audited), task metrics with baselines, judge calibration if used, ablation plan (change one thing), safety/refusal suite, human spot-checks. (6) SERVING: endpoint shape from 10.3 — TTFT/TPOT targets, batching mode (continuous for interactive), KV budget at target context and concurrency, quantized weights, cost model at stated utilization, canary/rollback. (7) MONITORING: drift (input and output distributions), latency/cost dashboards, feedback capture (edited responses as noisy labels — filter before reuse), retraining triggers, incident runbook. Quality GATES: ship only if (a) metric >= bar with margin, (b) p99 and cost within budget, (c) safety suite passes, (d) golden set shows no regressions — four gates, any failure = no ship.

**The frontier, priced.** MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS: total parameters large, ACTIVE per token fixed — 8-expert style model at 47B total / 13B active: weights (all loaded, fp16) = 47e9 x 2 B = 94 GB = 87.5 GiB (memory cost is TOTAL), while per-token compute tracks the active slice: 13/47 = 28% of a dense-47B's FLOPs. You pay memory for the whole routing table of experts and compute only for what you route — plus load-balancing aux losses (router collapse = hot expert = wasted capacity) and expert-parallel communication. LONG CONTEXT: rotary (RoPE) encodes relative position by rotation — extrapolation needs position remapping (position interpolation / NK/YaRN-style scaling) because attention scores were trained for seen relative distances; costs are arithmetic: KV grows linear in T (10.3: 4096 → 32,768 = 8x KV), attention FLOPs grow quadratically in T (5.4: 8x T = 64x the T^2 part) — hence sliding windows, chunked attention, sparse/linear attention research. MULTIMODAL: project patches/audio into the SAME token stream (connector + shared transformer) or keep modality-specific towers with alignment objectives (module 6.3); generation side: discrete tokens vs diffusion heads (8.4) — evaluation adds FID/CLIP-score plus preference, never replaces the human bar. ON-DEVICE: int4 weights (1.7B = 0.79 GiB) fit phones alongside activations and OS budget; but sustained throughput is thermal-bound and the CPU/NPU memory hierarchy punishes big KV — small context, aggressive caching, and distillation are the pattern; privacy/offline benefits are product features, not footnotes. The constants through ALL of it: data quality, honest evaluation, instrumentation, and cost accounting — this course, applied.

payload.title: Capstone gate checklist
rows: Metric >= baseline + margin on sealed, decontaminated test
One-command revert, canary %, alert thresholds defined

payload.code:
# ---- capstone budget sheet: requirements -> dollars ----
REQS = dict(requests_per_day=1_000_000, new_tokens_per_request=500,
            ttft_p95_ms=800, tpot_p95_ms=40, cost_per_1m_budget=0.60)

tokens_per_day = REQS["requests_per_day"] * REQS["new_tokens_per_request"]   # 5e8
tok_per_s_needed = tokens_per_day / 86_400                                   # 5,787 tok/s avg
gpu_tok_per_s = 2_000                                                         # measured, stated util
gpus = -(-tok_per_s_needed // gpu_tok_per_s)                                 # ceil -> 3
gpu_hours_per_day = gpus * 24
usd_per_day = gpu_hours_per_day * 2.00                                       # $2.00/GPU-h
usd_per_1m = usd_per_day / (tokens_per_day / 1e6)                            # $/M at that load
print(dict(tokens_per_day=tokens_per_day, gpus=int(gpus),
           usd_per_day=round(usd_per_day, 2), usd_per_1m=round(usd_per_1m, 3)))

# ---- MoE vs dense: memory TOTAL, compute ACTIVE ----
total, active = 47e9, 13e9
fp16_gib = total * 2 / 2**30          # 87.5 GiB loaded (all experts)
act_frac = active / total             # 0.277 -> ~28% of dense-47B FLOPs
print(fp16_gib, round(act_frac, 3))

payload.title: Write the rollback criteria before the first training step
payload.text: Gates defined after results arrive are negotiation, not engineering. Fix the metric bar, p99, cost ceiling, safety pass, and the revert command in the design doc — then the ship decision is a checklist anyone can run.

payload.title: Frontier architecture is not a requirement
payload.text: MoE buys compute-per-token at the price of memory, routing complexity, and serving machinery; 128k context buys retrieval breadth at the price of KV memory and quadratic attention. A distilled, quantized 7B fine-tuned on clean domain data beats a badly evaluated frontier model on every gate that matters — choose with arithmetic, not fashion.

payload.title: Run the capstone budget: traffic, experts, context, and gates
payload.problem: Service: 1,000,000 requests/day, 500 new tokens each; measured 2,000 tok/s per GPU; $2.00/GPU-hour; budget $0.60 per 1M tokens. (a) Tokens/day, average tok/s required, GPUs (ceil), GPU-hours/day, $/day, $/1M — does it pass the budget? (b) Add 30% headroom — new $/day and $/1M. (c) Alternative model: MoE 47B total / 13B active — fp16 weight memory, active-compute fraction vs a dense 47B, and what memory/compute conclusion a designer draws. (d) Context 4,096 → 32,768 for the GQA serving config of 10.3 (per-sequence KV, batch 8): KV memory now, and the attention-FLOPs multiplier. (e) int4 on-device: 1.7B weights in GiB, and the four gates this phone build must pass.

steps.title: (a) Traffic to dollars
steps.desc: tokens/day = 1e6 x 500 = 5e8. Average rate = 5e8 / 86,400 = 5,787 tok/s. GPUs = ceil(5,787/2,000) = 3 (4 would idle ~43%, so provision 3 with autoscale to 4 at peaks). GPU-hours = 3 x 24 = 72 → $144/day at $2.00. $/1M = 144 / 500 = $0.288/M — passes the $0.60 budget with 52% margin (headroom you can spend on quality: better eval, more retries).
steps.code_snippet: 5e8 tok/day ; 5,787 tok/s ; 3 GPUs ; $144/day ; $0.288/M OK

steps.title: (b) Headroom
steps.desc: +30%: 3.9 GPUs → provision 4 (round UP — you cannot rent 0.9 of a GPU), 96 GPU-h → $192/day; $/1M = 192/500 = $0.384/M — still inside $0.60. Alternatively keep 3 GPUs and accept queueing risk: the design doc must state which (headroom vs queueing p99) you chose and why; the p99 gate from 10.3 decides.
steps.code_snippet: 4 GPUs : $192/day ; $0.384/M (budget $0.60 — passes)

steps.title: (c) MoE arithmetic
steps.desc: Weights fp16: 47e9 x 2 B = 94e9 B = 87.5 GiB — ALL experts loaded (memory follows TOTAL params: needs tensor/expert parallelism, or int4 → 21.9 GiB, comparable to a dense 13-14B). Compute: active 13/47 = 0.277 → ~28% of dense-47B FLOPs per token — decode is bandwidth-bound (10.2) so the win shows up as fewer bytes streamed per token too, IF expert weights are fetched only when routed (irregular memory access is the systems tax). Conclusion: MoE = memory-heavy, compute-light per token — buy it when serving volume amortizes the machinery, not as a default.
steps.code_snippet: 87.5 GiB fp16 (21.9 GiB int4) ; active 13/47 = 0.277 FLOPs

steps.title: (d) Context scaling
steps.desc: T: 4096 → 32,768 = 8x. KV (linear): per-sequence 0.5 → 4.0 GiB; batch 8: 4.0 → 32.0 GiB (34.4 GB) — near the wall for an 80 GB card alongside weights and activations; mitigations from the lesson: GQA already applied, KV fp8/int8 (halve), sliding window (cap effective T), paged allocation (fragmentation). Attention FLOPs (quadratic): 8x T = 64x the T^2 term — prefill TTFT grows visibly; that is the true cost of "supports 32k".
steps.code_snippet: 8x T : KV x8 (32 GiB/b8) ; attention FLOPs x64

steps.title: (e) Phone build + gates
steps.desc: int4: 1.7e9 x 0.5 B = 8.5e8 B = 0.79 GiB of weights — fits a phone budget with activations/context in the remainder (and thermal limits cap sustained tok/s: bursty, cache-heavy design). Gates for shipping it: (1) quality — task metric >= baseline on the sealed, decontaminated set; (2) latency — p95 TTFT/TPOT on-device targets met under thermal steady state, not cold burst; (3) cost/UX — fits battery/memory budget (the mobile analogue of $/M); (4) safety + regression — on-device suite passes, golden set unchanged, one-command rollback via app channel.
steps.code_snippet: 0.79 GiB int4 ; gates: quality, thermal p95, resource, safety/rollback

payload.solution: (a) 5e8 tok/day, 5,787 tok/s, 3 GPUs, $144/day, $0.288/M — passes $0.60. (b) +30% → 4 GPUs, $192/day, $0.384/M — still passes. (c) MoE: 87.5 GiB fp16 weights (all experts) with 28% of dense-47B active FLOPs — memory-heavy, compute-light. (d) 8x context → 8x KV (32 GiB at batch 8) and 64x attention FLOPs — mitigate with KV quantization/sliding window/paging. (e) int4 = 0.79 GiB weights; ship only through the four gates: quality, thermal latency, resource budget, safety + rollback.

payload.title: Write and defend the capstone design
payload.prompt: Pick a real problem (campus document QA, code assistant, demand forecasting, medical-image triage — any domain). Deliver: (1) a design doc covering all seven sections with NUMBERS — quality bar vs baseline, p99, $/M at stated utilization, data provenance + split hygiene; (2) a scaled-down proof: fine-tune or prompt a small model, build a contamination-audited golden set, report task metrics + baselines + one ablation; (3) compress it (10.2): pick a quantization/distillation point on a measured quality-memory frontier; (4) a serving plan (10.3): batching mode, KV budget at your context/concurrency, TTFT/TPOT targets, cost sheet; (5) one frontier paragraph: you chose MoE / long-context RoPE / multimodal / on-device — or explicitly declined, with the arithmetic that decided it; (6) monitoring + rollback: dashboards, drift signals, gates, revert command. Be ready to defend every number.
payload.hint: The strongest documents read as arithmetic chains: requirement -> measurement -> budget -> gate. If a number has no source (measured, cited, or derived), it is a wish — cut it or measure it.

mistakes.mistake: Designing without pre-registered gates
mistakes.fix: Bars set after seeing results are negotiation. Write metric bar, p99, cost ceiling, safety pass, and rollback command BEFORE training — then the ship call is mechanical and reviewable by anyone.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting cost or latency without utilization and load
mistakes.fix: $/M at "ideal" throughput and mean latency at concurrency 1 both collapse under real traffic. State utilization, concurrency, prompt-length mix, and batching mode with every performance number — or the budget is fiction.

mistakes.mistake: Adopting a frontier architecture to look current
mistakes.fix: MoE doubles down on memory and serving complexity; 128k context multiplies KV and attention cost 8-32x. Quantify the requirement first (retrieval breadth? tokens/s?) — a distilled, quantized, well-evaluated small model usually wins the gates that matter.

mistakes.mistake: Eval suite assembled the week before launch
mistakes.fix: Contamination, judge bias, and missing baselines surface too late to fix cheaply. Build the golden set + baselines + judge calibration EARLY (module 7.1 decontaminate, 10.3 calibrate), run it in CI every change — the capstone is a continuous discipline, not a final exam.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Design an end-to-end deep learning system for a high-traffic text assistant: specify requirements (quality/latency/cost), data and split hygiene, model selection reasoning (including when NOT to use a frontier architecture), training instrumentation, evaluation suite, serving configuration, and monitoring with rollback. Include: traffic-to-dollars arithmetic for 1M requests/day at 500 tokens/request on 2,000 tok/s GPUs at $2/h; the MoE memory-vs-compute distinction for a 47B/13B-active model; and the KV/attention costs of going from 4k to 32k context.
payload.answer: Requirements: task + metric bar vs baseline with margin, p99 TTFT/TPOT at target concurrency, $/M ceiling at stated utilization, safety constraints, rollback criteria — all pre-registered. Data: consented sources, dedup/quality filters, labeling agreement, time/entity splits with a sealed decontaminated test set, PII handling. Model: capacity-vs-data evidence (10.1), compute view C = 6ND / D ≈ 20N (7.3), quantization target from 10.2 (e.g., int4 for decode bandwidth), and decline MoE/128k unless the arithmetic demands it — MoE 47B/13B-active loads 87.5 GiB fp16 (all experts = memory follows TOTAL) while per-token compute is 13/47 ≈ 28% of dense-47B: memory-heavy, compute-light, with routing/serving complexity as the tax; a distilled quantized 7B often clears the gates cheaper. Training: LR/accumulation schedule in optimizer steps, grad-norm/LR/scale traces from step 0, atomic full-state checkpoints, budgeted GPU-hours. Evaluation: golden set (contamination-audited — 5% leak can add +1.5 points), baselines, ablations, judge calibration with order-swaps if used, safety suite, CI regression. Serving: continuous batching for interactive use, KV budget = B x L x T x n_kv x d x 2 x bytes — 4k→32k is 8x KV (GQA batch 8: 4→32 GiB) and 64x attention FLOPs (T^2), mitigated by KV quantization, sliding windows, paged allocation; cost arithmetic: 5e8 tokens/day → 5,787 tok/s → 3 GPUs → $144/day → $0.288/M (4 GPUs at +30% headroom = $0.384/M), both under a $0.60/M budget. Monitoring: drift, latency/cost dashboards, feedback filtering, retraining triggers, canary + one-command rollback. Ship only through the four gates: quality, latency, cost, safety/golden-set — any failure blocks release.
payload.source: The capstone question: identical to defending this course's final project in an architecture review.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Seven sections: requirements (pre-registered gates) -> data -> model -> training -> evaluation -> serving -> monitoring/rollback.
Budget chain: 5e8 tok/day -> 5,787 tok/s -> 3 GPUs -> $144/day -> $0.288/M (4 GPUs w/ headroom = $0.384/M).
MoE: memory follows TOTAL params (87.5 GiB fp16 at 47B), compute follows ACTIVE (13/47 ≈ 28%).
Long context: KV x linear (8x at 32k), attention FLOPs x quadratic (64x) — pay in memory and TTFT.
Ship through gates only: quality, p99, cost, safety + golden set — with a rollback command already written.

questions.prompt: A MoE model at 47B total / 13B active parameters:
options: Loads ~87.5 GiB of fp16 weights (all experts) while running ~28% of dense-47B FLOPs per token
Is always smaller than a dense 13B
questions.explanation: Memory follows TOTAL (all experts resident: 47e9 x 2 B = 87.5 GiB); per-token compute follows the active slice (13/47 = 0.277) — memory-heavy, compute-light.

questions.prompt: Going from 4,096 to 32,768 context (8x) multiplies the attention FLOPs by:
questions.explanation: Attention over T positions is quadratic in T: (8)^2 = 64x for the attention term — while the KV cache grows linearly (8x).

questions.prompt: Serving 1M requests/day x 500 tokens at 2,000 tok/s per GPU ($2/h) requires about:
questions.explanation: 5e8 tok/day -> 5,787 tok/s -> ceil to 3 GPUs -> 72 GPU-h -> $144/day -> $0.288 per 1M tokens.

questions.prompt: The four ship gates for a capstone system are:
options: Quality, latency, cost, and safety/golden-set regression (plus a written rollback)
Training loss, val loss, test loss, leaderboard
questions.explanation: Any failing gate blocks release; rollback criteria are written before training so the ship decision is a checklist, not a negotiation.

courses.title: Generative AI Essentials
courses.subtitle: Forty deep lessons from generative foundations to a production GenAI spec — mechanics, models, reliability, cost, applied pipelines, safety and compliance
courses.description:
Most GenAI courses stop at the demo: a prompt that worked once, a slide about transformers, a list of tools. This one starts where those end. Forty lessons, ten modules, one exam bank and a capstone that forces the whole thing into a single defensible document — the spec you would actually put in front of a team.

It runs from the generative landscape (GANs, VAEs, diffusion, the transformer, foundation models) down into LLM mechanics — tokenization, embeddings, the sampling pipeline, the KV cache — then out to the decisions engineers actually make: open versus closed weights, small models versus frontier APIs, context windows, image/audio/video pipelines. From there it is reliability (hallucination, grounding, structured outputs, guardrails, evals), cost engineering (token arithmetic, caching, routing, quality-per-rupee), applied patterns (summarization that keeps the numbers, extraction, classification, code generation with tests as the oracle), safety and compliance (memorisation, copyright, data governance, DPDP and the EU AI Act), and a capstone that assembles all of it into a spec with a cost model, a failure register and a rollout plan.

**Who this is for:** anyone who has taken a basics GenAI course — or watched a demo — and wants the engineering underneath it. Developers shipping features, students preparing for AI rounds, product people who must evaluate a vendor's claim, and anyone tired of "the model said so".

**What you need:** basic AI literacy (you know what an LLM is and have used a chat assistant). No coding required — the Python snippets are read-only worked examples. You will write, not code, for the capstone.
outcomes: Distinguish generative from discriminative models and explain how the transformer plus foundation-model pretraining powers every modality
Trace the full sampling pipeline — logits, temperature, top-k/top-p — and the serving controls that steer and cut generation
Choose between open and closed weights, and between small and frontier models, using hard filters, a weighted rubric and a sensitivity check
Design image, audio and video pipelines including structured output contracts, with honest limits on each modality
Explain post-training — SFT, RLHF, DPO — and the alignment tax, red-teaming and training-cost realities as of 2026
Diagnose hallucination from the objective and apply grounding, structured-output contracts, guardrails and golden-set evals
Estimate and control token cost with batching, caching, routing and a quality-per-rupee framing
Ship applied pipelines: summarisation with number preservation, schema-bound extraction, classification decisions and codegen with tests as the oracle
Apply memorisation controls, the four-question copyright frame and the DPDP / EU AI Act obligation map to a real feature
Write an end-to-end GenAI spec — problem, metric, model, prompts, guardrails, eval, cost, failures, rollout — and maintain a currency system to keep it true
courses.about_course:
Ten modules, forty lessons, each lesson the same nine-step shape (objective, hook, concept, worked example, practice, common mistakes, exam/interview angle, quiz, summary) — so the rhythm never changes and the depth does.

Module 1 sets the landscape: what "generative" means as a technical distinction, the GAN-to-VAE-to-diffusion lineage, the transformer as the single architecture underneath, foundation models and what "multimodal" actually claims. Module 2 goes inside the machine: BPE tokenization from merge tables, embeddings as geometry, the sampling pipeline from logits to the chosen token, and the serving controls — system prompts, stop sequences, streaming, the KV cache — that decide cost and latency. Module 3 is the selection problem: open versus closed weights and what "open" really buys, when a 7B model beats a frontier call, context windows and their tradeoffs, and a weighted rubric with a sensitivity check.

Module 4 covers the other modalities — diffusion mechanics and prompting, speech pipelines, video and structured output. Module 5 is training and alignment: SFT, RLHF, DPO, red-teaming and the alignment tax. Module 6 is reliability: why hallucination happens from the objective, grounding, structured-output contracts, guardrails and evals. Module 7 is cost: token arithmetic, batching and caching, routing and latency, quality-per-rupee. Module 8 applies all of it — summarization with number preservation, extraction with schemas, classification decisions, code generation with tests as the oracle. Module 9 is safety, IP and compliance — memorisation, copyright, data governance, DPDP and the EU AI Act. Module 10 is the capstone and the frontiers: framing the spec, building the golden eval set, the cost model and failure register, rollout, and how to stay current without chasing announcements.

The through-line is arithmetic and falsifiability: every claim in this course is something you can check, cost or refute on your own data — and the exam, the quizzes and the capstone all test exactly that.
prerequisites: Basic AI literacy — you know what an LLM is and have used a chat assistant (any intro course, including a basics GenAI course, covers this)
No coding required: Python snippets appear as read-only worked examples you are meant to follow, not type
A notebook or doc for the capstone spec (the project is written, not coded)
Comfort with short technical prose and light arithmetic (token and cost estimates)
audience: Students and working engineers who took a basics GenAI course and want the engineering depth underneath the demos
Product, ops and support people who must specify, evaluate or govern a GenAI feature
Placement and interview prep for AI/LLM rounds — the exam bank mirrors the questions those rounds ask
Anyone evaluating model vendors, writing prompts at work, or being asked "should we use AI for this?"
courses.branch_label: AI/DS primary — open to all branches

exam_prep.target: AI/DS semester exams, placement AI rounds and GenAI interview prep — Generative AI Essentials (intermediate)

units.title: The generative landscape (M1)
units.summary: Generative estimates P(x)/the joint; discriminative estimates P(y|x). GAN = generator–discriminator game, failure = mode collapse; VAE = encode–bottleneck–decode, failure = blur; diffusion = add noise, learn to predict it, sample by iterative denoising. Transformer: self-attention token mixing + FFN channel mixing with residuals; encoder-only = understanding, decoder-only = generation, enc-dec = seq2seq. Foundation model = pretrained broadly once, adapted downstream; multimodal = a claim about actual input/output channels, audit not assume.
questions: Why can a generative model still be used for classification — and the reverse?
Name the characteristic failure of GANs and of VAEs, and why diffusion won.
What does a product’s "multimodal" claim actually assert? How do you audit it?

units.title: LLM mechanics, deeper (M2)
units.summary: BPE: characters → count adjacent pairs → merge most frequent until vocab size; merges ranked, applied in rank order; byte-level guarantees any input encodes; provider vocabularies differ → token counts differ → cost and context differ. Embeddings: meaning as geometry; cosine = angle not probability; domain mismatch and uncalibrated thresholds are the classic failures. Sampling: logits → temperature-scaled softmax → top-k/top-p pruning → renormalise → sample. Serving: roles/system prompt precedence, stop sequences (two failure modes), streaming vs time-to-first-token vs total time, KV cache growth makes long context per-token expensive.
questions: Walk the pipeline from logits to the appended token; what does each dial change?
Why do two providers tokenise the same sentence differently — and what does it cost you?
What is the difference between time-to-first-token and total generation time, and what does streaming change?

units.title: Model families and selection (M3)
units.summary: Open weights = parameters published, licence may still restrict, data/code not necessarily open; API-only hides hosting but adds ops. Small models win on: narrow stable task, high volume, cost linear in traffic, latency/offline/privacy constraints, clean labelled data — else frontier. Context windows: fit ≠ comprehension; lost-in-the-middle; prefill grows with length; retrieval top-k often beats naive full-dump. Selection: task+metric → hard filters → shortlist → golden-set eval → weighted rubric → weights-sensitivity check → recommendation with monitoring and rollback.
questions: Five conditions under which a small fine-tuned model beats a frontier API?
Why is "the window fits it" not a sufficient reason to full-dump 400k tokens?
Structure the model decision: what comes before the rubric, and what re-checks it after?

units.title: Image, audio and video (M4)
units.summary: Diffusion: train = add noise, predict it; sample = iterative denoising; steps trade time for quality; guidance scale = extrapolation between conditional and unconditional. Image prompting = subject/style/composition/lighting/format + negative channel; dialects differ; iterate one variable. ASR = speech→text (failure: accents, overlap, domain terms); TTS = text→speech; cloning needs consent as a technical control. Video = temporal latent diffusion/autoregression; cost scales with frames×duration; hard constraints on coherence. Structured output: schema, validation, retry, fallback — perception models returning boxes/JSON are not "images".
questions: What does the denoiser actually predict, and what does guidance scale trade?
Why is consent a technical requirement for voice cloning, not a policy footnote?
Video and structured output: what makes video expensive, and what contract does a boxes/JSON model need?

units.title: Alignment and training (M5)
units.summary: Pretraining → SFT → preference tuning. SFT: response-only loss masking, data quality over quantity, chat-template mismatch degrades behaviour; SFT vs RAG when the model "needs to know X". RLHF: preferences → reward model → PPO with KL anchor to reference; failures = reward hacking, sycophancy. DPO: implicit reward from log-probabilities, no reward model, no PPO; ORPO/KTO fit other feedback shapes; match method to data. Red-team with attack taxonomy → defence layers; alignment tax = capability lost to safety (refusals, softened behaviour); training cost realities and distillation as of 2026 — verify per release.
questions: What does response-only loss masking achieve in SFT, and what goes wrong without it?
Why does RLHF need the KL anchor, and what happens without it?
How does DPO differ from RLHF — and what is the alignment tax?

units.title: Reliability patterns (M6)
units.summary: Hallucination from the objective: plausibility not verification; generators = data gaps, forced choice, decoding, distraction, length; abstention ≠ refusal; calibration proxies = self-consistency, claim counts. Grounding: parametric vs in-context evidence; retrieve → assemble with provenance → answer from context → cite → abstain; two independent axes = retrieval relevance and generation faithfulness; limits = injection, distraction, latency. Contracts: prompt-only < JSON mode < schema-constrained decoding < tool calls; validate–repair–fallback bounded; shape ≠ truth. Guardrails (input filter, policy engine, output filter) guard live; frozen golden sets gate release; LLM-as-judge needs rubrics, order swaps, human calibration.
questions: Why does the training objective produce hallucination — and what is epistemic abstention?
Name the two independent failure axes of grounding and a metric for each.
Rank the output-contract ladder and say what schema validation cannot catch.

units.title: Cost engineering and applied GenAI (M7–M8)
units.summary: Pricing: input/output per million, output premium, multipliers = repeated system prompt, history growth, retries, tool loops, retrieval stuffing. Discount layers: async batch, provider prefix cache (byte-stable prefix), app exact cache (tenant-scoped, versioned), semantic cache (threshold + break-even). Routing: task tiers, cheap-first cascade with verification-gated escalation, TTFT vs total, p95 discipline. Quality-per-rupee: task metric on one golden set, cost per successful task, Pareto frontier, safety as gate never numerator. Applied: summarisation preservation contract + number-diff gate + map-reduce with fixed partial schema; extraction null policy + provenance spans + field-level P/R; classification volume math + measured-confidence routing + distillation; codegen tests-as-oracle with bounded feedback, human at review-and-merge; content review tiered by blast radius × reversibility × detectability.
questions: Compute a per-call token cost and name three multipliers that silently inflate the bill.
Design a four-layer caching strategy and say how each one fails.
Summarisation: why do numbers break, and what three-layer defence restores them?
When does LLM-prompting lose to a trained classifier — and how do you route on confidence?

units.title: Safety, compliance and the capstone (M9–M10)
units.summary: Memorisation: repetition + low entropy + no dedup → verbatim; five risk classes; canary probes bounded; controls at four layers. Copyright: train-side vs output-side vs vendor terms, kept separate; US fair-use differentiated, EU TDM opt-out reserved, India no explicit TDM exception — hedged as of 2026. Governance: data tiers → channels, Restricted barred from third-party tools; trace where an API call actually goes; enforceable acceptable-use policy. DPDP: fiduciary duties, demonstrable consent + notice, purpose limitation, children’s data, breach to Board; EU AI Act tiers attach to what the feature does and layer on top. Capstone: metric before model; golden set with binary safety gates; two-volume cost model; failure register with detection signals; phased rollout with rehearsed rollback; currency system with eval-first adoption.
questions: What makes a string easy to regurgitate — and where do the controls sit?
Split a GenAI copyright problem into its four questions.
What does DPDP require that "the vendor handles it" does not answer?
Why must every failure-register entry carry a detection signal, and what does eval-first adoption mean?

important_questions: Explain the generative vs discriminative distinction and why modern LLMs blur it. Give one example of each.
Walk the full sampling pipeline from logits to the chosen token, and say what temperature, top-k and top-p each change.
When does a small model beat a frontier API? Give five conditions and the routing consequence.
Why does summarisation damage numbers, and what three-layer defence restores them?
Design the validate–repair–fallback loop for structured extraction and say what schema validation cannot catch.
Separate a GenAI copyright problem into four questions and state what a dated decision record contains.
Write the seven parts of a production GenAI spec and defend metric-before-model ordering.

previous_year_questions.question: Explain how a transformer uses self-attention to connect distant words, and why this architecture scaled where recurrent networks stalled. (8 marks)
previous_year_questions.solution: Self-attention computes query–key–value interactions so every token can attend to every other in one parallel step, with residual connections and feed-forward layers stacked around it; positional information comes from encodings since there is no recurrence. It scaled where RNNs stalled because training is parallel over sequence positions (RNNs are sequential), gradients short-circuit through residuals, and the same block composes into encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants — which is why one architecture now powers chat, code, image and speech systems via foundation-model pretraining plus downstream adaptation.

previous_year_questions.question: A chatbot answers confidently wrong about a post-cutoff fact. Diagnose the failure from the training objective and give two response-side defences. (6 marks)
previous_year_questions.solution: Diagnosis: next-token training rewards plausibility, not verification — the fact was never in training (knowledge cutoff), and nothing in the objective penalises inventing a plausible stand-in. Defences: (1) grounding — retrieve the fact from an external store, answer from that context with provenance, and enforce a source-or-abstain contract; (2) epistemic abstention with calibration proxies — sample multiple answers (self-consistency) and abstain when they disagree or claims lack support. Note refusal ("I cannot help") is a different behaviour from abstention ("I do not know"); the failure here wants the second.

previous_year_questions.question: Estimate the monthly cost of an extraction pipeline processing 50k documents/day with 2k input and 300 output tokens each, at $2.5/M input and $10/M output. State one assumption that could make the real bill 5× higher. (6 marks)
previous_year_questions.solution: Per document: 2000×2.5/1e6 = $0.005 input + 300×10/1e6 = $0.003 output = $0.008. Daily: 50,000 × $0.008 = $400. Monthly (30 days) ≈ $12,000. A 5× inflation source: unbounded retry/tool loops or stuffing full document text plus a repeated system prompt into every call (retrieval stuffing / history growth) — the bill multipliers from the cost module. Real deployments log actual usage against the estimate and gate shipping on the gap.

bank.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a discriminative model from a generative model?
options: A discriminative model estimates how the data itself is distributed; a generative model learns the boundary between classes
A discriminative model learns the decision boundary between classes; a generative model learns the distribution of the data itself
Both estimate the same probability, differing only in model size
Generative models produce only images; discriminative models produce only labels
bank.explanation: Lesson 1.1: discriminative models estimate P(y|x) — where the decision boundary between classes sits — while generative models learn P(x) (or the joint), the shape of the data itself. Modern LLMs blur the line: a next-token generator can be steered into classification, and a classifier can be re-cast as a scorer inside a generative loop. The distinction is about what the objective learns, not what the product outputs.

bank.prompt: A GAN's generator keeps emitting the same few 'safe' images that reliably fool the discriminator, regardless of the noise sampled. This failure is called:
options: Mode collapse — the characteristic GAN failure
bank.explanation: Lesson 1.2: in the GAN game, if the discriminator only punishes one region of image space, the generator can converge to a single mode that always scores well — mode collapse. VAEs blur because the bottleneck plus pixel-wise losses average detail away; diffusion replaced both by training to predict added noise and sampling by iteratively denoising, which is stable to train and high-quality.

bank.prompt: Which pairing of transformer variant, typical use, and foundation-model claim is correct?
options: Encoder-only for generation, decoder-only for understanding, and any foundation model is automatically multimodal
All variants are interchangeable; the difference is only parameter count

Encoder-only for understanding/classification, decoder-only for generation, and a foundation model is trained broadly once, then adapted downstream — multimodal claims must be checked against actual inputs and outputs
A foundation model must be fine-tuned before any zero-shot use
bank.explanation: Lesson 1.3: encoder-only (bidirectional attention) suits understanding tasks like classification; decoder-only (causal attention) powers most chat LLMs; encoder-decoder bridges both for seq2seq tasks. Lesson 1.4: a foundation model is pretrained broadly for general behaviour and adapted to many downstream tasks — zero-shot included. Multimodal is a claim about the actual input and output channels (text-only input with image output is not omni), so audit the product, not the marketing.

bank.prompt: Why does the same sentence often produce different token counts on two providers?
options: Each provider trains its own BPE vocabulary and merge table, so the token boundaries differ
One provider counts characters, the other counts words
Tokens are always priced per word, so the count is cosmetic
One provider truncates the sentence before counting
bank.explanation: Lesson 2.1: BPE starts from characters, counts adjacent pairs, and merges the most frequent repeatedly until a target vocabulary size. Because each provider trains merges on its own corpus at its own scale, boundaries differ — especially for rare words, code and non-English scripts. That drives real cost and context-limit differences, not just cosmetic counting.

bank.prompt: Two sentence embeddings have cosine similarity 0.92. The honest interpretation is:
options: The sentences are 92% identical in meaning
The model is 92% confident they are duplicates
Their vectors point in nearly the same direction under the chosen metric — useful for retrieval only with a threshold validated on your domain
The sentences came from the same document
bank.explanation: Lesson 2.2: cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, not probability or identity. 0.92 means geometrically close under that model’s space — but domain mismatch, uncalibrated thresholds and corpus-inherited bias are the classic failures. Validate the threshold on a labelled sample from your domain before wiring it into a pipeline.

bank.prompt: Which statement about decoding and serving controls is correct?
options: Lowering temperature sharpens the distribution toward higher-probability tokens; a stop sequence cuts generation when its literal text appears; streaming improves perceived latency (time-to-first-token) but not total generation time
Temperature scales the context window, so a lower value fits more tokens
top_p = 1.0 removes low-probability tokens from the candidate set
Streaming reduces the number of tokens billed
bank.explanation: Lesson 2.3: temperature rescales logits before softmax — lower = sharper, more deterministic; top-k/top-p prune the candidate set then renormalise. Lesson 2.4: stop sequences terminate generation when a literal appears (classic failures: the sequence appearing inside content, or never appearing so generation runs long); streaming yields tokens as the KV cache fills, so time-to-first-token drops while total generation time does not.

bank.prompt: 'Open weights' means:
options: The trained parameters are published for download and self-hosting — licence terms may still restrict commercial use, and the training data or code need not be open
The training data, code and weights are all public
The model is free for commercial use without restriction
The model runs only in the browser
bank.explanation: Lesson 3.1: open-weight releases publish the parameters you can download and run, but the licence can still carve out restrictions (community licences with user caps, non-commercial clauses, acceptable-use terms), and you often get neither the training data nor the full training code. Fully open-source releases are a stricter, rarer subset. Read the actual licence text — the label alone tells you nothing enforceable.

bank.prompt: Which workload is the strongest case for a small (7B-class) fine-tuned model over a frontier API?
options: A high-volume, narrow, stable classification or extraction task with a fixed schema and clear labels
A one-off creative campaign with shifting briefs
Multilingual voice translation with long, unpredictable context
bank.explanation: Lesson 3.2: small models win when the task is narrow and stable (labels do not drift), volume is high (cost scales linearly with tokens, so per-call price dominates), latency or privacy/offline constraints bite, and a clean labelled set exists to fine-tune. Open-ended or shifting work keeps the frontier model’s advantage; route with a cascade when only some traffic is narrow.

bank.prompt: You must answer questions over a 400k-token document set with a model offering a 1M-token window. The most defensible first move:
options: Full-dump everything — the window fits it
Buy the largest model regardless of price
Fine-tune the model on the documents
Estimate fit and cost, remember lost-in-the-middle and prefill cost that grows with sequence length, and compare a top-k retrieval design against full-dump on your own golden set before choosing
bank.explanation: Lesson 3.3: capacity is not comprehension — attention quality degrades in the middle of very long contexts (lost-in-the-middle), and prefill cost grows with length even if the window "fits". Lesson 3.4: turn the choice into arithmetic — hard filters (window, compliance), then a weighted rubric scored on your own golden set, with a sensitivity check on the weights. Benchmark hype is not your metric.

bank.prompt: During diffusion sampling the denoiser predicts:
options: The noise that was added to the (latent) image at that step
bank.explanation: Lesson 4.1: training adds known noise to images and teaches the network to predict that noise; sampling starts from pure noise and iteratively subtracts the predicted noise. More steps trade time for quality; guidance scale extrapolates between the conditional (prompted) and unconditional predictions — higher guidance pushes harder toward the prompt at some cost to diversity.

bank.prompt: In image prompting, the negative-prompt channel is for:
options: Specifying content to steer away from, complementing the positive prompt
Replying to the model in natural language
Listing file paths of reference images
bank.explanation: Lesson 4.2: image prompts decompose into subject, style, composition, lighting and format levers; the negative channel names what NOT to include (e.g. blurry, extra fingers, watermark). Dialects differ across tools (natural language, flag-based, negative box), so map the same intent to each — and iterate one variable at a time so you learn what each change did.

bank.prompt: Which pipeline statement is correct?
options: ASR converts speech to text and TTS converts text to speech; voice cloning needs consent as a technical control; video cost scales with frame count and duration; perception models returning boxes or JSON need a structured output contract
ASR is text-to-audio and TTS is audio-to-text
Video is cheap because each frame is small
Structured output contracts only matter for pure-text tasks
bank.explanation: Lesson 4.3: ASR (speech to text) and TTS (text to speech) are two distinct stacks; cloning requires consent enforced as a technical control (verification plus provenance), not just a policy line. Lesson 4.4: video multiplies compute by frames and duration, making it the expensive modality; perception and multimodal pipelines that emit boxes, captions or records need a structured output contract (schema, validation, retry, fallback).

bank.prompt: In supervised fine-tuning of a chat model, response-only loss masking means:
options: The user's tokens are deleted before training
Loss is computed only on the assistant’s tokens, not the prompt or user tokens
Only the system prompt is trained on
Loss is masked whenever the response exceeds the context length
bank.explanation: Lesson 5.1: SFT sits between pretraining and preference tuning. With response-only masking, gradients flow only through the assistant’s reply so the model learns to produce good answers rather than re-learn to echo prompts. Data quality dominates quantity, and the chat template (role tokens, separators) must match the inference template exactly — a mismatch silently degrades behaviour.

bank.prompt: In RLHF, the KL penalty anchoring the policy to the reference model exists to:
options: Prevent reward hacking and degenerate drift while still improving the reward
bank.explanation: Lesson 5.2: RLHF learns a reward model from pairwise human preferences, then optimises the policy (PPO) to maximise reward — minus a KL-divergence term that keeps the policy near the supervised reference. Without the anchor, the policy exploits reward-model blind spots (reward hacking) and drifts into degenerate or sycophantic outputs. The anchor trades peak reward for stability.

bank.prompt: Which claim about preference tuning and alignment is correct?
options: DPO requires a trained reward model and PPO
Alignment tuning always improves benchmark scores

DPO skips the reward model by optimising preference pairs directly via an implicit reward from log-probabilities; alignment tuning trades some capability for safety (the alignment tax); red-teaming maps attacks to defence layers
Red-teaming is performed only by external regulators
bank.explanation: Lesson 5.3: DPO (and ORPO/KTO variants) converts preference pairs into a direct loss using an implicit reward from log-probabilities — no separate reward model, no PPO loop; match the method to the feedback shape you actually have. Lesson 5.4: alignment tuning extracts an alignment tax — refusals and softened behaviour can cost capability on borderline-but-legitimate requests; red-teaming is an in-house discipline mapping attacks (prompt injection, jailbreaks, data exfiltration) to defence layers, not a regulator’s job.

bank.prompt: The root cause of hallucination taught in this course:
options: The training objective rewards plausible next tokens, not verified facts
Models are deliberately trained to lie
bank.explanation: Lesson 6.1: next-token training never checked whether a statement is true — plausibility is the only signal. Fabrication generators: data gaps, forced-choice prompts ("answer yes or no" when unsure), decoding pressure, context distraction, and answer-length pressure. Response-side defences: abstention paths and calibration proxies (self-consistency sampling, claim counts) — note that refusal and epistemic abstention are different things.

bank.prompt: In a grounded QA system, the two independent failure axes are:
options: Retrieval relevance (right evidence retrieved) and generation faithfulness (answer supported by that evidence)
bank.explanation: Lesson 6.2: grounding separates parametric knowledge (weights) from in-context retrieved evidence, and answers should come from the retrieved context with provenance.
