Retrieval failure (wrong or missing evidence) and generation failure (unfaithful answer despite good evidence) are measured and fixed independently. Grounding is not a free lunch: injection risk, distraction by irrelevant chunks, and added latency all remain.

bank.prompt: Which statement correctly ranks output contracts and places the nets?
options: Schema-constrained decoding guarantees the shape by construction (beyond JSON mode); validate–repair–fallback is bounded; runtime guardrails catch bad requests and responses while frozen golden sets catch regressions before release; LLM-as-judge needs rubrics, order swaps and human calibration
JSON mode guarantees your exact schema
Guardrails and evals are the same mechanism
LLM-as-judge alone can approve a release
bank.explanation: Lesson 6.3: the contract ladder runs prompt-only JSON (advisory) < JSON mode (syntactic) < schema-constrained decoding (shape by construction) < tool calls (typed I/O); a validate–repair–fallback loop keeps repair bounded instead of open-ended. Lesson 6.4: runtime guardrails (input filter, policy engine, output filter) guard the live path; frozen golden sets gate releases. LLM-as-judge is a scale aid needing rubrics, order swaps and human calibration — never the sole approver.

bank.prompt: A call uses 2,000 input and 500 output tokens at $3 and $15 per million respectively. What is the cost?
bank.explanation: Lesson 7.1: input 2000/1e6 × $3 = $0.006; output 500/1e6 × $15 = $0.0075; total ≈ $0.0135. Note the output premium (here 5×) — output tokens usually dominate. Real bills then multiply by repeated system prompts, growing chat history, retries, tool loops and retrieval stuffing; log real usage against the estimate as a shipping gate.

bank.prompt: A nightly batch enrichment job and a real-time chat share a model. The best discount/latency pairing:
options: Route the nightly job through the async batch endpoint (patient work) and give the chat a byte-stable prompt prefix so provider prefix caching fires
Run both interactively at full price for consistency
Send the chat traffic to the batch endpoint
Disable caching to keep outputs fresh
bank.explanation: Lesson 7.2: batch APIs trade latency for a discount on patient work; provider prefix caching requires a byte-stable prefix (stable system prompt first, volatile user content last) and a minimum token count to qualify. Application-level exact caches (tenant-scoped, versioned keys) and semantic caches (similarity threshold plus break-even against a wrong answer) add further layers — each with its own invalidation rule and failure mode.

bank.prompt: Which practice makes a small-model cascade economically and safely sound?
options: Always start with the largest model to avoid failures
Escalate whenever the response is long
Judge quality by benchmark leaderboards alone

Verification-gated escalation measured on a shared golden set: route on task tiers, escalate when the cheap path fails a check, track cost per successful task, and treat safety as a gate — never a numerator
bank.explanation: Lesson 7.3: task-tier routing plus a cheap-first cascade with verification-gated escalation, with break-even arithmetic between the small and frontier paths. Lesson 7.4: compare candidates on one golden set with real unit costs, read the Pareto frontier over quality, cost and latency, and track cost per successful task with drift alerts. Safety conditions are gates that block an entry, never a term averaged into a score.

bank.prompt: A summary rewrites 'up to 20% concession' as '20% concession'. The failure class and the cheapest first gate:
options: A tokenizer artefact; regenerate at temperature 0
Qualifier loss; an automated number-diff between source and summary
A formatting issue; run a readability check
bank.explanation: Lesson 8.1: load-bearing words — "up to", "approximately", negations — are the first casualties of compression. The fix is an explicit preservation contract plus an automated number-diff gate (normalise digits, units and qualifiers, then diff). Long documents use chunk → map → reduce with a fixed partial schema and conflict rules, because errors compound through the passes.

bank.prompt: Fabricated invoice numbers appear in extraction output despite a valid schema. The strongest fix combination:
options: Raise the temperature for more variety
Absent-means-null in the prompt, schema-constrained decoding, and quote-verification of risky values with provenance spans
Remove the schema so the model can be creative
Ask the model to self-certify each value
bank.explanation: Lesson 8.2: a valid schema guarantees shape, not truth. Combine a null policy (absent field → null, never invented), schema-constrained decoding, and provenance spans that quote the source for each value so risky fields can be verified against the document. Evaluate with field-level precision and recall and a per-field error taxonomy — never by eyeballing sample rows.

bank.prompt: Which pair of decisions is defensible at production scale?
options: Prompt an LLM for 400k items/day regardless of cost; auto-merge generated code when tests are green
Train a classifier first for everything; review all content with equal intensity

High-volume stable labels → a trained or cascade classifier with calibrated confidence (LLM for the hard slice); generated code passes sandboxed tests before human review and never merges itself, while content review is tiered by blast radius × reversibility × detectability
Trust self-reported LLM confidence as the routing threshold; sample-audit at 10%
bank.explanation: Lesson 8.3: LLM prompting scales in cost linearly with traffic while a trained classifier front-loads cost — the volume math decides; route on measured confidence, not self-reported certainty, and run the distillation playbook (LLM-seeded labels, human-audited gold, small model, drift monitoring). Lesson 8.4: codegen uses tests as the only honest oracle with bounded error feedback and a human at review-and-merge; content pipelines tier human review by blast radius × reversibility × detectability instead of everything-or-nothing.

bank.prompt: Which text is most likely to be regurgitated verbatim from a model’s training data?
options: A serial number or API key repeated across thousands of pages (low entropy, repetitive, undeduplicated)
bank.explanation: Lesson 9.1: memorisation tracks repetition, low entropy and absent deduplication — a string appearing thousands of times in near-identical context is the easiest thing for weights to store and hand back. Canary-style probes can bound the risk but a negative result proves little; controls layer across what you send, vendor settings you verified, output-side deterministic scanning and incident response.

bank.prompt: Which practice survives the shifting copyright landscape?
options: Per-use dated decision records splitting train-side, ownership, output-infringement and vendor-term questions, checked per jurisdiction
Following the newest headline as if it were global rule
Assuming outputs are automatically owned by the user
Avoiding GenAI until all statutes settle
bank.explanation: Lesson 9.2: keep training-side and output-side questions separate, plus the vendor contract layer that can override both. The landscape as of 2026: US fair-use litigation is differentiated by use, the EU TDM exception carries an opt-out reservation, and India has no explicit TDM exception — all subject to change, so verify per jurisdiction with dates. Practical controls: rights hygiene for inputs, similarity checks on outputs, vendor terms read not assumed.

bank.prompt: An Indian consumer app with EU users ships an LLM feature. Which obligation set is correct?
options: DPDP applies only to Indian data; the EU Act bans all AI

DPDP: demonstrable consent plus notice, purpose limitation, breach notice to the Board; data tiers map to channels with Restricted barred from third-party tools; the EU AI Act risk tier depends on what the feature does (e.g. employment or credit = high-risk duties) — verify current text
Compliance equals publishing a privacy policy
Only the LLM vendor carries any duty
bank.explanation: Lesson 9.3: classify data into tiers mapped to approved channels — Restricted data never goes to third-party tools; minimisation and egress controls make the safe path the fast path. Lesson 9.4: DPDP puts fiduciary duties (demonstrable consent, purpose limitation, breach duties) on whoever determines purpose and means — usually you, not the vendor. The EU AI Act’s tier attaches to what the feature does (hiring, credit, exams = high-risk), and the regimes layer rather than replace each other.

bank.prompt: In a GenAI spec, what must exist before any model is tested?
options: The problem with its measured status quo, the metric with baseline, target, gates and counter-metrics, and the explicit out-of-scope — written while you still have no model opinions
bank.explanation: Lesson 10.1: the one-pager comes first — a problem statement with the current workflow’s numbers and cost of failure, a success metric with baseline, target, guardrail gates and counter-metrics, and explicit out-of-scope. Write the metric before you have model opinions so it cannot be reverse-engineered to fit a favourite. Then hard-filter and score three options on your own golden set, with a falsification condition stated up front.

bank.prompt: In a ten-item golden set, why are injection and PII-probe items critical and binary?
options: Safety conditions gate entry: a 90% pass means nine failures in ten — they never average into a score
They are easier to score automatically
They take less time to write
They count double toward the quality score
bank.explanation: Lesson 10.2: golden-set items need scoreable expectations; safety conditions (injection resistance, PII refusal) are gates that must pass on every run — averaging them into a percentage would hide the nine failures a 90% score implies. Keep the set frozen (never tune on the test), attach reason codes and fail paths to guardrails, and re-run the whole set on every change including vendor model updates.

bank.prompt: Which production posture is correct?
options: Mitigations without alarms are complete; migrate on announcement day to capture savings; usage dashboards alone prove quality

Every failure-register entry carries a detection signal with threshold and owner; rollout is phased with a rehearsed one-command rollback; model and vendor claims are verified on your own golden sets before migration — never on announcement day
Dashboards are optional once the canary passes
Rollback plans are written after the first incident
bank.explanation: Lesson 10.3: every failure-register entry carries a detection signal, threshold and owner — a mitigation with no alarm is incomplete; rollout is phased with entry gates, dashboards and a rehearsed rollback; the two-volume cost model (1k and 10k daily uses) keeps unit economics visible. Lesson 10.4: trends (agents, multimodal, on-device, open weights) are held at arm’s length as of 2026; run a currency system with ranked sources, cadence and an eval-first adoption rule — verify on your golden set, never on announcement day.

project.title: Spec a production GenAI use case
project.brief: Write a one-pager plus appendix that takes one real GenAI use case — yours — from problem to rollout. The one-pager: the problem with its measured status quo (how the work happens today, at what cost, failing how often); the success metric with baseline, target, guardrail gates and counter-metrics; the chosen model with a three-option comparison table scored on your own ten-item golden set; and the explicit out-of-scope. The appendix: (1) the prompt architecture — layered system contract, context packing, output schema — with guardrails placed by position, reason codes and fail paths; (2) the golden eval set: ten scoreable items covering the failure modes, with the safety items marked as binary gates; (3) the cost model at 1,000 and 10,000 daily uses, with assumptions visible, levers applied and cost per successful task; (4) the top-five failure register: failure, impact × likelihood, mitigation, and a detection signal with threshold and owner for every entry; (5) the phased rollout: entry gates, dashboards, a rehearsed rollback and named owners; and (6) the currency plan: which sources you watch, at what cadence, and the eval-first rule that decides when to migrate models. The claim you are defending is not that GenAI can do this — it is that you know when it fails, how you would see it, and what you would do next.
project.submission_hint: Public link (anyone-with-link view) to a document or repository, or a PDF attached to your submission — the one-pager plus appendix.

modules.title: Module 1 — The Generative Landscape
modules.summary: What "generative" actually means as a technical distinction, the GAN to VAE to diffusion lineage that produced today's image tools, the transformer as the one architecture underneath it all, foundation models and the modality map — plus what "multimodal" really claims.

lessons.title: Generative vs Discriminative: Two Ways a Model Uses Data
lessons.summary: The distinction that defines the field: models that learn decision boundaries versus models that learn the shape of the data itself — and why modern LLMs blur the line.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define generative and discriminative models in terms of the probability each one estimates
Classify six real AI products as generative or discriminative and justify each from its training objective
Explain why a generative model can still be used for classification, and give the reverse counter-example
Choose generative vs discriminative for three given business problems and defend the choice

payload.text: Two apps sit on the same phone. One tags your photos: "beach, dog, dinner" — it never invents a pixel, it only labels. The other, in the same minute, invents a photograph of a dog on a beach that never existed. Both are "AI", both were trained on images, but they were trained for fundamentally different mathematical jobs. That split — discriminative vs generative — is the fault line of the entire field, and every model you will meet in this course lives on one side of it.

**Two different questions about data.** A **discriminative** model learns P(label | input): given an image, how should I score each class? Its job is a *boundary* between classes. Logistic regression, SVMs, BERT-style classifiers, and the "is this spam?" layer in your email client are discriminative. A **generative** model learns P(input) (or P(input, label)): what does the data itself look like? How likely is this particular image, this sentence, this row? Because it models the whole distribution, it can *sample* — produce new data that never existed — and also answer questions like "how strange is this point?" (low probability = anomaly). Naive Bayes, Gaussian mixtures, GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, and every LLM are generative.

**What each one buys you.** Discriminative models go straight at the decision you care about; with labelled data they usually win on accuracy per unit of effort, because they spend all their capacity on the boundary. They cannot, by themselves, write a poem. Generative models spend capacity modelling everything about the data — including variation you may not care about — which is the price of being able to create, impute missing values, and detect anomalies. Generative models can also *classify* via Bayes' rule: if you know P(x | class) and P(class), you can compute P(class | x). The classic example is naive Bayes email filtering: count word frequencies per class, multiply, normalise — a generative model doing a discriminative job.

**The modern blur, and how to classify honestly.** Ask not "how is it used?" but "what objective was it trained on?" An LLM trained on next-token prediction over raw text is generative — even when you prompt it with "reply only SPAM or HAM", it *generates* the label as a token sequence rather than scoring classes internally. Reverse case: a semantic-search system that embeds documents and thresholds cosine similarity is doing discriminative-style separation with no generation involved. And a image classifier can be bolted onto a generative pipeline (detect, then regenerate) without changing what either model is. So the practical rule: **classify by the training objective, not by the user-facing trick.**

**Why the generative half exploded.** Discriminative deep learning peaked quietly in the 2010s (ImageNet, ad ranking, spam). The 2020s wave came from the generative side getting *good enough at scale* — transformers scaling next-token prediction to fluent text, diffusion scaling image synthesis to photorealism — so that sampling from P(data) now produces artifacts people actually want: essays, code, faces, music, voice. That is what "Generative AI" names: not a new mathematics of probability, but the point where modelling P(data) became useful enough to build products on. Every remaining lesson in this course is an elaboration of one of those two sentences: what the model estimates, and what it can do because of it.

payload.title: Generative vs discriminative: the working distinction
rows: P(x) or P(x, label) — the shape of the data
Naive Bayes, GAN, VAE, diffusion, LLM
Photo tagging, spam filter, fraud score
Accuracy on a fixed label set
Creation, anomaly scoring, flexibility across tasks
Spends capacity on detail you may not need; can hallucinate

payload.title: The one-question classifier
payload.text: When someone says "we built an AI that does X", ask: was it trained to score labels, or trained to reproduce data? The answer predicts its failure modes before you see a single demo.

payload.title: Generative does not mean truthful
payload.text: A generative model optimises likelihood, not correctness. Fluency is a property of P(text); truth is a property of the world. Confusing the two is the root of hallucination (covered in depth in Part II).

payload.title: Classify four systems — then watch a generative model do a discriminative job
payload.problem: Classify each as generative or discriminative: (a) a visa-application fraud scorer, (b) ChatGPT drafting an email, (c) a news-topic tagger, (d) an embedding model flagging near-duplicate support tickets by cosine > 0.92. Then hand-compute how a *generative* naive-Bayes tagger scores one ticket.

steps.title: Step 1 — classify by objective
steps.desc: (a) discriminative: trained on labelled fraud/not-fraud rows to score P(fraud | features). (b) generative: trained on next-token likelihood over text, sampled to produce new text. (c) discriminative: P(topic | headline). (d) borderline but treat as discriminative separation — it scores similarity against a threshold, never samples a new ticket.

steps.title: Step 2 — set up the toy naive-Bayes model
steps.desc: Two classes, refund requests (R) and delivery questions (D). Training counts: P(R)=0.5, P(D)=0.5. Word likelihoods: P("refund"|R)=0.40, P("money"|R)=0.30, P("refund"|D)=0.05, P("money"|D)=0.05.
steps.code_snippet:
P(R)=0.5  P(D)=0.5
P(refund|R)=0.40  P(money|R)=0.30
P(refund|D)=0.05  P(money|D)=0.05

steps.title: Step 4 — normalise to a posterior
steps.desc: Total = 0.06125. P(R | text) = 0.060 / 0.06125 ≈ 0.9796, P(D | text) ≈ 0.0204. A *generative* model (it modelled P(words | class)) produced a confident discriminative answer — same output shape, different internal job.

payload.solution: Four labels: discriminative, generative, discriminative, discriminative-by-similarity. The naive-Bayes walk-through scores 0.98 for the refund class — proving generation and classification are jobs, not mutually exclusive model species. Classify models by objective; predict behaviour from that.

payload.title: Audit your own AI stack
payload.prompt: List six AI features you used this week (photo tags, autocomplete, chat, transcription, recommendation feed, fraud alert). For each, write one sentence naming the objective you believe it was trained on, and one prediction about how it fails. Then find the one case where you are genuinely unsure — and say what evidence (docs, model card, demo behaviour) would settle it.
payload.hint: If the system only ever outputs a decision about your input, it is probably discriminative. If it can surprise you with something new, it is generative.

mistakes.mistake: Calling any tool that "uses AI" generative because it is new
mistakes.fix: Most production AI remains discriminative (ranking, scoring, tagging). "Generative" names a training objective — P(data) — not novelty or neural-network depth.

mistakes.mistake: Believing an LLM doing classification is a discriminative model
mistakes.fix: It generates the label as text from a next-token distribution. The objective never changed; you rephrased the task into its generative format.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming generative models are automatically better at decisions
mistakes.fix: For a fixed label set with good labels, a discriminative model is usually more accurate, cheaper and more debuggable. Generality is bought with capacity you may not need.

mistakes.mistake: Equating likelihood with correctness
mistakes.fix: A generative model reports how *text-like* something is, not whether it is true. High P(x) means familiar, not verified — the seed of every hallucination story.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Differentiate generative from discriminative models. Give one example of each in a modern product, and explain why an LLM prompt "classify this as SPAM or HAM" does not make the LLM a discriminative model.
payload.answer: A discriminative model estimates P(label | x): it learns the boundary between classes and is typically tuned for decision accuracy (e.g. an email spam scorer trained on labelled mail). A generative model estimates P(x) or P(x, label): it learns how the data itself is distributed, which lets it sample new instances and also, via Bayes, classify (e.g. ChatGPT generating text; or naive Bayes classifying from word likelihoods). Prompting an LLM to output SPAM/HAM changes the *task presentation*, not the training objective: the model still scores the next token from its learned text distribution and samples a label string. It never learned class-conditional boundaries; it learned text continuation and is being used as a classifier through prompting — which works, but inherits generative failure modes (fluency without calibration, sensitivity to phrasing).
payload.source: Standard ML interview screen; also a common MLOps/GenAI product-design discussion question.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Discriminative models learn P(label | x) — a boundary; generative models learn P(x) — the shape of the data, and can sample.
Generative models can classify (Bayes), but discriminative models cannot generate — that asymmetry is the whole difference.
Classify by training objective, not by how the product is used: prompting an LLM to label text does not make it discriminative.
The Generative AI wave = P(data) modelling scaled (transformers + diffusion) until sampling produced useful artifacts.
Likelihood is not truth: generative models measure text-likeness, which is why hallucination is possible at all.

questions.prompt: A discriminative model is best defined as one that estimates:
options: P(x) — how the input data is distributed
P(label | x) — the decision boundary given an input
P(x | y) only, with no way to score labels
The joint probability of every pixel in an image
questions.explanation: Discriminative models go straight at the conditional over labels — boundary learning, not density learning.

questions.prompt: An LLM is classified as generative because it was trained to:
options: Maximise the probability of the actual next token over raw text
Assign one of a fixed set of class labels
questions.explanation: Its objective is next-token likelihood over data itself — P(text) — which is what makes sampling new text possible.

questions.prompt: A naive-Bayes spam filter is sometimes called "generative" because it:
options: Models P(words | class) and P(class), then derives P(class | words) via Bayes
questions.explanation: It learns class-conditional data distributions — the generative route to a discriminative answer.

questions.prompt: The strongest practical reason to prefer a discriminative model for a fixed-label task is that it:
options: Spends all its capacity on the decision boundary, usually giving better accuracy per unit of effort when labels exist
questions.explanation: Modelling everything about the data is a cost; when you only need the decision, the boundary-focused model usually wins.

lessons.title: GANs, VAEs and Diffusion: Where Image Generation Came From
lessons.summary: Three generations of image synthesis — adversarial games, latent reconstructions, iterative denoising — intuitions for each and why diffusion won.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain the generator-versus-discriminator game behind GANs and name its characteristic failure (mode collapse)
Describe a VAE's encode-bottleneck-decode loop and why its samples come out blurry
Walk the diffusion training objective (add noise, learn to predict it) and the sampling loop (iterate denoising)
Identify which lineage member powers a given tool, including modern hybrids like latent diffusion

payload.text: Thisperson does not exist — the GAN-generated faces that fooled timelines around 2019. Two years later the same slot in the culture was taken by Stable Diffusion and Midjourney, which look nothing like those slightly glassy faces. Between those two demos sat a change of technology, not just of quality: the field moved from an adversarial game, through a probabilistic bottleneck, to a deceptively simple idea — corrupt data with noise, then learn to undo it. Today's image tools, as of 2026, are mostly that third idea, with pieces of the first two quietly inside.

**GAN (2014): learn by competing.** A **generator** G takes random noise and produces a candidate image; a **discriminator** D judges real training images vs G's fakes. They train in a minimax dance: G gets better at fooling D, D gets better at catching G. Intuition: an art forger and a critic, each sharpening the other. GANs produced the first startlingly sharp samples (StyleGAN faces), and their speed kept them alive in super-resolution and mobile filters. But the game is notoriously unstable — the two networks must stay in balance or training collapses — and **mode collapse** is the signature failure: G discovers one output that fools D and emits variations of it (one "safe" face forever), because the objective rewards fooling D, not covering the data. There is no likelihood, no principled measure of "how much of the data did I learn?" — just the game.

**VAE (2013): compress, then reconstruct.** An encoder maps the image into a small **latent** vector (a compressed code), a decoder rebuilds the image from that code, and training minimises reconstruction error plus a regulariser (the KL term) that keeps the latent space smooth and continuous. Two consequences you can see: (1) the latent space is *organised* — interpolating between two codes yields a coherent morph, which is why VAE latents became a control surface; (2) because the code is a lossy bottleneck and the loss is pixel-wise average, samples tend to look **blurry** — the model hedging across plausible reconstructions. VAEs never won the headline quality race, but they never left: they are the autoencoder that compresses pixels into the small latent grid that diffusion models actually run on inside tools like Stable Diffusion.

**Diffusion (2015–2020): corrupt, then uncorrupt.** Training has two halves. Forward: take a real image, add Gaussian noise step by step until it is pure static. Reverse: train a network to predict the noise that was added, given the noisy image (and, in modern tools, a text condition). Sampling flips the process: start from pure noise, ask the network "how much of this is noise?", subtract a bit, repeat 20–50 times until a coherent image emerges. The elegance is that the task is always the same simple regression ("predict the noise"), which trains stably at enormous scale — no adversarial balancing act — while step count at sampling time becomes a quality-versus-latency dial you can turn. GAN sharpness without the game, VAE-style compression without the blur.

**The lineage is not a replacement list.** Modern production is hybrid: a VAE first squeezes 1024×1024 pixels into a 64×64 latent (100× less compute), the diffusion transformer denoises there conditioned on text via cross-attention, and an adversarial loss is often added at the end for crispness. Credit where due: every ancestor is a component of the winner. As of 2026, flow-matching and rectified-flow training (used by models such as SD3 and FLUX-class systems) shorten the denoising schedule — fewer steps, similar quality — but they are descendants of the same denoise-the-noise idea, not a fourth lineage.

payload.title: Three lineages, three intuitions
rows: Generator fools a discriminator in a minimax game
Encode to a regularised latent bottleneck, decode back
Add noise in training; learn to predict it; iterate the removal
Stable training, quality/diversity control via steps
VAE latent + diffusion (or flow) denoiser + adversarial loss

payload.title: Why GANs did not disappear
payload.text: For real-time face filters, super-resolution on-device, and cheap one-step generation, a distilled GAN is still hard to beat. "Diffusion won" refers to headline text-to-image quality, not to every niche.

payload.title: Do not confuse lineage with a quality ranking
payload.text: A well-tuned VAE-variant can beat a lazy diffusion setup. Architecture sets the ceiling; data, conditioning and sampling settings decide where under the ceiling you land.

payload.title: Run a one-pixel diffusion step by hand
payload.problem: Simplify an image to a single pixel whose true value is 10. Forward diffusion with total noise-level ᾱ = 0.09 produces the observed noisy value x_t. The network is asked to predict the noise ε that was added. Compute the forward sample, run one perfect reverse step to recover x₀, then explain what changes when the sampler takes 40 small steps instead of 1 big one.

steps.title: Step 1 — forward noising arithmetic
steps.desc: The forward process gives x_t = √ᾱ · x₀ + √(1−ᾱ) · ε, with ε drawn as standard noise, say ε = 1.7. √0.09 = 0.3, √0.91 ≈ 0.954.

steps.title: Step 2 — what the network learns
steps.desc: The network never predicts "the image" directly; it predicts ε given x_t (and the text condition). A perfect network returns ε̂ = 1.7.
steps.code_snippet: network(x_t, text) -> noise_pred = 1.7

steps.title: Step 3 — one reverse step recovers the signal
steps.desc: x̂₀ = (x_t − √(1−ᾱ) · ε̂) / √ᾱ = (4.62 − 1.62) / 0.3 = 10.0 — the original pixel, from pure arithmetic on the predicted noise.

steps.title: Step 4 — why samplers take many small steps
steps.desc: Real networks predict noise imperfectly, especially when ᾱ is tiny (near-pure static). One giant step compounds the error; 20–50 small steps let each prediction be modest and correctable — the quality/latency dial every diffusion UI exposes. Guidance scale (Lesson 4.1) then pulls each prediction toward the text condition.

payload.solution: Forward: 4.62 from a true 10 plus 91% noise power. Perfect noise prediction inverts it exactly to 10.0. Iterative small steps exist because real predictions are imperfect — the whole engineering of samplers is error management across the reverse trajectory.

payload.title: Identify the machinery behind five tools
payload.prompt: For each, write which lineage (GAN / VAE / diffusion / hybrid) you believe dominates and why: (a) an "AI yearbook photo" phone filter running offline, (b) Midjourney or DALL·E-style text-to-image, (c) a face-swap video filter, (d) a text-to-video model, (e) an autoencoder inside an image-editing app that scales images down and up. Defend (e) especially — it is the quiet VAE.
payload.hint: Ask two questions per tool: does it run many denoising steps (diffusion), does it need a discriminator (GAN), does it compress to a latent code first (VAE)?

mistakes.mistake: Thinking diffusion models copy or collage training images
mistakes.fix: Training teaches a noise-prediction function over data statistics; sampling builds an image from new random noise. Memorisation can happen (a real research concern), but copying specific images is not the mechanism.

mistakes.mistake: Believing the GAN era simply ended
mistakes.fix: Diffusion won on controllable text-to-image quality; GANs persist where speed and on-device cost dominate (super-resolution, filters, one-step distilled generators).

mistakes.mistake: Assuming VAEs were replaced too
mistakes.fix: The VAE autoencoder is the compression stage inside latent diffusion pipelines — it decides the latent grid everything else runs on.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting 100 denoising steps to guarantee a better image
mistakes.fix: Beyond a point, extra steps add time, not quality — and can over-sharpen. Quality depends on model, conditioning, guidance and prompt together; steps are one dial of several.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain the diffusion training objective and the diffusion sampling procedure in one paragraph each. Why is this approach more stable to train than a GAN?
payload.answer: Training: take a real image, progressively add Gaussian noise to a randomly chosen timestep, and train a network to predict the added noise (or equivalently the clean image) given the noisy version, conditioned on text. The loss is a simple regression — never a game. Sampling: start from pure Gaussian noise and iteratively apply the learned denoiser over 20–50 steps to reveal an image. Stability follows because the network is trained on a fixed, well-defined corruption process with a plain regression loss; a GAN instead trains two networks in a minimax equilibrium that is fragile — imbalance causes mode collapse or divergence — and offers no likelihood to monitor. Diffusion trades that fragility for slower, iterative sampling, which modern samplers and latent-space tricks have made affordable.
payload.source: Standard generative-models exam question (GAN vs diffusion comparison) and ML research-screen favourite.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: GAN = generator vs discriminator minimax game: sharp samples, unstable training, mode collapse.
VAE = encode to a regularised latent bottleneck and reconstruct: smooth latent space, blurry samples, still the compressor inside modern pipelines.
Diffusion = add noise in training, learn to predict it, then iterate denoising at sampling time — stable regression, controllable steps.
Production text-to-image is hybrid: VAE latent + text-conditioned denoiser + optional adversarial polish.
Lineage is ancestry, not ranking: components of all three live inside today's tools; as of 2026, flow-matching variants shorten the same loop.

questions.prompt: The characteristic failure mode of GANs called "mode collapse" means:
options: The generator produces one narrow kind of output that keeps fooling the discriminator
The discriminator memorises the training set
The model runs out of GPU memory
questions.explanation: The game rewards fooling the critic, not covering the data — so the generator finds one safe output and iterates on it.

questions.prompt: VAE samples traditionally look blurry mainly because:
options: The images are stored at low resolution
The lossy latent bottleneck plus pixel-wise averaging hedges across plausible reconstructions
Too many denoising steps are applied
questions.explanation: Reconstruction losses over many plausible outputs produce their average — the classic blurry VAE look.

questions.prompt: In a diffusion model, the neural network is trained to predict:
options: The class label of the image
The noise added to a noisy image at a given timestep (optionally conditioned on text)
The final image in one pass
questions.explanation: One simple regression target — noise prediction — trained across all noise levels, then iterated at sampling.

questions.prompt: A modern latent text-to-image pipeline typically uses:
options: A GAN alone, with no autoencoder
A VAE to compress pixels into a latent grid, a text-conditioned denoiser in that latent space, and a decoder to pixels
A pure VAE with no denoising
questions.explanation: The ancestors became components: VAE compression, diffusion denoising, often an adversarial loss for crispness.

lessons.title: The Transformer: One Architecture for All of Generative AI
lessons.summary: Self-attention, the residual stack, and why the same block powers chatbots, image generators, speech models and code assistants.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe the transformer block: token mixing by self-attention plus channel mixing by feed-forward layers, stacked with residual connections
Distinguish encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants and name a current use for each
Explain two reasons transformers scaled where recurrent networks stalled
Map a new modality (time series, molecules, audio) onto the transformer recipe: tokenize, choose an objective, choose a variant

payload.text: Ask which architectures power: the chatbot answering you, the image you generated this morning, the transcription of yesterday's lecture, and the code autocomplete in your editor. The honest answer, as of 2026, is "basically one": a stack of transformer blocks with different tokens, objectives and heads bolted on. BERT for your search re-ranker, GPT-style decoder for chat, a vision transformer inside a diffusion model for images, a Conformer-flavoured encoder for speech — same skeleton, four jobs. This lesson is the skeleton.

**The block, in one pass.** A transformer processes a sequence of tokens (words, image patches, audio frames). Each token starts as an embedding plus positional information (an ID-to-vector lookup, Lesson 2.2, plus "you are position 17"). Then it enters a repeating block with two jobs. **Self-attention** lets every token look at every other token and compute a relevance-weighted blend of their information — content-based, not distance-based, computed for all positions in parallel. **The feed-forward network** then transforms each token's representation independently — the "think about what you gathered" step. A residual connection (add the input back to the output) and layer normalisation keep signals flowing across dozens of layers. Stack 30–90 such blocks and you get progressively more abstract per-token representations, ending in a projection to vocabulary logits (for generation) or to a task head (for classification).

**Three variants, one recipe.** *Encoder-only* (BERT lineage): bidirectional attention — every token sees both sides — trained by masking tokens and predicting them. It never generates; it produces rich representations, which is why it still runs search re-rankers, semantic-similarity encoders and classic NLU classifiers. *Decoder-only* (GPT, Llama, Claude, Gemini-class chat models): causal attention — each token sees only the left — which is exactly the next-token prediction shape. This variant won the assistant era because generation *is* its native mode, and because a single clean architecture scales predictably. *Encoder-decoder* (T5, BART): a bidirectional encoder feeds a causal decoder — natural for sequence-to-sequence jobs (translation, summarisation); less dominant now that prompt-only decoder-only models absorbed most tasks.

**Why they beat recurrence.** Old RNN/LSTM models shuffled information through a chain: a fact from token 1 had to survive 500 transformations to matter at token 500, and training could not parallelise over sequence positions (each step depended on the last). Transformers give every token a direct computational path to every other in one step, and — critically for the scaling era — **train all positions simultaneously**: a 100k-token document is one parallel matrix operation per layer, not 100k sequential ones. The bill is attention's quadratic cost in sequence length, which is why long contexts are expensive (Lesson 3.3) — a cost the field keeps paying because the benefits dominate.

**Beyond text: the same block, everywhere.** Vision: cut an image into 16×16 patches, treat each as a token (ViT), classify or generate. Inside image generators: modern diffusion uses a transformer denoiser (DiT) over latent patches rather than a pure convolutional net. Speech: chunk mel-spectrograms into frames and attend over them (Whisper-style encoders, Conformer hybrids). Code and math: still tokens — code has a next token. Even time series and molecules get the treatment after sensible tokenization. The recipe never changes: **decide what a token is, pick an objective (masked / autoregressive / denoising), pick a variant, scale.** As of 2026, attention remains the default even as efficient-attention and state-space (Mamba-style) architectures nibble at its edges — plan for transformers, watch the alternatives.

payload.title: One architecture, three variants
rows: Chat assistants, codegen, agents, tool calling
Translation, classic summarisation, some speech models

payload.title: The three-question modality test
payload.text: Faced with a new data type: (1) what is one token? (2) what is the training objective? (3) which variant? Answer those and you have sketched the system — this is how time-series and audio models were built from the NLP playbook.

payload.title: Why "attention is all you need" aged
payload.text: The 2017 title was about removing recurrence, not about attention being magic: the win was parallel training plus short gradient paths. Those two properties — not the name of the mechanism — are what made internet-scale training economically viable.

payload.title: Design a transformer for a modality you have never seen: weekly power-consumption series
payload.problem: A utility has 2 years of hourly smart-meter readings per household (17,520 numbers each) and wants (a) anomaly alerts and (b) next-week forecasts. Sketch the full transformer recipe: tokenization, objective, variant, heads, and the reason each choice follows.

steps.title: Step 1 — decide what a token is
steps.desc: Two workable options: (i) each hour is one token whose embedding is [value, hour-of-day, day-of-week, season] — sequence length 17,520 (chunk into 1-week windows of 168 tokens); or (ii) patch a week into 24 coarse tokens of 7 hours each. Choose (i) for clarity: token = one hour with calendar features attached.
steps.code_snippet: token_t = embed(value_t) + embed(hour_t) + embed(dow_t) + embed(month_t)

steps.title: Step 2 — pick the objective
steps.desc: Forecasting = autoregressive (predict next tokens from left context) or masked-span prediction (hide future hours, reconstruct them). For alerts, add a masked reconstruction loss: an anomaly is a future hour the model cannot reconstruct well — no labels needed.
steps.code_snippet: loss = next_hour_prediction  (+ masked_future_reconstruction for anomaly scoring)

steps.title: Step 3 — pick the variant
steps.desc: Decoder-only causal stack (GPT-style) for forecasting; the same backbone with a masked objective serves the anomaly head. Encoder-decoder is defensible for multi-step horizons, but a single causal model with an output head keeps serving simple.

steps.title: Step 4 — heads, eval, and the honest caveats
steps.desc: Regression head for the next value (and quantiles for intervals); anomaly score = reconstruction error threshold calibrated on clean weeks. Evaluate on a held-out season (holidays shift the distribution), and remember: the transformer learns patterns, not physics — a cold snap outside its training years can still fool it, exactly like an LLM's knowledge cutoff.

payload.solution: Hour-plus-calendar tokens, causal + masked objectives, decoder-only backbone, regression/anomaly heads, seasonal hold-out. The same four decisions built BERT, GPT, Whisper and DiT — the recipe is the transferable skill.

payload.title: Reverse-engineer five tools
payload.prompt: Pick five AI tools you know (chat, image gen, transcription, autocomplete, spam filter). For each, guess: variant (encoder-only / decoder-only / encoder-decoder / other), token type, and objective. Circle the two you are least sure about and say what experiment would reveal the answer (e.g. can it generate? can it see both directions of context?).
payload.hint: If the tool never produces output text token-by-token, encoder-only is a strong bet; if it streams generation, it is a causal decoder.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking attention only exists inside LLMs
mistakes.fix: Transformers run speech recognition, image classification, diffusion denoisers, recommendation re-rankers and protein models. LLMs are one variant serving one objective.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming BERT-style models were replaced by LLMs
mistakes.fix: Bidirectional encoders still dominate embedding and re-ranking duties: they see both directions, are cheaper than generators, and output vectors instead of text.

mistakes.mistake: Believing transformers "read" like humans — full document at once, understandingly
mistakes.fix: They compute relevance-weighted mixes of token representations per layer. Coherence emerges from that computation plus training data statistics, not from a comprehension faculty.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting attention cost to scale gently with context
mistakes.fix: Standard attention is quadratic in sequence length during prefill: doubling the document roughly quadruples that work. Long-context features are a compute decision, not a checkbox.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why did transformers replace recurrent architectures for large-scale language modelling? Answer with respect to (a) long-range dependencies and (b) training efficiency.
payload.answer: (a) Long-range dependencies: in an RNN, information from token 1 must pass through every intermediate state to influence token 500; vanishing signals make those paths unreliable. Self-attention creates a direct computational path between every pair of tokens in one step, with relevance determined by content rather than distance, so a pronoun can connect to its antecedent regardless of separation. (b) Training efficiency: recurrence is inherently sequential over positions — you cannot compute step t until step t−1 finishes — which caps data parallelism. Attention computes all positions at once, so batches and hardware are saturated and models can be trained on trillion-token corpora economically. The trade-off is quadratic cost in sequence length, which modern implementations (FlashAttention-style kernels, GQA, sliding windows) mitigate but do not erase.
payload.source: The canonical "transformers vs RNNs" interview question across ML and LLM roles.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: The transformer block = self-attention (mix information across tokens) + feed-forward (think per token), repeated with residuals and norms.
Encoder-only = bidirectional representations (retrieval, NLU); decoder-only = causal generation (assistants); encoder-decoder = sequence-to-sequence.
Transformers won on two levers: direct token-to-token paths and full-sequence parallel training — at the price of quadratic attention cost.
Any modality can be transformerised: define tokens, choose masked/autoregressive/denoising objective, choose a variant, scale.
As of 2026 attention is still the default; efficient-attention and state-space models are challengers, not replacements.

questions.prompt: The two core operations inside a standard transformer block are:
options: Self-attention across tokens and a per-token feed-forward network
questions.explanation: Attention mixes information across positions; the feed-forward layers transform each position independently — stacked with residuals and norms.

questions.prompt: A BERT-style encoder-only model is unsuited to free-form generation mainly because it:
options: Uses bidirectional attention and a masked-token objective, so it has no autoregressive left-to-right generation mode
questions.explanation: Its training shape produces representations, not a causal next-token loop — which is why it lives in retrieval and classification.

questions.prompt: Compared with RNNs, transformers train faster at scale primarily because they:
options: Compute all sequence positions in parallel instead of stepping through them sequentially
questions.explanation: Position-wise parallelism saturates GPUs — the economic unlock behind trillion-token pretraining.

questions.prompt: To apply a transformer to images, the standard move (ViT-style) is to:
options: Feed raw pixels one by one as characters
Split the image into patches and treat each patch as a token
Convert the image to English prose first
questions.explanation: Patch tokenization turns vision into a sequence problem — the recipe that also underlies diffusion transformers.

lessons.title: Foundation Models and the Modality Map
lessons.summary: Train once, adapt everywhere: what a foundation model is, how each modality is tokenised and generated, and what "multimodal" really claims about a product.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Define a foundation model in terms of broad pretraining plus many downstream adaptations
Build a modality map: for text, image, audio, video and code, name the token representation and the generation objective
Distinguish input multimodality, output multimodality and interleaved/omni behaviour with a concrete example of each
Audit a product's "multimodal" marketing claim and classify what it actually supports

payload.text: A vendor page announces: "our assistant is multimodal." Read the fine print and it accepts images and text but only returns text. Another claims video understanding, meaning it samples 1 frame per second and captions them. Meanwhile a live-voice assistant genuinely speaks, listens, and shows images mid-sentence. Same word, three very different systems. In this lesson you learn to decode that word — and the broader map of how foundation models cover text, image, audio, video and code.

**Foundation model = pretrain once, adapt many times.** The term names a training *strategy*, not a size: one model is pre-trained on broad, mostly unlabelled data spanning a domain (the internet, code repositories, image-caption pairs), acquiring general capabilities; then it is adapted cheaply to dozens of downstream jobs — by prompting, by in-context examples, by lightweight fine-tuning, by adding heads. Before this pattern, you trained a separate model per task (one sentiment model, one summariser, one tagger). Foundation models invert the economics: the expensive general learning is amortised across every product built on top, and adaptation costs a prompt rather than a training run. The same weights serve as assistant, extractor, tutor and reviewer — which is also why their failure modes travel with you from task to task.

**The modality map.** Every modality is handled by the same three moves: represent it as tokens (or continuous equivalents), choose an objective, decode back.

- **Text**: tokens are BPE subword IDs; objective is next-token prediction; decoding is sampling (Lesson 2.3). The reference implementation of the whole recipe.
- **Code**: still text tokens, but the corpus is repositories and the objective inherits execution semantics — code that compiles and passes tests is more frequent in the data than random token soup. Tool-added execution (running the code) is scaffolding around the model, not the model itself.
- **Image**: pixels are compressed by an autoencoder into a latent grid, then cut into latent patches (tokens); the objective is denoising (diffusion/flow) or sometimes autoregressive patch prediction; decoding runs the denoiser and the pixel decoder (Lesson 4.1).
- **Audio**: waveforms become mel-spectrogram frames or discrete codec tokens from an neural codec model; speech-to-text is encoder-decoder transcription, text-to-speech is a conditioning-then-vocoder pipeline, and music/voice generation conditions a generative model on text or a reference voice (Lesson 4.3).
- **Video**: the token explosion — a second of 24 fps video is 24 frames, each latent-patchable, plus optional audio tokens. Objectives add *temporal* consistency on top of per-frame denoising; decoding is expensive enough that clip length, resolution and cost are first-class constraints (Lesson 4.4).

**What "multimodal" actually means.** Three distinct claims, often blurred: (1) **multimodal input** — the model accepts images, audio or PDFs alongside text and fuses them into one context (vision-language models; you see it as "upload a screenshot and ask"). (2) **multimodal output** — it can produce non-text: an image, speech audio, a rendered chart. (3) **interleaved / omni** — the hard one: output alternates modalities within one turn ("here is the chart" + generated image + spoken narration), usually requiring every modality to be tokenised into the *same* sequence so one decoder handles all of it, with real-time streaming for voice. Cross-modal understanding (captioning an image, transcribing audio) is input-side; cross-modal generation is output-side. A product that only transcribes audio is multimodal-*input*. The word is real; the fine print decides which of the three you bought. As of 2026 the frontier labs ship omni-style voice models while most enterprise "multimodal" features mean images-in, text-out — audit before you architect.

payload.title: "Multimodal" without an output modality is half a claim
payload.text: Most assistants today are multimodal-input, text-output. If your use case needs the model to *speak back* or *draw*, verify output modality, latency, and whether modalities interleave in one turn or are separate API calls stitched by your code.

payload.title: Architect to the token boundary
payload.text: When products stitch modalities (transcribe → summarise → speak), your code owns the seams: timestamps, formats and error handling between stages. Native omni models move those seams inside the model — fewer failure points, less control.

payload.title: Audit a "multimodal assistant" claim before you build on it
payload.problem: A startup demo shows "the world's first multimodal tutor": upload a photo of a handwritten physics problem, get a typed solution, then hear a spoken explanation with a redrawn diagram. Decompose the claim into input/output/interleaved requirements, decide which parts need which modality machinery, and flag what you must verify before committing the product roadmap.

steps.title: Step 1 — split the flow into modality hops
steps.desc: Hop A: image + text in → typed solution (multimodal INPUT, vision-language model). Hop B: solution → speech (text-to-audio OUTPUT: TTS pipeline or an omni model with audio out). Hop C: redrawn diagram (image OUTPUT: diffusion model or programmatic plotting). Hop D: spoken explanation synced to the diagram (INTERLEAVED — the hard part).

steps.title: Step 2 — decide native vs stitched
steps.desc: If one omni model natively emits text + audio in one stream, Hop B merges into Hop A but the diagram likely still needs a separate image call (or code-generated plot). Most 2026 stacks are stitched: your backend orchestrates vision-LM → TTS → image gen, owning latency, caching and failure handling at every seam.

steps.title: Step 3 — verify the fine print
steps.desc: Questions to send the vendor: (1) does the model accept images natively or via OCR? (2) audio output: streaming or batch file? (3) any interleaved mode, or only sequential API calls? (4) rate limits and latency per hop? (5) handwriting quality on non-Latin scripts? Each answer changes feasibility more than the word "multimodal" ever did.

steps.title: Step 4 — restate the roadmap honestly
steps.desc: Write it back as: "vision-LM input (images) + separate TTS and image-generation outputs, orchestrated by our backend" — or "native omni, but diagram generation is separate". Now latency budgets, cost models and failure modes are visible. The marketing word never gave you that.

payload.solution: Four modality hops: image-in/text-out (input multimodal), TTS and image-gen (output multimodal), and a sync requirement (interleaved). The audit converts a slogan into an architecture with verifiable vendor questions and explicit orchestration seams.

payload.title: Draw your own modality map
payload.prompt: For three tools you use (e.g. a chat assistant, a note app with AI, a video platform), fill a mini table: accepted input modalities, produced output modalities, whether modalities interleave within one response, and one thing you would need to verify before building a feature on it. Then write one sentence defining "multimodal" that would survive a skeptical engineer's cross-examination.
payload.hint: Test a tool by uploading an image and asking it to *return* an image or audio — not just to describe it. Input and output asymmetry is where claims hide.

mistakes.mistake: Equating "foundation model" with "the largest model available"
mistakes.fix: It names a strategy — broad pretraining plus cheap adaptation — not a parameter count. Many small models qualify; some huge ones are single-purpose.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a multimodal input model can also generate that modality
mistakes.fix: Vision-language models typically read images and write text. Producing images or speech needs different machinery (decoders/generators) — always check both directions.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking video models are "just image models run in a loop"
mistakes.fix: Consistency over time — identity, lighting, physics — requires temporal modelling and is the dominant cost and failure source (Lesson 4.4).

mistakes.mistake: Believing code is a wholly separate modality with its own non-text machinery
mistakes.fix: Code is text tokens; what differs is the corpus and the evaluation signal (execution). Treating it as text keeps the whole token/sampling mental model in force.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define "foundation model" and distinguish multimodal input from multimodal output, giving one example of each and one example of interleaved behaviour.
payload.answer: A foundation model is a model pretrained on broad, general data to acquire widely reusable capabilities, then adapted to many downstream tasks cheaply (prompting, in-context examples, light fine-tuning) rather than trained per task — the economics are "expensive general training, amortised across products". Multimodal input means the model consumes non-text modalities (e.g. an image of a chart plus a text question, answered in text). Multimodal output means it produces non-text (e.g. generating an image from a caption, or synthesising speech from text). Interleaved behaviour — the strongest claim — means multiple modalities appear within a single response turn, such as an answer that mixes sentences, a generated diagram and spoken narration in one stream, which generally requires all modalities encoded into one token sequence handled by a unified decoder. Auditing which of the three a product actually supports is the practical skill: most assistants today are strong on input, text-only on output.
payload.source: Common product-design and ML-fundamentals question: "what exactly do you mean by multimodal?"

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Foundation models invert the economics: pay once for broad pretraining, adapt per task with prompts or light fine-tuning.
Every modality follows the same recipe: tokenize → objective → decode; text/BPE next-token is the reference case.
Code is text with a better corpus and execution signals; images are latent patches with denoising; audio uses frames/codec tokens; video adds temporal consistency and cost.
"Multimodal" hides three claims: multimodal input, multimodal output, interleaved/omni output — read the fine print.
When modalities are stitched by your backend, the seams (latency, formats, failures) are your engineering problem.

questions.prompt: A foundation model is best described as:
options: The largest model a lab has trained
A broadly pretrained model adapted cheaply to many downstream tasks via prompting or fine-tuning
A model that has been fine-tuned on foundation-stone data
Any model with more than 100B parameters
questions.explanation: The name describes the pretrain-once/adapt-many strategy, not a size.

questions.prompt: In a modern text-to-image system, images are represented as:
options: Latent patches from an autoencoder, denoised under a text condition
questions.explanation: Autoencoder latent compression plus patch tokenisation keeps sequence lengths tractable for the denoiser.

questions.prompt: An assistant that accepts photos and PDFs but only ever replies with text is:
options: Multimodal on input only, with text-only output
questions.explanation: Input and output multimodality are separate claims; this one supports only the input side.

questions.prompt: Interleaved (omni) multimodal behaviour means the model can:
options: Accept several file uploads at once
Emit different modalities within a single response stream — text, audio and images in one turn
questions.explanation: One response containing several modalities in sequence — the strongest form of the claim, requiring unified tokenisation or orchestration.

modules.title: Module 2 — LLM Mechanics, Deeper
modules.summary: Inside the tokenizer (BPE merges and ranks), inside the vector space (contextual embeddings), inside the sampler (logits, softmax, temperature, top-k, top-p worked by hand) and inside serving (system prompts, stop sequences, streaming and the KV cache that makes long context expensive).

lessons.title: BPE Tokenization Internals: How the Vocabulary Is Built
lessons.summary: Byte-pair encoding from the inside: counting pairs, merging by frequency, applying merges by rank — and why token counts differ across providers and languages.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe BPE training: start from characters, count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent, repeat until a target vocabulary size
Apply merge ranks to encode a word by hand and predict its tokens
Explain why byte-level BPE guarantees any input can be encoded, including typos and other scripts
Predict which of three texts will tokenize most and least efficiently, and connect that to cost and context limits

payload.text: Ask four different assistants "how many tokens is this?" and get four different numbers for the same paragraph. The tokenizer is not a formality — GPT-class models carry roughly 100k vocab entries, Llama-class models around 128k, Mistral-class around 32k, Qwen-class around 150k (all approximate, shifting with releases as of 2026). Those choices decide your bill, your effective context size, and why your name, your PIN, and your Tamil sentence behave oddly. This lesson takes the tokenizer apart and rebuilds it.

**The problem BPE solves.** Word-level vocabularies explode into millions of entries (every name, typo, inflection); character-level vocabularies are tiny but produce sequences so long the model drowns. BPE (byte-pair encoding), originally a data-compression trick, threads the needle: build a *subword* vocabulary from data by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols.

**Training, concretely.** Start with a corpus where every word is split into characters (byte-level variants start from bytes, covered below). Count every adjacent pair across all word *types* weighted by frequency. Merge the winner — the new symbol joins the vocabulary — and recount. Repeat until you hit the target vocabulary size (say 32k or 128k merges). Early merges create frequent short chunks (t, h, e, space-the); middle merges fuse common words (the, ing, re); late merges create whole rare words and domain terms. The result: frequent words survive whole, rare words split into reusable pieces, and unseen words still encode — awkwardly, but never by failure. Crucially, training produces a **merge table with ranks**: merges are applied at encode time *in rank order*, lowest first. Encoding is therefore deterministic: same tokenizer, same text, same tokens, always.

**Byte-level BPE: never fail.** GPT-2/3/4-family tokenizers operate over UTF-8 bytes rather than Unicode characters, with 256 byte slots always available as fallback. Any string — emoji, Sanskrit compound, a broken byte sequence — encodes to *something*. The cost: exotic characters consume several byte tokens each, which is one honest reason non-English text often costs more tokens than the same meaning in English. (Different families make different trade-offs: some use SentencePiece-style **unigram** tokenization — a probabilistic vocabulary learned by likelihood rather than a merge list — plus explicit byte fallback. Different algorithm, same economic consequences.)

**What else lives in the tokenizer.** Special tokens mark message boundaries (start/end of turn, system/user/assistant roles) via a **chat template** — the exact template your model expects. Feed a model the wrong template (or none) and it degrades silently: it was trained with those markers present. There is also a subtlety worth carrying forward: **the tokenizer is fixed before training and never learns**. Vocabulary size, language coverage and numeric chunking are frozen decisions that shape everything downstream — arithmetic reliability (digits chunked into non-positional groups), multilingual cost asymmetry, and code formatting quirks (leading spaces attach to tokens, so indentation-sensitive languages tokenize in a whitespace-dependent way). When a provider says "200k context", that is 200k of *these* units — roughly 150k English words, but fewer in less efficiently covered languages, more for digit-dense or base64 content.

payload.code:
# Tiny BPE: train a merge table, then encode with it
corpus = {"hug": 10, "hugs": 5, "unhug": 1}   # word -> frequency

# After counting weighted adjacent pairs:
#   (h,u)=16  (u,g)=16  (g,s)=5  (u,n)=1  (n,h)=1
# Merge the most frequent (tie -> first occurrence wins): "hu"
#   now (hu,g)=16  -> merge "hug"
#   now (hug,s)=5  -> merge "hugs"     # stop at vocab budget
merges = [("h", "u"), ("hu", "g"), ("hug", "s"), ("un", "h")]

def encode(word, merges):
    toks = list(word)
    for a, b in merges:                 # merges applied IN RANK ORDER
        i = 0
        while i < len(toks) - 1:
            if toks[i] == a and toks[i + 1] == b:
                toks[i:i + 2] = [a + b]
            else:
                i += 1
    return toks

print(encode("hugs", merges))    # ['hugs']
print(encode("unhug", merges))   # ['u', 'n', 'hug']
# An unseen word never fails: it degrades into known pieces.

payload.title: Tokenization efficiency varies by content
rows: Dominant coverage in most training corpora
More tokens than "123" looks like; hurts arithmetic

payload.title: Provider tokenizer tools are the authority
payload.text: Rule-of-thumb estimates are for mental math; anything billing- or limit-critical should go through the provider's official tokenizer counter. Cross-provider counts genuinely differ.

payload.title: Train a BPE merge table on a 3-word corpus, then encode
payload.problem: Corpus: "hug"×10, "hugs"×5, "unhug"×1. Target vocab = 4 new symbols. Run the BPE training loop (count pairs, merge, recount, tie-break by first occurrence), then encode "hugs" and "unhug" using the final merge table in rank order.

steps.title: Step 1 — count weighted pairs
steps.desc: Expand by frequency: (h,u) = 10+5+1 = 16, (u,g) = 16, (g,s) = 5, (u,n) = 1, (n,h) = 1. Winner: a 16-way tie between (h,u) and (u,g) — break by first occurrence, so (h,u) merges first.

steps.title: Step 2 — merge 1: "hu", then recount
steps.desc: Words become: hu+g (×10), hu+g+s (×5), u+n+hu+g (×1). New pairs: (hu,g)=16, (g,s)=5, (u,n)=1, (n,hu)=1. Winner: (hu,g).

steps.title: Step 3 — merges 2 and 3
steps.desc: Merge 2 creates "hug" (16). Now: hug×10, hug+s×5, u+n+hug×1 → pairs (hug,s)=5, (u,n)=1, (n,hug)=1. Merge 3 creates "hugs". Vocabulary now: base chars + hu + hug + hugs (budget reached; "un"/"nhug" never win).
steps.code_snippet: rank1: hu   rank2: hug   rank3: hugs

steps.title: Step 4 — encode by applying ranks in order
steps.desc: "hugs" → h,u,g,s → (rank1) hu,g,s → (rank2) hug,s → (rank3) hugs ⇒ ["hugs"]. "unhug" → u,n,h,u,g → (rank1) u,n,hu,g → (rank2) u,n,hug ⇒ ["u","n","hug"]. The trained word stayed whole; the other word fell back to pieces — exactly the intended behaviour for unseen text.

payload.solution: Merges in order: hu → hug → hugs. Encoding yields ["hugs"] and ["u", "n", "hug"]. The algorithm is just weighted pair counting plus rank-ordered substitution — deterministic, data-driven, and incapable of failing on any input at byte level.

payload.title: Predict, then verify
payload.prompt: Before using any tool: predict token counts for (a) "unbelievable", (b) "₹1,299.00", (c) your full name, (d) the Hindi sentence you know best, (e) a 6-line Python function. Then verify at least two with a public tokenizer page. Write down where your predictions were off and which of the five efficiency rules (Lesson table) explains each miss.
payload.hint: Expect name, currency, digits and non-Latin script to cost more than intuition suggests; smooth English prose to be cheapest.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the tokenizer as part of the neural network
mistakes.fix: It is a fixed, deterministic algorithm (counts and merges / a vocabulary model) chosen before training. The model never updates it — which is why its quirks are permanent.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming vocabulary size means linguistic completeness
mistakes.fix: Vocabulary is an engineering budget. A 128k vocab is 128k merge outcomes fitted to a corpus mix — coverage follows data frequency, not linguistic importance.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting identical token counts across providers
mistakes.fix: Different vocabularies, algorithms (BPE vs unigram) and chat templates produce different counts for identical text — always measure with the specific provider's tool.

mistakes.mistake: Blaming "the model" for numeric or multilingual tokenization weirdness
mistakes.fix: Digit chunking and language efficiency are frozen into the tokenizer. Mitigate with tool-using code for arithmetic and per-language budgeting for multilingual products.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the BPE training algorithm and explain why byte-level BPE is preferred over word-level or character-level tokenization.
payload.answer: Training: represent the corpus as character (or byte) sequences weighted by word frequency; count all adjacent symbol pairs; merge the most frequent pair into a new vocabulary symbol; repeat until the vocabulary budget is met. This yields a rank-ordered merge table. Encoding applies those merges in rank order, deterministically, so frequent words remain whole while rare and unseen words decompose into learned pieces. Byte-level encoding (over 256 UTF-8 bytes rather than Unicode characters) guarantees any input — typos, emoji, low-resource scripts — can be represented, removing out-of-vocabulary failure entirely. Compared with word-level schemes it keeps the vocabulary manageable (tens to low hundreds of thousands rather than millions) and covers unseen forms; compared with character-level it keeps sequence lengths short enough for context windows and attention cost, while giving the model meaningful subword units instead of raw letters.
payload.source: Standard NLP interview question (tokenization) and a favourite in LLM-infrastructure screens.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: BPE trains a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair; the output is a rank-ordered merge table.
Encoding is deterministic: apply merges lowest-rank first — frequent words stay whole, rare words fall back to pieces.
Byte-level BPE never fails on any input; exotic characters just cost several tokens.
Tokenizer choices freeze forever: they set multilingual cost, numeric behaviour, code whitespace quirks and chat templates.
Token counts are provider-specific — measure with the official tokenizer for anything billing- or limit-critical.

questions.prompt: BPE vocabulary training works by:
options: Listing every word in a dictionary and sorting by frequency
Starting from characters, repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair until the vocabulary budget is reached
Learning embeddings for each word jointly with the LLM
Splitting text at every punctuation mark
questions.explanation: Weighted pair counting plus iterative merging — a compression algorithm repurposed as a tokenizer.

questions.prompt: At encode time, a trained BPE tokenizer applies merges according to:
options: The rank order established during training (lowest rank first)
The order words appear in your prompt
questions.explanation: Rank order is what makes encoding deterministic and reproducible across runs and machines.

questions.prompt: Byte-level BPE is valuable mainly because it:
options: Guarantees any input — typos, emoji, other scripts — can be encoded using the 256 byte slots
Removes the need for a vocabulary
Makes multilingual text cost fewer tokens than English
questions.explanation: No out-of-vocabulary failure by construction; the trade-off is that exotic characters may consume multiple byte tokens.

questions.prompt: Why do two providers report different token counts for the same paragraph?
options: They use different vocabularies, algorithms and chat templates — tokenizer design is a per-provider engineering choice
Tokens are measured in words after 2024
questions.explanation: Distinct tokenizers partition text differently; counts are only meaningful relative to a specific tokenizer.

lessons.title: Embeddings in Vector Space: Meaning as Geometry
lessons.summary: Contextual vectors, cosine similarity and the retrieval machinery embeddings power — plus how the same geometry lives inside every layer of an LLM.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain how an LLM produces a contextual embedding for a token and how sentence embeddings are derived for retrieval
Compute and interpret cosine similarity on toy vectors with a chosen threshold
Distinguish embedding models (vector output) from generative models (text output) and where each fits in a pipeline
Diagnose three common embedding failures: domain mismatch, uncalibrated thresholds, and bias inherited from the corpus

payload.text: Search "how do I reset my password" in a modern help centre and you find the article titled "Change your login credentials" — no keyword overlap, yet it ranks first. Behind it: an embedding model turned both texts into vectors and cosine similarity did the matching. The same geometry powers semantic search, RAG retrieval, deduplication, clustering, moderation — and, one level down, the internal representations every LLM computation runs on. Two uses of "embedding", one idea: meaning as position in space.

**From IDs to coordinates.** A token ID is an arbitrary label — swapping numbers changes nothing. An *embedding* replaces the label with a dense vector (hundreds to a few thousand numbers) whose geometry is learned: tokens used in similar contexts land near each other. In an LLM, this is the input lookup — but the important move is that embeddings become **contextual**: the vector for "bank" is recomputed per sentence from everything around it, so "river bank" and "bank balance" occupy different positions. Layers above the input embedding transform these vectors further; the vectors a model attends over are the evolving, per-layer representations — this is what attention actually manipulates (Lesson 1.3).

**Embedding models for retrieval.** Separate from the LLM sit *embedding models*: networks trained so that related texts — across paraphrase, languages, even modalities (CLIP-style image/text models share one space) — end up close. Typical pipeline: embed the corpus once, store vectors, embed the query, take nearest neighbours by **cosine similarity** (the cosine of the angle between vectors — 1.0 identical direction, 0 orthogonal, insensitive to magnitude once normalised; equivalently, dot product on normalised vectors). Sentence-level embeddings are produced by pooling token vectors (mean pooling, a special summary token, or a model trained directly on sentence objectives) — pooling choice matters: an embedding model tuned for search beats naive averaging of an LLM's last layer.

**How similarity is used.** (1) Retrieval: top-k nearest chunks feed a generator (the R of RAG). (2) Deduplication and clustering: similarity above a high threshold ⇒ near-duplicate. (3) Classify-by-centroid: average embeddings per class, assign by nearest centroid — a discriminative use of generative-era geometry. (4) Reranking and moderation: cheap first-pass filter before an expensive model. Notice what never appears: a probability. Cosine 0.82 is *not* "82% relevant" — scores are model-specific, uncalibrated, and typically compressed into a narrow band (many models never produce values below ~0.3 for normalised text pairs), which is why thresholds must be set from your own judged pairs, not from intuition.

**Failure modes worth knowing.** *Domain mismatch*: an embedding model trained on web prose clusters legal clauses poorly — measure retrieval on your data. *Anisotropy / hubness*: real embedding spaces are "banana-shaped" — vectors cluster in a narrow cone, and some generic texts become near-neighbours of everything (hubs), skewing retrieval; mean-centring and Matryoshka-style dimension truncation are partial remedies. *Length and truncation limits*: models see a fixed token budget; long documents silently lose their tail. *Bias*: geometry faithfully reproduces corpus associations (Lesson 1.3 caveat applies). And the meta-point: embeddings are cheap, fast, non-generative and auditable — which is exactly why production systems use vectors for routing and retrieval while reserving the LLM for language.

payload.title: Embedding models vs generative models in a pipeline
rows: Fluent but wrong or hallucinated text

payload.title: A cosine threshold is a product decision
payload.text: 0.75 may be perfect for near-duplicate tickets and disastrous for cross-topic recall. Label ~100 query-result pairs, sweep the threshold, plot precision/recall — then pick. Never import a threshold from a blog post.

payload.title: Embeddings as a free classifier
payload.text: Before paying for an LLM call on a routing decision, try embedding + nearest centroid or similarity to labelled exemplars. It is often 95% as good at 1% of the cost, with the LLM reserved for exceptions.

payload.title: Compute similarities by hand and set a dedup threshold
payload.problem: Three 3-D toy embeddings (already normalised for simplicity): u = (1, 0, 0) — "reset password"; v = (0.8, 0.6, 0) — "change login credentials"; w = (0.5, 0.5, 0.707) — "enable two-factor auth". Compute cos(u,v), cos(u,w), cos(v,w). Then design a dedup rule for a ticket queue and state one risk of your chosen threshold.

steps.title: Step 1 — cosine for u and v
steps.desc: cos = (u·v) / (|u|·|v|) = (1×0.8 + 0 + 0) / (1 × 1) = 0.8. Two paraphrased tickets — strongly aligned.

steps.title: Step 2 — cosine for u and w
steps.desc: cos(u,w) = (1×0.5 + 0 + 0) / (1 × √(0.25+0.25+0.5)) = 0.5 / 1 = 0.5. Related domain, different intent — much weaker.

steps.title: Step 3 — cosine for v and w
