steps.desc: cos(v,w) = (0.8×0.5 + 0.6×0.5 + 0) / 1 = 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7. Interesting: v and w are closer to each other than either is to u — a reminder that intuition about "closeness" must be checked numerically.

steps.title: Step 4 — set the threshold, name the risk
steps.desc: For "merge obvious duplicates only": threshold 0.78 catches u–v (0.80) and misses v–w (0.70) — high precision, lower recall. At 0.68 you also merge v–w, risking over-merge of distinct intents. Recommendation: 0.78 for auto-merge, 0.68–0.78 routed to a human/LLM check — and validate both numbers on ~100 labelled pairs from your own queue, because real-model scores are uncalibrated.

payload.solution: cos(u,v)=0.80, cos(u,w)=0.50, cos(v,w)=0.70. Auto-merge at 0.78, human-check the 0.68–0.78 band, calibrate on labelled pairs — thresholds are data-driven product decisions, not constants of embedding space.

payload.title: Build a mini semantic-search test
payload.prompt: Pick 10 sentences from your own notes on one topic plus 5 unrelated sentences from a different topic. If you have access to an embedding tool/API: embed all 15, and for three probe queries write the top-3 neighbours and their scores. If not: hand-sketch where you would place them in 2-D and mark what a threshold of "close enough" would include. Report one surprising neighbour and your best explanation for it.
payload.hint: Look for a generic sentence (e.g. "This is important") acting as a hub — near many things because it fits many contexts.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing token IDs with embeddings
mistakes.fix: IDs are arbitrary integer labels with zero geometry; embeddings are dense learned coordinates where distance carries meaning. The ID is the index; the embedding is the content.

mistakes.mistake: Reading cosine similarity as a probability
mistakes.fix: It is an uncalibrated, model-specific angle score, often compressed into a narrow range. Convert to probabilities only via calibration on labelled data.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming one embedding model suits every domain
mistakes.fix: Retrieval quality is domain-dependent: legal, medical and code text need evaluation against your corpus, and sometimes a model fine-tuned for that domain, before deployment.

mistakes.mistake: Believing embeddings are objective, bias-free meaning
mistakes.fix: They are geometry fitted to corpus statistics — social biases appear as directions and neighbourhoods. Audit similarity behaviour on sensitive attributes before using them for decisions.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain how embeddings enable semantic search, including the similarity metric used, how vectors are typically stored and queried, and one limitation practitioners must handle.
payload.answer: Each document (or chunk) is converted by an embedding model into a fixed-size vector such that semantically related texts are close in that space; queries are embedded with the same model. Similarity — usually cosine similarity, equivalently dot product on normalised vectors — ranks documents by closeness, and the top-k are returned or passed to a generator. Vectors are stored in a vector index (exact search at small scale; approximate nearest-neighbour structures like HNSW for scale), often with metadata filters. Key limitation: scores are uncalibrated — "0.8" is not 80% relevant — so thresholds must be tuned on labelled pairs; additionally, domain mismatch can silently collapse retrieval quality, and long documents may be truncated or need chunking before embedding. Semantic search therefore improves but does not replace evaluation: you still measure whether the right chunk is retrieved for real questions.
payload.source: Core RAG/search engineering question; also appears in ML system-design interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Embeddings turn symbols into learned coordinates; modern LLM embeddings are contextual, recomputed from surrounding text.
Retrieval uses cosine similarity (or normalised dot product) over stored vectors queried by ANN indexes.
Embedding models output vectors cheaply and near-deterministically; LLMs output language expensively — different pipeline roles.
Cosine scores are uncalibrated: set thresholds from labelled pairs on your own data, never from intuition.
Geometry inherits corpus bias and suffers domain mismatch, truncation and hubness — evaluate, do not assume.

questions.prompt: In modern LLMs, a token's embedding is best described as:
options: A fixed lookup-table entry that never changes
A contextual vector recomputed from the surrounding sequence
questions.explanation: Contextualisation is the difference between static word vectors (word2vec era) and transformer representations.

questions.prompt: Cosine similarity between two embedding vectors measures:
options: The cosine of the angle between them — direction alignment, independent of magnitude
The probability that the documents are relevant
questions.explanation: Direction, not length, and definitely not a calibrated probability.

questions.prompt: Why must similarity thresholds be tuned on your own labelled pairs?
options: Scores are model-specific and uncalibrated — value ranges and semantics differ across models and domains
questions.explanation: A "good" score for one model/domain may be unreachable for another; calibration comes from data.

questions.prompt: The clearest division of labour in a RAG pipeline is:
options: The LLM embeds documents and the embedding model writes the answer
The embedding model retrieves candidate chunks by vector similarity; the LLM reads them and generates the answer
Both models generate text and vote
Embeddings are only used for billing
questions.explanation: Cheap vector matching for recall, expensive generation for language — each model doing the job its training supports.

lessons.title: From Logit to Token: Softmax, Temperature, Top-k and Top-p
lessons.summary: The full sampling pipeline with hand-worked numbers: raw scores to probabilities to the one token that gets appended.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Trace the decoding pipeline: logits → temperature-scaled softmax → top-k/top-p filtering → renormalisation → sampled token
Compute a softmax by hand and predict how temperature 0.5 reshapes it
Derive the exact candidate sets for top-k=3 and top-p=0.9 on a given distribution
Choose a decoding configuration for four different tasks and justify each choice

payload.text: Run the same prompt three times and the answers differ — except when temperature is 0 and they suddenly do not. Your JSON extractor fails at temperature 1 but passes at 0.1. A brainstorming tool feels "samey" at low settings and unhinged at high ones. None of this is magic: between the model's raw scores and the token you see sit a handful of arithmetic operations, each with a knob. This lesson runs those operations by hand so the knobs stop being folklore.

**Logits: raw scores.** The model's final layer emits one number per vocabulary token — the **logit** — for the next position. They are unnormalised: 4.2, 1.8, −0.3, … Positive, negative, any magnitude; alone they mean nothing.

**Softmax: scores into probabilities.** Softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum: pᵢ = e^zi / Σe^zj. Exponentiation makes everything positive and *amplifies differences* — a 1-unit logit gap becomes a 2.72× probability ratio — then normalisation forces the distribution to sum to 1, giving a usable "next token" distribution. (If all logits are equal, softmax returns uniform.)

**Temperature: reshape before you sample.** Divide logits by T before softmax. T < 1 sharpens: gaps inflate, the leader pulls away, the tail shrinks — toward greedy, deterministic decoding as T → 0. T > 1 flattens: gaps deflate, long-shots gain mass — variety and risk together. Note precisely what temperature is *not*: it does not add knowledge or creativity from outside the model; it re-weights the probabilities the model already holds, including bad ones.

**Top-k and top-p: cut the candidate set, then renormalise.** Top-k keeps exactly the k highest-probability tokens regardless of shape. Top-p (nucleus) keeps the *smallest* set whose cumulative probability reaches p — dynamic: two tokens when confident, hundreds when uncertain. In both cases the survivors are renormalised to sum to 1 before drawing the token. APIs apply them in a standard order: **logits → temperature → softmax → top-k/top-p filter → renormalise → sample**. Practically: tune temperature first, leave top-p at the provider default (0.9–0.95 is common) until you have a reason, and treat top-k as a belt-and-braces guard against tail garbage. Some open-source stacks instead expose **min-p** (keep tokens at least a fraction of the top token's probability), which scales with model confidence — same idea, different cut rule.

**Greedy, sampling, and what is rare where.** Greedy (argmax / T=0) is right for extraction, classification-style tasks and reproducible pipelines. Moderate sampling (T ≈ 0.3–0.8) suits chat and drafting. High T (≈ 1.0–1.3) is for genuine brainstorming where you *want* to be surprised. Beam search — the old workhorse of translation — is largely absent from chat LLMs, where diverse natural phrasing beats narrow likelihood maximisation. One honest caveat: T=0 is near-deterministic, not perfectly so — batching order and floating-point hardware can still flip ties.

**Two adjacent controls worth knowing.** *Repetition penalties* (and their cousins, frequency and presence penalties in several APIs) down-weight tokens already emitted, breaking loops before they start — useful at higher temperatures, dangerous at low ones (they can punish legitimate repetition like code identifiers). *Seed parameters*, where exposed, pin the RNG draw so identical settings replay identical samples — the backbone of reproducible prompt experiments. For offline evaluation, the professional default is the boring one: temperature 0, fixed prompts, version-pinned models — so that score changes mean model or prompt changes, not sampling luck. The knobs exist to shape a distribution; disciplined pipelines shape it once, then measure.

payload.code:
import math

logits = [4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -0.5]

def softmax(xs, T=1.0):
    e = [math.exp(x / T) for x in xs]
    s = sum(e)
    return [round(v / s, 3) for v in e]

softmax(logits)         # [0.627, 0.231, 0.085, 0.031, 0.019, 0.007]
softmax(logits, 0.5)    # [0.864, 0.117, 0.016, 0.002, 0.001, 0.0]

def top_p(ps, p=0.9):
    kept, total = [], 0.0
    for prob in sorted(ps, reverse=True):
        kept.append(prob); total += prob
        if total >= p: break
    n = sum(kept)
    return [round(v / n, 3) for v in kept]

top_p(softmax(logits))  # [0.665, 0.245, 0.09]  <- same as top-k=3 here

payload.title: Decoding presets that hold up in practice
rows: Repeatable, minimal deviation from the argmax
Maximum spread over the model's plausible options

payload.title: One dial at a time
payload.text: Changing temperature and top-p together makes experiments uninterpretable. Fix top-p at default, sweep temperature, compare three runs per setting — then touch top-p only if the tail still misbehaves.

payload.title: Hand-run the sampler on a six-token distribution
payload.problem: Next-token logits for candidates [A, B, C, D, E, F] = [4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, −0.5]. (1) Compute softmax at T=1. (2) Compute softmax at T=0.5. (3) Apply top-k=3 at T=1 and renormalise. (4) Apply top-p=0.9 at T=1. (5) Explain when top-p=0.9 would differ from top-k=3.

steps.title: Step 3 — top-k=3, renormalise
steps.desc: Keep A, B, C: mass = 0.627+0.231+0.085 = 0.943. Renormalised: [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]. D, E, F are now impossible — no matter their residual probability.

steps.title: Step 4 — top-p=0.9 and when they diverge
steps.desc: Cumulative: 0.627 → 0.858 → 0.943. Two tokens only reach 0.858 < 0.9, so the nucleus is {A, B, C} — identical to top-k=3 here. They diverge on flatter distributions: if probabilities were [0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1], top-k=3 keeps 75% of mass while top-p=0.9 must keep all five. Rule: top-k is fixed-count, top-p is mass-aware.

payload.solution: T=1: [0.627, 0.231, 0.085, 0.031, 0.019, 0.007]. T=0.5 concentrates to 0.864 on A. Top-k=3 and top-p=0.9 both reduce to {A, B, C} renormalised — they coincide here and split on flat distributions, which is exactly why nucleus sampling is the default adaptive guard.

payload.title: Run the sampler yourself
payload.prompt: Take one prompt you can run at adjustable settings ("Give five product taglines for a campus laundry service"). Run it at T=0, T=0.7, T=1.2 (top-p fixed). Record: overlap between runs, specificity, any invented claims. Then, using the code snippet above, compute softmax and top-p by hand for logits [2.0, 1.9, 1.8, 0.1] at T=1 and T=0.5 and describe how the nucleus changes.
payload.hint: Near-tied logits at T=1 give a broad nucleus; at T=0.5 the first two tokens usually swallow the budget.

mistakes.mistake: Raising temperature to make the model more accurate
mistakes.fix: Temperature re-weights existing probabilities; it cannot add facts or reasoning. For accuracy: lower temperature, ground the input, verify — never "temperature up for truth".

mistakes.mistake: Reading top-p=0.9 as "keep 90% of the vocabulary"
mistakes.fix: It keeps the smallest set covering 90% of the *probability mass* — often a handful of tokens when confident, hundreds when flat.

mistakes.mistake: Setting temperature, top-k and top-p all to extreme values together
mistakes.fix: Stacked filters interact: high T plus tight p/k starves variety; high T plus p=1.0 drags tail garbage in. Tune temperature first, keep p at default, use k/min-p as guards.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting T=0 to make output bit-identical everywhere
mistakes.fix: Greedy is near-deterministic: ties, batching order and hardware kernels can still change results. For reproducibility pin the model version too, not just the temperature.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A support-bot team reports creative, sometimes hallucinated replies at temperature 1.2 and robotic loops at temperature 0. Explain both mechanically and specify a corrected configuration for factual ticket responses.
payload.answer: Temperature scales logits before softmax: at 1.2 the distribution flattens, so long-shot tokens — including fabrications the model barely assigns probability to — enter the sampling pool with real mass, producing variety plus invention. At 0 the distribution collapses to its argmax, and once the model enters a phrase it tends to loop on the same high-probability continuation, giving repetitive, rigid text. Mechanism aside, both settings were mismatched to the task. Correct configuration for factual support replies: temperature 0–0.3 (deterministic extraction of grounded facts), top-p at the provider default (0.9–0.95) or slightly tightened as a tail guard, ground truth supplied in-context (ticket data, policy documents) with answers required to cite them, and validation of structured fields (order IDs, amounts) in code. Reserve higher temperatures for genuinely open creative features, never for fact-bearing ones.
payload.source: Classic applied-LLM configuration question; also common in chatbot tuning case interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Decoding pipeline: logits → divide by T → softmax → top-k/top-p filter → renormalise → sample → append.
Softmax turns raw scores into a distribution, amplifying gaps by exponentiation.
T<1 sharpens toward greedy; T>1 flattens toward the tail — re-weighting only what the model already believes.
Top-k is fixed-count; top-p is cumulative-mass and adapts to confidence — they coincide on peaked distributions.
Match decoding to task fidelity: 0–0.3 for extraction/code, ~0.5–0.8 chat, ~1.0+ brainstorming; tune one dial at a time.

questions.prompt: Before sampling the next token, temperature is applied by:
options: Adding noise to the embedding vectors
Dividing the logits by T prior to softmax, which sharpens (T<1) or flattens (T>1) the resulting distribution
Truncating the response length to T words
Selecting the top T vocabulary entries
questions.explanation: Temperature is a pre-softmax scaling of raw scores — the entire mechanism.

questions.prompt: Top-p (nucleus) sampling keeps:
options: The p highest-probability tokens by count
The smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, then samples within it
Exactly p percent of the vocabulary
The tokens above probability p individually
questions.explanation: Mass-based and adaptive — small nucleus when confident, wide when uncertain.

questions.prompt: With a peaked distribution, top-k=3 and top-p=0.9 may produce identical candidate sets because:
options: The top three tokens already cover ≥ 0.9 probability mass, so both cuts land on the same set
questions.explanation: When mass concentrates in the top few tokens, a count cut and a mass cut converge; they diverge only on flatter distributions.

questions.prompt: The most defensible configuration for deterministic JSON extraction is:
options: Temperature 0–0.2 with default top-p and schema validation in code
Any temperature, since JSON mode removes randomness
questions.explanation: Low temperature minimises deviation; schema validation is the real guarantee — sampling settings only reduce risk.

lessons.title: Steering and Serving: System Prompts, Stop Sequences, Streaming and the KV Cache
lessons.summary: The control surfaces and the physics: where instructions live, how generation is cut off, why text streams token by token, and why every token you keep makes the next one more expensive.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Place durable instructions, user input and examples into message roles with a clear precedence rationale
Design a stop sequence for a delimited output and predict its two classic failure modes
Explain streaming as a consequence of autoregressive compute, distinguishing time-to-first-token from total generation time
Size a KV cache for a given model shape and context length, and state why per-token cost grows with context

payload.text: Your chat UI writes like a person typing — because it *is* being computed like a person typing, one token at a time. Behind the curtain: a cache of key/value vectors ballooning with every token, a system prompt you cannot see steering every reply, and the option to slam generation shut with a magic string. All four — roles, stops, streaming, cache — are the same story: how a sequential probability machine is steered and paid for. This lesson is about the plumbing between the model and your product.

**Message roles: where instructions live.** Chat APIs structure input as a list of role-tagged messages: a **system** message (persistent instructions, persona, rules), **user** messages (inputs), **assistant** messages (model turns that get fed back). The system prompt is not a privileged kernel — it is earlier, structured text in the same context, so it usually dominates (training taught the model to treat it as authoritative) but can be degraded by long, conflicting, or manipulative user turns: prompt injection exploits exactly this. Practical rules: durable rules in the system prompt; volatile data in user messages; few-shot examples as explicit turns; re-state critical constraints near the end when context is long (primacy and recency both help); and never treat the system prompt as secret — it is extractable.

**Stop sequences: shutting generation off.** A stop string ends generation the moment the output matches it exactly — no tokens after. Perfect for delimited formats: generate rows until the literal END, or stop before a closing marker your code will add itself. Two classic failures: (1) the model emits *part* of the stop text and pauses mid-match semantics are fine (matching is on complete string), but a stop string that legitimately appears inside content (a row containing "END") truncates your data silently; (2) the model *never* emits the stop because it keeps elaborating — so always pair stops with a max-token cap and downstream validation. For hard contracts, schema-constrained decoding (Lesson 4.4 / Part II) beats string surgery.

**Streaming: compute made visible.** Generation is sequential — token n+1 cannot exist before token n is sampled. Streaming (Server-Sent Events over HTTP) delivers each piece as it is produced instead of waiting for the full string. What it changes: **time-to-first-token (TTFT)** becomes the perceived latency, even though total time is unchanged or slightly worse (per-chunk overhead). TTFT itself is dominated by **prefill** — processing your entire prompt through the network before the first output token. Long prompt ⇒ slow first token ⇒ streaming is the UX patch that makes it feel fast.

**The KV cache: why context costs memory.** Attention needs the keys and values of *every* previous token at every layer. Without a cache, each new token would recompute them all — quadratic waste. The KV cache stores them once per layer per token; each decode step just reads the cache and appends one entry. That is why generation is fast at all — and why long contexts are expensive: cache memory grows as layers × 2 (K and V) × KV-heads × head-dim × bytes × sequence length, i.e. **linear in context length for every concurrent sequence**. Compute per new token also grows with context (attention reads all prior entries), and prompt prefill is quadratic in length. Grouped-query attention (fewer KV heads sharing queries) exists precisely to shrink this cache. Operational consequences: long chats get slower and memory-hungry per session; servers cap concurrent long contexts; prefix caching (reusing the cache for a shared system prompt) cuts repeat cost — all direct fallout of one caching decision.

payload.title: Four levers, four mechanisms
rows: Earlier structured context, trained to be authoritative
Content contains the stop → silent truncation
SSE delivery of tokens as computed
Confusing fast TTFT with fast total time
Stored K/V per token per layer
Linear memory growth; slower per-token decode at long context

payload.title: Stop strings are content-sensitive, not structural
payload.text: They match raw output text — including places where the string is legitimate data. For anything a machine consumes, validate the parsed result and retry; use stop sequences as a fast-path optimisation, not your only guarantee.

payload.title: Design a stop-delimited exporter, then size its KV cache
payload.problem: A service streams inventory rows from a 7B-class model (32 layers, 8 KV heads via grouped-query attention, head dimension 128, bfloat16 weights) until the string END, capping at 8,192 tokens of context. (1) Specify the prompt contract and stop configuration, predicting two failure modes. (2) Compute KV cache memory for one 8k session. (3) Compute it for 32 concurrent sessions and state the serving implication.

steps.title: Step 1 — the contract
steps.desc: System: "One row per line: sku,qty,price. No header. Terminate with END." Stop: ["END"], max_tokens: 512, temperature 0. Validation downstream: each line parses as three fields; row count matches expected.
steps.code_snippet:
system: 'One row per line: sku,qty,price. End with END.'
stop = ['END']   max_tokens = 512   temperature = 0

steps.title: Step 2 — predict the failures
steps.desc: Failure A: a sku or product name contains "END" (e.g. BLENDER-END) → generation dies mid-data, silently. Fix: forbid the literal in the schema, or stop on a rarer token like <<STOP>>, plus row-count validation. Failure B: the model embellishes past the data ("As you can see…") and never says END → max_tokens cuts it off. Fix: cap + validator + retry with a stricter reminder.

steps.title: Step 3 — size one session's cache
steps.desc: Bytes per token = layers × 2 (K,V) × kv_heads × head_dim × 2 bytes = 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 B = 128 KB per token. For 8,192 tokens: 128 KB × 8,192 = 1,073,741,824 B ≈ 1.0 GB — for one sequence, weights excluded.
steps.code_snippet:
32 * 2 * 8 * 128 * 2 B = 128 KB/token
128 KB * 8192 = 1.0 GB per 8k session

steps.title: Step 4 — concurrency and the serving implication
steps.desc: 32 concurrent 8k sessions ≈ 32 GB of KV cache alone (an 8B model's weights are ~16 GB in bf16 — cache dominates!). Implications: long-context sessions cap concurrency; GQA (8 KV heads instead of 32) already cut this 4×; prefix caching amortises the shared system prompt; and per-token attention cost still grows with context, so long sessions slow down as they fill.

payload.solution: Contract: delimited rows + stop + cap + parse validation, with END-inside-data and never-ending elaboration as the named failure modes. Cache math: 128 KB/token → 1.0 GB per 8k session → ~32 GB for 32 sessions — the arithmetic behind every concurrency limit you have ever hit.

payload.title: Measure the two latencies
payload.prompt: Using any tool that exposes streaming: send one short prompt and one long prompt (paste a long document). Record time-to-first-token and total time for each, with and without streaming if you can toggle it. Write three sentences on why the long prompt's first token took longer even though the answer was short — naming prefill and the KV cache. If no API access, compute: at 50 tokens/sec decode, how long does a 600-token answer take, and how does TTFT of 3 s vs 0.5 s change the felt experience?
payload.hint: Answer length sets total time; prompt length sets prefill — and streaming only changes which of the two you feel first.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the system prompt as a secure, invisible channel
mistakes.fix: It is text in the same context: authoritative by training, but dilutable and extractable. Never store secrets in it; assume a determined user can elicit its contents.

mistakes.mistake: Using a stop sequence as the only output guarantee
mistakes.fix: Stops match raw strings and fail both ways (spurious match, or never emitted). Always add a token cap, downstream parsing and validation — preferably schema-constrained output for machine consumers.

mistakes.mistake: Equating streaming with faster generation
mistakes.fix: Streaming changes delivery, not compute: TTFT improves perceptually; total time is roughly unchanged (sometimes worse). Speed comes from shorter prompts, smaller models, batching — not from SSE.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming long context is free once the prompt is sent
mistakes.fix: Every generated token attends over all previous ones and lives in the KV cache: per-token compute and memory both grow with sequence length, and every session pays its own cache. Long context is a budget, not a licence.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why does the KV cache make long conversations memory-expensive, and why would removing it make generation hopelessly slow?
payload.answer: Attention at every layer needs the key and value vectors of all preceding tokens. The KV cache stores them once per token per layer (layers × 2 × KV-heads × head-dim × precision), so memory grows linearly with sequence length — for every concurrent sequence; an 8k-context session on an 8B-class model can consume on the order of a gigabyte by itself. Without the cache, each new token would have to recompute the K/V of the entire prefix through every layer — turning decoding into an O(n²)-per-token workload and making generation effectively unusable. So the cache is not optional: it trades linear memory for tractable compute. The engineering consequences are the ones you see in production — concurrency caps tied to total cache size, grouped-query attention to shrink cache entries, prefix caching for shared prompts, and the fact that per-token latency and memory still creep upward as a conversation fills its window.
payload.source: Serving/infra interview staple (also core material for LLMOps-style roles).

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: System prompts are authoritative-but-not-privileged context: durable rules go there, and injection/dilution remain risks.
Stop sequences cut decoding on exact string match — always paired with a max-token cap and downstream validation.
Streaming exposes autoregressive reality: TTFT is dominated by prompt prefill, total time by decode length.
The KV cache stores keys/values per token per layer: linear memory in context, for every session — the price of fast decoding.
Per-token compute also grows with context; GQA, prefix caching and concurrency caps are all responses to that arithmetic.

questions.prompt: The system prompt in a chat API is best described as:
options: A secure kernel channel users cannot influence
Persistent, structured instructions earlier in the same context — authoritative by training but still dilutable by later turns
A separate classifier run before the LLM
questions.explanation: Same context, privileged position — which is why injection and long-history drift still matter.

questions.prompt: A stop sequence causes generation to:
options: End the moment the output contains the exact stop string
questions.explanation: Hard termination on exact match — hence the twin risks of spurious matches inside content and never being emitted at all.

questions.prompt: Streaming reduces perceived latency mainly by improving:
options: Time-to-first-token visibility — tokens render as they are computed
questions.explanation: Delivery, not compute: the first tokens appear immediately; total time stays about the same.

questions.prompt: KV cache memory grows primarily with:
options: Sequence length — every token stores key/value vectors for every layer (times heads and precision)
questions.explanation: Linear in context per sequence; multiplied across concurrent sessions — the direct driver of serving memory limits.

modules.title: Module 3 — Model Families & Selection
modules.summary: Open weights vs frontier APIs in practical terms (license, hosting, control), parameter counts versus real capability and cost, context windows and their hidden quality tax, and a weighted decision framework you can run on any use case.

lessons.title: Open vs Closed Weights: Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek and the Frontier APIs
lessons.summary: What "open" really buys you, what an API-only model hides, and the three practical axes — hosting, cost shape, control — that decide deployments.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Distinguish open weights, fully open-source releases, and API-only models, and cite one real license caveat for each open family
Compare self-hosting and API access across deployment, data control, customisation, cost shape and ops burden
Choose a deployment mode for three scenarios with different privacy, scale and team constraints
State one operational risk of each option and a mitigation for each

payload.text: Two headlines from the last few years, both true: an open-weight release reset expectations of what a freely downloadable model can do — labs from Meta (Llama), Mistral, Alibaba (Qwen) and DeepSeek shipping weights anyone can download — while the best *fully-tuned product experience* remained behind GPT-, Claude- and Gemini-class APIs. "Open vs closed" is not a morality play; it is a deployment decision with line items: license text, GPU bills, data boundaries, and who patches the model at 2 a.m.

**Three categories, not two.** (1) **API-only** (GPT, Claude, Gemini families): you get inference, never weights. You trade control for a maintained product — quality tuning, safety layers, and infra are the vendor's job. (2) **Open weights** (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek families): weights (and usually an inference stack) are downloadable; you run them yourself or via hosted endpoints. License terms vary per model — some under Apache 2.0 (permissive, commercial-friendly), others under custom community licenses with clauses (e.g. monthly-active-user thresholds triggering terms, or acceptable-use riders). (3) **Fully open-source** in the strict sense (weights + training code + data recipe) is rare at frontier scale; when vendors say "open", ask which of the three you actually got. As of 2026, licenses and line-ups move fast — always read the specific model's license before shipping, not a blog summary of the family.

**The three practical axes.** *Hosting*: open weights run on your GPUs, in your VPC, or on a specialist host (vLLM-style serving stacks make this routine); API-only means data leaves your boundary unless the vendor offers contractual zero-retention, residency controls, or enterprise data agreements — which many do, but you must verify per vendor and tier. *Cost shape*: APIs bill per token (OpEx scales with usage, zero idle cost); self-hosting bills per GPU-hour (cost exists whether or not you use it — so unit economics favour self-hosting at steady high volume, and APIs at spiky or low volume). *Control*: open weights can be fine-tuned (LoRA on your schema and jargon), quantised (smaller, cheaper serving), inspected for known behaviours, and pinned forever; APIs give you a moving product — better on average each quarter, but version drift, silent behaviour changes, rate limits and policy filters you do not control.

**Capability reality check (as of 2026, hedged).** The strongest *closed* models still tend to lead open-ended reasoning, very long context, and polished safety tuning; but open-weight gaps have narrowed sharply per generation, and on narrow, well-specified tasks a fine-tuned open model often *beats* a frontier API outright (Lesson 3.2). Mixture-of-experts (MoE) releases have muddied "open catches up" claims too: an open MoE can have huge total parameters but modest active compute per token, so raw parameter bragging rights mislead. The professional habit: stop asking "is open as good?" and start asking "is open good *enough on my eval set*, at *my volume*, under *my constraints*?"

**The ops tax nobody puts on the slide.** Self-hosting means: model selection, quantisation choice, a serving stack, autoscaling, monitoring, red-teaming your own fine-tune, upgrading when a better release lands — engineering time that an API bills you for invisibly inside the token price. Many teams end up hybrid: open weights for the high-volume, data-sensitive core of the product; frontier API for the long tail of hard requests (Lesson 3.4 makes this arithmetic explicit). That hybrid is not indecision — it is the two economic models used where each is strong.
