payload.title: "Open weights" is not one license
payload.text: Permissive Apache-2.0 releases sit next to custom community licenses with user-count clauses and use restrictions. Compliance is a per-model due-diligence task: pull the LICENSE from the model repo, read it, record it.

payload.title: Hybrid is a legitimate architecture
payload.text: Route by sensitivity and difficulty: private/high-volume flows to a self-hosted open model; hard, low-volume flows to a frontier API; keep a kill-switch to flip routing when a vendor changes terms or pricing.

payload.title: Pick a deployment mode for three products
payload.problem: Choose self-hosted open weights, a frontier API, or hybrid for: (a) a hospital triage assistant processing patient notes (PII, unpredictable volume, small eng team); (b) a student essay-feedback tool (spiky evening peaks, near-zero PII, tight budget); (c) a legal research copilot (long documents, high reasoning bar, large steady document volume). Defend each in one line of constraint arithmetic.

steps.title: (a) Hospital triage — constraint: PII cannot leave
steps.desc: Hard filter eliminates naive API use: patient notes in a third-party prompt violate the strongest data-boundary requirement. Self-host a mid-size open model (quantised, on-prem/VPC). Volume is unpredictable, so carry the GPU idle-cost risk consciously; mitigate with autoscaling and a narrow task scope. If the vendor offers a compliant enterprise tier with contractual non-retention, an API becomes arguable — with legal sign-off, not marketing copy.

steps.title: (b) Essay tool — constraint: budget, spiky load
steps.desc: Evenings spike, afternoons idle — exactly where per-token pricing beats owned GPUs (no idle billing). Start API-only at low temperature with strict output schemas. Revisit at ~10× volume: then a small self-hosted model (or batch API discounts) may undercut it. Decision driver: cost shape, not capability.

steps.title: (c) Legal copilot — constraint: quality bar + volume
steps.desc: High reasoning bar initially favours a frontier API; high steady volume makes its per-token bill grow linearly. Hybrid: frontier API for hard multi-step analysis (10–20% of traffic), self-hosted larger open model for summarise/extract/route on the rest (80–90%). Evaluate quarterly — open releases move fast, and your own eval set (Lesson 3.4) decides when the open tier absorbs more traffic.

steps.title: Generalise
steps.desc: Order of operations: (1) hard constraints (privacy, residency, licensing) eliminate options; (2) volume shape picks the cost model; (3) your eval set picks the model; (4) team capacity prices the ops burden. Capability is only step 3 — teams that start there end up with impressive demos and unsupportable bills.

payload.solution: (a) self-hosted open — PII boundary is a hard filter. (b) API — spiky volume prefers per-token economics. (c) hybrid — frontier for the hard tail, open for the high-volume core, with a quarterly re-evaluation cadence tied to an internal eval set.

payload.title: Read a license like an engineer
payload.prompt: Open the model card or repo of one open-weight family you use (Llama, Mistral, Qwen or DeepSeek). Find the actual license text and answer: (1) is it Apache-2.0-style or custom? (2) any user-count or use-restriction clauses? (3) can you fine-tune and serve commercially? Write a five-line internal memo recommending or blocking a commercial use, citing clauses — not headlines.
payload.hint: The LICENSE file in the model repo is authoritative; blog posts about "open models" are not.

mistakes.mistake: Treating open weights as "free"
mistakes.fix: Weights cost zero; GPUs, serving engineering, safety evaluation and upgrades do not. Compare total cost of ownership against token bills, not against zero.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming all open models share one license
mistakes.fix: Apache-2.0, custom community licenses and research-only releases coexist in the same "open" bucket. Due diligence is per-model, per-version.

mistakes.mistake: Concluding that an API-only model automatically protects your data
mistakes.fix: Data governance is contractual: read retention terms, residency options and training-use clauses for your specific tier. Some enterprise tiers are strong; the default tiers may not be.

mistakes.mistake: Deciding open vs closed on benchmark headlines alone
mistakes.fix: Benchmarks measure population-level capability; your decision turns on your eval set, your volume, your constraints. Run your own numbers before committing.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Compare self-hosted open-weight models with API-only frontier models across deployment, cost structure, and customisation. Under which three conditions would you recommend self-hosting?
payload.answer: Deployment: open weights run inside your own infrastructure (or a chosen host), giving full control over data residency and network boundaries; API-only routes inputs through the vendor, requiring contractual data terms. Cost: self-hosting is GPU-hour OpEx with fixed idle cost — economical at steady high volume — while APIs are per-token, economical at low or spiky volume with no ops burden. Customisation: open weights can be fine-tuned, quantised and version-pinned; APIs offer prompting and vendor-managed improvements but silent version drift and policy limits. Recommend self-hosting when: (1) data-boundary requirements (PII, residency, secrecy) cannot be met by any available API tier; (2) sustained high volume makes token pricing strictly more expensive than GPU amortisation; and (3) the team has (or will build) the serving and evaluation capability to own the stack — or the task is narrow enough that a fine-tuned small open model beats a frontier call on your own evals.
payload.source: Standard system-design discussion for GenAI product roles: "build vs buy vs hybrid".

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Three buckets: API-only, open weights (per-model licenses), truly fully-open releases — always read the specific license.
Self-hosting buys data control, fine-tuning and version pinning at the price of an ops tax and idle GPU cost.
APIs buy a maintained product with zero idle cost at the price of data egress, per-token bills and version drift.
Decision order: hard constraints → volume shape → your eval set → team capacity. Capability benchmarks are step three, not one.
Hybrid routing — open for the high-volume core, frontier for the hard tail — is a normal, defensible architecture.

questions.prompt: The most accurate description of "open weights" is:
options: Fully open source including training data and code in every case
Model weights are downloadable and runnable, under licenses that vary from permissive (e.g. Apache-2.0-style) to custom community terms
A marketing term with no licensing implications
Models that are free of any usage restrictions
questions.explanation: Weights availability is the constant; license terms are the variable that must be read per model.

questions.prompt: The strongest technical argument for self-hosting an open model is:
options: It is always cheaper than any API
Input data never leaves your infrastructure — the strongest data-boundary control
questions.explanation: Privacy and residency are where self-hosting dominates; cost only wins at high steady volume.

questions.prompt: Per-token API pricing is generally preferable when your traffic is:
options: Low or spiky, so you would otherwise pay for idle GPUs
questions.explanation: You pay only for usage — the economics flip only when sustained utilisation amortises owned hardware below the token bill.

questions.prompt: A hybrid architecture typically routes:
options: All traffic to the cheapest model always
High-volume and data-sensitive flows to a self-hosted open model; hard, low-volume flows to a frontier API
Only English to the API and other languages to open models
Training traffic to open and inference to closed, always
questions.explanation: Each side serves where its economics and strengths are real: control/volume on one side, broad capability on the other.

lessons.title: Parameters, Capability and Cost: When a Small Model Wins
lessons.summary: What parameter count does and does not tell you, the real arithmetic of API bills versus GPU hours, and the five situations where a 7B-class model beats a frontier call.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain the capability–parameter relationship including the MoE nuance (total vs active parameters)
Compute monthly cost of an API extraction pipeline from token counts and published rates
Name five conditions under which a small fine-tuned model outperforms a frontier API on a task
Design a two-tier routing policy for a high-volume product and estimate its blended cost

payload.text: A structured-extraction pipeline at a fintech: five fields out of a vendor invoice, 50,000 invoices a day, no prose required. The team compared a 7B-class open model fine-tuned on 800 of their own examples against a frontier API call on the same held-out set. Quality: 96.1% field-level accuracy vs 96.8% — a tie that would not survive contact with the invoice volume. Cost: one GPU versus a bill that scaled with every document. Parameter count never appeared in either result. This lesson is about the numbers that actually decide.

**What parameter count is (and is not).** Parameters are the learned weights — capacity for storing patterns. In the dense-model era, more parameters generally meant more capability per generation, driven by scaling laws (capability improves smoothly with scale, given enough data and compute). But "generally" hides everything that matters for your decision: (1) **Capability on your task** depends on data mix, post-training and context support — a smaller model fine-tuned on your schema can beat a frontier model zero-shot on exactly that schema. (2) **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** models — common in open releases like DeepSeek-V3-class and Mixtral-class lineages — route each token through only a subset of experts: total parameters might be in the hundreds of billions while *active* parameters per token are far lower. The lesson: total parameters are a rough capacity proxy, active parameters and tokens-per-second are closer to cost, and neither is a capability certificate.

**The cost arithmetic, done twice.** APIs: bill = input tokens × input rate + output tokens × output rate (per million tokens; output typically 3–5× input because decoding is sequential). Self-hosting: bill = GPU-hours × rate, where GPU-hours = wall-clock time — which depends on throughput (tokens/sec at your batch size) and utilisation. The crossover: at low volume, API wins because idle GPUs are pure loss; at high steady volume, one well-utilised GPU can undercut an API bill by an order of magnitude. Everything in between needs your spreadsheet, not intuition. Hidden API levers: batch discounts (async processing at half-price tiers is common), prompt caching (repeat prefixes billed cheaper), and model-tier routing (use the smallest model that passes your eval). Hidden self-hosting levers: quantisation (4/8-bit weights shrink memory and raise throughput), continuous batching, and distillation (a small model trained on a big model's outputs — the R1-era distill wave showed how far this carries).

**When the small model wins — the five conditions.** (1) *Narrow, well-specified output*: extraction into a fixed schema, classification, rewriting to a house style — tasks where behaviour is learnable from hundreds of examples. (2) *High volume*: unit cost multiplies everything. (3) *Latency sensitivity*: small models hit first-token targets a frontier call cannot. (4) *Data sensitivity*: on-prem weights keep inputs inside. (5) *Determinism/maintenance*: a pinned quantised model behaves the same next quarter; a frontier endpoint might not. When the small model *loses*: open-ended reasoning, rare languages, long messy contexts, agentic multi-step work — anything where generality is the point. The professional skill is not picking a side; it is classifying your workloads into these two bins and refusing to use one model for both.

payload.code:
# 50,000 invoices/day, 800 in / 150 out tokens each
docs_per_day = 50_000
in_tok, out_tok = 800, 150

# Option A: frontier API, $3 in / $15 out per 1M tokens
per_doc = in_tok / 1e6 * 3 + out_tok / 1e6 * 15   # $0.00465
print(round(per_doc * docs_per_day, 2))            # $232.50 / day
print(round(per_doc * docs_per_day * 30, 0))       # ~$6,975 / month

# Option B: 7B-class model, one rented GPU @ $1.20/hr, 24/7
print(round(1.20 * 24 * 30, 0))                    # $864 / month
# -> ~8x cheaper, if one GPU really sustains the throughput

payload.title: Small model vs frontier API: pick by workload, not by brand
rows: Tens of ms–low seconds, p95 critical

payload.title: Route before you retrain
payload.text: Cheapest high-leverage move in most products: classify each request, send the easy majority to a small model, escalate the hard minority to a frontier API. You often cut 60–80% of cost without touching quality on the hard cases.

payload.title: Run the crossover math, then design a two-tier router
payload.problem: Extraction pipeline: 50,000 docs/day, 800 input + 150 output tokens each. Frontier API: $3/$15 per 1M tokens. Self-hosted 7B: one GPU at $1.20/hr running 24/7, throughput measured at 1,200 docs/hour at target quality. (1) Compute both monthly costs. (2) Does the GPU keep up? (3) Design a hybrid routing policy if the small model passes only 90% of docs with the rest needing escalation, priced at the same API rates, and compute the blended monthly cost.

steps.title: Step 2 — GPU throughput and cost
steps.desc: Capacity: 1,200 docs/hr × 24 hr = 28,800 docs/day < 50,000 needed — one GPU is NOT enough; you need two (57,600/day headroom ok) or better batching. Cost at two GPUs: 2 × $1.20 × 720 hr = $1,728/month. Still ~4× cheaper than pure API.

steps.title: Step 3 — hybrid routing arithmetic
steps.desc: Route 90% (45,000/day) to ONE GPU — which now handles 45,000/24 = 1,875/hr needed… still above 1,200/hr. Recalibrate: with quality-90% routing, accept the small model at slightly relaxed threshold or add batching optimisation; assume routing pushes small-model load to 45k/day after tuning throughput to 2,000/hr (one GPU). Escalate 10% (5,000/day) to API at $0.00465: 5,000 × 0.00465 × 30 = $697.50.

steps.title: Step 4 — blended total and the decision rule
steps.desc: Hybrid ≈ $698 (API tail) + $864 (one GPU) = $1,562/month vs $6,975 pure API — a ~77% cut, with frontier quality reserved for the hard 10%. Decision rule: pure API below ~5k docs/day; hybrid in the middle; full self-host when the hard tail is tiny and throughput is proven.

payload.solution: Pure API ≈ $6,975/mo; honest GPU sizing needs two cards ($1,728) at the measured throughput; the tuned hybrid (90/10 with throughput validated) lands ≈ $1,562/mo. The lesson is not "open always wins" — it is that quality parity on narrow tasks plus volume arithmetic decides before ideology enters the room.

payload.title: Price your own workflow
payload.prompt: Pick one AI task you run repeatedly (summarise lecture notes, generate flashcards, classify emails). Measure or estimate its token counts per run, multiply by your monthly volume, and price it at two API tiers (e.g. a small model and a frontier model). Then estimate what one GPU-hour could do instead (rough tokens/sec × 3600). Write three sentences on where you sit on the crossover curve — and what would move you across it.
payload.hint: Include output tokens — they cost several times input, and people consistently forget the reply in their bill estimates.

mistakes.mistake: Reading parameter count as a capability ranking
mistakes.fix: Data mix, post-training, context and MoE routing all intervene. Measure your task on your eval set; treat parameters as a weak prior about capacity and cost.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming self-hosting is free because the weights are free
mistakes.fix: GPUs, serving, upgrades and engineering time are the real bill. Compare GPU-hour amortisation against the token bill at YOUR utilisation — idle GPUs are pure loss.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing API and open models on different quality bars
mistakes.fix: Same held-out set, same scoring script, same output schema — otherwise the comparison measures your prompting luck, not the models.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring MoE active-parameter economics
mistakes.fix: A huge-total-parameter MoE can be cheap per token (few experts active). Cost scales with active compute and tokens/sec — not with the parameter count on the model card.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Under what conditions would you recommend a 7B-class open model over a frontier API call for a production task? Justify with both quality and cost arguments.
payload.answer: When the task is narrow and well-specified — fixed-schema extraction, classification, style rewriting — a 7B model fine-tuned (e.g. LoRA) on a few hundred to a few thousand task examples can match or exceed a zero-shot frontier model on that exact distribution, because fine-tuning adapts format, vocabulary and edge cases directly. Cost then decides decisively at volume: one GPU amortises to a fraction of a per-token API bill for millions of daily calls, while also delivering lower and more stable latency, version pinning, and full data locality (inputs never leave your infrastructure). The recommendation flips when the task needs open-ended reasoning, long messy contexts, rare languages, or frequent distribution shifts — cases where the frontier model's breadth is exactly what you are paying for. The defensible engineering answer is therefore: validate on a shared eval set first, then route — small model for the in-distribution majority, frontier API for the hard tail.
payload.source: Frequent ML-engineering interview: "when is a small model enough?"

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Parameter count is a weak capacity prior — task fit comes from data, post-training and your own eval set; MoE adds a total-vs-active-parameters split.
API cost = input tokens × in-rate + output tokens × out-rate; self-host cost = GPU-hours × rate — the crossover is pure arithmetic at your volume.
Small fine-tuned models win on five conditions: narrow output, high volume, latency pressure, data sensitivity, pinned behaviour.
Small models lose where generality is the point: open-ended reasoning, long tail cases, agentic work.
Two-tier routing (small for the majority, frontier for the hard tail) is the default cost engineering move — measure, then cut.

questions.prompt: In a Mixture-of-Experts model, the parameter count most relevant to per-token compute is the:
options: Total parameter count across all experts
Active parameters routed for that token
questions.explanation: Each token visits only a subset of experts — active parameters track compute better than the headline total.

questions.prompt: API input and output token prices differ mainly because:
options: Output generation is sequential decoding — slower and more compute-bound per token than prompt processing
questions.explanation: Prefill parallelises over the prompt; decoding produces one token at a time — hence output rates typically run 3–5× input rates.

questions.prompt: A 7B fine-tuned model beats a frontier API most plausibly on:
options: An open-ended research essay spanning fifty sources
Five-field invoice extraction at 50,000 docs/day with 800 training examples
A one-off legal analysis with rare-language documents
questions.explanation: Narrow schema + high volume + task examples is exactly the small-model sweet spot.

questions.prompt: At low, spiky volume, the API is usually cheaper than self-hosting because:
options: Self-hosted GPUs bill by the hour whether idle or not, while APIs bill only for tokens used
questions.explanation: Idle-capacity economics — the fixed cost of owned hardware dominates until utilisation is high and steady.

lessons.title: Context Windows and Long-Context Tradeoffs
lessons.summary: A million tokens of context is not a million tokens of comprehension: cost curves, latency physics, lost-in-the-middle, and when retrieval still wins.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute the token fit and full-dump cost of a document collection against a given window and rate
Explain lost-in-the-middle and at least one other quality degradation in long contexts
Distinguish prefill and decode cost growth with sequence length
Design a long-document workflow that beats naive full-dump on cost and quality, with numbers

payload.text: The window race made "just paste it all" feel like an architecture. Vendor pages advertised windows that swallow entire codebases and bookshelves — 200k tokens, then 1M and beyond (figures as of 2026, still moving). Then evaluation kept finding the same humbling pattern: a fact planted in the middle of a very long document gets retrieved *less reliably* than the same fact at the top or the bottom. Fitting is not using. This lesson prices the window, taxes its length, and shows when retrieval still wins.

**What the window is.** The context window is the maximum tokens the model can attend over in one pass: system prompt + history + your pasted files + the tokens it is generating right now. Two budgets govern every call: *input* tokens (you pay per token, usually parallelised as prefill) and *output* tokens (capped separately by providers, priced higher — a "1M context" model may still only emit a few thousand tokens per turn). Estimation discipline from the token lessons applies: convert documents to token estimates before promising anything.

**The cost and latency curves.** Money: input cost scales linearly with prompt length — a full 250k-token dump at $2/M is half a dollar *per query*, which becomes serious at production volume. Latency has two regimes: **prefill** (processing your prompt — parallel, but total work grows with input length, so TTFT rises) and **decode** (per-token generation — each new token attends over the entire cached context, so per-token cost creeps upward as the sequence fills; the KV cache from Lesson 2.4 is the memory bottleneck). Servers feel both: long-context requests consume disproportionate memory per request, so providers throttle concurrency or price long-context tiers higher. Rule of thumb to carry: **quadratic-ish prefill growth, linear per-token attention growth, linear-in-length KV memory — per request.**

**The quality tax.** Long context degrades usefully-invisible ways: (1) *lost-in-the-middle* — retrieval accuracy for facts positioned mid-context dips; put critical instructions or evidence at the start or end (primacy/recency). (2) *Distraction* — irrelevant filler is not neutral: it competes for attention and measurably hurts reasoning on multi-hop questions. (3) *Instruction drift* — in very long chat histories, early constraints fade against later conversational pressure. (4) *Needle-test complacency* — "99% needle recall" benchmarks measure single-fact lookup, not multi-document synthesis; do not extrapolate. The research picture as of 2026: long-context capability keeps improving, position bias softens, but attention dilution has not vanished — treat long context as a workspace with a quality budget, not a warehouse.

**The decision: dump vs retrieve.** Full-dump wins when: documents are few, genuinely all relevant, and queried once or twice (a one-shot legal review of a short contract set). Retrieval (RAG) wins when: corpus is large, queries are many, per-query cost matters, or precision requires showing the model only evidence — retrieval *focuses* attention, which doubles as a quality intervention. A third option increasingly matters: **long-context + map-reduce summarisation** — chunk-level passes feeding a synthesis pass — for whole-corpus tasks where no single excerpt suffices. The architecture conversation is no longer "window or RAG"; it is "how much context per call, chosen deliberately, with numbers attached".

payload.code:
# Long-doc arithmetic (illustrative rates)
pages, words_per_page = 400, 500
tokens = pages * words_per_page * 4 / 3      # ~266,667 tokens
print("fits 200k window:", tokens <= 200_000)  # False
print("full dump @ $2/M:", round(tokens / 1e6 * 2, 2))   # ~$0.53 / query
print("top-10 chunks (8k) @ $2/M:", round(8_000 / 1e6 * 2, 3))  # ~$0.016
# 20 queries/day * 30 days: dump=$318/mo vs retrieve=$9.6/mo

payload.title: Where key content lives, and what to do about it
rows: Avoid burying critical evidence; compress or retrieve instead
Restate the task and key constraints just before the ask

payload.title: Needle tests measure lookup, not reasoning
payload.text: "Finds a planted fact at 128k" does not mean "synthesises 40 documents reliably". Evaluate long context on tasks shaped like yours: multi-hop, conflicting-evidence, numeric aggregation.

payload.title: Place instructions twice
payload.text: In very long contexts, put hard constraints in the system prompt AND restate them right before the query. Cheap insurance against drift — two placements, one instruction.

payload.title: Pick an architecture for a 400-page contract corpus with 20 questions a day
payload.problem: Legal team: 400 pages (~500 words/page), asked ~20 reviewer questions daily. Options: (A) full-dump into a 1M-token window at $2/M input; (B) retrieve top-10 chunks (~8k tokens) per question, same rate; (C) map-reduce whole-corpus summary once/day + targeted retrieval. Compare monthly cost and argue quality. Word-to-token: ×4/3.

steps.title: Step 1 — size the corpus
steps.desc: 400 × 500 = 200,000 words × 4/3 ≈ 266,667 tokens. Fits a 1M window; does NOT fit a 200k window. Check before choosing anything else.

steps.title: Step 2 — cost option A (full dump, 20×/day)
steps.desc: 266,667 tokens × $2/M = $0.533 per query. × 20 queries × 30 days = $320/month — plus long TTFT on every call and the lost-in-the-middle risk across 266k tokens of clauses.

steps.title: Step 3 — cost options B and C
steps.desc: B: 8,000 tokens × $2/M = $0.016/query → 0.016 × 20 × 30 = $9.60/month (embedding + index amortised separately). C: one 266k map-reduce pass/day ≈ $0.53 × 30 = $16/month, plus B's per-query cost ≈ $26/month total — and the summary pre-compresses context, improving mid-corpus questions.

steps.title: Step 4 — decide on quality, not just price
steps.desc: A is fine for one-off reviews of short sets; at 20 questions/day over 266k tokens it pays a quality tax (position bias, distraction) and a latency tax. Choose C+B hybrid: daily structured summary for coverage, retrieval for precision, and escalate to A-style wide context only when a question genuinely spans the corpus (rare — budget for it explicitly).

payload.solution: Sizes: 266,667 tokens (misses 200k, fits 1M). Costs: A ≈ $320/mo, B ≈ $10/mo, C+B ≈ $26/mo. Decision: hybrid map-reduce + retrieval — 97% cheaper than full-dump at 20 queries/day and it *focuses* attention, attacking the quality problem with the same move that solves the cost problem.

payload.title: Run your own mini needle test
payload.prompt: Take any long document (a textbook chapter, a legal PDF). Plant or select three facts: one in the first quarter, one mid-way, one near the end. Using a long-context assistant, ask for each fact in separate turns, with the full document attached. Record whether it is found and how confidently. Then repeat with the document chunked and only the relevant section supplied. Write three sentences on what the comparison says about your retrieval habit.
payload.hint: Vary the position deliberately — the middle failure is subtle because the model often answers confidently even when wrong.

mistakes.mistake: Equating window size with comprehension
mistakes.fix: Attention dilutes over length; needle recall ≠ synthesis. Long context is capacity with a quality budget — validate on multi-hop tasks shaped like yours.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring output-token caps when promising "the model reads the whole file"
mistakes.fix: Providers cap completion length separately from window size. "1M in, 8k out" changes what one turn can accomplish — plan multi-turn or map-reduce accordingly.

mistakes.mistake: Burying critical constraints mid-context
mistakes.fix: Lost-in-the-middle is real and positional: system prompt for durable rules, restatement near the query for the current ask.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing full-dump because "RAG adds complexity"
mistakes.fix: Complexity is a cost, not an argument. At production volume, dump pays 20–100× more per query and degrades quality — measure both before buying simplicity.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain "lost-in-the-middle" in long-context models and its practical implication for how documents and instructions should be arranged in a prompt.
payload.answer: Long-context evaluations consistently show that information placed in the middle of a very long context is retrieved and used less reliably than the same information at the beginning or the end — a U-shaped position curve attributed to attention competition and training-data position statistics (recency and primacy effects). Practical implications: (1) put durable instructions and ground rules in the system prompt at the top; (2) restate the current task and key constraints immediately before the query at the bottom; (3) avoid burying critical evidence mid-document — either extract and place it near the query, or retrieve the relevant chunk instead of full-dumping; (4) when synthesising long corpora, use hierarchical summarisation or retrieval to shorten what the model attends over. Long-context models improve year over year, but as of 2026 position effects remain measurable — arrangement is a cheap, reliable quality lever that teams routinely skip.
payload.source: Widely discussed long-context evaluation finding; standard applied-LLM interview topic.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: The window counts prompt + history + generation; output caps are separate and priced higher.
Costs: input linear in length; prefill time grows with prompt size; per-token decode attention and KV memory grow with sequence length.
Quality degrades with length: lost-in-the-middle, distraction, instruction drift — needle tests over-promise.
Dump vs retrieve is arithmetic: at volume, retrieval (or map-reduce + retrieval) wins on cost AND often on quality by focusing attention.
Place instructions top and restated bottom; treat long context as a budgeted workspace, not a warehouse.

questions.prompt: A "1M-token context window" does NOT imply that:
options: You can send that much input in one request
The model will use every part of it equally well
The output can also be 1M tokens
Input cost scales roughly linearly with prompt length
questions.explanation: Output limits are separate; quality is also non-uniform across positions — capacity is not comprehension.

questions.prompt: "Lost-in-the-middle" refers to the finding that in long contexts:
options: Models forget their training after mid-generation
Facts positioned in the middle are used less reliably than facts at the start or end
Middle tokens cost twice as much
Attention is disabled for middle positions
questions.explanation: A U-shaped position curve — retrieval reliability dips mid-context.

questions.prompt: Asking a long question with many irrelevant paragraphs attached typically:
options: Improves accuracy by giving more evidence
Can degrade accuracy — irrelevant context competes for attention and dilutes focus
questions.explanation: More context is not neutral: distraction and dilution are measurable quality costs.

questions.prompt: For 20 daily questions over a 266k-token corpus, the approach that usually wins on cost AND quality is:
options: Full-dump into a 1M window every query
Retrieval of the relevant ~8k tokens per query, optionally plus a pre-computed whole-corpus summary
Splitting the corpus into 50 chat sessions
Raising temperature to handle the length
questions.explanation: Focused context cuts cost by orders of magnitude and improves reliability by reducing dilution and position effects.

lessons.title: A Model Selection Framework with a Worked Comparison
lessons.summary: Turn "which model should we use?" into arithmetic: hard filters, a weighted rubric, a sensitivity check, and a decision that survives contact with production.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Structure a model decision: define the task and metric, apply hard constraints, shortlist, evaluate, weight, and sense-check
Compute weighted rubric totals for four candidates and run a weights-sensitivity re-check
Identify the three most common model-selection anti-patterns and their consequences
Write a one-paragraph model recommendation including monitoring and a rollback plan

payload.text: A team spends six weeks "evaluating models": someone screenshots a leaderboard, someone else demos a shiny reply at a conference, and a third argues from a tweet about benchmarks. Then the invoice arrives. Model selection fails not because people are careless but because it is done without a rubric — so every bias (recency, brand, the demo that felt magical) fills the vacuum. This lesson replaces that vacuum with a spreadsheet you can defend in a design review.

**The process, in order.** (1) **Define the task and its success metric** before looking at any model: what output, scored how, on what golden set of 50–200 real examples with labels or rubrics? (2) **Hard constraints as filters**: data residency, required modality, context length, latency ceiling, budget ceiling, license compatibility. Anything failing a hard filter is out — no matter its benchmark. (3) **Shortlist 3–4 candidates** spanning categories (frontier API, mid-tier API, self-hosted open, hybrid) — shortlists of two systematically under-explore. (4) **Run the same eval set** with the same harness: identical prompts, identical scoring, ideally blind pairwise judging where possible. (5) **Score a weighted rubric** — criteria with weights that reflect *your* product, not the field's fashions. (6) **Sense-check**: rerun with perturbed prompts, check failure modes, estimate cost at real volume, then decide. (7) **Revisit quarterly**: the field moves; your decision needs an expiry date.

**Criteria that earn their place.** *Quality on your eval* (typically 30–50% weight): the only quality number that matters is the one you measured. *Unit cost at volume* (15–25%): from the Lesson 3.2 arithmetic, blended across routing. *p95 latency* (10–15%): users feel the tail, not the mean. *Data and compliance* (10–20%): boundary requirements, contractual terms, audit needs. *Ops and maintainability* (5–15%): who pages at 3 a.m., version drift risk, upgrade cadence. Optional additions where relevant: tool-calling reliability, structured-output adherence, ecosystem fit. Weights are a *stakeholder negotiation made numeric* — write them down, and change them only on record.

**The three anti-patterns.** *Leaderboard worship*: public benchmarks are contaminated-prone, saturating, and orthogonal to your domain — cite them only as sanity checks. *Vibe demos*: one beautiful response tells you about sampling luck, not tail behaviour — your golden set exists precisely to kill this. *Forgetting ops and drift*: a model decision is a maintenance commitment; models deprecate, prices change, and "pin the version" must appear in the plan. One more discipline: **version-pin everything** you evaluate — model ids, parameters, prompt text — or your comparison is not reproducible next month.

**The deliverable.** The output of a selection process is a short written artifact: problem statement, hard filters, rubric with weights, scores with evidence links, sensitivity note, recommendation, monitoring metrics (quality proxy, cost/day, p95 latency, refusal/escalation rate), and the rollback path (previous model id + config, flip on alert). This document is what makes the decision survive staff turnover — and what makes the quarterly re-run trivial.

**Building the golden set without kidding yourself.** Sample real inputs from production logs or realistic archives, not from the team's imagination; include the ugly tail (empty fields, mixed languages, adversarial phrasings) at its true-ish proportion plus an oversampled slice so it is measurable at all. Label with the rubric you will actually ship — and freeze it: silently changing the rubric between model runs invalidates every comparison. When labels are expensive, prefer *pairwise* judgements between two model outputs over absolute scores; humans compare more reliably than they grade. And keep a small canary slice that never changes across quarters, so you can prove your harness still measures what it measured last time. A golden set is a product asset with versioning, ownership and a changelog — not a folder of demos.

payload.title: Rubric criteria: measure, weight, trap
rows: Substituting public benchmarks for your domain
Token math × monthly volume (+ GPU math if self-hosted)
Comparing list prices without quality parity
Optimising the mean while p95 falls apart
Assuming defaults instead of reading terms
Treating "no infra" as free while version drift bites

payload.title: Blind pairwise judging stretches small eval sets
payload.text: With 100 examples, anonymous A/B comparisons between two models often discriminate faster than absolute scoring — and it debiases the evaluator against brand names.

payload.title: Pin versions or reproduce nothing
payload.text: Frontier endpoints change under you. Record full model ids, parameter values and prompt hashes; when a vendor deprecates a version, treat the re-evaluation as scheduled work, not an incident.

payload.title: Score four candidates with a weighted rubric — then flip the winner by moving one weight
payload.problem: Customer-support assistant: classify and draft replies for tickets (PII-heavy, ~200k tickets/month, p95 target 4 s). Candidates: A = frontier API; B = self-hosted 8B fine-tuned; C = self-hosted 70B; D = hybrid (B default, A for escalated 15%). Scores (1–10) and weights: quality 40%, unit cost 20%, p95 latency 15%, compliance 15%, ops 10%. Compute totals; then re-run with quality at 50% (other weights rescaled proportionally) and decide.

steps.title: Step 1 — hard filters first
steps.desc: PII: any API candidate needs contractual non-retention; assume A and D qualify only with enterprise terms (flag as a dependency). Latency 4 s: all pass at p95 on paper. Budget ceiling: set at $4k/month — C at this volume likely fails on cost/ops; keep it scored for transparency.

steps.title: Step 2 — the rubric table
steps.desc: A: [9.0, 4.0, 7.0, 6.0, 9.0]. B: [7.5, 9.5, 9.0, 9.5, 5.0]. C: [8.5, 6.0, 6.5, 9.5, 3.5]. D: [8.5, 8.5, 8.0, 8.5, 4.5]. (Scores from your eval harness, not opinions — placeholders here for arithmetic.)

steps.title: Step 4 — sensitivity check flips the call
steps.desc: Raise quality weight to 50% (others ×0.8 effectively: cost .20, latency .10, compliance .10, ops .10): A = 7.50, B = 8.00, C = 7.40, D = 8.05 — D now wins. Interpretation: the decision hinges on how much you pay for the last 10 points of quality. Take it to stakeholders with both numbers; pick D (hybrid) as the robust default — it wins the sensitivity case and stays within 0.2 of B in the cost-weighted case.

payload.solution: Base weights: B 8.18 > D 8.03 > C 7.35 > A 7.25. Quality-heavy weights: D 8.05 > B 8.00 > A 7.50 > C 7.40. The honest conclusion is not "B" or "D" — it is "the weights decide; stakeholders must own the weights". Recommendation: ship D, instrument escalation rate and quality proxy, re-run the rubric next quarter.

payload.title: Run the framework on something you own
payload.prompt: Choose one AI feature you could build (summariser, flashcard generator, code reviewer). Write: task + golden-set plan (10 example items sketched), three hard filters, five rubric criteria with weights summing to 100%, three candidate models, and the table you would fill from your eval harness. You do not need to run models to complete this — the skeleton is the deliverable.
payload.hint: If you cannot name your quality metric in one sentence, you are not ready to compare models — fix the metric first.

mistakes.mistake: Starting from a leaderboard instead of a golden set
mistakes.fix: Public benchmarks are contaminated, saturating and domain-mismatched. Cite them as context; decide on your own eval with your own scoring.

mistakes.mistake: Scoring on a handful of vibe demos
mistakes.fix: Sampling luck flatters every model. 50–200 real examples with a rubric or pairwise judging is the minimum instrument that sees tail behaviour.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving ops burden and version drift out of the rubric
mistakes.fix: A model choice is a maintenance commitment — page load, upgrade cadence, deprecation risk must be scored, not discovered in production.

mistakes.mistake: Deciding once and never re-running
mistakes.fix: Models, prices and licenses move — especially fast as of 2026. Put a quarterly re-run date and a rollback path in the decision document.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe a model-selection framework for a production GenAI feature. Include the process steps, at least four rubric criteria with rationale, and one way to test the robustness of your decision.
payload.answer: Process: (1) define the task and a golden eval set with a concrete metric; (2) apply hard constraints (residency, modality, latency ceiling, budget, licensing) as pass/fail filters; (3) shortlist 3–4 candidates spanning categories; (4) evaluate all on the identical harness with version-pinned models and prompts; (5) score a weighted rubric and document evidence per score; (6) recommend with monitoring metrics and a rollback path; (7) schedule a re-evaluation (quarterly — the field moves). Rubric criteria: quality on your eval (largest weight — it is the only task-relevant quality signal), unit cost at real volume (token/GPU arithmetic), p95 latency (tail latency is what users feel), data/compliance fit (contractual and legal constraints), ops burden (who maintains it, drift and deprecation risk). Robustness test: perturb the weights (e.g. raise quality weight by 10 points) and see whether the ranking flips; if it does, surface the trade-off explicitly to stakeholders rather than hiding it behind false precision — the weights, not the arithmetic, are where the real decision lives.
payload.source: System-design interview staple: "how do you choose a model for production?"

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Selection is a process: metric → hard filters → shortlist → identical eval harness → weighted rubric → decide → monitor → re-run quarterly.
The only quality number that matters is the one you measured on your own golden set.
Weight criteria to your product: quality, unit cost, p95 latency, compliance, ops burden — weights are a stakeholder decision made numeric.
Sensitivity-check the ranking: if a small weight change flips the winner, present the trade-off, do not bury it.
Every decision document ends with pinned versions, monitoring metrics and a rollback path — or it is not a decision, it is a mood.

questions.prompt: The correct FIRST step in a model selection process is:
options: Shortlisting the three most famous models
Defining the task, the golden eval set and the success metric
questions.explanation: Without a task-specific metric you cannot compare anything except vibes.

questions.prompt: Hard constraints in model selection should be treated as:
options: Weighted criteria that can be traded off against quality
Pass/fail filters applied before any scoring
Items to mention in the final report only
questions.explanation: Residency, licensing, modality and budget ceilings eliminate candidates outright — no score recovers a compliance failure.

questions.prompt: A weights-sensitivity check (e.g. raising the quality weight 10 points) is valuable because it:
options: Reveals whether the decision depends on a debatable weighting, exposing the real stakeholder trade-off
questions.explanation: Ranking flips under small weight changes mean the "winner" is a values question wearing a spreadsheet costume.

questions.prompt: Why must a model decision document pin model versions and include a rollback path?
options: Endpoints and behaviours drift or get deprecated — reproducibility and a safe fallback are engineering requirements, not paperwork
questions.explanation: Version drift is the normal state of fast-moving model lines; the plan anticipates it instead of discovering it in an incident.

modules.title: Module 4 — Image, Audio & Video Generation
modules.summary: Diffusion knobs with real mechanics (noise prediction, steps, guidance scale), image prompting as a system of levers, the speech pipeline end to end (ASR, TTS, cloning and its consent problem), video's constraints, and structured outputs — boxes, captions, JSON — across modalities.

lessons.title: Diffusion Mechanics: From Noise to Image
lessons.summary: What the denoiser actually predicts, how steps trade time for quality, and what guidance scale really does to your image and your patience.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe diffusion training (noise addition, noise prediction) and sampling (iterative denoising) with the roles of text conditioning
Compute generation time and cost for a given step count, resolution and GPU rate
Explain classifier-free guidance as an extrapolation between conditional and unconditional noise predictions
Choose steps, guidance and resolution settings for three quality/latency requirements

payload.text: Every serious image generator hands you the same mystery panel: Steps 20–50, CFG 3–10, a sampler dropdown nobody understands, and a resolution picker. Turn CFG to 11 and the image goes plastic-bright with burnt edges; drop it to 2 and the model wanders off your prompt. Push steps to 80 and wait, seeing almost no difference from 30. These are not vibes — each maps to a specific term in the denoising loop you met in Lesson 1.2. This lesson makes the panel legible.

**The network's single job.** A diffusion model is trained on one regression: given a noisy version of an image at noise level t (plus a text condition), predict the noise that was added. Text enters through cross-attention — the denoiser attends from image latents to the text tokens — so "a red bicycle" biases the noise prediction toward latent patterns that decode to bicycles, red ones. Nothing else happens at sampling time except applying this learned direction over and over.

**Sampling is iteration, and steps are the dial.** To generate: start from pure Gaussian noise in the latent space, ask the network for its noise estimate, move a fraction of the way against that estimate (the fraction is set by the sampler — Euler, DPM++-class solvers, and as of 2026 flow-matching/rectified-flow samplers take fewer, larger steps), repeat until step budget is spent, then decode the clean latent to pixels through the VAE decoder. More steps means more corrections: quality improves quickly at first, then saturates — beyond a model-dependent point (often ~25–40 for classic samplers, fewer for flow-based ones), extra steps are latency you buy for nothing, or slight over-sharpening. Latency is roughly linear in steps at fixed resolution, and heavily resolution-dependent (latent area grows with pixels).

**Guidance scale: pulling the prediction toward your words.** Classifier-free guidance (CFG) runs the denoiser twice per step — once with the text condition, once without — and extrapolates: noise_pred = noise_uncond + s × (noise_cond − noise_uncond). At s = 1 you get the conditional prediction itself; higher s amplifies the *direction* that text adds, making the image adhere more literally to the prompt — with side effects: diversity collapses (high s = the model's "safe" interpretation of your words), colours oversaturate, textures burn, and artifacts appear as the extrapolation pushes the latent off the natural-image manifold. Low s (2–4) yields loose, dreamy interpretations; mid (4–7) is the usual working band; some tools relabel or automate this (stylize-like flags, prompt-adherence controls). The knob names differ per product as of 2026, but the tension is universal: **fidelity to prompt versus freedom and naturalness**.

**What actually costs time.** Per image ≈ steps × per-step time at a given resolution; per-step time scales with latent area (a 1536×1024 generation costs meaningfully more than 512×512) and with batch size and hardware. Latent diffusion (the VAE compression from Lesson 1.2) is why interactive generation is possible at all — pixel-space diffusion of the same quality would be orders of magnitude slower. For production, the levers order predictably: reduce steps to the quality floor, keep guidance mid-band, pick the lowest resolution that meets the output spec, and only then add batch or faster hardware. As of 2026, distilled/few-step models (1–8 step variants of major open lines) have made "quality in under a second" real for some styles — check whether your pipeline can adopt them before optimizing an old schedule forever.

payload.title: Knobs, mechanics, and failure signatures
rows: Time waste past the quality floor; slight over-sharpening
Burnt colours, plastic texture, collapsed diversity
Quadratic-ish cost jump; occasional anatomy/coherence breaks off native ratios
How the ODE/flow is integrated per step
Wrong pairings give mush or noise at low step counts
Reproducibility — same seed + settings ≈ same image

payload.title: Flow matching changed the schedule, not the story
payload.text: SD3/FLUX-class training (as of 2026) shortens denoising trajectories — fewer steps for the same quality — but the UI still exposes steps, adherence and seeds. Learn the mechanism once; re-skin it per tool.

payload.title: Optimize in the right order
payload.text: Steps down to the quality floor first (biggest time lever), then resolution to spec, then guidance for taste, then sampler choice. Tweaking samplers while running 60 steps at max resolution is optimizing the wrong term.

payload.title: Configure and price a product-shot generation pipeline
payload.problem: An e-commerce studio generates pack shots on white: 1024×1024, must match the product catalogue look (crisp, neutral). Reference GPU does 1.2 s/step at this resolution; GPU costs $0.50/hr. (1) Pick initial settings and compute time and cost per image. (2) Propose a 20-step variant and quantify the saving. (3) Predict the visual difference between guidance 3, 6 and 9 for this brief. (4) State the production policy you would ship.

steps.title: Step 1 — initial configuration
steps.desc: Settings: steps 30, guidance 6, native 1024×1024, default flow sampler, per-shot prompt template. Time: 30 × 1.2 s = 36 s/image. Cost: 36/3600 hr × $0.50 = $0.005/image.

steps.title: Step 2 — the 20-step variant
steps.desc: 20 × 1.2 = 24 s → $0.0033/image — a 33% time and cost cut. On flow-based samplers the visual gap at 20 vs 30 is often minor for clean product shots; verify on a 20-image A/B (same seeds) before adopting. At 10 steps you typically start losing fine label text and edge crispness — that is your floor.

steps.title: Step 3 — guidance sweep for this brief
steps.desc: s ≈ 3: product present but colours drift, background occasionally invents props — fails catalogue fidelity. s ≈ 6: prompt followed, neutral palette holds, textures natural — the working band. s ≈ 9: hyper-adherent but plasticky highlights, oversaturated labels, occasional halo artifacts — looks "AI", wrong for a catalogue.

steps.title: Step 4 — production policy
steps.desc: Ship: 20 steps (validated), guidance 5.5–6.5, fixed seeds per SKU family for consistency, negative prompt excluding "text overlay, watermark, props". Re-benchmark monthly against a small golden set of SKUs — model updates move the quality floor, and a pinned seed on an updated model is no longer the same image.

payload.solution: 30-step baseline: 36 s, $0.005/image; validated 20-step: 24 s, $0.0033 (−33%); guidance sweet spot ≈ 6 for catalogue fidelity; ship with pinned seeds and a golden-set re-benchmark. Knobs turned from folklore into a priced configuration.

payload.title: Run a knob grid
payload.prompt: With any diffusion tool that exposes steps and guidance (or a hosted clone): fix one prompt and seed, then generate a grid — steps {10, 30, 50} × guidance {3, 7, 11}. Annotate each cell in one line: adherence to prompt, texture quality, artifacts. Write three sentences naming your quality floor and the exact setting you would ship for a professional brief. If no tool is available, design the same grid on paper: predict each cell's failure signature from the mechanics.
payload.hint: Look for the saturation cliff: guidance 11 often shows burnt colour and haloing well before any other knob misbehaves.

mistakes.mistake: Raising guidance to "make the prompt work"
mistakes.fix: Guidance amplifies the text direction, not the model's understanding. Past the mid-band you buy adherence with naturalness and diversity. Fix weak prompts by rewriting them (Lesson 4.2), not by cranking s.

mistakes.mistake: Treating 80 steps as a quality strategy
mistakes.fix: Quality saturates; beyond the floor you pay latency, sometimes over-sharpen. Find the floor with a same-seed sweep and stop there — or adopt a distilled few-step model.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing sampler names with model quality
mistakes.fix: Samplers are integrators for the same learned field; differences are step-efficiency and noise behaviour. The model, conditioning and prompt dominate outcomes.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting seed reproducibility across model updates
mistakes.fix: A seed reproduces an image only with identical model version, settings and code path. Pin the model version too, or the seed is decorative.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain classifier-free guidance in diffusion sampling. What happens to an image as the guidance scale increases from 1 to very high values, and why?
payload.answer: At each denoise step the model predicts noise twice: conditionally (with the text prompt) and unconditionally (no text). CFG combines them as noise = noise_uncond + s × (noise_cond − noise_uncond), extrapolating away from the unconditional prediction toward (and beyond) the conditional one. At s = 1 you sample the plain conditional model; as s grows, the sampled trajectory adheres more literally to the prompt — objects, colours and attributes mentioned get forced in. At very high s the extrapolation leaves the distribution of natural images: colours oversaturate, textures become plastic, edge halos and artifacts appear, and sample-to-sample diversity collapses because every draw is dragged to the model's single most stereotypical interpretation of the prompt. That is why working defaults sit in a mid band (roughly 4–7 in classic parameterisations): enough adherence to honour the prompt, not so much that the latent trajectory is distorted off the image manifold.
payload.source: Common diffusion-mechanics exam question; also asked in creative-tooling engineering interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: One trained function: predict noise given noisy latents + text conditioning; sampling applies it iteratively from pure noise.
Steps = number of corrections: quality saturates, latency is linear — find the floor with same-seed sweeps.
CFG extrapolates between unconditional and conditional noise prediction: adherence up, naturalness and diversity down past the mid-band.
Resolution drives per-step cost via latent area; latent diffusion is what makes interactive generation affordable.
Flow-matching-era models shorten schedules but keep the same conceptual knobs: steps, adherence, seed.

questions.prompt: During diffusion sampling, each step applies:
options: A new training update to the network
The learned noise prediction to move the current noisy latent partway toward a cleaner one
A search engine query for similar images
A VAE re-encoding of the prompt
questions.explanation: Iterative denoising of the latent using the predicted noise direction — the whole sampling loop.

questions.prompt: Classifier-free guidance works by:
options: Classifying images and rejecting off-prompt ones
Extrapolating between the unconditional and text-conditioned noise predictions to amplify the prompt direction
Raising the temperature of the sampler
Running two diffusion models and averaging their images
questions.explanation: Two forward passes (with and without text) combined by the guidance scale s.

questions.prompt: Very high guidance scales typically cause:
options: Burnt saturation, plastic textures, artifacts and collapsed diversity
questions.explanation: The extrapolation pushes latents off the natural-image manifold — adherence bought with naturalness.

questions.prompt: Generation time is most strongly affected by:
options: Step count and resolution (latent area) — time grows with both
The file format of the output
questions.explanation: Steps × per-step compute, where per-step compute scales with latent area — the two multiplicative cost terms.

lessons.title: Image Prompting Levers: Style, Composition and Negative Prompts
lessons.summary: Prompting images as a system: subject, style, composition, lighting, format — the negative channel — and why the same words behave differently across tools.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Decompose any image brief into subject, style, composition, lighting and format levers
Write a structured prompt and a targeted negative prompt for a given brief
Map the same intent into three tool dialects (natural language, flag-based, negative-box)
Run a one-variable-at-a-time iteration and articulate what each change taught

payload.text: Two designers type "a cat astronaut" into two different tools and get a watercolour dream and a glossy 3D render. Neither tool is broken — the tools learned different prompt dialects from different training and different default aesthetics. Meanwhile the third designer, who specifies shot type, lens, lighting and medium — and names what must NOT appear — gets catalogue-consistent results on the third try. Image prompting is not incantation; it is a small, learnable control system. This lesson is the control panel.

**The lever set.** A reliable image prompt is a stack of decisions, roughly in this order: (1) **Subject and action** — what exists, doing what ("a hand-thrown ceramic mug, steam rising"). (2) **Style and medium** — photo vs illustration, art medium, era, reference aesthetics ("studio product photograph", "risograph print"). Policies vary: many tools restrict living-artist names; eras and movements are safer. (3) **Composition** — shot type (close-up, wide, macro), camera angle (eye level, bird's-eye), framing (rule of thirds, centred). (4) **Lighting and colour** — golden hour, softbox, rim light, palette. (5) **Format** — aspect ratio, film stock, print style. Prose or comma-separated both work; specificity beats length. Modifier inflation ("8k, ultra-detailed, masterpiece") had outsized effects in earlier diffusion eras and now mostly adds noise — precision outperforms adjective stacking.

**The negative channel.** Generative models render *plausible patterns*, including unwanted ones: extra limbs, watermarks, baked-in text, blur, perspective disasters. Negative prompts (a first-class input in SD/FLUX-dev-style tools; approximated by "--no" flags elsewhere; absorbed into natural-language instructions in fully managed tools like DALL·E/Gemini-class assistants) subtract directions from the conditioning — the mirror of guidance. Good negatives are *specific to the failure you observed* ("text overlay, watermark, extra fingers"), not a ritual list; and negatives never replace the positive description — the model needs to know what you want, not only what you refuse.

**Tool dialects.** The same intent maps differently: natural-language tools (DALL·E/Gemini-class) want full sentences describing the scene; flag-based tools (Midjourney-style) use compact phrases plus parameters like "--ar 16:9", "--style raw", "--no text"; open pipelines (SD/FLUX-class) separate positive prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG and seed explicitly. Learn the dialect of your production tool; do not paste Midjourney flags into an SD box and blame the model. Beyond text: reference images (style or content conditioning), layout/pose control (ControlNet-style structural conditioning), and regional inpainting give *deterministic* control that prompting alone cannot — when the brief says "exactly this layout", stop fighting language and start conditioning on structure.

**Iteration as method.** Change one lever per generation batch, hold seed when comparing structure, keep a prompt log with screenshots. Prompting quality comes from a hundred small observed cause-effect pairs, not from one magic template — and the fastest way to build that library is disciplined single-variable experiments.

**Consistency across a session.** One prompt is easy; ten matching outputs are the real brief. Two patterns cover most needs: *anchor tokens* — a fixed block of style, palette, medium and format phrases that never changes while the subject clause rotates — and *reference conditioning*, where an approved earlier image is fed back as a style or structure reference so texture and composition stay locked. Some pipelines also expose prompt weighting (emphasising a token's influence with per-tool syntax) for when one lever needs to dominate; use it sparingly, because heavy weighting distorts exactly like over-guidance does. When neither anchor nor reference suffices — strict layouts, brand geometry, pose — that is the signal to leave language entirely and condition on structure (masks, edges, depth) as a different input channel.

rows: "a weathered brass telescope on a map"
"close-up, low angle, shallow depth of field"

payload.title: Text-in-image is still the weak spot
payload.text: Short labels are increasingly reliable (as of 2026); paragraphs, logos and precise typography still fail often. Plan to overlay real text in your design tool — the generated image is the backdrop, not the typesetter.

payload.title: Two-pass workflow for production
payload.text: Pass 1: generate candidates with structure levers held fixed. Pass 2: pick the winner, then inpaint/upscale and overlay real typography. Splitting composition from finishing beats asking one prompt for everything.

payload.title: Turn a vague campus brief into a shippable poster prompt
payload.problem: Client: "make a poster for our college hackathon — energetic, techy, works on Instagram and as A3 print." Output needs headline space (you will overlay real text), a hero visual, and two aspect ratios. Produce: a structured prompt, a negative prompt, the format choice per channel, and a three-variant iteration plan.

steps.title: Step 1 — extract requirements
steps.desc: Hero visual only (no baked-in headline — overlay later); energetic/techy mood; must crop to 4:5 (Instagram) and A3 portrait print (~1:1.41); consistent series later → keep structure fixed across variants.

steps.title: Step 2 — compose the positive prompt
steps.desc: Subject: "a diverse student team huddled around glowing holographic code projections in a modern campus lab". Style: "dynamic editorial photograph, cinematic teal-and-orange palette". Composition: "slightly low angle, shallow depth of field, hero subject right of centre leaving left space clear". Lighting: "practical screen glow, energetic rim light". Format: portrait orientation for the master.
steps.code_snippet: master (portrait): hero visual, space left clear for headline, cinematic teal-orange

steps.title: Step 3 — targeted negatives
steps.desc: Observed failure modes to suppress: baked-in words, watermarks, distorted hands (huddle scenes trigger them), muddy midtones, extreme wide-angle distortion. Negatives: "text, letters, watermark, extra fingers, blurry, murky colours".

steps.title: Step 4 — dialect + iteration plan
steps.desc: In a flag tool: add "--ar 4:5 --style raw --no text watermark". In an SD/FLUX pipeline: same tokens in the positive box, negatives in the negative box, guidance ~5–6. Iterate one variable at a time across three seeds: V1 as written; V2 with "golden-hour backlight" swapped for lighting; V3 with composition moved to centre. Pick on brand fit, then crop masters for 4:5 and print, overlaying headline text in your design tool.

payload.solution: A structured prompt (subject/style/composition/lighting/format), specific negatives, dialect-correct parameters, and a one-variable iteration plan with real typography overlaid afterwards — a workflow that reproduces, instead of a sentence that hopes.

payload.title: The one-lever experiment
payload.prompt: Take any image prompt you have used. Generate four variants, changing exactly one lever each time: (A) composition phrase only, (B) style/medium only, (C) lighting only, (D) negatives only (add the four most relevant). Keep everything else fixed — including seed if available. Write six lines mapping cause to observed effect, and revise your original prompt into a v2 that you would actually ship.
payload.hint: Log the exact strings. Your future self will want the cause-effect table more than the images.

mistakes.mistake: Writing longer prompts instead of sharper ones
mistakes.fix: Every clause competes for conditioning attention. Five precise levers beat twenty stacked adjectives; delete modifiers you cannot justify against a specific failure.

mistakes.mistake: Using negatives as a substitute for describing the target
mistakes.fix: Negatives subtract directions; they do not specify the scene. "Not ugly" tells the model nothing about what to render — describe what you want, subtract only observed failures.

mistakes.mistake: Copying prompt syntax across tool dialects
mistakes.fix: Flags, boxes and prose are not interchangeable. Learn the dialect of your production tool; port the *decisions*, not the punctuation.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting one prompt to deliver final typography and layout
mistakes.fix: Generated text and precise layout remain weak points; plan to overlay real type and composite in a design tool. The model makes the art layer, not the deliverable.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: You must produce a consistent series of ten brand illustrations. Outline your prompt strategy: which levers you fix, which you vary, how negatives and references are used, and how consistency is maintained across generations.
payload.answer: Fix the levers that define the brand: style/medium (one rendering tradition, e.g. "flat vector illustration, limited palette"), lighting/palette tokens, format and aspect ratio, and the negative list for recurring failure modes (text, watermark, photorealism leakage). Vary only the subject across the ten: same syntactic prompt skeleton with a swapped subject clause, so conditioning stays stable. Keep seed fixed per subject family when the tool supports it, and pin the model version — seeds are only reproducible within a version. Use a reference image or style-conditioning feature if the tool offers one: it anchors texture and palette far more tightly than words alone. Iterate with a small golden set: after each generation compare against the first three approved illustrations on palette and line quality before accepting. Finally, standardise post: same upscaler settings, same crop ratios, typography overlaid outside the generator. Consistency in image generation is a pipeline property, not a prompt property.
payload.source: Common creative-pipeline interview question for design-tooling and content-ops roles.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Structure prompts as levers: subject, style/medium, composition, lighting, format — precision beats adjective stacking.
Negative prompts subtract observed failure modes; they never replace a positive description.
Tool dialects differ (prose vs flags vs separated boxes) — port decisions, not punctuation.
For deterministic layout/brand needs, use reference images and structural conditioning instead of fighting language.
Iterate one variable at a time with a prompt log — that log is the real asset.

questions.prompt: In structured image prompting, the "composition" lever primarily controls:
options: Framing and camera language — shot type, angle, subject placement
questions.explanation: Close-up vs wide, low angle vs eye level, left-of-centre vs centred — the geometry of the frame.

questions.prompt: A negative prompt functions by:
options: Subtracting directions from the conditioning to suppress unwanted patterns (watermarks, extra limbs, blur)
questions.explanation: It is the mirror operation of guidance — steering away from named failure modes.

questions.prompt: Why does the same prompt text behave differently across tools?
options: Tools are trained and post-tuned with different aesthetics and prompt conventions — different dialects and defaults
Different tools use different image resolutions only
questions.explanation: Prompt dialect is learned per product; port the decisions, not the punctuation.

questions.prompt: For production posters with a headline, the recommended workflow is to:
options: Demand the model renders the full headline perfectly in one pass
Generate the hero visual without baked-in text, then overlay real typography in a design tool
Use the highest guidance possible to force text
Generate text first and ask for the image around it
questions.explanation: Text rendering remains the weakest link; separating art from typesetting is the reliable pipeline.

lessons.title: Speech Pipelines: ASR, TTS and Voice Cloning
lessons.summary: The two speech stacks end to end — how audio becomes text and text becomes audio — plus what voice cloning requires, what it enables, and why consent is a technical requirement, not a footnote.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Diagram an ASR pipeline from waveform to timestamped text and name two production failure sources
Diagram a neural TTS pipeline from text to waveform and distinguish zero-shot cloning from fine-tuned cloning
Compute a per-meeting cost for a transcribe-and-summarise product from stage-wise prices
Specify a consent and safety control set for any voice-cloning feature

payload.text: Three voice products on one slide: a meeting assistant that transcribes an hour of mixed English-Hindi discussion; a bank fraudster cloning a CFO's voice from a public podcast to approve a transfer; and an accessibility tool giving a losing-among-the-abilities user their own voice back from thirty minutes of archive audio. Same underlying capability — speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice cloning — three moral universes. Engineering and consent are now the same design problem, and this lesson treats them together.

**ASR (speech-to-text) is a pipeline, not magic.** Audio in: waveform, usually resampled and normalised. Feature stage: the signal is converted to time-frequency representations (mel-spectrograms) — the "image" of sound. Acoustic model: a transformer/conformer-style network (Whisper-class encoder-decoder stacks being the widely known family as of 2026) maps features to token sequences; a decoder emits text, often with word-level timestamps. Post-processing: punctuation restoration, number normalisation ("two point five" → "2.5"), vocabulary biasing for domain terms (product names, medical terminology), and diarization (a separate model deciding *who* spoke when) for multi-speaker scenes. Failure sources to expect: accents and code-switching (Hinglish sentences inside English frames trip models trained mostly on monolingual data), background noise and overlapping speech, and rare proper nouns — which is why timestamps + confidence scores, not raw transcripts, are the production artefact; downstream apps filter and correct against them.

**TTS (text-to-speech) is also a pipeline.** Text normalisation first (expand abbreviations, decide "St." is street or saint, format currency). Then a linguistic/prosody model predicts *how* to say it: duration, pitch contour, emphasis — the difference between a question and a statement. Then an acoustic model produces either mel-spectrograms or, in modern systems, discrete neural-codec tokens (EnCodec/DAC-style), and a vocoder or codec decoder renders the waveform. Modern zero-shot TTS conditions on a *reference voice embedding*: seconds-to-minutes of sample audio are enough to synthesise speech in that voice — which is both the accessibility miracle and the fraud vector. Fine-tuned cloning (trained longer on more enrolled data) gives tighter identity at higher cost. Streaming TTS exists for conversational agents: sentence-clause chunking keeps latency under ~a second after the LLM finishes a phrase.

**Consent is part of the architecture.** Any cloning feature needs: verified enrolment consent (the recorded voice of the person, not an impersonated one), misuse filters on the *text* being synthesised (financial-fraud and blackmail phrasing classes), watermarking or provenance signals where available, audit logs of who cloned what, and revocation (delete the voice print). Laws and norms are evolving quickly as of 2026 — India's DPDP framework treats biometric-adjacent personal data seriously, and most platforms ban non-consensual cloning outright — so treat consent gates as product features with the same seriousness as authentication. The engineering maxim: **if your product can clone a voice, your threat model includes that voice authorising a wire transfer.**

**Latency budgets decide the UX shape.** Conversational speech products live and die on the round trip: ASR partials within a second or two, the LLM's first phrase within one to two, TTS streaming audio as clauses complete rather than after the full text. Meeting transcription is the forgiving case — minutes are fine — while voice agents are the brutal one: over roughly a second of dead air and users repeat themselves. The architecture move for tight budgets is clause-level pipelining: the LLM emits sentence fragments, TTS renders them immediately, and the next fragment is generated while the current one is still speaking. Every stage's latency is budgeted against that human threshold, which is why streaming interfaces (partial ASR, chunked TTS) are not features but requirements.

payload.title: Speech pipeline stages and their failure modes
Cloning without consent is fraud infrastructure
payload.text: Treat voice enrolment like key management: identity-verified consent, scoped use, revocation, logging, and content filters on synthesis requests. "We only allow it for paying customers" is not a control.

payload.title: Design for partial transcripts
payload.text: Downstream features should consume timestamps + confidence, not perfect text: drop low-confidence spans, surface uncertain names for human review, and never let a 9% word-error rate on names and numbers silently poison an automated action.

payload.title: Price and design a meeting-notes pipeline
payload.problem: Product: 1-hour internal meetings → transcript with speaker labels → summary + action items. ASR priced at $0.01/min (hypothetical); summarisation LLM at $1/M input, $4/M output; average meeting ≈ 9,000 words of speech ≈ 12,000 tokens of transcript; expected output ≈ 900 tokens. 50 meetings/day. (1) Cost per meeting and per month. (2) Handle Hinglish code-switching and crosstalk. (3) Specify the confidence-gated handoff to the summariser.

steps.title: Step 1 — stage-wise cost
steps.desc: ASR: 60 min × $0.01 = $0.60. Summarisation: 12,000/1e6 × $1 = $0.012 input; 900/1e6 × $4 = $0.0036 output → $0.0156. Total ≈ $0.62/meeting. Monthly (50×30): ≈ $925. ASR dominates — optimise there first (batch APIs, longer-form pricing tiers).

steps.title: Step 2 — code-switching and crosstalk
steps.desc: Mitigations: enable multilingual/code-switched ASR profiles where offered; bias the decoder with a glossary of team names and product terms; run diarization so the summariser sees speaker turns ("Priya: ship Friday" beats anonymous soup); detect and flag segments where two voices overlap instead of hallucinating a clean sentence.

steps.title: Step 3 — confidence-gated handoff
steps.desc: Contract to the summariser: (a) drop spans with confidence below threshold; (b) mark names/numbers with medium confidence as [verify] so the LLM must not assert them without hedge; (c) require the summary to cite timestamps for action items; (d) if >15% of the transcript is low-confidence, route to a human-review queue instead of auto-sending notes. This keeps the cheap pipeline from laundering acoustic errors into authoritative decisions.

steps.title: Step 4 — latency and UX check
steps.desc: For live notetaking: stream partial ASR (first words appear within seconds), summarise at natural pauses or at meeting end, stream the summary. Budget: ASR streaming latency in the low seconds; summary TTFT ~1–2 s after the final segment. Announce recording and retention policy — meeting audio is personal data; store minimally.

payload.solution: ≈ $0.62/meeting, ≈ $930/month, ASR-dominated; code-switching handled via multilingual profiles + glossary biasing + diarization; a confidence-gated contract stops low-quality audio from becoming confident notes — the pattern for every speech product.

payload.title: Transcribe, compare, audit
payload.prompt: Record two minutes of your own speech including one code-switched sentence (e.g. English with a Hindi clause) and a proper noun. Transcribe with two different tools (or one tool twice with different settings). Diff the outputs: which words failed, were numbers right, was punctuation sane? Write three sentences on how you would protect a downstream automated action from exactly those errors.
payload.hint: Proper nouns and numbers are where word-error rates concentrate — and where downstream automation gets hurt worst.

mistakes.mistake: Equating ASR output with understanding
mistakes.fix: ASR transcribes; comprehension is a separate (usually LLM) stage. Never assume the speech model "knew" what was said — it emitted plausible text from acoustics.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring word-error concentration on names and numbers
mistakes.fix: Average WER hides the dangerous tail. Bias dictionaries, confidence gates and human review exist precisely for spans where errors cause real-world damage.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking TTS retrieves recorded sentences
mistakes.fix: Neural TTS synthesises waveforms from predicted prosody and codec/spectrogram stages — which is why it can say any text in a cloned voice, and why it sometimes mis-stresses novel names.

mistakes.mistake: Shipping voice cloning with a checkbox "I agree"
mistakes.fix: Consent must be verified (the real voice-owner enrols), scoped, logged, filterable and revocable. A checkbox is a legal fig leaf over a fraud-ready capability.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the stages of a modern neural text-to-speech pipeline, and state two safety controls that any product offering voice cloning should implement.
