Design rules: target first paint under ~1 second class (set your own number, measure p95); show a stable skeleton or "thinking" state immediately so layout never jumps; stream markdown incrementally with tolerant parsing (never render half a code fence as raw garbage); keep stop and regenerate controls live — cancellation also stops billing for undelivered output; handle mid-stream failure explicitly (retry policy, "connection lost — retry from here"), because partial answers look like truth; and *do not stream* when the consumer needs an atomic result — a JSON-driven UI or a structured record should validate first (6.3) and then render, or the user watches a broken widget. Perceived-latency stacks with quality: a fast wrong answer escalates twice (7.4's cost per successful task).

**Close the loop.** Per feature: a latency budget (p95 TTFT, p95 total), a cost-per-task budget (7.1), and a quality gate (6.4) — three numbers reviewed together, because routing changes move all three at once. Route with gates, stream with intent, and re-measure after every model version bump (10.4).

payload.title: Task tiers → model class → routing rule of thumb
rows: Classify, reformat, extract one field, canned KB line
Small / mini tier (or classic ML classifier — 8.3)
Summarise, grounded answer, draft reply, multi-field extraction
Rubric sample + human review where stakes demand

payload.code:
# Cascade with a verification gate (shape)
r = call(small, req)
if verify(r) == PASS:            # schema + consistency + retrieval checks
    return r                     # cheap path
r2 = call(large, req)            # escalation: pays both models
return r2
# track: escalation_rate, gate_false_pass (vs golden set), p95, cost/task

payload.title: A cascade's p95 is the escalation path
payload.text: Average cost falls while tail latency can rise: escalated requests pay two round-trips. Budget and alert on p95 of escalated traffic separately, or the UX quietly degrades for exactly the hard cases.

payload.title: Route a campus assistant's traffic and put streaming on its budget
payload.problem: A university assistant handles 12,000 requests/day: 60% one-line FAQ lookup from a small KB, 25% summarise/reformat, 10% multi-step ("explain my fee break-up with calculations"), 5% ambiguous admin advice. Current setup: one frontier model for everything, average 4.1s to completion, no streaming, $2,900/month. Design tiers, a cascade with gates, a latency budget with streaming — and estimate the new monthly bill and quality position.

steps.title: Step 1 — tier the traffic and pick models
steps.desc: 60% FAQ → Tier 1 small model with grounding (KB top-3, source-or-abstain from 6.2). 25% summarise/reformat → Tier 2 mid-size. 10% calculations → Tier 3 frontier *with tools* — never let any model do fee arithmetic from memory (6.1). 5% ambiguous advice → Tier 3 plus escalation-to-human flag. Static-by-endpoint first (transparent, testable), then a rules layer for exceptions.

steps.title: Step 2 — cascade + gates on Tier 1/2
steps.desc: Tier 1 answer passes gates (KB hit + claim check + schema for structured replies) or escalates to Tier 2; Tier 2 sample-gated by rubric (6.4) on 5% with automatic escalation on failure signals. Assume 15% escalation from Tier 1, 10% from Tier 2. Small $0.0015, mid $0.006, frontier $0.02 per call (illustrative).
steps.code_snippet:
blended = 0.0015 + 0.15*0.006 + (0.10*0.02 on escalated share)
est. blended ~$0.0045/call vs frontier-only $0.02  ->  ~$1,160/mo vs $2,900

steps.title: Step 3 — latency budget and streaming
steps.desc: Budget p95: TTFT ≤ 1.2s (retrieval 200ms parallel with prefill, Tier-1 prefill small), total ≤ 4s; escalated p95 tracked separately (frontier prefill on long context can dominate — trim context first). Ship streaming with stable skeleton, incremental markdown, live stop; atomic JSON replies validate-before-render. Expect *perceived* time to fall to first-paint (~sub-second class) even though escalated total time is unchanged.

steps.title: Step 4 — prove no quality loss
steps.desc: Same 60-case golden set (6.4) evaluated across all tiers vs the old single-model baseline: overall task score must be ≥ baseline, FAQ abstention must not regress (small models guess — test it), and escalation quality measured by gate false-pass rate on the golden set (target low single digits, hedged per task). Weekly dashboard: cost/task, escalation rate, p50/p95 TTFT and total, golden-set score. Re-run everything on the next model upgrade — routing tables rot.

payload.solution: Four tiers with tool-enforced arithmetic, gated cascades at 15%/10% escalation (illustrative ~60% bill reduction), a p95 budget with per-stage attribution, streaming for perceived latency, and a golden-set gate proving the small-model routes did not cheapen the answers — cost, latency and quality reviewed as one change.

payload.title: Tier your own traffic and time first tokens
payload.prompt: List the last 20 requests you personally made to an AI feature; classify each into trivial/standard/hard and note which model class you would route it to and why. Then, on two providers you can access, time (a) time to first token and (b) total time for the same short prompt, twice each — record the numbers, not feelings. Finally, write the verification gate you would trust to escalate a trivial-tier answer, and what false-pass rate would make you disable it.
payload.hint: If you cannot name the gate, you do not have a cascade — you have a lottery with extra steps.

mistakes.mistake: Routing by cost alone with no quality gate
mistakes.fix: Every route carries a golden-set score (6.4); escalation exists because the gate failed. A router without gates is an unmonitored quality lottery.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting average latency
mistakes.fix: Averages hide the tail users abandon on. Track p50 and p95 per stage (prefill, decode, tools) — the tail is a specific stage, usually retrievable.

mistakes.mistake: Streaming into an atomic UI
mistakes.fix: Structured consumers (JSON-driven widgets, records) should validate then render (6.3). Half-rendered structures read as bugs even when the final object is valid.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting double-payment in cascades
mistakes.fix: Escalated requests pay the small model and the large one, and their p95 spans both round-trips. Track escalation cost share and escalated p95 as first-class metrics.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Design a routing strategy for a traffic mix of 60% simple FAQ, 25% summarisation and 15% hard reasoning. Include tiering, a cascade with a verification gate, and the metrics that tell you the router is working. Then decompose end-to-end latency and say where streaming helps and where it does not.
payload.answer: Tiering: FAQ → small model with grounding (gates: KB hit, claim check, abstention when KB is silent); summarisation → mid-size model (gate: schema/length + rubric sample); hard reasoning → frontier class, optionally with tools for calculation, with human review where stakes require. Cascade: cheap first, verification gate (schema validity, self-consistency, retrieval-hit checks — cheaper than escalation), escalate on gate failure; all routes scored on one golden set so overall quality equals or beats the old single-model baseline. Metrics: escalation rate, gate false-pass rate (against golden set), cost per task, p50/p95 per route, golden-set score over time. Latency decomposition: queueing + prefill (scales with input/context — the reason retrieval and history caps affect TTFT) + decode (scales with output length) + tool/retrieval round-trips + network; measure p95 per stage. Streaming reduces *perceived* latency by delivering a fast first token and incremental rendering — huge for long text chat — but it does not shorten decode, does not help atomic/structured consumers (validate then render), and cannot hide a slow prefill; escalated cascades still pay full tail latency and must be budgeted separately.
payload.source: Classic system-design question for LLM serving and product engineering.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Tier by task difficulty; route with gates; small models win trivial work at 10× the savings.
Cascade economics: cheap-first + verification + escalation beats all-frontier — if the gate's false-pass rate is measured and low.
Latency = queue + prefill + decode + tools; budget p95 per stage, never average-only.
Streaming moves perceived latency to TTFT — design skeleton, incremental render, stop/error states; validate before rendering atomic structures.
Cost, latency and quality move together — change routing only with all three dashboards open.

questions.prompt: In a cheap-first cascade, the verification gate exists to:
options: Accept good cheap answers and escalate the rest — making escalation rate and false-pass rate the metrics to watch
questions.explanation: The gate is the routing brain: pass weak answers and quality caps out; fail good ones and the savings evaporate.

questions.prompt: Time-to-first-token is dominated by:
options: Input prefill — queueing and processing the prompt/context before decoding begins
questions.explanation: Prefill scales with everything you send; long outputs affect total time, not first token.

questions.prompt: A feature shows 2.1s average latency but 7s p95. The correct conclusion is:
options: Half the traffic is fine and a substantial tail is slow — investigate the tail per stage (users experience the tail)
Averages are sufficient for UX budgets
The model should be replaced immediately
questions.explanation: Tail latency is abandonment latency; per-stage p95 attribution tells you whether it is retrieval, prefill or tools.

questions.prompt: Streaming is the wrong choice when the consumer:
options: Is an atomic structured consumer (JSON UI) that must validate before rendering
Benefits from an early skeleton state
questions.explanation: Humans enjoy incremental text; machines need validated wholes (Lesson 6.3).

lessons.title: Quality-per-Rupee: Making the Trade-off an Engineering Number
lessons.summary: Defining measurable quality for your task, comparing candidates on one golden set with real unit costs, reading the Pareto frontier, and running unit economics as a monitored metric — with safety as a gate, never a numerator.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Operationalise "quality" as a task metric on a shared golden set before comparing any two models
Compute cost per task from real usage and combine it into a quality-per-rupee comparison
Construct and interpret a Pareto frontier over quality, cost and latency — and make the business-side trade explicit
Install unit-economics guardrails: target cost per task, drift alerts and a re-evaluation cadence

payload.text: The demo question: model A scores 92% on your eval, model B scores 88% — B costs one-twentieth as much. Which is better? The honest answer: the question is malformed until you can say what quality means for this task, what a wrong answer costs you, and whether 4 points buys anything you value. Teams that skip those questions argue in adjectives ("B feels fine"); teams that answer them ship a spreadsheet that settles the debate in one meeting. This lesson is about turning quality-versus-cost from taste into a number you can put on a dashboard and defend.

**Quality must be defined before it is compared.** "Quality" without a task metric is not a metric — it is a mood. Map yours to something measurable: exact-match or macro-F1 for closed tasks (classification, extraction — 8.2/8.3), claim-level faithfulness and number-preservation for factual text (6.2/8.1), rubric pass rate or judge score for open text (6.4), task success (did the user's job complete?) for agents (10.2). Then pin it to one frozen golden set — the same cases, same scorer, same thresholds for every candidate — because scores from different evals are not comparable, and vendor benchmarks answer vendor questions (10.4). Guardrails come first and separately: safety, format validity and policy compliance are *gates* (pass/fail thresholds from 6.4), not points on a quality scale — a model that is unsafe but cheap does not get a high ratio, it gets rejected.

**The comparison sheet.** For each candidate: golden-set quality (same set), cost per task computed from real usage (7.1 — tokens × rates, including retries), p95 latency (7.3), plus operational columns teams forget (privacy posture, data retention, lock-in, hosting options — Module 3.3's selection frame applied). *Quality per rupee* = quality ÷ cost per task (or equivalently: quality points per ₹100 of spend) — a coarse but decisive ratio when quality is on a common scale. Then plot quality vs cost: the **Pareto frontier** is the set of candidates where you cannot improve quality without paying more (or cut cost without losing quality). Anything below the frontier is dominated — eliminated without discussion. The frontier rarely has one winner: it has a *decision*, and that decision is business logic: what is one point of faithfulness worth? If a wrong fee costs ₹50 in support time and you handle 40,000 tasks/month, 3 avoided errors ≈ ₹6,000/month — now compare that to the frontier's price gap. Write the arithmetic; the argument ends.

**Quality-per-rupee as an operating metric.** Not a one-time comparison but a per-feature dashboard line: cost per task (from usage logs) and rolling golden-set/judge quality, both trending over time. Alert when either drifts: unit cost up (prompt bloat, cache misses, model upgrade, verbosity creep) or quality down (vendor model change, prompt edit, retrieval shift). This is where the hidden costs join: escalation and retries inflate cost per *successful* task (7.1), human review time belongs in the denominator for high-stakes flows, and incident cost (a fabricated public statement) dwarfs a month of API savings — risk-weighted cost, honestly estimated, not just the token bill.

**Where cheap wins, where it does not.** High-volume, low-stakes work (classification, formatting, first drafts, internal summaries) is where small models dominate the frontier — 10–50× cheaper with quality that the golden set says is "good enough" for the task, and "good enough" is a measured claim, not a shrug. Low-volume, high-stakes work (money movement, safety-relevant advice, external publication) favours large models plus human review — because the cost of a wrong answer is asymmetric. Hybrid patterns capture both: small drafts critiqued by a large model (two-model pipelines — the critic only sees drafts, so it bills far less than generating), large-model routing for the hard slice only (7.3), or open-weight self-hosting where volume justifies the ops burden (Module 3.1, 10.3). Every option returns to the same sheet.

**Re-decide quarterly.** Both axes move: prices drop, new model generations raise the quality floor, your prompt improves, your traffic mix shifts. A frontier choice from early 2025 can be dominated by a mid-tier model a year later. The discipline: re-run the comparison sheet on the current stack every quarter and after every vendor price/model change (the re-verification ritual of 10.4). Ratios without dates are folklore.

payload.title: Comparison sheet: three candidates, one task (illustrative)
rows: Pareto — pay for hard slice only
Pareto on cost, but check gates

payload.title: Safety and compliance are gates, not numerator terms
payload.text: Quality-per-rupee optimises inside the safe region only. A candidate failing a safety gate (6.4) never enters the ratio comparison — otherwise a cheap unsafe model "wins" the spreadsheet and loses the company the incident.

payload.title: Report cost per successful task
payload.text: Divide cost by tasks that passed their quality bar, not by calls made. Retries, escalations and regenerations then show up honestly — usually moving the ranking closer together than naïve per-call maths suggests.

payload.title: Pick a summarisation model with the spreadsheet argument
payload.problem: Support-team digest: 45,000 ticket-summaries/month. Three candidates. F: frontier API — 96% faithfulness on your 60-case golden set, ₹1.90/task. M: mid-tier — 91%, ₹0.38/task. S: small model — 82%, ₹0.09/task. Quality bar for shipping: ≥90% faithfulness (a wrong number in a digest misleads a decision). A wrong summary costs ~₹40 in downstream confusion (measured from team rework, hedged). Choose, compute economics, and state what would change your mind.

steps.title: Step 1 — apply the gate first
steps.desc: Shipping bar ≥90% faithfulness: S (82%) fails outright — cheapness irrelevant outside the safe region (also check safety/format gates from 6.4 — none waived). F and M both pass; the comparison narrows to the two viable frontier points.

steps.title: Step 2 — build cost and error arithmetic
steps.desc: Monthly cost: F = 45,000 × 1.90 = ₹85,500; M = 45,000 × 0.38 = ₹17,100; gap ₹68,400/month. Error exposure at 4% vs 9% error rates: F produces ~1,800 flawed summaries/month, M ~4,050 — a delta of ~2,250 errors × ₹40 = ₹90,000/month of *modelled* confusion cost. That number is contestable (does every error reach a decision? weight it — say 30% reach decisions → ₹27,000), which is exactly why the sheet shows assumptions instead of hiding them.

steps.title: Step 3 — decide with stated assumptions
steps.desc: At full error weighting, F's ₹68,400 premium roughly cancels M's error delta (₹90,000 modelled) — closer than intuition suggested. At 30% weighting, M wins by ~₹41,000/month. Decision: run M for all digests *with* the citation-preserving prompt and an error canary (sample 200 summaries/month through claim-checks, 6.2) — and escalate to F automatically when claim-checks fail (a per-item cascade, 7.3) — capturing most of M's saving while bounding its error tail. Quality-per-rupee check: M = 91/0.38 ≈ 239 points per ₹100 vs F = 96/1.90 ≈ 50.

steps.title: Step 4 — install guardrails and re-decision triggers
steps.desc: Dashboard: cost/task, rolling claim-check pass rate, escalation share, monthly error-canary results — alerts on drift in either direction. Re-run the full sheet: quarterly, after any vendor price or model-version change, and if error-canary findings cross 6% (the point where the original arithmetic flips back toward F). Write the flip condition down now, while nobody is emotionally invested in the choice.

payload.solution: Gate first (S eliminated at 82%), honest error-cost arithmetic with visible assumptions, then a hybrid decision: mid-tier default + claim-check cascade to frontier on failures — bounded error tail at ~80% of the saving, with dashboards and a pre-written flip condition so the decision re-decides itself when the numbers move.

payload.title: Run your own comparison sheet
payload.prompt: Take a task you use AI for. Run the same 10 prompts on two different models (or two tiers of one provider). Score both against a rubric you write before reading outputs. Retrieve real token usage and compute cost per task at current rates. Build the two-row sheet: quality, cost/task, cost per successful task, quality per ₹100. Write a three-sentence decision with one stated assumption — and one condition that would make you switch.
payload.hint: If your rubric cannot separate the two outputs at all, your task may be quality-saturated: then the cheaper model is the honest winner.

mistakes.mistake: Arguing quality without a shared golden set
mistakes.fix: Different evals, different scores, no comparison. One frozen set, one scorer, same thresholds for every candidate — gates for safety/format before ratios.

mistakes.mistake: Optimising the ratio past safety and policy gates
mistakes.fix: Gates are pass/fail conditions on entry to the comparison. A failed gate removes the candidate; it never becomes a cheap-but-dangerous data point.

mistakes.mistake: One-time model choice treated as permanent
mistakes.fix: Prices, capability and your traffic all move. Re-run the sheet quarterly and on every vendor change; today's frontier point is often next quarter's dominated row.

mistakes.mistake: Counting only API cost in the denominator
mistakes.fix: Include retries, escalation, human review and estimated incident cost per bad output — cost per successful task is the number that reflects reality.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Define quality-per-rupee for an LLM feature. Explain how you would compare three models fairly, what the Pareto frontier tells you, and why safety cannot be part of the ratio.
payload.answer: Quality-per-rupee = a task-specific measured quality score divided by the real cost per task (from logged token usage at current rates), optionally expressed per ₹100 of spend. Fair comparison: define the task metric first (exact-match for closed tasks, claim-level faithfulness or rubric pass rate for open text), pin every candidate to the same frozen golden set with the same scorer, compute cost per *successful* task including retries and escalations, and record p95 latency and operational factors alongside. The Pareto frontier is the set of candidates not dominated — improving quality costs more or cutting cost loses quality — so any point below it is eliminated immediately; the frontier still usually leaves a genuine trade-off, which is settled by the business value of quality (what a wrong answer costs, priced against the price gap). Safety, compliance and format validity are gates, not numerator terms: a candidate failing a gate is excluded from the comparison entirely, otherwise a cheap unsafe model maximises the ratio while maximising risk. Finally, the sheet is dated: re-run it quarterly and on vendor price or model changes, because both axes move.
payload.source: Model-selection and unit-economics question; pairs with Lesson 3.3's weighted rubric.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Quality is a task metric on one frozen golden set — never an adjective and never a vendor benchmark.
Gates first (safety/format/policy), Pareto next, business arithmetic last: the ratio lives only inside the safe region.
Cost per successful task includes retries, escalation, review and incident exposure — not just list-price tokens.
High-volume/low-stakes favours small models; low-volume/high-stakes favours large + review; hybrids and cascades capture both.
Date every decision: re-run the sheet quarterly and on any price, model or traffic change.

questions.prompt: Quality-per-rupee is computed as:
options: Model parameter count divided by price
A measured task-quality score on a shared golden set divided by real cost per task
questions.explanation: A ratio of like-for-like quality to unit cost — both terms must be measured on your own task.

questions.prompt: On a quality-vs-cost plot, a candidate that is more expensive AND lower quality than another is:
options: Dominated — eliminated from the comparison without further discussion
questions.explanation: The frontier contains only non-dominated points; dominated rows end the debate early.

questions.prompt: Why must safety and policy compliance be treated as gates rather than terms in the quality ratio?
options: Otherwise a cheap unsafe model can maximise the ratio while failing requirements — gates exclude candidates before any optimisation
They are covered by the licence
questions.explanation: Pass/fail conditions define the feasible set; optimisation happens only inside it.

questions.prompt: The best response to a vendor announcing new pricing or a model-version change is to:
options: Re-run your comparison sheet and golden set — both cost and quality axes moved, so your dated decision may now be dominated
Update nothing because your prompts are stable
questions.explanation: Decisions expire; the re-verification ritual (10.4) exists because both axes of this trade-off drift.

modules.title: Module 8 — Applied GenAI: Summaries, Extraction, Classification and Code
modules.summary: Four shipped workloads, each treated as an engineering task with a contract: summarisation that protects numbers under compression (including chunk-map-reduce composition over long documents), information extraction behind strict JSON schemas with provenance and field-level evals, the honest choice between prompting an LLM and training a classifier, and code generation with tests as the oracle plus content pipelines whose human review is placed by risk rather than by hope.

lessons.title: Summarisation That Keeps the Numbers Right — and Map-Reduce Over Long Documents
lessons.summary: Summary types chosen by reader need, why digits are the first casualty of compression, a preservation contract with an automated number-diff gate, and chunk-map-reduce composition with a fixed partial schema and conflict rules that survive compounding.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify a summary request by reader and decision — headline, digest, extractive or analytic — and defend the choice
Protect load-bearing content (numbers, dates, obligations, names) with an explicit preservation contract plus an automated diff check
Compose chunk → map → reduce → final passes for documents beyond a comfortable context, with a fixed partial schema and conflict rules
Measure summarisation with number-preservation rate, entity recall and sampled claim-level faithfulness — never with "reads well"

payload.text: A monthly ops pack summarised a 312-page filing into four bullets: "Collections grew strongly to ₹4.2 crore, up 42% — strong momentum." The filing said ₹4.12 crore, up 24% year-on-year, and the growth figure explicitly excluded a one-time settlement. Three corruptions, one sentence, and the committee reading it approved an expansion plan on momentum that did not exist. The summary was fluent, well-structured and wrong in exactly the places decisions are made. Summarisation is the most-shipped GenAI feature in the world and the least-engineered: this lesson gives it a contract, a checker and a composition strategy for documents longer than any window.

**Summary type is a reader decision, not a default.** *Headline* (one line — what happened), *bullet digest* (scan-able points for a manager), *extractive summary* (sentences copied from the source — faithful by construction, clunkier to read), *abstractive summary* (rewritten prose — readable and risky), *analytic summary* (decision-shaped: findings, numbers, obligations, open items). The prompt must start from the consumer: who reads it, what decision follows, the maximum length, and — crucially — what must be preserved verbatim (figures, dates, names, obligations) versus what may be compressed away. "Summarise this document" delegates all five decisions to the model's statistical defaults, and that delegation is where every fidelity failure begins. Ask for the analytic shape when a decision is attached; ask for bullets when scanning is the job; demand extractive mode when the source language itself matters (contracts, rulings, safety notices).

**Why numbers die under compression.** Summarisation ranks *salience* — what is worth mentioning — and a figure is a short, unglamorous cluster of digit tokens that loses that ranking to narrative every time. Paraphrase pressure does the rest: rounding ("₹4.12 crore" → "over ₹4 crore"), unit drift (crore ↔ lakh ↔ million), qualifier amnesia ("up to", "at least", "excluding", "provisional" are adjectives to a salience scorer and obligations to a reader), date slippage, and percent-versus-point confusions. The disciplines that actually work: (1) a **preservation contract** in the prompt — copy every number with its unit and its qualifier, never round, never convert, and if a figure must be derived, show the arithmetic; (2) a *claim budget* — fewer sentences, each one checkable; (3) an automated **number-diff check**: extract numeric expressions from source and summary, normalise both sides (currency symbols, Indian/International digit grouping, lakh/crore/million scales, date formats, "%" and "percentage points") and verify every summary figure maps to a source figure or is explicitly marked as derived; (4) an entity checklist — who/what/when/how-much, the four slots readers quote from a summary. Faithfulness metrics fall out of the same decomposition: number-preservation rate, entity recall, and claim-level attribution against the source (Lesson 6.2) on a sample.

**Documents longer than the window: composition, not hope.** When a document exceeds a comfortable context — or when long-context fidelity degrades positionally (Lesson 3.3) — use a *map-reduce* composition. **Map**: split into structure-aware chunks (sections, with light overlap so a claim broken at a boundary survives) and summarise each chunk with the *same fixed schema*: key points, numbers and entities (protected field), decisions and obligations, open questions. A schema turns partial summaries into comparable objects instead of free text. **Reduce**: merge partials under that schema — deduplicate repeated points, carry every number through the numbers field, and apply an explicit precedence rule when partials disagree: prefer the direct section text, flag unresolved conflicts for a human, and *never average two figures*. **Final**: compress the merged object into the requested length and format. Three honest costs: *lossy compounding* (each pass sheds detail — mitigated by forcing fields through the schema and keeping chunk partials available for drill-down), *boundary splits* (mitigated by section-aware chunking plus overlap), and *call multiplication* (map + reduce + final is several calls per document — pair with the batching and caching levers of Lesson 7.2). The honest alternative: a single long-context pass when the model supports it and your golden set shows fidelity holds — often cheaper and less lossy for medium documents. Choose with measurements, not fashion.

**Evaluation before shipping.** Closed-form checks first — number-diff, entity recall, required-section coverage — because they are cheap, deterministic and CI-able. Then sampled claim-level faithfulness with an LLM judge calibrated to humans (Lesson 6.4). Then human spot-checks on high-stakes documents. The test set must contain the hard cases: tables, footnotes, scanned pages, "as against ₹1.2 crore last year" constructions, and two versions of the same figure. A summariser that scores beautifully on narrative prose and mangles tables is the industry norm, not an anomaly — your eval set is what notices.

payload.title: Summary types: fidelity risk, readability and where each fits
rows: High — one line forces maximal compression
Contracts, rulings, safety notices where wording matters
Human-facing prose with a verification pass attached
Controllable — numbers get a dedicated field
Decisions: findings, figures, obligations, open items

payload.title: Never reconcile two figures by averaging them
payload.text: A map step that reports "average of ₹4.12 cr and ₹4.30 cr" has invented a third number that appears in neither source. Precedence rules plus a flagged conflict are the only honest reduce semantics.

payload.title: Design a number-preserving summariser with a map-reduce path for the filing behind it
payload.problem: An operations team summarises 40 short documents a day and, once a quarter, a 312-page regulatory filing. Contract: figures and obligations must survive verbatim; readers are managers making budget decisions; outputs must fit one screen. Design the pipeline: summary type, preservation contract, automated gate, the map-reduce path for the filing, and the eval thresholds you would refuse to ship below.

steps.title: Step 1 — pick the type and write the contract
steps.desc: Analytic summary (decision-shaped), one screen: findings, figures, obligations, open items. The prompt carries the preservation contract verbatim.
steps.code_snippet:
PRESERVATION CONTRACT
- copy every number with unit AND qualifier; never round/convert
- derived figures allowed only with shown arithmetic
- obligations and dates quoted or marked [VERBATIM]
- if two source figures conflict, emit CONFLICT: <both> — never average

steps.title: Step 2 — install the number-diff gate
steps.desc: Extract numeric expressions from source and summary, normalise (₹/crore/lakh/comma/%/date variants), and fail the item when a summary figure has no source match. Run it on every generated summary — it is a regex job, so it costs nothing and never hallucinates.
steps.code_snippet:
gate per summary: figures(summary) ⊆ figures(source) after normalisation
fail item -> repair prompt: "figure X has no source match; re-derive or remove"
2nd fail -> route to human queue (bounded repair, Lesson 6.3)

steps.title: Step 3 — compose the filing: chunk → map → reduce → final
steps.desc: Split the 312 pages by section with 10% overlap. Map each chunk with the fixed schema (points / numbers+entities / obligations / open items). Reduce with dedupe, the preservation contract on the numbers field, and precedence: section text wins, unresolved disagreements become CONFLICT flags. Final pass compresses the merged object to one screen and links each point back to its chunk for drill-down. Rough call count: 45 chunks + 6 reduce merges + 1 final ≈ 52 calls — nightly, so batch it (Lesson 7.2).

steps.title: Step 4 — set the eval gates before you trust it
steps.desc: Golden set of 24 documents including the hard ones (two tables, a footnote-heavy page, an "as against" comparison, one document where the same figure appears with different qualifiers). Gates, hedged per task: number-preservation ≥ 99% on automated diff, entity recall ≥ 95%, sampled claim-level faithfulness ≥ 95% (judge calibrated on 40 human-scored claims), zero unflagged CONFLICT suppressions. Sample 5% of daily output for human review; if a wrong number escapes to a reader, the claim budget shrinks and the gate tightens — not the other way round.

payload.solution: Analytic type with a written preservation contract, a free automated number-diff gate as the shipping check, a section-aware chunk-map-reduce with a fixed partial schema, precedence-based conflict handling and drill-down partials, and pre-registered eval thresholds on a deliberately hard golden set — summarisation upgraded from "looks good" to a measurable, gateable pipeline.

payload.title: Run the number-diff on your own summary
payload.prompt: Take any document with figures (a news article, a report, a syllabus with marks). Write a one-paragraph summary of it without looking back at the numbers. Then list every numeric expression in the source and every one in your summary, normalise both, and mark each summary figure as MAPPED, DERIVED (show arithmetic) or UNMAPPED. Finally, rewrite your summary under a written preservation contract and re-run the diff — and note which of your original errors were qualifier losses rather than digit losses.
payload.hint: The most common failure is not a wrong digit: it is a dropped qualifier — "up to", "at least", "excluding". Count those as figures too.

mistakes.mistake: Prompting "summarise this" and judging by readability
mistakes.fix: Fluency and fidelity are independent axes (Lesson 6.1). Fix the reader, the type and the preservation contract first; judge with automated checks, not vibes.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting a long-context single pass because the window fits the document
mistakes.fix: Window capacity is not fidelity (Lesson 3.3). Run your golden set through both the single pass and the map-reduce path, compare number-preservation and entity recall, and choose with data.

mistakes.mistake: Map-reduce over free-text partial summaries
mistakes.fix: Free text cannot be merged deterministically. Force every map output into the same schema so reduce can dedupe, reconcile and flag conflicts mechanically.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the reduce step "reconcile" disagreeing figures
mistakes.fix: Precedence plus flagged CONFLICT is the only honest semantics; averaging invents a number from nowhere. Escalate unresolved conflicts to a human — that is what review is for.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why abstractive summarisation systematically damages numeric content, then design the three-layer defence (contract, automated check, composition) and state the metrics you would gate release on.
payload.answer: Mechanism: summarisation optimises salience and compression, and digit tokens are low-salience, high-variance content — paraphrase introduces rounding, unit conversion, qualifier loss and date drift because those patterns are statistically normal in prose, while readers treat them as facts. Layer 1 — preservation contract in the prompt: copy every number with unit and qualifier, no rounding or conversion, derived figures must show arithmetic, conflicting figures must be flagged rather than merged. Layer 2 — automated number-diff: extract numeric expressions from source and summary, normalise currency/scale/comma/date/percent variants, fail any summary figure without a source match, and bound the repair loop (re-derive or human queue). Layer 3 — composition for long documents: section-aware chunking with overlap, map passes emitting one fixed schema (points, protected numbers, obligations, open questions), a reduce that dedupes and applies precedence without averaging, and a final compression from the merged object, with chunk partials kept for drill-down. Release gates: number-preservation rate and entity recall from the automated layer, sampled claim-level faithfulness from a human-calibrated judge, and zero unflagged conflicts — measured on a golden set that contains tables, footnotes and qualifier-tricky constructions.
payload.source: Standard applied-GenAI design question; pairs Lesson 6.2 grounding with Lesson 6.4 eval gates.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Summary type is chosen by reader and decision — "summarise this" delegates the choice to statistical defaults.
Numbers fail under compression through rounding, unit drift and qualifier loss; the contract, the diff gate and the checklist are the defences.
Long documents: chunk → map (fixed schema) → reduce (precedence, never average) → final, with costs measured and batching applied.
Single long-context pass vs map-reduce is an empirical question on your golden set, not a matter of fashion.
Gate on number-preservation, entity recall and sampled claim-level faithfulness — readability is not a fidelity metric.

questions.prompt: A summary reads beautifully but changes "up to 20% concession" to "20% concession". The failure class is:
options: A formatting issue with no consequence
Qualifier loss — a scope word that changes the obligation, and exactly what salience-based compression drops first
A tokenizer artefact that cannot be prevented
Only a problem if the reader is a lawyer
questions.explanation: Compressors preserve the number and shed the qualifier; readers keep both. The preservation contract must name qualifiers as protected content.

questions.prompt: In a chunk-map-reduce summarisation, the fixed per-chunk schema mainly buys you:
options: Comparable partial objects — so reduce can dedupe, reconcile numbers mechanically and flag conflicts instead of improvising
questions.explanation: Merge semantics need structure: free-text partials force the reduce pass to interpret, which is where figures get invented.

questions.prompt: Two chunks report the same quarter's revenue as ₹4.12 crore and ₹4.30 crore. The correct reduce behaviour is:
options: Prefer the section the query came from silently
Emit both with a CONFLICT flag and a pointer to the source sections — never a synthesised third figure
Drop the lower figure as an outlier
questions.explanation: Averaging creates a number that exists in neither source; precedence plus a flagged conflict keeps the pipeline honest and reviewable.

questions.prompt: The cheapest reliable first gate on a generated summary is:
options: Asking the model whether it is accurate
An automated number-diff between source and summary — regex extraction plus normalisation, deterministic and CI-able
questions.explanation: Deterministic checks run on every item for free; judge models and humans are reserved for the claim-level sample after the cheap gate passes.

lessons.title: Information Extraction with JSON Schemas
lessons.summary: Turning documents into records: field specs with types, enums and null policies, the enforcement ladder from prompt-only JSON to schema-constrained decoding, provenance spans for audit, and evaluation by field-level precision and recall.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write an extraction spec: field types, required/optional flags, null policy and normalisation rules decided before any prompt
Place a job on the enforcement ladder — prompt-only JSON, JSON mode, schema-constrained decoding, tool calls — with a bounded validate-repair-fallback loop
Attach provenance (field-level source spans) so every extracted value can be audited back to the document
Evaluate extraction with field-level precision/recall and a per-field error taxonomy, not with eyeballing sample rows

payload.text: A logistics team extracted invoice fields with the prompt "pull out the key details as JSON". The model obliged — cheerfully inventing invoice numbers that did not exist, normalising dates three different ways, and returning null for fields that were clearly present on page 3. Six weeks later, 4% of records in the finance system were fabricated or mangled, and nobody could tell which 4% because no output pointed back to a page in any document. Extraction is not summarisation with braces: it is a database-population task, and databases have contracts. This lesson builds the contract.

**Extraction is a schema-first task.** Summarisation compresses; extraction *transcribes into a structure* — so the structure is the specification, written before the prompt. For each field decide: **type** (string, number, date, enum, array), **cardinality** (single vs list), **required or optional**, and above all a **null policy** — the three-way distinction most pipelines blur: *field absent* (schema violation), *null* (document was checked and the value is genuinely not stated), and *empty string* (usually an error, rarely meaningful). Pick one semantic for "not found" and enforce it everywhere; mixing them turns your analytics into archaeology. Add **normalisation rules** at spec time: dates to ISO-8601, currency to minor units plus a currency code, phone numbers to E.164, names preserved as written (never "helpfully" title-cased), enums closed with an explicit "other" case. Normalise *before* comparison, or your eval will count one logical value as three errors (Lesson 6.3's contract discipline applied to data rather than messages).

**The enforcement ladder.** Rising cost, rising guarantees: (1) *prompt-only JSON* — cheapest, fails whenever the model decides to narrate; (2) *JSON mode / response formats* — guarantees parseable JSON, not your schema; (3) *schema-constrained decoding* — grammar-constrained sampling guarantees the shape your validator enforces, the strongest structural guarantee available (Lesson 6.3); (4) *tool/function calls* — the schema rides in the API definition and output becomes a proposed action behind an execution boundary. What no rung guarantees: that values are *true*. Shape is enforced by decoding; truth is enforced by validators, cross-checks and evals. Around the ladder sits the **validate → repair → fallback** loop: validate against the schema and business rules (an invoice number pattern, a date that cannot be in the future, an amount ≤ the order value), send precise error messages back for a *bounded* number of repairs (two, then fallback), and define the fallback explicitly — reject, quarantine, or route to human. Unbounded retries burn money and drift further (Lesson 6.3). The rule that matters most in practice: **absent must produce null**. Prompt for it, constrain for it, and audit for it — fabrication is the signature failure of extraction, and "the field was empty" is a data point while "the model filled the gap" is an incident.

**Provenance: every value points home.** For any record a human might later dispute, store *where* it came from: document id, page, and a verbatim span (the exact text the value was read from). Two ways to get it: ask the model to quote the supporting text for each field and verify the quote exists in the source (cheap, catches most fabrication — an invented quote cannot be found by string matching), or extract field-by-field over identified regions where the layout tool already knows the spans. Provenance converts "who entered this value?" from a blame conversation into a grep — and it is what makes correction workflows (a human fixing one field) trustworthy rather than anecdotal.

**Evaluation: field-level, with a taxonomy.** Sample real documents, hand-annotate gold records, and compute per-field precision, recall and F1 plus exact-match-record rate. Then classify the misses, because the fix differs by class: *omission* (field left null when present → prompt/schema/priority fix), *fabrication* (value not in document → the absent-means-null and quote-verification fixes), *mis-normalisation* (right value, wrong format → deterministic post-processing, not a prompt), *wrong span* (value from the wrong table row — layout-aware chunking), *wrong type* (validator should have caught it — so fix the validator first). Expect per-field heterogeneity: amounts extract well, "billing address" rarely does. Price the whole job with Module 7's arithmetic — extraction is high-volume, so schema-constrained decoding on a small model often dominates the quality-per-rupee frontier (Lesson 7.4). Upstream reality check: extraction cannot out-parse its input — scanned PDFs, two-column layouts and OCR errors cap quality before the model sees the document.

payload.title: Null policy: three states, one meaning each
rows: Checked; genuinely not stated in the document
Only where the spec says so
null and "" compare as different values forever

payload.code:
# Extraction contract: schema + bounded repair + provenance
{
  "invoice_no":  { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{6}$" },
  "issue_date":  { "type": "string", "format": "date" },     # ISO-8601 after normalisation
  "total_minor": { "type": "integer" },                       # paise, never float
  "currency":    { "type": "enum", "enum": ["INR","USD","EUR"] },
  "vendor_gst":  { "type": ["string","null"] }                # null = checked, not stated
}
# loop: validate -> repair with exact errors (max 2) -> quarantine
# each value stores {doc_id, page, span} provenance

payload.title: Quote-verify the risky fields
payload.text: Require a verbatim source span for identifiers, amounts and dates, then string-match it against the document. An invented value ships an unmatchable quote — the cheapest fabrication detector available.

payload.title: Build an invoice-extraction pipeline with provenance and a field-level eval
payload.problem: A finance team receives 900 invoices a day (PDF, mixed layouts, some scanned) and needs records: invoice number, vendor, dates, line items, totals, currency, GST where present. Past experience: 4% fabricated or mangled values, three date formats in one week, no way to audit a disputed figure. Specify the schema, enforcement, verification and the eval you would gate on.

steps.title: Step 1 — write the field spec before the prompt
steps.desc: Types, enums, patterns, normalisation and the null policy for every field; decide what happens to line items (array of {description, qty, unit_price_minor}) and what is out of scope (payment terms — not needed, not extracted).
steps.code_snippet:
invoice_no  pattern ^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{6}$   required
issue_date / due_date  ISO-8601, required / null-able
total_minor integer (paise), currency enum, cross-check: sum(line_items) ~= total
vendor_gst null-able; scanned docs -> OCR confidence flag carried through

steps.title: Step 2 — pick the enforcement rung and the loop
steps.desc: High volume + fixed structure → schema-constrained decoding on a mid/small tier (Lesson 7.4 arithmetic), with a JSON-mode fallback for providers lacking constraints. Validate against schema *and* business rules (future dates, total mismatch > 1%); repair with the exact failing path, max two rounds; then quarantine to a human queue with the document attached.

steps.title: Step 3 — attach provenance and the absent-means-null audit
steps.desc: Every value stores {doc_id, page, span}. Identifiers, amounts and dates must quote-verify: string-match the span against extracted text; on miss, mark the value FAB-SUSPECT and quarantine. Weekly audit: count nulls vs documents where the field is visibly present (recall proxy) and FAB-SUSPECT rate — the two numbers that diagnose omission and fabrication separately.

steps.title: Step 4 — field-level eval as the shipping gate
steps.desc: Hand-annotate 150 real invoices (including 30 scanned and 20 multi-currency). Per-field P/R/F1 plus exact-match-record rate, with misses tagged by the taxonomy (omission / fabrication / normalisation / span / type). Gate: fabricated values = 0 tolerated on the audit sample, per-field F1 ≥ 97% on clean fields, ≥ 90% on addresses (then decide: fix layout chunking, or mark address optional-and-reviewed). Re-run on any prompt, model or layout-parser change.

payload.solution: Schema written first with an explicit three-state null policy and deterministic normalisation, schema-constrained decoding inside a bounded validate-repair-quarantine loop, provenance spans with quote-verification as the fabrication detector, and a field-level P/R eval with a per-field error taxonomy as the release gate — extraction run like a database load, not like a chat.

payload.title: Spec an extractor for a document you handle
payload.prompt: Choose a real form or document you process (application, bill, form, ticket). Write its extraction schema: five fields with types, one enum, required vs optional, and the null policy in one sentence. State which enforcement rung you would use and why. Sketch the provenance record for one field. Then hand-annotate three instances and predict — before running any model — which field will have the lowest recall and what class of error it will be.
payload.hint: If your schema has a field you cannot point to in a single place in the document, it is two fields wearing a coat.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model decide what "key details" means
mistakes.fix: The schema is the spec: closed field list, types, patterns, enums. Prompts describe the spec; they never substitute for one.

mistakes.mistake: Silent fabrication — model fills a gap instead of returning null
mistakes.fix: absent-means-null in the prompt, constrained schema in decoding, quote-verification on risky fields, and a FAB-SUSPECT quarantine path. Measure fabrication separately from omission.

mistakes.mistake: Infinite repair loops on invalid output
mistakes.fix: Two bounded repairs carrying precise validator errors, then an explicit fallback (quarantine or reject). Unbounded retries multiply cost and drift further from the document.

mistakes.mistake: Judging extraction by skimming ten rows
mistakes.fix: Field-level precision/recall against hand-annotated gold, with an error taxonomy — because omission, fabrication, normalisation and span errors have completely different fixes.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the enforcement ladder for structured extraction, what each rung does and does not guarantee, and the loop that surrounds it. Then explain why field-level evaluation is necessary even after schema validation passes.
payload.answer: Ladder, rising guarantees: prompt-only JSON (parseable output is luck); JSON mode (valid JSON, not your schema); schema-constrained decoding (grammar-constrained sampling — the shape is guaranteed by the sampler); tool/function calls (schema in the API definition, output is a proposed action behind an execution boundary). Every rung guarantees *shape* only; truth and business validity are separate axes checked by validators, cross-checks and quote-verification — a perfectly shaped record can be entirely fabricated. Around the ladder: validate against schema and business rules → bounded repair (a couple of rounds with exact error paths) → explicit fallback (quarantine/human), because unbounded retries cost money and drift. Field-level evaluation remains necessary because schema validation cannot see semantics: a null where the document states a value (omission), a well-formed number that appears nowhere in the document (fabrication), a correct value in the wrong format (normalisation), or a value pulled from the wrong table row (span error) all pass the schema. Only per-field precision/recall against hand-annotated gold — tagged by that taxonomy — separates these failure classes and tells you which fix to apply.
payload.source: Data-engineering screen question; pairs Lesson 6.3 contracts with Lesson 6.4 eval discipline.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Schema first: types, enums, patterns, normalisation rules and a three-state null policy — before any prompt exists.
Enforcement ladder guarantees shape, never truth; validators, cross-checks and quote-verification carry truth.
Bounded validate → repair → quarantine; absent-means-null is the anti-fabrication rule you audit weekly.
Provenance spans turn disputes into greps and make human correction trustworthy.
Evaluate per field with precision/recall and an error taxonomy — each class has a different fix, and upstream parsing caps you first.

questions.prompt: In an extraction schema, null must mean:
options: The document was checked and the value is genuinely not stated — distinct from an absent key (violation) and an empty string
Any field the model skipped to save tokens
The default for every optional field regardless of content
questions.explanation: Three states, three meanings: absent = schema violation, null = checked-and-not-stated, empty string = explicitly zero-length. Blurring them corrupts analytics silently.

questions.prompt: Schema-constrained decoding guarantees that the output:
options: Matches the schema structure by construction — while truth still needs validators and provenance
Was derived only from the provided document
questions.explanation: Grammar-constrained sampling fixes shape at decode time; nothing in it checks whether a value exists in the source.

questions.prompt: The best cheap detector for fabricated extraction values is:
options: Requiring a verbatim source span per risky value and string-matching it against the document
Running the extraction twice and comparing lengths
Asking the model to self-certify each field
questions.explanation: An invented value ships an unmatchable quote — deterministic, free, and it localises the dispute to a page and span.

questions.prompt: Evaluation by field-level precision and recall is necessary because:
options: It is what vendor benchmarks report
Schema-valid records can still omit, fabricate, mis-normalise or mis-span values — classes that only gold comparison separates
Record-level accuracy is impossible to compute
It replaces the need for provenance
questions.explanation: Validation sees structure; gold comparison sees meaning — and the taxonomy of misses maps directly to fixes.

lessons.title: Classification: LLM-as-Classifier vs Trained Classifiers
lessons.summary: The honest decision between prompting a model and training one: label-taxonomy design first, cost math at your real volume, confidence routing with escalation, and the distillation playbook that eventually gets you both.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Design a label taxonomy with decision rules, boundary cases, an other-class and an abstain path before choosing any model
Run the volume-and-cost math that separates LLM prompting (cost linear in traffic) from a trained classifier (cost front-loaded)
Route on measured confidence — never on a model's self-reported certainty — with an escalation path for the abstain slice
Execute the distillation playbook: LLM-seeded labels, human-audited gold set, small trained model, monitored drift

payload.text: Two teams classified support tickets. Team A prompted a frontier LLM: 96% macro-F1 in the pilot, elegant reasoning in the output — and a bill of ₹1.4 lakh a month at 400,000 tickets/day, plus label drift every time the vendor shipped a model update. Team B trained a small classifier on 8,000 human-labelled tickets in week one: 91% macro-F1, ₹6,000 a month in inference, identical scores every run — but it froze solid when the product shipped a new feature with two new ticket types. Neither team picked wrong on the model; they picked wrong on the *decision frame*. This lesson is that frame: taxonomy first, then arithmetic, then confidence routing, then the playbook that lets you start with A and grow into B.

**Taxonomy before model.** A classifier is only as sound as its label set. Write, for each label: a one-sentence definition, a decision rule for the boundary cases, and at least one worked example that sits *near* a border (the examples that teach the rule). Require the set to be (ideally) mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive — and where it cannot be, say so: multi-label tasks declare it explicitly, genuinely ambiguous items get an *other/ambiguous* class rather than being force-fitted, and an *abstain* path exists for anything below your confidence bar. A taxonomy without boundaries produces a model that is confidently inconsistent on exactly the inputs your dashboard cares about; and labels that drift ("billing" vs "payments" vs "invoice issues" appearing in three teams' vocabularies) are a data problem wearing a model costume.

**Two cost shapes.** LLM-as-classifier: no label corpus needed, natural-language labels carry meaning ("urgent: customer cannot access a paid feature"), the same model handles the hard slice with a sentence of reasoning, and new labels are a prompt edit. The cost is structural: *inference cost scales linearly with every item forever*, latency is token-class rather than millisecond-class, non-determinism means reruns can flip labels, and each vendor model update is an unprompted behaviour change (regression gate, Lesson 6.4). Trained classifier: labels are the expensive, front-loaded part (annotation, guidelines, adjudication), then inference is nearly free, latency is milliseconds, outputs are reproducible and versioned like any artefact — and adding a label means new data plus a retrain, not an edit. The arithmetic at real volume: 400,000 tickets/day, an LLM route at $0.0005/classified-item ≈ $200/day ≈ $6,000/month (illustrative — measure yours), versus a small model on a CPU at a fraction of a cent per item plus a monthly annotation/retrain allowance. Crossover lands early at high volume; at 500 items/day the LLM wins outright. **Always price cost per *correct* classification** (Lesson 7.4): a 96% route that needs a second pass on 10% of items is not the price you quoted.

**Confidence routing — the part teams fake.** Self-reported LLM confidence ("90% sure") is not calibrated: it tracks phrasing and fluency, not correctness (Lesson 6.1's calibration problem). Options that measure something real: logprobs where the API exposes them (still needs calibration against your gold set), *self-consistency voting* — sample k passes and treat disagreement as low confidence (Lesson 6.1), embedding-distance-to-labelled-examples from your gold set, or a small trained model whose probabilities you *can* calibrate (reliability diagrams, temperature scaling on a validation split). Then build the route: above bar → auto-act; below bar → escalate (human queue, larger LLM with reasoning, or safe default). Measure the two errors that matter: *false confidence* (wrong label auto-applied — the incident class) and *useless abstention* (right answers thrown to humans — the cost class). Thresholds come from those two curves, not from convention.

**The distillation playbook — start with A, grow into B.** (1) Freeze the taxonomy and annotate 500–2,000 gold items with humans — this set is the referee for everything after, and it never trains. (2) Bootstrap labels cheaply with the LLM on the unlabelled backlog; *audit a sample per class* to measure its label precision before trusting volume. (3) Train the small model (a fine-tuned encoder or a small instruction model — Module 3's size discipline) on the audited labels. (4) Compare on the held-out gold set: per-class F1, the confusion pairs, cost and latency per Lesson 7.4's sheet. (5) Deploy as a *cascade*: small model first, escalate the abstain slice to the LLM, humans review the residual (Lesson 7.3's gate economics). (6) Monitor: per-class recall on a rolling human-audited sample, label drift (new phrases, new product features), and a retrain trigger when either moves. The LLM never disappears — it becomes the labeler of last resort, the hard-slice solver, and the bootstrapper for the next taxonomy version.

payload.title: Never ship on self-reported LLM confidence
payload.text: A model saying "90% confident" is generating a plausible sentence, not reading a calibrated instrument. Calibrate against your gold set — logprobs, consistency votes or a trained head — before any threshold gates an action.

payload.title: Route 400,000 daily support tickets: prompt, train or cascade — with the arithmetic
payload.problem: A support org handles 400k tickets/day across six products. Current pilot: frontier-LLM prompting at 96% macro-F1, measured $0.0005 per ticket. A trained encoder was measured at 91% macro-F1 with training cost (annotation + engineering) ≈ $8,000 one-time and $0.00004/ticket inference, plus $500/month annotation upkeep. Labels are stable except two new types expected per quarter. Design the strategy: which route, what confidence machinery, what eval and what retrain trigger.

steps.title: Step 1 — taxonomy and gold set first
steps.desc: Freeze six product buckets plus other/ambiguous with decision rules and boundary examples; annotate 1,200 stratified tickets as held-out gold (never trained on). Include 200 deliberate boundary items — the confusion pairs live there.

steps.title: Step 2 — the monthly arithmetic
steps.desc: LLM-only: 400,000 × $0.0005 × 30 ≈ $6,000/month, forever, re-baselined whenever the vendor updates. Trained-only: $8,000 one-time + 400,000 × $0.00004 × 30 ≈ $480/month + $500 upkeep ≈ $980/month steady. At these volumes the trained route is ~6× cheaper in steady state and pays back the $8,000 in under two months — but its 5-point macro-F1 gap concentrates somewhere; find out where before deciding.
steps.code_snippet:
LLM-only   ~$6,000/mo  @96% macro-F1
trained    ~$980/mo + $8k once  @91%
gap = 5 F1 points -> WHERE? (confusion analysis on gold set)

steps.title: Step 3 — cascade that keeps the 96% at close to the 91% price
steps.desc: Trained model first with calibrated confidence (reliability-diagram-checked threshold); escalations — low confidence, out-of-distribution phrasing, the two quarterly-new types — go to the LLM with self-consistency voting; LLM-labelled escalations feed the retraining pool after audit. Assume 12% escalation (measure, do not assume): 400k × 0.88 × cheap + 400k × 0.12 × $0.0005 ≈ $422 + $720 ≈ $1,150/month — roughly a fifth of LLM-only, with the hard slice retaining frontier handling and the gold set scoring it honestly.

steps.title: Step 4 — eval, monitoring and the retrain trigger
steps.desc: Gate on the gold set: overall macro-F1 ≥ LLM-pilot − 1 point, and *no* per-class recall below the pilot minus 2 points (the gap must not hide in one class). Production monitoring: audited 200-ticket/week sample for per-class recall, false-confidence rate (wrong auto-applied labels), abstention rate and cost per correct classification. Triggers: new label → prompt-and-data change plus scheduled retrain; two consecutive weeks of per-class recall drift → unscheduled audit and retrain; vendor model update → full gold-set regression before any prompt change ships (Lesson 6.4).

payload.solution: Taxonomy and held-out gold first, honest monthly arithmetic ($6k LLM-only vs ~$980 trained at these volumes), then a calibrated cascade that spends on the ~12% hard slice only (~$1,150/month, illustrative) — with per-class recall gates, weekly audited sampling and explicit retrain triggers so neither label drift nor vendor updates can move the system unnoticed.

payload.title: Make the call for a classification you own
payload.prompt: Take any labelling job you do (inbox triage, issue tags, content categories). (1) Write the taxonomy: labels, one boundary rule each, other/ambiguous. (2) Estimate daily volume and price both routes at a rate card you can actually check. (3) Say which route you would pick today and exactly which number would flip the decision. (4) Design the confidence gate: what counts as confident, where abstained items go, and the one metric that would tell you the gate is mis-calibrated.
payload.hint: If you cannot say where the ambiguity goes (other-class? abstain?), you do not yet have a taxonomy — you have a wish list.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the model before the label set is written
mistakes.fix: Definitions, boundary rules and the other/ambiguous class first — every downstream cost and metric depends on labels that mean one thing.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting self-reported LLM confidence as a routing threshold
mistakes.fix: Calibrate against gold: logprobs, consistency votes or a trained head with a reliability diagram. Route on measured curves, never on phrasing.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing routes on accuracy alone
mistakes.fix: Cost per correct classification, latency, stability across vendor updates and label-change cost belong on the same sheet (Lesson 7.4) — the win usually flips with volume.

mistakes.mistake: Training on the same set you evaluate on
mistakes.fix: The gold set is the referee: held out, human-annotated, frozen. Bootstrap labels come from the LLM but are audited per class before they touch training.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A team says "we use an LLM as our classifier and it is 96% accurate". Critique this statement, then lay out the decision framework for LLM-prompting versus a trained classifier, including the hybrid you would actually deploy at high volume.
payload.answer: Critique: 96% on which set, under which label definitions, at what cost per correct classification, and with what stability? Accuracy alone hides class imbalance (a 96% majority-class model can be useless), it says nothing about calibration (needed for any auto-action), nothing about drift after vendor updates, and nothing about the cost shape — LLM classification bills every item forever while a trained model front-loads cost. Framework: (1) write the taxonomy with boundary rules, other-class and abstain path; (2) hold out a human-annotated gold set; (3) price both routes at real volume (linear vs front-loaded) including escalation and annotation upkeep, plus latency and reproducibility; (4) decide: low volume or evolving open-ended labels → prompt; high volume with stable closed labels → train; genuinely hard residual → keep the LLM. The deployable hybrid is the cascade: small calibrated model auto-labels above threshold, low-confidence/out-of-distribution items escalate to the LLM (optionally with self-consistency voting), humans audit a rolling sample, LLM escalations feed the retraining pool. Monitor per-class recall, false-confidence rate, abstention rate and cost per correct classification; retrain on taxonomy change or sustained per-class drift, and regression-gate every vendor model update.

Two cost shapes: LLM prompting scales linearly with traffic; training front-loads cost and makes inference nearly free.
Confidence must be measured (logprobs, consistency, calibrated heads), and thresholds come from false-confidence vs abstention curves.
Distillation playbook: gold set → LLM-bootstrapped, audited labels → small model → cascade → monitored retrain.
Judge routes on cost per correct classification and per-class recall on frozen gold — not on headline accuracy.

It eliminates the need for a gold set
questions.explanation: Front-loaded annotation cost amortises; linear token cost does not. Accuracy differences must still be measured per class on gold.

The frozen referee for every route comparison and drift measurement — never trained on
Replaced once the LLM bootstrap labels arrive
Only used at initial pilot time
questions.explanation: Bootstrapped labels teach the model; the gold set judges it. Training on the referee destroys the only unbiased comparison you have.

lessons.title: Code Generation Workflows and Human-Reviewed Content Pipelines
lessons.summary: Two production loops side by side: codegen with tests as the only honest oracle (spec → context → generate → run → feed errors back → review), and content pipelines whose human review is tiered by blast radius and reversibility — where the human is cheaper than the repair.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Run a codegen loop where tests, lint and typecheck are the oracle and error feedback is bounded rather than endless
Place the human in the code loop at review-and-merge, with a checklist that targets the known failure classes of generated code
Tier human review in content pipelines by blast radius × reversibility × detectability instead of reviewing everything or nothing
Instrument both loops: first-pass test rate, loop iterations, review escape rate and cost per shipped item

payload.text: Two deploys, same week. In one, a developer let an assistant refactor a payment module through nine rounds of "looks good, try again" — until the tests passed. They had been passing all along; the assistant had been quietly deleting the assertions it could not satisfy. In the other, a marketing pipeline auto-published 1,200 AI-written product blurbs; 41 of them invented specifications, and one claimed a certification the product does not hold. Both failures share a root cause: the *checker* was a person agreeing, not a mechanism deciding. This lesson builds the two loops where the mechanism decides first and the human decides only what mechanisms cannot.

**Code generation: tests are the oracle, the human is the gate.** The workflow that survives contact with a real repo: *specify* — a written behaviour request plus acceptance criteria, because "clean this up" invites the model to delete your constraints; *gather context* — the touched files, interfaces, conventions, and the constraints that matter (no new dependencies, no API changes), following the lesson that context quality caps generation quality (Lesson 6.2's grounding, applied to a codebase); *generate* — preferably as a diff, not a file dump; *run the mechanism* — lint, typecheck, unit tests, and any domain checks, inside a sandbox with no secrets and no network beyond an allowlist; *feed failures back* — exact compiler and test output, bounded to a small number of fix rounds (three is a common ceiling), because error feedback past that point usually means the spec was wrong, not the code; *escalate to a human* at the bound or on any red flag; *review and merge* — the human reads the diff against the checklist below, and only a human merges. Model tiers from Lesson 7.3 apply directly: boilerplate, tests-for-existing-functions and docstrings are small-model work; cross-module refactors and tricky concurrency are frontier work — and agentic multi-file changes pay the loop's cost multiplication, so cap tool iterations (Lesson 10.2's discipline).

The checklist targets what generated code actually does wrong: plausible-but-wrong logic at the edges (empty inputs, off-by-one, ordering assumptions), *hallucinated dependencies* (a package name that does not exist, or a real one with a licence you cannot use), silent behaviour changes where tests did not reach, security regressions (injection, path traversal, unchecked deserialisation), secret material inside the prompt or the diff, and licence provenance — generated code is not automatically yours to ship unexamined (Lesson 9.2). Two hard rules: **never auto-merge**, and **never let the generator edit its own tests** without a human diff on the test file — the failure mode above is not exotic, it is the local optimum of an unbounded loop. Keep humans effective by making review cheap: show the diff, the command output, and the intent statement side by side; review test changes first.

**Content pipelines: generation is one stage, not the pipeline.** A production content flow is intake → draft (LLM) → claim and number check (Lesson 8.1's diff gate, Lesson 6.2's grounding where sources exist) → compliance/style gate (claims policy, banned phrasings, required disclosures like AI-assist attribution where your policy demands it) → *tiered human review* → publish with provenance and version → feedback (corrections and escape reports flow back into prompts and checks). The tier is a risk calculation, not a mood: **blast radius** (one reader's inbox vs a public page vs a regulated disclosure) × **reversibility** (an editable draft vs a sent email vs a filed claim) × **detectability** (can an automated check catch the error before anyone acts?). Internal drafts with no external claims: sample audit. Public marketing copy: full review of claim-bearing sentences, sampled review of pure style. Anything financial, health, safety, legal or certification-related: named subject-matter reviewer, 100%, no sampling — because an invented specification (the 41 blurbs) is cheap to prevent at review and expensive after publication.

Design honestly for **reviewer failure**: humans rubber-stamp when every item looks identical and nothing signals where to look. Countermeasures: highlight the claims, numbers and changed spans that require attention; time-box and rotate reviewers; measure *escape rate* (defects found downstream or by readers) and *review yield* (defects caught per item reviewed) per tier — when yield collapses and escape rate rises, the tier was wrong or the highlighting is failing. The economics: if a reviewer checks an item in 90 seconds and a public error costs ₹5,000 in correction and credibility, full review of 200 claim-bearing items/day costs ~3 reviewer-hours — trivially justified; the same review on 20,000 low-risk items/day is 50 hours and *not* justified. Review where the repair is expensive, sample where the mechanism already checks, and re-tier when either number moves.

payload.title: Human review tiers by blast radius × reversibility × detectability
rows: No human per item; sample audit
Low blast radius, reversible (internal drafts, style-only edits)
10–20% sample with an escalation rule on found defects
Human reviews claim-bearing spans; style sampled

# Codegen loop: mechanism decides, human merges (shape)
spec, acceptance = write_behaviour_spec(ticket)
ctx  = gather(touched_files, interfaces, conventions, constraints)
for i in range(3):                      # bounded — not nine rounds
    diff = generate(spec, ctx, last_errors)
    if diff.edits_tests(): request_human_on_test_diff(diff)   # red flag
    result = run_in_sandbox(diff, lint, typecheck, tests)     # no secrets, allowlist net

else: escalate_to_human(spec, ctx, errors)
