Compose a bounded repair prompt that includes the exact error and edits minimally
Choose a degradation path (fallback, human queue, loud failure) instead of looping forever

payload.text: A document pipeline validates every model response and "retries until valid" — three attempts, free-text repair prompt: "Something went wrong, please try again and make sure the JSON is correct." Median cost per document quadruples. One stubborn case burns nine attempts. And the repair keeps rewriting the four fields that were right while fixing one, so nothing downstream can diff the change. Validation without a repair contract is not reliability; it is an expensive coin flip with a compounding bill.

**Validator-first, always.** Write the checker before the prompt, because the checker defines what the prompt must produce and because its error message is the only useful input to a repair. Three layers, checked in order — stop at the first failure:

1. **Syntax layer.** `JSON.parse` (or your format's parser) on a defensively pre-processed payload: strip a surrounding markdown fence and a leading label in *code* — deterministic, free, instant — then parse. Fence-stripping is not a repair; it is cleanup, and burning a model call for it is paying for something a regex does in a microsecond.
2. **Shape layer.** Schema check: required keys present, no extra keys, types right, enums inside their domain, array lengths within bounds. If your provider already enforces the schema (Lesson 1), this layer mostly verifies what it enforces — cheap insurance against mode drift and version changes.
3. **Semantic layer.** Value claims: cross-field arithmetic (total equals the sum, discount equals rate times base), ranges (amounts non-negative, dates inside the document's window), existence (cited record ids appear in the dataset you provided), consistency with source (a quoted amount appears verbatim in the text). This layer never goes away, and it is where most surviving failures live.

**Three failure classes, three treatments.** *Syntax failures* (fences, preamble, truncation mid-stream) are handled deterministically where possible — strip, then, if still broken, a repair is justified. *Shape failures* (valid JSON, wrong structure: missing key, string where number belongs, enum misspelled) are the sweet spot for repair prompts: the error is precise and the fix is local. *Semantic failures* (structurally perfect, factually wrong) repair badly through prose — the model has no new information, so a retry is a fresh sample, not a correction. For semantics, re-ask with the source material re-anchored, add the missing constraint upstream, or route to a human; do not expect "fix the errors" to conjure the truth.

**The repair prompt contract.** A repair prompt is not an apology; it is a minimal-edit instruction with three components: (1) the failing output in full, (2) the exact machine error — the validator's own message, verbatim, not your summary of it, and (3) the minimal-edit rule: change only what the error names, preserve every other field byte-for-byte, output raw JSON only. Minimal edits matter for auditability (the diff is reviewable) and for stability (full rewrites re-roll every field, including the ones that passed). Cap attempts — one or two for shape, essentially zero for semantics — because every retry is a new coin flip and a new invoice line.

**Degradation, not loops.** Every loop needs an exit that is not "try again forever": fallback to typed defaults with a flag (`null, needs_review: true`), queue the record for a human with the error attached, or fail loudly so the caller decides. Unbounded retries multiply cost, latency and hallucination surface — and they hide upstream problems: a repair loop that fires on 6% of inputs is telling you the prompt needs a constraint or an example, not that you need a fourth attempt.

**Feed failures back.** Every validation error is golden-set material (Module 5, Lesson 4): add the failing input, classify the error, and fix the prompt once for the whole class. The repair loop is the seatbelt; the prompt is the driving.

payload.title: Failure class, detection and first treatment
rows: Strip fence/label in code; then repair
Repair prompt with the exact schema error
Re-anchor to source, fix prompt upstream, or human
Rarely — a retry is a fresh sample, not a correction

payload.title: Feed the validator its own error message, verbatim
payload.text: Models repair far better against "required property 'currency' missing; value must be one of INR|USD|EUR|UNKNOWN" than against "the JSON was wrong".

payload.title: Bound the loop and name the exit
payload.text: Unbounded retries multiply cost and let real defects hide behind luck. One or two attempts, then a typed fallback or a human queue — and log the error class so the prompt gets fixed once.

payload.title: Turn a retry-until-lucky pipeline into a bounded repair contract
payload.problem: An expense-extraction service parses model JSON for 40,000 receipts a day. Current handling: on any failure, re-prompt with "please return correct JSON". Symptoms: 3.2x cost on failing documents, inconsistent repairs, and no record of what failed or why. Redesign the loop end to end.

steps.title: Instrument first: classify a week of failures
steps.desc: Add the three-layer checker and log classes for seven days: 61% syntax (fences and a "Here is the JSON:" preamble), 31% shape (currency given as "Rs." breaking the enum; missing merchant key), 8% semantic (total disagreeing with line items). Only now do you know what to repair — instrumentation precedes repair, always.

steps.title: Kill the free failures in code
steps.desc: Strip fences and label preambles deterministically before parsing. One change removes 61% of model calls: those were never model failures, they were missing cleanup.

steps.title: BEFORE vs AFTER for the shape failures
steps.desc: BEFORE (weak): "Please try again and make sure the JSON is correct." — no error, no scope, invites a full rewrite. AFTER: the repair contract — exact error, minimal-edit rule, raw output — capped at one attempt, then a typed fallback so the pipeline keeps moving with a flag rather than a fabricated value.

steps.title: Route semantics upstream, close the loop
steps.desc: Semantic failures (8%) do not get repair prompts: the receipt image or OCR text is re-anchored at the top of a fresh extraction call with the constraint that was violated stated as a rule ("total must equal the sum of line_items; if the document does not print a total, set total to null"). Every failure from all classes lands in the golden set; the two recurring shape errors become schema enum fixes and a prompt line — so next month the loop fires on well under one percent.

payload.solution: Cost per failing document drops from 3.2x retries to one deterministic cleanup plus at most one targeted repair; the diff on repaired records is reviewable because edits are minimal; failures are classified, logged and converted into permanent prompt and schema fixes instead of recurring luck. The pipeline's reliability now comes from layers — cleanup, schema, semantics, bounded repair, typed fallback — rather than from hoping the next sample lands. That is what "making the contract hold" means: not that nothing fails, but that every failure class has one named, bounded, cheap response.

payload.title: Design the checker for your structured prompt
payload.prompt: For one prompt that returns structured data: (1) write the three-layer validator (parse, schema, semantic) with at least two semantic checks specific to your data; (2) draft the repair prompt with verbatim error and minimal-edit rule; (3) define the exit — attempts, fallback shape, and where the record goes; (4) list the three most recent real failures and which layer would have caught each.
payload.hint: If you cannot write two semantic checks, you have not yet decided what "correct" means for this output — that is the real finding.

mistakes.mistake: Burning model calls to strip fences and preambles
mistakes.fix: Deterministic cleanup belongs in code: strip, trim, parse. Reserve repair calls for failures a regex cannot fix.

mistakes.mistake: Repair prompts without the exact error or without a minimal-edit rule
mistakes.fix: "Try again" re-rolls everything; include the validator message verbatim and require unchanged fields to stay byte-identical — fixes stay local and diffs stay reviewable.

mistakes.mistake: Running repair loops on semantic failures
mistakes.fix: A structurally perfect wrong value gets no new information from a retry. Re-anchor to source, add the violated constraint upstream, or route to a human.

mistakes.mistake: Unbounded retries instead of a designed exit
mistakes.fix: Cap attempts, define the fallback (null plus flag, human queue, loud error), and log every class — otherwise cost and latency scale with your worst input while defects hide behind eventual luck.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe a validator-first pipeline for structured output, distinguishing the three failure classes and their treatments. Write the three components of a repair prompt and state when repair should be skipped entirely.
payload.answer: Pipeline: check in order and stop at first failure — (1) syntax: deterministic cleanup (strip fence/label in code) then parse; (2) shape: schema check for required keys, types, enums, no extras; (3) semantics: value checks — cross-field arithmetic, ranges, existence of referenced ids, verbatim agreement with source. Classes and treatments: syntax failures are cleaned deterministically and only repaired if still unparseable; shape failures are the repair sweet spot because errors are precise and fixes local; semantic failures get re-anchoring to the source, upstream prompt fixes or human routing, because prose repair has no new information to draw on. Repair prompt components: (1) the failing output in full, (2) the validator's exact error message verbatim, (3) a minimal-edit rule — fix only what the error names, preserve all else, raw JSON only. Skip repair when the class is semantic, when the attempt budget (one or two for shape) is exhausted, or when cleanup in code already resolves it; then degrade to a typed fallback with a flag, a human queue, or a loud error — and log every failure into the golden set so the class is fixed once in the prompt rather than repeatedly in the loop.
payload.source: Production reliability question; the standard discussion of LLM output validation and self-repair.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Validator-first: parse, then schema, then semantics — stop at the first failing layer, and record the class.
Syntax gets deterministic cleanup; shape gets a bounded repair prompt; semantics get re-anchoring or a human.
A repair prompt = failing output + verbatim machine error + minimal-edit rule, capped at one or two attempts.
Every loop exits somewhere: typed fallback with a flag, human queue, or loud failure — never endless retries.
Failures feed the golden set: the loop is the seatbelt, the prompt fix is the driving.

questions.prompt: Order of checks in a validator-first pipeline:
options: Parse (syntax), then schema (shape), then semantic value checks
Only schema — the provider handles the rest
questions.explanation: Cheap layers first and stop at the first failure: nothing else matters if the payload does not parse.

questions.prompt: The response parses and matches the schema, but total does not equal the sum of line items. Best response:
options: Repair prompt asking to fix the JSON
Check the arithmetic in code and re-anchor the extraction to the source (or set null and flag) — prose repair has no new information
Increase the temperature and retry five times
questions.explanation: This is a semantic failure: structurally perfect, factually wrong. Retry-as-repair just re-rolls; fix the anchor or route it.

questions.prompt: Which repair prompt is well-formed?
options: "Please try again and make sure the JSON is correct."
"Return correct JSON this time — be careful."
Failing output + exact validator error verbatim + "change ONLY the fields named; preserve the rest; raw JSON only"
A new copy of the original task prompt with no error information
questions.explanation: Repair needs scope (the exact error) and stability (minimal edits) — otherwise each attempt re-rolls every field, including the passing ones.

questions.prompt: 6% of inputs trigger a repair attempt every run. What does that primarily indicate?
options: The model needs a higher token budget
An upstream gap: the prompt or schema is missing a constraint or example for a whole failure class — fix it once instead of retrying forever
That retries should be raised to five
That the validator is too strict and should be disabled
questions.explanation: A recurring repair rate is a prompt/schema defect signal. Repair is the seatbelt; the permanent fix belongs upstream.

modules.title: Module 7 — Code Prompting: Specs, Tests, Debug Loops and Repo Context
modules.summary: Code is the one output you can execute, which makes it the most honest place to prompt. Spec-first codegen that blocks the common failure modes; test-first prompting where tests are the contract, plus refactoring prompts that state invariants; debug loops that demand diagnosis before patch, wired to the right repository context; and code review run as a structured prompt with a severity taxonomy.

lessons.title: Codegen: From Spec to Working Code
lessons.summary: The gap between "write me X" and working code is a specification. Write the spec the way you would brief a developer: signature, contract, constraints, edge cases — and know the failure modes before they show up.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Turn a one-line code request into a spec with signature, contract, constraints and edge cases
Name the common codegen failure modes and the spec line that prevents each
Ask for code against pinned versions instead of the model's memory of APIs
Judge generated code by execution, not by fluency

payload.text: A team lead asks, in chat: "write a Python function to parse dates." It returns instantly and confidently: a beautiful function using a helper from a library that does not exist in their pinned version, a signature that does not match how the rest of the codebase names arguments, and no handling for the format their logs actually use. The code compiles in the reviewer's mind. Then it hits CI. Twenty minutes of prompt-writing would have prevented twenty minutes of archaeology — and the lead already knew the requirements. They simply did not put them in the prompt.

**Why codegen punishes vagueness harder than prose does.** A vague prose request yields vague prose, which a human can salvage in place. A vague code request yields code that is *plausibly wrong*: right shape, wrong API, missing edge case, silent assumption. Code is executable, so its defects do not argue with you — they fail at three in the morning. The discipline is the one every tech lead already applies to a junior developer: you do not say "write something for dates"; you say what it does, what it takes, what it returns, and what must never happen.

**The spec skeleton for a codegen prompt.** Six slots, in the order a reader needs them:

1. **Task and signature.** One sentence of what it does, then the exact signature you want — parameter names, types, return type. Models match a declared signature reliably and guess one you will accept only occasionally.
2. **I/O contract.** Concrete input and expected output — at least one happy path in your real data format. Examples kill the ambiguity prose leaves open: "date" alone means at least three different things.
3. **Constraints.** What it must not do: no dependencies beyond those listed, no global state, no network calls, target language and library versions, house style ("match the repo: type hints, snake_case"). Constraints you omit become creative freedom you did not want.
4. **Edge cases you already know.** Empty input, nulls, unicode, timezone boundaries, duplicates, cycles — name them. This is the cheapest reliability available: every edge case you name gets handled instead of skipped for the happy path.
5. **Context snippet.** The neighboring code it must fit: the function it calls, the type it returns, ten lines of house style. Relevant lines beat volume — Lesson 3 is about selection, because pasted-unrelated context dilutes attention across everything you pasted.
6. **Verification ask.** "Give the two asserts you would run for the cycle and empty cases" or "list every assumption you made" — forcing assumptions into text turns silent guesses into reviewable lines, and the asserts become the run you were going to do anyway.

**The failure modes, named.** Treat these like Module 5's taxonomy: each has a signature and a first move. *Hallucinated APIs* — plausible methods that do not exist (pin versions, paste real usage, run it). *Invented dependencies* — a phantom package or helper module (ban new dependencies outright). *Silent scope change* — does more or less than asked because a degree of freedom was open (contract example). *Plausible-but-wrong logic* — off-by-one, sort order, boundary conditions (one worked example with real numbers). *Style drift* — correct logic in someone else's house (style constraint plus a snippet). *Version anachronism* — deprecated calls from training memory: APIs and provider tooling move, so verify against current docs and your installed versions rather than trusting recall.

**The verification layer.** Generated code is a proposal. In this domain — uniquely — the check is mechanical: compile, run, test. A prompt that ends with code and no instruction to execute outsources verification to whoever reads it next. Keep each ask small enough that its output can actually be checked: one function, one behavior at a time — Module 4's decomposition, applied where verification is free.

payload.title: Codegen failure modes and the spec line that blocks them
rows: Method looks real, does not exist
Pin library + version; paste real usage; run it
New package or phantom helper appears
"No new dependencies — stdlib and listed imports only"
Does more or less than asked
Contract example: exact input -> exact output
One worked example with real numbers
Style constraint + ten lines of neighboring code
State versions; re-verify when versions move

payload.title: Pin before you prompt
payload.text: "Python 3.12, pandas 2.x, no new dependencies" removes an entire class of confident nonsense — the model cannot reach for an API you told it does not exist here.

payload.title: Fluency is not correctness in this domain
payload.text: Beautifully formatted wrong code reads better, which makes it more dangerous. Execute the output; the run is the verdict, the review is commentary.

payload.title: Upgrade a one-line codegen request into a spec that ships
payload.problem: A developer needs a function that flattens nested org data (lists of dicts with a "reports" key) into spreadsheet rows. Current prompt: "write a Python function to flatten this JSON into rows." Three attempts: one with a nonexistent helper, one that recursed forever on a cycle, one that silently dropped the employee id column. Rebuild the prompt as a six-slot spec.

steps.title: BEFORE: the weak request, with its open degrees of freedom
steps.desc: A goal and nothing else — no signature, no column contract, no cycle policy, no dependency policy, no definition of a row. Each open slot is a coin flip the model takes on your behalf, and the three past failures map exactly to three unspecified slots.
steps.code_snippet:
BEFORE (weak)
"Write a Python function to flatten this JSON into rows for
 a spreadsheet. Make it clean and efficient."

Unspecified: signature, columns/order, cycle policy, depth
limit, dependency policy, what a "row" contains.

steps.title: AFTER, slots 1-2: signature plus one real I/O pair
steps.desc: Declare the signature and a concrete input/output example with actual values. The example pins column names, column order and depth-first row order — the things prose keeps vague and examples settle in one line each.
steps.code_snippet:
AFTER, slots 1-2 (signature + contract):

def flatten_org(root: dict) -> list[dict]:
    """Rows for export: depth-first, one dict per person."""

# in:  {"id":"E1","name":"Ada","dept":"Eng",
#        "reports":[{"id":"E2","name":"Lin","dept":"Eng"}]}
# out: [{"id":"E1","name":"Ada","dept":"Eng"},
#        {"id":"E2","name":"Lin","dept":"Eng"}]
# Columns and order exactly as above, always.

steps.title: AFTER, slots 3-4: constraints and named edges
steps.desc: Constraints close the creative freedom; the edge list converts known hazards into handled policies. Cycle handling is now a rule (track visited ids) instead of a hope, and the missing-id case becomes an explicit error rather than a silent drop.
steps.code_snippet:
AFTER, slots 3-4 (constraints + edges):
- Python 3.12, stdlib only: NO new dependencies.
- Depth limit 20; deeper -> ValueError with the path.
- Cycles: track visited ids; skip repeats, keep going.
- "reports" missing/null/[] -> leaf, no error.
- Person without "id" -> ValueError naming the name field.
- Pure function: no print, no I/O, no globals.

steps.title: AFTER, slots 5-6: context and verification, then run
steps.desc: Ten lines showing how rows are consumed downstream plus house style (type hints, docstring convention). Close with the verification ask: "give the two asserts you would run for the cycle and empty-reports cases." Then run the code and those asserts. Assumptions surface as text; defects surface as failures — before either reaches CI.

payload.solution: WHY the second version ships: the signature removed name-and-shape ambiguity; the I/O pair fixed column order and traversal order unarguably; the dependency ban killed hallucinated helpers by policy; the cycle rule prevented the infinite recursion the model had no reason to guess at; the missing-id rule turned a silent drop into a named error; the context snippet aligned style and consumption; and the verification ask plus execution closed the loop. Every one of the three past failures maps to a slot the weak prompt left open — codegen quality is spec quality, and execution is the only honest review.

payload.title: Re-spec a failed codegen
payload.prompt: Recall a code task that went badly with AI, or invent one you need. Write the full six-slot spec: signature, one concrete I/O example, constraints including a dependency ban, your named edge cases, a ten-line context snippet from a real codebase, and a verification ask. Run it, execute the result, and report which slot prevented which failure class.
payload.hint: If you cannot write the I/O example with real values, you do not yet know the contract — the model will guess it for you, and it will guess average.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for "a function that does X" with no signature or example
mistakes.fix: Declare the signature and one real input/output pair; examples settle names, ordering and formats that prose leaves as coin flips.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model invent dependencies and helpers
mistakes.fix: Ban new dependencies and paste how the project actually imports the library; then verify against your installed version, because docs and models both move.

mistakes.mistake: Reviewing generated code by eye instead of running it
mistakes.fix: Fluent wrong code is this workflow's most dangerous artifact. Compile, run, test — the run is the verdict.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for the whole feature in one request
mistakes.fix: One function, one behavior, one verification per prompt. Small outputs are the only outputs a human can honestly check.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Name four common codegen failure modes and the line of spec that prevents each. Explain why an I/O example with real values outperforms a paragraph describing the same contract.
payload.answer: Four failure modes with fixes: (1) hallucinated APIs — pin language and library versions, paste real usage from the project, execute the result; (2) invented dependencies — explicit constraint: no new dependencies, stdlib and listed imports only; (3) silent scope change — a concrete input-to-output example fixing columns, ordering and formats; (4) plausible-but-wrong logic (off-by-one, ordering, boundaries) — a worked example with real numbers plus named edge cases and stated policies (cycles, nulls, limits). An I/O example beats prose because prose underdetermines — "flatten", "clean" and "date" each carry several meanings — while an example is one unambiguous instance the model pattern-matches exactly, settling structure and formatting in a single line. Prose states intent; examples demonstrate the contract, and demonstrated behaviour consistently outweighs described behaviour (Module 3).
payload.source: Standard applied question in LLM-assisted development interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Codegen quality is spec quality: signature, I/O contract, constraints, named edges, context snippet, verification ask.
Learn the failure modes like a taxonomy: hallucinated APIs, invented dependencies, scope drift, wrong logic, style drift, version rot.
Pin versions and ban surprise dependencies; APIs and models both move, so re-verify on upgrade.
Examples beat prose for contracts: one real input/output pair settles what a paragraph cannot.
In this domain the run is the verdict — execute the output before you admire it.

questions.prompt: Which addition most reliably prevents a hallucinated-API failure?
options: Asking the model to be careful
Pinning language and library versions, pasting real usage from the project, then executing the result
Requesting the code in one block with no comments
Raising the temperature for more grounded output
questions.explanation: Pinning and real usage narrow the model to APIs that exist in your world; execution catches the residual.

questions.prompt: A generated function silently skips rows with missing ids instead of erroring. Which spec slot was missing?
options: A stated policy for that edge case — what must happen on missing ids
questions.explanation: Unnamed edge cases become happy-path defaults; policies for what must never happen belong in the edge-case slot.

questions.prompt: Why does one concrete input/output example usually beat a paragraph describing the contract?
options: An example is one unambiguous instance; prose underdetermines names, ordering and formats — and demonstrated behaviour outweighs described behaviour
Models cannot read prose about code
Examples remove the need to run anything
questions.explanation: Underdetermined prose is a per-field coin flip; an example pins structure and order exactly once.

questions.prompt: You have received generated code that reads convincingly. The correct next step:
options: Ask the model to approve its own code, then merge
Compile and run it against your named edge cases — the run is the verdict
Save it and test next sprint
questions.explanation: Execution is the only mechanical check this domain gives you for free; fluency is decoration.

lessons.title: Test-First Prompting and Refactoring Without Regressions
lessons.summary: Tests are the cheapest contract a model can produce — small, readable, executable. Generate and review them first, then generate code to satisfy them; and when old code changes, state the invariants that must survive.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Generate a focused test suite first and review it as the specification
Run a red-then-green loop where failing tests anchor codegen
Write refactoring prompts with explicit invariants, scope and acceptance checks
Detect tautological generated tests and correct them before coding

payload.text: Two engineers delegate the same task. The first says "write a parser for this config format and make sure it works" — gets code, argues about it for an hour, still cannot say whether the edge cases are covered. The second says "write five tests for this format first: these two should pass with these exact values, these three are the nasty ones" — reads the tests for ten minutes, corrects one wrong expectation, and the code is nearly an afterthought. One shipped a parser. The other shipped a parser and its specification.

**Why tests first.** A test suite is an executable spec in the most reviewable form the workflow produces: ten lines of test are faster to verify than three hundred lines of implementation, and they convert "looks right" into a binary run. The order of generation matters more than people expect. Tests written *after* code tend to mirror the code's assumptions — including its bugs, because the model writing them has just committed to those assumptions. Tests written *before* code, derived from your spec and I/O examples, constrain the implementation instead of ratifying it. That is test-first prompting: the model proposes the specification, you approve it, then the code arrives with somewhere to be right.

**The loop, concretely.** (1) Generate tests from the spec: give the signature, the I/O example, and the named edge cases; ask for exactly five to ten tests covering happy path, each named edge, and one case you did not name (models are good at proposing boundaries you forgot — a free edge-case audit). (2) *Review the tests like a contract*: is each expected value what you actually want? Is a policy encoded correctly ("cycle should skip, not throw")? Fix wrong expectations yourself — this is the ten minutes that saves the hour. (3) Generate the implementation against the approved tests: "make these tests pass; do not modify them." (4) Run. Red, then green — with a human approving the red.

**The tautology trap.** Generated tests can be vacuous: asserting what the code does rather than what the spec says, expected values copied from the implementation, every test passing on first generation, or ten happy paths and no negative cases. Red flags: tests that pass immediately (they may have been written to match a solution the model already had), assertions on incidental details (variable names, log output), and mocks so total that nothing real executes. The counter is structural: derive tests from *your* examples first, require expected values from your contract, and insist on at least one failure-path test per policy.

**Refactoring prompts: contract is "same behavior, different structure".** Refactoring is where vague prompts do the most damage, because the model helpfully "improves" behavior you were not thinking about: renaming a public function, swallowing an error it decides is edge-casey, dropping a guard as dead code. A refactoring prompt must state what *stays the same*, not just what changes:

1. **Invariants** — public API names and signatures unchanged; observable behavior identical, including error types and messages you depend on; no dependency changes.
2. **Scope** — exactly which function or files may change; "do not touch callers".
3. **Safety net** — attach the existing tests (or the test-first suite you just built) and require them to stay green; if no tests exist, this is your signal to generate them *first* — a refactor without tests is a rewrite with optimism.
4. **Acceptance** — ask for the minimal diff that achieves the stated goal, plus a list of any behavior risk the model sees while reading. Scope creep ("while I'm here...") is how refactors break things; forbid it by name.

The same split governs both halves of this lesson: your prompt states the contract, the model proposes artifacts, and the run decides. Tests are simply the cheapest contract artifact there is — which is why serious code prompting is test-first almost by default.

rows: 5-10 tests from your spec + I/O + edges
Read every expected value as a contract
Fix wrong expectations; add the policy test it missed
Implementation that must pass the approved tests
Do not let it edit the tests
Red/green is the verdict; failures feed the next round
Check the invariants and the diff, not the prose

payload.title: Test-first for a new helper, then an invariant-bound refactor

Both have failed before: the parser came back over-permissive, and a previous "cleanup" of the loader changed which error fires on a malformed key — breaking a downstream script that matched on the message.

steps.title: Test-first, BEFORE vs AFTER
steps.desc: BEFORE (weak): "write a flag parser and include some tests" — tests arrive after and beside a solution the model already imagined, so they ratify its choices. AFTER: tests-only prompt with expected values mandated from the spec (code block), forcing the specification artifact out first.

BEFORE (weak)
"Write a Python arg parser for --name, --flag. Include some

AFTER (strong, tests only — see extras for the full text)
- specs pinned, exactly 6 tests, each expected value mandated
- "Tests only — no implementation yet."  <- order is the point

steps.title: Approve the red: read six tests, fix one
steps.desc: Review takes minutes because the artifact is small. One test encoded "bare arg silently ignored" — wrong: your contract says ValueError. You correct the expectation. That correction, made now, is a spec decision; made later, it would have been a bug report.

steps.title: Generate the green, and forbid test edits

The stop clause converts disagreements into text instead of silent test edits — the model editing its own grading rubric is the failure mode this prevents.

steps.title: The refactor prompt: invariants first, then the goal
steps.desc: BEFORE (weak): "refactor the config loader to remove duplication — make it clean and pythonic" (previous run renamed a public function and changed an error message). AFTER: invariants, scope, safety net and acceptance stated before the goal — plus a demand to list behavior risks it notices.

AFTER (refactor):
INVARIANTS (must hold after the change):
  I1 public functions keep exact names + signatures
  I2 error types AND messages unchanged (scripts match text)
  I3 no new dependencies; no behavior change for valid configs
SCOPE: loader.py lines 40-120 only; do not touch callers.

Also: no "while I am here" improvements outside SCOPE.

payload.solution: The parser shipped as spec, not guesswork: six approved tests pinned permissiveness boundaries and error behavior before a line of implementation existed, and the stop clause kept the model from editing its own rubric. The refactor stated what must not change — names, signatures, error text, dependencies — which is precisely what the previous vague cleanup violated, and the attached suite plus minimal-diff acceptance made violations visible. Note the ordering principle behind both: contract artifact first (tests, invariants), implementation second, run last. Whether the artifact is a test file or a paragraph of invariants, you are doing the same thing — approving the specification before the code exists.

Then take one existing function you dislike and write its refactor prompt with invariants, scope and acceptance — and report which invariant did the most work.

payload.question: Explain why test-first prompting outperforms test-after prompting for LLM codegen, give three signs of a tautological generated test, and list the four components of a safe refactoring prompt.
payload.answer: Test-first wins because tests written after the implementation inherit its assumptions — the model ratifies the same choices (and bugs) it just made — while tests written first from your spec and I/O examples act as a binding contract the implementation must satisfy, and they are the smallest, most reviewable artifact in the workflow. Three tautological signs: tests that pass immediately (written to match an imagined solution); expected values copied from the implementation rather than your contract; assertions on incidental details or so heavily mocked that no real path executes — plus the tell of ten happy paths and no negative cases. lessons.title: Debug Loops: Error to Diagnosis to Fix, with the Right Repo Context
lessons.summary: Debugging prompts fail when they ask for a fix before a diagnosis. Build loops that supply evidence verbatim, demand hypotheses first, keep fixes minimal — and engineer exactly which repository context reaches the window.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Assemble a debug prompt with verbatim error, expected-vs-actual, repro and relevant code
Run a diagnosis-first loop that separates hypothesis generation from patching
Select and trim repository context so critical files are not diluted
Prime house style with a snippet instead of a paragraph of adjectives

payload.text: A developer pastes: "this doesn't work, can you fix it?" followed by forty lines of code with no error message. The model obliges with a confident patch that changes three things. Two rounds later, the actual bug — a timezone the code never handles — is found by a colleague in four minutes, because she asked "what did you expect, what happened, and show me the traceback." The model was not failing at debugging; it was being asked to guess instead of being given evidence. Guesses are cheap, and confident guesses are worse.

**Debugging is an evidence problem before it is a prompting problem.** A debugger withholds nothing: exact error, exact input, exact expectation, smallest reproducing case, the code involved, and what has already been ruled out. Strip any of those and the model does what models do — it completes the most statistically plausible scenario, which is often a *different bug entirely*. The weak debug prompt ("fix this") therefore has a characteristic failure: a fluent patch to code that was never broken.

**The debug prompt's five evidence slots.** (1) *Verbatim error* — the full traceback or message, unedited, including the line numbers; summaries discard the clue ("KeyError" alone hides which key). (2) *Expected vs actual* — one sentence each; without the expectation, "wrong" is undefined and any behavior can be argued either way. (3) *Minimal repro* — the smallest input and command that triggers it; if you cannot produce one, you have not isolated the bug, and the model cannot either. (4) *The involved code* — the failing function plus its immediate caller and the definitions it touches (Lesson 3's selection rules). (5) *Ruled out* — "already checked: config is correct, input parses, happens only in prod-like data." Ruled-out items stop the loop from re-proposing what you killed yesterday.

**Diagnosis before patch.** Structure the loop in three prompts, not one: first, "list the two or three most likely causes ranked, and for each give a one-line experiment that would confirm or kill it" — hypotheses with tests; second, once evidence picks a winner, "give the minimal fix for cause X only" — minimal means no drive-by refactors; third, "state the exact command to run to prove the fix, and what regression it could cause." This ordering exploits what models are good at (generating plausible explanations, widening search) while fencing what they are bad at (admitting uncertainty after committing to a patch). It also converts a wrong diagnosis into a cheap, visible step: you kill a hypothesis with its experiment instead of merging a patch that rewrites unrelated code. Bound the loop at two or three rounds; if evidence is not converging, the context is wrong or the problem is too big — widen the context or decompose (Module 5, class 8: stop wording, change structure).

**Repo-context engineering.** What reaches the context window decides what the model can see, and in code, position and relevance both matter (Module 1, Lesson 3). Four practices:

1. *Select, do not dump.* Include the failing file, its caller, and the interfaces it depends on — not the repository. Distant files dilute attention across everything pasted; a focused five-file context beats a fifty-file one for a localized bug. (Agentic coding tools auto-select context; the same principle governs what you hand them and what you check they gathered.)
2. *Trim to regions.* For a big file, paste the function and its neighborhood with a note on where it lives ("file: service.py, lines 80-140") instead of the whole file.
3. *Put the ask after the code.* Instruction and question at the end, adjacent to where generation starts — the edge placement that Part I established and long contexts keep proving.
4. *Prime style with an exemplar.* Two sentences of "match the house style" are weaker than ten lines of actual house style. Paste a representative function and say "match this: error handling, naming, comment density." Style is a pattern; patterns transfer by example (Module 3), not by adjective.

**The verification tail.** Every debug loop ends outside the model: run the repro, run the proposed confirmation experiment, run the suite. The loop closes when the evidence changes, not when the prose sounds right.

payload.title: Debug prompt anatomy
rows: Model patches a different, more common bug
"Wrong" is undefined; any fix can be argued
No isolation — the model guesses at scope
Fix breaks an interface it never saw

ERROR (verbatim, production):
Traceback (most recent call last):

    rows = key_by(ids)
KeyError: 'order_9182'

EXPECTED: every id in ids resolves (rows has 1:1 entries)
ACTUAL: KeyError on order_9182; 3 of 200 ids fail, always

RULED OUT: input csv parses; ids exist in source db;

CODE:
<sync.py:70-100>
...
</sync.py>

payload.title: Ruled-out is the most underrated slot
payload.text: Each dead hypothesis you state is one the loop cannot waste a round on — it converts prior work into prompt context instead of repeated archaeology.

payload.title: Never ask for the fix and the diagnosis in the same breath
payload.text: A patch-first prompt commits the model to a cause it has not argued for. Hypotheses with cheap tests first; minimal patch second; proof command third.

payload.title: Turn "it does not work, fix it" into a three-round evidence loop
payload.problem: A nightly sync intermittently fails with a KeyError. The developer's first two attempts: paste code with "it does not work" (received: a rewrite of the whole function), then paste code plus "fix the KeyError" (received: a try/except that swallowed it — the failure disappeared from the error log and reappeared as wrong data). Build the proper loop.

steps.title: Assemble the evidence: five slots filled
steps.desc: Full traceback, expected-vs-actual, the repro (only fails on ids imported after midnight — that pattern is itself evidence), the failing function plus its caller, and the ruled-out list. Round 1 asks only for ranked causes with confirmation experiments — explicitly no fix.

steps.title: Round 1 output: hypotheses you can kill cheaply
steps.desc: The model ranks: (1) duplicate ids collapsing in a dict — experiment: count len(ids) vs len(set(ids)); (2) stale id format from the midnight importer — experiment: regex the id shapes by import hour; (3) caller passing a generator it exhausts twice — experiment: log len at entry. Each is a one-line test; none involves rewriting code.
steps.code_snippet:
H1 dupes in dict build   -> count len(ids) vs len(set(ids))
H2 midnight id format    -> regex id shapes by import hour
H3 generator exhausted    -> log len(ids) at function entry

# experiment result: H1 wins - 3 duplicates, silent overwrite
# in the dict comprehension, last-seen wins and the orphaned
# key raises later at line 88.

steps.title: Round 2: minimal fix for the diagnosed cause only
steps.desc: Cause confirmed (H1), so the second prompt narrows hard: fix duplicate handling at dict construction, nothing else. The instruction forbids the two failure modes already seen: no wholesale rewrite, no swallowing — an explicit "do not add try/except that hides this" clause, because the previous attempt converted a data bug into silent corruption.
steps.code_snippet:
AFTER, round 2 (minimal fix):
Cause H1 confirmed. Fix ONLY duplicate-id handling in the dict
build: detect duplicates, keep an explicit policy (first-seen
wins), and raise with the offending ids if a duplicate appears
in the SAME input batch.
Do not refactor surrounding code. Do NOT wrap in try/except
that swallows KeyError. Output: the changed lines only + the
exact command to run to prove it.

steps.title: Round 3: proof and regression check, outside the model
steps.desc: The prompt asks for the proving command and the regression risk; you run them: repro with duplicated input (fails cleanly with ids named), the nightly dry-run, and the existing suite. Loop closed by execution — the evidence changed, not the prose.

payload.solution: The wrong-patch pattern (rewrite; swallow) never got a chance, because round 1 committed to no patch at all — only ranked hypotheses with one-line experiments, the shape of debugging that models are actually strong at. The confirmed cause made round 2 narrow enough that the fix touched the policy at dict construction and nothing else, and the explicit anti-swallow clause fenced the exact failure the developer had already shipped once. Repo context did its part: traceback verbatim, function plus caller, ruled-out items up front. Diagnosis first, minimal fix second, proof third — three prompts where the weak version used one.

payload.title: Run a diagnosis-first loop on a real bug
payload.prompt: Take a real unresolved bug (yours or a classic from your stack). Write the debug prompt with all five evidence slots filled honestly, including a ruled-out list. Round 1: ranked causes plus one-line experiments, no fix allowed. Run (or simulate) an experiment to kill one cause. Round 2: minimal fix for the survivor. Round 3: proof command plus regression risk. Report: which slot was empty in your usual debug prompting, and which round changed your mind.
payload.hint: If you cannot write a minimal repro, you are still in evidence-gathering — say so in the prompt instead of asking for a patch.

mistakes.mistake: "Fix this" with code attached but no verbatim error or expectation
mistakes.fix: Without evidence, the model completes the most common scenario for your snippet — usually a different bug. Five slots: error, expected/actual, repro, code, ruled out.

mistakes.mistake: Demanding diagnosis and patch in one prompt
mistakes.fix: The model commits to a cause before arguing for it. Hypotheses with cheap experiments first; minimal fix second; proof command third.

mistakes.mistake: Pasting the whole repository "for context"
mistakes.fix: Dilution: critical lines drown in distant code. Select the failing file, its caller and its interfaces; trim big files to the region; ask after the code.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a fix that hides the error (try/except, retry, swallow)
mistakes.fix: A patch that silences the signal while the data stays wrong is a regression. Require the fix to preserve error visibility and prove the original repro now succeeds.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: List the five evidence slots of a well-formed debug prompt, explain why the loop should request diagnosis before patch, and give two repo-context selection rules with the failure each prevents.
payload.answer: Five slots: (1) the verbatim error/traceback, unedited — summaries discard clues such as the exact key or line; (2) expected versus actual behavior, one sentence each — otherwise "wrong" is undefined; (3) a minimal reproduction — the smallest input and command that triggers the bug; (4) the involved code — failing function, its caller and touched definitions; (5) what has already been ruled out — so the loop cannot re-propose dead hypotheses. Diagnosis before patch because a patch commits the model to a cause it has not argued: ranked hypotheses with one-line confirmation experiments exploit the model's strength (plausible explanations) and fence its weakness (confident commitment), turning a wrong direction into a cheap killed hypothesis instead of merged damage; the minimal fix then targets the confirmed cause, and the proof command closes the loop by execution. Context rules: (1) select, do not dump — paste the failing file, caller and interfaces, not the repository — preventing attention dilution where critical lines drown in distant code; (2) trim large files to the relevant region and place the ask after the code — preventing position failures where the instruction is lost in the middle of a long paste.

lessons.title: Code Review as a Prompt — and Knowing What Review Cannot Do
lessons.summary: Run review as a structured prompt with a rubric, a severity taxonomy and an evidence rule — then remember the boundary: a model reviewer finds pattern violations cheaply and cannot prove novel logic correct. Tests and execution stay the final authority.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write a review prompt with a rubric, severity levels, evidence rules and a fixed output format
Separate pattern-level findings (strong) from logic-proof claims (weak) in model review output
Require a demonstrating test for every claimed bug before acting on it
Decide when review adds value versus when tests and execution answer the question

payload.text: A team adopts "ask the AI to review the PR" and, for two weeks, it is magic: every diff comes back with a list of findings, and everyone feels safer. Then a reviewer approves a diff because the AI list "looked thorough" — the list was six style nits and one false positive, while the actual defect sat in the one place neither the model nor the humans looked: a novel race in brand-new logic. Review had become a ritual: voluminous, confident, and systematically missing the class of problem that mattered most.

**Review is a prompt like any other: it needs a rubric, a contract and an evidence rule.** "Review this code" underspecifies the task the way "write about internships" underspecifies an essay: the model picks whatever dimensions are statistically popular, which produces generic findings. A structured review prompt names the dimensions, fixes the output format, and — the crucial addition — requires evidence.

**The four-part review prompt.** (1) *Rubric* — name the axes you care about, ranked: correctness against spec, edge and error handling, security (injection, path traversal, secrets in logs), concurrency where relevant, performance only where hot, readability and consistency with the pasted house style, test coverage of new behavior. Named axes stop the model from spending its findings budget on style nits by default. (2) *Scope* — the diff (preferred) or file, plus the spec or ticket it implements; findings must relate to the change. (3) *Evidence rule* — every finding cites the exact line or quotes the snippet and states the concrete failure scenario ("when input is empty, row 0 is read" — not "could be problematic"). A finding without evidence is noise, and a review that produces noise trains its readers to skim. (4) *Output contract* — findings ordered by severity with a fixed taxonomy, then a one-line verdict, then an explicit section for "what I could not check" — the honesty slot that names the model's own blind spots for this diff.

**The severity taxonomy.** *Blocker* — will cause incorrect behavior, data loss or a security hole in realistic conditions. *Major* — likely bug or contract violation under plausible inputs; fix before merge. *Minor* — real but bounded: dead code, duplicated logic, missing test for an edge case. *Nit* — style preference, naming taste. The taxonomy does real work: it forces ranking, which forces the model to spend its attention where you will spend yours, and it lets a busy human read blockers and stop. It also makes false positives legible — a "blocker" that turns out theoretical is a taxonomy violation you can push back on, rather than a vague disagreement.

**What model review is strong and weak at — know the boundary.** Strong: pattern-matching a large catalogue of known anti-patterns — SQL built by string concatenation, unbounded recursion, resource acquired without release, unchecked index access, secrets in code, missing null or error checks, API misuse against pasted docs, inconsistency with stated conventions. This is recall over a huge training distribution, and it is genuinely valuable at diff speed. Weak: *proving novel logic correct*. A fresh algorithm with subtle ordering or state handling can be flawless on every pattern the model knows and still be wrong — because correctness of new logic is established by execution, not pattern recall. Also weak: performance claims without measurements (treat as hypotheses), whole-repo consistency without the repo, and any claim about behavior the model cannot see (tests, runtime, data).

**The proving-test requirement.** For any finding labeled blocker or major, ask for a demonstrating test: the minimal input and assertion that would fail today. This single rule changes review quality more than any other. It converts claims into checkable artifacts; false positives die in ten seconds when you run the test; true positives arrive already encoded as the regression test you will keep. Findings the model cannot instantiate as a test downgrade — by contract — to "speculative", which is where most logic-proofs-from-prose belong.

**Where review sits in the loop.** Review is a cheap middle gate, not the final one: spec and tests first (Lessons 1-2), build and run, review the diff, then execute the proving tests for blockers. And when the question is "is this new algorithm correct", skip review as the primary tool — property tests, edge-case runs and a profiler answer that class of question mechanically. Review at its best is what a sharp colleague with infinite patience does at 1x speed: read for patterns you already know to fear, cite lines, rank by severity, and admit what it did not check.

payload.title: Severity taxonomy and the action it triggers
rows: Incorrect behavior, data loss or security hole in realistic conditions
Do not merge; require the demonstrating test to fail first
Likely bug or contract violation under plausible input
Fix before merge; test if it can be instantiated
Bounded issue: dead code, duplication, missing edge test
Queue; fix with the next change to the file
Optional; batch with style tooling, not with debate

  "reject uploads over 10MB with a clear error".
STYLE: house conventions (attached: 10 lines of exemplar).

RUBRIC (rank findings by this order):
  1 correctness vs the ticket, 2 edge + error handling,
  3 security, 4 test coverage of new behavior, 5 style

RULES:
- Cite the exact line for every finding.
- State the concrete failure scenario, not adjectives.
- Label each: blocker | major | minor | nit.
- For every blocker/major: give a minimal test that FAILS
  on the current code.
- End with: VERDICT (one line) and NOT CHECKED (what you
  could not verify: runtime, data, tests not shown).
- If nothing meets a level, say "no findings" for it.

payload.title: Ask for the proving test with every blocker
payload.text: Claims become artifacts: false positives die when you run them, true positives arrive pre-encoded as the regression test you keep.

payload.title: A thorough-looking finding list is not coverage
payload.text: Model review is pattern recall over known failure modes — novel logic still needs tests and execution. Never let a green-sounding review stand in for a run.

payload.title: From "review this please" to a review with a verdict you can act on
payload.problem: A PR adds an endpoint that applies a coupon to a cart. The team's current prompt: "review this code for any issues please." It returns nine bullets, mostly naming conventions, one vague "consider handling edge cases", no severities, no lines cited, and a closing "overall looks good!" that reviewers have started quoting in approvals. Restructure the review and handle its output.

steps.title: BEFORE: the weak review prompt and why its output is useless
steps.desc: "Review this code for any issues please" leaves rubric, scope, evidence and format all open — so the model defaults to popular, cheap findings (style) and generic advice ("handle edge cases") that names no edge, cites no line, and cannot be actioned or refuted.
steps.code_snippet:
BEFORE (weak)
"Review this code for any issues please."

Open: dimensions, scope, evidence, severity, format.
Result: 9 style nits, 1 vague edge advice, "looks good!"

steps.title: AFTER: rubric, scope, evidence rule, taxonomy, honesty slot
steps.desc: The structured prompt (see extras) names the rubric ordered by what matters, scopes to the diff against its ticket, requires line citations and concrete failure scenarios, fixes the severity labels, demands a demonstrating test for blockers/majors, and adds NOT CHECKED — the slot that stops confident omniscience.

steps.title: Process the findings: run the proving tests
steps.desc: Output: one blocker ("coupon applies twice when the cart is edited mid-request — no idempotency key"), two majors (stack trace leaks on invalid coupon; no test for the 100%-discount path), three minors, three nits, plus NOT CHECKED: "concurrent edit behavior, not visible in the diff". You run the blocker's demonstrating test: it fails today. The claim just became an artifact — and the test becomes the regression suite member that keeps the fix honest.
steps.code_snippet:
blocker test (model-provided, fails on current code):
  cart = apply_coupon(make_cart(total=1000), "SAVE10")
  cart = apply_coupon(cart, "SAVE10")          # re-request
  assert cart.total == 900   # FAILS: 810 (double-applied)

# after fix (idempotency key): test passes -> keep it.

steps.title: Handle the false positive and the honesty slot
steps.desc: One "major" (claim: unbounded memory on large carts) cannot be instantiated as a test and turns out theoretical for your size limits — by contract it downgrades to speculative and you note it in the PR, not the blocker queue. NOT CHECKED ("concurrent edit behavior") is not filler: it tells you exactly what the model could not see, so you assign a human to test concurrency — the review said where to look, which is more valuable than a fake green light.

payload.solution: The restructured review produced findings you could triage: ranked, cited, and — for the ones that mattered — executable. The proving-test rule did the heavy lifting: it killed a theoretical claim in seconds, converted the real defect into a permanent regression test, and made severity labels something you could argue with instead of take on faith. And the honesty slot converted the model's blind spot into a work item rather than a false assurance. Review had stopped being ritual and started being a gate: cheap to run, explicit about what it cannot do, and wired to execution as the final authority.

payload.title: Run a structured review on a real diff
payload.prompt: Take a recent change (yours or an open-source diff). Write the four-part review prompt: ranked rubric, diff scope, evidence rule (cite the line, concrete scenario), severity output plus NOT CHECKED. Run it. Triage: how many findings were blockers, could each blocker be instantiated as a failing test, and which severity label was wrong? Finally, name one question the review could not answer that only execution can.
payload.hint: If no finding cites a line, the prompt's evidence rule is missing — findings without citations are opinions.

mistakes.mistake: Unstructured "review this" prompts
mistakes.fix: Name the ranked rubric, scope, evidence rule and output contract — unspecified dimensions get statistically popular (usually trivial) findings.

mistakes.mistake: Treating every finding as equally actionable
mistakes.fix: Enforce the taxonomy: blockers block, nits batch into tooling. A flat list forces humans to re-rank by hand — the work you asked the model to do.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting logic-correctness claims from prose review
mistakes.fix: Novel logic is proven by execution, not pattern recall. Require a demonstrating test for blockers; downgrade uninstantiable claims to speculative.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting "the AI said it looks good" as approval
mistakes.fix: The verdict line is a summary of pattern recall over the shown context — no run, no data, no tests seen. Approval still means you ran it.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Specify the four parts of a structured code-review prompt and the severity taxonomy. Then state what model review is strong at, what it is weak at, and how the proving-test requirement changes how you triage findings.
payload.answer: Four parts: (1) rubric — named, ranked dimensions (correctness vs spec, edges/errors, security, tests, style) so findings are spent where you care; (2) scope — the diff (or file) plus the ticket it implements, findings tied to the change; (3) evidence rule — every finding cites the exact line and states a concrete failure scenario, not adjectives; (4) output contract — findings ordered by severity (blocker/major/minor/nit), a one-line verdict, and an explicit NOT CHECKED section naming what could not be verified. Strengths: recall over a huge distribution of known anti-patterns — injection via concatenation, resource leaks, unchecked access, API misuse, convention violations — at diff speed. Weaknesses: proving novel logic correct (correctness of new algorithms comes from execution, not pattern matching), performance claims without measurement, and anything outside the shown context. The proving-test requirement (a minimal failing test for every blocker/major) converts claims into artifacts: false positives die when you run them, true positives arrive pre-encoded as regression tests, and uninstantiable claims are contractually downgraded to speculative — so triage happens by execution rather than by prose confidence.
payload.source: Common question in AI-assisted development workflows: what can review automation actually guarantee?

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Structured review: ranked rubric, diff scope, evidence rule (cite line + scenario), severity taxonomy, NOT CHECKED slot.
Model review is pattern recall: strong on known anti-patterns, weak on proving novel logic correct.
Require a demonstrating test for every blocker/major — claims become artifacts that run.
Blockers block, nits batch into tooling; a flat finding list just re-ranks the work onto humans.
The verdict line is not an approval: no run, no data, no tests seen — execution stays the final authority.

questions.prompt: Which element most improves an LLM code-review prompt?
options: A ranked rubric, an evidence rule requiring cited lines, and a severity taxonomy with a NOT CHECKED slot
questions.explanation: Unspecified dimensions yield popular trivial findings; ranked rubric plus evidence plus taxonomy makes output actionable and triable.

questions.prompt: A review finding claims your new algorithm has a subtle ordering bug but cites no line and cannot produce a failing test. Correct handling:
options: Downgrade it to speculative by the proving-test contract, and verify ordering with a targeted test you run yourself
Delete the review and rerun until it disappears
Accept it — models are usually right about logic
questions.explanation: Claims that cannot be instantiated as tests are prose hypotheses; the run decides, not the phrasing.

questions.prompt: What is model review genuinely strong at?
options: Recall over a large catalogue of known anti-patterns — injection, leaks, unchecked access, API misuse — applied at diff speed
Verifying integration with systems it cannot see
questions.explanation: Pattern recall over training distribution is the real strength; proof and measurement need execution.

questions.prompt: The NOT CHECKED section of a review output is meant to:
options: Name explicitly what the reviewer could not verify (runtime, data, unseen tests) — converting blind spots into assigned human work
questions.explanation: A named blind spot is actionable; silence is a false assurance. Honest limits are what make the rest of the findings trustworthy.

modules.title: Module 8 — Long Context and Documents: Summarization, Chunking, RAG Prompts
modules.summary: Industrializing Module 1's context-assembly model. Summarization patterns chosen by purpose — map-reduce, hierarchical, key-point extraction — with the loss-compounding trap named; chunking strategies that split on structure, carry state and stitch honestly; the RAG prompt contract (context packing, citations, refusal branches, injection fencing); and the long-context traps — position, distractors, budget arithmetic — that break answers even when retrieval succeeded.

lessons.title: Summarization Patterns: Map-Reduce, Hierarchical and Key-Point Extraction
lessons.summary: Summarization is compression under a stated purpose, and the pattern you choose should follow that purpose — not the size of the document. Three patterns, where each wins, and how loss compounds when you chain them.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: State a summarization purpose (audience, decision, target) before choosing a pattern
Run map-reduce and hierarchical summarization with uniform per-chunk contracts
Choose key-point extraction over prose summarization when fidelity and verification matter
Predict where loss and distortion compound in a chained pipeline

payload.text: An analyst drops a 90-page annual report into chat: "summarize this." The answer arrives confident, well-organized — and confidently wrong in one place that matters: a risk disclosed on page 60, buried among near-identical risk paragraphs, never surfaced. The model did what was asked. Nobody asked what the summary was *for*, so the output optimized for looking complete, which is precisely how the one paragraph that would have changed a decision disappears.

**Purpose first, pattern second.** "Summarize" is an underspecified task (Module 5, class 1): no audience, no decision, no length, no inclusion rules — so the output converges on the statistically typical overview. Before any pattern, write three lines: *who reads this* (an executive, an engineer, a reviewer of claims), *what decision it feeds* (buy, reject, dig deeper, archive), and *what must never be dropped* (numbers, risks, dates, dissent). Those three lines then choose your pattern almost mechanically, and they turn evaluation from taste into checking: does the summary serve the stated decision?

**Pattern 1 — Single pass (when it fits).** If the document fits in the window with headroom for your output, one call with purpose, structure and constraints beats any pipeline: fewer failure points, no compounding loss, and full-document attention for cross-references. Give it a target shape — number of sections, what each must contain, a "top three findings" band — and require quotes for load-bearing claims so a human can verify them. Long windows make this viable for documents that used to require pipelines; verify your provider's current limits, and remember the window must hold input *plus* reserved output.

**Pattern 2 — Map-reduce.** Split into chunks; the *map* prompt summarizes each chunk independently; the *reduce* prompt combines the chunk summaries into the final one. This is the workhorse for content that exceeds the window, and its power comes entirely from *uniformity*: every map call must produce the same fixed fields (findings, numbers, risks, open questions — same order, same format), because heterogeneous chunk summaries cannot be combined reliably. The reduce prompt then works over structure, not prose: "merge these N blocks, dedup, preserve all figures with their chunk ids, flag conflicts."

**Pattern 3 — Hierarchical.** Chunk to section summaries, section summaries to a document abstract — a tree rather than a flat fan-in. It wins when document structure carries meaning (reports, contracts, specs with headings), because you can keep section titles and order as first-class data instead of hoping prose survives two compressions. The reduce stage operates over the tree, so you can also *query* the tree later (find the section mentioning X, then expand only that subtree) instead of regenerating the whole summary.

**Pattern 4 — Key-point extraction (when fidelity beats flow).** Sometimes prose summarization is the wrong artifact: for synthesis, comparison or audit, ask for *atomic points* instead — one claim per line, each with a quote and a source location. Extraction beats summarization for three reasons: points are checkable against the source (quote present? verbatim?), they dedup cleanly across documents, and they compose into the next stage without rewriting. This is the pattern that feeds multi-document synthesis (Lesson 4) and any summary whose outputs will be verified rather than admired.

**Where loss compounds.** Every hop loses what the prompt did not demand. In map-reduce, a detail absent from a map summary is *unrecoverable* — the reduce stage literally cannot see the original text; errors and omissions propagate and averaging blurs disagreements into mush. Mitigations that actually work: the map contract demands numbers, names and negatives explicitly (what is *at risk* is the first thing compression drops); chunk ids travel with every point so the reduce can attribute and a human can jump back; conflicts are *reported*, never smoothed; and at least one spot-check per run compares final points against source quotes. Chained pipelines are not "summarize twice for reliability" — they are lossy twice, which is why the pattern list starts with single-pass whenever it fits.

payload.title: Purpose picks the pattern
rows: Single pass with a findings band
Fits window; full cross-references; no compounding loss
Document far exceeds window, structure matters
Titles and order survive; subtree can be re-queried
Map-reduce with a uniform field contract
Parallel, composable — but every map loss is permanent
Points will be verified, compared or merged
Checkable, dedupable, composable — fidelity over flow

payload.code:
# MAP contract (identical for every chunk)
From <chunk id="3/7"> extract AT MOST 5 atomic points.
Each point: one claim, one VERBATIM quote (< 25 words),
one figure if present. Also: RISKS (may be empty),
OPEN_QUESTIONS (may be empty). Keep chunk id on every line.
No intro, no summary of the summary.

# REDUCE (over the 7 uniform blocks)
Merge into one set: dedup identical points (keep both quotes),
KEEP every distinct figure with its chunk id, list CONFLICTS
verbatim (same topic, different values) — never average them,
end with COVERAGE: one line per chunk on what was dropped.

payload.title: Demand negatives explicitly
payload.text: Compression drops risks, caveats and dissents first because they are statistically rare. "RISKS (may be empty)" as a named field is what keeps them alive through the map stage.

payload.title: Chained summaries compound loss irreversibly
payload.text: Anything absent from a chunk summary is gone — the reduce stage cannot see the original. Quote-bearing key points and chunk ids are the only things that make hops auditable.

payload.title: Rebuild a 90-page report summary from "summarize this" to a purpose-driven pipeline
payload.problem: A strategy team receives an annual report and asks "summarize this." Their complaint after three attempts: generic prose that reads fine, no figures with sources, risks missing, and no way to check any claim. Design the pipeline: decide single-pass vs hierarchical, and specify map and reduce properly.

steps.title: Write the purpose lines — they pick the pattern
steps.desc: Who: the strategy director deciding whether to renew a supplier contract. Decision: renew / renegotiate / walk. Must never drop: financial figures, named risks, contract dates, any dissent. From this: the report is 90 pages (check the window — if it fits with output headroom, single pass; if not, hierarchical over sections), and key-point extraction style beats prose for checkability.

steps.title: BEFORE: the weak prompt and its failure
steps.desc: One vague ask, output shaped by vibes. The three complaints map to three missing specifications: "reads fine" = no decision served; "no figures" = no figure field; "risks missing" = nothing named negatives.
steps.code_snippet:
BEFORE (weak)
"Summarize this annual report. Be thorough but concise and
 highlight the most important things."

Missing: audience, decision, must-keep fields, length shape,
quote requirement -> statistically typical overview.

steps.title: AFTER: single-pass version if the window allows
steps.desc: Fixed structure mirroring the decision, with quotes as the verification hook. This version is *checked*, not admired: every figure carries a page cite, so the director can spot-check in minutes.
steps.code_snippet:
AFTER (single pass):
Audience: exec deciding renew/renegotiate/walk.
Structure, exactly: 1) 3 key findings (one sentence each),
2) FINANCIALS table (figure, page) — every number VERBATIM,
3) RISKS — all named, no paraphrase collapse,
4) CONTRACT DATES (effective, renewal, exit), 5) DISSENT or
 gaps in disclosure (write "none found" if none).
Every claim outside quotes -> add (p. N). Max 600 words.
No new interpretation: what the report does not say -> "not disclosed".

steps.title: AFTER: hierarchical variant when it exceeds the window
steps.desc: Sections map through the uniform contract (extras block) into section summaries, then one reduce over sections with the same fixed bands as the single-pass version plus COVERAGE. Spot-check: pull three final points, jump to their chunk ids, verify quotes verbatim against the PDF. Loss audit, not vibes audit.

payload.solution: The purpose lines did the routing: a decision-shaped output with verbatim figures, page cites and a named RISKS band is checkable in minutes, and the "not disclosed" clause replaces the confident filler that made prior attempts read well and verify poorly. The hierarchical variant adds only what structure buys — attribution by chunk id, conflict reporting, a coverage line — while the quote requirement survives both hops. The difference from the weak version is not length or effort; it is that every field now exists because the decision needed it, and every claim can be walked back to a page.

payload.title: Run one summarization with a purpose header
payload.prompt: Take a real long document you need summarized. Write the three purpose lines first (reader, decision, must-never-drop). Choose single-pass, hierarchical or map-reduce and justify it in one sentence from the window size and document structure. Write the prompt with a fixed output structure that includes a negatives field and a quote-with-location rule. Afterward, verify three claims against the source and report: did anything the purpose lines named get dropped?
payload.hint: If your summary has no field for risks or dissent, compression will find a way to lose them — named fields are the only defense.

mistakes.mistake: Prompting "summarize" with no reader, decision or must-keep list
mistakes.fix: Three purpose lines first: they pick the shape, the fields and the pattern — and they convert evaluation from taste into a check.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing map-reduce for a document that fits in one pass
mistakes.fix: Extra hops add cost and permanent loss for nothing. Single pass when input plus output fits with headroom; pipelines only when the window forces them.

mistakes.mistake: Heterogeneous chunk summaries fed to a reduce stage
mistakes.fix: If each map call produces a different shape, the reduce stage is combining prose by vibes. One uniform field contract, same order, same format, chunk ids attached.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting a chained summary without quote-level spot checks
mistakes.fix: Loss compounds silently. Keep verbatim quotes plus locations through every hop and verify a sample — the only audit trail a lossy pipeline has.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe when single-pass, map-reduce and hierarchical summarization are each the right choice, give the map-stage contract elements that make reduce reliable, and explain why loss in a chained pipeline is irreversible.
payload.answer: Single pass: when input plus reserved output fits the window with headroom — full-document cross-references, no compounding loss, cheapest failure surface; give it a fixed structure mirroring the decision. Map-reduce: when content exceeds the window and is flat (no meaningful hierarchy) — parallel chunk summaries combined in a reduce; correct when chunks are independent. Hierarchical: when structure carries meaning (headings, sections) — section summaries to an abstract, preserving titles and order and allowing later subtree queries. Map contract elements: identical fixed fields in the same order for every chunk (findings, figures, risks, open questions), verbatim quotes with locations, chunk ids on every item, and no free-form narration — uniformity is what lets reduce merge structurally instead of by vibes. Irreversibility: reduce sees only what map emitted; any figure, caveat or dissent absent from a chunk summary is permanently gone (the original text is no longer in context), and averaging across hops blurs disagreements. Hence quotes, chunk ids, explicit negatives fields and spot-check audits as the only compensation.
payload.source: Applied NLP/LLM system design: long-document summarization pipelines.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Purpose lines (reader, decision, must-never-drop) pick the pattern and make the output checkable.
Single pass when it fits; hierarchical when structure matters; map-reduce for flat bulk; key-points when fidelity beats flow.
Uniform map contracts — same fields, quotes, chunk ids — are what make reduce a merge instead of a mood.
Chained pipelines compound loss irreversibly: negatives vanish first, so name them as fields and audit with quotes.
Key-point extraction with verbatim quotes beats prose summaries wherever claims will be verified.

questions.prompt: A document exceeds the window and its headings carry meaning. Best pattern:
options: Flat map-reduce with prose chunk summaries
Hierarchical: section summaries to an abstract, preserving titles and order
Ask for a longer window and single-pass it regardless
Sample three random pages and summarize those
questions.explanation: Structure-aware hierarchies keep section identity and allow subtree re-queries; flat fan-in discards the structure you needed.

questions.prompt: Why must every map-stage chunk summary follow the identical field contract?
options: So the reduce stage can merge structurally — heterogeneous prose summaries force combination by vibes and lose attribution
questions.explanation: Uniformity plus chunk ids is the entire composability guarantee of a fan-in pipeline.

questions.prompt: In a chained summarization pipeline, why are risks and caveats the first casualties?
options: Models dislike negative content by policy
They are statistically rare lines, so compression drops them unless a named field demands them — and once dropped at map, they are unrecoverable at reduce
Reduce stages filter them out deliberately
questions.explanation: Compression keeps what is frequent and central; explicit negatives fields and quotes are the only structural defense.

questions.prompt: Best artifact when summaries will be compared across documents and verified by a human:
options: Atomic key points, each with a verbatim quote and source location
The model's opinion of the document's quality
questions.explanation: Atomic points dedup, compose and check against source text — prose summaries do none of those reliably.

lessons.title: Chunked Prompting: Boundaries, State and Honest Stitching
