steps.desc: Load ordered history, append the incoming user message idempotently, assemble bounded history, call the provider, stream deltas to the client, then persist the assistant message with usage and finish reason — in a finally block, because failures bill too.

steps.title: Client: optimistic append, then reconcile
steps.desc: Render the user turn immediately with a client-generated id; the server echoes the canonical id on the SSE final event and the UI swaps. Refresh now reloads from the server store — the conversation outlives the tab.

steps.title: Read the cost curve from real usage
steps.desc: Log tokens-in per turn for 30 turns. You will see near-linear growth per turn and quadratic total. That curve is the argument for the window and summarisation policies of Module 4 — and for showing a per-session budget in your dashboards.

payload.solution: Memory became a design instead of an accident: roles assigned by stored fields, history rebuilt server-side each turn, usage captured on every path, and the client downgraded from source of truth to renderer. The quadratic curve is now visible in the ledger rather than surprising in the bill, which is exactly the insight you need before choosing a window size. And because prompt version and provider message id ride along with every row, this store will later double as the raw material for feedback and evaluation — one persistence decision paying off across three modules.

payload.title: Give your app real memory
payload.prompt: Persist every turn of an existing chat app to a store with role, usage and prompt version. Reload history after a hard refresh and confirm the conversation returns. Then plot tokens-in against turn number over 20 turns and state where your window policy should start — with the number that justifies it.
payload.hint: If you cannot answer what happened last Tuesday for a given user, your persistence is text-only — add the evidence columns before you need them.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming the provider remembers the conversation
mistakes.fix: Stateless means stateless: send every message you want considered, or build on a provider storage feature you have read the retention rules for.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping history only in the browser
mistakes.fix: A refresh wipes it. Server-side store with ids and TTL is the source of truth; the client renders it.

mistakes.mistake: Resending unbounded history forever
mistakes.fix: Cost and context both grow without limit. Apply a window, a summary at the boundary, and a per-session token budget (Module 4).

mistakes.mistake: Storing strings and nothing else
mistakes.fix: Add prompt version, model, usage, finish reason and timestamps now — retrofitting evidence columns after the fact loses every incident you wanted to inspect.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: The chat API is stateless — what must an application do to create the illusion of memory? Name the three memory scopes with examples, and derive why conversation cost grows quadratically with turn count.
payload.answer: It must persist the conversation itself and re-send, every call, exactly the messages it wants considered: append each user turn, call the model, append the reply, and rebuild the transcript in order with roles from stored fields — there is no server-side thread the model recalls. Three scopes: request scope (retrieved documents, tool results, current question — assembled per call, discarded after); session scope (the turn transcript plus any rolling summary — minutes to days, bounded by a window, resent each turn); user scope (preferences, entitlements, saved entities — durable structured rows injected deliberately, never raw history). Quadratic growth: if turn N re-sends roughly N prior turns at a constant average size, its input cost is proportional to N, and the sum over N turns is proportional to N squared — e.g. 30 turns averaging 800 tokens costs about 800 × 465 ≈ 372,000 input tokens across the session, with the system prompt paid 30 times. Windows, summarisation and prefix caching are all responses to that curve.
payload.source: Core architecture question in LLM app interviews: who owns conversation state?

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: The model conditions only on what you send; memory is persistence plus a resend policy.
Persist roles, usage, prompt version, finish reason and latency — the strings alone are not enough.
Three scopes: request (this call), session (the window), user (structured, editable facts).
Full-history resend makes cost grow quadratically — visible in your ledger, managed in Module 4.
Roles come from stored fields, never from parsing content; dedupe double-submits with message ids.
Retention and deletion are part of the design: what you cannot delete, you should not store.

questions.prompt: Which statement about chat APIs and memory is correct?
options: Providers keep a thread per user automatically for 30 days
Memory is enabled by setting a session flag in the request
Assistant messages are stored by the model for later recall
Each call conditions only on the messages sent; persistence and re-sending are the application's job
questions.explanation: Statelessness of the model is the founding constraint; every memory feature is app-side reassembly.

questions.prompt: User preferences such as plan tier and saved addresses belong in:
options: Request scope, fetched fresh each call
User scope — structured, durable, injected selectively and deletable on request
Session scope, inside the rolling transcript
The system prompt, written once forever
questions.explanation: Durable facts are data, not dialogue: structured storage keeps them editable, bounded and auditable.

questions.prompt: Why does a 30-turn conversation cost far more than 30 single-turn calls of the same length?
options: Each turn re-sends prior history, so input tokens sum to roughly N squared/2 times the average turn size
Providers charge more per token for long sessions
Streaming is less efficient for long chats
System prompts scale with conversation length
questions.explanation: Resending history is the mechanism; the arithmetic of re-paying the prefix each turn is what Module 4 manages.

questions.prompt: A chat app loses the whole conversation when the user refreshes the page. Root cause:
options: The model has a short memory
The system prompt was too long
History lived only in client-side state — no server-side message store backs it
questions.explanation: Refresh destroys anything not persisted; the client should render history, never own it.

lessons.title: The Architecture Map: Client, Orchestration, Model and Tools
lessons.summary: Where the LLM actually sits: a four-layer map with one layer that owns everything hard, and the LLM-as-a-function mental model with a taxonomy of failure modes you can classify and monitor.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Draw the four-layer architecture of an LLM app and assign responsibilities to each layer
Justify the orchestration layer with four concrete engineering reasons
Apply the LLM-as-a-function model: typed input, typed output, declared failure modes
Classify a reported failure as transport, contract, model-behaviour or application error

payload.text: A startup calls the provider directly from React components: the key sits in the browser bundle, each component assembles its own prompt, nothing is logged, and one screen quietly sent a system prompt with 60,000 tokens of pasted documentation on every scroll event. The bill appeared first, then a bad weekend. The model did exactly what it was asked. The bug was a missing layer — the place where keys, prompts, budgets and evidence were supposed to live.

**The four layers.**

1. **Client** — the web or mobile surface: input, streaming render, feedback capture, error presentation. It authenticates to you, shows states, and holds no provider key and no prompt logic beyond what display requires.
2. **Orchestration layer** — your backend service. It owns session state, context assembly, the provider call with its timeouts and retries, response parsing and validation, guardrails, logging and tracing, cost metering, quotas and fallbacks. This is the layer the rest of the course builds.
3. **Capability layer** — the things the orchestrator coordinates: model APIs, tools (functions, databases, search, third-party services), and data (documents, vector store, cache).
4. **Response path** — validation, persistence, then streaming back through the same layers with events the client can render.

**Why the middle layer is non-negotiable.** (1) *Secrets*: a key in the client is a key in the wild; the server injects it (Module 2). (2) *Policy and quotas*: per-user rate limits, spend caps, moderation, prompt-version routing must be enforced where the user cannot edit the code. (3) *Metering and evidence*: one place writes the usage ledger and the trace that makes incidents answerable (Lesson 3). (4) *Portability and evolution*: one seam to swap providers, change prompts under version control, or add caching — instead of forty call sites. Client-side calls fail all four at once, which is why they are a demo-only pattern.

**The mental model: the LLM is a function.** Not a colleague, not a search engine — an expensive, slow, non-deterministic function with a typed contract:

    answer, usage, finish_reason = f(messages, params)

Input: messages plus parameters. Output: a message, token usage, a finish reason. It is pure in the sense that it has no hidden memory of your last call (Lesson 3), impure in the sense that the same input can produce different outputs (Module 2 controls variance), and fallible in ways ordinary functions are not — it can violate its own apparent contract. That last property is the whole taxonomy.

**Failure modes, four classes.**

- **Transport failures** — the call did not complete: 401/403 auth, 429 rate limit, 5xx provider, timeouts, connection reset. Retryable or infra issues; belongs in the call layer with backoff (Module 2).
- **Contract failures** — the call completed but the payload violates the shape you required: malformed JSON, missing field, tool arguments that fail schema, text where a number belongs. Fixed by validation and repair, not by retrying blindly (Module 2).
- **Model-behaviour failures** — the call succeeded and the content is wrong: hallucination, refusal, ignored instruction, rambling, truncation from a length cap (finish reason length). These are quality signals; they need evaluation and UX handling, not a retry (Module 3 and Module 8).
- **Application failures** — your bug: wrong history assembled, stale prompt version, a tool that throws, a budget miscomputed. The most common class and the one logs exist to catch.

**The monitoring consequence.** Distinguish the call failing from the call succeeding with a bad answer. Status-code dashboards see only the first. Thumbs-down rate, validation-failure rate, refusal rate and truncation rate are how you see the second — which is where most real defects live.

**Mermaid.** The diagram below is the shape to keep in your head: the client talks to you, you talk to everything else, and the model is one swappable node among tools and data — not the centre of the design.
payload.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Client: input, streaming render, feedback"] -->|"auth + turn"| O["Orchestration: assemble, call, validate, persist, meter"]
  O --> M["Model API (swappable)"]
  O --> T["Tools: search, DB, 3rd-party APIs"]
  O --> D[("Data: sessions, usage ledger, docs")]
  O -->|"SSE deltas + final event"| C
  C -.->|"no key, no prompt logic"| O

payload.title: Failure taxonomy: who handles it, how
rows: Backoff, circuit break, surface typed error
Bad JSON, missing field, bad tool args
UX states, eval sets, prompt change under gate
Wrong history, stale prompt, tool exception
Logs, trace id, fix the code

payload.title: Name the layers in your code
payload.text: receive, assemble, call, validate, persist. When a stage has a name, its metrics and its tests have somewhere to live.

payload.title: Retrying a behaviour failure is how you burn a budget
payload.text: A refusal or a hallucination will usually repeat. Retry transport classes only; route behaviour classes to UX and evaluation.

payload.title: Classify five production incidents on the map
payload.problem: An LLM feature gets five bug reports in a week. The team retries everything three times, which helps nothing and doubles spend on two of them. Draw the architecture, then classify each report and assign the correct owner and response.

steps.title: Draw the map with your actual components
steps.desc: Client (React chat page) → orchestrator (one Express route) → capabilities (provider API, Postgres session store, a search tool) → response path (SSE back through the orchestrator). Mark where secrets, quotas and logs sit — if a component has no home on the map, it has no owner in an incident.
steps.code_snippet:
[Browser] --auth--> [Orchestrator] --key--> [Model API]
     ^                     |  \---> [Search tool]
     | SSE deltas          \----> [Session store + usage ledger]
     +---------------------------------+

steps.title: Classify: 401 after a key rotation
steps.desc: Transport class, call layer. Not your prompt, not the model. Response: rotation runbook with dual-key overlap and a spend alert (Module 2) — retries would fail identically because the credential is wrong.

steps.title: Classify: response missing the summary field
steps.desc: Contract class, validate layer — the call succeeded. Response: schema validation with one repair attempt (Module 2). Blind retries re-roll the dice on cost; the repair loop tells the model exactly what was missing.

steps.title: Classify: answer cites a policy that was deleted last month
steps.desc: Model behaviour (grounding) plus possibly application (stale system prompt). Response: check prompt version and retrieval freshness in the trace, then eval cases and UX citation affordances (Module 3) — not a retry.

steps.title: Classify: history assembled without the last user turn
steps.desc: Application class. Response: logs with trace id, unit test on the assemble stage (it is pure, so this is cheap — see code). This is the class that status-code dashboards never show and traces always show.

payload.solution: Four of the five incidents were invisible to a retry policy and one was invisible to a status-code dashboard — the exact blind spots the taxonomy removes. With layers named, each report now has an owner: transport to the call layer with backoff, contract to validation with repair, behaviour to UX and evaluation, application to traces and tests. The retry-everything reflex is replaced by a classification reflex, and the bill stops doubling during incidents. The architecture map is not decoration; it is the routing table for every problem you will have.

payload.title: Map and refactor
payload.prompt: Take an app that calls a provider directly from the frontend or from scattered handlers. Draw the four-layer map with your real components. Then extract one orchestrator module with named stages, move the key server-side, add a trace id to every log line, and re-file your last three bug reports against the taxonomy — noting which class each one actually was.
payload.hint: If you cannot point to the layer that owns retries, you do not have a retry policy; you have hope.

mistakes.mistake: Holding provider keys in the client
mistakes.fix: Keys live in server config or a secret manager and are injected by the orchestrator; the client authenticates to you.

mistakes.mistake: Retry-everything on any failure
mistakes.fix: Transport classes retry with backoff; contract classes repair; behaviour classes go to UX and evals — retrying a refusal just bills you twice.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a wrong-but-well-formed answer as an infrastructure error
mistakes.fix: It is a behaviour failure: monitor validity, refusal, truncation and thumbs separately from HTTP status codes.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping trace ids because logs exist
mistakes.fix: Without one id across client, orchestrator and provider call, you cannot reconstruct a single user-reported failure.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the four-layer architecture of an LLM application, give four reasons the orchestration layer must exist, and classify these failures: 401 from the provider; JSON missing a required field; a confidently wrong policy answer; history assembled without the last user turn.
payload.answer: Layers: (1) client — input, streaming render, feedback, error presentation, no secrets; (2) orchestration — session state, context assembly, provider call with timeouts and retries, validation, guardrails, logging, metering, quotas; (3) capabilities — model APIs, tools, data stores; (4) response path — validation, persistence, streaming back. The middle layer exists because: secrets must never reach the client; quotas, moderation and prompt routing must be enforced where users cannot edit code; one place must write the usage ledger and trace that make incidents answerable; and a single seam enables provider swaps, prompt versioning and caching instead of forty call sites. Classification: 401 — transport, fix credentials and rotation, do not retry until fixed; missing field — contract, validate and run one repair attempt; confidently wrong answer — model behaviour, handle with evaluation, grounding and UX affordances, never retry; history missing the last turn — application bug, caught by trace and a unit test on the pure assemble stage.
payload.source: System-design round for LLM application roles: draw the architecture and triage failures.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Client talks to you; you own the orchestration layer; the model is one capability among tools and data.
Orchestration earns its keep: secrets, policy, metering and evolution — four reasons, all fatal when missing.
The LLM is a function with a typed contract and four failure classes: transport, contract, behaviour, application.
Retry transport, repair contract, evaluate behaviour, trace application — one reflex per class.
Status codes see only call failures; validity, refusal and truncation rates are how you see bad answers.
One trace id across layers turns user reports into reconstructable incidents.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility must never live in the client layer?
options: Holding the provider API key and enforcing spend quotas
questions.explanation: Keys and enforcement belong where the user cannot edit the code; everything else listed is presentation.

questions.prompt: The API returns 200 with valid JSON that omits a required field. Which failure class?
options: Contract — the call succeeded but the payload violates your schema
Transport, because the data is incomplete
questions.explanation: Contract failures are handled by validation and repair; the transport did its job.

questions.prompt: A refusal or a confidently hallucinated answer should be handled by:
options: Distinct UX states plus evaluation and grounding work — retrying repeats the behaviour and bills twice
questions.explanation: Model-behaviour failures are quality signals: they need evaluation and presentation, not transport retries.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum evidence needed to reconstruct a user-reported failure across layers?
options: Provider status page during the incident
One trace id present in client, orchestrator and provider-call logs, plus prompt version and usage
questions.explanation: A shared id plus version and usage is what makes an incident reconstructable instead of anecdotal.

modules.title: Module 2 — API Engineering: Credentials, Parameters, Structure, Failure
modules.summary: The unglamorous layer that decides whether an LLM feature survives contact with production: credential patterns and least privilege, the five parameters that actually shape output and the tasks each belongs to, structured responses via schema and tool calls with validation and repair, and the failure engineering stack — error classes, backoff with jitter, rate limits, idempotency, and how much provider abstraction is worth building.

lessons.title: Credentials: API Keys, OAuth and Least Privilege
lessons.summary: A provider key is a bearer capability with your money attached. Where it lives, how it rotates, what a proxy buys you, and when enterprise OAuth or a gateway is the right shape instead.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain why an API key is a bearer capability and what blast radius that implies
Choose between client-held keys, a backend proxy and OAuth or gateway access
Design key rotation with a dual-key overlap window and per-environment separation
Apply least privilege in practice: scopes, spend caps, quotas and log redaction

payload.text: A developer pastes a provider key into a public Discord to help a friend debug. Within the hour, scripts are burning through the account; the usage dashboard climbs past four hundred dollars before anyone wakes up. The post-mortem said be more careful. The real lesson is structural: a bearer key grants everything to whoever holds it, so the design question is never how to hide the key harder — it is how few places hold it, how fast you can revoke it, and how small the damage is when (not if) one leaks.

**What a key is.** Nearly all chat APIs authenticate with a header: Authorization: Bearer followed by a long opaque string. That string is a bearer capability — no further identity, no scope narrowing, no way to tell which app used it unless you gave each app its own. Consequences follow directly: treat it like cash, assume it will eventually appear in a log or a repo, and design so that a leak costs bounded money and bounded time.

**Three deployment shapes.**

1. **Key in the client** — browser or mobile app calls the provider directly. Acceptable only for personal local tools. Extracting a key from a shipped bundle takes minutes; traffic inspection gets the rest. Do not ship it.
2. **Backend proxy — the default for product work.** The client authenticates to your API with your own session tokens; your server holds the provider key and forwards. Everything good lives here: per-user quotas, spend caps, unified logging, prompt versioning, cache hooks, and one seam to swap providers (Lesson 4). Your API becomes the thing to secure — rate limit it, authenticate it, and never let it become an open relay.
3. **Enterprise shapes — OAuth and gateways.** When access is on behalf of a user through a third-party platform (marketplace apps, org-managed seats), OAuth 2.1 with authorization code plus PKCE fits: short-lived access tokens, refresh tokens you can revoke, scopes that bound what the app may do. Some enterprise model platforms sign requests with cloud IAM credentials instead of static keys, and many organisations route every team through an internal LLM gateway that owns the provider keys so metering and policy are central. Exact mechanisms differ per provider and change often — verify current docs before you build against a blog post.

**Least privilege, concretely.** (1) Separate keys per environment — a low-limit dev key so experiments cannot drain prod's budget. (2) Separate keys per service or tenant where the provider supports it, so you can attribute usage and revoke one without a fleet-wide outage. (3) Spend caps and hard limits at the provider account: a monthly ceiling and alert thresholds are the only control that works while you sleep. (4) Anomaly alerts: a key that suddenly serves ten times its usual token rate, or appears from a new region, is compromised until proven busy. (5) Log redaction: never write the Authorization header or the key to logs, traces, error reports or client-visible payloads — one stray to_string of your request config has burned many teams.

**Rotation is a design, not an incident response.** Issue the new key, deploy it alongside the old, confirm traffic shifts, revoke the old, keep the rollback window. Dual-key overlap turns rotation from a Friday-night emergency into a Tuesday-morning deploy. Pair it with a written runbook: leaked key means revoke first, investigate second — the usage dashboard is readable after the bleeding stops.

**Hygiene list.** Keys in environment variables or a secret manager, never in code or config files committed to git (history counts — a rotated key still lurks in old commits). Pre-commit secret scanning. No keys in client-side code. Redact in exception handlers: HTTP libraries love to include request headers in error messages.

payload.title: Deployment shapes and what they buy
rows: Central policy, budget, audit across teams

payload.title: One key per environment is the cheapest safety rail you will ever install
payload.text: A dev key with a small hard limit turns a Sunday incident into a five-dollar learning experience.

payload.title: A key in a git commit is still live after you delete the file
payload.text: History keeps it. Rotate, then scrub if the repo is shared — deletion is not revocation.

payload.title: Contain a leaked key and redesign so it cannot happen again
payload.problem: A key from a staging environment is found in a public repository fork. Usage is spiking. Today there is one shared key for all environments, no caps, and the server logs full request configs. Contain the incident, then restructure.

steps.title: Contain: revoke, then investigate
steps.desc: Create a replacement key at the provider, set a hard monthly cap before deploying it, roll the service, revoke the compromised key, and only then read the usage dashboard. Every minute spent analysing before revoking is a minute of spend.
steps.code_snippet:
# runbook order - do not reorder
1. provider: create key B, set hard monthly cap
2. deploy: env now uses key B (dual-key overlap not needed - A is dead)
3. provider: revoke key A immediately
4. read usage dashboard: which endpoints, which hours, total cost
5. rotate any other secret that shared the commit history

steps.title: Attribute: give each environment and service its own key
steps.desc: Three keys now exist: dev (tiny cap), staging (medium), prod (real cap plus alerts). Each service that calls the provider gets its own so usage rows attribute to a caller and one leak costs one blast radius.

steps.title: Stop the bleeding next time: caps, alerts, scanning
steps.desc: Provider-side: monthly ceiling, 50 percent and 80 percent alerts, anomaly alert on token-rate spikes. Repo-side: pre-commit secret scanning that fails the commit on key-shaped strings. These are the controls that work while nobody is watching.

steps.title: Fix the observability leak
steps.desc: Audit every log line and error payload for header dumps; add a redaction helper in the HTTP client so an exception can never print the Authorization value. Then confirm: trigger a 400 locally and read the log — if the key appears, the fix is not done.

payload.solution: Revocation first turned a live incident into a cost report. The structural fix — per-environment keys with independent caps — means the next staging leak costs whatever staging is allowed to spend, not whatever a bored script can do at 3 a.m. Caps and anomaly alerts moved the detection from human luck to provider telemetry, and log redaction closed the quiet path where keys escape through stack traces. Least privilege is not a slogan here: it is the difference between one key with unlimited blast radius and five keys with five boring ones.

payload.title: Audit and re-key
payload.prompt: List every place your provider credential exists: repo, CI variables, hosting config, dashboards, laptops. Split into per-environment keys with caps. Set an alert. Then deliberately trigger an error and check your logs for leakage. Write the four-line rotation runbook you would follow at 3 a.m.
payload.hint: If you cannot name the monthly ceiling on your account right now, you do not have a budget — you have a hope.

mistakes.mistake: Shipping the provider key to browsers or mobile apps
mistakes.fix: Client authenticates to your backend; the backend holds the key. There is no client-side variant that is safe for production.

mistakes.mistake: One shared key for dev, staging and prod
mistakes.fix: Separate keys with separate caps: a staging experiment must never be able to drain the production budget.

mistakes.mistake: No spend cap or alerting at the provider
mistakes.fix: Your retry logic is not a budget. Hard ceilings and anomaly alerts are the controls that work while you sleep.

mistakes.mistake: Logging full request configs, including headers
mistakes.fix: Redact Authorization in HTTP clients and exception handlers; assume anything logged will be shipped to a third-party log service.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain why a provider API key is called a bearer capability, describe the backend-proxy pattern and what it buys beyond secrecy, and give a rotation runbook with a dual-key overlap.
payload.answer: Bearer capability: the key alone authorises the request — no further identity, no narrowing of scope, and no intrinsic attribution of which app used it. Whoever holds it can spend at the holder account rate limits allow, so leakage equals unauthorised spend until revocation. Backend proxy: clients authenticate to your API with your session credentials; your server injects the provider key server-side. It buys more than secrecy — per-user quotas and spend caps, unified usage logging and metering, cache and prompt-version hooks, moderation chokepoints, and a single seam for provider swap — while turning the security perimeter into your own API, which must itself be rate limited and authenticated. Rotation runbook: (1) issue key B and set its cap; (2) deploy B alongside A so traffic can shift gradually (dual-key overlap); (3) confirm traffic on B via usage attribution; (4) revoke A at the provider; (5) keep the rollback path until one full billing cycle is clean. For a suspected leak, skip the overlap: revoke first, investigate second.
payload.source: Standard question in LLM platform interviews: key management and blast radius.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: A provider key is cash with no scope: treat leakage as an unbounded spend event until revoked.
Client-held keys are demo-only; product work goes through a backend proxy you secure and meter.
Enterprise access adds OAuth with revocable scopes or central gateways — verify current provider docs.
Least privilege = per-environment keys, per-service attribution, hard spend caps, anomaly alerts, redacted logs.
Rotation is a deploy with a dual-key overlap, not a Friday-night emergency.
Revoke first, investigate second; history keeps deleted keys alive, so deletion is not revocation.

questions.prompt: Why is a provider API key dangerous by construction?
options: It is a bearer capability: whoever holds it can spend, with no further identity or scope
questions.explanation: No narrowing and no attribution means blast radius equals everything the account can do.

questions.prompt: Where should the provider key live in a production web assistant?
options: In the frontend bundle for simplicity
In the user profile so quotas can be checked client-side
Server-side in your orchestrator; the client authenticates to your API
In the system prompt so the model can manage it
questions.explanation: Server-side key plus your own auth is the default shape; the client is never a secret store.

questions.prompt: The safest sequencing for routine key rotation:
options: Delete the old key first, then deploy the new one
Rotate in the code but keep the old key as backup forever
Wait for an incident to justify rotation
Deploy the new key alongside the old, confirm traffic shifts, then revoke the old
questions.explanation: Dual-key overlap removes the all-or-nothing cutover; revoke only after the new key is proven in traffic.

questions.prompt: A staging key leaks and begins burning tokens. First action:
options: Revoke the key at the provider, then investigate the usage after the bleeding stops
Annotate the usage chart for later analysis
Add more logging to catch the source
questions.explanation: Containment is revoke-first: analysis waits until spend is stopped.

lessons.title: The Parameters That Shape Output
lessons.summary: Temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop and seed: what each one actually does, the task each belongs to, and the silent failures — truncation above all — that happen when parameters are set by folklore.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain the mechanism of temperature and top_p and why you normally tune one, not both
Match parameter profiles to extraction, drafting and brainstorming tasks
Detect truncation through finish_reason and handle it instead of shipping cut-off answers
Describe what seed does and does not guarantee

payload.text: An extraction pipeline scores 100 percent on its golden set in development and fails 8 percent of production tickets with unparseable answers. The prompt did not change. Someone did: a helpful colleague bumped temperature from 0 to 0.7 globally because a blog post said higher temperature makes models more creative, and creativity is good. The extraction task did not want creativity. It wanted the same answer every time.

**Sampling in one paragraph.** A language model produces a probability distribution over its next token; sampling picks from that distribution. Application parameters reshape the distribution before the pick. Understanding which knob changes which shape is the difference between deliberate settings and folklore.

**Temperature.** The logits are divided by T before the softmax: low T sharpens the distribution toward the most likely tokens (T near 0 approaches argmax behaviour), T of 1 leaves the trained distribution alone, and T above 1 flattens it, making rare tokens more likely. Practical bands, for typical general-purpose chat models: 0 to 0.3 for extraction, classification, SQL generation and anything you will parse; around 0.7 for conversational drafting; above 1 rarely, mostly for deliberate variation. Caveats worth internalising: temperature 0 is highly repeatable but not guaranteed bit-identical across runs or model revisions, because serving stacks batch and quantise differently — treat it as very low variance, not determinism.

**Top_p (nucleus sampling).** Keep the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, and sample only within it. It also trims the tail, for a different shape of control. Because both knobs narrow the same distribution, changing both at once makes it impossible to attribute a behaviour change — and providers ship different defaults, so read the default before assuming. The working rule: tune temperature first, leave top_p alone unless you have a specific reason and a test to verify it.

**max_tokens — the cap with a cliff.** This bounds output tokens only; input is billed separately. Generate past the cap and generation stops mid-sentence with a finish reason of length. Nothing throws. Nothing warns the user. You simply ship a truncated answer that reads like the model got tired — the most common silent failure in LLM apps. Fixes: set the cap with headroom above your longest expected answer; check finish_reason on every response; and build a handler — continue, re-ask for brevity, or show a truncated state — rather than pretending the answer was complete. Note for later: on some reasoning-style models the cap interacts with internal reasoning tokens, and per-message versus per-request semantics differ by provider; verify current docs.

**Stop sequences.** Hard terminators: generation ends when one appears, and the sequence is not returned. Useful to end structured output at a known marker or cap open-ended generation without guessing a token count. Traps: user content that contains the stop string cuts the answer short (never use user-controllable text as a stop), and stops cannot substitute for validation — they are a blunt cut, not a contract.

**Seed.** Where a provider supports it, a seed improves reproducibility of sampling for A/B tests and eval reruns. It is best-effort: model version updates, backend changes and concurrency can still shift output. Use seeds to stabilise experiments; never as a correctness guarantee or an idempotency mechanism (Lesson 4 covers the real one).

**The principle underneath.** Parameters reduce variance; prompts and structure reduce error. No setting of temperature makes a vague instruction specific, and the fanciest sampling cannot invent a field your schema forgot. Get the contract right first (Lesson 3), then choose the narrowest distribution that still does the job.

payload.title: Parameter cheat sheet
rows: Treating it as determinism or idempotency

payload.title: Check finish_reason before you render
payload.text: It is one field that separates an honest answer from a cut-off one. Wire it into metrics the day you ship.

payload.title: Temperature 0 is not a correctness guarantee
payload.text: Low variance, yes; identical output forever, no — model revisions and serving details still move underneath you.

payload.title: Tune an extraction endpoint by task, then debug the production failure
payload.problem: A ticket-triage endpoint extracts JSON from support text. In staging it is perfect; in production, 8 percent of responses fail to parse and users see a generic error. The team wants to raise max_tokens and add retries. Find the real cause with parameters and telemetry.

steps.title: Read the telemetry, not the vibes
steps.desc: The team logged errors but not parameters or finish reasons. Add three fields to every log line: model, full parameter set, finish_reason. One day of production data later, the failure rows are overwhelmingly finish_reason: length on responses whose JSON was cut mid-string — the cap was 120 tokens, the tickets got longer, and the schema grew a field.

steps.title: Right-size the cap with headroom
steps.desc: Measure the p95 of complete outputs (186 tokens), set max_tokens to 320, and keep the length check. The cap is now a guard against runaway cost, not a cause of silent truncation.

steps.title: Lock the sampling profile to the task
steps.desc: Extract endpoint pinned at temperature 0 and default top_p, with a code comment stating why — so the next helpful edit has to argue with a reason instead of a habit. Drafting endpoints keep their own profile in configuration, named per task, not one global value.

steps.title: Add the regression gate
steps.desc: Run the golden set on every parameter or prompt change. Truncation rate joins validity rate as a first-class metric: a change that fixes parse rate but doubles truncation is not a fix.

payload.solution: The failure was never the model being insufficiently creative — it was a length cap colliding with real ticket sizes, invisible because finish_reason was not logged. Instrument first, and the parameter discussion becomes evidence: raise the cap with headroom, pin temperature to the task, keep top_p untouched, and gate changes on a golden set that scores both validity and truncation. The deeper fix is organisational: named profiles per task replace folklore, so the next change to sampling has to be a decision with a measurement, not a vibe.

payload.title: Build a parameter profile and hunt truncation
payload.prompt: For one real endpoint, define a named parameter profile with a comment per choice. Log model, parameters, finish_reason and tokens_out on every call for a day. Report: truncation rate, p95 tokens_out, and whether your max_tokens has headroom. Then run the same 10 requests at temperature 0 and 0.7 and diff what changed.
payload.hint: If your logs cannot answer what parameters produced a given answer, you cannot debug drift — and you cannot A/B honestly.

mistakes.mistake: Raising temperature hoping for better accuracy
mistakes.fix: Temperature trades determinism for variety. Accuracy comes from the contract: prompt, schema, examples — then the narrowest sampling that still works.

mistakes.mistake: Tuning temperature and top_p together
mistakes.fix: Both reshape the same distribution; changing both destroys attribution. Tune temperature first, leave top_p at default unless testing one hypothesis.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring finish_reason and shipping truncated answers
mistakes.fix: Check it on every response, meter it, and route length results to a continuation or truncation-aware UI path.

mistakes.mistake: Treating seed as determinism or idempotency
mistakes.fix: Seeds stabilise experiments best-effort; real idempotency is keys and persistence (Lesson 4), not sampling.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain what temperature and top_p each control and why you normally change only one. What does a finish_reason of length mean, and how should an application respond? What does a seed guarantee?
payload.answer: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax: low values sharpen the distribution toward the most likely tokens, 1 leaves it as trained, above 1 flattens it toward variety. Top_p keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p. Both narrow the same distribution, so tuning both at once makes behaviour changes unattributable; the working rule is to tune temperature first and leave top_p at the provider default. finish_reason length means generation hit the max_tokens ceiling and stopped mid-answer: the response is a prefix, not an answer — so the app must check the field, meter truncations, and either continue generation, re-request a shorter answer, or present an explicit truncated state instead of rendering a cut-off reply as complete. A seed, where supported, is a best-effort request for reproducible sampling to stabilise evals and A/B comparisons; model revisions and serving changes can still alter output, so it is neither determinism nor idempotency.
payload.source: Applied question in LLM integration interviews: sampling parameters and their failure modes.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Temperature sharpens or flattens the distribution; top_p trims the nucleus; tune one, not both.
Named parameter profiles per task beat one global creativity toggle.
max_tokens is a cliff: finish_reason length means the answer is a prefix — check it every time.
Stop sequences are blunt cuts that can collide with user text; never use them as validation.
Seeds stabilise experiments best-effort; parameters reduce variance, contracts reduce error.
Log parameters and finish reasons with every call, or drift is invisible.

questions.prompt: An extraction endpoint fails intermittently with cut-off JSON. Most likely parameter cause:
options: max_tokens too small — generation stopped at the cap with finish_reason length
questions.explanation: A length-capped generation is a prefix; the fix is headroom plus a finish_reason check, not creativity settings.

questions.prompt: Which parameter change most directly increases answer variety?
options: Raising temperature or lowering top_p to widen sampling options
questions.explanation: Higher temperature flattens the distribution; top_p and temperature are the variety knobs — the rest do something else entirely.

questions.prompt: Why should temperature and top_p not be tuned at the same time?
options: Providers reject requests that set both
Both reshape the same sampling distribution, so simultaneous changes make behaviour differences unattributable
questions.explanation: One variable per experiment; otherwise you cannot say which knob caused the change.

questions.prompt: What does a seed actually provide?
options: Best-effort sampling reproducibility for evals and A/B tests, not a correctness guarantee
questions.explanation: It stabilises experiments where supported; model and serving changes still move output underneath.

lessons.title: Structured Responses: Schema, Tool Calls and Validation
lessons.summary: Applications need values, not prose. Choose between JSON mode, schema-constrained output and tool calls; design a schema the model can satisfy; then validate, repair once, and degrade gracefully — because structure shifts errors from syntax to semantics.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Choose among JSON mode, strict JSON schema and tool calls for a given output need
Design a flat, typed schema with enums that a model can satisfy reliably
Implement validate-then-repair-once with a degraded fallback
Explain why schema-valid output can still be semantically wrong

payload.text: A shipping app calls JSON.parse on every model response. It works in testing. Then a user pastes a returns request that begins with the words "Sure - here is the JSON you asked for" and the model helpfully wraps the object in a friendly sentence and a code fence. JSON.parse throws, the request is marked failed, and the user is told something went wrong — because an application trusted a probabilistic system to emit exactly one syntactic format with no enforcement behind it.

**Why structure is a first-class problem.** Your program wants a value: priority, category, list of clauses. The model speaks tokens. Without enforcement, every integration grows the same brittle stack — prompt says JSON, hope for the best, JSON.parse with a try, then a regex to strip a leading fence. That stack works until the day it does not, and the failure always lands on the user.

**Three mechanisms, three guarantees.**

1. **JSON mode / prompted JSON.** The API or your prompt asks for JSON only. Cheap and universal; it improves the odds dramatically; it does not guarantee syntax, and it certainly does not guarantee your schema. Always validate.
2. **Constrained structured output (response_format with a JSON schema).** The provider grammar-constrains decoding so the output conforms to your declared schema: valid JSON, correct types, required fields honoured. Feature surface varies — some providers restrict which JSON Schema keywords are supported, how additionalProperties behaves, or whether enums and nesting are fully enforced — so verify current docs for your model. This is the default choice when you need a value to consume.
3. **Tool or function calling.** You declare a function signature; the model returns structured arguments, optionally choosing to call it. Use tools when the structure is an action (write a row, call an API) or when you want the answer shaped as a call; use structured output when the structure is a value to display or store. Tool calls also stream as partial argument text — the same partial-parse problem Module 3 handles on the client. Part II, M6 goes deep on tools; here it is simply the third structure option.

**Schema design is prompt design.** The schema is instructions the decoder enforces syntactically, not semantics. Guidelines that measurably help: flat structures over deep nesting; enums for every closed set (never "a priority string"); explicit required lists; numbers as numbers so ranges can be checked; short, data-shaped field names (summary, not "the_summary_of_the_ticket_in_one_line"); and a modest field count — every field is a place for a hallucinated value. If the model must abstain, encode that: an answerable boolean or a null-by-default field beats free text for expressing ignorance.

**The failure taxonomy shifts.** With no enforcement you fight syntax errors. With enforcement you fight semantics: right shape, wrong content. Missing or empty fields, enum values chosen wrongly, entities that do not exist in the input, confident guesses where the source was silent. So the pipeline becomes: parse (now almost always safe) → validate against the schema (types, required, enums) → semantic checks you write (ranges, referential consistency, "this date appears in the input") → then a single repair attempt that feeds the validator error back as a user-role correction → then a degraded path that returns what is known plus an explicit flag. One repair, not five: repeated repair loops multiply cost and latency while chasing tails.

**Structure is not truth.** A schema-conformant object full of invented order numbers is still a hallucination — grounding and verification are separate problems (Module 4 and the RAG course). Schema removes a class of bugs; it does not remove the need for evaluation.

payload.title: Mechanism comparison
rows: Likely valid JSON; schema only if asked nicely
You need a value to consume — default choice
Arguments shaped as a function call
The structure is an action, or an agent loop

payload.title: Encode abstention in the schema
payload.text: An answerable flag or null-by-default field turns "I do not know" into a value your code can route on — far better than parsing hedged prose.

payload.title: Schema-valid is not accurate
payload.text: Constrained decoding fixes syntax, not truth. Keep grounding and evaluation in the plan; a perfect object of invented facts is still wrong.

payload.title: From hopeful JSON.parse to a validated, repairable contract
payload.problem: A support triage endpoint prompts for JSON and parses with try/catch; failures are generic errors. Rebuild it: schema, constrained output, semantic checks, one repair attempt, degraded fallback — and define the metrics that tell you whether it is working.

steps.title: BEFORE: the hopeful version and its three failure shapes
steps.desc: One prompt line saying return JSON, a bare JSON.parse in a try block, and an empty catch. Failures come in three shapes that all reach the user identically: preamble text before the object, a missing field the app dereferences, and a priority value like "ASAP" that is not in the enum your switch statement assumes.

steps.title: Declare the contract: flat schema, closed sets, abstention
steps.desc: Four required fields, enums for every closed set, boolean for the escalation decision, and additionalProperties false so stray fields cannot smuggle in. Flat by design: each nesting level is another place for empty objects.

steps.title: Constrain, validate, repair once
steps.desc: Request structured output against the schema; validate on arrival with a real validator; on failure, one repair call whose user message contains the exact validator issues. Cap repairs at one — further attempts mostly re-roll the same dice at full price.

steps.title: Degrade honestly, and measure
steps.desc: If repair fails, return a degraded marker that routes to a human with the raw text attached, never a generic error. Metrics: validity rate (schema pass on first try), repair success rate, degraded rate, and semantic-check failures — the last one is your true quality signal, because syntax is now nearly free.

payload.solution: The endpoint stopped failing at the syntax layer entirely and started failing at the semantic layer where failures are visible and actionable. One repair attempt converts most residual schema failures into successes at bounded cost; the degraded path turns the rest into human work with context instead of a dead user. And the metrics finally separate the two questions you care about: can the model produce the shape (validity rate), and is the content right (semantic failures, thumbs, downstream corrections)? That separation is what lets you change prompts and schemas with evidence instead of anxiety.

payload.title: Constrain one endpoint properly
payload.prompt: Take one place your app parses model text with regex or JSON.parse. Write a schema with enums and required fields, request constrained output, add validation and one repair attempt, and log validity and degraded rates over 50 calls. Name one semantic check you can write that the schema cannot express.
payload.hint: If a closed set of values exists in your code as a switch statement, it belongs in the schema as an enum — not in a prompt as prose.

mistakes.mistake: Prompting for JSON and parsing without validating
mistakes.fix: Prompts persuade; schemas constrain. Validate every payload with a real validator, including constrained outputs — semantics still need checking.

mistakes.mistake: Giant deeply nested schemas with twenty fields
mistakes.fix: Flat, few, typed fields with enums. Each field is a hallucination surface; each nesting level multiplies empty-object risk.

mistakes.mistake: Repair loops of five attempts
mistakes.fix: One repair with the exact validation errors, then degrade. Endless repair multiplies cost and latency while mostly re-rolling the same tail.

mistakes.mistake: Treating schema-valid output as accurate output
mistakes.fix: Structure is not truth: keep grounding, citations and evaluation in the loop, and measure semantic failures separately from syntax.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Compare prompted JSON, strict structured output and tool calling as mechanisms for machine-consumable responses. Give four schema-design rules and describe the validate-repair-degrade pipeline.
payload.answer: Prompted JSON asks the model for JSON via the prompt or a JSON mode: universal and cheap, but syntax and schema are best-effort — always validate. Strict structured output submits your JSON schema to the provider, which constrains decoding so responses conform to it (types, required fields, enums, subject to each provider’s supported subset — verify docs); this is the default when you need a value. Tool calling declares a function signature and returns arguments shaped as a call — right when the structure is an action, or inside an agent loop. Schema rules: flat over nested; enums for all closed sets; explicit required lists with numbers as numbers; modest field count with data-shaped names; and an abstention field such as answerable when the model may legitimately not know. Pipeline: validate against the schema, run app-written semantic checks, then one repair attempt that feeds validator issues back as a correction, then a degraded path that returns partial data with a flag and routes to a human — never a generic error. Metrics: first-try validity, repair success, degraded rate, semantic failures.
payload.source: Common LLM integration interview question: getting reliable structure out of a generative model.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Three structure options: prompted JSON (hope), strict schema (constraint), tool calls (actions).
Design schemas flat, closed and typed; every field is a hallucination surface.
Enforcement moves failures from syntax to semantics — validate, then check meaning yourself.
Repair once with the exact validator error, then degrade to a flagged human path.
A perfect object of invented facts is still wrong: structure is not truth.
Log validity, repair and degraded rates as first-class product metrics.

questions.prompt: What does strict structured output guarantee that prompted JSON does not?
options: That the content is factually correct
That the model will refuse off-schema requests
Conformance to the declared schema — valid JSON with the required types and fields
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding fixes syntax and shape; truth and accuracy remain separate problems.

questions.prompt: A ticket schema needs a priority from a fixed set. The right design:
options: A free string with a prompt hint listing the values
An enum in the schema, enforced by constrained decoding
A number from 1 to 10 with documentation
Three booleans the app converts to a priority
questions.explanation: Closed sets belong in the schema: prose hints are suggestions, enums are constraints.

questions.prompt: Validation fails on the first response. Best next step:
options: Send one repair request containing the exact validator issues, then degrade if it still fails
Retry the identical request up to five times
Return a generic error to the user
Strip the invalid fields and hope
questions.explanation: One targeted repair is cheap and informative; blind repeats re-roll the same dice, and silent stripping hides failures.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a semantic failure rather than a syntactic one?
options: The response is not valid JSON
Valid JSON with an order number that does not exist in the input
A trailing code fence around the object
questions.explanation: Shape is right, content is invented — the class that schema cannot catch and evaluation must.

lessons.title: Failures: Errors, Backoff, Rate Limits, Idempotency and Abstraction
lessons.summary: Every production LLM call eventually fails. Classify errors as retryable or terminal, back off with jitter and budgets, respect rate limits as backpressure, make submission idempotent, and decide how much provider abstraction is actually worth.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify provider and network errors into retryable, terminal and not-an-error classes
Implement exponential backoff with full jitter under a deadline budget
Handle 429 responses with Retry-After, queues and concurrency caps
Explain idempotency for LLM calls and weigh a thin provider adapter against lock-in

payload.text: A supposedly resilient client retries five times with no jitter. One provider blip hits a thousand in-flight requests; every one of them retries in lockstep at the same millisecond, the provider stays down longer, and the app turns a thirty-second blip into a ten-minute outage. Worse: for two endpoints, the timed-out request had actually succeeded upstream — so the retry bought two generations and took two side effects. Resilience without classification is just amplified damage.

**Error classes decide everything downstream.** A flat try/retry-everything policy is how outages get amplified. Sort errors first.

- **Terminal client errors (4xx, mostly).** 400 bad request, 401 bad or missing credential, 403 forbidden, 404 unknown model. Retrying changes nothing; the fix is in your code or config. Retrying these is how a misdeploy burns budget for an hour.
- **Rate and usage limits (429).** Retryable, but as backpressure, not hammering: honour the Retry-After header where present, queue locally, reduce concurrency. Distinguish the limit types — requests per minute, tokens per minute, concurrent requests — because the correct response differs: shedding load, delaying, or re-shaping batch sizes.
- **Server and network errors (5xx, timeouts, resets).** Retryable with backoff. One subtlety: a read timeout after the request was fully sent is ambiguous — the provider may have generated (and billed) the answer you never saw. Which is exactly why idempotency matters below.
- **Not errors: refusals and filter hits.** The call succeeded and the model declined or content was blocked. Handle as a domain outcome with its own UX (Module 3); never retry, because the second attempt usually behaves the same and bills again.
- **Contract failures.** Valid response, invalid payload (Lesson 3): repair once, do not retry blindly.

**Backoff recipe.** Exponential backoff with full jitter: sleep a random duration up to min(cap, base × 2^attempt) — randomised because synchronised retries are what turned your client into the outage. Bound it three ways: maximum attempts (three to five), a deadline for the whole user-facing request, and a retry budget (attempts × expected time must fit inside the deadline — a retry that would exceed the user's patience should fail fast with a typed error instead). Honour Retry-After overrides. Wrap the lot in a circuit breaker: after a threshold of failures to one provider, stop sending and fail fast or fail over for a cooldown, so a dead dependency does not consume every worker.

**Timeouts are two budgets, not one.** Time-to-first-byte (or first delta, when streaming) detects a hung connection early; total time caps runaway generations. Your proxy timeout must sit outside the client's, and each layer should time out before the layer above it, so the innermost failure produces a typed error rather than a dropped socket.

**Rate limits as design.** Client-side token buckets keep you under the provider's documented ceilings before you ever see a 429; per-user quotas keep one user from exhausting the shared budget; priority queues put interactive turns ahead of background batch jobs — the first taste of the cost engineering in Module 10.

**Idempotency.** The same request twice is two generations and two bills: LLM calls are not idempotent. Duplicates arrive from client retries after ambiguous timeouts, double-submits, and queue redelivery. The app-level answer: a client-generated idempotency key per logical action; a persistence check that returns the stored result if that key was already completed; and side effects keyed on the action id, not on the call. You cannot make sampling identical — you can make a user pay once for a message.

**Abstraction versus lock-in.** A thin internal interface — chat(request) returning normalised output, usage, finish reason and a small error taxonomy — buys provider swap for price, latency or availability, plus unified logging. The costs are real: lowest-common-denominator features (provider-specific caching controls, sampling extras and tool modes leak), streaming formats differ, and the adapter is code you maintain. Practical stance: do not build a multi-provider framework before you have a second provider; do design the seam — one module with normalised errors and usage — and keep an escape hatch to the raw client. Lock-in is a choice with a price; accidental lock-in forty call sites deep is just a default.

payload.title: Error classification and first response
rows: Fix credential or request; alert on sudden spikes
Backoff honouring Retry-After; queue and shed load
Full-jitter backoff inside a deadline; circuit break
Domain outcome with its own UX state

payload.title: Full jitter is not optional
payload.text: Randomised backoff is what stops your clients from synchronising into a thundering herd that extends the very outage you were defending against.

payload.title: A retry is a second purchase
payload.text: Ambiguous timeouts may hide a successful, billed generation. Idempotency keys and persistence are the cost control, not the retry counter.

payload.title: Harden a call path: classify, back off, break, dedupe
payload.problem: An assistant has naive try/catch retries, a fixed 60-second timeout, no idempotency, and direct provider calls in five services. During a provider incident it takes itself down. Harden the path and classify five incident symptoms correctly.

steps.title: Normalise errors at the seam
steps.desc: One adapter wraps the provider SDK and maps everything to a small taxonomy: auth, bad_request, rate_limit (with retryAfterMs), overloaded, timeout_ambiguous, refusal, other. Five services now branch on types instead of string-matching messages — and this module is the only place provider error shapes exist.

steps.title: Two timeouts, class-aware retries, a breaker
steps.desc: First-byte timeout of eight seconds, total of thirty. Retries only on overloaded and retryAfterMs-respecting rate_limit, full jitter, deadline-checked. Breaker opens after a run of failures and fails fast for thirty seconds — the app now degrades in one second instead of tying up workers for a minute.

steps.title: Make submission idempotent
steps.desc: The client generates an idem key per user message id. Submit checks the completed-actions table first: ambiguous timeouts now return the stored result instead of double-generating, and side effects (ticket created, email sent) key on the action id.

steps.title: Classify the incident symptoms
steps.desc: Five reports, five classes: burst of 401s after a rotation — terminal, fix credentials, no retries; 429s at traffic peak — backpressure, honour Retry-After, shed batch jobs; 500s from the provider — retry with jitter, breaker opens; user sees a policy decline — refusal, not an error, distinct UX; one response missing a field — contract, repair once. None of the five is helped by generic five-times retries.

payload.solution: The hardened path fails fast on what it cannot fix, backs off on what it can, and refuses to buy the same generation twice. The adapter turned provider-specific chaos into seven error kinds the whole system understands, which is also exactly the right amount of abstraction: one seam, normalised errors and usage, and an escape hatch to the raw client — enough to swap or fail over, not enough to become a framework you maintain forever. During the next incident the dashboard will show breaker state and rate-limit waits instead of a wall of worker timeouts, and the bill will show one generation per message.

payload.title: Write the classifier and the runbook
payload.prompt: Wrap your provider calls in one adapter that normalises errors into a small taxonomy with retryable flags and retryAfterMs. Add full-jitter backoff under a deadline, plus an idempotency check on your most expensive action. Then write the one-page incident runbook: which classes page a human at night, which shed load silently, and which never retry.
payload.hint: If your retry helper cannot answer is this retryable?, it is an outage amplifier wearing a safety costume.

mistakes.mistake: Retrying every failure including 400s, 401s and refusals
mistakes.fix: Classify first: terminal errors need fixes, refusals are domain outcomes, only overloaded and rate-limit classes deserve retries.

mistakes.mistake: Exponential backoff without jitter
mistakes.fix: Synchronised clients create thundering herds; full jitter spreads retries and shortens outages.

mistakes.mistake: One long timeout and no first-byte budget
mistakes.fix: Separate first-byte and total budgets; let each layer time out before the layer above so errors stay typed.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring ambiguous timeouts and duplicate submits
mistakes.fix: Idempotency keys plus a completed-actions store: one logical action bills and acts once, no matter how many transports failed.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Classify these provider responses and state the correct handling: 401, 429 with Retry-After, 503, a content refusal, and a valid JSON response missing a required field. Then explain full-jitter backoff, the two timeout budgets, and why LLM calls need application-level idempotency.
payload.answer: 401 — terminal: bad credential, no retry until fixed; alert if it appears in a burst. 429 with Retry-After — retryable as backpressure: wait at least the given delay, queue, shed non-interactive load; distinguish requests-per-minute from tokens-per-minute limits. 503 — retryable server failure: full-jitter backoff under a deadline, circuit-break if persistent. Content refusal — not an error: the call succeeded and the model declined; distinct UX, never retried. Missing required field — contract failure: validate, repair once with the exact issues, degrade. Full-jitter backoff sleeps a random duration up to min(cap, base × 2^attempt), which prevents clients retrying in lockstep and extending the outage. Two timeouts: first-byte (detects a hung connection, keeps TTFT honest) and total (bounds runaway generations), with each layer timing out before the layer above it. Idempotency: a single request can generate and bill twice under ambiguous timeouts, double-submits and queue redelivery; a client-supplied idempotency key plus a completed-actions store makes one logical action produce one generation and one set of side effects — sampling cannot be made identical, but billing and actions can be made once-only.
payload.source: Production reliability interview for LLM services: retries, limits and idempotency.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Classify before you retry: terminal, rate limit, server/network, refusal, contract.
Full-jitter backoff under a deadline; honour Retry-After; circuit-break a dead dependency.
Two timeouts — first-byte and total — with layers failing innermost-first.
Rate limits are backpressure: local buckets, per-user quotas, priority queues.
LLM calls are not idempotent: keys plus a completed-actions store make actions once-only.
Abstraction: one thin seam with normalised errors and usage, an escape hatch, no premature framework.

questions.prompt: A 401 from the provider should trigger:
options: No retry — the credential is wrong; fix configuration and alert if it bursts
A fallback to a second prompt
questions.explanation: Terminal class: the same request will fail identically until credentials change.

questions.prompt: Full-jitter backoff means:
options: Sleeping a random duration up to min(cap, base × 2^attempt), so retries do not synchronise
Sleeping a fixed doubling interval each attempt
Retrying instantly for the first two attempts
Waiting exactly the provider Retry-After, always
questions.explanation: Randomisation is the herd defence; Retry-After, when present, is a floor on top of it.

questions.prompt: Why do LLM calls need application-level idempotency even though they are read-only in appearance?
options: Providers bill twice for streaming calls
Models are non-deterministic, so idempotency is impossible anyway
An ambiguous timeout can hide a successful billed generation, and retries can duplicate side effects — one action must produce one generation
Rate limits count identical requests twice
questions.explanation: Generation is a purchase and often paired with actions; keys and persistence make the purchase once-only.

questions.prompt: The practical stance on provider abstraction is:
options: Build a full multi-provider framework on day one
Never abstract; hardcode one SDK everywhere
Abstract at the UI layer instead
Design one thin seam with normalised errors and usage, keep an escape hatch, and abstract further only when a second provider is real
questions.explanation: A single normalised seam buys portability and logging; premature frameworks buy maintenance.

modules.title: Module 3 — UX for AI: Streaming, Uncertainty, Errors and Feedback
modules.summary: The model is only half the product. This module covers the surface: token-by-token rendering that survives partial JSON, uncertainty affordances that stop discarding the model's own hedges, error states that map each failure class to distinct language and recovery, and the feedback and first-run loops that turn usage into evaluation data.

lessons.title: Streaming UI: Rendering Tokens and Surviving Partial JSON
lessons.summary: Deltas arrive one fragment at a time. Render them without layout thrash, decide how (and whether) to parse JSON before it is complete, and manage the client lifecycle: aborts, reconnects and honest truncation.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Build a token renderer that batches updates and avoids quadratic re-render cost
Choose a strategy for partial JSON: buffer-and-parse or incremental field build
Handle mid-stream death by keeping partial text and marking truncation
Manage lifecycle: abort on unmount, reconnect policy, accessibility of progressive text

payload.text: Two chat UIs sit side by side on the same network. The first re-renders the entire message on every token and re-parses a growing markdown string each time; scrolling stutters, the cursor jumps, and a half-finished table flickers like a broken sign. The second batches updates per frame and renders a stable surface that merely grows. Same model, same tokens, same backend — and users describe one as fast and the other as janky. In AI products, the renderer is part of the model experience.

**What the stream hands you.** Each server-sent event carries a delta: a fragment of the eventual message. The client accumulates deltas into a buffer and updates the view. The naive implementation — setState on every delta, re-render the whole thread, re-parse markdown from scratch — costs quadratically as the answer grows and fights the browser's layout. The working implementation treats rendering as an append pipeline.

**Rendering without thrash.** Three moves. (1) Batch: accumulate deltas into a plain string and flush to the DOM on animation frames or at a small token threshold, not per event — 60 updates a second is a ceiling, not a target. (2) Incremental markdown: a growing answer is an incomplete document; use a parser that tolerates unterminated code fences and tables, or render plain text until the stream ends and then do one rich pass — never full re-parse per token on long answers. (3) Scroll ownership: auto-scroll only while the user is at the bottom; the moment they scroll up to read, detach, and offer a jump-to-latest affordance. Clobbering a reader's scroll position mid-stream is the most common self-inflicted streaming wound. Add a blinking caret while streaming, stop it on done, and keep selection usable — users copy mid-answer.

**The partial JSON problem.** When the model streams structured output, every chunk is a prefix: {"na, then {"name":"Ad — invalid JSON at every intermediate point. You cannot JSON.parse until the end, and if your UI needs the values earlier, you need a different strategy:

1. **Buffer and parse at end.** Stream for feel, parse on completion, show a validating state for the tail. Simplest, usually right when the consumer needs the whole object (a form that appears when ready).
2. **Incremental field build.** Run a tolerant streaming-JSON scanner that emits key-value pairs as they close: complete a field when its closing delimiter arrives, render it, keep the unfinished one invisible. Libraries exist for this; writing one means handling escaped quotes, nested arrays and unicode boundaries. This gives progressive form fill.
3. **Item-wise flush for arrays.** For a streamed list of results, detect item boundaries and flush complete items — the user sees a growing list while the last item is still forming.

Tool calls (Part II) stream as partial argument text and hit the same problem server-side: do not act on arguments until the call event completes and validates.

**Lifecycle, the expensive part.** The stream is a live billed connection. Abort it when the component unmounts or the user navigates, or every closed tab keeps paying for tokens. Reconnects cannot replay mid-stream on most providers (some offer continuation by response id — verify current docs), so a dropped connection should render what arrived, mark it truncated, and offer continue or regenerate. On reconnect, guard against double-appending: deltas are not idempotent, so resume logic must track what was already applied.

**Accessibility.** Announce progressive text sparingly — screen readers should not read every token; announce on completion or at paragraph boundaries. Respect reduced-motion for the caret animation. And never rely on colour alone for the streaming state.

payload.title: Partial JSON strategies
rows: Accumulate, parse on done, one render
Streaming JSON parser emits closed fields
Lists of results arriving one by one

payload.title: Never JSON.parse a growing stream
payload.text: Parse at completion or with a real streaming scanner — there is no valid middle ground between those two.

payload.title: Unmount without abort is a slow leak of money
payload.text: Each abandoned tab that keeps streaming is tokens you buy for nobody. Abort is a cost control.

payload.title: Fix a janky streaming UI and a flashing JSON form
payload.problem: A research assistant renders streamed prose plus a structured citation list. Users report stutter, scroll fights, and a form that flashes undefined twice before appearing. Profile, then rebuild the render path.

steps.title: Profile: the per-token full re-render
steps.desc: The component holds the partial answer in state and maps over the whole thread list on every delta; markdown is re-parsed from scratch each time. At 80 tokens a second that is quadratic work and a layout pass per token.

steps.title: Batch the writes, isolate the growing node
steps.desc: Accumulate deltas in a ref, flush on animation frames, and update only the streaming message node — never the whole thread. Markdown switches to plain text while streaming and does one rich pass at done.

steps.title: Detach scroll from the user the moment they scroll up
steps.desc: Track atBottom; auto-scroll only while true; show a jump-to-latest chip when false. Selection stays usable so people can copy mid-answer.

steps.title: Tame the JSON: buffer, validate, then render fields
steps.desc: The citation list was parsing partial JSON every tick — hence undefined flashes. Now deltas accumulate silently, the object is parsed once on the done event, validated against the schema, and only then rendered. The user sees a stable placeholder, then a complete form.

payload.solution: Frame batching and node-local updates removed the quadratic cost; scroll detachment removed the fights; and parsing once at completion removed the flashing undefined values the partial-JSON bug always produces. The design rule behind all three: streaming is a live document, not a finished one — render what is stable, buffer what is not, and spend the expensive work (markdown, parsing, validation) once, at the done event. TTFT did not change by a millisecond, yet users now call the feature fast.

payload.title: Instrument and rebuild your renderer
payload.prompt: Measure your streaming UI: updates per second, time from delta to painted frame, and re-parse count per answer. Rebuild with frame batching, node-local updates and scroll detachment. Then break your own stream mid-answer and confirm the partial text survives with a truncated marker and a continue action.
payload.hint: If one token causes a full thread re-render, your cost curve is quadratic in answer length — fix that before touching the model.

mistakes.mistake: setState and full markdown re-parse on every token
mistakes.fix: Batch into frames, update only the growing node, re-parse rich formatting once at completion.

mistakes.mistake: JSON.parse on a growing stream
mistakes.fix: Buffer to done, or use a streaming JSON scanner that emits closed fields; nothing in between is valid.

mistakes.mistake: Forcing scroll to bottom while the user reads up
mistakes.fix: Auto-scroll only when already at the bottom; offer jump-to-latest once they leave it.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the stream running after unmount or navigation
mistakes.fix: Abort with a controller tied to component lifetime; treat orphaned generation as a cost bug.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why is partial JSON invalid mid-stream and what are two correct strategies for handling it? Name three practices that keep a streaming renderer smooth and one lifecycle rule that protects the budget.
payload.answer: A streamed object is a prefix of JSON at every intermediate point — {"na or {"name":"Ad are not parseable documents — so JSON.parse only becomes legal once the stream completes. Two correct strategies: (1) buffer-and-parse-at-end, accumulating deltas and parsing once on the done event (optionally with a validating placeholder state), which is simplest and right when the consumer needs the whole object; (2) incremental build with a tolerant streaming JSON scanner that emits fields as they close, enabling progressive form fill, at the cost of handling escapes and nesting. Smooth rendering practices: batch delta updates into animation-frame flushes instead of one state write per token; update only the growing message node rather than re-rendering the whole thread; parse markdown incrementally or once at completion rather than fully per token; and detach auto-scroll when the user scrolls up so they can read and copy. Lifecycle rule: abort the upstream stream when the component unmounts or the user navigates — abandoned generations bill someone, and that someone is you.
payload.source: Front-end interview topic for AI products: streaming render and partial structured output.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Stream render is an append pipeline: buffer deltas, flush per frame, touch one node.
