System, current turn, entities, active tools, safety

payload.title: Never cut a tool call away from its result
payload.text: A dangling call is not smaller context; it is context that lies about what happened.

payload.title: A flow remembered only in the window is a flow waiting to be truncated
payload.text: Keep step and collected fields in storage; let the model handle language inside the current step.

payload.title: Fix the loan assistant: ladder for overflow, state machine for flow
payload.problem: The loan assistant truncates oldest-first and lost the flow position on turn nine. Two changes: a ladder-based assembler with floors, and a state machine that owns step and collected fields outside the window.

steps.title: Name the real state of the flow
steps.desc: Today the flow lives in prompt text and hope. Rewrite it as explicit states (collect → verify → quote → confirm → done) with transition events and guards: identity check is code, income is a parsed number, quote math is deterministic. The model never decides where the flow is; it only extracts and speaks.

steps.title: Persist step and fields; assemble per step
steps.desc: Session row stores step plus collected fields. Each turn, assembly injects: system contract, the current step instructions only, collected fields as data, validation errors to fix, and recent turns for tone. Early conversational history can vanish entirely without harming the flow — which is the whole point.

steps.title: Add the ladder for the parts that still overflow
steps.desc: Document-heavy turns used to blow the window. The assembler now drops stale tool results first, replaces summarised middle turns with bullets, and floors system, entities and the current turn. A cut emits the omission marker so the model asks instead of assuming.

steps.title: Verify the old failure class is gone
steps.desc: Replay the turn-nine scenario: force an overflow mid-flow. The assistant continues from verify with the salary intact — the flow resumed from storage, the ladder cut only re-addable material, and no question was asked twice. Regression test: truncation cannot change flow behaviour.

payload.solution: Two different problems had one symptom. Flow amnesia was fixed by moving step and fields out of the window entirely — the state machine owns them, code guards transitions, and the model handles language inside a step. Overflow sloppiness was fixed by the ladder: re-addable material goes first, load-bearing components are floored, cuts are marked. Truncation still happens; it just no longer matters to correctness. That is the design target: not a context that never shrinks, but a system whose behaviour does not depend on everything surviving.

payload.title: Write your ladder and extract one flow
payload.prompt: Write the truncation ladder for your app with floors and overflow actions, then implement the assembler and force an overflow in a test: confirm the load-bearing pieces survive and the omission marker appears. Separately, pick one multi-step flow currently carried in conversation, extract it into a state machine with stored fields, and measure how much context per turn it removes.
payload.hint: Count how many tokens your flow instructions occupy per turn today; after extraction, the same flow usually costs a tenth of that — because it stops being re-explained to a forgetful model.

mistakes.mistake: Oldest-first truncation with no ladder
mistakes.fix: Order by re-addability: stale tool output first, load-bearing components floored, tool calls kept with their results.

mistakes.mistake: Cutting mid-conversation with no omission marker
mistakes.fix: Tell the model what was removed or instruct it to ask; silent gaps invite invented continuity.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model act as flow controller
mistakes.fix: Step, collected fields and transitions belong in code and storage; the model extracts and phrases inside a step.

mistakes.mistake: Protecting flow state by forbidding truncation
mistakes.fix: Move flow out and truncation stops being dangerous; the window is for language, not for your state machine.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe a truncation ladder ordered by re-addability for a chat app with tools, including what must never be cut. Then explain why multi-step flows should be state machines outside the context window, and what the model's role becomes.
payload.answer: Ladder: drop first the stale retrieved documents and old tool results (re-retrievable); then middle raw turns already covered by a summary; then old assistant replies the user can re-read (keep a gist); then early user turns compressed to intent bullets with requirements kept verbatim. Never cut: the current turn, the system contract, active tool schemas, extracted entity facts and the safety policy — with floors enforced in assembly, whole-message cuts only, tool calls kept with their results, and an omission marker so the model does not invent continuity. Flows become state machines because a flow remembered only inside the window is one truncation away from amnesia: the application stores step, collected fields and transitions; guards (parsing, checks, quote math) are deterministic code; and each turn injects only the current step instructions plus stored fields and recent turns for tone. Context stays flat with turn count, refreshes resume, transitions are testable, and the model's role narrows to what it is good at: extracting structure from messy language and speaking naturally inside the current step.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Truncation is policy: order cuts by re-addability, floor the load-bearing, mark the gaps.

The goal is not an unshrunk context — it is behaviour that survives shrinking.
Ladder plus state machine plus entities: three layers, three failure classes removed.

They are re-addable: re-fetching is cheap and deterministic, so they sit at the top of the truncation ladder
They confuse the attention mechanism entirely

questions.prompt: A flow assistant forgets which step the user is on after a long session. Best fix:
options: Store step and collected fields in your session store and inject only the current step — the flow leaves the window entirely
Repeat the full flow instructions every turn
Raise temperature so the model remembers better
questions.explanation: Durable flow state belongs in code; context carries language, not your state machine.

options: Say nothing so the answer looks clean
Include a marker such as [earlier turns omitted] or instruct the model to ask rather than assume continuity
Also drop the system prompt to compensate
questions.explanation: Silent gaps invite invented continuity; a marker converts uncertainty into an honest question.

modules.title: Module 5 — From Idea to First Working Slice
modules.summary: The bridge from integration knowledge to a shipped feature: the request lifecycle as named, testable stages; prompts as versioned application config instead of pasted prose; model and task fit decided by a feasibility spike and the smallest model that passes your eval — including the judgement call to not use an LLM at all; and the thin vertical slice with a mock path and a frozen baseline, which is what Part II builds on.

lessons.title: The Orchestration Layer: Anatomy of a Request Lifecycle
lessons.summary: Trace one request through named stages — receive, assemble, guard, call, stream, validate, persist — place cross-cutting hooks and trace ids correctly, and keep the pure stages unit-testable without a provider key.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Name the stages of an LLM request lifecycle and the responsibility of each
Place tracing, metering, moderation and caching hooks at the correct stage
Separate pure assembly from I/O so context building is unit-testable
Define the client-orchestrator API surface: typed SSE events and idempotent submission

payload.text: A team has one nine-hundred-line handler. It authenticates the user, builds the prompt, calls the provider, parses JSON, writes three tables and emits analytics — in that order, in one function. Nobody can unit-test the prompt assembly because testing it requires a live API key and a database, and nobody can change the retry policy without risking the parsing branch. The orchestration layer is not missing; it is interleaved. And interleaved is unfixable under deadline pressure, so it stays interleaved.

**Name the stages.** A request through an LLM feature has a fixed shape once you look for it. Naming the stages in code is what turns a handler into an architecture:

1. **Receive** — authenticate, validate the request shape (fail before spending), check per-user quotas, check the idempotency key (Module 2, Lesson 4).
2. **Assemble** — the pure function: session history plus system prompt version plus retrieved data plus the current input becomes final messages, parameters and a budget check (Modules 1 and 4). No I/O lives here; that is what makes it testable with fixtures.
3. **Guard (input)** — moderation, injection heuristics, PII redaction. Cheap checks that should not waste a generation (Module 9 deepens this; the hook belongs here now).
4. **Call** — provider call with the error taxonomy, timeouts and retries of Module 2. The only stage that knows provider shapes.
5. **Stream** — deltas forwarded to the client; optional per-chunk checks; abort propagation from client disconnect (Module 1, Lesson 2).
6. **Validate** — parse, schema-check, one repair attempt (Module 2, Lesson 3); finish_reason handling including truncation and refusal.
7. **Guard (output)** — moderation on the way out, because input filters do not see what generation produced.
8. **Persist** — append messages, record usage and prompt version, write the trace (Module 1, Lesson 3).
9. **Respond** — final stream event with usage, finish reason and trace id; close.

**Cross-cutting concerns attach to stages, not to vibes.** Tracing: one trace id created in receive, attached to every log and the provider call, returned to the client for support. Logging: structured events per stage, secrets redacted. Metering: usage written in persist regardless of outcome. Caching: a cache lookup naturally sits between assemble and call, keyed on the assembled request — which is why assembly purity pays off twice. When a concern has a stage, it has a test and a dashboard.

**The API surface between client and orchestrator.** One endpoint per logical action (for example POST sessions/:id/messages) that returns a typed event stream: delta events carrying text fragments; a final event carrying usage, finish_reason, prompt_version and trace id; an error event carrying a taxonomy kind, never a raw provider dump (Module 3, Lesson 3). The client sends a message id it generated, so submission is idempotent across double-clicks and flaky networks.

**Testing the layers you can test without money.** Assemble is pure: fixtures in, messages out, assert on the exact transcript, token pre-count and truncation decisions. Validate is pure: bad payloads in, taxonomy out. Call is thin enough to test against a mock provider (Lesson 4 builds one and reuses it). The stage that needs a live key shrinks to a few lines — which is the whole point.

**Keep the layer thin.** Orchestration is control flow and policy, not cleverness. Before any framework, prefer a directory of named functions with typed boundaries; frameworks earn their complexity when you actually have graphs, loops and recovery policies (Part II agents will). Build the seam first: one module where the stages live, one place where providers are swapped, one place where a stage gets a metric. The diagram below is the pipeline to keep in your head.
payload.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R["Receive: auth, validate, quota, idempotency"] --> A["Assemble (pure)"]
  A --> G1["Guard in"]
  G1 --> C["Call: retries, timeouts"]
  C --> S["Stream deltas to client"]
  S --> V["Validate: schema, repair, finish_reason"]
  V --> G2["Guard out"]
  G2 --> P["Persist: messages, usage, trace"]
  P --> F["Final event: usage, version, trace id"]

payload.title: If a stage has a name, it can have a metric
payload.text: p95 assemble time versus p95 provider time is the difference between debugging your app and guessing about someone else's.

payload.title: Validation after persist is a data bug generator
payload.text: Validate and guard first; persist only payloads you would defend in a post-mortem.

payload.title: Split the 900-line handler into named stages
payload.problem: One route does everything; a retry-policy change broke parsing last month. Refactor into stages without changing behaviour, and define what becomes testable at each step.

steps.title: Inventory the handler, assign each block a stage name
steps.desc: Read top to bottom and label: auth and body checks (receive), history load and prompt build (assemble), moderation call (guard in), provider request with a two-attempt retry (call), delta forwarding (stream), JSON parse (validate), second moderation (guard out), three inserts (persist), response write (respond). Nothing is rewritten yet — the labels are the design.

steps.title: Extract pure stages first
steps.desc: assemble moves to its own module with typed inputs and no I/O: history rows, prompt version, retrieved chunks, current text in; messages, parameters, token pre-count out. Now a fixture test locks the exact transcript — the first regression test the team has ever had for prompt behaviour.

steps.title: Wrap the provider call as the only aware stage
steps.desc: The adapter owns retries and the error taxonomy; every other stage now speaks normalised types. Changing retry policy touches one file and cannot reach the parsing branch, because parsing no longer lives next to it.

steps.title: Wire trace and final event, then measure
steps.desc: Trace id created in receive is attached to all logs and returned in the final SSE event. One week of stage-level metrics later: assembly is 12 ms, provider is 2.4 s p95 — the team stops blaming their own code for latency, and the retry-policy debate happens with evidence.

payload.solution: The handler became a pipeline with names, and each name unlocked the matching test: golden transcripts for assembly, scripted failures for the call layer, malformed payloads for validation. Retry policy changes now land in one file with a suite around them, and stage-level timing ends the finger-pointing about where latency lives. The refactor cost a day; the ongoing tax it removes — every future change negotiating with nine hundred interleaved lines — is unbounded. That is the orchestration layer paying for itself before a single new feature is built on top.

payload.title: Name your stages and test one pure stage
payload.prompt: Write the lifecycle table for your app: stage, responsibility, current owner, test. Extract assemble as a pure function with three fixture tests asserting the transcript and the token pre-count. Add a trace id that reaches the client final event. Report which stage was hiding the most bugs.
payload.hint: If assemble needs a network call, it is not assembly — it is retrieval wearing the wrong name; inject the results instead.

mistakes.mistake: Interleaving I/O, prompt building and parsing in one handler
mistakes.fix: Extract named stages; keep assemble and validate pure so they test without keys, mocks or databases.

mistakes.mistake: Validating and guarding after persist
mistakes.fix: Order matters: validate and guard first, persist only what you would defend later.

mistakes.mistake: No trace id across stages
mistakes.fix: Create it in receive, thread it through logs and the provider call, return it in the final event.

mistakes.mistake: Reaching for an agent framework before stages exist
mistakes.fix: A directory of typed functions is the right complexity until you genuinely need graphs, loops and recovery policies.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: List the stages of an LLM request lifecycle in order and give the responsibility of assemble and validate. Where do tracing, moderation and caching attach, and why must assemble stay pure?
payload.answer: Order: receive (auth, validation, quota, idempotency) → assemble → guard input → call (retries, timeouts) → stream deltas → validate (schema, repair, finish_reason) → guard output → persist (messages, usage, trace) → respond (final event). Assemble is the pure function that turns session history, prompt version, retrieved data and the current input into final messages, parameters and a token pre-count; validate parses the response, schema-checks it, attempts at most one repair and interprets finish reason. Tracing attaches at receive (one id for all logs and the client final event); moderation attaches twice — guard in before spending a generation, guard out on what generation produced; caching attaches between assemble and call, keyed on the assembled request. Assemble must stay pure because purity is what makes context building testable with fixtures — golden transcripts catch prompt and truncation regressions without a provider key, money or flakiness — and because a pure boundary is where a future provider swap or cache plugs in cleanly.
payload.source: Architecture interview for LLM feature roles: structure the request path.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Nine named stages turn a handler into an architecture you can test and measure.
Assemble and validate stay pure: fixtures in, transcripts and errors out, no keys required.
The call stage is the only provider-aware one — retries and taxonomy live there and nowhere else.
Guard in before spending, guard out before showing; persist only validated payloads.
One trace id from receive to final event is what makes incidents reconstructable.
Keep orchestration thin: named functions first, frameworks only when the graph earns them.

questions.prompt: Why must the assemble stage be pure (no I/O)?
options: It becomes unit-testable with fixtures: golden transcripts and token counts without keys, mocks or databases
It is faster than I/O by definition
questions.explanation: Purity buys deterministic tests for the layer where prompt and truncation regressions actually happen.

questions.prompt: Where should output moderation run?
options: Only on the user input, once
After validation, before persist and respond — generation can produce what input never contained
questions.explanation: Guard out catches what generation added; persist only payloads that passed it.

questions.prompt: The trace id should be created:
options: At the provider, and copied later
In receive, then attached to every stage log and returned in the final event
questions.explanation: One id from the edge inward is what ties a user report to the exact stages that ran.

questions.prompt: What is the right first abstraction for orchestration?
options: A multi-agent framework on day one
A directory of named, typed stage functions with one provider adapter — frameworks when graphs and recovery policies actually arrive
Direct provider calls from route handlers
questions.explanation: Stages give you tests and metrics; framework complexity is only justified by real control-flow needs.

lessons.title: Prompt-as-Code: Versioning, Templates and Drift
lessons.summary: A prompt changes product behaviour, so it is code: reviewable, versioned, tested and promoted under a gate. Externalise prompts into typed templates, know which version produced every response, and detect drift before your users do.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Externalise prompts into versioned, reviewable configuration with typed variables
Template safely: escape user data, default variables, fail on missing ones
Trace any response back to the exact prompt version that produced it
Promote prompt changes through an eval gate with a rollback path

payload.text: A support bot's best-performing prompt lives in a Google doc. Three engineers paste it into the code with three small edits each; production is running a fourth variant that nobody has written down. When quality dips on Thursday, the team cannot answer what changed, when, or where. The model version is the same. The prompt is unmanaged — and so the behaviour is unmanageable.

**A prompt is a behaviour change with no compiler.** Code changes go through review, tests and deploys; prompt changes can be equally behaviour-altering and arrive as a paste. The discipline is therefore borrowed wholesale from engineering, with one twist: your tests are evaluation cases, and your compiler is a gate you run yourself.

**Where prompts live.** Three options, chosen consciously. (1) Constants in code: reviewed with the code, versioned with the deploy — good default for most teams, with the cost that a wording fix rides a full release. (2) A prompt registry or config service: independent rollout, environment overrides, an admin trail — buy this when non-engineers change prompts regularly or you need per-tenant variants, and audit-log every edit. (3) Live console edits at the provider: fastest way to create the Google-doc problem; if you allow them at all, treat them as emergency-only, audited, and reconciled back into versioned source. Whichever you pick, prompt_version and model id must be logged on every completion — the attribution line without which nothing else is debuggable.

**Templates, not concatenation.** A template names its variables with types and defaults: locale, doc_text, user_name. Two safety rules carry most of the weight. First, escaping: user and document content is data — it is injected at data positions, wrapped in delimiters, and never interpolated into instruction positions or into JSON examples (a variable inside an example string breaks structure and invites injection). Second, validation: a template that renders with undefined in it is a production incident waiting for a deploy; fail the build when a required variable is missing. Typed template functions give you both for free.

**Versioning that supports rollback.** Immutable versions: returns-desk/v4 stays exactly what v4 was forever, so an old version can be re-run against new evaluation cases for reproducibility. A changelog line per bump answering why. Staging runs the same prompt as production — dev/prod prompt differences are fake tests. Rollback is then a config change, not an archaeology project.

**Drift, the quiet failure.** Four drift sources: a live console edit; a model auto-update under a stable alias (pin versions where providers allow, and re-run evals when they move — verify current docs); data drift, where yesterday's traffic looked nothing like your eval set; and copy creep, where well-meaning appends accumulate into sediment (Module 4, Lesson 1). Detection is mostly instrumentation: quality metrics per prompt_version (thumbs, repair rate, refusal rate, truncation rate), and a diff alert when the version serving production changes.

**The change loop.** Edit the template in review → run the golden set locally → bump the version with a changelog entry → promote through staging → canary a slice of traffic → compare the metrics that the change was meant to move, plus the ones it was not → promote fully or roll back. Twenty to fifty cases is enough to catch the regressions that matter; the loop costs minutes and replaces arguments with measurements. That loop is the habit that keeps prompt quality compounding instead of oscillating.

payload.title: Where a prompt can live
rows: Independent rollout, audit trail, per-tenant variants
New system to run and secure

payload.title: Version immutability is what makes rollback boring
payload.text: If v4 can still mean three different texts, you do not have versions — you have labels.

payload.title: A live prompt edit without an eval gate is a production deploy with no review
payload.text: Fast today, unexplainable on Thursday. Route every change through the gate, even the urgent ones.

payload.title: Externalise, version, and gate a prompt change
payload.problem: A returns-desk assistant has its system prompt as a template string in a handler, edited casually. An urgent wording fix goes out mid-week and quality dips. Restructure the setup and run the fix through a proper gate.

steps.title: Externalise with typed variables and delimiters
steps.desc: Move the prompt into a versioned module: policy document and user question arrive as named variables, with the document wrapped in delimiters and labelled as data. A missing variable now throws at build time instead of rendering undefined into production.

steps.title: Establish attribution retroactively impossible before
steps.desc: Every completion logs prompt name, version, model and trace id. The Thursday dip now has a query: compare thumbs and repair rates grouped by version over the week. Two versions were live at once — one from a canary that never fully rolled, one from a console tweak.

steps.title: Run the urgent fix through the gate
steps.desc: The wording fix becomes v6 with a changelog entry. Golden set (32 cases) runs pre-change: 29 pass. Post-change: 31 pass, but two citation cases regress — the brevity rule now conflicts with the citation requirement. The team fixes the constraint wording, re-runs, gets 32, and promotes.
steps.code_snippet:
$ prompt-gate run --version v6 --set golden32
  pass 29/32  regressions: cite_policy_window, cite_refund_rule
$ # fix constraint: citations are exempt from the 120-word cap
$ prompt-gate run --version v6b --set golden32
  pass 32/32  -> promote

steps.title: Canary, compare, and keep rollback one command
steps.desc: v6b goes to 10 percent of traffic; repair rate and thumbs hold; full promote. The previous version remains immutable, so rollback is pointing config at v5 — a decision that takes a minute at 2 a.m.

payload.solution: The prompt stopped being prose that happens to run in production and became a versioned artefact with attribution, a gate and a rollback. The gate earned its keep on the first real change by catching a cross-constraint regression the author could not see by reading — which is exactly what gates are for. And retroactive attribution answered the original Thursday mystery: two versions were live because nothing bound a response to the text that produced it. One logging line would have saved the week of argument.

payload.title: Version your prompts this week
payload.prompt: Externalise every system prompt into versioned modules with typed variables and delimiter-safe data injection. Add prompt_version and model to your completion logs. Build a five-case golden set for your most important prompt and run one proposed change through it. Report what the gate caught that reading did not.
payload.hint: If you cannot answer which prompt version produced last Tuesday's worst answer, stop and add attribution before anything else.

mistakes.mistake: Prompts in documents or live consoles
mistakes.fix: Reviewable versioned source with a changelog; console edits are audited emergencies that get reconciled back.

mistakes.mistake: No prompt_version on completions
mistakes.fix: Attribution is the foundation: quality per version, incident forensics and rollback all query that column.

mistakes.mistake: String-concatenating user data into instructions or examples
mistakes.fix: Typed variables at data positions, delimited and labelled as data; never inside instruction text or JSON examples.

mistakes.mistake: Shipping prompt edits without an eval gate
mistakes.fix: A twenty-case golden set in minutes replaces a week of arguing; canary and compare before full promote.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why should prompts be treated as versioned code? Describe template safety rules and the sources of prompt drift. Lay out the gated change loop.
payload.answer: Prompts change product behaviour as surely as code, so they need the same controls: review, immutability (a version label means one exact text forever), changelog with rationale, and rollback by pointing at the previous version. Template safety: typed variables with required-field validation so nothing renders as undefined; user and document content injected only at data positions, wrapped in delimiters and labelled as data — never interpolated into instructions or JSON examples, which breaks structure and opens injection. Drift sources: unaudited live console edits, provider model updates under stable aliases, input data that no longer matches the eval set, and copy creep from unreviewed appends. Detection: log prompt_version and model on every completion, watch quality metrics grouped by version, and alert on unexpected version changes. The gated loop: edit under review, run the golden set, bump version with changelog, promote through staging, canary a traffic slice, compare the metrics the change targeted plus guardrail metrics, then full promote or one-command rollback.
payload.source: Engineering-practice question: prompt management in production LLM apps.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Prompt changes are product changes: versioned, reviewed, gated, rollbackable.
Attribution first: prompt_version plus model on every completion, no exceptions.
Typed templates with validated variables; data injected delimited, never into instructions.
Drift is quiet: console edits, model updates, data shift, copy creep — instrument for all four.
The gate is minutes of compute that replace weeks of argument.
Immutable versions make reproducibility and 2 a.m. rollback boring, which is the goal.

lessons.title: Model and Task Fit: Feasibility, Choice and When Not to Use an LLM
lessons.summary: Before architecture, before UX, before memory: can the model do the task at all? Run a feasibility spike, pick the smallest model your eval passes, and have the honesty to choose deterministic code when it fits better.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Run a feasibility spike on representative cases and read the results as a decision
Choose a model by task fit across capability, structure support, window, cost and latency
Justify the smallest model that passes the eval with margin
Recognise tasks where deterministic code beats an LLM and pick the alternative

payload.text: A team spends six weeks building an LLM invoice-number extractor with retries, repair loops and a dashboard. A colleague replaces the happy path with a twelve-line regex and a line-item validation in an afternoon: faster, free, perfectly accurate on their corpus. Then the team is asked to extract policy exclusions from free-text clauses, and the regex approach is impossible. Same company, same week, two tasks — one where the LLM was an overpriced parser and one where it was the only tool that could work. The skill is telling the two apart before you build.

**Feasibility first, product second.** The most expensive mistake in this domain is building the shell — UI, memory, billing — and discovering at week six that the model cannot do the core task at 80 percent even with good prompts. The cheap alternative is a spike: ten to thirty representative cases with expected answers, hand-checked; run each through a strong model with a serviceable prompt; record success, failure modes, cost and latency per case. Then read the numbers as a decision rule, adjusting thresholds to your error cost: a typo in a marketing draft and a typo in a loan decision deserve different bars. Roughly, at or above the high nineties on hard cases with a simple prompt — build; mid-band — budget explicitly for structure, grounding and prompt work before committing; low with best effort — re-scope the task or decline it. A spike is days of work and saves months.

**Choosing a model, app-shaped.** Leaderboards are not your eval, and catalogs churn — verify current pricing and capabilities before deciding. The dimensions that matter to an application:

1. **Task capability on your cases** — judged by your spike, not reputation.
2. **Structure support** — if you need schemas or tools, the model must handle them well (Module 2, Lesson 3).
3. **Context window** — must fit your budget (Module 4, Lesson 3) with headroom; a bigger window is not better use of one.
4. **Cost envelope** — per-call cost times volume; output price matters most for verbose tasks.
5. **Latency envelope** — time-to-first-token and throughput against your UX budget (Module 3).
6. **Operational fit** — availability, data residency, enterprise terms, moderation and logging controls.

**The smallest-model principle.** Run the same eval set across a small, medium and large tier. Pick the cheapest that passes with margin, because quality is set by the eval — not by the tier you bought. Task dependence is real: routing, classification and short summaries often pass on small models; nuanced reasoning, rare formats and heavy instruction stacks do not. Note the scope: this is selection at design time. Dynamic per-request routing — small model first, escalate on difficulty — is cost engineering, and Module 10 owns it.

**When not to use an LLM.** The deterministic checklist: fixed-format parsing with learnable structure (regex or a real parser); arithmetic and lookups (models are bad calculators — use code and databases); policy decisions that must be explainable auditable rules; closed small label sets where a classical classifier beats a generative model on cost and latency; real-time constraints below model latency; extreme volume with narrow task mix where token cost dwarfs the engineering cost of a simpler solution. LLMs earn their place on open-ended language understanding, messy unstructured input, generation, judgement with context, and gluing systems together in natural language. Most durable architectures are hybrid: deterministic path first, LLM for the residue, human for the exceptions.

payload.text: Twenty cases, one afternoon, and you know whether the product is a product or a research project.

payload.title: Do not fall in love with the biggest model as a default
payload.text: It hides feasibility problems, doubles your latency and your bill, and often loses to a smaller model once structure is doing the heavy lifting.

payload.title: Spike a clause-extraction feature and choose the tier
payload.problem: A legal-tech team wants to extract exclusions and notice periods from insurance clauses. Stakeholders want a full app by next quarter. Run the spike, read the results, and decide tier and scope.

steps.title: Build 20 honest cases, not 20 easy ones
steps.desc: Sample across the real distribution: simple single-clause text, multi-clause walls, scanned-quality OCR noise, two cases with genuinely no exclusion present, and two adversarial ones where the exclusion is conditional. Expected answers written by someone who can check them — a spike against wrong labels is worse than no spike.

steps.title: Run three tiers, same prompt, same schema
steps.desc: Structured output with a flat schema: exclusions as string array, notice_days as integer, present as boolean. Results: small 9/20 (format collapse on multi-clause), medium 15/20 (three semantic misses, two schema repairs), large 19/20 (one conditional miss). Cost per case and p95 latency recorded alongside.

steps.title: Read failure modes, not just rates
steps.desc: The medium tier's misses are all conditional exclusions — a recognisable class. The fix candidates: a second pass that asks only about conditionals, and two targeted few-shot examples. The small tier's failures are structural, which is a different, harder problem. Failure mode beats average when choosing what to invest in.

steps.title: Decide with error cost in the room
steps.desc: Error cost here is high (missed exclusions in a compliance workflow), so the team picks large for the core extraction with a human review queue for anything flagged present-but-uncertain, plus medium for a cheap pre-screen on simple clauses. Re-scope: the two no-exclusion cases now short-circuit at the pre-screen — and the spike says the full app is feasible, with the budget attached.

payload.solution: In one afternoon the spike replaced a quarter of assumptions: the task is feasible, the difficulty is concentrated in one recognisable failure class, and the tier decision is grounded in error cost instead of vendor reputation. The hybrid choice — medium pre-screen, large core, human review on flagged uncertainty — is exactly the kind of design only the failure-mode data could justify. And if the results had come back at 40 percent, the team would have re-scoped before writing a line of app shell. That is the spike working: it makes the expensive news cheap and early.

payload.title: Run your spike
payload.prompt: Take your idea and write ten representative cases with expected answers. Run them through one strong model with a schema. Record pass rate, failure modes, latency and cost. Then run two other tiers on the same cases and name the cheapest tier that passes your bar. Finish with a one-paragraph go, re-scope or no-go decision that a skeptic could check.
payload.hint: If the expected answers are not written down before the run, you are grading on vibes — write them first.

mistakes.mistake: Building the app shell before proving feasibility
mistakes.fix: Spike with curl first: twenty cases, one afternoon, a written decision — then build.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a model by leaderboard or hype
mistakes.fix: Your distribution is not the benchmark: run your cases across tiers and let the eval pick the model.

mistakes.mistake: Defaulting to the largest model
mistakes.fix: It masks feasibility problems and doubles cost and latency; pick the smallest tier that passes with margin.

mistakes.mistake: Using an LLM for regex-shaped or arithmetic work
mistakes.fix: Deterministic first: parsers, rules, databases — LLM for the open-language residue that rules cannot reach.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe a feasibility spike for an LLM feature: inputs, measurements and decision bands. List six dimensions for model choice and four task shapes where deterministic code beats an LLM.
payload.answer: Spike: ten to thirty representative cases sampled from the real distribution, each with a hand-verified expected answer written before running; a serviceable prompt plus schema; measure per case pass or fail, failure mode class, latency and cost; then decide against bands adjusted for error cost — near-ceiling on hard cases means build, a mid-band means budget explicit work on structure, grounding and prompts before committing, a low band means re-scope or decline. Model choice dimensions: task capability on your cases, structured-output and tool support, context window versus your budget, cost envelope at your volume, latency envelope against the UX budget, and operational fit (availability, residency, moderation, logging). Deterministic beats LLM on: fixed-format parsing such as ids and dates; closed tiny label sets where a classical classifier is cheaper and auditable; arithmetic and lookups that must be exact; policy and legal decisions needing explainable rules; and high-volume narrow tasks where token cost dwarfs a simpler build. LLMs win on open-ended understanding, messy input, generation and judgement in context — and most systems are hybrid: rules first, LLM for the residue.

options: Switch to a larger model without re-measuring

questions.explanation: The spike exists to make the expensive news cheap and early; 55 percent is a scope decision, not a shipping detail.

lessons.title: The Thin Slice: Smallest End-to-End Path, Then Baseline It
lessons.summary: Ship one vertical path through every layer with a mock model for development, freeze a baseline of real cases before improving anything, and let measured bottlenecks — not trends — decide what to build next.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Scope a thin vertical slice that exercises every orchestration stage once
Build a mock provider path so development needs no keys or spend
Freeze a baseline case set with scores, latency and cost per case
Sequence the next build step from measured failure classes instead of enthusiasm

payload.text: Two teams get the same brief. Team A spends five weeks on the platform: an abstraction layer, a plugin registry, twelve configuration knobs and a beautiful chat UI — and no working use case. Team B ships a command-line tool that answers their domain question badly but end-to-end in week one, measures it against twenty real cases, and improves the prompt three times against that set. At week six, team A owns infrastructure and a demo; team B owns something people use. The difference was not talent. It was vertical versus horizontal.

**Thin means vertical.** A thin slice cuts one path through every layer — client (even a CLI counts), orchestration stages, provider call, validation, persistence — for exactly one use case, one model and a minimal prompt. It is thin because everything else waits; it is vertical because reality gets no delay. Horizontal work (platform, abstractions, dashboards nobody reads) is what teams mistake for progress in week one.

**Slice checklist.** (1) One concrete user job, phrased as a sentence with a verb and an object — answer support questions about our policy docs, not build an AI assistant. (2) An input path in its smallest form: paste text, one upload, one form field. (3) The orchestration stages from Lesson 1, even at sixty lines each. (4) A real provider call with server-side credentials (Module 2) and streaming if the answer is interactive (Module 1). (5) Validation for anything structured (Module 2, Lesson 3). (6) Persistence of messages and usage (Module 1, Lesson 3). (7) A way to run it today: a CLI, a single page, one endpoint with curl.

**The mock path.** Development against a live model is slow, expensive and non-deterministic — terrible for building UI and orchestration. So the call stage gets two implementations behind one interface: the real provider and a mock that replays canned responses. Build fixtures the way you would build test data: happy path, long answer, refusal, truncated stream, malformed JSON, 429. Those fixtures double as your first eval cases (Lesson 2 and Module 8). Where local open models can run on your machine, they are a third option for offline iteration — check current tooling before relying on them. The payoff is boring and enormous: frontend and orchestration work becomes free, fast and deterministic.

**The baseline is the memory of your product.** Before any improvement, freeze twenty to fifty real cases with expected behaviour, and score the current build: pass or fail per case, plus latency and token cost per case. Store it as JSONL in the repo — plain, diffable, reviewable. From that moment, every prompt tweak, model change or context change is a measured delta instead of a vibe: run, compare, keep or revert. A baseline also tells you what your failures actually are, because case-level scoring forces you to look at them one by one. Teams that skip the baseline spend the rest of the project arguing about whether things got better; they usually feel worse.

**Sequencing next steps by measured need.** The bottleneck your metrics name chooses the next module, which is exactly how this course orders Part II:

- Answers shallow or wrong on knowledge → grounding and retrieval (the RAG course).
- One-shot only, no continuity → memory done properly (Module 4 strategies).
- Users asking for actions → tools and function calling (M6).
- Output unreliable, structure failing → structured pipelines and extraction hardening (M7).
- Quality regressions shipping quietly → evaluation harness in CI (M8).
- Abuse, injection attempts, data exfiltration risk → safety layer (M9).
- Slow or expensive at volume → caching, batching, routing (M10).

**Definition of done for Part I.** You can state the architecture, persist state, control parameters, structure output, survive failures with classified errors, budget the window, version prompts, and measure a baseline. That is the floor. Part II adds tools, extraction pipelines, evaluation, safety and performance on top of a system that can already be measured — because you cannot improve what you cannot see, and you cannot trust what you have not baselined.

The UI-polish idea drops three places. Memory is not on the list at all — the slice showed no continuity failures yet.

payload.solution: Six weeks of horizontal platform collapsed into days of vertical slice, and the mock path made iteration free. The baseline turned the roadmap argument into a reading exercise: three failure classes, each with a known destination in the curriculum, and a UI idea demoted by evidence. That is the Part I close — a system that is measured end to end, with every improvement from here able to prove itself against a frozen set. Tools, extraction hardening, evaluation, safety and performance now have something solid to attach to.

payload.answer: A thin vertical slice is one path through every layer — client, orchestration stages, provider call, validation, persistence — for a single concrete user job with one model and minimal prompt; horizontal work builds platform, abstractions and dashboards before any use case works, which is how teams arrive at week six with infrastructure and no product. The mock provider implements the same interface as the real one and replays scripted fixtures: normal, long streaming, refusal, truncated, malformed JSON and 429 — making UI and orchestration development free, fast and deterministic, and turning each fixture into a labelled eval case. A baseline record is a frozen JSONL run of twenty to fifty real cases with expected behaviour, model, prompt version, score, failure class, latency and token cost per case; before it, improvements are feelings, and after it, every change is a measured delta. modules.title: Module 6 — Function Calling and Tools: Structured Intent, Real Actions
modules.summary: Tools turn a text generator into something that can act: JSON-schema contracts the model emits intent against, executed by your code and merged back into the transcript by call id. This module covers schema design and the routing-grade description that picks the tool, when a tool beats plain generation or a schema, parallel calls with deterministic merging, the preview-and-approve gate that stands between a hallucinated argument and an irreversible action, the deterministic-code-versus-model-judgement split, tool errors fed back as data inside a bounded loop, and streaming a tool round honestly to the UI.

lessons.title: Tool Definitions: JSON Schema, Naming and When Tools Beat Prompting
lessons.summary: The model never runs your code — it emits structured intent. Define tools as JSON Schema with routing-grade descriptions, walk the request → tool_calls → role:tool → request loop, choose between plain generation, structured output and a tool call, and treat every generated argument as untrusted input your server validates.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain the tool-calling loop: what the model returns, what your code executes and what re-enters the transcript
Write a JSON Schema tool definition with a routing-grade description, tight enums and honest required fields
Choose between plain generation, structured output and a tool call for any given requirement
Validate model-generated arguments server-side and return useful errors instead of trusting generated JSON

payload.text: A support team builds "search the policy base" with an instruction: when you need information, emit a line like <<SEARCH:my question>> and I will paste results. Week two, the model emits it inside a JSON field of a structured answer; week three it emits two tags on one line with different brackets; week four a user types the tag themselves and the regex fires against the user's own text. The team has accidentally rebuilt a protocol — with no schema, no ids and no validation. Function calling exists because that game has no winning move.

**Tools are structured intent, not code the model runs.** When you send tool definitions with a request, the model may answer with tool_calls instead of text: an array of calls, each carrying an id you generated nowhere, a name from your list, and arguments serialised as a JSON string. Your process parses that string, validates it, executes your own function — with your credentials, your permissions, your side effects — and appends one message per call with the tool role, the matching call id and the result as content. Then you request again. The loop repeats until the model returns an ordinary message, which is the final answer. Nothing about auth, validation or effect ever leaves your code. Field names differ slightly between providers (as of 2026, verify current docs), but the shape does not: decide → execute → feed back.

**The schema is the contract; the description is the router.** Most bad tool behaviour is a description problem, not a model problem. Three rules carry the weight. (1) Names are forever: lowercase, snake_case, verb-first, and stable — a rename orphans every trace, eval case and saved transcript that referenced it, and two near-twins like search_documents and lookup_policy will split calls arbitrarily. (2) The tool description is a prompt: say when to use it, when NOT to, and show one concrete example of a good argument; each property gets a type, a description and an example; closed sets become enums so a value outside the enum is a bug you can see instead of a string you must trust. (3) Keep it tight: three to six parameters, flat, one level of nesting at most — models drop fields inside deep trees, and every optional critical field becomes a silent default you did not choose. Mark everything you actually need as required, and set additionalProperties false where the provider's strict mode expects it (check current docs for your provider's exact constraints).

**The tool surface is a tax on every request.** Definitions ride along with each call: input tokens, prefill latency and the model's attention budget. Past a modest number of tools, selection accuracy measurably degrades — the numbers are provider- and era-specific, so the only honest answer is a routing eval over your own tool list (Module 8). If you carry a large surface, measure before trimming and after.

**Choose the mechanism deliberately.** Three ways to get values out of a model: plain generation, schema-constrained structured output, and a tool call. They are not interchangeable. Structured output is the model's judgement about input you already gave it — classification, extraction, scoring — with no side effect. A tool call is required when the value or effect lives outside the model: a system of record, a live API, anything that changes state, anything multi-step. Plain text is for prose you will show a human. Rule of thumb: system of record → tool; the model's wording → text; the model's judgement over provided input → schema. Reaching for a tool when a schema would do costs a round trip and a place to fail; reaching for prose when you need values costs you a parser.

**Failures, honestly.** Arguments arrive hallucinated regularly: an order id that does not exist, an amount in the wrong unit, a field the user never mentioned. From your server's point of view, tool arguments are user input — parse with a guard against malformed JSON, type-check and range-check them, then authorise: the order must exist AND belong to the signed-in user. Other recurring failures: the model calls a tool when a plain answer would do (fix with instructions, a smaller surface, or a forced tool_choice where the provider allows it); the system prompt contradicts a tool description and the model picks one (align them — they are the same contract); and the model answers from memory when it should have called (an eval case, not a vibe).

flowchart LR
  T["tools: JSON schemas on every request"] --> M["model decides: answer or call"]
  M -->|"tool_calls: id, name, arguments (JSON string)"| V["your code: parse, validate, authorise"]
  V --> X["your function executes with your credentials"]
  X -->|"role: tool, call id, result"| M
  M -->|"plain message, finish_reason stop"| F["final answer"]

payload.problem: A returns desk answers policy questions (grounded in three documents) and looks up order status (live DB). The current prompt says "output <<LOOKUP:...>> when you need the database". Redesign it as proper tools and show what the loop executes.

steps.desc: Policy questions are judgement over documents you paste into context — structured output or plain text with citations, no tool. Order status must come from the database — a tool, because the model has no idea what ORD-2026-00417 contains today. Two capabilities, two different mechanisms; the old instruction used one mechanism for both and got both wrong sometimes.
