The description names the exact situation to use it and the two situations not to — refunds and address changes belong to tools that do not exist yet, which is itself information.
steps.code_snippet:
name: "lookup_order"
description: "Fetch one order for the signed-in customer.\nUse when the user names an order id or asks about delivery status.\nDo NOT use for refunds, cancellations or address changes."
required: ["order_id"]   # no silent default for the one field the task needs

steps.title: Execute the loop and watch the first real call
steps.desc: The request returns one tool_call with arguments {"order_id": "ORD-2026-00417"}. Your code parses, validates the shape, checks the order belongs to this user, queries the database, appends the result as a tool message with the call id, and requests again. The second response is prose citing the real status. No regex, no protocol, no user-typed tags.

steps.title: Handle the argument the model invents
steps.desc: A second run returns order_id "ORD-2026-99999" — plausible, real format, no such row for this user. Instead of a crash or a lie, the tool returns a structured result: {"error": "not_found", "message": "No order matches that id for your account."} fed back as the tool message. The model then asks the user to re-check the id, which is the right behaviour and was reachable only because failure was data.

payload.solution: The protocol-without-schema became a schema with a contract: one name, a description that routes, required fields that cannot silently default, and a loop where every argument passes through validation and authorisation before touching a database. The invented order id — the failure that would have been a production incident under the regex design — became a tool result the model could reason about. That is the whole trade: tools do not make the model correct, they make its mistakes structured, visible and recoverable.

payload.title: Define your first real tool
payload.prompt: Pick one capability in your app that needs a system of record. Write its JSON Schema: name, description with a "do NOT use when" clause, three or fewer parameters, enums for any closed set, everything critical required. Then write the other side: the validation and authorisation checks your server runs before your code touches anything. Finally, list two capabilities that are plain schemas, not tools, and say why.
payload.hint: If your description does not mention one case where the tool is the wrong answer, it is not a router yet — it is a label.

mistakes.mistake: Parsing free-form text for command tags with regex
mistakes.fix: Use tool calls: ids, schemas and a typed message role give you structure the model cannot improvise around.

mistakes.mistake: Vague or duplicated tool descriptions
mistakes.fix: Describe when to use AND when not to; rename near-twins so routing stops splitting arbitrarily.

mistakes.mistake: Executing generated arguments directly
mistakes.fix: Parse guarded, validate shape and ranges, authorise against the session — arguments are untrusted input.

mistakes.mistake: Reaching for a tool when structured output would do
mistakes.fix: Judgement over supplied input is one schema-shaped response; a tool earns its round trip only when value or effect lives outside the model.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Describe the function-calling loop end to end: what a request with tools returns, what your code appends and why the loop terminates. Then give the three mechanism choices for getting values out of a model and the rule that picks between them.
payload.answer: Request with tool definitions → the model either returns an ordinary message (final answer) or tool_calls: an array of {id, name, arguments}, with arguments as a JSON string. Your code parses and validates those arguments, authorises them against the session, executes its own function with its own credentials, and appends one message per call with the tool role, the matching tool_call_id and the result as content; then it requests again. The loop repeats until a plain message arrives (finish_reason stop) — which is why every implementation needs a hard round cap as well. Mechanisms: plain generation for prose a human reads; schema-constrained structured output for the model's judgement over input already provided (no side effect); a tool call when the value lives in a system of record or the effect must happen in code. Rule: system of record or side effect → tool; model wording → text; model judgement over given input → schema. The description is the router: when to use, when not to, with examples; and generated arguments are treated as untrusted input — parse, type-check, authorise.
payload.source: Backend interview for LLM feature roles: "walk me through how function calling works."

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: The model emits intent; your code executes — auth, validation and side effects never leave your server.
Names are forever; descriptions route; critical fields are required; schemas stay flat and short.
Structured output for judgement, tools for systems of record and effects, text for prose.
Tool definitions ride along on every request: measure your routing accuracy before growing the surface.
Generated arguments are user input: parse guarded, validate, authorise against the session.
Errors should come back as structured tool results — that is what makes recovery possible.

questions.prompt: In the tool-calling loop, who executes the function?
options: Your code, after parsing and validating the model-generated arguments
The browser, on the user device
questions.explanation: The model only emits structured intent; execution, credentials and side effects stay in your process.

questions.prompt: Which requirement should become a tool rather than a structured-output schema?
options: Classifying a pasted complaint into a fixed set of themes
Extracting dates from a lease clause you pasted into context
Fetching today's stock level from your inventory database
Scoring an answer against a rubric you provided
questions.explanation: A value held by a system of record must be looked up; the model cannot know it, so retrieval is execution.

questions.prompt: The most common root cause of a model calling the wrong tool is:
options: A temperature that is too high
Vague, overlapping or missing "when not to use this" descriptions
A context window that is too small
questions.explanation: Routing happens from names and descriptions — the description is a prompt, and near-twins split calls arbitrarily.

questions.prompt: A tool_call arrives with order_id "ORD-99999" that does not exist for this user. Correct handling:
options: Return an exception to the user immediately
Send a structured not_found result back as the tool message so the model can respond or retry intelligently
Let the model invent a plausible order status instead
Log it and return an empty string as the tool result
questions.explanation: Failures are data: a structured error result lets the model recover, while also proving authorisation ran.

lessons.title: Parallel Tool Calls, Result Merging and the Deterministic Split
lessons.summary: One response can carry several tool calls. Run them concurrently without losing the call-id mapping, merge results in a stable order the model can reason about, stage dependent calls instead of guessing, and keep every deterministic decision in code while the model only judges.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Handle a response containing multiple tool_calls, preserving the id-to-result mapping under concurrency
Choose a merge strategy and a dependency order for fan-out results
Separate deterministic work (fetching, merging, computing) from model judgement (what to ask, what it means)
Bound fan-out: dedupe, cap concurrency and cap the result bytes that re-enter the transcript

payload.text: An assistant answers "compare our Basic and Pro plans for a 12-person team" by emitting three tool calls in one message. The app runs them one at a time, in whatever order they arrived in the response body, concatenates results in completion order, and streams them. Two of the three calls are slow; the answer opens with the Pro quote, compares it against nothing, then mentions Basic in a footnote. The model did not get dumber — its context was reordered, and the comparison logic in its head is order-sensitive.

**Parallel is a feature of the response, not of your loop.** Providers may return several tool_calls in a single assistant message, and the intended handling is to execute them concurrently — Promise.allSettled in JavaScript, asyncio.gather in Python — then post one tool message per call id, in any order, before requesting again. The invariant that matters is the mapping: every call id gets exactly one result, and results must never be attached to the wrong id. The cheapest way to break it is a shared mutable array filled in completion order while iterating later by position; the fix is a map keyed by id, built from the settled results. Concurrency limits still apply: gather with a semaphore, because the model's generosity is not your database's capacity.

**Merge order is a design decision.** When results re-enter the transcript, their arrangement is part of the answer's quality. Options, in increasing sophistication: (1) by call id — neutral, lossless, the safe default; (2) by declared intent — group related lookups in the order the model's question implied; (3) by domain priority — ground rules first, quotes second, live prices last, so the final reading order matches how you want the model to weigh them. Whichever you pick, make it deterministic: the same set of calls must produce the same arrangement tomorrow, or your eval runs will not reproduce. Cap each result too — a 40 KB table per call times five calls blows the window (Module 4) and buries the question; truncate per result with an explicit "truncated, 47 of 310 rows" marker rather than a silent cut.

**Dependency is the trap parallelism hides.** Some calls can only be issued once another has returned: you cannot fetch shipping options for a cart before you know the cart id. Detect this by looking at required parameters you already have versus need — if a call's argument would be null without a prior result, it belongs to the next round, not this one. Two honest options: let the model stage naturally (it issues cart lookup now, shipping next round — costs a round trip, keeps judgement with the model), or resolve dependencies in code (faster, but now you own planning logic you must test). Most apps should let the model stage and reserve code for what is truly mechanical. Never fabricate a placeholder argument to "run it in parallel anyway" — you are paying for a lookup against data you invented.

**The deterministic split, stated once.** The model judges: which tools to call, with what arguments, what the merged results mean, what to say. Deterministic code decides: what exists, what is authorised, how results are ordered, deduped, aggregated, sorted and truncated; all arithmetic; all policy. A clean test for the boundary — if two runs with the same inputs must produce the same value, it belongs in code. If it is interpretation of language or selection among options, it belongs in the model. When the model starts "merging" results in prose, you get arithmetic errors dressed as fluent sentences; when code starts "interpreting" results, you get brittle rules that cannot handle a new phrasing. Duplications are common: the model may emit the same call twice in one message (dedupe by name-plus-arguments hash before executing — same work, one round of tokens), and overlapping calls across rounds need an idempotency story (Module 2).
payload.diagram:
flowchart TD
  A["assistant message: 3 tool_calls"] --> B["dedupe by name + args hash"]
  B --> C["semaphore: cap concurrency"]
  C --> D1["call 1"] & D2["call 2"] & D3["call 3"]
  D1 & D2 & D3 --> E["map: call_id -> result (settled)"]
  E --> F["merge policy: stable, deterministic, per-result capped"]
  F --> G["one role:tool message per id"] --> H["next request"]
  X["dependent call: needs id from call 1"] -.->|"next round"| H

payload.title: Merge strategies and when each earns its keep
rows: Default for any set of independent lookups
Groups results in the order the question implied
Ground rules before live values before commentary
Answers where reading order shapes trust
Never as the only merge — ordering then drifts run to run

payload.title: Dedupe before you dispatch
payload.text: The same name-plus-arguments twice in one response is one lookup with two ids — pay once, answer both ids.

payload.title: Positional merging of concurrently completed calls is a correctness bug waiting for one slow request
payload.text: Key everything by call id; completion order is timing, not meaning.

payload.title: Compare two plans correctly under three-way fan-out
payload.problem: The plan-comparison assistant emits three calls: list_prices, list_limits and list_features for two plans. Results come back out of order and one fails with a timeout. Restructure execution so the answer is stable, complete and honest about the gap.

steps.title: Inspect the calls for dependencies and duplicates
steps.desc: All three take plan ids already present in the request — independent, so one round of concurrency is legal. None depend on another result, so nothing gets staged. On a run where the model emitted list_prices twice with identical arguments, dedupe collapses them to one execution and two id-keyed results.

steps.title: Execute concurrently with a cap, merge by declared intent
steps.desc: Three dispatches under a semaphore; each validates and authorises before touching pricing code. Merge policy for this question type is group-by-topic: prices, then limits, then features — the reading order the comparison needs — with each result capped at 2 KB and truncated markers intact.
steps.code_snippet:
calls: [list_prices, list_limits, list_features]  # independent -> one round
merge policy: topic order (prices, limits, features), deterministic
results capped: 2 KB each, "truncated: 47 of 310 rows" preserved

steps.title: Feed the failure back as data, not as a hole
steps.desc: list_limits timed out. Its id gets {"error": "timeout", "retryable": true} as the tool message — not a skipped entry, not an empty string. The model sees exactly which topic is missing and, on the next round, can retry that one call or answer with an explicit caveat.

steps.title: Read the second response
steps.desc: The model retries the limits lookup once, gets the data, and produces the comparison in the intended order with every plan line backed by a real result. If the retry had failed again, the answer would have stated the gap plainly — because the merged context said so, in an order the model could trust.

payload.solution: Concurrency with an id-keyed map, a deterministic merge policy and per-result caps turned a timing-dependent answer into a reproducible one. The timeout became information instead of a silence, which is the difference between a model that says "limits are unavailable right now" and one that quietly compares a price against nothing. And the deterministic split held: code ordered, deduped and capped; the model judged what the merged picture meant.

payload.title: Instrument one fan-out
payload.prompt: Take the last multi-call response your app produced (or design one for three independent lookups). Write the execution plan: concurrency cap, dedupe key, merge policy and per-result byte cap. Then write the dispatch code keyed by call id with allSettled-style handling, and name one call that must be staged to the next round and why.
payload.hint: If your merge order can differ between two runs with identical calls, it is not a policy yet — it is timing.

mistakes.mistake: Filling a shared array in completion order and reading it by position
mistakes.fix: Key results by call id; positional merging breaks the first time one request is slow.

mistakes.mistake: Issuing dependent calls in the same parallel round
mistakes.fix: Stage them: a call whose argument needs a prior result belongs to the next round — or to code, if you own planning.

mistakes.mistake: Unbounded fan-out and uncapped result sizes
mistakes.fix: Semaphore on concurrency, dedupe on identical calls, byte cap with explicit truncation markers per result.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model do the merging arithmetic
mistakes.fix: Deterministic split: code orders, dedupes and aggregates; the model only interprets language and chooses what to ask.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: A response contains four tool_calls and one is dependent on another. Describe correct execution, the id-mapping invariant, the merge decision, and where the deterministic-code/model-judgement boundary sits.
payload.answer: First classify: three independent calls run concurrently under a concurrency cap (a semaphore or bounded gather); the dependent call — whose required argument only exists after another returns — is staged to the next round (letting the model sequence it) or resolved in code if you truly own planning; never fabricate placeholder arguments to force parallelism. Invariant: results are stored in a map keyed by call id and exactly one tool message is posted per id — positional or completion-order merging corrupts the transcript under any timing variance. Merge strategy is explicit policy: by call id (neutral default), by declared intent (comparison order) or by domain priority — deterministic across runs, with each result byte-capped and truncation marked, since five 40 KB tables will bury the question. Dedupe identical name-plus-arguments calls before executing. Boundary: the model chooses what to call, with what arguments, and what results mean in prose; code does everything that must be reproducible — validation, authorisation, ordering, dedupe, arithmetic, truncation. Test: if two runs with the same inputs must yield the same value, it belongs in code.
payload.source: System-design round: "your assistant issues parallel tool calls — walk me through the handler."

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Several tool_calls per response is normal; execute concurrently under a cap, never unbounded.
The invariant is the id-to-result map — one tool message per id, key never position.
Merge order is policy: pick it deliberately, keep it deterministic, cap every result.
Dependent calls are staged to the next round; placeholders are invented data with a bill.
Dedupe identical calls and pay for one execution.
Deterministic split: code orders, dedupes and computes; the model selects and interprets.

questions.prompt: Under concurrent tool execution, results must be associated with calls by:
options: Completion order, since faster results are more relevant
The tool_call id each result was produced for
Array position in the original response
The tool name, which is unique per response
questions.explanation: Completion order is timing; only the id survives concurrency, retries and dedupe.

questions.prompt: A tool call needs an order_id that only a previous call returns. You should:
options: Pass null and let the model fill it later
Stage it to the next round (or resolve it in code if you own planning) — never fabricate the argument
Guess a plausible id to keep one round
Run it anyway; providers ignore missing fields
questions.explanation: Placeholder arguments mean paying for a lookup against invented data; dependencies belong to a later round.

questions.prompt: The deterministic-code vs model-judgement split says arithmetic and ordering belong in code because:
options: Two runs with the same inputs must produce the same value — that is what makes results testable and reproducible
Code runs faster than any model
Providers forbid the model from merging results
questions.explanation: Reproducibility is the test: anything that must be identical run-to-run lives in code, not in fluent narration.

questions.prompt: Four results of 40 KB each re-enter the transcript. The most likely consequence:
options: Nothing; results are not counted as tokens
The window overflows or the question gets buried — cap each result and mark truncation explicitly
Latency improves because context is cached
questions.explanation: Tool results are tokens like any other content; per-result caps with honest truncation markers protect the window.

lessons.title: Confirmation Flows: Preview, Approval and the Safety of Irreversible Actions
lessons.summary: Hallucinated arguments are normal, so destructive or outward-facing actions never execute straight through. Classify every tool by reversibility, build preview → approve → execute gates bound to the exact plan, and keep the model out of the job of deciding whether something is safe.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify tool actions into permission tiers by reversibility, blast radius and external visibility
Design a confirmation flow: preview, approval token bound to a plan hash, expiry and one-time use
Draw the boundary where model judgement ends and deterministic policy begins
Audit every gated execution with the plan, the approver and the outcome

payload.text: A demo assistant with an send_email tool processes "email the beta list about Friday's outage" — and the model, having been told in the system prompt that the outage was minor, fills recipients from a stale list in context: 14 emails to customers whose contracts were cancelled last month, each containing a confident sentence about downtime the company never had. The tool worked perfectly. Nothing between the model's invented arguments and the SMTP server ever asked a human.

**Not all tools are equal; treat them differently.** Classify every action on two axes: reversibility (can an operator undo it in minutes?) and blast radius (how many people see it or are affected?). That gives three practical tiers. Read: no side effect — lookup, search, calculation — always allowed within authz. Reversible write: creates or modifies something an authorised person can undo (draft created, cart updated, ticket tagged) — allowed, logged, undoable. Irreversible or outward-facing: sends, charges, deletes, publishes, external API calls with money or reputation attached — gated. The tier lives in code as a property of the tool, not in the prompt: the model does not get to reclassify delete_user as a reversible write because the conversation sounds confident.

**The gate: preview, approve, execute — bound together.** A confirmation flow is not a chat message saying "are you sure?". It is a small state machine with three properties that most implementations miss. (1) Preview shows the exact effect in human terms before approval: "Send to 14 recipients, subject 'Outage postmortem', body below" with the real list, the real body, the real amount — rendered from the arguments your code resolved, not from the model's prose description of them. (2) The approval is a token bound to a plan hash: SHA-256 of the canonicalised arguments plus the tool name plus the acting user. Executing re-computes the hash and refuses on mismatch — this closes the time-of-check/time-of-use hole where the model (or a prompt injection) swaps recipients between approval and execution. (3) The token is single-use with a short expiry (minutes, not hours) and is consumed atomically. Optional but wise for high blast radius: dry-run mode on the tool itself, so your preview calls the real validation path with a write flag off — previews that do not exercise the real checks are fiction.

**Where model judgement stops.** The model proposes: it decides an action is warranted and drafts the arguments. Deterministic code disposes: it validates shape, re-checks authorisation against current session state (not the one at preview time), enforces quotas and policy (Module 9), computes the resolved effect, and only then executes. Asking the model "is this safe to send?" is not a control — the same context that produced a risky plan will produce a reassuring answer about it. Three places people wrongly put the gate: inside the system prompt ("always confirm before sending"), inside the model's self-assessment, and in the UI as a yes/no with no binding to the arguments. All three are narrative, not mechanism.

**The audit line.** Every gated execution writes one record: plan hash, tool name, canonical arguments, who approved and when, request/trace id, and the outcome (executed, expired, hash mismatch, rejected). This is what turns an incident into a twenty-minute diagnosis instead of a week of archaeology — and what lets you later ask "how often did the model propose something a human had to correct?" as a product metric. Confirmation rate and correction rate are the health numbers of a tool-using app: a gate that approves 100% of plans forever is either a great filter or a rubber stamp, and the only way to tell is sampling what got approved.
payload.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P["model proposes: tool + args"] --> V["validate + authz + policy"]
  V --> R{"tier?"}
  R -->|"read"| E["execute"]
  R -->|"reversible write"| W["execute + log + undo path"]
  R -->|"irreversible"| H["resolve real effect from args"]
  H --> PR["preview to human: exact effect"]
  PR --> AP["approve: token = hash(plan) + user, TTL, single-use"]
  AP --> EX["re-hash, match, consume, execute, audit"]
  EX -.->|"hash mismatch / expired"| X["refuse + audit"]

payload.title: Permission tiers by reversibility and blast radius
rows: Authorisation only — always allowed inside the session
Create draft, tag ticket, update cart
Send email, charge, delete, publish, external API
Preview → human approval bound to plan hash → execute

payload.title: Approval rate and correction rate are your product metrics
payload.text: A gate approving everything forever may be a rubber stamp; sample what passed and you will know.

payload.title: "Are you sure?" addressed to the model is not a confirmation
payload.text: The model lives in the context that produced the risky plan; only a human with a bound token is a control.

payload.title: Gate the refund tool without stalling support agents
payload.problem: A support assistant can issue_refund up to ₹2,000. Agents want speed; finance wants accountability. Build the tier, preview and audit so that a hallucinated amount can never reach the payment provider.

steps.title: Classify and split the tool by amount
steps.desc: issue_refund is irreversible (money leaves). Rather than one tool with a weak prompt rule, split by blast radius: issue_refund (≤ ₹500, reversible only by finance ticket but small) logs with undo path — no, money is never "reversible", so the honest classification is: all refunds gated, with a lighter preview under ₹500 (one-click confirm, no second screen) and a full preview above it. The tier decision is a table in code, keyed on resolved amount — not on how the model phrases the request.

steps.title: Build the preview from resolved arguments
steps.desc: The model proposes {"order_id": "ORD-2026-00417", "amount": 499, "reason": "damaged item"}. Code resolves order, customer and prior refund total, then renders: "Refund ₹499 to Priya S. for ORD-2026-00417 (item: ceramic set) — ₹0 refunded previously". If the model had proposed amount 4999, the preview would show ₹4,999 against a ₹499 order and the discrepancy is visible to the approver before anything is consumable.
steps.code_snippet:
plan_hash = sha256("issue_refund|" + user_id + "|" + canonical(order_id, amount, reason))
preview  = "Refund {amount} to {customer} for {order_id} - previously refunded {prior}"
approval = single-use token, TTL 5 min, bound to plan_hash

steps.title: Approve once, consume atomically, re-hash on execute
steps.desc: The shift lead clicks approve. The database row is taken atomically (single-use), the hash is recomputed over the arguments as they stand now, and any mismatch — an argument edited after preview, an injected recipient swap — aborts to the audit log instead of the payment provider.

steps.title: Read the audit trail a week later
steps.desc: Eleven refunds executed; one expired because nobody was at the desk; one hash mismatch — a run where the model amended reason text between preview and approval, caught and refused. Confirmation rate 100%, correction rate one in thirteen: the number the team now watches, and the reason they sample approved plans monthly.

payload.solution: The gate is mechanism, not manners: tiered in code by resolved effect, previewed from arguments the code itself resolved, approved with a single-use hash-bound token, executed only after a re-hash match, and audited end to end. The hallucinated-amount path — the one that reached customers in the hook story — now dies at the preview, where a human sees the real number next to the real order. And because every proposal is recorded, the team can treat confirmation and correction rates as the health metrics they are, instead of assuming the gate works because nobody complained.

payload.title: Tier and gate one real action
payload.prompt: List every tool in your app and assign each a tier: read, reversible write, irreversible/outward. For the top tier, write the preview (what the human sees, rendered from resolved arguments), the plan-hash binding, and the audit record fields. Then find the one argument your model most often hallucinates and say which check catches it before execution.
payload.hint: If your preview text is generated by the model rather than assembled from resolved data, the preview can lie too.

mistakes.mistake: Executing outward-facing tools straight through with prompt-level "always confirm" instructions
mistakes.fix: Tier in code and gate with a mechanism; prompts describe intent, they do not enforce it.

mistakes.mistake: Confirmation not bound to the exact arguments
mistakes.fix: Hash the canonical plan (tool + user + args), single-use, short TTL; re-hash before execute to block TOCTOU swaps.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model judge whether an action is safe
mistakes.fix: The model proposes; code validates, authorises, enforces policy and computes the effect it will show a human.

mistakes.mistake: No audit record of gated executions
mistakes.fix: Persist plan hash, approver, outcome and trace id — the difference between a twenty-minute incident and a week of archaeology.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Give the three permission tiers for tools with an example of each, then describe a confirmation flow that is safe against argument swapping between preview and execution. Why is a model self-assessment not a control?
payload.answer: Tiers by reversibility and blast radius: read (lookups, searches) — authorised but ungated; reversible write (draft created, cart updated, ticket tagged) — executed with audit log and undo path; irreversible or outward-facing (send, charge, delete, publish) — gated. Gate design: resolve the real effect from the arguments in code (never from the model's description), show a preview rendered from that resolution, and issue an approval token bound to a SHA-256 plan hash over canonical arguments plus tool name plus acting user, with single-use consumption and a short expiry; at execution, take the approval atomically, recompute the hash over the current arguments and abort to the audit log on any mismatch — which defeats the time-of-check/time-of-use swap where arguments change after approval. Audit every outcome: executed, expired, mismatch, rejected. A model self-assessment is not a control because it runs in the same context that produced the risky plan: the system prompt asks for safety, the model says yes, and nothing independent verified anything — controls must be deterministic, outside the model, and bound to the exact effect.
payload.source: Safety/design interview: "your agent can send email and refund money — how do you ship it?"

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Tier every tool in code: read, reversible write, irreversible/outward.
Preview from code-resolved arguments — the model description of an effect is not the effect.
Approve a hash-bound, single-use, short-TTL token; re-hash before executing.
The model proposes, code disposes: validation, authz, policy and effects stay deterministic.
A human confirming without bound arguments is narrative, not mechanism.
Audit plans and outcomes; watch confirmation and correction rates as product metrics.

questions.prompt: Which tier does "send an email to a customer list" belong to?
options: Reversible write — the email can be recalled
Irreversible / outward-facing — gated with preview and approval
Any tier, decided by the model per request
questions.explanation: Outward-facing effects on people outside the system are the definition of the gated tier; recall is a myth in email.

questions.prompt: The plan hash in a confirmation flow exists to prevent:
options: Arguments changing between preview and execution (TOCTOU)
questions.explanation: Binding approval to a canonical hash of tool + user + args makes any post-approval swap fail the re-hash check.

questions.prompt: Asking the model "is this safe to execute?" is not a security control because:
options: It runs in the same context that produced the risky plan and has no independent authority
questions.explanation: A control must sit outside the thing being controlled; model self-approval is the risky plan vouching for itself.

questions.prompt: A preview that describes the effect in the model's own words is dangerous because:
options: The model writes longer prose than a template would
The same context that hallucinated the arguments will hallucinate the summary — previews must be rendered from code-resolved data
Models cannot describe side effects at all
questions.explanation: The preview is the last human checkpoint; if it narrates from the plan instead of resolving it, the checkpoint verifies nothing.

lessons.title: Tool Errors, Feedback Loops and Streaming Tool Rounds
lessons.summary: Every tool will fail. Classify the failure, hand it back to the model as structured data the next round can act on, keep the loop bounded so retries cannot become a cost incident, and stream a tool round to the UI without lying about what is happening.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify tool failures and return each as a structured tool result with a safe, actionable message
Bound the loop: round caps, per-tool retry budgets and no-progress detection
Design the streaming path for tool rounds: argument deltas, status events and final-answer streaming
Cancel in-flight tool work when the client disconnects, and account tokens across every round

payload.text: A PDF summariser exposes a search tool. One evening a dependency returns a 500 page; the raw HTML lands in the transcript; the model, unable to parse it, apologises and invents three citations; the app retries the same call with the same arguments nine times over four minutes at forty cents a round; the user closes the tab, but the loop does not notice and keeps going. Four failures stacked: unstructured error, hallucinated recovery, unbounded retries and no abort propagation. Each has a fix, and none of them is a better model.

**Errors are results, not exceptions.** An exception thrown away from the transcript throws away the only context the model has. Instead, every failure becomes a tool message with the call id and three fields: a stable error code your code branches on (not_found, invalid_argument, permission_denied, timeout, dependency_unavailable, quota_exceeded), a human-safe message that says what went wrong in plain language, and a hint the model can act on — "order_id must match ORD-YYYY-NNNNN" invites a corrected retry; "no order for this customer" invites asking the user instead. What must never cross back: stack traces, provider dumps, internal hostnames, SQL, secrets (Module 9 owns redaction; this is where it is enforced). The app also decides its own next step from the code: permission_denied is terminal for that call — do not offer the model a retry it is not allowed to succeed at.

**Bounds are what stop a feedback loop from becoming a cost incident.** Three nested limits, all in code. A round cap for the whole turn (six is a common ceiling for real tasks — verify yours with an eval), returning a graceful degraded answer when hit. A per-tool retry budget: the same tool with a materially different argument set may retry twice; identical name-plus-arguments after a retryable failure should be recognised as no-progress and stopped immediately, because repeating a deterministic failure is paying to be wrong. And a dependency circuit breaker: after N failures in a window, the tool reports dependency_unavailable for a cooldown rather than letting every user pay the latency of a dead service. When the budget is exhausted, the honest behaviour is a partial answer with a stated gap — not silent omission.

**Streaming a tool round without lying.** Tool calls stream too: the name and argument fragments arrive as deltas, and arguments are partial JSON until the final fragment — you cannot execute until the call is complete (finish_reason signals it; also verify provider behaviour on aborted argument streams). The UI contract that works: stream any assistant text the model wrote before calling (models may preface with "Looking that up…"), then emit a distinct status event per call — running search, fetching 3 results — then stream the final answer normally. Never render partial JSON as if it were a result, and never show a spinner where a specific status ("checking inventory…") is knowable. Client disconnects must propagate: an abort signal should cancel the in-flight HTTP request to the provider AND the dispatched tool execution, because a closed tab that keeps spending is both a bug and a bill. Usage accounting sums every round: prompt tokens grow with each re-send of the transcript plus accumulated tool results — which is why uncapped loops and 40 KB results (Lesson 2) compound into the same cost curve.

**Honest failure modes.** Truncated argument streams when a client or connection dies mid-call (the tool never ran — say so, do not half-run it); models that call a tool with a missing required field despite the schema (validate and return invalid_argument — the schema reduces, not eliminates, this); tool results so large the final answer degrades (cap at the source); and the classic: an error message so vague the model retries identically forever — which the round cap saves you from but the error design should prevent.

flowchart TD
  S["stream: assistant text deltas"] --> C["stream: tool_call name + arg deltas"]
  C -->|"call complete (finish_reason)"| V["validate + execute (cancellable)"]
  V -->|"success"| R["tool result"] --> N["next round"]
  V -->|"failure"| E["structured error as tool result"] --> N
  N --> Q{"round cap / no-progress / circuit breaker?"}
  Q -->|"ok"| S
  Q -->|"exhausted"| G["degraded answer with stated gap"]

payload.title: Harden the knowledge assistant: errors, caps, streaming
payload.problem: The assistant retrieves internal docs via search_docs and can summarise long files. A dependency outage produces the raw-500 story from the hook. Redesign the error path, the loop bounds and the streaming events.

steps.title: Turn every failure into a coded tool result
steps.desc: search_docs wraps its dependency: on 5xx it returns {"error": {"code": "dependency_unavailable", "message": "The document index is briefly unavailable.", "hint": "Answer from context if you can, otherwise say the index is down."}}; on an empty query, invalid_argument with the expected shape; on an ACL miss, permission_denied marked terminal. Redaction runs on the message field before it is serialised — stack traces and hostnames die at the boundary.

steps.title: Add the three bounds and watch a bad night replay
steps.desc: MAX_ROUNDS = 6 per turn; per-tool retry budget of 2 with same-key detection; circuit breaker opens after 5 dependency failures in 60 s. The outage replay now runs at most two attempts, then returns "the index is down — here is what I can say from this session" instead of nine paid rounds and three fabricated citations.

steps.title: Fix the streaming contract
steps.desc: Events: text deltas while the model narrates; a status event per tool call ("searching docs", "reading file X"); status done; then final answer deltas; final event carrying summed usage across all rounds, finish reason and trace id. Argument deltas are buffered and only executed on completion — a disconnect mid-arguments cancels the provider request and any dispatched tool, and the audit shows the call never ran.

steps.title: Verify with the failure fixtures from Module 5
steps.desc: Replay the six mock fixtures plus two new ones (dependency_unavailable, invalid_argument). All eight produce the right UI state, the right next round or a bounded stop, and usage that sums correctly. The eval case that used to fail with hallucinated citations now passes because the recovery is specified rather than improvised.

payload.solution: Failures became data with codes and hints, the loop acquired three independent bounds, and the stream told the truth about what was running. The outage that once cost nine rounds of spend and the user's trust now costs two attempts and one honest sentence — and because cancellation follows the disconnect, closing the tab actually stops the work. None of this required a smarter model; it required treating the tool loop as an engineered control system: bounded, observable and cancellable.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What must a tool error result contain and what must it never contain? Describe three bounds on a tool loop and the streaming event sequence for a round.
payload.answer: Contain: a stable error code for code to branch on, a human-safe plain-language message, and an actionable hint that lets the model choose a different next step; posted as a tool message with the correct call id. Never contain: stack traces, raw provider dumps, internal hostnames, SQL, or any secret — redaction runs before serialisation. Bounds: (1) a hard round cap per turn, after which the app returns a graceful degraded answer; (2) a per-tool retry budget with same-key no-progress detection so a deterministic failure is not repeated for money; (3) a circuit breaker that short-circuits a failing dependency for a cooldown instead of charging every request for its latency. Streaming sequence: assistant text deltas (any narration before the call) → per-call status events while argument deltas are buffered (nothing executes until the call is complete) → final answer deltas → a final event with usage summed across all rounds, finish reason and trace id; client abort propagates to both the provider stream and dispatched tool execution so a disconnected tab stops spending.

modules.title: Module 7 — Structured Extraction: Schemas, Validation, Documents and Doubt
modules.summary: Extraction is where an LLM stops being a writer and becomes a data source — which means the engineering changes completely. This module designs schemas the model can fill honestly (with citations back to the source text), validates every field with pydantic or zod and repairs once on failure instead of trusting, falls back gracefully when the model cannot comply, traces the document path from PDF through OCR to clean text and into fields, derives confidence the model cannot fake and forces an honest abstention, and resolves the same real-world entity across many records without merging the wrong two.

lessons.title: Schema Design for Extraction: Fields the Model Can Fill Honestly
lessons.summary: Extraction schemas are not database schemas. Design flat, enumerable, abstention-friendly shapes with a citation span per claim, decide where null and unknown and empty actually differ, and stop the three silent killers: defaulting, type drift and prose fields.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Design an extraction schema whose fields the model can fill correctly under pressure
Encode abstention and unknown as first-class values instead of forced guesses
Attach source spans so every extracted value can be checked against the input
Recognise the schema mistakes that produce silent wrongness rather than loud errors

payload.text: A fintech team extracts "amount" from uploaded invoices into a numeric column. The schema says number; the model, facing "₹1,25,000 (inclusive of GST)" and a line reading "Balance: NIL", returns the string "1,25,000" for one and the number 0 for the other. Both pass a try/except that only checks the key exists. Six weeks later, reconciliation finds 2,140 wrong rows and one very confident dashboard. Nothing failed loudly — the schema asked for a type and got a costume.

**A schema is a behavioural contract, not a storage plan.** Database schemas optimise for storage and joins; extraction schemas optimise for the model under pressure: long documents, ambiguous phrasing and the strong temptation to please you with an answer. Four design rules follow. (1) Flat over nested: one level of objects at most — field completion accuracy measurably drops as trees deepen, and your validator grows arms. (2) Enumerate everything enumerable: a status field with six possible values gets an enum, so an out-of-enum value is a visible bug rather than a string you must trust. Open sets (a product name, a clause quote) stay open strings — the mistake is forcing a closed enum on an open world, which just moves the guessing inside your allowed list. (3) Every field a human will check gets a citation span: the exact quoted substring plus its character offset (or page and bounding box for documents). A value without a span cannot be audited; a value with a span that does not appear in the input is a hallucination you caught for free. (4) Type hygiene: numbers are numbers, dates are ISO strings normalised by a stated rule, booleans are booleans — and the schema says so in the field description, because descriptions are instructions the model reads.

**Absence is three different facts.** present_and_extracted, absent_from_source (the document genuinely does not state it) and unreadable_or_uncertain (the scan is illegible in that region) are different outcomes with different downstream behaviour: the first populates a record, the second goes on the missing-field report, the third triggers a human or OCR review. A schema that collapses them all into null — or worse, into a default of 0 or empty string — manufactures data. Make abstention cheap and explicit: an optional field plus a reason enum is more honest than a required field that invites a guess. Instruct plainly in the field description: if the source does not state this, return null and record the reason.

**Type drift is the quiet killer.** The invoice story is the pattern: a numeric field receives a formatted string; a date field receives "end of month"; a boolean receives "yes". Two defences, layered. First, the schema description spells out the normalisation rule: amounts as plain decimal strings without symbols or separators, dates as ISO 8601 (yyyy-mm-dd), never a relative phrase. Second, your validator (Lesson 2) rejects on type rather than coercing silently — coercion is how a wrong value takes a seat in your database wearing a number costume. Note what does not work: asking the model in the system prompt to "be careful with types". Prompts lower the failure rate; only validators guarantee the floor.

**Design for the run, not the demo.** Big schemas degrade: as the field count grows, the model trades attention across fields and edge cases get abandoned quietly — so split documents into passes (core fields first, secondary fields in a second call over the same text) rather than one mega-object. Prose fields are a trap inside extraction: "notes" invites the model to summarise and editorialise, which it will do even when you asked for a quote — either drop the field or make it a verbatim span like every other claim. And always keep one field the model cannot invent: the source hash or document id your code attaches, so an extracted row can always be traced back to the exact bytes that produced it.

flowchart LR
  IN["source text (document, message, paste)"] --> SC["extraction schema"]
  SC -->|"fields + types + enums"| M["model extracts"]
  SC -->|"one span per claim"| M
  M --> V["validate: type, enum, span-in-source"]
  V -->|"all good"| OK["record + provenance"]
  V -->|"span missing / type drift"| R["repair pass (7-2)"]
  V -->|"absent / unreadable"| A["reason enum -> report or review"]

payload.code:
# an extraction schema designed for honesty, not for storage
from typing import Literal, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Span(BaseModel):
    quote: str = Field(description="Exact substring of the source text")
    start: int = Field(description="Character offset of quote in the source")

class InvoiceFields(BaseModel):
    invoice_number: Optional[str] = Field(
        description="Id printed on the invoice, e.g. INV-2026-00417. "
                    "null with reason=absent if the source does not state it."
    )
    amount_total: Optional[str] = Field(
        description="Grand total as a plain decimal string: digits and at most "
                    "one dot, no currency symbols, no separators. 125000.00, "
                    "never '1,25,000' or 'about 1.25L'."
    )
    due_date: Optional[str] = Field(
        description="ISO 8601 date yyyy-mm-dd. Never a relative phrase like "
                    "'end of month'. null if not stated."
    )
    currency: Optional[Literal["INR", "USD", "EUR", "GBP"]] = None
    amount_span: Optional[Span] = Field(description="Where the total appears")
    absent: list[str] = Field(
        description="Names of fields that are null, with reason: "
                    "absent_from_source or unreadable_or_uncertain"
    )

EXTRACT_PROMPT = (
    "Extract invoice fields from the text between <<< and >>>. "
    "Rules: quote spans must be exact substrings; if a field is not stated, "
    "return null and list it under absent - never guess.\n\n"
    "<<<\n{doc_text}\n>>>"
)

The redesign targets each: string-normalised amount with a stated rule, null-with-reason for absent, ISO-only dates, and a span per claim.

steps.title: Write the schema with spans and a reason enum

"Balance: NIL" -> amount_total=null, absent=["amount_total:absent_from_source"]
amount_span.quote must appear verbatim in the source, offsets checked by code

The validator checks the span offsets against the source bytes and confirms both quotes appear verbatim.

Compare the previous run: zeros and guesses had filled those rows and the gap was invisible. The schema change did not make the model smarter; it made honesty cheaper than guessing.

payload.solution: The new schema made every silent failure either impossible (type and enum rejection at the validator) or visible (spans that must exist in the source, abstention with reasons). NIL became an honest null with a reason instead of a zero that passed for data. And the paired-span rule gave reviewers their first cheap audit tool: any claim whose quote is not a verbatim substring is a hallucination caught by a string search, before a human reads it.

mistakes.mistake: Normalisation rules living only in the system prompt
mistakes.fix: Put them in field descriptions AND enforce them in the validator; prompts persuade, validators guarantee.

mistakes.mistake: Deeply nested extraction schemas
mistakes.fix: One level maximum; split a large extraction into ordered passes over the same text instead of one mega-object.

mistakes.mistake: Extraction values with no citation span

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Explain four design rules for extraction schemas and why absence must be modelled as three distinct outcomes. What are the defences against type drift?
payload.answer: Rules: (1) flat — at most one level of nesting, because field accuracy drops with depth and validation grows complex; (2) enumerable sets become enums, open sets stay open strings, because a forced closed list just relocates guessing; (3) one citation span (exact quote plus offset) per claim, because a value with no span cannot be audited and a span that is not a verbatim substring exposes a hallucination for free; (4) type hygiene stated in field descriptions — normalisation rules (plain decimal strings, ISO dates, no relative phrases) written where the model reads them. Absence is three facts with different downstream behaviour: extracted (populate the record), absent_from_source (missing-field report for the business), unreadable_or_uncertain (human or OCR review) — collapsing them into null or a default like 0 manufactures data. Defences against type drift: normalisation rules inside field descriptions, plus a validator that rejects mismatched types instead of coercing — prompts lower the failure rate, only validators guarantee the floor.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Extraction schemas optimise for a model under pressure, not for storage.
Flat, enumerable, abstention-friendly, one span per claim, source hash attached.
Absent, unreadable and extracted are three facts — never one null.
Normalisation rules belong in field descriptions; enforcement belongs in the validator.
Prose fields smuggle editorialising into data — quote or drop them.
Large extractions split into passes, not one mega-schema.

lessons.title: Validation, Repair and Fallbacks: pydantic and zod in the Loop
lessons.summary: The model will sometimes return wrong structure — so validate every extraction with a real schema library, repair exactly once with the error text fed back, and design the fallback chain for when the model simply cannot comply: partial records, human queues, honest rejects.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Validate model output with pydantic or zod as a hard gate before anything persists
Run one bounded repair round that feeds the validator error back as data
Design the fallback chain: repair, degrade to partial, route to human, reject
Instrument repair rate as a health metric that catches schema and prompt regressions

payload.text: A team trusts structured output mode and skips validation "because the schema is enforced". One model update shifts a field from string to string-array in their dialect; the extractor happily returns arrays where the database expects scalars; the ETL casts each value with a helper that turns lists into their first element via str()[1:-1] slicing. For two months, every multi-value field is stored as its first character. Enforced structure is not validated semantics — and the difference sat in one unchecked assumption.

**Structure enforced is not semantics guaranteed.** Providers can constrain output to match your schema — JSON mode, schema-constrained decoding, strict tool arguments (as of 2026 the names and guarantees differ; verify current docs). What that buys: you will receive parseable JSON of roughly the right shape. What it does not buy: a value that matches its type ("1,25,000" is a string; the schema wanted a plain decimal string), a span that actually appears in the source, an enum member the document supports, or a date that is not a relative phrase. So validation is your layer, always: parse, then check with a real library — pydantic in Python, zod in TypeScript — as a hard gate before anything persists. A validator is also where your business rules live: amounts in range, spans within source offsets, mutually exclusive fields, cross-field arithmetic.

**Repair once, with the error as data.** When validation fails, the cheapest fix is a second call that returns the failing payload plus the validator's error and asks for a corrected object only. Design details that separate a repair from a hope. (1) Bounded: one repair per object; a second failure goes to fallback, because repair loops are how a 2-cent retry becomes a dollar. (2) The feedback is precise: not "invalid JSON" but pydantic's actual message — field amount_total: value is not a valid number (input "1,25,000") — with the original document still in context. (3) The ask is narrow: return the corrected object, not a new full extraction; full re-extractions double tokens and invite new errors in fields that were fine. (4) Temperature stays low; repair is not the moment to get creative. Watch the trap: a repair that accepts any change may silently alter a value that was actually right and only mis-typed — so diff the repaired object against the original and keep original values when only the type changed, if your normalisation allows it.

**The fallback chain, decided in advance.** Repairs fail sometimes; that is normal, not exceptional. The chain: repair (once) → partial accept (persist the validated subset with per-field provenance, mark the record incomplete, queue the failed fields) → human review (the queue shows source text beside the failed field and the model's attempt) → reject the document with an honest reason. Which rung you jump to depends on error cost: a marketing-tagging pipeline can partial-accept almost everything; a compliance extraction partial-accepts nothing without review. The failure taxonomy matters here — syntax errors (should be near-zero with constrained output), type errors (your normalisation rules not followed), semantic errors (span not in source, arithmetic inconsistency) and refusals (model declines the document). Each class maps to a different rung and a different prompt or schema fix.

**Repair rate is a first-class metric.** Track repairs per field per prompt version (Module 5 attribution makes this queryable). A field whose repair rate jumps after a schema edit is a regression the demo never showed; a field stuck at 30 percent repair is misdescribed and needs a description or type redesign, not an infinite repair habit. Teams that watch only final-pass accuracy never see the money their repair loop is quietly spending — and never notice that half their "structured output" arrives via second chances.

flowchart TD
  O["raw model output"] --> P["parse (constrained mode)"]
  P --> V["pydantic / zod: types, enums, spans, business rules"]
  V -->|"valid"| OK["persist with provenance"]
  V -->|"errors"| RP["repair call #1: payload + exact errors"]
  RP --> V2{"valid?"}
  V2 -->|"yes (diffed)"| OK
  V2 -->|"no"| FB["fallback chain"]
  FB --> PA["partial accept + queue failed fields"]
  FB --> HR["human review"]
  FB --> RJ["honest reject with reason"]
  PA --> M["repair-rate metric per field, per prompt version"]
