payload.code:
# validate -> repair once -> fallback, with the diff guard
from pydantic import ValidationError

async def extract(doc_text: str, *, user_ctx) -> ExtractResult:
    raw = await model_extract(doc_text, schema=InvoiceFields, temperature=0)
    try:
        fields = InvoiceFields.model_validate_json(raw)
        return ExtractResult(status="ok", fields=fields)
    except ValidationError as err:
        pass

    # repair #1: narrow ask, exact errors, same document in context
    repaired = await model_repair(
        doc_text,
        payload=raw,
        errors=err.errors(include_url=False),   # field, message, input
        temperature=0,
    )
    try:
        candidate = InvoiceFields.model_validate_json(repaired)
        diff = value_diff(InvoiceFields.model_validate_json(raw) if False else None, candidate)
        keep = reconcile_type_only_changes(raw, candidate)  # type fixes ok, value swaps flagged
        audit("repair", field_diffs=diff, kept=keep)
        return ExtractResult(status="repaired", fields=keep)
    except ValidationError as err2:
        pass

    # fallback: validated subset only, failed fields queued with provenance
    partial = safe_subset(raw)                    # whatever validates cleanly
    queue_human_review(doc_text, failed=err2.errors(), attempt=repaired)
    metric("repair_failed", doc=user_ctx.doc_id, errors=[e["loc"] for e in err2.errors()])
    return ExtractResult(status="partial", fields=partial, needs_review=True)

payload.title: Feed the validator's exact error text back — vagueness produces vague repairs
payload.text: pydantic and zod already print the field, the message and the offending input; hand the model that, not a summary.

payload.title: Unbounded repair loops turn structure errors into cost incidents
payload.text: One repair per object; the second failure follows the fallback chain you decided in advance.

payload.title: Add validation and a repair budget to the invoice extractor
payload.problem: The extractor from Lesson 1 runs model → database with a shape check. A new document type breaks it in three ways: span offsets off by a page-header shift, amount as a list of candidate values, and one outright refusal. Build the loop and read the metrics.

steps.title: Put the validator in front of the database
steps.desc: pydantic gate on every extraction: types, enums, span-quote-must-appear check, amount parseable by your normalisation rule. The list-valued amount fails immediately with field amount_total: Input should be a valid string — the costume caught in one line, before any ETL helper can slice it.

steps.title: Repair once with exact errors
steps.desc: Second call carries the failing payload and the validator errors verbatim; the span-mismatch error shows the model its quote against the real location. Two of three documents come back corrected: amount collapsed to its single plausible value, span re-anchored. The diff guard keeps value changes visible in the audit.
steps.code_snippet:
repair ask: "Return only a corrected object. Errors:
- amount_total: Input should be a valid string (got ['9000', '9,000'])
- span[2].quote not found in source"
result: 2/3 valid; 1 still mismatches -> fallback

steps.title: Run the fallback on the third
steps.desc: Second validation fails; the chain partial-accepts the four clean fields with provenance, queues the span issue for human review with source text beside the attempt, and marks the record incomplete. Nothing incorrect reaches the database; nothing is silently dropped either.

steps.title: Read the dashboard a week later
steps.desc: Repair rate by field: due_date 18 percent — its description still confuses relative phrases, so the description gets rewritten (a schema fix, not a repair habit); amount_total 2 percent after the enum of candidate formats was removed in favour of the plain-decimal rule. Total repair spend: 0.4 cents per document, down from the unbounded-retry prototype that occasionally cost 12 cents and still failed.

payload.solution: Validation became a hard gate, repair became a bounded and precisely-informed second chance, and the fallback became a decision instead of a panic. The repair-rate metric did what final-pass accuracy never could: it named the misdescribed field (due_date) and priced the loop. And the refusal — the class where repair is pointless — went straight to a human, because the chain had already decided that in advance.

payload.title: Wire the loop and price it
payload.prompt: Add a real validator (pydantic or zod) in front of every persistence path in your app. Implement one repair round that feeds the exact validator errors back, then a partial-accept fallback with provenance. Log repair attempts per field with prompt_version. Report your repair rate, the worst field, and the one description you will rewrite because of it.
payload.hint: If you cannot answer "what did the repair change?", the diff guard is missing and value swaps will hide inside type fixes.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting constrained output as semantic validation
mistakes.fix: Constrained mode guarantees parseable shape; your validator still owns types, enums, spans and business rules.

mistakes.mistake: Repair loops with no bound
mistakes.fix: One repair per object, then the pre-decided fallback chain; loops are cost incidents with good manners.

mistakes.mistake: Vague repair feedback ("invalid output, try again")
mistakes.fix: Feed the exact field, message and offending input the validator produced.

mistakes.mistake: Persisting the repaired object without diffing it
mistakes.fix: Diff against the original; keep type-only fixes, flag value swaps in the audit before they become data.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why is schema-constrained output insufficient on its own? Describe the bounded repair design and the fallback chain, and explain what repair rate tells you that final-pass accuracy does not.
payload.answer: Constrained output guarantees parseable structure of roughly the right shape — not semantics: a string in a numeric field, an enum value the document does not support, a span that is not a verbatim substring, or a relative phrase in a date field all satisfy a shape check. So a real validator (pydantic/zod) gates every persistence path, enforcing types, enums, spans and business rules. Repair: exactly one second call carrying the failing payload plus the validator's exact errors (field, message, input) with the document still in context, asking for a corrected object only, at low temperature, with a diff guard that keeps value changes visible. Fallback chain, decided in advance: partial-accept the validated subset with per-field provenance and a review queue for failed fields; human review with source text beside the attempt; honest reject with a reason — which rung depends on the error cost of the domain. Repair rate per field per prompt version is a health metric: it prices the loop, catches regressions after schema edits and names misdescribed fields — a 30 percent repair field is a description bug, while a rising rate after a prompt bump is a regression that a final-pass-accuracy dashboard never shows.
payload.source: Data-pipeline interview: "walk me through what happens when extraction output does not validate."

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Constrained shape is not validated semantics — your validator is always the gate.
Repair once, feed exact errors as data, keep a diff guard on the result.
Fallback chain decided in advance: partial with provenance, human queue, honest reject.
Refusals never go through repair — they go to a human or a reason.
Repair rate per field per prompt version is the metric that prices the whole loop.
A permanently high repair field is a schema or description bug, not a model quirk.

questions.prompt: Schema-constrained output guarantees:
options: Semantically correct values for every field
Parseable structure of roughly the right shape — semantics remain your validator's job
That validation can be skipped entirely
questions.explanation: Shape is enforced at decode time; meaning, normalisation and provenance are still on you.

questions.prompt: The right number of repair attempts per extracted object is:
options: One — a second failure follows the pre-decided fallback chain
Three, matching the three most common error classes
questions.explanation: Bounded repair captures the cheap wins; unbounded repair is how a cent-level retry becomes a dollar-level habit.

questions.prompt: A repair returns a corrected object whose amount differs from the original by more than formatting. You should:
options: Accept it silently — the validator passed
Keep the original, since first outputs are more faithful
Diff it, flag the value change in the audit, and only keep type-only normalisations automatically
Run a second repair to see which one it prefers
questions.explanation: The diff guard is what stops value swaps from hiding inside legitimate type fixes.

questions.prompt: Repair rate for field due_date sits at 30 percent across thousands of documents. First action:
options: Add a third repair round for that field only
Rewrite the field description and normalisation rule — a chronically repaired field is misdescribed
Switch to a larger model for extraction
Mark due_date as always-null in production
questions.explanation: Repair rate names schema and description bugs precisely; paying to repair forever is the expensive way to avoid redesigning.

lessons.title: Documents to Text to Fields: The PDF and OCR Input Path
lessons.summary: Real extraction starts before the model: classify the document, parse text PDFs directly and route scans through OCR, clean without destroying layout meaning, keep provenance to page and offset, and treat parse quality as a measured gate — because garbage text produces confident garbage fields.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify documents and route each to the right extraction path: direct parse, OCR, or vision
Clean extracted text without destroying the layout signals extraction depends on
Preserve provenance: page numbers, offsets and region flags through every stage
Measure text quality before extraction and degrade honestly when the parse is poor

payload.text: A claims-processing team uploads 400 scanned forms to a PDF text extractor and runs their polished extractor on the result. The text layer is empty — the scanner wrote images, not text — so the extractor receives blank pages and returns null-everywhere records that pass validation (absent is a legal value!). Two weeks of "the model got worse" investigations end at a one-line fix: detect the empty parse and route to OCR. The model had not changed. The input path had never been built.

**Most extraction failures are input failures wearing the model's face.** The pipeline before the model has four stages, and each one can poison the fields. (1) Classify: is this a born-digital PDF with a real text layer, a scan, a photograph, a table-heavy financial statement, a multi-column newsletter? The class picks the path, and a cheap classifier (page-level text coverage, image ratio, or a small model) beats assuming. (2) Parse: text PDFs go through a layout-aware parser (pdfplumber, PyMuPDF, or a hosted document API — as of 2026 the hosted vision-document APIs are strong on layout and weak on your budget; verify current pricing); scans go through OCR (Tesseract for local, or a cloud OCR with word-level confidences); vision models can read pages directly when layout is too wild for text extraction — trading cost and latency for robustness. (3) Clean: normalise unicode, strip hyphenation across line breaks, drop page furniture (headers, footers, page numbers) by repetition detection — but keep paragraph breaks and table structure, because "did the total appear under a column" is layout, and layout is data. (4) Segment and extract: page-aware chunks with offsets, one extraction call per coherent region rather than one wall of text.

**Provenance is not optional.** Every extracted field should trace back to page number and character offsets (or bounding boxes where OCR provides them). Three reasons, all practical: the citation-span check from Lesson 1 needs offsets to verify against; human review needs to show the reviewer the right page region, not a 90-page wall; and when a parser is swapped or an OCR engine updated, provenance diffs tell you which fields moved. Carry it as a sidecar structure alongside the text: text, plus a map from offsets to pages, built once and threaded through cleaning — cleaning must therefore be offset-aware (removing a header shifts offsets; recompute rather than pretend).

**Measure text quality before you spend on extraction.** Three cheap signals: text coverage (characters of extracted text per page — near-zero means scanned images), OCR confidence distribution (a mean under 90 or a long low-confidence tail means expect field errors), and structural sanity (page count, presence of expected anchors like totals blocks). Gate on them: excellent → extract normally; marginal → extract but flag every field with a low-quality-source marker and route spans below threshold to review; poor → skip extraction, request a better upload or a human pass. This is the honest degradation the hook story lacked. Confidence propagation matters downstream: a field extracted from 70-confidence OCR is not the same fact as one from a clean text layer, and your record should say so.

**The long-document budget.** A 90-page contract at 40,000 tokens exceeds many windows and wrecks the rest of the budget (Module 4). Segment by structure — headings, numbered clauses, page boundaries — not by fixed character counts that bisect a clause mid-sentence; extract per segment with the schema; merge with provenance intact; and keep the global pass (what document is this, which sections matter) separate from the field pass. Watch the table trap: PDF tables flatten into noise in naive text extraction — detect table regions and use table-aware parsing, or a vision pass, because "row 4 column 2" is exactly where fields silently swap columns and still validate as numbers.
payload.diagram:
flowchart LR
  IN["upload"] --> CL{"classify"}
  CL -->|"born-digital"| P1["layout-aware parse"]
  CL -->|"scan / photo"| P2["OCR + word confidences"]
  CL -->|"wild layout"| P3["vision page read"]
  P1 & P2 & P3 --> Q{"quality gate"}
  Q -->|"ok / marginal"| C["clean, offset-aware"]
  Q -->|"poor"| H["request better upload / human"]
  C --> S["segment by structure + provenance"]
  S --> E["per-segment extraction (7-1, 7-2)"]
  E --> M["merge fields + page/offset spans"]

payload.title: Input class → path → what you must carry forward
rows: Page map, table regions, reading order
Quote boundaries, so replies are not merged with originals

payload.code:
# classify -> parse -> quality gate -> clean, with provenance intact
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class PageText:
    page: int
    text: str
    ocr_conf: float | None      # None for born-digital text
    char_to_page: list[int]     # offset -> page map, rebuilt after cleaning

def classify(path: str) -> str:
    coverage = text_coverage(path)          # chars of text layer per page
    if coverage < 5:   return "scan"         # essentially empty text layer
    if table_ratio(path) > 0.4: return "tables"
    return "digital"

def parse(path: str) -> tuple[list[PageText], float]:
    kind = classify(path)
    if kind == "scan":
        pages = ocr_with_confidences(path)          # word-level confidences
        mean_conf = mean(p.ocr_conf for p in pages)
    else:
        pages = layout_aware_parse(path)            # keep reading order + tables
        mean_conf = None
    return pages, mean_conf

def quality_gate(pages, mean_conf) -> str:
    total_chars = sum(len(p.text) for p in pages)
    if total_chars < 200 * len(pages): return "poor"      # e.g. empty parse
    if mean_conf is not None and mean_conf < 90: return "marginal"
    return "ok"

def clean(pages: list[PageText]) -> list[PageText]:
    furniture = detect_repeated_furniture(pages)   # headers/footers/page nos
    out = [strip_furniture_keep_offsets(p, furniture) for p in pages]
    return [dehyphenate(p) for p in out]           # offsets recomputed, never assumed

payload.title: Empty-parse detection is one line that saves weeks of misdiagnosis
payload.text: If extracted text is far below a page-count heuristic, you have a scan — route it or reject it, but never extract from nothing.

payload.title: Cleaning that shifts offsets without rebuilding the map breaks every citation span downstream
payload.text: Offset-aware cleaning, or a rebuild; never a silent edit.

payload.title: Build the input path for a mixed claims inbox
payload.problem: Claims arrive as born-digital PDFs, phone photos of paper forms and one notorious table-heavy spreadsheet export. Design the classification, parse, gate and provenance path so extraction receives usable text and reviewers receive page-cited fields.

steps.title: Classify before spending
steps.desc: A cheap first pass computes text-layer coverage and image ratio per upload: 68 percent born-digital (parse directly), 24 percent scans (OCR with confidences), 5 percent photos (vision page read), 3 percent table exports (table-aware parse). Each class gets its own path; each path emits the same PageText shape with provenance.

steps.title: Parse with structure kept, then gate
steps.desc: Digital pages keep reading order and table regions; OCR pages carry word-level confidences; a quality gate scores each document. One upload returns poor: its text layer is a single page of a 14-page scan set — the extractor is never called; the uploader gets a specific request ("pages 2–14 are images; re-upload or use scan mode") instead of a week of model-blaming.
steps.code_snippet:
gate: chars/page < 200 -> "poor"  -> no extraction, specific uploader message
gate: mean OCR conf < 90 -> "marginal" -> extract + low_quality flag + review threshold

steps.title: Clean offset-aware and segment by structure
steps.desc: Repeated headers and page numbers are stripped with offsets recomputed; hyphenated line-breaks are joined; paragraph and table structure survive. Segmentation follows numbered claim sections rather than fixed character windows, so a clause is never bisected; each segment carries its page map into extraction.

steps.title: Extract, merge, and show provenance in review
steps.desc: Fields extract per segment with spans; the merge resolves conflicts by preferring higher-quality sources (digital text over marginal OCR) and records source class per field. The review queue shows each flagged field beside its actual page region — reviewers now check a page image, not a text dump, and the marginal-OCR documents get eyes exactly where confidence was weakest.

payload.solution: The inbox stopped being one path pretending everything was clean text. Classification routes, the quality gate refuses to spend on garbage and says why, offset-aware cleaning keeps every citation honest, and provenance rides the whole way into the review queue — where a low-confidence OCR field is visibly a different kind of fact than a text-layer one. The blank-page mystery from the hook is now a one-line classification, caught before a single token is spent.

payload.title: Classify and gate one real document set
payload.prompt: Take five real documents from your domain. For each: measure text-layer coverage, classify the path you would take, and say what provenance you must carry. Implement the empty-parse check and the OCR-confidence gate, then show which of the five would extract, flag or refuse — and what the uploader sees in each case.
payload.hint: Print the first 200 characters of parsed text for each document; the garbage you see there is what your model will confidently structure.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming every PDF has a usable text layer
mistakes.fix: Classify by coverage first; scans go to OCR or vision, or they are refused with a specific message.

mistakes.mistake: Cleaning that destroys layout meaning or breaks offsets
mistakes.fix: Keep paragraph and table structure; strip furniture with offset recomputation, never silent edits.

mistakes.mistake: Extracting from low-quality text with no flag
mistakes.fix: Quality gate: marginal sources get per-field markers and review thresholds; poor sources skip extraction entirely.

mistakes.mistake: Fixed-size chunking that bisects clauses and tables
mistakes.fix: Segment by structure (headings, numbered sections, pages) and use table-aware parsing for tabular regions.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Outline the document-to-text pipeline with its four stages, the role of the quality gate, and why provenance must survive cleaning. What class of error does naive table flattening produce?
payload.answer: Stages: (1) classify — born-digital vs scan vs photo vs table-heavy, by text coverage, image ratio or a small classifier; (2) parse — layout-aware parser for text PDFs, OCR with word-level confidences for scans, vision page reads for wild layouts, table-aware handling for tabular regions; (3) clean — unicode normalisation, dehyphenation, furniture removal by repetition detection, while preserving paragraph/table structure and recomputing offsets whenever text shifts; (4) segment and extract — structure-aware chunks with page maps, per-segment extraction, merged with per-field provenance. The quality gate sits between parse and extraction: near-zero text per page means a scan (refuse or route, never extract from nothing), low mean OCR confidence means marginal (extract with a low-quality flag and review threshold), otherwise normal extraction. Provenance must survive cleaning because citation-span verification needs offsets, human review needs the right page region, and parser swaps must be diffable. Naive table flattening produces column-swap errors that still validate as numbers — the most dangerous class, because structure errors that pass a type check silently become wrong facts.
payload.source: Document-AI design question: "the extractor works on our test PDFs and fails on real uploads — diagnose."

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Classify, parse, gate, clean, segment — the model is downstream of all of it.
Empty-parse detection alone would have ended the hook story in one line.
OCR confidence is data: propagate it into per-field quality markers.
Cleaning is offset-aware; provenance (page, offsets) rides every stage into review.
Segment by structure, not by character windows; tables get table-aware handling.
Marginal sources extract with flags; poor sources are refused with a specific ask.

questions.prompt: A PDF returns almost no characters per page. The correct next step:
options: Raise max_tokens so the model can handle sparse input
Classify it as a scan and route to OCR or vision — or refuse with a specific uploader message; never extract from nothing
Retry the same parser; outages happen
questions.explanation: An empty parse is an input classification, not a model problem; extraction from nothing produces confident nulls.

questions.prompt: Why must character offsets be recomputed when cleaning removes a page header?
options: Otherwise every citation span downstream points at the wrong text, breaking audit and review
questions.explanation: Provenance is only as honest as its map; a shifted map mis-cites every field that follows.

questions.prompt: A document has mean OCR confidence of 84. Best handling:
options: Discard it — anything under 90 is useless
Extract normally; confidence does not affect field accuracy
Extract with a low-quality marker on fields, tighter review thresholds, and provenance recording the source class
questions.explanation: Marginal is not worthless — it is a different kind of fact that your record must honestly mark.

questions.prompt: The most dangerous consequence of flattening a PDF table into plain text is:
options: Longer output tokens and higher cost
Column swaps that still type-check as numbers — wrong facts that pass validation
The OCR engine refuses to process the result
Citation spans become impossible to store
questions.explanation: A value in the wrong column is still a valid number — the class of error that passes every structural check.

lessons.title: Confidence, Abstention and Entity Resolution Across Records
lessons.summary: Model-stated confidence is not calibrated — derive confidence from evidence instead: span support, run agreement and validator outcomes. Force honest abstention that routes to review, then resolve the same real-world entity across many records with deterministic normalisation first and model judgement only for the genuinely ambiguous pairs.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Distrust model-stated confidence and derive evidence-based confidence signals
Design abstention thresholds that route uncertain extractions to human review
Build an entity-resolution pipeline: normalise, block, match deterministically, escalate ambiguity
Keep resolution auditable: canonical ids, merge provenance and a reversible merge policy

payload.text: A CRM enrichment job extracts company names and asks the model to rate its own confidence 0 to 1. The ratings cluster at 0.9. "Acme Pvt Ltd" and "ACME PRIVATE LIMITED" and "Acme Pvt. Ltd. (Bengaluru)" resolve cleanly; "Acme" alone — which the model confidently resolves to the ₹400-crore Acme Industries — is actually the stationery vendor two blocks away. Three months in, the vendor receives enterprise pricing emails addressed to the wrong legal entity. The confidence field was never wrong, as far as the model knew. It was just not a measurement.

**Self-reported confidence is a tone, not a measurement.** Asked for a number, models produce a plausible one — anchored by training on human-like hedging, not by an internal probability you can calibrate. Treat it, at most, as one weak signal among several, and prefer evidence you compute yourself. Four signals that actually mean something: (1) span support — does each field have a verbatim quote that exists in the source (Lesson 1)? Absent span, lower confidence. (2) Validator outcome — did the value pass types, enums and cross-field checks, and did it need a repair? Repaired-at-once is slightly weaker than clean; twice-failed is weak. (3) Run agreement — extract twice at low temperature with a permuted field order; disagreement on a field is a real disagreement you can see. Cheap for the fields that matter, too expensive to run on everything (token cost doubles). (4) Source quality — the OCR and parse flags from Lesson 3, propagated per field. Combine them into a score you define and can defend, and always store the components, not just the sum: when a downstream review disagrees, the components say why.

**Abstention is routing, not refusal.** An extractor that always answers will guess; one that abstains well becomes a triage system. The design: every uncertain field carries a reason (low_span_support, cross_run_disagreement, low_source_quality, ambiguous_reference) and the record carries a review status derived from thresholds you set by error cost — a compliance pipeline routes anything below a high bar to humans; a research scraper lets low-confidence values through marked as provisional. The user-facing behaviour of abstention matters too: when the end user is a human reading the extraction, show "not stated in the document" proudly — it reads as competence, not failure. The failure mode to avoid is abstention theatre: a field abstains, a human approves it in one click forever, and you have built a slower guesser with extra steps. Measure the human-approval rate per field; if it is 100 percent at threshold, your threshold is theatre.

**Entity resolution: deterministic first, model last.** The same real-world entity arrives spelled a hundred ways — case, punctuation, legal suffixes (Pvt Ltd / Private Limited / LLC), transliterated cities, stray OCR errors. Resolution is a pipeline, and the order matters. (1) Normalise deterministically: casefold, unicode NFKC, strip punctuation, expand a fixed suffix table, standardise phone and address formats. This alone resolves the majority of pairs, free and auditable. (2) Block: generate candidate pairs by shared keys (normalised name, phone, domain, postal code) — comparing every record to every other is O(n²) and unnecessary. (3) Match with rules: exact normalised-key match merges automatically; rule-based scoring (name similarity plus corroborating keys like domain or phone) handles the rest, with thresholds for auto-merge, auto-non-merge and the ambiguous middle. (4) Escalate the middle to the model — with the two records side by side and a forced choice plus reason (same / different / cannot tell), never a bare yes. (5) Canonicalise: every merged record points at a canonical id, merges store their evidence and are reversible, and source records are never deleted. The trap to name: the model is worst exactly where you need it — short, generic names with no corroborating keys ("Acme" vs "Acme") are genuinely underdetermined, and the honest output is cannot-tell with routing to a human, not a confident pick. Never let an irreversible business action key off an unresolved ambiguous merge.
payload.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A["field extracted"] --> S{"span in source?"}
  S -->|"no"| L1["low_span_support"]
  S -->|"yes"| V{"validator / repair outcome"}
  V -->|"clean"| R["run agreement check (sampled)"]
  V -->|"repaired / failed"| L2["repair flags"]
  R -->|"agree"| C["confidence = f(components)"]
  R -->|"disagree"| L3["cross_run_disagreement"]
  L1 & L2 & L3 --> T{"threshold vs error cost"}
  T -->|"above"| P["persist; provisional flag optional"]
  T -->|"below"| H["human review queue with reason"]
  X["records"] --> N["normalise (deterministic)"] --> B["block candidates"] --> M["rules: auto-merge / auto-no / middle"]
  M -->|"middle"| Q["model: same / different / cannot tell"]
  Q --> K["canonical id + evidence + reversible merge"]

payload.title: Confidence components and what each catches
rows: Fabricated values with no source text
Doubles tokens — sample key fields only
Almost nothing reliable on its own
Free — keep as one weak feature

payload.title: Store the confidence components, not just the score
payload.text: When review disagrees with an extraction, the components tell you which signal lied.

payload.title: Irreversible actions must never key off an ambiguous merge
payload.text: Route cannot-tell to a human; "Acme" alone is underdetermined and confident picking is how vendors get enterprise pricing.

payload.title: Score extractions honestly and resolve the Acme mess
payload.problem: The CRM job trusts 0-to-1 self-ratings. Rebuild scoring from evidence and add resolution with an ambiguity rung, then read what changes in the queue.

steps.title: Replace the self-rating with component scores
steps.desc: Every field now carries span support (quote present in source?), validator outcome (clean, repaired, failed), cross-run agreement (sampled on 20 percent of fields), and source quality from the parse gate. The stored record has the components; the single score is a weighted function the team can argue about and change deliberately.
steps.code_snippet:
"ACME PRIVATE LIMITED" -> span yes, clean, agree, digital -> 0.97 -> auto-accept
"Acme" (ambiguous ctx)   -> span yes, clean, DISAGREE across runs -> 0.44 -> review queue

steps.title: Normalise and block before any model sees a pair
steps.desc: NFKC, casefold, punctuation strip, suffix table: Acme Pvt Ltd / ACME PRIVATE LIMITED / Acme Pvt. Ltd. collapse to the same key and merge automatically with the phone as corroboration. Blocking by domain and postcode cuts candidate pairs from 4 million to 12 thousand — the model never does the O(n²) work.

steps.title: Route only the middle to the model, with cannot-tell allowed
steps.desc: Rules auto-merge the top band and auto-separate the bottom; 38 pairs sit in the middle. The model sees each pair side by side with a forced choice. It returns cannot-tell on 11 of them — including bare "Acme" versus "Acme Industries", which now routes to a human instead of silently binding the stationery vendor to the enterprise account.

steps.title: Audit a month of merges
steps.desc: Auto-merge precision (sampled): 99.2 percent. Model middle-band: 24 merged, 3 separated, 11 human-resolved. Reversibility check: every merge has evidence rows and can be undone; two bad merges were undone in a day after a customer complaint — the feature that made finance comfortable enough to approve the rollout.

payload.solution: Confidence became measurements instead of manners — and the components, not a single number, explained every review decision. Resolution ran deterministic-first, so most pairs never needed a model, and the genuinely underdetermined cases got the only honest answer available: cannot-tell, a human, and a reversible merge trail. The confident wrong binding of the hook story is now a review-queue row, which is exactly where an underdetermined "Acme" belongs.

payload.title: Score and resolve on your own data
payload.prompt: For one extraction field, record the four evidence components and define a defensible weighted score; report how often it disagrees with the model's self-rating. Then run resolution on twenty duplicate-ish records: show which merged deterministically, which separated, and which landed in the ambiguous middle — and what you will do with each middle case before anything irreversible keys off it.
payload.hint: If your approval queue shows 100 percent one-click approvals, your abstention threshold is theatre — lower the bar or fix the field.

mistakes.mistake: Treating model-stated confidence as a calibrated probability
mistakes.fix: Compute span, validator, agreement and source-quality components; keep self-rating as one weak feature at most.

mistakes.mistake: Abstention with no routing — or routing nobody measures

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why is model-stated confidence unreliable, and which four evidence signals replace it? Outline the entity-resolution pipeline and say why the model belongs only at the final ambiguity rung.
payload.answer: Self-reported numbers are generated to sound plausible, not read from a calibrated internal probability — they cluster high and do not track real error rates. Replacement signals you compute: span support (the claim's quote exists verbatim in the source), validator outcome (clean versus repaired versus failed), cross-run agreement (a second low-temperature extraction with permuted field order — sampled where cost matters), and propagated source quality from the parse/OCR gate; store components so review disagreements can be explained, and keep the self-rating only as a weak feature. Resolution pipeline: deterministic normalisation (casefold, NFKC, punctuation, legal-suffix table, phone/address formats) resolves most pairs free; blocking by shared keys avoids O(n²) comparison; rule scoring with bands for auto-merge, auto-separate and a middle; the model sees only the middle, side by side, with same / different / cannot-tell forced and a reason — because short generic names with no corroborating keys are genuinely underdetermined and the model is worst exactly there. Canonical ids, stored evidence and reversible merges keep the whole thing auditable, and no irreversible action keys off an unresolved ambiguous merge.

Cannot-tell is a first-class answer for underdetermined pairs.
Merges keep evidence and stay reversible; nothing irreversible keys off the ambiguous band.

modules.title: Module 8 — Evaluation and Testing: Golden Sets, Judges, CI and Tracing
modules.summary: Part I baselined a slice; this module turns that into a discipline that scales. Build offline golden sets from real traffic with scoring functions you can defend; use LLM-as-judge where programmatic checks cannot go, with calibrated criteria and named bias traps; wire prompt and code regressions into CI behind thresholds rather than vibes; trace every request as spans with token accounting so failures are reconstructable; sample production honestly and legally; and run the eval-to-fix loop until quality compounds instead of oscillating.

lessons.title: Golden Sets: Offline Evaluation Your App Can Trust
lessons.summary: A golden set is your app's memory: real cases, expected behaviour, and scoring you can defend. Build one from production and incidents, score deterministically where you can, keep it versioned and held out, and read the numbers without fooling yourself about noise and overfitting.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Construct a golden set from real cases with expected behaviour written before running
Choose scoring: programmatic checks first, rubrics only where judgement is unavoidable
Version the set, hold out a slice, and resist overfitting to your own eval
Interpret results against noise: repeated runs, effect sizes and failure classes

payload.text: A team reports their assistant went from 78 to 94 percent in a week — then back to 81 the next week. The prompts barely changed. What changed was the set: three developers added cases they had just fixed, removed two that were "flaky", and regraded an old failure as a pass by reading it more generously. Their eval had become a mood with a number attached. The fix is not a better model. It is a set with provenance, held-out cases and scoring that does not depend on who is reading.

**What a golden case actually contains.** Four things, always: (1) the input as production would deliver it — full document, real mess, not a sanitised excerpt; (2) the configuration fingerprint: prompt version, model id, relevant retrieval or tool settings — because "did it pass?" is meaningless without knowing what ran; (3) the expected behaviour, written before the run — an exact answer where the task is closed (extraction, classification), a rubric of checkable properties where it is open (must cite two sources, must refuse medical advice, must not exceed 120 words); (4) a scoring function that turns output into pass or fail without a human deciding how to feel that day. A case missing any of the four is an anecdote, not an eval item.

**Scoring in order of decreasing honesty.** Programmatic first: exact or normalised match for closed tasks, field-by-field comparison for extraction, substring and regex checks for required or forbidden content, span-existence checks for citations, arithmetic checks for anything numeric, length and format constraints, refusal detection for out-of-scope probes. Each is deterministic, free and debuggable. Rubrics only where judgement is genuinely required — coherence of a multi-paragraph answer, helpfulness of tone — and there, write the rubric as checkable properties (does it address the actual question, does it hedge where the source is silent) rather than a 1-to-5 vibe scale. A hybrid case is normal: three programmatic checks plus one rubric line. What you must not do: let a model grade with no reference and no criteria — that measures agreeableness.

**Build the set from evidence, not from imagination.** Sources in order of value: production incidents and bugs (the case that broke you is worth ten invented ones); user feedback records from Module 3 (thumbs-down plus context is a labelled failure); the failure classes from your Module 5 baseline; adversarial inputs (injection attempts, refusal probes, out-of-scope requests); and a random production sample to keep distribution honest — because incident-only sets drift towards the exotic and forget that most traffic is boring. Sizes: 20–50 to start, 100–300 for a mature app; beyond a few hundred, maintenance cost beats marginal signal — better to keep 200 excellent cases than 2,000 stale ones.

**Version it, split it, and watch the noise.** The set lives in the repo as JSONL, diffed and reviewed like code — adding a case is a PR with a reason. Split into a dev set (you iterate against it freely) and a holdout set (run at release gates only); if you never look at holdout failures while tuning, it stays an honest estimate. Expect noise: even at temperature 0, provider-side nondeterminism means a single case flipping is not signal — run repeated trials on a sample to estimate your flip rate, compare changes on many cases, and treat one- or two-case deltas as nothing. Track failure classes, not only the pass rate: a total that holds while citation misses become formatting misses is a different app wearing the same number.

flowchart LR

  S2["thumbs-down feedback"] --> G
  S3["baseline failure classes"] --> G
  S4["random production sample"] --> G
  G["golden set (JSONL, in repo, versioned)"] --> SPL["dev split | holdout split"]
  SPL --> RUN["run harness: fixed prompt/model, low temp"]
  RUN --> SC["score: programmatic, then rubric"]
  SC --> REP["pass rate + failure classes + cost + latency"]
  REP --> D{"change worth it?"}
  D -->|"yes"| PROMOTE["commit case diffs, bump prompt version"]
  D -->|"no"| REVERT
  HOLD["holdout"] -.->|"release gates only"| REP

The citation-versus-accuracy trade that the pass rate hid is now visible, which is the real product of a golden set: not a number, but a classified picture of what your app does wrong.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: List the four components of a golden case, the scoring ladder in order, and five sources for case material. How do you handle eval noise and overfitting to your own set?
payload.answer: Components: input exactly as production delivers it; configuration fingerprint (prompt version, model, retrieval/tool settings); expected behaviour written before the run (exact values for closed tasks, checkable rubric properties for open ones); and a scoring function that does not depend on the reader's mood. Scoring ladder: normalised exact match → per-field comparison → structural checks (required/forbidden substrings, format, length) → programmatic semantics (arithmetic, span-in-source, citations resolve) → rubric lines with checkable properties — never a bare 1-to-5. Case sources: production incidents first (they are real), thumbs-down feedback with context, baseline failure classes, adversarial probes (injection, refusal, out-of-scope), and a random production sample for distribution honesty. Noise: pin temperature and the configuration fingerprint, run repeated trials on a sample to learn the flip rate, treat one- or two-case deltas as nothing and compare across classes. Overfitting: keep cases in versioned JSONL with a reason per addition, split into dev and holdout, and consult holdout only at release gates so it remains an honest estimate.

lessons.title: LLM-as-Judge: Criteria, Calibration and Bias Traps
lessons.summary: When scoring cannot be programmatic, a judge model can — if you design it like a measurement instrument: narrow criteria, reference-anchored rubrics, calibrated against human labels on a gold subset, with the known biases named and actively mitigated.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Design judge criteria as narrow, checkable dimensions instead of global quality scores
Calibrate a judge against human labels and measure agreement before trusting it
Name and mitigate the standard judge biases: self-preference, length, position, style
Decide where a judge may gate a release and where it may only inform

payload.text: A team replaces human review with a judge prompt that asks: "Rate the overall quality of this answer from 1 to 10." Scores land between 7 and 9 for everything, including answers that invented a policy. The judge correlates with nothing; nobody checks, because the dashboard looks rigorous. Two months later they discover the judge shares a model family with their generator — and their own model's drafts score a full point above a competitor's stronger model on identical tasks. The instrument was measuring fluency and family loyalty, and they had built a release gate on it.

**A judge is a rater, and raters need design.** The single global score is the trap: it collapses dimensions you actually care about into one number nobody can act on. Design instead as you would a human rubric: two to four narrow dimensions, each with checkable criteria and an explicit failure example. For a support-answer judge: correctness against the provided context (claims supported, nothing invented), instruction compliance (length cap, tone, required elements), and usefulness (answers the actual question — not a pivot to a related one). Each dimension gets its own verdict (pass/fail or a small ordinal), and the case passes only if the gates you chose pass. Give the judge the reference material — the source context, the expected properties from your golden case — because an anchored judge measures against evidence; an unanchored judge measures plausibility. Ask for a verdict plus quoted evidence from the candidate ("point to the phrase that violates the rule"), which both improves accuracy and gives you a debuggable artifact.

**Pairwise beats absolute when you are comparing versions.** Judging "is v4 better than v3" by two absolute score sets drowns in scale drift; presenting both answers side by side and asking which better meets the criteria (with ties allowed) yields more stable comparisons. Position bias — always preferring the first or second presented — is measured, not assumed: run each pair twice with order swapped and count order-flips; a judge that flips on position is not ready to gate anything.

**Calibration is the whole game.** Before trusting a judge, label a gold subset yourself: 50 to 150 cases across the pass/fail boundary, human verdicts recorded first. Then measure agreement: simple percent agreement plus something chance-corrected (Cohen's kappa for two raters, or percent agreement against majority when you use multiple judge runs). Targets are domain-specific — for a release gate you typically want high agreement on failures specifically (missing a real failure is the expensive error), which you check with the confusion matrix, not the headline agreement number. Where agreement is poor, fix the rubric (ambiguous criteria are the usual cause), not the judge model. Re-calibrate when the generator, prompt or judge model changes — a judge calibrated against v3 answers may not hold against v4.

**Name the biases and mitigate each.** Self-preference: judges favour outputs from their own model family (measurable, era-specific, so re-measure with your stack — as of 2026, cross-family judging or human spot-checks are the standing mitigations). Length bias: longer answers score higher on vague rubrics — constrain with explicit length criteria or normalise by asking the judge to check required elements rather than "thoroughness". Position bias: swap and average. Style-over-substance: polished prose wins on correctness dims — require evidence quotes for every verdict, and include deliberately correct-but-plain candidates in calibration. Sycophancy: judges agree with confident justifications — forbid justifications from the candidate influencing the verdict by structuring the prompt to judge criteria only. Each mitigation is cheap; the expensive mistake is shipping a gate and never testing which of these it suffers from.

**Where a judge may rule.** A calibrated judge can gate releases on dimensions it agrees with humans about, flag production samples for human review, and triage failures into classes. It should never be the sole judge of safety refusals (few edge cases, high stakes — keep humans in that loop), never grade its own family's outputs without a bias check, and never be reported without its calibration stats attached. The rule that keeps this honest: a judge number without agreement data is a number; with agreement data it is an instrument.

flowchart LR
  C["candidate answer"] --> J["judge: narrow dims + reference + evidence quotes"]
  R["reference / expected properties"] --> J
  J --> V["verdicts per dimension"]
  H["human labels on gold subset"] --> CAL["calibration: agreement + confusion matrix"]
  V --> CAL
  CAL --> G{"good enough for this use?"}
  G -->|"gates"| REL["release gate on agreed dims"]
  G -->|"informs"| TRI["triage + human review queue"]
  SWAP["order swap, 2x"] -.-> J

payload.title: Judge bias traps and the standing mitigations
rows: Cross-family judge or human spot-check; re-measure per era
Wordy answers win on vague dims
Explicit length criteria; check required elements, not thoroughness
First or second presented always wins
Run both orders; count flips; swap-and-average
Require evidence quotes; calibrate with plain-but-correct candidates
Structure the prompt to criteria only; ignore candidate justifications
Grade properties, not wording; allow equivalent phrasings

payload.code:
# judge design: narrow dims, evidence quotes, calibration stats
JUDGE_PROMPT = """Compare the candidate against the criteria and the reference.
Answer as JSON with one entry per dimension. For every verdict, quote the
exact candidate phrase that decided it. Judge criteria only - ignore how
confident the candidate sounds.

Dimensions:
1. supported_by_context: every factual claim appears in REFERENCE. fail if one claim is absent.
2. instruction_compliance: length <= {max_words}, contains required elements {required}.
3. answers_the_question: addresses the asked question, not a related one.

REFERENCE:
{reference}

QUESTION:
{question}

CANDIDATE:
{candidate}"""

def calibrate(judge_fn, gold):
    rows = [(judge_fn(g), g["human_label"]) for g in gold]
    agree = sum(1 for a, b in rows if a == b) / len(rows)
    kappa = cohen_kappa([a for a, _ in rows], [b for _, b in rows])
    cm = confusion([a for a, _ in rows], [b for _, b in rows])
    return {"agreement": agree, "kappa": kappa, "missed_failures": cm["fn"], "confusion": cm}

def judge_pair(judge_fn, a, b, criteria):
    # position bias check: run swapped; a flip means this pair is not gate material
    f1 = judge_fn(a, b, order="ab")
    f2 = judge_fn(b, a, order="ba")
    return f1 if not flipped(f1, f2) else {"verdict": "unstable", "flipped": True}

payload.title: Calibrate a judge for the support-answer task

steps.title: Rewrite the rubric into three narrow dimensions
steps.desc: The old single score becomes: supported_by_context (every claim traceable to the supplied docs), instruction_compliance (length cap plus required elements), answers_the_question (no pivot). Each verdict demands a quoted deciding phrase. Reference material — the actual doc excerpts — rides along with every judgement.

steps.title: Run against the gold labels and read the confusion matrix
steps.desc: Headline agreement: 84 percent, kappa 0.68. But the matrix shows the real story: the judge misses 8 of the 60 true failures (it passes invented claims) while over-failing only 3. For a release gate, missed failures are the expensive error — so this judge is not yet allowed to gate correctness alone.

agreement 0.84, kappa 0.68
confusion: TP 52  FP 3   (judge says fail)
           FN 8   TN 57
-> missed_failures=8: correctness gate NOT approved; compliance dim IS (0.95 agree)

steps.desc: Diagnosis of the eight misses: the judge accepted confident citations without checking them against the reference. The rubric change is mechanical — for supported_by_context, verify each quoted citation exists verbatim in REFERENCE before any other check. Re-run: agreement 0.92, kappa 0.81, missed failures down to 3. Compliance dimension already at 0.95 — approved to gate.

Self-family probe: mixed-family candidates, judge from a different family than the generator. Final permissions: gate release on compliance and correctness (with human spot-check of 10 percent of gate decisions), triage everything else, never sole-refusal judge.

payload.solution: The judge went from a 1-to-10 mood dial to an instrument with published agreement, a confusion matrix that named its worst error (missed hallucinations), a rubric fix that cut it, and explicit permissions: what it may gate, what it may inform, what it may never decide alone. That is the difference between a dashboard that looks rigorous and one that is.

lessons.title: Regression Tests in CI and Tracing Every Model Call
lessons.summary: Prompt changes and code changes need the same gates: deterministic tests for the pure layers, a bounded eval job for model behaviour with thresholds, and traces — spans around every stage and model call with token accounting — so when something regresses you can find it instead of reproduce it.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Split CI into key-free deterministic tests and eval gates with explicit thresholds
Design for flakiness: recorded fixtures, retries policy, quarantine and budgets
Instrument traces: spans per stage and model call with the attributes that matter
Do token accounting per request, user and prompt version — and debug from a trace id

payload.text: A prompt edit lands on Friday. Nobody notices the retrieval chunk order flipped until Tuesday, when support reports wrong refund windows. The engineer cannot reproduce it: their machine uses a different prompt file, the provider model alias silently updated, and nobody logged prompt_version, so no trace answers which of the three changes broke it. Three days of archaeology for a change that took four minutes — because tests ran only for the code, and traces existed only as printf debugging.

**Two gates, because there are two kinds of regression.** Deterministic tests cover everything that does not need a model: assembly and truncation logic (Module 5), schema validation and repair routing (Module 7), tool dispatch and gating (Module 6), error classification, budget math. Key-free, seconds-fast, run on every commit — and they should be the majority of your suite. The eval gate covers model behaviour: a bounded run over the golden set with a real or recorded model, run on prompt changes and nightly. Thresholds are explicit in the config: "no dimension may drop more than 2 points versus baseline; zero new failures on the holdout safety cases" — a gate without a written threshold is a report, and reports do not block merges.

**Flakiness policy is a design choice, made before it hurts.** Three tools. Recorded fixtures: replay recorded provider responses for the deterministic CI lane, so prompt-assembly and post-processing changes are tested without tokens, variance or keys — the live lane runs nightly or pre-release. A flip-rate-aware rule: mark known-flaky cases and judge by class-level thresholds rather than single cases (Lesson 1's noise discipline, enforced by the gate). And quarantine: a failing case that is a known model limitation goes to a labelled quarantine list with an owner — never deleted, because deleting failures is how a set rots into agreement. Retries: at most one eval retry on transport errors, never on scoring failures — retrying a failed score until it passes is the eval equivalent of grading on a curve.

**Tracing: spans that let you reconstruct one request.** One trace id created at receive (Module 5), then a span per stage — assemble, guard, call, validate, persist — with a nested span for every model call and tool execution carrying the attributes that actually answer questions: model id, prompt_version, temperature, input/output token counts, latency, finish_reason, tool name, cache hit or miss, validation outcome. Export to whatever backend you use (OpenTelemetry is the portable shape — as of 2026, provider and vendor support is broad but verify your stack). The debug workflow you are buying: a user reports a bad answer → trace id from the final event → span tree shows retrieval returned four chunks but assembly used two → the truncation ladder (Module 4) fired → attribute says budget 6k, used 6.1k. Ten minutes, versus Tuesday archaeology.

**Token accounting is cost observability.** Aggregate the usage attributes per request, per user, per prompt version, per tool round (Lesson 4 of Module 6 showed why rounds compound). Three numbers to dashboard: p95 tokens per request (window and cost health), cost per prompt_version (which release changed the bill), and per-user daily spend (the alarm that catches a runaway loop or a cost bomb — Module 9's threat, visible here first). Sample what you cannot afford to keep: head sampling for volume, tail-on-error always kept, PII redacted before export — traces are telemetry, not a second copy of user content. The habit that makes it all work: the trace id is returned to the client in the final event, so user reports and traces connect without anyone copying screenshots.

lessons.title: Sampling Production Traffic and the Eval-to-Fix Loop
lessons.summary: You cannot label everything, so sample deliberately: outcome signals, outliers and a random slice, redacted and consented. Turn labels into golden cases, classify failures, pick the fix the class deserves, and run the loop on a cadence with guardrail metrics that stop you optimizing one number into ruin.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Design a production sampling strategy: stratified signals plus a random slice, with privacy controls
Convert labelled production failures into versioned golden cases
Run the eval-to-fix loop: measure, classify, fix by class, gate, watch guardrails
Balance quality metrics against guardrails so one number cannot be gamed into ruin

payload.text: A team watches their judge score climb steadily for two quarters: 0.71 to 0.83. Costs per request tripled (the fix for every failure was "use the bigger model"), p95 latency went from 1.8 to 6.4 seconds, and thumbs-down rate — which nobody had wired to the dashboard — quietly doubled. The quality metric was optimised exactly as instructed, and the product got worse. The loop existed; the guardrails did not.

**Sampling is triage, and the signals pick the strata.** Four strata cover most needs. (1) Outcome signals: every thumbs-down, every repair event, every refusal, every round-cap hit — these are labelled for free and always worth reviewing. (2) Outliers: latency p99, cost per request, unusual tool patterns, high round counts — they catch the classes dashboards average away (the runaway loop, the 40 KB context). (3) Random: a small percentage of ordinary traffic, because signal-only sampling sees failures and forgets that most traffic is boring and possibly quietly broken in a way nobody thumbs down. (4) Targeted: new prompt version, new document type, new geography — the slices you need confidence in first. Ratios are yours to set; the discipline is that all four exist, because a random-only sample drowns in noise and a signal-only sample never measures the base rate.

**Privacy is a precondition, not a review item.** Production text is user content. Before anything enters a labelling queue: redact PII by detection plus your domain rules (names, emails, account numbers, anything your DPA forbids), drop or hash identifiers, respect retention settings (your provider agreement and your own policy both speak here), record consent posture, and keep raw text access logged and narrow — reviewers see the minimum, for the minimum time. A sample that fails privacy review teaches nobody anything because it never reaches an annotator. Keep the pipeline id: hashed user, trace id, prompt_version — enough to route and re-run, not enough to leak.

**From label to golden case.** When a failure is confirmed, it graduates: input (redacted) captured exactly as production delivered it, pre-written expectation of correct behaviour, scoring function, reason line naming the incident or feedback id, added to the repo via review — and the holdout gets a fresh copy of the class if that class was the gap. This is the mechanism by which your eval set tracks reality instead of your imagination: every production embarrassment becomes a permanent test. The set grows slowly and for reasons, which is exactly right.

**The loop, run on a cadence.** Measure (strata reviewed weekly) → classify (taxonomy: grounding, format, refusal misuse, tool error, injection attempt, latency, cost — extend it as reality adds classes) → pick the fix the class deserves (prompt contract for grounding, schema for format, routing for cost, guardrail for injection — each failure class has a home, which is why Part II's modules map to classes) → change one thing → gate on the dev set → canary → watch production signals for the version → promote or roll back. One change per cycle, so attribution survives. Cadence beats heroics: an hour a week compounds; a quarterly cleanup does not.

**Guardrails are the brakes on the loop.** Every quality target needs opposite-side metrics that must not move: quality up but cost per request, p95 latency, refusal rate, thumbs-down rate and safety-flag rate must hold or improve. Write them as explicit gate conditions ("judge +0.03 allowed only if p95 ≤ 2.5 s and cost/request ≤ baseline × 1.2"), because metrics without brakes are how a team tripled their bill while their dashboard smiled. Watch the meta-failure too: if the judge and production signals disagree — judge up, thumbs-down up — trust production and re-calibrate the judge (Lesson 2), because the judge grades samples you chose and users grade everything.

flowchart LR

payload.title: Run four weeks of the loop on the support assistant
payload.problem: The team has a judge, a golden set and no production loop: failures arrive as complaints, fixes arrive as panic. Install the sampling queue, the classification habit and the guardrails, then run a month.

steps.title: Stand up the strata and the redaction boundary
steps.desc: Weekly queue: 55 signal events (thumbs-down, repairs, refusals), 25 outliers (p99 latency, cost spikes, rounds ≥ 5), 20 random one-percent samples, 15 targeted at the new v7 prompt. Redaction runs before the queue — emails, phone numbers and account ids are stripped and ids hashed; reviewers see trace id and version, not identities.

week 1: 55 signal + 25 outlier + 20 random + 15 targeted -> redact -> label
labels: 22 confirmed failures across 5 classes
new golden cases: 9 (reason lines reference feedback ids F-2210..F-2244)

steps.title: Classify, then fix only what the class says
steps.desc: Classes: grounding 9, format 3, tool-loop 4, injection attempts 4, latency 2. The grounding class is largest → one fix: tighten the citation contract and chunk packing (not a model swap). Injection attempts go to the M9 backlog with concrete payloads. Tool-loop cases become three new eval cases plus a lower round cap. One change per cycle, so attribution survives.

steps.title: Gate, canary, watch with guardrails armed
steps.desc: The grounding fix passes dev (37/40, no class regressions) and canaries at 10 percent. Guardrails on the dashboard: judge +0.04, p95 2.1 s (under 2.5), cost/request 1.06× (under 1.2), thumbs-down down 18 percent. Two days, then promote. The injection and loop cases stay visible as classes, not as pressure to bundle unrelated fixes.

steps.title: Read the month
steps.desc: Golden set grew from 40 to 49 cases, every one with an incident or feedback reason. Thumb-down rate down, judge up, cost within bounds, and the two latency outliers traced to a 40 KB tool result — capped in M6 style, verified next week. The loop is now boring, which is what working looks like.

payload.solution: Sampling with four strata made failures arrive on a schedule instead of as emergencies; classification made each fix the one its class deserved; the reason-lined cases made the set track reality; and guardrails made sure the improvements could not quietly triple a bill. Four weeks of boring cadence out-produced two quarters of heroic firefighting — and the one number the old dashboard worshipped is now one line among six that must all hold.

payload.title: Start your weekly loop

Then write your guardrail block: four metrics besides quality, with the exact values that would block a promote.
payload.hint: If your quality metric can rise while cost triples with nothing to stop it, the loop is missing brakes, not steps.

mistakes.fix: Add a random stratum for base rate, outliers for the quiet blowups, targeted for new versions and types.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Name four sampling strata and why each exists. Describe the path from a production failure to a golden case, and explain how guardrails constrain a promote decision.
payload.answer: Strata: signal events (thumbs-down, repairs, refusals, round caps — labelled for free and always reviewed); outliers (p99 latency, cost, high round counts — they catch what averages hide); a random slice (the only measure of the base rate of problems nobody reported); and targeted slices (new prompt versions, document types, geographies — wherever confidence is needed first). Each exists because the others miss things: signal-only forgets the base rate, random-only drowns in noise. Failure-to-case path: redact PII and hash ids first (privacy is a precondition), label in the queue, confirm the failure, then graduate it into versioned JSONL — input as delivered, pre-written expectation, scoring function, reason line citing the incident or feedback id, added through review, with holdout refreshed for the class that was the gap. Guardrails: explicit gate conditions on the metrics that quality can damage — p95 latency ceiling, cost-per-request multiplier, refusal and thumbs-down rate caps — evaluated against baseline and a week of production signals; a candidate that wins on quality but breaches a guardrail is blocked and rolled back. Meta-rule: when judge scores and production signals disagree, trust production and re-calibrate the judge.

options: Swap to the largest model immediately, then re-measure everything
