lessons.title: Tokens and Next-Token Prediction
lessons.summary: An LLM reads and writes in tokens and does one thing — predict the next one. Everything else follows from that.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain what a token is and estimate token counts for English and Indian-language text
Describe generation as repeated next-token prediction
Predict two consequences of tokenisation: odd spelling/counting errors and cost differences across languages

payload.text: Ask some chat models how many times the letter "r" appears in "strawberry" and they have historically got it wrong — while writing a correct essay on photosynthesis in the same breath. That is not a random glitch. It falls straight out of how the model sees text: not as letters, but as chunks called tokens. Understand tokens and dozens of "weird AI behaviours" stop being weird.

**Tokens.** Before a model sees your text, a **tokenizer** splits it into tokens — common words, pieces of words, punctuation and spaces. "unbelievable" might become "un" + "believ" + "able". Each token maps to a number (an id in a vocabulary of roughly 50,000–250,000 entries). The model only ever sees and produces these ids.

**Rules of thumb (English):** 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of a word, so 1,000 words ≈ 1,300–1,500 tokens. Hindi, Tamil and other languages written in non-Latin scripts often take **more tokens per word** with many tokenizers, because the tokenizer saw less of that text during its construction. More tokens means higher cost, slower responses and less room in the context window for the same content — a real equity issue for Indian-language users that newer tokenizers are steadily improving.

**Next-token prediction.** An LLM is trained on one task: given the tokens so far, output a **probability for every possible next token**. Generation is a loop:
1. Read the prompt tokens.
2. Compute probabilities for the next token.
3. Pick one (Lesson 2.4 covers how).
4. Append it and repeat until a stop token or a length limit.

The model writes one token at a time and **cannot go back and edit** what it already produced — which is why asking it to "plan first, then answer" often helps.

**Why this explains odd behaviour**
- **Letter counting and spelling** — "strawberry" may be one or two tokens; the model never saw its individual letters during prediction unless it reasons step by step.
- **Arithmetic slips** — numbers are split into irregular token chunks; models trained to reason step by step, or given a calculator tool, do far better.
- **Pricing** — APIs bill per token, input and output separately (Module 3).

**Prediction is not lookup.** The model does not retrieve sentences from a database. It produces text that is statistically likely given its training — usually correct for well-documented facts, sometimes fluent fiction for rare ones.

lessons.title: Embeddings and Attention: How Meaning Gets In
lessons.summary: Words become points in a meaning-space; attention lets every token look at every other. The two ideas that make transformers work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain an embedding as a list of numbers that places meaning in space
Use cosine similarity intuitively to judge "how related" two pieces of text are
Explain attention as each token deciding which other tokens matter for it

payload.text: "The bank raised interest rates" and "We sat on the river bank" use the same word with two different meanings. You resolve it instantly from context. For decades computers could not. The transformer solved it with one mechanism — attention — that lets the word "bank" look at "interest rates" or "river" before deciding what it means. That same mechanism is why a model can follow a 50-page document.

**Embeddings: meaning as coordinates.** Each token is converted into an **embedding** — a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers. Think of it as coordinates in a huge "meaning space". During training, tokens used in similar contexts drift close together: "doctor" near "nurse" and "hospital"; "₹" near "rupee" and "price". Directions in the space can even capture relationships, which is why the famous example *king − man + woman ≈ queen* roughly works for some word models.

Whole sentences and documents can be embedded too. Two texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors even if they share no words — "How do I reset my password?" sits near "I forgot my login credentials". **Cosine similarity** measures the angle between two vectors: close to 1 = very similar meaning, near 0 = unrelated. This is the foundation of semantic search and RAG (Module 8).

**Attention: context decides meaning.** An embedding for "bank" starts the same in both sentences. In every transformer layer, **attention** lets each token compare itself with every other token in the context and pull in information from the ones that matter. Mechanically, each token produces a *query* ("what am I looking for?"), every token offers a *key* ("what do I contain?") and a *value* ("what I will share"). Query–key matches decide how much of each value flows in. After a few layers, "bank" near "interest rates" carries a finance meaning; near "river" it carries a geography meaning.

**Multi-head attention** runs many attention patterns in parallel — one head might track grammar, another who-refers-to-whom, another topic. **Stacking dozens of layers** builds rich, context-aware representations, and the final layer turns them into next-token probabilities.

**Why this mattered.** Earlier recurrent networks read text one word at a time and struggled to remember things far back. Attention looks at the whole context at once and parallelises well on GPUs — which is why transformers scaled. The cost: attention compares every token with every other, so compute grows quickly with context length, which is one reason long context windows are expensive.

payload.code:
# Cosine similarity of two embedding vectors (toy 3-D example)
import math

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    nb = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (na * nb)

doctor = [0.9, 0.8, 0.1]
nurse  = [0.85, 0.75, 0.2]
cricket = [0.1, 0.2, 0.95]
print(round(cosine(doctor, nurse), 3))    # ~0.99 — close in meaning
print(round(cosine(doctor, cricket), 3))  # ~0.30 — far apart

lessons.title: How a Chat Model Is Made: Pretraining to Preference Tuning
lessons.summary: Pretraining builds knowledge, instruction tuning teaches the assistant format, preference tuning shapes behaviour — and each stage leaves fingerprints you can see.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe the three main stages that turn a raw model into a chat assistant
Explain what RLHF / preference tuning optimises — and its side effects such as sycophancy
Distinguish fine-tuning from prompting and from retrieval as ways to adapt a model

payload.text: A raw pretrained model asked "What is the capital of India?" might reply "What is the capital of Pakistan? What is the capital of Nepal?" — continuing what looks like a list of quiz questions. It knows the answer; it just does not yet know it is supposed to *answer*. Turning that autocomplete engine into a helpful, careful assistant takes two more stages of training, and each one shapes the personality you meet in a chat window.

**Stage 1 — Pretraining (knowledge and skill).** The model learns next-token prediction on an enormous corpus — web pages, books, code, papers, and increasingly images and audio. This takes months on thousands of chips and costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars for frontier models. The result is a **base model**: broad knowledge and language ability, but no reliable habit of following instructions. Knowledge stops at the **training cutoff** date.

**Stage 2 — Supervised fine-tuning / instruction tuning (format).** The base model is trained further on curated examples of *instruction → good response*, many written or reviewed by people. It learns the assistant pattern: answer the question, follow the format, ask for clarification, decline clearly harmful requests.

**Stage 3 — Preference tuning (behaviour).** People (and increasingly AI systems guided by written principles) compare pairs of responses and mark which is better. The model is then optimised to produce preferred responses. Classic approach: **RLHF** — reinforcement learning from human feedback, using a reward model trained on the preferences. Newer methods such as **DPO** optimise on the preference pairs directly. Some developers also train against a written set of principles (a "constitution"). Reasoning-focused models get extra reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers (maths, code), which teaches them to work step by step.

**Fingerprints each stage leaves**
- **Cutoff** (pretraining): no knowledge of events after the data was collected, unless given search or documents.
- **Sycophancy** (preference tuning): human raters tend to prefer agreeable answers, so models can learn to agree with you — even when you are wrong. Push back on a correct answer and some models will cave.
- **Verbosity and hedging**: raters often reward thoroughness, so answers drift long.
- **Refusal boundaries**: safety training sets what a model declines — sometimes too much, sometimes too little.

**Three ways to adapt a model for your use**
- **Prompting** — instructions and examples at run time. Cheapest, fastest, first resort.
- **Retrieval (RAG)** — give the model your documents at run time. Best for facts that change or are private.
- **Fine-tuning** — further training on your examples. Best for consistent style, format or a narrow skill — not for teaching fresh facts.

lessons.title: Sampling, Context Windows, Cutoffs — and Why Models Hallucinate
lessons.summary: Temperature and top-p, what fits in context, what the model cannot know — the mechanics behind confident wrong answers.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain temperature and top-p and choose settings for factual vs creative tasks
Explain context windows, the "lost in the middle" effect and knowledge cutoffs
Explain the mechanical reasons hallucinations happen and the levers that reduce them

payload.text: In 2023 a lawyer in New York submitted a legal brief citing six court cases that did not exist — invented, with realistic names and citations, by a chat assistant. The judge was not amused. The model was not lying; it was doing exactly what it was built to do: produce plausible next tokens. This lesson shows you the mechanics, so you can predict when fluent fiction is likely — and stop it before it reaches anyone who matters.

**Sampling: how one token is picked.** The model outputs a probability for every next token. **Temperature** reshapes those probabilities: low (0–0.3) sharpens them so the top choice almost always wins — consistent, focused; high (0.8–1.2) flattens them — more varied, more creative, more error-prone. **Top-p** (nucleus sampling) keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (say 0.9) and samples from those, cutting off the long tail of unlikely tokens. Even at temperature 0, outputs can vary slightly between runs on many systems, so never rely on exact repeatability.

**Context window: the model's working memory.** Everything the model can use in one call — system instructions, conversation history, documents, and its own answer — must fit in the context window, measured in tokens (frontier models in 2026 commonly offer hundreds of thousands of tokens, some a million or more). Two practical facts: (1) when a long chat exceeds the window, older parts are dropped or summarised, so the model "forgets" early instructions; (2) even within the window, models tend to use information at the **start and end** better than material buried in the **middle** — the "lost in the middle" effect. Put key instructions and key facts where they will be used.

**Knowledge cutoff.** Pretraining data stops at a date. Without search or supplied documents, the model does not know about anything after it — and may not know that it does not know.

**Why hallucinations happen**
1. **Plausibility is the objective** — training rewards likely-sounding text, not verified truth.
2. **Sparse knowledge** — for rare facts (a small court case, a niche paper, a local college rule) the model has weak signal and fills gaps with a plausible pattern.
3. **Pressure to answer** — instruction tuning rewards being helpful; "I don't know" was historically under-rewarded, though newer models are better at abstaining.
4. **Missing or stale context** — the answer is not in the window, or it is past the cutoff.
5. **Compounding** — one early wrong token makes later tokens build on it.

**Levers that reduce them:** give the source documents (grounding/RAG); ask for quotes and citations you can check; allow "I don't know" explicitly; lower temperature for factual work; use search-enabled or tool-using modes for recent facts; and verify (Module 5). No lever reduces the risk to zero.

payload.title: Proof of work 2 — The token & temperature lab notebook
payload.text:
Pick the variant for your pathway. Save it in your AI.FIRST portfolio folder as PoW-02; the capstone defence draws on all twelve.

- **Explorer (no code):** Run the same three prompts (a fact, a summary, a creative task) at low and high temperature in an assistant that lets you set it, or by regenerating several times. Record differences and one hallucination you provoked on a rare fact.
- **Builder (code):** Call an LLM API at temperatures 0, 0.7 and 1.2 for the three prompts, 5 runs each. Log token counts and outputs to a CSV; measure how often the fact answer changes.
- **Leader (policy & strategy):** Write a one-page "settings policy" for your team: which tasks get which temperature, when grounding is mandatory, and who verifies outputs.

**Evidence that counts:** Raw outputs attached, a clear observation per setting, and one documented hallucination with the reason it happened.

payload.title: Diagnose the fabricated citation
payload.problem: An assistant was asked "Give me three Indian Supreme Court judgments on data privacy with citations." It returned one famous real case and two realistic but non-existent ones. Explain why, and redesign the request.

steps.title: Name the mechanism
steps.desc: The famous case has strong training signal. Lesser-known judgments are sparse, so the model generated plausible case names and citation formats.

steps.title: Name the pressure
steps.desc: The prompt demanded exactly three — the model filled the quota rather than saying it knew only one.

steps.title: Redesign
steps.desc: Use a search-enabled or legal-database tool; ask for links to the official judgment text; say "If you are not certain a case exists, say so"; do not fix a count.

steps.title: Verify
steps.desc: Open every cited judgment on an official source before use. No exceptions for legal, medical or financial claims.

payload.solution: Sparse knowledge + a quota + no grounding = fabrication. Grounded tools, permission to abstain and mandatory source checking fix the workflow.

payload.title: Provoke and prevent
payload.prompt: Ask an assistant (without search) for details of something real but obscure — a small local event, a minor research paper, your college's founding year. Record whether it fabricates. Then ask again with "If you are not sure, say you don't know" and, separately, with the facts pasted in. Compare the three answers.
payload.hint: Note whether the fabricated version sounds any less confident than the true one. Usually it does not.

mistakes.mistake: Treating confidence as a signal of accuracy
mistakes.fix: Fabricated answers are usually just as fluent and confident. Judge by sources and checks, never by tone.

mistakes.mistake: Pasting a long document and putting the key instruction in the middle
mistakes.fix: Put instructions and the question at the end (or both start and end) and keep only relevant material in context.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming temperature 0 makes the model truthful
mistakes.fix: Low temperature makes outputs consistent, not correct. A consistent fabrication is still a fabrication.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: Why do large language models hallucinate, and what would you do to reduce it in a product?
payload.answer: LLMs are trained to produce plausible next tokens, not verified facts. When the answer is rare in the training data, past the cutoff, or missing from the context, the model still generates something plausible. In a product I would ground answers in retrieved documents, require citations or quotes, explicitly allow "not found", use low temperature for factual tasks, add search or tools for recent facts, and run evaluations plus human review for high-stakes outputs.
payload.source: Probably the single most-asked GenAI interview question in 2024–2026.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Temperature/top-p control randomness; low for facts, higher for ideas — neither guarantees truth.
Context window = working memory; key content goes at the start or end.
Cutoff: no knowledge after the training data without search or documents.
Hallucination = plausibility without grounding; reduce with documents, citations, abstention, verification.

questions.explanation: Higher temperature flattens the distribution, increasing variety and risk.

questions.explanation: Start and end of context are used best.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest lever against hallucinated facts in a document-Q&A tool?
options: Grounding answers in supplied documents with quotes and allowing "not found"
questions.explanation: Grounding + citations + abstention is the core pattern.

questions.prompt: Temperature 0 guarantees:
questions.explanation: Consistency is not truth.

lessons.title: Model Families, Open vs Closed Weights
lessons.summary: Who builds the models, what "open weights" really means, and the trade-offs between using an API and running a model yourself.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Name the major model families and the organisations behind them, as of 2026
Explain the difference between closed models, open-weight models and fully open-source models
Choose between an API model and a self-hosted open-weight model for a given constraint

payload.text: A hospital in Pune wants AI to summarise patient notes. Its lawyers say patient data must never leave its own servers. A start-up in Bengaluru wants the best possible coding assistant and does not care where it runs. Same technology, opposite answers — and the deciding factor is not which model is "smartest" but whether you can download its weights.

**The main families (as of 2026 — this list changes every few months, so check current sources):**
- **Closed / proprietary frontier models** — accessed through an app or API, weights never released: OpenAI's GPT series, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, xAI's Grok and others.
- **Open-weight models** — weights downloadable, usually with a licence that sets conditions: Meta's Llama family, Mistral, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek, Google's Gemma, Microsoft's Phi, and many more.
- **Indian and Indic-focused efforts** — government-backed and start-up models focused on Indian languages and use-cases (for example under the IndiaAI Mission, and companies such as Sarvam AI). Worth tracking if you build for Indian users.

**Closed vs open weights vs open source**
- **Closed**: you send data to the provider; you get their latest quality, safety work and infrastructure; you accept their pricing, terms and data policies.
- **Open weights**: you can download and run the trained model on your own hardware or cloud, inspect and fine-tune it. Training data and code are often *not* released, and licences may restrict use (user-count caps, acceptable-use rules).
- **Fully open source** (rarer): weights, training code and data documentation are released under an open licence.

**The trade-off table you will actually use**
- **Data control**: open weights win — data can stay on your servers.
- **Peak quality**: closed frontier models usually lead, though the best open-weight models have often trailed by only months.
- **Cost at scale**: self-hosting can be cheaper at very high, steady volume; APIs are cheaper and simpler for most teams because you pay only for use and nothing for idle GPUs.
- **Effort**: APIs need an API key; self-hosting needs GPUs, serving software, monitoring, security updates and people who understand them.
- **Customisation**: open weights allow deep fine-tuning; many APIs also offer fine-tuning but within limits.

**Sizes matter.** "Small" models (a few billion parameters) can run on a laptop or phone and handle classification, extraction and simple chat well; frontier models handle hard reasoning, long documents and complex code. A common professional pattern is to **route**: send easy requests to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a large model (Lesson 3.4).

lessons.title: Multimodal AI: Vision, Voice, Images and Video
lessons.summary: Models that see, hear, speak and generate media — what they do well, how diffusion works, and where they fail.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Describe the main multimodal capabilities: image understanding, speech in/out, image and video generation
Explain diffusion — how image generators turn noise into a picture — at an intuitive level
Identify the typical failure modes of each modality

payload.text: A farmer in Vidarbha photographs a yellowing cotton leaf and asks, in Marathi, by voice, what is wrong. Within seconds a model replies, in spoken Marathi, with three likely causes and what to check first. Five years ago that needed four separate systems — speech recognition, translation, image classification, speech synthesis. Today one multimodal model can do it in a single conversation. It can also be confidently wrong about the leaf.

**Multimodal** models take in or produce more than text. The main capabilities in 2026:

**1. Vision (image understanding).** Upload a photo, a chart, a handwritten page or a screenshot; the model describes it, extracts text (OCR), reads tables, answers questions. Images are cut into patches and turned into tokens the transformer can attend over alongside text. *Strong at*: documents, screenshots, charts, everyday scenes. *Weak at*: exact counting of many objects, fine measurements, small text in low-resolution images, and specialist judgement (medical scans, structural cracks) without validation.

**2. Speech in and out.** Speech recognition (ASR) turns audio into text; text-to-speech (TTS) produces natural voices; newer **speech-to-speech** models converse in real time and can carry tone. Indian-language support has improved fast but still varies by language, accent and noise. *Risk*: realistic **voice cloning** from a few seconds of audio enables scams (Module 11).

**3. Image generation — diffusion.** Training: take real images, add noise step by step until they are pure static, and teach a network to **predict and remove the noise** at each step, conditioned on a text description. Generation runs that in reverse: start from random noise and repeatedly denoise, steered by your prompt, until an image emerges. *Weak at* (improving): exact text inside images, hands and counts, consistent characters across images, and anything requiring factual accuracy.

**4. Video and music generation.** Diffusion and transformer methods extended over time produce short clips and audio from text or images. Quality rose sharply in 2024–2026; consistency over longer durations and physics remain hard. These are also the core tools of deepfakes.

**Using multimodal well**
- Give the model **the image plus a precise question** ("Read the total amount on this bill and the date") rather than "what is this?".
- For anything consequential — medical, legal, safety, money — treat the output as a **draft to be verified**.
- Generated media must be **labelled** where it could be mistaken for real (and in many places, rules now require it — Module 10).

To generate, it starts from pure random noise and repeatedly removes predicted noise, guided by the text prompt, over tens of steps until a coherent image matching the prompt emerges.

lessons.title: Reasoning Models and Agents: What Changed
lessons.summary: Models that think before answering, and models that act — test-time compute, tool use, and the honest limits of both.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Explain what a reasoning model does differently and when the extra cost is worth it
Define an AI agent as a model in a loop with tools, and name what can go wrong
Decide whether a task needs a plain chat model, a reasoning model or an agent

payload.text: Ask an ordinary chat model a tricky maths olympiad problem and it answers in two seconds — often wrong. Ask a reasoning model and it "thinks" for forty seconds, tries an approach, notices a mistake, backtracks, and gets it right. Ask an agent to "find three internships matching my resume and draft applications" and it searches, reads pages, compares, and writes drafts over several minutes. These are different tools with different costs, and choosing the wrong one wastes either money or trust.

**Reasoning models (2024 onwards).** Instead of answering immediately, a reasoning model generates a long internal chain of intermediate steps first — planning, trying, checking, revising — and then gives a final answer. This uses **test-time compute**: spending more computation per question rather than only training a bigger model. They are trained with reinforcement learning on problems that have checkable answers (maths, code, logic), which rewards reasoning that actually reaches correct results.

*When it is worth it*: multi-step maths and logic, debugging and complex code, planning with constraints, careful analysis of long documents, and hard "think it through" questions.
*When it is not*: simple lookups, rewriting, short summaries, casual chat — you pay more and wait longer for no benefit. Many products now let you choose a "thinking" level or decide automatically.
*Honest limits*: longer reasoning can still reach wrong conclusions confidently; the displayed "thinking" text is not guaranteed to be a faithful account of how the answer was produced; and costs rise with thinking tokens.

**Agents.** An agent is a model placed in a **loop** with **tools**: it decides an action (search the web, run code, read a file, call an API, click in a browser), observes the result, decides the next action, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit is hit. Coding agents, research agents, browser agents and workflow agents all follow this pattern (Module 9 builds one).

*What agents add*: they can finish multi-step tasks, use fresh information and check their own work against reality (run the tests, read the page).
*What can go wrong*: errors compound over many steps; they can take irreversible actions (send, delete, pay); web pages can contain **prompt injections** that hijack them (Module 11); and costs and time are hard to predict. Good agent design adds permissions, confirmation before consequential actions, step limits and logs.

**The decision ladder**: plain chat → reasoning model → agent. Move up only when the task needs it.

payload.title: Chat vs reasoning vs agent
payload.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph CHAT["Chat model"]
    q1["Question"] --> a1["Answer"]
  end
  subgraph REASON["Reasoning model"]
    q2["Question"] --> t["Think: plan · try · check · revise"] --> a2["Answer"]
  end
  subgraph AGENT["Agent"]
    g["Goal"] --> d["Decide action"] --> act["Use a tool"] --> o["Observe result"]
    o --> c{"Goal met or limit reached?"}
    c -->|"no"| d
    c -->|"yes"| r["Report + evidence"]
  end

payload.title: Which tool for which task?
rows: Find the bug in a 300-line function
Book-keep: read 40 invoices, fill a sheet, flag mismatches
Research a company before an interview with sources

payload.title: Agents act — so they need brakes
payload.text: Never give an agent unsupervised power to send messages, spend money, delete data or submit forms on your behalf. Require confirmation for anything you cannot undo.

payload.title: Cost a reasoning call honestly
payload.problem: A plain model answers a coding question with 400 output tokens. A reasoning model uses 6,000 thinking tokens plus 400 answer tokens, billed as output. At a hypothetical ₹1 per 1,000 output tokens for both, compare cost — and decide when the reasoning model is worth it.

steps.title: Reasoning model
steps.desc: 6,400 tokens → ₹6.40 — 16× more (real prices for reasoning models are often higher per token too).

steps.title: Value the outcome
steps.desc: If the plain model is right 50% of the time and the reasoning model 90%, and a wrong answer costs a developer 20 minutes, the reasoning model is cheap.

steps.title: Route
steps.desc: Use plain models for easy questions and send hard ones to reasoning — or let a product's automatic mode decide.

payload.solution: 16× the tokens, but cost per correct answer — not cost per call — is the right measure. Reasoning models earn their price on hard problems and waste it on easy ones.

payload.title: Run the ladder
payload.prompt: Choose one hard question from your subject (a multi-step numerical problem or a tricky bug). Ask a plain chat model and a reasoning ("thinking") mode. Compare correctness, time and length. Then write which of five tasks from your week need chat, reasoning or an agent.
payload.hint: If both get it right, the problem was not hard enough to need reasoning.

mistakes.mistake: Using the most powerful mode for everything
mistakes.fix: Match the tool to the task. Reasoning and agents cost more and take longer; use them where steps and checking matter.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting the "thinking" transcript as a faithful explanation
mistakes.fix: Treat it as helpful but not guaranteed to reflect how the answer was produced. Verify the final answer independently.

mistakes.mistake: Letting an agent take irreversible actions without confirmation
mistakes.fix: Design human approval into any send, pay, delete or submit step.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What is the difference between a chat model, a reasoning model and an agent?
payload.answer: A chat model answers directly in one pass. A reasoning model spends extra computation generating intermediate steps — planning, checking and revising — before answering, which helps on maths, code and complex analysis at higher cost and latency. An agent puts a model in a loop with tools: it chooses actions, observes results and continues until a goal is met, which enables multi-step tasks but needs permissions, limits and human confirmation for consequential actions.
payload.source: Increasingly standard in 2025–2026 AI interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Reasoning models spend test-time compute thinking; worth it for hard multi-step problems.
Agents = model + tools + loop; they act, so they need permissions and brakes.
Measure cost per correct outcome, not per call.
Ladder: chat → reasoning → agent; climb only when needed.

options: A model in a loop that chooses and uses tools, observing results, until a goal or limit
questions.explanation: Loop + tools + observation.

questions.explanation: Many steps, files and verification.

lessons.title: Choosing a Model: Quality, Cost, Latency, Privacy
lessons.summary: A repeatable selection method with real token arithmetic, a small evaluation, and a written model-selection memo as your proof of work.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Compute monthly cost for an AI feature from token counts and per-million-token prices
Run a small comparative evaluation of candidate models on your own examples
Write a model-selection memo that a manager could approve

payload.text: A team ships a customer-support bot on the most powerful model available. It is brilliant — and the first month's bill is ₹4.2 lakh for a feature budgeted at ₹40,000. A smaller model would have handled 85% of the questions just as well. Choosing a model is an engineering and business decision, and it can be done properly in an afternoon.

**The four axes**
1. **Quality** on *your* task — measured, not assumed.
2. **Cost** — per-token prices × token volume, plus any hosting.
3. **Latency** — time to first token and total time; matters for chat and voice, less for overnight batch jobs.
4. **Privacy and compliance** — where data goes, whether it is retained or used for training, regions, contracts, and sector rules.

Add **context length**, **modalities**, **tool-use reliability** and **licence** where relevant.

**Token arithmetic.** API prices are quoted per **million tokens (MTok)**, separately for input and output; output is usually several times more expensive.
Monthly cost = requests × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) ÷ 1,000,000.

**Levers that cut cost without cutting quality**
- **Routing** — a small model for easy requests, a large one only for hard ones.
- **Prompt caching** — many providers discount repeated input (such as a long, fixed system prompt or document).
- **Batch APIs** — overnight, non-urgent jobs often cost much less.
- **Shorter outputs** — ask for exactly the format and length you need.
- **Trimming context** — send the relevant 3 pages, not the whole 300.

**A 30-example evaluation (do this every time)**
1. Collect 30 real examples covering easy, typical and hard cases (and a few nasty edge cases).
2. Write what a good answer must contain — a simple rubric.
3. Run 2–3 candidate models with the same prompt.
4. Score blind if you can (hide which model produced which answer).
5. Record quality, average tokens, latency and cost per 1,000 requests.
6. Pick the cheapest model that meets the quality bar — then re-check monthly, because prices and models change fast.

payload.title: Model selection workflow
payload.source:
flowchart TD
  R["Requirements: quality bar, budget, latency, data rules"] --> C["Shortlist 2–3 candidates"]
  C --> E["Run 30 real examples with one prompt"]
  E --> S["Score blind against a rubric"]
  S --> K["Compute cost per 1,000 requests"]
  K --> P{"Cheapest model that meets the bar?"}
  P --> D["Decide + write the memo"]
  D --> M["Monitor monthly: quality, cost, new models"]
  M --> C

payload.title: Prices are a moving target
payload.text: Real per-token prices change frequently and generally fall for a given capability level. Always use the provider's current pricing page and date your memo.

payload.title: Proof of work 3 — The model-selection memo
payload.text:
Pick the variant for your pathway. Save it in your AI.FIRST portfolio folder as PoW-03; the capstone defence draws on all twelve.

- **Explorer (no code):** Compare 2–3 assistant apps on 15 real tasks from your study or work. Score each on a rubric; include privacy settings you checked. One-page recommendation.
- **Builder (code):** Run a 30-example evaluation of 2–3 models through APIs with one prompt; log quality scores, tokens, latency and cost per 1,000 requests; recommend one model plus a routing rule.
- **Leader (policy & strategy):** Write a selection memo for a real team use-case: requirements, candidates, evaluation summary, monthly cost scenarios, data-protection review and a decision with a review date.

**Evidence that counts:** Your own scored examples, the cost arithmetic shown, and a decision a manager could sign. "Model X is the best" without evidence scores zero.

payload.title: The support-bot bill, fixed
payload.problem: Support bot: 60,000 conversations/month, average 2,000 input and 400 output tokens. Frontier prices (illustrative) ₹400 in / ₹1,600 out per MTok. Evaluation shows a small model (₹10 / ₹40) meets the quality bar on 85% of questions, which a cheap classifier can identify. Compute before and after.

steps.title: After
steps.desc: ₹1,836 + ₹12,960 ≈ ₹14,800/month — about 83% less, with quality held by the evaluation.

payload.solution: Routing cut the bill from ≈ ₹86,400 to ≈ ₹14,800 per month. The evaluation is what made the cut safe; without it, routing is a guess.

payload.title: Cost your own idea
payload.prompt: Pick an AI feature you would like to build. Estimate requests per month, input and output tokens per request, and compute monthly cost for a small, mid and frontier model using a provider's current price page. Add one cost-cutting lever and recompute.
payload.hint: Count tokens for one real example with a tokenizer tool, then multiply.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing by leaderboard rank
mistakes.fix: Leaderboards measure someone else's tasks. Your 30 examples decide.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that output tokens cost more than input
mistakes.fix: Constrain answer length and format; long outputs dominate many bills.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the privacy review because the demo worked
mistakes.fix: Check data retention, training use, regions and contract terms before real user data flows.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: How would you choose an LLM for a production feature?
payload.answer: Start from requirements: quality bar, budget, latency and data rules. Shortlist two or three models, run the same prompt over about thirty real examples including edge cases, score them blind against a rubric, and compute cost per thousand requests from token counts. Pick the cheapest model that meets the bar, consider routing easy requests to a smaller model, confirm privacy and licensing, then monitor quality and cost and re-evaluate as models change.
payload.source: A staple case question in AI engineering and product interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Four axes: quality on your task, cost, latency, privacy/compliance.
Cost = requests × (in × price_in + out × price_out) ÷ 1M.
Routing, caching, batch and shorter outputs cut cost without cutting quality.
A blind 30-example evaluation beats any leaderboard.

questions.explanation: Per-MTok, input and output priced separately.

"Routing" in model selection means:
options: Sending easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a larger model
Sending all traffic to one region

questions.explanation: Your own task is the benchmark that matters.

modules.title: Module 4 — Prompting & Context Engineering
modules.summary: I · Interact. The anatomy of a strong prompt, examples and output formats, reasoning and decomposition, and context engineering — documents, memory and a tested prompt library.

lessons.title: The Anatomy of a Strong Prompt
lessons.summary: Role, task, context, constraints, format, and a definition of done — the six parts that turn a vague wish into a reliable instruction.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Write prompts using the six-part skeleton: role, task, context, constraints, format, done-criteria
Diagnose a weak prompt and name which part is missing
Use system instructions versus user messages appropriately

payload.text: "Write about climate change" gets you a bland 500-word essay that could be about anywhere. "You are a science journalist writing for Class 10 students in Chennai. In 300 words, explain how rising sea levels could affect the city by 2050, using two local examples, one statistic with its source, and ending with one thing a student can do" gets you something useful. The model did not get smarter between those two prompts. You gave it what it needed.

**A prompt is a brief for a very fast, very literal colleague** who knows a lot but knows nothing about *your* situation. Most bad outputs are under-specified prompts.

**The six-part skeleton**
1. **Role** — who should answer: "You are a placement mentor who has reviewed 500 engineering resumes." Roles set vocabulary, depth and standards.
2. **Task** — one clear verb: summarise, compare, draft, critique, extract, explain, plan.
3. **Context** — the facts only you know: audience, purpose, background, the document itself.
4. **Constraints** — length, tone, reading level, what to avoid, what sources to use, "do not invent figures".
5. **Format** — bullets, table with named columns, JSON, an email with subject line, a numbered plan.
6. **Done-criteria** — how you will judge it: "Must include three options with costs" or "Flag any claim you are unsure about."

**System vs user instructions.** Many tools separate a **system prompt** (standing instructions: role, rules, format — set once, applied to every turn) from **user messages** (the specific request). In custom assistants and API calls, put durable rules in the system prompt and the changing request in the user message.

**Clarity beats cleverness.** Plain, specific instructions outperform "magic words". Modern models respond well to direct requests; you rarely need tricks. Delimiters help when you paste material: put documents inside clear markers (triple quotes or XML-style tags such as <report>…</report>) so instructions and data do not blur.

**Ask it to ask.** For bigger tasks add: "Before you start, ask me up to three questions if anything important is unclear." This one line fixes many under-specified prompts.

**Iterate like an editor.** The first output is a draft. Say precisely what to change: "Shorter by half, keep the statistics, make the tone warmer, remove the second option." Vague feedback ("make it better") gets vague changes.

payload.source:
flowchart LR R["Role
who answers"] --> T["Task
one clear verb"] T --> C["Context
facts only you know"] C --> K["Constraints
length · tone · sources · don'ts"] K --> F["Format
table · bullets · JSON"] F --> D["Done-criteria
how you will judge it"] D --> O["Output → you edit → iterate"]

<summary>

payload.title: Rebuild a failing prompt
payload.problem: A student asks: "Give me notes on DBMS normalization." The output is generic and too long for revision. Rebuild it with the skeleton.

steps.title: Role
steps.desc: "You are a DBMS professor preparing students for a semester exam and placement interviews."

steps.title: Task + context
steps.desc: "Create revision notes on normalization (1NF to BCNF) for a student who understands tables and keys but confuses 3NF and BCNF."

steps.title: Constraints + format
steps.desc: "One page. For each normal form: one-line rule, a 4-row example table that violates it, and the fix. End with a 3NF vs BCNF comparison table."

steps.desc: "Include two likely exam questions with model answers. Mark anything that varies across textbooks."

payload.solution: The rebuilt prompt specifies audience, scope, structure and verification. The output becomes a revision sheet rather than a textbook chapter — and it is checkable.

payload.title: Skeleton drill
payload.prompt: Take three prompts you actually used this week. Rewrite each with all six parts. Run old and new versions and record, for each, which output you would actually use and why.
payload.hint: Context and done-criteria are the parts people skip most often.

mistakes.mistake: Hunting for magic phrases instead of giving context
mistakes.fix: Specific context and clear done-criteria beat any trick phrase. Write the brief you would give a capable new colleague.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing instructions and pasted material without separation
mistakes.fix: Wrap pasted documents in clear delimiters so the model can tell data from instructions — this also reduces prompt-injection risk.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting the first draft
mistakes.fix: Iterate with precise edits. Prompting is a conversation with an editor's discipline.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: What makes a prompt effective? Give a framework.
payload.answer: An effective prompt gives a role, a single clear task, the context the model cannot know, constraints such as length, tone and sources, an explicit output format, and criteria for what a good answer must contain. Separate pasted material with delimiters, put standing rules in the system prompt, invite clarifying questions for complex tasks, and iterate with specific feedback.
payload.source: Asked in almost every role that uses AI tools, from marketing to engineering.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Six parts: role, task, context, constraints, format, done-criteria.
System prompt = standing rules; user message = this request.
Delimit pasted material; invite clarifying questions.
Iterate with precise edits, not "make it better".

questions.prompt: Which part of a prompt tells the model how you will judge the output?
questions.explanation: Done-criteria define what a good answer must contain.

questions.prompt: Where should standing rules for every turn of a custom assistant go?
questions.explanation: System prompts hold durable instructions.

questions.prompt: Why wrap a pasted document in delimiters?
options: So the model can separate data from instructions
questions.explanation: Clear separation improves accuracy and reduces injection risk.

questions.prompt: "Make it better" is weak feedback because:
options: It does not specify what to change
questions.explanation: Precise edits produce precise changes.

lessons.title: Examples, Few-Shot and Output Formats
lessons.summary: Showing beats telling: choosing good examples, controlling format with templates and schemas, and avoiding the traps examples create.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting appropriately
Choose examples that are varied, correct and representative
Request structured outputs (tables, JSON) that a spreadsheet or program can use

payload.text: A college office wants AI to tag 3,000 student emails as Fees, Exams, Hostel, Certificates or Other. With instructions alone, the model invents a sixth category called "Administrative" and tags half the inbox with it. Add five well-chosen example emails with their correct tags and accuracy jumps — and the invented category disappears. Examples are the most powerful lever most people never pull.

**Zero-shot** = instructions only. **One-shot** = one example. **Few-shot** = several examples (usually 2–8). Examples teach format, tone, granularity and edge cases faster than any description.

**Choosing good examples**
- **Varied** — cover different kinds of input, not five near-copies.
- **Representative** — match the real distribution; include the tricky cases (ambiguous emails, mixed languages, missing information).
- **Correct** — a wrong example is copied faithfully.
- **Balanced** — if four of five examples are "Fees", the model drifts towards "Fees".
- **Formatted exactly** as you want the output.

**Traps.** Models copy surface features: if every example is short, outputs get short; if all examples open with "Dear Sir", so will the output. Rotate examples, and test on inputs unlike the examples.

**Output formats that work downstream**
- **Tables** with named columns for human review.
- **JSON** for anything a program will read: give the exact keys and allowed values, and say "Return only JSON." Many APIs offer a **structured output / JSON schema mode** that guarantees valid JSON matching a schema — use it when available (Module 8).
- **Closed label sets**: list the allowed labels and add "If none fits, use Other — do not create new labels."
- **Reasons and confidence**: ask for a one-line reason and a confidence (high/medium/low) so humans can review the doubtful ones first.

**Template prompts.** For repeated tasks, write a template with placeholders — {email_text}, {course_name} — and fill them programmatically or by copy-paste. Templates make results consistent and testable, which is the bridge to the evaluation habit in Module 5.

payload.title: Few-shot classification flow
payload.source:
flowchart LR I["Instructions + closed label list"] --> X["5–8 varied, correct examples
input → label + reason"] X --> N["New input"] N --> O["Output in fixed format
label · reason · confidence"] O --> H{"Confidence low?"} H -->|"yes"| R["Human review queue"] H -->|"no"| S["Accepted → spreadsheet / system"]

payload.code:
Classify each student email into exactly one label:
Fees | Exams | Hostel | Certificates | Other
If none fits, use Other. Never invent new labels.
Return JSON only: {"label": "...", "reason": "...", "confidence": "high|medium|low"}

Example 1
Email: "Sir my semester fee receipt not generated after UPI payment"
{"label": "Fees", "reason": "payment receipt issue", "confidence": "high"}

Example 2
Email: "When will revaluation results of 5th sem come?"
{"label": "Exams", "reason": "revaluation results", "confidence": "high"}

Example 3
Email: "Need bonafide certificate for passport, also my hostel room fan is broken"
{"label": "Certificates", "reason": "primary request is bonafide; hostel issue secondary", "confidence": "medium"}

Email: "{email_text}"

payload.title: Mixed-intent inputs need a rule
payload.text: Example 3 shows a two-topic email. Decide the rule (primary request wins, or allow two labels) and show it in an example — otherwise the model decides inconsistently.

payload.title: Fix the drifting classifier
payload.problem: Your few-shot classifier labels 40% of emails "Fees" though only 20% are about fees. Your five examples were: Fees, Fees, Fees, Exams, Hostel. Diagnose and fix.

steps.title: Diagnose imbalance
steps.desc: Three of five examples are Fees — the model learned that Fees is the default.

steps.title: Rebalance
steps.desc: Use one or two examples per label, including Certificates and Other.

steps.title: Add hard cases
steps.desc: Include a mixed-intent email and a Hinglish email with the correct label.

steps.title: Measure
steps.desc: Hand-label 50 real emails; compare model labels; compute accuracy per label before and after.

payload.solution: Balanced, varied examples plus a measured check fixed the drift. Without the 50 hand-labelled emails you would not have known the classifier was wrong.

payload.title: Build a few-shot extractor
payload.prompt: Choose a repetitive task (extracting dates and amounts from bills, tagging feedback comments, converting notes to a table). Write a zero-shot prompt and a few-shot prompt with 4 varied examples. Test both on 10 new inputs and count errors.
payload.hint: Include at least one example where information is missing and show the expected output (for example null).

mistakes.mistake: Using near-identical examples
mistakes.fix: Vary length, wording, language mix and difficulty so the model learns the rule, not the surface.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the label set open
mistakes.fix: List allowed labels and give an explicit fallback; otherwise the model invents categories.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for JSON and parsing it blindly
mistakes.fix: Use schema/structured-output modes where available and validate every response in code.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: When would you use few-shot prompting, and how do you choose the examples?
payload.answer: Use few-shot when the task has a specific format, label set or judgement style that is easier to show than describe — classification, extraction, tone matching. Choose a small set of varied, correct, balanced examples that match real inputs and include hard and edge cases, formatted exactly as the desired output. Then test on inputs unlike the examples to make sure the model learned the rule rather than copying surface features.
payload.source: Common in AI-ops, data and product interviews.

payload.title: Lesson summary
points: Zero-, one-, few-shot: examples teach format and judgement fast.
Good examples are varied, representative, correct and balanced.
Closed label sets + fallback stop invented categories.
Ask for structured output; validate it; review low-confidence items first.

Including several worked examples of input and desired output in the prompt

questions.explanation: Imbalanced examples bias outputs.

lessons.title: Reasoning Prompts and Decomposition
lessons.summary: Step-by-step reasoning, breaking big tasks into chains, self-checking and critique loops — and when they help.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Use step-by-step and plan-first prompting for multi-step problems
Decompose a large task into a chain of smaller, checkable prompts
Use critique-and-revise loops while knowing their limits

payload.text: Ask for "a complete marketing plan for our college fest" in one prompt and you get a generic plan. Ask first for the audience analysis, then — using that — the message, then the channel plan with budget, then a critique of the whole plan against your ₹40,000 budget, and you get something you could actually execute. Same model, same afternoon. The difference is decomposition.

**Step-by-step reasoning.** Asking a model to work through a problem in steps before answering ("Think it through step by step, then give the final answer on the last line") improves results on multi-step maths, logic and analysis for many models — because each written step becomes context for the next prediction. **Reasoning models** (Module 3) do this internally; with them, you usually just state the problem clearly and let them think. For ordinary chat models, explicit step-by-step prompts still help.

**Plan first.** For long outputs: "First write an outline and wait for my approval." You catch structural problems before paying for 3,000 words.

**Decomposition / prompt chaining.** Break a big task into stages, each with its own prompt and checkable output:
1. Extract → 2. Analyse → 3. Draft → 4. Critique → 5. Revise.
Each stage is easier, can use the best model and settings for its job, and can be inspected. Errors are caught between stages instead of being buried in a wall of text.

**Self-critique and revise.** "Review your answer against these criteria: … List problems, then produce a corrected version." This often catches omissions and format errors. Its limit: a model checking itself shares its own blind spots — it may not catch a fact it is confidently wrong about. For facts, check against a source (Module 5), use a different model as reviewer, or run code/tests.

**Multiple attempts.** For hard questions, generating several independent answers and comparing them (self-consistency) surfaces uncertainty: if three attempts disagree, the question needs checking.

**Know when not to.** Simple tasks do not need chains. Over-engineering adds cost, latency and new places for errors.

payload.title: A five-stage prompt chain
payload.source:

payload.title: Chain the college-fest plan
payload.problem: Budget ₹40,000, 1,500 expected attendees, 3 weeks to go. Design a prompt chain that produces an executable promotion plan.

steps.title: Stage 1 — Audience
steps.desc: "List the 3 main audience segments for a tech-cultural fest at an engineering college in Jaipur, with what each cares about and where they spend attention." You check and correct.

steps.title: Stage 2 — Message
steps.desc: "Using these segments, propose one core message and one hook per segment."

steps.title: Stage 3 — Channels + budget
steps.desc: "Allocate ₹40,000 across channels for 3 weeks in a table: channel, segment, cost, expected reach, owner, deadline."

steps.title: Stage 4 — Critique
steps.desc: "Critique the plan: is the budget arithmetic correct, any segment unreached, any deadline unrealistic? List issues."

steps.title: Stage 5 — Revise and verify
steps.desc: "Fix the issues." Then you re-add the budget column yourself and confirm vendor prices with real quotes.

payload.solution: Five checkable stages produced a plan grounded in your context. The human checks after stages 1 and 5 — plus real vendor quotes — are what make it executable.

payload.title: Decompose your own task

mistakes.fix: Self-checks catch format and omission errors. Verify facts and numbers externally.

payload.answer: Prompt chaining splits a complex task into a sequence of smaller prompts — for example extract, analyse, draft, critique, revise — where each output feeds the next. It improves quality because each step is simpler and focused, lets you use different models or settings per step, and creates checkpoints where a human or code can verify intermediate results before errors compound.

lessons.title: Context Engineering: Documents, Memory and a Prompt Library
lessons.summary: What goes into the context window decides the answer. Curating documents, managing long chats and memory, and building a tested prompt library.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Curate the context a model receives: relevant documents, instructions placement, length budget
Manage long conversations, memory features and project/workspace knowledge safely
Build and version a personal prompt library with tested prompts

payload.text: Two students ask the same assistant to prepare them for a viva on their final-year project. One pastes nothing and gets generic questions. The other attaches the project report, the guide's feedback email and last year's viva questions from seniors — and gets a mock viva that feels uncomfortably real. "Prompt engineering" was the 2023 skill. By 2026 the skill that separates professionals is **context engineering**: deciding exactly what the model sees.

**Context engineering** = designing everything in the context window: system instructions, the user's request, retrieved documents, examples, conversation history, tool results and memory. The model can only be as good as what it sees.

**Curate documents**
- **Relevant, not everything** — 3 right pages beat 300 mixed ones; irrelevant text dilutes attention and costs tokens.
- **Clean** — remove headers, footers and boilerplate; keep tables as tables.
- **Labelled** — wrap each source: <source id="policy-2026">…</source>, so answers can cite them.
- **Ordered** — long documents first, instructions and question last.

**Long conversations drift.** Over many turns, early instructions fade or are truncated; errors from earlier turns get reused. Professional habits: start a **fresh chat for a new task**; when a chat gets long, ask for a **summary of decisions so far** and start a new chat with that summary; restate key constraints when they matter.

**Memory and projects.** Many assistants now offer persistent **memory** (facts about you remembered across chats) and **projects/workspaces** (a set of files and instructions shared by every chat inside). They are powerful for repeated work — and a privacy surface: review what is remembered, turn memory off for sensitive work, and never store passwords, IDs or other people's personal data (Module 10).

**A personal prompt library** turns one-off luck into a reusable asset:
- One entry per recurring task: name, purpose, the prompt template with {placeholders}, which model/settings, an example input and a good output, known failure modes, last tested date.
- **Version it** — when you improve a prompt, keep the old one and note what changed and why.
- **Test it** — keep 5 test inputs per prompt and re-run them when you switch models.

This is the habit that makes your AI use *reliable* rather than impressive-once.

payload.title: Proof of work 4 — The tested prompt library
payload.text:
Pick the variant for your pathway. Save it in your AI.FIRST portfolio folder as PoW-04; the capstone defence draws on all twelve.

- **Explorer (no code):** Build a library of 10 prompts for your recurring study or work tasks using the entry template. Test each on 3 inputs; record one improvement you made and why.
- **Builder (code):** Store 10 prompt templates as files in a Git repo with placeholders, plus a small script that runs each template on its 5 test inputs and saves outputs for comparison.
- **Leader (policy & strategy):** Create a team prompt library for 10 recurring team tasks with owners, approved data types (what may and may not be pasted) and a review cadence.

**Evidence that counts:** Before/after evidence for at least three prompts, version notes, and test inputs. A list of untested prompts copied from the internet scores zero.

As models got better at following plain instructions, quality became limited mainly by whether the right, clean, well-labelled information is present and well placed, so curating context now drives most of the gains.

modules.title: Module 5 — Verifying AI Output
modules.summary: R · Reliable — the heart of the course. A taxonomy of AI errors, lateral reading and source checks, verifying numbers, code and citations, and building a mini evaluation with golden sets and rubrics.

lessons.title: A Taxonomy of AI Errors
lessons.summary: Fabrication is only one of seven ways AI output goes wrong. Name the failure and you know the check.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Classify an AI error into one of seven types
Match each error type to the check that catches it
Decide how much verification a task needs from its stakes

payload.text: A student submits an AI-assisted report. The citations are real papers — but one says the opposite of what the report claims. The statistics are real — but from 2014, presented as current. The code runs — but silently drops rows with missing values. Not one of these is a "hallucination" in the made-up-fact sense, and every one of them would cost marks, money or trust. Verification starts with knowing what you are looking for.

**Seven error types**
1. **Fabrication** — invented facts, people, quotes, cases, papers, URLs. *Check*: does it exist in an authoritative source?
2. **Misattribution / misrepresentation** — a real source cited for something it does not say. *Check*: open the source and find the exact passage.
3. **Staleness** — correct once, outdated now (prices, rules, office-holders, versions, deadlines). *Check*: the date of the source; the official current page.
4. **Reasoning and calculation errors** — wrong arithmetic, a step that does not follow, unit mix-ups. *Check*: recompute independently; redo key steps.
5. **Omission** — the answer is right as far as it goes but leaves out a crucial exception, risk or option. *Check*: a checklist of what a complete answer must cover; ask "what is missing?" of a second source.
6. **Instruction failure** — ignored constraints: wrong length, wrong format, made-up labels, forbidden content. *Check*: compare the output against the brief line by line, or validate in code.
7. **Bias and slant** — one-sided framing, stereotypes, unequal quality across groups or languages. *Check*: counter-prompt ("argue the other side"), compare outputs across groups, consult diverse sources.

**Stakes decide depth.** A brainstorm for fest names needs no verification. A paragraph in your project report needs claims checked. Anything legal, medical, financial, safety-related, or published under your name needs **every** factual claim verified against primary sources — and a human who is accountable.

**The verifiable-claims habit.** Before checking, break the output into **atomic claims**: one checkable statement each ("The DPDP Act was passed in 2023"; "Penalty up to ₹250 crore"). Fluent paragraphs hide errors; lists of claims expose them.

**The professional stance**: you are the editor-in-chief. AI drafts; you sign. "The AI said so" is never a defence — not in a viva, not in a client meeting, not in court.

payload.title: Classify and check five claims
payload.problem: An AI summary for a client says: (1) "India's DPDP Act was enacted in 2023." (2) "It applies only to companies with over 100 employees." (3) "Penalties go up to ₹250 crore per instance." (4) "A 2021 NITI Aayog report found 87% compliance." (5) "Therefore most firms need no changes." Classify risks and choose checks.

steps.title: Claim 1
steps.desc: Low risk; check the official gazette or MeitY page. It is correct: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act received assent in August 2023.

steps.title: Claim 2
steps.desc: High risk of fabrication — no such employee threshold exists in the Act. Check the Act text. Cut.

steps.title: Claim 3
steps.desc: Check the Act's schedule of penalties; the maximum in the schedule is ₹250 crore. Verify the exact wording before quoting.

steps.title: Claim 4
steps.desc: Likely fabrication or misattribution — a 2021 report cannot measure compliance with a 2023 Act. Cut unless found.

steps.title: Claim 5
steps.desc: A reasoning error built on false claims 2 and 4. Cut and rewrite.

payload.solution: Only claims 1 and 3 survive verification. Claims 2 and 4 were invented and claim 5 depended on them. Splitting into atomic claims made this visible in minutes.

mistakes.fix: Plausibility is exactly what models optimise. Check against sources, not intuition.

mistakes.mistake: Verifying the citations exist but not what they say
mistakes.fix: Misattribution is common. Open each source and find the supporting passage.

payload.title: Exam / interview angle
payload.question: An AI tool produced a report for your manager. How do you verify it before it goes out?
payload.answer: I assess stakes first. For anything consequential I split the report into atomic claims, prioritise the risky ones — numbers, dates, names, legal or medical statements, and "studies show" claims — and verify each against a primary, current source, opening cited sources to confirm they actually support the claim. I recompute calculations, check completeness against what the report must cover, check the brief's constraints, test for one-sidedness, and cut or label anything I cannot verify. Then I own it.
payload.source: A defining question for AI-literate professionals; expect it in any AI-using role.

Each error type has a matching check.

Stakes set depth; you are accountable for what you submit.

lessons.title: Lateral Reading and Source Checking
lessons.summary: How professional fact-checkers verify: leave the page, check the source, trace claims upstream — with AI-era tactics for synthetic content.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Apply lateral reading to check a source in under five minutes
Trace a claim upstream to its primary source
Rank sources by authority and recency for a given question

payload.text: Researchers at Stanford compared professional fact-checkers with historians and university students on evaluating unfamiliar websites. The fact-checkers were faster and more accurate — not because they read more carefully, but because they barely read the page at all. Within seconds they opened new tabs to find out who was behind it. That habit — lateral reading — is the single best defence against polished misinformation, human or AI-made.

**Vertical vs lateral reading.** Vertical reading stays on the page and judges it by how it looks — design, tone, references. Polished sites, and AI-written text, pass that test easily. **Lateral reading** leaves the page: open new tabs and ask *who is behind this, and what do others say about them and this claim?*

**SIFT — a four-move routine** (developed by digital-literacy educator Mike Caulfield)
1. **Stop** — notice your reaction; do you know this source?
2. **Investigate the source** — who publishes it, what is their expertise and agenda?
3. **Find better coverage** — search the claim itself; do reliable outlets or official bodies report it?
4. **Trace to the original** — follow quotes, statistics and images back to where they first appeared.

**Source hierarchy (most to least authoritative for factual claims)**
- **Primary/official**: the law's text (India Code, the Gazette), the regulator (RBI, SEBI, UGC, AICTE), the court judgment, the dataset publisher, the company's own filing, the peer-reviewed paper itself.
- **Reputable secondary**: established news organisations with corrections policies, academic reviews, standard references.
- **Tertiary/aggregators**: encyclopaedias, explainers — fine for orientation, not for final citation.
- **Unverified**: forwarded messages, anonymous blogs, social posts, AI outputs.

**AI-era tactics**
- **Search the exact claim** in quotes; fabricated statistics often have zero independent mentions.
- **Check the date** on everything — staleness is a top error.
- **Reverse image search** suspected photos; check for AI-generation signs and provenance labels (for example C2PA "content credentials") where available. Absence of a label proves nothing either way.
- **Use AI to find, not to confirm**: AI search tools are good at locating candidate sources — then you open and read them.
- **Beware content farms**: whole websites can now be AI-generated, mutually citing one another. Many sources agreeing is meaningful only if they are independent.

lessons.title: Verifying Numbers, Code and Citations
lessons.summary: Recompute, test, and trace: the three checks for the outputs that most often look right and are wrong.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Verify AI-produced calculations with independent recomputation and sanity checks
Verify AI-written code with tests, edge cases and reading — not just "it runs"
Verify citations: existence, correct metadata, and support for the claim

payload.text: An AI assistant computes a home-loan EMI for a family: ₹42,000 a month. The real figure is about ₹45,000. A ₹3,000 gap sounds survivable until it is multiplied by 240 months — about ₹7 lakh — and the family has budgeted to the rupee. The model applied a slightly wrong formula and presented the result with two decimal places of false precision. Numbers, code and citations are where "looks right" is most dangerous — and where checking is most mechanical.

**Numbers: recompute, do not re-ask.** Asking the same model "are you sure?" mostly gets the same answer or a sycophantic change. Instead:
- **Recompute independently** — a spreadsheet, a calculator, or code you can read. Many assistants can run code; ask them to *compute with code and show it*, then read the code.
- **Sanity-check magnitude** — estimate roughly first. If ₹50 lakh at ~9% for 20 years "costs ₹2,000 a month", something is wrong.
- **Check units and definitions** — annual vs monthly rates, lakh vs million, percent vs percentage points, crore conversions.
- **Check the inputs** — a perfect calculation on the wrong figure is still wrong.

**Code: test it, do not trust it.**
- **Read it** — understand every line you ship; ask the model to explain any part you do not follow.
- **Run tests** — write (or ask for) unit tests that include **edge cases**: empty input, zero, negative numbers, missing values, very large inputs, wrong types.
- **Check silent behaviour** — dropped rows, swallowed exceptions, off-by-one loops, timezone assumptions.
- **Check dependencies** — AI sometimes suggests packages that do not exist; attackers have registered such names to distribute malware ("slopsquatting"). Confirm a package is real and reputable before installing.
- **Check security** — hard-coded secrets, SQL built from strings, missing input validation.

**Citations: three checks each**
1. **Exists** — find it in Google Scholar, the publisher's site, a DOI lookup, or an official repository.
2. **Metadata correct** — authors, year, title, venue match.
3. **Supports the claim** — open it and find the passage. This is the check people skip.

**Tool-assisted verification** is legitimate and powerful: code execution for maths, a second model as a critic, search for sources — as long as the final check rests on something independent of the original output.

    n1["Estimate magnitude"] --> n2["Recompute independently"] --> n3["Check units & inputs"]
  end
  subgraph CODE["Code"]
    c1["Read every line"] --> c2["Tests incl. edge cases"] --> c3["Check deps & security"]

payload.code:
# Verify an EMI independently: EMI = P * r * (1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1)
P = 50_00_000        # principal: ₹50 lakh
annual_rate = 0.09   # 9% per year
n = 20 * 12          # 240 monthly instalments
r = annual_rate / 12 # MONTHLY rate — the classic mistake is using 0.09 here

emi = P * r * (1 + r) ** n / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)
print(f"EMI: ₹{emi:,.0f}")                       # ≈ ₹44,986
print(f"Total paid: ₹{emi * n:,.0f}")            # ≈ ₹1.08 crore
print(f"Interest: ₹{emi * n - P:,.0f}")

# Edge-case tests for a function you were given
def emi_fn(P, annual_rate, years):
    r, n = annual_rate / 12, years * 12
    if r == 0:
        return P / n          # zero-interest loans must not divide by zero
    return P * r * (1 + r) ** n / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

assert abs(emi_fn(50_00_000, 0.09, 20) - emi) < 1
assert emi_fn(12_000, 0.0, 1) == 1_000
print("tests passed")

lessons.title: Build a Mini Evaluation: Golden Sets and Rubrics
lessons.summary: Turn "seems good" into a number: golden sets, rubrics, LLM-as-judge with care, and regression checks when prompts or models change.

payload.title: What you will learn
objectives: Build a golden set of test cases with expected outputs for an AI task
Write a scoring rubric and use it consistently, including with an AI judge
Run regression checks when a prompt or model changes

payload.text: A team improves its prompt for a college FAQ bot. Everyone agrees the new answers "feel better". Two weeks later students complain the bot now gets hostel-fee questions wrong — the new prompt had fixed tone and broken accuracy on one category. Nobody noticed because nobody measured. A 40-question golden set, run in five minutes before the change, would have caught it.

**An evaluation ("eval")** is a repeatable test of an AI system on fixed inputs, with a defined way to score outputs. It is how professionals know — rather than feel — whether something works.

**Golden set**: a fixed collection of test inputs with the expected output or the facts a good answer must contain.
- **Size**: start with 30–50 cases; grow to hundreds for important systems.
- **Coverage**: typical cases, hard cases, edge cases, adversarial cases (tricky phrasings, injection attempts), and **"should refuse / should say not found"** cases.
- **Real**: drawn from actual user questions where possible, with personal data removed.
- **Frozen**: do not tune your prompt by looking at the test answers over and over (that is overfitting again — Module 1). Keep a separate set for development.

**Scoring**
- **Exact or programmatic** where possible: correct label, valid JSON, number within tolerance, required keyword present.
- **Rubric** for open-ended answers: 3–5 criteria, each with a clear scale. For example: *Correct* (0–2), *Grounded in sources* (0–2), *Complete* (0–2), *Follows format* (0–1), *Appropriate refusal* (pass/fail).
- **Human review** of a sample — always, especially at the start.

**LLM-as-judge.** A capable model can score outputs against your rubric at scale. Use it carefully: give it the rubric, the reference answer and the output; ask for a reason before the score; check its agreement with human scores on 20–30 items before trusting it; and remember judges have biases (they often prefer longer answers, and can prefer answers from their own model family). Never let a judge grade without a reference for factual tasks.

**Regression testing.** Every time you change the prompt, the model, the retrieval settings or the documents, **re-run the golden set** and compare per category. A change ships only if it improves the target metric without breaking others. This is how AI work becomes engineering rather than hope.

payload.title: The evaluation loop
payload.source:
flowchart LR G["Golden set
typical · hard · edge · adversarial · refusal"] --> R["Run the system"] R --> S["Score
programmatic + rubric + human sample"] S --> C["Compare with previous version, per category"] C --> D{"Better overall and no category worse?"} D -->|"yes"| SHIP["Ship the change"] D -->|"no"| FIX["Revise prompt / model / retrieval"] FIX --> R SHIP --> MON["Add new real failures to the golden set"] MON --> G

rows: 2 = all facts match the reference; 1 = minor error; 0 = wrong
2 = every fact traceable to the cited document

Under 120 words, includes a link to the source page
Says "not in our documents" when the answer is absent

payload.code:
# A minimal golden-set runner (pseudo-real Python)
import csv, json

def score(output: str, case: dict) -> dict:
    must = [m.strip().lower() for m in case["must_include"].split(";") if m.strip()]
    hit = sum(1 for m in must if m in output.lower())
    refused = "not in our documents" in output.lower()
    return {
        "id": case["id"],
        "category": case["category"],
        "coverage": hit / len(must) if must else (1.0 if refused else 0.0),
        "refusal_ok": refused == (case["expect"] == "refuse"),
    }

results = []
with open("golden_set.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for case in csv.DictReader(f):
        output = ask_bot(case["question"])     # your system under test
        results.append(score(output, case))

by_cat = {}
for r in results:
    by_cat.setdefault(r["category"], []).append(r["coverage"])
print(json.dumps({c: round(sum(v) / len(v), 2) for c, v in by_cat.items()}, indent=2))

Pick the variant for your pathway. Save it in your AI.FIRST portfolio folder as PoW-05; the capstone defence draws on all twelve.

- **Explorer (no code):** Verify 20 claims from AI outputs you used this month: claim, error-type risk, source checked, verdict. Then build a 20-question golden set for one assistant you use and score it with a rubric.
- **Builder (code):** Build a 40-case golden set (CSV) for an AI task, a scoring script with programmatic checks plus an LLM-judge rubric, and report agreement between the judge and your own scores on 20 items.
- **Leader (policy & strategy):** Design an evaluation policy for your team: which AI uses need golden sets, minimum size, who reviews, when regressions run, and the ship/no-ship rule.

**Evidence that counts:** The actual log or golden set, scores by category, and at least one error or regression you found. "Everything passed" with no failures usually means the test was too easy.
